**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS, WHETHER LATIN OR GREEK, WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF THE COUNCIL OF TRENT (1545) FOR LATIN AUTHORS, AND OF THE COUNCIL OF FLORENCE (1439) FOR GREEK AUTHORS: A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST FIFTEEN CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH AND BEYOND, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND CORRECTED WITH THE UTMOST CARE; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST COPIOUS EDITIONS COMPLETED IN THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, YET POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY WITH RESPECT TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO HUNDRED AND MORE INDEXES OF AUTHORS AND WORKS—ALPHABETICAL, CHRONOLOGICAL, STATISTICAL, SYNTHETIC, ANALYTICAL, ANALOGICAL—CONCERNING EVERY POINT OF RELIGION, DOGMATIC, MORAL, LITURGICAL, CANONICAL, DISCIPLINARY, HISTORICAL, AND ALL OTHERS WITHOUT ANY EXCEPTION; BUT ABOVE ALL WITH TWO IMMENSE AND GENERAL INDEXES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH ONE MAY SEE AT A GLANCE WHATEVER not merely this or that Father, but every one of the Fathers, without a single omission, has written on any topic; THE OTHER, OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS, HAVE COMMENTED UPON EACH VERSE OF EACH BOOK OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM THE FIRST OF GENESIS TO THE LAST OF THE APOCALYPSE: A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its uniformity throughout the whole course of the Patrology, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered together in our Library from works and manuscripts belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**FIRST LATIN SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Innocent III; edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology, after the model of the Church herself, is divided into two parts, one Latin and the other Graeco-Latin. The Latin part, now fully published so far as its first series is concerned, consists in its bulk of two hundred and twenty-five volumes—or will do so shortly, once the indexes are completed—and sells for one thousand one hundred and twenty-five francs. The Greek has been printed in two editions. The first contains the Greek text together with a facing Latin translation and extends to one hundred and sixty-nine volumes, but without indexes. The second presents this translation alone, and is therefore contained within fifty-five volumes. Both had appeared in their entirety on 24 December 1860. Each Graeco-Latin volume is sold for eight francs, and each purely Latin volume for five francs only. In either case, however, in order that a purchaser may enjoy this advantageous price, he must buy the complete Greek or Latin collection—consisting of 326 volumes for the larger edition and 272 for the smaller edition without indexes; otherwise the size and difficulties of each volume will entail varying prices. Nevertheless, if anyone buys separately and complete either the Graeco-Latin collection or the same collection translated from Greek into Latin, then he will obtain each volume for nine or six francs respectively. These conditions apply to the series of the Patrology not yet printed.

# Special Indexes of the Latin Patrology

## Fourth Series of Indexes

[Col. 0009]

### [Preface]

Up to this point we have presented only the general indexes, of which our first volume consists. These indexes, although twenty-eight in number, are nevertheless nothing other than an introduction or preface to our unprecedented and, so to speak, gigantic undertaking, which we offer to the friends of patristic tradition. We must now undertake a new work; we must now furnish the special indexes. In this work we shall endeavor, so far as possible, to follow a logical order consonant with reason. Thus, in this fourth series, which contains thirteen indexes, we shall set before the reader in turn everything that the Holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers have said concerning God and His divine attributes; the Trinity and Providence; Creation; good and evil angels; the physical world; man; the human soul, its spirituality and immortality; human reason, its excellence and weakness; the earthly Paradise and the fall of the first parents. Thus the reader will immediately find, without labor, all the primary truths and everything which the Latin Patrology has handed down concerning them.

[Col. 0009]

## XXIX. INDEX CONCERNING GOD AND HIS VARIOUS ATTRIBUTES, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER AND PRESENTING WHATEVER THE FATHERS HAVE WRITTEN CONCERNING THEM

### Notice

In this index we treat of God in summary fashion. Yet, with a view to the reader’s greater advantage, we have established many headings, under which we set out separately—or indicate by the numbers of both volumes and pages—everything which the Fathers have said concerning God’s existence, essence, unity, foreknowledge, and His various attributes, so that with the aid of this index the reader may immediately and very easily find what is sought. At the end we have appended the books expressly treating of God that the *Patrology* contains. Moreover, in the outline of each heading we have observed the chronological order of the *Patrology*.

### [Index Concerning God]

#### I. On the Existence of God

God’s existence is proved from the creation of the world and of things: Tertullian, I, 375. God’s existence is demonstrated from the testimony of our soul, ibid., 376. The Romans worshipped the God of the Jews, ibid., 432. God’s existence is proved from motion, ibid., 590. The greater part of humankind knows the God of Moses, idem, II, 257. Works and benefits prove God, ibid., 265. In Paul’s time no one disputed concerning God, ibid., 270. God must first be known by nature, then recognized through doctrine, ibid., 266. Moses’ writing traces knowledge of God from the beginning of the world, from Paradise and Adam, not from Egypt and Moses as recent beginnings, ibid., 257. God, always known, was never hidden, because He has always shone forth, ibid., 285. We are taught about God by prophets and Christ, not by philosophers, ibid., 303. God is known to all through nature and conscience, ibid., 798.

God is discerned from the adornment of the whole world and from the order of times: Minucius Felix, III, 284.

All naturally know God: Arnobius, V, 1269.

Whoever denies God is judged foolish by public assent: St. Hilary, IX, 325 [Col. 0010]. God’s illustrious works bear witness that He exists, ibid., 761. Anyone who contemplates heaven will perceive that God exists, ibid., 668.

Nature itself recognizes its Creator by its own judgment: St. Ambrose, XVII, 68.

Knowledge of God is naturally present in everyone: St. Jerome, XXVI, 570.

How God is known from creatures: St. Augustine, XXXII, 782. Creation cries aloud that God is its Creator, ibid., 811. God must be sought by the authority of the Scriptures, ibid., 1315. The nations’ opinion concerning our God: idem, XXXIV, 1055. Rare is the kind of person who says in his heart, “There is no God”: idem, XXXVI, 613. No one dares say that God does not exist, even if he has dared to think it, ibid., 141. God is known to philosophers from creatures: idem, XXXVIII, 776. As the soul is understood from the motions and governance of the body, so God is understood from the governance of the world and the rule of souls, ibid., 1022. The true God is recognized through responses of oracles: idem, XLI, 651. What all nature teaches us concerning God: idem, XLII, 1061. Knowledge of God through creatures: idem, XLIV, 211.

God is known [Col. 0011] through the order of the world: Boethius, LXIII, 650.

God placed in human beings a testimony to the knowledge of Himself: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 771. How God is known from created things: LXXIII, 506. How He is known from the preservation of those same things: ibid.

One arrives at knowledge of God through creatures: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 706. We know God through visible things, 1107. We ought to infer that God exists from reason: idem, LXXVI, 403. The soul is raised from self-knowledge to the knowledge of God, ibid. God is known from His works, ibid.

By what arguments the fact that God exists is proved: Venerable Bede, XC, 1131.

God is known in various ways: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 220.

God can be known by experience alone: Guibert, CLVI, 353.

It is immediately evident to a rational mind that God exists more than all else: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 225. That there is a certain nature through which whatever exists exists, which exists through itself and is supreme among all existing things, ibid., 147. It is shown that that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists in reality, ibid., 249. In word God can be conceived not to exist; in reality He cannot, ibid., 228. That God truly exists, ibid., 227. That He is something best, greatest, and supreme among all existing things, CLVIII, 144.

Knowledge of God through creatures: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 28. One cannot arrive at knowledge of God except through self-knowledge, ibid., 826.

God’s existence is demonstrated: Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 673.

God is understood from the governance of the entire world, as the soul is understood from the governance of the body: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1328.

We apprehend God not by any knowledge but by faith alone: Alan of Lille, CCX, 601.

God’s existence and unity are proved: Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 791.

#### II. On the Essence of God

How varied were the philosophers’ opinions concerning God’s nature: Tertullian, I, 588. Philosophers declared God difficult to discover and describe, ibid., 509. Whence the name Θεός (*Theos*, “God”) is derived: idem, I, 590 ff. Before all things God alone existed: He was to Himself both world, place, and all things, idem, II, 160. Yet He was not alone in an absolute sense, since He had within Himself Reason and, in Reason, the Word, whom by thinking within Himself He made second from Himself, ibid. By His nature God does not know idleness; if He ceased, He would not be, ibid., 271. In God all things ought to be rational, as they are natural, ibid., 272. To judge God by our own perception is plainly foolish, ibid., 759.

Ancient poets and philosophers call God mind and spirit: Minucius Felix, III, 292.

“God” is His name: St. Cyprian, IV, 577. Epithets of God: Arnobius, V, 928.

God is rightly called by the name “Lord”: Lactantius, VII, 572.

God exists in such a way that He is always what He is: St. Hilary, IX, 269. God Himself is, is in Himself, is with Himself, is toward Himself, is His own to Himself, and is Himself all things to Himself, ibid.

The genus of God is to have no genus: St. Optatus, XI, 992.

When God is defined, He increases by the very act of His definition: St. Ambrose, XVII, 560.

What God’s essence is: St. Jerome, XXVI, 188. Apart from God, nothing can exist from itself, ibid., 488.

With God are supreme life and supreme reason: St. Augustine, XXXII, 591. What God is: idem, XXXIII, 439. What God is like cannot be comprehended by thought: idem, XXXIV, 790. It is no small part of knowledge to know what God is not before one can know what He is: idem, XXXV, 1588. What God’s nature is, ibid., 1876. What God is, ibid., 2213. God is a certain substance: idem, XXXVI, 844. In God are both the cause of subsistence, the principle of understanding, and the order of living: idem, XLI, 228. God is not of the same nature as the soul, ibid., 230. God is the supreme substance: idem, XLIV, 253. The true notion of God: idem, XLVI, 825.

What God is: St. Salvian, LIII, 29.

Description of God: Pope St. Leo, LIV, 194. God is supreme reason: idem, LV, 127.

The nature of God: Prudentius, LX, 667.

God, the origin of things: Dracontius, LX, 827. God, the origin of light: ibid., 698. God’s substance: Eugyppius, LXII, 619.

There is one essence, or nature, of deity: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 674. The true God is He who is God by nature; He is God by nature who has deity from the eternity of His birth, not from the grace of a gift, ibid., 214.

In how many senses Scripture speaks of God: Junilius, LXVIII, 21. On the significations of the divine essence: ibid., 21.

In Greek God is called “fear”: Cassiodorus, LXX, 741–742. How God is defined by some: ibid., 39.

In this life we perceive rather what God is not than what He is: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 713. What God’s being is: ibid., 1143. The divine substance receives neither loss nor increase: idem, LXXVI, 1048.

Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 259.

God has various names in Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 13.

God’s nature, which not even angels comprehend, is all the more inaccessible to human beings: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1423. God is truth not by accident but by essence [Col. 0012], ibid., 1399.

It can be explained not what God is, but what He is not: Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 709.

God is all things to all: Lanfranc, CL, 207.

On God and what God is: Manegald, CLV, 159.

God is one, individual, and simple nature: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 271. To one asking whence the supreme essence comes, the proper answer is: “From nothing,” that is, it was by no means made, ibid., 154. How God’s essence differs from created essence, ibid., 319. No nature is superior to God’s, ibid., 268.

God is substance: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 60.

What conception of God we ought to hold: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1073.

What God is: St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 801. An illustrious notion of God, ibid., 1057. God is that than which nothing better can be conceived, ibid., 796.

Whether God is universal or individual: Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 924.

#### III. On the Unity of God

God is one, who brought forth this entire mass from nothing: Tertullian, I, 375. God is unique, who created all things and fashioned man from the earth, ibid., 378. The supreme, great, and unique God must be believed in: idem, II, 201. If God exists, He must be unique, in order that He may belong to one alone, ibid. God is unique because of His infinite perfections, ibid., 249. God is one or none, ibid., 250.

God is one: Arnobius, V, 864. Only one God must be worshipped, ibid., 939.

God cannot be perfect unless He is one, so that all things may be in Him: Lactantius, VI, 123. God is one if there can be nothing else possessing so much power, ibid., 123. The world must be governed by the will of one, ibid., 125. The unity of God is established by the prophets, ibid., 127; by poets and philosophers, ibid., 129; by divine testimonies and the Sibyls, ibid., 138; by the testimonies of Apollo and the gods, ibid., 148. That God is one and cannot be many, ibid., 1019 ff. That God is only one, ibid., 1056. Philosophers’ opinions concerning God’s unity: idem, VII, 112–113.

God—God is one: St. Optatus, XI, 905.

One God, one name, one divinity, one majesty: St. Ambrose, XVI, 322. Common nature bears witness to one God; faith signifies one God; the magi believed in one God, ibid., 535. The unity of divinity is signified by unity of works, ibid., 534. The divine nature does not admit number, ibid., 799. Whatever God is, He is one, simple, and uncompounded, ibid., 1274. God is one and omnipotent, because His power is one, ibid., 566. Whatever departs from the confession of one God is regarded as dead: idem, XVII, 376. Without doubt God is one God of all, ibid., 80.

God is one or none: St. Phoebadius, XX, 15.

God is one by nature, many by positing: St. Gaudentius, XX, 855. There is one and only one nature of God, which truly exists: St. Jerome, XXII, 357. Natural and written law bear witness to one God: idem, XXIV, 408.

God is one: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1076; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 365; Pope St. Leo, LIV, 198; Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 999–1000. The unity of God: Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 107.

Testimonies concerning the one God: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 710–711. The authority of the Old and New Testaments demonstrates that there is one God, ibid., 362.

One must believe in God, first and last, one and three: one in substance, one in power, one in name: St. Columbanus, LXXX, 229.

To believe in three gods is profane: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXI, 141. The unity of God: ibid., 1294.

The deity is one: Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 472.

God is one: Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 18; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 238; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1072.

God is one in nature, not in person: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 527.

God is one to Himself and in Himself: St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 797. God is supremely simple, one, and immutable: CLXXXIII, 1169.

The supreme substance can have neither equal nor superior: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 897. That the supreme substance is identical with deity itself, and that God is not one except substantially, ibid., 898. That God is only one, ibid., 898, 902.

God is unique, free from every weakness or mutability: Alan of Lille, CCX, 451.

#### IV. On the Attributes of God

##### 1. God Uncreated and Eternal

We invoke God as eternal, true, and living: Tertullian, I, 441. God is eternal, before all time, ibid., 432. God’s motion is free and eternal: idem, II, 235. All things in God are natural and unbegotten, ibid., 271. What God purposed and revealed from eternity, He supplied beforehand through figures, enigmas, and allegories during the intervening course of ages, ibid., 483. God alone is without origin, ibid., 468.

God, as parent of all, has neither beginning nor end: Minucius Felix, [Col. 0013] III, 309.

That which has neither rising nor setting is divine, ibid., 309.

Is He not alone unbegotten, immortal, and everlasting? Arnobius, V, 928.

That good which all things seek, since God by His own nature always is, has no origin and therefore no beginning: Constantine the Great, VIII, 405.

Nothing is before God, nothing derives from elsewhere, nothing is outside Him: St. Hilary, X, 431. From the Scriptures one learns that God is eternal, ibid., 28.

God alone is perfect, omnipotent, everlasting: St. Zeno, XI, 391.

It belongs to that God who always is to be: St. Ambrose, XV, 1823. God has neither beginning of days nor end: idem, XIV, 126. This is God’s true name: to be always, idem, XVI, 914. He who is and always is, is God, ibid., 614. God alone is without process, because in every perfection He is always eternal, ibid., 619. It is proper to God not to have begun, but always to be the same thing which He always is: idem, XVII, 516.

God without beginning and end: Rufinus, XXI, 341.

God alone, who is eternal, truly possesses the name of essence: St. Jerome, XXII, 457. God alone is always what He was: idem, XXIII, 344. God has no beginning: idem, XXIV, 437.

God’s eternity: St. Augustine, XXXII, 664. God is and truly is, and by the very fact that He truly is, He is without beginning and end: idem, XXXVII, 1743. God remains with Himself; in Himself is full and perfect eternity: idem, XXXVIII, 1073. God alone is eternal, ibid., 208. God is wise and eternal, not by participation in wisdom and eternity, but by the wisdom and eternity of which He Himself is the author: idem, XL, 16.

God alone is truly eternal: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 453, 620.

God exists before time: St. Patrick of Ireland, LIII, 835. God’s eternity: ibid., 835; Eugyppius, LXII, 646. God properly is, because He has neither past nor future: Cassiodorus, LXX, 645.

God disposed all things from eternity: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 986. God’s eternity is explained: idem, LXXIX, 628.

If the supreme nature had an end or beginning, it would not itself be true eternity: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 167. The supreme nature is without beginning and end, ibid., 164. God is eternity, ibid., 322.

God’s attributes: St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 67, 68, 104. On God’s eternity, ibid., 71, 75.

God alone is properly eternal: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1530.

There is one supreme substance, which exists from itself and, for that very reason, from eternity and without any beginning: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 895. That God is uncreated, ibid., 901.

God is eternal, invisible, incomprehensible—the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 795.

God’s throne is eternity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 269. God is after all things, not in time, but in eternity, ibid., 270.

##### 2. Infinite and Immense

God is immense: Tertullian, I, 376. Every place is in God, not God in a place, because He is the final boundary of the universe: idem, II, 175. God is within the abysses and stands everywhere, but by power and might, ibid., 184. God is perfect in all things, ibid., 274, 304.

God is infinite, immense, and known to Himself alone as great as He is: Minucius Felix, III, 341.

God is above all things, containing all things, immense: Novatian, III, 889.

Fear, desire, envy, and covetousness do not apply to God: Lactantius, VII, 124.

God is everywhere: St. Hilary, IX, 682. God is wholly, always, and everywhere, ibid., 863. God is the same and whole everywhere, ibid., 629. How God is poured around and through all things, ibid., 774. God, infinite and immense, cannot be understood or displayed by the brief utterances of human speech: idem, X, 522. God’s immensity, ibid., 253. The infinite God is poured around and infused into all things, ibid., 28. All things are within God, and outside Him there is nothing capable of containing Him, ibid., 71.

Though God is immense, He contains the measure of all things: St. Ambrose, XIV. The incomprehensible splendor of divinity overwhelms the senses of our body: idem, XV, 1703. God, who is always everywhere, does not move from place to place: idem, XVI, 572. In God all things are equal by the immensity of infinity: idem, XVII, 384.

God is enclosed by no place, because He encloses all things in His fist and palm: St. Jerome, XXIV, 653. God is everywhere and wholly everywhere: idem, XXVI, 472.

God is present everywhere, not through spatial extension, but through the power of His majesty: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1277. God is present everywhere: idem, XXXVI, 952; XXXVII, 1125. God is wholly everywhere, divided nowhere: idem, XXXVIII, 367, 560. God is present everywhere and sees all things, ibid., 441. God’s substance is not circumscribed by quantity, ibid., 157.

There is no place without God: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 396. God alone is infinite and eternal, ibid., 620.

God is present everywhere, always whole: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 296. He who is wholly everywhere cannot be contained in places: idem, 582.

God is immense and present everywhere: Prudentius, LIX, 661; LX, 147.

God can be enclosed in no place: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 244. God’s immensity is diffused throughout every place without quantity, ibid., 684. God is immense in power, not in bulk, ibid., 512, 513, 696.

God’s [Col. 0014] presence is everywhere: St. Benedict, LXVI, 380. How God is present everywhere, ibid., 478.

God is wholly present everywhere: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1148, 328, 889. God is enclosed by no determination of place, ibid., 592.

God’s immensity is described: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1126, 1139. God is immense without spatial extension, eternal without beginning and end: idem, LXXVI, 805. There is no place where God is not, ibid., 1211.

On God’s immensity and omnipotence: Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 733; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 541.

God is wholly everywhere: Alcuin, CI, 642; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 281, 1413.

God is uncircumscribed, wholly everywhere, nowhere less and nowhere greater: Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 707.

God is everywhere in different ways: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 381.

God fills all things, is incomprehensible, and is wholly everywhere: Guibert, CLVI, 484.

God will have no end, whether willing or unwilling: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 164. On God’s immensity: ibid., 780; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1074.

God exists essentially, and truly exists in every creature, place, and time—and how: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 223.

God is immense: St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 796. God is everywhere, but in various ways: idem, CLXXXIV, 23. Creatures proclaim that God is everywhere, ibid., 23.

God is everywhere: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 272; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 632; Walter, CCIX, 572; CCX, 601.

##### 3. God Is Spirit

God is spirit, entirely free from every bodily concretion: Tertullian, I, 399. Platonists called God incorporeal; Stoics, corporeal, ibid., 517. God Himself is invisible and at the same time visible: idem, II, 170. What are God’s hands, feet, and eyes? ibid., 303.

God can neither be seen, being brighter than sight; nor comprehended, being purer than touch; nor assessed, being greater than the senses: Minucius Felix, III, 290; St. Cyprian, IV, 576.

God lacks bodily features: Arnobius, V, 953. God is not male, though His name is masculine, ibid., 945. God is incorporeal, ibid., 757, 928. God is free from quantity and quality, ibid., 755. God is without position, movement, and disposition, ibid., 755.

God is without a body: Lactantius, VI, 153. God is the light of the human mind: idem, VII, 74. Whether God has any figure, ibid., 82.

God is not bodily in our sense: St. Hilary, IX, 683, 719, 430. God is invisible and cannot be seen in this life, ibid., 554. What are God’s heart, hands, and eyes? idem, X, 439.

God is spirit: St. Ambrose, XIV, 257. There can be no bodily representation of the incorporeal God, ibid., 131. God has nothing bodily in His substance: XV, 1749; St. Jerome, XXV, 77.

“If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: He can. If you ask how I know, I answer: because it is read in the most truthful Scripture: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart’”: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 612. How God is seen, ibid., 625. God is not something corporeal, nor anything that can be formed by our thought: XXXVIII, 369. What are God’s face, hands, and feet? ibid., 366. God is defined by no bodily form: idem, XL, 188. It is proved that God is not a body: idem, XLI, 230. Whatever is corporeal, and whatever mutable is encountered even among spiritual things, is not God: idem, XLII, 958. The eyes of flesh cannot behold divinity: idem, XLIV, 92. There is no sex in divinity, ibid., 405.

God alone is incorporeal: Cassian of Marseilles, L, 683.

No bodily form is to be conceived in the nature of deity: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 347.

God is incorporeal and invisible: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 376.

God is incorporeal: Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1018.

God cannot be seen with bodily eyes: Prudentius, LIX, 924.

God is an incorporeal substance: Boethius, LXIV, 1410; LXV, 162.

God’s ears and eyes: St. Benedict, LXVI, 229.

God is invisible and incomprehensible: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1140. Who believed God to be corporeal: idem, LXXVI, 636.

God is spirit and not soul: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 84.

To what extent eyes, ears, hands, and anger may be attributed to God: Blessed Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 727.

The error of those who attributed a body to God is refuted: Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 704.

God does not have members: Guibert, CLVI, 484.

God is the supreme spirit: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 229. The supreme essence is spirit, not body nor anything sensible, ibid., 161. Supreme wisdom is nothing other than supreme spirit, ibid., 183.

God is incorporeal: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 199. God is truly spirit: idem, CLXIX, 363.

### 4. God Simple

Some deny to God His proper attributes, simplicity and power; Tertullian, I, 1201.---God is simple and must not be conceived after the manner of human beings; St. Hilary, X, 338. God is free from composition; id., IX, 720. God is supreme simplicity; id., X, 166, 253, 268. What are the attributes of God, who is supremely simple? ibid., 305.---God neither suffers defect or diminution, nor admits addition; St. Ambrose, XIV, 319. [Col. 0015] Whatever God is, He is one, simple, and uncompounded; St. Ambrose, XVI, 1274. God is of a simple nature; ibid., 553. In the Godhead there are neither limbs nor parts; these are expressed on account of the unity of the Godhead; ibid., 757. God possesses, and cannot lose, what He possesses naturally from divine majesty; ibid., 662. God cannot be understood as composite; id., XVII, 510.---The simplicity of God; St. Augustine, XLI, 231. God is said figuratively to have a soul, as also bodily limbs; ibid., 534. God has neither sex nor age nor determinate bodily limbs; ibid., 134. God is a most simple nature; id., XLII, 1076. God is simple and manifold; ibid., 928, 929.---God alone is truly simple; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 488.---No succession of times is ascribed to God; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 518.---God’s nature is simple and in no way composite; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 167.---God is supremely simple, one, and immutable; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 797; CLXXXIII, 1169.---God is one and incorporeal; Galterus, CCIX, 572.

### 5. God Immutable

God must be believed immutable and incapable of being formed, in order that He may be eternal; Tertullian, II, 190. God alone is blessed by the attribute of incorruptibility; ibid., 304.---God must be believed immutable; Novatian, III, 892.---Everything divine—that is, God—is immutable; Candidus, VIII, 1013.---God’s eternal immutability; St. Hilary, IX, 1066. God is not subject to change; ibid., 268.---God alone is perfect, omnipotent, and unchangeable; St. Zeno, XI, 391.---Since God is immutable, why is He said to be angry? St. Ambrose, XIV, 366. God does not think as human beings do, so that a new decision should replace a former one; ibid., 366. God’s will is immovable, but human beings are mobile—and why; id., 1175. God’s decision is not changeable; ibid., XVI, 1159. God remains immutable; id., XVII, 75.---God does not change; St. Jerome, XXV, 1473. God alone is immutable by His nature; id., XXVI, 320.---God, supremely good and immutable, is the Creator of all mutable natures; St. Augustine, XXXII, 599. To believe is to believe that God is immutable nature and the supreme good; ibid., 634. He does not think rightly about God who does not believe Him both omnipotent and unchangeable in no respect whatsoever; ibid., 1224. God is a certain most excellent and immutable nature; id., XXXIV, 357, 362. God is the immutable good; ibid., 384. God’s counsel is unchangeable; ibid., 300. God’s life is immutable; id., XXXV, 1548. Disturbance has no place in God; id., XXXVI, 92. God’s very substance is that which has nothing mutable, where nothing is past as though it no longer were, nor future as though it were not yet, and where there is only “is”; id., XXXVII, 1311. God is immutable; id., XXXVIII, 986; XL, 360; XLI, 220, 362; XLII, 518. God is neither extended by bulk nor diminished by division; id., XLI, 280. God acts by immutable counsel and will; ibid., 366, 367. In the substance of the supreme good no temporal mutability can be found; id., XLII, 594. God alone is immortal because He alone is immutable; ibid., 768.---God alone is immutable and good; Cassian, L, 667.---The principles of all things are eternal and immutable in God; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 717. God is immutable; ibid., 284.---With God the order of things is unchangeable; Pope St. Leo, LIV, 368.---God’s decrees are immutable; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 567.---God is immutable; Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 995.---God is immutable; Eugyppius, LXII, 576, 724. God does not vary with time; ibid., 734. God is immutable; ibid., 851; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 513; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 349; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 601; LXXIX, 663. God alone is free from mutability; LXXV, 1003; LXXVI, 324, 1143. God is immutable by nature and by will; id., LXXVI, 640. God is not subject to mutability; id., LXXIX, 438.---In God there is nothing subject to change; Alcuin, C, 716.---God’s judgment is immutable; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 522.---God changes times, not counsels; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 249.---The supreme essence is in no way mutable; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 178. God is immutable; ibid., 419; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 154; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 592; CLXX, 251; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 799, 800; Godefridus, CLXXIV, 427; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 220; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1169; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 349; Galterus, CCIX, 572; Alan of Lille, CCX, 451.

### 6. God Free

God’s motion is free and eternal; Tertullian, II, 235. Freedom, not necessity, belongs to God; ibid., 212.---By God’s will those things that occur in the world occur; Arnobius, V, 895.---For God, His will is law and the right to give; St. Ambrose, XIV, 1035. The divine will is the foundation of the universe; ibid., 134. God’s will is power; id., XV, 1636. God’s will is the strength of nature; id., XIV, 149. God’s word is will; God’s work is nature; ibid., 141.---Nothing occurs apart from God’s will, even when it goes against His will; St. Augustine, XL, 279.---God has a twofold will; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, [Col. 0016] 428.---God’s will is compelled by no necessity and subject to no necessity; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 419. God’s will is manifold; ibid., 583. By His will alone God made all things from nothing; ibid., 222. This is God’s will, from which, through which, and in which are all things; ibid., 413.---God accomplished what He willed, not through another, but through Himself; Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 450.

### 7. God Omnipotent

For God, to be able is to will, and not to be able is not to will; moreover, what He willed He both could do and showed forth; Tertullian, II, 166. Weakness and falsehood do not belong to God; ibid., 774. Nothing is impossible to God except what He does not will; ibid., 756. God must be believed under no other rule than that He is believed able to do all things; ibid., 809. Examples of divine power; ibid., 810.---The rule of truth requires that, before all else, we believe in God the Father and omnipotent Lord; Novatian, III, 886.---It belongs to God alone to do all that He wills; St. Hilary, IX, 757. His works bear witness to God’s greatness; ibid., 790. God’s works are effected powerfully; ibid., 857. God’s power manifests itself certainly by deeds whose rationale is hidden from us; id., X, 78.---God alone is perfect, omnipotent, and unchangeable; St. Zeno, XI, 391.---What cannot He do who can do all things, except what He does not will to be able to do? St. Ambrose, XV, 1494. God does not wish to share dominion with others; ibid., 1370. God is one and omnipotent because power is one; id., XVI, 566. Nothing is impossible to God; ibid., 532.---God’s power is proclaimed; id., XXIII, 556. All things are possible to God; ibid., 517. God’s power is commended; St. Jerome, XXIII, 385. God’s majesty and power; id., XXIV, 406. In what God’s omnipotence chiefly prevails; ibid., 492. God’s power is shown in small living creatures; id., XXV, 964. God founded the earth by strength; ibid., 625. How God’s sovereignty, power, and kindness are to be understood in the creation of things; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 228. God needs no creature in order to be better, more powerful, or happier; id., XXXVI, 896. God is omnipotent; id., XXXVIII, 1060, 1067. No one denies that God is omnipotent, not even a pagan; ibid., 1131. Every creature serves God, willingly or unwillingly; id., XL, 279. God, being good, would not permit any evil to occur unless He were omnipotent; ibid., 279. No force overcomes God’s will; id., XLI, 389. How God does whatever He wills; ibid., 752.---God’s omnipotence is infinite; Cassian of Marseilles, L, 135.---By God’s omnipotence all things are preserved and subsist; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 467.---God is omnipotent; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 371.---God made all things by His will; Eugyppius, LXII, 622. God’s will is most powerful; ibid., 798.---God’s power is no less than His will; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 660. Deity alone possesses full power; ibid., 287. God can do as much as He wills; ibid., 162. In God there is no weakness; ibid., 294. God’s will is always fulfilled, because His power is in no way overcome; ibid., 441.---Nothing is impossible to God; Cassiodorus, LXIX, 478.---God is omnipotent; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 541.---God is omnipotent because He made all things; St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 127.---No one can resist God’s power; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1139. In God is the power of death and life; id., CIX, 17.---God is omnipotent; Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 130.---God can do all things, whether He does them or does not do them; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 609.---God’s omnipotence; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 780. The supreme nature is omnipotent; ibid., 164.---On God’s omnipotence; Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 486.---That God is supremely powerful; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 900.

### 8. God Supremely Wise; on His Knowledge

Nothing is sudden to God, because nothing is undisposed of by God; Tertullian, II, 323.---Why God’s knowledge is wonderful; St. Hilary, IX, 800. How God’s knowledge embraces all things; ibid., 463. The creation of the world reveals God as wise; id., X, 173. God’s knowledge is perfect; ibid., 56.---There is in God a certain womb, the fatherly secret-place of wisdom, which neither angels nor the nature of any creature could penetrate; St. Ambrose, XVI, 654. God is wise above all; ibid., 148.---God is ever immortal and wise; St. Jerome, XXIII, 542. God alone is wise; ibid. God founded the earth by wisdom; id., XXV, 627.---God is wisdom, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are wise are wise; St. Augustine, XXXII, 869. God is wise and eternal, not by participation in wisdom and eternity, but by that wisdom and eternity of which He Himself is the author; id., XL, 16.---Nothing is new to God’s eternal wisdom; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 435.---God always acts in all things by reason and judgment; St. Salvian, LIII, 45.---God’s judgments are incomprehensible; St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 254.---God’s decree and wisdom are infallible; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 738.---How God’s wisdom is manifold; Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 294.---What God’s wisdom and knowledge are; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 99.---God’s strength and wisdom; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1021, 1070.---God alone is wise in the proper sense; Peter Lombard, [Col. 0017] CXCI, 1530.---That God’s wisdom is so supreme that each perfection is itself perfect; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 900.

### 9. God Supremely Good

God’s goodness always accords with reason; Tertullian, II, 273. God alone is good; ibid., 300.---God is best from what is His own, just with respect to what is ours; ibid., 812. Though good by nature, God is nevertheless also just; ibid., 984.---What and how great God’s patience is; St. Cyprian, IV, 624.---By God’s goodness that which is rightly bound is preserved; Arnobius, V, 865. God is impartially kind to all; ibid., 939. God denies His kindness to no one; ibid., 781.---In what sense anger is ascribed to God; Lactantius, VII, 89, 131.---In God there is nothing but what is good and eternal; St. Hilary, IX, 657. God’s goodness toward those who fall through weakness; ibid., 529. From our birth we learn that God is good; id., X, 173.---It is proper to God to be good; St. Ambrose, XV, 1326. God is good in His entirety; man only in part; ibid., 1785. How God is good to all; id., XIV, 839. God’s goodness extends to all, His severity to few; id., XV, 1323. How great is God’s love for us; id., XIV, 608. God’s goodness wills no one to perish; id., XVII, 91. Three things in God preserve the order of time—past, present, and future: goodness, mercy, and justice; ibid., 1005.---Why a good God chastises the righteous; St. Gaudentius, XX, 838.---God is good through Himself; Rufinus, XXI, 820.---What God’s clemency is; St. Jerome, XXIII, 544. God’s great clemency is praised; id., XXIV, 345. Great is God’s clemency; id., XXV, 840. God is kind and severe; ibid., 689.---God is good by His nature; id., XXVI, 445.---Creatures subsist and are brought to perfection through God’s goodness; St. Augustine, XXXII, 845. By God’s grace all things subsist; ibid., 846. God’s goodness does not permit anything to be brought by corruption to the point of non-being; ibid., 1349. On God’s goodness and justice in the differentiation of human beings; id., XXXIII, 832.---How God’s sovereignty, power, and kindness are to be understood in the creation of things; id., XXXIV, 228. God made all things out of goodness, not necessity; id., XXXVII, 1745. God is the good of all goods, the good from which all good things come; ibid., 1742. All creatures proclaim testimony to God’s goodness and greatness; ibid., 1865. God is good by the property of His nature in such a manner that He cannot be corrupted; id., XLV, 1536.---What God’s goodness is; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 263.---God is the supreme good without quality; Claudianus Mamertus, LIII, 779.---In God is all fullness of goodness and all the tranquility of goodness; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 800.---God is wholly good and goodness itself; Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1018. God is not the author of the evil that He permits; ibid., LIX, 700.---God’s goodness and justice; Dracontius, LX, 831. God’s goodness toward human beings; ibid., 733. God’s kindness and clemency; ibid., 826.---God is kind; Eugyppius, LXII, 615. God’s goodness, justice, and power; ibid., 640.---God’s patience leads us to repentance; St. Benedict, LXVI, 236.---God is supremely good, full of benevolence, free from envy, and ignorant of malice; St. Gall, LXXXVII, 89.---God does good to the good and the evil; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 248.---God alone is truly good by nature; St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 137.---Nothing is better than God, nor is anything good found without Him; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1472.---God’s essence is nothing other than goodness; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 803.---God’s kindness and severity toward the sinner; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 662.---God is every good; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1063.---God’s goodness toward sinners; Gillebertus, CLXXXIV, 527.---In what sense God is the author of good and evil; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 857.---God alone is eternal and good in the proper sense; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1530.---God is properly called love; Peter Cantor, CCV, 274.

### 10. God Supremely Just

God is a just and severe judge; Tertullian, II, 302. God’s justice is the fullness of His very divinity; ibid., 300. Though good by nature, God is nevertheless also just; ibid., 984; Arnobius, V, 864.---God cannot be charged either with injustice or with an evil will; St. Hilary, IX, 343. God’s justice is not diminished through mercy; ibid., 860. Justice regulates God’s goodness in its manner of use, not in its bestowal; ibid., 859.---God is just in all things, wise above all, perfect in all things; St. Ambrose, XVI, 148. God is neither unjust, nor is His decision mutable; ibid., 566. Three things in God preserve the order of time: goodness, mercy, and justice; id., XVII, 1005. God’s justice belongs to the mystery of God; ibid., 79. God is just because He has given what He promised; ibid., 56.---If God is just, why are infants, ignorant of their elders’ deeds, afflicted by diverse evils? Zacchaeus Christianus, XX, 1104.---In what sense God is said to be just toward good and evil persons; Rufinus, XXI, 675.---What God’s justice is; St. Jerome, XXIII, 563.---On God’s goodness and justice in the differentiation of human beings; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 832. God is just both when He condemns and when He has mercy; id., XXXVII, 1922. Great is God’s love of justice; id., XLIV, 712.---God is merciful and just; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 413.---God is the source of justice; Eugyppius, LXII, 842.---God’s justice is to be feared; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 158.---God is holy and just; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 16.---God’s judgment, though hidden, is nevertheless just; Servatus Lupus, CXIX, 551.---God judges in equity, that is, without respect of persons; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXL, 248.---God’s works are both just and kind; Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 337.---God’s justice is nothing other than God Himself; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 378.---God judges justly; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1007.---God alone is just; Adam the Scot, CXXXIX, 352.---With God there is no respect of persons; Peter Cantor, CCV, 200.---God is just; Galterus, CCIX, 572.

### 11. God Supremely Holy

Perversity and deceit do not belong to God; Tertullian, II, 166. God is not the cause of sin; ibid., 296. God alone is without sin; ibid., 720.---God is not the author of evil; Arnobius, V, 895, 897.---God’s holiness does not withdraw itself from human aid; St. Hilary, IX, 862.---He is without sin; St. Ambrose, XVI, 808. How anger and indignation are in God; id., XVII, 65.---God alone is true; every human being is a liar; St. Jerome, XXIII, 584. God alone is without sin; ibid., 561.---God is the author of no sin, even the slightest; St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1397.---God cannot sin; Eugyppius, LXII, 818. God is light; ibid., 687.---God alone is holy; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 61. Guibert, CLVI, 484.---God is supreme truth; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 167.---God alone is holy, good, and just; William, CLXXXIV, 1202.---God is not the author of evils; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 949.

### 12. God Supremely Merciful

What God’s mercy and patience are; Lactantius, VII, 137.---God is especially to be praised for His mercy; St. Hilary, IX, 861. What God’s mercy and patience are; ibid., 560. God’s justice is not diminished through mercy; ibid., 860.---How the earth is full of God’s mercy; St. Ambrose, XIV, 911. Three things in God preserve the order of time—past, present, and future: goodness, mercy, and justice; id., XVII, 1005.---God’s mercy is concealed and His wrath displayed, so that people may cease from sinning; St. Jerome, XXIV, 210. God alone is merciful, compassionate, and patient by essence; Cassiodorus, LXX, 721.---What God’s mercy is; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 104.---God is just and merciful; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 88.---That no one can be saved except through God’s preceding and following mercy; St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 187.---God never forgets His mercy; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1115.---What God’s mercy is; Servatus Lupus, CXIX, 628.---Why God is merciful; Guibert, CLVI, 837.---God’s mercy and justice; Goffridus, CLVII, 184; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 735.

### VII. On God’s Foreknowledge

God neither condemns His past judgments nor is ignorant of the future; Tertullian, II, 311.---For God, future things are as accomplished facts; St. Hilary, IX, 664. How God knows or does not know the future; ibid., 260. God’s foreknowledge; ibid., 449. To know the future belongs properly to God; id., X, 330.---It belongs properly to God to know what has passed and to know the future; St. Zeno, XI, 463.---With God all future things are present, and all hidden things manifest; St. Ambrose, XIV, 958. With God there is nothing that may be called future; id., XVII, 260. What God’s foreknowledge is; ibid., 134. God’s judgment by foreknowledge is just; ibid., 136. God judges according to justice, not according to foreknowledge; ibid., 134. How God predestined those who are saved; ibid., 427. God chose Paul while he was persecuting, knowing beforehand that he would become good; ibid., 136.---God’s foreknowledge does not err; St. Gaudentius, XX, 864.---What God’s foreknowledge is; St. Jerome, XXIII, 415. Knowledge of future things belongs to God alone; id., XXV, 499.---How God’s foreknowledge does not remove free will from those who sin; St. Augustine, XXXII, 1272. God’s foreknowledge does not cause us to sin otherwise than by free will; ibid., 1273. God, who knows beforehand, does not compel people to sin and therefore punishes sins justly; ibid., 1275. God knows all things immutably; id., XXXIV, 334. God does nothing that He did not know beforehand from eternity that He would do; id., XXXVII, 1416. With God everything is present; id., XL, 15. What knowledge and foreknowledge are in God; ibid., 136. What God’s will was concerning the salvation of Adam, whom He had foreknown would sin; ibid., 281. God by foreknowledge sees past and future things immutably; id., XLI, 334. God’s foreknowledge, like His judgment, is certain and fixed; ibid., 472. God’s foreknowledge knows future things beforehand; id., XLIV, 845.---God’s foreknowledge embraces all times; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 718. God’s foreknowledge does not impose necessity on the will; ibid., 719.---Knowledge of the future belongs to God alone; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 258.---God’s foreknowledge does not forcibly impel human wills either toward right actions or their opposites; Faustus of Riez, LVIII, 815. In God, foreknowing is one thing and predestining another; ibid., 816.---Why God created the human being whom He knew beforehand would transgress; Eugyppius, LXII, 637. God’s foreknowledge is true and immutable; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 610. In God alone is foreknowledge of those things which truly will be, not of things which will not be; ibid., 610. God knew beforehand all human sins; id., 175. What belongs to God’s predestination; ibid., 654.---Nothing new occurs contrary to God’s foreknowledge; Cassiodorus, LXX, 764. He recognizes our deeds and thoughts even before we exist; ibid., 984. Through foreknowledge God distinguishes us—and how; ibid., 592.---God saw and decreed future things from eternity; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 986. In God’s foreknowledge the times of every life are immovably fixed; ibid., 1013. Things are not seen by God because they exist; rather, they exist because they are seen; id., LXXVI, 163. The certainty of divine foreknowledge; id., LXXIX, 393. The certainty of divine predestination; ibid., 393.---God, foreseeing future things, praises them as though already completed; Rabanus Maurus, CVII. God does not speak in order that something may occur; rather, because it will occur, He foretells it; id., CXI, 865.---God’s foreknowledge and predestination are eternal and immutable; St. Remigius of Lyons, CXXI, 989. God’s predestination imposes necessity for evil on no one; ibid., 995.---God knows all things before they occur; Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 325. What God’s foreknowledge is; ibid., 702.---On God’s foresight and providence; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 74, 75, 76.---For God there is nothing future and nothing past; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 101.

### VIII. Books Treating of God

*Book on the Anger of God*; Lactantius, VII, 80.---*Book on the Unity of God*; St. Augustine, XLII, 1193. One book *On the Essence of Divinity*; ibid., 1200.---*Conflict concerning the Triune and One God*; Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 239.---*Poem on God*; Dracontius, LX, 679.---Catholic proposition on the Unity of God; Boethius, LXIV, 1249.---*Monologion on the Essence of Divinity*; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 142. *Dialogue on the Existence of God*; ibid., 224.---*Treatise on the Harmony of God’s Foreknowledge, Predestination, and Grace with Free Choice*; ibid., 507. *Book on the Will of God*; ibid., 581.

## XXX. INDEX ON THE TRIUNE GOD, OR ON THE TRINITY, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER, BRINGING BEFORE THE EYES WHATEVER THE FATHERS WROTE ON THIS MYSTERY

### Notice

In this index we set forth various judgments of the Fathers concerning the concept and existence of the Most Holy Trinity, and concerning the three divine persons—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We further enumerate the various errors concerning that mystery, and the books by which the Fathers attempted to refute them. As in the preceding index, in every chapter we follow the chronological order of the *Patrologia*.

## [INDEX ON THE TRINITY]

### I. The Concept and Existence of the Most Holy Trinity

All the Scriptures show the distinction and demonstration of the Trinity; Tertullian, II, 166. The Trinity, rationally considered, establishes truth; ibid., 158. In the Trinity unity is ordered: three, not in state but in rank; not in substance but in form; not in power but in appearance—yet of one substance and one power; ibid., 157.---The mystery of the Trinity was manifested in the last times; St. Cyprian, IV, 815. The three are one; ibid., 366.---The three divine persons are inseparable because of the unity of nature; St. Dionysius, V, 108.---The mystery of the Trinity was hidden from the Jews; St. Hilary, X, 147. It is ineffable and incomprehensible; ibid., 53. Knowledge of the Trinity is sufficiently conveyed in baptism; ibid., 49. Apostolic men were always zealous to explain and defend the mystery of the Trinity; ibid., 652. The false designation of the Trinity among certain Easterners; ibid., 656.---The names of the Trinity: what they are; St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 911, 962. The three persons are indicated at the beginning of Genesis; ibid., 1047.---Trinity signifies a distinction of persons; unity, power; St. Ambrose, XIV, 963. Clear testimony for proving the coeternal and perfect Trinity; id., XV, 1625. Those who affirm a Trinity of one will thereby affirm a Trinity of one power; ibid., 1036. Although the Godhead is indivisible, the person is distinct; ibid., 1722. In the creation of the world the operation of the Trinity shines forth; id., XIV, 138. We confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in such a way that in the perfect Trinity there is both fullness of divinity and unity of power; id., XVI, 531. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one nature and one knowledge; ibid., 769.---The mystery of the Trinity; id., XVII, 754. The term “Holy Trinity” is a great mystery and secret; ibid., 522. The Trinity’s mystery is proved from the Apostle; ibid., 1004. In the Trinity we believe that the three names and three persons are of one essence, one majesty, and one power; ibid., 551. Both Unity in Trinity and Trinity in Unity exist; ibid., 514. The mystery of the Trinity, though immense, is enclosed within the nature and power of the one God; ibid., 245. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one dominion, one deity, and one omnipotence; ibid., 804.---The three persons of the Holy Trinity appear in the mystery of Christ’s baptism; St. Chromatius, XX, 330, 331.---The Trinity’s nature is undivided; St. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, XX, 946.---The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity; St. Jerome, XXIII, 170. The mystery of the Trinity was unknown to the ancients; ibid., 431. By what means the unity of the Trinity is taught; ibid., 120 ff. Confession of the Trinity among Christians; ibid., 1090. The confession of the Trinity: holy mountain and doctrine of truth; id., XXIV, 541. In the mystery of the Holy Trinity there is nothing obscure; id., XXV, 1039, 1401. Outstanding exposition of the Holy Trinity; id., XXVI, 497.---The faith of the Trinity is expounded; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 453. What faith teaches concerning the Trinity; id., XLII, 694, 716, 823, 945. What is to be maintained concerning it; XXXIII, 744, 458; XL, 193; XLIII, 497. Explanation of the Trinity; id., XXXIV, 21. The mystery of the Trinity cannot be explained even by angelic words; id., XL, 659. The Trinity is one God; id., XXXV, 1682, 1683; XXXVI, 83; XXXVIII, 64, 453, 614, 620. The Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; yet together all are one Lord God; id., XLII, 741. The whole Trinity is one God, not three gods or three omnipotent beings; id., XXXIV, 355, 1059, 1063, 1071. The Trinity’s wondrous simplicity; id., XXXIII, 745. The substance of the whole Trinity is one; id., XXXV, 1862. The Trinity is one Lord, not three lords; one God, one substance, three persons; id., XXXVIII, 64, 65.

The persons of the Trinity; id., XXXIII, 1028. The persons of the Trinity are neither confusedly one nor separately three; ibid., 750. The persons of the Trinity are inseparable; id., XXXV, 1870, 1871. The persons of the Trinity are distinguished by various properties and names; id., XXXII, 976, 1077, 1336; XXXIV, 128. The distinction of the persons of the Trinity arises from relation to another; id., XLI, 325. What is said relatively in the Trinity; id., XLII, 919. “Trinity” is not said relatively; ibid., 919. Those things which are said relatively to one another in the Trinity properly belong to the individual persons; what is said of them in relation to themselves is said individually, not of the three in the plural; ibid., 947. In order that the Trinity, though inseparable, may nevertheless be understood as Trinity, much is said separately concerning the individual persons; id., XXXIII, 744. The Trinity is no less in each individual person than in all, nor greater in all than in each individual person; ibid., 750.

The coeternity of the Trinity; id., XLII, 909. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one power, one substance, one deity, one majesty, and one glory; ibid., 814. The nature of the Trinity is immutable; id., XXXIV, 389. The whole Trinity is invisible; id., XLII, 758, 854, 866, 881.

The Trinity’s works are the same; id., XXXVIII, 704. Its works are inseparable; id., XXXIII, 75, 745, 878; XXXV, 1557, 1559 ff., 1781, 1902; XXXVIII, 356, 459, 1063; XL, 251, 463, 684; XLII, 308, 686, 691, 694. Sacred Scripture measures the Trinity’s act not by a difference of powers but by the ineffability of its works; ibid., 697. The Trinity’s power and operation are indivisible; id., XXXVIII, 356, 459, 703. The Trinity created the world; id., XXXIV, 232. Every creature receives being, form, and order from the Trinity; ibid., 128. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the threefold Unity, the one Trinity—alone are Creator; id., XXXVIII, 986. In humanity’s creation, the plurality of persons and singularity of divinity are shown; ibid., 703. In the Trinity certain works belong to one person, but not without the cooperation of the others; ibid., 357, 459, 463.

The Trinity is represented in created things; id., XLII, 932. Traces of the Trinity in creatures; id., XLI, 300. The Trinity is indicated in all God’s works; ibid., 338. The mystery of the Trinity is indicated in Genesis; id., XXXII, 847; XXXVIII, 26; XL, 167; XLI, 345.

A likeness of the Trinity in the name; id., XXXVIII, 362; XLI, 339, 342; XXXII, 849. How the Trinity is shown in the mind; id., XLII, 1040, 1044, 1048. The image of the Trinity in each person’s memory, understanding, and will; ibid., 1088, 1090. A trace of the Trinity also in the outward human being; ibid., 983. A trace of the Trinity in vision; ibid., 985, 991. Whether and how, from the trinities shown in the human being, it may be demonstrated that God is Trinity; ibid., 1064, 1065. The Trinity is illuminated by analogies; id., XL, 189, 658, 692.

There are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—yet the Trinity itself is one God; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 490. There is no disparity in the supreme Trinity; ibid., 488.

The mystery of the Trinity is explained; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 358, 401 ff. In the Trinity there is a distinction of persons, but unity of essence; ibid., 208. Why certain things are attributed to the individual persons; ibid., 404. The Trinity’s works are undivided; ibid., 412.

How the mystery of the Trinity was depicted in the basilica erected by Paulinus; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 336. How it was represented in churches; ibid., 880 ff. How Victricius preached it to the nations; ibid., 355.

The Trinity is taught from several passages of Scripture; Eugyppius, LXII, 654.

What the Trinity is, ibid., 934. Analogies of the Trinity, ibid., 927. — On the unified Trinity of the Godhead; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 238. On the distinct persons, ibid., 246. On the unified and everlasting substance of the Trinity, ibid., 268. — The Trinity is one God, yet three persons; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 574. One nature in God and three persons, ibid., 498. The Trinity of persons in God revealed to Isaiah, ibid., 204. Testimonies concerning the Trinity, ibid., 714, 715, 500, 352. The Holy Trinity is proved by the example of the human soul, in which are memory, understanding, and will, ibid., 520, 521. In creatures there is Trinity in Unity; therefore much more so in God, ibid., 504. When one God is spoken of, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one nature is to be understood; when Trinity is spoken of, three persons, ibid., 361. One power and Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ibid., 406. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit act inseparably, ibid., 401. The image of the Trinity in the human soul, ibid., 726, 727. An indication of the Trinity in fire, ibid., 777. Man was made in the image of the Trinity, ibid., 368. The works of God are common to the whole Trinity, ibid., 300. The Catholic faith concerning the Trinity, ibid., 719, 720. In the Trinity there are certain properties proper to the persons, ibid., 574. “Hold most firmly and do not doubt in any way that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are by nature one God,” ibid., 694. What are the proper attributes of the individual persons of the Trinity, ibid., 759.

On the essence of the Trinity; the same author, LXVII, 908. — On the meanings of “Trinity”; Junilius Africanus, LXVIII, 21. — The mystery of the Holy Trinity explained; Cassiodorus, LXX, 367, 511, 590. The teaching of the Catholic Church concerning the Trinity, ibid., 23, 397. The Scriptures transmit knowledge of the Holy Trinity, ibid., 1131. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one principle, ibid., 794. — The Unity of the Trinity demonstrated in Scripture; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 515 ff. The fathers of the Old Testament did not openly preach the mystery of the Trinity, ibid., 979. — God is Trinity; St. Columbanus, abbot, LXXX, 230. — On faith in the Trinity; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 913, 1227. Profession of faith of the Council of Nicaea concerning the Trinity; the same author, LXXXIV, 98. That the Trinity is to be believed and preached, ibid., 184. — That we may believe, worship, and confess the Trinity in persons and unity in substance; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 587. — On the Unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of Unity; Alcuin, CI, 14. — Faith is that by which we believe in one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 269. — Whence the Trinity is so called, and what it is; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 26. All Scripture of the Old and New Testament, divinely inspired . . . intimates that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, ibid., 26. — We believe most firmly that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are by nature one God, ibid. On faith in the Holy Trinity: how it is to be held by priests and preached; Rodulphus of Bourges, CXIX, 704. — Great and incomprehensible is the mystery of the Holy Trinity; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1036. — On the essence of the Trinity, that is, on the distinction of persons and unity of substance; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 19. How the persons are distinguished in the Trinity, ibid., 27. — How the mystery of the most sacred Trinity shines forth in the image of the sun; Othlo of St. Emmeram, CXLVI, 247. Guitmund’s confession concerning the Holy Trinity; the same author, CXLIX, 1495. — On the unity and Trinity of the most holy Godhead; Guitmund of Aversa, CXLIX, 1495. — What faith in the Trinity is common to Latins and Greeks; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 285. How indivisible unity and unassociated plurality agree in God, ibid., 288. It benefits every person to believe in threefold unity and one Trinity, ibid., 221. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet there are not three gods, but one God, ibid., 278. — What the Catholic writers have judged to be the proper attributes of the divine Trinity; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 60. Three persons in God, ibid., 68. — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 172. On the Holy Trinity, ibid., 973. If Moses had written nothing further, this alone which is written at the beginning of this book could suffice for the affirmation of our faith: that we ought to worship one God in three persons, ibid., 975. The person of the Father is one thing, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, ibid., 976. These three persons are not three gods, but Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, ibid., 976. For God, the Word of God, and the Spirit of God are three persons and one God, ibid., 983. — Clearly, the Father is principle, the Son is principle, and the Holy Spirit is principle. Yet there are not three principles but one principle, just as there are not three gods but one God; Rupert, CLXIX, 18. — On the Trinity; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1076. On the various names distinguishing the persons of the Trinity by their properties, ibid., 1078. On the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ibid., 1080. On the distinction of the persons of the most holy Trinity through particular determinations, ibid., 1082. Whether the properties of the persons are the persons themselves, ibid., 1085. — How God is one and three, demonstrated by comparison with the sun; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1109. How the Trinity is understood to be one God, ibid., 1010. On the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ibid., 1111. — On the distinction within the Trinity; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 50. On the names distinguishing the persons of the Trinity, ibid., 52. [Col. 0023] On the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ibid., 54. That nothing concerning the Holy Trinity is said accidentally, ibid., 55. — The same substance, altogether simple and indivisible, which is the Father is also the Son and the Holy Spirit; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1057. When Moses was treating of the creation of the whole world, he mentioned God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit immediately in the very opening of Genesis, ibid., 990. Certain works are specially attributed to one person, although the works of the whole Trinity are proclaimed indivisible, ibid., 992. That the sum of faith lies in divine unity and Trinity, ibid., 1698. He shows what he himself thinks concerning unity and Trinity, and defends it by reason and authority, ibid., 1699. Some things are customarily held to belong to one person and not another; some things are said of one and understood of all, ibid., 1702. He proves that philosophers were not without salvation or knowledge of the Trinity, ibid., 1712. — That God is both simple and threefold; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 797. That no inequality whatsoever is to be admitted in the Trinity, but complete equality, ibid., 1057. He recounts and refutes Abelard’s impious doctrines concerning the Holy Trinity, ibid., 1055. — On the mystery of Trinity and Unity; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 525. How the trace of the Trinity appears in creatures, ibid., 530. How the image of the Trinity is in the soul, ibid. On the distinction of the three persons, ibid., 546. On the equality of the three persons, ibid., 573. — On the most holy Trinity; Master Baudinus, CXCII, 972 ff. On the equality of the three persons, ibid., 997. Whether the properties of the persons are the persons themselves or God, ibid., 1011. — How, from consideration of the property of shared love alone, a trace of the Trinity may be perceived; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 927. That supreme equality exists in that Trinity, ibid., 928. On the three appropriations to persons in the Trinity, ibid., 991.

That a person should never forget fervently to invoke one God in three persons; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 449. The true faith is that one God in the Trinity of persons, and that same Trinity in one God, should be gloriously honored, ibid., 1069, 1070. — In the unity of the divine substance there are three persons, or hypostases: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Walter the theologian, CCIX, 577. The mystery of the Trinity is explained by the likeness of the human soul, ibid., 584. — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equal in power and nature; Alan of Lille, CCX, 604. The Trinity of persons is the unity of the Godhead, ibid. The works of the Trinity are indivisible, ibid., 650. — The manifold distinction of persons in the Trinity; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 875. On this name, “Trinity,” ibid., 919.

## II. On God the Father

A Father must have a Son in order to be Father; Tertullian, II, 165. The Father is the whole substance; the Son, however, is a derivation and portion of him, ibid., 164. — That God is Father of the Word; Constantine the Great, VIII, 405. — It is proper to the Father to be unbegotten; St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 102. — The Father begot in himself another from himself, namely from that unbegotten substance of his; St. Zeno, XI, 395. The Father rejoices in the Son, shining forth in one original co-eternity with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 392. — “Father” is the proper name of one who begets; St. Ambrose, XVI, 563. Father and Son are one, not by confusion of person but by unity of nature, ibid., 531. — Therefore God must be believed to be the Father of his only Son, our Lord, not investigated; Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 341. — Therefore that which is neither born nor made is the Father; St. Ambrose, XVII, 512. — The Father always begets, and the Son is always born; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1047. The Father himself is wisdom; the same author, XLII, 936. The Father is light, the Son is light, the Holy Spirit is light, ibid., 939. In what respect God the Father is greater than the Son, ibid., 746.

Father is principle and Son is principle, but not two principles; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 318. — The eternal Father has an eternal Son; Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 979, 1000. — The Father of truth, that is, the origin of the Son; Eugyppius, LXII, 745. The person of the Father is prior, ibid., 709, 710. — The Father is God; Boethius, LXIV, 1249. The Father is the principle of generation, ibid., 89. — God the Father is not the author of the Trinity, but of the Son and Holy Spirit; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 821, 822. — We believe in one God, the almighty Father; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 139. — When asked about the Father, answer, “God.” When asked about the Son, answer, “God”; Alcuin, CI, 15. The Father is not God without the Son, ibid., 17. The Father is not God from God, nor light from light, ibid. It is necessary to believe that the Father is full and perfect God, ibid., 18. The Father is one, and the Son another; nevertheless, the substance of Father and Son is not different, ibid., 19. God did not make the Son, but begot him from his own substance, equal to himself, ibid., 32. As the Father is life, so also the Son is life, ibid., 33. We do not say that the Father is from the Son, as the Son is from the Father; indeed, the Father is from no one, [Col. 0024] ibid., 1055. The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeding, ibid., 1060. God the Father from himself ineffably and without beginning begot the Son, ibid., 1061. — He could not have been Father eternally if he had not had the Son eternally; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 21. It must be believed without any doubt that the Father is full and perfect God, ibid., 22. — The person of the Father is God; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 266. The Father is father, begetter, and unbegotten, ibid., 269. — The question is asked whether the Father begot the essence; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 535. Whether the Father begot the Son by will or necessity, and whether God is unwilling or willing, ibid., 539.

## III. On God the Son

The Son of God is true God, to whom all the names of the true God are attributed: Tertullian, I, 399, 404, 415; II, 161, 176, 183, 422, 802. He is like and equal to his eternal Father, most high and almighty, ibid. He came forth from the Father as a ray from the sun and a stream from a fountain, the same author, II, 163. — The Son is one person and the Father another; Novatian, III, 936. — The Word is consubstantial with the Father; Pope Dionysius, V, 109. The Word was not formed or made, but begotten from all eternity, ibid. — That the Son is not a God distinct from the Father; Lactantius, VI, 538. — The Son is not inferior to the Father in time or nature; St. Hilary, X, 32. The Son’s Godhead is established from Hosea, ibid., 122; from Isaiah, ibid., 123. The Son of God is neither an emanation nor a part of the Father, ibid., 496. He is said to be begotten from the womb in order to show that he was born from the Father’s substance, ibid., 168. He is from the Father’s substance and within the Father’s substance, the same author, IX, 936. The Son is Son in power, substance, Godhead, and generation, ibid., 809. The Son is one with the Father, not merely in unity of will but also of power, ibid., IX, 801. — The Son of God is proclaimed God, equal to the Father; St. Zeno, XI, 385, 394, 403. — That the Son of God is almighty, and that the omnipotence of Father and Son is one, as their Godhead is one: Faustinus and Marcellinus, XIII, 62. — “If anyone shall not say that the Word of the Lord, the Son of God, is God like his Father”; Pope St. Damasus, ibid., 361. We believe in the Son, who is not the Father but has a Father from whom he is begotten, not made, ibid., 1049. — The eternity and Godhead of the Word are established from the opening words of John’s Gospel; St. Ambrose, XVI, 821. By various arguments it is proved that the Son of God is true God, ibid., XV, 553. In Father and Son there is no distance of Godhead, but one majesty; the same author, XVI, 575. The Son of God possesses immortality by nature and substance, not by temporal grace but by everlasting Godhead, ibid., 656. The Son possesses all that the Father possesses: eternity, majesty, Godhead, and so forth, ibid., 567. The foundation of our faith is this: the Son of God is begotten, ibid., 561. The Son comes forth from the Father as God from God, ibid., 778. The Son is Son without beginning, the same author, XVII, 512. There was no time when the Son existed without the Father, ibid., 516. We confess that the Son of God the Father—only Son of the Most High and only God—is one God with the Father and Holy Spirit, ibid., 522. — The Father is not without the Son; Phoebadius, XX, 24. — The everlasting generation of the Son of God is to be understood in these words: “Today I have begotten you”; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 71. The Son of God is God, the same author, XL, 628, 640. — The Word of God is God, not a creature; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 289. — The Son has Godhead equal with the Father; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 769. — It is proved in many ways that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 354. — The Son is God; Boethius, LXIV, 1249. — That the Son is God equal to the Father; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 749. The Son is called true God in such a way that the Father is not called truer God, ibid., 366. — The Son is the radiance of light and a spotless mirror; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 702. — The Son is consubstantial with the Father; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 379.

## IV. On the Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Holy Trinity: Tertullian, II, 163. The third name of the Godhead and third rank of majesty, ibid., 196. He is of the same nature as the Father and Son, ibid. — Belief in the Holy Spirit; Novatian, III, 943. — The Holy Spirit is not a part of the Father or Son; St. Hilary, X, 519. He receives from the Father and the Son, ibid., 656. — The Holy Spirit has one substance, power, Godhead, majesty, and will with the Father and Son: St. Zeno, XI, 428. — On the Holy Spirit: Faustinus, XIII, 76. — The Holy Spirit is called Lord; St. Ambrose, XVI, 747. It is proved that the Holy Spirit has all that God has, ibid., 810. By various arguments it is proved that the Holy Spirit is neither a creature nor mutable, ibid., 719. The Holy Spirit knows all things and has one knowledge with the Father and Son, ibid., 767. The operation of the Father and Holy Spirit is the same, ibid., 772. The Holy Spirit, like Father and Son, is creator [Col. 0025] of all things, the same author, 749, 755. The Holy Spirit is proved to be God, XVII, 200, 1004. From eternity he proceeds inseparably from Father and Son, the same author, 674, 947, 1015. — The Holy Spirit is not a creature; St. Jerome, XXIII, 106. The Holy Spirit is the third person distinct from Father and Son, ibid., XXVI, 274; St. Augustine, XLI, 337, 338. — The Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father is God; St. Augustine, XXXII, 1321; XXXVIII, 1071; XL, 258, 634; XLII, 697, 722, 742, 752. The Godhead of the Holy Spirit is established, XXXIII, 1046. — The Holy Spirit is consubstantial and coeternal with Father and Son, XXXV, 1816; XLII, 928. — The Father gave the Holy Spirit life to proceed from the Son as he proceeds from himself; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 489. — The Godhead and nature of the Holy Spirit explained; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 401, 404, 412. The Holy Spirit is from the Father truly, properly, and from the divine substance, and is true God, LVI, 689. — One must not doubt that the Holy Spirit is God, since his glory with Father and Son is inseparable; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 637.
