# XXXI. INDEX CONCERNING DIVINE PROVIDENCE AND ITS BENEFITS TOWARD HUMAN BEINGS, SETTING OUT IN LOGICAL ORDER THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING IT

## IX. On the existence of Providence

God’s providence was acknowledged by Plato and the Platonists, and denied by Epicurus and his followers; Tertullian, I, 517. God is governor of the whole world; the same author, II, 599. — That the world was created by God and is ruled and governed by him; Minucius Felix, III, 284. — God, Lord and ruler of the world, and all things are governed by his will and command; St. Cyprian, IV, 548. Nothing can happen except what God has either done or permitted to be done, ibid. — On Providence; Lactantius, VI, 293, 740. The providence of God shines forth from the arrangement of natural things, ibid., 743, 746. On the creation of man and the arrangement of the world, ibid., 749. On the origin of the world, the nature of things, and God’s providence; the same author, VII, 100. — God’s providence is established from the order and arrangement of natural things; Constantine the Great, VIII, 416. — The things in which God’s providence and goodness are signified; St. Hilary, IX, 872. Against those who deny God’s providence, ibid., 856. — God cares for and watches over human beings; St. Ambrose, XIV, 487. Testimonies to God’s providence, ibid., XIV, 1473. God’s providence toward human beings; the same author, XIV, 216, 217. Some philosophers wrongly denied it, ibid., 407. — An objection against divine providence, derived from the fact that the wicked and the good alike experience tribulations, is resolved; St. Gaudentius, XX, 840 ff. — Providence is attacked on account of the apparent disorder of the world, the prosperity of the ungodly, and the adversity of the righteous; Zacchaeus, XX, 1104. It is defended, ibid. Another objection is drawn from infants ignorant of evil yet afflicted by different evils, ibid., 1105. — Not all things happen by chance, nor does varying fortune play among human affairs; rather, all things occur by God’s judgment; St. Jerome, XXIII, 1083. All things are done by God for the benefit of human beings and are not arranged apart from his will, ibid., 1075. God commanded the elements to serve human use, so that, seeing these things, people might understand that providence exists, ibid., 1039. Those ignorant of the truth are not ignorant of providence, the same author, XXV, 1125. God’s providence is established, the same author, XXV, 1286. Those who deny providence are reproved, ibid., 1351. — Some deny providence; St. Augustine, XXXII, 1273. Others, in a wicked error, believe that God’s providence is either weak, unjust, or evil, ibid. All things are ruled by divine providence; the same author, XXXIV, 977. Arguments for divine providence, ibid., 337. The twofold operation of providence, ibid., 379. Whatever occurs occurs by the order and laws of providence, the same author, XXXVII, 1946. No sea is so deep as this thought of God: that the wicked flourish and the good suffer; the same author, XXXVII, 1176. The governance of things belongs to God, the same author, XXXVIII, 318. The Epicureans denied, while the Stoics maintained, that human affairs belong to the care of the gods, the same author, XLI, 601. — That nothing occurs in this world without God; Cassian, XLIX, 582. — God’s providence is attacked because of the apparent disorder of this world; Fastidius, L, 385. Examples establishing God’s providence, ibid., 388, 390 ff. — God arranged all things as he willed, yet wisely; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 619. God rules without weariness the world which he created, ibid., 622. — On the governance of God; St. Salvian, LIII, 30 ff. — God has always provided for the human race; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 203. — God’s providence is established; Eugyppius, LXII, 765. — What providence is; Boethius, LXIII, 814. — On matters belonging to the governance of the world; Junilius, LXVIII, 28; Primasius of Hadrumetum, ibid., 688. — Nothing happens to human beings without God’s counsel, although it is hidden; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 986. Providence is described with particular excellence, ibid., 1126. — Divine providence administers all things in a most certain order; Bede the Venerable, XCI, 84. — God’s providence demonstrated from the order of the world; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 1121. — All things subsist in God and are governed by him; St. Prudentius of Troyes, CXV, 998. We in no way doubt that by God’s eternal providence and most omnipotent foreknowledge all things are ordered, arranged, administered, destined, ruled, and governed in ways fitting to each, ibid., 1021. — All things are immovably subject to eternal ordination; St. Remigius of Lyons, CXXI, 993. On God’s eternal providence, ibid., 1098. — On God’s providence; [Col. 0028] St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 605. — All things are ruled by none other than God; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 222. God has care for all things, ibid., 857. All things are subject to God’s ordering, ibid., 525. — On God’s providence; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 979. That God disposes all things and considers the end of all, ibid., 981. — Providence defined; Honorius, CLXXII, 1139. Established, ibid., 1136. — God’s providence is twofold: toward his own and toward others; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 218. — On divine providence; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 590. All things are ruled by divine providence; the same author, CLXXXIV, 28, 29. — On divine providence: Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 146; Robert Pullen, ibid., 714; John Barest, the same author, CXCIX, 444, 446.

## II. On the object of divine Providence, or Providence in the temporal and spiritual order

At God’s command all things are set in motion: springs gush forth, rivers flow, waves rise, all things bring forth their offspring, winds are compelled to blow, and so forth; Novatian, III, 898 ff. God’s providence operates not only with individual human beings, but also through cities themselves and states, indeed through the whole world, ibid. — The world is governed by God’s providence; Minucius, III, 284. — A marvelous reason governs the world and all its parts, as we see; Lactantius, VI, 745. — God cares for and watches over human beings; St. Ambrose, XIV, 847. Whatever is observed in rational or even irrational living creatures is ascribed to divine providence; the same author, XV, 1472 ff. All birds of the sky neither sow nor reap, and God feeds them, ibid. He who feeds birds—would he not feed human beings, whom he made in his own image and likeness? ibid. — God’s providence governs this world; St. Gaudentius, XX, 840. — God governs all things; St. Jerome, XXIII, 499. God has care for all nations, the same author, 1005. The order of God’s providence, dispensing every kind by an ineffable judgment; the same author, XXIV, 189. God’s providence extends even through human beings individually; the same author, XXV, 1286. — Divine providence reaches to each individual; St. Augustine, XL, 37. God’s providence extends to humanity, to lower things, and even to the least things; the same author, XXXII, 978; XXXVII, 1446, 1892, 1943. There would be no justice among human beings if God did not care for human affairs, the same author, XL, 38. God has care for all, especially for the righteous, the same author, XXXVII, 450, 456. The hidden administration of God, by which he also gives growth to trees and herbs, the same author, XXXIV, 379. God’s providence in the governance of things and the ordering of evils, the same author, XXXVIII, 318, 692. — Divine providence administers all things in a most certain order; Bede, XCI, 84. God’s care for all things, the same author, XCII, 35. — God creates all things, gives life to all things, and governs all things; Alcuin, C, 565. — God’s care for human beings and all creatures; Haimo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 687, 688. What God’s providence has determined concerning humanity, the same author, 736. — It is proved that the whole world is ruled by God’s providence; Ratramnus, CXXI, ibid. — All things are ruled and governed by God; Atto, CXXXIV, 248. — God governs heavenly and earthly things; St. Bruno of Segni, CLIII, 235. — God’s providence toward all created things; St. Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1312. — God’s great care for all creatures; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1499. — Divine providence governs all things; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 28, 29. Human conduct is subject to divine providence; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 337. God crowns some and condemns others; he never errs. He tests some and approves others; he orders all, the same author, XXXVIII, 118. As good, he creates all natures; as just, he orders all wills, the same author, XXXIV, 380. — God’s providence, ruling and administering the whole creation, both natures and wills, and so forth; Eugyppius, LXII, 649.

## III. On errors concerning divine Providence
Those who have denied divine providence: Lactantius, VI, 740.---Many people attribute the distinctions and adornments of all things to nature; others assign them to fate or to chance occurrence: Constantine the Great, VIII, 412.---Many deny that God takes care of human actions: St. Hilary, IX, 856.---Divine providence is denied by certain philosophers: St. Ambrose, XIV, 268. Some deny providence: St. Augustine, XXXII, 1272. Some acknowledge it in a thoroughly perverse manner, ibid.---The Epicureans deny that God cares for human affairs, XLII, 376.---For there was an error of certain persons: that God governs only heavenly things, while earthly things are turned about by the mere chance of fortune: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 235.

IV.---Works Treating of Providence.

All things are governed at the nod of the one God: Minucius Felix, III, 284, 297; Novatian, III, 898.---On Divine Providence: Lactantius, VI, 120, 1019, 1036; VII, 100.---A metrical discourse on God’s providence: Decius Ausonius, XIX, 839.---On God’s providence: St. Jerome, XXII, 802.---All things are governed by divine Providence: St. Augustine, XXXII, 977; XXXIV, 336, 379. # XXXII. GENERAL INDEX OF CREATION, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER WHATEVER THE HOLY FATHERS HAVE SAID CONCERNING BEINGS CREATED IN THE BEGINNING.

## NOTICE.

In this Index, following the order of creation, we shall in turn set forth: I, what it is to create and what is the nature of creatures; II, whose work creation is; III, what philosophers’ opinions concerning creation have been; IV, the creation of angels; V, the creation of light, or the first day of creation; VI, the second day, or the creation of the firmament; VII, the work of the third day; VIII, the fourth day, or the creation of the sun, moon, and stars; IX, the creation of birds and fishes, or the fifth day; X, the sixth day, or the creation of beasts; XI, the seventh day.

## [GENERAL INDEX OF CREATION.]

### What it is to create, and concerning the nature of a creature.

How creation and birth differ: St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 493 ff.---Things created from nothing have within themselves the necessity of not existing, idem, IX, 1057.---What *creatio* means among Greeks and Latins: St. Jerome, XXVI, 509. How creation and possession differ, idem, 471.---To create and to found are the same thing: St. Augustine, XL, 184. In Scripture, “to create,” “to found,” “to establish,” and “to make” are used interchangeably and in one and the same sense: St. Augustine, XLII, 632, 633. No creature can create: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 602. Men therefore cannot fashion anything out of nothing, because they work through a body: St. Augustine, XL, 90. By “to create” we mean to institute something new, so that what did not exist is seen to come into being: Cassiodorus, LXX, 365. What the difference is between making and creating: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1044. What it is to create: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 202; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 734; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1029.

Every creature is bounded by the limits of its own nature: St. Ambrose, XVI, 723. Every creature is mutable, ibid., 720; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 687.---What is a creature? Augustine, XLII, 1162. Every created thing is from nothing, and, as it were, not from nothing, idem, XL, 1018. Of itself it always tends toward nothingness, idem, XLII, 1162. Whatever creatures are, they are life in God, idem, XXXV, 1387; XXIV, 332. Before all things were made, they existed in the knowledge of their Maker, idem, XXXIV, 332. How creatures existed in God’s wisdom before creation, idem, XLII, 674. All creatures are in God’s Word, idem, XXXV, 1674.---How creatures existed in God before they were made: Alcuin, C, 745, 746. A creature was made not from God’s nature but from nothing, idem, XXXIV, 247. To have been made from nothing is the same as not being God’s nature, idem, XLV, 1479. Creatures possess within themselves the limit of their nature, whereby they are not what God is, idem, XXXIV, 309. A creature is neither consubstantial nor coeternal with God, ibid., 247.---Paul shows that a creature is neither alien to God nor nevertheless of the same substance as he: St. Augustine, XLII, 583. Created things and the Creator do not have one nature, idem, XL, 761, 773.---No creature has anything from itself: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 325. Creatures do not possess simple and absolute being, ibid., 184. Creatures are said to exist not simply and absolutely, but scarcely, ibid., 181.---The causes of all creatures existed eternally in God: Hildebert, CLXXI, 1120.---Every creature of God is good: St. Jerome, XXII, 729. Creatures were created good by God [Col. 0030]: St. Jerome, XXII, 503.---How all creatures are good: St. Augustine, XLII, 580, 593, 538, 743; XXIV, 32; XLV, 1537.---No nature of creatures is evil: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 683; Gennadius, LVIII, 995, 1035.---Everything created is good: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 883.---That creatures were created good by the good God: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 348.---Every creature, by the nature proper to it, can be subject to sin: St. Ambrose, XVI, 731.---The lowliness of creatures is demonstrated, that the incomparable sublimity of God may appear: St. Jerome, XXII, 806. Every creature, except God, is subject to defect: St. Jerome, XXIII, 333.---Of itself, a creature always tends toward nothingness: St. Augustine, XLII, 1162.---What has been made from nothing hangs upon nothing: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1033. In comparison with God, creatures are as though they were not, idem, LXXV, 1144. Whatever in created things is compared with God becomes empty and nothing, idem, LXXVI, 751.---A creature, in relation to God, is nothing and does not possess immortality: Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 807.

## II.---Whose work creation is, and concerning the motive of creation.

The Word through whom all things were created: St. Victorinus the martyr, V, 311; Faustinus, XIII, 41.---How creation belongs jointly to the Father and the Son: St. Hilary the bishop, X, 112. All things were created with the Father speaking and the Son making, idem, IX, 880. God created all things in the Son, and afterward brought forth each thing at will from the treasures stored within himself, ibid., 496. Created things testify to the greatness of their Creator, ibid., 563. All the world’s creations testify to God’s magnificence by the unchangeable ordering of their respective functions, ibid., 580.---Every creature exists from the will, through the operation, and in the power of the Trinity: St. Ambrose, XVI, 764.---All creatures have from God their being: St. Jerome, XXVI, 488.---God made the whole creation not through any creature, but alone: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1758. The creature cries out from every side, “God made me,” idem, XXXVI, 205. Creatures cry, “He made us”; their cry is their form, idem, XXXII, 783. All creatures were made by God through his Son, idem, XLII, 579. The Father’s command that all things be made is nothing other than the Father’s Word, through whom all things were made, ibid., 685. Why, in the creation narrative, the Son is mentioned sometimes as Principle and sometimes as Word, idem, XXXIV, 248. The opinion of certain people is refuted: that God made all things by the Word, but made man, as more excellent than the rest, with his own hands: XXXVI, 158. God established the whole creation through the Son in the unity of the Holy Spirit: XXXIII, 221, 241. The creation of the world is the work of the whole Trinity: XLII, 129. Every creature receives being, form, and order from the creating Trinity: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 129. In the creature are traces of the Trinity, XLI, 342. The Holy Trinity is indicated in the beginning and completion of the creature: XXXIV, 251. The beginning of spiritual creation and eternal wisdom, XXXIV, 250. Creatures are traces and signs of God: XXXII, 1264. All God’s works bear witness to God’s goodness and greatness: XXXVII, 1580.---God alone is Creator, not the angels, although they apply their operation to things generated in the world: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 447. It has always been known to all that God is the author of all things and that he wisely ordered everything as he willed: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 619.---Creation and our re-creation are from the whole Trinity: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 616.---God formed all things from nothing by the almighty power of his Word: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 238.---The creation and government of the whole world are to be ascribed to God: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 229.---Creation and sanctification are from the Holy Spirit: Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 314. It may be understood that God made heaven and earth in his only-begotten Son: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 13. How all things are from God: Lanfranc, CL, 144. God made from nothing all things that are: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 805. God made all things from nothing by his will alone: idem, 224, 445, 780. Creatures are most clear signs of God: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 204. Every creature was both made through the Son and re-formed through him: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1573. In creating heaven and earth and their adornment, the Trinity had no model other than itself: idem, CLXVII, 199. In creatures are signs of the Trinity and of its attributes: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1084. The one principle of all things that exist, move, and live is God: Ernald, abbot, CLXXXIX, 1515. All created things are from the Father, and yet through the Son: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1605. All things were created through Christ: CXCII, 264. The greatness of creatures demonstrates God’s immensity: Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 800.

The sole cause of things to be made was God’s mercy: St. Hilary, IX, 772. God established created things not for his own benefit, but for that of creatures, idem, 269. God created all creatures from his goodness alone, not from need: St. Augustine, XXXII, 845. Why God willed to make the world, XL, 18. There is no other cause of the world’s creation than that good things should be made by the good God, XLI, 334. Plato acknowledged this, ibid., 336. For what purpose the world was made: Lanfranc, CL, 167. Matter was created for the praise of God and the benefit of man: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 33. The benefit of creation is considered: St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 239. Why and how God created the world: Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 771.

## III.---Opinions of philosophers concerning creation.

Philosophers maintain that this world is unbegotten and unmade: Tertullian, II, 809. They maintain that the universe consists of contraries: Tertullian, II, 657. Pythagoras said that the world was uncreated: Tertullian, I, 333. According to Simon Magus, it was established by angels: Tertullian, II, 62, 708. Plato taught that the world was made by God: Tertullian, I, 333; II, 1033, 667. The Stoics hold that matter flowed forth through God as honey through honeycombs: Tertullian, II, 236.---Various opinions of philosophers concerning the world: Arnobius, V, 824, 865, 898.---Aristotle believed the world eternal: Lactantius, VI, 315, 735. The error of the ancients concerning the eternity of chaos: Lactantius, VI, 297. Cicero’s opinion concerning the creation of the world, ibid., 121. Democritus asserted that all things came about by chance: Lactantius, VI, 120, 760. Epicurus’s opinion concerning the world’s creation: Lactantius, VI, 120. Heraclitus says that all things were born from fire: Lactantius, VI, 309. Plato acknowledged that the world was generated: Lactantius, VI, 755. Thales said that water was the principle of all things: Lactantius, VI, 133.---Some assert that the world was formed by chance movements: St. Hilary, IX, 251. Those who suppose the world to arise either from a chance concurrence or from God are refuted: St. Hilary, IX, 880.---Those who asserted that the world was constituted and adorned by God from pre-existing matter: St. Zeno, XI, 390, note 1.---Aristotle posits two principles of things, matter and form, and a third alongside them called the efficient principle: St. Ambrose, XIV, 123. Plato believes the world to be incorruptible and neither created nor made: St. Ambrose, XIV, 123. What other philosophers thought concerning it, ibid. Thales said that all things consist of water, idem, 125. Most pagans wish the world to be coeternal with God, as though it were a shadowy image of divine power: St. Ambrose, [Col. 0032] XIV, 131. A reply to those who attempt to establish the eternity of matter from the words of Scripture: St. Ambrose, XIV, 135. Most people said that the world was ungenerated: St. Ambrose, XIV, 841.---The Platonists believed the world to have been made and yet to exist from eternity: St. Augustine, XLI, 311, 319, 320, 359. Epicurus imagined innumerable worlds to be generated and dissolved by chance movements of atoms: St. Augustine, XLI, 320. Various and conflicting opinions of philosophers concerning the world’s unity, beginning, and so forth: idem, 601. Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Simon Magus, Menander, and Saturninus asserted that the world was not made by God: St. Augustine, XLII, 26.---The Priscillianists maintain that the world was made by an evil ruler, XLII, 44. How and from what the world was fashioned according to the Manichaeans, XLII, 113. The Seleucians hold that the matter of the elements from which the world was made was not made by God but is coeternal with God, XLII, 41.---The Priscillianists believed that the world was made last so that souls which had previously sinned might be cleansed, XLII, 668, 674, 675.---The pagans believed that the world was made by God but administered by gods whom God had made: XLI, 318.---Various opinions concerning the origin of the world: XXXV, 2316.---Against those who dare to assert that matter is coeternal with God: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 380.---The errors of philosophers who held that the world was never created or would never end are properly overthrown: Cassiodorus, LXX, 717.---Philosophers’ opinions concerning the creation of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 443; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 53.---Philosophers posit three principles: God, matter, and archetypal ideas: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 33. Plato said that there are three principles: matter, form, and artificer, CLXXVI, 79.---The first chapter of Genesis abolishes and confounds everything philosophers thought concerning the world: Ernald, abbot, CLXXXIX, 1515.---For Plato there are three principles; for Aristotle, three principles concerning the creation of the world: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1027.---Plato knew that God created all things: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 314.

## IV.---On the Creation of Heaven and Earth . . . What the Days of Creation Were Like . . . The Creation of Angels.

Whether the world was made from eternal matter: Lactantius, VI, 124, 297, 926. The world as a divine fabric, idem, 307.---God prepared the world from eternity simultaneously and all at once: St. Hilary, X, 458.---Moses’ view concerning the beginning of things, the author of the world, and the creation of matter: St. Ambrose, XIV, 124. The world has its beginning from God, idem, 126. A reply to those who try to establish the eternity of matter from the words of Scripture: idem, 135.---Verse 1 of Genesis chapter 1 is defended against detractors who ask what God was doing before the world’s creation and why he suddenly resolved to create the world: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 174; XXXII, 815.---On the creation of heaven and earth: Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 748; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 443.---On prime matter: when, where, and of what kind it was created: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 34.---In what “beginning” God is to be understood as having made heaven and earth: St. Ambrose, XIV, 127, 130; St. Jerome, XXIII, 937; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 174, 247; Bede, XCI, 13; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 443; Walafrid Strabo, XCIII, 68; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 54; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 253, 255; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1029.

The measure of one day is a period of twenty-four hours: St. Ambrose, XIV, 144.---What the days and nights of creation are: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 231. It is impossible to conceive the first days of the world’s creation, much less to speak of them: St. Augustine, XLI, 322. How one day was completed both in creation and after the creation of light, XXXIV, 253. How day and night could have existed before the creation of the sun, XXXIV, 231, 275. It is not proved that day and night before the creation of the sun were produced by the emission and contraction of light, XXXIV, 258. How day, evening, and morning should be understood in the history of creation, XXXIV, 314, 317. All things were made simultaneously, yet were nevertheless made through six days, XXXIV, 319. How the six days of creation are to be understood, XXXIV, 295, 309, 314, 323, 338; XLI, 322.---In what sense God is said to have created all things simultaneously: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 614.---How creation was made over several days, ibid. And thus one day, namely twenty-four hours, was completed: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 18.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 449.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 71. What those six days of creation signify: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 57, 58; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 160.---Whether, if all these things were made in one day, they were made over six days: Wicbodus, XCVI, 1137.---Evening is the end of the day, while morning is the end of the night; joined together, these two make twenty-four hours and complete one day: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 255.---Some say that God made everything whatsoever simultaneously; others distinguish the work over six days and say that this distinction is figurative: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 33. Though God could make everything in a moment, he distinguished his works over six days, not because of his own lack of power, but for the instruction and example of rational creatures: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 33. Yet it seems to some that those distinctions of things were made not at intervals of time but simultaneously: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 89. Over six days the kinds of things were distinguished from that matter: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 90.---It is therefore clear that God worked, according to Moses, for six days upon everything contained within heaven’s circuit, not that it might be well with himself, but that others might share in his goodness: Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 717.---They say that the interval between one work and another was as great as that contained in the spaces of six days: Ernald, abbot, CLXXXIX, 1517.---This was not made all at once, as some Fathers seem to hand down, but through the successive courses of six days, as the Catholic faith maintains: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1040.---Whether God completed the works of the six days simultaneously or successively: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1.

But God created angels and archangels before he formed man, preferring spiritual things to earthly things: St. Victorinus the martyr, V, 305. Yet God completed his works before he created angels and fashioned man, lest perhaps they might falsely assert that they had been his helpers: St. Victorinus the martyr, V, 306.---Angels were created before times and ages: St. Hilary, X, 612.---The creation of angels: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 222. It is understood through the light made on the first day, idem, 228. Angels are not coeternal with God, yet they have not undergone the vicissitudes of time, XXXII, 831. Whether angels could always have existed, XLI, 363. When angels were created, XLI, 324, 347. Whether the creation of angels preceded that of the world, XLI, 345. Scripture did not expressly state the creation of angels, XLI, 324. The angelic creature was the first of all things created, XXXIV, 326. Angelic nature is the day first established, XXXIV, 334. How angels were created, or are not coeternal with God, if they are understood to have always existed, XLI, 364. Under what conditions discussion of the creation of angels is permissible, XLI, 345.---Angels were created first among all creatures: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 664. In what sense angel and man were created together, idem, 644.---The angels who were created in the beginning with heaven and earth: Bede the Venerable, XLI, 14; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 445.---On the creation of angels: Wicbodus, XCVI, 1107, 1115, 1118.---God made two things before all time: the angelic creature and unformed matter: Walafrid Strabo, XCIII, 69.---The fiery heaven, which was immediately filled with angelic spirits: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 55.---By the name “heaven” are understood incorporeal beings, such as angels, and all spiritual things not seen by us: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 254. For they themselves were the morning stars which praised God at the creation of the world, idem, CLXXII, 255.---Who knows for how many years or five-year periods the angels praised their Creator before the world? Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 34. On the creation of things, especially of angels: idem, CLXXVI, 79.---God created the angel immediately with heaven, and in heaven: Robert Pullus, CXXXVI, 719.---Before heaven and earth were created, service of angelic brightness was not lacking to the Creator, and that spiritual nature preceded bodily nature in origin: Ernald, abbot, CLXXXIX, 1517.---The time of angelic creation: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1030.---When angelic nature was made: Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 941. Where angelic nature was made, idem, 942. What angelic nature was like when made, idem, 943. What angelic nature was like afterward, idem, 944.

## V. On the Creation of Light, or the First Day of Creation.

In the beginning God made light, and divided it by the twelvefold number of hours into day and night: St. Victorinus the martyr, V, 303.---Light is created; it is separated from darkness and approved; and why light was called day and darkness night: St. Ambrose, XIV, 141.---Created light is twofold, spiritual and bodily: St. Augustine, XLVIII, 405, 611. Various difficulties concerning the light created on the first day, idem, XXXIV, 254. Whether light was the first creature, ibid., 248. What the light made in the beginning was, ibid., 227, 228, and what kind it was, 322. Whether it was bodily or spiritual, ibid., 232, 248. Whether God said, “Let there be light,” temporally or in the eternity of the Word, ibid., 232, 269. Nor is it said, “And so it was made,” ibid., 292, 317. How the division between light and darkness is to be understood, ibid., 228. Whether “Let there be light” was said in time or without time, ibid., 251.---It befits God’s works that he should begin the adornment of the world with light: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 16. In what places light was made, ibid., 17. On the creation of light, idem, XCIII, 209.---Did God say, “Let there be light,” during the day or before every day? Wicbodus, XCVI, 1117. Whether this light is visible or invisible, ibid., 1118. “Light was made,” that is, angelic creation, because then they began to know or understand their Creator, ibid. Why God praised light alone and not night, ibid., 1120. What it is to divide light from darkness, ibid.---What is meant by the words, “God said: Let there be light”: Alcuin, C, 520. Why do we read that light was created on the first day? ibid.---Where light was first commanded to come into being: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 447.---On the creation of light and what sort it was: Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 71; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 55.---What is understood by light: Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 37.---What is this light said to have existed before the sun, moon, and stars? St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 149. The mystical meaning of light, ibid., 151.---That the light which was made is an angelic creature: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 206. That the angelic creature is called light not by resemblance but in reality, ibid., 207.---Light is said to have been created in the place where the sun rises: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 34.---On the creation of light: Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 738.---What sort of light was created on the first day: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1041. Where this light was made, ibid.

## VI.---On the Creation of the Firmament, or the Second Day of Creation.

The firmament is created in order to separate waters from waters: St. Ambrose, XIV, 146. The firmament is not the same as heaven, and it is wrongly denied that real waters remain above it, ibid., 148. “Heaven” is a general name, “firmament” a particular one, ibid., 152.---The waters as divided by the firmament: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 181. The firmament is the same as heaven, ibid., 232. Not every firmament is heaven, ibid., 233. What the firmament of heaven is, ibid., 238. What the firmament in the midst of the waters is. Some deny that waters are above the starry heaven, ibid., 263.---On the creation of the firmament: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 18. What the cause of this division of waters was, ibid., 20. On the second day of creation, idem, XCIII, 210, 249; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1122.---The firmament was made on the second day, and the waters were divided above and below the firmament: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 449; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 72. On the second day God set the firmament, namely the holy Scriptures, in the Church, ibid., 73.---The firmament is created: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 56.---What is the firmament but the strength of the Scriptures? St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 992.---Which is the firmament created by God? St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 151. Whether the upper waters, with the firmament placed between, changed their nature, ibid. What the firmament in the midst of the waters signifies spiritually, ibid.---What the firmament is or of what it consists: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 219. What those waters above the firmament are, ibid. Why God called the firmament heaven, ibid., 224. What the second day is, ibid., 225.---What the firmament created on the second day is: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 35; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 741, 742.---On the distinction of the second day, on which the firmament was made; and of what matter the firmament was made: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1042. Why God was silent concerning the goodness of the things created on the second day, ibid.

## VII.---On the Work of the Third Day.

In the gathering of the waters the figure of the Church is expressed: St. Ambrose, XIV, 155. The earth, previously invisible beneath waters poured over it, appeared when those waters flowed together into one place . . . how wonderful that all waters could be contained in one place and that their boundaries could be fixed for them by God, ibid., 158. How God prepared a place for waters spread throughout the whole world, ibid., 161. Why fodder for cattle was created before food for man, ibid., 167. That harmful things are produced with useful things not without reason, ibid., 171. Seeds never properly degenerate, since not their kind but their perfection is changed, ibid., 173. On the growth of trees, ibid., 175 ff.---How and when trees were created: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 275. They were created on the third day according to rational causes, ibid., 259. A certain heresy said that water was not created by God but was coeternal with him, idem, XLII, 45. It is impiously denied that waters were made by God, idem, XLI, 348. When water was created, idem, XXXIV, 250. The gathering of waters is their formation, ibid., 181, 232. How the waters were gathered, ibid., 255; XLII, 612. On those who think waters were not created, idem, XLI, 347.---On the third day of creation: Bede the Venerable, XCVII, 211, 251; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1125.---On the third day waters are commanded to be separated from the earth, and the earth to sprout: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 451.---On the third day the waters are gathered; the mystical meaning [Col. 0035] of this gathering: Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 75; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 993; Guibert, abbot, CLXI, 44 ff.; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 152. The earth producing green grass and making seed is the Church, and the examples and teaching of the apostles and martyrs, ibid., 153.---On the gathering of the waters: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 226, 227. On what was said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” ibid., 229. On the third day, ibid., 232.---On the third day the waters were gathered into one place: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 35; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 748.---On the distinction of the third day: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1042. Where the waters were gathered, ibid.

## VIII.---On the Creation of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, or the Work of the Fourth Day.

The sun was created by the Son of God: St. Ambrose, XIV, 189. Fruitfulness was bestowed upon the earth by God, not by the sun, ibid. The luminaries were made for signs, but not for nativities, ibid., 192. The greatness of the sun and moon is proved from the fact that they appear alike to all, ibid., 200. Many things said of the sun also apply to the moon, ibid., 202.---Origen’s error concerning the sun, moon, and stars: St. Jerome, XXII, 800.---Of what the luminaries and stars were made: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 265. Why they were made on the fourth day, ibid., 235, 273. How they distinguish between day and night, since God had already divided between light and darkness, ibid., 236. The luminaries dividing night from day allegorically, idem, XXXII, 854. How luminaries and stars serve for seasons and signs, for days and years, idem, XXXIV, 183, 274, 275. What the moon was like when created, ibid., 275. The Manichaeans taught that the sun was made from good fire, idem, XLII, 35. They say that the sun is God and a part of God, ibid., 597. Philosophers say that the sun is everlasting, idem, XXXIII, 379. Why was the sun created if the first light sufficed to make day? idem, XXXIV, 254. It is not surprising that it is larger than the other stars, idem, XXXIII, 80. How the preceding three days could have existed without the sun, when we now see that day passes with the sun’s rising and setting, while night comes to us through the sun’s absence as it returns to the east from another part of the world, idem, XXXIV, 183.---How, if light had preceded, the sun is now said to have been appointed for illumination: Eustathius, LIII, 922. How the sun has dominion over the day, ibid., 931.---The creation of the sun, moon, and stars: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 21 ff. On the fourth day of creation, idem, XCIII, 212; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1127.---The luminaries are commanded to be made, and were made on the fourth day: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 452; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 56.---The luminaries created in heaven: what they signify: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 993; Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 46; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 154.---On the fourth day, on the luminaries, and on the power of the greater luminary: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 232, 234. Why, in saying “and the stars,” God did not add, “and let them be for signs and seasons”; and on the same fourth day, and what the fourth day is, ibid., 238.---On the fourth day God made the sun from the aforesaid light or fire, improving it with form and brightness: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 35.---The sun, moon, and stars are created: Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 751.---On the adornment of the fourth day, when the luminaries were made: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1043.

## IX.---On the Creation of Birds and Fishes, or the Work of the Fifth Day.

A special prerogative is granted to the sea: St. Ambrose, XIV, 205. By the power of the words, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” far more creatures were produced in the sea than on land, ibid., 207. The manifold manner of reproduction among fishes, ibid., 208. Why fishes are so well supplied with teeth, ibid., 210. Particular dwelling places are prescribed for each kind of fish, ibid., 217. On the fishes of the Atlantic Sea; likewise on salt, coral, and certain other things. On account of these, but especially on account of navigation, the sea surpasses the lands, ibid., 220. On the creation of birds, ibid., 224.---How birds are understood to have been created by God from waters: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 183.---On the creation of birds and fishes: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 25 ff. On the fifth day of creation, idem, XCIII, 213, 254; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1128.---On the fifth day animals are commanded to be brought forth from the waters, and the animals themselves are blessed: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 456.---What the fishes and birds created on the fifth day signify: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 993; Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 48 ff.; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 155.---On the fifth day, and what the fifth day is: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 239. On what was said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul,” ibid., 239. Why, when the waters brought forth all birds [Col. 0036], they cannot also live under water, ibid., 240. Why it was not said, “God saw the birds or creeping things, that they were good,” but, “He saw that it was good,” ibid., 244.---On the fifth day fishes and birds were made from waters: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 35; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 756.---On the adornment of the fifth day: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1043.

## X.---On the Sixth Day. Creation of Animals.  
*(The Creation of Man is treated elsewhere.)*
To treat of the nature of beasts: Ambrose approaches the subject, XIV, 243. The law of generation implanted in living creatures by God’s word persists through the succession of species, ibid., 245. On the remarkable instinct of certain animals in avoiding what harms them and pursuing what benefits them, ibid., 247. Why the Lord created some beasts with shorter and others with longer necks, ibid., 253. The strongest and fiercest beasts were subjected to humankind by the Creator; yet the tiniest animals are a terror and destruction to them, ibid., 255.---All animals are subject to humankind because of intellect: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 186. God fashioned the beasts of the field on the sixth day by an operation distinct from that by which he created all things simultaneously, ibid., 342. Why beasts harmful to one another were created, ibid., 289. On the creation of venomous animals, ibid. On the creation of insects, ibid., 288. Why blessing was granted only to aquatic creatures, as it was to humankind, ibid. That beasts now harm humankind is a punishment of the first sin, XLIV, 657, 663. In paradise beasts would neither have died nor been savage, XLV, 1307. The opinion concerning the transformation of beasts into humans and humans into beasts, XXXIV, 445.---On the creation of beasts: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 27; XCIII, 215. Whether venomous animals, when they were first created, possessed venom as they do now, ibid., 256; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1132.---On the earth’s being commanded to bring forth animals on the sixth day: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 458.---What is understood by earth, cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth: Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 51.---Why so many poisonous, deadly things hostile to humankind were created by God: St. Bruno of Signi, LXIV, 156.---Why cattle, or animals of the earth, are assigned to the work of the sixth day together with humankind: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 244. On the threefold kind of cattle, creeping things, and beasts, ibid., 245.---On the sixth day the earth brought forth animals of diverse kinds: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 35; CLXXVI, 89; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 759.---On the adornment of the sixth day: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1043.

XI.---On the seventh day of creation.

On the seventh day God rested from all his works, and blessed and sanctified it: St. Victorinus the martyr, V, 306.---How God is said to have rested: St. Ambrose, XIV, 272.---The rest of the seventh day allegorically understood: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 189. In what sense God is said to rest, ibid., 302. The question whether God himself could properly have rested, ibid., 303. How both propositions are consistent: that God rested on the seventh day and that he continues to work even now, ibid. Another way of reconciling Scripture concerning God’s rest and his continuous operation, ibid., 304. Why God sanctified the day of his rest, ibid., 305. God’s rest from his works on the seventh day, ibid., 306. Why the seventh day had morning but not evening, ibid., 308. Whether the seventh day was created, ibid., 310. Why the seventh day was sanctified by God, id., XXXVIII, 80. The seventh day having no evening, ibid. In what sense God may be understood to have completed his work on the seventh day: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 34. How he is said to have rested, ibid. How God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, ibid., 35. Why God blessed the seventh day, on which he created nothing, id., XCIII, 218; Wicbodus, XCVI, 1136.---How the statement read in Genesis, “God rested on the seventh day,” etc., agrees with that in the Gospel, “My Father is working until now”: St. Julian, XCVI, 599; Alcuin, C, 517.---The completion of the world on the seventh day: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 464.---In what sense God rested on the seventh day: Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 82.---Why God rested on the seventh day: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 59.---As God is read to have rested from his work on the seventh day, so, after their labor, the bodies of the righteous are believed to rest in their tombs and their souls in joy: Honorius of Autun, CLXXVI, 259.---How God is said to have rested on the seventh day and yet to work until now: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 90.---How God is to be understood to have rested: Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1043. How God is to be understood to have completed his work on the seventh day, ibid.

[Col. 0037]

XXXIII. INDEX ON ANGELS, indicating everything the Fathers wrote: I) on their creation; II) on their fidelity, confirmation in grace, and reward in glory; III) on the hierarchy and on the name, nature, and properties of each order; IV) on spirituality, immortality, and other supernatural endowments; V) on their mission from God to humankind; VI) on their functions in heaven and on earth, especially their care and concern for the human race, both in spiritual and temporal matters.

I.---On the creation of angels.

Sacred Scripture has not explicitly set forth their creation. Why Moses was silent concerning it. Opinions are reported concerning its time: whether before, in, or after the words of Genesis, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; whether when he said “Let there be,” or only on the day when he made humankind. Yet all agree on this: that the angelic creature was created first of all. It is shown that both good and evil angels were created, or transferred, in heaven; that they were made in the likeness of God; that they were truly morning stars; that they were in grace, directed toward blessedness, but not yet in blessedness. Their number is unknown to us. Their various designations—such as heaven, firmament, light, mountains, waters, gold, kings, princes, consuls, governors, and so forth—and the explanation of these. Ancient writers, poets, and philosophers, etc., did not deny their existence.

II.---On the fidelity of angels, their confirmation in grace, and their reward in glory.

The angels were created endowed with free choice and a right will. They knew that they could either change this will or persevere in it, and that they would justly be punished if they sinned. Therefore, although all knew what they ought to will or not will, and that they ought not to will what those who transgressed willed, the good angels, more zealous for the justice they possessed than for what they did not possess, and steadfastly remaining in it, merited the firmness of eternal perseverance and a blessedness which they had previously received in a lesser degree. Then, by grace and their own merit—not by nature nor by the misfortune of the wicked—they attained all that they could attain, and were made immutable and confirmed in every good. Thus, recognizing that the saying addressed equally to them applies, “What have you that you did not receive?”, and that they did not possess even their initial uprightness of will from themselves, they merited that they should be unable to will anything else or to cease willing that uprightness. Hence it is clear that God gave angels the ability to abandon justice, so that in a certain manner they might give justice to themselves; and he granted them glory beyond the recompense of their own labor.

III.---On the angelic hierarchy, and the name, nature, and properties of each of its orders.

Angels are not equal among themselves; rather, one differs from another in power and rank, as do the sun, moon, and stars. For there are nine orders of heavenly essences. Their first arrangement consists of Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones; the middle of Dominations, Principalities, and Powers; the last of Virtues, archangels, and angels. That is, all these spirits are distinct in persons, arranged in dignities, and have stood in their order from the beginning. Thus there are among them names, offices, merits, and degrees which we may conjecture and distinguish. We must therefore suppose that angels excel in knowledge of the divine judgments, and that those believed to be assigned individually to individual human beings are called angels; that archangels preside over angels, and, foremost in knowledge of God’s inward counsels and fully aware of the divine mysteries, are sent only for especially great and weighty causes; that above them are Virtues, by whose mighty command or action signs and prodigies, wrought in or from the elements, appear for the admonition of mortals; that Powers are superior to these, by whose strength the tyrannical malice of demons is cast down, repressed, and rendered ineffectual, and the malignity of this air is restrained, so that it may not harm as much as it wishes and may not work evil except so as to benefit; that Principalities are set over these also, by whose governance and wisdom authority, dominion on earth, the rights of kingdoms, and the heights of dignities are, at the will of the Almighty, established, apportioned, ruled, bounded, transferred, curtailed, and changed; that Dominations so surpass all the foregoing orders that, in comparison with them, all the others appear to be ministering spirits, and the acts of the latter are referred to these as to lords; that Thrones have ascended still higher, at a distance even from Dominations, being called Thrones because they sit, and sitting because God sits in them, pours himself into them, and reveals his secrets to them, that through them these may be transmitted to those below. This sitting is supreme tranquility, most placid serenity, and peace surpassing all understanding. Thus they are most like the Almighty, who sits upon the Thrones—the Lord of Hosts—judging all things with tranquility, in fullest gentleness, serenity, and peace. We must further suppose that the Cherubim draw and pour forth streams of knowledge from the very fountain of wisdom, the mouth of the Most High; and that the Seraphim, spirits wholly inflamed by the divine fire, set all things aflame, so that the individual citizens are individual lamps burning and shining: burning with charity, shining with knowledge. Hence their inequality is clear, etc.

IV.---On the spirituality, immortality, and other supernatural endowments of angels.

Since in the angelic orders nature is the subtler in proportion as the image of God is more distinctly expressed in them, this section shows that all angels are the likeness of God, light, incorporeal, spirits, powerful in themselves, glorious, blessed in the vision of God, perfect in their kind, ethereal in body, everlasting through immortality, incapable of suffering—not created so, but made so by grace, not by nature; pure in mind, kindly in affection, loving toward themselves, devout in religion, whole in chastity, undivided in unanimity, secure in peace, adorned with every knowledge, beautified with every loveliness, wise with regard to the one God; that they are present everywhere in an instant, know all things because they behold all things in God, and certainly can without difficulty accomplish all that they wish to do; that all things are accessible to their subtlety; that they are immeasurably rational, participants in the eternity, truth, and will of God, etc., etc. This article also treats of their mutual similarity, etc.---It is not omitted that Christ restored them, so that after his coming they learned many things which they had previously not known, etc., etc.

V.---On the mission of angels from God to humankind.

[Col. 0041]

As is known to all, the name “angel” is a name of office and operation, not of property and nature. Although all orders of heavenly spirits are generally called angels, since all may be sent without distinction, the name properly belongs only to those who are sent, including Seraphim when they are sent, whose name is interpreted as “burning” or “setting aflame.” For God has often worked through good angels. Taking on a true body, frequently in human form and with real flesh of its own kind, they appeared to human beings to announce notable divine purposes. First, indeed, to Adam, when a Cherub was stationed before Paradise armed with a flaming sword to prevent his entrance. Three appear to Abraham, Sarah, and Lot, and are received as guests; through them Sodom is overthrown. They are sent to Jacob, Manoah, etc.; to the Blessed Virgin Mary and to her spouse St. Joseph. Isaiah the prophet was purified by a Seraph. Raphael, Gabriel, and Michael are named. The angel of the Pool of Bethesda is known. Lazarus’s soul is carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. They announced the births of John and Christ; they ministered to Christ in the wilderness; they saw him risen and ascending into heaven, etc., etc. In the Acts of the Apostles diverse missions and visions of angels are read; in the Temple at Jerusalem angelic voices were heard forewarning its overthrow and complete ruin, etc., etc.

VI.---On the office of angels in heaven and on earth, especially their care and concern for human beings, both in spiritual and bodily matters.

God has never ordained anything better, whether for himself or for us, [Col. 0042] than angels. For these spirits in heaven serve God’s eternal command sweetly and generously; they sing to him without end and never turn away from contemplating him. Seeing in God the unchangeable truth, they direct their wills according to it. It is explained how, while always seeing God, they nevertheless unceasingly desire to look toward him, etc. With regard to us, they may be called members of God; they are his eyes, by which he looks mercifully upon us. Their merit consists in desiring our good; for this purpose they range through the whole world to aid us. Above all, they surround the sacred Eucharist of the altar with trembling. They afterward admonish us to repent. They rejoice over spiritual athletes who fight bravely; they stand, fly with wings, and fight for us. All things serve us through them; they furnish us with consolations; they rejoice in our redemption; their protection is present to the tempted and the weak, and especially to those who are dying. Then, at the hour of death, they prepare the way before us; all of them, like a guardian angel joining themselves to that angel, lead souls to heaven and assign them places, etc., etc.

XXXIV. INDEX ON GUARDIAN ANGELS.

The angels of God are also our angels. According to Sacred Scripture, the nations are divided according to their number. Hence there are public and private guardian angels. They possess a certain kinship of spiritual consanguinity with the human race. The guardianship of guardian angels protects empires, kingdoms, provinces, cities, villages, religious communities, and churches, etc. They stand beside all the faithful everywhere; each person has his own guardian angel, who helps us against spiritual wickednesses. For our weakness could not withstand so many and such great spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places unless angels had been assigned for our protection. The protection of guardian angels is necessary for us. Zealous, desirous, and solicitous for our salvation, they console, visit, and help us; they preside over our prayers; in eager service they carry our desires and prayers to God; they call us their brothers. Here too it is explained that their service is needed by the dying; that our souls are carried to heaven in their hands, etc., etc.; that we ought to have the greatest confidence, reverence, and devotion toward them; that their assistance is to be sought; and that offending them is to be avoided as much as possible, etc., etc.

## XXXV. INDEX CONCERNING DEMONS

This presents, in logical order, everything that the Fathers have handed down to us: I. concerning their fall and the names then imposed on them; II. concerning the prerogatives or gifts they lost; III. concerning those retained, as naturally and fundamentally inherent in their nature; IV. concerning the punishments inflicted upon them, whether they dwell in the air, in hell, or among human beings; V. concerning their attacks upon human beings by divine permission.

### I.—Concerning the fall of demons and their names

Demons fell, through their own free choice, from the nine orders of angels. They were unwilling that God alone should rule; they wished to be like God. Thus they sinned: by disorderly desiring more than they had received, by desiring an advantage which they ought not to have desired, and by refusing to desire what they ought to have desired. Yet the entire explanation of this perverse will and fall is that God did not give them perseverance, and did not give it because they did not receive it … etc. It is plainly shown that they were good in the beginning, but through their own fault made themselves unjust, etc. The names by which they are designated include Devil, Leviathan, Serpent, Lion, North Wind, Night, etc.

### II.—Concerning demons’ prerogatives lost through their fall

If the apostate angels did not wholly lose, through their fall, the spiritual properties with which they were created and which the faithful angels augmented through their merit, how immensely they mutilated them! Their moral endowments—intelligence, power, knowledge, and so forth—were from that time made subject to and limited by God’s command. What they possessed for the highest and greatest things was reduced to the lowest. The more exalted the nature of these spirits had been, the more base it became.

Accordingly, it is shown that after their ruin they fell from heaven; lost truth and justice; became fixed in malice; were intent upon nothing except malice and wickedness; and so forth. They have no freedom to do good, but are hardened, as the punishment for their crimes, in the greatest ill will. Thus, in the broader sense, they fell both from what they were going to receive and from what they had already received; but in another, stricter and narrower sense, they fell only from what they were going to receive.

### III.—Concerning demons’ retained prerogatives and gifts

Although the transgressing angels lost holiness, truth, justice, and other supernatural gifts, they nevertheless did not lose spirituality, immortality, agility, and so forth; nor the keen capacity of angelic nature, or the other properties fundamentally inherent in that nature. They still possess very great knowledge, understanding, penetration, subtlety, and fineness for assaulting both elements of the human being.

For, the more subtle their nature is than that of humans, the more skilled they are than any human being in every art … Yet they do not know everything; nor do they know future things except insofar as they infer them from what has occurred, whether by the subtlety of their nature, the experience of time, or as much as God permits them to know. Nor can they do what they wish, nor will they ever be able to do so wholly. They are completely effective for evil, yet not to the extent that they wish, but to the extent that God or the good angels permit them. Thus, for example, through their arts and deceits, oracles and miracles were produced which the pagans attributed to the skill of their gods, etc., etc.

Nor is their strength to be feared: by our own will we submit ourselves to them, etc. They were conquered by Christ through the cross; Christians likewise overcome them by adjurations, prayers, fasts, etc. Finally, it is shown there that, because of Adam’s sin, we are all placed under the power of demons; nevertheless, whatever may be delivered to them by God’s judgment cannot be outside the law [Col. 0047] of God’s power, under which they themselves are established … etc. Hence, in the stricter sense of the fact, they retained whatever they had received, where the question concerns only more or less.

### IV.—Concerning the punishments inflicted upon demons

Since the apostate angels could not be restored, because they fell voluntarily and sinned unforgivably—because their fault was judged the more damnable in proportion as their nature had been more exalted—Lucifer and his princes were cast out of heaven into hell, eternally confirmed in their fall. Other companions were cast into this dark air, which is for them as a prison, in which are the spiritual forces of wickedness and in which, as in hell, they suffer a burning punishment …

Moreover, their obstinacy shut against them every path of mercy … Here it is shown that, wrapped in eternal fire whether in the air, on earth, or in hell, they are prepared for eternal punishments, and that in such condemnation there is nothing but God’s just judgment … At the end of the world nothing but torments awaits them; nor will any power or privilege, left to them until that time over human beings or the air, remain to them, etc.

### V.—Concerning demons’ attacks upon human beings

Demons are permitted to attack us outwardly and inwardly, for our exercise. For the sake either of testing or of vengeance, God permits them to tempt us through the agency of the flesh, and each person according to his disposition. They customarily join battle with the soul because of the association of substance and the difference of nature. They insinuate their evil ways into us; they are ever present to our thought, speech, and action, in case they may find something from which they can become accusers before the tribunal of the righteous Judge. Hardly any human being is without a demon. It is sport to them to draw us from vice into vice …

Moreover, whenever God is angry with this world by any scourge, he sends them as agents of vengeance; yet they are restrained by the divine will, lest they harm as much as they wish … Since, therefore, they tempt us by countless suggestions, because it is sweet to them that we sin, so that they may glory in our sins, we must resist them and implore God’s help. We should remember that they do not harm one who is unwilling, and do not wound those who resist them, but crown them; and that we have renounced the devil, his pomps, and his angels; etc., etc.

## XXXVI. INDEX CONCERNING THE DURATION OF THE WORLD AND ITS END, CONTAINING VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS

### I.—Concerning duration

“You should know that the decline of the age and the time of Antichrist are approaching.” St Cyprian, IV, 350. “The second coming of Christ is drawing near to us.” St Cyprian, IV, 388. “The world itself now speaks and bears witness to its decline by the evidence of its failing condition.” St Cyprian, IV, 546. “Now the end of the world is near.” St Cyprian, IV, 561. Opinions of philosophers concerning its antiquity and duration. Lactantius, VI, 781. “When the six-thousandth year has been completed, the consummation must take place.” VI, 781, 783, 1006. “So that at the end of the sixth thousandth year every evil may be abolished from the earth.” VI, 783. The ancients believed that the end of the world would come together with the end of the Roman Empire. St Optatus, XI, 1153. “When the seventh and thousandth year begins, those who truly believe in the faith will be freed from the world.” St Hilarianus, XIII, 1105. After Antichrist has been killed, when the total of six thousand years has been completed, there will be a resurrection of all the saints while the world still survives. Hilarianus, XIII, 1105. “After the seventh and thousandth year Satan will be released from his prison.” Hilarianus, XIII, 1106. The period from Christ’s ascension to the end of the world is denoted by a thousand years. St Ambrose, XVII, 930. “For in six thousand years, if five hundred years are assigned to each hour of the day, the time of the faith of the Gentiles will consequently be called the last hour.” St Jerome, XXV, 1186. “The end of the world is near.” St Augustine, XL, 667. “That is, after the toil of six thousand years—since humanity was created …—when six thousand years, as though six days, have been completed, there follows, as it were, a seventh, Sabbath day in the final thousand years, for celebrating that Sabbath by the saints who have risen.” St Augustine, XLI, 667. No one knows the final time of the world—the day or hour. St Augustine, XXXIII, 899, 900, 901, 902, 903. Christ did not reveal the day of judgment to the apostles. St Augustine, XXXVI, 906. Some think it will occur after a fixed number of thousands of years. St Augustine, XXXVIII, 576. St Augustine does not venture to count the times until the Savior’s coming expected at the end. St Augustine, XXXIII, 899. Some said that the world’s end would occur after six thousand years. St Augustine, XXXVIII, 576.

[Col. 0050] “When the sixth millennium of years has been completed, it will rest in the seventh millennium, the world then ceasing from every secular work.” St Augustine, XXXV, 2320. The six ages of the world. St Augustine, XXXIX, 1920; XL, 742, 749. “Now the end of the age is at hand.” St Augustine, CXL, 1187. Some understand this in such a way that they make six thousand years like one day and divide it into twelve parts, as though hours, so that the final five hundred years appear to constitute the last hour. St Augustine, XXXIII, 910. The belief that the world would last seven thousand years was held by some. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 729, note. That is, the sixth millennium of years, however much it may be prolonged until the end of the age, whose latter periods are now passing, etc. Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 914. Cassiodorus’s opinion concerning the end of the world. Cassiodorus, LXIX, 515. “You behold this world, which a nearby end is pressing upon.” St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 694. “Why do you not consider that the world is at its end?” St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 884. “In the work of the six days are shown the works of six thousand years. For a thousand years are compared with one day before God … The Sabbath of those days is the time of the seventh thousandth year, and the rest of the future kingdom and age, where there will no longer be any activity of things, but only the rest of the saints.” St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 523. Whether Christ knew the end of this world. Bede the Venerable, XCII, 265. “In these six thousand years there ought to be five hundred years, and when evening comes after the twelve hours of this day, then, after twelve times five hundred years—that is, six thousand years—have been completed, the eternal recompense of the just Judge should be brought forth.” Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 674. Nor were there lacking those who thought that the course of this age, which also revolves through seven days, was to end in seven thousand years; Augustine refutes them. Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 674.

### II.—Concerning the signs of the end of the world and the fire of the final conflagration
At the end, astonishing prodigies will occur throughout all the elements of the world. Lactantius, VI, 785. On the devastation of the world and its prodigies. Lactantius, VI, 790. [Col. 0051] On the last times. Lactantius, VI, 1188. Fire will descend from heaven, and all human beings will be consumed. Hilarianus, XIII, 1106. The two sickles signify that fire by which the whole world is to be destroyed. St. Ambrose, XVII, 896. The cities of the nations will fall; with that fire which will precede the face of the Lord as he comes for judgment, all nations will be destroyed. St. Ambrose, XVII, 909. When the end of the world is imminent, purgatorial fire will burn many while purifying them; but, acquitted before judgment, they will be received into the company of the saints. St. Ambrose, XVII, 931. Fire will come forth from heaven, because, when the Lord comes for judgment, fire will go before him; it will consume not only the whole host of the ungodly, but the world itself as well. XVII, 932. Behold: the earth, the air, the sea, and the other elements will be consumed by fire. St. Ambrose, XVII, 933. Earth and heaven—that is, the appearance of earth and heaven—will be changed by fire from their present form, so that they may be refashioned into another, much better and more beautiful form. St. Ambrose, XVII, 934. What signs are to be sent beforehand. Zacchaeus Christianus, XX, 1161, 1162. In the middle of the night, while all are secure, the consummation of the world will come. St. Jerome, XXII, 974. The sign of the Lord’s coming is that the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world . . . and we see that this has either already been accomplished or will be accomplished shortly. St. Jerome, XXVI, 177. We can infer the world’s final time from its signs. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 903, 909. The signs of the judgment’s imminently future coming have existed since apostolic times and yet do not cease to coincide with the last days and to be signs. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 913, 914. [Col. 0052] Nearly all the signs of judgment foretold by the prophets have been fulfilled. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 576. The end of the age will not come before the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 900. The world is reserved for the final fire, for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly persons. St. Augustine, XIII, 684. Antichrist, whose time is followed by the day of the Lord. St. Augustine, XLI, 685. The form of this world will pass away in the conflagration of worldly fires. Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 921. As the same end of the world approaches, many things threaten which did not exist before: namely, changes in the air and terrors from heaven, etc. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1293. On the conflagration by fire through which this world is said to perish. St. Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 518. Thus some say that, at the consummation of the age, when fire descends, it will indeed begin from the higher places, so as gradually to descend to the lower. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 829. Luke’s account of the fire of Sodom gives us occasion to understand that this world is to be burned by fire. CCX, 829. For when the resurrection has taken place and Christ comes for judgment, fire will immediately follow; it will burn up the world and devour sinners. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 715. Fire will blaze fifteen cubits above all the mountains. Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 778.

## BOOKS TREATING OF THE END OF THE WORLD

A short work on the duration of the world. St. Hilarianus, XIII, 1097. A treatise on meditating upon the plagues that will occur near the end of the world. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 201.

## XXXVII. INDEX CONCERNING THE CREATION OF HUMANITY, SET OUT IN LOGICAL ORDER: EVERYTHING SAID ABOUT IT BY THE HOLY FATHERS

Humanity is the Creator’s handiwork: Tertullian, I, 514. Created by God from nothing: ibid., 524.---Holy Scripture teaches that humanity was God’s final work, and was thus introduced into this world as into a house already prepared and furnished: Lactantius, VI, 305.---The origin of humanity has this dignity: it was fashioned not by a hand but by the hands of God: St. Hilary, IX, 565.---Why humanity was created after all the other creatures: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1129. Why it was not praised immediately upon being created by God: ibid., 310. How great is humanity’s dignity in its creation, and what does this teach it? Id., XVII, 1015.---According to the Jews, Adam was created at a mature age: St. Jerome, XXII, 902.---At what age or stature Adam was created: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 348. Adam and Eve were not first formed on that spiritual day initially created: ibid., 341. Why humanity is called God’s principal work: ibid., 347, 348. God made humanity, like everything else, through his Word: ibid., 371. Adam was formed only in the manner contained in the primordial causes: ibid., 349, 351. Humanity was made invisibly, causally, and potentially on the first day of creation, but visibly on the sixth day: ibid., 343, 344, 346, 347, 349; 410. The origin of Adam and Eve according to the Manichaeans: id., XXXII, 1375. The Manichaeans say that Adam was created by the prince of darkness: id., XLII, 569. The creation of humanity: id., XXXIV, 186, 241. The creation of humanity expounded allegorically: XXXII, 858. Why, in the creation of humanity alone, it was said, “Let us make”: id., XXXIV, 291. Why it is not said of humanity’s creation, “and so it was made”: ibid., 292. Humanity created on the sixth day: id., XLII, 257.---Whether humanity was formed in mature manhood or would have grown through intervals of time: St. Eucherius, L, 905.---The creation of humanity: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 622.---On the creation of the first human being: Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 656.---Why humanity was made last, after the creation: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 350.---The creation of humanity: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 163.---Humanity’s prerogatives in the establishment of things: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 900. Humanity was made on the sixth day: id., LXXVI, [Col. 0052] 1230. The first human being was so created that, by not sinning, he could pass without death into the homeland of the angels: id., LXXV, 664; Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 753. What was the first human being’s bread in paradise: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 607.---That the rational creature, angels and human beings alike, was created simultaneously: Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 750.

On the condition of the first human being: ibid., 753.---On humanity: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 559.---Why “Let us make” is said in the creation of humanity: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 28 ff. Humanity is God’s own work and handiwork: id., CLXVIII, 627.---God wished to make humanity outside paradise, so that humanity might understand that it was placed in paradise by grace, not by nature: Hugh of St. Victor, CXXXV, 39. Adam was immediately made, without any progressive development of his limbs, at mature manhood: id., CLXXVI, 92. The formation of the first human being: its allegorical meaning: id., CLXXV, 639. Humanity is composed of a twofold substance: Tertullian, II, [Col. 0053] 452, 850.---Humanity comprises two natures, spiritual and earthly: St. Hilary, IX, 720. According to the body, formed from earth: ibid., 566. According to the soul, made from no foreign substance: ibid.---Various difficulties arise if Adam’s soul was not created before it was breathed into his body: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 370.---Before sin, Adam’s flesh was created so immortal that, assisted by the supports of temporal nourishment, it would remain free from death and pain: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 32; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 463.---The flesh of the first human beings was created immortal and incorruptible in such a way that they might preserve that same immortality and incorruption of theirs by keeping God’s commandments: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 32.---The human being was made of the substance of body and soul: Alcuin, C, 5, 521.---The whole human being is improperly described as consisting of both substances: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 139.---For one must not believe that the soul, being spirit, light, and pure, was made from mud: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 55.---Perhaps the human body was formed through the ministry of angels: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 37. What the first human being was like in body when created: id., CLXXVI, 275. God formed the human body from the mud of the earth: ibid., 92.---Why humanity was made from mud: Garnerius, CXCIII, 277.

Humanity created in the image of God the Son: Tertullian, II, 168. Fashioned after the likeness of the Son and the Spirit: ibid. Made in the image of God, that is, of Christ: Tertullian, II, 802.---Humanity made in God’s image not in bodily features, but in freedom and power of choice: Tertullian, II, 290.---Adam, whom he perfected in his own image and likeness: St. Victorinus the Martyr, V, 306.---The human soul made in God’s image: St. Hilary, IX, 566. Humanity was chiefly made in God’s image in that it surpasses irrational creatures: id., 30. Why humanity was made in God’s image: CLXXVII, 1119, 1120.---Humanity, by the dignity of its soul, was made after the particular likeness of the individual persons: Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 761. Humanity’s end is eternal life: XXXIV, 144. By whom, why, and for what humanity was created: XL, 849. Humanity was chosen so that it might either use created things or rule over them: St. Hilary, IX, 426.---The strongest and fiercest beasts were subjected to humanity by the Creator: St. Ambrose, XIV, 255.---Humanity’s power over beasts: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 187.---Ruling beasts, in allegory: ibid. If, placed in such honor, a person does not understand so as to act rightly, that person will be compared to those same insensate animals over which he was set: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 30. It is asked for what benefit humanity received dominion over fish, birds, and all animals of the earth: id., XCI, 31. It is worth asking why even now humanity does not rule over all animals: ibid.
