The reason why they were brought to him was this: he was to be lord over all of them, and therefore it was fitting that he should assign them names according to his own judgment: id., CLXXV, 40.---God does not set one human being over another, but only over insensible or irrational creatures, so that humanity may take them into its power: Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 762.---Dominion over everything on earth and in the waters was given to humanity: Abbot Ernaldus, CLXXXIX, 1534.

### On the Creation of Woman

Woman was not made in God’s image: St. Ambrose, XVII, 240, 259.---Woman made from man: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1784. She was made in God’s image: id., XXXIV, 293. She was made outside the six days of creation: ibid., 343. The formation of woman was accomplished by no one other than God: id., XXXIV, 403, 404. Why woman was formed from man: id., XLI, 372, 376. Woman was made as a helper for the sake of offspring: id., XXXIV, 395 ff. Woman was made so that man might rule over her: ibid., 450. The formation of woman is mystically called a building: ibid., 402, 403. The formation of woman, in the manner in which it is narrated, occurred so that something might be foretold: ibid., 402. The formation of woman mystically signified the formation of the Church: ibid., 407, 408.---It is asked whether the woman formed from the man’s side received her soul from his soul: St. Eucherius, L, 909.---In the beginning God created one woman: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 30. Woman was created in God’s image insofar as she too possessed a rational mind: ibid., 30. Since Adam needed a wife, could this not have been accomplished otherwise than by removing a rib from him while he slept, from which a wife might be built? Id., XCIII, 275.---Why woman is said to have been built from the side of the sleeping man, rather than fashioned from earth: Alcuin, C, 522.---On the making of woman from Adam’s rib: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 482. That woman was made from the man’s side ought to be believed necessary, in order to commend the force of their union: ibid., 484.---On the formation of woman: Hildebert, CLXXI, 1119.---It should be noted that what was taken to make woman was taken neither from the man’s head nor from his feet, lest she be thought his mistress if from the head, or his slave if from the feet: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 40. It was fitting, therefore, that she be taken from the middle—that is, from the rib—so that she might be understood as his companion: ibid. On the formation of woman: id., CLXXVI, 92.---For just as the other persons derive their being from the Father, so in human creation woman derived her being from being created out of man, not man out of woman: Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 761.

## XXXVIII. INDEX CONCERNING THE HUMAN SOUL, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY THE FATHERS ON THE SOUL’S ORIGIN, NATURE, IMMATERIALITY, FACULTIES, IMMORTALITY, EXCELLENCE, ETC., ETC.

### Notice

In this Index, providing at once for the reader’s usefulness and convenience, we shall establish a number of divisions, as follows: I, on the existence and origin of the human mind; II, on its nature; III, on its immateriality; IV, on its various faculties; V, on its immortality; VI, on the union of the soul with the body and on its seat; VII, on its excellence; VIII, on the soul’s present state; IX, on its state in death and after death; X, we shall cite books expressly treating of the soul; XI, finally, as in an appendix, we shall address the question of animal souls. But, lest this Index become too long, we have not reproduced every statement of the Fathers word for word, but have indicated only the volume and page numbers where the reader may most easily find the desired passages.

## [INDEX CONCERNING THE HUMAN SOUL]

### I. On the existence and origin of the human mind

The human soul, created and descending not from God but by God, is God’s image, for it has the same motions and perceptions as God, though not such as God has. It is maintained that souls did not exist before they were sent into bodies; that they are not transmitted by propagation, but are created and infused when the body has been formed. Various opinions concerning its origin, and errors relating to it, are also listed here.

### II. On the nature of the human soul

The soul is a simple substance; rightly, then, it is called, as it were, *anaima* (ἀναίμα), that is, altogether distinct from blood, since after the body’s death it is manifest that its substance remains complete. Some say that the soul is so called because it animates and gives life to the substance of its body. It is called *animus* because its exceedingly swift thought ranges about with rapid motion like the wind; it is called *mens* from *mēnē* (μήνη), that is, “moon,” because, although it is changed by varied alternation, it restores itself to what it was by a certain perfected renewal. It is also called spirit, either because it breathes forth what it wills, fills all things, is wholly present throughout the world, and is unmoved in place; or because it is a subtle substance, invisible to us; or because life among mortals is sustained by that which is emitted and received throughout the whole body. It is one soul which, when it contemplates, is spirit; when it senses, sensation; when it knows, *animus*; when it understands, mind; when it distinguishes, reason; when it consents, will; when it remembers, memory; when it gives life to the limbs, soul. Various opinions about the soul’s nature are reported, and various errors refuted.

### III. On the soul’s immateriality

The soul is spirit, as the day itself is light; it is incorporeal and immaterial, and therefore cannot be dissolved. It does not grow in children, flourish in youth, or diminish in old age. It retains nothing bodily in itself: it has neither length, breadth, nor depth; spiritually it considers many things both distant and near, thinks on heavenly things, and desires to know certain lofty things concerning God himself, the supreme God, etc.

### IV. On the properties or faculties of the soul

The soul is rational and free, capable of knowledge and understanding, always active and exercised. In the body the soul has three affections: rational, concupiscible, and irascible; it consists of a threefold power—vital, sensory, and rational; it is vigorous in reason, strong in counsel, and preeminent in intelligence. The soul treats of divine things, understands human matters, naturally tends upward, possesses by nature faculties and as it were instruments for knowing and loving, and has seven powers as well: *animus*, mind, imagination, opinion, reason, intellect, and memory, etc.

### VI. On the seat of the soul and its union with the body

How the soul adheres to the body cannot be comprehended. It is not contained in the body as something is in a vessel or in a place; rather, it is simultaneously wholly present in every part of the body, neither smaller in smaller members nor greater in larger ones, but wholly present in all and wholly present in each. It gives life, sensation, and governance to all these things through a threefold operation, etc.

### VII. On the excellence of the soul

The human soul, marked with God’s image, adorned with his likeness, espoused by faith, endowed with the Spirit, redeemed by blood, capable of blessedness, heir of goodness, participant in reason, bears a certain trace of the Trinity; it reflects the greatness and uprightness of the Image or Word; nothing is more powerful than it, nothing more exalted, etc.

### VIII. On the soul’s present state in the spiritual order; the necessity and means of sanctifying it

The soul is God’s chariot, having good and bad horses; adorned with the flowers of virtues, it is a garden, or has within itself a sprouting paradise; it is a city fortified by Christ and besieged by the devil; it is God’s temple and altar. It wastes away when sin is diminished; it grows fat when sins are accumulated. Once it has attached itself to desires, it can with difficulty rise again to the height from which it descended, without God’s favor. With God alone and in God alone the soul is happy; given over to temporal pleasures, it continually burns with desire and cannot be satisfied. The soul’s nourishment is the will of God. The soul dies in three ways: by thought, by deed, and by persistence in evil, etc., etc. In this article, as we have already said, lest the Index be too long, we indicate only the volumes and columns of the Fathers’ passages treating of the soul’s present state and the necessity and means of sanctifying it; the reader may consult these passages with profit.

## IX. On the State of the Soul at Death and after Death

When the soul of a righteous person departs from the body, it sees all its good works and therefore rejoices. Immediately the angel who guarded it receives it and places it before the throne of God. But when the soul of a sinner begins to be released from the bonds of the flesh, it is crushed by bitter terror and torn by the stings of a biting conscience: it recalls the forbidden deeds it has committed and grieves; it strives to remain but is compelled to go; it is ashamed, etc.

After death, if the soul of the righteous has nothing to be purified, it immediately flies to heaven; but the sinful soul is cast down into hell, etc. Here also various opinions concerning metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls, are set out and refuted. With respect to the punishments of the sinful soul and the rewards of the righteous, let the reader consult the indexes on heaven and hell.

## XI. On the Soul of Brute Animals

No animate creature exists without sensation, and nothing sentient exists without a soul, Tertullian, II, 775.---Whether animals possess mind, and who have attributed one to them, Lactantius, VII, 93. Their intelligence and foreknowledge of the future, the same author, VI, 765. Their souls are dissolved by death, ibid., 321; who have attributed reason to them, ibid., 917.---A soul is present even in cattle, St Augustine, XLII, 1057, 1061; the souls of beasts live but do not understand, ibid., 975, 979. Beasts lack intellect, the same author, XXXVI, 480; XXXVII, 1939. Beasts perceive, remember, and desire, the same author, XLII, 999; images are present in one part of the souls of brute animals, ibid., 979.---The souls of animals come into being with the very birth of the flesh and end with the death of the flesh, but are not governed by reason, Gennadius, LVIII, 984.---The animal is a friend of reason, Dracontius, LX, 723.---The souls of brute animals, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1231.---What animal souls are, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1076.---The soul of a brute animal does not live except so long as it gives life, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 239.---The souls of brute animals perish together with them, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 739.---Why the spirit of a brute animal is called natural and vital spirit, and whether it is animate or inanimate, Alanus of Lille, CCI, 330, 331.

[Col. 0059]

# XXXIX. INDEX ON HUMAN REASON AND ITS EXCELLENCE, POWER, AND WEAKNESS, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER WHATEVER THE HOLY FATHERS HAVE SAID ON THESE MATTERS

## Notice

In this Index we follow a logical order of subjects. Thus, after defining reason, we set forth its existence, ends, and excellence. But since among these endowments of human reason very many defects arise, we then take up its weaknesses and their causes, either reporting the various opinions of the Fathers concerning all these matters, or at least indicating them by the numbers of volumes and columns.

## I. Definition of Reason

Reason is a movement of the mind capable of distinguishing and connecting the things learned, St Augustine, XXXII, 1009.---Reason is the gaze of the mind contemplating truth, the same author, XXXIII, 626; XXXVIII, 255; XL, 786.---Reason belongs to the soul, situated above bodily things and below spiritual things, the same author, XL, 808.---Reason is the power of the soul which discerns and judges all things, the same author, XL, 809.---Reason is a movement of the mind by which it is led to the hidden things of truth, [Col. 0060] Cassiodorus, LXX, 1284.---Reason is a certain movement of the mind, sharpening the sight of the intellect and distinguishing true things from false, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 82.---Reason is nothing other than intellect, through which we are made like God and the angels, Guibert, CLVI, 33.---St Bernard’s excellent threefold definition of reason, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 341 and 351.---Reason is a certain power that distinguishes good from what is not good, Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 946.

## II. The Existence of Reason

The human soul is rational.

Man is endowed with reason in order to perceive and admire creation, Lactantius, VI, 749; VII, 122; Venerable Bede, XCI, 30.---The end of reason is the knowledge of God, Lactantius, VII, 14; St Hilary, IX, 527; St Zeno, XI, 126; St Ambrose, XVI, 1132; St Jerome, XXVI, 504; XXIII, 116; XXX, 720; Hincmar, CXXV, 131; [Col. 0062] St Anselm, CLVIII, 401; Blessed Ado, CLX, 1081.---The end of reason is the worship to be rendered to God, Lactantius, VI, 749; VII, 93, 14; St Hilary, IX, 828; St Augustine, XL, 812; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 586; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 946; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 254.---Reason was given to man so that he might be an imitator of God, St Leo, LIV, 168; LV, 125; St Anselm, CLVIII, 803; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 773.---Reason was created so that man might not be good in and of himself, Eugyppius, LXII, 933.---Reason was given to man in order that he might distinguish good from evil, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 427; St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 337, 803; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 946.---Reason was given to govern and guide the whole of human life, Alcuin, CI, 614.---God made human nature rational, so that it might order the irrational creation according to God’s will, St Anselm, CLVIII, 806.---Reason was created so that man might attain supreme happiness, St Anselm, CLVIII, 804; Rupert, CLXVII, 259; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1107; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 721; CLXXVII, 93; Hermann, CLXXX, 13.---God joined reason to the human body in order to show an example of the union between spirit and God, Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1107.---God adorned man with reason in order that he might excel all animals, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 341, 773.

### 1. With Respect to Natural Truths

### 3. With Respect to Moral Truths

### 4. The Excellence of Reason Expressed Generally

## V. The Weakness of Reason

### 1. With Respect to Natural Truths

The causes of natural things are inaccessible to reason, Arnobius, V, 892; Lactantius, VI, 414; VII, 54, 60, 61, 62, 64; Constantine the Great, VIII, 419; St Hilary, IX, 718; St Zeno, XI, 318, 402, 445; St Jerome, XXIII, 1075; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 835; LXXVIII, 990; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1011, 1015.---The soul is full of mysteries beyond reason, Lactantius, VII, 62, 68; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 361; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 835; Guibert, CLVI, 36.---Many works of creation are inscrutable to reason, St Zeno, XI, 455, 456; St Ambrose, XIV, 249; XVI, 1339; Zacchaeus, XX, 1092; St Jerome, XXVI, 504; St Augustine, XLI, 352; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 620; Cassiodorus, LXX, 657; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 331; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 869.---Knowledge is uncertain and vain, St Augustine, XL, 29; Manegaldus, CLV, 155; St Anselm, CLVIII, 761; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1277; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 478; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 667.---Reason cannot teach us where we go or whence we come, St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 1422.---Reason is deceptive concerning natural truths, Manegaldus, CLV, 154.---Understanding of things comes from God, Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 17.

### 2. With Respect to Supernatural Truths

The infinite greatness of God is inaccessible to the mind, Tertullian, I, 509, 806, 809, 810; II, 759.---The intellect cannot apprehend the goods promised to the elect, Lactantius, VI, 638.---In matters of God the mind fails, St Hilary, X, 33, 230, 385; IX, 718, 855, 58, 149, 94, 143.---Man cannot possess knowledge of heavenly things, St Hilary, X, 107.---In God there are mysteries incomprehensible to reason, St Ambrose, XVII, 511; St Jerome, XXX, 561, 700; St Augustine, XXXIV, 790; XXXII, 661; XLII, 1120.---Reason cannot explain the miracles of the Gospel, Cassian, L, 136.---The judgments of God are impenetrable, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 687; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 157; Salvian, LIII, 38; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 619, 457.---Truths perceived by reason cannot confer eternal life, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 246.---Reason can do little concerning divinity, Boethius, LXIII, 818; Eugyppius, LXII, 933, 880; Primasius, LXVIII, 419; Cassiodorus, LXX, 1067.---Reason apprehends God’s acts, but by no means his substance, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1031; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 99.---For a human being to speak about God is like a blind person discoursing about light, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 403, 439; LXXV, 708, 686, 679.---God is incomprehensible, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 613; CXII, 418; Haymo, CXVIII, 558; Abbot Lupus, CXIX, 493; John Scotus, CXXIII, 362, 413, 844, 1158.---The perfections of God exceed the human mind, Gezo, CXXXVII, 376; Manegaldus, CLV, 157; St Anselm, CLVIII, 320, 210, 608, 609, 581; Rupert, CLXVII, 1248; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1246.---Philosophers have been unable to apprehend the supreme truth, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXXI, 581.---The incarnation and redemption exceed the powers of reason, Herveus, CLXXXI, 610.---The knowledge of God surpasses every intellect, the same author, CLXXXI, 1188.---Divinity is an abyss to reason, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 323; Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 836; Gualter, CCIX, 586; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 535, 444, 539.

### 3. With Respect to Moral Truths

Reason left to itself soon confuses the notions of good and evil, Tertullian, I, 653; St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 246; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 421; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 667; Innocent III, CCXVII, 1038.---Philosophers could not, by themselves, possess the notion of justice, St Zeno, XI, 281.---On the insufficiency of natural law, St Ambrose, XVII, 155; Rufinus, XXI, 692; St Jerome, XXX, 675, 720; St Augustine, XXXVI, 673; XXXVII, 1574; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 239; Gennadius, LVIII, 991; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 141; Lanfranc, CL, 110; St Bruno, CLIII, 40; Rupert, CLXVIII, 131; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 348, 692; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 559, 560; CLXXVI, 301; Herveus, CLXXXI, 636; Gerhoh, CXCIII, 1177; Wolbero, CXCV, 1052; Peter of Celle, CCII, 924.---In rational nature there is ignorance concerning what ought to be done, St Augustine, XL, 244.---No one understands his own faults, Rufinus, XXI, 714.---Holy counsels do not arise from free will without the grace of God, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 243.---Through sin there is in reason ignorance of the good, Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 318.---Through the darkness of the mind man is drawn into sin, Garnerus, CXCIII, 370.---The light of God is necessary if we are to distinguish between good and evil, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 1178.---In reason there is ignorance of good and evil, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 769, 770.

## VI. Causes of the Weakness of Reason

### 1. Cause: Original and Actual Sin

Through sin the soul is blinded, St Fulgentius, LXV, 539; St Hilary, IX, 944; St Ambrose, XIV, 462; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 664; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 126, 653; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 767, 768, 787, 870; LXXVI, 317, 916; LXXIX, 556; Venerable Bede, XCII, 510, 767; XCIII, 492, 514, 696, 890; Herveus, CLXXXI, 613; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 567; CLXXXIV, 1066; Adam of Prémontré, CXCXIII [probably CXCVIII], 246.---Original sin is for us a bond of error, St Ambrose, XVI, 125.---Evil knowledge comes to us from sin, the same author, XVII, 964.---The light of wisdom withdrew from the sinner, Rufinus, XXI, 748.---Because of sin, the soul suffers wretched ignorance, St Augustine, XLIV, 180.---Original sin is an impediment to the knowledge of things, the same author, XLV, 1268.---Error is the punishment of original sin, the same author, XLI, 784.---Sins veil the clarity of truth, the same author, XXXII, 1311.---In Adam’s sin man was stripped of understanding, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 237.---From original sin comes ignorance contrary to reason, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1294.---Sins take away the light of wisdom, the same author, LXX, 347.---The sinful man hides himself in the night of error, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 774, 775.---Because of sin the soul no longer recognizes the good which it seeks, the same author, LXXVI, 158.---Man fell in paradise, and the light of the mind departed from him, the same author, LXXVII, 317.---Man lost the light of reason through sin, the same author, LXXIX, 614.---God withdrew knowledge of the truth from those who departed from him, Venerable Bede, XCII, 510.---The imperfection and diminution of reason came about through the first man, the same author, XCIII, 528, 737; Bishop Amulo, CXVI, 118.---Sin overthrew the order of knowledge, John Scotus, CXXII, 843.---Once innocence was lost, errors became deeper, Hincmar, CXXV, 191.---Original sin removed man from the true light, the same author, CXXV, 131.---“The light of your countenance upon us” was darkened in Adam, St Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 165.---The first punishment of sin is profound ignorance, St Odo, CXXXIII, 524.---Reason was weakened through Adam’s sin, St Bruno, CLII, 803; St Anselm, CLXIII, 320, 434.---Reason was handed over to sin as a plaything, Guibert, CLVI, 160.---Before sin there was understanding without error, Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 348.---Before sin there was more perfect knowledge, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXXV, 441.---As sin increases, error grows, Herveus, CLXXXI, 613.---Fallen man is darkened, Aelred, CXCVIII, 246.

### 2. Cause: Pride of Mind
Reason, when it errs, wishes to be regarded as prudence, St. Hilary, X, 158.---Through pride philosophers went astray, St. Zeno, XI, 318 and 319; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 777; XXXII, 707; XXXIV, 440; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 139; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 536; St. Bruno, CLIII, 25; Alan of Lille, CCX, 133.---Through pride Adam fell into darkness, St. Ambrose, XV, 1283; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 237, 238; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 564; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 1422.---Truth is opposed to pride, St. Ambrose, XV, 1783.---Pride, the mother of heretics, St. Jerome, XXV, 858; St. Augustine, XXXII, 142; XXXVIII, 280; St. Anselm, CLXVIII, 554; CLIX, 123; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 923, 924; Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 126; Garnerius, CXCIII, 153.---Pride blinded the Jews, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1778; St. Bruno, CLXIV, 181, 186; CLXVIII, 130.---By pride man is driven into darkness, St. Augustine, XLIV, 206.---Pride blocks the ears of the heart, ibid., XLIV, 618.---God denies truth to the proud, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 437; LXXVI, 269, 595; Amulo, CXVI, 118; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 233; CXLV, 576, 577, 700; Guibert, CLVI, 165; Rupert, CLXIX, 670; see Hildebert, CLXXI, 688; Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 770.---Pride says, “I do not do good because I do not know [it],” Amulo, CXVI, 121.---An exposition of the errors into which the proud man falls, St. Odo, CXXXIII, 242 ff.; Manegaldus, CLV, 157, 158.---Reason is submerged in folly, Manegaldus, CLV, 155.---Through pride the mysteries are rejected because they are incomprehensible, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 263.---The mind ruined by the weapon of pride, ibid., CLVIII, 869.---Because of pride, you disdain either to see or to know, Rupert, CLXVIII, 573.---Pride rules and resists reason, see Hildebert, CLXXI, 190.---Ignorance is the punishment of self-exaltation, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 301.---From pride there arises a mind devoid of reason, ibid., CLXXVI, 999 and 1000.---The human mind deceived through pride, Garnerius, CXCIII, 112.---The proud refuse to learn, Innocent III, CCXVII, 1022.

### 3. Cause: the concupiscence of the flesh

X, 345; St. Zeno, XI, 343; St. Ambrose, XIV, 599; St. Augustine, XLI, 242; XXXII, 1009; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 452, 491; Cassiodorus, LXX, 1284; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 418; see Bede, XCI, 214; XCIII, 513, 522, 633; John Scotus, CXXII, 844; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 403; St. Bruno, CLII, 793, 1082; CLII, 184; Guibert, CLVI, 88; Rupert, CLXVII, 287; CLXVIII, 1244; see Hildebert, CLXXI, 348; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 1001; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 821; Anonymous, CCXIII, 919; Innocent III, CCXVII, 999, 1012.---Vices and lusts overwhelm truth, St. Hilary, IX, 527, 839; Cassian, XLIV, 1025; Boethius, LXIII, 770; Eugyppius, LXII, 596; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 712, 714; St. Paschasius, CXX, 82; John Scotus, CXXII, 849, 874; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 870; Rupert, CLXIII, 572.---On the conflict between flesh and spirit, St. Zeno, XI, 342; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 832; Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1188; Wolbero, CXCV, 1225; Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 700; Alan of Lille, CCX, 141, 142.---Luxury turns aside from true faith, St. Ambrose, XVI, 626.---Sexual lust engulfs the mind, St. Augustine, XLIV, 373 and 374.---The mind capable of truth is free from vices, ibid., XL, 299.---The mind, weighed down by the mass of the body, cannot long adhere to the heavenly light, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 832.---Many do not wish to know, lest they be compelled to do good, Amulo, CXVI, 139.---Lust does not wish to apprehend the light, Hincmar, CXXII, 349.---Concupiscence weighs down the mind, St. Bruno, CLII, 794.---The reprobate person's judgment cannot be convicted by knowledge through any proofs, Guibert, CLVI, 165.---Wisdom flees the carnal mind, Rupert, CLXVII, 1629.---There are two causes of darkness: anger and a softer affection, St. [Col. 0067] Bernard, CLXXXIII, 755.---Unlawful sadness produces the mind’s wandering, Garnerius, CXCIII, 153.---From gluttony of the belly comes dullness [Col. 0068] of understanding, Garnerius, CXCIII, 153.---Luxury deceives the mind, ibid., CXCIII, 154.

## XL. INDEX OF THE EARTHLY PARADISE, IN WHICH, LEAVING ASIDE THE QUESTION OF ORIGINAL SIN, IS NOTED EVERYTHING THAT THE FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING THE HISTORY OF EDEN, FROM ADAM’S TRANSLATION INTO IT UNTIL HIS EXPULSION; THAT IS: 1) WHAT TOOK PLACE BEFORE, 2) WHAT TOOK PLACE DURING, AND 3) WHAT TOOK PLACE AFTER THE FALL OF THE FIRST PARENTS THEREIN

### I. Before the Fall

In this part Genesis, chapter 2, from verse 8 to the end, is explained: namely, the planting, trees, and rivers of the earthly paradise; Adam’s introduction; the command not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—not because the tree itself was rational by nature or possessed knowledge of good and evil, but because in it Adam could experience and know the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience; the bringing forward and naming of the animals; the sleep, prophecy, and formation of Adam and the woman; their lack of shame—that is, Adam and Eve, preserving the propriety of angelic dignity, were naked indeed of earthly garments, but clothed with the splendour of immortality; and the moral and physical condition of Adam and Eve while they dwelt innocently in that most delightful place. That is, they had been placed in the earthly paradise in order to be good and happy, without any assault of the flesh, free for good and evil, so that, if they bound themselves by the bonds of love to obedience toward their Creator, they might at length pass into their heavenly homeland without bodily death. For they had been created mortal, so that if they sinned they could die; and immortal, so that if they did not sin they could also not die; and so that, through the merit of free choice, they might attain the blessedness of that region in which they could neither sin nor die.

### II. During the Fall

Under this heading Genesis, chapter 3, verses 1–9, is treated: namely, the permission and manner of the devil’s temptation and seduction of Adam and Eve. For God had said, “You shall die by death”; Eve said, “Lest perhaps we die”; finally the serpent said, “You shall by no means die.” Thus Eve immediately ate from the forbidden tree; Adam too was deceived through the woman and likewise ate. Finally, the opening of their eyes, their shame, and their fig-leaf coverings are treated. Hence, while both sought likeness to divinity, they fell and lost the gifts of immortality; and, having lost charity, they were found evil. That is, the prince of vices, when he conquered them, stripped those made in God’s image, armed with chastity and ordered by temperance, of these gifts and such great goods, and destroyed them together . . .

### III. After the Fall

An explanation is given of Genesis, chapter 3, verses 8–24: namely, God’s walking in paradise and his questions to Adam and Eve, with their confession and excuse; the curse upon the serpent and the promise of the Saviour; the punishments inflicted upon Adam and Eve; the skins of animals, the expulsion from paradise, the cherubim, and the flaming sword.
