## XLI. INDEX OF ORIGINAL SIN, OR OF THE FALL OF THE FIRST PARENTS, IN WHICH EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY THE FATHERS IS SET FORTH IN ANALOGICAL ORDER

Lest this index should overlap twice in one place, it is only mentioned here and will be placed below under the Index of Sins. Let the kindly reader consult it there.

## FIFTH SERIES OF INDICES

[Col. 0071]

### [PREFACE]

In this fifth series, comprising eleven indices, we shall present everything concerning Holy Scripture insofar as it is the word of God and the foundation of all religion. First, indeed, we shall report everything that the Fathers said concerning the inspiration, authenticity, truthfulness, and so forth of the Scriptures. Next we shall append all general commentaries on Scripture; all explanations of the various chapters of each book and of the more notable passages. Thereafter there will appear an exegetical index of every verse, from the first of Genesis to the last of Revelation, according to the canonical order of the books, so that at a single glance the reader will see all the writers—often two or three hundred in number—arranged chronologically from Tertullian to Innocent III, who have elucidated or commented on this or that verse of Scripture. Furthermore, indices will be appended concerning allegories, figures, and parables of both the Old and New Testaments. Finally, the more distinguished men and women of both Testaments whom the Fathers mention in their writings will be set out in alphabetical order. Once this has been done, not one word, or even one iota, of Scripture cited in the *Patrologiae Cursus* will escape us; and if elsewhere we have promised labours more than Herculean, this series alone will prove the truth of that promise.

[Col. 0073]

## XLII. SCRIPTURAL INDEX: THAT IS, AN INDEX REPORTING EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY THE FATHERS CONCERNING THE INSPIRATION, AUTHORITY, EXCELLENCE, ETC., OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS

### NOTICE

We have determined to append this index as a necessary preface, as it were, to the three indices that follow, by whose aid access to them will be easier and more certain. In this index, then, we shall in turn discuss the inspiration, authority, excellence, and integrity of Holy Scripture; its canon, authors, versions, interpretation, and various senses. Moreover, we shall speak of the division of Scripture, namely, the Old and New Testaments and all the books of each; finally, we shall report general treatises on Holy Scripture. Thus the reader will be able, with no little advantage, to survey at a single glance all the sayings of the Fathers concerning the sacred books.

### [SCRIPTURAL INDEX]

### I. On the inspiration of Holy Scripture

The divinity of Holy Scripture is demonstrated, Tertullian, I, 388 ff.---The divine Scriptures, ibid., III, 1059.---The books of the Old Testament were published by men filled with the divine Spirit, ibid., 378.---Why divine Scripture is called *theopneustos* (θεόπνευστος, God-breathed), St. Ambrose, XVI, 803.---All the words of Scripture are divinely inspired, St. Jerome, XXII, 431.---All Scriptures are inspired by the Holy Spirit, ibid., XXIV, 332.---The Scriptures were produced by the Holy Spirit, ibid., XXV, 1222.---The sacred writers spoke by one Spirit, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1175, 1176.---In Scripture God himself speaks, ibid., XXXII, 864; and the Apostle demonstrates this, ibid., XLII, 646.---Holy Scripture is God’s written bond, ibid., XXXVII, 1880.---Holy Scripture is the venerable pen of God’s Spirit, ibid., XXXII, 747.---The Scriptures are divinely inspired, ibid., XLII, 1175, 1183.---They are like letters sent to us by God, ibid., XL, 1050.---Things inserted into the Holy Scriptures by the divine Spirit, Cassian, XLIX, 728.---God is the author of the Holy Scriptures, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 880.---All Scripture is divinely inspired, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 749; St. Lawrence of Novara, LXVI, 105.---How we prove that the books of our religion were written by divine inspiration, Junilius, LXVIII, 42.---How it may be proved that Scripture is divine and delivered by God, Cassiodorus, LXX, 19.---All books of divine Scripture shine with the heavenly light and power of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 1109.---Holy Scripture is called the language of God, ibid., 540.---The Holy Spirit speaks through the sacred writer things which belong to the Spirit; and the writer himself writes within himself of things belonging to God, as if of another, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 518.---The sacred writer is the pen by which the sacred books have been written by the Holy Spirit, ibid., 517.---The inspiration of Holy Scripture, ibid., LXXIX, 19.---In Scripture one hears not the voice of prophets and patriarchs, but that of God, ibid., LXXIX, 148.---The Holy Spirit is believed to be the author of those same Scriptures, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 750.---The Holy Spirit fully inspired the New and Old Testaments into the holy Church, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 139.---Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored all these books and corrected all the volumes of the prophets, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 366.---These are the writers of the sacred books, speaking by divine inspiration, ibid., 367; CXI, 110.---The Holy Spirit is believed to be the author of those same Scriptures, ibid., CVII, 367.---Ezra the scribe, after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans and the Jews had returned to Jerusalem, inspired by the divine Spirit restored the library of the Old Testament, ibid., CXI, 121.---Separated individually in separate cells, as some assert, they interpreted everything by the Holy Spirit, ibid., 122.---The Scriptures are inspired by God, ibid., CVIII, 1134.---All Scripture of the Old and New Testaments is divinely inspired, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 752.---It is called fiery because it is inspired by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 33.---All Holy Scripture, canonical Scripture, is one book, tending toward one end; it proceeds from one God and was written by one and the same Spirit, Rupert, CLXIX, 18.---For Holy Scripture was never brought forth by human will; rather, holy men of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke, ibid., 1091.---Holy Scripture is a voice from [Col. 0074] heaven, ibid.---Which writings ought uniquely to be called Scriptures of divinity, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 9.

### II. On the authority of Holy Scripture and its truthfulness
Scripture’s majesty and authority. Tertullian, I, 386 ff., 446, 469; II, 167. The authority of the divine Scriptures is to be followed, idem, III, 1058, 1065, 1114. Scripture’s authority, St. Hilary, IX, 1045. The authority of Greek manuscripts of Sacred Scripture is greater, St. Ambrose, XVI, 839. The authority of the Scriptures is to be followed, St. Jerome, XXIV, 122. Neither the error of fathers nor that of ancestors is to be followed, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches, ibid., 743. If what may be called well-intentioned lies are admitted into the holy Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? idem, XXII, 648. Whether a writer of the Holy Scriptures ought to have lied, ibid., 566. The authority of the Scriptures wavers if their writers could have lied for a beneficial purpose, ibid., 567. On the canonical authority of Scripture, composed by the divine Spirit, St. Augustine, XLI, 318. He recognizes the necessity of faith and the authority of the Scriptures, idem, XXXII, 722. The Manichaeans remove the authority of the Scriptures altogether when they accept some things and reject others, idem, XLII, 508, 597; XLV, 1008. The divine authority of Sacred Scripture, idem, XXXII, 723, 842, 852; XLII, 249. Scripture’s wondrous authority, idem, XLI, 357, 359, and its most exalted authority, ibid., 318. Holy Scripture is placed upon the highest and heavenly summit of authority, idem, XXXIII, 277, 278. It must be believed that the authors of the canonical books alone made no error in writing anything, ibid., 276, 284, 285. The authority of canonical Scripture yields to no one, idem, XLI, 517, 678. How the authority of the Scriptures is to be proved, ibid., 245, 248, 283, 284, 452, 485, 486, 517, 626. How great the authority of Scripture is in the narration of events, idem, XLI, 599, 600. The authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, commended by Christ and his apostles, idem, XLII, 637, 638, 647. Scripture’s authority is not to be blamed because of the sins it recounts; indeed, it is to be praised and loved, ibid., 438, 439, 440. The Scriptures which are called canonical in the Church must be believed without any doubt, idem, XXXIII, 598. Christ wished nothing to be believed contrary to the confirmed authority of the Scriptures, idem, XLII, 284. What the authority of divine Scripture prescribes, or what the universal Church regularly observes, must be observed, idem, XXXIII, 202. Faith totters if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers, idem, XXXIV, 35. Those who attribute any falsehood to Holy Scripture attempt to break its authority, idem, XL, 404. No man, however holy and learned, is to be compared with the authority of canonical Scripture, idem, XLIV, 381. If a line of reasoning is offered against the authority of the divine Scriptures, however acute it may be, it deceives by its plausibility; for it cannot be true, idem, XXXIII, 588. Scripture is supreme truth, idem, XXXIII, 839, 860. When Scripture takes some testimony from an author, it does not thereby endorse that author’s other writings, idem, XXXIV, 738. Scripture is heaven, whose authority, like a firmament, is set in the Church and spread throughout the whole [Col. 0075] world, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 288. The authority of Sacred Scripture is indubitable, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 314. The divine Scriptures preserved by the Hebrews furnish testimony against those very enemies of evangelical truth, St. Maximus of Turin, LVIII, 355. On the authority of the Scriptures, Junilius, LXVIII, 20. Which books possess complete authority, ibid.; which possess intermediate authority, ibid.; which possess no authority, ibid. Which authority of Scripture is to be followed first in the Churches, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 139. To whom recourse must be had when the authority of Sacred Scripture is not at hand, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 283. On a most obscure matter one must not argue without the authority of the divine Scriptures, ibid., 314. On the authority of the divine Scriptures and tradition, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 84. On the authority of the books of Sacred Scripture, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15. Nothing of authority will remain to the canonical Scriptures if falsehoods are admitted into them, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 50. Equal authority is not owed to the Scriptures and to their expositions, ibid., 51.

### III.—On the excellence of the Holy Scriptures

By the preaching of the Scriptures Christians renewed their hope and confidence, Tertullian, I, 489. The harmony of all the Scriptures, idem, II, 632. Greater strength will be given, and the understanding of the heart will work more and more as one searches the old and new Scriptures, St. Cyprian, IV, 677. The Scriptures contain nothing unworthy of their author, St. Hilary, IX, 768. Whatever is in them is lofty, divine, rational, and perfect, ibid. Nothing is wiser or more eloquent than the Scriptures, ibid., 543. How much knowledge the Scriptures impart to us, ibid., 396, 397. All Scripture calls us to hope for heavenly goods, ibid., 548. Through the Scriptures God has instructed us in the knowledge of himself, idem, X, 171. Refreshed by God’s utterances, the soul contains within itself, as it were, nourishment for eternal life, idem, IX, 549. Let divine Scripture be your way, St. Ambrose, XV, 1394. It builds up everyone, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1157. The word of God has feasts: some more substantial, such as the Law and the Gospel; others sweeter, such as the Psalms and the Song of Songs, idem, XV, 1517. The books of the heavenly Scriptures are good pastures, ibid., 1390. God filled them with saving precepts by which the weakness of the soul might be healed, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1012. They are the remedy for every weariness and the one refuge in temptations, ibid., 819. Divine Scripture is Wisdom’s banquet, idem, XVI, 71. God walks in paradise when I read the divine Scriptures, ibid., 1154. Our faith is the price of Scripture, ibid., 1043. The more abundantly it is chewed over in the heart, the more health-giving sweetness it offers to the mind, idem, XVII, 866. It is exceedingly sharp for cutting away vices, ibid., 926. It is bread for souls, ibid., 831. It is nourishment and life, ibid., 662.

It is Scripture’s custom to call people to repentance, St. Jerome, XXIV, 235. The teaching of the Scriptures is a most firm wall, idem, XXV, 1267. Scriptural learning brings virgins to blossom, ibid., 1489. Through the Scriptures God made known all mysteries, idem, XXVI, 452. When Scripture is useful to its hearers, ibid., 322. The fruit of meditating upon the Scriptures, ibid., 439. Arm yourself with knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh, idem, XXII, 1078, 124. The majesty of divine Scripture is to be admired, idem, XXIV, 596.

The praise and dignity of Sacred Scripture, St. Augustine, XXXII, 854; XXXIII, 508, 524. The dignity and excellence of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, idem, XLII, 74. Sacred Scripture excels all other writings, idem, XLIII, 128. A comparison of Sacred Scripture with profane writings, idem, XXXIV, 64. Faith is conceived from the Scriptures, idem, XLI, 646. Scripture’s great excellence over secular literature, idem, XXXII, 748. Sacred Scripture is sweeter than all worldly delights, ibid., 810. In the Scriptures there is satiety without disgust, idem, XXXVIII, 30. Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth terrifies the attentive, by its truth feeds the great, and by its friendliness nourishes the little, idem, XXXVIII, 323. The simplicity of Sacred Scripture, idem, XXXII, 686, 723, 847. The wondrous depth of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 723, 810, 832, 1315; XXXIII, 516. The harmony of the Scriptures, idem, XLX [sic], 600. Although the Scriptures have different writers, all nevertheless agree with one another so that they are found to have been spoken, as it were, with one voice, idem, XLII, 249. Scripture’s hidden depths are especially effective in sharpening love for truth, etc., idem, XL, 320. In the Scriptures, some matters concern faith and teaching alone, while others concern the ordering of morals, idem, XXXIV, 887, 888, 889. Scripture asserts nothing but the catholic faith concerning things past, present, and future, ibid., 71. Nearly every page of the Scriptures sounds forth nothing other than Christ and the Church spread throughout the whole world, idem, XXXVIII, 289; XLII, 463. The Old Scripture exists only to commend Christ’s coming and foreshadow the Church, idem, XL, 313, 315. The New Scripture narrates Christ and exhorts to love, idem, XL, 375. How Scripture forms human morals, idem, XXXIV, 71. Every sickness of the soul has its remedy in the Scriptures, idem, XXXVI, 357. God’s Scripture fortifies us against scandals, idem, XXXIII, 266, 267, 270. All Scripture tends to this one end: that faith, hope, and charity may be built up in the soul, idem, XLII, 951. We read the prophetic and apostolic books for the recollection of our faith, the consolation of our hope, and the exhortation of our charity, ibid., 294. The fullness and end of Scripture are love of God and neighbor, idem, XXXIV, 34, 39. All the Scriptures teach you nothing other than self-restraint from this world, so that your love may run toward God, idem, XXXVIII, 264, 695. The usefulness of the Scriptures, idem, XXXVI, 564. Scripture, covered with figures and sacraments, is heaven veiled in clouds, idem, XXXVII, 1908, 1909. Why Scripture is called a two-edged sword, idem, XLI, 692. The Scriptures are like lamps lit in the night of this age, idem, XXXV, 1662; XXXVIII, 1567. Sacred Scripture is a cloud, idem, XXXVI, 137; XLII, 266. Sacred Scripture is a mirror, idem, XXXVII, 1388; XLII, 438, 440; XLIII, 89; XL, 702. A divine treasure, idem, XXXVIII, 1481; XL, 670. To what extent the books of the Old Testament are still useful, idem, XLII, 237, 238; XLIV, 138.

Divine Scripture is compared to a rich and fertile field, Cassian, XLIX, 723. Demons are to be driven away by the authority of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 1233.

By reading the divine Scriptures we acquire the food of the everlasting utterance, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 564. The Scriptures call us back from the seductions of the world, ibid., 340.

All branches of knowledge are inferior to Holy Scripture, Eugippius, LXII, 628. On the power of divine Scripture, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1131. The Holy Scriptures contain nothing superfluous, ibid., 17. Nothing vain is contained in the Sacred Scriptures, ibid., 1139. The power of Sacred Scripture, Cassiodorus, LXX, 22, 1131. Sacred Scripture is the pasture of the faithful people, ibid., 698. Why divine Scripture is called “dripping honeycombs,” ibid., 1077.

Sacred Scripture is called a river in which a lamb may walk and an elephant swim, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 613. It is called now food, now drink, ibid., 540; harvest and riches, ibid., 1088. Sacred Scripture is called field and vineyard, ibid., 1150; a lamp, idem, LXXVI, 107, 848; the Church’s bow, ibid., 133. Scripture is called a tower from which a thousand shields hang, ibid., 971. Sacred Scripture is to be preferred far above all other books, ibid., 135. Its excellence, ibid. Those who, in reading Sacred Scripture, do not seek love of God and neighbor feed upon grass and bark, ibid., 149. In Sacred Scripture God teaches us everything that he teaches us to know, ibid., 271. Sacred Scripture resembles a wheel: it rises and descends, ibid., 829. Scripture builds up in every respect, ibid., 831. Sacred Scripture is compared to heaven, ibid., 883. Sacred Scripture resembles flint, from which fire is struck even though it is cold, ibid., 1058. Sacred Scripture is a mountain indeed, idem, LXXIX, 474; fire, ibid., 475; a spring and a well, ibid., 513, 515. Sacred Scripture is the foundation of the Church, ibid., 146. Sacred Scripture is symbolized by the name of a cart, ibid., 202.

Sacred Scripture surpasses all knowledge and teaching beyond any comparison, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 790. Through the precepts of Sacred Scripture we are restored to life, though we lay dead in sin, ibid., 791. Sacred Scripture is Christ’s table, Alcuin, C, 630. On the preeminence of the Holy Scriptures and the end to which all knowledge ought to be directed, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 379. Nothing else is comparable with these sacred writings, idem, CXI, 106. The reading of the Holy Scriptures is no small foreknowledge of blessedness, idem, CXII, 1233. For in them, as in a mirror, a person can consider himself—what he is like or whither he is tending, ibid. Constant reading purifies the soul, instills fear of hell, and urges the reader’s heart toward heavenly joys, ibid. The reading of the Holy Scriptures bestows a twofold gift, ibid., 1234. It instructs the mind’s understanding, ibid. It draws a person away from worldly vanities and leads him to the love of God, ibid. Clearly, all the Holy Scriptures were written for the salvation of souls, so that by them we may advance in the knowledge of truth, ibid., 1234. On the commendation of Sacred Scripture, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 25. Scriptures are called rains by analogy, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 678; balances, ibid., 926; a table, ibid., 975; heavens, ibid., 1039.

The purity of Sacred Scripture, Guibert, CLVI, 178.

Sacred Scripture contains the authority for every truth that reason gathers, St. Anselm, *Cant.*, CLVIII, 528. Whoever seeks to live piously meditates on Holy Scripture, ibid., 596.

The Gospels and the Apostles’ Epistles, the books of Moses and of the prophets, are set before us like dishes filled with every delight, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 406.

To read Sacred Scripture is to celebrate a feast, [Col. 0077] Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 813. Sacred Scripture is the road to heaven, idem, CLXVII, 366. It is signified by the dove, ibid., 441. The opening of Sacred Scripture is signified by the richness of the earth or the abundance of grain and wine, ibid., 461, 462. Sacred Scripture is the paradise of delight, ibid., 607. By reading the Sacred Scriptures we explore the excellent land, ibid., 875. Sacred Scripture is the land of the living, ibid., 958. It engenders love in the soul, ibid., 1575, 1576. Prophetic Scripture is signified by the early rain, and apostolic Scripture by the latter rain, idem, CLXVIII, 92. Sacred Scripture is called gold and silver, ibid., 248. Scripture’s pure speech shines like silver and gleams like gold, ibid., 1557. That the holy Scripture of the Old Testament is that field, and why it is fittingly signified by the name of a field, idem, CLXIX, 15. That this treasure of Sacred Scripture is not in one part of the field, but throughout the whole field, ibid., 16. Sacred Scriptures are sometimes customarily signified by the name of waters, ibid., 1091. They are also customarily compared to thunder, ibid. The reading of Scripture is a guardian of chastity, Hildebert, CLXXI, 197. Scripture is a watchtower, a guard, and a table, ibid., 515; a crowned table, ibid., 350; our mirror, ibid., 374; bread for the soul, ibid., 588, 678. Sacred Scripture is the storehouse of grace, ibid., 394. Sacred Scripture is saving water which washes, refreshes, and cools, ibid., 663. It is the way of salvation, ibid., 712. The pastures of Sacred Scripture are holy, ibid., 780. Sacred Scripture is the treasure of shepherds and Christians, ibid., 818. The excellence of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 862. Sacred Scripture provides remedies against temptations, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 60, 167. Sacred Scripture is compared to the kingdom of God, ibid., 154. Meditation on Holy Scripture nourishes sweetness of spirit, ibid., 721. Scripture is a sacred harvest, ibid., 1059. That divine Scripture is distinguished from other writings, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 11. On the fruit of divine reading, ibid., 20. What fruit Sacred Scripture receives from other writings, and what it bestows on them, ibid., 20. On the subject matter of divine Scripture, ibid., 24; and CLXXVII, 376. Sacred Scriptures are sacred vessels, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 762. The four functions of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 178. The whole intention of the Scriptures seems to tend toward this: that we may believe, hope, and love, Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 154. Holy Scripture is a lamp, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1096. Divine Scripture is a table richly supplied, ibid., 637. Scripture is refreshment for the good, ibid., 1483. Why Sacred Scripture is called the fiery law, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 755. The continual reading of Holy Scripture: its fruits, benefits, and other praises, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVII, 629. That Sacred Scripture also contains the best rules of civic life, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 740.

### IV. On the integrity of Sacred Scripture and its alteration

The authority, integrity, and antiquity of the Old Testament cannot be doubted, Tertullian, I, 384. The interpolation of the Scriptures—how great a sacrilege it is, idem, II, 51 ff. Their adulteration always accompanies variation in doctrine, ibid. The adulteration of the Scriptures and of their expositions is to be identified wherever a difference of doctrine is found, idem, II, 51, 146. He corrupts the Scriptures in some cases by hand, and in others the expositions by their sense, ibid., 52. The integrity of the Scriptures, ibid., 51. The alteration of the Scriptures by heretics, ibid., 52, 515. Marcion rejects and corrects the Sacred Scriptures, ibid., 758. He separated the New Testament from the Old, ibid., 268. Philosophers corrupted many things drawn from the Scriptures, idem, I, 515, 520. Anathema to anyone who adds anything to the divine Scriptures or takes anything away, St. Ambrose, XVI, 927. Some Latin copies of Scripture were falsified by faithless persons, ibid., 752. Heretics attached certain false things to the divine Scriptures and removed certain things from them, idem, XVII, 968. St. Jerome answers those who reproached him because he had altered certain passages from the New Testament already received, XXII, 431. If the Scriptures are not received intact, the gates are opened to every error or crime, St. Augustine, XLII, 1145. The Manichaeans contended that certain false statements had been mixed into the canonical Scriptures which they accepted, idem, XLV, 1337. They shamelessly taught that the Scriptures had been corrupted, idem, XLII, 69. By whom the Manichaeans believed them to have been corrupted, ibid., 70. The Donatists boast that they saved the Scriptures from fire, idem, XXXVIII, 310. Augustine exhorts Jerome to restore the Septuagint version, greatly corrupted and divergent, to its true form, idem, XXXIII, 241, 807. The books of Scripture guarded by Catholic teaching are not falsified, idem, XL, 70. The Latin translation of the Scriptures varies so greatly in different codices that it can scarcely be tolerated, idem, XXXIII, 291. The idioms of Sacred Scripture must in no way be rashly altered, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1126. The language of Sacred Scripture must remain uncorrupted, ibid., 1127. The words of Scripture must not be changed in order to preserve the rules of Latin expression, ibid., 1128.

### V. On the canon of the Holy Scriptures

Notes on a fragment by an unknown writer concerning the canon of the Holy Scriptures, Tertullian, III, 169. A headless fragment by an unknown writer concerning the canon of the Holy Scriptures, ibid., 173. Which Scriptures Hilary held to be canonical, St. Hilary, IX, 240, 241, note. A decree on books to be received and not received, elucidated from unpublished documents, Anonymous, XIX, 787. The order of the Old Testament begins, 791. The order of the prophets begins, 791. The order of the historical books begins, ibid., 792; likewise the order of the Scriptures of the New Testament which the holy and catholic Church receives, ibid. Which books are received in the canon, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 501, 626. Every Scripture which does not accord and agree with the ecclesiastical canon, we not only do not receive, but also condemn as alien to the truth of faith, Bachiarius, XX, 1034. Canon of the Scriptures, St. Jerome, XXIII, 246. Canon of the books of the Old and New Testaments, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41. What canonical and apocryphal Scripture is, idem, XLI, 470. Which Scriptures are canonical, as established by a council, idem, XXXIII, 233. None are to be received besides those received by the Church, idem, XXXIX, 2176. The books of Scripture are received in the number transmitted by the authority of the Church, idem, XLV, 1718, 1733. Canonical books, idem, XXXIV, 40. We receive the New and Old Testament in that number of books which the authority of the Catholic Church transmits, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 513, 514. Canon of the Holy Scriptures, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 504, 721, 871. Whether the canon of Scripture was established by the Synod of Nicaea, ibid., 429, 430. A decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas—note on the order of the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. Which books do not rank among canonical Scriptures, Junilius, LXVIII, 17. What is the fullness of the New and Old Testament which the Catholic Church receives in the canon, according to the ancient tradition of predecessors, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 155. Which books are received in the canon, idem, LXXXIV, 652. Which books are contained in the canon of each Testament, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 140. That all books of holy authority ought either to be kept in memory or not be wholly unknown, ibid. On the books of the two Testaments, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 383. On canonical and noncanonical books, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 20 ff. What the canonical Scriptures are, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338. The order of the Old Testament received and venerated by the holy and Catholic Roman Church, arranged by Pope Gelasius together with seventy bishops, ibid., 983. A decree, made with seventy bishops, concerning apocryphal writings, ibid., 984. Decrees on books to be received or not received, written by Pope Gelasius, Burchard, CXL, 715. On the order of the books of the Testament, which Pope Gelasius held in a council at Rome with seventy bishops, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276. On the order of the books of the New Testament which the holy Roman Church holds and the universal Church observes, ibid. That canonical Sacred Scripture of both the Old and New Testaments is bounded by its own definite limits, ibid., 313. Which books have been received by the Church, ibid., 1101. On the number of the books of the Old and New Testaments, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 320. On the order and number of the books, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 778. On the number of the books of sacred utterance, idem, 185; CLXXV, 15.

### VI. On the authors of the divine books

On divine writers, Junilius, LXVIII, 20. We know the writers of the divine books from their titles and prefaces, ibid.; or from their titles alone, ibid.; or from the tradition of the ancients, ibid. On the writers of the sacred books, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 747; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365; CXI, 106; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 16; CLXXVI, 779. On the authors of the New Testament, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 781. Which Scriptures are authentic, ibid., 786. Which Scriptures are apocryphal, ibid., 787.

### VII. On translations of the Holy Scriptures

The books of Scripture translated from Hebrew into Greek, Tertullian, I, 378 ff. At the request of King Ptolemy, seventy elders translated the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew letters into Greek, St. Hilary, IX, 262. Their venerable and ancient authority, ibid., 539. It is not safe to depart from their translation, ibid., 529, 751. Among the variety of translations, the Septuagint is preferred, ibid., 742. Hilary composed two translations of Scripture together, ibid., 878. The Church follows the readings of the seventy men more closely, St. Ambrose, XV, 1325. On a new translation of the Old Testament made after the Septuagint, St. Jerome, XXII, 665. The fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, idem, XXIII, 665. The preeminent authority of the seventy translators, idem, XXII, [Col. 0079] 566. Hilary translated into Latin the homilies on Job and many treatises on the Psalms, ibid., 572, 603. Origen interpreted the Scriptures well in many places, ibid., 603. Origen compiled the Hexapla of four editions and mixed Theodotion’s edition into the Septuagint edition, idem, XXIII, 459. The Septuagint edition in Daniel differs greatly from the truth and is rightly rejected by the Churches, ibid., 455. The seventy translators were corrected and translated by Jerome, ibid., 447. How the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion render the text of Scripture, ibid., 452. They are received by the Greeks, ibid. They are contained in the Hexapla, ibid. The sixteen books of the prophets, which I translated into Latin from the Hebrew language, idem, XXII, 512. I recently translated Job into our language, ibid. Eusebius of Vercelli translated into our speech the commentaries on all the Psalms by the heretical man Eusebius of Caesarea, ibid., 603. Aquila’s first edition, idem, XXIV, 719. Aquila’s second edition, ibid., 740. The common translation of the Septuagint differs from Hebrew truth and from the other editions, ibid., 126, 239. Augustine, dissuading Jerome from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew and exhorting him to restore the Septuagint version, greatly corrupted and varying, to its true form, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 241. Aquila translated Scripture from Hebrew into Greek, idem, XLI, 603. At what time, ibid., note. The Jews prefer Aquila to the other interpreters, ibid., 470. Greater trust is to be placed in Greek copies of the Gospels, idem, XXXIV, 1259. Augustine calls the Septuagint translation the Vulgate, idem, XLI, 489. Various translations of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 603. There are very few interpreters of the divine Scriptures in Latin, but innumerable ones in Greek, idem, XLII, 214. Why certain things are found in the Septuagint version which are not in Hebrew codices, and conversely, idem, XLI, 604. Hebrew codices and the Septuagint version are both to be used, ibid., 605. Why the seventy translators differ from the Hebrew, idem, XXXIII, 243; XXXIV, 1139; XLI, 604. The Septuagint edition distinguished by asterisks and obeli, idem, XXXIII, 753. This translation was commissioned by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, idem, XLI, 235. The extent of the authority of the seventy translators, idem, XXXIV, 595; XLI, 450, 470, 603; XXXIII, 243, 290. Why Augustine does not wish Jerome’s translation of the Septuagint from Hebrew to be read in church, idem, XXXIII, 290. The Septuagint version was in use in Latin churches, idem, XLI, 604. The Old Latin translation and the Greek translation of the seventy interpreters are commended, idem, XXXIV, 46. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated the sacred utterances from Hebrew into Greek, idem, XLI, 603. St. Jerome translated all the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew codices into Latin, Gennadius, LVIII, 1059. He rendered Daniel and Job into the Roman language in a finished translation, ibid. Jerome made Matthew’s Gospel, from Hebrew, Roman [Latin], ibid., 1060. Alone among all Romans he commented upon all sixteen books of the prophets, ibid. By what arrangement of God’s providence the Scriptures of the Old Testament were translated from Hebrew into Greek speech, so that they might become known to all nations, Eugippius, LXII, 1018. Translations of the holy books by St. Jerome, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1116, 1117, 1118, 1119, 1124. The Vulgate translation is derived from Hebrew and Arabic speech, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 645. The new translation is preferred to the old translation of Scripture, ibid., 174. The seventy translators issued the first edition after Ezra, from Hebrew into Greek, under Ptolemy, king of Egypt, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 747. After this Aquila issued the second edition, and Theodotion and Symmachus the third and fourth, ibid., 748. Origen found the fifth and sixth editions and compared them with the other aforementioned editions, ibid. Jerome the priest alone translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech, ibid. On the Septuagint version, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 366; CXI, 121. After this Aquila issued the second edition, and Theodotion and Symmachus the third and fourth, ibid. He found the fifth and sixth editions, ibid. Translators of the Bible, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 23. On the translation of Sacred Scripture used by St. Bruno, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 19. On the various translations of Sacred Scripture, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 17; CLXXVI, 780, 781.

### VIII. On the use, interpretation, and various senses of Sacred Scripture

The sense of Scripture requires the guidance of a definite interpretation, Tertullian, II, 22. Simplicity itself commends the common senses, ibid., 799. The Jews recited the Scriptures openly, with tax-exempt freedom, idem, I, 381. They were read in Christian assemblies, ibid., 477. Christians did not conceal them, nor could they, ibid., 446. That heretics are to be admitted to no discussion whatsoever based on the Scriptures, idem, II, 28, 30, 31, 50. Aristeas’s testimony concerning the Greek [Col. 0080] translation of the Old Testament, idem, I, 380. The recitation of Sacred Scripture in the palace, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 73. How it is fitting to read, hear, and sing the Scriptures, St. Hilary, IX, 550. Jews, when reading the sacred books, do not dare touch them with the hand, but place a cloth beneath them, ibid., 728. The spiritual senses of Scripture are not invented, ibid., 685. Those who believe that all things must be understood according to the letter are refuted, ibid., 779, 783. Scripture is rich in senses, ibid., 987. The allegorical sense takes nothing away from the truth of the letter, ibid., 758–954. From where the understanding of the Scriptures is to be sought, idem, X, 107. Scripture, pregnant with mysteries, demands a skilled and pious reader, idem, IX, 753. Moral uprightness is a preparation for investigating God’s testimonies, ibid., 504. To understand the mysteries of the old Law one needs a heavenly teacher and very great merits of faith, ibid., 610. Study of the Scriptures should be persistent, but their understanding must be awaited from God, idem, X, 49. Grace is necessary for understanding them, idem, IX, 501. The understanding of the Scriptures is to be sought from what precedes or follows, idem, IX, 282. One must examine the force of words no less than that of things, idem, IX, 966. Individual matters must be distinguished according to persons, times, and so forth, ibid., 754. Scripture does not customarily repeat the same things in two forms of expression, ibid., 716. Knowledge of Christ is the key of the Scriptures, ibid., 236.

Meditation on Scripture is especially necessary for priests, St. Ambrose, XV, 1344, 1345. First the prophet is read, then the apostle, and thus the Gospel, in which the words are clear and the precepts more forceful, ibid., 1443. We should exercise ourselves in its unwearied use, and why, ibid., 1370. All divine Scripture is either natural, mystical, or moral, St. Ambrose, XV, 65. The mystical sense is sharper; the moral sense sweeter, ibid., 1351. Solomon expressed the moral subject more fully in Proverbs, the natural in Ecclesiastes, and the mystical in the Song of Songs, idem, XIV, 511. They customarily put past things in place of future or present things, ibid., 445. Let us employ ourselves day and night in a kind of arena of the heavenly Scriptures, idem, XV, 1370. Eat their food daily, so that you may not hunger but be filled, ibid., 1517. Sacred Scripture is a sea containing profound senses within itself, idem, XVI, 880.

Sacred writings are called a snare for those who interpret them wrongly, Rufinus, XXI, 688. One must pray in interpreting the Scriptures, St. Jerome, XXII, 364. A carnal understanding of Scripture is the occasion of many evils, idem, XXVI, 407. The literal sense does not help, ibid. Some refuse to understand them spiritually, ibid., 422. Read the divine Scriptures often; indeed, let sacred reading never be laid aside from your hands, idem, XXII, 533. How difficult it is to understand divine Scripture, and especially the prophets, ibid., 512. It is not the work of one and the same person to test gold coins and the Scriptures, to taste wines, and to understand prophets or apostles, ibid., 604. On the study of the Scriptures, ibid., 540. He first exhorts to the reading of divine Scripture, ibid., 1204. Knowledge of the Scriptures cannot be possessed together with the riches of the world, idem, XXIII, 936. We do not learn any arts without a teacher; yet to many the teaching of Scripture alone seems so cheap or easy that it needs no instructor, ibid., 1037. How the Old and New Testaments should be read, ibid., 1104. What he observes in interpreting the Scriptures, idem, XXV, 1164. In citing the Scriptures, the apostles follow not the words but the sense, ibid., 1056. The misuse of Scriptural testimonies is condemned, ibid., 1028. It is a great danger to interpret the Scriptures in the Church, idem, XXVI, 322. Some prefer to follow Jews rather than apostles in expounding the Scriptures, ibid., 383. It is customary for them often to set down a Hebrew word together with its interpretation, ibid., 374. What asterisks and obeli signify in the interpretation of Scripture, idem, XXII, 928.

Two kinds of disagreement in interpreting the Scriptures, St Augustine, XXXII, 838. Against those who rashly reject others’ method of interpretation, ibid., 839. How Scripture is understood in various ways by learned persons, ibid., 841. He considers that very great authority should be accorded to interpreters of Scripture, id., XXXIII, 112. The true senses of Scripture are revealed by the Holy Spirit, id., XXXII, 844. To what extent knowledge of animals, plants, and so forth—especially of the heavenly bodies—contributes to understanding the Scriptures, id., XXXIV, 56. An ambiguity in Scripture in one language is removed by another, id., XXXVII, 1536. What obelisks or asterisks signified in Greek manuscripts, id., XXXIV, 590; XLI, 604. Why strokes or obeli and asterisks were sometimes placed in the edition of the Seventy Translators, id., XXXIII, 261. How the Scriptures should be read, id., XXXVIII, 354, 74; XXXIV, 262. Study of sacred Scripture requires a humble and gentle mind, id., XXXIV, 64, 66. An explanation of Scripture that is not understood should be sought from God, id., XXXV, 1539, 1540; XXXIV, 89. Understanding of Scripture is not to be expected in an unusual manner, id., XXXIV, 17. Whoever cannot understand Scripture should give honour to God’s Scripture and fear to himself, ibid., [Col. 0081] 261. When sacred Scripture is not understood, how it should be read, id., XXXV, 1536. He whose heart is full of charity comprehends the Scriptures without any error and retains them without any labour, id., XXXIX, 1533. Augustine advises beginning the reading of Scripture with the Apostles, id., XXXIII, 508. From whom an exposition of sacred Scripture should be sought, id., XXXII, 1311. No one ought to judge sacred Scripture, ibid., 859. Scripture was expounded in church, id., XLI, 77. The treatment of Scripture is a great and arduous task, id., XXXIV, 19. Two vices are hostile to the treatment of Scripture, id., XLII, 845. Rules for understanding Scripture, id., XLIII, 673; XXXVIII, 26, 30, 46, 149, 180, 198, 450, 456, 470, 556, 609. A fourfold method of treating the Scriptures of the Old Testament, id., XLII, 68. How Scripture is to be understood and explained, id., XLI, 473. Rules for attaining the true sense of Scripture, id., XL, 344, 345. Various interpretations of sacred Scripture can at the same time be true, id., XXXII, 838, 844. Which sense should be regarded as the more excellent, ibid., 844. In all Scripture the utmost care must be observed, so that the exposition of the divine mystery may accord with faith, id., XL, 55. Study, prayer, and reading of the Scriptures are necessary for a priest, id., XXXIII, 88, 89. How great reverence is owed to the Scriptures, id., XXXIX, 1739. What sort of reader Scripture requires, id., XXXIV, 36. How one should devote oneself to the study of Scripture, ibid., 42. The usefulness of diversity of interpretation, ibid., 43. From what source a fault of interpretation may be corrected, ibid., 44. From what source knowledge of an unknown word or unknown expression is to be derived, ibid., 45. What sort of soul the study of sacred Scripture requires, ibid., 64. The obscurity of Scripture is useful, id., XLI, 332. Why some things in Scripture are closed and others open, id., XXXVIII, 849, 196; XXXVI, 159, 160; XXXVII, 1189, 1907. The hidden places of Scripture are especially effective in sharpening love of truth, etc., id., XL, 320. Amid all the abundance of Holy Scripture we are fed by its clear passages and exercised by its obscure ones, id., XXXVIII, 450. Scripture is a forest because of the darkness and shaded recesses of its mysteries, id., XXXVI, 214. Pious faith and humble inquiry are necessary to its understanding, id., XXXVIII, 336. We ought not to be content with the surface of the Scriptures, id., XXXIII, 920. In the obscurities of Scripture its expositors are not to be followed rashly, ibid., 922. Sacred Scripture is reproved only rashly when it is not understood, id., XLII, 77, 91. When sacred Scripture is not understood, what should be done, id., XXXV, 1722, 1726, 1727, 1741. Obscure passages of Scripture are to be explained from clearer ones, id., XXXIV, 79. The obscure things of Scripture are revealed to the meek and humble, id., XXXVII, 1907. Scripture is received differently by the pious and the impious when it is obscure, id., XXXV, 1721, 1722. Scripture capable of bearing a double sense is not to be interpreted with hasty assertion, id., XXXIV, 260. Nothing prevents the same passage of Scripture from being understood in various ways, ibid., 80. An uncertain passage is explained rather through other passages of Scripture than by reason, ibid. Obscure passages of Scripture are to be explained by other manifest and least doubtful passages, id., XXXVIII, 264; XXXIX, 1634; XLI, 332, 333. In the difficulties of Scripture, honour God’s word; defer understanding in piety, id., XXXVII, 1907. Honour in it what you do not understand, and honour it all the more the more veils you perceive, id., XXXVIII, 336. Piety and humility are more required for the divine Scriptures than acuteness of intellect, ibid. Before you know why something was said, believe that it ought to have been said as it was said, id., XXXVII, 1915. Hold fast and devoutly receive the clear matters of Scripture, that the obscure matters may rightly be opened to you, id., XXXVIII, 290. The very desire to understand is prayer before God, ibid., 820. Augustine confesses that in the Holy Scriptures themselves he knows far more that he does not know than he knows, id., XXXIII, 222. Scripture may fail to be understood because of ambiguous or unknown signs, id., XXXIV, 42. Ambiguity in Scripture is either in proper words or in figurative ones, ibid., 65. Hebrew, Syrian, Egyptian, and other names occurring in sacred Scripture had been interpreted by Augustine’s time, ibid., 62. In Scripture everything said or done is to be understood literally, figuratively, or in both ways, id., XXXVIII, 556. There are three kinds of expression in Scripture, id., XLII, 846. From what source knowledge of an unknown word or unknown expression is to be derived, id., XXXIV, 45. How indefinite propositions in Scripture are to be understood, id., XXXVIII, 450. It uses the plural for the singular, id., XLI, 519. At times it uses “many” for “all,” ibid., 696. Many things are spoken of as though already done when they are still only in hope, id., XXXIII, 842. Scripture narrates future things as past, id., XXXVII, 1476. It uses the future for the past and the past for the future, id., XL, 305, 705. There is no book of Scripture which, by extracting and tearing away certain sentences, does not appear contrary to itself, id., XXXVIII, 332. Passages of Scripture apparently contrary are reconciled, ibid., 764, 180, 213, 283, 372, 791, 804. Why Scripture speaks in figures, id., XL, 663. In matters which it recounts figuratively, some things may be received according to the meaning of the figures and some according to faith in the events performed, id., XXXIV, 247. What cannot be expounded literally in Scripture is figurative and mystical, ibid., 401, 430. How metaphorical modes of speech in sacred Scripture are to be understood, ibid., 166. What rule should be maintained in explaining allegories, id., XXXVI, 116. A spectacle divinely displayed in the senses of Scripture, id., XXXVI, 298; XXXVIII, 322. To remove ignorance of signs, knowledge of languages is necessary, especially Greek and Hebrew, id., XXXIV, 42. Rule concerning passages of Scripture in which actions of good persons now contrary to morals are praised, ibid., 78. Before all else, the genre of expression must be considered, ibid. The same word does not signify the same thing everywhere, ibid. Nothing prevents the same passage from being understood variously, ibid., 80. An uncertain passage is more safely made clear through other passages of Scripture than through reason, ibid. Knowledge of tropes is necessary, ibid. The seven rules of the Donatist Tychonius are examined, ibid., 81 ff. In obscure passages of Scripture nothing is to be asserted rashly, ibid., 260. A rule for understanding the allegories of Scripture, id., XXXVIII, 198.

Some things in the Scriptures are so clear that they need no supporting interpretation. Cassian, XLIX, 722. Others, however, are so obscured by mysteries that, in investigating and understanding them, they reserve for us an immense field of exercise and diligence, ibid. By what study a monk can attain knowledge of Scripture, ibid., 250. Some have attained the sense of Scripture in dreams, ibid., 972. By what stages one arrives at it, ibid., 965 ff. If you wish to arrive at true knowledge of the Scriptures, you must first attain an unwavering humility of heart, ibid., 970. Constant reading of Scripture is recommended, ibid. Many twist it to alien meanings, ibid., 515. The literal and figurative senses of Scripture, ibid., 723. The mystical sense is manifold, ibid., 961, note. How knowledge of Scripture is acquired, ibid., 249, note. — Understanding of the Scriptures must be merited by good works. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 418. The usefulness of Scriptural obscurity, ibid., 437, 519. — Who is an interpreter of Scripture, St Leo the Great, LIV, 918. The canonical Scriptures to be read in church, id., LVI, 428. Reading the divine Scriptures is necessary. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 277. What we ought to know in observations for understanding Scripture: some matters are commanded universally, others, etc. Eugyppius, LXII, 964. On modes of expression, knowledge of which he declares necessary for resolving Scriptural obscurities, ibid., 966. On the seven rules of Tychonius, by which he says that those diligently striving to understand Scripture are greatly assisted, ibid., 967.

What is to be observed in understanding Scripture. Junilius, LXVIII, 42. With what study holy Scripture ought to be read together with expositors. Cassiodorus, LXX, 1138. Obscure passages of Scripture are elucidated through others, ibid., 1107. Absurd words found in Scripture are to be corrected by Hebrew or Greek codices, ibid., 1129. Scripture has the custom of speaking allegorically, ibid., 468. Sacred Scripture often uses the plural number for the singular and conversely, ibid., 191. Sacred Scripture often uses future things in place of past things, ibid., 69. — With how much discernment sacred Scripture should be read, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 807. In it we must seek sometimes the letter, sometimes the spirit, ibid. Sacred Scripture should be read in such a way as to benefit ourselves and others, ibid., 887. Christ himself taught us to interpret sacred Scripture figuratively, ibid., 1131. How manifold is the sense of sacred Scripture, id., LXXV, 45. How obscure and difficult it is, id., LXXVI, 882. The letter of Scripture sometimes contradicts itself, id., LXXV, 633. Understanding of sacred Scripture is acquired through humility and assiduity in reading, ibid., 633. The path by which one arrives at understanding the sense of Scripture, ibid., 736. Those who know how to discern the manifold senses in the sacred Scriptures abound in delights, ibid., 1132. The obscurity of sacred Scripture moves us to investigate its deeper meaning, ibid., 37. Heretics do not eat the marrow of sacred Scripture but gnaw its bark, id., LXXVI, 749. — The usefulness of sacred Scriptural obscurity, ibid., 829. The book of sacred Scripture is opened and unfolded by God’s hand, ibid., 882. In sacred Scripture the truth of history must first be established; afterwards the sense of allegory must be sought, ibid., 1302. A manifold sense lies hidden in the same Scripture, ibid., 845. Sacred Scripture is difficult to understand, ibid., 986. Sacred Scripture deserves reverence even when it is not understood, id., LXXIX, 20. The letter of Scripture without the spirit is not only dead but also killing, ibid., 268.

On expositors of the divine Scriptures, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 808. That they should not search the sacred utterances too deeply, ibid., 810. Scripture is to be understood not only historically but also mystically, St Isidore, LXXXIII, 528. — Its individual sentences, namely those of sacred Scripture, have manifold senses, Alcuin, 652. The allegorical and historical senses, ibid., 559. And the moral sense, id., CI, 1080.

[Col. 0083] The obscurities in which sacred Scripture is enveloped, and the fact that no one may read it rashly; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 380. On the method of reading the sacred Scriptures, ibid., 383. On unknown signs, ibid., 385. A method of determining whether an expression is literal or figurative, ibid., 389. On the varying signification of words, consisting in opposition and diversity, ibid., 390. On reading the divine writings, id., CXII, 1193. The fourfold sense of Scripture, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 33. Whether the literal sense is more worthy than the other senses of sacred Scripture, ibid., 37, 38. From what one must begin, ibid. What should be called the literal sense of sacred Scripture and what the spiritual sense, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 39. Whether every text of sacred Scripture is expounded in the fourfold sense mentioned above, ibid. Whether a text of sacred Scripture has only one literal sense or sometimes several, ibid., 41. Given that one text sometimes has several senses, which of them is to be preferred over another, ibid., 43. Whether an effective argument can be drawn from every literal sense, ibid., 44. The literal sense can be compared with the other senses in two ways, ibid. His response to the saying, “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life,” ibid., 47. Through the literal sense not only history but also things to be done are obtained, ibid. The literal sense is the foundation, ibid., 48. In sacred Scripture many things are handed down parabolically, ibid. From whom study of sacred Scripture begins, ibid., 49. The tropological, allegorical, anagogical, and literal senses, ibid., 57, 63. The seven rules for interpreting Holy Scripture, Walafrid Strabo, XCIII, 31, 32. Only canonical Scriptures are to be read in churches. Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338.

Scripture is to be interpreted from tradition. Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 339. Against a corrupt interpretation of divine Scripture. Othlonus, CXLVI, 77. Bishops and pastors ought to teach the people sacred Scripture. John of Rouen, CXLVII, 142, 233. Four rules are to be applied in expounding the sacred Scriptures. Guibert, CLVI, 25. History, allegory, tropology, anagogy, ibid. Study of sacred Scripture is enjoined above all. St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 1064. All ought to approach questions concerning the sacred page with the utmost caution, ibid., 265. How and at what time the books of the Old and New Testament ought to be read. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 277, 1103. How the divine Scriptures ought to be read and interpreted. St Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 173. Scripture’s profundity is understood only through faith in Christ, Rupert, CLXVII, 983. Holy Scripture, in matters of faith, is to be interpreted not according to one’s own opinion but by reason and authority. Hildebert, CLXXI, 1067. Four matters are to be observed in sacred Scripture, ibid., 634. What is not expounded in sacred Scripture by Scripture itself is reserved for the prelates of the Church to expound, ibid., 767. What is not understood in sacred Scripture is to be left to the Holy Spirit, ibid., 767. Pleasures hinder understanding of Scripture, ibid., 768. Scripture has a literal, spiritual, and intellectual sense. Godfrey, CLXXIV, 999. On the threefold understanding. Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 789. Not everything found in divine discourse, but only certain things, are to be forced into the said threefold interpretation, id., CLXXV, 12. The necessity of literal and historical interpretation, ibid., 13. How divine Scripture should be read for the correction of morals, id., CLXXVI, 794. How sacred Scripture should be read by those seeking knowledge in it, ibid., 799. On treating divine Scripture in three ways, id., CLXXVII, 205. On interpreters of sacred Scripture, CLXXVI, 780. On study of the divine Scriptures, ibid., 777. On the seven rules, ibid., 791. On the mystical places, times, and events of sacred Scripture, id., CLXXV, 23. On difficulties in sacred Scripture, ibid., 25. The threefold sense of Scripture: historical, moral, mystical. St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 714. Whether and how several senses of the same Scripture are to be admitted, ibid., 1027. To misuse Scripture is devilish, ibid., 186. The Church’s judgment is infallible in the use and application of Scripture, ibid., 94. Scripture must be searched seriously and diligently, id., CLXXXV, 211. A pious aspiration toward Christ for obtaining understanding of sacred Scripture, id., CLXXXIV, 762. The sense of Scripture is often opened to those who pray, ibid., 976. On reading Scripture, ibid., 1194. Senses not at variance with the rule of faith, or not too discordant with the context of the reading, are not to be rejected. Guerric, CLXXXV, 177. The necessity of secular learning for understanding sacred Scripture is shown. Gratian, CLXXXVII, 206. Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ, ibid., 210. To whom the understanding of Scripture is opened. Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1276. Scriptural obscurity is useful and not to be reproved, ibid. Sacred Scripture admits manifold exposition. Richard of St Victor, CXVI, 269. Holy Scripture contains four senses, of which the literal is sometimes more difficult than the spiritual. Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 630. With what simplicity Scripture is to be [Col. 0084] explained. Peter Cantor, CCV, 33. Its interpretation should not depend upon our will, but rather the reverse, ibid., 240. Sacred Scripture has a threefold sense: historical, tropological, allegorical. Alan of Lille, CCX, 209.

## IX. On Allegories in Sacred Scripture

Certain allegories of sacred Scripture. St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 100 ff. Allegories throughout the whole of sacred Scripture. Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 850 ff. Allegories in the Old Testament. Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 635 ff. Allegories in the book of Genesis from the beginning of the world to Abraham, ibid. On the remaining mysteries of Genesis from Abraham to Moses, ibid., 643; in the remaining books of the Pentateuch, and first in Exodus, ibid., 653. Allegories in the books of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, ibid., 670 ff.; in the First Book of Kings, from Hannah to David, ibid., 681. ## X. On the Division of Sacred Scripture

Division of sacred Scripture. St Augustine, XXXV, 1745. All Scripture is divided into two Testaments, Old and New, id., XXXIV, 246, 247. Sacred Scripture divided into four parts. St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 834. Into how many books the Old Testament is reckoned. Alcuin, CI, 1120. How the first order of the Law is to be understood, ibid., 1124. What the second order is, ibid. What the third order is, ibid. The Hebrews, with Ezra as author, reckon the Old Testament according to the number of their letters as twenty-two books, dividing them into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, in which there are nine books, ibid. Some, however, assign Ruth and *Cinoth*, called in Latin the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, and make twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, ibid. Among us the fourth order of the Old Testament consists of those books which are not in the Hebrew canon. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 10. In the New Testament, moreover, there are two orders, ibid. Others distinguish the Old and New Testament into seventy-two books, ibid. The first books of the Law, those of Moses, are five, ibid.; these are followed by sixteen historical books, ibid. There are sixteen prophetic books, ibid., 105, 106. After these come eight books of verses, which among the Hebrews are written in different metres, ibid. There are forty-five books of the Old Testament, ibid. Of the New Testament the first are the four Gospels, ibid.; these are followed by fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, to which are joined the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude, ibid. The Acts of the Twelve Apostles, the seal of all these being the Apocalypse of John, ibid.

## II. On the Old and New Testament

The Old Testament pertains no less to Christians than to Jews. Tertullian, I, 386. Why and how, Tertullian, I, 394. The Old Testament was buried in Christ, id., II, 973. The passing away of the Old and the succession of the New, ibid., 415. The New Testament had to be sealed on the platform on which the Old had been written, ibid., 414. Among the Israelites the Apostles unsealed the Old Testament and sealed the New, ibid., 849. Marcion separated the New Testament from the Old, ibid., 43. Hebrew books of the Old Testament, deposited at Alexandria, id., I, 379.

Why the covenant—the law given to the Jews—was called by that name by the prophets. Lactantius, VI, 514. That the Old and New are different, ibid. That the Old was not perfect but the New completed, ibid., 515. Moses established the Old Testament in writing. St Hilary, IX, 262. Division of the Old Testament into twenty-two books, ibid., 241. The doctrine of the Old and New Testament is the same, ibid., 431.

The name of sacred law is attributed not so much to Moses’ Pentateuch as to the other books of the Old Testament and even to those of the New. St Zeno, XI, 338, note; I, 387, note 3. The covenants of the old and new law signified by Jacob’s ladder, ibid., 428; by the sword sharpened on both sides, ibid. They are compared with a scribe’s pen, ibid., 429. They are explained by the two coins in the mouth of the fish caught by Peter, ibid., 430. They are confirmed from the two coins given by the Samaritan to the innkeeper, ibid., 431. They are designated by Moses and Aaron, ibid., 510. One cannot be useful without the other, ibid., 430.

The New Testament was in the Old Testament. St Ambrose, XV, 1250. The old covenant in type, the new in truth, id., XIV, 331. Shadow in the Law, image in the Gospel, [Col. 0085] truth in heavenly things, id., XVI, 94. The day of the Old Testament has passed; the new day has come, on which the New Testament was consummated, ibid., 1141. The Old Testament is not contrary to the New, id., XVII, 243. It was a shadow of the New Testament, ibid., 832. In the New Testament we hold the pledge of divine grace, id., XIV, 331. Whoever drinks of the New Testament is not merely a river, but rivers of living water will flow from his belly, id., XVI, 1210. The grace of the New Testament is the peace of the Old, ibid., 1138. Why it is called the New Testament, id., XVII, 889.

Nothing is discordant in the Old and New Testament. St Jerome, XXII, 366. Ezra, restorer of the Pentateuch, id., XXIII, 190. Christ the Lord is author of both Testaments, ibid., 451. There are many things in the New Testament from the old books that are not found in the Septuagint, ibid., 456. Heretics who mutilate the Old Testament, ibid., 575. Heretics denying the Old Testament, id., XXV, 168. Both Testaments belong to one God, ibid., 1297. We are commanded to believe in both instruments—that is, the old and the new—with equal veneration, id., XXIII, 1101. Eternal punishments are prepared for those who by no means join the two Testaments, ibid., 1104. The two Testaments are joined in unity, id., XXIV, 97. The New Testament is strengthened by testimonies of the Old, ibid., 271.

The two Testaments. St Augustine, XXXVIII, 36. Why one covenant is called old and the other new, id., XLIV, 221, 222, 597. Both Testaments hidden before Moses, id., XLIII, 122. The Old Testament was revealed through Moses, id., XLIV, 596. Various names for the Old Testament, ibid., 595. What the Apostle calls by the name “Old Testament,” id., XXXII, 632. The name “Old Testament” is used in two ways, id., XLIV, 327. To what extent the books of the Old Testament are still useful, id., XLII, 237, 238; XLIV, 138. The Old Testament is useful even for convicting Gentiles, id., XLII, 328. The books of the Old Testament pertain to Christians, ibid., 52. Why a veil is said to have been placed in the reading of the Old Testament, id., XLIV, 219. What Augustine thought about the Scriptures of the Old Testament and their authors, id., XLII, 73. The authority of the Old Testament is now maintained not in imitation of Jewish servitude but in testimony to Christian freedom, ibid., 240, 243. Cerdon despises the Old Testament, ibid., 29; the Severians despise it, id., 30. The Old Testament is from God, id., XLIV, 594. In the Old Testament there are many things that offend the minds of those ignorant of and inattentive to themselves, id., XLII, 67. What the Manichaeans object to in the books of the Old Testament, id., 73. Faustus thought the Old Testament should be rejected for a twofold reason, id., 217. The calumny of the Pelagians concerning the Old Testament, id., XLIV, 591.

Why the precepts of the Old and New Testaments differ, id., XLII, 449. In the Old Testament a distinction must be made between precepts for doing the life and precepts signifying the life, ibid., 228, 236, 243, 501, 504. The Old Testament contains such precepts of righteousness as we are still commanded to observe, id., XLIV, 222, 594. The Old Testament is useful, and has the greater authority for preaching Christ because it came to us through the Jews, id., XLII, 329. Why the more severe punishment of the Law prevailed in the Old Testament, id., XXXIII, 660. The Manichaeans do not receive the Old Instrument; they assert that the New is corrupt, id., XLV, 1009, and falsified, id., XLII, 38, 501, 506, 514. Concerning the New Testament, Manichaeans are less able than Catholics are concerning the Old to answer objections, ibid., 244. How it is proved that the New Testament belongs to the Apostles, ibid., 509. The God of both Testaments is one and the same, ibid., 622, 623, 660, 661, 662, 663; XXXVI, 931. The Manichaeans slandered the two Testaments as not agreeing with one another, id., XXXVII, 1893, but as mutually opposed, id., XXXVIII, 23, 26. The Old and New Testaments are not contrary to each other, id., XLII, 622. The harmony of the two Testaments, id., XXXIII, 218. The order of each is wonderful, id., XXXII, 1334; XXXIV, 136. The New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made manifest in the New, ibid., 623, 633. The New was hidden in the Old as fruit in the root, id., XXXVI, 914. What the Old Testament prefigured, id., XLII, 448. To those who understand it rightly, the Old Testament is a prophecy of the New, ibid., 302, 328. The New Testament was foretold in the Old, id., XXXII, 619. It was foreshadowed in the Old, id., XXXVII, 1070, 1305; XLII, 448, 449, 623. In the New Testament the obscurities of the Old are revealed and the predictions fulfilled, ibid., 518. In the Old Testament grace lay hidden, veiled and concealed, which was revealed in the Gospel of Christ, id., XLIV, 216, 217. When the revelation of the New Testament was made, ibid., 597.

The distinction between the Old and New Testaments, id., XXXIII, 540; XXXVI, 930; XLIV, 220, 226, 227, 228; and their harmony, id., XXXVIII, 37. The briefest and clearest difference between the two Testaments: fear and love, ibid., 207; XLII, [Col. 0086] 158. The law of the Old Testament is a ministry of death and condemnation; the law of the New, a ministry of Spirit and righteousness, id., XLIV, 219. The New Testament pertains to charity, id., XXXV, 2074; the Old to fear, ibid., and to the old man, ibid., 1636. It promised carnal things, ibid. The harmony of both Testaments lies in the precept of charity, id., XXXII, 1316, 1322, 1325. The promises and sacraments of the Old and New Testaments differ, id., XXXIV, 732. The promises of the Old Testament differ from those of the New, id., XXXVI, 327, 931; XXXVII, 1145, 1466, 949. Only earthly happiness is openly promised in the Testament properly called Old, id., XLIV, 328. The Old Testament has temporal promises but spiritual meanings, id., XXXVIII, 37. The New Testament is promised in the Old, id., XLIV, 328. The promise of the New Testament was made through Ezekiel, id., XLV, 1264, 1265, 1266, 1267, 1271. Why the Old Testament promised earthly goods whereas the New promised heavenly goods, id., XLII, 162, 163. In the Old Testament the prefiguration of our possession is known; in the New, possession itself is held, ibid., 157. The Old Testament bears servants, the New free persons, ibid., 622. The two Testaments signify two lives and two hopes, ibid., 304. Who belong to the New Testament and who to the Old, id., XLIII, 122; XLIV, 593. The saints of the Old Testament belong to the New, id., XLII, 456, 656; XLIV, 591. Christians serving God in hope of a carnal reward belong to the Old Testament, id., XXXVIII, 32, 40. How both Testaments pertain to the Israelites, id., XLIII, 255.

The grace of the New Testament, id., XXXIII, 542. A book on the grace of the New Testament, ibid., 539. No mention of the New Testament occurs in the old books except in Jeremiah, id., XLIV, 221, 222. Christ is mediator, sealer, guarantor, witness, inheritance, and co-heirs of the Testament, id., XXXVII, 1130. Injury is done to the New Testament if it is made equal to the Old, id., XLIV, 329. The New Testament is to be preferred to the Old in dignity, id., XLI, 662. The Old Testament is compared to barley, id., XXXV, 1594. In the two Testaments, Old and New, the rule of discipline has been handed down to us, id., XXXII, 1334. Christ removed the exceedingly heavy yoke of many observances of the Old Testament, id., XXXVIII, 594. In the New Testament Christ wished discipline to be gentler, ibid., 1413. The two Testaments commend God’s mercy, id., XXXIV, 634. The Old Testament is signified by the former tablets, ibid., 653, 755, 756. The sign of the Old Testament is circumcision in hidden flesh; that of the New, the cross upon the free forehead, id., XXXVIII, 876.

The two Testaments are prefigured in Sarah and Hagar, Isaac and Ishmael, id., XXXIV, 566; XXXVI, 302; in the two spies at Jericho, id., XLIII, 638; in the holy place and the Holy of Holies, id., XXXIV, 635; and in the two cherubim of the ark, ibid., 634. The sign of the New Testament: the red heifer, ibid., 732. The two Testaments are signified by two men carrying a cluster of grapes, id., XXXIX, 1799; Christ being in the middle of the two, ibid. The two Testaments are two breasts from which the saints are nourished, id., XXXV, 2417. The New succeeded the Old Testament as wine succeeds water, id., XXXIX, 1919, 1920, 1921.

The Spirit of the Old and New Testament is one, and their harmony one, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 693. The testimonies of the two Testaments concerning Christ wonderfully accord with one another, ibid., 245.

Paulinus calls the two Testaments the lips of God, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 218. The Old and New Testament depicted in paintings in the basilica of St Felix, ibid., 666, 667.

One faith of the New and Old Testament, St Fulgentius, LXV, 445. No one ought to reject the Old Testament because he sees that its sacraments have ceased, ibid., 434. Both Testaments in Scripture under the names of an old and a new friend, ibid. New wine: the New Testament, ibid.

The harmony of both Testaments, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 835. What one Testament signifies, the other presents, ibid., 836. The Old Testament understood spiritually and the New remain unchangeable, ibid., 837. How greatly the New Testament excels the Old, ibid., 979. Christ is the end of both Testaments, ibid., 981. The distinction between the Old and New Testament, ibid., 1042. The Old Testament is called a shadowed mountain, ibid., 669. The Old Testament is signified by the wheel which appeared upon the earth to Ezekiel, ibid., 833. The two Testaments are two wheels, id., LXXIX, 188. The harmony of both Testaments is signified by the two cherubim above the mercy-seat, with wings spread and facing one another, id., LXXVI, 835.

On the Old and New Testament, St Isidore, LXXXII, 229. The whole content of both Testaments is distinguished in a threefold way: history, morals, and allegory, ibid., 230.

On the Old Testament, Alcuin, CI, 1120. On the New Testament, ibid., 1128. The Old Testament restrains the lust of the flesh; the New, even that of the mind, id., C, 1098. The Old Testament is indicated by the twenty-four elders and the throne, ibid., 1117. [Col. 0087] The Old and New are figured by the bow, ibid., 1123.

All the books of the New and Old Testament agree with one another, St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 320.

The two Testaments are signified by the two cherubim, Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 702, 1153; by the two mountains, id., CLXVIII, 741.

Why it is called a Testament, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 210. On the two Testaments, ibid., 208. Each Testament is divided into three orders, id., CLXXVI, 778. What distinctions exist between the two Testaments, id., CLXXV, 626, 627.

Why one is called the Old Testament and the other the New, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 461, 462. Why we retain the authority of the Old Testament while not observing its rite, ibid., 461.

The translation of the Old Testament into the New, id., CXCI, 398. The New Testament is better than the Old, id., CXCII, 460. The two Testaments do not have the same promises, sacraments, and precepts, ibid. The difference between the two Testaments, ibid., 461. The Old Testament is signified by the denarius, id., CXCI, 1298. The Old and New Testament are a two-edged sword, ibid., 1258. The Old Testament divided into three orders, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1259.

## XII. On the Books of the Old Testament
Books of the Old Testament: twenty-two or twenty-four, St. Hilary, IX, 241. Order of the Old Testament, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Order of the prophets, ibid. Order of the historical books, ibid., 792. Prologues to the books of the Old Testament, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 156 ff., 747. Into how many books the Old Testament is counted, Alcuin, CI, 1120. Into how many divisions these books are divided according to the Hebrews, ibid., 1123, 1124. Whether there are more books of the Old Testament, ibid. Whether further books from the Old Testament are found, ibid. The Hebrews, with Ezra as author, receive the Old Testament in twenty-two books, according to the number of their letters, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 105. When and at what season the books of the Old Testament should be read, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 277. On the books of the Old Testament, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15; CLXXVI, 782. How many books Sacred Scripture of the Old Testament has, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 697. For there are forty-two books of the Old Testament, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 320.

### On Genesis

The five books of Moses, St. Hilary, IX, 241. The books which the religion of the Hebrews handed down as having been written by Moses and the prophets, id., X, 28. Paradise is the book of Genesis, in which the virtues of the patriarchs spring up, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1154. On Genesis, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Genesis is received among the canonical books, St. Innocent I, XX, 501. Preface to the *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, St. Jerome, XXIII, 935 ff. Subjects treated in Genesis, id., XXII, 545. Genesis offers much concerning the nature of things, id., XXIII, 179. Genesis is the head of all books, ibid., 938. What it is called among the Hebrews, ibid., 939; XXVI, 387. Genesis is received among the canonical books, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 504, 721, 891; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. Moses wrote the Pentateuch, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 747. On Genesis, ibid., 159, 155. Moses, author of the five books which among the Greeks are called the Pentateuch, Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 235. On Genesis, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. Moses first issued the cosmographical account of sacred history in five volumes, which is called the Pentateuch, Alcuin, CI, 1125. What Genesis contains, ibid., 1121. Moses first wrote the Pentateuch, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365. Moses wrote the book of Genesis, id., CVIII, 1001; CXI, 105, 106. On Genesis, id., CVII, 365; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 778; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 201; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15, 16; id., CLXXVI, 186, 778. What reason Moses had for writing the history of the divine law, Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 111. The question is raised where Moses published his books, ibid., 112. The Holy Spirit is faithfully believed to be the author of Genesis, ibid., CXV, 111.

St. Hilary, IX, 241. Sedulius, XIX, 791. St. Innocent I, XX, 501. Subjects treated in Exodus, St. Jerome, XXII, 545. Exodus, in which almost everything by which the Church is instructed is expressed figuratively, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 183. Exodus among the canonical Scriptures, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15, 16; id., CLXXVI, 186, 778.

On the book of Joshua, St. Jerome, XXII, 545; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 504, 721, 871; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. Among the historical books, Junilius, LXVIII, 16. St. Hilary, IX, 241. One book of Judges, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Among the prophetic and canonical books, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15; CLXXVI, 186, 778.

### On the Book of Ruth

St. Hilary, IX, 241. One book of Ruth, Sedulius, XIX, 791. It is received in the canon, St. Innocent I, XX, 501; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41. It seems rather to belong to the beginning of Kings, ibid. It is placed among the canonical Scriptures, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 504, 721, 871; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. Ruth among the historical books, Junilius, [Col. 0089] LXVIII, 16. On the Book of Ruth, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 156, 161, 746. The Hebrews append this little book to the Book of Judges, ibid. The Latins maintain that it belongs more correctly to the corpus of the Book of Kings, ibid. ### On the Book of Kings

Four books of Kings, St. Hilary, IX, 241; Sedulius, XIX, 791; St. Innocent I, XX, 581 [probably 501]; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 47; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 504, 721, 871; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. Among the historical books, four books of Kings, Junilius, LXVIII, 16. Books I and II of Kings are ascribed to Samuel, ibid., 20, 268, 17 note. Four books of Kings, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 157. On the Book of Kings, ibid., 161. Four books of Kings are contained in the canon of both Testaments, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. What is in the Book of Kings? Alcuin, CI, 1121. Why it is called *Malachim*, ibid., 1125. Who first brought this book together into one volume, ibid. David wrote the continuation of Samuel to the end; Jeremiah issued the whole of *Malachim*, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 747. Four books of Kings, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365. Samuel, which is the first of Kings, id., CXI, 105. *Malachim*, which is the second of Kings, ibid. What the Book of Samuel describes, ibid., 107. From where it received its name, ibid. Who composed it, ibid. Why the book *Malachim* is so called, ibid. How the Book of Kings is divided among the Latins and among the Hebrews, ibid., 111. Subject matter of the books of *Malachim*, ibid. Samuel, that is, First and Second Kings, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; *Malachim*, that is, Third and Fourth Kings, ibid. Four books of Kings, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15, 16; id., CLXXVI, 186, 779.

### On Paralipomenon

St. Hilary, IX, 241. Two books of Paralipomenon, Sedulius, XIX, 791; St. Innocent I, XX, 502; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 505, 721, 871; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537.
