Two books of Paralipomenon are contained in the canon of both Testaments, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. What is in Paralipomenon, Alcuin, CI, 1121. Paralipomenon, which among the Hebrews is one book, not two, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21. Two books of Paralipomenon, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338. Two Paralipomenon, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15. What *Paralipomenon* means in Latin and Hebrew, id., CLXXVI, 186, 779.

### On the Book of Job

St. Hilary, IX, 241. One book of Job, Sedulius, XIX, 792; St. Innocent I, XX, 501. Job begins in prose, proceeds in verse, and ends in ordinary prose, St. Jerome, XXII, 545. It sets out all the rules of dialectic by proposition, assumption, confirmation, and conclusion, ibid. Every individual word in it is full of meanings, ibid. Job, the athlete of the Church before Christ, seems to write against the future Origen, id., XXIII, 381. From the prologue to Job, ibid., 452. On the Book of Job, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 505, 721, 871. One Book of Job, Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. How the book of the prophet Job should be read, Eugippius, LXII, 626, 627. One Job, Junilius, LXVIII, 17. Who was the author of the Book of Job? St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 515. Its author is the Holy Spirit, id., 517. By whose inspiration Job described his own struggles, ibid. On the Book of Job, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 163. The Hebrews think Moses wrote the Book of Job; others, one of the prophets, id., 747. It is contained in the canon of both Testaments, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. What is in Job? Alcuin, CI, 1121. Who was the author of the Book of Job? id., 1126. Its beginning and end among the Hebrews are composed in prose; all its middle portions proceed in heroic metre, ibid. On the Book of Job, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365. Author of the Book of Job, ibid.; CXI, 107. [Col. 0090] On the subject matter of the Book of Job, id., 112. First among the nine Hagiographa is Job, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21. One Job, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15. Some believe that the Book of Job was written by Moses, others by one of the prophets, and still others by Job himself, ibid., 16. In the order of the Hagiographa nine volumes are contained: first, Job, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 186.

### On the Psalter: the Author of the Psalms

The book of Psalms is not David’s alone, St. Hilary, IX, 232. They belong to those whose names they bear, ibid., 233. Those without a name belong to the person named in the title of the preceding psalm, ibid. Whether the author of the same psalm should be said to be David or Asaph, St. Ambrose, XIV, 837. All writers of psalms included examples, or certain sayings of their predecessors, in their writings, ibid., 924. It should indeed be known that holy David composed these 150 psalms by the revelation of the Spirit of God, Rufinus, XXI, 644. Although David sang all the psalms, St. Jerome, XXVI, 824. Whether all the psalms contained in the Book of Psalms are by David, St. Augustine, XLI, 547. Sure indications establish that the psalms belong to the prophet David alone, Cassiodorus, LXX, 14. Ten prophets wrote the Psalter, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 747. David alone composed all the psalms, Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 483. Authors of the Psalms named in their titles, Alcuin, CI, 1126. On the authors of the Psalter, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365, 366; CXI, 107. There are also those who say that Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah wrote [psalms], ibid. Whether David composed all the psalms, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 841. David issued the Book of Psalms, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 16; CLXXVI, 780.

### On the Titles of the Psalms

Various titles of the Psalms, St. Hilary, IX, 243. They were added by the Seventy translators, ibid., 843. The title is an index of the matters to be treated, ibid., 292. It shows of what matters the psalm consists, ibid., 246. Titles of the Psalms that direct us toward understanding, ibid., 642. Title and psalm mutually lend each other authority, ibid. A title which indicates history does not exclude spiritual understanding, ibid. The purport of all the titles prefixed to the psalms, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 641 ff. Eleven psalms that have no titles, St. Jerome, XXIII, 408. Psalms without a title, id., XXII, 407. What is a title but a key? id., XXVI, 834. By the title the meaning of each Psalm is understood, ibid. The title of a psalm is, as it were, the psalm’s herald, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1804; Cassiodorus, LXX, 424. On the uniformity of the titles’ inscriptions, ibid., 16. The inscriptions of the Psalms must be considered by allusion, ibid. Why proper names are placed in the titles of the Psalms, ibid., 300. Why “for the end” is so often repeated in the titles, id., 103. Explanation of various titles, Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 139. Ezra prefixed titles to the Psalms, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 990—and did so by the Spirit of God, id., 1213. Gerhoh, CXCIII, 636. On the titles of the Psalms, ibid. Individual psalms are found marked beforehand by their own proper titles, ibid., 637.

### On the Subject Matter, Excellence, and Usefulness of the Psalms

Almost all the Psalms assume the person of Christ, Tertullian, II, 167. They represent the Son speaking to the Father, ibid. The Psalms sing the Gospel history, St. Hilary, IX, 235. The Psalms teach us the perfect knowledge of God and obedience, ibid., 584. The Psalms are prophecies of evangelical mysteries, ibid., 235. The Psalms do not announce only matters of their own time, ibid., 643. In them there is nothing low or commonplace, ibid., 610. Nothing but prophecy, ibid., 838. Some think that the person of Christ is applicable to scarcely any of the psalms, ibid., 352. The Book of Psalms especially breathes the grace of God, St. Ambrose, XIV, 922. Praises and virtues of the Psalms, ibid., 924. What psalm is not a remedy for the sinful conscience? ibid., 1009. In this Book of Psalms are the advancement of all and a certain medicine for human salvation, ibid., 923. David, our Simonides, Pindar and Alcaeus, and likewise Horace, Catullus, and Serenus, gives voice to Christ on the lyre and raises him from the dead in the ten-stringed psaltery, St. Jerome, XXII, 547. The whole Psalter is nothing but prayer to God in all works, St. Jerome, XXIII, 501. Power and usefulness of the Psalms, St. Augustine, XXXII, 767. The Psalms: honeyed letters from the honey of heaven, ibid., 768. The Psalms are our mirror, id., XXXVI, 248. The Psalms are called David’s harp, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 515. What its subject matter is, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 844. Its intention, ibid. Its method of treatment, ibid. The subject matter of this book is the whole Christ, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 59. What its method of treatment is, ibid. Subject matter of the Book of Psalms, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 630. Its intention, ibid. Its method of treatment, ibid., 631.

### On the Division, Number, and Order of the Psalms

Ezra, compiler of the Psalms into one book, St. Hilary, IX, 234. Ancient traditions concerning Ezra as compiler of the Psalms, [Col. 0091] ibid., 238. The Book of Psalms is one, not five, ibid., 232. The Psalms were undivided among the Hebrews, collected into one by Ezra, and arranged in order by the Seventy, ibid., 238. What the three fifties of psalms signify, ibid., 239. The Psalms among the Hebrews lack order and number, having been collected by Ezra into one volume, ibid., 237, 238. The Psalter seems to be divided into five books, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1085 ff. Ezra the scribe, who supplied the titles, arranged the psalms otherwise than they had been dictated, Rufinus, XXI, 644. Some have said that there are five books of Psalms, but the authority of canonical Scripture proves that there is only one, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1961. Number of the Psalms, St. Benedict, LXVI, 472. Division of the Psalms, ibid., 471. Division of the Psalms according to the ancient Fathers, Cassiodorus, LXX, 504. On the fivefold division, ibid., 16. On the arranger of the Psalms, Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 482. This book consists of 150 psalms, not without a reason of deeper mystery, Walafrid Strabo, XCIII, 843. Likewise, through three fifties a threefold division of the Psalms is made, ibid., 844. The Book of Psalms is one, not five, ibid. The order of the Psalms differs from the order of history, ibid. Ezra was the first to collect these psalms into one volume and to arrange them in order and number, Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 136. Order of the Psalms, ibid., 141. Of how many psalms this book consists, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 57. How it is divided, ibid. Whether the Book of Psalms is one or several, ibid., 57, 58. On the order of the Psalms, ibid., 59. Who arranged the psalms in this way, id., 60. Ezra arranged the Psalms, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 636.

### On the Use, Interpretation, and Various Senses of the Psalms

Singing of the Psalms, Tertullian, II, 660; id., I, 1194. The key of the Psalms is faith in Christ, St. Hilary, IX, 236. Some are easy, others difficult to grasp, ibid., 291. For their understanding, it helps to know who is speaking and about whom, ibid., 247, 248. They are shut and sealed to learned and unlearned alike without the key of faith, ibid., 235, 236. Each has its own keys, ibid., 246, 247. The spiritual understanding of the Psalms cannot be rejected, ibid., 685. A psalm can be understood spiritually even if its title presents history, ibid., 642. Psalms are to be sung always and everywhere, ibid., 550. Though the whole body of all the Psalms is one, natural, mystical, and moral senses nevertheless flourish in it, St. Ambrose, XIV, 966 ff. A person ought not to end the day without the celebration of the Psalms, ibid., 223. Certain Psalms are so much the deeper as they seem the more open, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1501. Psalter translated from the Hebrew by St. Jerome, id., XXXIII, 1077. Origen, Eusebius, and many others who interpreted the Psalms are listed, ibid., 262. Among the Latins, two translations of the Psalter are in use and honour: namely, the Roman and the Gallican, Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 481. Why it is used in the Church more frequently than all others, ibid., 483; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 842. On interpretation of the Psalms, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 22. On censures directed against Bruno’s interpretation of the Psalms, ibid., 23. Why this Scripture is used more than the others in ecclesiastical offices, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 57. David chose four thousand men to sing psalms not only with their voices but also with musical instruments, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 632. David himself also struck the harp with the singers in the house of the Lord, ibid., 633.

### On the Composition of the Psalms

In what language the entire Psalter was composed, Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 480. All the Psalms among the Hebrews are composed in metrical verse, Alcuin, CI, 1126; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 108.

### On the Inspiration of the Book of Psalms

The author of the Psalms is the Spirit of God, St. Hilary, IX, 792. Holy David composed these 150 psalms by the revelation of the Spirit of God, Rufinus, XXI, 644. David issued his prophecy by the prompting of the Holy Spirit alone, without any external assistance, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 53. Inwardly taught by heavenly inspiration, he was filled by the Spirit speaking in him, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 938.

### On Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, etc.

St. Hilary, IX, 241. Although Solomon is said to have sung innumerable songs, he nevertheless left only one, the *Song of Songs*, which the Church received, St. Ambrose, XIV, 923. Three books of Solomon: one on Proverbs, another Ecclesiastes, the third on the Song of Songs, id., XV, 1529. Three books of Solomon, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Five books of Solomon, [Col. 0092] St. Innocent I, XX, 501. Three books of Solomon were received into canonical authority, St. Augustine, XLI, 554; XXXIV, 41. Solomon wrote Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 505, 871; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 747; Alcuin, CI, 1126; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 366; CXI, 108; Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338; Rupert, CLXVII, 1232; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 16; Wolbero, CXCV, 1013. In the Book of Proverbs Solomon treated the moral sphere more fully, the natural in Ecclesiastes, and the mystical in the Song of Songs, St. Ambrose, XIV, 511. One Book of Proverbs, Sedulius, XIX, 791; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; XLI, 554. Proverbs of Solomon, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 721. Three books of Solomon: Proverbs, etc., Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. On Proverbs, Junilius, LXVIII, 18. What is taught in Proverbs, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 164. Three books of Solomon: Proverbs, etc., St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. From where the Book of Proverbs derives its name, Alcuin, CI, 1126. What Proverbs contains, ibid., 1122. On the Book of Proverbs, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 108; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 1125. Subject matter of Proverbs, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 1127. Proverbs of Solomon, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15. Solomon composed parables, ibid., 16. The Proverbs of Solomon are called *parabolai* in Greek and *masloth* in Hebrew, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 186. The Book of Proverbs invites to faith, Ecclesiastes to hope, and the Song of Songs to charity, Rupert, CLXVII, 1232. In Proverbs he speaks of moral uprightness, Wolbero, CXCV, 1013.

### Ecclesiastes

One book, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Ecclesiastes offers much concerning the nature of things, St. Jerome, XXIII, 479. There is no ambiguity about it, ibid., 527. Ecclesiastes is a book which, in the judgment of the Hebrews, deserved authority, ibid., 1116. It is the book of Solomon doing penance, ibid., 1021. Some wrongly think that this book urges us to self-will and luxury, ibid., 1014. It does not urge luxury, nor does it fall into the doctrine of Epicurus, ibid., 1106. On Ecclesiastes, St. Augustine, XLI, 554. The Jews possess Ecclesiastes among the canonical books of the sacred writings, ibid., 661; Eugippius, LXII, 767. [It is possessed] by Christians, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. What difference there is between *Ecclesiastes* and *Ecclesiasticus*, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1117. In Ecclesiastes he examines the nature of things, etc., St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 164. Ecclesiastes is contained in the canon of both Testaments, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. What is in Ecclesiastes, Alcuin, CI, 1122. From where Ecclesiastes derives its name, ibid., 1126. On Ecclesiastes, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365, 366. Subject matter of Ecclesiastes, id., CXI, 113. From where it is named, ibid., 108. In the number of canonical books, Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; Wolbero, CXCV, 1013.

### Song of Songs

St. Hilary, IX, 241. One Book of the Song of Songs, Sedulius, XIX, 791; St. Augustine, XLI, 554; XXXIV, 41; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 18. Subjects treated in the Song of Songs, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 164, 165. Our teachers report that among the Hebrews there was an observance that no one was permitted to read this book unless he were already a man of perfected knowledge and tested faith, ibid., 165. What the Song of Songs contains, Alcuin, CI, 1122. Why it is called the Song of Songs, ibid., 1126. What was the reason why the Song of Songs was sung, ibid., 1010. Three things are to be considered in this book: its matter, intention, and final cause, ibid., 1012. In this book nothing is to be understood carnally according to the letter, ibid. In the Song of Songs he sings of the rational ordering of divine mysteries, ibid., 1013. Four speaking persons are introduced in this book, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 409.

### On the Book of Wisdom

The Book of Wisdom is ascribed to Solomon, Tertullian, II, 544. Among the Latins it is regarded as Solomon’s; among Greeks and Hebrews, as the Wisdom of Sirach, St. Hilary, IX, 827. Easterners regard it as the word of the Lord, ibid., 673. One Book of Wisdom, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Five books of Solomon, St. Innocent I, XX, 501. The Book of Wisdom is inscribed with Solomon’s name, St. Jerome, XXIV, 616. The Jews do not receive the Book of Wisdom into canonical authority, St. Augustine, XXXII, 638; XXXIII, 199. One book, called Wisdom, is said to be Solomon’s by a certain resemblance, id., XXXIV, 41. The Book of Wisdom possesses the authority of canonical Scripture, id., XLIV, 980, 981. Great and learned men who dealt with the divine utterances long before Augustine used the authority of the Book of Wisdom, id., 1019, 1020. Five books of Solomon, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 504, 871. Likewise, one Book of Wisdom, Vigilius of Thapsus, [Col. 0093] LXII, 537. Some add the book called Wisdom, Junilius, LXVIII, 18. On the Book of Wisdom, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 165. The Book of Wisdom is said to have been issued by Jesus son of Sirach, ibid., 158. It is marked beforehand with Solomon’s title, ibid. It is contained in the canon of both Testaments, St. Ildephonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews, Alcuin, CI, 1127. The Jews affirm that it is by Philo, ibid. Jerome says that the same Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews, nor was it received among the canonical Scriptures by the ancients, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 672. Five books of Solomon, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 338. Wisdom of Solomon, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15, 16. In the 130th canon of authority the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon is not written, id., CLXXVI, 186.

### On Ecclesiasticus

One Book of Ecclesiasticus, Sedulius, XIX, 791. Five books of Solomon, St. Innocent I, XX, 501. Another, entitled *Ecclesiasticus*, is said to be Solomon’s by a certain resemblance, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 41. On Ecclesiasticus, id., XLI, 554. Ecclesiasticus is not in the Hebrew canon, id., XL, 165. Five books of Solomon, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 505, 871. One Book of Ecclesiasticus, Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 537. On Ecclesiasticus, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 165. Ecclesiasticus is said to have been issued by Jesus son of Sirach, ibid., 158. It is marked beforehand with Solomon’s title, ibid. Ezra’s book despised the trifles of philosophers, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1074. One Book of Ezra, Sedulius, XIX, 792. Two books of Ezra, St. Innocent I, XX, 501. On Obadiah; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 18. On Obadiah; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 171; St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140; Alcuin, CI, 1127. What is in Obadiah? ibid., 1123; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 117. Obadiah; idem, 108; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21. At what time Obadiah prophesied; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 119. The prophet Obadiah; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 16.

Jonah.—One book of Jonah; Sedulius, XIX, 791. The subject matter of the Book of Jonah; St Jerome, XXII, 546. How [the name] is interpreted; idem, XXV, 1117. At what time he prophesied; ibid., 1119; St Augustine, XLI, 583, 587. He announced not wrath but mercy; idem, XXXIX, 1610. Jonah prophesied Christ not so much by speech as by a certain passion of his own; idem, XLI, 587. On Jonah; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 18; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 171; St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140; Alcuin, CI, 1127. What is in Jonah? ibid., 1123; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 117. On Jonah; ibid., 108; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 127; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 16.

Micah.—One book of Micah; Sedulius, XIX, 791. What he announces; St Jerome, XXII, 546. In the order of the prophets according to the Septuagint translators, he is third; idem, XXV, 1151. Sixth according to the Hebrew; ibid. At what time Micah prophesied; St Augustine, XLI, 583. What Micah, Jonah, and Joel prophesied that accords with the New Testament; ibid., 586. On Micah; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 18; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 172; Alcuin, CI, 1127. What is in Micah? idem, 1123; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 117. On Micah; ibid., 108; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276. How [the name] is interpreted; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 439. On Micah; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 16.

Nahum.—One book of Nahum; Sedulius, XIX, 791. The matters with which he treats; St Jerome, XXII, 546. How [the name] is interpreted; idem, XXV, 1231. In the Hebrew, Micah is placed after Jonah, and Nahum follows Micah; ibid. At what time he prophesied; ibid. What predictions concerning the salvation of the world in Christ are found in Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk; St Augustine, XLI, 587. On Nahum; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, etc., as in the preceding entry.

Habakkuk.—One book of Habakkuk; Sedulius, XIX, 791. The subject matter of the Book of Habakkuk; St Jerome, XXII, 546, 547. What he prophesied and at what time; idem, XXV, 1274. What predictions concerning the salvation of the world in Christ are found in Habakkuk; St Augustine, XLI, 588. On Habakkuk; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721, etc., as in the preceding entries for the other Fathers.

Zephaniah.—One book of Zephaniah; Sedulius, XIX, 792. The subject matter of the Book of Zephaniah; St Jerome, XXII, 547. How [the name] is interpreted; ibid. He prophesied in the days of Josiah; idem, XXV, 1339. What Zephaniah, by the prophetic Spirit, foretold concerning Christ and the calling of the Gentiles; St Augustine, XLI, 591. At what time he prophesied; ibid. On Zephaniah; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721, etc., etc. For the other Fathers, as in the preceding entries.

Haggai.—One book of Haggai; Sedulius, XIX, 792; St Jerome, XXII, 547. Concerning what he prophesies; idem, XXV, 1338. What he prophesied and at what time; St Augustine, XXXVII, 1467. These two prophets, [Col. 0096] Haggai and Zechariah, were filled with the Holy Spirit; ibid. On the prophecy of the prophet Haggai; idem, XLI, 593. He was a prophet during the Babylonian captivity; idem, XXXVII, 1917. He prophesied Jerusalem’s restoration; ibid. A passage of Haggai is defended against the Manichees; idem, XXXVIII, 330. Haggai does not support the Donatist schism; idem, XLIII, 670. Haggai; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721, etc., etc., as in the preceding entries for the other Fathers.

Zechariah.—One book of Zechariah; Sedulius, XIX, 792; St Jerome, XXII, 547. Zechariah the prophet is obscure and the longest among the Twelve; idem, XXV, 1417. Origen wrote two volumes on this prophet; ibid., 1418. Hippolytus likewise published commentaries; ibid. What Zechariah prophesied and at what time; Augustine, XXXVII, 1467, 1917, 1940; XLI, 593. On Zechariah; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721, etc., etc., as in the preceding entries for the other Fathers.

Malachi.—One book of Malachi; Sedulius, XIX, 792. He openly prophesies Israel’s rejection and the calling of the Gentiles; St Jerome, XXII, 547. Various opinions concerning the prophet Malachi; idem, XXV, 1541. Origen wrote three volumes on this book; ibid., 1543. Whether he is the same as Ezra or different from him; ibid., 1541 ff. Whether he was an angel in a human body; ibid., 1399. At what time he prophesied; ibid., 1542. Malachi, or the prophet Malachi, is called “Angel,” and by some is believed to be Ezra the priest; St Augustine, XLI, 699. What he prophesied and at what time; ibid., 593. On Malachi; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 721; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 18; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 174; St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140; Alcuin, CI, 1123, 1127; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 108, 118; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21. The Hebrews think Malachi to be Ezra the prophet and priest; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 277. He prophesied at the same time as Haggai and Zechariah; ibid. Some thought him an angel by nature clothed in flesh; ibid. Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 815. On Malachi; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 16.

On the Maccabees.—Tertullian, II, 606; St Cyprian, IV, 668, 743; idem, III, 800. The Second Book of Maccabees, formerly read constantly by Christians in time of persecution; Lactantius, VII, note 391. The Second Book of Maccabees is cited; St Hilary, X, 582. The First Book of Maccabees is cited; Lucifer of Cagliari, XIII, 959, 964, 966. On the Second Book of Maccabees; ibid., 981, 982; St Ambrose, XIV, 632, 633, 634, 635. On the First Book of Maccabees; idem, XVI, 81, 82. On the Second Book of Maccabees; ibid., 83, 84. Two books of Maccabees; Sedulius, XIX, 792; St Innocent I, XX, 501. The Jews do not have the books of Maccabees, if [they are reckoned] in the same manner as the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; St Augustine, XLIII, 729. Yet they have not uselessly been received by the Church, if they are read or heard soberly; ibid. The Church holds them as canonical; idem, XII, 596; XXXIV, 41. On the Second Book of Maccabees; idem, XL, 593. Two books of Maccabees; St Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 505, 871; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; Junilius, LXVIII, 17. On the Maccabees; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 174, 175; St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. What is to be understood in the books of Maccabees; Alcuin, CI, 1123. By whom the books of Maccabees were written is by no means established; ibid., 1128; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 367. Two [books] of Maccabees; ibid., 365, which, although the Jews separate among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ nevertheless honours and proclaims; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 105. The subject matter of the books of Maccabees; ibid., 119. Although the Hebrews do not regard them as canonical, the Church nevertheless regards them as canonical because of the powerful and wonderful sufferings of certain martyrs; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 21, 22. Two books of Maccabees; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 276. They are indeed read, but are not written in the canon; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 15; CLXXVI, 186. Their author is by no means established; idem, CLXXV, 17.

Baruch.—One book of Jeremiah together with one [book] of Baruch; Sedulius, XIX, 791. The little book of Baruch is joined to the Septuagint edition and is not held among the Hebrews; St Jerome, XXIV, 680. Interpretation of Baruch; idem, XXVI, 445. Baruch is sixth, as Jerome says in the prologue to Jeremiah; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 22. Prolegomena.

XIII.—On the Books of the New Testament.

On the Gospel: its inspiration.—The Evangelists, as the divine Spirit supplied them with an abundance of sayings and of every event, wrote the Gospel without any labour; St Ambrose, XV, 1534. They did not speak by their own power, nor did all relate all the same things; rather, the grace of the Holy Spirit bestowed upon them the things which they should speak, etc.; idem, XIV, 787, 788. In the Evangelists the Holy Spirit speaks; idem, XIV, 787, 711. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they wrote the Gospels; St Jerome, XXVI, 221. The Evangelists proceed wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit leads them. The teaching of the Holy Gospel [Col. 0097] is divinely inspired; St Maximus of Turin, LVI, 750, ibid. The four Evangelists, breathed upon by the fire of the Holy Spirit, wrote; Rupert, CLXIX, 920.

Its authority, excellence, etc.—The authority of the Gospel; Tertullian, II, 363. The Gospels mutually lend one another completeness; St Hilary, X, 376. The Gospel contains all truth; St Ambrose, XV, 1466. It excludes the imperfection of philosophy; idem, XIV, 469. It is a teaching not only of faith but also of morals; idem, XV, 1493. In the Gospel is the perfection of goodness; in the Law, instruction in equity; ibid., 1817. Shadow in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in heavenly things; idem, XIV, 1031. Through hidden mysteries the Law announces Christ, but does not show him face to face as the Gospel does; idem, XV, 1300. The Law is, as it were, a figure for us; the Gospel, as it were, light and the seal of truth; idem, XIV, 1116. The Gospel shines as a lamp’s path in the shadow—that is, in this age; ibid., 817. The Gospel possesses forgiveness, by which sins are pardoned; idem, XVI, 1255. In the Law is servitude; in the Gospel, freedom; ibid., 1089. In the Law is sacrifice; in the Gospel, mercy; ibid., 483. As far as a servant is from a master, so far is the Gospel from the Law; idem, XVII, 52. The Gospel is the discipline of Christians; ibid., 867. Paul declares his glory to be in it; ibid., 230, 231. It is preferred to the Law; St Jerome, XXIII, 251. And why is it to be preferred? ibid., 525. The Gospel’s perfection; idem, XXIV, 566, 753. All things are recapitulated in the Gospel; idem, XXVI, 36. The authority of the Evangelists; St Augustine, XLII, 213. What the Evangelists wrote ought to be reckoned as written by Christ; idem, XXXIV, 1070. *Evangelium* in Latin means “good news” or “good announcement”; idem, XXXVIII, 266, 740; XLII, 210, 214. The authority of the Gospels; idem, XXXIV, 1041. Augustine would not have believed the Gospel except because of the authority of the Church; idem, XLII, 176. One ought to hear the Gospel as though the Lord himself were present; idem, XXXV, 1632. The Gospel is Christ’s mouth; idem, XXXVIII, 784. The Gospel is the rod of Christ’s power; idem, XLI, 551. The wine preserved at the wedding; idem, XXXV, 1459. The Gospel is a teacher for grown persons; the Law, for little ones and a pedagogue; idem, XL, 37. The Gospel teaches us what we ought to love, despise, do, avoid, and hope for; idem, XXXVIII, 1357. The four Gospels are like the four-horse chariots of the New Testament, over which Christ presides; Cassiodorus, LXX, 1093. The four rivers of Paradise are the four Gospels sent to all nations for preaching; St Isidore, LXXXIII, 216; Christianus, CVI, 1265. The Gospel surpasses all the pages of divine Scripture; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 355. The Gospels surpass all pages of the divine Scriptures in their authority; Angelomus, CXV, 108. The majesty of the Gospel surpasses the Law, the Prophets, and apostolic writings; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 26, 27.

On the harmony of the Gospels.—The Gospels do not disagree; St Jerome, XXVI, 38. How Matthew and Luke are reconciled; ibid., 121. The same [Matthew] and John do not differ from one another; ibid., 209. The Evangelists vary while preserving the truth of the narrative; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1117, 1130, 1153. Their writings are not contrary to one another; idem, XLII, 515. In setting forth Christ’s genealogy, they do not disagree with one another; ibid., 217. The Evangelists’ agreement concerning the division of Christ’s garments; idem, XXXV, 1947. One may safely believe that there is no discordance of the Gospels until it is understood [otherwise]; idem, XXXVIII, 336. Four books on the harmony of the Evangelists; idem, XXXIV, 1042 ff. On the agreement of Matthew and Luke in the Lord’s genealogies; idem, XXXVIII, 332. The generations of the Lord are variously counted by the Evangelists without falsehood; ibid., 350. Why they are counted through Joseph and not through Mary; ibid. Why Matthew counts downward, but Luke upward; ibid., 351. Variation without disagreement among the Evangelists in the history of the resurrection; ibid., 1130. Variation without falsehood among the Evangelists; ibid., 1153. On the Evangelists’ agreement in the miracle of the five loaves; Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 821. On the rod; ibid., 823. On the alabaster jar of ointment; ibid., 826. On the hour of the Lord’s passion; ibid. On the two thieves; ibid., 831, etc., etc. On the harmony of the Evangelists; Taio of Saragossa, LXXIX, 790. That the Gospels do not disagree with one another; Freculf, CVI, 1154. Four books on the harmony of the Evangelists; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 11 ff.

On the number and canon of the Gospels.—Very many wished to write a Gospel, but only four were received; St Ambrose, XV, 1538. Wealthy heresy composed many Gospels; poor faith held to this Gospel alone which it possessed; ibid., 1770. Though heresies have many Gospels, they do not have one [true Gospel]; ibid., 1534. Pseudo-Gospels; ibid., 1533. The four Gospels which the Holy and Catholic Church receives; Sedulius, XIX, 792; St Innocent I, XX, 502. Four Gospels selected from many and handed down to the churches; [Col. 0098] St Jerome, XXVI, 221. Several wrote Gospels; ibid., 15. These were the beginnings of various heresies; ibid. False [Gospels] published by certain persons; ibid. The Gospel of the Nazarenes and of Ebion; ibid., 78. The Gospel according to the Egyptians; ibid., 221. [The Gospels] according to the Apostles, Thomas, and Matthias; ibid. That many Gospels had been written by many persons; ibid. There are four Evangelists because there are four regions of the world; St Augustine, XXXV, 1045; XXXVII, 1359. The four Gospels are four drachmas by which we are freed from the exaction of this age; ibid., 1783. On the four books of the Gospel; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 429, 505, 721, 871; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537. The four rivers of Paradise are the four Gospels sent to all nations for preaching; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 216. These four Gospels were ordained by God because of the world’s four quarters and were shown beforehand by the prophets many ages ago; Christianus, CVI, 1264. Matthew’s Gospel is first, because it was made in the time of Gaius; ibid., 1265. Mark’s is second, written in Rome in Greek in the time of Claudius; ibid. Luke’s is third, in Achaia, in Greek speech; ibid. John’s is fourth, in Asia, in the city of Ephesus, in Greek speech, in the time of the emperor Nerva; ibid. There are four Gospels; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365; CXI, 105; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 338. On the Gospel canons; Odo of Cambrai, CLX, 1118; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 784.

On the authors of the Gospels.—Luke and Mark, from the apostles, wrote the history of the Gospel; Tertullian, II, 363. The Gospel Instrument has as authors apostles—John and Matthew—or apostolic men—Luke and Mark; ibid. Mark, Peter’s interpreter, wrote the Gospel, which is ascribed to Peter; ibid., 367. Matthew, the most faithful commentator on the Gospel, as companion of the Lord; ibid., 789. The reason John had for writing the Gospel; St Hilary, X, 190. Luke wrote the Gospel in historical style, and why; St Ambrose, XV, 1528, 1530. Luke is reported to have written the Gospel; idem, XVII, 441.

Matthew and John, of whom the former composed his Gospel in Hebrew and the latter in Greek; St Jerome, XXIV, 98. The four Evangelists; St Jerome, XXVI, 18. Why the forms of animals are assigned to them; ibid. Luke wrote his Gospel in regions of Achaia and Boeotia; ibid. Luke briefly narrated those things which seemed worthy of Christ’s Gospel; idem, XXVI, 328. Mark wrote his Gospel more according to the reliability of the events than their order; idem, XXVI, 18. Matthew published his Gospel in the Hebrew language: why? ibid. John’s Gospel was written against the doctrine of Cerinthus and the Ebionites; idem, XXIII, 623. At the request of the bishops of the Church; ibid. John was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write the Gospel; idem, XXVI, 19. The order in which the Evangelists wrote; St Augustine, XXXIV, 1043. There are four Evangelists because there are four regions of the world; ibid.; XXXVII, 1359. The four Evangelists are understood in the four living creatures of the Apocalypse; idem, XXXV, 1666. The Evangelists are called heavens; idem, XXXIV, 870, 873; XXXVI, 154. The angels are the Lord’s feet; idem, XXXVII, 1167. Arrows; idem, XXXVI, 150. They are signified in the angels ascending and descending; idem, XLII, 268. The order of the Evangelists and their manner of writing; idem, XXXIV, 1043. Matthew, together with Mark, directed his attention to Christ’s royal person; Luke to his priestly person; ibid., 1044. John took care to express his very divinity; ibid., 1045. John’s aim in writing the Gospel; ibid., 1375, 1377. He spoke more sublimely than the others concerning the Lord’s divinity; idem, XXXV, 1662. Matthew is said to have written in the Hebrew tongue; idem, XXXIV, 1044, 1139. The others in Greek; ibid. Why the Gospels have four writers; idem, XXXV, 2392. Why among them Matthew is first, Luke second, Mark third, and John fourth; ibid. Matthew is the first writer of the New Testament; idem, XL, 858. The Evangelists are likened to the four rivers of Paradise, watering the Church with most pure teachings; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 561. The Evangelists are designated under the form of the four living creatures; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 625, 893; Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 788; Alcuin, CI, 1129. Why Matthew bears in himself the figure of a man; ibid., 1133. Why Mark bears the figure of a lion; ibid. Why Luke bears the appearance of a calf; ibid. Why John has the likeness of an eagle; ibid. Matthew wrote his Gospel in the time of Gaius; Christianus, CVI, 1265. Mark [wrote] in Rome in Greek in the time of Claudius; ibid. Luke wrote his Gospel in Achaia in Greek speech; ibid. John [wrote] his in Asia, in the city of Ephesus, in Greek speech, in the time of the emperor Nerva; ibid. John wrote his Gospel under compulsion from the bishops of Asia; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 355. Where and in what language Luke wrote the Gospel; ibid., 894. Matthew wrote for Jewish believers; ibid., 895. Mark for penitents; ibid. John for the perfect; ibid. Luke for Greek believers; ibid. Matthew is signified by the Gihon, Mark by the Tigris, Luke by the Euphrates, John by the Pishon; Christianus, CVI, 1265. [Col. 0099] By what the four Evangelists are figured; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 109, 119; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 64; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 780; Rupert, CLXIX, 928.

On the Acts of the Apostles.—Luke is reported to have written the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles; St Ambrose, XVII, 441. One book of Acts of the Apostles; Sedulius, XIX, 792. The Acts of the Apostles are received in the canon; St Innocent I, XX, 502. The Acts of the Apostles seem to convey bare history and to contain the infancy of the Church; St Jerome, XXII, 548. Every word of this book is medicine for a languishing soul; ibid.

Certain Manichees reject the Acts of the Apostles; St Augustine, XXXIII, 1033; XLII, 69, 368, 505. They are unwilling to believe this book as well; idem, XXXIV, 1262. The reading of the Acts of the Apostles is celebrated in the Church; idem, XLIV, 962, note 2. The Book of Acts is recited in the Church every year; idem, XXXV, 1433. The Book of Acts is customarily read from the Sunday of Easter; idem, XXXVIII, 1426. On the Acts of the Apostles; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 428, 721, 871; Junilius, LXVIII, 16; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 178. Who composed the Acts of the Apostles; idem, 750; Alcuin, CI, 1130; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 367; CXI, 110. The subject matter of Acts of the Apostles; idem, CXI, 120. To what in the New [Testament] the Acts of the Apostles correspond; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 24; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 277; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 15.

On the Fourteen Epistles of Blessed Paul.—Paul wrote his Epistles in Greek; Tertullian, I, 1186. Cerdon receives neither all nor all parts of the Apostle’s Epistles; idem, II, 70. Paul’s Epistles were mutilated by Marcion; ibid., 470. The aim of the Epistle to the Galatians; ibid. Ecclesiastical order is treated in the Epistles to Titus and Timothy; ibid., 524. Summary of the Epistle to the Galatians; Victorinus, VIII, 1145. Summary of the Epistle to the Ephesians; ibid., 1235.

The varying order of Paul’s Epistles; St Ambrose, XVII, 497. Paul writes to the Romans in four ways; ibid., 46. The reasons for which he wrote to the Corinthians; ibid., 183. Before this Epistle he had written another to the same persons; ibid., 210. Why he wrote to the Colossians; ibid., 421; and to the Thessalonians, ibid., 441; and to Timothy, ibid., 461; to Philemon, ibid., 503.

Paul’s Epistles number fourteen; Sedulius, XIX, 792; St Innocent I, XX, 502; St Jerome, XXIII, 617. The Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Romans: to whom and why it was written; St Jerome, XXVI, 395. It contains nothing contrary to the Epistle to the Galatians; ibid. The Epistle to the Galatians was subscribed in Paul’s own hand but written out by another; ibid., 434. The matter of Galatians and Romans is the same; ibid., 309. A certain difference is noted between the two; ibid. The Epistle to the Ephesians is obscure beyond all others; ibid., 505. Both Epistles of Paul to Timothy, [and those] to the Hebrews and Titus, are rejected by certain heretics; ibid., 555. From where the Epistle to Titus was written; ibid. Some reject the Epistle to Philemon; ibid., 599. They are refuted; ibid. The Epistle to the Hebrews is placed outside the number by most persons; idem, XXII, 548. Whose it is believed to be; idem, XXIII, 617. It was not held among the Romans; ibid., 669. The Epistle to the Hebrews was not received by the Latins; idem, XXIV, 94. Why it is opposed and doubtful; ibid., 99. It is not received among the canonical Scriptures; ibid., 121. It was not received by all; idem, XXVI, 475. It is received among ecclesiastical [writings]; ibid., 578.

Some denied that the Epistle to the Hebrews was by the apostle Paul; St Augustine, XLI, 500. The Epistle to the Hebrews is uncertain to some, but is held among the canonical books by the Eastern churches; idem, XLIV, 137. Distinguished defenders of the Catholic rule have used the Epistle to the Hebrews as a testimony; idem, XL, 235. The Epistles to the Romans and Galatians are compared with one another; idem, XLIV, 733. On the fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul; idem, XXXIV, 41; St Leo the Great, LVI, 429, 721, 871; Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 778; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 176, 749; St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. Who wrote Paul’s Epistles; how many they are; where they were written; and where they are read; Alcuin, CI, 1129. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365, 367; CXI, 105, 110, 119, 120. From where the Epistle to the Romans was written; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 469. For what reason; ibid. Haymo, CXVII, 364. The First Epistle to the Corinthians, written from Ephesus; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 519. For what reason; ibid. Haymo, CXVII, 509. The Second Epistle to the Corinthians, written from Troas through Titus; ibid., 551. For what reason; ibid. Haymo, CXVII, 667. The Epistle to the Galatians; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 569; Haymo, CXVII, 669. The Epistle to the Ephesians; Walafrid Strabo, CXVII, 699. The Epistle to the Philippians; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 601. The Epistle to the Colossians; ibid., 609. The First Epistle to the Thessalonians; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 615; Haymo, CXVII, 765. The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians; Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 619; Haymo, CXVII, 777. The First Epistle to Timothy; [Col. 0100] Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 623. The Second Epistle to Timothy; ibid., 633. The Epistle to Titus; ibid., 637; and Haymo, CXVII, 809. The Epistle to Philemon; Walafrid Strabo, 641. The Epistle to the Hebrews; ibid., 643; Haymo, CXVII, 809, 819, 821. Fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 338; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 277; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 15; CLXXVI, 186.

Among all writers of epistles, Paul perhaps excels in three or more respects; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1297. It should be known that Paul wrote fourteen Epistles; ibid., 1298. What they signify; ibid. Whether the Epistle to the Hebrews is by Blessed Paul; ibid., 1299. Whether it bears Paul’s title; ibid. In what language it was written; ibid. On the order of the Epistles of Blessed Paul; ibid., 1299. What the general subject matter of all the Epistles is; ibid., 1302. Their intention and manner of treatment; ibid. ff.

On the Seven Canonical Epistles.—The canonical Epistles number seven; Sedulius, XIX, 792. Received in the canon are three Epistles of John, two Epistles of Peter, the Epistle of Jude, and the Epistle of James; St Innocent I, XX, 502. The Catholic Epistle of Blessed Peter is noted; St Jerome, XXIV, 685. Jerome calls the Second Epistle of Blessed Peter canonical; ibid., 636. The Epistle of Jude is among the canonical Scriptures; St Augustine, XXXV, 1831. ### On the Apocalypse

The Apocalypse of John unfolds the order of times. Tertullian, II, 830. The author of the Apocalypse is the same John who wrote the Gospel. St. Hilary, X, 192; note, 191. Some wished to cut the Apocalypse out of the catalogue of the divine Scriptures. St. Ambrose, XVII, 964. This Scripture concerns not only future time but also the past, ibid. Who its author is, ibid., 765. It is divided into seven visions, ibid., 767. The Apocalypse of John the apostle: one book. Sedulius, XIX, 792. St. Innocent I, XX, 502. The Apocalypse was written long after the Passion of the Lord. St. Jerome, XXII, 487. It is difficult and obscure, ibid., 543. It is not unsealed except by Christ, ibid. The Apocalypse has as many mysteries as words, ibid., 548. The Apocalypse contains boundless mysteries of future things, idem, XXIII, 247. Those who have interpreted the Apocalypse, ibid., 625. — The book of the Apocalypse: how obscure it is. St. Augustine, XLI, 683. The Alogi do not accept the Apocalypse, idem, XLII, 31. Augustine doubts whether Pelagius accepted the Apocalypse, idem, XXXVIII, 1376. The Apocalypse of John. St. Leo the Great, LVI, 429, 505, 871. Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 537. The Apocalypse of John is greatly disputed among the Easterners. Junilius, LXVIII, 18. On the Apocalypse. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 178, 160. St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 140. Who composed the Apocalypse, at what time, and where. Alcuin, CI, 1130. What is contained in the Apocalypse, ibid., 1131. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 365, 367; CXI, 105, 110, 120. Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 24. Rabanus Maurus, CXXX, 338. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 277. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 15; CLXXVI, 186. On the island of Patmos he wrote the Apocalypse with his own hand. St. Martin of León, CCIX, 253. The Apocalypse surpasses the other prophecies, ibid., 300.

[Col. 0101]

## XLIII. GENERAL INDEX OF COMMENTARIES ON THE SCRIPTURES, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF THE SACRED BOOKS, FROM GENESIS TO THE APOCALYPSE, CHRONOLOGICALLY RECORDING ALL EXPOSITIONS FOUND IN THE *PATROLOGIA LATINA*

### Notice

In this Index we mention only general commentaries or explanations on any books of Scripture, omitting everything which pertains to individual chapters or to more notable passages; for these will constitute the following Index. We follow the canonical order of Sacred Scripture, and, in each article, the chronological order—that is, that of the volumes. When the same author has issued several writings on the same Book, we distinguish them only by intervening dashes, but return each writer to a new line so that confusion may not arise. The first chapter, as a prologue to this Index, presents all treatises on the Sacred Scriptures; thus everything relating to the Holy Books will be open to the Reader at a single glance.
