## XLV. EXEGETICAL INDEX OF ALL VERSES OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM THE FIRST OF GENESIS TO THE LAST OF THE APOCALYPSE, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE CANONICAL ORDER OF THE BOOKS, CHRONOLOGICALLY PRESENTING THE VARIOUS COMMENTARIES AND ELUCIDATIONS OF THE FATHERS ON EACH VERSE

### NOTICE

That exegetical index of all verses of Holy Scripture, which stands out among the others like a giant, is mentioned here only because we have not yet completed it, and because, on account of the breadth of its materials and the importance of its contents, we have resolved to publish it separately; it will alone comprise one volume. Let the reader not take this amiss: it will shortly come to light.

[Col. 0123]

## XLVI. INDEX OF ALLEGORIES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT, ARRANGED IN ANALOGICAL ORDER AND, WITHIN THAT ANALOGY, OBSERVING ALPHABETICAL ORDER; SETTING FORTH VARIOUS EXPLANATIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS

### NOTICE

In this Index we first set forth everything dealing with the nature, division, and usefulness of allegory. We then establish thirteen headings, successively presenting allegories which pertain: I, to God; II, to Christ; III, to the Virgin Mary; IV, to angels; V, to evil spirits; VI, to the Church; VII, to the sacraments; VIII, to the Apostles and the righteous; IX, to Gentiles and Hebrews; X, to heretics and sinners; XI, to virtues and vices; XII, to the last things of humanity; XIII, to Holy Scripture. Within each heading we preserve alphabetical order, so that the matters sought may immediately be at hand for the reader.

## [INDEX OF ALLEGORIES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT]

[Col. 0123]

### PREFACE: On the Nature, Division, and Usefulness of Allegory

**ALLEGORY** is when one thing is said and another is signified: Victorinus Afer, VIII, 1185; St Jerome, XXIV, 629; XXV, 161; XXVI, 389; Junilius Afer, LVIII, 19; Cassiodorus, LXX, 223, 698, 1271; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 330.—Allegory is so called when one thing appears to be expressed in the sound of the words and another to be signified in the understanding: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1347; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 147.—Allegory is a trope in which one thing is understood from another: St Augustine, XLII, 1068, 1069; Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 25.—Allegory foreshadows, in things truly done, the form of another sacrament: John Cassian, XLIX, 963.—Allegory is when, through what is set forth as signified by the letter, something else accomplished either in the past, present, or future is signified: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 11.—Allegory is called, as it were, *alieniloquium* [speaking of another thing]: ibid., 11.—There are several kinds of allegory, among which is that called enigma: St Augustine, XLII, 1068.—Allegory is fourfold: that of history, deed, speech, and sacrament: ibid., XXXIV, 166.—Allegory is recognized in four ways: first, according to transference or metaphor: “The Lord was angry”; second, according to imagination or hypotyposis: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho”; third, according to comparison or likeness: “The kingdom of heaven is like”; fourth, according to proverbial mode: “Drink water from your own vessels”: St Justus of Urgell, LXVII, 19.—Allegory is nothing other than spiritual understanding; spiritual knowledge, moreover, embraces three kinds: tropology, allegory, and anagogy. Tropology is moral explanation directed to amendment of life and practical instruction; allegory is when things truly done are said to have foreshadowed the form of another sacrament; and anagogy is that which ascends from spiritual mysteries to certain more exalted and more sacred secrets of heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 331.—Allegory is called, as it were, *alieniloquium*, because one thing is said and another signified; it is subdivided into simple allegory and anagogy. Allegory is when one invisible event is signified through a visible event; anagogy, that is, “upward speech,” is when an invisible event is disclosed through a visible one: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 11.

Everything that is figuratively suggested to us moves us and kindles love more than if it were set forth bare, without any likenesses of sacraments; and whatever is intimated through allegorical signification moves, delights, and is honoured more than if it were stated most plainly in literal words: St Augustine, XXXIII, 214.—Unless certain things in Scripture are softened by allegorical explanation and made pliable by the testing of spiritual fire, they will by no means reach the wholesome nourishment of the inner person without the disaster of corruption: John Cassian, XLIX, 725.—What, placed in plain view, did not move one so greatly, is drawn out through the uncovering of some allegory: Eugippius, LXII, 858.—Allegory is an instrument by which the soul is raised to God: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 473; Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 405.—By means of what is known and not repugnant, allegory understands something unknown: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 473.—Divine meanings are clothed in things known to us, through which allegories are formed; and, while we recognize the outward words through the thing, we reach the inward understanding: ibid.—Allegory is concerned especially with the mysteries of our faith, which are believed more than understood: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI.—Christ himself employed allegory in the Gospel: St Augustine, XLII, 70.

## ARTICLE I. Allegories Pertaining to God

**HIDING.** God is said to hide his face when he conceals the knowledge of himself from certain peoples among the nations, as we see now fulfilled in the case of the Jewish people: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 734.

**ABYSS.** The eternal judgment of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 52.—The incomprehensibility of God’s judgments: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 284.—In Scripture the name “abyss” denotes the ineffable judgments of God: Alcuin, C, 23.

**SEVEN HEIFERS** sacrificed by Abraham signify the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 425.

**HUSBANDMAN.** God is our husbandman: St Augustine, XXXVI, 804.—God is called a husbandman: St Eucherius, L, 742.—God the Father is called the heavenly husbandman: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 366; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 855.

**WINGS.** Divine protection: St Eucherius, L, 748.—Wings: the mercy of the Lord; and truth: the commandments of the Lord: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857.—By the covering of wings the divine word signifies the protection of God’s mercy: St Hilary, X, 392.—God is said to have wings because, in the manner of a bird, he gathers and cherishes his elect beneath himself as chicks: St Eucherius, L, 733.—Mercy and charity are, as it were, the Father’s wings, under whose protection one fittingly asks to be sheltered: Cassiodorus, LXX, 120.

**WALKING.** God is said to walk, not by passing from place to place—for it is impious to believe this—but his walking is delight in the hearts of the saints; or certainly, God’s walking is his passing from place to place in his holy preachers: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 735.

**ANGEL.** The Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 51.

**SOUL.** The power of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 852.

**YEARS.** God’s eternity: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 741.

**WATER.** By the name “water” the Holy Spirit is understood: St Augustine, XXXIV, 216; XXXVII, 1353.—Water signifies both the people and the Holy Spirit: St Augustine, XXXIV, 79.—In Holy Scripture, the name “water” sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 742.—Waters customarily denote the Holy Spirit: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 100.—Water: the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 861; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 198.—By water the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified: St Gregory the Great, XXV, 960.—Water: the streams of the Holy Spirit: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 293.—Water: the infusion of the Holy Spirit: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 279.—Living water: the grace of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 353.—Water: a symbol of grace: St Augustine, XXXIV, 737.

**BOW.** The purpose of divine threatening: St Eucherius, L, 738.—The Holy Spirit: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 324.

**SILVER.** Silver signifies the divine utterances: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 859.

**ARMS OF THE LORD.** His help toward the saints: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.

**BRACELET.** Divine mercy: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.

**INSPIRATION** is understood as God’s breathing toward eternal happiness, and the decline of the shadow as the unceasing night of this mortality: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1156.

**EARS.** God is said to have ears because he hears all things and nothing is concealed from him in silence: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731.—The ears of the Lord, when he deigns to hear: ibid., 737.—The ear of God: his power and mercy: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.

**GOLD.** Divinity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.—The brightness of divinity: [Col. 0126] Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 303.—Gold and silver signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1524.

**SOUTH WIND.** The Holy Spirit: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 869; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 901; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 56; Alan of Lille, CCX, 82.—The south wind signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 262.—The south wind signifies the Holy Spirit: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1175.—By the south wind, which is indeed a warm wind, the Holy Spirit is fittingly denoted, since whoever is touched by it is freed from the coldness of his iniquity: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 436, 623, 799, 938; LXXIX, 516.

**STAFF.** God’s mercy: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.—A sign of divine judgment: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 339.

**BASES.** Divine counsels: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 874.—Golden bases signify God’s counsel and inflexibility in judging: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 927.

**REED.** God’s ordering: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.

**PEBBLE.** The word of the Lord: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 880.

**DARKNESS.** A covering for divine secrets: St Eucherius, L, 739.

**CUP.** In God there is a cup of wrath and a cup of life, just as there is wine which gladdens the human heart and wine which pierces the human heart with compunction: St Hilary, LX, 385.—The judgment of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.

**HEAT.** The fervour of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 880; St Bruno of Würzburg, CLXII, 100.

**HEAD OF GOD.** We must understand it as the very essence of his divinity, which goes before and to which all things are subject: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 730.

**CEDAR.** Divinity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.

**HEAVEN.** Heaven, protecting the earth on every side, is an image of divine mercy: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1331.—Heaven: God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.—Heaven: heavenly judgment; divine speech: Garner of St Victor, CCXIII, 30.—Heaven is called the most holy Trinity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 63.

**KNOWING.** God’s knowing is making people know: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 736.

**DOVE.** The Holy Spirit: St Eucherius, L, 748; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 71; Alan of Lille, CCX, 63.—In the dove, according to prophecy, the Holy Spirit must be understood: St Hilary, IX, 1036.—The dove: a symbol of the Holy Spirit: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1001.—The dove: a type of the Holy Spirit: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 336.—The dove: the Holy Spirit; the gifts of that same Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.

**PILLAR OF CLOUD.** A figure of the Holy Spirit instructing the faithful: St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 168.—The pillars of Christ’s litter are the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Alan of Lille, CCX, 75.

**KNIFE.** God’s commandments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.

**CHARIOT OF GOD.** The seat of God: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.

**DESCENDING.** God is said to descend into the world when he works something new in human nature which had not existed before: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 734.

**RIGHT HAND OF THE LORD.** It signifies the glory of the Father and eternal blessedness: St Eucherius, L, 732.—The right hand signifies God’s loving-kindness: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1068.—God’s right and left hands signify eternal and temporal salvation: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1214.

**FINGER.** The Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 910; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 312, 416, 627.—The finger of God is understood as the Holy Spirit; for he himself wrote who dictated what was to be written: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 732.—The finger of Christ indicates the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the word of preaching: Venerable Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 561.—Fingers: the Holy Spirit and the gifts of that same Holy Spirit: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 200.—The Holy Spirit is called God’s finger because of the distribution of goods bestowed by him: St Eucherius, L, 738.—Fingers are understood as the distribution of the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 160.—Fingers are divisions of graces: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1255.

**RICHES.** Contemplations of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911.

**SLEEPING.** God is said to sleep when faith in him does not keep watch but sleeps amid the prosperity of this world and in the hearts of certain faithful persons; or certainly, God’s sleeping is his delayed help to those in distress: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 737.

**EPHI.** The measure of three measures is a type of the most holy Trinity and of the Incarnation: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 286, 287, 298, 676.

**FACE OF GOD.** Knowledge of his divinity for all: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731.—Face: God the Father; God’s foreknowledge; knowledge of God; God’s goodwill; God’s knowledge; God’s protection; God’s attentive regard: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 920.

**SICKLE.** Divine judgment: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 921.

**QUIVER.** God’s hidden judgment: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 919.

**POTTER.** The name of potter is not inappropriately applied to the Creator: Venerable Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 289.

**FIRMAMENT.** God’s protection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 929.

**RIVER.** The Holy Spirit and his gifts: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 295.

**SWORD.** Divine vengeance upon the impious: St Eucherius, L, 738.

**FRUIT OF GOD’S VINEYARD.** God: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1260.—The fruit of God’s vineyard is blessedness: ibid., 1262.

**LIGHTNING.** The stirring of divine terror: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 60.

**SMOKE.** The beginnings of God’s threatening: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.

**CORD.** Divine commandments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 937.

**HEN.** The wisdom of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 939; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 75.

**SWORD.** In Jacob’s vision, the sword is the Holy Spirit, having one hilt—that is, one substance, power, divinity, majesty, and will of the Father and the Son—while bearing two edges, that is, the two Testaments: St Zeno, XI, 42.—Sword: vengeance, or the word of the Lord: St Eucherius, L, 738.—Sword: God’s wrath; God’s words: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 940.—Swords are the words of God: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1144.

**HAIL.** The Lord’s threatenings: St Eucherius, L, 739.

**STEPS.** The gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 942.

**MAN.** God the Father: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 955; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 135.

**FIRE.** The Holy Spirit: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 966; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 277.—Fire: God, the Holy Spirit: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 355.

**IMAGE.** Deity itself: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 969.

**RAIN.** It signifies God’s wrath: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 867.

**HARDENING.** God is said to harden the hearts of certain evil people, not because almighty God hardens their hearts by his power—for it is impious to believe this—but because, in accordance with their deserts, he does not take away the hardness of heart by which they themselves, in committing every evil, turn themselves aside: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 737.

**INTESTINES.** The hidden words of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 971.—God’s hidden and mystical commandments: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 228.

**ANGER.** God is said to be angry, not by a movement of mind or by any disturbance—which cannot happen to him at all—but because he is said to inflict just vengeance upon the offending creature, that is, upon impious persons and sinners: namely, to render to them what they deserve. This divine vengeance is called his fury: ibid., 736.

**LAMP.** The gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 981.—Burning lamps denote the illuminations of sevenfold grace: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 648.

**LION.** God as judge: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 983.

**BOOK.** God’s foreknowledge: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 987.

**LILY.** The brightness of divinity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 986.

**LINE.** God’s hidden judgment: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 987.

**TONGUE OF GOD.** Mystically it signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father revealed his secret to human beings: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 176.

**SPEAKING.** God’s speaking is invisibly inspiring his will and right understanding into the minds of saints, without the sound of a voice or any noise; or revealing future things, as in the holy prophets: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 735.

**SEVEN LAMPS.** The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 635; CXI, 605; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 1028; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 731; Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 698.

**MORNING STAR.** Divine speech: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 43.

**LIGHT.** The brightness of divinity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 979.—Light: God the Father: ibid., 990.

**LIGHT.** God the Father: ibid., 990.

**MORNING.** The illumination of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 992.

**HAND OF GOD.** His power is understood; likewise, his scourge: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 732.—The hand of the Lord: his threats or vengeance: ibid., 738.—The hand of the Lord signifies [Col. 0128] God’s power: Alcuin, C, 607.—Hand: divine consolation; the force of heavenly power; God’s power; God’s dispositions: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 993.

**SEA.** Divine speech: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 287.

**HONEY.** Deity itself: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997; Alan of Lille, CCX, 81.

**MELODY.** The inner person is constituted, as it were, through seven distinctions of voice, by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1103.

**MOUNT PARAN.** God the Father: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 629.—A mountain denotes divinity: Venerable Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 47, 48.

**WOMAN.** The wisdom of God: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 140.

**NECKLACE.** God’s wisdom: Alan of Lille, CCX, 61.

**NOSTRILS OF GOD.** His inspiration into the hearts of the faithful: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731.

**CLOUDS.** The veil of God’s mysteries: ibid., 739.

**SINEW.** The divine essence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1005.

**NOT KNOWING.** God’s not knowing is his reprobating certain reprobate persons: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 736.

**CLOUD.** The Holy Spirit; divine consolation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.—A cloud suggests heavenly grace: Venerable Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 190.

**FORGETTING.** God is said to forget when he has mercy upon certain impious persons and sinners: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 737.

**EYES OF THE LORD.** Divine inspection is understood: St Eucherius, L, 737.—God is said to have eyes because he sees all things and nothing is hidden from him; or eyes are understood as a gracious regard: ibid., 730.—Christ’s eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1086.—The sevenfold Spirit is signified by the seven eyes of God: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 768.—Eye: perfect knowledge of God; the Holy Spirit: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 166.

**FRAGRANCES.** The fragrance of scents displays the sweet goodness of God: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 802.

**OIL.** By the name “oil” the Holy Spirit is denoted: St Fulgentius, LXV, 278; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1011.

**OLIVE.** The Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1011.—The two olive trees are the two gifts of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 731.

**MOUTH OF THE LORD.** It is understood as his speech or command: St Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731, 738.

KISS, a gift of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1014.---A kiss is understood as the Holy Spirit: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1007.

God is said to SHOW his face when, through the regard of his grace, he instils himself into the heart of those whom he wills and pours in his love: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 734.

The EYELIDS of the Lord signify his hidden and incomprehensible judgments, or his spiritual speech in the divine books: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 731.---The eyelids of God are his judgments which test the children of men: same author, ibid., 737.---Eyelids, the judgments of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 170.

The BREAD of life is the teaching of God: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 795.---The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are understood through the seven loaves: Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 490.

The PARADISE of delight is the will of God: Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 795.

FATHER: God the Creator; the First-formed Man [Protoplastus]: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1023.

The FEET of God are the firm foundation of his power, because he is present everywhere and all things are subject to him: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 733.---The feet of the Lord, the steadfastness of eternity: same author, ibid., 738.

RAIN: the Lord’s precepts or commandments, because they water the earth—that is, human beings: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.---Rain signifies saving teaching: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1120.---The love of God is a kind of spring rain of virtues, beneath which both blessed willing germinates and holy action bears fruit: Cassiodorus, L, 100.

God is said to REPENT, not because, in the human manner, he repents of deeds already done; for he who knows things before they happen cannot repent of acts that have been committed. Rather, God’s repentance is to change his decrees and to alter into something else what he had previously done otherwise: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 736.---God’s not repenting is never to change his decrees: same author, ibid.

FRAGRANT FRUITS, the advent of God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 348.

The PROPITIATORY [mercy-seat] is called the divine majesty: Alanus, CCX, 240.

God is said to DEPART and pass over to others, because he is accustomed to do something not locally or visibly, but by an invisible, hidden, just judgment: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 735.

REFRESHMENT, God’s protection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.

RIVULETS, the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1040.

A ROMPHAEA [sword], vengeance, or the word of the Lord: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.

DEW, the Word of the Lord: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.---Dew, the grace of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1040.---The dew of heaven signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 461.---Dew signifies the Holy Spirit: same author, ibid., 1120.---Dew, a symbol of divine grace: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 38.

ARROW: the word of God; God’s rebuke; the Lord’s acts of vengeance; the Lord’s precepts; God’s threats; God’s blows: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1044.---Arrows, divine precepts: St. Eucherius, L, 738.---Arrows in the hand of the mighty one are the words of God’s teaching: Alcuin, C, 579, 620.

BLOOD, the wrath of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.

God is said to have SHOULDERS because he carries the weak members of the Church, as though upon his shoulders: St. Eucherius, L, 733.

SHIELD, divine protection: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 321.

God is said to SIT, not bodily in a human fashion, but by his power to preside rationally over every creature: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 734.

PATH, the stricter precepts of God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 264.

SEVEN. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are understood through the seventh hour: Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 620.---The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are designated through the first seven books of Holy Scripture: same author, ibid., 1064.---The number seven signifies the activity of the sevenfold Spirit; the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 448.

BOSOM, the substance of the Godhead; God’s grace: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1054.

SUN, God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1057.

SOUND, the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1059.

SPIRIT, God himself; divine inspiration: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1056.

God is said to STAND when he patiently sustains us who are weak—that is, his creation—unto repentance and conversion: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 735.

STAR, the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.

TIMES, the fitting dispensation of the divine will: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 741.

DARKNESS, the hidden judgments of God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 378.

The number THREE signifies faith in the most holy Trinity: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 442.

TREASURE, God’s providence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1066.

TORRENT, the wisdom of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1068.---The overflowing of the Holy Spirit: same author, ibid.; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 297.

God is said to PASS OVER when he withdraws from the hearts of certain persons, in whom he was formerly believed through faith, and passes to others, after faithlessness or any sin has subsequently crept in: St. Eucherius, L, 735.

The THREE CHILDREN bear the figure of the Trinity: St. Zeno, XI, 522, 524.

WHEAT, the Word of God: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 742.

TROWEL, divine protection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1070.

TRUMPET, the manifest voice of the Lord: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.

TURTLEDOVE, the Holy Spirit: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 748; Garner of St. Victor, CXCVII, 71.

BREASTS signify the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 841.

SHADOW, divine protection: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 741.

JONAH’S BOOTH signifies divine consolation: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 436.

OINTMENT is the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 23.---Ointment, the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.---The best ointment is the grace of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 841.---Ointments are God’s spiritual gifts: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 56.

WOMB, the substance of the Father: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1086.---The grace of God: same author, ibid., 1086.---God’s womb, his incomprehensible judgments, which cannot be searched out: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 733.---The secret place from which he brought forth the Son: [Col. 0130] same author, ibid., 738.---The secret bosom of God’s grace; God’s counsel: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 225.

VESSEL, understanding of the Godhead; God’s approval: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.

God’s BELLY is understood as the hidden origin of his substance: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 733.

WINNOWING-FAN, the examination of God’s justice: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 742.

WIND, the gifts of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1071.---The burning wind signifies the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 197.

The FOOTSTEPS of the Lord, signs of his hidden works: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.---Footsteps, God’s operations; God’s visitations; God’s presence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1076.

GARMENT, divine works: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1075.

WAY, divine precepts: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1077.---Way, God’s actions: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 260.

God’s SEEING is approving good deeds; in another sense, God’s seeing is, by knowing, to reprove human evils; likewise, in another sense, God’s seeing is to make us see: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 735.

God’s WATCHING is manifestly showing himself in defence of his elect: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 737.

WINE, the mystery of the Godhead; the fervour of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.---Wine signifies the power of the Holy Spirit: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 794.

ROD, the signification of kingship or the correction of discipline: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.---Rod, the abiding word; divine chastisement; divine persecution: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.

FILLET, divine precepts: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1082.

VOICE, divine exhortation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1083.

God is said to be JEALOUS when he frequently chastises, corrects, and scourges his creature, whom he does not wish to perish, and by scourging brings it back to himself: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 736.---God is also said to be jealous when he wishes to leave no sin unpunished: same author, ibid., 736.

## ARTICLE II. Allegories concerning Christ

ADAM. Christ is the second, heavenly Adam: St. Hilary, IX, 669; St. Augustine, XLV, 1512; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 239, 249, 570.

Our SUMMER is Christ’s advent; our winter, Christ’s hiddenness: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 217.

THE LAMB is Christ, through whom we have been redeemed and made alive: St. Cyprian, IV, 653.---The Lamb is said of Christ as man: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 432.---The typical lamb, slain as a figure of Christ: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 932.---The paschal lamb, Christ: St. Cyprian, IV, 561; Lactantius, VI, 530; St. Ambrose, XIV, 437, 648, 1107; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 547; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 336, 339.---The paschal lamb, a type of Christ to be incarnate: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1280.---The Passion is figured in the sacrifice of the paschal lamb: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 253.---Christ is a lamb to us, but a goat to the Jews: St. Ambrose, XIV, 648.

The ALTAR is called the Godhead itself, Christ’s flesh, the humanity of the Word: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 856. The altar of earth is Christ in the Incarnation: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 404.

The ANGEL of God who addressed Hagar is God: he is both Son and angel of God and God: St. Hilary, X, 113.---The Angel is the Son, the Angel of Great Counsel, and Lord and God: same author, ibid., 116.---The Angel seen by Moses in the bush is Lord and God: same author, ibid., 119.---He appeared to Jacob in the form of an angel in order to show that he was the messenger of Great Counsel: St. Phoebadius, XX, 46.---Christ was the Angel who wrestled with Jacob: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 306; XXXVII, 1936; XXXVIII, 682.

WATER. Christ’s humanity is compared to water: St. Gaudentius, XX, 985.---The bitter waters have the figure of the killing letter and of the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1031.

ARK. In Noah’s ark some things are referred to Christ and some to the Church: St. Augustine, XLII, 274, 275.---Noah’s ark signifies Christ and the Church in all respects: same author, XLI, 472, 477.---It signifies the incarnation of the Saviour: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 145.---It was a figure of Christ’s humanity: Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 428.---A figure of Christ’s Body: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 669.---The ark of the covenant, a type of Christ’s human nature: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 241.---The ark of the testament is a figure of the Body which the Lord assumed: St. Hilary, IX, 737; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 232.

SILVER. Christ’s humanity is signified by silver: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1423.

The RAM sacrificed by Abraham was a figure of Christ: St. Ambrose, XIV, 448; St. Augustine, XLI, 511.---The reddened ram was a figure of Christ and the martyrs: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 635.---The ram caught by its horns, a figure of Christ crucified: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 244.---The ram caught in the brambles is Christ amid the blasphemies of the Jews: Abbot Rupert, CLXIII, 859.

God is said to ASCEND when the Son led into heaven the flesh assumed from us: St. Eucherius, L, 734.

ASCENT. Christ’s exaltation is called an ascent; he himself is the one who ascends: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.---The ascent of the palm tree was Christ’s ascent onto the cross: Abbot Wolbero, CXLV, 1235.

The SPRINKLING of blood according to the Law, purifying the people through faith, is a sacrament of the future sprinkling from the Lord’s blood: St. Hilary, IX, 338.

GOLD signifies the incarnate wisdom of God: Alcuin, C, 1114.---Gold is Christ’s royal power: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.

BIRD. Christ’s yoke is compared to birds’ feathers: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 598.

BEARD. Christ’s divinity is called a beard: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.

CHARIOTS. Through the chariots by which Christ rides forth savingly, Isaiah signifies the course [or movement]: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 646.

CLUSTER carried by the scouts from the land of promise, a figure of Christ: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1037; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 214; Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 275; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1082.---The cluster hanging from wood is surely Christ from the wood of the cross: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 845.---Christ on the cross, a cluster placed upon a pole: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 786.---The cluster signifies the sweetness of Christ’s resurrection: Abbot Walbero, CXCV, 1080, 1084.

BUTTER, Christ’s humanity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 877.

REED, the eternity of the divine Word: Garner, CXLIII, 425.

The LORD’S SANDALS mystically signify his Incarnation: St. Eucherius, L, 733; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 772; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 97.---His humanity is signified through sandals: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 918.

A BURNING STONE signifies Jesus Christ: Alcuin, C, 1106.

CUP is called Christ’s Passion: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879; Garner of St. Victor, CXCLIII, 457; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 143.

FIELD is Christ’s human nature: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 64.

LAMPSTAND signifies the Lord’s body: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.---The Incarnate One, together with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, is signified by the lampstand with seven lamps: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 705.---The golden lampstand signifies Christ, crowned with glory on account of the Passion: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 728.

BASKET. By the basket of consummation we understand the Lord’s tongue: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 331.

The NEW SONG is called the Lord’s Incarnation, by which the world was filled with saving rejoicing and through which the angels resounded in tuneful voices of praise: Cassiodorus, LXX, 226.

ROE DEER is a type of Christ: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 98.---By roe deer are understood Christ’s members: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1094.

COALS, the virtues which were in Christ: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.

FLESH. Christ was figured in the flesh supplied to the people of Israel in the evening, and in the loaves supplied in the morning: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 616.

The PROVISION concerning hidden murder mystically denotes the Saviour: Rabanus Maurus, CXIII, 913.

CAVERN, the wound in the Lord’s side: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 890.---The cavern of the wall signifies the wound in Christ’s side: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 70.

WAX CANDLE, an image of Christ: St. Augustine, XLVI, 819.

CHRIST is called the second Adam: St. Hilary, IX, 669; St. Augustine, XLV, 1512; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 239, 249, 570; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 679.---Fat: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.---Bronze: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 315.---Lamb: St. Cyprian, IV, 561, 653; Lactantius, VI, 530; St. Zeno, XI, 511, 517; St. Ambrose, XIV, 437, 648, 1107; St. Jerome, XXV, 462; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 547; XXXV, 1839; XXXVI, 763; XXXVIII, 45, 133, 1209; XLVI, 828; St. Eucherius, L, 745; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 336, 339; Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 675, 757; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 560; LXXIX, 209; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 432; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 802; CXII, 855; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 517, 567, 615, 1336; CLXVIII, 566; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 402; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1045.---Lamb and Lion: St. Augustine, XLVI, 828.---Husbandman: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, [Col. 0132] 800.---Alpha and Omega: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 673; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1179; LXXIX, 626.---Altar of the Church: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1017.---Friend: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 622; CLXIX, 11.---Almond tree: Ven. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 559.---Angel: St. Augustine, XLII, 772; St. Eucherius, L, 739; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 851; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1505; Ven. St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 232.---Tower of strength: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 725.---Turtledove: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 71.---Anointed with a full horn: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 462.---Ointment: St. Jerome, XXV, 462.---Grape: St. Ambrose, XIV, 681; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 109; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 554.---Cow: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1072.---Mountain and valley: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1597.---Bar: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 470, 473.---The bar of the tabernacle joining the two Testaments: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 695.---Vein: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.---Wind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1071.---Hidden word: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 705.---Good word: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 437.---Worm: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 174; St. Eucherius, L, 754; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236; CXII, 1075; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 891; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 720; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 671; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 229; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 130.---Crown of the head: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 162.---Way: St. Jerome, XXV, 162; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1077; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 289; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1024; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 260; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 702.---The way beside which a snare is set by evildoers: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1244.---Vineyard: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1079; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 870.---Man: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 90; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 639; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 137.---A man surrounded by a woman: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 23.---Rod: St. Augustine, XL, 698; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 596; CLXVIII, 852.---Both rod and flower: St. Hilary, IX, 283; St. Jerome, XXV, 462.---Vine: St. Ambrose, XIV, 681; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1839; St. Eucherius, L, 745; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 367; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 593; Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 831, 836; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 925.---Calf: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1153; XXXVIII, 45; St. Eucherius, L, 753; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 625; LXXIX, 463; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1158; CXII, 1082; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 262; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 757, 1438; CLXVIII, 1577; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 101.---Vulture: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 885; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 67; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 266, 1239; CXII, 1083; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 83.

Christ is compared to:

- A lamb: Alan of Lille, CCX, 231.
- A bee: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 41.
- Noah’s ark: Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 803.
- A silkworm weaving silk: Alan of Lille, CCX, 243.
- A golden lampstand: Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 176.
- A she-goat: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 497; Alan of Lille, CCX, 68.
- A burning and dead coal: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1020.
- A wax candle: Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 65.
- A stag: St. Ambrose, XIV, 811; Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 65.
- A cithara: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 655.
- A hen: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1116.
- A drop: Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 329.
- A fawn: Alan of Lille, CCX, 68.
- A kid: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 384.
- A sheep: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 41; Alan of Lille, CCX, 231.
- Bread: [Col. 0137] Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 384.
- A plane tree: Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 591.
- Rain: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 384.
- Dew: the same, ibid.
- Rich land: Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1088.
- Thunder: the same, ibid., 886.
- A timbrel: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 222.
- Ointment: Guerric, CLXXXV, 68.
- Wind: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 75.
- A violet: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 668.

Christ is designated by Noah’s ark: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 758; Alan of Lille, CCX, 241.---By the pillar of cloud: St. Ambrose, XV, 1251.---By a honeycomb: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1497.---By Moses’ rod: St. Ambrose, XV, 123.

Christ is prefigured in the slain lamb: St. Leo, LVI, 1136; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 497.---In the ram seen by Abraham: St. Ambrose, XLV, 448, 479; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 244; XLI, 511.---In the three birds: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1299.---In the cluster carried by the scouts from the land of promise: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1082.---In the scapegoat: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 420.---In the flesh given at evening and the bread given in the morning to the people of Israel: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 616.---On Mount Gilead: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 118.---In the tree of life: St. Augustine, 701.---In the loaves of presentation: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 517.---In the fish caught in the Tigris: St. Optatus, XI, 990.---In the serpent raised up by Moses: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1578; XXXVIII, 1342; XLV, 1138; Alcuin, C, 510; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 661; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 492.---In the calf sacrificed in the court of the tabernacle: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 346.

Christ is represented in balsam: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 938.---In the slaughtered kid: Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 203.---In the hydrus [water snake]: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 771.

Christ is signified by a suckling lamb: St. Gregory, LXXIX, 200.---By the four living creatures: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1683.---By water that irrigates or washes: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 175.---By the cluster brought from the land of promise: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1037; Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 214; Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 275.---By various flowers: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 190.---By a goat: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 818.---By a wooden hammer sounding upon a board: Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 150.---By manna: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 633; XXXV, 1603.---By fish: Ven. Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1101.---By a pail: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 902.---By a red cow: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 704.

Christ’s flesh is called:

- An altar: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 856.
- Haircloth: the same, CXII, 894.
- Diadem: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1071.
- House: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 589.
- Shoulder: the same, CXII, 959.
- Beast of burden: ibid., 973.
- Bed: Alan of Lille, CCX, 65.
- Robe: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1060.
- Earth: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 239.
- Earthen vessel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1066.
- Censer: ibid., 1070.
- Tunic: ibid., 1069.
- Golden urn: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 884.
- Garment: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1076.
- Heifer: ibid., 1082.

Christ’s body is called:

- House: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 395.
- Food: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 917.
- Flask: ibid., 979.
- Manna: ibid., 995.
- Marrow: ibid., 997.
- The mountain upon which the righteous rest: St. Hilary, IX, 301.
- Zion: the same, ibid., 297.
- Temple: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1064; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 685; Alan of Lille, CCX, 202.

Christ’s divinity is called:

- Altar: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 856.
- Gold: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 922.
- Beard: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.
- Head: ibid., 884.
- Column: ibid., 899.
- Pillar of fire: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 637.
- Right hand: Alan of Lille, CCX, 67.
- Throat: the same, ibid., 90.
- Hook: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 240.
- Mouth: the same, CXII, 1014.

Christ’s humanity is called:

- Altar: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 856.
- Butter: the same, CXII, 877.
- Head: ibid., 884.
- Column: ibid., 899.
- Pillar of cloud: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 637.
- Diadem: Alan of Lille, CCX, 233.
- House: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911.
- Potter’s house: Ven. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 290.
- Horse: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 916.
- Thigh: ibid., 923.
- Grain: ibid., 943.
- Hook: ibid., 947.
- Garden: Alan of Lille, CCX, 91.
- Hyssop: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1088.
- Milk: Alan of Lille, CCX, 81.
- Left hand: the same, ibid., 67.
- Lamp: the same, ibid., 233.
- Cloud: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 49.
- Wall: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1022.
- Sardonyx: ibid., 1046.
- Tabernacle: ibid., 1062.
- Earth: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 239.
- Shadow: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.
- Urn: ibid., 1086.
- Garment: ibid., 1073.
- Belly: ibid., 1071.
- Clothing: ibid., 1075.
- Rod: ibid., 1081.
- Christ’s humanity is compared to the belly and ivory: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1198.

Christ’s incarnation is called:

- Betrothal: Alan of Lille, CCX, 77.
- Fringe: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 928.
- Manger: ibid., 1027.
- Root: ibid., 1036.
- Footstool: ibid., 1043.
- Shadow: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 382.

[Col. 0138] Christ’s Passion is called:

- A bundle of myrrh: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 920.
- Fragment: ibid., 922.
- Purple: ibid., 1034.
- Redness: ibid., 1041.
- Blood: ibid., 1045.
- Torrent: ibid., 1068.

ASHES: the consummation of the Lord’s Passion, ibid., 895.

CITHARA signifies Christ’s humanity: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 901.---The cithara signifies the glorious Passion, which, with its strings stretched and its bones counted, sounded forth the strength of endurance in a certain intellectual melody: Cassiodorus, LXX, 404.---Christ fastened to the cross is compared to a cithara: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 655.

SCARLET DYE: the Lord’s Passion: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.

THE HILL of the Son’s right hand is the eternal loftiness of the Redeemer: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 351.

THE SERPENT, Moses’ rod having been made into it, signifies Christ’s death: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 584.

THE DOVE shows us the grace of baptism: St. Phoebadius, XX, 46.---The dove sent out from the ark: Christ sent to the Jews: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 509.---The dove: the Lord’s gentleness: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 71.

COLUMN. Christ’s divinity is a column, and likewise his humanity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 899.---By the column, Christ’s humanity is signified to us: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1157; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 641.---The pillar of fire shows the gift of the Holy Spirit: St. Phoebadius, XX, 46.

BANQUET. Christ’s supper at the feast of Passover was prefigured by the banquet which Lot made for the angels: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 408.---Joseph’s banquet for his brothers was a figure of the banquet of the body by which the Jews were united in covenant: ibid., 535.

HEART: Christ’s soul; Christ’s wisdom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.

HORN denotes divinity: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1256.

LEG: the courses of the Lord’s incarnation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.---Christ’s legs are preachers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 90.

THE DEDICATION of the temple signified Christ’s Resurrection: Cassiodorus, LXX, 202.

CHRIST’S BETROTHAL: his incarnation: Alan of Lille, CCX, 77.

CHRIST’S RIGHT HAND is his divinity; his left hand, his humanity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 67.

DIADEM is the name for the flesh that Christ assumed for us, by which, in dying, he destroyed the dominion of death, and by which also, in rising, he bestowed upon us the hope of rising: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1071.---Christ’s diadem: his human nature: Alan of Lille, CCX, 233.

DAY. Christ is fittingly called “day” in the mystery, whose apostles are the twelve hours: St. Ambrose, XV, 1759; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 650.---Day belongs to those to whom Christ is present; night to those to whom he denies himself: St. Ambrose, XV, 1292.---The brightness of Christ’s conduct: day: Garner, CXCIII, 370.

HOUSE is the Savior’s flesh assumed in the holy Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 389.---House: Christ’s humanity: the same, CXII, 911.

GOD’S SLEEPING is when the only-begotten Son of the Father deigned to die for us in assumed flesh: St. Eucherius, L, 737.

THE TWELFTH MONTH designated for the slaughter of the Jews represents the final age of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 665.

IVORY: the incorruption of Christ’s flesh: the same, CXII, 913.

ELECTRUM: a type of our redemption: the same, CXI, 478.

EMMANUEL. Christ is rightly called Emmanuel because that which Emmanuel signifies came: that is, “God with us”: Tertullian, II, 337; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 385.

HORSE. Christ’s humanity: horse: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 916.

THIGH has the same meaning in the Psalm as Christ’s incarnation: Cassiodorus, LXX, 320.---Christ’s thigh: his humanity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 923.

WINDOWS: Christ’s miracles: ibid., 924.---The windows and lattices through which the Beloved looks upon us are his divinity: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1109.

THE SON OF GOD appeared to Abraham, but in the form of a human body, in order that it might be shown that in the last times he would come as a human being: St. Phoebadius, XX, 36.

FISCELLA (BASKET). The Lord’s manger is prefigured in Moses’ basket: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 646.

FLAME OF FIRE. Christ appeared to Moses in the bush, in a flame of fire, in order to show himself as light to believers and as judgment to unbelievers: St. Phoebadius, XX, 46.

FLOWER from the rod: the Son of Mary, who is called Jesus Christ: Tertullian, II, 788.---The flower is denoted by Nazareth: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 372.---The flower: Christ’s glorious flesh: Alan of Lille, CCX, 69.

[Col. 0139] CREVICES OF THE ROCK: Christ’s wounds: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCII, 1071; Alan of Lille, CCX, 70.---Christ’s wounds, namely the marks of the nails and of the lance’s blow: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1066.---Christ’s wounds are the crevices of the rock and the hollow of the wall: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 615; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1071.

HEN. Christ’s charity is very like the nature of a hen: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 543.

CHEEK. By the cheeks of the bridegroom are understood Christ’s modesty, mercy, severity, or the appearance of his countenance: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1086.---The Savior’s modesty is denoted by the cheeks: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.

GIANT is Christ, of twofold nature: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 396.

SWORD: the word of God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 322.

GRAIN: Christ’s humanity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.---Christ was a tree when he rose again, who was a grain when he died: St. Eucherius, L, 745.

STEPS signify the coming of the Son of God and his return to the Father: St. Eucherius, L, 734.

THROAT: Christ’s teaching: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 946.---Christ’s divinity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 90.

HOOK is called the divinity of the Son of God: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 240.

HERMON. The dew of Hermon is Christ’s grace: Alcuin, C, 637.

FAWNS bear the type of Christ’s body and soul: Alan of Lille, CCX, 98.

GOAT. The two goats offered in fasting figure the two offices of Christ: namely, Christ who was to suffer and Christ who was to provide nourishment for the faithful in the Church: Tertullian, II, 331. Some understood Christ and Barabbas by the two goats: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 818.---The two goats signify Christ and Antichrist: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 1577.

KID. Christ is a lamb to us, but a kid to the Jews: St. Ambrose, XIV, 648.---The kids offered by Isaac prefigure the Savior’s coming in the flesh: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 588.

GARDEN is Christ’s human nature: Alan of Lille, CCX, 91. The garden bed of this garden is the soul: Alan of Lille, CCX, 91.

HYSSOP, dipped in the blood of the victim, was customarily sprinkled seven times over the leper’s body, signifying that the stains of sins are effectually to be washed away by the precious blood of the Lord and Savior: Cassiodorus, LXX, 364.---Christ’s blood is signified by hyssop: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 206.---Hyssop signifies faith and the humility of Christ’s Passion: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 692.

FIRE. Christ’s humanity is signified by the cloud that overshadowed by day, and his divinity by the fire that shone by night: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 730.

YOKE is called Christ’s dominion: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 972.

STONE. Christ is the stone cut from the mountain; when he lies low, he strikes down the one who stumbles against him, but when he comes in exaltation, he crushes the proud: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 567, 681.

THE BREADTH of the temple signifies Christ’s charity: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1147.

WOOD. By the wood of Moses, water is cured from the defect of bitterness into the wholesome quality of sweetness; that wood was Christ, healing from himself the waters of baptism: Tertullian, I, 1209.---That bitter waters become sweet when wood is received into them was a sign that the bitterness of the nations would at some time be changed, through the wood of the cross, into the use of sweetness: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 76. Christ was aptly compared to a fruit-bearing tree because of the cross that he undertook for human salvation: Cassiodorus, LXX, 30.---The woods of Lebanon: Christ’s members: Alan of Lille, CCX, 83.---The tree of life in the midst of Paradise is Christ in the midst of his Church: St. Ambrose, XVII, 778.

LILY AMONG THORNS: Christ among the Jews: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1094.

THE HEAVENLY LIGHTS are likened to Christ’s wounds: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 968.

WOODEN MALLET sounding upon a board signifies Christ upon the cross: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 150.

POMEGRANATE. Christ is understood under the name of pomegranate: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 361.

PUNIC APPLE / POMEGRANATE signifies Christ’s Passion: Alan of Lille, CCX, 93.---The blood of Christ is called a pomegranate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 932.

MORNING: Christ’s coming; likewise, the coming of the Judge: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 368.---Morning is called the time of the Incarnation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 992.---The time of the Resurrection: ibid.---Christ’s Resurrection is called morning: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

MANNA. By the hidden manna may be understood Wisdom, which is Christ: St. Ambrose, XVII, 781.---Manna signifies Christ’s flesh: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 869.---Manna was a figure of Christ, the heavenly bread: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 554; XXXIX, 1155.

HAND. By the hand of the beloved is understood all the strength of his power: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1185.

JAW signifies Christ’s Passion: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 486.

MERCHANT. Christ is the merchant who carried our price in a sack; he was struck by the lance, the sack was split open, and the price of the world flowed out: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 178, 179.

MIDDAY denotes the time of the Passion: Alan of Lille, CCX, 59.

MOUNTAIN. Christ is continually called a mountain in the Scriptures: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 74, 77, 517; XXXVIII, 45.---The mountain moved into the sea is Christ proclaimed to the nations by the apostles: ibid., XXXVIII, 554.---Mountains signify Christ by reason of the loftiness of his virtues: St. Eucherius, L, 742.---As laws were given on the mountain, so too were the commandments of Christ the Lord given on the mountain: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 767.

MYRRH. By myrrh are denoted Christ’s Passion and burial: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1060.---Myrrh signifies the bitterness of the Passion: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1080.

NARD is a type of the Lord’s Passion: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1078.

NOSTRILS. Christ’s foreknowledge is denoted by the name of nostrils: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1004.

MIST. Christ’s humanity is like a mist covering the whole earth: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 50.

CLOUD: Christ’s ascension: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007. Christ’s humanity is signified by the cloud that overshadowed by day: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 730.

THE EIGHTH. By “for the eighth” is signified the Lord’s second coming, when, the week of the age ended, he shall come to judge the world: Cassiodorus, LXX, 59.

OIL. Christ’s name is compared with oil: Nicholas, CLXXXIV, 831.

DOOR. The door in the side of the ark is a type of the wound in Christ’s side: Guerric, Abbot, CLXXXV, 140.

CLOAK: the height of Christ’s humanity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018.

STAKE. Christ’s pillar is signified by the stake of the vine: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 644.

WALL signifies the Savior’s body: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 401.

PASSOVER is a figure of Christ’s passage to the Father: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 766.

SPARROW.---The two sparrows of Leviticus 14 are Christ’s divinity and humanity: Rupert, Abbot, CLXXII, 811.

SHEPHERD. Christ is the true shepherd, and those who would not be fed by him death shall feed upon: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1164.

FOOT. Christ’s example is a foot: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1025.---By the feet of the Son of God is understood the Incarnation: St. Eucherius, L, 733.---The Lord’s feet signify his Incarnation, but his hands his power: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 812.

ROCK. What is said in the prophet Isaiah, “He will bring forth water for them from the rock,” is fulfilled in the Gospel when Christ, who is the rock, is opened by the stroke of the lance: St. Cyprian, LV, 379.

THE ROBE REACHING TO THE FEET and the mitre in Zechariah signify Christ’s coming in glory: Tertullian, II, 330, 331.

THE BACK PARTS. The Incarnation of the Son of God is understood: St. Eucherius, L, 733.

PSALTERY: a fitting likeness of the adornment of the Lord’s body: Cassiodorus, LXX, 342.

PURPLE is called Christ’s Passion: Alan of Lille, CCX, 100.---The purple color signifies the mystery of the Lord’s Passion: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1071, 1073, 1096.

THE CHARIOTS OF AMMINADAB are Christ’s principal virtues displayed in the Incarnation: Alan of Lille, CCX, 95.

RAHAB, hanging a scarlet cord in the window, bore beforehand the mystery of Christ’s blood: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 545.

ROOT: the Lord’s Incarnation, root: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 342.

BRANCH of the green olive denotes Christ’s most holy flesh: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 1016.

DEW signifies the Word of the Lord: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 328.---Christ is as dew in the Virgin’s womb: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 201.

SACK is the body of Christ Jesus, when he deigned to die for us: Cassiodorus, LXX, 206.

SACRIFICES. Christ was prophesied in the ancient sacrifices: St. Augustine, XCII, 347.

[Col. 0141] SHARP ARROWS are the words of the Lord and Savior: Cassiodorus, LXX, 321.

BLOOD: Christ’s Passion, blood: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 212.

SAPPHIRE: Christ’s miracles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1044.

PATH. The purpose of the Incarnation, path: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 264.---Christ’s ascension, path: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1049.

SERPENT raised up by Moses: a type of Christ crucified: St. Ambrose, XVII, 34; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 729.---The bronze serpent foretold Christ the Lord freeing people from the bite of the devil: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 780; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 340.

SUN: Christ’s Resurrection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1057.

FILTH in Zechariah signifies Christ’s first coming in weakness: Tertullian, II, 330, 331.

BULL. “Its beauty is that of a bull; its horns are the horns of a unicorn”: by these words Christ was signified—fierce to some as Judge, gentle to others as Savior: Tertullian, II, 346.

TIME. Christ and the Church are figured in the very times of the Judges and Kings: St. Augustine, XLII, 271.---The present times display the name of Christ and the Church just as past times announced them: ibid., 285.

POTSHERD. Let us not think that Christ’s power is inappropriately compared with a potsherd: Cassiodorus, LXX, 158.

TABOR especially signifies the Lord’s coming: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 362.

CENSER is a symbol of Christ suffering: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 856.

INCENSE. The Magi from the East offered incense, myrrh, and gold to the Lord as it were, the conclusion of sacrifice: Tertullian, I, 672.

WINEPRESS Christ alone trod: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1162.

TORRENT. Christ’s wisdom is aptly compared to a torrent: Cassiodorus, LXX, 254; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 154.

BREASTS denote Christ’s divinity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 100.

SHADOW is called Christ’s humanity and protection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.

COW: the weakness of the Incarnation: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 96.---By the red cow delivered to the priest for sacrifice is figured the incarnate Lord, who made himself a sacrifice for our redemption: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 703.

A POTTER’S VESSEL broken signifies Christ’s death: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 291.

VEIL OF THE LAW. Christ lies hidden in the veil of the Law as the kernel in barley beneath the husk: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 725.

PRIVATE PARTS. Christ’s weak flesh is signified by Noah’s uncovered private parts: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 954.

WORM. Christ, called “a worm and not a man,” denotes the humility of his future incorporation: St. Gaudentius, XX, 989; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 547.

EVENING: the time of the Incarnation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1076.

GARMENT. Christ came from Bozrah with garments dyed: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 136.

THE CLOTHING of the Son of God is his flesh: St. Eucherius, L, 733.

WAY is called Christ; likewise the passage of his humanity and his particular coming to the heart: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 260.

WINE. Christ’s divinity is compared with wine: St. Gaudentius, XX, 985.---Wine: Christ’s blood: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.

ROD. Christ himself is the flower from the rod which came forth from the root of Jesse. Christ’s humanity is signified by Moses’ rod: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 584.---Moses’ rod changed into a serpent was a figure of the Lord’s Passion: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 933; XXXVIII, 67; XLII, 880.---Moses’ rod was a figure of the wood of Christ’s cross: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1061.---The power given to Christ is signified by Moses’ rod raised over the Red Sea: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 641.

VINE. The pruning of the vine: Christ’s self-emptying: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 637.---Vine leaves denote Christ’s words: ibid., 852.

CALF: a type of Christ’s human nature: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 650.

## APPENDIX TO ARTICLE II. Allegories concerning the Cross.

CROSS is called: altar: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 366.---Apple tree: John Algrinus, CCVI, 808; Alan of Lille, CCX, 105.---The cross is denoted by the apple tree: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 541.---The tree of the cross brought forth the fruit of salvation and life: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 953.---Noah’s ark: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 770.---Staff: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.---Hook: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 102.---Bed: Gilbert, CLXXXIV, 655.---Wood: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.---Wood making waters sweet: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 655.---Little ship: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1005.---Mercy seat: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 771.---Oak of Tabor: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, 439.---Royal seal: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 727.---The bridal seat in which Christ joined the Church to himself: ibid., 656.---Ladder and gate of heaven: Alan of Lille, CCX, 224.---The cross is properly called the ladder of heaven, because through it the Lord Jesus Christ, accomplishing and completing all mysteries, brought all the mysteries back to the Father and to Adam, and opened the way to heaven for all who follow him: St. Zeno, XI, 433.---The sole way to heaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 740.---Balance: Rupert, Abbot, CLXXII, 1612.---The balance of Christ’s body, that is, of the Church: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 672.---Sycamore: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1053.---Sycamore, or foolish fig tree: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 438.---Bar: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.---Rod: ibid., CXII, 1081; St. Augustine, XL, 698.---Rod of power: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 761.

By the name of wood the holy cross is denoted: St. Eucherius, L, 741; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 329.---By the name of palm tree: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1017.---By the name of the Winepress: ibid., 1068.

The wood of the cross is called: altar: ibid., 856.---Tree: ibid., 865.---Cedar: ibid., 891.---Figures of the cross were the paschal lamb, the sign of the paschal lamb’s blood, and the sign of the cross: Lactantius, VI, 530.---Wooden altar. The mystery of the cross is signified by the wooden altar: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1488.---Ehud. The cross is denoted by the hilt of Ehud’s sword: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 270.---Noah’s ark: St. Augustine, XL, 334.---Cluster of grapes. Christ upon the cross: a cluster placed upon a pole: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 786.---The cross prepared for Mordecai: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 660.---Gideon. The cross foreshadowed in Gideon: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 769.---Isaac. Isaac, carrying the wood, was a figure of Christ bearing the cross: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 429.---Jacob. The cross is signified by Jacob’s crossing of his hands over Ephraim and Manasseh: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 548.---The juniper tree beneath which Elijah was: ibid., 1245.---Wood cast into the waters to make them sweet: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1031.---The Lord Jesus Christ was aptly compared to a fruit-bearing tree because of the cross that he undertook for human salvation: Cassiodorus, LXX, 30.---Christ reigned from the wood—not from that tree of Paradise by which the devil seemed to hold the human race captive, but from this wood, from which liberty lifted up its head and rose into life. For upon that tree hung the death of transgression; upon this shone forth the faith of confession. That tree led down to hell; this sends up to heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 360.---Moses stretching out his hands: St. Augustine, XLII, 901.---So long as Moses stretched out his hands, the proud audacity of Amalek was crushed down, foretelling the cross of the most blessed Passion: Cassiodorus, LXX, 959.---Palm tree: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 536; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 947; Alan of Lille, CCX, 221.---The stake by which Jael pierced Sisera’s brain: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1136.---Samson’s pillars: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 285.---Serpent. The serpent suspended upon wood was a type and shadow of Christ hanging on the cross for our salvation: St. Ambrose, XVII, 34.---The tablets written by God’s finger, a type of the cross: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 606.---Terebinth. Christ’s cross was signified by the terebinth where Jacob buried the foreign gods, because our sins were buried in Christ’s flesh: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 501.---The tambourine of Mary the prophetess: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 1022.---The Greek letter Tau (T): St. Augustine, XXXIV, 804; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1101; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1038.---Aaron’s rod: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 730.---Moses’ rod: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 686; Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1061.---The rod by which the rock was struck: Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 188; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1617.

The cross is signified by the two pieces of wood gathered by the widow of Zarephath: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1241.---The outer ends of the cross are a bull’s horns: Tertullian, II, 346.---The arms of the cross are called horns: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.---The arms of the cross are horns in Christ’s hands: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1618.---The cross had two timbers: one, the tongue of the Jews; the other, the hand of the Gentiles: Rupert, Abbot, CLXXII, 884.

The two timbers of the cross are signified by the actual striking of the rock: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1612.---The sign of the cross: bark: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904.---The sign of the living God is the sign of the cross: Alcuin, C, 1129.---The banner of the cross is a shield: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 895.

## ARTICLE III. Allegories concerning the Blessed Mary.

ARK OF THE COVENANT prefigures nothing other than Mary: St. Ambrose, XXII, 689.

SPICES. Mary’s virtues are compared with aromatic spices: Alan of Lille, CCX, 82.

DAWN. Mary is like the dawn: Alan of Lille, CCX, 94.

HEAD of the Blessed Mary: Christ: Alan of Lille, CCX, 100.

CASTLE can be a symbol of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 959.

THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN is compared with Mary’s faith: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 120.

NECK not stretched out signifies Mary’s humility: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 944.---The neck of the Blessed Mary is her obedience: Alan of Lille, CCX, 60.---It is her teaching: ibid., 99.

DOVE. The properties of the dove are applied to the Blessed Mary: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 884.

DAY. Mary is day, as is the angel Gabriel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.

IVORY. Mary’s body is compared with ivory: Guerric, CLXXXV, 117.

LEAVEN. Mary’s faith is leaven: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 801.

SEALED FOUNTAIN: the Virgin’s womb: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 106.---Mary is called a fountain sealed by the Holy Spirit, both in body and in mind: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 898.

FOUNDATION. Mary is the foundation of our faith: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 1149.

CORD. Mary is signified by the scarlet cord that Rahab bound in the window: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 887.

THROAT. The Blessed Mary’s meditation is compared with a throat: Alan of Lille, CCX, 101.

JERUSALEM denotes the Blessed Mary: Alan of Lille, CCX, 202.

ENCLOSED GARDEN: the Virgin’s womb: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 106.

LIPS of the Virgin Mary signify her teaching: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 884.

BED. The womb of the Virgin Mary is called a bed: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 858.---Solomon’s bed prefigured the Blessed Mary: Alan of Lille, CCX, 75.

LEBANON. Mary’s virginity is compared with Lebanon: Gilbert, CLXXXIV, 89.

LILY AMONG THORNS: the Blessed Virgin among the daughters of the synagogue: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1093.---Mary and Joseph: two lilies: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 871.

MANNA. Mary is manna—delicate, bright, sweet, and virgin—which, as though descending from heaven, poured forth food sweeter than honey for all the peoples of the churches: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 330.

MARY: a full field: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1074.---Aqueduct: ibid., CLXXXIII, 439.---Dawn: Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 124.---Rising dawn: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 936; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 896.---Castle: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 32; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1083.---Hill of incense: Alan of Lille, CCX, 80.---Neck: Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 122.---Beloved dove: Alan of Lille, CCX, 93.---Mystical dove: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 37.---House of divine Wisdom: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 957; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 674.---House of Wisdom: Alan of Lille, CCX, 261.---Potter’s house: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 290.---Chosen as the sun: Alan of Lille, CCX, 94.---Fountain: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1008; Alan, CCX, 76.---Sealed fountain: Alan of Lille, CCX, 95.---Foundation of our faith: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 1149.---Garden of spices: Alan of Lille, CCX, 95.---Enclosed garden: ibid., 82.---Garden of delights: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 876; Guerric, Abbot, CLXXXV, 119.---Garden of nuts: Alan of Lille, CCX, 95.---Discoverer of grace: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 415.---Lentil: Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 35.---Lily among thorns: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 754; Alan of Lille, CCX, 247.---Moon: Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 124.---Mother of charity: St. Bernard, CLXXIII, 922.---Mother of the nations: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 950.---Middle of the earth: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 327.---Queen of mercy: ibid., CLXXXIV, 1059.---Mountain: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 310.---Mountain of myrrh: Alan of Lille, CCX, 80.---Mighty woman: St. Bernard, [Col. 0144] CLXXXIII, 63.---Little ship: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 603.---The business of the ages: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 327.---Olive tree of the field: Alan of Lille, CCX, 247.---Planting of a rose in Jericho: Alan of Lille, CCX, 247.---Full of grace and knowledge: ibid., 87.---Gate of heaven: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1010.---Greatest gate of heaven: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 70.---Ezekiel’s gate: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 753.---Eastern gate: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 905; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1011.---Knowing God’s secrets: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 857.---Christ’s sister and bride: Alan of Lille, CCX, 80, 81.---Star: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 719; Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 124.---Star of the Sea: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 719; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 440.---Temple of the Lord: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 63.---Chamber of holiness: ibid., 67.---God’s treasure: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 395.---Throne of God: Guerric, Abbot, CLXXXV, 189.---Royal throne: ibid., 117.---Dining chamber of the divine counsel: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 67.---Tower of David: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 888.---Gideon’s fleece: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 64.---Summit of the mountains: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 47.---Flowering rod: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 62, 432.---The rod from which Jesus the flower came forth: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 41.---Virgin and martyr: Guerric, CLXXXV, 117.---A little rod of myrrh and incense spices: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 986.

The Virgin Mary is called: battle-line of armies: Alan of Lille, CCX, 91, 94.---Noah’s ark: ibid., 91, 94.---Castle: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 885.---City: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 897; Alan of Lille, CCX, 200.---Heaven: St. Peter Damian, CXCIV, 861.---Litter: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 925.---Basket: ibid., 929.---Treasury of virtues: Alan of Lille, CCX, 53.---Enclosed garden: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 896.---Jerusalem: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 205.---Alan of Lille: CCX, 91, 94.---Wool: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 980.---Lily [printed *Litium*]: Alan of Lille, CCX, 64.---Mountain: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1001.---Mountain of myrrh: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 205.---Woman: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1002.---Egg: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 1456.---Palace: Alan of Lille, CCX, 53.---Paradise of the heavenly King: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 895.---Gate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1031.---Gate of heaven: Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1010.---Gate of the sanctuary: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1493.---Prophetess: ibid., 1307.---Fair and blessed woman: ibid., CLXVIII, 851.---Queen of angels: ibid., CLXX, 205.---Bush: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1041.---Jacob’s ladder: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1010.---Sun: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1057.---Christ’s sister: Alan of Lille, CCX, 107.---Mirror of humility: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 205.---Star: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.---Shunammite: Alan of Lille, CCX, 96.---Tabernacle: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1062; Alan of Lille, CCX, 53.---Earth: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.---Temple: ibid., 1064.---Chamber: ibid., 1063.---Tower: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 205.---Fleece: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.---Rod: ibid., 1081; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1031.---Little rod of smoke: Alan, CCX, 74.

The Virgin Mary is compared with Noah’s ark: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1016, 1019.---Dawn: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 719.---A field: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 41; Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1093.---A castle: Alan of Lille, CCX, 190, 201.---The Church: Alan, CCX, 60.---The city of Jerusalem: ibid., CCX, 190, 201.---The moon: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 719.---The burning bush: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1017.---The sun: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 720; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 760; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 430.---The earth: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 748, 1007.---Tartarus: Alan, CCX, 60.---A rod: Alan, CCX, 190.---The rod of Jesse: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 720.---Mary is likened to a palm tree: Alan of Lille, CCX, 100.---Mary is called simply “our Lady”: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 210.---Mary was the apostles’ teacher: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 916.---The name of Mary unfolded from the treasury of Divinity: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 508.---Mary giving birth is, in the moral sense, Wisdom bringing forth the fruit of salvation: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 310.---Mary is terrible to demons: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 720.---Mary bore a certain type of our souls: St. Maximus of Turin, [Col. 0145] LVII, 269.---Mary denotes the faithful soul: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 638.---Mary denotes a religious congregation: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 335.---Mary and Joseph morally denote reason and conscience respectively: ibid., 367.

NECKLACE. The Blessed Mary’s necklace is Christ’s obedience: Alan of Lille, CCX, 60.

MOUNTAIN denotes the Blessed Virgin Mary: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1091.

THE WOMEN listed in the book of Genesis were figures of Mary: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 1022.

NARD denotes the Blessed Mary’s flesh, and also her renown: Alan of Lille, CCX, 61.

THE BLESSED MARY’S EYES are the active and contemplative life: ibid., CCX, 99.

FRAGRANCE. Mary’s good fragrance is Christ; but Christ is an evil fragrance to Eve: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 854.

PARADISE. The womb of the Virgin Mary is Paradise: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 837.

LITTLE GIRL. Mary is called “little girl” and as having no breasts: Alan, CCX, 107.

SKIN. Mary’s beauty is like Solomon’s skins: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 846.

ROCK. Mary is rightly called a rock: Guerric, CLXXXV, 119.

RAIN is a symbol of the Blessed Virgin Mary’s humility and chastity: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 1006.

POLE. Mary is figured by the pole: Alan, CCX, 201.

GATE is Mary, who remained ever closed before the Prince’s entry—that is, Christ’s—and remained closed forever after his departure: St. Ambrose, XVII, 948.---The gate denotes the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 385.---It was a gate accessible to God alone: Alan, CCX, 85.

DEW. Mary’s conception by the Holy Spirit is signified by the dew lying in the wilderness: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 1328.

ROSE. Eve is a thorn; Mary a rose: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1020.

BUSH: a prefiguration of the Virgin Mary: St. Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 513.

TEMPLE. Mary is a kind of temple in which we are to dwell: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 367.

EARTH. Mary is the earth giving the fruit of blessing: Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 115.

CHAMBER signifies the womb of the holy Virgin Mary: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 390; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 413.

BREASTS. Mary’s two breasts are virginity and fruitfulness, as two twin fawns: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 889.---The Blessed Mary’s breasts are humility and virginity: Alan of Lille, CCX, 107. Charity is denoted by the Blessed Mary’s breasts: CCX, 79. The Blessed Mary’s breasts denote flesh and soul: ibid., 98.

WOMB. The Virgin Mary’s womb is called the wilderness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.

FLEECE is Mary, from whose fruit saving garments are woven for the peoples: St. Ambrose, XVII, 614.---The womb of the Virgin Mary is Gideon’s fleece: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 661.

ROD. Mary is Aaron’s rod: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 721, 760.---Mary was figured by Aaron’s rod: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 883.---The rod from the root is Mary from David: Tertullian, II, 788.---The Virgin Mary is the rod of Jesse’s root: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 310; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 112, 113.---Mary is the rod; Christ, the flower: St. Ambrose, XV, 1561; St. Augustine, XL, 698; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 1454; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 392; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 826, 827.

VIRGIN and star of the sea: a type of divine grace: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 231.

FRUIT-BEARING VINE is the humility of the Blessed Virgin: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 989.

SCARLET BAND signifies the words of the Blessed Mary: Alan, CCX, 78.
