St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 355.---Our sisters: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 647, 648.---Stars: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.---Tabernacle: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1062.---Temple: ibid., 1063.---Thrones: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.---God’s garment: Rupert, elsewhere, CLXVII, 212.---Our neighbours: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 897.---Watchmen: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.---Man: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 137.---Virtues/powers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.

Angels signify God most high: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 658.---Faith: ibid., 778.---Angels bear the world: ibid., 1006.---They are signified by the abyss: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1013; by the altar: ibid., 1091.---Angels are compared to winds: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1348.---Guardian angels are called cedar trees: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 430.---By the name “angels” the angelic choir itself is denoted: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.

WATERS in heaven are called the hosts of angels, by whom the higher regions of heaven are covered: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 987.

GOLD is called the wisdom of the first angel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.

HAIR. By the hair of the head we must typologically understand holy angels or virtuous elect persons: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 709.

HEAVEN is the understanding of angels, the assembly of heavenly spirits, angels: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.---Angelic understanding is a kind of heaven: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 278, 787.

BRONZE. The strength of angels is called bronze: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 918.

HOST. The multitude of angels is a host.

[Col. 0147] FIRMAMENT: the confirmation of angelic nature after the fall of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 36.

LILY: angels, by reason of the brightness of righteousness: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

MONTHS: the orders of angels are months: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997.

MOUNTAINS may be understood as angelic ministries and the virtues and powers of heaven, through whose ministry ascent to the heights is granted us: St. Hilary, IX, 655. The mountains around us are angelic fortifications which defend us: ibid., 682.---By the name of mountain is signified the loftiness of angels: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1141, 1142.---The mountains around Jerusalem are angels: ibid., 1650.

The NINE names of Ezekiel’s stones are the nine orders of angels: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1250.---The number nine: the nine orders of angels: Garner, CXCIII, 450.

SAPPHIRE. The brilliance of angels is sapphire: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1044.

HEDGE. The guardianship of angels is a hedge: ibid., 1049.

SEAL is the first angel: ibid., 1053.

TEMPLE is the capacity of angelic and human understanding: ibid., 1063.

## ARTICLE V. Allegories concerning evil spirits

ABYSS: the devil’s cunning: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 284.

EGYPT. What is understood by the name of Egypt but the multitude fallen from the heavenly dwellings? And what is meant by Pharaoh, king of Egypt, but the devil himself, author of darkness? St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 187.

STRANGER. Demons are called strangers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857.

BREATH (*halitus*; source reads *alitus*): the devil’s suggestion: ibid., 856.

AMALEKITES: a figure of evil spirits: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 299.

AMMON. The people of sorrow, or Ammon, may not inappropriately be understood as the devil and his angels: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1187.

ANGEL: an evil spirit: the same, CXII, 851.

SOUL: the will of the devil: ibid., 852.

EAGLE. In Sacred Scripture, under the term “eagle” are understood evil spirits, snatchers of souls and ambushers: the same, CX, 694; CXII, 862.

NORTH WIND. The devil and his angels are figuratively placed in the north, as Christ is in the south: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 561.---The devil and his co-apostate angels are called the north wind: St. Eucherius, L, 739.---The devil is customarily called by the name of the north wind, because he binds the hearts of the nations as with the cold of numbness: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 26, 798, 939; LXXIX, 515.---The devil comes from the north, and is the prince of our reproach: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 231.---The sides of the north: the devil’s nation: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 842.

WEAPONS: the devil’s wickedness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.---The devil’s deceits: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 318.

ASPS: evil spirits: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.---The devil’s hidden cruelty: ibid.---The devil’s suggestions: ibid.

ASSYRIA is the same as the devil, because he draws many into guilt and descends with all his multitude to the gates of hell: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 916.

BIRD: evil spirits: Rabanus Maurus, LXXV, 872.

BABYLON is the city of the devil: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1510.

WAR: the devil’s temptation; the resisting adversary; the adversary’s suggestion; the evil one himself: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 874.

BEASTS of the earth are evil spirits: ibid., 875; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 991, 1182.

GILL: the devil’s power: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 874.

CARTILAGE: the devil’s members: ibid., 887.

WHELPS: demons: ibid., 889.

WHALE, or Leviathan, prefigures the devil: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 644, 824.

CANAANITE. The devil is signified by the Canaanite fighting against Israel: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 875.

CITIZENS: demons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.

CRY: the devil’s violent temptation: ibid., 881.

SHIELD. The devil’s resistance is a shield: Garner, CXCIII, 321.

HILL is the devil, cast off because of pride: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1038.

HEART: the devil’s cunning: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 902.

RAVEN is a symbol of the devil: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 253.

[Col. 0148] BEDCHAMBER: the devil’s rest: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904.

GUARDIANS: evil spirits: ibid., 905.

DEMONS are deservedly represented by swine: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 198.---Demons are denoted by the name of tempest: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 854. Demons are called slanderers: ibid., 991.---Demons are signified by dragons: ibid., 1013.

TEETH: the persecutions of demons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 907.

DESERT: demons: ibid., 909.---Evil spirits are called desert: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 268.

DEVIL: accuser at the Judgment: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 871.---Adversary: ibid., 268; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.---Angel: ibid., 851.---A solitary wild boar: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 306.---North wind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 842.---Northern region: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 741.---Armed man: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 865; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 988.---Rider: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.---Asp: ibid., 868; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 340.---Author of scandals: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 202.---Bird: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.---Nocturnal bird, hating vigils and anathema: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1159.---Basilisk: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 874; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 340.---Behemoth: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 875.---Beast: ibid.---Ox: ibid., 877.---Corpse: ibid., 878.---Darkness: ibid., 879.---Slanderer: ibid., 880; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 450.---Head: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.---Head of the ungodly: Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 971; Rupert, CLXVIII, 641.---Head and beginning of all iniquity: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 279.---Head and prince of all evils: St. Agobard, CIV, 155.---Whelp: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 889.---Whale: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 824; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.---Hill, cast off because of pride: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1038.---Serpent: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900.---Damascus: ibid., 906.---Doe: ibid., 906.---Dragon: St. Eucherius, L, 754; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 104; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 74, 340, 375; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1755.---Dragon lying in wait: St. Augustine, XXXV, 879; XXXVI, 438, 867; XXXVII, 1168.---Dragon, enemy of the Church: ibid., 1381.---Edom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 915.---Exactor: ibid., 918; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 980.---Exactor of a most evil inheritance: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 268.---Smith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 919.---Smith blowing persecutions against the servants of God: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1340.---Strong man: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 931.---Giant: ibid., 916.---Man: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 754.---Terrible one: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1097.---Ancient enemy: the same, LXXVI, 601.---Enemy of man: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 178.---Hyena: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 954.---Anvil: ibid., 970.---Hell: ibid., 970.---Founder of pride: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 268.---Inventor of death: ibid.---Inventor and cause of every evil: St. Agobard, CIV, 280.---Stone: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 980.---Stone of darkness: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1233.---Hunter’s snare: St. Bruno of Asti, CLII, 1122.---Thief: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1063; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 761.---Lion: St. Augustine, XXXV, 879; XXXVIII, 1209; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 74, 340, 375; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1755; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 237.---Lion in attack, dragon in ambush: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 438, 867; XXXVII, 1168.---Lion and ant: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 702.---Leviathan: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.---Lucifer: ibid., 989.---Wolf: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 319.---Hammer: Cassiodorus, LXX, 690; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997.---Hammer of the heavenly Craftsman: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 483.---Kite: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 999.---Moab: ibid., 1000.---Mountain: the same, CXI, 359.---Mountain which cast itself into the heart of Judah: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1137.---Death: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1002.---Mulberry tree: ibid., 1002.---Scoundrel: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1649.---Night: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.---Father: ibid., 1023.---Father of lies: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 267.---Partridge: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1027.---Pirate: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1649.---Fish: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1030.---Lead: ibid., 1034.---Gate of death: the same, CXI, 385.---Overseer of death: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 223.---Prince: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1029.---Prince of the prison: Rupert, CLXVII, 522.---Prince of our reproach: the same, CLXIII, 231.---Prince of the proud: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 857.---Prince of worldly pleasures: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 61, 63.---King: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1088.---Most cruel king: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1114.---King of vices: Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 852.---Scorpion: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 754.---Serpent: ibid.; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1051.---Saw: ibid.---Servant: ibid.---Spirit: ibid., 1056.---Proud one: ibid., 1061.---Shadow of death: Cassiodorus, LXX, 169.---Bar: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.---Bar which strikes to death: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 645.---Wind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1074.---Viper: St. Eucherius, L, 754.---Man: ibid.; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080.---Calf: ibid., 1082.---Fox: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 514.

The devil is called Addition: Rupert, CLXVII, 1631.---Stranger, because he is alien to the Lord’s kingdom: Cassiodorus, LXX, 785.---Wild boar: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---Antichrist: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 306.---Eagle: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 69.---North wind: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 806; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 59.---Asp when it strikes secretly; basilisk when it openly spreads poisons: Cassiodorus, LXX, 654.---Assyria: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1079.---Bird: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 65.---Staff: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.---Basilisk when it openly spreads poisons: Cassiodorus, LXX, 654.---Beast: St. Eucherius, L, 748; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 428, 581, 670.---Ox in its members, that is, in heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 201, 208.---Slanderer: Cassiodorus, LXX, 508.---Dog: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 752.---Captivity: Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 925.---Raven: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 748.---Day: ibid., 761.---Dragon: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1277.---Dragon when it swallows up the negligent with impious voracity: Cassiodorus, LXX, 654.---It is called dragon because it breathed into Eve, the first woman, poison through deadly persuasions: ibid., 739.---Exactor, whose voice is the temptation of wretched suggestion: St. Gregory the Great, LXX, 676; LXXVI, 555, 563, 1297.---False reasoner: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 90.---Usurer: Cassiodorus, LXX, 785.---Thief: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1442.---Man: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 135.---Man insofar as he is stained by sins: Cassiodorus, LXX, 156.---Man, not by nature but by guilt and infirmity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 957.---Evil man: Cassiodorus, LXX, 994.---Enemy of man: St. Paulinus of Nola, 294.---Lion: Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 846; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 700; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 290.---Lion when it persecutes the innocent: Cassiodorus, LXX, 654.---Wolf: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 748.---Lie: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 790.---Soldier: Cassiodorus, LXX, 331.---Kite: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 82.---Death: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 556; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 97.---Fly: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---Night: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 376.---Dark gates: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 490.---Leopard: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 748.---Destruction: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 97.---Partridge: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---Gate of death: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 490.---Frog: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 752.---King: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 147.---Foolish king: Alcuin, C, 687.---Serpent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 645; Alcuin, C, 709.---Ancient serpent: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 239, 471.---Job, the tempter: St. Hilary, X, 723.---Bear: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---Scorching wind: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 54, 406, 814.---Man: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 137.---Bird of heaven: St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVI, 95.---Foxes: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 752; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 96.

The devil is called asp: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 129.---Behemoth: ibid., 123.---Bassia [reading uncertain]: ibid., 106.---Ox: ibid., 94.---Serpent: St. Jerome, XXV, 1052; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 126.---Winding serpent: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 35.---Day and night: ibid., 641.---Dragon: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 124.---Lion: St. Jerome, XXV, 1052; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 36, 646; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 108.---Wolf: ibid., 115.---Myrmicoleon (“ant-lion”): St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 36, 646.---Night: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 641.---Solitary night: ibid., 644.---Regulus: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 127.---Axe: St. Jerome, XXXV, 137.---Serpent: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 124.---Saw: St. Jerome, XXIV, 137.---Tiger: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 36, 646; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 113.---Bear: St. Jerome, XXV, 1052.---Rod: St. Jerome, XXIV, 137.---He is denoted by the name Behemoth: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 691.---By the name Pharaoh: the same, LXXIX, 187.---By the name Philistines: ibid., 205.

He is signified by the name eagle: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1181.---By the name north wind: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 832.---By the name beast: Venerable Guibert, abbot, CLVI, 301.---By the name strong and mighty one: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 695, 910.---By the name death and hell: the same, XLI, 681; Alcuin, C, 431.

The devil is represented, or signified, by the king of Egypt: Rupert, CLXX, 73.---By Ammon: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1187.---By an eagle: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1181.---By the north wind: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 534; Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 889; Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1175; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 83.---By the rider of the horse: Rupert, CLXVII, 645.---By Assyria: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1169; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 233, 670; CLXIX, 1365.---By the king of Babylon: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1500.---By the whale or Leviathan: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 644, 824.---By the Chaldeans: Rupert, CLXVIII, 972.---By the Canaanite fighting against Israel: the same, CLXVII, 875.---By Goliath: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 302.---By Herod: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 961.---By the lion: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, [Col. 0150] 1086, 1097, 1104; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 983.---By Leviathan: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 644, 824; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1102.---By the wolf: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 223.---By mountains and hills: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 49.---By the mountains of Gilboa: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1039.---By Nimrod: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 366.---By the partridge: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 249.---By Pharaoh: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1349; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 569.---By a fish: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1102.---By creeping things: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1186.---By Sihon: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 212; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1040.---By Sisera: Rupert, CLXVIII, 1031.---By the king of Syria: ibid., 1263.---By a fox: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.

The devil is compared to wild beasts because he is always delighted by human ruin: Cassiodorus, LXX, 162; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 110.---To a pot which cooks the meat it has taken in: Cassiodorus, LXX, 779.---To a partridge: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 718.

DAY. The devil, or apostate angel, is called day; imitation of the devil is shadow: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 741.

ETHAN is interpreted in the Hebrew language as “strong,” which signifies the devil: Cassiodorus, LXX, 532, 628.

HOST: an assembly of demons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 918.

GALL is the persuasion of demons: ibid., 923.

SONS of the devil: sinners: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 210.---Foreign sons are devils: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 195.

FLAME: the devil’s instigation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 921.

RIVER. A river is the devil’s teaching: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 291.

PIT is called the damnation of the devil: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 409.

SMOKE: the devil’s temptation: the same, CXII, 933.

FOUNDATION: the devil’s hidden things: ibid., 935.

THIEVES: evil spirits: ibid., 937.

SWORD: evil spirits: ibid., 942; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 322.

A DISTANT NATION signifies the devil: Rupert, CLXVIII, 249.

HOOK, in an evil sense, is understood as the devil: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 240.

TERRIBLE ONES are demons: ibid., CXII, 958.

OUR ENEMIES are the devil and his angels: St. Agobard, CIV, 275.

UNGODLY ONE: the ancient enemy: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 970.

UNJUST ONE. The devil is most unjust and deceitful: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 180.

STONE: the devil, who is hard through impenitence and weighty through iniquity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 980.

SPECTRES are demons: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 486.

THIEVES are evil spirits: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 983.

LION. The devil as tempter is represented in the insatiable lion: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1086, 1097, 1104.---Demons are called lions: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 80.

HAND: the devil’s temptation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 994.

JAW: the devil’s malice: ibid., 997.

MOUNTAINS crushed by Christ signify the devil and his followers: St. Hilary, LX, 418. Mountains: evil spirits: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1001. The devil is signified by mountains and hills: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 49. The devil is denoted by the mountains of Gilboa: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1039.

NOSTRILS: the devil’s instigation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1004; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 171.

SINEWS: the devil’s devices: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1005.

The devil is always eager to harm: St. Agobard, CIV, 182, 184.

RAZOR. The devil is a razor of deadly cutting: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 261.---The devil’s subtle suggestions rightly deserve to be called razors: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 409.

EYES: the devil’s counsellors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1010.

POT: the devil’s malice: ibid., 1011.

MOUTH: the devil’s cunning: ibid., 1013.

GATES: evil spirits: ibid., 1014.

EGGS: the counsels of demons: ibid., 1015.

CLOTHS are the devil’s worldly pomp: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 268.

PARTRIDGE, a deceitful and unclean bird, signifies the devil: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 249.

HAIRY ONES are unclean spirits: the same, CXII, 1027.

SWINE: unclean spirits: ibid., 1032.---Swine, a symbol of evil spirits: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 206.

GATES of death are the devil’s: St. Bruno of Würzburg, [Col. 0151] CXLII, 71.---Hostile powers are called a gate: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 402.

FROGS are demons and spirits of demons: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.

CREEPING THINGS are unclean spirits: the same, CXII, 1039.

ROARING: the devil’s savagery: ibid., CXII, 1041.---The devil’s suggestion: ibid.

SABEANS. Demons are denoted by the Sabeans: Rupert, CLXVIII, 971.

The movements of this world and the waves of the surging sea are compared, according to prophetic and allegorical interpretation, with the sway of the ruling devil: St. Hilary, IX, 316.

ARROWS are called the devil’s: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 502.

SCORPIONS: demons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1060.

AXE. In the Scriptures and prophets the devil is called axe, saw, and rod: St. Jerome, XXIV, 137.

LEFT HAND: reprobate angels: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1055.

TIGER signifies the devil’s cunning, the devil himself: the same, CXI, 219.

SHADOW. A shadow is imitation of the devil: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 382.

VIPER: the devil’s temptation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1079.

That CALF which Moses broke is the devil’s body: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1026.

BIRDS: evil spirits: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1083.---Birds of heaven signify demons: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 80, 1468; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 357.

VOICE: the enemy’s suggestion: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1083.

FOXES: evil spirits: ibid., CXII, 1084; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1182.---Demons are signified by the name of foxes: St. Hilary, IX, 406.---Mystically, a fox signifies the deceitful devil: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.---The devil is a species of fox: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 514.---Demons are called foxes because of malice, but birds because of pride: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1468.

## ARTICLE VI. Allegories concerning the Church

HEAP. The Church’s womb is compared to a heap of wheat: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1094.---A heap of wheat signifies the multitude of the faithful: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1230.

THE BUILDING of the tabernacle and of the temple denotes one and the same Church of Christ: Venerable Bede, XCI, 737.

EGYPTIANS despoiled of their riches by the Hebrews are a figure of Christians advancing through pagan learning: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 64.---Christians who either cause schisms or heresies, and inflict upon the Church of God whatever afflictions they can, become Egyptians: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 384.

FIELD. God’s land, God’s field, is the Church: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 314.---By the name of field the universal Church can be denoted: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1150.---The two persons in the field are clerics who govern the Church: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1279, 1730.

WATERS of the sea signify the Christian people: Cassiodorus, LXX, 226.

NOAH’S ARK. Let us see whether, according to the type of the ark, there will also be in the Church a raven, a kite, a wolf, a dog, and a serpent; certainly an idolater is not included in the type of the ark.

No animal is represented as an idolater. What was not in the ark should not be in the Church: Tertullian, I, 696.---If anyone who was outside Noah’s ark could escape, then one who remains outside the Church could escape: St. Cyprian, IV, 503.---Noah’s ark bore the figure of the Church, in which all were saved: St. Hilary, LX, 874.---The Church, like Noah’s ark, is tossed about in this life: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 847.---As Noah’s ark contained every kind of animal, so the Church contains every nation: the same, XXXVII, 1358.---The beasts of every kind gathered into Noah’s ark declare nothing other than that human beings of every kind are to be gathered into the unity of the Church: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291.---Just as Noah’s ark, when the world was shipwrecked, kept unharmed all whom it had received, so Peter’s Church will present unharmed all whom it embraces: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 722.---Noah built the ark of incorruptible wood; Christ builds the Church from human beings who will live forever; this whole ark shows forth the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 515.

The ARK of the Covenant was a figure of the Church, covered all around with gold, because those who possess wisdom should not keep it only within, but should preach it outwardly by displaying it: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 308.

[Col. 0152] ARCTURUS. By the name Arcturus the radiance of the universal Church is expressed: St. Eucherius, L, 741.---Arcturus, set upon the axis of heaven, shining with the rays of seven stars, ever revolving and never setting, signifies the universal Church, which in John’s Apocalypse is represented by seven churches and seven lampstands: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 866.---In Arcturus, which illuminates the spaces of night throughout its circuit without setting, the whole Church together is denoted: the same, LXXVI, 517; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 273.---The circuit of Arcturus denotes the labours of the Church militant: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 704.

COURTYARD. Entrance into the courtyard denotes entry into the holy Church: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 707.

DAWN is called the Church, which is changed from the darkness of its sins into the light of righteousness: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 648.

SOUTH WIND signifies the holy Church set ablaze by the warmth of faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 262.

BABYLON. The Church drawn from the Gentiles is called Babylon: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.

STAFF of the Lord denotes the discipline of the holy Church: St. Eucherius, L, 738.

WAR. The continuous wars between the kings of Judah and Israel signify nothing other than that the holy Church, which persists in the unity of faith, is at war with heretics and schismatics: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 486.

BETHEL is interpreted “house of God,” which is aptly called the Church, because the Lord dwells in it when our hearts are cleansed through faith: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 338, 501.

LAMPSTAND signifies the holy and divine Church; the seven lamps placed upon the lampstand signify the mystery of the Church in its sevenfold form: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

HAIR of the Church is its peoples: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493.

KIRIATH-JEARIM. The Church of the Gentiles is signified by Kiriath-jearim, that is, “city of forests”: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1085.

SHEEPFOLDS. Just as sheep signify religious persons who are meek and live innocently, so sheepfolds signify the holy Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 407.

CEDAR mystically signifies the holy Church: ibid., CXI, 317.

CELLAR. The Church is the wine-cellar in which charity is ordered: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1062.

CITY. By the illustrious and redeemed city, redeemed by Christ’s blood, is understood the Church, which is also called a dove because of the simplicity of the multitude believing in it: St. Jerome, XXV, 1374.---By city is understood the Church; by the streets of the city, spiritual men; and by its broad ways, secular men: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 502.

HEAVEN is the Church; the earth itself is the Church’s enemies: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 380, 388, 394.---The Church of the elect is called heaven: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 553, 651.

NECK signifies the union of the members with the head: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 512, 622.

The SAPPHIRE COLOUR denotes the triumphant Church, the purple colour the Church militant: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 704.

DOVE. The Church of the elect is called one dove: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 529.

BODY. The Church is Christ’s body and spouse, purified by him through medicinal afflictions: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 25.---The Church is one body, whose head is Christ: Regino, abbot, CXXXII, 359.

HANNAH’S HORN is the power of the holy Church: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 62.---The horn of Christ’s kingdom signifies the Church’s exaltation: ibid., 462.

RIB. The Church is built from Christ’s rib: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1076.

BEDCHAMBER is the Church, Christ’s body: St. Ambrose, XV, 1206.

GUARDIANS of the Church are the prophets, apostles, and successors of the apostles: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1099.---Guardians of the Church: apostles and preachers: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 108.

CYPRUS. By Cyprus the universal Church is denoted: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 428.

TEETH. By the Church’s teeth is understood the firm stability of its teachings: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1090.---The Church’s teeth are preachers: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493.---The Church’s words are called teeth: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 907.

HOUSE. For the pious, the Church is a house; for the pious, heaven is a homeland: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1163.---The Church is a house whose abundance is the overflowing of graces; the torrent of delight is the Holy Spirit: St. Ambrose, XIV, 962.---The house of God which King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 133.---The Church, the house of Israel, is struck by waves: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 272.

[Col. 0153] The CHURCH is called a field: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1279, 1730; XXXVIII, 46; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1150; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 856; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 256.---The field of God: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1744; the Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 924.---Roe deer: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 501; St Bernard, CLXXXV, 180.---Sheepfolds: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 407.---Cedar: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 317.---Hinds: St Augustine, XXXIV, 880.---Henna (cyprus): St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 428.---Flood: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1354.---The fig tree putting forth its unripe figs: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 499.---Gilead: the same author, LXXVII, 77, 94.---Garden: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 530.---Islands: Rupert, CLXVIII, 670.---Jerusalem: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 379; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 60.---Judaea: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 339.---Moon: St Ambrose, XIV, 204, 678; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 365; Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 755; Cassiodorus, LXX, 735; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 665, 992; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 638.---The mule on which Solomon sat: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1146.---The woman who gives birth to daughters in pain: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 496.---Ships: the same author, CXI, 372.---Paradise of delight: St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 161.---Mount Paran: St Augustine, XXXIV, 775.---Sacrifice offered from fine flour: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 258.---Mount Zion: Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 758; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 53, 70; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1345; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 362; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 480, 1287.---Tabernacle: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 708; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 60; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 624; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 669.---The temple built by Solomon: St Ambrose, XV, 1585; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 599.---Earth: the Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1014.---Solomon’s ivory throne, surrounded by lions: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 195, 477.---Christ’s seamless tunic: Cassiodorus, LXX, 161.---Christ’s undivided tunic: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 110.---Garment of the high priest: St Augustine, XXXIV, 687.---Vineyard: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 305.

The Church is compared to the dawn: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 530.---To a body: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1134.---To a herd of goats: St Ambrose, XV, 1432.---To a garden: St Ambrose, XV, 1839.---To an enclosed garden: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1160, 1170.---To islands: Cassiodorus, LXX, 683.---To Lebanon: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1202.---To the moon: St Gaudentius, XX, 861; St Augustine, XXXVI, 132; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 488; Cassiodorus, LXX, 76, 1082; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 374; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 149; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 259.---To a pomegranate: St Ambrose, XIV, 180.---To a Punic apple [pomegranate]: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 508.---To the sea: Cassiodorus, LXX, 663.---To myrrh: ibid., 1069.---To the eyes of a dove: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1072.---To a palm tree: ibid., 1096.---To the sun: ibid., 1082; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 530.---To Joseph’s many-coloured tunic: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 901.---To a turtledove: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1059; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1290.---To a wine-skin: Cassiodorus, LXX, 228.---To grapes trodden underfoot: the same author, ibid., 395.---To a garment: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1287.---To the vineyard which benefits more from being dug about and is multiplied by pruning: Cassiodorus, LXX, 582.

The Church, espoused in Paradise at the beginning of the world, prefigured in the Flood, proclaimed by the Law, called by the prophets, long awaited the splendour of the Gospel: St Ambrose, XV, 1201.---The Church began to be in gardens after Christ had suffered in gardens, ibid., 1524.---Christ is the foundation and head of the Church: St Augustine, XXXIX, 1615.---The Church grows daily into God’s temple, and the whole body is built up from that very head: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 282.---The Church, Christ’s bride, whose bridal chamber is adorned with the gold of faith, the silver of wisdom, the gems of virtues, the veils of holiness, the roses of modesty, the lilies of chastity, and the violets of purity: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 262.---In the Synagogue, while the Jews were darkening it, the Church was made dusky: ibid., 412.---The Church is Christ’s sister: sister, bride, beloved, dove, spotless one: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1075, 1082, 1092.---The Church of the Gentiles is called deserted: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1130.

FACE. The face of the bride is the public assembly of the Church, distinguished by the diverse character of professions, dignities, and orders: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1148.

WOMAN. The bride’s two women are the Church’s two peoples: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 534.

LITTER. The litter which Solomon made for himself is the Church: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1148.

[Col. 0157] FIG TREE. False Christians are very bad fig trees: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 307.

FAITH, the gates of the Church: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 99.

DAUGHTER. The Church is called daughter of the multitude on account of the multitude of peoples flocking together: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1095.---The churches of the apostles are daughters of kings: St Augustine, XXXVI, 508.---The daughters of kings are souls, or churches, converted through the preaching of the apostles: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 188.---The daughters of Jerusalem are churches: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 74.

SONS of God’s servants are sons of [lacuna] the whole Church, which is Christ’s body and is the mother of all fathers and of all sons: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 284.---The sons of Korah, that is, the sons of the cross, are Christians: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 314.---Christians are sons of those cast down, that is, of the prophets: ibid., 473.

RIVER of God: Christians are so called: ibid., 243.

FRUITS of the Church are her children, especially martyrs: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 514.

The FOUNDATIONS and gates of the Church are the apostles, as also the prophets: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1103.

CHEEKS of the Church are preachers: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 193.

STEPS of the Church are the swift preaching of the apostles, through whom the Gospel resounded throughout the whole earth: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1093.

WHIRLPOOL. By a whirlpool is understood the manifold preaching of the expositors of the holy Church: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 303.

GARDEN signifies the holy Church, in which various kinds of virtues are produced: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 530.

INDIA, which lies in the eastern region and first receives the rising of the sun, can signify the primitive Church established among the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 335.

ISLANDS are the churches of God, battered by the various waves of temptations: St Eucherius, L, 742. Churches are designated by the name of islands: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 971.

JUDAEA signifies the holy Church, in which the Lord is always praised by right faith, devout confession, and good works: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 339.

The JUDGMENT of carnal Israel is a type of the Church, which, as a stranger and unknown, believed in repentance and desired to hear wisdom: St Hilary, IX, 666.

BEASTS OF BURDEN signify ecclesiastical flocks, which are nourished with suitable refreshment—some with milk, others with solid food—as shall seem fitting to the steward: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1037.

OATH. In God’s oath to Abraham is prefigured the seed of the Church, which extends beyond number: Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 747.

LIPS of the Church are preachers: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493.---The doctors of the Church are the bride’s lips: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 300, 611.

The LEFT hand signifies the consolations which Christ promised the Church, but the right hand glory: Rupert, CLXVIII, 862.

BED. By Solomon’s bed is understood the present Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1070.

LEVERET signifies the people of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 777.

The LILY among thorns is the Church among the daughters of this age: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1094.

The MOON represents the mystery of Christ and the Church: St Ambrose, XIV, 204; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 365; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 665, 992.---The Church is compared to the moon, which grows in peace and diminishes in persecution: St Gaudentius, XX, 861.---The Church, situated in this mortality of the flesh, is marked in the Scriptures by the name of the moon because of that very mutability: St Augustine, XXXIII, 209.---The Church is called the moon because it shines in the night of this world: St Eucherius, L, 739.---We compare the Church to the moon, because, like the moon, it shines among the nations and borrows light from the Sun of righteousness and from Christ’s rays: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 488; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 273.

POMEGRANATES: the Church, composed of many nations, or possessing diverse graces: St Eucherius, L, 742.

The HANDS of the Church are holy persons: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1226.

SEA. The persecutors of the Church are signified by storms at sea: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1470.

The NUMBER ONE THOUSAND signifies one faith, one baptism, one God: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1178.

MOUNTAIN. By the name “mountain” are signified the Synagogue and the Church: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 267.

MULE. The Church is signified by the mule on which Solomon sat: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1146.

WOMAN. Through faith, the Church is that strong woman of whom the Proverbs speak: the same author, CLXIX, 146.

[Col. 0158] WORLD. The creation of the world is a figure of the formation of the Church: St Augustine, XXXII, 850.

The WALLS of Jerusalem are assemblies of the Church established throughout the whole world: St Ambrose, XIV, 883.

SHIPS are churches which sail through the storms of this world by the wood of the cross: Cassiodorus, LXX, 772; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 372.

NINEVEH bears the image of the Church, in which our people from the Gentiles were already dwelling: St Zeno, XI, 449.---Nineveh, the great city, city of foreigners, is a figure of the twofold Church: Tyconius the African, XVIII, 39.

NOAH. The Church is prefigured in the blessing of Noah’s sons: St Augustine, XLII, 265.

MARRIAGE, the calling of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1008.

The EYES of the Church are preachers: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 507, 508.---The eyes of the Church, or of the faithful soul, are consideration of temporal misery and everlasting blessedness: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1230.

POURED-OUT OIL is the spreading of Christ’s name through the Church: ibid., 1043.

BORDER. The border of the garment of the Lord the Saviour signifies the Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 956.

BONES. The bones and strength of the Church are the apostles: St Augustine, XXXVI, 175; XXXVII, 1297.

SHEEP signify the Christian people: Cassiodorus, LXX, 77.---The sheep and oxen that Solomon sacrificed signify the multitude converted to the Lord: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1174.

PARADISE. By paradise is signified the Church, but by the trees of paradise the doctors of the Church: St Ambrose, XVII, 812.---Paradise is the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 479.---Moreover, paradise is planted “in the beginning,” because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, who is the beginning of all things. The river going forth from paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain, who waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of baptism: ibid.

The WALLS of the Church are clergy and laity: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 417.

FEET. The lowest members of the Church are called feet: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 233.

That ROCK cut from the mountain in Daniel is the Church: Tertullian, II, 330.---The rock upon which the Church was promised to be built is Christ himself: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1238.

The GATES of the Church are the gates of chastity and righteousness: St Ambrose, XV, 1694.

The FIRSTFRUIT of the Church was Abel: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1421.

The universal Church is called the MOST BEAUTIFUL of all women: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1190.

ORPHAN. The people of the Church are called an orphan: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 808.

ROOT. Christ is the root of the Church: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 211.---The roots of the Church are the prophets planted by the operation of the heavenly King: Cassiodorus, LXX, 582.

RULER. Christ is the ruler of the Church: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 272.

QUEEN. The Church of the Gentiles, by believing in Christ, became a queen: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1175.

STREAM. The explanations of the Church are called a stream: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 296.

The SACRIFICE offered from fine flour foretells the figure of the Catholic Church: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 258.

THE SECOND DAY AFTER THE SABBATH. The Church is prefigured by the second day after the Sabbath: St Augustine, XXXVI, 532.

The NUMBER SEVEN signifies the universality of the Church: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 448.

MOUNT ZION designates the Church: Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 758; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 53, 70; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1345.---Zion is called the Church because contemplation is fixed there in contemplative virtue: Cassiodorus, LXX, 38.---The Church is called Mount Zion and the holy of holies, whose inhabitant is Christ: ibid., 696.---“From Zion shall go forth the law,” that is, from the holy mountain which is the Church, which has raised its head throughout the Roman world under the whole heaven: St Optatus, XI, 996.---Zion, the city of all the elect: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 16.---In Zion is the image of the present Church; in Jerusalem, the image of the future Church: St Augustine, XXXVI, 70, 122; XXXVII, 1107.---Zion, the present Church; Jerusalem, the heavenly city: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 71.

BRIDE. The Church, Christ’s bride, left her mother the synagogue in order to cleave to him: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 570.

STARS are Christians; the sterile sand, Jews: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1220.

The TABERNACLE of the Lord is a type of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 158.

The TEMPLE built by Solomon was a type of the Church: St Ambrose, XV, 1585.

[Col. 0159] TIME. Christ and the Church are prefigured in the very times of the Judges and Kings: St Augustine, XLII, 271.---The present times display Christ’s name and the Church, just as past times proclaimed them: ibid., 285.

TENT, the holiness of the primitive Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.

FRANKINCENSE. The garments of the Church are compared to frankincense: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1077.

WINEPRESS. On account of the tribulations it suffers, the Church is called a winepress: St Eucherius, L, 742.

TUNIC. The Church of Christ is the Lord’s tunic, woven not with threads but with verses; not with warp but with compunction; not with wool but with grace: Cassiodorus, LXX, 270.---The unity and charity of the Church are Christ’s tunic: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 235.

The TOWERS of the Church are priests: St Ambrose, XIV, 261.

The BREASTS of the Church are the Law and the prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 956.---The breasts of the Church are knowledge of truth and love of virtues: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1163.

GRAPE. Christians are compared to grapes trodden underfoot: Cassiodorus, LXX, 395.

The MOST HIGH VEHICLE is the Church: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1146.

The BELLY of the Church consists of the unlearned and simple: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 89.

The GARMENT of the Lord is understood as the holy Church, which is joined to him through faith and love: St Eucherius, L, 733.

WIDOW. The Church is despised by the world but truly espoused by Christ: Alcuin, C, 636.

VINEYARD. The Church is compared to the vineyard which benefits more from being dug about and is multiplied by pruning: Cassiodorus, LXX, 582.---The vineyard prefigures the Church, which grows only through persecutions: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 305.---The vineyards of Engaddi are the congregations of the Church: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 996.

MAN. The man of the Church is the Redeemer of humankind: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 62.

ROD. The two rods in the prophets signify the Church and the Synagogue: St Jerome, XXII, 683. The two rods of which Isaiah speaks designate both peoples, Gentiles and Jews: the same author, XXXV, 518.

The STRENGTH of the Church is its love: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1698.

## ARTICLE VII. Allegories concerning the sacraments

LAMB indicates repentance: the Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 903.

WATER. Baptism is signified by water: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---Just as the people escaped the power of the king of Egypt by passing through water, so the nations are freed from the world through water: Tertullian, I, 1209. Baptism is the water which flowed for the people from the accompanying rock. For if the rock is Christ, then without doubt we see baptism blessed in Christ through water: ibid., 1210.---The water of sprinkling signified baptism, which would benefit both Jews and Gentiles: St Augustine, XXXIV, 735, 736.---The water of baptism is Christ’s tomb, in which we are healed from sins: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1269.---The waters of contradiction are called waters of baptism: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 387.---The waters of Christ’s redemption are the sacraments: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 190.

ARK. Just as Noah’s ark, after all the vices of sinners had been overwhelmed, was borne on high, so the Church is borne near to heaven by the font of baptism: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 574.---The ark placed upon the new enclosure indicates that the grace of the New Testament is infused into minds renewed in baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 84.

BIRD. One given life by holy baptism is like a bird flying out of Egypt: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 177.

BAPTISM is called water: St Eucherius, L, 742.---Flood: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911, 914; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 748.---Fountain: St Eucherius, L, 742.---Basin: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 977.---Lebanon: ibid., 985.---Laver: ibid., 991.---Morning: St Eucherius, L, 741.---Sea: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 995.---Cloud: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 748.---Baptism is prefigured in the book of Genesis: St Ambrose, XVI, 392; St Augustine, XL, 133.---Baptism is a figure of death and burial: St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 544.---Baptism destroys the proud and makes them humble: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 767.---Christ’s baptism signifies our justification: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 394.

HAIR. The sacraments of the Law are called hair: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.

FLESH is sometimes used in the Scriptures for “wife”: St Augustine, XXXV, 1395.

[Col. 0160] CASSIA signifies baptism and faith: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 659.

DELUGE was an image of baptism: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1046.

ASHES. Repentance is called ashes: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 362.

CIRCUMCISION formerly held the place of baptism: St Augustine, XXXIII, 845.---The sacrament of circumcision prefigures the baptism of our time: the same author, XLIV, 403, 504, 833.---Circumcision of the flesh was commanded by the Law because original sin could not be more aptly signified as removed through Christ, the author of regeneration: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 472.---Circumcision is a type and figure of baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 561.

CISTERN. Baptism is the Bethlehemite cistern: the Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 507.

FLOOD. Baptism is compared to the Flood: Tertullian, I, 1209; Cassiodorus, LXX, 202; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 129.---Baptism is called a flood: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911, 914; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 748.---The Flood sometimes signifies baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 329.---The Flood was a figure of baptism: St Ambrose, XVI, 423; St Augustine, XLII, 263; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 342.---After the Flood, the dove as herald announced peace to the earth; by the same dispensation, when our flesh emerges from the washing after its former offences, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies to it: Tertullian, I, 1209.---The Flood happened once as a comparison to baptism, because baptism cannot be repeated: St Optatus, XI, 894.

ELIJAH. Elijah’s sacrifice was a figure of baptism: St Ambrose, XVI, 175.

ENGADDI, “spring of the kid,” signifies baptism: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1061; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 493; Alcuin, C, 645; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 428; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1083.---Penance is signified by the name Engaddi: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 916.---Engaddi signifies the baptism of the Gentiles and the tears of sinners: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 996.

SONS of baptism are called sons of the sea: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 177.

RIVER: one river signifies baptism, another persecution: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 245.

FOUNTAIN. Baptism is the fountain of the house of David: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 794.

KID. Penance is denoted by the name of a kid: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 953.

HYSSOP. Baptism is denoted by the name of hyssop, ibid., 1088.

INFANT. Anyone regenerated by baptism is called an infant: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 145.

The ISRAELITES, promising that they would not drink from the wells of King Sihon, are a type of Christians who renounce the devil in baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 720.

JORDAN. By the Jordan is signified the journey to the promised land; likewise by baptism, the journey to the promise of the heavenly kingdom: St. Chromatius, XX, 330.---The turning back of the river Jordan was a figure of baptism: St. Ambrose, XV, 1548.---Jordan is taken for baptism: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 815.

LAVER. By the bronze laver, or laver, is principally understood the water of baptism, by whose washing all who enter the gates of the Church must be cleansed: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 215.

JAR: the faith of baptism: ibid., CXII, 979.

HIDING-PLACES is the name given to the sacraments of God: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 191.

LEBANON. Baptism is figured by Lebanon: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 510.

WASHING. Christ’s baptism at the beginning of his preaching was prefigured by Aaron’s washing at the beginning of his consecration: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1368. The baptism of the sevenfold Spirit was prefigured in Naaman’s seven washings: ibid., CLXX, 108.

MANNA was a figure of Eucharistic bread: St. Ambrose, XV, 1462.

MARAH. Baptism is Marah: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 252.

SEA signifies baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 311; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1035.---The molten sea was made as a figure of the Savior’s laver, by which we are cleansed for the remission of sins: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 171.---The molten sea set at the right side of the Temple signifies that baptism flowed from Christ’s side: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1166.

MELCHIZEDEK. Melchizedek’s sacrifice in bread and wine is a figure of the Christian sacrifice: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 505.

The TABLE of Christ is the holy Eucharist: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 819.

The MASS was figured by the sacrifice of the red heifer: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 705.

[Col. 0161] MYRRH. Myrrh is a symbol of penance: St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 48.

NAAMAN. The grace of baptism was figured by Naaman’s healing from leprosy: St. Ambrose, XVI, 420, 421, 423; Rupert, CLXVIII, 1263.---The baptism of the sevenfold Spirit was prefigured in Naaman’s seven washings: ibid., CLXX, 108.---Penance was figured in Naaman: St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 61.

By the name of SNOW baptism is signified: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 739.

DOOR. Baptism is the door placed in Noah’s ark: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 342.

CLOAK. Penance is called a cloak: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018.

BREAD is called the Eucharist, ibid., 1020.---Penance is called bread baked under ashes: Alan of Lille, CCX, 208.

ROOTS. The sacraments are compared to roots: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 981.

ROSE. In the Eucharist the rose is plucked, that is, the blood of the Lord’s body: St. Ambrose, XV, 1390.

RED SEA. The Red Sea signifies baptism: St. Cyprian, IV, 414; St. Zeno, XI, 510; St. Ambrose, XIV, 867; XVI, 420, 421, 423; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 764; St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 507; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 162.---As the Jews enter the Red Sea once only, so too our baptism, of which the sea was a figure, is to be received once only: St. Ambrose, XVII, 18.---The drowning of the Egyptians in the Red Sea is a figure of the abolition of sins in baptism: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 37.---The Red Sea is a figure of the water of baptism, which, mingled with blood, came forth from Christ’s side: Cassiodorus, LXX, 588.---Baptism in the cloud and in the sea was consummated into Moses: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 66.---The baptism of the Israelites was figured by their crossing through the Red Sea: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 917; XXXVII, 1037, 1411, 1420, 1760; XXXIX, 1562, 1635, 1637; XL, 335, 695; Cassiodorus, LXX, 531; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1162; LXXIX, 491; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 9.---As the Jews reached the wilderness after the sea, so after baptism we reach paradise, that is, the Church: St. Zeno, XI, 519.---Those are truly said to be redeemed by the Lord who throughout the whole world are freed from great and broad Egypt, as though through the Red Sea—that is, baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 307.---The divisions of the Red Sea signify Christ’s baptism, in which divisions occur, so that it is life to some and death to others: life to believers, death to persecutors, ibid., 389.---As the people of Israel were saved through the Red Sea when Pharaoh was drowned, so the Church of the Gentiles, through baptism, was freed from the devil’s service and brought into the true land of promise and evangelical liberty: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1059.---The crossing of the Red Sea was a figure of the Eucharist: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1659.

SILOAM. Baptism is signified by the waters of Siloam, ibid., 1291.

DARKNESS. The laments of penance are called darkness: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 378.

OINTMENT is called penance: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.

WOMB. The water of baptism is a womb and a tomb: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1648.

BELLY. The font of baptism is called a belly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1071.

SPRING is called the renewal of life through baptism or through resurrection: St. Eucherius, L, 741.

CLOTHED is the name for one possessing the garment of baptism; naked, however, for one lacking the sacrament of baptism: ibid., 756.

ARTICLE VIII. Allegories relating to the apostles and the righteous.

All the GARMENTS OF AARON are the faithful of the last times: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1026.

FIR TREE: a holy contemplative: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 336.

THE UNTIMELY BORN: the saints before the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.

ABYSS means the preachers of the Word: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 984.---The college of apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.---In Scripture, abysses are the wise hearts of human beings: Alcuin, C, 423.

HAWK: any holy person: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 748; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 81.---Hawk, any elect person: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 853.

HEAP OF WITNESS: the multitude of martyrs: ibid., CXII, 854; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 917.---The heap of witness is the teaching of the holy Fathers: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1149.

VINEGAR-BOWL. The apostles are compared to a silver vinegar-bowl: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXIV, 745.

BATTLE-LINE: the unity of the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.

[Col. 0162] YOUNG WOMEN are souls of the elect renewed through baptism: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 482, 529.---They are souls of the saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1026; Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 39.---The apostles are called young women: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 329. Those who love God are called young women, ibid., 214.

BRONZE: the footwear of the apostles: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 727. Bronze signifies the prophets, ibid., 728.---Bronze: the voice of preachers, the obscure preaching of the ancient Fathers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 315.

SUMMER signifies youth: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1223.

SUMMER: any perfect person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 91.

EGYPTIANS. The despoiling of the Egyptians figures that a Christian ought to borrow the learning of philosophers: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 955.

FIELD is the mind: Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 225.---The faithful soul is compared to a field: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 789.

EWE-LAMB is the active life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 855.

LAMBS: the apostles: St. Eucherius, L, 752.---Lambs, the saints: ibid.; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 202, 855.---Lambs signify the faithful: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 337.---A lamb signifies the harmless life of any Catholic: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 202. A lamb: the apostles, holy persons, the simple and innocent: ibid., CXII, 855.

FARMER: doctors of the Church, ibid., 855.

WINGS: the virtues of the saints: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---The thought of a holy person; the virtues of the saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857.

ALTAR: the life of the righteous, ibid., 856.

FATTED ANIMALS: the Fathers of the New Testament, ibid., 857.

FRIEND: any one of our neighbors, our mind, holy preachers, other saints, ibid., 857.---Friends united in God: St. Eucherius, L, 755.---The friends of God are apostles and patriarchs: Cassiodorus, LXX, 990.---Pastors are called the most beloved friends of the Bridegroom: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1154.

HANDMAID: the humble preachers of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 858. Handmaids sent to the citadel signify that Christ chose weak and despised preachers to gather faithful peoples to the heavenly homeland’s lofty edifices: ibid., CXI, 710.

ANGEL is said of John the Baptist: ibid., CXII, 851.---Of any priest: ibid.; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 116.---The angels ascending and descending on Jacob’s ladder signify those advancing and declining: St. Zeno, XI, 432; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 224.---By the name of angels in Holy Scripture are signified the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem assumed among human beings; the body of the faithful; any righteous person; preachers or priests: St. Eucherius, L, 739.---The holy preachers of the Church, because they announce the glory of the heavenly homeland, may be understood by the name of angels: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 725; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 250; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 83.---Angels are said to be holy John the Baptist, preachers, saints, prelates of the Church, and priests: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 27.

SOUL is taken for life: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 973.---The soul is king and priest: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 276.---The soul is a virgin and a harlot: ibid., 329, 330.---The faithful soul is compared to a field and a garden: Adam the Scot, CXCIII, 789.

LIVING CREATURES. Each of Ezekiel’s living creatures fittingly corresponds to one Evangelist: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 625, 803; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 505; CXII, 859; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 969; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 93.---The Evangelists are signified by the four living creatures, because they were to spread the Gospel through the four regions of the world: Alcuin, CI, 1120, 1133.---The living creatures full of eyes round about and within signify the saints: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 109, 803; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 93. Living creatures: Evangelists, righteous persons, the simple in the Church, ibid.---Ezekiel’s four living creatures signify the pastors of the Church: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1099.---The wings of Ezekiel’s living creatures are the virtues of the saints: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 297.

The FOUR RINGS of the ark signify the four Evangelists: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 758.

YEAR: the multitude of the redeemed: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 858; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 858.

OUTER DEFENSE-WALL: the prophets: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 394.

BEE: the humble: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859.

The APOSTLES reaped what the patriarchs sowed: Abbot Rupert, CLXXIII, 376.

WATER denotes the Christian people: Eugippius, Abbot, LXII, 1041; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 48.---Water figures human thought: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 189.---Good minds are called water: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 279.---Water: blessed souls, saints, devotions: [Col. 0163] Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---Waters customarily signify the minds of those following faith: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 100.---Waters are merits in human beings: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 408.---The waters of the sea signify doctors from among the Gentiles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 320.---Preachers are denoted by waters: Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 941.---They are compared to waters: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 194.---The upper waters signify the good who are to be saved; the lower waters, the evil who are to be damned: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 637.

EAGLE. John the Evangelist is compared to an eagle: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 815; Alcuin, CI, 1133; Rabanus Maurus, CX, 694; CXII, 862; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 857; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1681.---Eagles: the saints: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---In Sacred Scripture, by the term “eagle” are signified the most subtle understandings of the saints, and John the apostle and Evangelist: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 694.---Eagle: John the Evangelist, the soul, a lofty power of this age, the soul of the elect: ibid., CXII, 862; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 69.---The soul is compared to an eagle: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 368.---The ancient Fathers are compared to eagles: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 623.

NORTH WIND sometimes means one of the elect converted to faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.

TREE: a human being is known by the fruit of his works: St. Eucherius, L, 742.---Adam is compared to a tree: Alan of Lille, CCX, 246.---A tree is any person perfect in faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 865.---Trees are a type of those eminent in holiness: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 31.---A tree: those who aspire to what is lofty: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 333.---A human being is an inverted tree: Guerric, CLXXXV, 107.

ARK. The soul of the righteous person is the ark of the covenant: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1191.---Noah’s two-storied ark signifies contemplatives and active persons: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1279.---The ark and winepress signify the afflictions of the saints: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 255.

NARROW WAY: the way of the perfect: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 315, 316.

ARCTURUS signifies the ancient Fathers: ibid., CLXVIII, 317.

BOW: an Evangelist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 862.

HERON may signify the souls of the elect: ibid., CXI, 246.

THRESHING-FLOOR: an ecclesiastical doctor; a holy mind: ibid., CXII, 864.

SAND: the elect, ibid., 849; the humble, ibid., 864.

LITTLE GARDEN-BED: any humble person, ibid., 866.

SILVER: martyrs; the life of preachers, ibid., 863.---Writers of the divine utterance: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 311.---The apostles are like silver: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 714.

RAM. By the ram must be understood the first order of priests within the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 778.---Ram: the priestly order, the holy apostles, prelates in the Church, all rational persons: ibid., CXII, 863; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 103.---A ram can indicate prelates who lead by example: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1072.---Rams signify apostles or leaders of churches: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1026; XXXVI, 785; XXXVII, 749, 1414; St. Eucherius, L, 752; Eugippius, Abbot, LXII, 757; Cassiodorus, LXX, 178, 990; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 764, 1148; St. Agobard, CLV, 224; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 778; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 746, 1238; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 284.---The apostles are called rams and their successors the sons of rams: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 128, 243.---Rams are doctors of the Church: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 527.---Rams are prelates: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1731.---By the name of rams are shown the priests whom instruction in apostolic doctrine, accompanied by the fragrance of prayers, leads on to zeal for martyrdom: St. Hilary, IX, 434.

WEAPONS: the miracles of the saints: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 318.

HERDS: doctors or rulers of the Church; the college of patriarchs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 866.

BRACELET: the works of superiors, ibid., 864.

AROMATICS: holy persons; the good works of the saints, ibid., 866.

LIMBS: the inward members of the Church, ibid., 865.

SMALL ALTAR: the human heart, ibid.

FIELDS: subjects, ibid., 867.

ASCENT: the affliction of martyrs, ibid.

The LORD’S COLT is a gentle people: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 272, 310.

SHE-ASS: all heavenly souls; the simple: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.---Those living simply: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 90.---The soul of the righteous person is compared to a she-ass: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 23.---Doctors are called shining she-asses: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1028.

ASS: a faithful soul: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 88.

[Col. 0164] STARS: holy persons in the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.

COURTYARD: the breadth of the faithful; prophets and apostles, ibid., 868.---The court of the tabernacle signifies the life of the patriarchs: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 746.---The outer court of the tabernacle denotes beginners and novices: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 706.---Courts signify those already in the inner sanctuary of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 390.

FOWLER. The apostolic preacher is a fowler who strikes with the reed of divine speech the minds of young people flying through their deeds: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 498.

CHARIOTEER: any preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 871.

EAR: a doctor of the Church, ibid.

DAWN is the mind of a righteous person which, abandoning the darkness of its sin, now breaks forth into the light of eternity: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1158; St. Eucherius, L, 741.---Dawn: one who newly begins good works; the life of the righteous; a holy mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 869.

GOLD: the splendor of the saints in heaven; faithful souls; the assembly of martyrs; the life of a priest; good conduct; the faithful people; the splendor of those who despise the world; the keenness of subtle intellect; the eternal life of the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.---The good are like gold, the evil like hay: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1375.---By gold is signified the life of the righteous: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1212.---The knowledge of the apostles is compared to gold: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 746.---Gold is called the understanding of one who works well, a faithful soul: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 303.---By princes who possess gold, the apostles are meant: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 670.

SOUTH WIND: a preacher; the assembly of martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 869.---Any fervent spirit: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 56.

AUTUMN signifies youth: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1223.

BIRD: the human soul; spiritual persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 871.---The soul is like a bird; the word of God is like a snare: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 294.---Birds are called the human mind, the minds of spiritual persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 65.

AXLES: the hearts of the saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXIII, 871.

BEARD: the assembly of apostles, ibid., 873.---The apostles are aptly called a beard: Cassiodorus, LXX, 956.---The apostles are denoted by the name of beard: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1733.---The apostles are Aaron’s beard: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1026.---In Aaron’s beard, which first received the ointment flowing down from the head, are signified the apostles and martyrs, in whom the strength of the head stands forth both in sacrament and in example: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 382.---The apostles are called Christ’s beard or hair: Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 614.

BASES are holy doctors who administer the laver to us by their life: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 445.---By bases are signified the apostles and apostolic persons, ibid., 173, 443.---Bases: apostles, preachers, Fathers of the Old Testament, ibid., CXII, 874.---The apostles are the bases of the Church: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 727.---The bases set beneath the capitals are the foundations of the apostles and prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 711.---Bases: doctors, prophets, intentions of the soul: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 411.

BATH: the two substances of a human being: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 874.

The BLESSING of the apostles was figured in the blessing of Zebulun and Naphtali: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 990.

BEAST: anyone converted from sin: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 875.

The number TWO signifies those perfect in charity: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 439.

OX: the labor of a preacher; the wise multitude of doctors: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 94.---Ox: preacher, Luke the Evangelist, patriarchs, prelates, all perfect persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 877.---Oxen signify the apostles: St. Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 201, 208; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 854.---The twelve apostles are signified by the twelve oxen carrying the sea of the Temple, ibid., 1168.---Oxen mystically signify the labor of preaching: Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 165.---Oxen signify preachers: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 370; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 666.---Oxen signify those who work good: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 971.

CLUSTER OF GRAPES: holy preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 876.

The ARMS of Christ are the prophets: Cassiodorus, LXX, 133; Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1150.---The apostles: Cassiodorus, LXX, 133; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 201.---Christ’s arms, the apostles and prophets, are like a bronze bow: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 96.

TRUMPET: preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 877.

[Col. 0165] BUTTER: the teaching of the patriarchs, ibid., 878.

BOX TREE. The box tree signifies those who, although they do not rise to the heights of virtues or bear fruit, nevertheless are ever green in the faith of their parents: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1275.

REED: any preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.---Reed: the skill of doctors; writers of sacred discourse: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 425.

TREADERS are the apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 279.

FOOTWEAR.---Preachers are denoted by footwear: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 918.

CUP: the tribulation of saints; the passion of martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.

FURNACE: the tribulation of the righteous, ibid., 882.

BELL. Preachers are in many respects compared to bells: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 19.

FIELD: the minds of the faithful: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 882.---Fields: saints; likewise, on account of the equality of the righteous people: St. Eucherius, L, 742.---Gentle persons are called fields: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 350.---Fields denote active persons; fields are those who do not abandon earthly things: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 337.

CHANNELS: the mountains of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 883.

LATTICES signify the first patriarchs: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 865.---The lattices through which the Beloved looks through the wall were the ancient Fathers: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1109; they are the teachings of the apostles, ibid., 1110.

LAMPSTAND: the dignity of a preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 882.---The apostles are compared to lampstands: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 652.

DOG: any penitent person, the weak, apostles, reprovers, good preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 883; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 102.---A dog’s tongue signifies the words of the wise person: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 969.---By the dogs of the flock are signified holy doctors who have stood as guardians of the faithful: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 145, 1302.---The apostles are called dogs, keeping faith with the Lord and barking against enemies: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 833; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 453.---The dogs of the Church are doctors: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 351.

HAIR: the order of preachers; the faithful peoples: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.---By the bride’s hair are signified peoples: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 507.---Hair signifies subjects: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 118, 121.

ROE DEER: the virtues of souls: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 885.---Roe deer signify the dignity of holy souls: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 355.---The ancient Fathers are signified by roe deer and stags: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 863.---Roe deer and stags are patriarchs and prophets: Alan of Lille, CCX, 68.---By roe deer are understood the members of Christ, namely doctors: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1094.---Roe deer and fawns are doctors: Alan of Lille, CCX, 74.---Those lively in spirit are denoted by roe deer and stags: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 68.

HEAD: any ruler; the mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 804.---The heads of the people, priests, heart, religious persons: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1092.

COALS: saints, righteous persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.---The prophets are called coals of desolation: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLI, 655.---Coals: hidden saints, any holy person: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 359.

HINGES: preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.

FLESH: a weak person, the whole human being, Christ’s disciples: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 886. Flesh: human nature: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 207.

CHESTNUT TREE can signify the company of continent persons, who by bodily chastity bring forth many fruits of virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515.

CASTLE: our mind, ibid., CXII, 885.

CAMPS: holy persons, ibid., 889.

FLOODGATES: apostles, ibid., 890.---Prophets: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 655.---Prophets and apostles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 180.

WHELP: apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 889. The apostles are whelps of a lioness: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 537.---Whelps signify subjects: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1140.

CEDAR: the loftiness of the saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.---Cedar signifies prophets and apostles: ibid., CXI, 517. Cedars: apostles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 161; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 641, 838.---Apostolic persons, ibid., 838.---Doctors, ibid., 641, 838.---Prelates, ibid., 641.---Martyrs: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 306.---Martyrs are fittingly compared to cedars, for in the Church of Christ they are established on the loftiest summits: Cassiodorus, LXX, 582.---Cedars: persons of higher power: St. Eucherius, L, [Col. 0166] 742.---The cedars of Lebanon are called kings: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 128.

HIND: doctors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, [reference defective].---Doctors are signified by hinds: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1166.

STAG: saints: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---A faithful soul, the ancient Fathers, great contemplatives, saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.---A stag signifies the faithful person in many respects: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 415.---By stags are signified the ancient Fathers: St. Gregory the Great, LXXXIX, 501; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 863.---Patriarchs and prophets: Alan of Lille, CCX, 68.---Preachers: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 116.---Those lively in spirit: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 68.

HAIR-SHIRT: a type of the penitent person: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 343.

CIRCUMCISED PERSON. In the circumcised person is understood the Christian who is circumcised in heart: St. Prosper, LI, 774.

CISTERN: the human heart: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.

CITIZENS: the faithful, ibid., 897.

CITY, understood morally, signifies the soul: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 258.---City: a holy soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 897; Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 379.---The human soul: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 389.---The heart of a holy person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 897; Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 608.---The faithful of the Church: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1328; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 389.---The faithful are a city because of their gathering together: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1453.---The city of God is the totality of creation: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 26.---The city of Judah is the soul: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 977.

KEY: the powers of doctors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 881.

NAIL. Nails: the corrections of saints, ibid., 881.

CLERICS are figured by the Levites: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 669.

HEAVEN is called the soul: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1204.---A faithful soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 276.---The soul of the righteous: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 508; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 30.---A holy soul: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 917.---The priesthood: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 30.---The lofty life of saints, ibid.---Any one of the faithful can be heaven: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1243.---The apostles are called heavens: St. Ambrose, XV, 1369; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 157, 288; XXXVII, 1121, 1243, 1573, 1626, 1864; St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 33; LXXVII, 76, 592, 627; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 898; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 636, 748; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1632, 1743; CLXVIII, 56, 81; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 185; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 287.---Doctors: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 864.---The elect: ibid., LXXVI, 438.---Evangelists: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 154, 170.---The righteous: ibid., 136, 275, 276; XLI, 698; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1004, 1099.---Preachers: St. Eucherius, L, 410; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 420, 550; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1406; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 192; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 287.---Saints: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1256; XXXVI, 157, 159; XXXVII, 370, 891; XLI, 698; St. Eucherius, L, 738.---The wise in the Church: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 287.---The wiser persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.---Spiritual persons: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 380, 388; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 287.---Elders: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 206.---Heaven may appropriately be understood as priests, Pharisees, or doctors of the Law: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 864.---The apostles are called now heavens, now Cherubim, now clouds: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 748.---The foundations of heaven are called those upon whom the kingdom of heaven is built up among saints and faithful persons: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1049.

HILL signifies the perfect life of faithful subjects: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 290.---A hill is the life of any religious person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 880.---The apostles were called hills: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 785.---Martyrs are fittingly compared to hills: Cassiodorus, LXX, 449.---Hills: saints before the Law, martyrs, holy persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900.---By hills are signified the righteous: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 48.---Prelates: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1238.---Preachers, ibid., 991.---Prophets are compared to hills: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1014.---The mountains of the heavenly Jerusalem are the apostles, but the hills the other saints: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 310.---Hills: saints of lesser merit: St. Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 365; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1282.

NECK of the bride signifies preachers: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 534.---The lofty eloquence of doctors: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1029.---Neck: the order of preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.---The doctors of the Church are the neck and ivory tower: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1095.

PURPLE COLOR signifies the afflictions of the married state: [Col. 0167] Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 729.---Sapphire color signifies clerics, ibid., 727.---Green color, laypeople, ibid.
