DOVE: the simple person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.---On account of its simplicity, the dove figures the soul that is Christ’s bride: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 498.---The dove in the clefts of the rock signifies the simple soul strengthened in Christ’s wounds, ibid., 499.---The dove sent out by Noah signifies evangelical preachers: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 357.---The apostles are doves at their windows: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1006, 1095.---The doves at their windows are prelates of the Church: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1149.

The PILLAR of cloud and fire signifies prelates who restrain the wicked now by terror and now the good by gentleness: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 786.---The souls of the righteous are called pillars: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1027.---The apostles are called pillars: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 950; XXXVII, 1831; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 283.---The apostles were called pillars: they wavered at the Lord’s Passion and were made firm at the Resurrection: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 950.---The apostles are God’s pillars: ibid., XL, 692.---Pillars of the Church: St. Ambrose, XV, 1264; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 853; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 483.---The apostles are signified by the pillars of the tabernacle: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 964.---The apostles are deservedly compared to pillars: Cassiodorus, LXX, 357.---The doctors of the Church are pillars: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 90.---Doctors are denoted by silver pillars: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1070.---Silver pillars signify the apostles: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 727.---The patriarchs are pillars of the Jews: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1494.---Pillar: preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.---The pillars in the portico of Solomon’s Temple signify the apostles and all spiritual doctors: strong, assuredly, in faith and work, and raised to heavenly things by contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CLX, 433.---The pillars from which the tent was suspended are holy doctors, whose head is Christ: ibid., CVIII, 178.---Pillars: any person strong against the devil’s temptations; the foremost preachers; Evangelists: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 411.---The pillars raising and supporting the tents on high are the doctors and preachers of the Church: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 695, 707.

LOCKS OF HAIR: companies of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900.---The hair of the head, which is Christ, consists of prophets or apostles: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1192.

COMMENTARIES: doctors of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 892.

HARMONY: the discourse of doctors, ibid., 901.

CONCUBINES. Doctors of the Church are compared, some to queens and others to concubines: Alcuin, C, 658, 665.---The concubines of prelates are souls: John Algrin, CCVI, 642.

COUNSELORS and judges are the apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1279.

CONSULS: holy preachers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 151.

BASKET: the hearts of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.

COOKS are priests, because, when they speak to the elect faithful in the fervor of the Spirit, they cook food for the mind as though by fire: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 273.

HEART: prelates: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.---The heads of the people, priests, heart, religious persons: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1092.

HORN: saints; the powers of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.---Preachers are signified by bowls and the horn of the altar: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 773.---The horns of the altar signify the strength of the apostles, ibid., 775.

CROWN: the assembly of apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.---Crown: the multitude of saints, ibid.---The Lord’s crown signifies the assembled company of disciples surrounding him: Cassiodorus, LXX, 148.

BARK: the outward utterances of the Fathers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 347.

CURTAIN: a holy person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.

RAVEN: a preacher, ibid., 902; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 76.

BOWL: the order of preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.

GRIDIRON: the heart of any saint, ibid., 888.

HAIRS OF THE HEAD: Christ’s apostles: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 282.

LEG. Holy doctors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.---By legs are understood the apostles, through whom Christ traversed the whole world: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 524.

BEDCHAMBER. The heart of the righteous is a bedchamber: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 123.

CULTIVATION: saints who are cultivated by God: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

CHARIOT: the company of saints; a gentle prelate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.

[Col. 0168] **GUARDIANS.** The apostles are called guardians of the Church: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1156.—Guardians of the walls of Jerusalem: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 970.—Teachers, guardians: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.—Guardians of the city: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1081; Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 236.—Pastors are called guardians and cultivators of the vineyard: Bernard, CLXXXIII, 409.—Prelates, guardians of the city: id., CLXXXIV, 1232.

**CUPS,** the humble recipients of doctrine: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.

**CUP,** hearers in the Church of Christ, ibid., 895.

**CYPRUS:** in the Church, every holy soul: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1172.

**DEER,** saints: St Eucherius, L, 751.

**DANIEL** signifies the contemplative person: Alan of Lille, CCX, 248.

**DENARIUS:** the number denotes human nature: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 452.

**TEETH,** apostles: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 178.—Preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1222; CXII, 907; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 178.—The apostles, Christ’s teeth: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1069.—The apostles, teeth of the Church: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 614.—The strong in the Church: id., CLXVII, 555.—Preachers: id., CLXVIII, 614.

**DESERT,** the holy mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 908.—By the desert one may understand the person who has forsaken the world: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 85.—The human heart: ibid., 170, 377.

**RIGHT HAND,** the righteous person, a friend: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.

**RIGHT HAND,** the elect: St Eucherius, L, 732; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 198.

**DAY,** redeemed human beings: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.—The spiritual teacher; the soul of the elect: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 370.—The apostles are the days of the age: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1111.

**FINGER,** workers of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 910.

**FINGERS.** By the fingers of God are understood the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit, by his inspiration, writes the books of the Law and the Prophets: St Eucherius, L, 732.

**GODS.** The apostles are called gods: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 840.

**RICH MAN,** the faithful person abounding in spiritual goods: St Eucherius, L, 756.—Innocent persons are mystically rich: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 388.

**THE TEACHERS** of the Church are the Church’s breasts, teeth, eyes, neck, bosoms, and clusters: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1074.

**THE MOST LEARNED.** The apostles, martyrs, and priests are signified by the most learned men of Israel surrounding Solomon’s bed: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1136.

**LORD,** any prelate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911.

**HOUSE,** the human mind: ibid., 911.—The soul: John Algrin, CCVI, 170.—The house of Christ consists of apostles, priests, and ministers of the altar: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 482.—The humble heart is Christ’s house: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 100.

**BACK,** rulers of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 912.—Subjects: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 201.

**TWELVE:** the apostles, like the twelve hours of the day: St Augustine, XXXVI, 650.—The twelve patriarchs, distinguished in twelve tribes; the twelve springs of the wilderness; the twelve stones of the Jordan raised from its bed, were a figure and form of the apostolic company: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 645.—The twelve oxen which bore the bronze sea represent the whole order of pastors: St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 33, 475.—The twelve apostles are the twelve sons of the true Jacob; these are the twelve princes of the people of Israel; these are the twelve springs found at Elim; these are the twelve encampments from Rameses to Sinai; these are the twelve stones in the priestly garment; these are the twelve loaves of presentation; these are the twelve scouts sent by Moses; these are the twelve leaders of the people who entered the land; these are the twelve stones of the altar; these are the twelve stones raised from the Jordan; these are the twelve stones brought into the same place; these are the twelve officers of Solomon; these are the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea; these are the twelve lion cubs on Solomon’s throne; these are the twelve stars in the bride’s crown; these are the twelve foundations; these are the twelve gates of the city of God; these are the twelve months of the year; these are the twelve hours of the day: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 891.—The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are the twelve apostles and all their followers in doctrine within the Church: id., CVIII, 149.—The twelvefold number of the apostles, through the threefold division of four, supplies and forms for us the four-horse chariot through which the whole Trinity is driven throughout the whole world by apostolic impulses: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 645.

**LEADER,** the apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 913.—The apostles are called leaders of the sheep, the chief members of the shepherd: St Augustine, XXXVI, 785, 916; XXXVII, 1849.—The apostles are leaders of the tribes: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 854.—Leaders are holy preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 448.

**DRUNKENNESS,** the inward fullness of the saints: id., CXII, 914.

[Col. 0169] **IVORY,** the life of the holy Fathers: ibid., 913.

**ELIM.** The twelve apostles are figured by the twelve springs of Elim: St Ambrose, XVII, 18; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 367; St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 267; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 655; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1019.—The twelve springs of Elim and the seventy palm trees signify the teachers of the Christian flock—namely, the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples: St Ambrose, XVII, 18.

**HORSE,** the apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 916.—The preacher: ibid., 916; Garner, CXCIII, 87.—The bodies of the elect: ibid., CXCIII, 87.—A holy man: St Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 916.—Horses, preachers: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1174.—Preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 213; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 219.—Saints: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1173; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1064.

**HEDGEHOG,** one who fears God: St Eucherius, L, 751.—Hedgehogs, penitents: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 917.

**FOOD,** any saint: ibid., 917.

**ETHERS,** Fathers of the New Testament: ibid.

**SWARM.** The apostles are signified by the swarm of bees coming forth from the lion’s mouth: Rupert, CLXVII, 1044.

**THRESHED OUT.** The apostles were called “threshed out”: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1159.—By “sons of those threshed out” are understood the apostles, the sons of the prophets, whose prophecy was overshadowed by many coverings; the preachers of the Gospel revealed it by threshing it out: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 373.—The apostles are called sons of those threshed out because they are sons of the prophets: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1674, 1677.

**THRESHERS** are the apostles: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1329.

**ARMY,** holy martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 918.

**SCOUTS,** preachers: ibid., 918; Rupert, CLXVII, 1008.—Reprovers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 918.—The apostles, scouts of the faith and truthful men: Rupert, CLXVIII, 214.

**CRAFTSMAN.** What is meant by the craftsman who labours day and night, if not preachers? Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1035.

**FACE,** the preacher: id., CXII, 920.—The prelate: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 184.

**BUNDLE.** The apostles are the bundle which Christ bound with the bond of charity on the day of Pentecost and upon which he founded the Church: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 374.

**DRIPPING HONEYCOMB.** The lips of the devout soul are a dripping honeycomb: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 486.

**THIGH,** saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 923.

**WINDOWS,** teachers of the Church: ibid., 924.—The faithful: ibid.—Contemplative minds: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 409.—Prelates of the holy Church: ibid., 409.—Prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 865.

**HAY,** one simple in faith; the work of the good: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 924.—Hay, the steadfastness of converts: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 312.

**LITTER** is the holy soul: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 442.

**IRON,** holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 925.

**FIG TREE.** The righteous soul is compared to a fig tree: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 58.

**FIG,** the human race; the human mind: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 341.—The fig signifies religious persons gentle in character: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1070.

**POTTERS** who work in plantations and hedges are understood as none other than holy teachers, who shape and fashion the vessels of the Lord: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 366.—By the name of potters holy preachers are signified: ibid., 1036.

**DAUGHTER,** the faithful soul: St Eucherius, L, 755.—Daughter, the weaker members of the Church, the infirm: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 927.—The daughters of Jerusalem are called the holy Fathers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 87.—Holy souls: ibid., 94.—The daughters of Judah are the souls of confessors: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 195.

**SON,** the people of believers: St Eucherius, L, 755.—Son, any member of the Church, the apostles, holy men, human beings created by God: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 927.—The apostles are called sons of mother Jerusalem: St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 525.—Sons of the bridegroom: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1845.

**FRINGE,** human ways of life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 928.—Fringe, our minds: ibid.

**FIRMAMENT,** the apostles: St Augustine, XXXIII, 853; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 100; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 185.—The prophets: id., CXLII, 100.—The apostles are called the bones, or firmaments, of Christ’s body: St Augustine, XXXVI, 168; XXXVII, 1297.—The teachers of the Church are the firmament of truth: Gilbert, CLXXXIV, 90.

**FLOWERS,** souls beginning in goodness: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 347.—The good apostles are flowers which have poured forth the fragrance of their various writings and works: St Ambrose, XV, 1276.

[Col. 0170] **RIVER,** the human race: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933.—Preachers: ibid.; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 295.—The apostles, rivers lifting up their voice: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1187.—By rivers are called the sayings of the ancient Fathers: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 71.—Preachers are called rivers: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 656, 681.—Princes: ibid., 730.—Rivers signify human beings: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1202.

**STREAM,** the course of the human race; the sayings of the Fathers: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 291.—The rivers of the earth are the wise of the world: Rupert, CLXVIII, 637.—The four Evangelists are prefigured in the four rivers of paradise: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 572, 790.—Holy preachers are likened to a stream: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 828.—Prelates are signified by the river Tigris: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 618.

**LEAF.** A person who fell from the tree in paradise is compared to a leaf: St Eucherius, L, 742.

**FOUNTAIN,** the human soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 929.—The mind of the righteous: ibid., 931.—Preachers: ibid., 929.—The apostles of Christ are fountains because, like most pure springs, they abound with the grace of preaching: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 319.—The four Evangelists are denoted by four fountains flowing from the rock: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 334.—The apostles are the fountains of the Church: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 964.

**OPENINGS OF THE ROCK** are the four Evangelists: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1115.

**ANT,** the provident or workers: St Eucherius, L, 752. The ant is compared to the wise person: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 357.—Ants are like human beings: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 493.

**STRONG MEN.** The apostles are strong and pure in faith: Rupert, CLXVIII, 201.—The apostles are the Lord’s strong men, weak in flesh but strong in spirit: ibid., 559.—The apostles were the three mightiest men after David, that is, Christ: id., CLXVII, 1139.—The mighty men surrounding Solomon’s bed are patriarchs and prophets who defend the Virgin’s womb both with the natural and the spiritual sword: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 878.—The teachers of the Church are signified by the sixty mighty men: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1070.

**BROTHER,** a Christian, a good person, Christ’s kinsmen: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 921.—The apostles are called brothers: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 240.

**WHEAT,** the elect soul: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 430.—The righteous person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 938.

**LIGHTNING,** miracles of the saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 60.—The preacher gives light like a lamp and rouses like lightning: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 359.—Lightning, preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933.

**FOUNDATION,** the apostles, preachers, defenders of the Church, supreme princes of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935.—Foundation, the faithful and holy apostles: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 400.—The apostles are called foundations: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1095.—Foundations of the Church: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1103; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 731.—Foundations of the heavenly city: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1101.—The prophets are called foundations of the heavenly city: ibid.—Foundations of the Church: ibid., 1103.—Foundations of the world: id., XXXVI, 150.

**GILEAD,** a multitude of martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 939.

**HEN.** The preacher ought to be likened to a hen: Peter Cantor, CCV, 197.

**COCK** signifies a holy man or an evangelical teacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.—Cock, the order of teachers, the company of apostles: id., CXII, 939.—Cock, a holy preacher: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 73.—By the name of cock are signified holy preachers who, amid the darkness of the present life, endeavour by preaching—as though by singing—to announce the coming light: St Eucherius, L, 748; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1730.—The office of the cock and that of the preacher are alike: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 816.

**GERIZIM** indicates the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 362.

**TREASURY,** the mind of a holy man; a prelate of the Church: id., CXII, 943.—Treasuries are the hearts of teachers which preserve the riches of knowledge: id., CXI, 945, 957, 959, 981, 982; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 414.

**GEBAL** indicates the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 362.

**CHEEKS,** holy martyrs, high priests, good workers, modest prelates: id., CXII, 943.—Cheeks, spiritual Fathers: CXI, 151; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 183.

**THE KNEES** of Christ are the apostles: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1223; Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 466.—Worshippers of Christ are signified by knees: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1497.

**GIANT,** a saint, prelates, princes of the earth, a strong person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 946.

**CLODS,** holy men: ibid., 945.—The diverse orders of the elect, united through charity: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 248.

**GRASSES,** hearers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.

**HAIL,** the rebuke of the saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 66.

**FLOCK** is understood as the congregation of the faithful, leaving behind its former manner of life in baptism: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 204.—Flock, the assembly of the elect saints, the company of the perfect, the order of penitents, the orders of saints: id., CXII, 945.—The preachers of the Church are called the flock of prophets: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 293.—Flocks of goats are the prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 883.

**CRANES** can signify those who, living communally in monasteries, nevertheless do not disdain to follow the guidance of one person: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 244.

**HELMSMAN.** Peter is signified by the helmsman of the ship in Jonah: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 408.

**THROAT,** the human heart; the preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 946.

**REINS.** The prelates of the Church are the fiery reins of the chariot: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 555.

**DWELLING PLACE.** Sent preachers and angels are God’s dwelling place: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 333.

**SAND,** the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 949.

**SPEAR,** the apostles: ibid., 948.

**GRASS,** every spiritual person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 950.—Support for preachers: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 419.

**HERODIUS** [heron], every perfected person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 955.—The person of the elect: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 82.

**THE LAND OF HAVILAH** signifies the difficulties of novices’ involuntary conversion: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 617.

**WINTER** signifies old age: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1223.

**JERUSALEM** signifies peaceful souls: Alan of Lille, CCX, 76.

**FAWN,** saints according to the variety of graces: St Eucherius, L, 751.—Female deer and fawns are teachers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 74.

**SWALLOW** represents those repenting for their sins: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252.

**KIDS** signify the reprobate: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 337.—When Isaac is commanded to bring two tender and good kids, teachable and innocent souls are signified: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 588.—The two kids customarily offered on the altar denote Saint James and Saint Stephen: id., CX, 998.

**MAN,** the preacher, the righteous person, Matthew, the human race, the patriarchs: id., CXII, 955.—Because he began with human generation, Matthew is rightly figured by a man: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 815; Alcuin, CI, 1133; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 71.—Spiritual men are called “man”: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 135.

**THE THIRD, SIXTH, NINTH, AND ELEVENTH HOURS** signify adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepit age: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 370.

**ENCLOSED GARDEN** is the devout soul: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 513.—The holy soul, a garden of delights: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 269.—The faithful soul is denoted by a garden: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 789.—The good disposition, a garden of delight: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 506.—The garden of nuts is the hearts of the saints: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 531.—The bridegroom’s gardens are the hearts of saints, fortified by watchfulness and flourishing through chastity: ibid., 399.

**SHOULDERS** are the proclamations of the prophets: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 959.

**GROUND,** the holy mind: ibid., 958.—The mind of the elect: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 248.

**HYADES** signify holy preachers: St Eucherius, L, 741.—Holy teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1087.

**JARS,** the hearts of the faithful: ibid., 1088.—The four Evangelists are represented in Elijah’s four jars: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 785.

**IBEXES,** preachers, perfected men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 966.

**FIRE** is said of spiritual persons when they burn in spirit and kindle those whom they exhort: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 290.

**WATERLESS PLACES** are called chaste minds: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 217.

**CHILD,** any elect person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 970.

**MERCHANTS,** prophets: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 971.

**DARTS,** the words of saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 320.

**GATEKEEPERS** are called the apostles: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 727.

[Col. 0172] **GATE,** all the elect: Rabanus, CXII, 965.

**JERUSALEM,** Christ’s present Church: ibid., 965.—Jerusalem denotes the congregation of the righteous or the soul: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 21, 159.—Through love of God, every saint becomes a citizen of Jerusalem: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 597.

**JORDAN,** the order of the baptized: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 971.

**JUDGES,** the apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1279.—Prelates of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 973.

**BEAST OF BURDEN,** the obedient: St Eucherius, L, 752.—The soul, every faithful person placed under discipline, is called a beast of burden: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 85.—Preachers; the simple: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 973.

**RUSH,** every hearer: ibid., 973.

**RIGHTEOUSNESS,** the righteous: ibid.

**YOUNG MEN,** those eager for God: St Eucherius, L, 755.—The strong: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 974.—Martyrs: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 987.

**LIPS** of God are called the prophets: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1114.—The lips of Christ are holy preachers: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 171.—The bride’s lips are the preachers of the divine Word: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1151.

**MILK** indicates those who are weak yet devoted to good works: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 694.—The life of laypeople is signified by milk: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 748.

**BOTTLE,** our bodies: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 462.

**LAMP,** any simple person; the hearts of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 981.—Any saint: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 457.—Lamps signify the radiant hearts of saints, ever shining with the light of knowledge: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.—The apostles are the mouth of the lamp: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 231.

**WOOL,** the meek: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 980.—Wool and linen signify the ancient priesthood: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 41.

**STONE** signifies apostles or holy men, or works of virtue themselves, and sometimes the order of superiors in the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 462.—Stone, preachers, minds of saints, religious persons, apostles: id., CXII, 981.—The faith of martyrs is a stone: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1505.—Strong minds are called stone: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 350.—Stones, apostles: St Augustine, XXXVI, 166; Alcuin, C, 590; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 138.—The apostles, stones of the Church: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 616.—The twelve stones from the bed of the Jordan were a type of the twelve apostles: St Jerome, XXII, 887; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1013.—The prophets, stones of Zion: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1303.—The stones set in the foundation of the Temple are properly prophets and apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 138.—The stones of the sanctuary are religious persons: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1296.—Stones, saints: St Eucherius, L, 742.—The saints are stones which roll upon the earth, smooth, enduring, and, by their roundness, like the courses of wheels: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 713.—Four-cornered stones are any saints whose life knows how to stand firm in prosperity and adversity: id., CX, 951.—All who believe in Christ Jesus are called living stones: id., CVIII, 648.—The faithful are called living stones because of faith: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 383.

**COFFERED CEILINGS,** the simple in the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 982.

**SNARE.** The soul is, as it were, a citizen; the word of God, as a snare: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 294.

**STONE-CUTTERS,** teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 983.

**SIDE,** the crown of the righteous; the mind: ibid., 982.

**LIONESS,** the human mind: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 110.

**BED** is called the conscience filled with good works: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1008.—The secure and free mind: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 11, 17.—The bed of holy men is the pursuit of the contemplative life: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1090.

**EMBASSY,** the tears of penitents: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 984.

**AMBASSADOR,** the preacher: ibid., 984.

**LION,** the animal of Saint Mark: St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 496; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 815; Alcuin, CI, 1133; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 71; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 573; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 208; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 108.—Lion, one spiritually strong: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 983.—It signifies the righteous person: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1280.—Lion signifies prelates: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1140.—Lion, Mark the Evangelist, the security of the righteous, the severity of teachers: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 108.—The two lions standing beside each hand represent the Fathers of both Testaments, who through strength of mind have learned well to rule both themselves and others: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 197.

[Col. 0173] **LEVITES** were a figure of clerics: St Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 513.

**LEBANON** signifies the Temple: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 927.—Lebanon, the powerful of this world: ibid., 897.

**WOOD,** the human soul: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 329.—The human heart: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.—Examples of the Fathers: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 329.—The righteous person: St Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 329.—The strong minds of the Fathers: ibid., 329.—Penitents: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 986.—Holy men: ibid., 986.—The woods of Lebanon are holy men: Abbot Rupert, CXXVIII, 881.—The teachers of the Church are signified by the wood of shittim: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 579.

**LILY,** the perfect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 986.—The sweet-smelling lily, the life of the saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 421.—The lily among thorns is the faithful soul among daughters of wickedness: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1094.—Lilies are called imitators of Christ: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 141.—Lilies are the righteous: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 182.—Lilies denote the purity of those living well: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 474.

**THRESHOLD,** Fathers of the New Testament: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 464.

**TONGUE,** preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.

**SHORE,** the faithful: ibid., 987.

**PLACE,** the human mind; the hearts of the righteous: ibid.

**LOCUST,** preachers: ibid., 988.—In the locust may be understood the united fellowship of anchorites: CXI, 778.

**LAMP,** the bridegroom’s friend: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989.—The apostles: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1311, 1566.—The righteousness of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989.—Preachers: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 198.—John the Baptist was the lamp of the Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 131.—A burning and shining lamp: St Hilary, IX, 591; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 349.

**MORNING STAR,** the way of the righteous: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 43.—A holy man: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989.

**LIGHT,** the apostles: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1311, 1566; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 990.

**LIGHTS.** Teachers are lights that separate light from darkness: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 441; Cassiodorus, LXX, 664.

**MOON** signifies every creature: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 992.—By the moon a fool is signified: Cassiodorus, LXX, 582.—Virgins are compared to moons: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 703.

**WOLF,** one who fears God: St Eucherius, L, 751.—The wolf signifies the blessed Paul: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 223.

**LIGHT.** By the name of light every righteous person is understood: St Eucherius, L, 741.—Light, apostles, faithful: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989.—The apostles are the light of the world: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1701.—The light of the world, apostolic men: St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 509.

**WALL** can be understood as the doctrine of the apostles: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1116.

**THE TEACHERS** of the world are the apostles: St Agobard, CIV, 114.

**POMEGRANATES,** companies of the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 992.

**POMEGRANATE,** those holding one faith; martyrs: ibid., 992.—Pomegranates signify martyrs: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 536; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 1083, 1084; Alan of Lille, CCX, 95.—Pomegranates signify perfect believers: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 495.—By the taste of pomegranates, love for the holy martyrs is signified: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1101.—Martyrs, and likewise religious communities, are signified by pomegranates: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 186, 187.

**BREASTS,** preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 992.

**JAWS:** the young are martyrs born from the Gentiles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1048.

**MORNING** signifies childhood: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1053.

**HANDS,** an intimate friend, martyrs, members of Christ, good workers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 993.—The hands of Christ the worker are the good: Alan of Lille, CCX, 89.

**SEA** denotes the penitent heart: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 434, 1120.—The human heart, like the sea: ibid., 124.

**PEARL,** righteous human beings: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 996.

**MARTYRS** are the fruit of the Church: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 514.—The cheeks of Christ: ibid., 523.—Martyrs are rightly compared to cheeks, which are red from the shedding of blood: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1074.

**MALE,** the human spirit, every person, the rational faculty of the soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 996.

**MOTHER,** the preacher, Eve: ibid., 996.

[Col. 0174] **MEDIATOR** between God and humanity is the prelate: Peter Cantor, CCV, 175.

**MARROW,** royal nobility: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 219.

**HONEY,** holy souls: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997.—Honey signifies the life of the faithful: Alan of Lille, CCX, 240.

**MEMBERS,** the weak in the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997.—The saints, members of Christ: St Ambrose, XIV, 1043.—The apostles are Christ’s more excellent and active members: ibid., 1159.—Bishops are members of Christ’s body: St Agobard, CIV, 267.

**MONTH,** the multiplication of the faithful, orders of spirits, gatherings of souls: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 383.—By the name of months, a gathering of souls or the perfection of the saints: St Eucherius, L, 741.

**HIRED LABOURER,** any righteous person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 998.

**MIDDAY** signifies youth: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1053.

**HARVEST,** the abundance or multitude of the faithful: St Eucherius, L, 742.

**REAPERS** are the apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 279.

**THE MERCY** of God toward the elect is figured by the manna in the ark: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 759.—The apostles are called men of mercy: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 412.

**THE MEEK** are the humble, but the harsh are proud: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1786.

**MOUNTAIN; MOUNTAINS,** apostles: St Augustine, XXXVI, 347, 517, 781, 817, 882; XXXVII, 1355, 1650; St Eucherius, L, 742; Cassiodorus, LXX, 253, 446, 507, 618, 812; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 668; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359; CXII, 1001; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 241, 322; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 310; Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 48, 49; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 252; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1122.—The apostles, eternal mountains: St Augustine, XXXVI, 961; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 283.—Mountains of spices to which Christ flees: St Ambrose, XV, 1524.—Mountains of God: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 185.—Mountains of the heavenly Jerusalem: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 254, 310.—Mountains round about Jerusalem: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1650.—Great mountains: XXXVI, 961.—The apostles are called Mount Sinai: ibid., 817.—The knowledge of the apostles is compared to mountains: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 887.—Mountains, the good: St Augustine, XXXVI, 349.—The good, whose head is Christ; the evil, whose head is the devil: ibid., 519; XXXVII, 1257.—The illustrious and spiritual: id., XXXVI, 437.—The contemplative: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 337.—Devout persons: ibid., 476.—The devout mind: ibid., 477.—Those who seek only heavenly things: ibid., 337.—Dispensers of the word: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1479.—Patriarchs: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1014; Alan of Lille, CCX, 68.—Preachers: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1650, 1651; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1001; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 991.—Prelates: ibid., 1238.—Prophets: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1650; Cassiodorus, LXX, 507, 618, 812; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 283; Alan of Lille, CCXI, 68.—The devout, through whom Scripture is dispensed: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1651.—Men eminent in the Church through outstanding holiness: id., XXXVI, 904.—Holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359, 365.—All eminent and elect men: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 136.—Saints by reason of the loftiness of their virtues: St Eucherius, L, 742.—Mountains of spices, saints: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 959.—The mountains of Bethel are saints: Alan of Lille, CCX, 72.

**LITTLE MORTAR,** the human mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1002.

**WOMAN;** the human race, the faithful soul, holy souls, subjects: ibid., 1012.—A woman is a type of the soul softened by grace: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 934. The soul is compared to a woman: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1171.

**WORLD.** The faithful soul is called a world: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 279.

**GOLDEN ORNAMENTS.** The sayings of saints are signified by little golden ornaments: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 853.

**WALL,** virtues of the soul; princes of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1003.

**MYRRH** signifies martyrs: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 213.

**MYRTLE,** the disposition of a tranquil mind; the compassionate: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 422.

**NARD,** the sweet-smelling life of saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 424.

**LITTLE BOAT** denotes the spiritual congregation: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 909.—The humbled soul: ibid., 920.

**SHIP,** the soul, the human heart, the ancient Fathers, rulers: Rabanus Maurus, CXXII [probably CXII], 1004.—Human life is like a ship: [Col. 0175] Peter Cantor, CCV, 40.—The holy Fathers are compared to ships bearing fruit: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 884, 886.—Ships signify souls saving themselves and others: Venerable Abbot Guibert, CVI, 325.

**SINEW,** the virtues of the soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1005.

**NEST,** exalted rest for the saints: St Eucherius, L, 748.—Holy men; the mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1006.

**SNOW,** a holy man: ibid., 1006.—The lofty hearts of saints: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 63.

**RAZOR,** any preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.

**NIGHT,** the manner of life of laypeople; the adversity of a saint: ibid., 1007.

**CLOUDS,** apostles: St Augustine, XXXVI, 347, 520, 814, 833, 980; XXXVII, 1212, 1235; XLI, 532; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 27, 83, 406, 1006; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.—Teachers: Alcuin, C, 713.—The righteous: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 49.—Preachers: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 289; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1149; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 289, 328; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 192, 363; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 49.—Prophets: St Eucherius, L, 738; Alcuin, C, 713; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 223; Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 15; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 49.—The saints are clouds; Moses was a cloud and spoke, as it were, as a cloud; likewise Isaiah was a cloud: St Jerome, XXV, 628.—Clouds, saints: St Eucherius, L, 738.

**MESSENGERS.** The apostles are signified by the messengers sent by David to Nabal: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1413.

**NUT.** The life of the righteous is rightly compared to a nut: Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 655.

**NIGHT-RAVEN,** a holy man despised by unbelievers: St Eucherius, L, 748.—The night-raven signifies the sinner doing penance: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 371.

**REFINED GOLD,** human holiness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1009.—The perfect mind: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 306.

**EYE,** the contemplative mind, an intimate friend, peoples: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1009.—The eyes of Christ, the apostles: St Augustine, XXXVI, 1114; Cassiodorus, LXX, 625; Alcuin, C, 363; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 970.—Teachers of the Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1086; Alcuin, C, 563.—The eyes of Christ’s body, apostles and priests: St Hilary, IX, 809.—By the eyes of God are understood the holy and learned: Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 410.—The eyes of the Church, apostles: St Augustine, XXXIV, 843; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1162.—Teachers: Cassiodorus, LXX, 664, 1095; Gillebert, CLXXIV, 156.—Prelates: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 118; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1148, 1231. The eyes of the Holy Spirit are teachers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 88.

**OLIVE TREE,** a saint abounding in fruits of mercy: St Eucherius, L, 742.

**OIL OF GLADNESS** is the charity of the saints in heaven: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 654.

**OLIVE,** the merciful: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 337.—The Mount of Olives, patriarchs and prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 805.

**WILD ASS,** a hermit: St Eucherius, L, 751.—The solitary righteous person: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 116.

**WORKERS,** the apostles, or preachers of the Gospel: St Eucherius, L, 756.

**NOBLES,** teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1012.

ORIONS, rising in the severity of winter, signify the holy martyrs: St. Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1012.

RISING, a holy mind, a faithful soul, ibid., 1013.

MOUTH, a preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1013.—The mouth: a preacher, the knowledge of teachers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 173.—The mouth of the Lord consists of prelates and masters: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 173.

BONE, strength of mind, virtues of the soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1014. Martyrs are rightly compared to bones: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1030.—Dry bones returning to life show the people of Israel to be restored to their own land, or the resurrection of Jews and Christians: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 859, 860.—Bones: all who are strong: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 214.

DOOR, contemplatives, the order of hearers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1014.—Preachers, ibid., 1014.—Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 406.—Priests, through whom believers enter the Church: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 956.—The apostles are called the doors of the Church: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 470.

SHEEP, faithful peoples: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—The simple and meek: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 405.—The chosen Christian people, id., CXI, 201.—Subjects, id., CXII, 1014.—The redeemed human being, good persons, ibid., 1015. All simple persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 105.—Martyrs are rightly compared to sheep: Cassiodorus, LXX, 313.—The faithful are sheep because of their meekness: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1153.—The sheep of the house of Israel are innocent [Col. 0176] souls: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 195.

PEACEFUL ONE, every saint, preachers, lovers of concord: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1016.

CHAF﻿F, holy men, ibid., 1018.

PALM TREE, the righteous person, ibid., 1017; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 556.—The seventy palm trees signify the seventy disciples: St. Ambrose, XVII, 18; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 320.—Martyrs are signified by the palm tree: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 655.

BRANCHES, apostles, true believers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1017.—Vine-shoots: apostles or saints: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

EYELIDS, prelates of the Church, prudent men of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 166.

BREAD, a holy man, apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1021.—Breads from heaven: righteous persons: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 263.

CLOTHS, examples of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1021.

PARADISE, a holy soul: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 265.—The soul of the righteous: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1589.—The conscience of the righteous: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1072.

THE BRIDEGROOM’S FRIENDS (paranymphs) of the bride, the Church, are prelates: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 107.

THE PARENTS of Christ are priests: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1093.

WALL, the hearts of subjects: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1022.—The wall: the nature of humanity: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 401.

LITTLE ONE, humble and simple in mind: St. Eucherius, L, 755.

SPARROW, a holy man, and elsewhere any Christian: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—The solitary sparrow in Scripture mystically signifies the penitent sinner: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 371.—Sparrow: a holy man, every convert: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1022.—The humble; the twofold substance of man, ibid.

SHEPHERD, an apostle: St. Eucherius, L, 756.—The apostles are called the first shepherds: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 764.—Shepherds are the apostles or other rulers of the Churches: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1254.

FATHER, prelates, superiors, id., CXII, 1023.—The apostles were called Fathers: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 513; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXVI, 1152.

POOR MAN, the humble person: St. Eucherius, L, 756.

PAVEMENT, every hearer: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1023.—The humility of hearers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 420.

CATTLE, the righteous person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1024.—Cattle: all simple persons less endowed with subtlety in reasoning: St. Eucherius, L, 752.

PELICAN, a holy man devoted to solitude: St. Eucherius, L, 748; Alcuin, C, 588; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1026.—The pelican mystically signifies the penitent sinner: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 371–372.

SKIN, holy women, the bodies of martyrs, the ancient Fathers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1026.—The examples of preceding Fathers are figured by the skins of dead animals: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1041.

FEATHERS, the admonitions of prophets, the contemplations of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1026; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 765.

BAG, the understanding of the apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1027.

STRANGER, every person who despises the world, ibid.

FOOT: every preacher, friend, apostles, the weak, actions of saints, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1025.—The apostles are Christ’s feet: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 578; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 87.—The feet of God: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 238; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 805.—The feet of the Lord: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1167; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 805.—The feet of the Lord are preachers: St. Eucherius, L, 733; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 632; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1101.—Feet: one who supports by helping, one who runs to tasks imposed upon him, apostles, preachers, ministers of works done for the weak: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 233.

ROCK, a steadfast man, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1028.

QUIVER, counsels of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 919.

BOWL, the human soul, teachers: ibid., 926. Preachers are signified by bowls: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 773.

SPICE-SELLERS are called apostles: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1195; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 89.

HAIRS, the humility of penitents: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1028.

FISHERMEN, apostles or teachers: St. Eucherius, L, 756.—The apostles, fishers of men: St. Augustine, [Col. 0177] XXXVI, 781.—Fishermen: preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1030.

FISH, faithful people, priestly and royal power: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1030.—Fishes: saints: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

PLANT, Abel, the first righteous man: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 258.

PLANE TREES, holy men, every contemplative: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1020.

STREET, hearers, worldly persons, the hearts of the elect, ibid., 1020.

CARTS. The apostles are the oxen and carts of the Church: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 856.

PLEIADES signify the elect: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1029; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 44; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 703.

FRUITS, the fruits of saints in virtues: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—Fruits: marks of humanity, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, 1030.

GATE, preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1031; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 402.—Good teachers, ibid., 402.—A preacher is mystically the gate of the city: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 585.—The gates are the apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 385; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 425.—Holy teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 385.—Prophets: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 425.—The gates of the Church: the apostles: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1103.—Prophets: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1330.

PORTICO, the ancient Fathers: Rabanus Maurus, 1032.

BEARERS OF THE CHURCH: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 856.

DOORPOSTS, the body and soul of man: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1032.

PRINCE, a prelate, apostles, rulers of the Church, ibid., 1029.—Princes: those who rule their own thoughts: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 155.—Apostles: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 834.—The princes of Judah: apostles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 255. The apostles are called most mighty princes: CLXXIV, 501.

THE STEWARD of the vineyard is a preacher: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 135.

PROPHETS. Preachers are called prophets: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 718.—The apostles are called sons of the prophets: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 68.

BULWARKS OF THE CHURCH, teachers: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 511.

NEIGHBOURS, those near in faith and those who show mercy to the needy: St. Eucherius, L, 755.

THE MIGHTY, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1032.

CHILD, every innocent person, ibid., 1032.—Children: those who serve the heavenly commandments, the tender stage of beginners, innocent persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 145.

BATTLE. The battle and victory of the martyrs were prefigured in Gideon’s battle: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1748.

YOUNG, saints: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—The apostles, young ravens: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 541.—A young one: apostles, people from the Gentiles, hearers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1833.

PUPIL OF THE EYE, the elect, ibid., 1034.

PURPLE consists in the shedding of the precious blood of martyrs, id., CXI, 578.

CHARIOT. Virgins are signified by the chariot of white horses: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 739.—The apostles are signified by the chariot of red horses, ibid., 744.—Chariots: apostles, holy teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1037.

FOUR. Just as Moses divided the divided people of God on earth into four camps, so the Apostle describes four orders of saints in heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 604. The number four signifies the four Evangelists: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 444.

ROOT, the soul of man, man’s suggestion: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1037.—The nature of humanity: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 343.

BRANCHES, holy preachers, ibid., 356.

THE PILOTS of the ship are the apostles: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 411.

QUEEN, devout souls: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1038.—The soul ruling the senses: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 992.—The souls of prelates are queens: John Algrin, CCVI, 642.—Teachers of the Church are figured by queens: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 93.

KINGDOM, a holy mind, the different orders of the faithful: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1038.—The heart of the righteous is the kingdom of God: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 254, 580.

RULE, the eloquence of philosophers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1039.

REMNANT. The apostles are the remnant of Jacob: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 593.

KING, a preacher, a holy man, prelates: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1037.—Apostles, preachers, holy men: Garner [Col. 0178] of St. Victor, CXCIII, 147.—Kings are apostles or other saints who know how first to govern themselves well and then the Church subject to them: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 708.—Preachers are called kings: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 980.

RHINOCEROS, every strong person: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—One powerful in this world: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 121.

STREAM, preachers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 296.—Streams: preachers, peoples, faithful persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1040.

DEW signifies the teaching of the apostles: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 494.—Of preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 328.

ROSE, because it is red with a glowing colour, signifies martyrs: St. Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528; CXII, 1040.

WHEEL, preachers, ibid., 1041.—By Ezekiel’s four wheels the four Evangelists are signified: id., CX, 635.

ROARING, the lamentation of the penitent, the anxieties of prelates: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1041.

CLIFFS, preachers, the powerful of the world, ibid., 1042.

LITTLE SACK, the heart of the penitent, ibid., 1043.

SACKCLOTH, the mind of man, ibid.

CURTAINS, rulers of the Church, ibid., 1043.—The office of prelates is signified by the curtains of the tabernacle: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 766.

ARCHER, every preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1943.

ARROWS, apostles: St. Eucherius, L, 738; Cassiodorus, LXX, 71, 330.—Prophets: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 738.—The apostles are to some vessels of death and sharp arrows: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1106.—The arrows of the Lord: apostles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 65.—Evangelists, ibid., 93; Cassiodorus, LXX, 128.—The apostles are God’s arrows, swift in flight, wounding the faithful, piercing, rebuking, flying: St. Hilary, IX, 702.—Arrows are the sayings of preachers: St. Bruno the Carthusian, 828.—The preacher’s words are sharp arrows: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 640.

SALT. The apostles are called the salt of the earth, the light of the world, and a lamp of the house on a lampstand because of the outstanding and conspicuous works of their faith: St. Hilary, IX, 809.—Priests are compared to salt: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 191.

WILLOWS, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.—Willows, on account of their greenness: good persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 336.

THE BOOKS OF SOLOMON prefigure teachers of the Church in peace: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 331.

THE APOSTLES are called SAVIOURS: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 331.

BLOOD, examples of martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.

SAPPHIRE, every saint: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 353.

SARDONYX, a holy man: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1046.

STONE, a strong mind, ibid., 1047.

FOOTSTOOL, every person serving God in good action, ibid., 1043.

SPARK, examples of the righteous, words of preachers, ibid., 1055; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 359.

SCORPION, teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1060.

CARVING, examples of saints, ibid., 1061.

AXE, a good man, ibid., 1047.

SEAT. The apostles are called the thrones or seats of God: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1625.—Seats are saints, because the Lord sits in them and through them decrees his judgments: St. Eucherius, L, 739.—Seat: a holy mind, apostles, the conduct of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1048.—A holy soul, the seat of wisdom: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 544.—A soul adorned with virtues is the seat of God: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1061.

SEED, good people, chosen men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1048.

OLD MAN, every perfect person, ibid., 1049.—Old men: consummate righteousness: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 755.

THE SEVENTY disciples represent the seventy palm trees: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXVI, 267.

SERAPHIM. The apostles are seraphim: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1299.

BARS. Prelates are called the bars of the gates of the Church: St. Bruno the Carthusian, XLII, 1408.

SERPENT, prudent persons: St. Eucherius, L, 754.

THE SERVANTS of God are kings: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 697.

SHEKEL, our body and soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1053.

SEAL, the confirmation of the elect, the people of old, ibid., 1053.

FOREST, this world, the human mind, ibid., 1054.

[Col. 0179] MUSTARD, the strength of the faithful man: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 430.

FINE LINEN, a pure mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 430.

BOSOM, our mind, that which is ours, ibid., 1054.

ZION. A weak soul, not yet perfect, is called Zion: Adam the Scot, CXVIII, 298.

SUN, the intelligence of the wise, the brightness of preachers: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 862; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 37.—Preachers, the priestly order, a wise person, one exalted in the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1057.

WATCHMAN, a preacher, ibid., 1050.

EAR OF GRAIN, the sayings of the Fathers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 434.

THORN, a preacher: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1056.

SPIRIT. Figuratively, all spiritual persons in the Church are called spirits; they become angels when they become preachers and messengers of truth: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 290.—Spirit: our mind, the human soul, our reason, human strength, every spiritual person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1056.—The soul is called spirit: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 155.

SPOILS, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1059.

BRIDE of God, the soul: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 708.—Bride of Christ, the soul: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 849.—The faithful soul: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 643.—The faithful are the bride because of love, id., CLXXXIII, 1133.

BASKETS, the hearts of teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1059.

STACTE, our mind, ibid., 1047.

WARP, the human soul, ibid.

STARS, apostles: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 405; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 51.—Preachers: Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 51.—Preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.—A star: apostles, prelates, virtues of saints, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.—Stars: saints or learned persons, or those who instruct unto righteousness: St. Eucherius, L, 739.—Stars: ancient prophets, apostles, preachers, the righteousness of saints: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 41.

DROP, preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1057.

DRIPPINGS, faithful persons, ibid., 1057.

STAKES, counsels of saints, ibid., 1061.

FURROWS, the hearts of saints: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—Holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1061.

TABERNACLE, our mind, ancient saints, ibid., 1062.—The hearts of saints are called tabernacles, id., CXI, 589.

TABLETS, apostles, id., CXII, 1062; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 826.—Cedar tablets signify saints: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1254.

ANKLES. The apostles are signified by ankles: Rupert, CLXVII, 1497.

BULLS, the Fathers of the Old Testament: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1063; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 100.—Leaders of peoples: St. Eucherius, L, 752.

TEMPLE, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1064.—The soul of the righteous; the faithful people: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 398.—The temple of the Lord is a holy and immaculate mind: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 93.—The faithful soul is a kind of temple to be sanctified for God: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 369.

TENT, every saint, the congregation of saints: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.—The apostles are figured by the tent at the entrance of the tabernacle: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 327.

EARTH, a saint, a subject, the household, the lesser members of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.—The soul of the righteous, the human soul, the subject people: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 239.—By the name earth are understood those occupied in earthly actions who come to eternal life through alms and tears: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—Prelates are called earth: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1179.—The righteous person is signified by heaven, the sinner by earth: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 275–276.—Earth: earthly persons, id., XXXVII, 370.

BRIDAL CHAMBER, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1063.—Every person loving God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 413.

TREASURE, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1066.

THRONE. The faithful soul is denoted by the throne: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1125–1126.—Thrones are saints: St. Eucherius, L, 739.—Apostles: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1625.—Holy preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1069.

CENSER, good workers, apostles, ibid., 1070.

BEAMS, teachers: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1061; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1067; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 64.

DYES, philosophers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1067.

THUNDER, every preacher, ibid., 1068.

[Col. 0180] TOPAZ, holy men, ibid.—One full of many virtues: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 354.

TORRENT, preachers: St. Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1068; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 237.

BEAM, apostles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1063.

THREE HUNDRED. Preachers are signified by the three hundred men who were with Gideon: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 168.

WHEAT, saints or God’s elect: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

TRUMPET. John the Evangelist: a trumpet of horn, silver, and gold: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 726.—A preacher is figured in the trumpet: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 976.—The apostles are trumpets: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 477.—Malleable trumpets signify endurance: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 712.

TOWER. The apostles are towers: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1320.—Martyrs are rightly compared to towers: Cassiodorus, LXX, 913.—Preachers in the Church are like towers: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 196.

TURTLE-DOVE, a holy man: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—The apostles are turtle-doves: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1065.

THE SAILORS AND PILOTS OF TYRE are compared with the prelates of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 782.

BREASTS, preachers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 221.

ELM. The elm signifies secular persons who are less fruitful, yet support others living well from their resources: Wolbero, abbot, CXXV, 1275.

THE NAVEL of the Church consists of preachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085, 1228.

WINE-SKIN, the hearts of spiritual persons, ibid., 1086.

WIFE, the wisdom of the righteous, ibid., 1087.

COW, every faithful person in the Church: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—Holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1072.—The minds of the faithful: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 96.—The cows carrying the ark of the Lord signify preachers: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1083.

VALLEY, the humble, the humble sayings of the Fathers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 258.

VESSEL, prophets, people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.—The following are called vessels: a holy preacher, every disciplined person, the capacity for understanding, holy Fathers, the souls of faithful peoples, our consciences, our bodies: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 451.

BAR, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.—Teachers in the Church are signified by bars of shittim wood: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 700; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 706–707.

HUNTERS. The apostles are hunters: Alcuin, C, 564.

WINDS, the souls of saints: St. Eucherius, L, 739; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1074; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 75; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 51.—The winds are the apostles, whose preaching ran through the whole world like a swiftest wind: Cassiodorus, LXX, 963.—Evangelists: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 785.

SPRING signifies childhood: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1223.

FOOTSTEPS. The apostles are Christ’s footprints: Cassiodorus, LXX, 119.

GARMENT, the order of the faithful, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1075.—Garments indicate good subjects: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 187.

CLOTHING, every person striving for purity, Christ’s martyrs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1076.

CLOTHED, one possessing integrity of faith or the garment of righteousness: St. Eucherius, L, 756.

WAYS are the apostles, through whom one comes to life: Alcuin, C, 598, 629.

TRAVELLERS, holy men: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1077.

THE VICARS of Christ are the apostles: St. Agobard, CIV, 128.

VILLAGES, religious persons, citizens of heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.

WIDOW, the soul: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 143. The soul of the righteous is compared to a widow: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 92.

WATCHMEN are the holy apostles and the other teachers of the Church: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1068.—Holy shepherds: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.—Watchmen guarding the city are holy teachers: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1123.

VINEYARD, faithful peoples: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 507; CXII, 1079; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 934.—A soul fruitful in virtues: Garner of St. Victor, CXIII, 341.—A vineyard in flower: novices in religious life: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1083.—A vineyard which has blossomed signifies those further advanced: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1083.—The guardians of the vineyard were patriarchs, prophets, kings, and leaders: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 958.—Souls are signified by vineyards: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1056.—Those fervent in spirit are compared with vineyards, ibid., 1070.—The first [Col. 0181] faithful are compared with vineyards in bloom, ibid., 1068.—The apostles: the vineyard leased and cultivated by them: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 545.

VINE-DRESSERS are called preachers: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 48.—Prelates of the Church, ibid.—Apostolic men: Rupert, CLXVIII, 48.

WINE, every contemplative person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.

VIOLETS, confessors: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

MAN, the robust and spiritual: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080.—Every perfect man, perfect men: Garner of St. Victor, CXIII, 193.—“Man” is taken for what is strong, “woman” for what is weak: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 259.—The apostles are signified by the two men carrying a cluster on a pole: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 738.

ROD, the congregation of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.—The human race is compared to Moses’ rod: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 684.

VIRGIN, a holy soul: St. Eucherius, L, 754; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080.—Virgins are forms of Christ: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 517.

INWARD PARTS, the minds of human beings: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.—Inward parts: those who serve spiritual sacraments in the Church: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 228.

GLASS, the state of the citizens of heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1082.

CALF, saints: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—A holy preacher: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 101.—Luke bears the appearance of a calf: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 815; Alcuin, CI, 1133; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 909; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 133; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 101.

THE LIVING, the righteous: St. Eucherius, L, 756.

FLIGHT, the saints’ passing beyond themselves into God: St. Eucherius, L, 748.

BIRDS, holy souls, rulers of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.

## ARTICLE IX. Allegories concerning Gentiles and Hebrews

HEAP. The heap of mercury: an unbeliever: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.

ADVERSARY, the unbelieving people, ibid., 872.

EGYPT, the Gentile world, ibid., 915; Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 63.

FIELD, Gentile identity: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 256.—The Jewish and Gentile people: a field: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.

FARMER. The leaders of the Synagogue are farmers, ibid., 853.

HANDMAID, the effeminate minds of the Jews, ibid., 859.

ANIMALS were the nations devoid of true religion, id., CXI, 199.—The animals among whom Christ was recognized were the two thieves, that is, the Church from Jews and Gentiles, that is, the two Testaments: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 629.

JEWS are called ANTICHRISTS: St. Agobard, CIV, 94.

WATER enclosed by five porticoes: the Jewish people shut within the Law: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1065.—The water of contradiction can denote the Jews: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 851.—Peoples, the soft hearts of the Jews, unbelief: water: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 284.—By the force of waters Scripture signifies the rage of peoples: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 369.—Many waters are unbelieving peoples, whether attacking from without or lying in wait within, ibid., 410.—Many waters are called the crowds of Gentiles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 289.—Waters signify peoples: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 747.

NORTH WIND, the Gentile world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 59.

ARK. Just as Dagon fell while the ark of the Lord stood, so, when the Testament of the Lord came to the Gentiles, the idols that possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 28.

ARCHONS. God calls the archons of the Jews “archons of Sodom”: Tertullian, II, 339.

ARCTURUS, the Gentile people: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 430.—The unbelieving people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 862.

THRESHING FLOOR, the extent of the Gentile people, ibid., 865; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 993.

SAND, the Gentile people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 949.—Unfruitful unbelievers, ibid.—The sand of the sea denotes the people before the Law, unfruitful: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1111.—The sands of the sea signify the innumerable multitudes of nations: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

[Col. 0182] RAM, the leadership of the peoples who follow: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 103.

HERDS. By herds may be signified the synagogues of the Jewish people, which bore the yoke of the Law and supplied their hearers with the milk of simple teaching: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 404.

REED, the Gentile people: id., CXII, 949.

SHE-ASS. In the she-ass is figured the people of the Gentiles, now subject to Christ: St. Ambrose, XIV, 416.—The Synagogue: a she-ass: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.—The Gentiles are signified by the she-ass: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 347.—Balaam’s she-ass, speaking with a human voice, is a figure of the conversion of the Gentiles: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 200.—Balaam’s she-ass bears the type of the Gentile world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 731.

ASS, the Gentile people: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1675; St. Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 405; CXII, 867; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 651.—By asses is signified the simplicity of the Gentiles: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 527, 578, 1149; LXXVI, 770–771; Rupert, abbot, CLVII, 1271; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 88.—The ass represents the people under the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 88.—The folly of the Jews: an ass: id., CXII, 867.

ASP. The Jews are figured in the asp: Cassiodorus, LXX, 105.

COURT, the unbelieving people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.

GOLD, the wisdom of the Gentile world, ibid., 870.

SOUTH WIND, the Jewish people, id., CIX, 398; CXI, 262; CXII, 869.—The south wind: Judaea: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 56.

BABYLON. The Church from the Gentiles is called Babylon: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.

BEARD, the Jewish people, ibid., 873.

BEAST is called the Church from the Gentiles, ibid., 875.—The beasts of the forest are understood as the nations: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291.

OX, the Jewish people: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1675; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 629; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 94.—A straying ox represents the nation from the circumcision: Rabanus Maurus, CXIII, 921.—The humility of the Israelites is signified in oxen, id., CXI, 578.—Oxen signify the Jewish people and the Synagogue: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 629. Jews and Gentiles: oxen: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 876.

CLUSTER. Gentiles and Jews are signified by the two men carrying a cluster on a pole: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 874.

CORPSES mystically signify the bodies of unbelievers: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 195.

REED, the Gentile world, id., CXII, 879, 882.

CAMEL is the Jew swollen with pride, such as the scribes and Pharisees, id., CVIII, 883.—The Gentile people, the life of the Samaritans: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 92.—By camels are signified vicious Gentiles and Samaritans: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 536, 545; LXXVI, 770.—Gentiles may be represented by camels: Rabanus Maurus, CXX, 405.

FIELD, the Jewish people; uncultivated nations, id., CXII, 882.—The Gentile world: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 257.

DOG is called Jew or Gentile: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—The Gentiles were called dogs by the Jews: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 702; XXXVII, 486, 679.—The Jews are figured in dogs: Cassiodorus, LXX, 413.—Nations and Jews: dogs: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 883; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 102.

CAPER-BUSH, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 885.

GOATS are called the righteous coming from the Gentiles: St. Eucherius, L, 752.

HEAD, the Jewish priesthood, the leadership of the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.—The summit of the Jewish priesthood: head: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 158.—The heads of Christ’s enemies are the Jews: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 96.

SEDGE, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 887.

CARMEL, the carnal purification of the Jews, ibid.

CHAINS, the harsh laws of the nations, ibid., 890.

PUPS signify Gentiles, id., CXI, 224.—Gentiles and Jews, CXII, 889.

CEDAR, the kingdom of Judaea: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 334.—Gentiles and Jews: cedars: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.

STAG signifies the Jewish people: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 541.

HAIR-CLOTH, Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 894.

CURLS, companies of peoples, ibid., 896.

CITIZENS, persecuting Jews, ibid., 897.

CITY, Gentiles and Jews, ibid.

THE LAME: Jews who, holding the Old Testament carnally, rejected the grace of the New: Cassiodorus, LXX, 136.

[Col. 0183] HEAVEN is said of the Jewish people: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 30.

COLUMN, leaders of the Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 899.

CONCUBINES. The Jews are signified by David’s concubines: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 287.

SPOUSE. The Gentile world is virgin and spouse: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII.

HEART, priests of the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.

RAVEN nourishing Elijah prefigures the conversion of the Gentiles: St. Hilary, IX, 874.—The raven sent out by Noah signifies the Jewish people: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 317.—The Fathers who venerated idols bore the figure of ravens, pursuing dead and unclean things; their young, that is, their children, call upon the true God and are nourished by the food of the Holy Spirit: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 419.—Ravens: Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 902.—Gentiles and Jews: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 76.—Ravens: Gentiles; young ravens: children of the Gentiles: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1911–1912.

DAMASCUS. The Roman empire is called Damascus: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 906.

SHRINES signify the superstitions of the Jews: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 132.

DESERT, the Gentile world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 908.—Judaea, ibid., 908; Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1131.—Judaea and the Gentile world: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 268.—The Jews are called the desert of Kadesh: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 748.

DEVIL. Jews are called vessels of the devil: St. Agobard, CIV, 78.—Children of the devil, ibid., 111.

BELOVED, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911.

DISC. The conversion of the Gentiles is prefigured by the mystical disc: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1248.

RICH MAN, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911.

HOUSE, Jews and Gentiles, ibid.—The house of Israel is understood as the Synagogue: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 320.

DRAGON, the most wicked leaders of the Jews; Gentiles: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 124.—Jews and Gentiles: dragons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 906.

DROMEDARY, the Gentile world, ibid., 912.

EDOM, the Jewish people and the Gentile world, ibid., 914.

THE LORD’S CAVALRY was the Israelite people: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1060.—The devil’s cavalry: the synagogue of unbelievers, ibid., 1064.

WILDERNESS. Judaea and the Gentile world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 953.

ETHIOPIA, the Gentile world, ibid., 918; Rupert, CLXVIII, 677.

THE SCOUTS OF HOLOFERNES—what are they but the philosophers of the Gentiles and curious investigators of human disciplines? Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 566.—The twelve scouts bore the image of the scribes and Pharisees who turned the Israelite people away, lest they trust that they could attain the grace of the divine promise through Christ: id., CXI, 54.

DREGS. The Jews are the dregs of the living God: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 701.

WILD BEAST, the savagery of the Jews, the Gentile world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 924.

FIG TREE, a type of the Synagogue: Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 54.

FIG TREE bears the type of the Synagogue: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1065; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 70.—The unbelieving Synagogue is called a fig tree: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—Fig tree: Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 926.—The fig tree signifies especially the Jewish people: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1066.—The fig tree having leaves but lacking fruit: Jews and Pharisees possessing words, not deeds: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 264.

DAUGHTER, Judaea: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 927.—By the daughter of Edom, interpreted “bloody” or “earthly,” the Synagogue of the Jews is expressed: id., CXI, 1261.

SONS, Jews and Gentiles, id., CXII, 927.—By the sons of men the Jews may be understood: Cassiodorus, LXX, 104.

END, Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 932.

RIVER, Jews and Gentiles, ibid., 933.

HAY. In the Old Testament, all humankind was hay devoured by the ox of the devil: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 642.

THE STRONG, Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 931.

LEAVES, the kings of Judaea: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 347.

FRUITS. By the name “fruits” are understood converts, whether Jews or Gentiles: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 434.

FROST. The cold Synagogue is called frost: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.

[Col. 0184] NATION, the Jewish people, Gentiles, and those living as Gentiles: ibid., 944.

GENTILES and Jews beginning to believe are signified by Tyre, Sidon, and Gomorrah: Rupert, CLXVIII, 1516.

ICE. The cold Synagogue is called ice: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 940.

CLODS, the hard hearts of unbelievers: ibid., 945.—The respective bodies of individual orders in Judaea are clods: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 248.

GOMORRAH. God calls the Jewish people the people of Gomorrah because of similar impiety: Tertullian, II, 339.

HAIL. The cold Synagogue is called hail: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.

FLOCK, unlearned peoples: ibid., 945.

GOATS signify unbelievers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 59.—The two kids which Isaac is commanded to bring signify the adoption of the two peoples: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 588.

IVY has the type of the Jewish people, which once flourished but did not long remain in its former greenness: id., CXI, 528.

HERMON, the Gentiles: id., CXII, 953.

WINTER, the coldness of unbelief: ibid.

HE-GOAT. The Gentile people is denoted by the name of he-goat: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—Gentiles are called he-goats: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 203.—The two he-goats are the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles: ibid.

GARDEN. Judaea, a garden of nuts: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1218.—The garden of nuts signifies the universality of humankind: ibid.

IDUMAEA. Gentilism is called Idumaea: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 966.

WICKED MAN, the Jewish people: ibid., 970.

INDIA, the world: ibid.

JUDGES are called Jews: ibid., 973.

BEASTS OF BURDEN. The Jews are represented by irrational beasts of burden: Cassiodorus, LXX, 344.

PLATE, the hearts of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 979.

WOOL. The Jewish priesthood is signified by wool: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 41.

STONE, the Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 981.—A stone signifies the Jewish people or the hardness of the Gentiles’ heart: id., CXI, 462.—Stone: the hard hearts of the Gentiles: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 350.—The nations are called the stones of the field: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 830.—They are called stones because they worshipped stones: id., XXXVII, 679.

SIDE, unbelieving peoples, Jews, Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 982.

A DEAD LION denotes the people of the circumcision: Alcuin, C, 703.—The Jews: lions: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 983.

WOODS, the Gentiles: ibid., 986.

LINEN, the Gentiles: ibid., 987.—The Jewish priesthood is signified by linen: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 41.

LOCUST. In the locust there was a figure of the Gentile people: St. Ambrose, XV, 1578.—By the name of locusts are denoted the Jewish people or converted Gentilism: St. Eucherius, L, 748. Some interpret the locust as the multitude of the nations: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 778.—Nations and Jews: locusts: id., CXI, 988.

MUD, the Jews: ibid., 991; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 276.

WALL, the Jewish kingdom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 992.

MIDIANITES are a type of Gentiles persecuting the Church: id., CVIII, 1154.

MANDRAKE. The fruitfulness of the nations in the progress of faith is signified by the fragrance of mandrakes: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 949.—Mandrakes signify Gentiles and Jews: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1240.

HAND, the Jewish people; persecution by the Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 993.

SEA, Gentilism: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 937; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 996; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 331, 349; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 371; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 287.

MOTHER, the Jewish people and the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 996.

MOAB, Gentilism: ibid., 996.

MOUNTAIN, Gentilism: ibid., 1001.—The Jewish people: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 252.—The mountain from which the stone was cut: the Jewish kingdom: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1270.—Mountains signify the Jewish people, or the Jewish scribes: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359.

SHIPWRECKED MAN. An unbeliever is often termed in the Psalms by the name “shipwrecked man”: St. Hilary, IX, 316.

SHIP. Christ chose Peter’s ship and abandoned that of Moses—that is, he rejected the faithless Synagogue and received the faithful Church: St. Ambrose, XVII, 677.

MIST, filling the house of the Lord, suggests the proud pontiffs and teachers of the Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 185.—The hearts of unbelievers: mist: id., CXII, 1005.

SNOW, the hearts of unbelievers: ibid., 1006.

WEST, unbelief: ibid., CXII, 1010.

EYES. The teachers of the Jews are called eyes: id., ibid., 1009.

OLIVE, the Jews: ibid., 1011.

WILD OLIVE is called a Gentile: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

POT. The Synagogue is called a pot: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 459.

WILD ASS is called the Jewish people: St. Eucherius, L, 751.—The Jews are represented by wild asses: Cassiodorus, LXX, 732.—The wild ass: Gentile and Jew: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1012; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 116.

EAST, a Jew: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1012.

DRY BONES coming to life show that the people of Israel will be brought back into their own land, or the resurrection of Christians: id., CX, 859, 860.

SHEEPFOLD, the Synagogue: ibid., 1015.

SHEEP. Believers from among the Jews: sheep: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 105.

CHAFF. Condemned unbelievers are called chaff: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018.

PAPYRUS, the Synagogue: ibid., 1021.

The peace which the Amorites made with Samuel signifies the union of Gentiles and Jews effected in Christ: id., CIX, 34.

CATTLE, peoples: id., CXII, 1024.

ROCK. By the Rock the hardness of the Jews is to be understood: Cassiodorus, LXX, 813.

POOL, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1030.

STREET, a multitude of peoples: ibid., 1020.
