LEAD. The Synagogue: ibid., 1034; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 318.

PORTICO, the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1031.

BOYS, the Jews: ibid., 1032.

COLT, Gentilism: ibid., 1033.

RHINOCEROS, the proud Jewish people: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 121.

DEW, unbelief: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1040.

WHEEL, this world: ibid., 1041.

The BURNING BUSH, not consumed, signified the Jewish people: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

JEWISH PRIESTHOOD is a whitewashed wall: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 331.

WILLOWS. The Jews are those willows on which the instruments of song were hung: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 127.

HEDGE, Gentile peoples: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1041.

SERVANT, the Jewish people: servant: id., ibid., 1051.

SEAL, the Gentile people: id., ibid., 1053.

FLINT, the Gentile people: ibid., 1054.

WILDERNESS, Gentilism: ibid., 1059; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 269.

THORNS OF THE WORLD signify the sins by which the Jewish people, fiercely aroused in their transgressions, burned as though with a rebuking fire: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.

SHUNAMMITE. The Shunammite signifies the Synagogue, before Christ’s coming captive in the devil’s bond and despised by God: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1093; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1061.

SYCAMORE, the Jewish people: ibid., 1053.

The SYNAGOGUE is sinful and is the mother of Antichrist, who will be born from it: id., CVIII, 1171. The Synagogue: mother-in-law: id., CXII, 1057.—Sister: St. Eucherius, L, 755.—Ostrich: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 79.

TABERNACLE denotes Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1062.—Tabernacles are the privileges of the Jews: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 363.

BULLS, the Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1063.—The leaders of the Jews are signified by bulls: Cassiodorus, LXX, 157.

TENT, the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.

EARTH. The Synagogue and Gentilism: earth: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 239.—Earth: the Israelite people, the company of the scribes and priests of the Synagogue, Gentilism: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.

The TWO SMOKING FIREBRANDS are a type of two kingdoms destined to end: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 248, 249.

TYRE denotes Gentilism: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 832, 1078.

BREASTS. Jews and Gentiles: breasts: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 221.

UNICORNS are called Jews because they accept a single Testament: Cassiodorus, LXX, 200; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 747.

WOMB is the name given to the Synagogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1066.

COW. Cows signify the Jewish people: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1362.—The Jews are called a cow: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1072.

FLEECE signifies the Jewish people: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 992; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1036.

BRAMBLES are called Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1074.

VILLAGE, Gentile peoples: ibid., 1078.

VINE signifies the people of Israel and the Jewish people: CXI, 507. The Synagogue; the Church from among the Gentiles: id., CXII, 1079.—The Synagogue is called a vine: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 786.—The Jews are called God’s vine: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1065.—Gentiles and Jews beginning to believe are signified by flowering vines: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 949.—The flowering vines which give fragrance are the nations that, having heard the word of faith, spread the fragrance of good works: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1113.

ROD. Nations and Jews are signified by two rods: Rupert, CLXVIII, 786.

VIRGIN, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080.

MEN OF BLOOD are rightly called the Jews, who condemned the blood of the Innocent One by a sacrilegious crime: Cassiodorus, LXX, 411.

CALF, the Jewish people: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1082.—The Jews are called calves because, ignorant of God’s yoke, they indulge in unconsidered and shameless wantonness: Cassiodorus, LXX, 157.

## ARTICLE X. Allegories concerning heretics and sinners

FIR TREES, powerful and unfruitful persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.

MISCARRIED CHILDREN, human imperfection: ibid.

ABYSS signifies the multitude of the wicked: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1732.—Abyss: the darkness of the wicked man, and every utterly despairing person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 852.—The abyss is called the despairing mind, the hearts of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 284.

HAWK, every rapacious person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.—The officials and exactors of prelates are likened to hawks: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 93.

VINEGAR, every sluggard: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.

Every FLATTERER is a traitor: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 142.

EGYPT is always taken to mean this world: St. Jerome, XXII, 487.—Egypt is frequently used as a figure of the whole age, from which one must depart spiritually: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 326.—Egypt is this world, which afflicts the Christian people with diverse calamities: Cassiodorus, LXX, 964.—It signifies affliction, which does not otherwise release the souls of the faithful unless they are burdened in it by harsh labours: Cassiodorus, LXX, 964.—Every sinful nation is called Egypt and Ethiopia, from species to genus: Tertullian, I, 635.

AIR, the mind of every worldly person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.—The instability of worldly minds: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 48.

BRONZE, a hard heart: ibid., 315.

ETHIOPIANS signify sinners: ibid., 918; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 271.

ETHIOPIA, the assembly of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 918.

FIELD, the life of every negligent person: ibid., 854.

LAMBS denote wanton persons: CXI, 202; CXII, 855.

FARMER, every reprobate person: ibid., CXII, 855.

WINGS, the thoughts of the hypocrite, the desires of the rapacious: ibid., 857.

AMORITE. By the Amorite a part of reprobate humanity is denoted: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 214.

CORNER, the hearts of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859.

SOUL. A soul desiring fleshly things is compared to a woman who has no husband as ruler: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 479.

ANIMAL, the carnal man: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—Animals signify brutish people, thinking only of earthly things: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 199. Animals: the covetous; the two thieves crucified with Christ: id., CXII, 859.

ANTICHRIST, the head of all wicked persons: St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 69.—The tail of Behemoth: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 646.—Cerastes and serpent: ibid., 596; Alcuin, C, 564.—A man assumed by the devil: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 648, 700, 709.—A condemned man: ibid., 428.—A sinful man: ibid., 486.—The devil’s sword: ibid., 726.—A lion in his lair: Cassiodorus, LXX, 88.—King of pride: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 741.—A vessel of damnation: ibid., 93.—A vessel of the devil: id., LXXVI, 428, 716.—Antichrist is likened to the head of an asp and the tongue of a viper: id., LXXV, 1090.

BEE, an unclean sinner; detractors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859.

WATER, the pleasures of the reprobate: ibid., 860.—By the name waters are understood sinful peoples: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1644.—The waters of contradiction are persecuting peoples: id., ibid., 1865.—We should understand waters and abysses as the wicked: Cassiodorus, LXX, 730.

EAGLE signifies philosophers and sophists: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 378.

NORTH WIND, unbelieving or evil persons: St. Eucherius, L, 739.—By the name North are denoted sinners: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1019.—Persons to be rejected: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 961.—North: the coldness of sinners: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 59.—The North is the forerunner of evil: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 760.

SPIDER, human frailty: St. Eucherius, L, 754; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.—The confidence of hypocrites is rightly said to resemble spiders’ webs, because everything for whose attainment they toil is scattered by the wind of mortal life: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 845.

TREE, the mass of the reprobate; heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 865.

BOW, the snares of those who strike: id., ibid., 862.—Of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 324.

SAND, the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 849, 949.—By the name sands of the sea are understood weak and carnal persons in the Church: St. Augustine, XXXII, 336.

RAM, heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 863.—Rams signify wicked leaders: id., CXI, 1202.

EAR OF GRAIN, reprobate rich persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 436.

ARMS, the heart of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.

ARMED MAN, every proud person; tyrants: ibid., 865.

REED, a sinner, or one weak in faith, or in some temptation: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—The unstable, the vicious: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 949.—Reed: the carnal mind: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 427.

RIDER, a lover of this world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.

SHE-ASS, the flesh, or a people lacking knowledge of God: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—The lustful; wanton impulses: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.—The asses of Kish are sinful souls: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 249.

ASS, anyone serving the weak; the sluggishness of fools: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.—The ass is a type of those desiring earthly affairs: id., CIX, 37.—By the name asses are sometimes denoted the sluggishness of fools, sometimes the immoderate lustfulness of wanton people: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 537, 578, 1149; LXXIX, 79; St. Eucherius, L, 752; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 88.

ASP, every reprobate person; the deceitful: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.—An asp is one who disdains to hear the word of God: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 129.—The obstinate and stubborn are like an asp: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 236.

GOLD, the wisdom of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.

BIRD, every unstable person: ibid., 871.—A talkative soul is compared to a variegated bird: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 967.—Proud persons are called birds: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 65.

The BUILDERS OF THE TOWER OF BABEL are a type of the proud: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 813.

BABYLON signifies this world: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 336; XXXVII, 1659; Alan of Lille, CCX, 248.—Babylon and Jerusalem are figures of the righteous and the reprobate: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 773.—Babylon has the devil as king; Jerusalem has Christ as king: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 773.—Babylon began from Cain, Jerusalem from Abel: ibid., 733, 773.—Who belong to Babylon and who to Jerusalem: ibid., 733.—Babylon, a type of the society of the wicked: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 337.—Babylon is called the city of the devil: id., XLI, 550; XLIII, 56.—Babylon is an earthly habitation, and its rivers are all temporal enticements, whether in conduct or in opinions: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 390.—Babylon is called the city of the reprobate, the wicked mind, the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.—The wretched daughter of Babylon is itself the same as Babylon; in its progeny it is both mother and daughter—mother by begetting, daughter by succeeding—certainly unhappy and wretched, since it is begotten and begets for destruction: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 392, 396.

The BABYLONIAN CITY is the society of all the lost, and itself possesses an earthly kingdom: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 208.—Through love of the world, every wicked person labours at the building of Babylon: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 597.

BEAST, the irrational mind; the society of the reprobate; any simple-minded persons; unbelievers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 875.—Beasts: savage persons: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—Beasts: the host of Antichrist’s preachers; the irrational mind: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 106.

OX, the madness of the lustful: id., ibid., 94.—Oxen: the senselessness of fools; the life of each person at work: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—The madness of the lustful, or the devil in his members—that is, heretics—is compared to an ox: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 201, 208.

CLUSTER, the ungodly: id., CXII, 867.

ARM, Antichrist: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 192.—The pride of Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.

CORPSE denotes anyone fallen into sin: ibid., 878.—Corpses are called the bodies of unbelievers: St. Eucherius, L, 756.

REED, hypocrite: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.

DARKNESS, the confusion of error and of the mind: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 381.

CAMEL, rich persons respectable in worldly goods, or distorted in their morals: St. Eucherius, L, 752.

CAMON. Heretics or evil Catholics may appropriately be understood under the name Camon: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1177.

FIELD, those humbled from the swelling of pride: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 257.

DOG, negligent preachers: St. Eucherius, L, 754.—An shameless sinner; a most worthless person; detractors; evil preachers devoted to talkativeness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 883.—Flatterers; heretics: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 102.

HEAD, a proud person, Antichrist, the enemy’s concupiscence, the exaltations of the proud: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.—The heads of Christ’s enemies are heretics: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 96.

COALS, sinners, wicked persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.—Minds cold in sins: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 359.

SEDGE-BED, the life of hypocrites: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 887.

FLESH, Antichrist: St. Eucherius, L, 754.—Carnal persons, the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 886.—The body of death: St. Augustine, XLIV, 676.—The Lord’s reprobate disciples: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 207.—A domestic enemy, an instrument of the devil: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 504.—The fox’s den: ibid., 456.—In Scripture flesh is used for the earthly human being: St. Ambrose, XIV, 261.—For corruption: St. Augustine, XLII, 250.—Those who live in the world according to the flesh are called by the name “flesh and blood”: St. Augustine, XXXII, 631.—By the name “flesh and blood” may be understood either carnal prudence or corruption: St. Augustine, XLV, 1602.

CASTLE is the sinful soul: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 872.

FORTRESS. The devil uses our flesh as a fortress: ibid., 81.—Camps: persecutors: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 889.

CHAIR. The chair of the ungodly is a chair of pestilence, because by its contagion it infects even the will of a religious mind: St. Hilary, IX, 253.

TAIL, Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 890.

CAVERN, the heart of the wicked; the preachings of heretics: ibid., 890.—A wicked heart: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 275.

CEDAR, every proud person; powerful secular persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891.—Cedar signifies proud heretics or philosophers: id., CXI, 517.—Cedar: the proud power of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 334.—In Sacred Scripture the name cedar denotes the rigid arrogance of the wicked or their proud power: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 649, 1166.—Cedars: the proud and exalted: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

WAX, every sinner: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.

CERASTES, Antichrist: ibid., 893.

HIND, a negligent preacher: ibid., 893.

NECK, the exaltations of the proud: ibid., 893.

WHALE, the proud height of worldly dominion: ibid., 893.—Carnal persons are denoted by great sea-creatures: Venerable Abbot Godefrid, CLXXIV, 461.

FOOD, the possession of hypocrites: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.

[Col. 0189] HAIRCLOTH, the coarse minds of human beings: ibid., 894.—Haircloth: a type of the penitent person: id., CXI, 343.

ASHES signify the emptiness of human frailty: ibid., 280. Ashes are a figure of sinners: ibid., 1222. Ashes: a sinner: id., CXII, 895.

CISTERN, the wicked mind: ibid., 896.—Heretics are cisterns: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 289.

CITY is said to mean the thoughts of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 389.—The sinful soul is called a city of blood: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 570.

Every FLATTERER is blind in mind: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 142.

HEAVEN. By the name heaven are understood spiritual and carnal persons in the Church: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 264. By the name heavens are denoted weak persons: id., XXXVII, 1959.

HILLS, the proud: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 286.

SERPENT, Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 126.

DOVE, a fool: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.

CONCUBINES, imperfect souls: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 934.—The souls of the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.—Vain preachers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 93.

THE INTERCOURSE of Lot’s daughters with him is a figure of those who misuse the Law: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 720.

COUNSELLORS, wicked teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.

THE CONVENTICLES OF HERETICS should be called not churches but councils of the devil: St. Leo, LVI, 887.

HORN, an opponent of the Law; the defenses of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.

BODY, the multitude of the reprobate: ibid., 902.

RAVEN, a figure of sinners: St. Hilary, IX, 874; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 253.—Raven: the obstinate and shameless: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 902.—Ravens are irreligious men clothed inseparably in the blackness of sins and never shining forth with any brightness of conversion: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1037.—The raven signifies the blackness of sinners or demons, or the sinner’s slowness to repent: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252.

BEDCHAMBER, gatherings of evil persons: id., CXII, 904.

GNAT, Barabbas the robber: ibid., 905.

STALK, every dissembler: ibid., 904.—Stalks: hypocrite: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 436.

CHARIOT is the soul which has good or evil horses: St. Ambrose, XIV, 727.—Pharaoh’s chosen chariots signify tyrants persecuting Christians: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 639.

SKIN, every reprobate person; every weak person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905.—Skin: one devoted to outward care: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 205.

CYMBAL, the preaching of Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 895.

DOG-FLY, the malice of the wicked: ibid., 895.

DAMASCUS is called the mass of the reprobate: ibid., 906.

TEETH, detractors: ibid., 907; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 885.—Those who bite: ibid.—Persecutors of the good: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 178.—Persecutors of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 907.—Wicked preachers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 178.

WILDERNESS, the ungodly; the wicked mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 938.—The heart of the sinner may be called a wilderness: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 986.—Wilderness: the heart of unbelievers; the doctrines of heretics: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 268.

DETRACTORS are compared to swine and dogs: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 194.

DAY, the prosperity of the wicked; the condition of evil persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.

FLOOD signifies the error of heretics: id., CXI, 329.

RICH MAN, a lover of the world: id., CXII, 911.

HOUSE denotes the hearts of the reprobate; the house of the devil, the gathering of all evil persons: id., CXI, 389. House: the wicked soul: id., CXII, 911.—The embittering house is the house of the disobedient: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1259.—The exterminated house can aptly be called the synagogue of heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 907.

BACK, wicked subjects; the mind of the reprobate: id., CXII, 912.

DRAGON, Antichrist: ibid., 906; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 124.—An open persecutor: St. Eucherius, L, 754.—Evil persons: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 124.

LEADER, wicked teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 913.—Leaders: authors of errors: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 151.—Leaders: heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 448; CXII, 913. Jews, or wicked teachers: id., CXI, 448.

KID, a sinner; the reprobate: id., CXII, 914.

ELEPHANT signifies a sinner monstrous in crimes and filthy in the ugliness of his misdeeds: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222; St. Eucherius, L, 748.

[Col. 0190] HORSE, every irrational person: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—Carnal power: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 213.—The ungodly, the blind, a persecutor, a type of heretics, Antichrist, the lustful, the proud and rich: id., CXII, 916. Horses are understood as sinners and lustful people: id., CXI, 213.—By the name horses the life of the wicked is denoted: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1173.

HYRAXES, a weak people who made themselves homes in the rocks: St. Eucherius, L, 751.

OUR EVE, our flesh: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 459.

FACE, the foreknowledge of Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 920.

FLOUR, the thought of the wicked: ibid., 921.

BUNDLE, the gatherings of the condemned: ibid., 920.

EMBER, the wicked mind: ibid., 923.

HAY, every carnal person: ibid., 924.

IRON, the malice of the wicked: ibid., 925.—Iron is called one who does not abandon the malice of harming: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 312.

FIG, heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 926.

DAUGHTER, worldly persons: ibid., 927.—The preachings of heretics: constructed daughters: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1259.

SON, heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 927.

PIPE, the words of wicked persons: ibid., 929.

FLOWER, the tender and unwise: ibid.

WAVES, persecutors; the malice of the wicked: ibid., 935.—The paths of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 303.

RIVER, the crimes of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933.—The doctrine of heretics: Rupert, CLXVII, 1760.—Rivers: unbelieving peoples: St. Eucherius, L, 742.

STREAM, the flow of false believers: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 291.—The river of Egypt: the corruption of human nature: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 841.

MONEYLENDERS are compared to Judas and the devil: St. Ambrose, XIV, 984.—To the sea: ibid., 765, 776.

LEAVES are evil persons; the leaves of the fig tree signify evil persons: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 145.

OPENING, the wicked mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 230.

FURNACE, Antichrist: ibid., 931.

PIT is the condemnation of sinners; pit: the condemnation of Antichrist: id., CXI, 409.

PITFALL, deceit or a snare leading to death; heretical deception: ibid.

FRUIT, Antichrist: id., CXII, 938.

SMOKE, the doctrine of heretics: ibid., 935.—The reprobate are like smoke, dust, and wax: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1142.

SLING, the instability of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935.

FOUNDATION, the exaltations of the proud: ibid. The foundations of the mountains: the hopes of the proud: id., CXI, 359.

THIEF, a heretic; every hidden enemy: id., CXII, 937.—Heretics are called thieves: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1089.

GLUTTONS are called sinners of the earth: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 45.

HUNCHBACK, every covetous person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 946.

GIANT, proud persons; those in despair: ibid.—The curious are compared to the giants of old: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 31.

SWORD is called a persecutor; Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 94.—The flattering persuasion of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 322.

GRAVEL, the unstable mind; the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 942.

HAIL, the hard and cold hearts of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 66.

STEPS, the actions of the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 945.

FLOCK, the gathering of sinners: id., CXI, 204.—The gatherings of the reprobate: id., CXII, 945.

GRIFFINS may signify the ferocity of persecutors and the pride of the proud: id., CXI, 222.

PILOT. The curious preacher is like the nauseated pilot of a ship: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 40.

DROP. Drops: the opinions of heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 947.—Heretics are compared to dew and drops of the night: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 223; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1181.

HERETICS, corrupt in mind: St. Eugyppius, LXII, 763. Ever discordant: ibid., 597. Heretics belong to Antichrist: ibid., 779.—Like the heads of a hydra: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 919.—Shapeshifters and hypocrites: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1091, 1093.—Foxes to be caught: John Algrin, CCVI, 316.—Heretics are called muddy water: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1392. Savage—indeed, beasts—in the Church of God: ibid., 965.—Ravening wolves: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 318.—Stiff-necked bulls: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 965.—The venom of asps: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 698.—Little foxes demolishing the Lord’s vineyard: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 215.—Foxes: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 677; Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1118.—Heretics are compared to adulterers: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1077.—To serpents: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1372.—Heretics are signified by Samson’s foxes: Alan of Lille, CCX, 212.—Heretics dig a well of calumny and schism: Abbot Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 196.

SPEAR is called the doctrine of heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 948.—A spear: the raging persecution of the wicked: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 327.

GRASS denotes carnal persons: ibid., 419.

HEROD, dissemblers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 961.

HE-GOAT indicates the spirit of the sinful human being: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 1069.—He-goats: sinners: St. Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 246.—Antichrist is signified by the he-goat: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 819.

SWALLOW, the proud: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 954.

KID, sinners, the pleasure-loving, the reprobate: ibid., 953.—Kids: sinners: St. Eucherius, L, 752; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 286.—Antichrist is signified by the kid: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1802.

MAN, a wicked person; Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 955.—Man is called every carnal person: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 135.

DROPSICAL MAN, every avaricious person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 953, 1088.—The avaricious person is like a dropsical man: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 106.

Every AVARICIOUS PERSON is an idolater: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 51.—Whatever can be said of idols and idolaters can rightly also be said of heresies and heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 735.

FIRE is called the deceit of Antichrist: id., CXII, 966.

WICKED MAN, every reprobate person; Antichrist: ibid., 970.—The ungodly are signified by the Philistines: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 661.

HELL, all the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 970. The inventors and constructors of perverse doctrines are heresiarchs: id., CIX, 943.

THE DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM are weak souls: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1205; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 321.

JOB. Heretics are signified by Job’s friends: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 252, 756; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 50.

JUDGES are called evil prelates: id., CXII, 973.

BEAST OF BURDEN, one lacking understanding or eloquence: St. Eucherius, L, 752.—Beasts of burden: the lustful: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 973.—Beasts of burden are called carnal people, brutish minds, persons duller in understanding: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 85.

LIZARD, the way of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 979.

LAKE is called the depth of sins: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 803.

LEFT HAND, the reprobate: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 199.

LAMIAE. Heretics are compared to lamiae: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 816; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 442; Alan of Lille, CCX, 113.

LAMP, the deceits of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 981.

STONE, an ungodly person: ibid., question 81.—Stones: the foolish and hard-hearted: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—The unrepentant heart is said to be like a stone: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 250, 547. Evil ministers are called stones scattered at the head of all streets: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1199, 1200.

CEILINGS signify hearers: Alan of Lille, CCX, 64.

The SNARE or bird-trap of hunters is the love of this life; the pain of this snare is escaped by sparrows—that is, all humble believers—through the protection of heavenly election: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 369.

BRICK, the earthly mind; the lustful mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 982.

LIONESS, the proud or headlong: St. Eucherius, L, 748.

CAULDRONS represent vain persons: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 496.

EMBASSY, the reconciliation of sinners: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 984.

ENVOY, the preachers of Antichrist: ibid., 984.

LAW-GIVER, Antichrist: ibid., 984.

LION, every cruel person; Antichrist: ibid., 983.—Antichrist; every ravager: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 108.—Lions are the leaders of Babylon who made the land of Judaea a wilderness and destroyed that city by fire: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 815.—The lairs of lions are the hearts of the perverse: Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1160.

LEPROSY. In the examination of leprosy diverse heretics are represented: [Col. 0192] St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 774.—The bitterness of heretics is signified by death in leprosy: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1263.

LEPERS, heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 803.

HARE, every wicked person yet learned in the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 984.

LUSTFUL PEOPLE are called sinners of the earth: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 46.

WOOD, the exalted person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.—Woods: the wicked: ibid., 986.—Sinners assigned to fire: St. Eucherius, L, 742.—Woods are called the exalted heart, the unjust person: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 329.

TONGUE, heretical doctrine; worldly doctrine: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 985.

PLACE, the heart of adolescents: ibid., 987.

LOCUST, flatterers; heretics: ibid., 988.—Vain people: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 346.—Locusts: peoples; the tongue of flatterers; or the life of preachers: St. Eucherius, L, 748.—The falsehood of heretics is represented by the locust: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 605.

SPEECH. The doctrines of heretics are forms of speech and sacred chatter: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 4271.

LOT. Heretics are signified by Lot’s wife: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 668.

LAMP, the glory of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989.

MOON is called the instability of fools: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 40.

LUPUS (WOLF), any rapacious person: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 115.---The wolf signifies heretics or deceitful men: St Eucherius, L, 748; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 233.---Wolves are tyrants: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1088.---Evil prelates are wolves among lambs: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 570.

MANUS (HAND) denotes the power of Antichrist, the enemy’s cunning: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 993.

MARE (SEA) signifies persecutors of the Church: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1126; Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 315.---All unbelievers: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1748.---Sinners agitated by the waves of vices: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 311.---Wicked people; the pleasure of worldly persons: idem, CXII, 995.---The sea, as a figure, denotes this age, bitter through falsehood and turbulent with waves: St Augustine, XXXVI, 1478. The sea is like secular life: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 292. The human race, deeply inquisitive through the vice of the first man, stormily swollen and unstably fluid, is compared with the sea: St Augustine, XXXII, 911.---The reprobate are signified by the deserted sea: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 822.---The sea’s depth: the heart of the ungodly: St Augustine, XXXVI, 782.

MEMBRA (MEMBERS), the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 997.

MERCENARIUS (HIRELING), hypocrite: ibid., 998.---Hirelings are those serving the Lord not solely for divine love but for temporal reward: St Eucherius, L, 756.

MERETRIX (HARLOT), the sinful soul: St Eucherius, L, 756.---The defiled soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 998.

MERIDIES (MIDDAY), the ardour of carnal persons: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 388.

MESSIS (HARVEST), the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 998.

MILVUS (KITE) signifies the rapacious or the proud: St Eucherius, L, 748.---Kites: the rapacious: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 999.

MOAB, the wicked person: ibid., 1000.---Heretics are called Moab and the sons of Ammon: Rupert, CLXVIII, 665.

MONOCERON (UNICORN), any proud or violent person, or one holding to a single Testament: St Eucherius, L, 748.

MONS (MOUNTAIN), proud persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1001; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1120.---By mountains is shown the pride of persecutors: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 586.---Mountain: a heretic: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 252.---Heretics are called mountains of the world: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 363.---Mountains signify persons who both seek the heights of this world and, by senseless superstition, have led astray the rich and the powers of this world; they signify heretical doctrine and the heretics themselves: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359.---By mountains are prefigured the ungodly, who swell with proud efforts and attain, through an obstinate heart, the hardness of rocks: Cassiodorus, LXX, 691.---By mountains are denoted sinners: Alan of Lille, CCX, 215.

MORTUI (THE DEAD), sinners or unbelievers: St Eucherius, L, 756.

MULIER (WOMAN), voluptuaries: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1002.---Carnal minds: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 976; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 140. By the strange woman is understood the perversity of heretics, alien from Christ and the members of the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 690.---The foolish and clamorous woman is heresy, plainly contrary to wisdom: ibid., 711.

MULUS (MULE), any sluggard: idem, CXII, 1003.

MUSCAE (FLIES) signify Egyptians because of their filth: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1396.---The reprobate: idem, CLXVIII, 1287.---Dead flies are heretics: idem, CLXX, 37.

[Col. 0193] MUSTELA (WEASEL), the life of wicked persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1004.

MYRICA (TAMARISK), the life of the ungodly: ibid., 999.

NAVES (SHIPS) are called lovers of the world: ibid., 1004.

NEMUS (GROVE), the life of wicked persons: ibid., 1005.

NITRUM (NITRE), the perverse mind: ibid., 1006.

NIX (SNOW), any sinner: ibid., 1006.---The cold hearts of the wicked: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 63.---Hypocrites are said to be like snow: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 435.

NOCTUA (OWL), a deceptive mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.

NOVACULA (RAZOR), every ungodly person: ibid., 1007.---The fraud and deceit of Antichrist are expressed in the razor: idem, CXI, 610.---The persecutor is like a razor: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 870.

NOX (NIGHT) is called heresy: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 859.---The life of false Christians: ibid., 859.---The life of sinners: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 788.---Night may be called a life spent in ignorance: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 465.

NUBES (CLOUDS), blindness of mind; the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1007.---All who are unstable; the proud heart: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 49.---Clouds are called the times of the wicked: St Eucherius, L, 738.---A cloud set before the eyes is a figure of the density of sinners: St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1178.

NUDUS (NAKED), lacking divine help or good works: St Eucherius, L, 756.

OBSTETRICES (MIDWIVES) are called sinners: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1009.

OCCIDENS (WEST). The sons of the West signify the ungodly and sons of darkness; likewise, persecutors of the Churches: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1154.

OCULUS (EYE), a heretic; preachers of Antichrist: idem, CXII, 1009.---The eye denotes wicked counsellors and wicked prelates: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 166.

OLEASTER (WILD OLIVE), a fruitless man: St Eucherius, L, 742.

OLEUM (OIL). Flatterers are poisonous oil: Bernard, CLXXXIII, 194.

OLIVA (OLIVE), hypocrite: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1011.

OLLA (POT), the reprobate mind: ibid., 1011.

OLUS (VEGETABLE). Vegetables denote the rich: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 784.---The ungodly are compared with hay and vegetables: Cassiodorus, LXX, 257.

ONAGER (WILD ASS), heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1012; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 116.---Heretics are like wild asses because, in their pleasures, they are estranged from the bonds of faith and reason: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1149.---The wild ass is every arrogant person, that is, a lover of vainglory: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 213.

ONOCENTAURUS (ONOCENTAUR), any reprobate and lustful person: idem, CXII, 1011.---The wanton and proud: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 121.

OS (MOUTH), preachers of Antichrist: ibid., 173.

OSSA (BONES), the more evil members in the body of Antichrist; the strength of worldly dignities: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 214.

OVES (SHEEP), reprobate persons; the wanton impulses of the flesh: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1014.

PALEA (CHAFF), sinners: St Eucherius, L, 752.---Chaff denotes the unstable: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1018.---The wicked: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 435.

PALIARUS (PALIURUS / CHRIST’S THORN), any person exceedingly powerful in malice: ibid., 429.

PALUDES (MARSHES), communities of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1019.

PANIS (BREAD), a sinner; heretical doctrine: ibid., 1021.

PARDUS (PANTHER), a sinner: St Eucherius, L, 748.---Any vicious person; a hypocrite: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1022.---A panther, variegated with the spots of sinners: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 114.---Heretics are like the panther: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 153.

PARIES (WALL) signifies the pretence of hypocrites: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 401.---The whitewashed wall is the ancient priesthood: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 331.

PASSER (SPARROW), unstable: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1022.

PECUS (CATTLE), a heretic, sinner, or covetous persons: ibid., 1024.

PELICANUS (PELICAN) denotes the sinner who, dwelling in the heart’s desert of this world and caught by the wretched allurements of this life, delights in the poison of diabolical persecution: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 608.

PELLIS (SKIN), movements of the flesh; the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1026.---Fools, evil subjects, gross human minds: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 202.

PES (FOOT), ministers of the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.

PHARETRA (QUIVER) denotes the machination of the wicked: ibid., 919.

PILOSUS (HAIRY ONE), one devoted to excess: ibid., 1028.

PISCIS (FISH), inquisitive persons: ibid., 1030.---Fishes: sinners: St Eucherius, L, 742.---Fishes denote the inquisitive and philosophers: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 666.

[Col. 0194] PLATEA (STREET), the glory of the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1020.

PLUMBUM (LEAD), weighed down by the burden of sins: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 318.

PORCI (SWINE) are called unclean and lustful persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 206.---Despisers of truth; evil persons: idem, CXII, 1032.---The lustful person is compared with a pig: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 265.

PORTA (GATE), the doctrines of heretics; wicked teachers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1031.---Evil teachers: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 402.---Heretics and false teachers are expressed by the name “gates”: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 385; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 71.

POTENTES (THE POWERFUL), the proud: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1032.

PRAEDA (PREY), the praise of hypocrites; the souls of the wicked: ibid., 1027.

PRAEDONES (ROBBERS), plunderers: ibid., 1027.

PRINCEPS (PRINCE), the proud; heretics: ibid., 1029.---Princes: authors of heretical perversity: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 155.

PRUNAE (COALS), the hearts of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1035.---Coals: minds burning with earthly desire: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 361.

PULVIS (DUST), sinners: St Eucherius, L, 742; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 332, 357.---Lightness of mind; every unstable person; a sinner; the frailty of man: idem, CXII, 1033.---The inconstancy of sinners; the weakness of the human condition: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 250.

PUTEUM (WELL), a heretic: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1035.

QUERCUS (OAKS) are called lustful persons: ibid., 1036.

RADIX (ROOT) denotes the offspring of the wicked: ibid., 1036.

RAMUS (BRANCH), wicked persons: ibid., 1037.

RANA (FROG) prefigures the talkativeness of heretics: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 297.---Frogs: heretics: St Eucherius, L, 734; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228; CXII, 1037; St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 247.---Flatterers are likened to branches: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 140.

REGULUS (BASILISK), Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1039; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 127.

REMIGES (ROWERS). Evil prelates are like evil rowers: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 531.

REX (KING), the wicked; the proud: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1037.

RHAMNUS (BUCKTHORN): nettles, thorns, thistles, paliuri, and plants full of prickles signify the harsh, deceitful, proud, and all wicked persons whom no good or gentle person can touch or correct without the sting of pain: St Eucherius, L, 742.---By the buckthorn, rightly, the type of Antichrist is signified: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1171; CXII, 1037.

ROTA (WHEEL), the conduct of the reprobate: ibid., 1041.---The ungodly, while they roll about in evil thought, become like wheels: Cassiodorus, LXX, 590.

RUGA (WRINKLE), all pretenders: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1041.

RUPES (ROCK), every hardened person: ibid., 1042.

SACCULUS (LITTLE SACK), the negligent mind: ibid., 1043.

SAGITTAE (ARROWS), the deceits of the wicked: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 326.

SALICES (WILLOWS), proud persons barren in good works: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.---The reprobate on account of barrenness: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 336.

SALTATRIX (DANCING WOMAN). By the dancing woman, what better can we understand than the crowd of heretics, which, because of the instability of its mind, now chooses this thing, now that, and never knows how to remain in the state of truth? Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 820.

SANGUIS (BLOOD), malicious persons: idem, CXII, 1045.

SCIRPUS (RUSH), the life of hypocrites: ibid., 1057.---Any hypocrite: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 428.

SCUTUM (SHIELD), the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1061.

SEMEN (SEED), evil persons; the inciter of a holy man: ibid., 1048.

SENEX (OLD MAN), hardened in malice: ibid., 1049.

SEPULCRUM (TOMB), the body of a sinner containing within itself a soul dead through vices: St Eucherius, L, 757.---Tomb: the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1050.---The hypocrite is like tombs: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 812.

SERPENS (SERPENT), malicious people: St Eucherius, L, 754.---The serpent deceiving Eve is a symbol of heretics: St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 291.---A talkative man is called a serpent: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1229.---Disturbers of peace are denoted by the serpent in paradise: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 623.---Serpents are heretics: St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 493.

SERVUS (SERVANT), any person tempted: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1051.

SILIQUAE (PODS), secular doctrines: ibid., 164.

SINISTRA (LEFT HAND), reprobate people: ibid., 1055.

SOMNUS (SLEEP), any hypocrite: ibid., 1059.

SPELUNCA (CAVE), the wicked mind: ibid., 1050.

SPINA (THORN), preachers; heretics: ibid., 1056.

SPIRITUS (SPIRIT), the sinner’s desire; human pride: ibid.

[Col. 0195] SPOLIA (SPOILS), sinners: ibid., 1059.

STAMNUM (TIN), a pretender to holiness: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 318.

STELLA (STAR), hypocrites: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.---Stars: the hypocrisy of hypocrites: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 41.

STELLIO (SPOTTED LIZARD), every wicked person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1052.

STERCUS (DUNG), the hidden malice of the heart: ibid., 1053.

STERQUILINIUM (DUNGHILL). The hypocrite is compared with a dunghill: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 63.

STIPULA (STUBBLE), those dry toward faith, or the spirits of the dead: St Eucherius, L, 742.

STRUTHIO (OSTRICH) denotes every heretic or philosopher: St Eucherius, L, 748.---A hypocrite: ibid., 748; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 79.---An ostrich: every negligent preacher; pretenders: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1061.

SUDES (STAKES), the wicked: ibid., 1061.

SUPERBIA (PRIDE), a kind of heretics: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1089.

SUS (SWINE), a worldly person: Alan of Lille, CCX, 238.---An unclean sinner: St Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1061.

SYCOMORUS (SYCAMORE), the folly of the world: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 338.

TABERNACULUM (TENT) denotes the flesh of the ungodly; the crimes of the reprobate: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1062.

TALPAE (MOLES), that is, either [uncertain: *la*] or heretics who do not see the truth: St Eucherius, L, 754.

TAURUS (BULL), the proud: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 100.---The bull’s neck: pride; heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1063.---Heretics are compared with bulls: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 757.

TELA (WEB), the state of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1064.

TENEBRAE (DARKNESS) denotes sinners: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 378.

TENTORIUM (TENT), all the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.

TERRA (EARTH) denotes man himself or a sinner: St Eucherius, L, 742.---Earth signifies sinners: Alcuin, C, 590.---Earth: those who think earthly thoughts; Antichrist: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1065.---Earth is called the sinful soul, the sinner, those occupied with earthly things: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 239.---Dry ground: unfruitful persons: St Eucherius, L, 742.

THESAURUS (TREASURE), the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1066.

TIGRIS (TIGER), hypocrite: ibid., 1066; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 113.---Female arrogance: St Eucherius, L, 748.

TINEA (MOTH), any heretic: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1067.---Heretical perversity: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 133.---Heretics are compared with the moth that corrupts everything: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 51.

TORRENS (TORRENT), inventors of heresies: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 237.---The torrents of iniquity are the multitude of wicked people troubling the Church: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 91.

TRIBULUS (THISTLE), heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1067.

TYRUS (TYRE): the sailors and pilots of Tyre are compared with heretics: idem, CX, 782.

ULMUS (ELM), any worldly person: idem, CXII, 1085.

ULULAE (SCREECH-OWLS) are called the wicked: ibid., 1084.

UMBRA (SHADOW), any ungodly person: ibid., 1085.---The wicked: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 382.

URSUS (BEAR), savage leaders or plotters: St Eucherius, L, 748.---Any cruel or unclean person: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.

UTER (WINE-SKIN), the minds of the wicked: ibid., 1086.

UTER (WINE-SKIN). By the wine-skin we understand the flesh of this death: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 350.

VACCAE (COWS), persons full of carnal vices: St Eucherius, L, 752.---Foolish souls: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1082.---Cows signify souls susceptible to seduction: St Augustine, XXXVI, 836.

VALLIS (VALLEY), the minds of the wicked: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1072.

VAS (VESSEL), heretics; reprobate persons: ibid., 1073.

VENTER (BELLY) denotes an ungodly exactor: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 634, 635.

VENTUS (WIND), malice: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1071.

VESICA (BLADDER), the swelling of one growing proud: ibid., 1077.

VESPER (EVENING), Antichrist: ibid., 1076.

VESTIS (GARMENT). By a woollen garment hypocrites are signified: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 936.

VIA (WAY). This world is called the way of sinners: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 61.

VIDUA (WIDOW), the wicked soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.---The heretical people: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 143.

VILLA (ESTATE), the mass of the ungodly: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.

VINEA (VINEYARD), the life of the negligent person; a hypocrite: ibid., 1079; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 341.

[Col. 0196] VINUM (WINE) denotes the pleasures of the damned: Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 228.

VIPERA (VIPER), wicked persons: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 128.

VIR (MAN), the soul’s error; heretics: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1080.

VIRGO (VIRGIN), the wicked mind: ibid.

VISCERA (INWARD PARTS), the pride of the wicked: ibid., 1081.

VISIO (VISION), the life of hypocrites: ibid.

VITIS (VINE), every person overthrown: ibid.

VITULA (HEIFER), the wicked mind: ibid., 1082.---The carnal mind: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 99.

VITULUS (CALF), the lascivious: St Eucherius, L, 752.---Our brutish and vicious flesh is signified by the calf: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 925.

VOLUCRES (BIRDS), all proud persons: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1083; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 127.---Birds denote the vain: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 677.---The birds of heaven are called proud persons: St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 68.

VULPES (FOXES), flatterers: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1080, 1081, 1089.---Detractors: ibid., 1081, 1089.---Deceitful persons: ibid., 1084.---Heretics: St Eucherius, L, 752; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 452; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 500; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225; CXII, 1084; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 1089; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1086, 1089; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 773.---The cunning sinner: St Eucherius, L, 752; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.---Persecutors: idem, CXII, 1084.---Seductive spirits: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1089.

VULTUS (COUNTENANCE), the wicked mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1083.

VULTUR (VULTURE), any rapacious person: ibid.

ZIPHAEI (ZIPHITES) denote sinners flourishing in this world: J. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 212.

## ARTICLE XI. Allegories relating to virtues and vices. I. Virtues.

ABIES (FIR), the height of contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 853.---Contemplation; heavenly virtues: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 336.---The fir signifies the virtues of contemplation, ever rising to the heights: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1275.

ABYSSUS (ABYSS), the judgment of human reason: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 284.

ACERVUS TRITICI (HEAP OF WHEAT), the increase of virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.

ACUS (NEEDLE), the piercing of sorrow: ibid.

ADEPS (FAT), spiritual desire, abundance, the goodness of the inward will: ibid.

AER (AIR), empty utterance: St Eucherius, L, 739.

AES (BRONZE), good action, strengthening: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 917.---Perseverance: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 728.---True fortitude; constancy in long-suffering: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 315.

AESTAS (SUMMER), a prefiguration of future joy: St Eucherius, L, 741.---Charity: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1060.

AGER (FIELD), a good work, the office of preaching, outward ceremonial observance, the heavenly homeland: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 854.---The Christian life is compared with the cultivation of a field: St Augustine, XL, 693.

AGGER (MOUND), clouds of temptations: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 271.

AGNA (EWE-LAMB), the active life: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 202; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 106.

AGNUS (LAMB), the active life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 855; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 768.---The lamb denotes simplicity, gentleness, and patience: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 903.

ALAE (WINGS): the soul’s two wings are knowledge and devotion: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 352.---Nature and grace: ibid., 356.---Hope and fear: ibid., 764.

ALOE (ALOES), the virtue of continence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857. Aloe and myrrh signify the mortification of the flesh: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1173.

ALTARE (ALTAR), devotion of heart, the secret place of heaven, the mind’s hidden sanctuary, faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 856.---The altar of God is our faith: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXIV, 277.---The altar of incense denotes action: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 758.---The bronze altar of sacrifices denotes the sacrifice of penitence: ibid., 768.

ALTITUDO (HEIGHT), the loftiness of rewards; prosperity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 857.

AMOR (LOVE) is the gate of death or life: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 809.

[Col. 0197] AMPHORA (AMPHORA), measure in contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 858.---An amphora of wine denotes the beginning of charity: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 46.

ANAGLIPHA (CARVED RELIEFS), varieties of good works: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859.

ANIMA (SOUL), the human soul, doctrine, intention: ibid., 852.---Soul: that which is loved more dearly; the mind’s intention: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 157.

ANIMALIA (ANIMALS), thoughts raised up from the earth: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 93.

ANNULUS (RING) denotes the seal of faith, or the germ of eternal blessedness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 848, 858.---A golden ring denotes eternal blessedness: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 749.

ANTRUM (CAVERN), thought: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 276.---Caverns: the heart’s secrets: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 859.

APIS (BEE), an image of the righteous: St Augustine, XLVI, 819.---A form of virginity or wisdom: St Eucherius, L, 748.---A sign of virginity and fruitfulness: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1254.

AQUA, AQUAE (WATER, WATERS), abundance: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 563.---Charity: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1353.---The grace of compunction: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 783.---Knowledge: Venerable Guibert, Abbot, CLVI, 534; Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1375.---Knowledge of preaching: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 960.---Sacred knowledge: idem, LXXVI, 100.---Prosperity: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 947.---Unformed spiritual life: St Augustine, XXXIV, 250.---Water: wisdom, compunction, human knowledge, worldly abundance, the historical sense, eternal refreshment, laments of humility: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---Water is called tribulation, holy knowledge, flowing speech, waves of sorrow, laments of humility: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 279.---A certain power subject to reason, by which God and truth are known through reason, has rightly been called water by divine authority: St Augustine, XXXIV, 232.

AQUILO (NORTH WIND), adversity: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 208.---Old age: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---The north wind signifies the harshness of threats: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1175.

ARATRUM (PLOUGH), the cultivation of righteousness; a good example: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.

ARBOR (TREE), humble knowledge of God, robust faith, good will: ibid., 865.---The bad tree signifies intention: Alan of Lille, CCX, 309.

ARCUS (BOW), human strength; the virtue of patience: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---Judgment: Alan of Lille, CCX, 205.

ARENA (SAND), the distress of this life, the instability of this age, love of the world, the frailty of things: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864, 949.

AREOLAE (LITTLE GARDEN-BEDS), the sweetnesses of virtues: ibid., 866.

ARGENTUM (SILVER), spiritual speech; poetic fictions: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 862.---Silver denotes knowledge: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 427.

ARIES (RAM) bears the form of gentleness: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 1031.

ARMA (ARMS), spiritual virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.---Human protections; the necessities of the present life: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 318.

ARMILLA (BRACELET), actions belonging to the Decalogue: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.

AROMATA (AROMATICS), pure thoughts, the sweetnesses of prayers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 866.---Good works: Alan of Lille, CCX, 83.---Aromatics are a symbol of virtues: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 797.---Sweet and holy affections are the bride’s aromatics: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 199.

ARUNDO (REED), weak help: St Eucherius, L, 742.

ASCENSUS (ASCENT), progress in the spiritual life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 867.

ASINA (SHE-ASS), the simple thoughts of the heart: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 90.

ASPIS (ASP). Temptation concerning the necessities of life is compared with an asp: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 240.

ATRIUM (COURTYARD), the course of the world, the commandments of charity, the secrets of heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 868.---The heavenly kingdom, present life, charity, contemplation, eternal life: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 416.---Courtyards signify the entrance of faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 39.

AURIS (EAR), the heart’s understanding; inward contemplation: idem, CXII, 871.---The ear of the heart is a gate: Alan of Lille, CCX, 582.---A ringing in the ears signifies love and fear of God: Venerable Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 430.

AURORA (DAWN) denotes humility: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 711.

AURUM (GOLD), the splendour of the heavenly homeland, the beauty of good spirits, the virtue of charity, spiritual wisdom, temporal eminence, the virtue of patience, the brilliance of secular pomp: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 870.---Gold: the splendour of the heavenly city, charity, the brightness of temporal glory, the splendour of holiness, natural ability: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 303.---Gold signifies faith: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1242.---The perfection of virtues: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 831, 832.---Excellence in holiness: St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 39.---Wisdom: St Augustine, XXXIV, 633; XXXVIII, 331; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 492; St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 427; CLXXXV, 46.---Knowledge of truth: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 684.---By gold wisdom and by silver prudence are figured: St Augustine, XXXVI, 911.---Gold signifies faith, but silver the eloquence of speech: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVII, 1346.

AUSTER (SOUTH WIND), the ardour of charity: St Augustine, XXXIII, 361.---The warmth of faith: St Eucherius, L, 739.---Holy devotion, the holiness of religious conduct, the secret place of heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 869.---Prosperity: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 208.---The gentleness of blandishments: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1175.

AZIMA (UNLEAVENED BREAD), purity of mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 872.

BACULUS (STAFF), the law of righteousness, pastoral cares: ibid., 873.---The discipline of the law, the support of consolation, pastoral care: St Eucherius, L, 738; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 344.

BALTEUS (BELT), continence, the virtue of continence, mortification of the flesh, unity of faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 873.

BARBA (BEARD), confidence: ibid.---An indication of virtue: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 884.---The adornment of virtue; confidence in one’s own virtue: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 789.

BASES (BASES). The golden bases are wisdom and goodness, on which stand the marble columns, that is, mercy and truth: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1200.

BDELLIUM, a black aromatic tree, signifies prayer: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 617.

BINARIUS NUMERUS (THE NUMBER TWO), the two commandments of charity, understanding and operation, two works of compunction: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 439.

BITUMEN (BITUMEN), the strength of charity; virginity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 876.

BOS (OX), good work, gentle thoughts: ibid., 877.---Good action: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 94.---The ox is the form of obedience: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 1033.

BOTRUS (CLUSTER OF GRAPES), spiritual joy; the work of righteousness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 876.

BRACHIUM (ARM), the work of charity; vigorous works: ibid., 875.---Action: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 192.---The arm denotes work and strength: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXVI, 978.---Arms denote works: Alan of Lille, CCX, 106.

BUTYRUM (BUTTER), the contemplative life, the fruitfulness of good action, the richness of spiritual virtues, the anointing of penitence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 877.

BUXUS (BOX TREE), the greenness of faith: ibid., 878.

BYSSUS (FINE LINEN), a type of chastity: idem, CXI, 578. Righteousness, affliction of the flesh, virginity, the array of virtues, outward worship: idem, CXII, 876.---Fine linen is a symbol of purity of heart: Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 388.---Twisted fine linen, morally understood, is continence of the flesh: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 695.

CADAVERA (CORPSES) are called our prayers: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 878.

CAELATURAE (ENGRAVINGS), works of virtues: ibid., 892.

CALAMUS (REED), the brilliance of temporal glory: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 425.

CALCEAMENTA (SHOES), affections and advances: Alan of Lille, CCX, 97.---A shoe: action, outward goods, mortifications of the members: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 880.

CALCANEUM (HEEL), the end of our action; our progress: ibid.; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 238.

CALOR (HEAT), the sweetness of charity; desire for righteousness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 880.

CAMELUS (CAMEL), arrangements of earthly matters; distorted and swollen thoughts: ibid., 882; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 92.---By camels, which have something clean when they chew the cud and something unclean when they do not at all divide the hoof, good dispensations of temporal matters may be understood: St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 590.

CAMINUS (FURNACE), charity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 882.

CAMPUS (PLAIN), the broad life: ibid.

CANCELLI (LATTICES) denote obscure doctrine: Alan of Lille, CCX, 69.

CANDELABRUM (LAMPSTAND), contemplation; the state of the body: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 882.---The lampstand denotes the purity of inward contemplation: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 757.

CANDOR (WHITENESS), innocence; the beauty of the heavenly homeland: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 882.

CANTUS (SONG). Preaching is denoted by song: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1037.

CAPILLUS (HAIR), subtlety of thoughts; superfluous thoughts: [Col. 0199] Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.---Hairs are most subtle thoughts: Rupert, Abbot, CLXVIII, 885.---Flowing thoughts of the mind; superabundant earthly substance: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 163.---Thoughts: Alan of Lille, CCX, 77, 92.---The hairs of the head are the counsels of the heart: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 398. The bride’s hairs are holy meditations: ibid., 451.

CAPRA (GOAT), contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 886.

CAPREA (ROE DEER) figures contemplation: Alan of Lille, CCX, 92. The roe deer and the fawn are the endowments of the glorified body: ibid., 71.---By stags and roe deer are understood faith, hope, and charity: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 496.

CAPUT (HEAD), faith, principle, the beginning of temptation, excellence, intention: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 884.---The head denotes the mind: Alan of Lille, CCX, 77.

CARBONES (COALS) are called the fire of charity, or of examples, or of penitence: St Eucherius, L, 738.---By coals may be understood prayers kindled by the fire of charity: Cassiodorus, LXX, 903.---Coals: the ardours of penitence, the burnings of charity, good examples: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.

CARBUNCULUS (CARBUNCLE), the light of great knowledge: ibid., 887.

CARDO (HINGE) can signify the firmness of right faith: idem, CXI, 400.

CARMELUS (CARMEL), knowledge of mysteries: idem, CXII, 887.

CARMEN (SONG), praise of God, heavenly glory, inward consolations: ibid.

CARO (FLESH), humble doctrines: ibid., 886.---Sensibility of heart: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 207.

CASEUS (CHEESE), firmness of mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 888.

CASIA (CASSIA), signifies exaltation: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 829.

CASTRA (CAMP), spiritual virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 889.

CATENAE (CHAINS), afflictions, spiritual virtues, present tribulations: ibid., 890.

CATHEDRA (CHAIR), good doctrine: ibid., 889.

CAUDA (TAIL), perseverance; the end of the age: ibid., 890.

CAUMO (BURNING HEAT), zeal for faith: ibid.

CEDRUS (CEDAR), faith in Christ: ibid., 891.---The loftiness of heavenly glory, hope, one made steadfast in the love of God, the height of virtues: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 334.---Cedar wood is a symbol of our hope, which ought firmly to dwell in heavenly things: St Augustine, XXXIV, 734.

CELLA VINARIA (WINE CELLAR) denotes contemplation: Alan of Lille, CCX, 66.---It is ecstasy: ibid.

CERVIX (NECK), good freedom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.---The uprightness of freedom: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 161.

CHARITAS (CHARITY), a faculty of the soul: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 741. The fruit of the vine: ibid., 1070.---Charity is called a burning pebble: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1035.---A house: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1083.---The single eye: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 407.---Charity is denoted by the bow: St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1041.---By gold: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 832.---By the sun’s brightness: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 711. By laughter: ibid., 716.---Charity is figured in the scarlet band: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 891.---Charity is like oil: Godfrey, Abbot, CLXXIV, 526, 533.

CHORUS (CHOIR), concord: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898.---The choirs of camps are assemblies of virtues: Alan of Lille, CCX, 97.

CIBARIA (PROVISIONS), spiritual refreshments; things pertaining to bodily sustenance: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 894.

CIBUS (FOOD), the communion of life; the doctrine of inward consolation: ibid., 893.---The soul’s food is penitence and doctrine: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1109.

CILICIUM (HAIRSHIRT) signifies the harshness and compunction of sinners: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 280; CXII, 894.

CINCINNI (CURLS), a gathering of thoughts: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 164.---Curls denote thoughts: Alan of Lille, CCX, 85.

CINGULUM (GIRDLE), the vigour of righteousness: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.

CINIPHES (GNATS), unrest of heart: ibid.

CINIS (ASHES), failure, penitence, humility, the corruption of mortality, the perfection of good works: ibid., 895.---Worldly care: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 362.

CINNAMOMUM (CINNAMON), humility: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.---The habit of penitents: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1172, 1258.

CIRCULUS (CIRCLE), heavenly protection: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.

CITHARA (HARP), right action, the active life, mortification of the flesh, joy, the sweetness of consolation: ibid., 897.

CIVITAS (CITY), human conduct, bodily senses: ibid.---City is called the heavenly homeland: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 389.

CLAMOR (CRY), the desire of the righteous: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 881.---A cry in God’s ears is vehement desire: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 247.

[Col. 0200] CLAUSTRUM (ENCLOSURE). Paradise is called an enclosure: idem, CLXXXIV, 1058.

CLAVI (NAILS), the commandments of charity, reason and understanding: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 881.

CLIBANUS (OVEN), good love: ibid., 894.

CLYPEUM (SHIELD), an exculpatory word, the defences of virtues, the virtue of patience: ibid., 895.---The fortification of virtues: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 321.

COCCUS (SCARLET), the ardour of charity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898; Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1151.---Scarlet twice dyed is love of God and neighbour: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 695.---The scarlet colour denotes charity: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 701.---The scarlet cloak denotes the twofold love of God and neighbour: Rupert, Abbot, CLXX, 160.

COELUM (HEAVEN), holiness of life; lofty modes of contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 287. Heaven is understood as holiness: ibid., 277.---The heavens concern the signification of a serene understanding of truth: St Augustine, XXXIV, 264.---By the higher regions of heaven charity is to be understood: idem, XXXVII, 1342.---By the first heaven humility, by the second charity, and by the third contemplation is understood: Wolbero, Abbot, CXCV, 1020.

COENA (SUPPER), the sweetness of contemplation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 892.

COGNITIO (KNOWLEDGE), approval; knowledge: ibid., 901.

COLLUM (NECK), the speech of preaching, the mind, faith, boldness, final exaltation: ibid., 898.---The neck is called humility: Alan of Lille, CCX, 81.---By the name “neck” understanding is denoted: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 984.

COLOR (COLOUR), the beauty of religious life; secular eloquence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900.---White colour is an indication of glory and joy: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 412.---Diversity of colours is diversity of virtues: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 766.

COLUMBA (DOVE), simplicity: St Eucherius, L, 748. — The active life; groans of repentance: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 898. — The dove, a symbol of charity and simplicity: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 972. — Of humility: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1001. — The dove signifies wisdom: St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 622. — The dove released from the ark signified virtue: St Ambrose, XIV, 391. — In the dove is displayed simplicity of heart: St Fulgentius, LXV, 581; St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 529. — A good intention is denoted by the dove: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 286.

COLUMNA (COLUMN), uprightness of faith; the inward virtues of the mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 899. The pillar of fire signifies a guilty conscience tortured; the pillar of cloud, a good conscience giving refreshment: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 786. — The two columns in Solomon’s Temple signify mercy and judgment: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1165. — The four columns are the cardinal virtues: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1027. — The five columns signify the five external senses: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 753.

COMAE (HAIR), thoughts of the mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 900.

COMEDERE (TO EAT), to learn; to fulfil: ibid., 901.

COMPAGES (JOININGS), intentions: ibid., 900.

COR (HEART), reason; will; sublime contemplation; thoughts: ibid., 901.

CORNU (HORN), strength; the defences of virtues: ibid., 903. — The horn denotes patience: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 978. Virtue: ibid., 1110. — Horns signify the new life: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 640.

CORONA (CROWN), victory; the reward of the kingdom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.

CORPUS (BODY), any one of our actions: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 157.

CORTEX (BARK), pleasures; historical senses: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904. — The historical sense; the covering of humility: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 397.

COSTAE (RIBS), spiritual strength; the faculties of the soul: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 224.

CRINES (LOCKS OF HAIR) denote thoughts: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 181.

CROCUS (SAFFRON), charity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904. — Abstinence is compared to saffron: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 719.

CRUS (LEG), good desires; supports of stability: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 905. — The bridegroom’s two legs are mercy and truth: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 927.

CUBILE (BEDCHAMBER), a good mind; heavenly rest; the rewards of the saints.

CUBITUS (CUBIT), good action; the multiplicity of the active life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904. — Action: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 194.

CULMUS (STALK), the state of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904.

CULTRUM (KNIFE), keenness of understanding: ibid., 905.

CYMBALUM (CYMBAL), services of charity: ibid., 895.

CYPHUS (CUP), heavenly doctrine; the law: ibid.

[Col. 0201] CYPRUS (HENNA), the refreshment of heavenly grace: ibid., 896.

DENTES (TEETH), inward faculties: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1222; CXII, 907; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 178. — Strengths of virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 907. — Teeth signify understanding: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 124. — Spiritual exercises: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 92.

DESERTUM (DESERT), holy manner of life; heaven: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 908.

DEXTERA, DEXTRA (RIGHT HAND), grace; salvation of the soul; good action; contemplation; patience; prosperity; exaltation in virtues; eternal life; favour: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909. — Everlasting life; that which is held of great value: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 198. — The right hand signifies power or piety: St Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 844. — Favour: ibid., 944. — Eternal things; resurrection: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1103. — Prosperity: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 56. — The right hand denotes happiness: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1426. — Mystically, the right hand denotes good works: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 729.

DEXTRALIA (RIGHT-HAND ORNAMENTS), ornaments of good works: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909.

DIES (DAY), justice; faith; prosperity. By “days” is also understood the illumination of divine grace through the various gifts of virtues: St Eucherius, L, 741. — Day: time; illumination of the mind; brightness of inward rest; inward goods: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 909. — The brightness of the future life; clarity of understanding: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 370. — A day signifies reward: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1156.

DIGITUS (FINGER), discernment; moderation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 910. — Fingers: discernment: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 200. — Fingers denote discerning works: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 86.

DILUCULUM (DAWN), the coming of inward brightness; zeal: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 910. — Knowledge of truth: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 366.

DIVITIAE (RICHES), counsels: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911. — The keen points of counsels: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 309.

DOMUS (HOUSE), the heavenly homeland; the delight of favour; diverse orders; a good conscience: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 911. — Conscience; the fabric of virtues: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 395.

DORMITIO (SLEEP), the rest of life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 913.

DORSUM (BACK), patience: ibid., 912.

EBRIETAS (DRUNKENNESS), the joy of supernal grace: ibid., 914.

EBUR (IVORY) is said to be chastity and strength: ibid., 913.

EDOM. — By the daughter of Edom is expressed the host of all persecutions of the Church: ibid., CXI, 1261.

EDUS (KID), groaning; repentance: ibid., CXII, 914.

ELATAE (ELEVATED [THINGS]), the spiritual triumphs of palms: ibid., 915.

ELECTRUM (ELECTRUM). Peace is compared to electrum: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 494.

ENSIS (SWORD), the rigour of repentance; the rigour of continence; the keenness of preaching: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 915.

EQUUS (HORSE), secular honour; works; thoughts: ibid., 916. — Temporal dignity; right intention: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 87. — The horses of the chariot of prudence are the five external senses: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 521.

EREMUS (WILDERNESS), an austere, secure, and tranquil life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 953.

ESCA (FOOD), simple doctrine; desire; sacrifices of the law: ibid., 917. — Clean and unclean foods signified that by alms all things are made clean: St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 775.

ESEBEN, a contrite heart: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 917.

EXITUS (DEPARTURE), compunctions; abandonment of sin: ibid., 919.

FACIES (FACE), intention; good conscience; action: ibid., 920. — Mind; intention and knowledge of the mind; thought of God; the presence of a thing; the punishment of chastisement: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 184.

FARINA (FLOUR), a pure thought: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 921.

FAUCES (THROAT), branches of knowledge; meditations of the heart; words: ibid., 923.

FAVILLA (GLOWING EMBER), remembrance of mortality: ibid.

FAVUS DISTILLANS (DRIPPING HONEYCOMB), the sweetness of merits: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 496.

FEMINALIA (BREECHES), insignia of chastity: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 923.

FENESTRA (WINDOW) is the hearing of faith or the understanding of the heart; sight, hearing, smell, and the other senses of the flesh; the thought of the flesh; or the mind’s own intention: ibid., CXI, 401. — Windows indicate our senses: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXXIV, 844; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 409. — Manifest doctrine: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 67.

FENUM (HAY), concupiscence: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1242. — A transitory thing; temporal supports: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 924.

FERMENTUM (LEAVEN), charity: ibid.

FERRUM (IRON), the gift of understanding; preaching; tribulation; [Col. 0202] harsh speech; spiritual strength; the necessity of the present life: ibid., 925. — Strength; the dart of preaching: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 342.

FESTUCA (MOTE), disturbance of mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 925.

FETUS GEMELLI (TWIN OFFSPRING) signify the two commandments of charity: that is, love of God and of neighbour: ibid., CXI, 202.

FICUS (FIG TREE), sweetness of mind; charity: ibid., CXII, 926.

FIDES (FAITH) is a lamp: Bernard, CLXXXIV, 522. — Faith is signified by a little boat: St Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1554. — By the first day: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 607. — Faith is compared to Lebanon: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 197. — The pupils of the eye: St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 741. — Shadows: ibid., CLXXXIII, 944.

FILIAE JERUSALEM (DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM) denote virtues: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 76.

FILIUS (SON), good works: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 927. — Virtues are signified by Job’s daughters: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 966.

FINIS (END), fulfilment; death of the flesh; inward thoughts; the extremity of the world: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 932.

FISTULA (PIPE), suggestion: ibid., 929. — Humility is expressed by a pipe: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1172, 1258.

FLAMMA (FLAME), knowledge; temporal glory; good preaching: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 921.

FLOS (FLOWER), the beauty of the world; the tenderness of first youth; the beginning of a good work: ibid., 929. — The flower of the garden: virginity; the flower of the field: martyrdom; the flower of the bridechamber: good action: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1009. — Flowers: an example of justice, or the beginning made by those who act well: St Eucherius, L, 742. — The glory of the present life; human favour: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 347. — Flowers denote faith: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1025. — Flowers denote those who are beginning, fruits those who are perfect: ibid.

FLUCTUS (WAVES), fear of God: St Eucherius, L, 742. — The turmoil of temptations: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 303.

FLUENTA (STREAMS), abundance of virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 936.

FLUMEN (RIVER), instability of the age; the transitory things of this world; tribulations: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933. — Actions of the world: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 295.

FLUVIUS (RIVER), abundance of inward refreshment; secular life; secular wisdom: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 934. — The course of mutability: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 291. — A river denotes heavenly grace: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 200. — The river going out from paradise denotes grace: Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 249. — The four rivers of paradise are the cardinal virtues: Venerable Godefrid, CLXXIV, 147.

FOLIUM (LEAF), the word of doctrine; or clothing and adornment together with the protection of divine grace: St Eucherius, L, 742. — Instability: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 939.

FONS (FOUNTAIN), spiritual doctrines; gifts of inward grace: ibid., 929. — Gifts of spiritual grace; streams of truth: Garner of St Victor, CXCVIII, 299. — The sealed fountain is wisdom: Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 186.

FORAMEN (OPENING), inward compunction; spiritual gifts: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 930. — Hidden inspiration: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 86. — FORNAX (FURNACE), tribulation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 931.

FORTES TRES DAVID (DAVID’S THREE MIGHTY MEN) signify wisdom, humility, and strength: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 167.

FOSSA (DITCH), humility; patience: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 932; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 275.

FOVEA (PIT), rejection of earthly things; a hiding place of defence: ibid., 274.

FRENUM (BRIDLE), affliction of the flesh: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 925.

FRIGUS (COLD), adversity: ibid., 937.

FRUCTUS (FRUIT), reward; example; justice; holy preachings; spiritual virtues: ibid., 938. — Fruits denote works: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1025.

FRUMENTUM (WHEAT), spiritual work; virtues; the word of doctrine: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 938. — The greenness of eternal recompense; spiritual work; inward understanding of sacred speech; virtues; words of preaching: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 430.

FULGOR (SPLENDOUR), renewal of mind: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 933.

FULGUR (LIGHTNING), threatening against sinners; the terror of fear; miracles: ibid. — Lightnings express the divine terrors or threats written in the divine law: ibid., CXI, 277.

FUMUS (SMOKE), beginnings of future compunction: St Eucherius, L, 738. — Compunction; brevity of life: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935. — Compunction; murky uncertainty: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 359. — Contrition is signified by the vapour of smoke: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1676. — Smoke signifies the compunction of tears: ibid., 1291.

FUNDAMENTUM (FOUNDATION), faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935.

FUNICULUS (CORD), faith; our thought; subtlety of preaching: ibid., 937.

[Col. 0203] FUNIS (ROPE), favourable outcomes; the hardships of the age: ibid., 936.

GALBANUS (GALBANUM), the virtue of prayer: ibid., 939.

GALEA (HELMET) is said to be good action: ibid., 940.

GALILAEA (GALILEE), which is interpreted as “wheel” or “a migration made,” signifies revelation and sometimes the course of life: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 340. — Galilee: change of life: ibid., CXII, 947.

GALLINA (HEN) signifies wisdom, or the holy Church: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1152; St Eucherius, L, 748; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 348. — Hen: the soul: St Eucherius, L, 748.

GELU (FROST), the harshness of tribulation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 943.

GENAE (CHEEKS) signify outward bearing: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 924. — Cheeks denote modesty: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 93.

GLADIUS (SWORD), holy preaching; sharp intellect; temporal tribulation; separation; resistance; persecution: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 940. — A blow at close range; temporal tribulation: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 322. — The tongue is called a sharp sword: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1258. — The rigour of discipline is signified by a sword: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1197.

GOMOR, the virtue of discernment: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 946.

GRANDO (HAIL), a word of correction; severe tribulation; affliction: ibid., 943.

GRANUM (GRAIN), the word of faith: ibid.

GRESSUS (STEPS), good works; holy merits; spiritual progress: ibid., 945.

GURGES (WHIRLPOOL), the onset of persecution: ibid., 946.

GUTTAE (DROPS), distress: ibid., 947. — The dark drops of nights are wisdom: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 85.

GUTTUR SPONSI (THE BRIDEGROOM’S THROAT), inward savour: Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 518. — Preaching: St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 537.

HABITACULUM (DWELLING-PLACE), the heavenly Jerusalem; action: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 948.

HAEDI (GOATS). — The eyes and ears are signified by goats: St Bernard, CLXXXII, 957.

HAMUS (HOOK) is said to be preaching: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 947.

HASTA (SPEAR), preaching; royal power; persecution: ibid., 948. — The dart of preaching: Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 327.

HERBA (GRASS), delight, or certain rudiments of the progressing soul: St Eucherius, L, 742. — The verdure of faith; virtues; good knowledge; action; temporal support; worldly glory; plainer ordinances: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 950; Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 419.

HIEMS (WINTER), servile fear: St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1060.

HINNULI (FAWNS), spiritual virtues: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 954.

HIRCUS (HE-GOAT), works of repentance: ibid.

HIRUNDO (SWALLOW), constancy in prayer: ibid.

HODIE (TODAY), all time: ibid., 964.

HOLOCAUSTUM (WHOLE BURNT OFFERING), the contemplative life: ibid., 961.
