ACETUM. Vinegar expresses the old law, which, long persisting among the former people and corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, could not preserve its native flavor: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1208.

ADEPS, the simple sense of Scripture: idem, CXII, 852.

ADVERSARIUS, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 872.

AGER, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 854; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 256.---The breadth of Sacred Scripture can be signified by the name *field*: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1150.

ALAE, the two Testaments: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---The three pairs of the seraphim’s wings signify the three senses of Scripture: Alan of Lille, CCX, 270.

ANNULUS. The book of the Gospels is called a ring: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 858.---In the four rings by which the altar was carried, the four books of the Evangelists may quite fittingly be understood: idem, CVIII, 210.

AQUA signifies Sacred Scripture: Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 42, 50, 56; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 902; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 279.---Water signifies the Old Testament: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 909.---The hidden utterance of the prophets and Christ’s holy preaching are called water: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 860.---The bitter waters of the West prefigure the letter and the law: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 76.---The water of wisdom is the divine word: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 878.---Dark water is called the Scripture of the prophets and apostles: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 93.---Water denotes knowledge of Scripture: St. Eucherius, L, 741; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 783.

ARBOR. Sacred codices are called a tree: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 333.

ARCA signifies spiritual knowledge of Sacred Scripture: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 202.

ARCTURUS, the Old Testament: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 862.---The old law: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 47.

ARCUS, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 862; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 324.---By the name *bow*, in sacred discourse the divine utterances themselves are signified: St. Gregory the Great, [Col. 0223] LXXVI, 133.---The Lord’s bow is called the New and Old Testament: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 65, 230.

ARGENTUM denotes the divine utterances: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 233, 506; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 311.---Sacred Scripture is the Lord’s gold and silver: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 248.---Gold signifies the inward sense of Scripture, but silver the outward: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 853.---The brilliance of divine eloquence: silver: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 863.

ARUNDO, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 949.

AURUM signifies the law and the prophets: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1413.

BASES of columns are the books of the law and the prophets: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 394.

BINARIUS NUMERUS indicates the two Testaments: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 439.

BRACHIUM. The truths of Scripture are signified by the heart and arm: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 954.

BUTYRUM denotes the tropological sense of Sacred Scripture: Alan of Lille, CCX, 240.

CALAMUS, Sacred Scripture: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 425.

CALIGO is called prophecy: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.---Darkness is the depth of the Scriptures: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 92.

CALIX, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 879.---The two Testaments must be understood through the two cups, one belonging to the lamb, the other to the mystery of the body: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1360.

CAMELI. Abraham’s ten camels are the ten commandments of the law: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 437.

CAMPI. The divine Scriptures are called fields: St. Eucherius, L, 741.

CANALES, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 883; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 303.

CANCELLI through which the Beloved looks through the wall are the teachings of the Gospels: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1110.

CANISTRUM, in which loaves are offered, signifies Holy Scripture, in which is the refreshment of spiritual food—evangelical doctrine mingled and combined with the oil of gladness, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 624; CXII, 882.

CAPITELLA, the two Testaments, ibid., 885.

CARO, the teachings of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 886.

CASEUS denotes the allegorical sense of Sacred Scripture: Alan of Lille, CCX, 240.

CATARACTAE, the profound teachings of Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 890.

CATHEDRA, Sacred Scripture: Hugh of St. Victor, CXCV, 510, 511.

CELLA VINARIA, the Mosaic law: Alan of Lille, CCX, 66.---Sacred Scripture is figured by the wine-cellar: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 495.

CELLARIA REGIS, the law and the Gospel: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1036.

CERA, the old law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 893.

CHERUB, the two Testaments, ibid., 891.---The two cherubim in Moses’ tabernacle are the two Testaments: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1153.---The two cherubim of the ark of the covenant signify the Testaments: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 759.

CISTERNA, Sacred Scripture, sacred books: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 896.

CIRCULUS, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 896.

CLAVIS, the opening of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 881.

CLERI, the two Testaments, ibid., 892.

CLYPEI, the ten commandments of the Decalogue: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1074.

COELUM is called Sacred Scripture: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1341, 1909; St. Eucherius, L, 738; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 891; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 276.---Sacred Scripture is compared to heaven: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 562.---The heavens are the books of both Testaments: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 112.---The Gospel books are rightly called heavens because they contain Christ the Savior: Cassiodorus, LXX, 75.

COLLIS. Sacred Scripture resembles a hill: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 288.

COLLUM. Sacred discourse is designated by the name *neck*: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 190.

COLUMNA, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 899.

COMAE of Christ’s head, the truths of Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 922.

CONCUBINA, the old law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 901.

CONDENSA. The dark or covered portions of divine Scripture are called *thickets*: St. Eucherius, L, 741.

CORNU, the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 903.

[Col. 0224] CORUSCATIONES, the splendors of the Gospel: St. Eucherius, L, 738.

COTURNIX, the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 904.---Quails have the figurative sense of the history of the law: idem, CXI, 250.

CURRUS DEI is called the fourfold character of the Gospels: St. Eucherius, L, 737.

DELICIAE denote the divine utterances: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 907.

DENTES in the Church are the expositors of Sacred Scripture: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1150.

DIGITUS, the four Gospels: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 910.

DIVITIAE, the words of the law, ibid., 911.

EMUNCTORIA denote the two Testaments, ibid., 915.

EXPLORATORES denote the two Testaments, ibid., 918.

FACIES, the old law, ibid., 920.

FAVUS is an image of the divine Scriptures: St. Augustine, XLVI, 819.---The literal sense of Sacred Scripture: honeycomb: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 922.

FEMEN. The joining of the thighs: the concord of the two Testaments: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1227.

FERCULUM OF SOLOMON is Sacred Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 880.

FERMENTUM: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 924.

FEX, the letter of the law, ibid., 925.

FICUS bears the image of the law, ibid., 926; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 469.

FIRMAMENTUM. Sacred Scripture is mystically called the firmament: Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 185.

FLUMEN, the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935.---The four rivers watering paradise prefigured the four Gospels of Christ: St. Cyprian, IV, 412.

FLUVIUS, the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 934.---Sacred writers are compared to a river: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 513.

FONS, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 929.

FORCEPS, the two Testaments, ibid., 931.

FRAGMEN, the more secret things of the law, ibid., 922.

FRUMENTUM, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 938; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 430.

FUNDA, the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 935.

GALAAD signifies Sacred Scripture, in which the covenant and pact established between God and humankind is read: idem, CXI, 360; Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1149.

GEMELLI FETUS, the two Testaments, ibid., 1150, 1155.---Twin offspring denote the allegorical and moral senses of Scripture: Alan of Lille, CCX, 78.

GLADIUS BIS ACUTUS, the Old and New Testament: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1234.

GUTTUR OF THE BELOVED is understood as the sound of Sacred Scripture: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1203.---By the bridegroom’s throat is understood the testament of Christ through which he speaks to us: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 525.

HEDERA signifies the letter of the law: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 436.

HERBA, the teachings of the Old Testament: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 950.---Knowledge of Scripture is called grass: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 419.

HIEMS. Through winter is meant the severity of the law: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 498.

HOEDI, the two goats brought by Esau to Isaac, signify the two Testaments: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 460.

HORDEUM. The letter of the law is called barley: St. Eucherius, L, 741.---The Old Testament is called barley: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 432.

HORTUS is Sacred Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 960.---The sacred books are the gardens of the devout: St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 210.---By gardens is signified the loveliness of the Scriptures: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1268.

HUMUS, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 958.

IGNIS. Scripture is called fire: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 475.

IMBER MATUTINUS ET SEROTINUS, evangelical teaching: Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 291.

JANUA, the understanding of Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 965.

LABIA CHRISTI, the two Testaments: Cassiodorus, LXX, 113; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 86.---God’s lips are mystically understood as the concord of both Testaments: St. Eucherius, L, 731.

LAC. Sacred teaching is designated by milk: Alan of Lille, CCX, 240.---The teaching of the law is called milk: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 978.---Sacred Scripture is a drink of milk: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1208.---The threefold sense of Scripture [Col. 0225] is designated by milk: Alan of Lille, CCX, 240.

LAGENA anointed with oil denotes the prophetic books: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 311.

LAPIS is called the law: idem, CXII, 981.---The words of Scripture: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 350.---David’s five stones against Goliath prefigure the five books of Moses: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 53.

LATUS, the two Testaments: idem, CXII, 982.

LENTICULA signifies Sacred Scripture, in which the promise of the Holy Spirit is contained: idem, CXI, 602.

LEO, the severity of the law: idem, CXII, 983.

LEX, the Old Testament, the book of Psalms, ibid., 984.

LIBER, the Old Testament and the Gospel, ibid., 787.

LILIUM, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 986.

LIMEN, the assembly of the Old Testament, ibid.---Knowledge of Sacred Scripture: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 404.

LUCERNA, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 989; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1087; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1296.---Knowledge of the law: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 364.---Prophecy is a lamp prepared before Christ to illuminate the way: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 381.

LUMINARE. The New Testament may be called the greater light, and the Old the lesser light: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 441.

LUX, knowledge of the law: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 361.

MANNA. Sacred Scripture is called manna: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 995.---Manna figures the Gospel: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 551.

MARE is called the Gospel: St. Ambrose, XIV, 212.---The sacred Scriptures are called the sea: St. Eucherius, L, 741.

MEL. The mystical sense of Scripture is compared to honey: Alan of Lille, CCX, 209.

MENSA, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 998; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 114; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 965.---Sacred Scripture: a table made a snare for the Jews: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 261.---Sacred Scripture is a table richly supplied: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 637.---Christ’s table is Sacred Scripture: Alcuin, C, 630.---The Christian’s table is the law and Sacred Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 622.---Sacred Scripture is the Lord’s table: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 992.---The four tables for the burnt offering, built of squared stones, are the four Gospels: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1046.

MERIDIES, Holy Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 998.

MESSIS, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 998; Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 432.

MICAE, Sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 999.

MONS, Sacred Scripture, ibid., 1001.---Sacred Scripture is a shadowy mountain, dense in its teachings and shadowy in its allegories: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 474.---Sacred Scripture is designated by the name *mountain*: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 252.---The two airy mountains are the two Testaments: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 785; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 739.---Mountains denote the divine books: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359.

MUSTUM is called the mystical sense of Scripture: Alan of Lille, CCX, 104.

NAVIS. The two Testaments are called a ship: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1004.

NUBES, radiant divine utterances: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 93.

OBOLUS. By the ten obols demanded as the price for the soul of each individual, nothing more fitting can be understood than observance of the law’s Decalogue: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 214.

OSTIUM. Understanding of the word of God: a door: idem, CXII, 1014.

PALEAE, the teachings of Sacred Scripture, ibid., 1018.

PALLIUM. The letter of the Old Testament is called a cloak, ibid., 1018.---The Gospel of Christ is Elijah’s cloak: Rupert, CLXVII, 1258.

PANIS [BREAD], sacred teaching: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1021.---The books of the Law, ibid.---Scripture is compared to bread: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 209.---Bread is a type of divine Scripture: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 952.---By the unleavened loaves, or unleavened cakes mixed with oil, understand the apostolic books: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 311.

PANNI [CLOTHS], the commandments of the Law, id., CXII, 1021.

PALPEBRAE [EYELIDS]. The Scriptures are denoted by eyelids and by rain: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 678.

PARABOLAE [PARABLES]. By Solomon’s three thousand parables is understood the fullness of faith delivered by Christ in the Law and in the Gospels: Rabanus Maurus, CLX, 152.

PARIES [WALL], sacred Scripture, id., CXII, 1022.

[Col. 0226] PECUNIA [MONEY] denotes the divine utterances: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 308, 309.

PELLIS [SKIN], the literal sense of Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1026.

PENNAE [WINGS], the two Testaments: St. Eucherius, L, 748.---The wings of the silvered dove signify the sacred Scriptures: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 527.

PHARETRA [QUIVER], sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 919.---The Father’s quiver is sacred Scripture: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1158.

PICTURA [PICTURE]. Sacred Scripture is like a picture: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 473.

PLAUSTRUM [WAGON]. The Gospel is the wagon upon which the ark of the covenant was carried: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1126.

PLEIADES. The grace of the Testament is called the Pleiades: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 44.

PLUVIA [RAIN]. The words of the holy apostles are called rain: St. Eucherius, L, 739.---The early and latter rain signifies prophetic and apostolic Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 92.---The Scriptures are denoted by rain: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 678.

POMA [FRUITS], prophecies and commandments of both Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CVI, 1030.

PORTA [GATE] signifies the canon of the Old Testament and sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 385.---Knowledge of sacred Scripture is called a gate: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 402.

PORTICUS [PORTICO], the books of the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1031.

POSTES [DOORPOSTS], the books of the Gospels, ibid., 1032.

PRAESEPE [MANGER], sacred Scripture, ibid., 1027.

PROPUGNACULA [BULWARKS], the defences of the Scriptures, ibid., 1032.---Silver bulwarks are the defences of divine utterances: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1153.

PUTEUS [WELL], sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1035.---True Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXII, 424, 454.---The books of Scripture: Garner of St. Victor, CXCVII, 300.

QUADRANS [QUADRANT]. The fourfold understanding of sacred Scripture is called a quadrant: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1036.

QUADRIGAE [FOUR-HORSE CHARIOTS] of Amminadab are the four Gospels of Christ: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 635, 638; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 79; Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1221.---The four Gospels are, as it were, the four chariots of the New Testament, over which Christ himself presides as charioteer: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1093.

QUATERNARIUS [THE NUMBER FOUR] denotes the four Gospels: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 444.

RAMUS [BRANCH], sacred teaching, sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1037.

REFECTIO [REFRESHMENT] of the soul is sacred Scripture: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1116.

REGNUM [KINGDOM], sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1038; Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 154.

RESTICULA [CORDS], God’s commandments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1040.

RIVULI [RIVULETS], the sayings of sacred Scripture, ibid.

RIVUS [STREAM], the Gospel books: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 296.

ROS [DEW] signifies evangelical teaching: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 494.

ROTA [WHEEL] having four faces is sacred Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1585.---The Old and New Testaments are a wheel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1041.---The wheel within the wheel is the New Testament within the Old: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1058.

SAGITTAE [ARROWS], sacred Scripture: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 326.

SALTERIUM [PSALTERY], the old Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1045.

SAXUM [ROCK]. The literal sense of Scripture is compared to a rock: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 209.

SCALA [LADDER] of Jacob signifies the two Testaments, which, woven together with evangelical precepts, have customarily raised believing persons who do God’s will to heaven, as it were by certain steps of observance: St. Zeno, XI, 428.---Jacob’s ladder was a figure of the two Testaments: Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 499.

SEGES [HARVEST] is to be called sacred Scripture: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1059.

SERAPHIM signifies sacred Scripture: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 269.

SICLUS [SHEKEL], the old Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1053.

SILVA [FOREST], the old Law, ibid., 1054.

SPECULUM [MIRROR]. The sacred Scriptures are a mirror: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 788.---The Gospel is the mirror of priests, ibid., 1085.

SPICAE [EARS OF GRAIN], the sayings of sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1055.

SPOLIA [SPOILS], divine utterances, ibid., 1059.

STATERA [BALANCE]. The Scriptures are denoted by a balance: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 926.

[Col. 0227] SYMPHONIA [HARMONY], the preaching of the Gospel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1054.

TABULAE [TABLETS] of the Testament, written by God’s hand, broken and restored, are a figure of the Old and New Testaments, id., CVIII, 872.

TECTUM [ROOF], the subtlety of sacred Scripture, id., CXII, 1064.

TERRA [EARTH]. Sacred Scripture is compared to earth: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 181.

TONITRUA [THUNDERS] are called the voices of the Gospel: St. Eucherius, L, 738.

TORRENS [TORRENT], the streams of the sacred books: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 297.

TURRIS [TOWER] with bulwarks signifies sacred Scripture: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 809.

TURTUR [TURTLEDOVE]. The preaching of the Gospel is signified by the voice of the turtledove: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 868; Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1112.

UBERA [BREASTS] are the two Testaments: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1084.---The mystical words of sacred Scripture, ibid.---The words of sacred utterance: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 221.---By the bridegroom’s breasts is understood the sweetness of the Gospel: Cassiodorus, LXX, 1057.

UMBRA [SHADOW], the harshness of the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1085.

UTER [WINE-SKIN], the letter of the Law, ibid.

VACCA [COW], the red heifer, a sign of the New Testament: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 732.

[Col. 0228] VAS [VESSEL], sacred Scripture: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 238.---The sacred Scriptures are sacred vessels: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 762.

VELUM [VEIL], the obscurity of sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1073.

VENA [VEIN], sacred Scripture, ibid.

VESTIS [GARMENT], sacred Scripture, ibid., 1076.

VIA [WAY]. The Gospel is the way; the lamp shines in the shadow, that is, in the world: St. Ambrose, XIV, 816.

VILLAE [VILLAGES] are called the obscurities of sacred Scripture: Alanus of Lille, CCX, 102.

VINEA [VINEYARD], sacred Scripture: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1079.---The sacred codices are called a vineyard: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 341.

VINUM [WINE], knowledge of the Law, the word of the Gospel: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1078.---The truth of sacred Scripture is compared to wine: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 240.

VIRGA [ROD], the terror of the Law: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.---The two rods signify the covenant of God with humankind, made twice: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 786.

VIRTUS [POWER], the Gospel of preaching: St. Ambrose, XV, 1353.

VISIO [VISION], revelation: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1081.

VOLATUS [FLIGHT], understanding in the Scriptures: St. Eucherius, L, 748.

[Col. 0227]

XLVII. INDEX OF NEW-TESTAMENT ALLEGORIES, ARRANGED IN ANALOGICAL ORDER AND, WITHIN EACH ANALOGY, IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER, AND REPORTING VARIOUS EXPLANATIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS.

In this Index we have observed the same order as in the preceding one; therefore, if he wishes, the kindly reader may consult the notice to Index XLVI of this present Index.

ARTICLE I. Allegories concerning God.

AGRICOLA [FARMER]. God is the farmer; we are his cultivated field: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1555.

COLUMBA [DOVE], signifying the Holy Spirit, descends upon Noah as upon Christ in the Jordan: St. Jerome, XXII, 660.---By the dove and the fiery tongues under which he appeared, the Spirit shows that charity is to be given us by his gift: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 580.---The dove is a figure of the Holy Spirit: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1145; Alcuin, C, 757, 769, 773.---The whole dove appearing to Christ signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1590.

CORNUA [HORNS] seven denote the sevenfold operation of the Spirit: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1121.---The operation of the sevenfold Spirit is signified by the seven horns, ibid., 1121.

FIGULUS [POTTER] is God: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1465.

FUMUS [SMOKE]. The glory of the Trinity is called smoke, by which the Jews were blinded: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1113.

FUR [THIEF]. God, the heavenly Judge, is compared to a thief: Alcuin, C, 1110.

LAMPADES [LAMPS] seven signify the sevenfold Spirit: Alcuin, C, 1117. The Holy Spirit is compared to lamps, ibid.

LIGNUM [TREE] of life is the wisdom of God the Father, ibid., 1103.

NUBES [CLOUD] in the Red Sea, a figure of the Holy Spirit: Peter [Lombard], CXCI, 1617.

OCULI [EYES] of Jesus mystically denote the gifts of his Spirit: Alcuin, C, 821. The eyes represent the Holy Spirit who enlightens the Church, ibid., 1098.---The seven eyes signify the sevenfold operation of the Spirit: Alcuin, C, 1121.

OLEUM [OIL] denotes the Holy Spirit: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 841.

[Col. 0228] PEDES [FEET] of God signify eternal stability: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 378.

SEDENS [THE ONE SEATED]. The person of the Father is signified by the one seated upon the throne, but that of the Son by the right hand of the one seated: Alcuin, C, 1120.

SEPTEM [SEVEN]. The sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit is denoted by the number seven: Alcuin, C, 1097.

STELLAE [STARS]. The seven stars are the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, ibid., 1109.

ARTICLE II. Allegories concerning Christ.

ADOLESCENS [YOUNG MAN] can be understood as a figure of Christ’s humanity: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1083.

AGNUS [LAMB]. Christ is called a lamb because, offering himself, he redeemed the world: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1121.

AGRICOLA [FARMER]. Christ as man is the vine; as God, the farmer: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1839.

ALPHA. Christ is Alpha and Omega because he is the beginning and the end: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1095.

ALTARE [ALTAR], concerning which John speaks in the Apocalypse, is Christ’s humanity: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 472.

ANGELUS [ANGEL] moving the water of the pool was a figure of Christ: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 690.

ARCA [ARK] of the Testament, the incarnation of Christ: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1029.

AURUM [GOLD], the beginnings of redemption: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 259.---By gold, power is shown, ibid., 269, 283. In the gift of gold, royal dignity is displayed: St. Sedatus, LXXII, 773.

CALCULUS [SMALL STONE]. Jesus Christ is signified by the white stone: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1106.

CALIX [CUP] indicates the Passion of the Lord: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 948.

[Col. 0229] CANTICUM [SONG]. Christ sang the new song: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1122.

CHRIST is called a heap of twenty measures: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1363.---The full age at which all shall rise again: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 337.---Lamb: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1121; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 756.---Lamb of God: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 650.---Male lamb: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 259.---Farmer: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1839.---Alpha and Omega: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1095.---Altar: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1329.---Altar of God: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1126; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 768.---Altar of the Church: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1017.---Angel: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 976; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 394.---Angel ascending from the rising of the sun: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1129.---Angel descending from heaven: Rupert, CLXIX, 1148.---Mighty angel descending from heaven in a cloud: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1143.---Angel casting a stone into the sea: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1156.---Great angel, ibid., 975.---Angel of great counsel, ibid., 959.---Apostle: St. Agobard, CIV, 56.---Altar of the temple: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 973.---Barachias, “blessed of the Lord,” ibid., 950.---White stone: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 283, 284.---Head of the Church: St. Agobard, CIV, 62; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 178.---Our head: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 434.---Crown of martyrs, ibid., 707.---Son of David: St. Hilary, IX, 1004, 1047.---The Desired One of all ages: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 35.---Day: St. Ambrose, XV, 1759.---Lord of lords: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1169.---The Lordly man: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 582.---Emmanuel: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 117, 118.---Bishop of bishops: St. Agobard, CIV, 196.---Flower of virgins: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 707.---Fountain of life: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1654, 1113.---Mighty in humility: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 43.---Grain of wheat and grain of mustard: St. Ambrose, XV, 1747.---Grain to be put to death and multiplied: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1766; XXXVI, 720.---Grain multiplied by death, id., XXXVIII, 1397.---Grace of those who are continent: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 707.---Man who went abroad: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1106.---Image of God: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 235.---Sinless: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 412.---Incomprehensible: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 332.---Door: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 780, 1647.---Just and justifier: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 558.---Jasper: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 865.---Pure and white stone: Venerable Rupert, CLXIX, 1130.---Stone laid as a foundation: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 733.---Stone beneath Jacob’s head: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 865.---Lion, ibid., 756.---Lion because he conquered the devil: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1121.---Lion of the tribe of Judah, ibid., 1121.---Book: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 544.---Tree of life: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 870.---Lamp, ibid., 854.---Light, ibid.---Enlightening light: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1782.---Light of life, ibid., 1654.---Light of the world, ibid., 1652; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1148.---Unquenchable light: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1375.---Hidden manna: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1105.---The pearl for which all things must be sold: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1371.---The evangelical pearl, to be compared with the abundance of all good things: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 276.---Mediator: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 283, 284; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 437; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 975, 976.---Mediator of God and humankind: St. Hilary, IX, 989.---The sole mediator between God and humankind: St. Agobard, CIV, 202.---Our mediator: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 127.---Most merciful: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 499.---Gentle toward us, harsh toward himself, ibid., 240.---Mountain: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 215.---Great and high mountain: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1194.---The sole mountain from which help comes to us: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 622.---The sole one free from sin: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 253.---Wall against the enemy’s snares: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1440.---Mouth of the Father: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 590.---Doorkeeper: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1728.---Door, ibid.---St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 319; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 121.---Door opened to believers: Blessed Alcuin, C, 884, 1111, 1116.---The door which the key opens, ibid., 1111.---Sheep: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1728, 1735.---Bread: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1612; XXXVIII, 265, 325, 1463; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 320.---True bread: St. Augustine, 1602, 1607.---Bread of angels: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1105.---Heavenly bread foreshadowed by manna: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 45, 1551.---The heavenly bread eaten by true Israelites, ibid., 1551.---Bread descending from heaven: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 563.---Paraclete: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1828.---Shepherd, ibid., 1728, 1734; [Col. 0230] XXXVIII, 308, 1647.---Good Shepherd: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 328; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 829.---Shepherd of shepherds: St. Agobard, CIV, 196.---Supreme Shepherd, ibid., 197.---Householder: Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1154.---Peace: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 170.---Rock, id., XXXV, 1729, 1736; XXXVIII, 45, 1238, 1348.---High priest: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 501.---Drink: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1612.---Reward: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 539.---Price, ibid.---Our price: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1591.---Beginning, ibid., 24.---Root of David: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1121; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 928.---Our refreshment: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 495.---King of kings: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1166.---Priest according to the order of Melchizedek: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 487.---Axe laid to the root: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1164.---Sun: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1126; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1214.---Sun of righteousness and truth: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 206.---Bridegroom of the Church: St. Agobard, CIV, 189.---Morning star: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 890.---Temple: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1329; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 973.---Truth: St. Agobard, CIV, 113.---Truth in promise: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 404.---Way: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 244.---Way in example: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 404.---Man: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 259; Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 401.---Our man, ibid., 434.---Rod: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1109.---Eternal life: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1610, 1818; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 404.---Life of the sacraments: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 92.---Vine: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1839, 1841; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 323.

Christ is compared to a she-ass and her colt: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 33.---To a thief: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1110.---To a hen: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1330; XXXVI, 526; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 791.---To a grain of wheat: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 950.---To a grain of mustard: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1084.---To a lamp: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 428.---To a branch cut from a tree, ibid., 24.---To a woodworm, ibid., 500.

Christ is called a sheep carrying a sheep upon his shoulders back to the fold: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 194. Christ at his birth is a holy child, prophet, and angel: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 394. Christ is the way in example, truth in promise, life in reward, ibid., 404. Christ in Mary is light in wax, ibid., 611. Christ’s flesh is called ark, tabernacle, cloud, and diadem, ibid., 636. Christ on the cross is king and priest, ibid., 696. Christ left his mother by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and by cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 620.

CIBUS [FOOD]. Christ’s food is virtue; Christ’s food is strength: St. Ambrose, XV, 1687.

CITHARAE [HARPS] of the elders figure Christ’s Passion: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1122.

CLAVIS [KEY] of David is to be understood as Christ’s Incarnation: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1111.

COLLIS [HILL]. The seven hills are the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 586.

EQUUS [HORSE], white, is a symbol of Christ’s humanity: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1123.

FACIES [FACE] of a man denotes the Incarnation: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 940.---A face, as it were, is Christ’s Passion, ibid., 942.---Christ’s face shining like the sun, ibid., 659.---The Redeemer’s Incarnation is manifested by the face of the angel shining like the sun: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1099.

FERMENTUM [LEAVEN]. Christ is denoted by the leaven put into three measures of meal: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 772.

GALILAEA [GALILEE] denotes the Lord’s transfiguration: Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 201.

GRANUM [GRAIN]. Christ is denoted by a grain of mustard: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 772.

HOMO [MAN] descending into Jericho represents Christ: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 570.

IRIS [RAINBOW], signifying the bow of the world’s reconciliation through the Incarnation, is a figure: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1116.---The rainbow above Christ’s head is his divinity, ibid., 1143.

JASPIS [JASPER] denotes Christ’s divinity, in which all things live, ibid., 1116.

LIBER [BOOK]. The book sealed with seven seals is a type of Christ: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 279.---Christ alone is worthy to open the book: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1120.

LEO [LION] of the tribe of Judah is Christ of David’s seed, ibid., 1121. The resurrection is figured in the lion, ibid., 1118.

[Col. 0231] LUCERNA [LAMP] is a type of Christ’s humanity: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 924.

MAGI. The Magi’s gifts signify gold, a king; incense, God; myrrh, a man: St. Hilary, IX, 923; St. Ambrose, XVI, 244, 535; Juvencus, XIX, 98; Sedulius, ibid., 605; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 620; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 264, 272; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1112; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 716.---The gifts which the Magi offered to the newborn King contain the precious gifts which the Saviour himself, reigning in heaven with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, received from the nations: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 261.---In incense the Magi acknowledge Christ as God, in gold as king, and in myrrh as man: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 147.

MANUS [HAND] of the mighty angel is the working of our salvation: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1144.

MEDIATOR [MEDIATOR] of God and humankind is the angel holding a golden censer in his hand, namely Christ, ibid., C, 1135.

MONS [MOUNTAIN]. Christ, proclaimed to the nations by the apostles, is the mountain moved into the sea: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 554.

MYRRHA [MYRRH] foretells Christ’s resurrection and ours from the dead: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 259.---Myrrh denotes incorruptibility, ibid., 269, 283.---In the form of myrrh, the humanity to be buried is shown: St. Sedatus, LXXII, 773.

NOE [NOAH]. Christ was figured in Noah, and the world in that ark: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1464.

OREB [HOREB] is a type of Christ: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 89.

PEDES [FEET]. Christ’s coming into the world is denoted by feet: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 140.

PISCIS [FISH] was Christ, providing the disciples with life-giving food, but is changed into a serpent for the Jews: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LII, 354.---The fish which first came up, having a stater in its mouth, is a figure of Christ: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 600.

PRIMOGENITUS [FIRSTBORN]. Christ is rightly called firstborn, because no dead person rose before him: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1093.

RUGITUS [ROARING] of Christ is like that of a lion: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1008.

SAMARITANUS [SAMARITAN], merciful, denotes Christ: Venerable Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 269.

SAPIENTIA [WISDOM]. Christ, the wisdom of God, is present everywhere: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1659.

SARDINUS [SARDIUS] signified the Redeemer’s humanity: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1116.

STELLA [STAR], morning, figures Christ, ibid., 1109.---According to the mystery of the Incarnation, he is a star: St. Ambrose, XV, 1569.

TESTIS [WITNESS], faithful, is rightly affirmed of Christ: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1093.

THABOR [TABOR], which is interpreted “coming light,” is a type of Christ incarnate: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 38.

THUS [INCENSE], the worship of true religion and the superstition of idols destined to cease: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 259.---Christ’s priesthood is shown by incense, ibid., 269, 283.---In the vapour of incense, divine majesty is displayed: St. Sedatus, LXXII, 773.

UNCTIO [ANOINTING] of priests figures Christ’s anointing: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1090.

VINEA [VINEYARD] is so called from the vine which is Christ: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 928.

ARTICLE III. Allegories concerning angels.

ANIMALIA [LIVING CREATURES] and elders in the Apocalypse are angels: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1123.

MESSORES [REAPERS] are angels, who bind the tares into bundles for burning when they associate like with like in similar torments: the proud with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the avaricious with the avaricious: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 381.

OCULI [EYES]. Angels are denoted in the Church by eyes: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1098.

SEDES [SEATS] set in heaven are the holy angels: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 746.

ARTICLE IV. Allegories concerning evil spirits.

ANGELI [ANGELS], four standing at the four corners of the earth, signify the body of the ancient enemy: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1128.

DIABOLUS [DEVIL] is called the angel of the abyss: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 992.---Accuser: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1020.---Dragon: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1467.---Great dragon: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 670; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 860.---Red horse: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 943.---Destroyer: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1141.---Murderer, ibid., 872.---Hell: [Col. 0232] Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 947.---Lion: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1731.---Wolf, ibid.---Wolf in the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 887.---Liar and father of lies, ibid., 906.---Great mountain: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 780.---Death, ibid., 943.---Father of the Jews, ibid., 562.---Prince of this world: Blessed Alcuin, C, 940; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 562.---Satan: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 670.---The night-time sower of seed: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 560.---Ancient serpent: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 670; Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 800.

EQUUS [HORSE], red, is the body of the ancient enemy: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1124.

GLADIUS [SWORD], the great sword given to the rider upon the red horse, figures the devil’s power, ibid.

PHARAO [PHARAOH], that is, the devil, is killed in the waters: when the people have been baptized, he himself is overwhelmed with his army: St. Hilary, IX, 762.

SEDENS [RIDER] upon the red horse is the devil, who takes peace from the earth: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1124.

VOLUCRES [BIRDS] of heaven, we have learned, are very often the name given to unclean spirits: St. Hilary, IX, 957.---Demons are birds: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 839.

ARTICLE V. Allegories concerning the Church.

ABEL. The Church began with Abel: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 307.

ANGELUS [ANGEL] who appeared to John, together with the apostle, prefigures the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1091.---The seven angels of the Churches mentioned in the Apocalypse are the seven Churches: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 81.---Angels indicate the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1135.

ANIMA [SOUL] is a figure of the Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 387.---The soul of the Church is the Holy Spirit: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 407.

ANIMALIA [LIVING CREATURES], four, figure the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118, 1119, 1124.

ARCA [ARK] of Noah signifies the Church: St. Ambrose, XV, 814; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 166, 167, 743.

AREA [THRESHING FLOOR] is the Church, in which there is now wheat, not without chaff: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1174.---By the Lord’s threshing floor is understood the Lord’s Church, vigorously and widely spread throughout the whole world, id., XXXIV, 127.

BETHLEEM [BETHLEHEM] was a type of the whole Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 133, 134; Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 81.---Bethlehem mystically is the Church: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 188.

CANDELABRUM [LAMPSTAND]. The Church is signified by the lampstand: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1398.---The seven lampstands denote the sevenfold Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1097.

CANTUS [SONG] of the Church, a great voice from heaven: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1055.

CIVITAS [CITY] of Christ is the Church founded upon Christ: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1193.

COENACULUM [UPPER ROOM] signifies the holy Church: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 590.

COLUMBA [DOVE] is a type of the Church: St. Ambrose, XV, 1587.

COLUMNA [PILLAR]. By the pillar of cloud mentioned in the Apocalypse, we may understand the Church, ibid., 863.

CONJUNCTIO [UNION]. The mystery of the union of man and woman foreshadows the union of Christ and the Church: Victorinus the African, VIII, 1289.

CORONA [CROWN]. The Church has golden crowns: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117.

COSTA [RIB] of Adam, built into a woman, is a type of the Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 647, 648.

CRUX [CROSS]. The Church is exalted by Christ’s cross: St. Augustine, XL, 688.

DOMUS [HOUSE] strengthened with seven pillars is a type of the Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 41.---The house of Simon the leper is a type of the Church, ibid., 878.

ECCLESIA [CHURCH] is, or is called, the Lord’s field: St. Augustine, XL, 685.---God’s field, at first thorny, ibid., 688.---Christ’s blessed field: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 274.---Field of blood: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1573.---A two-pound weight, weighing and forgiving human sins: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1125.---A fortress set upon a mountain: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 390.---City: Blessed Alcuin, C, 906; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 733.---City of God: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 588.---City of the Lord: Rupert, abbot, CLVIII, 1474.---Unconquerable city: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 495.---City set upon a mountain: St. Chromatius, XX, 340–341; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 802.---Heaven: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXXVI, 1282; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 744.---Dove: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 258.---Pillar of truth: [Col. 0233] Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 353.---Body, ibid., 195, 197.---God’s creature, ibid., 72.---House: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 733.---House of Jacob and house of Joseph, ibid., 401.---House of Judah: St. Jerome, XXII, 817.---House of obedience: Blessed Alcuin, C, 906.---Family of Christ: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 834.---Lightning: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1330.---Jerusalem: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 733.---Mother: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 264; Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 625.---Woman clothed with the sun and moon: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1039; CLXX, 36.---Woman giving birth: id., CLXIX, 743.---Woman giving birth in sorrow: Blessed Alcuin, C, 955.---Christ’s sheepfold: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1721.---The faithful’s own fold: Blessed Alcuin, C, 304.---Sheepfold of sheep: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203.---One fold and one shepherd: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 793.---Christ’s eternal kingdom: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 308.---Kingdom of God: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 733; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1680.---Kingdom of heaven: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1118, 1154.---Dragnet, ibid., 1116.---Seat of Christ’s majesty: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 602.---Christ’s seat in heaven: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 906.---Zion: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 733.---Christ’s mother-in-law: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 373.---Bride: Blessed Alcuin, C, 786.---Bride of Christ: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 264; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 741; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 70.---Heavenly stability: St. Augustine, XL, 259.---Temple of God: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1112, 1119.---Holy temple: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 368.---Temple of the tabernacle: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 1111.---Christ’s wife: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 300.---Garment made white above snow: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 214.---The Lord’s vineyard: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 132.---Virgin: Blessed Alcuin, C, 786; Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 625.

The Church is compared to a field: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 738.---To Noah’s ark: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 819.---To a lampstand: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 705.---To a cloud: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117.---To the seamless tunic: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 538.---To a vine: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 694.---The Church is denoted by heaven and by a seat: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1116.---The Church is signified by the throne, the living creatures, and the elders surrounding it, ibid., 1121, 1133.---The Church is called fair as the moon, chosen as the sun: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 185.---The Church with Christ is one flesh: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 214.---The Church of the elect is denoted by the world enrolled by Augustus, whose cardinal points are the prelates: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 236.

JERUSALEM. The Church is signified by Jerusalem: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 135.

LAPIS [STONE]. The Church is the small stone cut from the mountain without hands which occupied the whole face of the earth: St. Victorinus the African, V, 87.

LUNA [MOON], the Church as moon: now bright in prosperity, now dark in adversity: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 759.

MANUS [HAND] of the Church signifies a presbyter: St. Chromatius, XX, 350.

MONS [MOUNTAIN] is a figure of the Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 214, 699, 796.

MULIER [WOMAN] seeking the drachma, a figure of the Church inviting to repentance: St. Ambrose, XV, 638.---The Canaanite woman, who is the mother of the Gentiles, prays to the Lord for her daughter—that is, the Church: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 740.---The Canaanite woman signifies the holy Church to be gathered from the Gentiles, ibid., 740; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 75.---The woman suffering a flow of blood is the Church, which, wounded by the sin of the first man, was wholly flowing with blood, wholly running down by origin into death: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 300; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 880.---The adulterous woman signified the Church from the Gentiles: Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 602.

NAVICULA [LITTLE BOAT], sprinkled by the waves, bore the figure of the Church, because it is disturbed on the sea—that is, the world—by waves, that is, persecutions and temptations: Tertullian, I, 1214.

NAVIS [SHIP] is a type of the Church: St. Hilary, IX, 957; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 360; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 28.

OCULUS [EYE] of the Church denotes a bishop: St. Chromatius, XX, 350, 367.

OLIVAE [OLIVE TREES], two, are the two witnesses, or the Church, because of anointing: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1147.

PANIS [BREAD]. The Church is denoted by bread: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 189.

PARADISUS [PARADISE] signifies the Church: St. Ambrose, XV, 778.

PATHMOS [PATMOS]. The straits of the Church are figured by the island of Patmos: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1095.

[Col. 0234] PEDES [FEET] of Christ figure his flesh specifically, but more generally the whole Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1097.

PETRA [ROCK]. The Church is founded upon the rock: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 560, 561, 562.

PISCATIO [FISHING]. The Church is figured in the fishing before and after Christ’s Passion: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1158, 1161, 1164, 1167; XLIII, 196, 397, 632.

SAMARITANA [SAMARITAN WOMAN], a type of the Church: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 66.---The Samaritan harlot is the Church gathered from the Gentiles: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 481.

SENIORES [ELDERS], twenty-four, figure the universal Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1119.

SEPTENARIUS [THE NUMBER SEVEN] indicates the universal Church, ibid., 1092.

STELLAE [STARS], seven, are the Churches which the Apostle names in their own titles: St. Victorinus, V, 319.

TUNICA [TUNIC] of the Lord, seamless, declares the Church’s unity: St. Cyprian, IV, 505.---The integrity of Christ’s body and his seamless tunic prefigured the integrity of the Church: Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 875.

VAS [VESSEL]. The Church is figured in the vessel shown to Peter: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 802.

VESTIMENTA [GARMENTS]. The Church is figured in the garments of Christ transfigured: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 490.---The Church is clothed in white garments: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117.

VIDUA [WIDOW]. The Church, as a widow of the Law, married Christ: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 278.

VIRGO [VIRGIN]. The whole Church is one virgin: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 70.

ARTICLE VI. Allegories concerning the sacraments.

AMBULATIO [WALKING]. Christ’s walking upon the waters signified baptism: St. Augustine, XXXV, 694.

AQUA [WATER] signifies baptism, ibid., 2026.---The water flowing from Christ’s side figured the water of baptism: St. Anselm, CLIX, 255.---The many waters are understood as the gift of baptism which Christ sent forth through the apostles: St. Victorinus, V, 319.

BAPTISMUS [BAPTISM], the day of redemption: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 300.---A figure of death, ibid., 210.---The first gate of the Church, opened through Christ: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 76.

BETHLEEM [BETHLEHEM], called the city of bread, brought forth for us that heavenly bread and that drink by which those who have been satisfied and made drunk shall forever taste eternal joys: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 259.

CURATIO [HEALING] of the man born blind was a figure of baptism: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1272.

JOHN. John’s baptism was a figure of Christ’s baptism: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 629; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 544.

LANCE may signify the opening of the sacraments: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 639.

WASHING. Through the washing, the Christian is a son of God: St. Ambrose, XV, 1760.

MANNA signified the heavenly bread and the altar of God: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1612.—The hidden manna, the sacrament of the Eucharist: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 642.

SEA is Christ’s baptism, ibid., 610.—The Red Sea signifies baptism: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1723; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 796.—The crossing of the Red Sea, a figure of baptism: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1618.—Baptism is signified by the sea of glass: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1107.—The sea of glass around God’s throne is a figure of baptism: the same author, CLXX, 314.

DEATH of the Egyptians signifies the washing away of sins: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1723; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1617.

DOOR. Baptism and penitence are called the Lord’s door: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 432.

BREAD. The Eucharist is called the bread of angels: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1618.

POOL of Bethesda, a figure of baptism: Tertullian, I, 1205.

## ARTICLE VII. Allegories concerning the apostles and the righteous.

ANGEL ascending from the rising of the sun signifies the prophet Elijah, who will precede the times of Antichrist in order to restore the Churches: St. Victorinus, V, 350.—The angels are the preachers of the Church and are signified by the seven stars: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1099.—Angels signify the apostles, [Col. 0235] Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 804.—The Evangelists, ibid., 1096.—The angels of the gates of Jerusalem are teachers of the Church, ibid., 853.—The seven angels are preachers, ibid., 1111.

LIVING CREATURES. The twenty-four living creatures are the twenty-four Fathers: twelve apostles and twelve patriarchs: St. Victorinus, V, 324, 325.—By Ezekiel’s four living creatures are understood the four Evangelists: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1046, 1665; Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118, 1119; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 969; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1152.—The living creatures around God’s throne are Catholic teachers: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 314.

ANTIPAS, the faithful witness, figures all martyrs: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1104.

EAGLE. John is prefigured by the eagle: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1665; St. Eucherius, L, 796; Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 335; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 750; Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 301.—Christ’s disciples are called eagles: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 814, 815.—The souls of the righteous are compared to eagles: St. Ambrose, XV, 1781.

TREES. In Scripture, the states of souls are signified by trees: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 160.

RAMS. The apostles are called rams: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1579.

GOLD tried by fire, the choir of saints: St. Victorinus, V, 318.

OXEN are called apostles and prophets: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1470.

DOGS licking wounds are preachers: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 390.

HAIR signifies the saints of the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1098.

CENTURION. The figure of a perfect mind is most beautifully signified by the Gospel centurion: John Cassian, XLIX, 673.

CANAANITE WOMAN, an image of the penitent soul: Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 192.

STRINGS. The apostles and holy patriarchs are like strings stretched on harps through afflictions: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1091.

HEAVEN is called the soul of the righteous: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1283.—Heavens are called preachers, ibid., 1224.—The apostles are rational heavens: Abbot Rupert, XXXV, 1664.—The apostles and prophets are denoted by the name “heavens”: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1664.

COLUMN. Both preachers and good hearers are columns in God’s temple: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1112.—The faithful are columns of the Church, or of truth: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 353.

BODY. The faithful are Christ’s body, ibid., 236, 290.

CUPS are prophets and teachers of the Law: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1106.

RIGHT HAND of the angel signifies preachers: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1100.

TWELVE. The twelve apostles are the twelve foundations of the city; the twelve oxen supporting the bronze sea; the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel; and the twelve springs at Elim: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 402.—The twelve lions bearing Solomon’s throne, the twelve stones of the altar, and the twelve hours of the day: ibid., 100, 401, 402.

HORSES. The apostles are horses and chariots of salvation: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 758.

FACE. The elect may be understood by a face shining like the sun: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1122.

FOUNTAIN. A fountain of waters indicates the abundance of God’s gifts in the saints, ibid., 1134.

LIGHTNING, the apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1395.

FOUNDATIONS are called prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1195.—The twelve apostles are the foundations of the city: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 402; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1197.

MAN. Matthew bears the form of a man: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1665; St. Eucherius, L, 796; Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 335; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 750.

HOURS. The apostles are hours; Christ is the day: St. Ambrose, XV, 1759.—The twelve apostles are like the twelve hours of the day: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1750; Blessed Alcuin, C, 807; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 402.

ISLANDS are persons of lesser righteousness: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1127.

STONES. The apostles are the stones mentioned in Joshua: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 401; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1367.

AMBASSADORS of peace are Christ’s apostles: the same author, CLXIX, 810.

LION. Mark is prefigured under the form of a lion: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1665; St. Eucherius, L, 796; Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118; [Col. 0236] St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 335; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 750.

LOCUSTS are the food of prophets: St. Ambrose, XV, 1578.

LAMPS. The prophets are lamps among God’s people: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1583.

LIGHT. The apostles are called the light of the world: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 232, 233, 234; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 753.

WOMAN giving birth signifies a penitent: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 331.

CLOUDS signify apostles: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 958.—Preachers: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1094.—Saints: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 405.

EYES figure the Church’s preachers: Alcuin, C, 118.—The eyes of the living creatures are the spiritual lights of the elect, ibid., 1118.

SHEEP at the right hand signify the elect: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 862.

PALMS signify the victory of the elect: Alcuin, C, 1133.

FEET of Christ are the apostles, who, forged through the Passion, preached his word throughout the whole world: St. Victorinus, V, 319.

BOWLS are apostles and apostolic men: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1106.

FISH. The fish which first came up, having a coin in its mouth, is a figure of St. Stephen the protomartyr: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 601.

STREETS of the holy city are saints of lesser merit: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 866.

LABOUR PAINS. Labour pains, forgotten after giving birth, denote the blessed soul: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 337.

STEWARDS. Preachers are the stewards of the vineyard, ibid., 135.

BRANCHES. The grafted branches of the wild olive are patriarchs and prophets: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1486.

KINGS. The members of Christ—that is, the faithful—are kings and priests, because their head is king and priest: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1093.

SALT. The apostles are called the salt of the earth: St. Chromatius, XX, 337; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 231, 232.

SAMARITAN WOMAN at the well, an image of the penitent soul: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 229.

THRONES placed in heaven are perfect teachers and prelates, established and ordained through mercy in the holy Church: Richard, CXCVI, 746.

ELDERS. The twenty-four elders are all the holy and perfect teachers of the Old and New Testaments: Richard, CXCVI, 747.—They are called twenty-four elders because of the gravity of maturity, ibid.—The apostles are called elders: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 909.

SERAPHIM. The two seraphim are apostles and prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 198.

SERVANTS. Preachers are the servants of the Lord who invites to the wedding feast: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 612.

SMYRNA is translated into Latin as “their song,” that is, the song of the elect: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1096.

BLOODY SWEAT of the Lord signified the sufferings of martyrs: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 520.

SEVEN THUNDERS are the seven oracles of the prophets: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1009.

NEW WINESKINS are called apostles: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 380; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1480.

VESSELS. The faithful are compared to earthenware vessels: Alcuin, C, 1100.

SEERS. The prophets are called seers: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1228.

IRON ROD signifies the governance of preachers: Blessed Alcuin, 1108.

CALF. Luke is announced in the calf: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1665; St. Eucherius, L, 796; Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 335; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 750.

CHRIST’S golden girdle, the choir of saints: St. Victorinus, V, 318.

## ARTICLE VIII. Allegories concerning Jews and Gentiles

MANY WATERS are understood to be peoples: St. Victorinus, V, 319; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1528.

DAUGHTER of the ruler of the synagogue signifies the Jewish people: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 485, 486.—The ruler’s daughter is the synagogue: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 302; Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 290.

SHE-ASS or colt of a she-ass signifies the human race: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 57.—By the name of the she-ass the Gentile world is signified [Col. 0237]: St. Ambrose, XV, 1759; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 607.—The Lord rode the colt of the she-ass as a figure of the Gentile people: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1257.—The she-ass and her colt brought to Christ are figures of Jews and Gentiles: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 700, 701; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 544.

ASS, a figure of the Gentiles: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 453.—In Sacred Scripture we often see the nations signified by the name “asses”: St. Hilary, IX, 1019.

OUTER COURT of the temple signifies Jews and Gentiles to be expelled from the Church: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1146.

BEAST means a multitude of peoples: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1132.

BETHANY, “house of obedience,” signifies the people of the Gentiles: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 104.

OX. By the ox the Jews are signified: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 453.

BLIND MAN. The blind man beside the road, crying out to Jesus, represented the human race: Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 94.—The man blind from birth signifies the human race, ibid., 114.—The man blind from birth prefigured the Gentiles: the same author, CLXIX, 587.—The blind man of the Gospel is the Jew who, in the synagogue and in the village of ignorance, was held and sat oppressed by the blindness of ignorance: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 666.—The two blind men sitting beside the road signify both peoples, Jews and Gentiles, drawing near to Christ through faith: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 76.

DOG. The Gentiles are figured by the dogs licking Lazarus’s sores: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1352.—In the Gospel, Gentiles are called dogs by Christ: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 411.—Dogs are Jews: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 513.

FLESH. The Jews are called fleshly and pleasure-seeking: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 286.

CHAIR of pestilence is philosophy, the Pharisee, and the heretic: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 325.

CEDRON signifies the hardness of the Jews: Venerable Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 788.

CENTURION prefigures the believing people from among the Gentiles: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 857; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 349.

HORSES. The Gentiles are called horses driven by the devil: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1000.

FIG TREE on which Christ, being hungry, found no fruit is the synagogue of the Jews: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 384.

FIG TREE. By the fig tree without fruit we understand the synagogue and assembly of the Jews: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1044.

RIVERS signify the Gentiles: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 981.

HAY is a type of the Gentiles: St. Hilary, IX, 948.

WOMAN WITH A HEMORRHAGE figured the Gentile people: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 486.

STONES are called Gentiles: St. Cyprian, IV, 377; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 159, 160.

LEPER signifies the Jewish people: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1461.

LOCUSTS were a figure of the Gentile people: St. Ambrose, XV, 1578.—Of the Jews: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 154.

MAGI seeking Christ by the star were a figure of the Gentiles: St. Hilary, IX, 923; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1334.—The calling of the Magi signifies the calling of the Gentiles: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 394.

SEA. The Gentiles are signified by the sea: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 981, 1057; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 780, 824.

TWO WOMEN GRINDING, one of whom is taken and the other left, are a type of the synagogue and the Church: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 193.

MUTE MAN healed by Christ, a type of the Gentiles: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 390.

CHRIST’S EYES were Jews and Gentiles: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 284.

OLIVE signifies the Jews: Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 143.

PARALYTIC, a figure of the Jewish people: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 285.

SINFUL WOMAN. The sinful woman washing, anointing, and wiping Christ’s feet is a type of the Church to be called from the Gentiles: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 278.

PHARISEE. The Pharisee who invited Christ, but anointed neither his head nor his feet, is a type of the synagogue, ibid.

SWINE signify the Jews: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1472.

PUBLICAN bears the type of the Gentile people: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 285.

SAMARITAN. The Gentile people is figured by the Samaritan: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 572, 599.

[Col. 0238] SCORPIONS of the earth are called the enemies of Israel: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 987.

TWELVE STARS are the twelve tribes of Israel, ibid., 1011.

BULLS signify the Gentiles: the same author, CLXVIII, 1574.

OLD WINESKINS, Jews; new wineskins, Christians: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 289.

VESSEL. The salvation and reception of all Gentile peoples within the Church was figured by the vessel shown to Peter: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 802, 1036.

VINEYARD of the Lord, the house of Israel: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1168.—The vineyard of Sodom, the Jews, ibid., 791.

VIPER-BROOD. The Jews are a brood of vipers: by the death of the mother and the killing of the father, when they kill Christ they burst open the womb of their mother, the synagogue: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 287.

VINE. The Jewish nation is called an alien vine: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 713.

## ARTICLE IX. Allegories concerning heretics and sinners.

ABYSS and earth, reprobate persons: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1178.

EGYPT and Sodom signify the iniquity of the persecutions in the time of Antichrist: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1149.—Egypt signifies the world from which God calls his own: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1341.—The Egyptians are the impenitent, ibid., 979.

WINGS of locusts signify the proud learning of heretics: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1140.

FOUR ANGELS bound in the great river Euphrates are the whole body of the reprobate: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1141.

OUTER COURT of the temple signifies heretics to be expelled from the Church, ibid., 1147.

BEAST ascending from the abyss figures Antichrist, ibid., 1148; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1063.

DOGS whom the Apostle expels outside are figures of heretics: Tertullian, II, 289.

STAGS. Heretics are stags: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 257.

HERD of bulls among the cows of the peoples are heretics, ibid., 1017.

DEMONS. Heretics are signified by demons, ibid., 1465.

BLACK HORSE signifies false fathers, ibid., 944.—The black horse signifies the hunger of the wicked: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1125.—The pale horse signifies the envy of heretics: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 946.

THE DESTROYING KING of the locusts, a type of heretics: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1141.

FURNACE. Antichrist persecuting the Church is compared to a great furnace, ibid., 1139.

THIEF is a heretic: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 720.

JERUSALEM is called Sodom and Egypt, ibid., 1030.—A harlot, ibid., 1037.

MAN who fell among robbers represents the sinner: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 866.

DECEIT. The teaching, wickedness, and deceit of heretics are so called: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 458.

JEWS. Heretics are signified by the name “Jews”: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1104.

BURDOCKS. Heresies are burdocks and thorns: John Cassian, L, 14.

LEPERS signify sinners: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLXVIII, 661.—The nine lepers mystically signify heretics: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIX, 322.

LOCUSTS. The locusts going forth from the smoke of the pit of the abyss indicate heretics: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1139; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 783.

WOLVES signify heretics: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 420; St. Ambrose, XV, 1711.

SEA OF GLASS is directed against false persons and hypocrites: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 918.

WOMAN is a type of human frailty: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 152, 361.—The bent state of the sinful soul is signified by the bent woman of the Gospel: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 447.

CHAFF are those who are imbued with the mysteries of the same faith as the elect, but differ from their solid perfection either through the lightness of their works or through the emptiness of faithlessness: Blessed Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 774.—Chaff signifies sinners: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 166.—Proud persons: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1361.

HIDDEN LOAVES are the errors of heretics: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 377.

[Col. 0239] PARALYTIC. Mystically, the paralytic is the person dissolved and without good works: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 327.—The paralytic signifies one who is becoming spiritually lukewarm: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 116.—A spirit weakened by sins, ibid., 609.—The human race, ibid., 604.

ALIEN SHEPHERDS are heretics: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 607.

PARTRIDGE. Heretics are compared to the partridge: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 376.

PLANTS of death are heretics: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 716.

SERPENT is called the error of heretics: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1418.

STARS falling from heaven are those who seem holy and who will fall into wickedness in that time of Antichrist: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1127.

EARTHQUAKE of the sixth seal foretells the final persecution of Antichrist, ibid., 1126.

WIND. The teaching of the wicked is like wind and storm: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 204.

STEWARD accused before his master, a person abusing God’s gifts: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 524, 530.

VINE. Disobedient Adam is compared to an alien vine, ibid., 831.

FOX. Herod, a fox: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 251; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 776.—Heretics are compared to foxes: St. Jerome, XXV, 110; St. Ambrose, XV, 1707, 1710; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 857.

TARES are those who do not even deign to hear the words of faith: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 774.—Tares signify heretics: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 493, 494.

## ARTICLE X. Allegories concerning virtues and vices.

### I.—Virtues.

SIX WINGS are the works of mercy: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 918.

ANGEL appearing to Joseph, Mary’s husband, signifies inward inspirations: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 321, 325.

ANNA the prophetess is a type of the devout soul that benefits itself and its neighbour: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 354.

WATER, lowly water changed into wine, signifies that the mortal substance of humanity is to be changed in the resurrection into glory: St. Ambrose, XVII, 620; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 608.

GOOD TREE and bad tree in the Gospel, the two wills of human beings: St. Augustine, XLIV, 370, 461, 667, 668, 672, 754; XLV, 454, 1455, 1458.

STEWARD OF THE FEAST signifies discernment at a banquet: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 435.

SILVER is the word of preaching: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 678.

REFINED GOLD is charity: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 740.

BETHLEHEM mystically signifies a religious community: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 398.

REED given to John to measure God’s temple tropologically signifies divine preaching: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1146.

CANA OF GALILEE is zeal for revelation: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 398.

FLESH signifies weakness: Blessed Lanfranc of Canterbury, CLI, 303.

CHARITY is the mother of all goods: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1602.—The source of goods, ibid., 1658.—Charity, the root and foundation of all virtues: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 158.—Charity, the activity of the right path, ibid., 194.

EYE-SALVE is humility: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 901.

DOVE signifies works of piety: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1387.

HEART. What is a priestly heart but the ark of the covenant? St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 933.

CRYSTAL. Faith is compared to crystal: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118.

WHITE HORSE is the word of preaching sent into the world with the Holy Spirit: St. Victorinus, V, 328.

REPUTATION. The good fragrance of reputation, directed to the edification of one’s neighbour, is signified by the star leading the Magi to Jesus: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 402.

FLAME. The love of God is signified by a flame of fire: Alcuin, C, 1098.

SMOKE is the effect of incense: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 986.—The smoke of the pit, the wisdom of this age, ibid.

WHITE GEM, adoption as a child of God: St. Victorinus, V, 322.

SWORD of the mouth is speech: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1005.

SHOULDER signifies labour: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 657, 662, 664.

[Col. 0240] WATER JAR. Faith is like a water jar for drawing grace: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 577.

JORDAN is a type of humility: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 396; Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 397.

BED signifies boldness and security: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1107.

TEN LEPERS signify our inner and outer senses: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 575.

LITTLE BOOK received from the angel’s hand is preaching: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1145.

BOOK sealed with seven seals, wisdom: Gilbert, CLXXXII, 186.

CLOTH is a symbol of purity of heart: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 783.

WASHING of feet signifies the cleansing of the affections, ibid., 784.

MOON signifies charity: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLI, 540.

HIDDEN MANNA is immortality: St. Victorinus, V, 322.

HAND signifies the active life: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 250.

PEARLS. Religion is compared to pearls: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1131.

LITTLE BOAT signifies faith: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1554.—Simon’s boat is a symbol of the humbled soul: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 464, 608.

NEW NAME written on the stone is “Christian”: St. Victorinus, V, 322.

EYE signifies the intention of the mind: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 250.—The contemplative life, ibid., 251.—The eyes of the soul are understanding and affection: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 164.—The raising of the eyes is intention, ibid., 626.

SWEET SPICES are prayers: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 757.

OIL. Charity is signified by oil: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 841.

OLIVE GROVE. The Mount of Olives signifies mercy: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 23, 26.

BONES signify firmness: Blessed Lanfranc of Canterbury, CLI, 303.

FEET signify the thoughts of the mind, ibid., 366.

BOWLS. Charity is understood by golden bowls: Blessed Alcuin, 1098.

FISH signifies faith: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 320.

ROOTS of trees are thoughts, ibid., 161.

NET cast into the sea, a type of mercy: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1042.

SALT is used figuratively for wisdom: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 231, 232.

LADDER. The Beatitudes are that ladder of Jacob whose top reached from earth to heaven: St. Chromatius, XX, 328.

THE NUMBER SIX signifies perfection: Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 752.

SOLITUDE is a lamp which shines upon the whole world, set upon the candlestick of the wilderness: St. Eucherius of Lyons, L, 709.—This solitude is the city which cannot be hidden, built on the mountain of the desert, which by its image gave the heavenly Jerusalem to the earth, ibid.

GOLDEN CENSER is faith: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 973.

TRUMPET. Charity is compared to a trumpet because it summons to spiritual warfare: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1116.

SEAMLESS TUNIC signifies faith: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 360.—Charity: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 283.

VESSELS. Hearts are signified by vessels: Blessed Lanfranc of Canterbury, CLI, 629.

WEDDING GARMENT is charity: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 615.

VOICE of many waters signifies charity: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1098.

### II.—Vices.

EAGLE is called blood: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1117.

EAR signifies the desire for human praise: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXXIV, 794.

CAMEL represents worldly affections, ibid., 695.

EMMAUS signifies imperfection and lukewarmness, ibid., 807.

BLACK HORSE signifies famine: St. Victorinus, V, 329.—The pale horse and the one seated upon it, Death, signify great plagues and mortalities, ibid.—The red horse foretells future wars, ibid.

DREGS denote sinful action: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 791.

[Col. 0241] LANTERN signifies sinful consent, ibid., 791.

BED is called great tribulation: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1108.

LEPROSY of the body, an image of lust: Adam Scotus, CXCVIII, 411.

SEA signifies the present age: Blessed Alcuin, C, 819, 995.

HARLOT. The great harlot of the Apocalypse specifically signifies Rome, which was then persecuting God’s Church: St. Ambrose, XVII, 915.

PARALYSIS signifies harmful thoughts: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 128.

TWO GATES through which the devil enters: covetousness and fear: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 204.

PIT of the abyss is falsehood: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 986.

KINGDOM of the devil is the world: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 297.

BLOOD figures sin: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1107.

TARES are an evil thought: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 233.

## ARTICLE XI. Allegories concerning our last things.

CEDAR. In Sacred Scripture, by the name cedar is sometimes expressed the lofty excellence of heavenly glory, and sometimes the height of heavenly glory: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1166.

EARTHLY JERUSALEM is a figure of the heavenly Jerusalem: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 68, 69.

HOUR of supper signifies the faith of the world: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1231.

RAINBOW signifies the judgment preceded by the flood and followed by fire: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117.

JASPER signifies the green pastures of paradise, ibid., 1116.

BED is called eternal punishment, ibid., 1108.

MOON. The heavenly Jerusalem is described as perfect like the sun and moon: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 954.

NAZARETH is a heavenly garden: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 94.

ONE SHEEPFOLD of all may be understood as heaven, ibid., 321.

PARADISE is eternal life: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1103.

SUN. The heavenly Jerusalem is described as perfect like the sun and moon: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 954.

BALANCE in the hand of the rider is the scale of examination: St. Victorinus, V, 329.

VINEYARD of the Lord is called the heavenly paradise: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 140.

## ARTICLE XII. Allegories concerning Sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0242]

WINGS of the four living creatures figure the sayings of the two Testaments: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118.—Sacred Scripture is expressed by three wings: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 918.

LIVING CREATURES. The four living creatures are the four Gospels: St. Victorinus, V, 324; St. Ambrose, XV, 1253.—The twenty-four living creatures are the twenty-four books of the prophets: St. Victorinus, V, 324.

WATER. Sacred Scripture is compared to waters and thunders: Abbot Rupert, CLIX, 1090.

FLYING EAGLE is called Sacred Scripture, ibid., 984, 1051.

BOW held by the rider on the white horse figures the New and Old Testaments: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1123.

SHOE. The Gospel is called a wedding shoe: St. Ambrose, XV, 1582.

EYE-SALVE signifies divine commandments: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1114.

SWORD signifies the preaching of the Old and New Testaments, ibid., 1099.

OPEN LITTLE BOOK is the grace of the New Testament, ibid., 1144.—The little book received from the angel’s hand is Sacred Scripture, ibid., 1145.

BOOK written within and without signifies the Old Testament, which was given into Christ’s hands: St. Victorinus, V, 327.—The book written within and without seems to contain both Testaments: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1120.

LIGHT. Sacred Scripture is light upon earth: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1204.

CHRIST’S BREASTS are the two Testaments: St. Victorinus, V, 318.

EYES. The preaching of the Old and New Testaments is figured by the eyes of the four living creatures: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118.

DOOR of the Lord is the Old and New Testament: Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 432.

BREAD signifies Sacred Scripture: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 462.

ELDERS. The Old Testament is indicated by the twenty-four elders and the throne: Blessed Alcuin, C, 1117.

THUNDERS. The preaching of the Old and New Testaments is expressed by voices and thunders, ibid.

SEVEN TRUMPETS indicate the perfect preaching of the Old and New Testaments, ibid., 1135.

VOICE of waters is called Sacred Scripture: Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 858.—Sacred Scripture is called a voice from heaven, ibid., 1090.

[Col. 0241]

# XLVIII. EXEGETICAL INDEX OF FIGURES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT, ARRANGED ANALOGICALLY, WHILE PRESERVING WITHIN EACH ANALOGY BOTH THE ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS AND THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS.

## NOTICE.

In this Index, as also in the following one, for the usefulness and convenience of the reader alike, we have established various divisions and have reduced all the figures discussed by the Fathers to five headings: I, figures relating to Christ; II, those relating to the Church; III, those relating to the apostles and the righteous; IV, those relating to Jews and Gentiles; V, those relating to heretics and the ungodly. Moreover, lest anything escape the reader, we have added an Appendix in which we have collected all figures that express either the devil or the two Testaments. In each article we have observed an alphabetical order of subjects, so that whatever anyone may seek will be found at once.

# [INDEX OF FIGURES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT.]

## PREFACE.

### What a figure is, and its division.

A figure is antiphrasis, when words are spoken through their opposite: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 634.—A type or figure is the manifestation, through actions considered as actions, of unknown present, past, or future realities: Junilius Africanus, LXVIII, 33.—There are four kinds of types:

1. Pleasant things signify pleasant things; for example, Christ’s resurrection is a type of our resurrection.
