2. Sad things signify sad things; for example, the rejection of angels is a type of the rejection of the wicked.
3. Sad things signify pleasant things; for example, Adam’s transgression is a type of the Saviour’s righteousness.
4. Pleasant things signify sad things; for example, baptism is a type of Christ’s death.

Junilius Africanus, LXVIII, 34.

## I.—Figures that prefigure Christ.

[Col. 0243]

AARON the priest prefigured Christ the priest; and his rod, miraculously putting forth shoots, prefigured Christ’s flesh, which is called a rod by the prophet. For it flowered when dry, because it rose after death: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1060; XVI, 560; XVII, 25; St. Jerome, XXII, 545; St. Prosper, LI, 779; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1244; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109; Alcuin, C, 637; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1034; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1368.

ABEL, shepherd of sheep, offering from the firstborn of his flock, prefigured Christ, the good shepherd of souls, offering the sacrifice of his passion; and, innocent though slain by his brother’s impiety, represented Christ the innocent one, sacrificed by his Jewish brethren: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1061; XVII, 813; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 145, 460, 461; St. Leo, LV, 118; LVI, 1136; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 355; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359; Eugyppius, LXII, 672; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 515; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 99; Blessed Alcuin, C, 768; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 674; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 173; Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 328, 343.

ABRAHAM, leaving his kindred, wandering in foreign lands, and sacrificing his only son upon the mountain, represented the Saviour coming into this world and dying for the life of the world: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 133; St. Prosper, LI, 746; St. Leo, LV, 148; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 551, 563; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 100.

ACHIMAAS, whose name is interpreted “beauty,” bears the type of the Saviour, because all who shine in the holy Church with the splendour of virtues receive it from the fullness of his light: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 404.

ACHINOE, whose name is interpreted “the brother’s rest,” rightly figures Christ; for he is our brother, who, rising for us, called us brethren: St. Gregory the Great, LXXXIX, 404.

ACHITOB, “brother and good,” is a figure of Christ: our brother because he shares our nature; good because he freed from eternal death the nature which he assumed: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 404.

ADAM, formed on the sixth day, represents Christ born in the sixth age of the world; and as all die in Adam, so in Christ they are made alive. When God cast Adam into sleep in order to make a wife for him from his side, Adam bore the type of Christ sleeping upon the cross. In Adam’s side, Christ’s opened side was shown: Tertullian, II, 782.—St. Ambrose, XV, 1611; XVII, 98, 813.—St. Jerome, XXII, 1101.—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 684; XXXV, 1401, 1463; XXXVI, 461, 668; XXXVII, 1381; XXXIX, 778; XLIV, 462; XLV, 1171, 1223, 1225.—St. Prosper, LI, 735.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 378.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 99.—Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 121.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 52.—St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 506.—Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 161.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 284.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 215.

ADONIRAM, interpreted “my Lord is exalted,” is an apt type of our Lord: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 137.

AMINADAB is called Christ because he is king and priest: St. Ambrose, XVI, 290.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 532.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 938.

AMOS, a shepherd and countryman, is a type of Christ, who, transferred from the pastoral office over sheep—that is, from the governance of the Hebrews—now feeds other flocks among the Gentiles: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

AOD, using either hand as his right, figures Christ: Venerable Hildebert, CLXXIV, 270.

ASER, interpreted “blessed,” points to the Lord Jesus Christ, whose bread is rich in the mouths of believers because he provides delights for kings; that is, he gives the sacraments of his body and blood to the saints, who are rightly called kings because they govern well either themselves or those subject to them: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 46.

BANAIAS, killing a lion in a pit, is a type of Christ and the Church: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 137.

BENJAMIN, interpreted “son of the right hand,” is our Lord Jesus Christ, most beloved of the Father: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 262, 281.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 48.

BOAZ, a mighty man and of great wealth, kinsman of Elimelech, was our Redeemer, who was related to the law and to the lawgiver, because he was promised through the law, was born from the stock of the patriarchs, and according to the flesh derived his origin from the Jewish people. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1205.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 674.

[Col. 0244] KORAH prefigured the people to be redeemed through Christ’s Passion, because Korah is interpreted “baldness,” just as our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1069.—St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1097.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1003.

KISH, who is called “hard,” signifies not only the elect, but even the Redeemer himself; for no one proved harsher toward himself. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 249, 282.

CYRUS the king designates the Lord Savior both by name and by deeds; this is established not by our conjecture but by the utterly plain words of Isaiah the prophet. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 536.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1521.

DAN, whose name is interpreted “judgment” or “judge,” is referred to him who is awaited as Judge of the living and the dead. Rufinus, XXI, 322.

DANIEL, cast into the lions’ den and delivered by God, represented Christ the Lord handed over by the Jews. St. Prosper, LI, 809, 810.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1511.

DAVID, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand,” set forth the image of our Savior: whether because, under the persecution of the Jews, he endured unjust persecution; or because, strong of hand, he conquered and bound the strong devil, and distributed his spoils throughout the whole world. Thus, through almost all the events of his life, he prefigured Christ, and was a type both of the good things Christ bestowed upon us and of the evils which Christ himself suffered from the reprobate. St. Hilary, IX, 844.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 251, 314, 861, 883; XV, 1506; XVII, 833.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 73, 148, 154, 245, 302, 305, 315, 600, 603, 619, 628, 646, 663, 664, 713, 716; XXXVII, 1238, 1845; XLII, 458.—St. Prosper, LI, 378, 380, 797, 799.—St. Leo, LVI, 1136.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 248, 249, 250, 251.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 35, 43, 193, 1015.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 461, 505, 509, 642.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 634; CI, 133.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 49, 58, 342; CXI, 58.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 65.—St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 147, 210, 213, 230, 300.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 624, 1111.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 691.—St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 507.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1090, 1097, 1104, 1107, 1133, 1135, 1136; CLXVIII, 1566; CLXX, 20, 96, 143.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 298, 498.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1078.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1251.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 389.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 231, 536.

ELIAKIM, whose name is interpreted “resurrection of the Lord,” designates no one better than our Redeemer, who said: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 350.

ELIJAH, whose name is interpreted “God the Lord,” or “my God,” or “mighty God,” signifies Christ the Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord is strong, the Lord mighty in battle.” When that same prophet went into the wilderness, was fed by ravens, and was taken up into the aerial heaven, he represented Christ, fed by angels in the wilderness and ascending into the heavens; and likewise in many circumstances of his life. St. Cyprian, IV, 615.—St. Ambrose, XVII, 834.—St. Prosper, LI, 803.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1217.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 206, 207.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1256; CLXX, 248.—Venerable Hildebert, CLXXIV, 1089.

ELIMELECH is interpreted “my God”; and who can more fittingly be called by this name than our Savior? Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1199, 1201.

ELISHA, whose name is interpreted “salvation of the Lord,”—who else is he but his Son, who is everywhere called Savior? That same prophet, casting himself down in order to raise the dead man, represented Christ, who, descending from heaven and humbling himself, healed our mortality, etc. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1274; XVII, 834.—St. Prosper, LI, 804.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 895.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 912.

ENOCH, translated to heaven, prefigured Christ’s Ascension. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1217.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 223.

ESAU, from whose seed came Job, signifies Christ among the Gentiles through faith. St. Prosper, LI, 750.

EZRA figures the house of God—that is, its restoration through Christ the Lord. St. Prosper, LI, 813.

HEZEKIAH, whose name is interpreted “one who lays hold of the Lord,” or “strength of the Lord,” prefigured Christ when he broke the bronze serpent and thus removed many abuses of idolatry. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 252; CXI, 63.

EZEKIEL was a type of Christ: both when he is called “son of man,” and when, thirty years old, he saw the heavens opened, as the Gospel tradition relates concerning Christ; and when he stands beside the river Chebar, etc. St. Jerome, XXV, 698.—St. Prosper, LI, 812.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 796, 797.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.—Rabanus [Col. 0245] Maurus, CX, 647; CXI, 67.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1422.

GAD represents Christ, who at his second coming will fight against Antichrist. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.

GIDEON, who went into battle with three hundred men, bore a type of Christ, who won victory over the world in the sign of the cross; for the number three hundred is contained in the letter T, which displays the form of a cross; and likewise in other circumstances. St. Prosper, LI, 786.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1157, 1158, 1163, 1172; CXI, 56.—Peter Damian, CXLIV, 893.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1035; CLXVIII, 17.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 34, 655.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1092.

ELKANAH prefigured Christ, and his sacrifice represented Christ’s Passion. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 21, 30.

ISAAC, born by promise as a type of the Savior, surrendered by his father as a sacrificial victim, and himself carrying the wood for the sacrifice, prefigured the suffering Christ; and likewise in various circumstances of his life. Tertullian, II, 346.—St. Zeno, XI, 427.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 319, 428, 446, 501, 1061; XVII, 133, 464.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 1464; XXXVI, 244, 245, 603; XXXVIII, 133; XLI, 511; XLII, 772, 810, 852.—St. Prosper, LI, 696, 745, 746.—St. Leo, LVI, 1136.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 356, 799.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 318, 359.—Eugyppius, LXII, 675.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 569, 573, 574.—Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 401.—St. Bruno of Asti, CXIV, 198.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 323, 397, 401, 448, 458, 465; CLXIX, 95, 101.—Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 684.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 135.

JABEZ, that master of scribes and singers, whom can he signify better than our Redeemer, who is the true master of holy teachers and of those who rightly sing praises to God? Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 295, 296.

JACOB, whose name is interpreted “supplanter,” prefigured Christ when descending into Egypt, when wrestling with the angel, when having a vision, and when marrying Laban’s daughter. St. Hilary, IX, 878.—St. Zeno, XI, 428.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 624.—St. Jerome, XXV, 930.—St. Prosper, LI, 751, 756.—St. Leo, LVI, 1136.—St. Maximus of Turin, LXII, 608.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 437.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 563.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 591, 610; CXI, 38.—St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 506.—Rupert, abbot, CLVII, 490; CLXIX, 100; CLXX, 23.

JAIR, whose name is interpreted “enlightening,” signified Christ, the true light. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1176.

JEHOIACHIN prefigured Christ. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 341.

JEPHTHAH AND HIS DAUGHTER. Jephthah, sacrificing his daughter after his victory, displayed the figure of the Redeemer, who, departing from the presence of his brethren—that is, the Jews—received sovereignty among the Gentiles. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1817.—St. Prosper, LI, 789.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1177; CXI, 57.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1040.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 33.

JEREMIAH the prophet, by both words and deeds, figured Christ’s death and Passion. St. Jerome, XXV, 666.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1365; CLXX, 122.

JEZREEL signifies Christ’s seed. Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 30.

JOSHUA SON OF NUN, Moses’ minister and high priest, set forth in both name and action a type of Christ, Savior of the world. For just as he led the people of Israel into the land of promise, so the Savior has led us to the truth and will place us in the kingdom of glory. St. Hilary, X, 463.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 1154; XVI, 651.—St. Jerome, XXV, 1391.—St. Augustine, XLII, 328.—St. Prosper, LI, 782.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 195, 630.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 115.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 118, 137, 1120; CIX, 1090; CXI, 54, 65.—Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 187.

JOTHAM, whose name is interpreted “perfect,” was a type and figure of Christ. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 513; CXI, 62.

JOB—righteous, truthful, wealthy, tempted by the devil, losing his possessions and children, covered with sores, urged by his wife to sin, enduring his friends’ insolence, sitting on the dung-heap, recovering health, etc., etc.—presents an image of Christ, who endured things like all these for us. St. Zeno, XI, 441, 442.—St. Jerome, XXVI, 623 and following.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 525, 532, 576, 583, 1063; LXXVI, 237.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1607; CLXVIII, 963, 967.

[Col. 0246] JONAH in every respect held and fulfilled the type of the Savior: whether when he fled from the presence of the Lord, when he himself became the cause of his being cast into the sea, or when plunged into the depths and emerging unharmed on the third day. St. Hilary, IX, 473.—St. Zeno, XI, 418.—St. Jerome, XXII, 546.—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 384.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 303.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 357.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 404, 405.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 474, 475, 477, 532, 553.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 402; CLXX, 125.

JONATHAN, a figure of Christ. St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 761.

JOSEPH—whether dreaming, cast into the pit of death, sold by his brothers, taken into Egypt, or feeding the hungry Egyptians, etc., etc.—through all the events of his life represented Christ, Savior of the world. Tertullian, II, 346.—St. Cyprian, IV, 689.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 405, 644, 645, 649, 688, 1096, 1110.—Paulinus of Milan, XX, 727.—Rufinus, XXI, 328.—St. Jerome, XXII, 462; XXV, 1493.—St. Prosper, LI, 752, 753, 755, 756.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 595.—St. Leo, LVI, 1136.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.—St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 166.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1217.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 792.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 622, 624, 629, 663; CIX, 223.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 218.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 448, 506, 524, 526, 535, 576; CLXX, 107.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 1148, 1151.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 651.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 760, 1025; CLXXXV, 141.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 231, 236.

JOSIAH prefigured Christ suffering for us, who casts down vices, pulverizes what has been burned, and throws it into the torrent of this world. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 63.

JUDAH, a lion’s whelp, prefigures the Lord Savior, as one sprung from a leonine lineage, namely, born from the royal stock. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 721.—Rufinus, XXI, 301, 302.—St. Jerome, XXV, 1493.—Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 694.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 43.

LOT, righteous and hospitable in Sodom, who deserved to escape safely from that fire which was a likeness of the coming judgment, bore a type of the body of Christ. This body, in all the saints, now groans among the wicked and impious, does not consent to their deeds, and at the world’s end will be delivered from association with them, when they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 556; CXI, 36.

MALACHI, whose name is interpreted “angel of the Lord,” prefigured the Savior, who is called the Angel of Great Counsel. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

The ANGEL appearing to MANOAH and standing in the flame of the altar must be understood rather to have signified that Angel of Great Counsel in the form of a servant—that is, in the humanity which he was to assume—not one who would receive sacrifice. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1192.

MATTATHIAS signifies the Lord Savior, who is prince of God’s people and defender of his elect. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1163.

MELCHIZEDEK the king, offering bread and wine, represents Christ’s kingdom and priesthood, whose sacrament of body and blood is offered under the appearance of bread and wine. St. Cyprian, IV, 376.—St. Leo, LV, 148.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 889.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1064.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 320.—St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 754.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 188.—Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 460.

MOSES, who freed his people from the slavery of the Egyptians, represented Christ, Savior of the world, through almost all the events of his life. Tertullian, I, 667; II, 347.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 319.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 743.—St. Prosper, LI, 759, 761, 777, 782.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 17, 18, 84, 86.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1034.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 576.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 260, 1151.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 492.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 306.

NAHSHON, whose name is interpreted “serpentine,” was a figure of Christ. St. Ambrose, XV, 1222.

NABOTH, dying, is a most fitting type of Christ falsely accused by rulers and fixed to the cross. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 217; CXI, 65.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1251.

NEBUCHADNEZZAR dreamed of the precious stone—that is, Christ. Blessed Alcuin, C, 1129.

NOAH, whose name is interpreted “rest,” drunk from the vine and stripped naked in his house—who could fail to see in him a figure of Christ? He was made drunk when he suffered; he was stripped naked when he was crucified; and this took place in his house, that is, among his own people and the household of his blood, namely the Jews. For then the mortality of his flesh was laid bare. Ham, seeing this nakedness—that is, Christ’s Passion—mocked; and the Jews, seeing Christ’s death, derided it, etc., etc. St. Cyprian, IV, 375.—St. Ambrose, XV, 1610.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 1022; XLI, 472.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 200, 359.—St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 164.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 102.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 320, 525.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 185.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 340, 346, 362; CLXX, 151, 231.

HOSEA the prophet prefigured Christ. Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 17, 158.

UZZIAH prefigured Christ, who took into his body the Church from the fornication of the Gentiles. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.

OTHNIEL, striking the city of Kiriath, represented Christ. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1623.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 272.

SOLOMON foretells the figure of Christ, who built a house for the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem, not from wood and stones but from holy human beings; to hear whose wisdom the queen came from Ethiopia—that is, the Church from the Gentiles. And likewise in many other respects. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1668.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 186; CXI, 59.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1141.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 521, 759.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 147, 672, 912.—Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1274.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 75.

SAMSON, in his birth, life, and death, represented Christ in many ways. St. Ambrose, XVII, 774.—St. Jerome, XXVI, 454.—St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1646; XLVI, 820.—St. Prosper, LI, 790, 792.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 254, 264.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 491, 1173.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1194, 1197, 1198.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 928.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1043.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1090.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 275.

SAMUEL prefigured Christ the Lord: leader, priest, prophet, reprover of priests, etc. St. Cyprian, IV, 689.—St. Prosper, LI, 795.—Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 43.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 428.

SAUL, in his persecution, bore Christ’s type in many respects. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 250.

SETH, whose name is interpreted “resurrection,” signifies the risen Christ. St. Augustine, XXXIX, 445, 460, 461.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 101.

TOBIAH THE SON bore the image of our Lord Jesus Christ, who illuminates by the brightness of his power a figure hidden and blinded by the darkness of the law. St. Prosper, LI, 815.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 66.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 1101.

ZARAH, whose name is interpreted “rising,” was a figure of Christ. St. Ambrose, XV, 1600.

ZECHARIAH, the high priest, bore a type of Christ. St. Ambrose, XV, 1542.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 699.

ZERUBBABEL, a type of the Savior, who brought the people back from captivity and built the temple from living stones. St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 170.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 697.

II.—Figures concerning the Church.

AARON, a type of bishops, bears the image of the Church, which he fittingly compared to a very strong mountain: it surpasses others in holy honor and stands firm in the solidity of faith. His rod signifies the true priesthood. Cassiodorus, LXX, 554.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 536.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 669.

ABEL, sacrificed, is a type of the firstfruits of the Church and of the Christian people. St. Ambrose, XIV, 318.—St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1589.

ABIGAIL, by going beforehand in prayer to David, bore the type of the Church in the sacrifice of the altar. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1113; CLXX, 39.

ABIMELECH, the house of the Gentiles, prefigured the Church. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 415.

ABRAHAM, concealing his wife Sarah, was a type of the Church, Christ’s hidden bride; and by his priesthood the royal priesthood of the new law was figured. St. Augustine, XLI, 424.—St. Prosper, LI, 743.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.

ADAM, type and guardian of the Church. St. Ambrose, XV, 1632.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 536.

HANNAH, barren, guarding and keeping what she prayed the Lord for from the very recesses [Col. 0248] of her breast, not with a clamorous petition but modestly and silently, bears the type of the Church, formerly barren but now abundantly fruitful. St. Cyprian, IV, 522.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 27, 62, 90.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.

EHUD, judge in Israel, is a type of the good prelates of the Church. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1131.

NOAH’S ARK was a prophecy of our times, prefiguring the Church of Christ. St. Jerome, XXII, 1054.—St. Augustine, XLI, 598.

BENJAMIN is called the land of the Church. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 262.

BATHSHEBA, while bathing unclothed in the spring of Kidron, pleased David and was compelled to come to the king’s embrace; her husband was killed by royal command. So also the Church—that is, the gathering of the faithful—is known to be united to Christ the Lord through the washing of holy baptism, once the filth of sins has been cleansed. Cassiodorus, LXX, 358.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 66.

DAVID, eating the loaves of offering, is a type of kingship and priesthood. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 601.—St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 755.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 696.

DEBORAH, who, after Sisera the devil had been conquered, proclaimed a song of heavenly glory, mystically revealed to us the rising of the Church which was to arise from the Gentiles. St. Ambrose, XVI, 249.—St. Prosper, LI, 785.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.

ENOSH, invoking the name of the Lord, signifies the Church living in hope until it reaches blessedness. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 101.

EPHRAIM is a type of the Church. St. Hilary, IX, 388.

EZRA, unfolding the parable, figures the Church. St. Prosper, LI, 814.

ESTHER, whose name is interpreted “hidden,” and who by another name was called Edissa, that is, “mercy,” designates the Church of the Gentiles. Because of the chastity of faith, she pleases God in the hidden place of her heart and finds mercy and grace before God’s eyes more than the synagogue of the Jews, which through Hosea is deservedly called “without mercy” because of its impiety. St. Jerome, XXII, 547; XXV, 1337.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 646.

EVE, mother of all the living, brought forth from Adam’s ribs, signifies that from the side of Christ, asleep in death upon the cross, the sacraments of salvation would come forth—namely, blood and water—from which the Church, his bride, would be formed. St. Ambrose, XVII, 813.—St. Jerome, XXII, 1101.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 215; XXXVI, 461; XXXVII, 1673.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 357.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 326.—St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 163.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 99.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 484.—St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 506.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 215.

EZEKIEL prefigured the person of those set over the Church. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 45, 46.

HEBER, who preserves his own speech (*loquela*) while the other languages are divided, prefigured the Church, in whose bosom is unity. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

ISHMAEL, playing with Isaac, was a figure of the persecution of the Church. Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1040.

ISRAEL is called the Church—that is, “he in whom God is,” and “one seeing God.” St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 255.—St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 212.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 459.

ISSACHAR signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which submitted its shoulder to bear the burden of the cross. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 44.

JACOB prefigures the people of the New Testament. For just as Jacob was earlier than his brother in blessing although born afterward, so the Christian people preceded the earlier people of the synagogue in the steps of faith. St. Jerome, XXII, 888.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1015.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 689, 962.—St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 202.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 459.

JAEL, that foreign woman of whom prophecy said that victory would be achieved by a woman’s hand, bears the figure of the Church gathered from foreign nations. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1136.

JAPHETH signified hearers in the Church. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 362.

JEPHTHAH’S DAUGHTER, mourning for sixty days over her virginity, signified the Church as daughter and virgin. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1189.

JOSIAH’S HOUSE figures the Church, where Christ is crowned. Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 746.

JUDAH designates the Church. Cassiodorus, LXX, 358.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 191.

[Col. 0249] JUDITH, after completing her prayer, taking off her mourning clothes and putting on garments of gladness, is a sign of the holy Church. Although it may sometimes display penitence for its sins, still, through hope of forgiveness and of future reward, it greatly cheers its anxious mind. St. Jerome, XXV, 1337.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 365, 575.

THE SEVEN MACCABEES AND THEIR MOTHER designate the Church in its sevenfold form, which crowned a multitude of martyrs for Christ. St. Cyprian, IV, 669.—St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1380.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.

MORDECAI, clothed in sackcloth and mourning the decreed destruction of the Jews, figures the teachers of the Church. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 654.

MARY, Moses’ sister, striking the timbrel with the women, was a type of the Church, which, singing a hymn with all the churches she has borne, leads the Christian people into heaven. St. Zeno, XI, 510.

THE HARLOT whom Samson married, and the two harlots disputing before Solomon about the child, bear the type of the Church and the synagogue. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 92, 1640.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 358.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 127 and following.

MICHAL, a figure of the Church. St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 488.

MOSES’ ETHIOPIAN WIFE signifies the Church of the Gentiles, on whose account the synagogue is covered with leprosy. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.

THE WOMAN among the wives of the prophets who had two sons designates the holy Church of two peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile, like a mother of two sons. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 228.

NOAH figured the clergy and rulers of the Church. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1731.

NAOMI AND HER DAUGHTERS-IN-LAW bear the figure of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which married Christ, the Son of God born from the Jewish people. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1201, 1221.

ORPAH is interpreted “her neck.” What, then, is designated by Orpah but believers from the Jews, who are fittingly called by the name of “neck”? For they were the first, after the Lord’s Resurrection, to receive the strength of faith and the vigor of good works. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1202.

PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER, who gathered up Moses after he had been exposed upon the riverbank, is the Church of the Gentiles, which finds Christ at the river of the saving washing. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 52.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1159.

RACHEL, called “God’s ewe,” at first barren and beautiful and stealing her father’s idols, foreshadowed Christ’s Church. St. Ambrose, XVI, 289, 1237.—St. Jerome, XXII, 1055; XXV, 930.—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 209.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 563.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 607, 763.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 61, 62.—St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 825.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1009.

REBEKAH, descending from the camel to meet Isaac, etc., figures the Church coming from Gentile life. St. Ambrose, XIV, 452, 455, 617; XVI, 1245.—St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1673; XXXVIII, 38.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 770.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 459.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 135.

MOSES’ BUSH represented the Church. St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 687.

RUTH: just as she slept at Boaz’s feet, so spiritual Ruth, namely the Church, slept at Christ’s feet, when, resting as it were in hope of his incarnation—from which she believed certain salvation would come to her—she patiently awaited him. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1202, 1214, 1215.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 62.

THE QUEEN OF SHEBA, stirred up to come from the farthest bounds of the South and desiring to hear Solomon’s wisdom, already then represented the Church from the Gentiles that was to come, longing for Christ. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 168.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 472.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1175.

SOLOMON, whose name denotes peace, was a type of the Church. St. Jerome, XXVI, 419.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 186.

SAMSON prefigured Christ’s Church in its beginnings, suffering persecutions. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1126.

SARAH, restored untouched to Abraham by Abimelech, is an illustrious type of the holy Church. St. Ambrose, XIV, 434, 436.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 560.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 25.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 196.

THE WIDOW OF ZAREPHATH is the Church, which is never diminished by the grace of Christ’s body and the anointing of chrism. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 808.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.

SHEM signified the teachers of the Church. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 362.

ZIPPORAH bears the type of the Church from the Gentiles, which teaches the circumcision of the foreskin of her son—that is, of the Gentile people—by the sharpest rock, that is, by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or by that Rock of which the Apostle says, “But the Rock was Christ”; that is, she teaches the stripping off of the old man with his deeds. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 27.

SUSANNA figured the Church, which the Jews falsely accuse as an adulteress. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 66.

TAMAR was a type of the Church, which is not rightly married to Judah, because, when Christ came, Judah, reborn in the Church’s bosom by the spiritual wave of baptism, was to become her son, not her husband. St. Hilary, IX, 437.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 358.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 67.—Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 241.

THE WIDOW to whom Elijah was sent foreshadowed Christ’s Church. St. Ambrose, XV, 1626; XVI, 235.—Likewise, the widow mourning her dead son. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 324.

ZEBULUN signifies the Church, which, dwelling beside the waves of this life, endures all the temptations and storms of the world and, through its teachers, summons peoples of every nation to attain the virtues and render praises to the Lord. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 723.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 44.

III.—Figures prefiguring the apostles and the righteous.

AARON denotes devotion. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 334.

OBADIAH designates all preachers of the faith who refresh believers with the nourishment of the sacred Scriptures. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

ABEL, carrying a lamb for sacrifice to God, just as the Lamb is offered, prefigures also the righteous who endure persecution from the ungodly. St. Augustine, XLI, 456, 614.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 502.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1752.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 480.

ABISHAG THE SHUNAMMITE is an image of divine grace and charity; and her fourfold gift signifies the fourfold gift of wisdom. Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 231, 312, 313, 825.

ABRAHAM, offering his only-begotten son, is a type of religious offering and of the devout man. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 82, 83.—Blessed Lanfranc, CLI, 118.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 328, 480, 821.

ADAM is a type of reason. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 344.—Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 363.

HAGGAI is a figure of the saints who, in the life of this pilgrimage, declare to us the future time of deliverance. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

AMALEK, who is commanded to be struck and destroyed twice, signifies that the preacher ought to advance those whom he instructs in the chaste life to the perfection of virtue. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 407, 410.

HANNAH, Samuel’s mother, is a figure of Christian religion and grace. St. Augustine, XLI, 528.

ARIOCH, whose name is interpreted “leading into solitude,” signifies zeal for uprightness and the rigor of strict severity. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1243.

ASHER: “rich bread.” Some think this was said because of Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who, together with Simeon, is reported in the Gospels as the first to have prophesied about the Lord; and who, by the faith of her prophecy, as it were gave food to the princes—that is, to the apostles—and to the other believers, in the things which had been prophesied concerning him. Rufinus, XXI, 325.

BENJAMIN, a ravening wolf—that is, Paul, born from the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee, circumcised on the eighth day—eating in the morning when he was young, and giving food in the evening when, having become a believer, he supplied spiritual nourishment to the churches established by him. Tertullian, II, 148.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 660, 692; XV, 1273.—Paulinus of Milan, XX, 731.—Rufinus, XXI, 333.—St. Jerome, XXV, 724, 862.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 664; CVIII, 1144; CXI, 48.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 232.

BATHSHEBA, a figure of the Virgin Mary. Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 1026.

DANIEL, serving God in celibacy, set forth a figure of God’s servants, that is, monks and continent persons who do not misuse earthly wealth. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1771; XL, 714, 717.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, [Col. 0251] 114.—Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 643, 725.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 1113.—Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1243.

DAVID represents the upright, contemplative, and humble person; and through him we rightly understand the holy soul, which slew within itself him who “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 626.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 551.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1060.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 467.—Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 195.

DEBORAH, whose name is interpreted “bee,” signifies the sweetness of prophecy and the pleasantness of heavenly doctrine. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 56.

ELKANAH, Samuel’s father, persevering in prayer, prefigured those steadfast in devotion. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 14.

ELIJAH, sent to the widow of Zarephath, and his double spirit, prefigures the apostles sent to the Gentiles. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1240.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 322.

ELISHA, following Elijah and asking for his double spirit, represents the apostles following Christ and the soul thirsting for God. St. Prosper, LI, 803.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1254, 1255; CLXX, 248.—Godefridus, abbot, CLXXIV, 334.

EZRA bears the type both of the apostles and of the preachers of Christ’s Gospel, who, after the faithful depart from the Babylon of this world and return to the land of promise, restore and rebuild God’s spiritual edifice daily by words and examples. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.

EVE is a figure of the Blessed Virgin Mary. For just as Eve caused us to be condemned through the fruit of a tree, so Mary released us through the fruit of a tree, because Christ too hung upon the wood as fruit. Tertullian, II, 782.—St. Ambrose, XVII, 692.

HEZEKIAH designates all the saints to whom, for the acquisition of heaven, the five books of Moses and the ten commandments of the Decalogue were given. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.

EZEKIEL, the eminent prophet, lying for forty days upon one side, while prefiguring the coming captivity, brings about deliverance; this sacred number took upon itself iniquities in order to destroy them, entered into captivities in order to release them, suffered bonds in order to loosen them. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 635.

GIDEON bore the type of the penitent. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 705.

HABAKKUK is the faithful people, set upon the heights and contemplating the Lord upon the cross. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

ISAAC, a type of religious offering and of the children of promise. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 566.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 83.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 148.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 481.

ISAIAH signifies the evangelists and apostles, and proclaimed all Christ’s mysteries as though present. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.

ISRAEL—that is, “the man who sees God”—signifies the elect and the contemplative life. Blessed Alcuin, C, 1105.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1130, 1138.

ISSACHAR, a symbol of religious profession, and, because his name is interpreted “reward,” a type of the apostles, who ought to be regarded as the reward of the Son of God. Rufinus, XXI, 317.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 482.

JACOB, through the various circumstances of his life, prefigured the elect and their virtues, as well as the kingdom of heaven, etc. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 567; XXXVII, 1597, 1598, 1771, 1772, 1936; XXXIX, 34, 35, 687; XLI, 518. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 10, 11. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 84, 352.—St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 586.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1558.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1030, 1136, 1138.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 820.—Peter Cantor, CCV, 77.

JAPHETH, a type of the apostles and preachers. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 362.

JOTHAM, just as he withdrew by flight while his remaining brothers were killed, signifies that no one will be able to escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he withdraws by flight and ascends the mountain of blessing. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1172.

JOB signified married persons and penitents; but his sons signified the apostles. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1732.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 535.—Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 643, 725.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1113.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 705.

JOEL signifies those who begin to know the mystery of the door of faith and of divine knowledge. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

JEHOIADA, who is substituted in Ahithophel’s place, signifies that, when Judas transgressed and fell from the apostleship, the twelfth place did not remain empty; rather, in the place of the transgressor, [Col. 0252] Matthias—humble and faithful—succeeded, being appointed by Peter and the other apostles. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 406.

JOSEPH, a type of the apostles, chastity, and grace. St. Hilary, IX, 923.—St. Prosper, LI, 754, 757.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 146.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 199.

JOSIAH, a type of the elect. Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.

JOSHUA signifies the chaste and those who preserve baptismal whiteness. Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 587.

JUDAH, insofar as can be understood, was partly a type of the prophets, partly of the patriarchs and Fathers, who, on account of God’s righteousness, regarded all human beings as sons. St. Zeno, XI, 435.

LEAH, whose name is interpreted “laboring,” is a figure of the active life. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1046.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 449.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 84.—St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 303.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 474.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 755, 1276.

LOT, fleeing Sodom, signifies both religious persons and saints who at the end of the age will be delivered from the burning of the impious. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1044.

MACHIR, whose name is interpreted “he will restore,” and who is the firstborn of Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, signifies the earlier people from whom descended the leaders—that is, the apostles and doctors of the primitive Church. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1144.

MORDECAI signifies the teachers of the Gentiles, and especially the blessed Apostle Paul, who testifies that he too was of the stock of Jemini, that is, of the tribe of Benjamin. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 646.

THE SONS OF MATTATHIAS signify the apostles and martyrs. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1141.

MOSES denotes discernment. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 334.

NAAMAN, a figure of the worldly man converted to better things. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 220.

NABOTH prefigures all the righteous. Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 25.

NEHEMIAH is a type both of the apostles and of the preachers of Christ’s Gospel, who, after the faithful have departed from the Babylon of this world and returned to the land of promise, rebuild God’s spiritual edifice by renewing it daily through words and examples. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.

NAPHTALI bears the figure of the apostles and preachers who, leaping like a stag, raise both themselves and their hearers to heavenly things. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 727.—Rufinus, XXI, 327.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1144.

NOAH, a type of the elect. Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 643, 725.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 821.

ORPAH AND RUTH. Some, after receiving the grace of baptism and fellowship in the faith, relapse backward into their former errors; Orpah, who returned to her gods and to her people, bore their type. Others, however, with settled purpose and diligent zeal follow the grace they have received; Ruth represented their figure. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1204. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1026.

PHINEHAS signifies holy teachers who strike Jews and heretics with the spiritual sword. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 110.

RAHAB, a figure of the most chaste Virgin Mary. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1025.

RACHEL, whose name is interpreted “the principle of sight,” sets before us the contemplative life. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1046; XLII, 432.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 954; LXXVI, 449.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 303.

SAMSON, by his hair, signifies all the elect; by visiting his wife, the preaching of the apostles. St. Ambrose, XVII, 774.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1048.

SAMUEL represents John the Baptist. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1091.

SARAH provides an image of prudence. Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 334.

SHEM, a figure of the prophets and apostles who are born from his stock. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

ZEPHANIAH signifies those who, through the secret of contemplation, attain perfection of merits. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.

TAMAR figures the blessed Virgin Mary. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1022.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 384.

TOBIAS, a type of prudence. Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 331.

URIAH THE HEBREW, a type and example of ardor and devotion to the common good. Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 485.

ZEBULUN: the hunters are none other than the Lord’s apostles, some of whom were from his tribe. Rufinus, XXI, 317.

ZECHARIAH, whose name is interpreted “mindful of the Lord,” and who was [Col. 0253] the son of Shelemiah, prefigures the teachers of the Gentiles, appointed by the apostles and the first preachers of the Gospel to preach to the Gentiles. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 397.

#### IV.—Figures relating to Jews and Gentiles

AARON, speaking with Moses against Pharaoh, signifies the law and the old priesthood; in dying, he teaches the passing away of that priesthood. Abbot Rupert, 581, 888.

ABEL signifies the Christian people from among the Gentiles. Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 669.

ABIGAIL, of whom Scripture relates that she was a most prudent and beautiful woman, bears the type of that people who, converted from the Jews to the faith, deserved to please the Lord. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 64.

ABRAHAM, by his calling, figures the land of the living that was to belong to the Christian people, and, by his seed, the same people as to be multiplied like the stars. St. Prosper, LI, 742, 743.

ABSALOM bears the type of the Jews who raised rebellion against the true David, envying him and plotting against his rule. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 642.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 107; CXI, 59.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1105.—Abbot Rupert, CLXXVII, 1077.

ACHIOR, leader of the Ammonites, signifies the pagans who, when they saw the holy Church overcoming through faith and steadfastness the ferocity of its enemies and persecutors, were shaken by overwhelming fear, fell from the obstinacy of their pride, and were compelled by extreme terror to venerate the holy Church. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 576.

AHITHOPHEL denotes the Jews, once most beloved because of the prerogative of the Fathers and most illustrious through converse with God, but who, scandalized by the Incarnation and Passion, became most cruel enemies. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 408.

ADONIJAH, David’s elder son, who through the arrogance of pride wished to succeed his father in the kingdom, indicates the Jewish people, who appear to be like the elder son because they received the law first. Despising the Gentile people, who were called later through God’s grace, they supposed that the Lord would reign with themselves alone. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 425.

HAGAR and her son prefigured the synagogue and the carnal adherents of the Old Testament. St. Augustine, XLI, 512.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 491.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 547.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 388, 503.

HAMAN, a type of the Jews, who killed the prophets and did not fear to kill the Lord of the prophets himself and his apostles. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 652.

AMMON, whose name is interpreted “son of my race,” or “a troubled people,” represents the Jews. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 380.

ASAPH is interpreted “synagogue,” signifying that portion which believed, not that which remained obstinate. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1347; XXXVI, 916, 929, 970, 1011, 1051.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.

ASHER predicts holy men who will come from the synagogue, whose bread is rich—that is, prophetic teaching abounding in the nourishment of the Holy Spirit. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 726.

BILHAH, a figure of the law of the Old Testament, which the people of Israel defiled by transgression. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.

BALAAM, whose name is interpreted “vain people,” seems to bear the character of the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 729.

BARAK seems to bear the form of the earlier people, who were the first of all called through prophecy and invited to hear God’s sayings and receive the gifts of the divine law. They did indeed shine and gleam for a brief time in the splendor of the law; but they did not remain long, nor could they attain the unbroken brightness of light. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1135, 1143.

CAIN, offering gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth, a fratricide and accursed man, prefigured both the synagogue and the earthly, deicidal Jews. St. Ambrose, XIV, 317, 318; XVII, 813.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 442, 705, 997; XL, 688; XLI, 445, 258, 259, 260.—St. Prosper, LI, 737.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 793.—Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 115.—Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 669.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 100.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 504.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 402.

HAM, Noah’s son, is a type of the Jews who mocked Christ incarnate and dead. Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 675.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

CANAAN, condemned to a curse for his father’s offense, presents the posterity of the Jews, accursed because of Christ’s Passion. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

[Col. 0254]

DELILAH, whose name is interpreted “little poor woman” or “bucket,” signifies the synagogue that crucified Christ at Calvary. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 57.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1050, 1112.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 281.

DINAH, a figure of the synagogue, or of the soul which the devil corrupted when he found it occupied with outward concerns. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.

THE BOYS MOCKING ELISHA, a figure of the Jews who mocked Christ on the cross and were captured by Titus and Vespasian. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.

EPHRAIM, a figure of the Gentiles, who through the patriarch’s blessing was set above the greater people of the Jews. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 283.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1144.

ESAU, a type of the Jewish people, in whose place the Christian people, figured by Jacob, is received. St. Ambrose, XV, 1485; XVII, 364.—St. Jerome, XXV, 1001.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 437.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 829.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1136, 1139.—Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 515.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 102.

GAD bears the type of the elect Jews, who became, as it were, certain leaders of the new people and brought them into the land once promised. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 726.

GILEAD, whose name is interpreted “heap of witness,” denotes the Jewish people, which can aptly be called a heap of witness, or a people girded about, because, possessing the Old Testament written in the law and prophets, it trusted that by this it would be safe and fortified on every side. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1146.

HARBONA, the eunuch who revealed the cross prepared for Mordecai, signifies the teachers of the law, who made known, by reading that very law, the Jews’ deceit and everything contrary to the divine commands. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 660.

HEBER figures the Hebrew nation, whose primacy Christ handed over to the Christian people. St. Prosper, LI, 741.

ELI, rejected, and his sons signify the extinguished posterity of the earlier priesthood and the succession of the new priesthood. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 91.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 58.

ER, Judah’s first son, is the first people, that is, the Hamites: all those most powerful men and kings who had corrupted the whole world through the violence of power and lust. St. Zeno, XI, 435.

HOLOFERNES is the dominion of the Gentiles, which persecuted Christ’s Church. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 546.

ISAAC, conceived by promise and born contrary to the hope of barren old persons, prefigures the calling of all nations. St. Augustine, XLI, 605.—St. Prosper, LI, 696.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 793.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.

ISHMAEL, born of the slave woman, represents the Jewish people. St. Ambrose, XVII, 363.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 793.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.

ISSACHAR, the strong ass, bears the type of the Gentile people, which, before it had the Lord as its rider, was brutish and impatient of the reins, carried along by its own will. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 724. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 336.

JACOB, signifying the people of the Gentiles, lived as a simple man in tents, because the elect from the Gentiles strove to please God through faith alone and good will. St. Ambrose, XVII, 818.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 506; XXXVIII, 55.—St. Prosper, LI, 392, 752.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 840, 1028.—Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 515.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 502.

JAPHETH signifies the Gentile people dwelling in the churches of the Israelites. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

JEHU denotes the dominion of the Gentiles. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 61.

JOTHAM, the younger son of Jerubbaal, who fled in order to escape the enemy’s sword, is a figure of the remnant of Israel’s people who, through Elijah’s preaching, will believe in the last times and escape Antichrist’s sword. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1171.

JOB’S OVERTHROWN HOUSE was a figure of the synagogue. When that house fell, it crushed the children, because when Judaea fell into the cruelty of the Lord’s Passion, it overwhelmed the apostles’ faith with the terror of despair. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 582.

JOSEPH signifies the Gentiles. St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1029.

JUDAH, a type of the unbelieving Jewish people. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1082.

LABAN, a type of the law and the devil, from whose body Christ took to himself two wives, namely, the Jews and the Gentiles. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.

[Col. 0255]

LEVI, both the progenitor and figure of the chief priests who crucified Christ. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.

LEAH, bleary-eyed and fruitful, displays the sacraments of the synagogue, which, with the weak eyes of its heart, could not behold God’s mysteries. St. Ambrose, XV, 1488.—St. Jerome, XXII, 1055; XXV, 930.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 475, 503.

LOT bears the character of the law. Those who use it with a carnal understanding bring forth works of unbelief; his two daughters signify Samaria and Jerusalem, which commit fornication in the law through the adultery of unlawful teaching. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 106.

MANASSEH, a type of the earlier people. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.

MARY, Moses’ sister, presents the likeness of the synagogue, leprous because of detraction and murmuring against Christ, whose blood it sold. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 53.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 947.

MICHAL, despising David as he danced, prefigures the synagogue blaspheming Christ. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1112, 1126.

NAAMAN, described as commander of the king of Syria’s army, could signify nothing more fittingly than the Gentile people, who throughout the world held sovereignty through military might and enjoyed worldly splendor. St. Ambrose, XVII, 834.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 231.

NABAL, of whom it was said that he was a harsh, very wicked, and malicious man, bears the type of the Jewish people. Some of them, intoxicated by a grape of gall and a cluster of bitterness, continually resisted the Holy Spirit with stiff necks and uncircumcised hearts; following a carnal understanding of the law, they became foolish. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 64.

NOAH, in his three sons the nations are figured which Christ the Lord found scattered and gathered together. St. Prosper, LI, 741.

AHAZIAH signifies the Jewish people, and especially the leaders of the synagogue, who, given over to sins and vices, repelled—and indeed persecuted—the truth. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 65.

ONAN, Judah’s second son, is a type of the Jewish people, to whom it is commanded to raise up seed for its brother: that is, to stir up the other nations, devoted to idolatry, to God’s worship. St. Zeno, XI, 436.

UZZIAH THE LEPROUS, a figure of the Jews who bear their disgrace on their forehead. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.

THE PHILISTINES, keeping watch over Samson seized in Gaza, signify the Jews placing a guard at Christ’s tomb. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1173.

RAHAB, a type of the Gentile world. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1008.

REHOBOAM AND JEROBOAM represent the division of the Jews at Christ’s coming: one part will follow Christ, the other Antichrist. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.

REUBEN, the firstborn, figures the people who violated the bed of God the Father when they fastened Christ’s flesh to the cross’s gibbet. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 717.—Rufinus, XXI, 313.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.

RUTH, gathering barley from the ears, a type of the steadfastness of converted Gentiles. St. Prosper, LI, 795.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1206, 1207, 1209.

SAMSON, killing the lion, a type of the Jews. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 265.

SAMUEL signifies the succession of the new priesthood, the old priesthood having been rejected. St. Augustine, XLI, 532, 533.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 91.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.

THE WIDOW OF ZAREPHATH prefigured the Gentile world. Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 326; CLXX, 106.

SAUL suggests the rejection of the Jewish people, or its jealousy, by which it strove through unjust judgment to destroy David—that is, Christ. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 58.

SERON, commander of the Syrian army, represents the dominion of this world. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1150.

SIMEON AND LEVI signify the scribes and Pharisees, who wage war against the Lord not by battle with weapons but by cunning craft. Paulinus of Milan, XX, 719.—Rufinus, XXI, 315.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 551.

THE SON OF THE SHUNAMMITE, a figure of the human race, upon which Christ breathed the sevenfold Spirit. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.

TAMAR, carrying twin sons in her womb, bore two peoples. The one born later first put his hand out of the womb, because the people of the Gentiles was indeed previously indicated through the prophets but was revealed later. Therefore the midwife [Col. 0256] bound its right hand with scarlet, because that same people was marked with the sign of Christ’s blood upon the cross. St. Isidore of Seville, CLXXXIII, 108.

TOBIAS bears the image of the ancient law, whose eyes Jewish swallows blind, while the Jewish swallows, wrongly understanding the mysteries of light, blind them. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 66.

URIAH, sent with letters in order to be killed, is the Jewish people carrying the law through which it dies. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 67.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1135; CLXX, 294.

QUEEN VASHTI represents the Jewish people, which seemed to reign as a queen because it was found to excel the other nations in the worship of one God. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 642.

ZECHARIAH demonstrates the Gentile people. Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 834.

#### V.—Figures representing heretics and the impious

ABADDON, king of the locusts, is a type of heretics. Blessed Alcuin, C, 1141.

ABIMELECH, son of a slave woman and king of sedition-makers, bears the character of Antichrist, the head and prince of all the wicked. He also prefigures Judas the traitor, through whom the devil acted deceitfully against our Redeemer, who is truly King. St. Prosper, LI, 788.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1175; CIX, 59; CXI, 56.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 388, 392.

ABIRAM, KORAH, AND DATHAN, who separated themselves from Moses and Aaron and tried to usurp sacrifice, signify the perversity of heretics and the destruction of those who divide themselves from Christ’s priests and the fellowship of the Church and receive profane sacrifices. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 110.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 681; CXI, 53.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 814.

ABSALOM, while cruelly pursuing his father David, was carried by the force of his mule into a thick oak, its branches binding his neck, and was suspended high in the air, in a certain prefiguration of the Lord’s betrayer. For just as Judas, entangled in a noose, ended his life, so David’s persecutor breathed his last with his throat constricted. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 97; XXXVII, 1847.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 43.—St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1097.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 807; CXI, 59.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 647.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1136.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 72, 752.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 77.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 801, 816.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 558.

AHAB, who reigned in Samaria, represents heresiarchs who lead a crowd of the lost along the byways of error and plunge them into death’s everlasting abyss. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 60.

ACHAN, who coveted the accursed thing from Jericho, signifies the wicked Christian who, after receiving the faith, desires worldly habits or the enticements of the world. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 54.

ACHARIS, whose name is interpreted “bitter,” represents heretics, rightly called bitter because they did not deserve to be filled with divine grace. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 898.

AHITHOPHEL, who withdrew from David and went over to Absalom, signifies heretics who, leaving the path of truth, join themselves to the ancient enemy and follow error. He likewise represents Judas the traitor. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 107, 406.

ADAM, fleeing from paradise, represents the person fleeing from truth. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 165.

HAGAR, the slave woman fleeing from Sarah’s face, a figure of heretics and of the flesh. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 32.—St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 233.

ALCIMUS, defiler of the law and betrayer of his country, represents those who do not fear to profane God’s Testament through wicked sects and disturb God’s Church. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1183.

AMALEK signifies the spirit of fornication and the vice of lust. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 397, 407.

HAMAN THE PROUD signifies both the devil and the arrogance of this age’s powerful men, who abuse the benefits bestowed on them by divine mercy and disdain to have as companions in grace their neighbors, whom they have as partners in nature. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 652.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 169.

AMMON, whose name is interpreted “son of sorrow,” signifies heretics and all those predestined for Gehenna, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, as befits a people of sorrow. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 396.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1187; CXI, 380.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 384, 815.

[Col. 0257]

ANTIOCHUS, the most wicked king who persecuted God’s people, prefigured Antichrist, who will persecute Christ’s people. St. Cyprian, IV, 669.—St. Jerome, XXV, 568.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 651.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1411.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1132.

ARCHELAUS, a type of boastfulness. Adam the Scot, 331.

ASAHEL bears the type of those whom violent fury seizes and drives headlong; they must avoid that same onset of fury with all the greater caution, the more madly they are carried away. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 77.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 76.

ASSUR, a type of Antichrist. Rabanus Maurus, CX, 818.

BALAAM, whose name is interpreted “variegated people,” signifies heretics and those who, having knowledge of God through faith, are darkened and fall through evil deeds; at the same time, worldly persons who curse religious persons whom they neglect to imitate. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 110.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1105.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 337.

BALAM bore the type of priests who sell ecclesiastical matters for gain. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 895.

BAAL-PEOR, a type of Antichrist. Abbot Rupert, LXVII, 908.

CAIN, a figure of Antichrist and of evil people who persecute the righteous. St. Augustine, XLI, 456.—St. Gregory the Great, XXVI, 484.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1752.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 813.

HAM, exposing his father’s nakedness, prefigured heretics. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 362.

CHUSHAN-RISHATHAIM, oppressor of the Jews, mystically signifies any tyrant. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1126.

KISH’S SHE-ASSES, sinful souls. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 249, 282.

DELILAH, a figure of the sinful soul and of concupiscence. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 287.—Adam the Scot, XCVIII, 815.

DAN prefigures Antichrist, who will be like a serpent in the way and a horned viper in the path, because, against those walking in the way and path of God’s commands, he sets himself up as an obstacle, so far as lies in him, armed against them with a twofold device. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1079.—Paulinus of Milan, XX, 725.—Rufinus, XXI, 321.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 661, 662.

DINAH, a type of the sluggish soul deceived by the devil’s arts. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 108.

DOEG THE EDOMITE, a figure of Judas and Antichrist; for as Doeg was David’s adversary, so Antichrist will be Christ’s. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1646.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 373.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1106.

ELEAZAR, who died after killing an elephant, bears the character of arrogant people who wish to do something bravely, yet do so not with a simple but with a proud mind, and are cast down defeated in their undertakings. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1174.

ENOCH, Cain’s son, building a city, signifies the impious as founded only in this life. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 100.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 813.

ESAU is a figure not only of those who deny the faith but also of those who persevere in evil works until life’s end; he also signifies the gluttonous and carnal. St. Ambrose, XIV, 317.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 527.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 438.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 190.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 814.—Peter Cantor, CCV, 332.

GOG, a type of pride, aptly denotes heretics. Rabanus Maurus, CX, 868, 871.

GOLIATH, a figure of the proud. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 333.

ELIHU, a type of faithful but proud teachers, who speak with sound understandings indeed, but are carried away into foolish words of self-exaltation. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 527; LXXVI, 252, 452.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.

ISHMAEL signifies the birth of those who are slaves of sin. St. Ambrose, XVII, 363.

JACOB, descending into Egypt, figures Adam’s fall; and, prevailing over the angel, those persecutors prevailing over Christ. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1022.—Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 71.

JEROBOAM, a type of heretics. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1237; CLXIX, 331.

JEZEBEL represents eternal death and heretics. Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1245; CLXIX, 881.

JEHOAHAZ, whose name is interpreted “held back,” signifies wicked rulers chosen by the people of the land—that is, carnal persons devoted to earthly desire—who, in accordance with their own habits, consent to their vices. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 530.

JOB’S THREE FRIENDS prefigure heretics who, under the appearance of consoling, pursue the aim of seducing; his wife, who [Col. 0258] provokes him to curse, represents the perversity of carnal persons. St. Jerome, XXV, 619.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 526, 621, 729.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 50.

JORAM represents those who were instructed in the Church’s mysteries after being imbued with the Catholic faith and regenerated by Christian baptism, but who, abandoning faith’s truth, follow the errors of heretics. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 61.

LABAN signifies this world and ecclesiastical prelates who seek gifts. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 607.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 441, 481, 958.—Peter Cantor, CCV, 83.

LAMECH, whose crime Christ washed away, signifies both heretics and a figure of this world. St. Jerome, XXII, 1053.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 101.

LOT bears the type of a vicious multitude, and his wife that of those who, called through God’s grace, later look back and strive to return to what they had left. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 36.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 374.—Peter Cantor, CCV, 210.

LYSIAS, the most savage enemy of the Jews, who holds the dominion of the pagans, signifies those who harass God’s Church with the most grievous persecutions. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1224.

MICHAL, despising the humbled David, is a type of those who follow Christ in profession but Antichrist in deed. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 87.

NAAMAN THE SYRIAN AND LEPER, a figure of the proud and lustful person. Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 411.

NABAL denotes ecclesiastical prelates seeking gifts. Peter Cantor, CCV, 83.

UZZAH, supporting the ark when it leaned aside, represents those who approach the sacred Eucharist unworthily. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 339.

PHARAOH, a type of vain glory. Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 332.

THE CHIEF OF THE COOKS, who overthrew Jerusalem’s walls, signifies that all who serve the desires of the belly destroy the soul’s virtues. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.

REHOBOAM signifies the division of heresies, from which Christ gathers sheep. St. Prosper, LI, 801.

REUBEN denotes heretics who defile souls through incest, and concupiscence. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 87.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 550.

SAMSON, invincible when his hair was preserved but captive when it was cut, is a type of the sinner. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 264.

SAUL prefigures evil shepherds, the pride of powerful men, and death. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 53, 55.—St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 695.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1060.

ZEDEKIAH signifies rich people and sinners who, captured by the devil, lose the eyes of understanding. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.

TIMOTHEUS bears the type of heretics who continually strive, both by themselves and through the help and support of others, to destroy the faith of Christ and the truth of the Gospel. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1242.

## Appendix

In this Appendix, so that nothing may escape the reader, we have included every figure that anciently prefigured either the devil or the two Testaments, and which the holy Fathers mentioned; namely:

### I.—Figures denoting the devil

ALEXANDER prefigured the devil as tempter. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1130.

AMALEK. St. Cyprian, IV, 662.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.

HAMAN, seeking to be worshipped. Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 106.

AMMON, whose name is interpreted “their sorrow.” Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 371; CX, 372.

ASSUR, the rod of God’s wrath and the staff of his indignation. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 383; CX, 818.

BENHADAD. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 236.

CAIN, a fratricide from the beginning. St. Hilary, IX, 648.

CANAAN, evil kings. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1147.

CHUSHAN-RISHATHAIM, oppressor of the Jews. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1126.

EGLON, whose name is interpreted “rolled” or “orbited.” Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 55.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 270.

GOLIATH, the proud one. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 52, 53; CXI, 58.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1098.

[Col. 0259]

HOLOFERNES, head of the wicked. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 546.

LABAN, whose name is interpreted “whitening.” Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 606.

MOLOCH. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 462.

NEBUCHADNEZZAR, prince of confusion. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 272; CXI, 65.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1344; CLXX, 338.

NIMROD. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

UZZIAH, the leprous king. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 246.

PHARAOH, who attempts to destroy God’s people. St. Zeno, XI, 510.—St. Prosper, LI, 761.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 637.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 978; CLXXXIV, 577.

RABSHAKEH. Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 73.

[Col. 0260]

SIHON, king. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 719, 850.

SISERA. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.

URIAH THE HITTITE. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.

### II.—Figures prefiguring the two Testaments

ABRAHAM’S TWO SONS signify the two Testaments. Victorinus of Africa, VIII, 1185.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 2133.

HAGAR AND SARAH. St. Jerome, XXII, 1055.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 388.

THE TWO SPIES. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111.

JACOB’S TWO WIVES, one free, the other a handmaid. Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 691.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.

[Col. 0259]

XLIX. EXEGETICAL INDEX OF FIGURES OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, ARRANGED BY ANALOGY, WHILE WITHIN EACH ANALOGY PRESERVING AT ONCE THE ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS AND THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS.

I.---Figures relating to Christ.

THE ANGEL moving the water signifies Christ; for when the angel descended the sick person was healed, and when Christ descended the world is healed. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.

THE FOUR EVANGELISTS, under the appearances of the four living creatures, figuratively set forth Christ. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116.

JOHN, by the figure of the eagle, signifies that Christ, after the resurrection of the flesh, flew up into heaven. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

JOSEPH, the Virgin Mary’s spouse, indicates Christ, who was appointed as guardian of the holy Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

LUKE, through the mystical appearance of the calf, proclaims Christ sacrificed for us. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

MARK, beginning from the wilderness, assumes the figure of the lion and proclaims Christ’s unconquered kingdom and power. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

MARTHA, who is described as anxious amid continual service, may not inappropriately figure the assumed humanity of Christ. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 959, 960.

MATTHEW, announcing the Redeemer as born and suffering, appears in the likeness of a human being. St. Isidore of Seville, CLXXXIII, 117.

PETER AND JUDAS are the two eyes of Christ, which that new Samson lost when Peter denied him three times at the voice of the maidservant at the door, and when Judas, who betrayed him, hanged himself with a noose. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 284.

THE BRIDEGROOM signifies Christ, who at the wedding with the Church changes water into wine, because believers, through the grace of the washing, pass over to the glory of the Passion. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.

II.---Figures denoting the Church.

THE APOSTLES bear the type of the whole Church. They received a like power in remitting sins, having the form of the patriarchs, who through preaching begot peoples for Christ throughout the whole world. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

THE DAUGHTER OF THE RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which, after the preaching, believed in Christ and deserved to receive salvation. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

THE CANAANITE WOMAN represents the Church from the Gentiles, which, like a dog, seeks crumbs from the teaching of the apostles and prophets. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 487, 486, 544.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXIII, 118.---Her daughter likewise was a type of the Church. St. Hilary, IX, 1604, 1005.

[Col. 0260] THE SEVENTY-TWO DISCIPLES signify the enlightenment of the whole world through the Gospel. They are sent two by two, on account of the preaching of love for God and neighbour, or on account of the two Testaments of the mysteries—namely, the Church of God. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

THE ETHIOPIAN EUNUCH, who had come to worship in Jerusalem, represents the Church from the Gentiles, which stood outside because it had not found knowledge of the Law and the Prophets. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 228, 229.

LAZARUS RAISED FROM THE DEAD is a figure of the Church of God. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 872.

MARY, Christ’s Mother, signifies the Church, which, a virgin betrothed to Christ, conceived us from the Spirit and, though a virgin, also gave birth. St. Ambrose, XV, 1555.---St. Augustine, XL, 660.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

MARY AND MARTHA. With respect to the present time and the future, the Church is figured by Martha and Mary. For Martha represents the Church in this life, receiving Christ in her heart and labouring in works of righteousness; but Mary, seated at Jesus’ feet, represents it in the age to come, ceasing from work and resting. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1341.---Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 121.

MARY MAGDALENE AND THE OTHER MARY bear the type of the Church: one name is doubled in two women, because here the Church, coming from two peoples, is figured as one from two peoples—that is, Jews and Gentiles—because the first are last and the last first. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 412, 415, 432, 468.---Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 228.

WOMEN OF THE GOSPELS. Very many women mentioned in the Gospel represented the Church in various ways, namely:

The woman hiding leaven in flour. St. Ambrose, XV, 1749; XVI, 498.---The woman infirm for eighteen years. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 126.---The adulterous woman. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII.---The woman to whom the risen Christ said, “Do not touch me.” St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1144, 1153.---The woman who entered the Pharisee’s house. St. Ambrose, XV, 1339.---The woman suffering from an issue of blood. St. Ambrose, XVI, 476; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 821; XXXV, 1644.---The Samaritan woman. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 110.---The woman anointing Christ’s head and feet. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1110.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 171.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 938.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.---The widow casting two coins into the treasury. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1043.---The mother of Zebedee’s sons. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 944.

PETER AND JUDAS. Peter bears the person of the Church, which has the power to forgive and retain sins and to bring human beings back from hell; Judas, however, bears the image of Babylon destined for condemnation. Cassiodorus, LXX, 785.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

THE FOUR OR FIVE THOUSAND MEN fed with the loaves are the peoples of the Church, [Col. 0261] nourished by the five senses of the body and the two Testaments; or they are the Church of the Gentiles, which extends through the four regions of the world and is renewed by grace. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 120, 121.

III.---Figures signifying the righteous and the virtues.

THE APOSTLE JOHN is a type of the contemplative life, just as Peter is of the active life. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 670.

JOSEPH, Mary’s husband, signifies the elect and the soul continually growing in virtue. Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 224, 310.

THE UNJUST JUDGE makes known how great hope one who continually entreats the Lord ought to have, since even before the ears of an unjust judge the repeated persistence of an entreating widow prevailed. The widow herself also signifies the Church, which by its perseverance seeks vengeance against the devil or heretics. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.

LAZARUS, buried in the tomb and raised by Christ, is a figure of the sinner whom Christ calls back to life. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1306; XXXVIII, 433.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 645.

THE MAGI, coming to Christ from afar, are both a type of converts and the firstfruits of the Gentiles. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 677, 678.

MARY, betrothed to Joseph, figures the faithful soul, which is to become the mother of Jesus. Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 639, 640.

MARY AND MARTHA: the former represents the contemplative life, the latter the active life and the pastors of the Church. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 449, 877.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 512.---Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 200.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 624; CLXXXIV, 1004.
