THE PARALYTIC signifies the soul weakened by vices in its body. Healed by Christ’s grace, it immediately rises, carries the bed of the flesh back to the house of virtues, and no longer returns to vices. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

THE APOSTLE PETER signifies the order of preachers, the elect, leaders, and the active life. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 600, 604, 607.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 670.

THE WIDOW WOMAN, casting two small coins into the treasury, is the faithful soul keeping in the treasure of its heart the fruit of love for God and neighbour. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.---The son of the widow of Nain, whom Christ raises and restores to his mother, represents sinners whom Christ heals through grace and restores to the Church. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.

IV.---Figures referring to Jews and Gentiles.

THE MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH, sent to the pool of Siloam, signifies the human race healed through the waters of baptism.---The blind and mute man possessed by a demon signifies those who are converted from idolatry to faith in the Lord.---The blind man sitting by the road signifies the Gentile people, which through Christ deserved the brightness of faith.---The two blind men sitting beside the road signify both peoples drawing near to Christ through faith. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119, 127, 128.

THE CENTURION indicates the faith of the Gentiles, which humbly asks healing for its sick son; and his son, like the daughter of the Canaanite woman, signifies the Gentiles, whom Christ, though he does not visit them bodily, saves through faith in the word. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 118.

THE DEMONIAC freed from the legion represents the Gentile people enslaved to the worship of many demons. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

ELIZABETH holds the type of the old Law, or prophecy, just as her husband Zacharias holds that of the old priesthood. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 74.

THE EUNUCH OF QUEEN CANDACE represents the synagogue. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 520.

HEROD AND PILATE, made friends because of Christ, signify the two peoples, divided but made harmonious with one another through Christ’s Passion. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.

THE MAN WITH A WITHERED HAND is the synagogue, unfruitful in works of mercy. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 120.

JOHN THE BAPTIST, whose name is interpreted “in whom is the grace of God,” represents both the old and the new Law. St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 331.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 1001.

THE TWO THIEVES ON THE CROSS signify both peoples: one blasphemes Christ hanging on the cross; the other, a Gentile, rebukes the Jews. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 130.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1342.

POOR LAZARUS is a figure of the Gentile people, whom divine help raises up all the more because it trusts less in the resources [Col. 0262] of its own strength. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 341.---Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 315.

LAZARUS FOUR DAYS DEAD signifies the world raised on the fourth day of death: the first day, the inheritance of death drawn from Adam; the second, transgression of the natural law; the third, violation of the law that was given; the fourth, contempt for Gospel preaching. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.

THE LEPER indicates the human race, stained by the contagion of sin. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 118.

THE MAGI signify the peoples of the Gentiles, who would come to know the light of faith; by the sacramental gifts they indicate Christ as God through frankincense, as a man who suffered and was buried through myrrh, and as king of all ages through gold. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 117.

MARY MAGDALENE, as a sinner, prefigured Gentile life. Rupert, abbot, CLXIX, 650.

MATTHEW THE TAX COLLECTOR bears the type of the Gentile people. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 285.

THE ADULTEROUS WOMAN is a figure of the synagogue. Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 845.

THE PHARISEE AND THE TAX COLLECTOR. The Pharisee praying in the Temple is the Jewish people, which exalts its merits from the justifications of the Law; the tax collector is the Gentile people, confessing sins and justified by the Lord because of humility. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.

THE CHIEF PRIEST tearing his garments is the Hebrew people, stripped of priesthood and deprived of its divided kingdom. His servant, whose ear is cut off, is the Israelite people made a servant because of unbelief. It loses the right ear when it passes to the left through its literal understanding; but the Lord restores the hearing of faith in those who believe. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.

THE SAMARITAN WOMAN is the synagogue, which Christ urges to receive the grace of washing, or understanding of the Law. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.

SIMON OF CYRENE, upon whom they laid the cross to carry, is the people of the Gentiles, which, foreign to the Law, becomes obedient in the Gospel. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.

SIMON THE LEPER is the Gentile people, cleansed by the Redeemer. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 128.

PETER’S MOTHER-IN-LAW, sick with fever, indicates the synagogue inflamed by carnal desires, whose daughter is given to Peter to govern. St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 118.

THOMAS THE UNBELIEVING is a type of the Jews. Rupert, abbot, CLXX, 239.

ZACCHAEUS is the Gentile people: small in merits, but raised up through the wood of the cross, it contemplates Christ’s mystery. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.

V.---Figures relating to heretics and the ungodly.

BARABBAS, released by Pilate to the Jews, figures Antichrist, whom they, in their error, deserved to receive in place of Christ. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 129.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 819.

THE BLIND signify those who do not at all understand the faith which they believe; THE LAME, those who neglect to fulfil the saving commandments; THE MUTE, those who do not confess Christ’s faith; and THE DEAF, those who do not render obedience to the commandments. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 118.

HEROD represents the devil; or the Gentiles wishing to extinguish Christ’s name from the world; or likewise the luxury and pride of kings. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 118.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 677.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 856.---Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 398.

THE MAN WITH A WITHERED HAND signifies the soul barren in works of mercy; but he who often falls into fire or water signifies the world, ever seized by the fire of desires and the water of pleasures. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 120, 121.

THE DROPSICAL MAN figures those burdened by the overflowing stream of carnal pleasures. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 126.

JUDAS is called an agent of the devil, and is a new Absalom hostile to his father. St. Hilary, IX, 712, 838.

LAZARUS, Christ’s dead friend, is the soul buried beneath earthly sins. St. Augustine, XL, 59.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1242; CLXX, 119.---Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 741.

THE TEN LEPERS are heretics who possess the diversity of schisms and are therefore sent to the priests to receive the sacrament of unity. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.

[Col. 0263] THE SHEPHERDS OF THE FLOCKS FLEEING are leaders of the ungodly, who, fleeing faith, nevertheless preach virtues which they marvel at. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

PILATE is a type of all judges who would [Col. 0264] condemn those whom they considered innocent. St. Ambrose, XV, 1828.

THE REJECTED SCRIBE signifies those who seek Christ’s faith not for the Lord’s sake but for worldly gain. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 119.

[Col. 0263] Should the reader desire fuller material, let him consult the Index of Homilies and Sermons, especially those on the Scriptures; there he will find other figures explained.

[Col. 0263]

L. EXEGETICAL INDEX OF THE PRINCIPAL PARABLES OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, ARRANGED AT ONCE IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS AND IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS, IN WHICH ARE PRESENTED THE VARIOUS EXPLANATIONS OF THEM FOUND IN THE *Patrologia Latina*.

PROEM.

Definition of a parable.---Parables are likenesses of things compared with the matters under discussion. Rufinus, XXI, 840.---St. Jerome, XXV, 161.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 546; XXXVI, 852.---Salonius, LIII, 967, 968.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 623, 1277.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 38.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 239.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 939; CVIII, 723; CX, 694, 698.---St. Ivo of Chartres, CXLII, 259, 290.---St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 847, 1030.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 191.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 614, 1553.---Peter Lombard, CXCI, 724.

Division.---The Lord’s parables must be understood according to both likeness and unlikeness. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1358.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 550, 551.

Usefulness.---A parable presents likenesses of matters commonly encountered in human life, so that a hearer may be equipped, through the teaching of comparison, with zeal for action. St. Gaudentius, XX, 973.---St. Jerome, XXVI, 132.---St. Augustine, XL, 320.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 469.---Salonius, LIII, 968.

PARABLE I.---A FRIEND ASKING HIS FRIEND AT NIGHT FOR LOAVES FOR A GUEST. Luke 11:5.

That man who at midnight asked his friend for three loaves expresses the likeness of anyone who, amid tribulation, asks the Lord to give what is necessary. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 598.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1721, 1722.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 630.---St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 618–620.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 543–545.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 125.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 473, 474, 519, 520.---Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1339.---Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 305, 306.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 224–226.---Haymo, CXVIII, 530–534.---Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1902.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 149–152.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 658.---John Algrin, CCVI, 745.---Innocent III, CCXVII, 427, 438.

PARABLE II.---THE RICH FEASTER AND LAZARUS THE BEGGAR. Luke 16:19.

The rich man clothed in purple and fine linen signifies the pride of the Jews, once flourishing in the splendour of empire or the eminence of honour. The beggar covered with sores shows the Gentile people, humbled by confessions of sins. The five brothers of that rich man tormented in hell are understood as the Jews, who are placed under the five books of the Law. Tertullian, I, 680.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1768, 1771.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 639; XXX, 575.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1350; XLVI, 921, 923.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 529–532.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 308.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1301; LXXIX, 1222.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 126.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 533; XCIV, 268.---Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1362.---Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 348–352.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 294–297; CXI, 81.---Haymo, CXVIII, 589–595.---Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1962.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 422, 793.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 822.---Robert [Col. 0264] Pullus, CLXXXVI, 824, 825.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 337–340.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 833, 834.

PARABLE III.---THE RICH MAN CONGRATULATING HIMSELF ON HIS MANY RICHES. Luke 12:16.

The rich man whose field produced abundant fruits signifies the person given over to luxuries and abounding in sins. The Lord rebukes him as he immoderately desires to sin more and more, saying: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” Tertullian, I, 1161; II, 432.---St. Cyprian, IV, 533.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 611, 612.---St. Jerome, XXV, 679; XXIX, 632, 633.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 490.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 307.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 1020.---Alulphus, LXXIX, 1214, 1215.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 125.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 491, 492.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 1518; CLXX, 323.---Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 574.---Hervaeus, monk, CLXXXI, 76.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1799.---Peter Cantor, CCV, 338.

PARABLE IV.---THE HOUSE FOUNDED UPON THE ROCK. Matthew 7:24; Luke 6:48.

The rock is Christ, the originator of the apostles. The house of which he spoke is the dwelling-place of our body. Therefore, let us build our house upon this rock—that is, upon Christ; that is, let us sanctify our body, so that when the rivers and wind come—that is, the onset of persecution and the storm—we may be assailed but not fall. Sand, however, means nothing other than heresies, which are tossed about by every storm. Whoever, therefore, builds his house upon this sand—that is, upon heresy—is foolish; for immediately the rivers and winds—that is, the onset of persecution—will come, and he will at once fall. St. Jerome, XXVI, 50.---Arnobius, LIII, 574.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 118.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 75.---St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 329.

PARABLE V.---THE LOST DRACHMA, WHICH, WHEN THE WOMAN SEEKING IT HAS FOUND IT, SHE REJOICES WITH HERSELF AND HER OWN HOUSEHOLD. Luke 15:8.

The woman is divine wisdom; the ten drachmas are the nine orders of angels together with the addition of human nature. For the woman had ten drachmas when God created human beings and angels in his image; but she lost one when man departed from the likeness of his Creator. Yet Wisdom lit a lamp in order to seek it when it appeared in the flesh; for the lamp is light in an earthen vessel—that is, the Word in the flesh. When that light shone among human beings, it overturned the house, because it disturbed human consciences by consideration of their guilt. Thus the drachma is found when the likeness of the Creator is restored in man. Tertullian, I, 1242; II, 993.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 635, 636.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 637.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1344.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 641, 643.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 302.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1246, 1249.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 121.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 521.---Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 360, 361.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 77.---Haymo, CXVIII, 613, 615.---Hugh of [Col. 0265] St. Victor, CLXXV, 820.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 303.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 757.---Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 977.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 629.---Innocent III, CCXVII, 645, 810.

PARABLE VI.---LEAVEN PUT INTO THREE MEASURES OF FLOUR. Matthew 13:33; Luke 13:21.

That woman who took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened is either evangelical preaching or the Church gathered from diverse nations. It took the leaven—that is, the knowledge and understanding of the Scriptures—and hid it in three measures of flour, so that spirit, soul, and body, brought into unity, might not disagree among themselves, but, when two or three come together, might obtain from the Father whatever they ask.

Many interpret this woman as the Church, which mingles a person’s faith with three measures of flour, with belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and, once this has been leavened into one, it leads us not to knowledge of a threefold God, but of one divinity. Likewise, because the measures of flour do not have a distinct nature in each, they lead to unity of substance. Pope St. Sixtus, V, 87.---St. Hilary, IX, 994.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 227.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1749, 1750; XVII, 628–630.---Juvencus of Aquileia, XIX, 214.---St. Jerome, XXVI, 91, 92; XXIX, 559, 635; XXX, 552.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1326; XXXVIII, 641.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 477, 479.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 514.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 287.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 120.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 67, 507.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 948, 949, 950; CXI, 76.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 133.---St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 498.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 191, 250.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 794.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 228–231.

PARABLE VII.---THE UNFRUITFUL FIG TREE, WHICH IS ORDERED TO BE CUT DOWN. Luke 13:6.

The man who planted a fig tree in his vineyard is Christ, who established the synagogue among the Jewish people. When the Lord ordered it cut down as if useless, the apostolic cultivators make for it a trench of humility, manure is applied—that is, confession of sins—and thus, by believing at the last, it will be changed for the better and will yield abundant fruits of righteousness. PARABLE VIII.---TWO SONS: ONE REPENTING AND OBEYING HIS FATHER; THE OTHER PRETENDING TO OBEY. Matthew 21:28.

These two sons, sent to work the vineyard, show the type of the two peoples. The first, sent, is called the people of the Gentiles, through understanding of nature, to the cultivation of the divine work; yet, scorning this call, it was stubborn and denied that it would go. But when the Lord came, it corrected its earlier stubbornness by subsequent obedience. The second son, the Jew, sent through knowledge of the Law, answered: “Whatever the Lord shall say to us, we will do.” But he is condemned because he not only transgressed in his profession of the Law, but stretched out parricidal hands against the very Lord of the vineyard. St. Hilary, IX, 1040.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 287.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 569; XXX, 557.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 317.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 122.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 94.---Christianus Druthmarus, CVI, 1436.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1047; CXI, 78.---Haymo, CXVIII, 237, 238.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 247, 794.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1565.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 797.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 384.

PARABLE IX.---THE PRODIGAL SON. Luke 15:11.

“A certain man,” that is, God the Father. “Two sons,” Jews and Gentiles, because the Law was first given to the Jews. “Give me my portion,” that is, the present life. “He divided the substance,” that is, he gave freedom of choice to both peoples. “He set out into a far country,” that is, far from God. “Living luxuriously,” [Col. 0266] that is, worshipping idols. “A severe famine,” that is, famine of God’s word. “To one of the citizens,” that is, to a philosopher. “In his estate,” that is, in the world. “To feed swine,” that is, he lived after the manner of beasts. “And on husks,” that is, to fill the belly but not grow fat. “Swine,” that is, fools. “The hired servants of my father,” that is, those who are the humbler servants of God. “Are filled with bread,” that is, with teaching. “I have sinned in heaven”: this is said by those who have the devil as father, who sinned in heaven. “Moved by mercy,” that is, he came in the flesh. “To his servants,” that is, to the apostles. “The first robe,” faith which Adam lost. “A ring,” that is, the cross upon the forehead. “Shoes,” that is, the Gospel. “The fatted calf,” that is, Christ from the two laws. “He was dead,” that is, Adam. “He came to life again,” that is, through baptism. “He was lost,” that is, in despair. “He was found,” that is, in hope. “The elder son,” that is, the Jews. “In the field,” that is, in unclean desire. “Music and dancing,” that is, prophecy and the Gospel, etc. Tertullian, I, 1242.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 637.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1756–1760.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 637; XXX, 574.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1374.---St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 395.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 197.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 825.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 303.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 1066.---Alulfus, LXXIX, 1218.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 126.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 522; XCIV, 375, 510.---Paul Winfrid, XCV, 1257.---Haymo, CXVIII, 247–253.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 414–420.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 201, 210.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 820.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 305–310.

PARABLE X.---THE UNJUST JUDGE AND THE WIDOW. Luke 18:2.

That unjust judge, who did not fear the Lord but nevertheless heard the widow continually entreating him, is a likeness demonstrating how great hope one who unceasingly entreats the Lord ought to have, since the repeated persistence of an entreating widow prevailed even before the ears of an unjust judge. The widow herself may signify the Church, which by its perseverance seeks vengeance against its enemies, that is, the devil or heretics. St. Jerome, XXIX, 640, 641.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1358.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 316.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 550; XCIV, 314.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 81.---Haymo, CXVIII, 696–698.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 383.

PARABLE XI.---THE PRECIOUS PEARL. Matthew 13:45.

The good pearls which the merchant seeks are the Law, the Prophets, and knowledge of the Old Testament. But the one precious pearl is knowledge of the Saviour, the sacrament of his Passion, and the mystery of his Resurrection. When the merchant has found it, he despises all the mysteries of the Law and Prophets and the former observances in which he had lived blamelessly as refuse and rubbish, in order to gain Christ. This does not mean that finding one new pearl is a condemnation of the old ones, but that in comparison with it every other jewel is of lesser value. St. Cyprian, IV, 608.---St. Hilary, IX, 995.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 229.---St. Jerome, XXVI, 95; XXIX, 559; XXX, 552.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1371.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 331.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 528.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 288.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1115.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 69.---Christianus Druthmarus, CVI, 1376.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 954.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 133.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 504.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 192, 1067, 1070.---Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1564.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 719.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 794.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 687.---St. Ogerius, abbot, CLXXXIV, 1131–1133.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 235.---John Algrin, CCVI, 629.---Innocent III, CCXVII, 799.

PARABLE XII.---TEN MINAS DISTRIBUTED TO SERVANTS FOR TRADING. Luke 19:12.

The servant who, having received one mina, gained ten signifies teachers who, having received the grace of the Gospel, made good use of the ten precepts of the Decalogue and by teaching gained many people in faith; therefore, when the Lord comes, they will be praised because they made a profit. But the servant who gained five from one signifies those who, keeping God’s commandment, attain knowledge of the Law written in the five books of Moses and, by teaching, lend it out for the use necessary to salvation. But the one who kept the single mina in a cloth shows the person who treated the gift of grace entrusted to him delicately and idly. He rightly loses the grace bestowed upon him, because through negligence he disdained to preach, so that the gain which he had worked for might be increased. St. Hilary, [Col. 0267] IX, 1038–1061.---Lucifer of Cagliari, XIII, 975.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1792, 1794.---St. Jerome, XXIX, 642.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 1359.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 337.---Alulfus, LXXIX, 1229.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 127.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 562; XCIV, 472.---Smaragdus, CII, 540.---Christianus Druthmarus, CVI, 1512, 1516.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 82.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 435, 438, 852, 1058.---Godfrey, abbot, CLXXIV, 773, 780.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 485, 488.

PARABLE XIII.---THE WEDDING OF THE KING’S SON, TO WHICH THOSE INVITED NEGLECTED TO COME. Matthew 22:2; Luke 14:16.

The king who made a wedding for his son is understood to be God the Father, who joined virgin flesh, from the Virgin, to Christ. The servants sent to summon the invited are the apostles and prophets, who called the Jews through the Law and the Gospel. But those Jews, at one time oppressed by earthly pleasures, at another by the burden of the flesh and the Law, despised the solemnity of the Lord’s coming; hence they judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, while the Gentiles are shown to have entered. The angry king, who sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city, is God the Father, who raised up Vespasian, emperor of the Romans; he devastated the people with the sword and utterly overthrew the city of Jerusalem with all its inhabitants, so that it can no longer wage war. The man without a wedding garment at the banquet, who was silenced when the king spoke and whom he orders the servants to take away and cast into the outer darkness, is the one who indeed rests with the others in faith; but if on the day of judgment he is found to have the garment of flesh stained with works, he is immediately ordered to be taken by angels and plunged into the Gehenna of eternal fire. PARABLE XIV.---LABOURERS HIRED AT VARIOUS HOURS OF THE DAY, RECEIVING THE SAME WAGE. Matthew 20:1.

The master of the household who hires labourers for the vineyard and promises the wage of a denarius is Christ, who calls all to the cultivation of faith, promising them the reward of perfect blessedness. The labourers hired at the first hour are those who have pursued the cultivation of faith from the earliest elements of childhood; those at the third hour are those who came to faith in adolescence; those hired at the sixth hour are those who believed in the age of youth; those who came at the ninth hour are those who, declining from youth into old age, received Christ’s grace; and those at the last hour are those who, already decrepit and at the very end of their lives, came to Christ when called. Yet they receive a reward of eternal blessedness equal to that of the former: Christ preserves justice in those who laboured from the first hour of their birth, while bestowing mercy on those who laboured for one hour of life. ## PARABLE XV.—THE LOST HUNDREDTH SHEEP, WHICH THE SHEPHERD SOUGHT AFTER LEAVING THE NINETY-NINE. Luke XV, 4; Matthew XVIII, 12.

The man who has a hundred sheep, leaves the ninety-nine, seeks the lost sheep, and, having found it, bears it back upon his shoulders, represents Christ. Leaving the ninety-nine companies of angels in heaven, as the good shepherd he found among the Gentiles the sheep lost in Adam, and bore it back to Paradise on the shoulders of his cross. ## PARABLE XVI.—THE GOOD SHEPHERD, THE HIRELINGS, AND THE SHEEP. John X, 2.

The good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep is Christ himself, who, becoming man for humankind, died on the cross. The sheep are human beings, both Gentiles and Jews, all of whom Christ wishes to gather into one fold. The hirelings are evil shepherds, who do not seek the gain of souls but crave earthly advantages, delight in the honour of prelacy, and rejoice in temporal profits. The wolf is the evil spirit, namely the devil, who tears apart the minds of the faithful in temptation: drawing one toward lust, inflaming another with avarice, raising another up in pride, dividing another through anger, goading this person with envy, tripping up that one through deceit, and so forth. ## PARABLE XVII.—THE MASTER WHO MERCILESSLY DEMANDS FROM A SLAVE A DEBT ALREADY FORGIVEN. Matthew XVIII, 23.

That man and king to whom the kingdom of heaven is compared, who settled accounts with his slaves, is our Redeemer, who settles accounts with his servants when, strictly examining, he weighs the merits of each. This slave, who owed ten thousand talents, is the Jewish people, whom their Lord delivered into the power of foreign nations because of their transgressions of the Law; but afterwards, moved by mercy, he ended their captivity. Thus freed from captivity, the Jewish people not only gave no thanks to their Redeemer, but did not hesitate to harass their fellow slave, that is, the Gentile people, as though it were subject to them. The fellow slaves who reported the servant’s insolence to the Lord are the apostles and preachers of the Gospel. In anger, the Lord handed him over to the torturers, that is, into the hands of the Romans, who ravaged all their land and destroyed Jerusalem from its foundations. ## PARABLE XVIII.—THE PHARISEE AND THE TAX COLLECTOR. Luke XVIII, 9.

The Pharisee praying in the Temple is the Jewish people, who exalt their own merits on the basis of the justifications of the Law. The tax collector, however, is the Gentile people, who, standing far from God, confess their sins. One withdrew unjustified through pride; the other, humbled in confession, deserved to draw near and was exalted. ## PARABLE XIX.—THE NARROW GATE OF HEAVEN, THE CONSTRICTED WAY OF SALVATION. Luke XIII, 24.

The hall of salvation is entered through a narrow gate, because toil and fasting are necessary in order to overcome the allurements of this deceitful age. The gate is not called narrow and the way constricted because Christ’s yoke is harsh and his burden heavy, but because few are willing to bring their labours to completion. Broad is the worldly way toward the pleasures that people desire; narrow is the way opened through labours and fasts. Many walk by the broad way; few find the narrow one. We do not seek the broad way, nor is there any need of finding it: it offers itself of its own accord and is the way of those who go astray. But not everyone finds the narrow way, and those who find it do not immediately enter upon it; for many, having found the way of truth, are captured by worldly pleasures and turn back midway on the journey. ## PARABLE XX.—CHILDREN SINGING AND LAMENTING IN THE MARKETPLACE. Matthew XI, 17.

Those children who sit in the marketplace singing and lamenting signify the generation of the Jews. The marketplace is the Lord’s precinct, or the synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, in which the ordinances of heavenly commands were kept, and where they spoke to their equals. By the word “dancing” are meant neither theatrical motions nor undulating twists of the body, but the eager devotion of the heart and the religious agility of the limbs. ## PARABLE XXI.—THE NET CAST INTO THE SEA. Matthew XIII, 45.

This net is the holy Church: it has been entrusted to fishers, and through it each person is drawn from the waves of this present world to the eternal kingdom, lest he be submerged in the depths of eternal death. It gathers fish of every kind, because it calls to forgiveness of sins the wise and the foolish, free persons and slaves, the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak. But the shore signifies the end of this world; the net, the holy Church which was being drawn. The good fish—that is, good people—are then received into vessels, that is, led into eternal dwellings; but the bad are cast out, namely into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Alternatively: the net is the preaching of the Gospel, which draws all good and evil persons to the Church; the sea is the world; the shore, the end of the age; fish gathered into vessels, the saints admitted to heaven; fish cast out, the reprobate thrust down into hell.---St Hilary, IX, 996.---Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 229, 230.---St Jerome, XXVI, 95; XXIX, 559; XXX, 552.---St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 331.---Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 288.---St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1116.---St Paterius, LXXIX, 1041.---Alulfus, LXXIX, 1161.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 70.---Christian Druthmar, CVI, 1376.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 954; CXI, 240.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 134.---St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 506.---Remigius of Lyons, CXXI, 1006.---St Odo, abbot, CXXXIII, 493.---St Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 192.---Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 719.---Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 761, 795.---Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 235.

## PARABLE XXII.—THE SAMARITAN TREATING THE MAN WHO FELL AMONG ROBBERS, POURING OIL AND WINE INTO HIS WOUNDS. Matthew XVIII, 23.

The man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho is understood to be Adam in the human race. Jerusalem, the city of peace, is that heavenly Jerusalem from whose blessedness he fell. Jericho is interpreted “moon” and signifies our mortality, because it is born, grows, ages, and dies. The robbers are the devil and his angels, who stripped him of immortality and, having inflicted wounds—that is, having persuaded him to sin—left him half-alive: in the respect in which a human being can understand and know God, he is alive; in the respect in which he wastes away and is weighed down by sins, he is dead, and is therefore called half-alive. The priest and Levite who, having seen him, passed by, are the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament. The Samaritan is Christ; the binding of the wounds, the restraining of sins; the oil, the consolation of good hope; the wine, the exhortation to act bravely; the beast, Christ’s flesh; the inn, the Church; the next day, the resurrection; the two denarii, the two commandments of charity; the innkeeper, the apostles; and so forth. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 593.---St Ambrose, XV, 1717–1719.---St Jerome, XXIX, 629; XXX, 573.---St Augustine, XXXV, 1340.---St Fulgentius, LXV, 931.---St Paterius, LXXIX, 1062.---St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 124.---St Eligius, LXXXVII, 627.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 468.---Abbot Smaragdus, CII, 446.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 449; CXI, 80.---Abbot Godefridus, CLXXIV, 370.

## PARABLE XXIII.—THE SOWER WHOSE SEED FELL: SOME BY THE WAYSIDE, SOME UPON ROCKY GROUND, SOME AMONG THORNS, SOME UPON GOOD SOIL, AND PRODUCED A HUNDREDFOLD, SIXTYFOLD, OR THIRTYFOLD CROP. Matthew XIII, 4.

The seed is the word of God; the sower is Christ God. “He went out to sow”: coming forth from the bosom of the Father, he came into the world and sowed the word of truth, either himself or through those whom he appointed. That which fell by the wayside was trampled by passers-by and snatched away by birds—that is, by demons. That which fell on rocky ground fell into hearts taught by no studies of discipline and softened by no testing of temptations: they hear only the sweetness of the word and delight for a time in the heavenly promises, but fall away in time of temptation. That which fell among thorns is choked by worldly care. That which fell upon good soil is the faithful conscience of the elect, which bears fruit and brings forth a crop. ## PARABLE XXIV.—THE SERVANT WATCHING BY NIGHT AND AWAITING HIS LORD’S RETURN FROM THE WEDDING. Luke XII, 36.

The Lord returning from the wedding is Christ, coming from heaven to judge. He will knock by foreshadowing death; he will make his watchful servants recline—that is, be refreshed in eternal rest, being satisfied by the illumination of his own light. ## PARABLE XXV.—THE COSTS TO BE CALCULATED BEFORE WAR AND BEFORE BUILDING A TOWER. Luke XIV, 28.

The man building a tower and the king preparing for war signify Christ’s disciple, who must consider the end in all things, and must anticipate by diligent reflection everything that is done. The tower to be built is the tower of humility, which is constructed not by gathering expenses but rather by distributing them. The opposing king represents the supreme Judge, to whom the Christian must send an embassy: his tears; send works of mercy; sacrifice upon his altar offerings of propitiation; and so forth. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 633.---St Jerome, XXIX, 636.---St Augustine, XXXIV, 990; XXXV, 1343.---St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1274.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 517, 518.---Abbot Smaragdus, CII, 532–534.

## PARABLE XXVI.—THE MUSTARD SEED. Matthew XIII, 31.

The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel and the knowledge of the Scriptures that leads to life. The man who sows is either the Saviour, who sows in the minds of believers, or the person himself, who sows in his own field, that is, in himself and in his heart. The mustard seed is the preaching of the Gospel, which is the least of all forms of learning, since it preaches humble things and is despised by philosophers. Yet this preaching, which seemed small in its beginnings, when it has been sown either in a believer’s soul or in the whole world, does not rise into a vegetable but grows into a tree, so that the birds of heaven—which we ought to understand as either the souls of believers or the powers consecrated to God’s service—come and dwell in its branches. I think that the branches of the Gospel tree grown from the mustard seed are the various doctrines, in each of which one of the aforementioned birds finds rest. ## PARABLE XXVII.—TALENTS DISTRIBUTED TO SERVANTS: FIVE GIVEN TO ONE, TWO TO ANOTHER, AND ONE TO A THIRD. Matthew XXV, 14.

The man departing on a journey, who entrusted his goods to his servants, is Christ, who, returning to heaven after his resurrection, entrusted Gospel grace to Gospel merchants for investment. But in the five talents given to him, the first servant received the five books of the Law, which he increased through the teaching or observance of the Ten Commandments. In the two talents, the second received the two Testaments; by piously administering them in their moral and mystical senses, he doubled them. Under the figure of the one talent, the third obscured the gift of grace received in earthly pleasures and was therefore cast into hell, because he produced no fruit from it. Others understand in the first servant the five senses of heart and body received, in the second understanding and action, and in the one talent reason. ## PARABLE XXVIII.—THE TREASURE HIDDEN IN A FIELD. Matthew XIII, 34.

The treasure is heavenly desire. The field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of heavenly study. Certainly, the person who, having sold everything, buys that field, renounces fleshly pleasures and through the observance of heavenly discipline tramples down all earthly desires, so that nothing which flatters the flesh may be permitted and the spirit may not shrink from anything that destroys the carnal life.

Alternatively: the treasure is either God’s word, which is seen to be hidden in Christ’s flesh, or the holy Scriptures, in which the knowledge of the Saviour is laid up. When someone has found it in them, he must despise all the advantages of this age, so that he may possess what he has found. What follows—“when a man has found it, he hides it”—is said not because he does this out of envy, but because, through the fear of one guarding and unwilling to lose it, he hides in his heart what he has preferred to his former riches; and so forth. ## PARABLE XXIX.—THE UNJUST STEWARD, MAKING FRIENDS FOR HIMSELF FROM THE MAMMON OF INIQUITY SO THAT, WHEN DEPRIVED OF HIS OFFICE, HE MAY BE RECEIVED BY THEM. Luke XVI, 1.

The wasteful steward whom his master orders removed from the stewardship, and who, defrauding his master, remitted to his master’s debtors a portion of what they owed so that he might have a means of living in the future, is set before us as an example. For if the man who defrauded his master and provided for his future from another’s property deserved to be praised by his master, how much more can we please Christ if we show mercy to the needy from our own resources, by whom we may be received into eternal dwellings.

Alternatively: the rich man is Christ; the steward, any human being; to waste the goods, evil use of reason; “he called him,” death; the account of stewardship, judgment; “I cannot dig,” sincere confession; “I am ashamed to beg,” the sinner’s shame; and so forth. ## PARABLE XXX.—THE VINEYARD LET OUT TO TENANTS, WHO KILLED ITS MASTER’S SERVANTS AND SON. Matthew XXI, 33.

The man who planted the vineyard represents God, who founded Jerusalem. In it he built a tower and dug a winepress—that is, the altar and the Temple—and surrounded it with a hedge, that is, fortified it with the protection of angels. The tenants to whom he let the vineyard are the people of Israel, who possessed Jerusalem under divine worship. The servants sent at the time of the fruits and killed by the tenants are understood to be the prophets, whose blood was shed by the Jews when they demanded from them the fruit of justice and of the Law. The son sent last, whom the tenants cast out of the vineyard and killed, is Christ, whom the Jews crucified, casting him outside the gates of Jerusalem. The tenants whom the Lord of the vineyard destroyed are understood to be the same Jewish peoples, who formerly, as it appears, were scattered and killed. But the other husbandmen to whom the vineyard is ordered to be transferred signify the apostles, or the successors of the apostles; and so forth. ## PARABLE XXXI.—THE TEN VIRGINS: FIVE WISE AND FIVE FOOLISH. Matthew XXV, 1.

The five wise virgins are understood as all holy souls, which, because they admit no corruption of heart through the five bodily senses, are accordingly counted by the number five. The five foolish virgins, who have no oil in their vessels, are those souls which indeed possess bodily integrity but do not preserve within their conscience the testimony of a good work, while they glory before people in outward appearance and not before God in the heart. Therefore, because they do not bear in the vessels of their breasts the brightness of the mind, when the Lord comes they are shut out from the joy of his kingdom.

Alternatively: the bridegroom and bride are Christ and the Church; lamps, the light of shining souls; oil, the fruit of good work; vessels, human bodies; sellers, priests; wedding, the assumption of immortality; the bridegroom’s delay, the time for repentance; the sleep of those awaiting him, the rest of believers; the cry at midnight, the sound of the trumpet at the final judgment; and so forth. ## PARABLE XXXII.—THE TARES WHICH THE ENEMY SOWED OVER THE SEED. Matthew XIII, 24.

The sower is Christ; the field, the world; the good seed, the children of light; the tares, the children of iniquity; the sleeping people, negligent prelates; the enemy, the devil; the grass springing up, its fruit progressing toward better things, his good work; the harvest, the consummation of the age; the reapers, the angels; [Col. 0274] the binding of the tares into bundles indicates that the associates in one crime will share one punishment; the wheat, the saints; the barn, the heavenly dwelling. Moreover, in this parable of the tares Christ teaches good will, caution, patience, discernment, longsuffering, and justice; and so forth. ## LI. INDEX OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND WOMEN OF THE OLD TESTAMENT, TREATED IN ONE WAY OR ANOTHER BY THE FATHERS IN THEIR WRITINGS; ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY NAME, BUT WITHIN THIS ALPHABET THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS IS PRESERVED.

## NOTICE.

In this Index, as also in the following one, so that it might not be unduly prolonged and thus delay rather than assist the reader, we have not listed absolutely all persons, nor either all the names or all the places where they occur in the *Patrologia*. For to accomplish this, we would have needed to do nothing other than transcribe again and again nearly the whole writings of certain Fathers. Rather, we have recorded only the principal instances, presenting no text but indicating volume and page by numbers; should the reader wish to consult them, he will find what he seeks. At times the reader is referred to the bold numbers inserted into the text.

[Col. 0273] **AARON**, brother of Moses and renowned companion in miracles, the first priest of the Lord under the Law, whose rod, chosen by lot, blossomed with leaves and bud. At the age of one hundred and twenty-three years, he died on Mount Hor by the Lord’s command, and there he lies buried. CLXVIII, 17, 838, 878, 1310; CLXIX, 94, 95, 100; CLXX, 77, 179, 568, 579, 580.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 50, 459, 615 and following.---Hervéus, CLXXXI, 1647, 1648, 1659.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 472.---Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1364, 1365, 1368, 1374, 1375; CXCII, 146, 147, 491–493, 497.---Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1009.---Abbot Volbero, CXCV, 1047.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 643, 1037, 1039, 1040.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 289, 331, 332, 480, 481.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1091, 1094, 1097, 1102, 1108.---Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 633, 898.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 79, 255.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 748.---Alan of Lille, CCX, 206, 207, 261.

ABSALOM, David’s son, after killing his brother, fled to Talmai, king of Geshur; recalled, he attempted to seize his father’s kingdom, but Joab pierced him with three spears as he fled and hung entangled in a tree. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 807; XXXVI, 73, 97; XXXVII, 1847; XLIII, 720.---St. Fulgentius, LXV, 616.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 412.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 443.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 105, 107; CXI, 39.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 714, 1077.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 72, 73.---Peter Lombard, CXCI, 77.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 816, 817.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1336, 1338.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 817.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 917.

AHAB, the impious king of Israel, tyrannizes Naboth; he is pierced by a weapon, and, according to Elijah’s words, dogs lick his blood. Tertullian, II, 378, 990.---Philastrius, XII, 1127, 1136.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 735, 754, 1097, 1098.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 308.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 811; XXXVI, 1001.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 224–226 and following.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 452.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 60.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 176.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1243, 1248.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1378.

ACHAN, who coveted and stole from the accursed things of Jericho, was stoned in the valley of Achor. St. Augustine, XLIII, 743.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 374, 375.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 291; CXI, 54.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 146, 366.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 586.

AHAZ, king of Judah, born of the righteous father Jotham, fell into faithlessness and the crime of idolatry; having plundered the house of the Lord and the houses of kings and princes, he gave gifts to the king of the Assyrians, and yet it profited him nothing. St. Jerome, XXII, 673 and following.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 248; CXI, 62, 377.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 511, 765, 766.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1264, 1405.

AHIJAH, also called AHIMELECH, priest of the Lord, gave David the loaves of the Presence and Goliath’s sword; he perished by being pierced through. St. Ambrose, XV, 1645, 1646.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 362.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 145.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 648.

ACHIOR, leader of the Ammonites, is handed over into the hands of the children of Israel and becomes a Jew. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 553, 554, 576, 611, 612, 629.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 48.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1264.

ACHISH, king of Gath, before whom David feigned madness and who gave him the city of Ziklag. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 301, 302, 305, 308, 315.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 403.

AHITHOPHEL, David’s counsellor, attached himself to Absalom, gave impious counsel, and afterwards hanged himself. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 97.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 107, 406.

ADAM, the first-formed man and tiller of Paradise, chief of the human race and of transgression, made in God’s image and set over the whole creation; he gave names to creatures and received authority to rule over them. But, on account of transgression, he was cast out of Paradise, and, groaning as a labourer, inhabited a land made desolate by thorns. After the course of nine hundred and thirty years, he returned to the dust from which his flesh had arisen, and lies buried in the place Arbre. Tertullian, I, 1248, 1257, 1277; II, 272, 286, 290, 293, 297, 314, 315, 599, 601, 665, 723, 883, 900, 904, 958, 990, 1038.---St. Cyprian, IV, 620, 629, 634, 675, 840.---Lactantius, VI, 322, 323.---St. Hilary, IX, 258, 261, 404, 437, 438, 484, 648, 669, 779, 780, 839, 871, 930, 960, 979, 1020, 1075; ADDO, born in Samaria, was sent to Jeroboam while he was sacrificing to a calf. He came by the word of the Lord and rebuked him as he sacrificed. As he returned home, a lion killed him on the road because of his disobedience; Bethel contains his burial-place and that of the prophet who had deceived him. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 146.

ADONIJAH, David’s son, who sought his father’s kingdom but perished by being killed. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 125, 126.

ADONI-BEZEK, an impious king, was captured and killed by the Israelites. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1112; CXI, 55.

AGAG, king of the Amalekites, captured by Saul, was killed at Samuel’s command. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 441.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 434.

HAGAR, Sarah’s maidservant, bore Ishmael by Abraham, the prince of a great people. St. Hilary, X, 113, 114, 463.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 328, 491.---St. Jerome, XXV, [Col. 0278] 975, 976; XXVI, 390.---St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 32; XLI, 512.---St. Fulgentius, LXV, 595.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104, 242 and following, 218.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 543, 561.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 122.---Haymo, CXVI, 926.---Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 94.---St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 652.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 387, 421.---Abbot Volbero, CXCV, 1040.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1096, 1103.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 742.

HAGGAI, born in Babylon, came to Jerusalem while still a young man; he saw part of the building of the Temple, and rests gloriously buried beside the tombs of the priests. St. Hilary, X, 694, 695.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 1063.---St. Jerome, XXV, 1419.---St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1053, 1467; XLI, 593, 1917; XLIII, 670.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 911.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115, 145, 173.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 843.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 543, 561; CXI, 69, 371.---Haymo, CXVII, 211 and following, 222.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1522; CLXIX, 1378.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1481.

AHIJAH, the prophet at Shiloh who cut a cloak into twelve pieces and foretold evils to Jeroboam’s wife. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 789.

ALEXANDER, king of the Macedonians. St. Jerome, XXV, 503, 504.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1129–1131.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1397, 1398.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1496.

AMALEK, son of Esau, against whom Joshua fought and whom he defeated while Moses prayed. Cassiodorus, LXX, 377.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 409–412.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109, 299.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 84, 945; CIX, 1144; CXI, 53.

HAMAN, an Amalekite, favoured by the king of Persia and hostile to the Jews, died miserably by hanging. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1110.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 652.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 745, 746.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1000, 1380, 1381 and following.

AMASA, son of Abigail, David’s sister, and commander of the army under Absalom. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 252.

AMAZIAH, son of Joash, avenged his father’s murder, defeated the Edomites in war, and perished after being captured. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 62.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1316.

AMMINADAB, son of Aram and father of Nahshon. St. Ambrose, XV, 1222; XVI, 290.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 201, 453, 572.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 938.

AMMON, son of Lot and his daughter, from whom came the Ammonites. St. Jerome, XXV, 1001, 1002.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 818; XXXVII, 1053.---Salvian, LIII, 54.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1128, 1129, 1187; CIX, 97, 103, 371, 372; CXI, 63, 380.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1332–1335.

AMOS, shepherd and rustic, from the town of Tekoa, whom the Lord sent to the people of Israel, commanding him to go to Samaria and there prophesy the things that were to come. King Amaziah repeatedly afflicted him with blows; at last his son Uzziah, piercing his temples with a bar, killed him by a cruel death. St. Jerome, XXII, 463; XXIII, 894, 924; XXIV, 21–23; XXV, 989–991, 993.---St. Prosper, LI, 542.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115, 144, 170.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 68.---Haymo, CXVII, 107 and following.---Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 415.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1401.

HANANIAH, who prophesied against Jeremiah. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70, 1015.

HANNAH, who was first barren and afterwards made fruitful, mother of Samuel. Tertullian, II, 389.---St. Cyprian, IV, 522, 542, 689.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 368.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 27, 58, 62, 110, 111.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112, 392, 425, 426.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 12–16; CXII, 1100.---Angelomus, CXV, 248, 249 and following.---Haymo, CXVI, 699.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1296.

ANTIOCHUS, king who destroyed the Temple and overthrew Jerusalem, setting up an idol upon the altar of the Lord. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1125, 1133, 1134, 1138, 1139, 1173, 1176.

ARAM, also called Ram, son of Hezron and father of Amminadab. St. Jerome, XXIII, 926.

ARPHAXAD, king of the Medes, defeated by Nebuchadnezzar. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 541, 599, 601.

ARTAXERXES, king of Persia, who permits Israel to build the Temple. Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 706.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1483.

ASA, son of Abijah, king of Judah, who removed idols and was father of Jehoshaphat. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 487; CXI, 59.

ASAHEL, Joab’s brother, remarkable for swiftness of body. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 77.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 76, 77, 506.

ASAPH, David’s singer. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1347; [Col. 0279] XXXVI, 916, 929, 970, 1011; XXXVII, 1035, 1051.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 335, 332; CXI, 70.---Haymo, CXVI, 195.---St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1058.

ASHER, remarkable for riches, filling princes with delicacies. St. Ambrose, XIV, 686, 687.---Rufinus, XXI, 325.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107, 135.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1131.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 597; CVIII, 1114; CXI, 46.

AHASUERUS, king of Persia, who took Esther as his wife. St. Jerome, XXIII, 579.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 636, 661, 662, 670.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 748.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1383.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 964.---Thomas the Cistercian monk, CCVI, 176.

ASSUR, whose name means “rod of the Lord’s wrath.” Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 583, 632; CX, 818.

ATHALIAH, daughter of Omri king of Israel; she reigned six years and destroyed almost the entire royal stock. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 498; CXI, 61.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 616.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1270; CLXVIII, 879.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1397.

AZARIAH, a native of the land of Sabatha, was sent as prophet to King Asa; he died and was buried in his own small field. St. Prosper, LI, 541.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 146.---St. Agobard, CIV, 136.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 787, 789.

BILHAH, Rachel’s maidservant and Jacob’s concubine, whom Reuben defiled through the crime of incest. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108, 261.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 550.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1005 and following.

BALAAM, hired to curse Israel, was taught by the Lord what he ought to say and blessed it. Tertullian, I, 456.---Philastrius, XII, 1134.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 338, 1156 and following.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 972.---St. Augustine, XL, 136.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, in sermons 27, 159.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 263, 265, 282.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 399, 434, 882, 903, 1132; LXXVII, 68, 69, 111.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 110.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1104, 1105.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 725, 727, 729, 746, 765, 795, 1122; CXI, 53.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 107.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 493 and following.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 433.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1146, 1149 and following, 1153 and following.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 337, 814.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1236, 1238.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 80.---Peter of Blois, CCVII, 824.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 871.

BALAK, king of the Moabites, who incited Balaam to curse Israel. St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1810.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 357.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1105.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 80.

BILDAD. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 526, 622.

BALE. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 537.

BELSHAZZAR, king of Babylon, to whom Daniel explained the words inscribed upon the wall. St. Jerome, XXIV, 158; XXV, 518, 521.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 968.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1510; CLXIX, 1357.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 80.---Abbot Volbero, CXCV, 1048.

BARAK, whose name means “lightning,” judge of Israel, who, aided by Deborah, routed Sisera. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 380, 381.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1134–1136, 1143; CXII, 804.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1026, 1031, 1034.---Hervéus the monk, CLXXXI, 1656, 1657.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1275.

BARUCH, son of Neriah, who, at Jeremiah’s dictation, wrote out a book to be read to the people. St. Hilary, X, 127, 156.---St. Zeno, XI, 410, 411.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 679, 680; XXVI, 445.---St. Augustine, XLI, 591.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 56, 1071, 1072.

BETHUEL, son of Nahor, father of Rebekah. St. Ambrose, XIV, 580.

BEN-HADAD, son of Hazael, king of Syria. St. Salvian, LIII, 136.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 213, 236.

BENJAMIN, later in birth than his brothers, whose birth brought death to his mother. He is the ravening and bloodthirsty wolf who, upon the base of his lot, pours out the blood of the victim in the morning, and at evening distributes food to princes and priests. Rufinus, XXI, 333.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 834, 1022.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 580.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 262.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107, 135, 267.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 617, 640, 665; CVIII, 1144; CXI, 48.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1006.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 532, 534.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 88.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 773.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1123, 1140.

BARZILLAI, who supplied King David with food. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 214.

BATHSHEBA, Uriah’s wife, whom David loved; when she became his wife, she bore Solomon. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 411, 430.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1020.

BOAZ, son of Solomon, took Ruth as wife; by her he begot Obed. St. Ambrose, XV, 1602, 1603.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1205; CVIII, 1207, 1216.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 62, 90.---Gerhoh, CXCIII, 1501.

CAIN, Adam’s son, who killed his brother Abel and became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. St. Cyprian, IV, 641.---St. Hilary, IX, 648.---St. Zeno, XI, 314.---Philastrius, XII, 1116, 1261.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 315 and following, 329, 330, 350, 351, 353 and following, 357, 359–361, 864, 1040; XVI, 819, 881; XVII, 756, 976, 980.---Juvencus, XIX, 350, 351.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 944, 915; XXV, 920, 1146.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 396, 548; XXXV, 2013; XXXVI, 442, 705, 733, 773, 997; XLI, 437, 438, 441, 444, 445, 456, 460, 461, 463, 465, 469; XLII, 134, 258, 260; XLIII, 34, 319; XLV, 1556.---St. Prosper, LI, 697, 698.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, in sermons 4, 96, 109, 147, 172.---Anonymous, LIX, 524.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1053.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 100, 223 and following.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 501; CIX, 716; CXI, 32, 33.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 98.---Angelomus, CXV, 146, 148.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 787.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 388.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 78 and following.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 172, 174 and following.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 322, 327, 334; CLXVIII, 815, 816.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 45, 640 and following.---Abbot Volbero, CXCV, 1263.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 813.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1078.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 53, 387.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 215, 216.

CALEB, son of Hezron, explorer of the land of Canaan. Philastrius, XII, 1288.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 630.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 278.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 115.---Haymo, CXVI, 937.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 879, 1390.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1268 and following.

KETURAH, whose name means “fragrant with spices,” whom Abraham took as his wife after Sarah’s death. St. Ambrose, XIV, 328.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 566; XLI, 512.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 253.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 579.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 205.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 202.

HAM, whose name means “hot,” the middle of Noah’s three sons; he mocked his father’s nakedness, and for this was cursed. Tertullian, II, 66.---Lactantius, 327, 328.---Philastrius, XII, 1224.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 363, 408, 409, 412, 414.---St. Jerome, XXII, 677, 678.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 55; XXXVII, 1398; XLI, 477, 478.---Anonymous, LIX, 526.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103, 235–237.---Alcuin, C, 532.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 525; CVIII, 454; CXI, 34.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 112, 113.---Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 78.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 185 and following.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 360.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1087.

CANAAN, Ham’s son, cursed by Noah; from him came the Canaanites and the land of Canaan, which was afterwards promised to Abraham. St. Ambrose, XIV, 409, 414.---St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1394, 1751; XLI, 478, 499, 524.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 20; CXI, 94.

CHUSHAN-RISHATHAIM, king of Syria, who ruled over Israel for eight years. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1122.

KORAH, a rebel against Moses, swallowed up by fire. St. Cyprian, IV, 513.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 464, 482, 493, 514, 525, 533, 605; XXXVII, 1056, 1069.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 680, 681; CIX, 1089; CXI, 53, 71, 72.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 814.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1230.

CYRUS, king of the Persians, who permitted the captive Israelites to return to Judaea and restored to them the vessels formerly taken away by Nebuchadnezzar. St. Jerome, XXV, 45, 46, 536.---St. Augustine, XLI, 117, 583.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 810.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 535, 536; CXI, 336.---Haymo, CXVI, 942.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 152; CLXIX, 167–169, 1371, 1373–1375.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1470.

DELILAH, Samson’s wife, who shaved his head and thus took away his strength. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 57.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1050.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 275, 276 and following.

DAN, Jacob’s son, from whose seed came Samson, who held the sceptre of Israel: a strong Nazirite and conqueror of enemies, lying in wait like a serpent along the paths of the Philistines and, like a basilisk, laying waste their cavalry by the breath of his mouth. St. Ambrose, XIV, 684, 685, 1079.---Rufinus, XXI, 321.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 596; LXXIX, 142.---St. Isidore of Seville, [Col. 0281] LXXXIII, 107, 135.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 661, 662; CIX, 26; CXI, 44, 378.

DANIEL the prophet, born in Upper Beth-horon of the tribe of Judah, of noble family, chief of all the Chaldeans, and flourishing in royal descent and the nobility of his native country. He lived one hundred and ten years, and was buried in the royal cave, alone in captivity with glory. St. Hilary, X, 172, 463.---St. Zeno, XI, 117, 118.---St. Jerome, XXII, 463; XXIII, 308, 454, 455; XXV, 120, 498, 499, 505, 725.---Dexter, XXXI, 570–572, 579–591.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 899, 901, 904, 911; XXXIV, 461, 462; XXXV, 2039, 2191; XXXVII, 1731; XXXIX, 2027; XL, 716; XLI, 593; XLIV, 159.---Peter Chrysologus, LII, in sermon 131.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 376.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 1114.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 535; LXXVI, 277, 546, 797, 862, 976.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 143, 169.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1122, 1127.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 265; CXI, 67.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1499 and following, 1518 and following; CLXVIII, 1392; CLXIX, 1069, 1368, 1371.---Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1282, 1290.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1113.---Peter Lombard, CXCI, 81.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1243, 1246, 1296, 1298, 1306.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1447.---Alan of Lille, CCX, 248.

DARIUS, king of the Persians, who overthrew the Babylonian empire and took Daniel with him and brought him to the Medes, where he was held in the highest honour. Tertullian, II, 614.---St. Hilary, X, 694, 870.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 459; XXIV, 158; XXV, 518, 535, 536, 1418, 1419.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 143.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 848.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 535, 536; CXI, 336.

DATHAN, punished by the Lord, perished by fire with Abiron and Korah, whom see. St. Cyprian, IV, 513.---St. Hilary, IX, 484.---St. Jerome, XXV, 1087.---St. Salvian, LIII, 47.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 402.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1230.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 80, 134.

DAVID, both king and prophet, sprung from the tribe of Judah, son of Jesse, born in Bethlehem, a boy and shepherd of sheep; younger than his brothers in age, but superior in virtue; called by the Lord to kingship and anointed king by the prophet; a warrior in youth, singular in combat, glorious in triumph, seasoned in victory, patient in adversity, prudent in dangers, grieving over his own sin and mourning at another’s death, inclined to repentance, quick to pardon, mild under insult, and ready to show mercy. In the fortieth year of his reign and the seventieth of his age, he completed the last day of his life and was buried in his own city, Bethlehem, where also our Lord Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh. Tertullian, II, 14, 305, 388, 624, 937, 990.---St. Cyprian, IV, 641, 667, 782.---St. Hilary, IX, 321, 322, 337, 338, 358, 374, 375, 397, 398, 401, 403, 404, 515, 517, 519, 520, 535, 545, 546, 549, 550, 554, 555, 558–560, 567, 570–576, 585, 594–597, 602, 606, 609, 622, 623, 626–628, 632–936, 639, 641, 665, 699, 728, 729, 733, 734, 737–740, 816, 833, 834, 838, 840, 844, 985.---St. Zeno, XI, 320, 321.---St. Optatus, XI, 980, 981.---Philastrius, XII, 1256.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 599, 600, 813, 824, 844, 848, 851, 853, 854, 857–865, 874, 875, 883, 884, 887, 889, 890, 894, 899, 902, 907, 908, 956, 1009, 1015, 1016, 1041;
