DEBORAH, prophetess and wife of Lapidoth, who with Barak defeated Sisera through the power of the Lord. St. Ambrose, XVII, 248, 249.---St. Jerome, XXVII, 227.---St. Augustine, XLI, 572.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 380, 381.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 423.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1134, 1126, 1138; CVIII, 632, 638; CIX, 1144; CXI, 56.

DINAH, Jacob’s daughter, whom Shechem the prince violated. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 108, 667, 668.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 614; CXI, 42.

DOEG, Saul’s servant, who betrayed the priest Abimelech and slaughtered the priests of the Lord. St. Ambrose, XV, 1646.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 601.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 429.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 59, 70, 321, 322.

EGLON, king of the Moabites, whose name is interpreted “turned” or “an orbit.” Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1129; CIX, 1130; CXI, 55.

ELKANAH, whose name is interpreted “possession of God.” St. Cyprian, IV, 689.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 21, 30.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 425.—Venerable Bede, XCI, 499.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 12, 13, 77.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 248.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1061.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXV, 681 and following.—Gerhoh, CXIV, 1009.

ELEAZAR, Aaron’s successor. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1204.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 434.

ELEAZAR, martyr. St. Cyprian, IV, 671, 672.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 632, 633.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 16; CXII, 53.

ELEAZAR, soldier. St. Ambrose, XVI, 82.—St. Gregory, LXXVI, 119.—Rabanus Maurus, CLX, 1174.

ELEAZAR, son of Amminadab. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 452, 453.

ELIJAH the Tishbite, high priest and prophet, a dweller in the wilderness, full of faith, supreme in devotion, strong in labours, diligent in activity, endowed with outstanding intelligence, trained in the exercise of discipline, constant in holy meditation, and undaunted by fear of death: he struck down tyrants, slew sacrilegious persons, and shone forth through many signs of miraculous power. At last he ascended, snatched up to heaven in a fiery chariot; he is to come at the end of the world to fight Antichrist. Tertullian, II, 413, 636, 711, 733, 735, 881.—St. Hilary, IX, 622, 1032, 1058.—Philastrius, XII, 1126, 1127, 1168, 1232, 1281.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 319, 697, 700, 710, 720, 731; XV, 1508, 1548, 1585, 1694; XVI, 107, 204, 205, 235, 239, 477, 834, 835, 1097, 1135.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 244, 307, 308, 380, 381, 383, 558, 580; XXV, 334, 1082, 1447.—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 521, 871, 872; XXXIV, 396, 397, 702, 725; XXXV, 1408, 1416, 2181–2183, 2230; XXXVIII, 1335; XXXIX, 1823, 1825, 2263; XLI, 704; XLV, 1598.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LI, sermons 27, 43, 92, 131, 136, 147, 150, 151, 166.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 452, 575, 578.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 377.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 796, 872, 964, 965, 1053; LXXVI, 101, 102, 178, 557, 948, 1216, 1217; LXXIX, 67, 236, 321, 535, 573.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113, 110, 270, 418.—Venerable Bede, XCII, 376; XCIII, 447.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 519, 1122.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 431; CIX, 206, 207 and following, 223, 568, 1100, 1101; CXI, 1078, 1085.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 607.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 177 and following, 496 and following.—Haymo, CXVIII, 881.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1239, 1243, 1254; CLXVIII, 306, 836, 885, 1391; CLXIX, 1026, 1027, 1324–1328; CLXX, 105.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 334.—Hugh of St. Victor, CXXXV, 708, 709 and following, 712; CLXXVII, 690, 691.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, [Col. 0283] 718, 719, 763, 764.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 823.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1378, 1379 and following, 1387.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 825.

ELIEZER, Abraham’s faithful servant, who brought Rebekah from Mesopotamia to be Isaac’s wife. St. Augustine, XLI, 502.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 536.

ELIMELECH, kinsman of Boaz. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1201, 1202.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1058.

ELIPHAZ, one of Job’s three friends. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 526, 621, 695.

ELISHA, Elijah’s disciple, from the town of Abel-meholah, descended from the tribe of Reuben. Glorified with Elijah’s double spirit, he shone forth through very many and great signs of miraculous power. He turned the Jordan, divided for his passage, backward by checking its waters; by immersing a vessel, he restored the barren waters of Jericho to fruitfulness; with a word he handed over boys who mocked him to beasts to be suddenly devoured; he caused blood-red waters to flow for the destruction of enemies; meanwhile, by a word he made a barren woman fruitful in conception and raised her dead son; he cleansed Naaman of the marks of leprosy by washing in the Jordan; he also inflicted cursed leprosy upon his disciple; he made iron from an axe, sunk in the Jordan, float when wood had been cast into the waters; he struck the Syrian enemies with blindness; he foretold death to an unbeliever, put the enemy to flight by the sound of chariots, dispersed a siege, and drove away famine. Finally, after his death, he gave life to a lifeless corpse. His tomb is still shown today in the city of Sebastia, worthy of ample honour and held in worthy veneration. St. Hilary, IX, 787.—Philastrius, XII, 1232.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 244, 1029; XV, 1508; XVI, 169, 178, 834 and following, 957, 1197, 1198.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 2183, 2230; XXXIX, 1826, 1827, 1832, 2263.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 465, 466, 657.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 417.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 796, 797, 894, 895; LXXVI, 217, 218, 759, 790, 791.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113, 141, 419, 420.—Venerable Bede, XCIII, 447; XCIV, 1237.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 213, 223 and following, 243, 244; CXI, 67.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 612, 615.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 497, 517.—Haymo, CXVIII, 891, 907.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1248, 1254, 1258, 1260; CLXVIII, 305, 306, 879, 1109; CLXIX, 1026, 1324, 1328, 1329.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 334.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 715; CLXXVII, 691.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 80.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 823.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1380, 1388 and following, 1399.

ELIHU, one of Job’s three friends, who spoke arrogantly against him. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 50.

HEMAN, son of Joel, one of the singers whom David, at the bringing of the ark, appointed over the others for singing. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.

ENOCH, son of Jared, seventh from Adam, pleasing to God, ignorant of evils and unacquainted with death; unable to bear the afflictions caused by wicked men, he was withdrawn from the world’s destructive contacts and deserved to be transferred alive to the place from which the first-created man had been expelled. He was taken away at three hundred and sixty-five years of age. He remains in the body to this day; at the consummation of the world, together with Elijah, he will return to the mortal condition of life. Tertullian, I, 665, 684, 1307, 1308; II, 601 and following.—St. Hilary, IX, 748, 1032.—Philastrius, XII, 1300.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 282; XVI, 204, 205, 1097.—Juvencus, XIX, 351.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 236, 381, 580, 615; XXV, 1087, 1147; XXVI, 573, 574.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 397; XXXV, 2154; XL, 1037, 1134, 1144; XLI, 447, 460, 462; XLII, 262, 598; XLIV, 398; XLV, 1581.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 377.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 671; LXXVI, 922, 969, 1216, 1217.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 100, 102, 131.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 519, 1122.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 223, 1084; CXI, 33; CXII, 223, 791, 794.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 100, 101.—Haymo, CXVIII, 891.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 490, 491.—Philip of Harvengt, CCVIII, 1013, 1014.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 260, 341, 343.

ENOSH, son of Seth, who was the beginning of calling upon the name of the Lord. St. Jerome, XXVI, 354.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 101.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 32.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 102.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 341, 343.

EPHRAIM, Joseph’s offspring and Israel’s adopted son, left in the testamentary blessing among the number of the patriarchs; younger in age than his brother, but preferred through the greater grace of blessing; stronger than all the tribes, and an unconquered ruler among his brothers. St. Hilary, IX, 388.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 558, 571, 580, 779.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 24.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107, 136.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1144; CIX, 14; CXI, 49, 1102.

ESAU, son of Isaac by Rebekah, Jacob’s brother, who sold his birthright for food and was afterwards deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him. St. Cyprian, IV, 621, 634.—St. Hilary, IX, 623.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 317; XV, 1485.—Juvencus, XIX, 366 and following.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 373, 919, 978; XXV, 334, 1009, 1010.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 579; XXXVI, 715; XXXVII, 1772.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 563.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 437, 438, 607, 608, 627.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 689, 690, 959; LXXVI, 557, 829.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 255.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 582, 583, 613, 619; CVIII, 1136, 1139; CIX, 717; CXI, 1485, 1486.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 150.—Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 102.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 272.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 208.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 449 and following, 465, 491.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 632; CLXXVI, 1213.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1518; CXCII, 505.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 814.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1111, 1121.—Peter the Chanter, CCV, 62.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 813.

EZRA, priest of God, who by many is called Malachi, that is, “angel of God.” He was a writer of sacred history and a second giver of the law after Moses; for after the captivity he restored the law, burned by the nations, and invented the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. He brought Israel back and caused Jerusalem to be rebuilt. He died and was buried with his fathers, interred in Jerusalem. St. Hilary, IX, 234.—Philastrius, XII, 1232.—St. Ambrose, XVI, 1074; XVII, 219.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 190, 344, 345.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 2191; XLI, 596.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 146, 174.—Venerable Bede, XCI, 859, 873, 876, 908.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 305, 311; CXI, 70.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 706, 711.—Haymo, CXVII, 23.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1288, 1289, 1378.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 730.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 77.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1483.

ESTHER, queen, daughter of Mordecai’s brother, of the stock of Benjamin, was carried captive from Jerusalem to the city of Susa, and, because of the beauty of her appearance and the conspicuous excellence of her virginity, was joined in marriage to the king of the Persians. In order to free her people from danger, she offered herself to death; and she persuaded the king that his friend, who had wickedly urged action against the people of God, should be handed over to the cross. She rescued the nation, free from destruction, and delivered it from slavery. She lies buried in Susa, a city of the Medes, in which she also reigned. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1197.—St. Jerome, XXXIII, 412.—St. Augustine, XLI, 596; XLIV, 569.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116, 147.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 416, 653; CXI, 66.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 739 and following.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 877; CLXIX, 1381, 1389, 1390; CLXX, 106.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 733 and following.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1489.—Thomas, Cistercian monk, CCVI, 176.

ETHAN the Ezrahite, son of Cush, one of King David’s singers. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 312; CXI, 70.—Haymo, CXVI, 195.

EVE, formed from the rib of sleeping Adam, mother of the human race, who was first seduced by the serpent, ate from the tree of life, and thus ruined all her children. Tertullian, I, 1257, 1277; II, 65, 723, 782.—St. Zeno, XI, 277, 300.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 279, 289, 290, 298, 301–303, 310, 311, 1040; XV, 1205, 1407, 1408, 1613, 1614, 1622, 1632; XVI, 311, 312.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 942, 943.—St. Augustine, XXXII, 713; XXXIV, 207, 212, 215, 445, 446; XXXVIII, 1439, 1475; XXXIX, 1984, 1985, 1991, 2104; XLIV, 442, 864; XLV, 1564, 1566.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 254.—Anonymous, LIX, 523, 524.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 606.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 99, 131, 217, 220.—Paul the Deacon, XCIV, 1208, 1210.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 474, 482, 484; CVIII, 1148; CXI, 31.—Haymo, CXVIII, 928.—Hincmar, CXXV, 818.—Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 62.—St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 411.—Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 70 and following, 497, 589.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 164 and following.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 281 and following; CLXVIII, 867, 886.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 360, 361, 427, 475, 478, 939, 1014, 1091, 1131.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 40, 597, 639, 640.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 458; CLXXXVI, 749, 750.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 215, 341, 342.—Gerhoh, CXCIII, 1505.—Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 363.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 583.

HEZEKIAH, son of the impious Ahaz, was nevertheless a pious king; he broke the bronze serpent; he sent messengers to the prophet Isaiah; and for his good work fifteen years were added to him. St. Hilary, IX, 575, 643, 644.—St. Jerome, XXII, 463; XXIII, 308.—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 801; XXXIV, 351; XXXV, 2187; XLI, 578.—Cassian, XLIX, 405–408.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1003; LXXVII, [Col. 0285] 17; LXXIX, 140, 286.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 225; LXXXIII, 114, 420–422.—Venerable Bede, XCIII, 449.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 252, 255, 256, 258, 260, 261, 264, 517, 765; CXI, 63.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 621, 622.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 528, 529, 532, 533.—Haymo, CXVI, 696, 899, 900.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 24, 879.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 640, 641.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1411, 1412.

EZEKIEL, priest, son of Buzi, born in the land of Sarira, is called “son of man” as a type of Christ. Carried captive with Jehoiachin to Babylon, he prophesied to the captives, reproving their offences and, moved by zeal for God, denouncing all their crimes and shameful deeds. The leader of the people of Israel killed him because Ezekiel had rebuked that leader for the impiety of sacrilege with priestly severity and authority. He was buried by the people in the field of Maurim, in the tomb of Shem and Arphaxad. St. Cyprian, IV, 482.—St. Hilary, X, 463.—St. Optatus, XI, 979.—St. Ambrose, XVI, 296; XVII, 945.—St. Jerome, XIX, 38, 298, 471, 698, 703, 735.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 772; XLI, 592; XLIV, 1273, 1281.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, sermon 166.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 230.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 204, 797, 798, 868–870, 929, 934–936, 948, 949; LXXVII, 45, 46, 126; LXXIX, 247, 264, 484.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 143, 168, 169.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1118; CI, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CX, 497, 554, 555, 558, 561, 595, 647, 750, 957.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 42.—Haymo, CXVI, 195.—St. Anselm, CLVIII, 632.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1443 and following.—Peter the Chanter, CCV, 185.

GAD, Jacob’s son by Leah, ready for the battle-line, who fights against enemies and nations on behalf of his brothers left beyond the Jordan, and triumphs victoriously with a strong arm. St. Ambrose, XIV, 685.—Rufinus, XXI, 323.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107, 135.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1131.

GIDEON, son of Joash, from the tribe of Manasseh, born in the wilderness, liberator of the people, and father of many sons; strong in hand, vigorous in counsel, testing by signs the tokens of future victory and God’s power in the fleece. With three hundred men he triumphed valiantly over Amalek. He judged Israel for forty years, died an old man, and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah, of the family of Ezri. St. Ambrose, XVI, 703–707, 738.—St. Jerome, XXIV, 140; XXVII, 237.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 809, 813–815; XXXVI, 521, 833, 907; XXXIX, 1616; XLIII, 398.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 564–567.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 138, 381–383.—Venerable Bede, XCIII, 424, 425.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1156, 1159, 1166–1171, 1182; CXI, 56.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1035.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 678, 679 and following; CLXXVII, 705, 1092.—Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1656, 1657.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 497.—Garnerius, CXCIII, 232, 233.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 822.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1298.—Peter the Chanter, CCV, 40, 138, 147, 173.—Thomas the monk, CCVI, 545.

GEHAZI, Elisha’s disciple and servant, who through greed inherited the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 233.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1265.—Peter the Chanter, CCV, 81, 134, 135.

GOLIATH, the Philistine giant, whom David struck down with a stone in his pride. Philastrius, XII, 1225.—St. Augustine, XXXVI, 302; XXXVIII, 197.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 450, 781, 782.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 52, 53; CXI, 58.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 313.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1100.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1311.

HEBER, in whose house the original language remained when the other languages were divided, and from whom the Hebrews were named. Philastrius, XII, 1219, 1235.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 2323; XLI, 598.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103.

ELI, high priest, who was rejected because of his sons’ wickedness, since he neglected to rebuke them; and, after the ark had been captured, he fell from his seat and died with his neck broken. Philastrius, XII, 1124.—St. Ambrose, XVII, 209.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 2239; XXXIX, 2321.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 557, 570; LXXIX, 134, 140, 141, 362.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112, 393.—Venerable Bede, XCI, 505, 509, 515, 516, 524; XCIII, 431.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 13, 20–22, 25, 27; CXI, 58.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 250.—Samuel of Morocco, CXLIX, 341.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1070, 1072; CLXIX, 881.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 683.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 815.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1298.

ER, son of Judah, whose name is interpreted “leather-worker.” St. Zeno, [Col. 0286] XI, 435.—St. Augustine, XLII, 156.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 289.

HIRAM, king of Tyre, who supplied Solomon with very many things for building the Lord’s temple. Venerable Bede, XCI, 739.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 420, 453, 474.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 346.

HOLOFERNES, commander of Nebuchadnezzar, whom Judith killed while he was besieging Bethulia. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 546, 572, 573, 575, 602, 608, 627.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 748.

HABAKKUK, prophet, of the tribe of Simeon, was born in the field of Bethsachar and descended from a glorious stock of ancestors; he prophesied, died, and was buried in his own field. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1135.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 308, 533, 534, 562, 886, 895, 902; XXV, 38, 1275.—St. Augustine, XLI, 587.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, sermon 68.—Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1164.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115, 145, 172.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 69; CXII, 1111, 1128.—Haymo, CXVI, 705.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1469.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1059.

ISAAC, son of Abraham, born in the land of Canaan by promise, called the everlasting seed; renowned for chastity in married life, ready for grace and prepared to forgive. He did not drive away those who excluded him by arms, but conquered through patience; he received penitents with kindness; and through love of God he carried honour for his parent so far that he voluntarily approached the altar to be sacrificed, and, as a figure of Christ, did not refuse death. He died at one hundred and eighty years of age and was buried beside his father. St. Cyprian, IV, 629, 689, 802.—St. Hilary, IX, 350.—St. Zeno, XI, 418–420, 423, 429.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 319, 428, 446, 447, 501, 539, 1061.—St. Jerome, XXII, 237, 969, 975; XXIV, 618.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 566, 569; XXXVI, 244, 245; XXXVIII, 31, 38, 44, 133; XLI, 438, 505, 510, 511; XLIV, 714.—St. Prosper, LI, 696.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 799.—Cassiodorus, LXIX, 884.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 671, 918; LXXVI, 408, 763, 770, 771, 789, 829, 970; LXXVII, 188, 189, 595; LXXIX, 477.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104, 133, 248, 252, 253, 255.—Venerable Bede, XCII, 797.—Paul the Deacon, XCIV, 1211–1213.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 549.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 565, 573, 574, 580; CXI, 37; CXII, 329, 331, 334.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 149, 152.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 200 and following.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 199 and following, 205 and following.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 95, 101, 104.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 630.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1377; CXCII, 146, 147, 493.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 135, 481, 821.

JESSE, father of David. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 463, 464.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 52; CXI, 58.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 99.

ISAIAH, prophet, son of Amoz. Such was the excellence of his holiness and life that he is said to have possessed only one tunic, and that of haircloth; when this too was afterwards cast off on account of the people’s sin, he covered his limbs with sackcloth. Finally, laying this aside as well, in accordance with the Lord’s command he went about among the assembly of the peoples with his body and feet bare; thus he endured summer heat, winter frosts, and storms of rain, both obeying God’s commands and lamenting the sins of the people. He commanded the shadow to descend backwards through fifteen steps. By his oracle King Hezekiah obtained a postponement of death. Manasseh, however, cut him in two from the crown of his head through the middle and destroyed him by a cruel punishment. St. Cyprian, IV, 802.—Potamius, VIII, 1415, 1416.—St. Zeno, XI, 428, 429, 462 and following, 472.—St. Ambrose, XV, 1535, 1800; XVI, 813, 1180.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 847; XXIV, 18, 19, 22, 33, 91, 95, 150, 188, 189, 279, 286, 338, 384, 546, 547; XXV, 104, 592.—Dexter, XXXI, 212, 213.—St. Augustine, XXXV, 1779; XXXVIII, 259; XLI, 582, 585; XLIII, 503.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 293.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 862, 869; LXXVII, 20, 854; LXXIX, 293, 349, 350, 356, 590.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 141, 166, 167.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 64; CXII, 1091.—Haymo, CXVI, 695, 718.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1271 and following; CLXVIII, 12, 879.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 765.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 1111.—Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 17 and following.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 823.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 730.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 793.

ISHBOSHETH, son of Saul, who reigned over Israel for ten years, and whose name is interpreted “man of confusion.” St. Jerome, XXIII, 532.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1325.

ISHMAEL, son of Abraham by Hagar, and prince of the Ishmaelites. St. Jerome, XXIII, 967; XXVI, 388, 392.—St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1603; XXXVIII, 33; XLI, 439.—St. [Col. 0287] Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 538.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 390, 419.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 146, 147.—Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1040.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1096, 1109.

ISSACHAR, son of Jacob, diligent in the labours of the earth, possessing Galilee and offering gifts to kings from the fruits of his blessing. St. Ambrose, XIV, 683.—Rufinus, XXI, 319.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106, 135.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1131.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 43.

JACOB, son of Isaac, born in the land of Canaan, beloved of his mother, supplanter of his father, humble and simple, and dwelling in an innocent household. After he had seized the blessing of the firstborn, obedient to his mother and fleeing his brother’s wrath, he became an exile and endured long servitude; yet, though he lacked the fellowship of men, he deserved the company of angels. He prevailed in wrestling with the Lord; he saw God face to face; driven by lack of food, he entered Egypt with his noble offspring. Having completed one hundred and forty-seven years, he paid nature’s debt and was buried with his fathers. Tertullian, I, 1208; II, 356, 357.—St. Cyprian, IV, 667.—St. Hilary, IX, 336, 482, 658, 707, 755, 756, 878; X, 119, 141, 354, 380, 381, 658.—St. Zeno, XI, 316, 428, 432, 433.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 317, 329, 597 and following, 601, 615, 621, 624, 628, 641; XVI, 56, 960, 1049, 1050, 1085, 1216, 1320, 1321, 1343, 1344; XVII, 818, 843, 844.—Juvencus, XIX, 366, 368 and following.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 413, 528, 988; XXIV, 657, 807, 875; XXV, 924, 825, 930, 1244; XXVI, 545.—St. Augustine, XXXII, 739; XXXVI, 506, 527, 987, 1015; XXXVII, 1597, 1598, 1771, 1772, 1936, 1937; XXXVIII, 34, 37, 39, 41, 45, 47, 55, 56, 557, 681, 1275.—St. Prosper, LI, 696.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, sermons 70, 73, 131, 147, 154.—St. Leo the Great, LIV, 241.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 608, 799.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 437, 607, 608 and following.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 671, 672, 674, 690, 959; LXXVI, 408, 563, 789, 829, 830, 955, 970; LXXVII, 33, 474, 668, 980, 981; LXXIX, 52, 132, 133, 402, 633.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 134, 255–258, 264, 266.—Venerable Bede, XCII, 397.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 549, 552, 1105.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 582, 589, 591, 605, 609, 610, 615, 616, 645, 647, 650, 654, 666; CXI, 38, 339, 357.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 150, 155 and following, 162, 174.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 206.—Haymo, CXVIII, 909.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1004 and following.—St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 204, 205 and following, 216 and following.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 449 and following, 465, 470, 474, 497, 541, 548; CLXVIII, 359, 360, 878, 1312, 1313, 1332, 1385; CLXIX, 95, 101, 108.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 100.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 58, 59, 489 and following, 650, 652, 654; CLXXVI, 1213; CLXXVII, 641, 642, 697, 698.—Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1653.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 756, 1276; CLXXXV, 167.—Peter Lombard, CXCI, 896; CXCII, 493–495.—Garnerius, CXCIII, 159, 231.—Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 1270.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 821.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1113, 1121, 1140.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 343.—Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 858, 1155.

JAEL, wife of Heber, who pierced the temples of Sisera, commander of the Canaanites, with wood, and thus won the victory. Venerable Bede, XCIII, 423.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1136; CXI, 56.—St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1081.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1033.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1275.

JAPHETH, son of Noah, whose name is interpreted “breadth,” and who is therefore called the father of the nations. St. Hilary, X, 1033, 1034.—Philastrius, XII, 1245.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 363, 412; XVI, 1169.—Juvencus, XIX, 352.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103, 236.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 532.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 525, 526; CIX, 281.—Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 109.

JECHONIAH, son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, himself also king, whom Jeremiah calls “Childless.” St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1076; XXXVIII, 341.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 862.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 725.

JEHU, son of Jehoshaphat, king of Israel, who killed Jezebel and the seventy sons of Ahab. St. Augustine, XL, 520.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 232, 238, 498.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 685.—Haymo, CXVII, 13.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 886.

JEPHTHAH the Gileadite, fortunate in battles, overcoming natural affection by endurance of mind. For he had vowed to God that, if anything first met him as he returned after victory, he would sacrifice it. Returning from the enemy as victor over the Ammonites, lest he be defiled by the stain of perjury, he fulfilled his promised vow and sacrificed his daughter, who had come to meet the victor. He judged Israel for six years, died, and was buried in the city of Gilead, which is in the half-tribe of Manasseh. St. Ambrose, XIV, 858; XVI, 168, 169, 267, [Col. 0288] 351; XVII, 266.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 242, 373; XXIV, 735; XXVII, 261.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 810, 812, 814, 817–819; XLI, 35, 815, 816, 820.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, sermon 55.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 139, 388 and following.—Venerable Bede, XCIII, 428.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1040.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 33.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 680; CLXXVII, 323–327, 329 and following.—Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1659.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 344.

JEREMIAH, descended from the priestly tribe, in the village of Anathoth, three miles from Jerusalem; a priest established in Judah and a prophet consecrated among the nations; known before he was formed, sanctified before he came forth, and admonished to remain a virgin. He began to preach as a boy, reproving the people for their sins and frequently urging them to repentance; but by the cruelty of the raging faithless populace he was often afflicted and bound, even cast into prison, thrown into a pit, and encircled with chains; at last, at Tahpanhes in Egypt, he was stoned by the people. Tertullian, II, 137.—St. Hilary, IX, 233, 1032; X, 156.—St. Zeno, XI, 410, 411.—Philastrius, XII, 1232.—St. Ambrose, XVI, 354; XVII, 561.—St. Jerome, XXIII, 415, 566, 567; XXIV, 61, 681, 682, 845, 846, 854, 855, 867; XXV, 104, 587–589, 592, 624, 640, 665, 724.—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 846; XXXIV, 344; XXXVII, 1917; XLI, 236, 582, 583, 591; XLV, 1429.—Cassian, L, 85.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 176.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 636; LXXVI, 797, 862; LXXVII, 20, 197, 256, 854.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 142, 167, 168, 422.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1122, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 76, 77, 797, 798, 959, 960, 1050, 1051.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 9 and following, 40.—Haymo, CXVII, 12, 222; CXVIII, 891.—Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 449.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1363, 1365; CLXVIII, 879.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 289.—St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 333.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.—Hugh of Éleran, CCII, 257.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1105.—Peter the Chanter, CCV, 39, 40, 172, 173, 185.—Peter of Blois, CCVII, 362.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 793.

JEROBOAM, who separated the ten tribes from the house of David and from the temple of God, and led them into idolatry. St. Ambrose, XVI, 217.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, sermon 27.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 398.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 170.—St. Agobard, CIV, 233.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 199, 1099; CXI, 59, 64.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1276; CLXIX, 361; CLXX, 581.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 511.

JESUS, high priest. St. Jerome, XXIII, 288, 562.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 65.

JESUS, son of Sirach. Philastrius, XII, 1171.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 165, 166.

JETHRO, priest of the Midianites, whose daughter Moses took as wife. St. Ambrose, XIV, 329.—St. Augustine, XXXIV, 619.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 87, 88.

JEZEBEL, the impious wife of the impious King Ahab, who killed the Lord’s prophets; after her death she was torn apart by dogs. Philastrius, XII, 1127.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 585; XVI, 344, 345, 1210.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1106, 1107.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 65.—Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 881, 882, 886, 1067.

JOAB, son of Zeruiah, David’s sister, commander of the king’s army. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 715.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 112.

JOASH, son of Ahaziah, who alone escaped when the royal family was killed, and, though king of Judah, perished when murdered by his own servants. Cassian, XLIX, 458.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1171, 1172; CIX, 513; CXI, 58.

JOTHAM, son of Uzziah, king of Judah. St. Jerome, XXIV, 101, 102.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1171, 1172; CIX, 513; CXI, 58.

JOB, son of Zerah, of Bozrah, king of the Edomites; a Gentile man, renowned in faith, supreme in humility, exceptional in hospitality, gentle in discipline, lavish in almsgiving, rich in possessions but suddenly made poor, wealthy in children but suddenly bereaved. He was handed over to temptation, but against temptation was armed with the breastplate of faith; he became glorious in the contest, even-tempered in suffering, bore the loss of all things, yet glorified God amid torments, and for such patient virtue was raised up by a twofold reward at the end. He lived one hundred and forty years after his affliction, and the total days of his life were two hundred and forty-eight years; he died and was buried in his own region. Tertullian, I, 1271; II, 105.—St. Cyprian, IV, 588.—St. Hilary, IX, 328, 473, 537, 562, 618; X, 723, 724.—St. Zeno, XI, 316, 317, 439–442 and following.—St. Ambrose, XIV, 278, 798, 801, 808, 829, 1019, 1054; XV, 1371, 1396, 1397, 1624; XVI, 1021; XVII, 134.—St. Jerome, XXII, 677; XXIII, 381, 382, 539, 592, 885, 890, 971; XXV, 724; XXVI, 527.—St. Gaudentius, XXXI, 835, 837.—St. Augustine, XXXII, 1329; XXXIII, 242, 540, 1103; XXXV, 1697, [Col. 0289] 2007, 2023, 2361; XXXVI, 220, 255, 327, 539, 660; XXXVII, 1150, 1151, 1207, 1255, 1382–1384, 1612, 1732, 1758, 1794, 1881; XXXVIII, 147, 264, 500, 569; XXXIX, 1511, 1692, 1739, 1813, 1841, 1842, 1844; XL, 615, 632, 704, 716, 719; XLI, 37, 609; XLIV, 159, 161, 162, 283, 305; XLV, 1652, 1820, 1823.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 455.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 316.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 515–525, 528–537, 542, 554, 562, 566–568, 572, 576, 579, 583, 584, 599, 603, 606, 608, 610, 616, 634, 635, 637, 661, 691, 695, 699, 773, 776, 779, 781, 782, 801, 809, 830, 881, 882, 917, 954, 968, 969, 976, 981, 991, 994, 999, 1000, 1040, 1064, 1074–1080, 1136; LXXVI, 104, 204, 205, 213, 233, 236, 237, 249 and following, 356, 534, 753, 754, 769; LXXVII, 741; LXXIX, 643.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108, 136, 163.—Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1121, 1282.—Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 50, 111, 1236.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 747, 748, 790, 805, 822, 838.—Haymo, CXVIII, 909.—St. Odo, abbot, CXXXIII, 109 and following.—Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 433; CLXVIII, 961, 963, 968, 970, 971, 978, 983, 1001, 1009, 1104, 1105, 1107, 1150 and following; CLXIX, 63, 76, 86; CLXX, 381.—Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1281.—Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 946, 947, 1113.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 705.—Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1561.—St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 471, 829.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 339, 498.—Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 534.—Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1169, 1182, 1186.—Peter of Blois, CCVII, 795, 826.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 154, 157, 165, 166.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 344.

JOBAB, who is thought to be the same person as Job. St. Jerome, XXIII, 996.—St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 516.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 287.

JOEL, the prophet, who was of the tribe of Reuben, was born in the district of Beth-horon, where he also died in peace and was buried. St. Augustine, XLI, 583, 587.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 186.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115, 144, 170.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1122.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 35; CXI, 68.---Haymo, CXVII, 97 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 205.

JONADAB, son of Rechab, of the family of Jethro, distinguished by the austerity of his life and father of the Rechabites. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 875, 876, 890.---Cassian, XLIX, 1174.---St. Agobard, CIV, 214.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 932.

JONAH, son of Amittai, was sent to proclaim to the Gentiles; having been sent, he despised the mission; despising it, he fled; fleeing, he slept. Because of him the ship was endangered, but the shipmaster found him hidden; the great fish swallowed him when he was cast out and vomited him forth when he prayed. Having been cast forth, he preached destruction. Yet he was grieved at the city's repentance and begrudged the salvation of the Gentiles; he rejoiced also beneath the shade of the green ivy, and grieved when it suddenly withered. Tertullian, II, 840, 999.---St. Hilary, IX, 473, 1007, 1008.---St. Zeno, XI, 324, 444–450.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 222, 1129; XV, 1723; XVI, 1001.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 576; XXIV, 854; XXV, 928, 1110, 1117, 1119, 1121, 1122, 1145, 1372, 1373.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 242, 291, 382–384; XXXIX, 1610; XL, 666; XLI, 583, 587.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, in Sermon 37.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 357, 358, 602, 603, 814, 815.---St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1047.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 746; LXXIX, 391, 632.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 115, 144, 171.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 68.---Haymo, CXVII, 127 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 402, 415, 417, 318; CLXX, 118, 119.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1108–1110.

JONATHAN, son of Saul, whose death in battle David, his friend, mourned with love. Tertullian, II, 378.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 179.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 331.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 316.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 557; LXXIX, 337, 338, 359–363, 369, 380, 381, 399.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 410.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 442.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 42, 54, 1187.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 553, 554, 561, 662.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 299, 300 ff., 313, 334.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 688 ff.

JEHOSHAPHAT, son of Asa, king of Judah, sent men to teach the true worship of God in the cities of his kingdom. St. Jerome, XXIII, 558.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 91.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 225, 280.---St. Agobard, CIV, 97.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 492, 493; CXI, 60.---Haymo, CXVII, 105.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 879.

JOSEPH, prince of Egypt, son of Jacob by Rachel, born in the land of Canaan, blessed as Israel’s firstborn and receiving Reuben’s primacy; beloved by his father and, above all the others, sole heir of the paternal possession. Out of jealousy he was carried off by his brothers and thrown into a pit; through envy he was sold; he became humble even to slavery, patient even to imprisonment, and chaste even to suffering. He became wise in interpretation, prudent in counsel concerning the future, a partner in the kingdom, provident in organizing abundance, and a just distributor during famine—ready to repay evil with the grace of good recompense, since he did not repay his brothers’ injury but, having driven away famine, supplied the aid required by necessity. He held rule in Egypt for eighty years; and, having completed one hundred and ten years of life, he closed his final day. Tertullian, I, 596; II, 346, 626, 937.---St. Cyprian, IV, 629, 641, 667, 689, 802.---St. Zeno, XI, 299, 316.---Philastrius, XII, 1251, 1254.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 641–645, 652, 653, 656–659, 666, 688, 856, 1098, 1099, 1110; XV, 1371, 1414, 1610, 1625; XVI, 43, 56, 108, 118, 122, 124–126, 362, 884, 885, 1086, 1181.---Juvencus, XIX, 368, 372 ff.---Rufinus, XXI, 327, 328 ff.---St. Jerome, XXII, 463; XXV, 1493; XXVI, 193, 527.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 98, 461, 582, 588, 593, 594; XXXV, 2163; XXXVI, 1021; XXXVII, 1037, 1404; XXXVIII, 1439; XXXIX, 1509, 1592, 1765, 1766, 1768, 1770, 1773, 1924; XLI, 563.---Cassian, XLIX, 1077.---St. Prosper, LI, 299, 625.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 580.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 585, 745; LXXVI, 408, 545, 546, 1054, 1055, 1217; LXXVII, 937.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 107, 134, 270, 273.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 365; XCIV, 1272.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1132.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 621, 623, 629, 633, 635, 643, 649, 668, 669; CIX, 718; CXI, 44.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 168, 170 ff., 182.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 242.---Haymo, CXVI, 195; CXVIII, 909.---Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 114 ff.---St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 592; CXLV, 661.---Samuel the Moroccan, CXLIX, 342, 343.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 311, 328 ff.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 218 ff.---Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1654.---St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 69, 829, 962.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 495.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 272, 289, 821, 822.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1116, 1125 ff., 1139, 1141.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 729, 1037.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 169.---Thomas, Cistercian monk, CCVI, 549.---Alanus of Lille, CCX, 231, 236.

JOSIAH, son of Amon, king of Judah: he celebrated the Passover and, wounded by archers, departed from life. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1376, 1398.---St. Jerome, XXV, 121.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 801; XLI, 548.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 266, 267, 270, 527, 528, 1106, 1107.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 824.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1415 ff.

JOSHUA, son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, was born in Egypt; disciple of Moses, successor to his authority, and victor in a new warfare. In order to secure victory, he commanded the heavens that the sun should stand still. He also caused the course of the Jordan to halt for his crossing. He brought down Jericho’s impregnable walls by the sound of trumpets being blown. He overthrew the kingdoms of the Canaanites, destroyed their kings, and alone led the people of God into the land of promise, which he allotted by lot. He presided over Israel for twenty-seven years, died at the age of one hundred and ten, and was buried in his city of Timnath-serah. Tertullian, II, 343, 622, 937.---Lactantius, VII, 459, 501, 659, 956.---St. Hilary, X, 463.---St. Zeno, XI, 351.---Philastrius, XII, 1128, 1288.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 895, 1154; XV, 1463; XVI, 130, 651, 674.---St. Jerome, XXV, 1391; XXVIII, 199.---St. Gaudentius, XXXI, 873.---St. Augustine, XXXII, 821; XXXIX, 1553; XLI, 522, 568; XLII, 271.---Cassian, XLIX, 938.---Anonymous, LIX, 529.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524; LXXVI, 408, 970; LXXIX, 67, 195, 630.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 138, 371.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 911; XCIII, 417.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1121, 1125.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 130, 137, 778, 1118, 1120, 1124; CIX, 1090–1092; CXI, 54, 112.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 242.---Haymo, CXVI, 937; CXVIII, 891.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 736, 998, 999, 1019, 1022; CLXVIII, 879, 1390; CLXIX, 117.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 671.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1241, 1260, 1268, 1271.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1010.---Alanus of Lille, CCX, 343, 344.

JUDAH, distinguished by a royal line of succession, to whom the leadership in wars and the kingdom over Israel were entrusted; he gave his own name to the people. Mighty as a lion in royal strength and resplendent in the brilliance of power, his imperial posterity did not cease until Christ, like a lion’s cub, sprang from his stock and ascended, and the hope of the Gentiles, proceeding from a virgin womb, shone forth wondrously. Lactantius, VII, 473.---St. Zeno, XI, 434, 435, 439.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 678, 679, 856; XV, 1610.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 79.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 812; XXXVI, 540, 835, 865; XLII, 439, 456, [Col. 0291] 457.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 358.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106, 135, 268.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 625, 627.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1023, 1028.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 652.---St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 89, 809.

JUDITH, widow, daughter of Merari, of the tribe of Simeon, great-hearted in glory and surpassing men. For the salvation of her people she offered herself to death and did not tremble before royal fury; for she killed the ruler while he slept and, preserving her chastity, brought back to her fellow citizens the triumph of victory. She lived one hundred and five years and was buried in the cave of her husband Manasseh in the city of Bethulia. St. Ambrose, XVI, 169, 170, 246, 1197.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 412.---St. Augustine, XLI, 583.---St. Fulgentius, LXV, 319, 320.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116, 148.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1127.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 541, 543, 558, 565, 567, 568, 570–572, 589, 593, 597, 618, 621, 622, 624, 627, 628, 634, 646; CXI, 66.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 755 ff.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 743 ff.; CLXXVII, 1169, 1172, 1175.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1475.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 1184, 1183.

LABAN, father of Leah and Rachel, whom Jacob took as wives. St. Ambrose, XIV, 582, 623.---St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1763; XLII, 432.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 563; LXXVII, 981.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 260.---Rabanus Maurus, CVI, 606, 607; CXI, 42.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1004.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 83.

LAMECH, whose name is interpreted “striking,” killed Cain; and afterward he himself confessed to his wives that he had committed this deed. St. Hilary, IX, 1022.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 360.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 101.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 33.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 154.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 101.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 175.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 333; CLXVIII, 816.

LEVI, founder of the priestly lineage, joined with the tribe of Judah by mixture of descent, yet divided throughout all Israel; lacking the boundary-line of his own allotment and dwelling in every allotment of his brothers. St. Ambrose, XIV, 677.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 135.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 984.

LEAH, daughter of Laban and wife of Jacob, to whom she bore many children. Juvencus, XIX, 368.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 799.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 764; LXXVI, 954; LXXVII, 449.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 259 ff., 264 ff.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 797.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 601; CLX, 1219; CXI, 40.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 1004–1006.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 474.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 755, 1276, 1277.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 2, 6.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1116.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 119, 575.

LOT, son of Aram, kinsman of Abraham, father of Moab and Ammon, born among the Chaldeans; a righteous and hospitable man, who lived piously and chastely in Sodom among a wicked people. On account solely of his office of hospitality, he was even made host to angels; he escaped the sulphurous destruction and burning of the Sodomites, and afterward remained in the city of Zoar, which lies beside the Dead Sea. Tertullian, II, 602.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 424, 426, 440, 441, 457; XV, 1339; XVI, 214.---Juvencus, XIX, 355 ff., 359, 363.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, in Sermons 10, 12, 42.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 464.---St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 662.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 750; LXXVII, 102, 103, 855, 856.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 134, 245.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 555; CXI, 36.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 130, 133.---Haymo, CXVIII, 911.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 117, 118.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 374, 413.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 646 ff.; CLXXVI, 1023, 1024.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1041.---Gerhoh, CXCIII, 752.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1101.---Alanus of Lille, CCX, 344.

THE MACCABEAN LEADERS, namely Judas and his brothers, who waged a glorious war against the enemies of the people of God. Tertullian, II, 606.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 2192; XLV, 1733.---St. Valerian, LII, 746, 747.---St. Maximus of Turin, 691–698.---Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 1293 ff.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 748 ff.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1505 ff.---Hugh Eterianus, CCII, 198.

THE SEVEN MACCABEAN BROTHERS, steadfast in faith, strong in hope, most constant observers of the divine law, patient amid the bitterest torments, brutally slain by King Antiochus with their mother for the law of God, deserved the crowns of martyrdom. St. Cyprian, IV, 354, 668, 671.---St. Zeno, [Col. 0292] XI, 378.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 633, 636.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 911, 1066.---St. Gaudentius, XXXI, 948, 949 ff.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 156; XXXV, 2192; XXXVI, 389, 855, 856, 868; XXXVII, 1945; XXXVIII, 202, 1300, 1377, 1379, 1380; XLI, 596; XLIII, 729; XLV, 1733.---St. Leo the Great, LIV, 241; LV, 520.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116, 148, 174, 175, 423.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 451.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1236, 1237; CXI, 66.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 1422.

MALACHI, born in Sophah after the people’s departure, was a just man and handsome in appearance. The Jews assert that he was called Malachi, that is, “angel of the Lord,” because whatever he foretold was immediately confirmed by an angel coming from heaven. He died while still very young and was buried in his own field. St. Jerome, XXV, 1541; XXVI, 124.---St. Augustine, XLI, 593, 699.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 115, 145, 174.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 69.

MANASSEH, “enlarged among thousands,” mystically endured tribute together with his father Joseph. These are the fathers of the apostles and leaders of the Jewish people, the tribes of Jacob and the illustrious offspring of Israel. When dying, their father left them the grace of sanctification in place of abundant riches; and, while Joseph ruled in Egypt, they ruled there too, where after a long repose of life they died and were buried. St. Hilary, IX, 388.---St. Ambrose, XVII, 988, 989.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 1079; XXV, 1340.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 820; XXXVI, 719, 1022.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 580.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 136.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1131.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 265, 522; CXI, 49, 63.---Haymo, CXVI, 195; CXVIII, 928.---Abbot Rupert, CLXX, 585.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1415.

MORDECAI, Esther’s defender and guardian, was taken captive to Babylon and received the highest honour from the king. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 645, 660.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 744.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 193, 879; CLXIX, 1000, 1379, 1380, 1382, 1384.

MIRIAM, sister of Moses and Aaron, was struck with leprosy as punishment because she had murmured against Moses, the meekest of men. St. Zeno, XI, 310.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 1203, 1204.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 885.---St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1638.---St. Salvian, LIII, 46.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 109.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 400, 405.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 661, 662, 664, 666, 850; CXI, 53.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 652, 869, 872.---Gerhoh, CXCIII, 1026.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1227, 1232.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 134.

MATTAN, priest of Baal. St. Augustine, XXXII, 633.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 725.

MATTATHIAS, high priest, who showed zeal for the defense of religion and fought stoutly for it. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1140, 1143, 1148.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 879.

METHUSELAH, son of Enoch, who alone lived on earth for 969 years. St. Hilary, X, 537.---Juvencus, XIX, 351.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 947.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 518; XLI, 449, 454; XLIV, 398.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 510, 511; CXI, 33.

MELCHIZEDEK, king of Salem, first priest of God Most High and offerer of the true sacrifice, whose origin is secret. Returning after his victory, Abraham was blessed by him. In the type of the true sacrifice, he was the first to offer bread and wine from the fruits of the earth to God as an oblation, because priesthood and kingship truly belonged to the firstborn, before Aaron exercised the priesthood. After the Flood he founded the city of Salem, that is, Jerusalem, in which he ruled; he died at the age of six hundred. St. Cyprian, IV, 375, 376.---Philastrius, XII, 1186, 1231, 1282, 1303.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 475; XVI, 404, 438, 607.---St. Jerome, XXII, 676 ff.; XXIII, 961.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 769; XXXIV, 567; XXXV, 2325–2329; XLI, 500.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 798.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 890.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 104, 132, 239.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 536, 1062, 1063 ff.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 540; CVIII, 505; CXI, 35.---Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 100.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 127.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 188, 189, 1127.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 377, 378, 380; CLXVIII, 1313; CLXX, 583.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1094.---Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 670, 671.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 218.

MICAH, the prophet, was born in Moresheth of the tribe of Ephraim. Because he repeatedly rebuked Ahab for sinning, he died after being thrown from a great precipice under Ahab’s son Joram. He was buried in his own country beside Polyandrum, near Nain. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1234.---Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1164.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 145, 172.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 216, [Col. 0293] 490.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 610.---Haymo, CXVII, 141 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 118.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 511.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 169.

MICHAL, daughter of Saul, who was given to David as wife. She saved his life by lowering him through a window, but mocked him as he danced before the Lord. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1179.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 681.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 85, 86.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1313.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 60.

MOAB, son of Lot, whose descendants were cursed by God. St. Hilary, IX, 389.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 739; XXXVII, 1052.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 379; CXI, 36.

MOSES, son of Amram, of the tribe of Levi, leader and prophet of Israel, adopted son of the king’s daughter and friend of God, master of Pharaoh: he delivered the people of God from the Egyptians’ yoke and ruled them in the wilderness for forty years. Distinguished by many victories and miracles, he died at the age of one hundred and twenty. Tertullian, I, 382, 386, 387, 403; II, 85, 257, 305, 326, 346, 456, 600, 602, 622, 697, 763, 835, 876, 937.---St. Cyprian, IV, 481, 662, 684.---St. Zeno, XI, 376.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 124, 125, 245, 319, 329, 1132; XV, 1301, 1449, 1462, 1471, 1510; XVI, 111, 112, 161, 171, 302, 479, 1136, 1226, 1228; XVII, 39, 40, 823.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 238, 240, 241, 307, 577; XXIV, 97, 98, 697; XXVI, 259, 330, 376, 391, 420.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 96, 521, 610, 611; XXXIV, 18, 597, 599, 614, 619, 633, 656, 684, 716, 743; XXXV, 1403, 1779, 2170–2172, 2174, 2198, 2222; XXXVI, 889, 933; XXXVII, 1141, 1265, 1267, 1329, 1414, 1788, 1789, 1802, 1857; XXXVIII, 59, 63, 64, 81, 161, 198, 199, 687, 758; XXXIX, 1553, 1554, 1635, 1781, 1789, 1813, 2026, 2262; XL, 662, 663; XLI, 565, 568, 596, 599, 662; XLII, 229, 320, 321, 323, 325, 326, 330, 334, 443, 444, 450, 452, 461, 568, 811, 812; XLIII, 305.---Cassian, XLIX, 862.---St. Peter Chrysologus, in Sermons 43, 66, 69, 83, 126, 131, 147.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 250.---St. Fulgentius, LXV, 595.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 526, 643, 644.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 796–798, 872; NAAMAN, commander of the forces of the king of Syria, whom Elisha cleansed from leprosy. St. Optatus, XI, 1061, 1062.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 1222, 1627.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 797.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 141.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 377; XCIII, 454; CIV, 1237.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 231, 232.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 505.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1263.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 220, 221.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 719, 720.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 411.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1391.

NABAL, a wicked and avaricious man, whose wife Abigail pleased David. St. Ambrose, XVI, 1067.---St. Salvian, LIII, 52.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 64.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1114.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 696.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 83, 336.

NABOTH, whom Ahab, at Jezebel’s instigation, had stoned because he would not give him his vineyard. St. Ambrose, XIV, 731, 759; XV, 1800; XVI, 163, 345, 1092, 1097, 1098.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 259.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 224.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 217; CXI, 65.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 488, 489.---Haymo, CXVII, 13.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 22, 25, 26, 879; CLXIX, 1378, 1379.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1383.

NEBUCHADNEZZAR, most powerful king of Babylon, [Col. 0294] who because of pride dwelt among wild beasts for seven years. Tertullian, I, 1248, 1269; II, 611, 731.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 843.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 325, 398, 796, 816; XXXV, 2391; XXXVIII, 1381; XXXIX, 150.---St. Salvian, LIII, 110.---Anonymous, LIX, 532.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 688; LXXVI, 625, 745; LXXVII, 18.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 116, 162.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1129.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 272, 276, 301, 372, 545, 556, 604, 611; CX, 803; CXI, 65, 836, 1102.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 691; CXIV, 42.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 542.---Ekkehard, CLIV, 545.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1500, 1505, 1507; CLXVIII, 346; CLXIX, 1000, 1066, 1068, 1342, 1343 ff., 1356, 1358.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1232, 1233, 1273 ff., 1312, 1314, 1315.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1420.

NADAB, son of Aaron, perished, consumed by fire together with his brother Abihu. St. Hilary, IX, 483.---St. Salvian, LIII, 45.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 341, 342, 344.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 325.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 792.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1203.

NAHUM, the prophet, of the tribe of Simeon, was born at Elkosh, beyond Beth-harim, and died there; he lies in his own tomb. St. Augustine, XLI, 587, 588.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 145, 172.---Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1123.---Haymo, CXVII, 167 ff.

NATHAN, a prophet from the Gibeonites, who taught King David the law of God and revealed the sin in which he had transgressed with Bathsheba; he consecrated Solomon as prince by anointing him. He died an old man in his own country and was buried with honour. St. Hilary, IX, 384.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 796, 798; LXXVII, 53.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 145.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 1095.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 573 ff., 654.

NEHEMIAH, of the tribe of Judah, who, with Zerubbabel under King Darius, rebuilt the Temple of the Lord, constructed Jerusalem’s walls, restored Israel to its former condition, and renewed both religious worship and the law of the priests and Levites; he was buried in Jerusalem. St. Ambrose, XVI, 173, 174.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 147.---Venerable Bede, XCI, 883, 884, 886 ff., 921, 923.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 70.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 713.---Haymo, CXVII, 23.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 879; CLXIX, 1378, 1379.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 1145.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1485, 1488.

NAPHTALI, son of Jacob, most abundant in the richness of the land and abounding in the teaching of the law. St. Ambrose, XIV, 687; XVI, 1098.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 835.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106, 135.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 1131.

NIMROD, a mighty and vigorous hunter, was the first to seize an unprecedented tyranny over peoples, and himself undertook, in impiety against God, to build a tower. Philastrius, XII, 1224.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 406, 415.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 955.---Paulus Orosius, XXXII, 758.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 551; XLI, 491.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 103, 237.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 528, 530; CXI, 35.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 366.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1087.

NOAH, son of Lamech, tenth from Adam, second father and restorer of the world; eminent in righteousness, long-suffering in hope, wise in action, and the sole righteous man on earth. Commanded, he built the ark; warned, he entered it; nor did he shrink from the waves of the Flood. He died in his nine hundred and fiftieth year. Tertullian, I, 1307 ff.; II, 310, 600, 601.---St. Cyprian, IV, 258, 503.---Philastrius, XII, 1244, 1264, 1303.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 361, 363, 377, 382, 393, 417, 701, 1006; XV, 1610; XVI, 59, 1181.---St. Jerome, XXII, 677, 678; XXIII, 236, 948.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 111, 272; XXXVII, 1358, 1731; XXXIX, 1611, 1952, 1953, 2028, 2068; XL, 717; XLI, 477, 598; XLII, 262, 266, 267.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, in Sermons 12, 14, 69, 147, 160, 163.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 576, 602.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 535, 671; LXXVI, 976.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 102, 132, 229 ff., 235.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 527, 562.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 513; CIX, 281, 1085; CXI, 53.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 110, 111.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 162.---Haymo, CXVIII, 891.---St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 44.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 88, 98.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 177 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 341 ff., 349, 362; CLXIX, 87, 91, 286, 1266; CLXX, 150, 231, 582.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1112, 1113.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 48 ff., 653, 644; CLXXVII, 694, 704, 1089.---Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1646, 1647.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 491.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1082, 1087.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 255.---St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 618.

NAOMI, wife of Elimelech. St. Ambrose, XVI, 245.---St. [Col. 0295] Augustine, XLI, 465.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1201, 1205, 1210, 1211, 1221.

AHAZIAH, son of Ahab, who persecuted God’s prophets, especially Elijah. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 221; CXI, 65.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 70.

HOPHNI AND PHINEHAS, both sons of Eli the high priest, who perished when they were killed in battle against the Philistines because of their crimes. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 29–30.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 279.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 21, 27; CXI, 58.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 281.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 366.

ONAN, son of Judah, who took Tamar, his brother’s wife, to raise up offspring for him, but frustrated her so that she would not become a mother; for this reason he was punished by God. St. Zeno, XI, 436.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 268.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1023, 1027.

HOSEA, the prophet, of the tribe of Issachar, was born at Belemoth and buried in his own land. St. Jerome, XXIV, 22, 122; XXV, 819, 950.---St. Augustine, XLI, 584; XLII, 459.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114, 144, 169, 170.---Haymo, CXVII, 11 ff., 222.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 18.

OTHNIEL, son of Kenaz, defeated the king of Mesopotamia, delivered the people of Israel from slavery, and judged them for forty years. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1111, 1125, 1127, 1128.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 1024.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 173.

UZZIAH, king of Judah, who, taking to himself the office of priests, was punished with leprosy when he wished to burn incense. St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 114.---St. Agobard, CIV, 135, 181.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 246, 503, 512, 562.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1316.---Peter the Chanter, CCV, 134.

PHARAOH, king of Egypt, who oppressed Israel with slavery and, as he pursued the people fleeing after Moses had delivered them, perished with all his army, drowned in the waters. St. Hilary, IX, 762.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 421; XV, 1300, 1455.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 339, 619, 620, 657; XXV, 277.---St. Augustine, XXXIII, 219; XXXIV, 498, 501, 601; XXXV, 2080, 2081; XXXVII, 1750, 1771; XXXVIII, 72, 73; XLI, 521; XLIV, 911.---St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1044.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 587, 916.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 108, 288 ff.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 634, 644, 647; CVIII, 27, 28; CX, 795, 796, 798, 800, 811, 814, 820, 821; CXI, 52.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 205.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 234, 244 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 525, 565, 569, 588, 625; CLXVIII, 1394; CLIX, 61, 62, 1146.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 332.

PEREZ, son of Judah by Tamar. St. Ambrose, XV, 1597, 1601.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1023, 1024.

PENINNAH, wife of Elkanah, who bore him many children. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 27.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 248 ff.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1296.

PHINEHAS, a priest, son of Eleazar the priest, son of Aaron. In zeal for the Lord, he pierced with a weapon the shameless Zimri, who was having intercourse with a Midianite prostitute, together with the prostitute; and he earned the perpetual priestly fillets and the reward of sacrificial offerings among Israel’s generations, because, inflamed with zeal of divine love, he appeased the Lord’s wrath by striking. St. Jerome, XXIII, 512; XXVII, 205.---St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2263.---St. Prosper, LI, 305.---Anonymous, LIX, 537.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 872; LXXVI, 91.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 110, 138, 426.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 408.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 21.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 881.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1240.---Alanus of Lille, CCX, 261.

THE THREE YOUTHS, distinguished by royal descent, glorious in memory, instructed in learning, equal in faith, steadfast in devotion, incorrupt in body, sober in mind, judges of provinces and leaders of regions; mindful also of their ancestral laws, and in no way defiled by Gentile foods or things sacrificed to idols, they sustained life on legumes and vegetables. By the strength of virtue they despised death, did not worship the rite of idols, overcame the most savage king by the strength of faith, quenched the conflagration of the blazing furnace, and amid dreadful flames thick with darkness sang a hymn with voices raised openly. They lie together in Babylon, placed beneath a single cave and buried with great veneration. St. Cyprian, IV, 353, 427, 490, 667.---St. Zeno, XI, 522, 523.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 399; XXV, 511, 512.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1161.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 146.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 879; CLXIX, 1353, 1354, 1368; CLXX, 128.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 498.

RACHEL, daughter of Laban, wife of Jacob, mother of Joseph and Benjamin. St. Cyprian, IV, 689.---St. Hilary, IX, 923.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 222, 223, 262, 289, 1237.---Juvencus, [Col. 0296] XIX, 368 ff.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 237; XXV, 930.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1046; XLII, 432.---St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 799.---St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 209.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 75, 564, 764, 954; LXXVII, 449.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 105, 140, 259 ff., 264 ff.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 607, 617, 763, 903; CXI, 40, 773.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 126, 216 ff.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 84, 133, 144, 145.---St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 303, 590, 1004–1006.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 217.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 474.---St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 755, 1276, 1277.

RAHAB, the prostitute, who received as guests the scouts sent into the city of Jericho and thereby saved them; as her reward, when the city was captured, she was saved together with her household. St. Ambrose, XV, 1020, 1598, 1776; XVI, 674, 675; XVII, 698.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 243.---St. Augustine, XL, 540, 541 ff.---St. Fulgentius, LXV, 514, 515.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 619.---Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 371, 374.---Venerable Bede, XCIII, 417.---Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 61.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 887, 1315; CLXX, 76.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1024–1026.---Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1656.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1261.

REBEKAH, daughter of Bethuel and wife of Isaac, to whom she bore twin sons, namely Esau and Jacob. Tertullian, II, 598, 904.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 432, 453; XV, 1245; XVI, 1216.---Juvencus, XIX, 364 ff.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 254.---St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1673; XXXVIII, 38; XXXIX, 1757, 1758.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 770, 829.---St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 252, 253.---Blessed Alcuin, C, 549.---Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 569, 571, 573, 578, 580, 590.---Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 153.---Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 201, 202 ff.---Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 98.---Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 200.---St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 199, 200 ff.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 439–441, 443, 447; CLXVIII, 1312, 1313; CLXIX, 101, 104.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 647 ff.---Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 135, 136.---Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1107, 1109.

ROBOAM, son of Solomon, whom he succeeded. During his reign Israel was divided into two parts, resulting in the kingdom of Judah, over which Rehoboam ruled, and the kingdom of Israel, over which Jeroboam ruled. St Jerome, XXIV, 61.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 681.—Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 707.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1372.

RUBEN, Israel’s firstborn son, older than his brothers in age but lesser in number of descendants; he defiled his father’s bed and so lost the rank of the firstborn dignity. Rufinus, XXI, 314.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 106, 135, 267.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 1130.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 618; CVIII, 1145; CIX, 309; CXI, 43.

RUTH, a foreign woman from the Gentile people, a Moabite by nation, whom Boaz took as wife and from whom David was subsequently descended. St Ambrose, XV, 1601–1603.—St Augustine, XL, 435.—St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 848.—St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 660.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 112, 390, 391.—Venerable Bede, CI, 1121.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1201, 1206, 1208, 1212, 1215, 1221; CX, 465; CXI, 111.—Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 66, 89.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1057, 1100, 1315, 1316; CLXVIII, 1315; CLXX, 76.—Godefrid, abbot, CLXXIV, 1026.—Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 688; CLXXVII, 1063.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 123.

QUEEN OF SHEBA, who, stirred from the remotest regions, came to hear Solomon’s wisdom. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 815.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII [printed LXXXIIII], 113, 417.—Venerable Bede, XCIII, 446.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 464.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1175.—Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 181.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1369.

SHALMANESER, king of the Assyrians, who fought against Samaria and deported Israel, together with King Hoshea, among the Assyrians. St Jerome, XXIV, 379.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 725 and following.

SOLOMON, David’s son by Bathsheba, called the wisest of men and the consecrator of the Lord’s Temple: fortunate in empire, inferior to his father in merits, beloved by God, wise in judgment, just in decision, and peaceful in his kingdom. He asked for and obtained wisdom, so that he might know the ordering of the world, the powers of the elements, the natures of animals, and human thoughts. He also set moral conduct in order, discovered the natures of things, and revealed the mysteries of Christ and the Church. His beginnings were good, but his end evil; for, after the glory of many virtues, corrupted by love of women, he both lost the wisdom he had received and was plunged, in a lamentable fall, into the depths of idolatry. He reigned forty years, lived fifty-two years, and was buried in Bethlehem, the city of his father. St Hilary, 695, [Col. 0297] 708, 826, 947, 948, 955.—St Ambrose, XIV, 857, 892, 894, 895, 1133; XV, 1289, 1290, 1417, 1592, 1593.—St Jerome, XXII, 673 and following, 682, 683; XXIII, 243, 288, 512, 1011–1013, 1023, 1031, 1116; XXIV, 61.—St Augustine, XXXIV, 77, 78, 453, 466; XXXVI, 94, 901; XXXVII, 1135, 1667, 1668; XLI, 540, 541, 554; XLII, 285, 450, 453, 459.—St Peter Chrysologus, in sermons, 48, 163.—Cassiodorus, LXX, 113.—St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 556, 998; LXXVI, 199, 998; LXXVII, 101.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 113, 140, 161, 413 and following, 416, 417.—Venerable Bede, XCI, 737; XCIII, 441 and following.—Blessed Alcuin, 658, 669, 725; CI, 1123, 1126, 1127.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 187; CIX, 130, 132, 133 and following, 186, 269, 468, 1096, 1097; CXI, 51, 101.—Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 584, 658, 674.—Angelomus of Luxeuil, CXV, 397, 408 and following.—Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 48, 65, 67.—Hincmar, CXXV, 817.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1141, 1145, 1176, 1178; CLXVIII, 877, 878, 880–882, 1207.—Godofrid, abbot, CLXXIV, 759.—Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 115, 116, 703, 704; CLXXVII, 696, 697, 714, 715, 868 and following.—St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 86, 234.—Richard of St Victor, LXCVI [probably CXCVI], 223 and following.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1347 and following, 1369, 1370.—Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 623 and following, 630 and following, 643–645, 658, 659, 1002.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 75.

SAMSON, son of promise, born to his father Manoah, from the tribe of Dan, called a Nazirite, liberator of Israel, and strongest of all men. He killed a roaring lion and took a honeycomb from the dead animal’s mouth; he also lifted the bars of the gates upon his shoulders and set them on a mountain summit. By tying fire to foxes’ tails, he burned up the entire country of the Philistines; when bound, he broke the cords and slew a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone. He tore apart bonds woven of sinews as though they were woollen threads. Afterwards, deceived by the greed of a seductive woman, he lost the power of his strength when his hair was cut. Then, without delay, after his eyes had been gouged out, he shook the columns of the temple and perished beneath its collapse together with his enemies. He judged Israel for twenty years and was laid in his father’s tomb. Philastrius, XII, 1122.—St Ambrose, XIV, 892; XVI, 744–746, 985 and following, 993; XVII, 774, 775.—St Jerome, XXII, 678; XXIII, 241, 921.—St Augustine, XXXV, 2177, 2202; XXXVII, 1041, 1126; XXXIX, 1639; XL, 702; XLI, 35, 39, 576; XLIII, 731.—St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 264.—St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 787; LXXVI, 1133, 1134.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 111, 139, 389, 390.—Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1193, 1196 and following; CXI, 57; CXII, 804.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1041, 1043.—Godefrid, abbot, CLXXIV, 275, 276 and following.—Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 263, 680.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1285 and following.—Alan of Lille, CCX, 212, 344.

SAMUEL the prophet, son of Elkanah, of Ramah, from the tribe of Ephraim, numbered with Moses among God’s priests; consecrated to the Lord from his very cradle, diligent in ministry, a leader among the people, and a seer in the Temple. At his word the heavens obeyed, clouds gathered, and rain was poured forth. This conqueror of enemies set up the Stone of Help; this man first anointed a ruler in the kingdom. He was buried in his own town, Ramah, which is in Bethlehem. SHIMEI, of Saul’s household, who cursed David but obtained pardon for the injury he had inflicted; after David’s death he was condemned to death by Solomon. St Augustine, XLIV, 906.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 106, 108.

SENNACHERIB, king of Assyria, who, during Hezekiah’s reign, attacked all the fortified cities of Judah. St Jerome, XXIII, 558; XXIV, 379.—Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 258, 519.—Haymo, CXVI, 777, 896, 900.—Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 347; CLXIX, 1339.

SIMEON, leader of the scribes and avenger of violated chastity; having no inheritance, but dwelling in the tribe of Judah as a participant in its possession. St Ambrose, XIV, 676, 677; XV, 1610.—Rufinus, XXI, 315 and following.—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 135.

TOBIAH, son of Ananiel, from the tribe of Naphtali, of the town of Cibel, which is in the region of Galilee. He was carried captive by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, to Nineveh. Pre-eminent in the fear of God, magnificent in deeds, glorious in mercy, and devoted in care for burials: while he buried the dead and fed the poor, he was deprived of sight through blindness; and, after darkness, with his eyes opened, he attained the light of brightness. ## LII. ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED INDEX OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND WOMEN OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, TREATED IN ANY MANNER IN THE WRITINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS, WHILE PRESERVING THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS WITHIN THE ALPHABET

ANDREW, whose name means “handsome,” Simon Peter’s brother; according to John, the first [called], but according to Matthew, second after the first. BARNABAS, also called Joseph, a native of the city of Cyprus, founded by Cyrus king of the Persians; having received the apostolic office among the Gentiles with Paul, he was afterwards separated from Paul because of the disciple John, also surnamed Mark, yet nevertheless carried out the work of Gospel preaching entrusted to him. BARTHOLOMEW the apostle, whose name derives from the Syriac language, received Lycaonia as his allotted field of preaching and translated the Gospel according to Matthew into the Indians’ language for them. At last, in Albanum, a city of Greater Armenia, he was flayed alive by exceedingly cruel barbarian peoples and was thus buried in the earth. JACOB, father of Joseph, the husband of the Virgin Mary. Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 258.—St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 169.—Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 76.—Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1595.

JAMES, SON OF ALPHAEUS, first bishop of Jerusalem, surnamed the Just, son of the sister of the Mother of the Lord, and hence called the Lord’s brother; a man of light and a worker of truth, and of such great holiness that people eagerly desired to touch the fringe of his garment. While he was preaching Christ the Son of God in Jerusalem, he was thrown down from the Temple by the Jews, crushed with stones, and buried there beside the Temple. Josephus testifies that he possessed such holiness and veneration in Judaea that Jerusalem is believed to have been destroyed because of his killing. JAMES, son of Zebedee, brother of John, fourth in order, wrote to the twelve tribes that are dispersed among the nations; he preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and the western lands and shed abroad the light of preaching at the meeting-place of the world. He died, struck down by the sword of Herod the tetrarch. Buried in Marmarica. ## JOHN THE BAPTIST

John the Baptist, son of Zechariah, of the tribe of Levi, born in Jerusalem; conceived at an angel’s announcement; forerunner of Christ, herald of the Judge, prophet of the Most High, voice of the Word, friend of the Bridegroom, witness of the Lord, lamp of the Light, boundary of the prophets, beginning of baptism. At his birth, he took away the voice of his father who had foretold him and loosed the function of his father’s tongue. Before he was yet born, he prophesied Christ; he greeted him in the womb, recognized him in the dove, and pointed him out in the wilderness. His clothing was camel’s hair, his dwelling the desert, and his fare honey and locusts. When he forbade Herod to violate his brother’s marriage, he was consigned to the darkness of prison. The king’s daughter demanded his head from her mother as the prize of her dance; and he, drunk amid his cups, gave the severed head to the daughter who wickedly demanded it.

## JOHN, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST

John, apostle and evangelist, son of Zebedee, brother of James, a virgin chosen by the Lord and more beloved than the rest; he reclined also upon the Master’s breast and drank the streams of the Gospel from that sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast itself. At Christ’s command he succeeded Christ in Christ’s place, when, as the disciple received the Master’s Mother, he himself was in a manner left as another son in Christ’s stead. While preaching Christ’s Gospel in Asia, he was banished by the Emperor Domitian to the island of Patmos, where he also wrote the Apocalypse. In his life he performed very many miracles. At last, worn out by extreme old age, when he felt that the day of his departure was at hand, he is said to have ordered a grave dug for himself; there, bidding farewell to the brethren and having prayed, he entered the tomb alive, and then rested in it as though in a little bed, at Ephesus.

## JOSEPH

Joseph, son of Jacob, of the tribe of Judah and the family of David; a craftsman, betrothed to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and reputed father of Jesus Christ.

## JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA

Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and disciple of Jesus, who came to Pilate and requested Jesus’ body; wrapping it in a clean linen cloth, he placed it in a tomb which he had cut out of rock.

## JUDAS ISCARIOT

Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve apostles: an avaricious man, who betrayed his Master with a kiss and handed him over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. But afterward, moved by repentance, he threw the silver into the Temple and hanged himself with a noose.

## JUDAS, BROTHER OF JAMES

Judas, brother of James, evangelizing in Mesopotamia and the interior regions of Pontus, tamed by his teaching the fierce and untamed peoples, as though they possessed the natures of beasts, and subjected them to the Lord’s faith. He was buried at Berytus, a city of Armenia.

## LAZARUS

Lazarus, brother of Mary and Martha, friend of Christ, whom the Lord raised from the tomb after four days, when he already stank.

## LUKE

Luke of Antioch, evangelist and author of apostolic history; by nation a Syrian, by profession a physician, trained in Greek speech. Most authorities report that he was a proselyte and did not know Hebrew letters. Yet he was Paul’s disciple and his inseparable companion in travel. From his earliest youth he was most chaste and carried out the work of Gospel preaching. He died in the seventy-fourth year of his life and was buried in Bithynia.

## MARK

Mark, evangelist, disciple of Peter and his son in baptism. Some report that his Gospel was dictated by Peter at Rome. It is said that, lest he be promoted to the priesthood, he cut off his own thumb. He first occupied the see of Alexandria and first founded the churches of Egypt, flourishing in such virtues of learning and self-restraint that all Christ’s disciples followed his example. He died in Alexandria in the eighth year of Nero and was buried in tranquil repose.

## MARTHA

Martha, sister of Mary and Lazarus, who, when she received the Lord into her house and was busily occupied with much serving, was told by Jesus: “You are anxious and troubled about very many things; but one thing is necessary.”

## MATTHEW

Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who also took the surname Levi from his tribe; called by Christ from the tax collector’s office, transferred from a life of sin. He first evangelized in Judaea, afterward preached in Macedonia, and rests in the mountains of the Parthians.

## MATTHIAS

Matthias, one of the seventy disciples, was substituted for Judas Iscariot among the twelve disciples. He was chosen by lot and alone had no surname. To him is assigned the preaching of the Gospel in Judaea.

### NATHANAEL

Nathanael, a native of Cana in Galilee, a true Israelite in whom there is no guile; Philip brought him to Christ. He was one of the Lord’s disciples, and many consider him identical with Bartholomew.
