### PAUL

Paul, formerly Saul, apostle of the nations, advocate of the Jews, called by Christ from heaven: he who fell to the ground sighted rose up blind; from a persecutor he became a chosen vessel, from a wolf a sheep; among the apostles last in calling, first in preaching. Under the Law, a disciple of Gamaliel; in the Gospel, a servant of Christ. His native city was Tarsus, and his tribe Benjamin.

In the second year after the Lord’s Ascension he was baptized and was granted the dignity of the apostleship. Labouring more than all the rest, he scattered the grace of the word far more widely than they, and by his preaching fulfilled evangelical teaching. Beginning from Jerusalem, he advanced as far as Illyricum, Italy, and the Spains, and made Christ’s name known among the nations of many peoples to whom it had not previously been declared.

These miracles of his are known: caught up on high, he ascended to the third heaven; plunged down below, he spent night and day in the depths of the sea; he condemned the spirit of Python that was leading astray, commanding it to depart; he restored the life-giving spirit to a dead young man; he struck a magician with blindness; he restored to a lame man his proper gait. He neither felt nor feared the bite of a dreadful serpent, but consigned it to the fire to be burned; he also healed Publius’s father of fevers by prayer.

For Christ’s love he endured many sufferings and severe bodily torments: first, persecutions by Jews [Col. 0310], the miseries inflicted by Gentiles, labour, hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, shipwrecks, and a thousand dangers; the rage of beasts, beatings, the darkness of prison, the tortures of chains, filth, and bonds. Amid these things he was bound by the Jews, handed over to the Gentiles, stoned nearly to death, lowered in a basket through a wall, beaten with rods, subjected to punishments, and, while bound in prison, released when an earthquake occurred. Finally, Nero put him to the sword on the day on which Peter also was crucified. He was buried at Rome on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion.

### PHILIP

Philip, from the town of Bethsaida, whence Peter also came, preaches Christ to the Gauls; he leads barbarian peoples, neighbouring darkness and joined to the swelling Ocean, to the light of knowledge and the harbour of faith. Then, in Hierapolis, a city of the province of Phrygia, he died crucified and stoned; and, his body having been buried upright, he rests there with his daughters.

### PONTIUS PILATE

Pontius Pilate, governor of Judaea for the Romans, who condemned innocent Christ to death; afterward, having been sent into exile by Tiberius, he killed himself.

### SIMON PETER

Simon Peter, son of John, brother of Andrew, born in the village of Bethsaida, in the province of Galilee, which is beside Lake Gennesaret. The first interpretation of his name, Bar-Jonah, is “the direct generation of the Law.” Peter in Christ is the foundation of the Church. Cephas is the primacy and headship of Christ’s body. Simon, son of John, is the incorruptible regeneration of virginity. Although he is reckoned third according to John, according to Matthew he is chosen first; and not without reason, since he is the prince of the apostles: the first confessor of the Son of God; disciple and shepherd of the human flock; rock of the Church, keeper of the keys of the kingdom, lover of the Lord, and denier. Praised in confessing, puffed up in presuming, fallen in denying, purified in weeping, approved in confessing, crowned in suffering: his name is given from his deed, and his title is bestowed from the merit of his authority.

He preached the Gospel in Galatia, Pontus, Cappadocia, Bithynia, Asia, and Italy, and shone forth in these signs of power. With suspended step he trod the raging sea; as he passed by, his shadow [Col. 0313] gave life to the dead; he restored to the lame their former function, and returned paralysed limbs to their proper condition. Besides these things, he raised a dead widow; sentenced Ananias and Sapphira, guilty of faithlessness, to death; and dashed Simon, as he ascended heavenward by magical arts, down to the ground.

After founding the Church of Antioch, under the Emperor Claudius he went to Rome against that same Simon Magus. There he preached the Gospel for twenty-five years and held the episcopate of that city. In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion, Nero Caesar crucified him in the city of Rome head downward, as Peter himself wished, and he was buried in the Vatican.

### SIMON ZELOTES

Simon Zelotes, who was formerly called the Canaanite, fervent with zeal for the Lord, Peter’s equal in surname and like him in honour, received the primacy of Egypt and, after James the Just, held the see of Jerusalem. After one hundred and twenty years, under Trajan, he was deemed worthy to undergo the suffering of martyrdom by the cross. He lies in the Bosporus.

THOMAS, apostle of Christ, called Didymus, and, according to the Latin language, Christ’s twin and like the Savior: unbelieving when he heard, faithful when he saw. He preached the Gospel among the Parthians and Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Indians, who thundered forth in the eastern region; penetrating into the remotest parts of the nations, he carried his preaching there as far as the [Col. 0316] heading of his Passion. For he died, pierced by lances, in the Indian city of Calamina, where he was honorably buried. SIXTH SERIES.

[Col. 0317]

[PREFACE.]

In this sixth Series we deal with Religion in its more general sense: namely, insofar as it is a society between God and man, embracing their reciprocal relations and therefore God’s rights and human duties; with divine Revelation to human beings and its possibility, usefulness, and necessity; with Prophecies and Miracles, and their nature, marks or characteristics, and evidentiary force. We then set forth the various errors which both pagans and philosophers raised against religion. Finally, since the Holy Fathers—especially those who lived in the earliest centuries—attacked these errors in writings both polemical and apologetic, we append various indices of these writings.

[Col. 0317]

LIII. INDEX OF RELIGION CONSIDERED IN GENERAL, IN WHICH THE VIEWS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING IT ARE SET OUT IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER.

NOTICE.

The doctrine of religion considered generally rests upon these words of the Apostle: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; even his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20); and upon these words of the Psalmist: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). That is: God, who is invisible by nature, permits himself in some manner to be seen by displaying his power through some likeness. For when we behold ourselves and created things, we are raised to admiration of the Creator, acquire knowledge of the divinity, and through ourselves and what has been made marvel at the power of the Maker. In created things there lies an open indication of knowledge of God. By this God has wonderfully impressed his image upon our inner person; and just as he furnished human beings in himself an example of good works, so he placed in them a testimony to the acknowledgment of himself, so that, when his image is considered either in us or in creatures, knowledge may be gained of him whose image it is.

It must therefore be confessed naturally and necessarily that not only in ourselves and in all things, but in each individual thing, a certain image and trace of Deity shines forth; that in the magnitude of the universe, as in a human face, divine power is observed; in the beauty of things, wisdom; and in their usefulness, goodness. All things consist in these invisible things of God—namely power, wisdom, and goodness—and are governed through them. For power creates, wisdom governs, and kindness preserves. Yet, just as these are ineffably one in God, so they cannot be separated in operation: power creates wisely through kindness, wisdom governs kindly through power, and kindness preserves powerfully through wisdom.

Hence, in a wonderful order, God so instills understanding of himself that he withdraws it, and so withdraws it that he instills it. Therefore, in all created things the Creator shines forth in many ways: always known, always understood, always heard, because he is never hidden and never absent. Since, then, he is wonderful in majesty, venerable in wisdom, and lovable in goodness, a threefold cord arises between the Creator and the rational creature, which is not easily broken: that he may be feared, honored, and loved. We are born on this condition: that we render just and due service to God who begot us, know him, and follow him. By this bond of piety we are both bound and rebound. Hence Religion itself took its name from *religare*, “to bind again,” and is so called because through it we bind ourselves again to God and bind our souls together, as it were into one bundle, for divine worship by the bond of service; or because it entails care and ceremonies directed to a certain higher nature, which they call divine.

This is clearly inferred from the fact that knowledge of God has always existed on earth. For what profit is there in knowing God if it is not in one’s heart to love and fear him? As a master demands service from his slave, and as one human being compels another to submit and obey, so by the law of humanity and of natural power it belongs to human beings to be joined with God in fear and love, because he is Lord and Father. These two are one reality and force under two names, the one situated in disposition and the other in action. For God alone is the source of religion; he alone must be dedicated in the mind and consecrated in the heart, accompanied, on our part, by some form of outward submission.

In conclusion, religion considered generally is the knowledge and worship of the true God, leaving aside the question in what manner and rite he should be worshiped, provided that he is worshiped—or believed to be worshiped—even if the true God is worshiped and honored by a false and unworthy worship. This also admits that it does not harm each person to worship what he has judged to be the true God, since religion taken generally is, beyond other things, voluntary, and no necessity can be imposed upon anyone to worship what he does not wish.

This Index touches upon these principles and conclusions of natural law, including the point that, in addition to reason, temples should be built, sacrifices offered, and thanks given to God for those things which he himself has bestowed; that beyond worship in fragrance, blood, prayer, and invocations, and beyond the testimony of the soul looking toward heaven and tending toward God, there ought also to be a perfected order of justice in human duties; that one should strive for piety and, in [Col. 0319] observances of good works, rise beyond them through purity of mind; so that there may be wisdom, a spirit of gratitude, a nature desirous of fellowship and human society, and finally in us a disposition to will what God commands, to refuse what he forbids, and to live in his sight in relation to himself, to our neighbor, and to ourselves.

[Col. 0319]

LIV. INDEX OF DIVINE REVELATION, ARRANGED ANALOGICALLY AND PRESENTING THE VARIOUS VIEWS OF THE FATHERS CONCERNING IT.

NOTICE.

In this Index, so that the matters sought may more readily come before the reader, we shall classify them under different questions. Thus we shall ask: (1) What is Revelation? (2) Has it existed? (3) Is it useful, indeed necessary? (4) Is it consistent with truth? (5) Is it contrary to human reason? (6) Is it threefold, namely Primitive or Natural, Mosaic, and Evangelical? Moreover, under each heading we shall report the various views of the Holy Fathers in chronological order; or rather, for the sake of brevity, indicate them summarily at the beginning of each article.

If an Arabic numeral should sometimes fail to refer to the columns of our edition, the kind reader should consult the boldface numerals inserted in the text. What I say of this Index may perhaps need to be said of certain others, though very rarely.

[INDEX OF DIVINE REVELATION.]

[Col. 0319]

I.—What is Revelation?

Revelation is the vision of things themselves, and a kind of admonition from without, by which, through the Holy Spirit, something is suddenly disclosed at any time. Victorinus the African, VIII, 1151, 1248.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 1145.---St. Augustine, XLII, 171, 172.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 892, 1310.---Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 202.

II.—Has Revelation existed?

The Lord himself has always come down to converse with human beings; from the beginning he conversed with the patriarchs and prophets, [Col. 0320] already teaching what he would do at the end.---We have no need of divination, since the divinity itself has disclosed truth to us.---All things are full of divine testimonies.---We profess what Truth itself has deigned to reveal through divinely inspired Scriptures so that it may be believed.---The Gospels and the Epistles of the Apostles, the books of Moses and of the prophets, are set before us all as certain dishes filled with delights. Tertullian, II, 61, 174, 317, 328.---Lactantius, VI, 118, 127, 763.---Emperor Constantine, VIII, 552.---Victorinus the African, VIII, 1152, 1252, 1263.---Pope Liberius, VIII, 1397.---St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 615; X, 96, 237, 295, 448, 506, 733.---St. Ambrose, [Col. 0321] XIV, 125, 1180; XVI, 718, 743; XVII, 523.---St. Phoebadius, XX, 20.---St. Jerome, XXIII, 135, 136; XXIV, 119, 729, 732, 906; XXV, 521.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 125; XXXVI, 541; XXXVIII, 602.---Cassian, L, 450.---St. Leo the Great, LV, 52.---Deacon Paschasius, LXII, 9.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 65.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 7; LXXVI, 712; LXXVII, 712.---Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 788.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 24.---Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 524.---St. Odilo of Cluny, CXLII, 1000.---Durandus of Troarn, CXLIX, 1401.---St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 11.---St. Bruno of Segni, CLIV, 1034.---St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 938.---Peter Lombard, CXCII, 224.

III.—Is Revelation useful, indeed necessary?

A human being cannot attain knowledge of truth by himself unless taught by God.---Human beings neither knew what truth itself was, nor how, where, or with what disposition it was to be sought.---We can in no way know the rationale of heavenly things.---Human beings could not know the mystery of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus except through Revelation.---While philosophers rage in their eagerness to contradict, while they even defend their own falsehoods, they overthrow the truths of others also; not only has truth escaped them, but they themselves have especially lost it through their own fault.---The Law is spiritual, and Revelation is needed for it to be understood.---In Sacred Scripture God teaches whatever it is fitting for us to know.---Revelation is useful for consolation and sanctification.---What is remarkable in the Gospel is that it supplies words for every condition of human life, so that each person may attain eternal salvation in his own state.---Sacred Scripture is the way to heaven, a paradise of delight.---The Law was a day which, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, taught worship of the one God, showing what we owe God and what our neighbor; what punishment is reserved for sins and what reward for virtues.---The strength of the Church is the truth of Revelation. Tertullian, II, 50.---Lactantius, VI, 267, 350, 432, 734, and throughout Book VII.---Victorinus the African, VIII, 1261.---St. Hilary, IX, 987.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1693; XVI, 617; XVII, 765.---St. Jerome, XXII, 1543; XXIV, 16, 27, 156–158, 160, 434, 511, 543, 607, 1120.---St. Augustine, XXXIV, 121, 128, 554; XXXVI, 357; XXXVII, 581, 1481; XL, 951; XLII, 821.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 66, 331, 490, 517.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 747, 1267 ff., 1378; LXXVII, 712.---Blessed Alcuin, XCIX, 384, 460.---Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 675; CX, 311.---Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 366.---John Scotus, CXXII, 296.---Othlo, CXLVI, 174.---Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 365.---St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 362.---St. Bruno of Segni, CLIV, 1129, 1257; CLV, 62.---Venerable Abbot Guibert, CLVI, 125.---St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 264.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 76, 248.---Hildebert of Tours, CLXXI, 564, 1101.---Hervaeus the monk, CLXXX, 1606.---St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 938.---Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 65.---Absalon, abbot, CCXI, 22.

IV.—Is Revelation consistent with truth?

Nothing is more delightful than the revelation of truth, and nothing is to be preferred to the word of God.---Believe him who does not deceive; nor is he a deceiver who gave the Law.---The rule of truth is expressed through the oracles of divine speech.---We must believe that the oracles of the supreme God are true; for divine utterance is shown by the faithful of the holy Church to be right and true.---It is impious to suppose that the Scriptures lie, for the words of the Scriptures are divinely inspired.---Sacred Scripture is the venerable style of the Holy Spirit.---The truth of Sacred Scripture is supreme.---That Law which was given through Moses is beyond reproach, because it consists in perfect truth.---All books of the divine Scriptures shine with heavenly light and with the power of the Holy Spirit.---The Evangelists never depart from truth and never speak falsehood; whatever they say is true, just, pure, and exceedingly credible.---Sacred Scripture is God’s voice to human beings and therefore cannot lead into error. Tertullian, I, 378, 659; II, 405.---St. Cyprian, IV, 561.---St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 96, 144, 416.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 145; XV, 1501.---Rufinus, XXI, 677, 690.---St. Philastrius, XXII, 1267.---St. Jerome, XXV, 323, 545, 808; XXVI, 481; XXIX, 134.---St. Augustine, XXXII, 839; XXXVI, 1159; XXXVII, 747; XXXVIII, 692.---St. Prosper, LI, 473.---Cassiodorus, LXX, 66, 538.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 8, 13.---St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, CXVI, 136.---Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1130.---Abbot Smaragdus, CII, 28.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 238, 409; CXI, 26, 889; CXII, 1072.---Hincmar of Reims, [Col. 0322] CXXVI, 119.---St. Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 279.---St. Bruno of Segni, CLIV, 83, 97.---Abbot Rupert, CLXIX, 8.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 21.

V.—Does Revelation oppose reason?

Our faith is founded upon word and reason; for Revelation, far from destroying natural reason, on the contrary perfects it, as a kind of aid sent by God.---Human reason and divine Revelation are like two lights kindled from the same sun, illuminating the same road. They are two full sisters, who love to join hands with each other and willingly and kindly offer human beings assistance, so as to lead them to one and the same end.---Reason and divine Revelation derive their origin from the same source, which is God, and tend toward the same one end.---There are two modes, two paths, two kinds of manifestation through which the hidden God has, from the beginning, revealed himself to the human mind: namely, human reason and divine revelation.---Reason discovers God within itself and from things external; Revelation, however, discloses to us what was unknown concerning God and strengthens faith in those divine attributes already known. St. Hilary, X, 76, 95, 143.---Faustinus, XIII, 39.---St. Ambrose, XV, 1535; XVI, 665, 780; XVII, 964.---Abbot Gezo, CXXXVII, 376, 380.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 441, 442.

VI.—Revelation is threefold, namely:

I.—Primitive or natural.—God gave Adam definite commands, and every age from the foundation of the world was instructed by God’s teachings.---All nations and all regions of the world first received the natural law.---Natural law was given to all, and before the written law it remained in the hearts of the godly.---God did not cease to distribute bread—that is, the word—to his faithful, in the earliest ages as well as in the latest.---To every rational spirit the Father of lights gave a certain twofold power: one is reason, the other affection; reason, by which we discern, and affection, by which we love; reason for truth, affection for virtue. These are the two sisters betrothed by the Lord. Tertullian, II, 599.---Lactantius, VI, 322.---St. Hilary, IX, 631.---St. Philastrius, XII, 1270.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 1242.---St. Gaudentius, XX, 891.---Rufinus, XXI, 781.---St. Jerome, XXIV, 283; XXV, 1576.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 500.---Peter Chrysologus, LII, 111.---St. Leo the Great, LIV, 202, 204.---Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 32–36.---Abbot Wolbero, CXCV, 38.---Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 3.

II.—Mosaic.—God is believed to have given the Law through Moses to one people.---The law of Moses was written by God.---Moses may be called the law of God’s mouth, through whom the Lord spoke and gave the Law.---Through Moses the Lord had summoned heaven and earth as witnesses while giving his law to the people.---Tertullian, II, 599.---St. Hilary, IX, 928.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 433, 703, 967; XV, 1328; XVI, 1254; XVII, 1008.---Rufinus, XXI, 373.---St. Jerome, XXII, 916; XXIV, 10, 70, 316, 318, 362; XXV, 916.---St. Augustine, XXXV, 615; XXXVI, 1574; XXXVII, 198; XL, 262.---St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 394.---St. Prudentius, LX, 99.---Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 790.---Venerable Bede, XCII, 658.---Rabanus Maurus, CX, 627; CXII, 443.---Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 366.---St. Bruno of Segni, CLV, 119.

III.—Evangelical.—The rule of faith was instituted or revealed by Christ.---The Master came in signs: the heavenly Teacher and the Founder of perfect truth.---The evangelical precepts are nothing other than divine teachings, and evangelical doctrine, preached through the Apostles, was given from heaven.---The law is threefold: human or natural law, Mosaic law, and evangelical law, which teaches us to pardon one who sins, pray for sinners, and love enemies.---Tertullian, II, 26 ff.; III, 960.---St. Cyprian, IV, 519.---Emperor Constantine, VIII, 508, 936.---St. Ambrose, XIV, 1408; XV, 1320, 1408.---Rufinus, XXI, 705.---St. Jerome, XXII, 124, 168, 205, 401, 714; XXIV, 130, 247, 319, 322, 526; XXV, 13, 275.---St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1130; XLII, 116.---St. Prosper, LI, 475, 479.---St. Leo the Great, LIV, 422.---St. Prudentius, LIX, 617, 865.---St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 649, 1004.---St. Gregory the Great, LIV, 422.---St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 883, 1580.---Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 791.---Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 986, 1009; CX, 238; CXI, 22.---Hincmar of Reims, CXXVI, 128.---Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 191.---Flodoard of Reims, CXXXV, 500.---St. Anselm, CXLIX, 593.---Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 243, 561.---Hervaeus, CLXXX, 1690.---Reinerus, CCIV, 49.---Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 5.---St. Martin of León, CCIX, 162.

[Col. 0323]

LV. INDEX OF PROPHECIES, ANALOGICALLY ARRANGED, PRESENTING THE VARIOUS VIEWS OF THE FATHERS CONCERNING THE CONCEPT OF PROPHECY, ITS USEFULNESS, ITS DIVINITY OR INSPIRATION, ETC.

NOTICE.

This Index treats: (1) the concept of prophecy and its usefulness; (2) the divinity or inspiration of prophecies; (3) the characteristics or forms of prophecies; (4) the prophets and their life; (5) the principal objects of prophecies: first, the Blessed Virgin Mary; second, Christ; third, the Church.

[INDEX OF PROPHECIES.]

[Col. 0323]

I.—On the concept of prophecy, its usefulness, or excellence.

The prophets are so called from their office of speaking beforehand: Tertullian, I, 378.---Prophecy is instituted either for the knowledge of its hearers or for the innocence of their will: St. Hilary, IX, 395. How the prophetic books are mountains, 655.---Prophecy is the announcement of the future: St. Ambrose, XIV, 676. God’s truth must be gathered from the oracles of the prophets, 961. Prophecy is the first proof that our faith is rational, XVII, 157.---The books of prophets and apostles are free from every error: St. Jerome, XXII, 937. Every prophecy is called a vision, XXV, 928.---A prophet of God is nothing other than a herald of God’s words to human beings who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 601. The prophets were called seers because they saw future things not with the body but with the spirit, XXXIII, 620. Three kinds of prophets, XLII, 348. Prophecy is a lamp kindled to show the way, XXXVII, 1854. Prophecy serves every kind of faith, hope, and charity, XXXIV, 35. Why everything pertaining to the knowledge of God or upright morals was handed down to God’s people not through contests of argument, but through prophetic voices, XLI, 602. Prophetic speech is more effective for strengthening faith, XXXVIII, 256. The prophets are the foundations of the heavenly city, XXXVII, 1101; the foundations of the world, XXXVI, 150; the foundations and gates of the Church, XXXVII, 1103; the stones of Zion, 1303; lamps, XXXV, 1583; mountains, XXXVI, 1024; XXXVII, 1650; clouds, XXXVI, 136.---Prophecy was a lamp for those walking in darkness: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 381. The authority of prophecy is not human but divine, ibid., 371.---On prophecy: Junilius, LXVIII, 17.---The prophets are called merchants: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 69; likewise clouds, ibid., 407; and bases of the Church, ibid., 458; mountains, ibid., 668. The Apostles rest upon the prophets, who illumine them, ibid., 458. Why it is called prophecy, ibid., 786. The order of prophecy, ibid., 788. Why prophets are sometimes called teachers in Sacred Scripture, LXXVII, 30, 472. The office of prophets is to reveal hidden things and foretell the future, LXXIX, 290.---Two kinds of them: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 116. There are many kinds of prophesying, CXI, 985. What prophecy is, CIX, 611; CXVI, 195.---Why prophets were called seers: St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 330.---The prophets’ office: Lanfranc, CL, 199.---Very many kinds of prophecy: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 639. It is called a vision, CLIII, 434. The prophets are called the lips of God, CLII, 1114.---The prophets are called such because they were deemed worthy to foreknow the incarnation of the Son of God: Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 369. Prophets called seers, CLXIX, 1228. There are three times of prophecy, ibid., 831.---There are three kinds of prophecy: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 356.---The prophets are clouds: Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 16.---Why prophecy is the first gift in the enumeration of graces: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1500. Who are called prophets, ibid., 336.---Definition of prophecy: Alan of Lille, CCX, 113; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 830.

II.—On the divinity or inspiration of prophecies.

The prophets were flooded with the divine Spirit: Tertullian, I, 378. Christ always spoke in the prophets, II, 328. He is the seal of all the prophets, ibid., 632.---The sayings of the prophets are God’s words: St. Hilary, X, 412. The author of prophetic speech is the divine Spirit, IX, 792.---The Lord spoke in the prophets, and therefore they could not err: St. Ambrose, XV, 1809. They did not always prophesy, but did so [Col. 0324] when the grace of the prophetic Spirit was poured into them, ibid., 1366. They prophesied in an ecstasy of mind, filled with God’s Spirit, XIV, 1059; and how this occurred, ibid., 484. The prophets received the Spirit and saw Christ, XVI, 815.---God spoke in the minds of the prophets: St. Jerome, XXIV, 20. God spoke in the prophets and in the Gospels, XXV, 1222. God’s utterance came to them inwardly, ibid., 1289. Whence the obscurity of the prophets arises, ibid., 1244. The oracles of the prophets are from God, not from human beings, XLI, 602. The prophets were filled with the Holy Spirit, XLII, 644. Prophets are instructed either by God’s wisdom or by angels, XLI, 319. When the prophet speaks in his own person, the Lord himself speaks through him, XXXVI, 662. In them Christ sometimes speaks in the person of the head, sometimes in the person of the body, XXXVII, 1784. Why many books of prophets are not received as canonical, XLI, 598.---Prophets are sometimes inspired through angels: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 450. Some prophets, speaking from their own spirit, are corrected by the Holy Spirit and rebuke themselves, LXXVI, 793. The difference between true and false prophets, ibid., 794. It should be understood that those who possess the spirit of prophecy, by sometimes speaking openly about themselves and at other times uttering words about themselves as though concerning others, show that not the prophet but the Holy Spirit speaks through the prophet, ibid., 799. The prophets speak in God’s person, ibid., 873. A true prophet speaks God’s words, not his own, ibid., 891. The spirit of prophecy is not always present to prophets, LXXV, 597, 807; LXXVI, 792.---The spirit of prophecy is not always at hand for the minds of prophets: Alcuin, CI, 465.---The prophets, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, were made ready and prompt in writing: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1072.

III.—On the characteristics or forms of prophecies.

Prophets sometimes announce future events as though already past: Tertullian, II, 326. They wrote many things figuratively, through allegories, riddles, and parables, ibid. Whether they preached everything through images, id., 821. Not all of them always employ an allegorical form, id., 822.---They spoke of certain future things in the past tense: St. Hilary, IX, 665. Prophecy records events still to be done as things done, id., 403, 686. Although prophetic speech uses the ordinary usage of human language, it nevertheless does not contain the same meaning that lies open to common understanding, id., 645. Future things were present to the prophets, XIV, 1000; XV, 1318, 1370. Things to come are revealed to them by the Spirit as though present, XIV, 725; XVI, 551.---The prophets foretell future things and reveal the Scriptures: St. Ambrose, XVII, 249, 254.---They understood what they said and did not speak in ecstasy: St. Jerome, XXIV, 19. In the prophets everything is full of riddles, id., 629. The prophets understood what they said concerning Christ, though not as the apostles did, id., 1274. In the Minor Prophets there is admirable brevity and greatness of meaning, XXVI, 602. The obscurity of prophecy and the difficulty of explaining it, XXV, 946. The spirit of prophecy foretells future things even through evil persons, XXXV, 1757. The gift of prophecy is granted even to the wicked, XXXVII, 1343. It can be given to one rejected, envious, and ungrateful, XL, 138. What prophecy is more certain, id., 129, 130. How true prophets were distinguished from false ones, XLI, 601, 602. How prophets and seers foretold future things, XXXIV, 1059. Various ways in which the spirit of prophecy affects prophets, XL, 129, 130. Prophets sometimes predict evils as though wishing for them, XXXVI, 328. By the figure of an imprecation prophets customarily foretell future things, just as they often sang of things to come in the figure of the past tense, XXXIV, 1265. Why they generally pronounce future things thus [Col. 0325], as though they were past, XXXVI, 75, 485. It is affirmed that the prophets also foretold Christ, XLII, 254. Filled with Christ, they proclaimed Christ, XXXVII, 1845. The prophets foretold Christ as God and man, XXXIII, 522. Prophetic books, when Christ is not understood, are insipid and foolish, XXXV, 1459. Prophecy concerning Christ was not lacking in any former age, ibid. All prophecy concerning Christ extended to all nations, id., 1462, 1463. At one time their oracles concern the heavenly Jerusalem, at another the earthly Jerusalem, and at another both, XLI, 525.---The prophets spoke of future things as past: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 368.---The saints of the Old Testament promised Christ by prophecy, both in deeds and in words: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524. Prophets say many things with the intention of prediction, not with the wish to curse, LXXVI, 347. In how many ways prophets are touched by the spirit of prophecy, id., 788. Prophets join the word they utter outwardly to the word they hear inwardly, id., 796. Why prophets sometimes speak of themselves as though of others, id., 799. Prophets see many things at once which they are compelled to recount successively, id., 833, 856. Prophecy declares not only future things, but also past things, LXXV, 671.---What the four Major Prophets treat: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 112, 113.---Prophets often put the past for the future: St. Bruno, bishop, CXLII, 183. Prophets speak of future things as though of present and future things, CLII, 639.---All the sayings of the prophets are testimonies concerning Christ: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1179. The sayings of the prophets were obscure before Christ, id., 712.

## IV.—On the Prophets and Their Life

The prophets were men worthy of righteousness and innocence: Tertullian, I, 378. They always suffered in the world for divine religion, II, 636.---They were neither mad nor deceitful: Lactantius, VI, 128.---The life of the prophets accords with the Gospel: St. Ambrose, XV, 1598. How the faith of the prophets may be demonstrated, XLII, 285, 290. By what criterion it is to be judged whether prophets lived well or badly, id., 280. It is wrongly denied that there were prophets before Christ, id., 643, 648. From what point the era of the prophets takes its beginning, XLI, 523. The prophets flourished especially when the Roman kingdom began and the Assyrian failed; why this was so, id., 584. The people of Israel had prophets down to the time of Darius, id., 583, 584. It did not have them after the restoration of the Temple, id., 606. The prophets are older than the pagan philosophers, id., 596, 597; later than the theological poets, id., 597. Prophets were not thieves and robbers, XXXV, 1720. Which prophets are to be regarded as robbers and thieves, XLII, 322. There were many prophets, but the writings of only a few are preserved, XLI, 583. Why prophets are called Major and Minor, ibid. Certain prophets are called Minor because of the brevity of their books, XXXIV, 927. All prophets are below John, XXXVIII, 1302.---Not all prophets attain the merit of holiness: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 399. The prophets were stars producing rain, id., 405. The prophets apprehended divine knowledge more fully than Moses, id., 980.

## V.—On the Principal Subjects of Prophecies

### 1. On Mary, the Virgin Mother of Christ

The rod is from the root; Mary is from David: Tertullian, II, 788.---Beautiful things were prophesied concerning Mary under the figure of the Church: St. Ambrose, XVI, 326. By “the woman” in this passage we may understand blessed Mary, XVII, 876. By the eastern gate the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary is prefigured, id., 948.---That which is shut and sealed bears the likeness of the Mother of the Lord, mother and virgin: Jerome, XXIII, 254. Let Isaiah speak the mystery of our hope and faith: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son,” etc., id., 254. Some aptly understand by the shut gate, through which the Lord God of Israel alone enters, and by the prince for whom the gate is shut, the Virgin Mary, who remained a virgin both before and after childbirth, XXV, 430.---On Christ born of a Virgin: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 819.---In this rod blessed Virgin Mary was undoubtedly foretold: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 204.---Isaiah’s prophecy that a virgin would bear a son, whose name is Emmanuel, was fulfilled in Mary: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 235.---Mary was a rod—bright, slender, and virgin—who, like a flower, brought forth Christ in the integrity of her body, id., 310.---She is also called manna in the same sense, because she was splendid, sweet, and virgin; like food coming down from heaven, sweeter than honey, she flowed forth to all the peoples of the Churches, id., 330.---There can be no doubt that the rod of Jesse’s root, namely blessed Mary, brought forth the shoot of her nature—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—from the material of her flesh: Vigilius of Tapsus, LXII, 113.---The enclosed garden may be understood as Mary, Mother of the Lord: St. Justus of Urgell, LXVII, 978.---Isaiah’s oracle concerning a virgin who would bear a child was fulfilled in Mary: Bede, XCIV, 32. Some understand the words, “I shall place enmities,” etc., of the Virgin in whom God was born, id., XCI, 215.---From several prophetic oracles it is proved that supreme virginity ought to be joined with the glory of motherhood: St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 64.---Some have understood the words, “I shall place enmities between you and the woman,” of the Virgin of whom the Lord was born: Wicbodus, XCVI, 1164; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 496.---The woman clothed with the sun is blessed Virgin Mary: Alcuin, C, 1152.---Some aptly understand the shut gate, through which the Lord God of Israel alone enters, and the prince for whom the gate is shut, as the Virgin Mary: Rabanus Maurus, CX, 1003.---Psalm Thirty-Fourth is sung for the feast of blessed Virgin Mary; those matters which may be referred especially to Mary: Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 911.---That, under the occasion of the mercy by which he was delivering the besieged people, he might announce that his Son would be born of a Virgin: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 758.---When it is said, “The Lord himself will give you a sign,” it must be something new and marvelous. But if a young woman, as the Jews wish, and not a virgin, will bear a child, what kind of sign can it be called? id., 761. Therefore, O house of David, let that child who is born of a virgin now be called Emmanuel by you, id., 762.---The rod came forth from the root of Jesse, because the Virgin Mary sprang from the lineage of David: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 779.---According to the oracle of that most holy prophet, a certain virgin was to conceive and bear a son; and this virgin was good Mary: Abbot Goffridus, CLVII, 244. This gate of the Temple, and Temple of the Lord, is Mary, the most blessed and incomparable Virgin, from whose womb came to us the image of God the Father, ibid., 248.---That most holy land, namely the Virgin Mary, gave its fruit, whom, at the angel’s announcement, she conceived by faith and love, ibid., 249.---The honorable and praiseworthy woman, the Virgin Mary worthy of God, is called the house of the Lord, in which the eastern gate is said always to remain shut, ibid., 250.---It is certain that many centuries before Mary’s birth or conception Isaiah, inspired by the Holy Spirit, said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” etc.: St. Anselm, CLIX, 304.---That rod which produced such a flower from itself was, without any dissent, the Virgin Mary, ibid.---There are many daughters of kings, but one queen, by whom we understand blessed Virgin Mary: St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 857.---“Hear, daughter, and see,” etc. Although this may suitably be understood of the whole catholic and universal Church, I shall nevertheless expound it particularly of blessed Virgin Mary, id., 858.---Not inappropriately may the Virgin Mary be called the city of God, id., CLXV, 1021.---The Virgin Mary is rightly called daughter of Jerusalem, ibid. It signified that this glorious virgin, who according to Isaiah was the rod from the root of Jesse, bore the flower, that is, Christ, id., 1022.---The Virgin Mary is prefigured by the garden in which were diverse flowers of virtues, ibid. “A woman shall encompass a man”: that is, the Virgin Mary shall carry in her womb Christ, whom the whole world cannot contain, ibid.---“I saw the gate in the house of the Lord shut,” which the Lord entered and left, and left shut, because she was a virgin before and after childbirth, ibid.---By prophetic utterances the house of David was assured that God had promised and sworn to David that Christ would be born of his seed, as he says there among other things: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc.: Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 539.---“You are an enclosed garden, O Mother of God,” id., 896.---Behold prophecy and figure. Jesse was David’s father; Jesse’s root is the Jewish family. The rod is Mary; the flower, her Son: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 392.---Likewise Aaron’s rod, which produced nuts without seed, signifies Mary, who gave birth to Christ without seed, id., 393.---Concerning this gate of the Virgin the Lord said to Ezekiel: “This gate which you see shall be shut and shall not be opened,” ibid.---Mary is called beloved in the Song of Songs because she bore the Father’s secrets: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 501. “Our vineyard has blossomed,” that is, Mary bore Christ, in the Song of Songs: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 503.---Praise of the Son concerning the Mother, id., 505.---The words of the Virgin follow, desiring Christ to come into her: Song of Songs, id., 508.---There follows the praise of the Church converted from the Jews, marveling at the Virgin’s glory, id., 515.---The Virgin’s promise: Song of Songs, id., 516.---Christ speaks to the faithful concerning his Virgin Mother: Song of Songs, ibid.---Ezekiel also saw the ever-shut gate through which the King of kings alone passed and which he left shut (Ezek. XLIV).---Holy Mary is the gate of heaven, who was a virgin before childbirth and in childbirth, and remained a virgin after childbirth: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 905.---The Virgin’s conception and childbirth are rightly called a sign, for she became a mother in such a manner as not to lose the seal of virginity: Herveus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 99. “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse”: the rod is Mary; Mary’s flower is Christ, id., 140.---Isaiah sets forth the greater mystery of this great miracle, saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1): St. Bernard, abbot, CLXXXIII, 63. In this testimony of Isaiah, however, understand the flower as the Son and the rod as the Mother, id., 64.---The prophetic saying also seems quite aptly to correspond to Gideon’s deed, where it is read: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece,” ibid.---Let us also hear Jeremiah foretelling something new to the old: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). Who is this woman? And who is this man? ibid.---But see whether Isaiah does not also most clearly explain this new thing of Jeremiah, he who above expounded Aaron’s new flowers: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” id., 66.---On the entire and perfect beauty of blessed Virgin Mary: “You are wholly beautiful,” etc. (Song IV): Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 482.---The holy and perpetual gate is also the virgin, as is found said in the same Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened” (Ezek. XLIV, 2): Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 186.---Accordingly, although the song of love—that is, Solomon’s epithalamium—is referred specially and spiritually to the Church, it is referred most especially and most spiritually to the glorious Virgin: Alan of Lille, CCX, 53.

### 2. On Christ Our Lord

On Christ’s birth from a Virgin, Isaiah the prophet: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14): St. Jerome, XXIV, 102; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 819; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 761; Rupert, abbot of Tuit, CLXVII, 1304; Herveus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 99.

On Christ’s birth from a woman, Jeremiah the prophet: “A woman,” he says, “shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22): St. Jerome, XXIV, 880; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1039.

On Christ laid in a manger, Isaiah the prophet: “The ox,” he says, “has known its owner, and the ass the manger of its Lord” (Isa. I, 3): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 820.---And Habakkuk: “In the midst of two animals you shall be made known” (Hab. III, 2, according to the Septuagint): St. Jerome, XXV, 1309; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 820.

On Christ adored by the Magi, David said: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. LXXI, 10): Rufinus, XXI, 939; St. Jerome, XXVI, 1029; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 820; Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 865; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 663.---Likewise Isaiah: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold, incense, and precious stone,” etc. (Isa. LX, 6): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 820.

On the flight into Egypt, Hosea the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hos. XI, 1): Rufinus, XXI, 1016; St. Jerome, XXV, 915; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 821; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 602; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 79; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 170 ff.; and Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt; and Egypt’s idols shall be moved at his presence,” etc. (Isa. XIX, 1): St. Jerome, XXIV, 181, 250; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 807.

On Christ’s miracles, Isaiah the prophet: “Behold,” he says, “our God shall repay judgment; he himself shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf shall hear,” etc. (Isa. XXXV, 4): St. Jerome, XXIV [printed “XVIV”], 376; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 822; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 894.

On Christ walking upon the sea, David the prophet: “Your way is in the sea and your paths in many waters” (Ps. LXXVI, 20): St. Augustine, XXXVI, 981; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 823; Cassiodorus, LXX, 553; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 994; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 720.---Habakkuk also says: “Scattering the waters of his course, the deep gave its voice” (Hab. III, 10): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 823.

On Jesus being borne upon an ass, Zechariah the prophet: “Say,” he says, “to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving; he himself is meek, sitting upon a yoked ass and a young colt” (Zech. IX, 9): St. Jerome, XXV, 1483; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 823; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 250; Rupert, abbot, CLXVIII, 769.

On the insults directed against Jesus, the crown of thorns, his cross, and wounds. Through Isaiah the prophet: “I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them,” etc. (Isa. L, 6): St. Jerome, XXIV, 477, 478; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 825; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 973; Herveus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 471.---And Jeremiah says: “He shall give his cheek to one striking him; he shall be filled with reproaches” (Lam. III, 30): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 825.---David himself says: “I was turned in my affliction while the thorn is fastened” (Ps. XXXI, 4), ibid.---“They pierced my hands and feet; they numbered all my bones” (Ps. XXI, 17): Rufinus, XXI, 723; St. Augustine, XXXI, 175; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 825; Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 353; [Col. 0328] Cassiodorus, LXX, 159; Bede the Venerable, CXIII, 595; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 266; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 722; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 768; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 234; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 1012.---Isaiah the prophet: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7): St. Jerome, XXIV, 508, 509; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 825; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 990; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1338; Herveus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 493, 494.---Jeremiah says: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. XI, 19): St. Jerome, XXIV, 756; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 825.

That Christ was crucified between thieves. “He was counted among the wicked, he who committed no sin; by whose bruise we have all been healed” (Isa. LIII, 12): St. Jerome, XXIV, 512; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 826; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 994; Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1339; Herveus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 496.

That his garments were divided and they cast lots for his tunic. Through David the prophet: “They divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. XXI, 19): Rufinus, XXI, 723; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 176; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 826; Cassiodorus, LXX, 161; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 266; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 235; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 1024.

On Christ, who was given gall and vinegar to drink. Through David the prophet: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22): St. Hilary, IX, 481; Rufinus, XXI, 927; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 858; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 826; Cassiodorus, LXX, 486; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 425; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 498; St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 261; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 959; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 636.

That sun and moon were darkened during Christ’s Passion. Joel the prophet: “Before his face the earth shall be confounded and heaven moved; the sun and moon shall be darkened,” etc. (Joel II, 10): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 827.

On the burial of Christ the Lord and his resurrection, David the prophet: “I became as a man without help, free among the dead, like the wounded sleeping, cast forth in tombs” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5–6): St. Augustine, LXXXVII, 1111, 1112; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 827; Cassiodorus, LXX, 624; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 493; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1100; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 1036; Odo of Asti, CLXV, 1248; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 812, and elsewhere. “You shall not leave,” he says, “my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10): Rufinus, XXI, 698; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 145; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 827; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 691; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 742; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 175.

Hosea the prophet says: “He has given us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us,” etc. (Hos. VI, 3): St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 828.

On Christ’s ascension into heaven, David the prophet says: “He ascended on high; he led captivity captive,” etc. (Ps. LXVII, 19): Rufinus, XXI, 917; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 829; Cassiodorus, LXX, 469; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 948; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 611. And elsewhere: “He ascended above the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII, 11): Rufinus, XXI, 704; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 829; Cassiodorus, LXX, 126; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 247; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 190.

On the second coming of the Son of Man, David the prophet says: “God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not be silent. Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. XLIX, 3): Rufinus, XXI, 844; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 569; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 849; Cassiodorus, LXX, 349; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 365; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 854; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 874; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 476.

### 3. On the Church

Christ also summons this bride to himself through Solomon, from the calling of the Gentiles. For you have read: “Come, bride, from Lebanon” (Song IV, 8): Tertullian, II, 382.---That the Church, formerly barren, would have more children from the Gentiles than the Synagogue had previously had: St. Cyprian, IV, 688.---The Holy Spirit also designates this Church in the Song of Songs, speaking in the person of the Lord: “My dove, my perfect one, is one,” etc. (Song VI, 9): St. Cyprian, IV, 500.---The Holy Spirit points out and announces this house in the Psalms, saying: “God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII, 7), id., 506.---We have always understood this mountain, its name, and even that of the city itself to mean the Church, which is called Christ’s body; the Lord says in the Psalms: “But I have been established king by him over Zion,” etc.: St. Hilary, IX, 414.---“Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King,” etc. Why it is the joy of the whole earth is clearly stated: because the Lord Jesus gathered the Church to himself from sinners: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1147.---In it is the Church of the Lord, which is the city of the great King, id., 1148.---“They shall be filled with drink from the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV). Therefore the house is the Church: St. Ambrose, XIV, 962.---“And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun,” etc. This woman signifies the Church: St. Ambrose, XVII, 875.---“And I saw the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven from God,” etc. The city Jerusalem is the Church constructed from all the righteous, id., 937.---The prophets made preparations; the apostles laid the foundations of the Church, id., 380.---“You shall crush his head,” etc.—The woman is the Church; the serpent, the devil: St. Jerome, XXVI, 840.---The voice of the Church against heretics (Ps. X), id., 845.---Psalm XXIII contains the voice of the Church praising Christ, XXVI, 884.---Psalm XXIII sometimes contains the voice of the Prophet speaking of the Church, id., 886.---Psalm XXIV sometimes has the voice of the Church in supplication, id., 889.---“The queen stood at your right hand.” The Prophet now speaks to the Church itself: St. Jerome, XXVI, 959.---God the Father gave his Son in Zion, that is, in the holy Church, id., 979.---“Glorious things have been said of you, city of God”; yet we understand this city itself to be the Church gathered from the Gentiles, id., 1081.---The Prophet speaks to the Church and says to her: “The dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you,” id., 1084.---The Psalm, “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” refers to the Church, id., 1257.---“Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear,” etc. (Isa. LIV, 1). The barren woman is the Church without Christ her husband: XXVI, 391; XXIV, 515.---“And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the top of the mountains”; this is understood of Christ’s Church, id., XXIV, 43.---When the nations were shaken, the chosen things of all nations came, and the glory of the house of the Lord was filled, which is the Church of the living God, etc., id., XXV, 1404.---“How beautiful are your feet in your sandals, daughter of the prince” (Song VII). The holy Church is called daughter of the prince because through Christ’s preaching it is regenerated into new life, id., 533.---“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII, 5). The holy Church comes up from the wilderness because, placed in the exile of this pilgrimage, it stretches in mind and thought toward heavenly joys, id., LXXIX, 540.---“Our little sister has no breasts” (Song VIII, 8). Christ calls the Church sister because he said of the apostles themselves: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10). But the sister was little and had no breasts when the Church existed only in the apostles, id., 543.---“Who shall find a strong woman? Her value is far from, and from the uttermost bounds.” The strong woman is called the catholic Church: Bede the Venerable, XCI, 1039 ff.---The Song of Songs is referred to the Church, id., 1087 ff.---“A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. XII). The Church of Christ, surrounded by light, treads down temporal glory, id., XCIII, 165.---“Upon her head a crown of twelve stars.” The Church’s head is adorned by the number twelve of the apostles, id., 166.---“Come, I will show you the bride, the Lamb’s wife” (Rev. XXI). He calls the Church bride and wife, which, remaining immaculate, continually bears spiritual children for God, id., 195.---Chapter XII of the Apocalypse refers to the Church: Alcuin, C, 1152.---“She shall crush your head” (Gen.). The woman crushes the serpent’s head when the holy Church drives away the devil’s snares and poisonous persuasions as soon as they are detected at their very beginning, etc.: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 495.---“And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. II). This mountain is indeed the mountain of the Lord’s house, that is, of the Church, which is the Lord’s house founded upon Christ: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 729.---“Arise, put on your strength, Zion; put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, holy city” (Isa. LII). This may also be referred to the present Jerusalem, that is, the Church, id., 982.---“Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear,” etc. (Isa. LIV). The Church, deserted among the Jews, may also be called barren, because when the Lord came it did not bear her children, id., 993.---“The Desired One of all nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory” (Hag. II). Therefore, after Christ came, the house of the Lord was filled—that is, the Church, which is God’s house built of living stones, id., CXVII, 217. A prophecy concerning the establishment of the holy Church, consisting both of Jews and Gentiles, id., 248.---Solomon composed this little book, the Song, about the marriage of Christ and the Church, id., 295.---The holy Church is signified by heaven, and likewise by the woman (Rev. XII), id., 1089.---Or again, the white cloud signifies the Church (Rev. XIV), id., 1111.---The woman (Gen. III) here means the Church. What Isaiah foretold concerning the Church: St. Augustine, LXI, 585, 586. By this concise expression Haggai prophesies Christ and the Church more clearly: “Yet once more, a little while, and I shall shake heaven, earth, sea, and dry land,” etc., id., 593. Zechariah on Christ and the Church: “Rejoice,” he says, “daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem; behold, your King shall come to you,” etc., id., 594. Malachi, prophesying the Church which we see propagated through Christ, speaks very clearly to the Jews in God’s person: “I have no pleasure in you,” etc., id., 594. On the prophecy of Daniel and Ezekiel that agrees with Christ and the Church, id., 592. That the Church of Christ itself was foretold: whence it is said, “A throne of glory is exalted, our sanctification” (Jer. XVII, 10, 12), XLII, 289. What mountain but that which, according to Daniel’s prophecy, grew from a little stone and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole earth (Dan. II, 34), ibid. “I am the Church,” of whom in the same Psalm it is said, and as a fact what was to be is foretold: “The Queen stood at your right hand,” etc., id., XL, 175. Thus Isaiah speaks, beginning from Christ’s humility and afterwards turning to address the Church: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear,” id., XXXIV, 1065.---The prophet teaches that Mount Zion is now the Church, saying: “I, the Lord, shall raise up Zion among the nations,” etc.: Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 329.---We read in the same apostle the saying concerning the Church: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear,” etc.: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 469.---“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” This is the voice of the Church coming to Christ in the kiss: St. Justus of Urgell, LXVII, 963. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” Christ pronounces twice beautiful the Church, which he made a friend of his peace by a kiss, id., 968. “He brought me into the wine-cellar”: the Church is brought into the wine-cellar when that apostolic assembly is filled with the Holy Spirit, id., 970. “My dove in the clefts of the rock.” The Church is called a dove for no other reason than that it is without guile and is filled with the Holy Spirit, id., 972. “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” The Church comes up through the wilderness when the people of the Gentiles, occupying the multitude of believers by faith, makes progress, id., 974, 975. “He made its columns of silver.” The supports of the Church are prepared from learned men or apostles, id., 975. “Our sister is little and has no breasts”: the Church coming from the Gentiles, etc., id., 991.---“A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet”: that is, the Church clothed with Christ, trampling all mutable things for love of him: Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 872. “And upon her head a crown of twelve stars,” that is, upon the Church: he says that the Church, immediately founded, was adorned in its beginnings by the number twelve of the apostles, id., 873. “Come, I will show you the new bride, the Lamb’s wife,” that is, the Church, id., 923. Hence Isaiah (ch. III): “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains and shall be lifted above the hills,” ibid.---“Who is this who comes forth as the dawn rising?” (Song VI, 9). The Church of the elect rises like the dawn, since it leaves the darkness of its former perversity and turns itself toward the brilliance of new light: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 648. The Church is aptly described as compared to the dawn, which is changed through the knowledge of faith from the darkness of its sins into the clear light of righteousness, LXXVI, 62. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14). The Church is the king’s daughter, begotten to good works by the preaching of spiritual rulers, LXXV, 853. “They reap a field not their own and gather the vintage of the vineyard of one whom they have violently oppressed” (Job). The whole Church may be designated by the name of field or vineyard, id., 1150. “The city shall be built for the Lord,” etc. (Jer. XXXI, 38). No one is ignorant that the city of the Lord is the holy Church, LXXVI, 333. “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXXI, 3). It is the city itself, namely the holy Church, which is to reign in heaven but still labors on earth, id., 938. “Behold, even the moon does not shine,” etc. (Job). What is signified by the moon but the Church as a whole, id., 21. “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden” (Song IV, 5). He who blows through God’s garden, that is, the holy Church, id., 799. “A woman clothed with the sun and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. XII, 2). Since the holy Church is protected by the splendor of heavenly light, it is clothed as it were with the sun; and because it despises all temporal things, it presses the moon beneath its feet, id., 731. “Who is this who comes forth?” etc. (Song VI, 9). The holy Church comes forth like the dawn rising at the Last Judgment, LXXIX, 530. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song). The holy Church, longing for the coming of the Mediator of God and men, prays to the Father that he may send his Son, etc., id., 478. “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song I, 3). The Church of God is like a certain house of the king; and this house has a gate, an ascent, a dining-room, and chambers, id., 483. How the words “I am black, but beautiful” are referred to the Church, id., 486. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song II, 12). What is meant by the turtledove but the Church? id., 499. “I shall arise and go about the city” (Song III, 2). What is meant by the city in this passage but the Church, id., 502. “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” (Song III, 6). The Church lives in the wilderness in this world, while exiled from the kingdom it dwells among beasts, namely demons, id., 504. “My sister, my bride, is an enclosed garden” (Song IV, 12). The holy Church is a garden because, while it bears many peoples in faith, like good soil it brings forth beautiful flowers, id., 513.---He speaks of the one to whom the devil is opposed: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 66.---In the Song, the bridegroom is God and the bride is the Church: Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1189. The woman (Rev. XII) signifies the Church: as a woman gives birth and nurses, so the Church brings human beings to the light and faith, and nourishes them with every divine word, id., 1543.---The voice of the Church to Christ (Song): St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 1235. For this woman (Rev. XII) is the Church, which, clothed about with the beauty and brightness of the sun, has drawn many lovers to herself and after herself by the light of her radiance, CLXV, 667, [Col. 0332] 888.---What Isaiah and Daniel foretell concerning the Church: Rupert, abbot, CLXVII, 1282. That woman (Rev. XII) signified the holy Church, CLXIX, 1040; CLXX, 34.---The Church, Christ’s bride, desires the coming of the bridegroom (Song): Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 359.---Solomon, divinely inspired, sang the praises of Christ and the Church (Song): St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 788. How the bride, that is, the Church, desires to be drawn after the bridegroom, that is, Christ (Song 3), id., 872. On the blackness and beauty of the bride, that is, the Church (Song I, 4), id., 899.---How the Church finds the riches of divine mercy in the openings of Christ’s wounds (Song II, 13). The woman, namely, clothed with the sun (Rev. XII), signifies the holy Church, which is clothed, covered, and fortified on every side by Jesus Christ, her bridegroom and defender: St. Martin of León, CCIX, 365.

[Col. 0331]

LVI. INDEX OF MIRACLES ARRANGED IN AN ANALOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS

NOTICE

In this Index we treat: I. miracles considered generally; II. miracles of the Old Testament; III. miracles of the New Testament; IV. miracles following the apostolic age—that is, those which the Fathers themselves performed, or heard from other trustworthy persons and recorded in their writings; V. all false miracles, or, more properly, prodigies, however astonishing, which were spread abroad through the craft and art of demons, especially before Christ’s advent; VI. finally, we give alphabetically the names of the Fathers who in the foregoing articles are indicated only chronologically.

I.—On miracles considered generally.

Since this question extends more broadly and without fixed limits, and treats of the possibility, existence, cause, reason, manner, evidentiary force, and so forth, of miracles—and since one may investigate the authors of miracles, whether acting in their own name, as if they were God, or in another’s name, if they are merely sent—while no miracle stands unless divinity is at work, by an argument that can be pressed against anyone performing wonders, in this notice we shall submit Christ alone, as it were, to the balance. Nothing ever was, nor can any testimony be better suited to establishing and irrefutably proving our purpose. Therefore, with Arnobius we boldly say:

“Was he then a mortal, or one of us, at whose command, at whose voice uttered in ordinary and everyday words, weaknesses, diseases, fevers, and other bodily torments fled? Was he one of us at whose command foul blemishes, immediately driven away, obeyed and left harmony of colour to limbs disfigured by stains? Was he one of us at whose light touch issues of blood stopped and immoderate flows were restrained? Was he one of us from whom dropsical waters fled, whom penetrating fluid avoided, and whose swollen entrails subsided through healing dryness? Was he one of us who commanded the lame to run? Was he one of us who, by a single intervention, healed a hundred or more persons afflicted with various disabilities and diseases? At his mere word raging and maddened seas became calm; the whirlwinds and tempests of storms obeyed him. He set his foot unstained upon the deepest gulfs; he trod upon the surface of the sea, while the waters themselves marvelled and nature entered into service. With five loaves he fed five thousand followers; and, lest those unbelieving and obstinate people should think it a trick, he filled twelve baskets with fragments left over. Was he one of us who commanded souls long since departed to return to their bodies, those buried to come forth from their tombs, and those dead for three days to be freed from the wrappings of embalmers? Was he one of us who perceived what each person turned over in mind, what they kept hidden beneath obscure thoughts, in the hearts of the silent? Was he one of us who, when he uttered one voice before diverse peoples speaking in discordant tongues, was thought to employ the familiar sounds of words and the language proper to each? Was he one of us who, when he delivered the duties of a definite religion to his followers, suddenly filled the whole world and revealed, through the disclosed immensity of his name, both how great he was and who he was? Was he one of us who, after laying aside his body, manifested himself openly in light to countless persons, whose name when heard drives away harmful spirits and imposes silence upon prophets? These powers he not only accomplished by his own strength; what was still more exalted, he granted many others, with devotion to his name, to experience and perform them. For since he saw that we would be deniers of deeds done by him and of divine work, lest there be any suspicion that he had bestowed those gifts and benefits by magical arts, from that immense multitude of people who followed his grace in wonder he chose fishermen, workmen, country people, and such ignorant persons, so that, sent among various nations, they might perform all those miracles without any disguises or aids. What do you say, O unbelieving, difficult, hard minds? Did that Capitoline Jupiter give such power to any mortal?”

So many and so great powers therefore demonstrate irresistibly, as all acknowledge, that miracles are the chief sign and final seal on earth for proving divine action and divine purposes.

TERTULLIAN.—He creates all things from nothing, I, 334. God commanded them to be made by the Word, ordered them by reason, and established them by his power, 375. Christ’s miracles prove him to be God and man, 400. God is the first author of every motion, 590. God is lord and author of nature, II, 83. For God, to be able is to will, and not to be able is not to will; whatever he willed, he both could and showed, 166. He for whom there is no nature has no natural instruments at his disposal, 266. Every position, condition of the elements, effect, motion, state, rising, and setting of individual things are judgments of the Creator, 299. Nothing is impossible to God except what he does not will, 756. We ought to believe miracles, 760. To raise a dead person is nothing other than to make him whole, 878. Fasts obtain a change of nature, 963.

ST. CYPRIAN.—Christ is the power of God, reason, wisdom, and glory, III, 578. By the word and command of his voice Christ expelled demons from people, strengthened paralytics, cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, gave walking to the lame, restored the dead to life, compelled the elements to serve him, the winds to be subject, the seas to obey, and hell to yield; thus the Jews, who believed him to be human only because of the humility of his flesh and body, judged him a magician because of the freedom of his power, 580. Miracles are sometimes performed by outsiders, 1181, 1192. It avails nothing to perform miracles unless one walks in observance of uprightness and justice, IV, 511.

COMMODIANUS.—A poem against the ridiculous inventions concerning the gods of the heathen, V, 201 ff. One must believe in Christ and the resurrection, 220, 221, 222.

ANTONIUS.—In his Poem against the Gentiles, he describes the miracles of creation, V, 278 ff.

[Col. 0333]

ST. VICTORINUS, MARTYR.—He celebrates God’s power in the work *On the Making of the World*, V, 301 ff. He praises and explains the visions and revelations of the Apocalypse, 317 ff.

ARNOBIUS.—He demonstrates that Christ’s miracles are true, V, 781 ff. His miracles, especially at the time of his death, show how great his power is, 791. The truth of Christ’s miracles is proved from exceptionally ample witnesses, 792; likewise from the rapid spread of the Christian religion, 793. Pagans who object that Christ assumed human nature and was killed in a human way are refuted, 800, 801.

LACTANTIUS.—Human thought cannot attain God’s plans and ordinances, VI, 113. He cannot be comprehended in any way, 152. His power and majesty were proclaimed by Plato, 153. He is truly omnipotent, 153. He made all things from nothing, 298. He alone, together with the Son, possesses power over all things, 338. Nothing is closed or secret to God, 724. On his ineffable power even over incorporeal things, 800. God raised up princes who overthrew the impious and bloody dominions of tyrants and provided for the human race, so that now, as though the cloudiness of the past time had been scattered, a pleasant and serene peace might gladden the minds of all. Now, after the violent whirlwinds of so great a storm, calm air and desired light have shone forth. Now, appeased by the prayers of his servants, God raises up by heavenly aid those who lay fallen and afflicted. Behold, now, the conspiracy of the impious having been extinguished, he wipes away the tears of mourners; and those who fought against God lie fallen; those who overthrew the holy temple have fallen in a greater ruin; those who tortured the righteous have poured out their guilty souls under deserved heavenly blows and torments—later indeed, but severely and justly. For God had deferred their punishments in order to provide in them great and wonderful examples, from which posterity might learn both that God is one and that he is the avenger who inflicts fitting punishments upon the impious and persecutors, VII, 191, 192.

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT.—God is the source of all things that come into being, VIII, 405. From him all things contained within the compass of the world receive the cause of their subsistence and life, VIII, 405. Most people assign the cause of this distinction and ordering of all things to nature; others attribute it to fate or chance, ascribing the power governing such matters to fate. They do not understand that, when they name fate, they utter indeed a name but designate no action and no substance. For what can fate itself be in its own right if nature has produced all things? Or what are we to judge nature to be if the law of fate cannot be violated? But from the fact that what is called a fatal law is said to be a law, whereas every law is the work of some lawgiver, it is sufficiently evident that fate itself, if indeed it is a law, is God’s work and invention. All things therefore are subject to God, and nothing is without his power. Yet we do not object to fate being regarded and understood as God’s will, 412, 413.

ST. HILARY.—The possibility of miracles is maintained, IX, 411, 412; and inferred from the creation of man, 566. God’s revelations to human beings, 619. All magnificent and excellent works testify that there is a God, 761. Miracles performed bodily, IX, 761. God alone works miracles, IX, 772. Christ’s works testify who he is, 810. The holiness of God’s works establishes faith in his words, 862. Christ’s deeds do not submit to the natural perceptions of minds, X, 34. God is not subject to the laws of nature, from whom all nature receives its law, 339.

ST. ZENO.—Christ’s works must be believed, XI, 389. The begetter of the ages became the immortal Son of the Virgin; he dies, himself, for man, XI, 403. Christians must believe in the resurrection of the flesh, 377, 378, 381.

ST. OPTATUS.—One must believe that the Son of God was born according to humanity through the Virgin Mary, suffered, died, and was buried, and after these things rose again, XI, 885. St. Optatus recognized Christ’s wonderful and real presence in the Eucharist, 765.

ST. AMBROSE.—Moses could neither be deceived nor deceive. For, educated in every learning of the Egyptians and supported by royal resources, he desired to be formed and instructed in all disciplines of secular wisdom. Although he received his name from water, he nevertheless did not think that all things consisted of water, as Thales said. Although brought up in the royal court, he preferred for the love of justice to undergo voluntary exile rather than, at the summit of tyranny, gain the enjoyment of sin. Moved by a natural love of equity, he withdrew into the wilderness of Ethiopia. There, removed from other concerns, he devoted his whole mind to divine knowledge, so that he might see the glory of God face to face. Thus Moses, not in the persuasion of human wisdom or in the deceptive disputations of philosophy, but in the demonstration of Spirit and power, as a witness to divine work, dared to say: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” XIV, 124, 125. Matter is from God; through him comes the operation that bound and constrained all things into himself, because when he wills, all things endure and subsist through his power; their end returns to God’s will and they are dissolved at his judgment, [Col. 0334] XIV, 131, 132. The creature does not give the law but receives it and keeps what it has received, XVI, 133. Nothing is impossible to God, XVI, 147. If in this creation of the world there are things that appear difficult for us to understand and incomprehensible to our intellect, we ought not to condemn them by a certain rash judgment, XVI, 277. By the wiser serpent through whom the woman was deceived is to be understood that adversary who possesses only the wisdom of this world, XVI, 301. How the devil tempts man, XIV, 302, 306. Many things are not to be measured by our intellect, but judged from the height of divine ordinance and the Word; nor should one doubt or criticize that the devil was in paradise: there is miracle in the elements, instruction in the mysteries, XIV, 1633. Miracles among the nations before Christ were rare, or nonexistent, 1663. It is not granted to everyone to merit miracles of divine power, but to those whom the pursuits of religious devotion support, XVI, 240, 241. People who raised the dead did not do so in their own power, but in Christ’s name, 595. Miracles performed by Saints Gervasius and Protasius cannot be denied by Arians, 1025.

ST. JEROME.—Nothing false is said in the sacred Scriptures, XXII, 566. What we have heard and seen, our fathers also reported to us, XXII, 566. No one doubts that what is written truly happened, as though the letter sounded one thing and the Spirit held another hidden thing, XXII, 698. Objections against miracles are answered, XXII, 900. In the greatness of signs, not a change of nature but God’s omnipotence is demonstrated, XXII, 901.—Arguments against miracles, XXIII, 348. There are many magical deceptions and innumerable snares by which human souls are caught; but we shall stop our ears lest we hear the voices of enchanters, and shall disregard the songs of sirens, XXII, 719. The force and power of miracles are demonstrated, XXIII, 348. Why signs are performed among barbarian peoples through God’s servants, XXV, 527. The error of the Gentiles, who think those beings gods whom they see above themselves, XXV, 504.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—God is tested when miracles are demanded, not for salvation but for experiment, XXXII, 802. Why miracles occur in some places and not in others is God’s counsel, XXXIII, 269. Things wonderful are no longer wonders through the habit of seeing them, XXXIII, 372. God delivered the three men from the fire and Daniel from the lions in order to provide for the salvation of those kings by whom they were handed over to those punishments, XXXIII, 425. All God’s wonders are not believed by unbelievers because their reason is not apparent, XXXIII, 454. Many need to be aroused to faith in invisible things by visible miracles, XXXIII, 454. Miracles are daily produced in the natural world, but become cheap through familiarity, XXXIII, 519. Miracles are not signs of wisdom, XXXV, 1307. God daily performs miracles at which people do not marvel, XXXV, 1450. He who performs miracles apart from truth is nothing, XXXV, 1501. God preserved certain unusual things which he had made in order to awaken sleeping people, XXXV, 1450. All that the Lord Jesus did serves not only to awaken our hearts by miracles, but also to build them up in the doctrine of faith, XXXV, 1458. In miracles Christ provided more for the salvation of souls than for bodily health, XXX, 1527. Miracles admonish the human mind to understand God from visible things, XXXV, 1592, 1593. Miracles strengthen faith, XXXV, 1752. Miracles have their own language, XXXV, 1593.
