Miracles are Christ’s works and words; Christ performed some miracles which no one else performed, while others performed some which he did not perform, XXXV, 1860, 1861. In performing miracles the apostles did not claim their Lord’s power for themselves, XXXVII, 1197. Miracles were performed differently by Christ and differently by the saints, 1432, 1440. How a Christian himself performs miracles in another person who performs them, 1707. By bodily miracles Christ built up faith, XXXVIII, 339. The Church’s later faith without miracles is more praiseworthy, 539. Christ now performs greater miracles, 540. The Lord’s miracles are in bodies and souls, 591. Christ’s miracles were performed for their signification, 592. If you begin to investigate the reason for miracles by human judgment, beware lest you lose faith, 1157. Why not all obtain miracles of healing, 1299. God knows how he ought to commend his miracles; he knows how to act lest they become cheap, 1299. Some miracles are at times performed even by wicked people, such as saints cannot perform. Why miracles are sometimes allowed to be done by evil persons and sometimes not; miracles are rightly performed by magicians and saints for different ends and by different power; differently by good and differently by evil Christians, XL, 91, 92. Miracles were performed through the simple faith of piety, not through incantations, XLI, 286, 291.—How many miracles were performed in the Old Testament to commend the worship of God, 286. Magical miracles deceive most human senses merely in appearance, by imaginary illusion, 295. The miracles of gods are not to be compared with ours, 295. Those who say that miracles [Col. 0335] reported in sacred Scripture are false are answered, 296, 297. A thing has not failed to exist, nor will it fail to be, merely because no explanation can be given, 714. The miracles of the Gentiles were performed either with the help of magical arts or by demons themselves, 717. Many things done by human beings through the use of creatures seem miraculous, 718. Miracles are still performed in Christ’s name, 760, 769. Miracles now performed are not made illustrious by glory as great as that of the first miracles, 760. In miracles there is a kind of divine eloquence, 770. Whether miracles occur through the operations of martyrs or only through their prayers, 771. The miracles of martyrs and false gods are compared, 772. What miracles are properly so called, 879. How miracles are performed cannot be comprehended by man, 881. Whether miracles occur in no manner at all, 63, 64. Why they do not occur now, XLII, 90. What a miracle is and how many kinds there are, 90. In miracles the entire reason of the deed is the will of the doer, 519. Truth alone performs miracles, 876. It is more powerful to be joined to the Almighty by a devout will than, through one’s own power and will, to be able to do what those who cannot do such things tremble at, 957.

JOHN CASSIAN.—God’s grace consists not in wonders but in humility, XLIX, 1004. It is a greater miracle to drive from oneself the fuel of lust than to expel demons from other bodies, 1007. How greatly integrity of life itself surpasses miracles, 1008.

ST. PROSPER.—Why Christ’s miracles were not performed among those who would believe but were performed among those who would not believe is inscrutable, LI, 198. The authority of prophecy is not human but divine, 371. Prophecy was a lamp in darkness, 381. Wonders which God alone has performed, 387, 388. God performs some miracles through angels and people, 388. Those for whom they are beneficial see God’s wonders, 442. God’s daily wonders, visible and invisible; one must pass from visible to invisible things, 445.—Miracles are not contrary to nature, although they appear so to us, 469.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—To whom miracles are to be granted, LII, 222. Signs to the demon, 222. The powers of miracles are from God, 334. A singular miracle: not seeing what has been seen, not knowing what has been known, not believing what has been believed, 430. Evidence of belief from the miracles of Christ’s disciples, 435. Miracles show Christ to be God, 480. Miracles weary the Jews and do not profit them, 486, 487. What Christ’s miracle accomplished, 493.

AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS.—On the oracles of the pagans, LIX, 959. Christ’s miracles, LX, 104. The power of performing miracles communicated by God to martyrs, 292. Miracles at the tombs of martyrs, 291, 407.

ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA.—Miracles performed by Christ provoked the Jews not to believe but to blaspheme, LXI, 410. Every miracle of both the Old and New Testament plainly declares that all things are subject to God, not to fate, 607.

EUGYPPIUS.—Why miracles do not occur; that they nevertheless occur even now; why the disciples at first performed wonders, LXII, 803, 804.

JUNILIUS.—On the authority of the divine Scriptures, which abound in miracles, LXVIII, 20. How all things were created by God’s nod, 25.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—Miracles ought not to be examined by intellect, LXXV, 738. Why we should marvel at miracles, though God’s wonderful works have become cheap to us through their very familiarity, 738. Why Christ performed miracles by day and devoted himself to prayer at night, 760. Those who despise invisible things can be moved by visible miracles, LXXVI, 410, 721. Miracles are necessary for holy preachers, 410, 827. The miracles of saints illuminate the darkness of our insensibility, 410. Signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers, 420, 1082, 1215. Miracles do not produce the same effects in everyone, 423. The violence of tyranny was broken by the miracles of saints, 469. God broke the rigid powers of this world not by words but by miracles, 573. At the end of the world miracles will be withdrawn from the Church of God, 721. The miracles of saints are our defenses, 972. They are not certain proofs of holiness, 998, 1215. How the miracles of the elect differ from those of the reprobate, 998. The sole rationale in miracles is the power of the doer, 1034. Miracles granted to the weak, 1082. Christ’s miracles show one thing by power and speak another through mystery, 1082. What miracles following true faith ought to be understood as, 1215. Miracles sometimes prove holiness but do not create it, 1215. Why the tombs of martyrs are made illustrious by miracles, 1257. The Church’s power of miracles is vindicated from the Old and New Testament, LXXVII, 134, 139, 140. Miracles recorded in sacred Scripture surpass every faith, 139. Examples of virtues must be preferred to miracles, 141. By the miracles of the Fathers may be understood both astonishing works of virtue and signs, 143. Frequent miracles at martyrs’ tombs prove that their souls live, 329. Miracles are sometimes performed by the reprobate, 1141.

Finally, the reader will permit us to quote in full this remarkable testimony of this Father concerning the wonders of God:

“[Col. 0336] Who can sufficiently search out the wonders of almighty God?” says the holy Doctor (LXXV, 737). “It is enough that he created all things from nothing; that the very fabric of the world is ordered by a wonderful power; that the earth is balanced over the abyss; that all this universe, visible as it is, exists from invisible things; that he made man—if one may so speak—a second world gathered together in brief, yet rational; that, constituting him from soul and flesh, he united spirit and clay in an unsearchable ordering of power. Thus, of these things we know some and are others; nevertheless we neglect to marvel, because things wonderful by incomprehensible investigation have become cheap to human eyes through familiarity.

“Hence, if a dead person is raised, everyone leaps up in amazement; yet every day a person who did not exist is born, and no one marvels, although all certainly agree that to create what did not exist is greater than to restore what existed. Because Aaron’s dry rod blossomed, all marvelled; every day a tree springs from dry earth, and the power of dust is changed into wood, and no one marvels. Because five thousand people were fed with five loaves, all marvelled that food increased in their mouths; every day grains of seed scattered abroad are multiplied into the abundance of ears, and no one marvels. Seeing water once changed into wine, all marvelled; every day moisture of the earth, drawn into the root of the vine, is changed into wine through the cluster, and no one marvels.

“Therefore all things are wonderful which people neglect to wonder at, because familiarity dulls them for consideration. But amid these things it must be known that divine miracles ought always to be considered with diligence and never examined by intellect. For often human understanding, seeking and not finding the reason of certain things, plunges itself into an abyss of doubt. Thus some people consider the bodies of the dead reduced to dust; and, since they cannot infer by reason the power of resurrection, they despair that these can return to their former state. Wonders, therefore, are to be believed by faith, not investigated by reason; for if reason laid them open to our eyes, they would not be wonders.

“But when perhaps the mind wavers concerning these things, it is necessary that it recall things which it knows by experience but nevertheless does not grasp by reason, so that by the argument of a similar matter it may strengthen a faith which it finds shaken by its own subtlety. When considering the dust of human flesh, the mind of some is troubled and despairs how dust may return to limbs, reconstituting a living body by the outlines of its members; how that dryness of earth may grow green through living limbs and distinguish itself through their appearances and forms. Certainly this cannot be comprehended by reason, yet it can readily be believed from an example. For who would believe that an immense tree could arise from one grain of seed, unless experience established this as certain? For in the great smallness of a single grain, and in its almost complete lack of apparent differentiation, where lies hidden the hardness of wood, the pith softer or harder than wood, the roughness of bark, the greenness of root, the taste of fruits, the sweetness of scents, the variety of colours, the softness of leaves? Yet because we know this by experience, we do not doubt that all these things come forth from one grain of seed. What then is difficult in dust returning to limbs, when we daily behold the Creator’s power, who wonderfully creates trees from a grain and, still more wonderfully, fruits from trees? Hence the greatness of divine works can be neither examined by quality nor numbered by quantity.”

LIVES OF THE FATHERS.—The power of miracles, LXXIII, 160, 161. Miracles occur through prayers, not through the commands of saints, LXXIII, 163, 164. Miracles through garments and blessed oil, LXXIII, 252, 253. By what power miracles occur, LXXIV, 14. Miracles as a pledge of doctrine, LXXIV, 104. Why miracles occur in the Church, LXXIV, 238.

TAIO, BISHOP OF CAESARAUGUSTA.—What is sufficient for a human being to investigate concerning God’s wonders, LXXX, 741. God performs great and unsearchable things, LXXX, 742. God’s miracles are to be believed by faith, not investigated by reason, LXXX, 742. Miracles were necessary at the beginning of the Church, LXXX, 871. Unbelievers placed holiness in miracles, LXXX, 806.

ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—The power of works has been given to the Church, LXXXIII, 591. The world had to believe by means of miracles, LXXXIII, 592. When Antichrist comes, miracles will cease in the Church, LXXXIII, 592. The distinction between miracles, portents, signs, prodigies, and monsters, LXXXII, 470, and LXXXIII, 56.

SEDULIUS SCOTTUS.—Signs of virtues give greater authority to signs, CIII, 17. What a sign is, CIII, 48. Faith takes no account of nature, because it knows him who moves it to be all-powerful, CIII, 50.

ST. AGOBARD, BISHOP OF LYONS.—On the illusion of signs, CIV, 24. Saints perform wonders not as causes but as means and instruments, CIV, 26. On the intervention of angels and the devil in human actions, CIV, 180, 183.

[Col. 0337]

Divine worship must not be rendered either to angels or saints, although miracles are sometimes performed through them, CIV, 203.

RABANUS MAURUS.—On various superstitions of the Gentiles, CVII, 392. God’s will is the foundation of the universe, CVII, 414. By miracles someone can become famous, but not holy, CXI, 104. Various monsters said to have appeared, CXI, 197 ff.

ST. EULOGIUS.—The Lord appropriately grants the world the true signs of miracles through his servants, because, in his foreknowing divinity, he knows that those who await them nevertheless derive profit thereby, and knows that workers of powers do not labour in vain, so that at least those who reject the saving commands of the sacred law may yield to the novelty of prodigies. . . . When God’s providence works miracles either for the faith of believers or for the future faith of those present, we should not so much marvel at them in admiration as consider with provident discernment whether the workers of those signs excel, having expelled vices, in uprightness of character; whether, dead to the world, they live to God; whether, because of that true charity which surpasses all gifts of charisms, they count all worldly attachments as nothing; whether they ascribe the power received not to their own glory but to the benefit of its giver; whether, with attentive ears of the heart and having received the admonition of the true teacher, they rejoice not because demons are subject to them but because their names are written in heaven. Therefore, in those authors of prodigies, this enumeration of virtues rather than the effect of signs itself is what ought to be admired; and it is the more preliminary indication of the way to seek the kingdom—not what makes us publicly conspicuous and notable as standard-bearers—because holiness, fear of the Lord, and the worship of the heavenly kingdom proceed only from the fit and perfect. . . .

Especially in the first centuries of the Church, God’s power granted the world the distinguishing glory of miracles, so that by the powers of prodigies it might either mitigate the madness of raging persons which wearied the constancy of the blessed, or convert from the error of unbelief the incredulous race which, with hardened hearts, rejected the ordinances of the heavenly Scriptures. At that time it was often necessary that God’s witnesses should shine preeminently in signs of powers, since they strove to establish Christianity, still raw and spread through the age, firmly at its roots in the hearts of believing peoples—now by instruction of words, now by exercise in the Scriptures, now by the showing of signs, now even by the illustrious trophies of sufferings. . . .

That the exercise of signs is not fitting for every time, and that not all are found worthy of contemplating heavenly powers, can readily be perceived by comparing the events performed by the apostles. When they wished to preach the good news to the Asians, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:6–7); and he who had commanded that the Gospel be proclaimed to every creature (Mark 16:13), knowing that in Asia no one existed worthy to receive evangelical truth, by the foreknowing authority of divinity prevented the disciples from seeking their salvation, since they were going to reject the word of life in an arrogant spirit and would not listen because they would despise it. . . .

Now indeed, although the heavenly dispensation has not entirely withdrawn miracles from among us, they are not displayed openly and repeatedly as in former times. Yet this is done by a wonderful dispensation, so that in one matter both divine mercy and justice may be fulfilled. For when, with the powers of signs withdrawn, the holy Church appears somewhat more lowly, then both the reward of the good increases, who venerate her in hope of heavenly things and not because of present signs; and the mind of the wicked is sooner revealed against her, since they neglect to follow the invisible things which she promises when they are not held fast by visible signs. For signs of powers are neither given to all nor to be exercised everywhere at any time. At the end of the age (St. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIV, no. 7), signs of powers will be absent from the Church. For, by the terrible ordering of hidden providence, before Leviathan appears in that condemned man whom he will assume, signs of powers will be withdrawn from the holy Church. Prophecy is hidden, the grace of healings is removed, the power of prolonged abstinence is diminished, the words of teaching fall silent, and the prodigies of miracles are taken away, CXV, 748, 749, 750.

There also, and throughout the *Memorial of the Saints*, the *Document Concerning Martyrdom*, and the apologetic book on the martyrs, it is irrefutably shown that martyrdom is a true miracle, properly so called: when martyrs, with exultant minds, rejoice in the prospect of suffering; regard punishment as of little account; resound with hymns; sound forth praises; render psalms; persist in prayer, so that, with the Lord’s favour, they may be strong enough to win victory; when they are visited by angels, their chains burst apart, and so forth. . . . CXV, 735–870.

HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT.—The power of miracles is not from man but from God, CXVII, 620. We perform miraculous signs in a fragile body; while healing others, we ourselves become sick, 624. [Col. 0338] The Holy Spirit himself is the pledge to believers, because from him they receive the working of miracles, 766. Demons are driven away by invocation of Christ’s name, 707. The Lord’s disciples performed signs and miracles in order that they might be known to have been sent by God, CXVIII, 14. At the end of the world the Church will not shine with the splendour of miracles, 18. Whenever the Lord’s miracles are read, they are not to be taken as examples but rather admired and venerated, 126.

ST. GREGORY VII, POPE.—In the Appendix is given the Life of St. Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and there it is said: “St. Anselm performed many wonders both living and dead. Indeed, his good disciple also performed them. Master in God and disciple in God—and in his most blessed master, Gregory VII—the disciple, as is said, performs more. Nor is this surprising. For Peter performed more than Christ, certainly not by his own power, but because, denying himself, he followed Christ. So also this venerable Father of ours, St. Anselm, because he imitated in all things his devout master, St. Gregory VII, works many powers. For we know many whose life was most holy, yet who did not display the power of miracles. But this man, not only because he lived a religious life, but rather because he carried out faithful obedience, hating with perfect hatred the party of the excommunicated and loving and defending the unity of Catholics, confirms by miracles what he taught by speech. Therefore all of you who have thus far obeyed the commands of Lord Pope Gregory in Catholic unity, rejoice and exult; and say to those who have turned back and abandoned the footsteps of truth, that they may now believe deeds, what they formerly refused to believe words,” CXLVIII, 921.

VALCANDUS, MONK.—Christian discernment ought rather to seek and attend to the works which make each person holy than to those which show him to be holy. It delights indeed in the visible deeds of saints, but nevertheless desires by every means to reach their invisible deeds, and, thirsty, prefers to quench its thirst from the spring rather than from the stream. Hence the Lord says: “Do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). This we merit by holiness of soul, not by the display of miracles, especially since on the day of judgment he will say to many who have performed many powers in his name: “I do not know you” (Matt. 11:29). From this the faith of the Church more ardently seeks what those whom it venerates were like in the invisible virtues of the soul than what they were like in visible signs, which are indeed milk for little children, not solid food for the perfect. But as one passes from milk to solid food, so the imperfection of our faith, nourished by signs, is at length brought to the solid virtues of the soul, so that it no longer needs to suck, but to chew the cud, CLI, 632.

St Bruno, founder of the Carthusian Order.—How the power of God, once resplendent in such great miracles, is despised by some. CLII, 722. God works and confirms the words of St Bruno by the signs that follow, 722. The voice of God has set wonders upon the earth, CLIII, 838. Christ made the apostles powerful not only in preaching but also in miracles, 955. Their preaching would not be believed unless they worked miracles, ibid. God’s illumination occurs through miracles, 1021. By the miracles of preachers earthly-minded people were moved, 1029. The Church had its beginning through Christ’s preaching, the working of miracles, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, 1166. Those who end their lives in peace, however praiseworthily they have lived, are not counted in the catalogue of saints without a definite manifestation of miracles, 77. Some have fallen away and yet have power to perform miracles, ibid.

Radulphus Ardens.—There are two things which the Lord promised to those believing in him: namely, that they would perform divine works, and that they would obtain from the Father whatever they asked in his name, CLV, 1367. To heal the sick merely by one’s shadow, as happened through Peter, is greater than to heal by the touch of a garment’s fringe, as happened through Christ, 1367–1368. It is greater and more wonderful that a dead man should be raised by a mortal man—even a dead one—than that he should be raised by almighty God, 1367.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent.—Signs and visions serve repeatedly not the benefit of those through whose ministry they occur, but that of others, CLVI, 616. Just as true deeds of saints redound to God’s honour, so false ones turn to disgrace, 620. Faith is very often the cause of miracles, 663. One should not readily believe every miracle, 662–664. Whether devils inhabit this world, 672.

St Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.—Miracles which God alone performs are always wonderful, CLVIII, 446. God works many things through created beings which they would by no means do according to their own ordinary use and proper nature, 445.

St Bruno, bishop of Segni.—Miracles are to be attributed to the finger of God alone [Col. 0339], CLXIV, 721. Miracles of divine mercy, 1112. The splendour of miracles is greater than the splendour of fire, and the fame of miracles shines much farther than the flame of lamps, 759.

Hermann, a Jew converted to Christianity.—For the conversion of a soul, one should neither ask God for a sign nor greatly desire one. For it is certainly most easy for his omnipotence, without any miracle, to convert whom he wills; and a sign visibly displayed outwardly is useless if he himself does not work invisibly by grace in the human heart. Faith persuaded by miracles has either no merit or very little, CLXX, 814.

Hugh of St Victor.—The multitude and depth of God’s wonders, CLXXVI, 613. God is wonderful in his saints, more inwardly than outwardly, 622. On the manifold kinds of vision, 646. That God can do all things, CLXXVII, 68. It is greater to make something out of nothing than to make more out of something, 286. To reduce something to nothing is possible to God alone, 287.

Venerable Hervaeus, monk of Bourg-Dieu.—There are three kinds of visions, CLXXXI, 19. Signs are displayed in the spirit through certain likenesses of bodily things, 20. The apostles were adorned by the beauty of virtues and the brilliance of miracles and preaching, 745. Faith does not seek rational explanations of what it ought to believe, but reckons all things possible to divine power, knowing that nothing is impossible to God, 831. Outward miracles are performed in order to lead human minds to inward things, so that, through what is visibly shown to be wonderful, the invisible things may be believed to be still more wonderful, 966.

Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.—Among the charisms of the Holy Spirit, the grace of miracles holds no small dignity, since it contains such great usefulness in itself: chiefly through it the world was delivered from the darkness of unbelief and endowed with the eternal light of truth; and even now, in the hearts of many faithful people to whom it is sometimes granted to see this, faith is increased, hope grows, and truth is confirmed, CLXXXIX, 852.

John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres.—Why a *praestigium* is so called, and who is called its author, CXCIX, 406. Who magicians are and whence they are so called, 407. On the kinds of magic, 407. Who are enchanters, diviners, soothsayers, natural philosophers, image-makers, conjecturers, astrologers, fortune-tellers, and augurs, ibid. That the significations of natural things are not to be despised, 407 and 418.

Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury.—Although the holy prophets were illuminated by the Holy Spirit to see or foresee certain things, yet, as human beings, they were permitted to remain ignorant of many things which God did not reveal, CCIV, 574. On the necessity of miracles, 586.

II.—On the miracles of the Old Testament.

III.—Likewise, on the miracles of the New Testament.

Since these two inquiries would have required an account of all the miracles of Holy Scripture—miracles more frequently recounted requiring frequent repetition—and since this excessively burdensome task is supplied by the general index *On the Words of Holy Scripture Contained in the Writings of the Fathers*, an index which alone, it is thought, will conclude the final volume of the *Patrology*, we refer readers to this index, which is in truth a concordance of the writings of the Fathers. For it is readily understood that, once one knows where the Fathers have treated the word “Sodom,” for example, or “Cana,” and so forth, there one will find an account of the miracles of the destruction of Sodom, and so on with the rest.

IV.—On miracles performed after the apostles.

Here are indicated: first, miracles which the holy Fathers performed or heard of, possessing the force of Christ’s and the apostles’ miracles and “the same manifestation of the Spirit for the common good”—that is, whatever belongs to the word of wisdom and knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, workings of powers, prophecy, discernments of spirits, kinds of tongues, and interpretations of utterances (1 Cor. 12:7–11); second, likewise, mighty deeds bearing the seal of divinity.

As one example selected from thousands of this latter class of miracles, let the deaths of the persecutors of the Roman pontiffs suffice (Lactantius VII, cols. 190–276). Therefore let it not be taken ill if, with due reverence, we write here certain matters in French, as they were recently published (7 and 14 September 1861) by the well-known weekly periodical *Le Rosier de Marie*.

“Rome sacrifices her Pontiffs!! At the head of the list of persecutors stands the name of the all-too-famous Nero. This prince, the shame of thrones and the vassal of crime, after murdering his mother, slaughtering his wife, killing his concubine, sending an innumerable multitude of innocents to death, setting fire to the four corners of Rome, and singing in an actor’s costume amid that vast conflagration, signed the first edict of persecution against Christians and enrolled the apostle St Peter among the martyrs . . . But suddenly everyone rises up: friends, enemies, people, army. The Senate assembles in tumult and issues this decree: that a post shall be raised in the middle of the public square; that the tyrant shall be dragged there naked and loaded with chains; that his executioners shall beat him with rods until he expires; and that his body shall finally be hurled into the Tiber . . . Abandoned by all, struck by a servant, Nero falls. Domitian, the second persecutor of the Church and executioner of Pope St Anacletus, perishes, murdered by his officers and his own wife. Trajan stains his imperial purple with the blood of Popes St Clement and St Evaristus; he does not arrive at Rome, where triumphal arches and garlands await him, but breathes his last after an illustrious defeat beneath the unknown walls of obscure Selinus. Hadrian dared to number St Alexander and St Sixtus among the martyrs . . . He died from the consequences of a meal. Valerian, defeated and taken prisoner in a battle fought against Shapur I, king of Persia, was drenched in insults by that cruel victor. For seven years Shapur dragged him from city to city, burdened with heavy chains. Whenever he wished to depart, he had him brought near, compelled him to kneel, ordered him to bend still lower; then, setting his foot on his loins, shoulders, or head, he sprang from there onto his horse or into his chariot. Nor was this all: when death came to end the miseries of the unfortunate old man, Shapur had him flayed. He ordered his skin to be stuffed with straw, so as to preserve its human form; dyed red, to show that it had borne the imperial purple; and hung at the gate of a temple . . . What then had Valerian, once so powerful a prince, done? He had caused Popes St Stephen and St Sixtus to be put to death.”

Likewise, we have as a miracle what is said of Julian the Apostate in the aforesaid publication:

“One day, a powerful man, scorning all prophecies and wishing to prove them false, undertook to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem and restore Judaea to its former glory. What happened? A deadly arrow pierced the heart of the audacious impious man. Staggering, he gathered a handful of blood and, hurling it furiously toward heaven, cried: ‘You have conquered, Galilean!’ Then he fell lifeless.”

Having set these matters forth, we append notices which often include such things, supported by greater or lesser evidence. Taken together, though individually they say almost nothing, they bring great evidentiary force to the cause to which they are adapted and devoted—namely, in support of our religion, following the progress of its chain of miracles.

Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage.—Christians are as numerous as we are denounced to be. They cry out that the city is besieged, that Christians are in the countryside, villages, and islands; they lament, as though it were a loss, that every sex, age, condition, and even rank is passing over to this name, I, 262–264. Glabrio, exposed by Trajan to a most savage lion, overcame it with God’s help and by his own courage, and was afterwards himself killed; in the Notes, 264. At Christ’s death, daylight was withdrawn while the sun was marking the middle of the world; Tertullian says to the pagans: “You have the account of this cosmic event in your secret archives,” 401. “We are but of yesterday, and we have filled everything belonging to you—cities, islands, fortified places, municipalities, meeting-places, the very camps, tribes, divisions, the palace, senate, and forum; we have left you only your temples,” 462, 463, 570, 571, 704. The Seventy Interpreters—this happened before Christ and the apostles—separately translated the text and all arrived at the same meaning and the same wording, I, 380. Torn and bloodied Christians cry out: “We worship God through Christ,” 403 and 865.

Martyrdom is a battle in which Christians contend before pagan tribunals at the peril of their lives, and conquer when they are killed. “We become more numerous whenever we are mown down; the blood of Christians is seed,” I, 535, 704. A woman attended the theatre and returned with a devil; after being exorcised, she was freed, 657. Marcus Aurelius, having through the prayers of Christian soldiers obtained rain from God, ordered more severe penalties against those who accused followers of Christ, 295, 707. Vigellius, Saturninus, and Claudius Lucius, persecutors of Christians, display divine vengeance in their deaths, 702. If former disasters are compared, lighter calamities now occur, since God has received the Christian world, 486. The life of Christians, in its holiness, is a continual miracle: “See,” the pagans say, “how they love one another,” 280, 465, 471, 472, 700. Severus, Antoninus’s brother, sought out the Christian Proculus, procurator of Euhodia, who had once cured him by means of oil, and kept him in his palace, I, 703. An unclean spirit commanded by any Christian to speak confesses itself to be a demon, 413, 700. How great is Christians’ power over demons: 413, 463, 624, 677, 700, 703; II, 112. The devil confesses that he is the devil, I, 631, 655, 977, 1164, 1205, 1256, 1312; II, 54, 102, 106, 296, 297, 301, 576, 620, 673, 916. The devil’s reply, when challenged during an exorcism about a Christian woman whom he possessed in the theatre: “I found her on my own ground,” I, 657. The existence of demons is affirmed, I, 405, 413, 434, 447, 646, 677, 700, 703; II, 97, 693, 700, 717, 732, 748. Some Christians were tested by fire, others by the sword, others by beasts, II, 125.

Holy martyrs Felicity and Perpetua: *Visions and Passion of the Holy Perpetua, Felicity, and their Companions*, III, 47–58. When holy Felicity, pregnant and suffering in childbirth because of the natural difficulty of the eighth month, was in pain, one of the prison attendants said to her: “You who are now in such pain, what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts, which you despised when you refused to sacrifice?” She answered: “Now I suffer what I suffer; but there another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I too shall suffer for him,” 47–58. To St Peter, shortly to be crucified at Rome, Christ appeared and said: “I am going to be crucified again”; in the Notes, III, 47. On the martyrdom of St Polycarp, 44. John, immersed in boiling oil, suffered nothing; in the Notes, 90.

Minucius Felix.—It is repeatedly and emphatically affirmed that every magical art and all incantations vanish through the sign of Christ’s cross and Christians’ adjurations, and that all deceptions of demons are repelled. Demons adjured by the one true God shudder unwillingly within afflicted bodies, and either depart immediately or gradually disappear, according as the sufferer’s faith assists or the healer’s grace breathes upon them, III, 326. On the martyrdom of St Agnes, *Dissertation on Minucius Felix*, 536. Boys and little women, through patience in suffering inspired from above, mock crosses, tortures, beasts, and all the terrors of torments, 353. The remarkable martyrdom of Biblias, 487.

Pontius, deacon.—Martyrdom of St Cyprian, 1482–1506.

St Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr.—Fishermen were changed; afterwards even very many senators were changed; Cyprian was changed, IV, 75. “After, through the help of the water of rebirth, the stain of my former life had been washed away, and a serene and pure light from above had been poured into my cleansed breast; after, with the Spirit breathed from heaven, a second birth restored me as a new man: then, in a marvellous manner, doubts at once began to be confirmed, closed things opened, dark things made bright; what had seemed difficult was given power, what had been thought impossible became possible; so that one could recognize as earthly what had previously been carnally born and lived subject to sins, and as belonging to God what had now begun to be animated by the Holy Spirit,” 200–201. Demons are driven by Christians out of the bodies of the possessed, 203, 555. No Christian resists when arrested, however exceedingly numerous the Christian people may be, 557. Martyrs rejoice amid torments, 559. There is something great in gifts if a person is crowned with that by which he thinks himself crowned, should he perhaps die as a martyr, 794. Such is the power of martyrdom that through it even the person who wished to kill you is compelled to believe, 795. On the revelation of the head of St John the Baptist, 931, 940.

Arnobius.—Polycarp, a most steadfast and flourishing martyr, was burned to death; Notes, V, 747. Peoples, tribes, and nations who saw these things performed before their eyes believed them and handed them on as matters to be believed by posterity, 792. The whole world was filled with Christian religion in a short time, 793. Heralds of the Christian religion, sent throughout the entire world, offered their limbs and entrails to be torn apart, 794. Simon Magus is reported to have been hurled down from the lofty air by St Peter, 828.

Lactantius.—It could not happen that divine reason should become known to human beings by themselves; therefore God did not permit humanity, seeking the light of Wisdom, to wander for long and roam without any fruit of labour through inextricable darkness. At last he opened their eyes and made knowledge of truth his gift, so that he might show that human wisdom is nothing and point out to one wandering and straying the way to attain immortality, VI, 113. The Sibyl foretold Christ and other matters of the Christian religion, 491–498; 505–513. Just as Christ, while he lived among human beings, put all demons to flight with a word and restored minds disturbed and maddened by evil assaults to their former senses, so now his followers expel those same unclean spirits from human beings by their master’s name and by the sign of his Passion. For when sacrifices are offered to their gods, if someone bearing the sign upon his forehead is present, the rites by no means obtain favourable results: “Nor can the consulted prophet give responses,” 532 and 886. Christians prefer to be tortured and killed rather than cast incense, grasped with three fingers, into the brazier, 610–611. When demons occupy human bodies and torment souls, Christians adjure them and drive them away in the name of the true God. On hearing this, they tremble, cry out, and declare that they are being burned and beaten; and, when asked who they are, when they came, and how they crept into a human being, they confess. Thus compelled and tortured by the power of the divine name, they depart, 623. When Nero was already emperor, Peter came to Rome and, working certain miracles by God’s own power, granted him by God, converted many to righteousness and established for God a faithful and enduring temple, VII, 195–196. Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God upon his shields and thus enter battle. He did as commanded, and, with the letter X set crosswise and its topmost point bent round, he marked Christ on the shields. Armed with this sign, the army takes up its weapons. The enemy advances to meet it without its emperor and crosses the bridge. The battle-lines clash frontally. The fighting is vigorous on both sides. Neither side knows flight. An uprising occurs in the city . . . Then suddenly the people cry aloud that Constantine cannot be defeated, 261. As Licinius slept, an angel of God stood by him, warning him to rise quickly and pray to the most high God with his whole army; victory would be his if he did so. After these words, when he seemed to himself to rise, and to stand with the one who warned him, that one then instructed him how and with what words he should pray, 264. Very many marvels are reported in the work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, 190–275.

Eusebius Pamphilus.—The emperor Constantine declared that at the midday hours, while the sun inclined toward the west, he saw with his own eyes in the sky a trophy of the cross formed from light, placed above the sun, bearing this inscription: “By this conquer,” in the *Life of Constantine*, VIII, 22–23. Just as in the days of Moses and the once-devout nation of the Hebrews God cast Pharaoh’s chariots and army into the sea and covered them with waves, so indeed Maxentius, persecutor of Christians, and all around him—soldiers and guards—fell like a stone into the deepest whirlpool of the Tiber, 25–26. Wherever the sign of the cross was present in battle, victory was won, 38. Of those bearing the cross, whoever fled was killed; whoever remained faithful escaped unharmed, 39. Constantine obtained victory while praying in his tent, 40.

Fortunatus.—St Hilary drives serpents from the island of Gallinaria; raises an infant who died without baptism; obtains by prayer the death of his daughter Abra and his wife, IX, 190–192. By the aid of St Hilary’s relics, the dying Probianus is healed; two lepers are cleansed by dust from the tomb. A contracted hand is healed, sight is restored to a blind person, a woman’s withered hand is made sound, many miracles occur in one girl, and miracles occur through a candle, 195–199. In St Hilary’s presence, heretical devices cannot succeed, 190.

St Zeno.—He healed the daughter of the emperor Gallienus from an evil spirit; brought oxen and their driver, who had been submerged, back from the sea; freed many from a pestilential enemy; raised a dead man taken from a river; destroyed many idols by frequent fasts; his power over demons was great, XI, 131, 154. In the city of Verona, on the feast of St Zeno the martyr, when the waters of the River Adige rose as high as the upper windows of his church, they could not enter it, displaying the martyr’s power, 155.

St Optatus.—Julian the Apostate, a profane and sacrilegious emperor, died by God’s just judgment, XI, 969. The Donatists ordered the Eucharist to be poured out for dogs, not without a sign of divine judgment; for the same dogs, inflamed with madness, tore their own masters—guilty, like thieves, of the holy body—with avenging teeth, as though they were strangers and enemies. They also threw a flask of chrism out of a window in order to break it; and although their casting it down assisted its fall, an angelic hand did not fail to lower the flask by spiritual conveyance. Though thrown down, it could not feel the fall; guarded by God, it came to rest unharmed among the rocks, XI, 972. On the martyrdom of Saints Donatus and Marculus, 1015.

St Paulinus.—The voice of a child is reported to have sounded among the people: “Ambrose bishop”; and at the sound of that voice the mouths of the whole people turned and cried aloud, “Ambrose bishop,” *Life of St Ambrose*, XIV, 29. A certain paralysed woman, lying in bed, was carried in a little chair to St Ambrose, and was healed when he prayed and laid his hand upon her, 30. St Ambrose was seized by the clothing by an Arian virgin seeking to drive him from the church. He warned her to fear God’s judgment, lest some evil befall her. The outcome confirmed his words: on the following day he accompanied her corpse to the tomb, repaying insult with grace; and this struck fear into all, 31. Euthymius maliciously prepared a cart in which to drag the kidnapped St Ambrose into exile; but by God’s just judgment Euthymius himself was carried in that cart into the exile he had prepared for St Ambrose, ibid. [Col. 0343] Saints Protasius and Gervasius reveal themselves as martyrs to St Ambrose; when their bodies were raised, a blind man received light and bodies possessed by unclean spirits were cured, returning home with the greatest joy, 32, 37, 93. A certain Arian, seized and tortured by an unclean spirit, began to cry that he wished those who denied the martyrs or did not believe in the unity of the Trinity taught by Ambrose might be tortured as he himself was tortured. But the Arians present, stunned by this utterance, killed the man by plunging him into a pool, adding murder to their unbelief, 32. A man belonging to the Arian heresy saw in church an angel speaking into the ears of St Ambrose as he preached, so that the bishop seemed to announce the angel’s words to the people, 33. Demons confess that not only can they do nothing against St Ambrose, but they cannot even approach the doors of the house in which Ambrose stayed, 34. A certain Arian carrying a sword came as far as St Ambrose’s chamber to kill him; but when he raised his hand with drawn sword, his right arm, stretched out in the air, remained stiffened. Then, after confessing that Justina had sent him, the arm which had stiffened when wickedly raised was healed through the confession, ibid. A boy afflicted by an unclean spirit came to Milan and was not possessed while with St Ambrose; but upon returning he was again afflicted. When the exorcists asked why the spirit had not appeared in him while he was at Milan, the devil confessed that he had feared St Ambrose and therefore withdrawn for a time, waiting in the place from which he had departed until the boy returned, ibid. Emperor Theodosius had promised pardon to the citizens of Thessalonica; but, while the counts acted secretly with the emperor, very many innocent people were killed. When St Ambrose learned of this, he refused the emperor entrance into the church and did not judge him worthy either of the Church’s assembly or communion in the sacraments until he had performed public penance, 35, 36, and 57–59. One possessed by a demon is healed by St Ambrose, 38–39. There are still certain similar miracles in the following passages, 40–46. Valentinian, the prefect, is punished for his insults against St Ambrose, 91. During Titus’s siege of Jerusalem, on the days of Passover the Temple shone every night as though it were day; other marvels were heard, such as a voice from the east saying, “Let us depart from here,” and so forth, XV, 2187–2192. On the discovery and miracles of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, etc., 2100, 2206; XVI, 337–338. On the blind man who received sight, 10191 and 026.

Sulpicius Severus.—In the *Life of St Martin* and in the *Dialogues*, many miracles performed through the intercession of St Martin, and so forth, are read, XX, 159 and 222.

Rufinus of Aquileia.—In the *History of the Monks*, innumerable miracles are reported; see it, XXI, 391–463. A dialectician philosopher is confounded by the simplicity of a certain elder, 469–470. Paphnutius the confessor heals the sick by prayer alone, restores sight to the blind, and heals paralytics, 471. When thieves came by night to the sheepfolds of Bishop St Spyridon to steal sheep and remained bound by certain invisible chains, in the morning he set them free and dismissed them. His daughter Irene had died after receiving a deposit; the person who had entrusted it demanded it back from her father. Since it could not be found—for no one knew where it was—Spyridon hurried to his daughter’s grave and called her by name. Then she said from the grave, “What do you want, father? . . .” “Where did you put the object entrusted to you?” Pointing out the place, she said, “There you will find it buried”; and the father found the object and gave it to the person demanding it, 471. St Helena, Constantine’s mother, makes her way to Jerusalem and proceeds to the place indicated to her by a heavenly sign, in order to find Christ’s true cross. She found three crosses lying in disorder; although the title was present, it did not sufficiently clearly identify the Lord’s instrument of execution. A woman, worn down by severe illness, happened to lie half-dead. Macarius, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, said: “Bring here all the crosses which have been found, and God will now reveal to us which bore the Lord.” After prayer he applied one of the three crosses to the half-living woman, then the second; they had no effect and did nothing. But when he applied the third, the woman suddenly opened her eyes, rose up, recovered the steadiness of her strength, and began to run through the whole house, more lively than when she had been healthy, declaring the Lord’s power, 475–478. Bishop Frumentius among the Indians received from God such grace of powers that apostolic signs were performed through him, and an infinite number of barbarians were converted to the faith, 478–480. A captive woman, having poured out prayer to God, heals the sick little child of a certain noblewoman by invoking the name of Christ God. The parents are converted to the faith; the report spreads; the king himself and the queen of the place summon the captive woman, and they, with the entire kingdom, are converted to Christ, and a church is built, 480–482. St Athanasius, hidden for six years in a dry cistern, escaped after being betrayed, warned by the divine Spirit on the very night when men were coming to seize him, 491. Miracles concerning the attempts of Jews, deceived by Julian, who wished to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem: by an earthquake and fire kindled by God, the Jews were thwarted in their unlawful undertaking, 505–506. A ball of fire running through the middle of a street at Jerusalem moved back and forth, and the sign of the cross appeared on everyone’s garments. These terrifying signs resulted in the destruction of the Jews, 506. A man with all his limbs, especially his feet, withered, was anointed with oil in the Lord’s name and healed; his soles were strengthened. A blind man received sight at the cell of the absent St Macarius. A lioness from nearby brought her cubs to St Macarius; when he understood that the beast was pleading for her cubs’ blindness, he asked God to restore their sight. When it had been restored, they followed their mother back to the cave, 511–512. Unclean spirits are driven out of a girl by five Fathers carried to a certain island of Egypt, and the island’s people are converted to Christ, 513–514. “Woman, where are you hurrying so quickly?” said a certain prefect. “To the field,” she said, “where the Catholic people are assembling.” “Have you not heard,” he said, “that the prefect is going there to kill everyone he finds?” “I have heard,” she replied, “and therefore I hurry, that I may be found there,” 514. How many powers and miracles the disciples of St Antony performed, 517. The empress Justina receives the exile she had prepared for God’s priests, 525.

St Jerome.—A lion came to the monastery at Bethlehem over which St Jerome presided, limping on three feet and holding up the fourth; its sole had been wounded by thorns. It was healed and recovered. Having become tame, it kept company with an ass, and together they performed the household work in the fields. The ass was stolen by merchants. After some time they returned to the neighbourhood, leading the aforesaid ass loaded with merchandise, together with many camels. When the lion saw the thieves of the ass, it drove them away and forced the ass and camels before it to the monastery. The Fathers marvelled, rejoiced that their ass had been returned, and were troubled about the booty of camels. Soon the merchants came and confessed that they had indeed once stolen the ass, and described the lion’s rage against them when it saw them in the fields. Then, peace having been made, they left the ass and took their camels and possessions with them, proceeding on their journey, *Life of St Jerome*, XXII, 204–214. Those wishing to die were not permitted to be killed. Thus one martyr, victorious amid racks and red-hot plates, was smeared with honey and placed beneath the blazing sun with his hands tied behind his back, so that he who had overcome burning pans might yield to the stings of flies. Another, entangled in the soft bonds of garlands, was placed on a bed piled with feathers amid white lilies and red roses. A beautiful prostitute began to embrace his neck with seductive caresses . . . What was Christ’s soldier to do, and where could he turn? Pleasure overcame the man whom tortures had not conquered. At length inspired from heaven, he bit off his tongue and spat it into the face of the woman kissing him; and so the greatness of the pain that followed overcame the sensation of lust, XXIII, 20. As Paul rested at night, it was revealed to him that there was another, far better than himself, farther on, whom he ought to go and see, 22. After Paul and Antony had exchanged a holy kiss and greeted one another by name, as they conversed, they saw a raven alight upon a branch of a tree. It then flew gently down and set a whole loaf before their astonished faces. After it had departed, Paul said: “Come now, the Lord has sent us a meal—truly kind, truly merciful. For sixty years now I have always received a half-loaf; but at your arrival Christ has doubled the ration for his soldiers,” 25. Paul asks Antony to fetch the cloak of St Athanasius in order to wrap his body after death, 26. Antony sees Paul, gleaming in snowy whiteness, ascending on high amid companies of angels and choirs of prophets and apostles, 27. When Antony was distressed because he had no hoe with which to dig the earth, two lions came running from the interior desert, their manes flowing down their necks. They halted in a straight run beside the body of blessed Paul. Waving their tails ingratiatingly, they lay down around Antony’s feet; roaring with a great growl, plainly so that he might understand that they mourned as best they could. Then not far away they began to scrape the ground with their paws, and, throwing up sand in rivalry, dug a space large enough for one person. Immediately, as though demanding payment for their work, with ears moving and heads lowered, they came to Antony, licking his hands and feet. He recognized that they were asking his blessing . . . Afterwards he ordered them by a gesture of his hand to depart, 27–28. St Hilarion puts the mockeries of demons to flight by signing the cross of Christ upon the forehead, 31. Robbers coming by night to St Hilarion could not find the place of his cell from evening until sunrise, [Col. 0345] 33. A barren woman has a son through St Hilarion’s intercession, 33–34. A blind woman brought to St Hilarion receives sight, 35. A charioteer, struck by a demon in his chariot, became completely rigid, and St Hilarion heals him, ibid. Marsitas, possessed by a demon, is healed by St Hilarion, ibid. Likewise a paralytic, 36. Other similar miracles of St Hilarion are reported, 37–39, 46, 49–50.

Lucius Dexter.—Miracles of St James the Apostle in Spain, XXXI, 115. St Veronica comes to Rome and dies there, renowned for miracles, 161. St Mary Magdalene dies in Gaul, renowned for miracles, 255. St Eutychus, whom St Paul had raised after he fell from a window, dies a martyr in Spain, 299.

S. AUGUSTINE.—To Monica, the mother of St. Augustine, anxious and grieving over her son’s wicked ways, it was said in a dream: “Where you are, there your son also will be”; and a certain bishop answered her: “Go away from me; as surely as you live, it cannot be that the son of such tears should perish,” XXXII, 692, 693. “I was weeping,” says St. Augustine, “in the most bitter struggle of my heart, and behold I heard a voice from a neighboring house, chanting and repeatedly saying, ‘Take up, read; take up, read.’ I arose and opened the book, to read the first passage I should find; I read the passage on which my eyes first fell: ‘Not in reveling,’ etc.; and at once all the darkness of doubt fled away,” 762. A miracle performed through the aid of Severinus the bishop’s niece, XXXIII, 426. By a vision God revealed to St. Ambrose the place in which lay hidden the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, XXVII, 770. The body of St. Stephen was revealed by divine disclosure through St. Ambrose, XXXVIII, 1299, 1438. This discovery was attended by many miracles. “I was at Milan,” says St. Augustine; “I learned of miracles that had occurred. A blind man, very well known to the whole city, received sight; he ran, had himself led there, and returned without a guide,” 1299. Through St. Stephen’s prayers Paul and his sister Palladia were healed, as follows: A certain woman had ten children; the eldest afflicted her with grievous and intolerable wrongs, and even laid hands upon her. The other children, present, kept silence. The mother, proceeding to the font of sacred baptism, asked God that, exiled from their country and wandering through foreign lands, they might frighten all mankind by their example. Immediately trembling of the limbs seized the eldest son; and within one year—preserving the order in which they had been born—the same punishment overtook them all. The second son obtained healing at the shrine of the glorious martyr Lawrence. Paul, sixth in order, together with his sister, after they had been admonished by a divine vision concerning their future recovery, received healing: Paul was praying at the place where, at Hippo Regius, stands the memorial shrine of the holy martyr Stephen; suddenly he fell down; shortly afterward he rose and found that the trembling was no longer in his body. While St. Augustine was preaching, the people began to cry out from the shrine of St. Stephen, “Thanks be to God! Praise to Christ!” Amid that uninterrupted cry Palladia, Paul’s sister, who had been healed, was brought to the apse. When they saw her, the people, with joy and tears, prolonged their shouting for some time, with no words interposed, but only a tumultuous outcry, 1443, 1444, 1446; XLI, 769, 770. Very many miracles are related in Book XXII of *The City of God*, XLI, 763–771.

JOHN CASSIAN.—The power of the Lord’s Cross against demons, XLIX, 700.—Miracles of Abbot Abraham, 1000. A demon openly confesses that he spread heresies through Arius and Eunomius, 715, 716. For various reasons demons possess human bodies, 707. On demons, 197, 238, 560, 602, 681, 695, 698, 707, 712, 733, 751, 752, 761.

ST. HILARY OF ARLES.—On the miracle of St. Genesius, martyr of Arles, I, 1273–1276.

IDATIUS.—Appearance of the Savior’s Cross in the East under Constantine the Great, in the year 351, LI, 909.

MARCELLINUS.—Signs in heaven in the year 389. The marvelous revelation of St. Stephen’s relics, made to the presbyter Lucian in the year 415, LI, 923.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—All who are afflicted with fevers, pestilences, or the bite of a rabid dog and come to the tomb of St. Peter Chrysologus are healed; in the *Life*, LII, 39, and frequently elsewhere.

POPE ST. LEO.—Attila and Genseric are restrained from hostile intent by the dignity and appearance of Pope St. Leo, and suddenly prepare to depart, LV, 280.

VICTOR OF VITA.—Two brothers die as martyrs, LVIII, 244. A woman torn by harsh tortures so that she was thought dead, upon being touched by a certain virgin who arrived, was immediately healed, 244. Very many miracles are related, 234–260. The martyrdom of St. Julia, 579–580 and 391–420. Sixty confessors, among whom was St. Reparatus Vigilius, speak as they had spoken before, although their tongues had been cut out, 245.

[Col. 0346] DRACONTIUS.—Peter’s greatest miracles, LX, 856. He confounds Simon Magus flying through the air, 858.

PAULINUS OF NOLA.—Gennadius was renowned for power over demons, LXI, 71. A miracle performed at the discovery of the Holy Cross removes every doubt, 329. Valgius was saved from shipwreck, 399, 400. Many other miracles are related, 671, 672, and 909.

ST. SEVERINUS.—A certain man laid at St. Severinus’s feet his son, afflicted by a daily sickness. Then, after prayer had been offered, he who had been brought in half-alive immediately rose, to his father’s astonishment, and at once returned in complete health; in the *Life*, LXII, 1192. Through St. Severinus’s prayers a leper is cleansed by divine help, 1292; and very many other miracles are cited in the *Life*, 1170–1200.

GUIBERT.—St. Eleutherius raises the tribune’s son; he himself, bound in chains, is freed by an angel; he gives sight to a blind man and heals a leper; an angel, at his request, reveals to him the sin committed by Louis, king of the Franks, LXV, 67–69. At the burial of St. Eleutherius’s body, a blind and mute woman recovered sight and speech, 75. At the elevation of his body, a dead man was raised; two blind persons received the sight of their eyes; three paralytics were healed; a lame man was strengthened and walked, leaping, 75–79. By his intercession Feriolus, who was imprisoned, was released, and Libertinus was raised from death; and in the city of Tournai, to which his body was translated, new miracles occur day after day through the merits of this saint, 80–82.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.—On the miraculous discovery of the head of St. John the Baptist, LXVII, 419–454.

ST. CAESARIUS OF ARLES.—A boy is raised through his prayers; in the *Life*, LXVII, 1015. Elpidius the deacon, harassed by a diabolical assault, is freed by St. Caesarius from that affliction; in the *Life*, 1016. A paralytic woman, contracted in all her limbs, is healed; in the *Life*, 1018. Several other miracles are related, 1018–1020. Innumerable other miracles, performed by St. Caesarius both during life and after death, are indicated, 1025–1042.

AURELIUS CASSIODORUS.—The Emperor Constantine, considering what god might assist him in war, saw in sleep the sign of the Cross brilliantly displayed in heaven; and angels stood by the astonished beholder of the vision, saying: “O Constantine, conquer by this.” It is also reported that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the Cross, and commanded him to make a likeness of it and possess this aid in battle, by which he might win the rights of victory. Eusebius Pamphilus reports, having heard the emperor himself state this under oath, that about midday, when the sun was already declining, he and the soldiers then with him saw a sign of the Cross made of light, together with an inscription saying, “Conquer by this,” LXIX, 888. The sign, transformed into a standard of the Cross and called the Labarum, was displayed in battle before all the ranks; and marvelously, under divine governance, the enemies’ arrows were fixed in the sign, while the standard-bearer immediately escaped through the dangers, 888, 889. Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine, warned in a dream, hastened to Jerusalem and sought there for Christ’s tomb. When the Lord’s monument had been openly revealed, three crosses buried near it appeared, together with nails and a title inscribed in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” It is said also that a dead man rose at the touch of the Cross, and that a woman exhausted by a long illness, touching the true Cross, was healed, 936, 937. On the marvels which happened when the Jews, through the instigation and support of Julian the Apostate, began to rebuild the temple of Jerusalem, and on the causes for the cessation of the work, 1058, 1059. A miracle concerning demons fleeing at the signing of the Cross, 1030. Julian the monk, a most holy elder, knew in prayer of the death of Julian the Apostate at the hour when he was struck down, 1061. A missile suddenly hurled, passing through Julian the Apostate’s arm, was embedded in his side. From this wound he met the end of life. But who inflicted the most righteous wound is still unknown. They say, however, that when he had been wounded, he at once filled his hand with his own blood and threw it into the air, saying: “Galilean, you have conquered,” 1066. Other miracles are described, LXX, 1297.

ST. GREGORY OF TOURS.—In the *Life of St. Gregory, Bishop of Tours*, Abbot Odo, his biographer, records many miracles, LXXI, 115–130. Likewise the books of miracles: *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, 705; *On the Miracles of St. Julian*, 800–828; *On the Glory of the Confessors*, 828–912; *On the Miracles of St. Martin*, 913–1010; *Lives of the Fathers*, 1010–1096. The history of the Seven Sleepers, 1107–1118; the *Life of Abbot Aridius*, 1118–1150.

VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS.—*Life of St. Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, LXXII, 55–78; LXXXVIII, 454–479. On St. Maurice and his companions, on St. Hilary, Medard, etc., 108–130. On St. Martin, 328–333. *Life of St. Hilary of Poitiers*, 440–454; *Lives of Saints Albinus, Paternus, Radegund, Amantius, Remigius, Medard, Marcellus, Leobinus, and Maurilius*, 482–576.

LIVES OF THE DESERT FATHERS.—The *Life of St. Paul the First Hermit*, by St. Jerome; the *Life of Abbot Antony*, by St. Athanasius; the *Life of the Monk St. Hilarion* and the *Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk*, by St. Jerome; and the lives of others contain many miracles, LXXIII, cols. 89–882. The *Sayings of the Elders* and the *Lausiac History*, which follow, likewise relate innumerable miracles, 882–1234. Philotheus or Theophilus, the *Spiritual Meadow*, Heraclides’ *Paradise*, and Palladius’ *Lausiac History* likewise relate many miracles, LXXIV, 15–394. At the end of the aforesaid volumes, LXXIII and LXXIV, the subject index gives in detail the names and deeds of each saint. Whoever wishes knowledge of these matters should consult that index; lest we become too lengthy, we ought not to provide it here, nor elsewhere where we merely indicate the *Lives of the Fathers*.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—In his two *Lives*, one by Paul and the other by John the deacons, many miracles performed by him are related, LXXV, 41–242. Likewise in the four books of the *Dialogues*, where the lives and miracles of the Italian Fathers are treated, LXXVII, 150, 430.

ST. AUGUSTINE, ENGLISH BISHOP.—Many miracles are read in his *Life*, written by the monk Goscelin, LXXX, 43–94.

PAUL OF MÉRIDA.—The *Life of the Fathers of Mérida* contains many miracles, LXXX, 118–164.

VARNAHARIUS (ST.).—The *Acts* of the triple martyrs Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus relate many miracles performed by them, LXXX, 185–195. The *Life and Martyrdom of St. Desiderius* likewise contains many miracles, 195–198.

SISEBUT.—The *Life and Passion of St. Desiderius the Monk* has appended certain miracles performed by St. Desiderius during life and after death, LXXX, 377–384.

ST. SULPICIUS.—His *Notice* relates many miracles performed by him both during life and after death, LXXX, 575–592.

ST. ISIDORE.—Certain miracles performed by him after death are related in the *Prolegomena*, LXXXI, 147, and in the *Appendix*, 943–967, and LXXXII, 19–56.

ST. DESIDERIUS OF CAHORS.—Twelve distinct miracles are related in his *Life*, LXXXVII, 239–246.

ST. FRUCTUOSUS.—Miracles are related in his *Life*, LXXXVII, 460–470.

ST. ELIGIUS OF NOYON.—His miracles are read, LXXXVII, 482–593.

JONAS.—*Life of St. Columbanus*, LXXXVII, 1012–1046. *Life of St. Eustace*, 1046–1056. *Life of St. Attala*, 1056–1062. *Life of St. Bertulf*, 1061–1069. *Life of St. Burgundofara*, 1070–1083. *Book of the Miracles of St. John, Abbot*, 1083–1088. There, throughout, more frequent miracles performed by these saints are found; to any reader they will seem wonderful and astonishing.

ST. ADAMNAN.—On the life, revelations, and apparitions of holy Columba, LXXXVIII, 726–776.

ST. ALDHELM.—Faricius writes many miracles concerning him in the *Life of St. Aldhelm*, LXXXIX, 64–88.

ST. BONIFACE.—His *Life*, written by Willibald, contains many miracles, LXXXIX, 604–664.

THE VENERABLE BEDE.—His *Ecclesiastical History* relates certain miracles performed by various holy men, which may be seen in the index to that history, XCIV, 23–292; XCV, 132–138 and 222–234.

ST. LEODEGAR.—A great light, like the circle of a wheel, descended from heaven and shone over St. Leodegar’s head. Then all who saw this sign trembled and said: “What is this, lord, which appears above your head: a most brilliant light, sent from heaven in the form of a circle? We have never seen anything like it in our lives,” XCVI, 343. The history of his translation relates certain miracles then performed at his tomb, 344–346. The lives and miracles of five holy abbots and of St. Cuthbert, 713–789. The appearance of St. Michael and miracles performed, 1387–1394.

ST. ILDEFONSUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO.—His life and miracles are related, XCVI, 43–54. The Blessed Virgin Mary appears to and speaks with St. Ildefonsus, 50.

KING DAGOBERT.—Three martyrs appeared to him in dreams, XCVI, 1398.

CLOVIS, KING OF THE FRANKS.—On miracles shown to him, XCVI, 1438.

DIONYSIUS, PRIEST.—He reports that a certain monk always lit a lamp before the image of holy Mary ever-Virgin, and upon returning after the third, fifth, or even sixth month found it unextinguished, XCVIII, 1205.

ST. LUDGER.—The *Life of Abbot St. Gregory* by St. Ludger, and the acts of St. Ludger written by Altfrid, contain miracles concerning both St. Gregory and St. Ludger, XCIX, 749–795.

[Col. 0348] ALCUIN.—On the life of St. Martin of Tours: as a catechumen, he clothed a poor man in the winter cold with half his cloak; and in that same portion of the cloak, divinely enlightened, he saw the Lord Jesus clothed amid the angelic hosts on the following night, CI, 659. A certain catechumen attached to him was suddenly snatched away by death while the holy man was absent; St. Martin, pouring out prayers, raised him and, after restoring him to life, baptized him. He likewise restored to life by holy prayers another man who had hanged himself with a rope in a field. A third, the weeping son of a certain woman, he raised by prayer alone in the sight of the people, 659, 660. He turned aside a falling pine tree from himself by opposing the sign of the Cross, and made the astonished crowd believe in Christ. He placed himself upon the roof of a certain house against flames, so that the harmless roofs might not be injured by the fire that burned an idolaters’ shrine; and another temple, dedicated through ancient error to demons, which human hand could not overthrow, he overthrew with angelic assistance. Elsewhere, while overthrowing pagan rites, he was attacked with a sword by a pagan; he bared his neck to the striker’s blow, but the impious man fell backward and, recognizing his own impiety, sought pardon from the saint. When another man was raising a stroke against the saint’s head, the weapon slipped from his hands. A paralyzed girl, whose whole body was disabled, he restored to her former health before the people by the application of blessed oil. By laying on of hands he freed a proconsular official’s servant from a demon, etc., etc., 660, 661. A certain blind man met St. Vedastus, asking him to restore the light of his eyes through the prayers of his holiness. St. Vedastus poured forth prayers and, trusting in divine mercy, placed his right hand, with the sign of the Cross, before the blind man’s eyes, saying: “Lord Jesus, who are the true light, who opened the eyes of the man born blind, open also the eyes of this man, so that this people now present may understand that you alone are God, who work wonders in heaven and on earth.” Immediately the blind man, having received sight, went rejoicing on his way, 670. Miracles of St. Richarius, 690–694. Miracles of Willibrord, 702. The miracle concerning Christ who was to come, seen by Caesar Augustus, 1174.

EGINHARD.—History of the translation of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, and various miracles which followed it among deaf and mute persons, the crippled, and other sick people, CIX, 537–590. Miracles through the intercession of Saints Protus, Hyacinthus, and Hermes in the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, CIV, 590–594.

HILDUIN.—The passion of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and miracles related concerning the same, CVI, 23–50.

DUNGAL.—Demons roar before the relics of saints, CV, 474. A blind man is healed by the power of the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, 475. A miracle performed at Milan in the times of Augustine and Ambrose, 477.

AGNELLUS.—In the *Pontifical Book*, containing the lives of the Roman pontiffs who flourished from St. Apollinaris to St. George—that is, Saints Apollinaris, Aderitus, Eleucadius, Martianus, Calocerus, Proculus, Probus, Dathus, Liberius, Agapitus, Marcellinus, etc., etc.—many miracles are related as performed by them during life or after death, CVI, 475–750.

JOSEPH THE PRIEST.—In the history he supplied concerning the translation of the bodies of Saints Ragnobert and Zeno, many miracles are related, CVI, 891–904.

RABANUS MAURUS.—Miracles are performed through the relics of St. Alexander and certain other saints, CVII, 44–68. He himself performed many miracles; for it is reported that by his prayers he gave sight to two blind men, enabled four lame men to walk, cast demons out of several human bodies, and was distinguished by many other miracles; in his *Life*, 94. St. Maximinus, presiding over the church of Aix, shone forth in many and diverse miraculous powers, CXII, 1494. On the miracles of the sisters Mary and Martha, 1495–1508.

WALAFRID STRABO.—In the *Life of Abbot St. Gall* he relates innumerable miracles, during the saint’s life and after his death, CXIV, 979–1030. Likewise in the *Lives* of Saints Othmar, Blathmac, and Mamma, 1031–1062. Visions of angels and demons in the metrical *Life of Wettin*, 1068–1082. On the miracles of St. Leodegar, 1143–1151.

OLDRIC, BISHOP OF LE MANS.—Many miracles are found in his *Life*, CXV, 29–106.

ST. EULOGIUS.—He sets forth thirty-six distinct miracles performed at the two translations of the holy martyrs George, Aurelius, and Nathalia, CXV, 948–960.

HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT.—It is said that, to fulfill the desire of Abgar, king of the Edessenes, the Lord in some measure impressed his face upon a linen cloth and sent it to him, so that he who could not be seen in his own form might at least be seen through an impressed image. Thus Thaddaeus, the disciple sent to Edessa, had the privilege of bringing there the aforesaid image of the Lord; it remained there for a long time, until it was carried to Constantinople with the other relics, CXVIII, 825. Agabus, one of the prophets, prophesied concerning a coming famine under Claudius, 826.

[Col. 0349] When divine vengeance pressed upon the Jews, it did not allow Pilate either—who, in the death of Christ, performed the office of an unjust judge—to go unpunished. Thus, tortured by Gaius with many disasters and evils, he finally pierced himself with his own hand and condemned himself to death, 827. Herod, the murderer of James, the Lord’s brother, while giving spectacles at Caesarea in honor of Caesar, clothed with extreme arrogance in a garment wonderfully woven with gold and silver, was suddenly called a god by the amazed people because of the radiance of the gleaming metal; they begged him to be propitious. But because he did not check this acclamation and pride, he was immediately struck by an angel and seized with incredible pain and swelling of the belly; looking at his friends, he said: “Behold me, your god; behold, I am immediately struck down and taken from life,” 828. The fraud of Simon Magus exposed and extinguished by St. Peter, 828. Nero, the most cruel emperor, who advanced to such a degree of crime that he became a parricide against his mother, his brothers, his wives, and all those nearest to him by blood, and committed incest, persecutes Christians especially, 830. At the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus Vespasian, the church of the faithful that had assembled in Jerusalem, having received a divine response, forestalled the destruction and emigrated beyond the Jordan to a town named Pella. Then an incredible slaughter of the Jews occurred; first, an intolerable plague of dreadful and unheard-of famine was divinely sent, so severe that wars and killings were committed between parents and children as they struggled to snatch food from one another not only from their hands but from their very mouths. At last they spared neither straps nor belts nor even their shoes; some even ate stalks of old hay. Moreover, an abominable deed occurred there, not previously heard of either among Greeks or barbarians. A certain woman named Mary, when the peril of famine grew severe and she was wholly exhausted by hunger amid the enemy’s plundering, following the worst counsel, slaughtered her little son, who was at her breast, and roasted him over a fire; she consumed one half and reserved the other. But when the raiders soon entered, having detected the odor of the flesh, she offered them a portion, saying: “This is my own offspring; do not become more scrupulous than a mother or more tender than a woman; eat, for I have eaten first.” Immediately the entire region was filled with the report of so wicked a crime. Not long afterward the magnificent and most famous city of Jerusalem was taken. How great its devastation was can scarcely be comprehended in writing: eleven hundred thousand persons killed by famine and the sword are reckoned there, apart from chosen young men reserved for triumph because of their bodily beauty, and other persons assigned to Egyptian labor, to cutting marble, or to extracting metals, or sold in chains into slavery throughout the provinces; their number amounted to ninety thousand, 832, 833. Also, at that time, during the destruction of Jerusalem, a heifer brought for sacrifice on the feast day of Unleavened Bread gave birth to a lamb in the hands of the ministers. The gate in the court of the inner sanctuary, though so heavy that scarcely twenty men could close it, secured with bars and bolts, opened of itself at night. Chariots and companies of armed men were also seen borne through the air, and many other things, 833. The words of St. Ignatius the martyr are related, 837. On St. Polycarp, the distinguished martyr, 840. Marcus Aurelius makes war upon the Sarmatians and Germans; when his army was endangered by thirst, certain Christian soldiers present implored God. Through their supplications a copious rain poured from heaven refreshed the army, while frequent flashing bolts of lightning drove the enemies away from a distance, 845. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, turned water into oil when, by chance, oil was lacking for the lamps on the solemn day of the Paschal vigil, 846.

ST. ANSGAR.—He relates many miracles performed by St. Willehad after death; after such a narration he says: “Lest the account become too lengthy and burdensome to readers, we have omitted these and many other things, which nevertheless are commonly reported among the people by the mouths of very many persons. His body, magnificently placed in the basilica, shone with innumerable indications of miraculous power; and day by day, through the merits of the blessed man, manifold signs of miracles there increase,” CXVIII, 1022–1032.

ST. LUPUS OF FERRIÈRES.—There are certain miracles in the *Life* which he wrote of St. Maximinus, CXIX, 665–680; many indeed in the *Life of St. Wigbert*, 680–694.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS.—He relates certain marvels in the passion of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius, CXX, 1489–1507; likewise in the *Lives* of St. Adalhard and Abbot Wala, 1508–1556 and 1557–1650.

WANDALBERT.—Many miracles are related in the *Life of St. Goar*, CXXI, 639–658; likewise in the *Translation of the Relics of the Holy Martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria*, 673–682; and in the book *On the Miracles of St. Othmar*, 779–795. Likewise in the metrical *Life*, *Translation*, and *Elevation* of St. Amandus, 931–977.

ST. ADO OF VIENNE.—A certain leper, in the people’s sight, was cleansed of leprosy by the touch of St. Desiderius, bishop of Vienne. From the day when St. Desiderius entered the island on which he endured exile, a little lamp full of oil, which had been lit by his hand through divine power, remained unfailing, always burning and making its undiminished fullness evident to all; and anyone of whatever sickness who was anointed by the holy bishop from that liquid immediately departed healed, CXXIII, 437.

[Col. 0350] An empty little vessel of wine was immediately found full, through St. Desiderius’s confidence in the goodness of God and the generosity of the Creator, 438. Queen Brunhild, who ordered St. Desiderius cruelly killed, was herself, by God’s just judgment under King Clothar, tied to untamed horses by her arms, her legs spread apart, and torn limb from limb, 439.
