Miracles occur at St. Desiderius’s tomb. A certain poor man, contracted in every limb and, further, shaken by a grave affliction of trembling limbs, was carried in a wicker basket to the shrine of St. Desiderius and immediately returned uninjured in perfect health, ibid. A man named Claudius had a daughter who had long limped in one leg; he came and entrusted his daughter to St. Desiderius to be healed; once she had been anointed with his oil, she became completely sound and lost the distortion of her lameness, ibid. It cannot be said how many blind persons there received unaccustomed sight, how many demoniacs were cleansed, lame persons healed, and persons suffering from various illnesses cured in various ways. Moreover, if anyone with faith carries away a splinter from the wood by which that holy head was pierced and by which the martyr died, through his merits they are freed from toothache, from the attack of various fevers, or from other illnesses [lacuna]. A woman afflicted for many years by an unclean spirit was dragged there by the hands of her relatives; as soon as she reached St. Desiderius’s place, she was immediately healed by divine power, 439, 440, 441. A man blind from birth received unaccustomed sight at St. Desiderius’s tomb, in the presence of the whole church. And afterward the Lord worked many things there through his servant, which, if anyone wished to write them all, would fill a volume of great length, 444, 442. St. Theuderic builds a cell by means of a miracle, 446. An angel appeared to St. Theuderic, designating for him a secluded place in which to build a monastery, 447. The Lord glorified St. Theuderic through miracles, so that many persons vexed by malignant spirits and held by various illnesses were healed through his prayers, 448. When St. Theuderic’s body, placed in a bier, was to be carried to burial, it could not be moved from the spot; but once it was decided that it should be carried to his own monastery rather than to the other place first determined upon, it was immediately moved with such ease that it seemed to have no weight at all, 448. When a blind man touched the covering of St. Theuderic’s bier, blood immediately flowed from his eyes and he received sight, 449. A certain man, so contracted in his limbs that the soles of his feet adhered to his buttocks, returned on his own feet from the holy tomb, 450. At the translation of St. Bernard, when the limbs of this holy bishop were raised from the tomb, they seemed to the elders to be washed with wine, from which many benefits were afforded to the sick. We saw demoniacs and lunatics, having drunk of this liquid, recover their strength after the demonic assault had been calmed, 451, 452. Seven other miracles are related with their proofs and circumstances, 451, 452.

USUARD OF SAINT-GERMAIN.—Many miracles are listed in his *Martyrology*, 599, etc.

ADREWALD.—History of the translation of St. Benedict and of miracles, CXXIV, 901–948. *Life of St. Aigulf*, 956–968. Miracles of St. Germanus, 1208–1270.

ADREWALD, MONK.—Miracles of St. Benedict, 905 and following. Miracles of St. Aigulf, 965 and following.

ODO OF BEAUVAIS.—How the relics of Saints Maximus and Julian are made illustrious by miracles, 1124.

HERIC, MONK.—Miracles of St. Germanus, 1161–1211 and following.

HINCMAR OF RHEIMS.—*Life of St. Remigius of Rheims*, CXXV, 1130–1188.

ST. BERTARIUS.—St. Scholastica, bowing her head into her hands and pouring streams of tears upon the table, changed the serenity of the air into rain so that her brother St. Benedict would not yet leave her; and she said to him: “Behold, I asked you, and you would not hear me; I asked my Lord, and he heard me,” CXXVI, 983, 984. When St. Benedict had returned to the monastery, he saw the soul of that same sister leave her body in the form of a dove and penetrate the hidden places of heaven, 986.

V. — On False Miracles.

It is certain that Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, performing astonishing signs in order to overthrow, if possible, even God’s elect; that demons, as subtle spirits, can be everywhere in an instant; that the whole world is one place to them; and that they can know as easily what is done everywhere as they can report it. Hence their swiftness is believed to be something divine. They seem to be the authors of what they announce. Through dwelling in the air, proximity to the stars, and intercourse with the clouds, they know heavenly matters and promise certain predictions of seasons; hiding also beneath the names and images of the dead, they produce belief in divinity by certain signs, and imitate deity itself when they steal divination. They further hid themselves in pagan temples, beneath statues and images, that they might thus obscure truth with darkness, direct the flights of birds, regulate lots, produce oracles mingled with numerous falsehoods, and accommodate ambiguities to events. Nor is it surprising that formerly they knew God’s plans, since they received them while prophets preached; nor that they know them even now, since they snatch them up when readings of Holy Scripture resound. Unable to distinguish their deceits from truth, profane people thought that empire, victories, wealth, prosperous outcomes, and deliverance of the state from imminent dangers were granted by them. Hence the Romans and all other pagans maintained that their gods were true gods, because they had again and again demonstrated their divinity and omnipotence by astonishing signs, miracles, prophecies, oracles, divinations, and certain deeds which appeared to surpass all the powers of created things.

And these things, which they thought had occurred outside the customary order of nature, had so bewitched their eyes and minds that they were entirely convinced that they must be attributed to the power of the gods alone. But what follows shows that this argument is advanced and pressed only by those who did not know the true cause of those effects. Once empty prejudices had been set aside, they could have recognized that all these things had been done by the extreme agility of demons, by evil arts, tricks, frauds, and illusions through which these lying and impure spirits utterly deceived unwary people. To this must also be added the fact that the pagans could not deny that many acts similar to the extraordinary deeds of their supposed gods had been performed by persons devoted to magic through the tricks and frauds of these same demons. Who, then, unless mad, would for that reason call them true gods? The nature and weight of the arguments by which the Fathers refuted these things may be seen in the works of the early Fathers: namely, Tertullian, *Apology*, I, 404–432, and *Dissertations*, 874–899; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, III, 312–331, and *Dissertations*, 589–645; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, IV, 568–575; *To Demetrianus*, IV, 541–564; Commodian, *Poem against the Gods of the Gentiles*, V, 202–282; Arnobius, *Disputations against the Nations*, V, 714–1290; Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, VI, 330–341, and *Dissertations*, 823–1016; and so forth.

TERTULLIAN. — Croesus, king of Lydia, sent messengers to various oracles of the gods to consult them and ask what he himself was doing in Lydia. When he had received the responses of each, he approved none except that of Delphic Apollo, who declared by this answer the things he was in fact doing: “He has cooked together a tortoise and a lamb cut into pieces in a bronze cauldron, with a bronze lid placed upon it,” 409, 878. When the same Croesus was considering making war on the Persians, he consulted Delphic Apollo, whose temple he had adorned with countless riches and offerings, about the future outcome of that war, and received this entirely ambiguous answer: “Croesus, having crossed the Halys, will destroy a great force of wealth,” 409, 878. Likewise Pyrrhus, when he consulted the oracle, received this ambiguous answer from the prophet: “I say that you, Pyrrhus, can conquer the Romans,” 409, 877–878. The apparition of the Castors means that demons assumed the likeness of Castor and Pollux, and thus by their innate swiftness announced at Rome, on the very day it was won, the famous Roman victory over King Perseus, 410. A Tuscan woman carrying water in a sieve, 409 and 876. Claudia moving a ship with her girdle, 410, 876.

[Col. 0357] A beard made reddish by touch: Castor and Pollux appeared to Lucius Domitius, so that he might announce the victory to the people and Senate; and, as proof of divine majesty, his beard was changed from black to ruddy and bronze-coloured, 410 and 876. On Romulus’s ascent into heaven, 402 and 863. Goats and tables divining through the deceptions of demons, 411. Aesculapius prolongs the life of Socordius, Thanatius, and Asclepiodotus, 413, 414, and 883. Goats and tables give oracles, 410, 879, 880, 881, 882. Mercury was believed to cure, by appropriate remedies, men afflicted by the assault of demons, 413, 887. Despair and destruction, as a cause of glory and fame, were among the Romans a standard of courage: Empedocles gave his whole self to the fires of Mount Etna at Catana; Dido, founder of Carthage, gave herself to the pyre rather than a second marriage; Regulus, lest one man should live in place of many enemies, endured crosses with his whole body; Mucius willingly left his right hand upon the altar; an Attic courtesan, when the executioner was already weary, finally spat out her bitten-off tongue into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might spit out her voice as well, lest she be able to confess her fellow-conspirators even if she wished, once overcome; and so forth, 532–533. Cleonymus Pyctes was healed in a dream, II, 729. False visions through dreams, 727–731.

MINUCIUS FELIX. — Miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, dreams, and other extraordinary events among the pagans did not proceed from the power of their gods but from demonic frauds and deceptions, III, 297–298. The wonderful, monstrous miracles of the pagans: the many-formed Scylla, the manifold Chimera, the regenerating Hydra, the Centaurs, Jupiter, Apollo, Isis, Ceres, 299. On Romulus, Juba, Alexander, and others, 301–302, 310. Flaminius and Junius are said to have lost their armies because they did not think it necessary to await the most solemn sacred dance of the chickens; nor should the rashness of the Roman consul Claudius in the First Punic War be forgotten. Since he obtained no auspice of good omen, he ordered doves, exhausted by fasting, to be placed before him on the route he was to take, after wheat grains had been scattered, so that he might alleviate the unfavourableness of the auspice at least by their omen. When they refrained still more diligently from food, he ordered them to be thrown into the river, “so that they might drink, since they would not eat”; and, drowned in the river, they showed that the consul with his army was to be drowned. Such indeed was the subsequent outcome. Yet Regulus, Mancinus, and Paulus observed religion, and events turned out badly for them. Caesar, however, although auguries and auspices opposed his sending ships to Africa before winter, disregarded them; and he sailed and conquered all the more easily. But what, and how much, should I relate about oracles? 320–321. On Pyrrhus, Croesus, and others, 610.

ST CYPRIAN OF CARTHAGE, bishop and martyr. — A woman, walking barefoot amid harsh snows in severe winter, was neither hurt nor distressed by her wandering; it was discovered that she did such things through an evil spirit, III, 1162–1165. Dreams and foolish visions, IV, 407. Among individual nations and provinces, the various religion of the gods changes. On Alexander the Great, and so forth, 568–575. Demons by their breath inspire the breasts of prophets, direct the flights of birds, produce oracles, always mingle falsehood with truth, are deceived and deceive, disturb life, trouble sleep, and so forth, 572–574.

COMMODIAN. — He treats in verse the ridiculous miracles accepted by the pagans: for example, that Saturn devoured his children and, when Jupiter was born, ate a stone in place of the infant; the stones cast into the empty world by Deucalion and Pyrrha; and so forth, V, 204 and following.

ARNOBIUS. — The pagans alleged many miracles performed by the gods and answers given about future events: that a miracle had been performed on account of the Circensian Games while plague devastated the city; that the plague had at last been calmed because of the statue of Aesculapius; that the Capitol had been struck by lightning and the statue of Jupiter cast down from its place; and so forth, V, 604–607. On astonishing things attributed to Aesculapius, Mercury, and others, 964–971. On the razor cut by the augur, on Juno, Claudia, Ceres, and so forth, 972. On Aesculapius of Epidaurus, and so forth, 1278–1280. “But,” the pagans say, “the Great Mother, summoned from Phrygian Pessinus by similar commands of the prophets, was salutary to the people and a cause of great rejoicing. For an enemy long powerful was driven from possession of Italy; by glorious and illustrious victories the city’s former honour was restored; the boundaries of the empire were extended far and wide; the right of liberty was taken from countless nations, cities, and peoples, and the yoke of slavery imposed; and many other things accomplished abroad and at home established with irresistible firmness the name and majesty of the nation,” 1283–1284.

LACTANTIUS. — And indeed many things worthy of wonder may be enumerated. First, that when Attus Navius, the chief augur, warned Tarquinius Priscus not to undertake anything new unless he had first obtained augural sanction, the king, disparaging confidence in his art, told him to report, after consulting the birds, whether what the king had conceived in his mind could be done. When Navius affirmed that it could: “Take, then,” said the king, “this whetstone and cut it apart with a razor.” Navius took it without hesitation and cut it. Then there is the story that Castor and Pollux, during the Latin War, were seen beside the Lake of Juturna washing the sweat from their horses, when their shrine adjoining the spring opened of its own accord. The same pair, during the Macedonian War, are said to have appeared, mounted on white horses, to Publius Vatienus as he came to Rome at night, announcing that on that day King Perseus had been defeated and captured—a fact which letters from Paulus confirmed a few days later.

Also marvellous is the tradition that the statue of Womanly Fortune spoke more than once; likewise that of Juno Moneta, when Veii had been captured and one of the soldiers sent to transfer her asked jestingly and playfully whether she wished to move to Rome, replied that she did. Claudia too is presented as an example through miracles. When the Idaean Mother had been summoned in accordance with the Sibylline books, and the ship in which she was carried had stuck in the shallows of the Tiber and could not be moved by any force, Claudia—always thought unchaste because of her excessive bodily adornment—is said to have prayed, kneeling, to the goddess that, if she judged her chaste, she should follow her girdle. Thus the ship, which all the young men had been unable to move, was moved by one woman. Equally wonderful is the report that, when plague raged, Aesculapius summoned from Epidaurus freed the city of Rome from its enduring pestilence.

Sacrilegious persons can also be numbered, upon whom the gods were believed to have avenged their injuries by immediate punishments. Appius Claudius the Censor, because contrary to an oracle he transferred the rites of Hercules to public slaves, was deprived of sight; and the family of the Potitii, which had handed them over, was extinguished within a year. Likewise the censor Fulvius, when he removed marble roof-tiles from the temple of Juno Lacinia in order to roof the temple of Equestrian Fortune which he had built at Rome, lost his reason and, after his two sons serving in Illyricum had died, was consumed by extreme sorrow. Turullius, prefect of Mark Antony, after building a fleet at Cos from the sacred grove of Aesculapius which he had cut down, was later killed in that same place by Caesar’s soldiers. To these examples is added Pyrrhus, who, after taking money from the treasury of Proserpina of Locri, suffered shipwreck and was dashed upon shores near the goddess, so that nothing except that money was found unharmed.

Ceres of Miletus likewise greatly increased the reverence accorded her among men. When Alexander captured the city and soldiers burst in to plunder her, an oncoming flash of fire suddenly put out the sight of them all. Dreams also occur which seem to show the power of gods. Jupiter is said to have appeared in sleep to Tiberius Atinius, a commoner, and commanded him to report to the consuls and Senate that at the most recent Circensian Games the performer who danced before the procession had displeased him, because one Antonius Maximus had led a whipped slave to punishment under a fork through the middle of the circus; therefore the games had to be repeated. When Atinius neglected this command, he lost his son that same day and was himself seized by a grave illness. When he saw the same apparition again asking whether he had sufficiently weighed the penalties for neglecting the command, he was carried in a litter to the consuls; after setting forth the whole matter in the Senate, he recovered his bodily strength and returned home on his own feet.

No less remarkable was the dream by which Caesar Augustus is said to have been saved. When, in Brutus’s civil war, he was suffering severely from illness and had decided to abstain from battle, an appearance of Minerva appeared to his physician Artorius, warning that Caesar should not remain in the camp on account of bodily weakness. Therefore he was carried into battle in a litter, and on that same day Brutus captured the camp. Many further similar examples might be adduced; but these suffice concerning them, VI, 288–292. The whole art and power of magicians consists in the breathings of demons. When invoked, these demons deceive human sight with blinding illusions, so that people do not see the things which are and think that they see those which are not. These polluted and ruined spirits wander over the whole earth and make the destruction of men a consolation for their own destruction. They therefore fill all things with snares, frauds, tricks, and errors. They cling to individual people, occupy every house door by door, and assume for themselves the name of household spirits. Since they are subtle and incomprehensible spirits, they insinuate themselves into human bodies and, secretly working within the organs, corrupt health, provoke diseases, terrify minds with dreams, and shake intellects with madness, so as to compel people under these evils to have recourse to their aid, VI, 332–333.

Wandering and unchaste demons, in order to trouble all things and spread error over human hearts, sow and mingle falsehoods with truths. Hence the stone was cut by the augur’s razor; Juno of Veii replied that she wished to move to Rome; Womanly Fortune announced danger; the ship followed Claudia’s hand; and Juno when stripped, Proserpina of Locri, and Ceres of Miletus punished sacrilegious persons; likewise Hercules punished Appius, Jupiter Atinius, and Minerva Ceres. Hence the serpent summoned from Epidaurus freed the city of Rome from plague, 337–341.

EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS. — Apparitions were seen in the cities subject to Licinius, VIII, 38.

JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS. — The constant opinion of the ancient Christians was that demons hid beneath statues and images, XII, 1613. On Serapis, the Palladium, and others, XII, 1011–1024.

CASSIODORUS. — Licinius, intending to fight Constantine, hoped for victory through divinations and sacrifices. It is said that he then tested the divination of the Milesian and Didymaean Apollo; and, when he consulted him about the war, the demon replied in these two verses written in Greek by Homer:

> “Old man, warrior youths greatly watch over you,  
> and your life is loosed, and cruel old age will receive you.”

LXIX, 891. After the death of Julian the Apostate, magical practices were discovered. Those entering the temple found strange images of the emperor; they saw a woman hanging by her hair with her hands extended, whose womb he had opened in order to inspect Persian victory in her liver. At Antioch they say that many chests in the palace were found filled with human heads, and that innumerable corpses had been sunk in wells. After his death, all cried together: “Most foolish man, where are your prophecies? God and His Christ have conquered,” 1003–1004.

ST GREGORY THE GREAT. — A certain wealthy Roman, after abandoning his wife, had been excluded from communion by St Gregory, bishop of Rome. Bearing this most grievously and unable to nullify the authority of so great a pontiff, he sought the aid of magicians. Persuaded by great gifts that they could by their spells arrange for a demon to be sent, and for the pontiff’s horse to be tormented until it and its rider were endangered, they confidently promised it. Delighted by this promise, the wicked judge allowed the magicians to stand beside the route on which the pontiff was going to proceed to the station, in an elevated place, so that they might see passers-by without being seen by them.

When, from the processions of mourners and those carrying cloths, the magicians recognized the great pontiff, they sent in a demon and caused his horse to be so violently tormented that it seemed it could never be held by its rider or by the grooms. Then St Gregory, recognizing through the revelation of the Holy Spirit the demonic attack, freed the horse from its immediate madness by the holy sign of the cross; and, ordering the evildoers to be brought down from their hidden height, he punished them with perpetual blindness, LXXV, 104.

ALCUIN. — At one time St Vedastus visited on horseback a certain woman devoted to God, and, having mounted his horse, was preparing to return home. But the aforesaid woman, following in the footsteps of the father as he rode, offered her son to St Vedastus. When he received the child, the horse became savage and, gnashing its teeth here and there, kicking with its feet, and raging with its whole body, began to race across the field with unwonted violence. But when St Vedastus prayed, the boy was unharmed and the horse was restored to its gentleness. The mother received her son, sound and laughing, into her arms from the ground. Yet St Vedastus thereafter chose to travel not by horse but by a most gentle ass. Thus, by God’s mercy, the temptation of the malignant enemy was turned for him into an occasion of honourable praise, and the horse’s pride, caused by a demon, became for St Vedastus a lesson and teacher of humility, CI, 687–688.

HAYMO. (From St Augustine, Epistle 86.) — A certain Simon of Samaria, the head of all perversity and origin of every heresy, was raised up under the emperor Claudius by magical arts and the help of demons; in the city of Rome he was decreed to be a god and received the honour of a statue, set up between the two bridges of the river Tiber, bearing also an inscription in Latin words: “To Simon the holy god.” But he did not endure long, once the fraud had been divinely exposed, CXVIII, 828. At Alexandria the huge temple of Serapis was thrown down. In it was such an immense image of Serapis that its right hand touched one wall and its left another; this monster was said to have been composed from every kind of metal and statue. They said that on appointed days it was greeted by the sun, because it had been contrived so that, through a tiny window, a ray of the sun would shine directly upon its mouth and lips before the people watching. At the same time, an image of the sun made from exceedingly fine iron was moved downward by a lodestone fixed above in the ceiling and drawing it, and then was raised higher, as though to greet Serapis. But when Christians rose to overthrow this image, they were for a little while deterred by fear, because the pagans confidently asserted that, if a human hand touched it, the earth would immediately split open and dissolve into chaos, and heaven would fall headlong [Col. 0360]. Then, behold, one of the soldiers, burning with faith, seized a battle-axe and struck it against the cheek of the crafty old impostor . . . Thereupon Serapis was torn apart and burned; and then the fraud was discovered: through underground passages a prophet entered the statue to deliver oracles, and many other pagan deceptions were then exposed, 873–874.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona. — How the devil can perform certain marvels by magical arts, CXXXVI, 153–154. The power to do so comes to them only by God’s permission, 154. You have, on St Augustine’s authority, that demons can do much through that angelic nature of theirs—things which they nevertheless cannot do when forbidden by God—but can do nothing unless power is granted from above—whether to deceive the deceitful, as the Egyptians, whose like are those who either venerate the devil’s deceptions as divine or seek them as beneficial, although far more detestable than these are those who practise them, indeed those through whom they are practised, as though they were powers, 157.

OLIVA, bishop of Vic. — Since demonic possessions have a certain appearance of miracle, although they occur only by God’s permission, and since after the third century of the Church no other false miracles are adduced save the astonishing acts performed by bodies tormented or possessed by demons, it may suffice at last to recount one outstanding example of the demons’ audacity and cunning in deceiving souls which devote themselves to evil. It is the example of holy Afra and her companions, prostitutes, who, on account of their manner of life, although they were not visibly mad as the possessed commonly were, nevertheless were truly possessed, being bound in diabolical chains. This will appear when the demon claimed them for his own power and maintained that they were his property.

There was a bishop Narcissus in the time when Diocletian’s madness prevailed. Not knowing where to enter, he fled into the house of a prostitute named Afra, together with his deacon Felix. When hope appeared for the amendment and conversion of Afra and her companions, and Narcissus and Felix were praying, there appeared a certain Egyptian, blacker than a raven, naked and covered over his whole body with the sores of elephantiasis. He began to bellow and say: “O holy bishop Narcissus, what have you to do with my dear Afra? What have you to do with my handmaids, whom I have always kept in my friendship? Your God loves clean souls and clean bodies; these women are now mine and cannot belong to another. Do I enter where chastity reigns? Do I find a place where the spirit of chastity is? Why have you entered here, where bodies are defiled and souls polluted?”

Then Narcissus said to him: “I command you, unclean spirit, to answer what I shall ask you. Tell me, accursed one: do you know my Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth, tempted, scourged, and so forth?”

The demon answered and said: “Would that I had been permitted not to know this! For at the hour when he was crucified, our Prince fled from before his face and cast himself into the temple of God; and therefore the veil of the temple was torn, then the rocks, and so forth, because our prince was crucified by him, was seized, and bound with fiery chains.”

Narcissus answered and said: “What is the name of your prince?”

The demon said to him: “His name is Satan.”

Narcissus said: “Tell me: what sin did our Lord Jesus Christ commit, that he suffered such things?”

The demon said: “Did he commit sin?”

Narcissus said: “And why did he who never sinned suffer so much?”

The demon answered: “He suffered not for his own sins, but for another’s.”

Narcissus said: “By your own mouth you condemn yourself, unclean spirit. Therefore, since you know that my Lord Jesus Christ was killed not for his own sins but for the sins of others, depart from these women, since he suffered for those who flee to his faith and grace.”

The demon said: “Why does the holy law teach and command that no one take another’s property, while you, who are holy, take what is mine? Why do you take from me souls which I have gained for myself?”

Narcissus said: “You are both breaker and thief, accursed and inveterate one, from the beginning; for you separated these souls from their Creator and Lord. I now hold you as a thief and restore the creature to its Creator.”

The demon answered him: “I too am his creature; therefore restore me also to my Creator.”

Narcissus said: “You yourself have confessed with your own mouth that Christ suffered for human sins. If he had suffered for the sins of men in such a way that he also suffered for the demon, I would restore you to your Creator. But now he suffered for human sins in such a way that he bound your prince in hell and stripped him of his dominion.”

The demon said: “Now command me to remain here this night.”

Narcissus said: “If you can remain with us, remain.”

The demon said: “If you stretch out your hands to heaven, bend your knees, and sing psalms to your God, I cannot remain here.”

Narcissus said: “May it never go well with you, unclean spirit. Not I alone, but all these people will bend their knees with me all night before our Lord and sing his praises together with us.”

Then the demon, uttering a most hideous howl in a dreadful voice, appeared nowhere, CXLII, 593–597.

ST GREGORY VII, pope. — In the Life, or Passion, of St Tiemo [Col. 0361] it is read: When the martyr Tiemo had been cruelly tortured amid torments and had died, men tried to lift the holy martyr’s limbs from the ground. But God made them weighty, like the huge foundations of mountains, and not even the smallest member of a finger could be lifted by any contrivance of the gentile crowd. When the king heard of this miracle, he and his followers were terrified that they had perpetrated so unheard-of a murder. Having taken counsel, he sent to his adviser, the most abominable idol named Machmit. He reported what had happened and asked what still ought to be done. The idol is said immediately to have given this reply:

“Great and mighty is the God of the Christians, for after death he grants his witnesses life in the kingdom of heaven. Behold, it is clear that the man whom you killed was his most intimate friend, and therefore you can have no power over those limbs. Therefore, since you cannot do so, grant permission to the Christians that they may zealously bury him honourably as their greatest Father, and may rejoice that, having deserved to have him as bishop while he lived, after death they have him as a worthy patron.”

The returning messengers conveyed to their king the answer which they had heard, CXLVIII, 903–904.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres. — The finger of God, as certain writers have thought fit to say, stirred up Vespasian, ravager of Judaea and father of Titus, the pious destroyer of Jerusalem, by miraculous signs to execute vengeance among the nations. (For our part, we consider these miracles fabricated, or rather false.) For while he was not yet emperor, a man of the people, blinded in his eyes, and another man lame and weak in the leg, came together before him as he sat upon the tribunal, praying for help in their infirmity, because it had been shown to them in sleep that the former’s sight would be restored if Vespasian looked upon him, and the latter’s weak leg strengthened if he deigned to touch it with his heel. At his friends’ entreaty, though unwilling, he tried both; and the result did not fail, CXCIX, 426.

What need be said of necromancers, whose impiety, God being its author, has now everywhere become contemptible of itself, except that those are worthy of death who endeavour to borrow knowledge from death? As for diviners from birds, augurs, soothsayers, female Pythonists, haruspices, and others whose number makes their enumeration tiresome, it is superfluous to compose a longer discussion, since none of these now comes forth into the light; if any does exist, he practises works of darkness in hiding. Haruspices, as has been said, divine in part from the entrails of animals. Palm-readers also boast that they know truths concealed in the wrinkles of hands. Consultation of Pythonists is all the more ruinous because in them the deceit of evil spirits is more manifest; whether they lie or not, they always intend harm. At times they deceive from a desire to deceive, at times because they themselves have been deceived by the error of their blindness; yet they work incessantly to appear fully aware of future things. Hence they strive to obscure oracles by ambiguity of words, so that, when found false or deceptive, they may seek to protect their deception with some covering of plausible argument. Thus indeed they do not cease from deceiving until they plunge their hearers into ruin. For whose benefit, since the beginning of the world, have the answers of seers been—Croesus’s, Pyrrhus’s, or anyone’s, whether before or after them?

The Theban commander, while hoping for victory from the oracle, is pierced by his brother’s sword. Yet his grandfather Laius seemed to have promised success in war. For what else could this mean, after many evasions, than:

> Victory for Thebes is certain.

But lest, after the commander’s death, he should be charged with lying, he added, to cover his deceit with an ambiguous token of truth and so protect his malice:

> Alas for me! The father conquered by swords. . . .

Croesus confidently believes that, if he crosses the Halys, the greatest kingdoms will be made subject to him on the faith of the oracles. But when events turned out contrariwise, deceitful Apollo freed himself from the charge of lying by the equivocation of a single little word. And Pyrrhus? Having defeated the Romans, whom he had often routed in battle by valour, he promises himself dominion through Phoebus’s favour; but, being irretrievably overthrown, he turned the blame upon himself, because he had understood the oracle’s ambiguity to his disadvantage, etc., 461–462.

[Col. 0362]

ST MARTIN OF LEÓN, priest. — Before we bring this question concerning false miracles to an end, we shall adduce a testimony admirably arranged, so that the end may crown the work. When it is properly understood, as we have already noted in the works of the earliest Fathers, it will shine forth wonderfully that very many miracles of pagans, heretics, and even schismatics must be attributed to demons, and that no credence should then be given to them, whatever they may wish to prove. Accordingly St Martin of León says:

“Good angels are so confirmed by grace that they cannot sin; and evil angels are so darkened by vice that they cannot live rightly. Although evil angels are thus obstinate in malice, they are not wholly deprived of lively perception. For, as St Isidore teaches, demons possess a threefold sharpness of knowledge: by the subtlety of their nature, partly by the experience of times, and partly by revelation from the higher spirits. Magical arts also are practised through this knowledge, although both their knowledge and their power are given by God, whether to deceive the deceitful, to admonish the faithful, or to exercise and test the patience of the righteous.

“Thus blessed Augustine says: ‘I see what may occur to weak-minded thought as to why such miracles are performed by magical arts. For Pharaoh’s magicians also made serpents, and many other things besides. But this is more to be wondered at: how did the power of the magicians, which could make serpents, wholly fail once it came to the tiniest flies—that is, gnats (*sciniphes*)? Why, then, could the magicians not make gnats, except because there was present the greater sovereignty of God forbidding it through the Holy Spirit?’ This the magicians themselves confessed, saying: ‘This is the finger of God’: that is, God’s manifest power works these miracles.

“This vanity of magical arts, as blessed Isidore says, prevailed for many centuries throughout the whole world by a tradition of evil angels, through a certain knowledge of future and hidden things and through their evocations. Haruspicy, augury, and the practices called oracles and necromancy were also invented. Nor is it surprising in regard to magicians’ tricks, since their arts of maleficence advanced so far as even to resist Moses with most similar signs, changing rods into dragons and waters into blood.

“The first of the magicians was Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, slew in battle. Aristotle wrote of him; the contents of his books show that he himself composed two hundred thousand verses. Many centuries later Democritus enlarged this art, at the same period when Hippocrates’ medical discipline flourished. A certain most famous sorceress, Circe, is also said to have changed Ulysses’ companions into beasts (Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII, 70). We likewise read of a sacrifice which the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus; whoever partook of it was changed into the forms of beasts.

“Hence it clearly appears beyond all doubt what that noble poet writes of a certain woman who excelled in magical arts; for he says:

> Behold, by spells she promises to release the minds  
> Whom she chooses; but to send harsh cares into others;  
> To halt waters in their rivers, and turn the stars backwards;  
> And summon the nocturnal shades. You will see the earth  
> Bellow beneath your feet and ash-trees descend from the mountains.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 487.

“What more? If it is lawful to believe, the Pythoness called forth the soul of the prophet Samuel from the depths of hell and presented it to the sight of the living—if indeed we believe it to have been the prophet’s soul, and not some phantasmal illusion wrought by Satan’s deceit.

“Prudentius likewise says of Mercury:

> He is said thereby, by the guiding power of his wand,  
> To have recalled extinguished souls to the light . . .  
> Yet to have condemned others to death.

“And shortly afterward he adds:

> For a harmful art knew how, by magical murmur,  
> To call forth tenuous shapes,  
> And skilfully to enchant sepulchral ashes,  
> And likewise to strip others of life.

“In all the things mentioned above, therefore—and we say the same—there is an art of demons, arising from a pestilential fellowship of human beings and evil angels. Hence all such things are to be avoided by Christians and utterly rejected and condemned with every execration,” CCVIII, 566–567.

[Col. 0363]

## VI.—ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF THE FATHERS COLLECTED IN THE PRECEDING INQUIRIES SOLELY IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

[Col. 0363] Abbo (St), CXXXIX. Adalbert, CXXXVI. Adamanus (St), LXXXVIII. Adam of Bremen, CXLVI. Adam the Persian, CCXI. Ademar, CXLI. Ado (St), CXXIII. Adrewald, CXXIV. Adso, CXXXVII.
