## LVII. MYTHOLOGICAL INDEX, OR AN ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED INDEX OF THE GODS, GODDESSES, AND PAGAN SUPERSTITIONS

### Notice

In this Index we list, in alphabetical order of names, all the gods and goddesses to whom pagans of old rendered divine worship, a practice which the Fathers very often reproached them for. The Roman numeral refers to the volume and the Arabic numeral to the column where these various superstitions are attacked or even ridiculed.

### [MYTHOLOGICAL INDEX]

## A

**ABEONA**, a goddess. Tertullian, I, 600. — St Augustine, XLI, 128, 196.

**ABROXAN**, whom Basilides said was the supreme God. Tertullian, II, 62.

**HAWK**, worshipped by the Egyptians. Lactantius, VI, 786.

**ACDESTIS**, fabulous birth. Arnobius, V, 1089. — Acdestis, despiser of gods and men, ibid., 1089, 1090, 1091, 1095. — He inspires terror in the gods, ibid., 1089. — He loves Atys, ibid., 1090, 1091. — He deprives himself of manhood, ibid., 1091. — His death, ibid., 1110, 1113.

**ACHAMOTH**, Valentinus’s Aeon. Tertullian, II, 68, 564, 568, 571 ff.

**ACHERON**, a river. Arnobius, V, 831.

**ACHERUSIAN ENTRANCES.** Arnobius, V, 1141.

**ACHAEAN GODS.** Wars between the gods of the Achaeans and Trojans. Tertullian, I, 351.

**ACINAX.** The Scythians worship the *acinaces* [short sword] as a god. Arnobius, V, 1185.

**ACRISIUS** was buried in the earth in the citadel of Larissa. Arnobius, V, 1173.

**ACTAEON**, the horned hunter. Arnobius, V, 986. (Text and note.)

**ADEONA**, a goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 128, 196.

**Apollo tended the flocks of King Admetus.** Tertullian, I, 352.

**ADONIS.** Arnobius, V, 1059, 1266. — Adonis changed into a boar by Mars. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1004.

**ADORATION OF RULERS.** Arnobius, V, 940.

**AEACUS.** Arnobius, V, 1167. — Aeacus, judge of the underworld. Lactantius, VI, 804.

**AEGERIA**, the nymph regarded as Pompilius’s wife. St Augustine, XLI, 233.

**EGYPTIAN GODS.** Every superstition derives from Egypt. Tertullian, I, 640. — Authors to consult concerning Egyptian superstitions. Lactantius, VI, 282. — The Egyptians were the first to teach metempsychosis, ibid., 405. — On their worship of animals, ibid., 620, 786. — They consecrated sheep and beasts: Tertullian, I, 418; they worshipped them, ibid., II, 596. — They condemned to death those who killed one of them, ibid., I, 418. — The Egyptians’ gods: ibis and crocodile, ibid., II, 302. — Egyptian bulls as high priests, ibid., 928, 953. — Egyptian hierophants, ibid., 260. — Egyptians are superstitious. Arnobius, V, 958–959. — By law they prohibited anyone from making public the place where the hidden Apis lay, ibid., 1176. — Egyptians were the first to begin observing and worshipping the stars. Lactantius, VI, 328. — They worshipped the sun under Jupiter’s image, ibid., 621.

**AENEAS**, how undeservedly he was called pious and a god. Tertullian, I, 599. — He betrayed or abandoned his country, ibid., 598. — Cowardly, he did not appear after the battle of Laurentum, ibid., 599.

**AEONS** of the Valentinians. Tertullian, II, 47, 68. — Of the Ophites, ibid., 64.

**AIR.** Worship of air among the Assyrians and certain peoples of Africa. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 989.

**AESCULAPIUS.** Aesculapius’s birth: Arnobius, V, 760, 944; Lactantius, VI, 160. — His upbringing, ibid., 160. — Son of Apollo and Coronis, or Pharonis, or Arsinoe, born with uncertain paternity. Tertullian, I, 352; Arnobius, V, 1279. — The deeds by which he deserved divine honours. Lactantius, VI, 160. — A holy god: Arnobius, V, 1279; a physician: Arnobius, V, 770, 1245; St Augustine, XLI, 128; St Isidore, LXXXII, 314. — Discoverer of herbs. Arnobius, V, 760, 764. — Guardian and protector of health. Arnobius, V, 770, 781, 912, 1279. — Summoned from Epidaurus to Rome. Arnobius, V, 1279; St Augustine, XLI, 254. — When Aesculapius sailed to Rome, an Epidaurian serpent accompanied him [Col. 0366]. St Augustine, XLI, 294. — Aesculapius both man and god, ibid., 254. — Why he perished struck by lightning. Lactantius, VI, 160. — Struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt on account of medicine and greed. Tertullian, I, 352; St Cyprian, IV, 225; Arnobius, V, 1048. — The Athenians worshipped Aesculapius and his mother. Tertullian, I, 605. — A temple consecrated to Aesculapius on a mountain of Libya. St Augustine, XLI, 254. — His priests wore a pallium. Tertullian, II, 1031. — And sandals with rattles, ibid. — They ministered standing. Tertullian, I, 612. — A cock consecrated to Aesculapius. Tertullian, II, 648; Lactantius, VI, 97. — Questioned by Christians, he will confess that he is a demon. Tertullian, I, 413. — Aesculapius prolongs the lives of Socordius, Denatius, and Asclepiodotus, although they were to die the next day. Tertullian, I, 413. — Bearded Aesculapius. Lactantius, VI, 273. — Aesculapius’s grape-harvest. Arnobius, V, 1263. — Aesculapius with a staff. Arnobius, V, 1213. — Three Aesculapiuses, ibid., 1031.

**AFFERENDA**, a goddess. Tertullian, I, 601.

**AGDIR** or **ABDIR**, a stone or goddess worshipped in the form of a stone image. Lactantius, VII, 496 (note). The same as the stone which Saturn is said to have swallowed in place of Jupiter. Lactantius, VII, 497 (note).

**AGDUS**, a stone god. Lactantius, VII, 496.

**AGENORIA**, a goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 122, 125.

**Αἰγιοχός** (*Aigiochos*), an epithet of Jupiter: “Aegis-bearing.” Lactantius, VI, 240.

**ALAGABUS**, a stone god. Lactantius, VII, 497 (note).

**ALBANA**, a goddess. Tertullian, I, 600.

**ALBUNEA**, a Sibyl. Lactantius, VI, 144.

**ALBURMIS**, a god. Tertullian, I, 290. — Discovered by Metellus, ibid., II, 266.

**ALCIDES.** Arnobius, V, 1266.

**ALCMENA.** Arnobius, V, 924, 1043, 1126.

**ALECTO**, a Fury of the underworld. St Augustine, XLI, 88.

**ALLEGORIES CONCERNING THE GODS.** Arnobius, V, 1147 ff.

**PROFANE ALTARS.** St Cyprian, IV, 152.

**AMALTHEA**, the nymph believed to have nursed Jupiter as an infant. Lactantius, VI, 240.

**AMALTHEA**, the Cumaean Sibyl. Lactantius, VI, 143.

**AMBROSIA**, the food of the gods according to the poets. Lactantius, VII, 282.

**AMMUNDAS.** Commodianus the African, V, 215.

**AMPHIARAUS.** Oracle of Amphiaraus at Oropus. Tertullian, I, 730.

**AMPHILOCHUS.** Oracle of Amphilochus at Mallus. Tertullian, II, 730.

**AMPHION.** The story of Amphion. St Augustine, XLI, 570.

**AMPHITRITE.** Arnobius, V, 1054.

**AMPHITRYON.** Arnobius, V, 1265.

**ANTAEUS.** The story of Antaeus. St Augustine, XLI, 570.

**ANTELII**, demons. Tertullian, I, 684; II, 97.

**ANTINOUS**, a god. Tertullian, I, 600; II, 266.

**ANTIQUITY** considered very many authors to be gods as well. Tertullian, II, 649.

**CAVE OF JUPITER** in Crete. St Cyprian, IV, 225.

**ANUBIS**, a god. Tertullian, I, 597; St Augustine, XXXII, 750. — Anubis, a god with a dog’s face. Arnobius, V, 1214.

**APIS**, third king of the Argives. St Augustine, XLI, 563. — Apis became Serapis, the greatest god of the Egyptians. Tertullian, II, 261; Arnobius, V, 761; Lactantius, VI, 235; St Augustine, XLI, 563; St Isidore, LXXXII, 323. — Apis has a bull’s head. Lactantius, VI, 472. — Egypt worshipped the bull in honour of Apis. St Augustine, XLI, 563. — Apis was a symbol of Joseph. Lactantius, VI, 235. — Where he was worshipped, ibid., 621. — Buildings of Apis in Egypt. Tertullian, II, 261. — Authors to consult concerning him. Lactantius, VI, 621. — Among the Memphites he was a symbol of the moon, ibid.

**APOLLO**, twofold. St Augustine, XXXII, 983. — Apollo, delicate and beardless [Col. 0367]. Tertullian, I, 574. — He tended King Admetus’s flocks. Tertullian, I, 352; St Cyprian, IV, 225; Arnobius, V, 1054; St Augustine, XLI, 571. — Among the Greeks Apollo is called **πυραῖος** (*pyraios*, “of the fire/pyre”). Tertullian, I, 684; II, 97. — Apollo’s oracles, ambiguous and deceitful, ibid., 408. — Worshipped at Delphi because he killed a dragon, ibid., II, 85. — His priests do not marry, ibid., 1284. — He did not defend Delphi from Pyrrhus, ibid., 607. — The Apollinarian games, ibid., 638. — Apollo: Arnobius, V, 747; St Isidore, LXXXII, 314, 319. — Enriched, he deceived men through the ambiguity of his response. Arnobius, V, 1028. — Robbed by brigands, ibid., 1209. — Apollo Clarian, Didymaean, Philesian, Pythian, ibid., 747–748. — Son of Latona, ibid., 1054. — Pythian, ibid., 748, 968, 985. — Sminthian, ibid., 985. — Divine, ibid., 1209. — Musician, ibid., 1245. — Not always worshipped at Rome, ibid., 929. — Apollo, Liber, and Sol are one deity, ibid., 985. — The pagans considered the testimonies of Milesian Apollo divine. Lactantius, VI, 138. — His testimony concerning God, ibid., 149. — Why he was called Sminthius, ibid., 151. — Why he performed a shepherd’s task, ibid., 161. — With Neptune he built the walls of Troy, ibid., 161; St Augustine, XLI, 79. — How he killed Hyacinthus, ibid., 161. — Why called Milesian, ibid., VI, 484. — His testimony concerning Christ, ibid., 485. — Colophonian Apollo, ibid., 148. — Apollo worshipped by the Milesians. Lactantius, VII, 443. — Apollo’s shameful deeds. Lactantius, VI, 160–161. — Apollo, brother of Diana and also said to be the Sun. St Augustine, XLI, 207. — Apollo ignorant of the future, ibid., XLI, 79. — Oracle concerning Pyrrhus, ibid., 94. — Apollo’s oracle disparaged Christ, ibid., 620, 653. — Cumaean Apollo is said to have wept for four days, ibid., 86. — What the haruspices said about Apollo’s weeping, ibid., 86. — Apollo fought for the Trojans, ibid., 79. — Why Apollo holds arrows, ibid., 207. — Why musical games were instituted for Delphic Apollo, ibid., 569. — Apollo is painted as an ephebe, ibid., 184. — Apollo, god of medicine together with Aesculapius, ibid., 129. — Diviner and physician, ibid., 207. — Apollo, son of Latona, tended King Admetus’s cattle with Hercules, ibid., 571. — Distinct from the Apollo who delivered oracles, ibid., 571.

**APOLLONIUS OF TYANA.** St Augustine, XXXIII, 383, 514. — Much greater than Jupiter, ibid., 533. — Some attempted to compare Apollonius of Tyana with Christ or even to rank him above Christ, ibid., 533.

**APOTHEOSIS**, a solemn procession. Tertullian, I, 451. — Its origin. Lactantius, VI, 192 ff. — Authors to consult concerning its rites, ibid., 193.

**WATER.** Pagans believed that water had healing power through religious rites. Tertullian, I, 1205. — Their “widowed waters,” ibid., 1204. — The devil broods over them in streams and springs . . . imitating the things of God, ibid., 1205. — Pagans purified villas, houses, and whole cities by sprinkling water carried round them, ibid., 1204 ff. — In the Apollinarian and Eleusinian games, they immersed themselves in water for regeneration and exemption from punishment for their perjuries, ibid., 1205. — Worship of water among the Egyptians. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 984.

**EAGLE**, why dedicated to Jupiter. Lactantius, VI, 183. — On its worship among the Egyptians, ibid., 787.

**AQUILICIUM**, sacrificed to Jupiter. Tertullian, I, 487.

**GODS OF THE ARABS.** Tertullian, I, 418. — Arabs worshipped a stone as a god. Lactantius, VII, 494.

**ALTARS OF THE GODS.** Tertullian, I, 347. — Inscriptions naming the gods to whom they were dedicated were written upon the altars, ibid. — Those who breathed over altars, ibid., 413. — Prostitution was conducted even among the pagans’ altars, ibid., 363.

**TREES** planted around the temples of the gods. Tertullian, I, 315.

**ARGENTINUS**, a god, son of the god Aesculanus. St Augustine, XLI, 103.

**ARGIUS**, a god. Tertullian, I, 606.

**ARGUS**, son of Apis, king of the Argives. St Augustine, XLI, 564. — After death Argus began to be regarded as a god, ibid., 564.

**ARIADNE** depicted among the stars. Tertullian, II, 142. — Ariadne’s garland of gold and Indian gems, ibid., 85.

**THE BOW-BEARERS**, Diana and Apollo. Arnobius, V, 760.

**THE BOW-BEARING DELIAN**, Apollo. Arnobius, V, 1042.

**ARSINOE.** Arnobius, V, 1055.

**HARUSPICES.** Tertullian, I, 495. — Haruspices of both gods and the dead, ibid., 347. — Haruspices consulted concerning the death of the Caesars, ibid., 459. — Compared with magicians and soothsayers, ibid., 495, 642.

**Pagans worshipped asses with Epona and Isis.** Tertullian, I, 577.

**The gods of the Assyrians did not protect their kingdom.** Tertullian, I, 608.

**ASTAROTH** and **ASTARTE**, names of Juno. St Augustine, XXXIV, 797.

**ASTARTE**, or Atargatis, Syrian goddess. Tertullian, I, 418.

**ASTROLOGERS.** The arts of astrologers, like those of haruspices, augurs, and magicians, were transmitted by the fallen angels and forbidden by God. Tertullian, I, 459. — Astrologers censured [Col. 0368], ibid., 268; II, 671. — They consulted demons concerning the future death of the Caesars. Tertullian, I, 459.

**ASTRONOMERS.** An astronomer observes Volatica. Tertullian, II, 1050.

**ATABYRIAN JUPITER.** Lactantius, VI, 248.

**ATHENS.** The god of the Athenians, Numentinus. Tertullian, I, 1596. — Minerva did not defend Athens against Xerxes, ibid., 607.

**ATHUS**, son of heaven and earth and father of Saturn. Tertullian, I, 601.

**ATLANTEAN OFFSPRING.** Arnobius, V, 965.

**ATLANTIC NEPTUNE.** Arnobius, V, 727.

**ATLAS**, astrologer and king of Mauretania. St Augustine, XLI, 599. — Why he is imagined to carry heaven, ibid., XLI, 565. — Mount Atlas worshipped as a god by its inhabitants. Lactantius, VII, 404.

**ATTALUS**, king of Phrygia, sent to Rome the stone received as the Great Mother. Arnobius, V, 1283–1284.

**ATTIC IDOLATRY**, what it was. Tertullian, I, 255. — Attic mysteries. Tertullian, I, 474.

**ATYS** or **ATTIS**, a god from Pessinus represented on the stage. Tertullian, I, 576. — Attis, the sun. Arnobius, V, 1157. — His story, ibid., 1095. — His birth, ibid. — Atys, handsome, ibid., 1063, 1093. — Loved by the mother of the gods, ibid., 1093. — Castrated, ibid., 771. — Deprived of his male organs, ibid., 1095, 1154. — Who Atys was. Lactantius, VI, 205. — His loves with Cybele and the nymph Sangaris, ibid. — Atys, a handsome castrated youth. St Augustine, XLI, 185. — The story of Atys, ibid., 215.

**AUGURS**, their origin. Lactantius, VI, 613. — St Isidore, LXXXII, 312.

**AUGURIES** mocked by Cicero. St Augustine, XLI, 136. — Auguries and auspices among the Romans. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 253. — How empty they are, ibid., 320. — Auguries forbidden. St Cyprian, IV, 325. — Auguries held in esteem among pagans. Lactantius, VI, 287. — Their inventor, ibid., 288.

**GOLDEN APPLES** taken from the Hesperides. Arnobius, V, 1122.

**AUSPICES OF VICTORY.** St Cyprian, IV, 33. — St Isidore, LXXXII, 312.

## B
BAAL, a name of Jupiter. St Augustine, XXXIV, 797. BABYLONIAN fires. St Cyprian, IV, 120. BACCHANALIA, monstrous rites. Arnobius, V, 1118.—The Bacchanalia instituted in honour of Father Liber. St Augustine, XLI, 571.—Prohibited by the senate in the city of Rome, ibid.—Tertullian, I, 304, 306. BACCHANTS or BACCHAE: whence they were so called. Lactantius, VI, 163. BACCHUS and Apollo, the same as the Sun. Arnobius, V, 985.—Bacchus called Δεοσάφης (*Deosaphēs*, “god-wise”) among the Arabs. Lactantius, VII, 494.—In what form he was worshipped by them, ibid.—His worship was at times under the figure of a column, ibid., 498.—By what deeds he acquired divine honours, id., 164.—His loves, ibid.—Why he was called Indian, ibid.—His retinue on the Indian expedition, ibid., 164, 995.—The discovery of wine is not to be attributed to him, ibid., 213, 327.—By whom his rites were introduced into Greece, ibid., 247.—Why they were called Orphic rites and Orgies, ibid.—What authors should be consulted concerning them, ibid.—The rites of Bacchus formerly suppressed. Tertullian, I, 304, 306.—The frenzies of the Bacchanalia, in which they spared not even dead Christians. Tertullian, I, 461. BAUBO received Ceres as a guest and cheered her by exposing her private parts. Arnobius, V, 1133, 1134, 1135, 1150. BELENUS, god of the Norici. Tertullian, I, 419, 596. BELLEROPHON: his story. St Augustine, XLI, 570. BELLONA. Arnobius, V, 751.—Goddess of wars, ibid., 972.—Wife of Mars. St Augustine, XLI, 191.—A temple of Bellona established at Rome, ibid., 105.—The rite for celebrating her sacred ceremonies. Lactantius, VI, 234.—Bellona’s priests were consecrated with blood. Tertullian, I, 321.—The dark garment and gloomy fleece worn over the head by those initiated into this goddess’s rites, II, 1045. BELUS. How ancient his rites at Edessa were. Lactantius, VI, 229.—Older than the Trojan War, ibid., 250.—Who he was, contemporary with Saturn, ibid. BERECYNTHIA. Arnobius, V, 1107. BOEOTIA had the oracle of Trophonius. Tertullian, II, 730, 1039. BOETULI, stones among the Phoenicians. Lactantius, VII, 495.—A temple was built for them in the East, ibid., VII, 469. BONA DEA, the same as Fatua Fauna. Tertullian, I, 36.—Lactantius, VI, 245. THE BULL APIS, god of the Egyptians. Tertullian, I, 129; St Augustine, XLI, 564.—Its priests observed continence. Tertullian, II, 928. BROMIUS, the same as LIBER. BUBONA, goddess responsible for the care of oxen. St Augustine, XLI, 140. [Col. 0369] Businis and his graveyard altars. Tertullian, II, 1041.—Busiris. St Augustine, XLII, 601.—A tyrant, son of Neptune by the mother Libya, id., XLI, 570.—He sacrificed his own guests to his gods, ibid., 570. BYTHOS (“Depth”), Valentinus’s Aeon. Tertullian, II, 68, 551, 666.

## C

CABIRI, gods: where they were worshipped. Lactantius, VI, 194. CACA, a goddess worshipped by the Romans. Lactantius, VI, 226. CACABULUS of Saturn. Tertullian, I, 344. CADUCEUS of Mercury. Tertullian, I, 576. CAECULUS, a god. Tertullian, I, 606. CAESARS: the Romans called them gods and mocked them. Tertullian, I, 583.—Altars, temples, priests, and a sacred couch were assigned to Caesar beside those of the gods, ibid., 247.—Why the deeds of the Caesars were not worshipped by Christians, ibid., 452. CALVA, Venus the Bald. Lactantius, VI, 225. CAMILLA: Diana mourned her. St Augustine, XLI, 86. CAMOENA teaches singing. St Augustine, XLI, 122. CANDELIFERA, a goddess. Tertullian, I, 600. CANTHERII, pack-horses worshipped by the pagans. Tertullian, 365. A GOAT is sacrificed to Liber. Arnobius, V, 1244. THE CAPITOL, the council-house and temple of all demons or gods. Tertullian, I, 646.—Which gods were rejected from the Capitol. Tertullian, I, 373.—One was not permitted to enter the Capitoline temple without paying tribute, ibid., 345, 574.—In calamities the Romans called upon Heaven at the Capitol, ibid., 487. CARDEA, a goddess. Tertullian, I, 683; II, 97.—Cardea, the goddess set over the hinge of a door. St Augustine, XLI, 119. CARMENTES, who sing fates to those ignorant of them. St Augustine, XLI, 122. THE GOD DELVENTIUS of the people of Casinum. Tertullian, I, 420. CASTOR AND POLLUX. Castor, son of Jupiter. Tertullian, II, 378.—Horses were allotted to Castor and Pollux by Mercury, id., I, 641.—Why Castor and Pollux were called the Tyndaridae. Lactantius, V, 130.—Abductors of other men’s brides, ibid., 161.—The poets’ fabrication about them, ibid., 162.—Their various appearances, ibid., 289.—Castor and Pollux enrolled among the gods. St Augustine, XLI, 134. THE CASTORS, gods. Tertullian, I, 606; Arnobius, V, 761, 924.—Their three kinds, ibid., 1031.—Apparitions of the divine Castors. Tertullian, I, 409.—Eggs are assigned in honour of the Castors, id., II, 639. CATABOLIC spirits. Tertullian, II, 698. CATIUS, a god who makes people *cati*, that is, sharp or acute. St Augustine, XLI, 128. CECROPIANS. Arnobius, V, 1132. CEPHEUS, delineated among the stars by Aratus. Tertullian, II, 142. CERBERUS. The story of Cerberus. Arnobius, V, 1142.—St Augustine, XLI, 570. CERES, born in the region of Trinacria. Arnobius, V, 760.—Ceres, worshipped as discoverer of grain. Tertullian, I, 334; Arnobius, V, 764, 912; St Isidore, LXXXII, 320.—Ceres with breasts. Arnobius, V, 950, 1213.—She pointed out grain; she did not institute it. Tertullian, I, 334.—Ceres’ chariot was drawn by serpents, ibid., 341.—Dark garments please Ceres, id., II, 1045.—The rites of Ceres. Arnobius, V, 909; St Augustine, XLI, 185, 210.—For initiates of Ceres, the entire attire is white; the privilege of fillets and caps. Tertullian, II, 1045.—The priests of Ceres, with their husbands’ consent, are widowed by an amicable separation. Tertullian, II, 953.—Women devoted to African Ceres voluntarily renounce marriage and grow old unmarried, id., II, 928. Cerealian games, id., I, 638.—Ceres passionately loved Jason. Arnobius, V, 1059.—They maintain that Ceres is the Great Mother, or Earth, and Juno. St Augustine, XLI, 207.—Ceres and Liber are placed in charge of seeds, ibid., 207.—Milesian Ceres. Lactantius, VI, 291. CHAOS: what it is. Lactantius, VI, 131.—Whether all things came forth from it, id., VI, 132.—The error of the ancients regarding its eternity, ibid., 297. CHARIS (“Grace”), Valentinus’s Aeon. Tertullian, II, 551. THE CHARITES (“Graces”), goddesses. Tertullian, II, 85. CHIRON teaches Aesculapius medicine. Lactantius, VI, 160. CHLORIS, wife of Zephyrus. Lactantius, VI, 219. CHRYSIS, priestess of Juno. Arnobius, V, 1209. THE CIMMERIAN Sibyl. Lactantius, VI, 142. CINXIA, a goddess. Arnobius, V, 972, 979, 1186. CIRCE, daughter of the Sun. Arnobius, V, 1029.—Circe, the most famous sorceress. St Augustine, XLI, 573.—She transformed Ulysses’ companions, ibid., 575. CLOACINA, a goddess. Tertullian, II, 266.—Lactantius, VI, 220.—St Augustine, XXXIII, 84.—Whence she was so called. Lactantius, VI, 220; St Augustine, XLI, 118.—Tatius dedicated Cloacina as a goddess, id., XLI, 190.—The name Cloacina assigned to Venus, ibid., 118. COCYTUS, a river. Arnobius, V, 831. [Col. 0370] COELESTIS, goddess of the Africans. Tertullian, I, 419, 596.—Beasts assigned to her, ibid., 341.—The goddess Coelestis was held in the highest honour among Africans and Carthaginians. St Augustine, XXXVI, 752; XXXVII, 1270; XXXVIII, 624; XLI, 75.—The goddess Coelestis, Promiser of rains. Tertullian, I, 413.—The shameful rites of the heavenly goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 75. HEAVEN: they make it the father of Saturn. St Augustine, XLI, 209.—They assert innumerably that Heaven is Jupiter, id., 210. COLLATINA, a goddess set over hills. St Augustine, XLI, 118. THE SPRING OF COLOPHON, demonic in nature, makes persons possessed by a nymph (*lymphatici*). Tertullian, II, 734. CONCORDIA, a goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 105, 132.—Concordia was vainly regarded as a goddess by the Romans, ibid., 106.—A temple of Concord was made on the site of seditions and killings, ibid., 105, 106. THE CONSENTES, gods. Arnobius, V, 995, 996; Lactantius, VI, 199.—The Consentes gods summoned into Jupiter’s council. St Augustine, XLI, 130. CONSEVIUS, a god. Tertullian, I, 600.—His office, ibid. THE CONSUALIA, festivals. Tertullian, I, 637. CONSUS, a god. Tertullian, I, 600.—God of counsel. Tertullian, I, 637; St Cyprian, IV, 310; Arnobius, V, 967; St Augustine, XLI, 122.—The same as Equestrian Neptune. Tertullian, I, 637, 640; Lactantius, VI, 712; St Augustine, XLI, 61.—Discovered by Romulus. Tertullian, II, 266.—Circus games consecrated to him. Lactantius, VI, 712.—The shrine of Consus in the circus. Tertullian, I, 637.—Why the Consualia, the circus games, were so named. St Augustine, XLI, 61.—His altar was buried underground in the circus, beneath the first turning-posts. Tertullian, I, 637, 640. CORYBANTES. Lactantius, VI, 187.—Foul rites employed in the worship of the Corybantes. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1006. CORYBANTIAN bronze instruments. Tertullian, I, 426.—Corybantian rites. Arnobius, V, 1120. THE CROCODILE worshipped by the Egyptians. Tertullian, II, 302. WORSHIP OF DEMONS. Commodianus Afer, V, 203. THE CUMAEAN or CUMAN Sibyl. Lactantius, VI, 143.—She sang many things about Christ. St Augustine, XLI, 580.—Perhaps the Cumaean prophetess heard in the Spirit something concerning the one Saviour, id., XXXIII, 1073.—The Cumaean poem, id., XXXIII, 393; XXXV, 2089.—Poems attributed to the Cumaean Sibyl, published under the name of the Erythraean, id., XLI, 580. CUNINA, the goddess who attends the cradles of infants. St Augustine, LXI, 118, 122. CUPID. The origin of this god. Lactantius, VI, 207; St Isidore, LXXXII, 322.—Which poets wrote *The Triumph of Cupid*. Lactantius, VI, 896. CYBELE, a goddess represented in theatres. Tertullian, I, 570.—She sighs for Attis, the disdainful shepherd, ibid., 359.—She migrated to Rome, ibid., 424 and following.—She did not know of the death of the emperor Aurelius, ibid., 425.—Beasts assigned to Cybele, ibid., 341.—The archigallus poured out his own blood to her, ibid., 425. Her rites celebrated by Galli priests. Lactantius, VI, 206.—Her various names, ibid., 233.—The rite for celebrating her sacred ceremonies, ibid., 234.—Her female ministers called *Melissae* (“Bees”), ibid., 248.—Why she was called goddess of the mountains. Lactantius, VII, 404.—Likewise called Πυλήνη (*Pylēnē*) or Σιπυλήνη (*Sipylēnē*), ibid.—She is also the sacred stone called Agdus in the region of Phrygia, ibid., 496.—Properly called Lady, ibid., 572. CYNEGIUS, son of Flora. St Augustine, XL, 157, 591. CYNOCEPHALUS (“Dog-head”), one of the Roman divinities. St Augustine, XLI, 59.—Cynocephalus came from Egypt to Rome, ibid., 87. CYTHEREAN VENUS. Arnobius, V, 1046.—Mother of the Cupids, ibid., 973.—Her statues. Arnobius, V, 1191.

## D
DAEDALUS. The story of Daedalus. St Augustine, XXXII, 894; XLI, 570.

DAEMONS. Some called daemons by the name of gods. St Augustine, XLI, 255.—St Isidore, LXXXII, 315.—How a daemon was made a god from a human being. St Augustine, XLI, 252.—Daemons are called, not simply gods, but gods of the nations, id., XXXVII, 1757.—Some daemons are greater, others more contemptible, ibid., XXXVII, 1375.—Some distinguished daemons from gods, id., XLI, 257.

DANAE. Arnobius, V, 1147, 1265.—Whether she was deceived by a shower of gold. Lactantius, VI, 170.—What Jupiter’s desire for intercourse with Danae by means of a golden shower signifies. St Augustine, XLI, 571, 572.

DAPHNE. Arnobius, V, 1055.

GODDESSES. Commodianus the African, V, 212.—Gentle goddesses. Arnobius, V, 1208.—They give birth, ibid., 948, 949, 950, 962.

DECIMA (goddess). Tertullian, II, 713.

DOLPHINS were vowed to Neptune. Tertullian, I, 639.

DELVENTIUS, god of the people of Casinum. Tertullian, I, 120.

DEMOPHILE, Sibyl. Lactantius, VI, 143.

DEUCALION and Pyrrha. Arnobius, V, 1089.

[Col. 0371] **Δευσάρης** (*Deusares*), the name of Bacchus among the Arabs. Lactantius, VII, 494.

DIANA, goddess of the Scythians. Tertullian, II, 136, 953.—Diana is represented as a virgin, id., I, 574; as scourged, I, 358.—Diana, Ceres, and the Moon are heads of one god. Arnobius, V, 986.—Diana with her thighs half-covered, ibid., 1214.—Driver through the woods, ibid., 1042.—Huntress, ibid., 1149.—Her shrine, ibid., 1174.—Three Dianas, ibid., 1031.—Tauric Diana. St Cyprian, IV, 226.—How suspect Diana’s virginity is. Lactantius, VI, 209.—Human sacrifices offered to her among the Taurians, ibid., 230.—Why she was called Thoanthea, ibid., 229.—She was among the deities of sailors, ibid., VI, 237.—The origin of her title Trivia, ibid., VI, 354.—Called Nemorensis and wanderer of the mountains, id., VII, 493.—Where the image of Tauric Diana, carried off by Orestes, lay, ibid., 498.—Diana is regarded as Apollo’s twin sister, the Moon, and ruler of roads. St Augustine, XLI, 207.—Why she is called a virgin, ibid., 207.—The pagans interpret Diana as virtue, id., XXXIV, 1059.

DICE, or Justice, goddess of the pagans. Lactantius, VI, 392. The same as Astraea and Themis, ibid.

DIESPITER, god. Tertullian, I, 600; Arnobius, V, 924, 1087.—His function. Tertullian, I, 600.—He violates Ceres, his mother. Arnobius, V, 1122.—Diespiter, a surname of Jupiter. Lactantius, VI, 190.

GODS. The Idaean Mother of the Gods. St Cyprian, IV, 226.—Some gods are natural, others instituted by human beings. St Augustine, XLI, 183.—They derive their origin from Saturn. Tertullian, I, 329, 601.—From Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, according to Varro, ibid.—How fables concerning the gods gained force. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 306.—The very frenzied lust that boils over into many divine powers. St Augustine, XLI, 211.—To call the gods of the nations members of the one great God is sacrilegious wit, id., XXXIII, 83.—Error in the making of gods, id., XLI, 250.—Heraclitus believes that the gods are from fire, Pythagoras from numbers, Epicurus from atoms, id., XLI, 181.—Anaximenes, from air, XLI, 236.—Plato considers them made by one God, id., XLI, 775.—Trismegistus says that some gods were made by the supreme God, others by human beings, id., XLI, 247.—The mythical race of gods invented by poets is rejected. Tertullian, I, 395 ff., 408 ff.—They said that the gods were dead heroes. Tertullian, I, 594.—Human beings were made gods either because of virtue and certain distinguished exploits, Tertullian, I, 334; or because of benefits bestowed on humankind, ibid.; or because of things invented, id., I, 606.—How persons, though they had been human, came to be named gods. Lactantius, VI, 192.—Which gods were made from human beings. Arnobius, V, 992.—Gods are said to be made by human beings when invisible spirits are, through a certain art, joined to images. St Augustine, XLI, 247, 250, 251.—Unbelief is the cause of this error, id., XLI, 250.—It is easier for a human being to cease being human than for the gods made by a human being to be gods, id., XLI, 250.—Even if later Roman times did not establish dead human beings as gods, they nonetheless did not cease to worship those already established as gods, id., XLI, 581.—Gods made at human discretion. Tertullian, I, 344, 347, 596.—Not without a decree of the senate, id., I, 290, 304 ff., 344, 375, 575.—Nor without Caesar’s consent, id., I, 429.—Gods and household vessels were customarily fashioned from the same material, id., I, 339.—They were made from the meanest material. Arnobius, V, 1195, 1196; and from stones, Arnobius, V, 1490, 1191, 1192.—How they came to be believed gods. Lactantius, VI, 156.—Authors to be consulted concerning them, id., VI, 177.—The beginning of their worship, id., VI, 247.—How they acquired divine honours, id., VII, 111.—When images of gods were established. St Augustine, XLI, 581.—For what purpose they were devised, id., XLI, 198.—The existence of gods cannot be proved even by certain alleged signs, miracles, and oracles. Tertullian, I, 395 ff., 408 ff.—On gods and goddesses. Commodianus the African, V, 212.—The philosophers’ opinion concerning the gods. Lactantius, VI, 120.—Philosophers held differing opinions concerning the nature of the gods. St Augustine, XXXIV, 123.—Xenocrates invented a twofold kind of gods, and Dionysius, Arcesilaus, and Varro another, threefold kind. Tertullian, I, 587 ff.—That is, physical, mythical, and civic or popular; ibid.—They are refuted, ibid.—The natural philosophers demeaned the gods, Tertullian, I, 502, because they said that they were the elements of the world, id., I, 589.—Gods are made of corruptible matter according to Plato. Arnobius, V, 865.—Mortal and dissoluble, ibid., 1163, 1164.—Gods are living beings according to Plato. St Augustine, XLI, 241.—Plato assigned male gods to heaven and female gods to earth, then later confused them, id., XLI, 87.—According to Plato, the gods are enclosed in heavenly bodies, id., XLI, 794.—It is a great benefit to gods made by the supreme God to have immortal bodies, ibid., XLI.—God promised the gods everlasting continuance in heavenly bodies, id., XLI, 794.—Plato finally judged the gods to be good, id., XLI, 126, 237.—Others likewise, ibid., 247, 235.—The Platonists perhaps called good gods holy angels, id., XLI, 275, 276.

The Platonists considered many gods ought to be worshipped, id., XLI, 277.—Why Plato deprived only evil gods, or daemons, of the pleasure of theatrical games, ibid., XLI, 239.—The Stoics hold that the contests of opposing pursuits are the province of daemons, not gods, id., XLI, 262.—Varro’s opinions concerning the gods are ambiguous, id., XLI, 208.—He rejected popular belief concerning the gods, id., XLI, 137.—Varro vainly attempts to assign gods to heaven and goddesses to earth, id., XLI, 218.—Varro wished litigation and legal judgments to be alien to gods, id., XLI, 567.—Porphyry subjected the higher gods to disturbances. St Augustine, XLI, 304, 305.—And maintains that they are subjected through theurgy, id., XLI, 288.—Apuleius distinguished them from the taint of disturbances, id., 304.—The Stoics distinguished them, id., XLI, 262, 263.—Why, id., XLI, 304.—Porphyry said that gods can be bound by incantations, id., XLI, 304, 305.—The sharpest minds suffer straits in interpreting fables about gods, id., XLI, 209.—The more intelligent and serious Romans recognized that the things proclaimed about gods are vain, id., XLI, 136.—It is human to form an opinion on what concerns the nature of gods; it is God’s to know, id., XLI, 208.—Euhemerus wrote that the gods had once been human beings, id., XLI, 284.—Vergil and Cicero thought so, id., XXXIII, 84.—Cicero admits it, id., XXXIV, 1056.—Leo, an Egyptian priest, declares it and disclosed it to Alexander, id., XXXIV, 1056–1057; XLI, 229.—This makes it more credible, id., XLI, 208, 217, 253, 254. History and memorials testify that such gods were human beings. Tertullian, I, 328.—It is certain that many of them reigned, id., I, 428.—The civic or popular class of gods is rejected. Tertullian, I, 595 ff.—Their bodily forms: human, goat-like, bovine, those of birds and other animals, id., I, 374, 574 ff., 577.—They were mere human beings. Tertullian, I, 328; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1349.—Certain gods have particular guardianships, permissions, and powers. Arnobius, V, 912.—Guardian gods, id., V, 970.—Patrons of arts, id., V, 966 ff.—Native gods, id., V, 754, 922.—Of both sexes, id., V, 944, 1286.—They have birthdays, id., V, 1270, 1271.—They dwell in images. Arnobius, V, 1201.—Enclosed in temples, id., V, 1201.—They dine and drink in the palaces of heaven, id., V, 1068.—They go to the Ethiopians for dinner, id., V, 1170.—They are treated to sumptuous dinners, Arnobius, V, 1251, 1252.—They suffer from stomach upsets, id., V, 1251, 1252.—They delight in mimes, id., V, 1265, 1266.—They fall asleep, id., V, 1262.—They wage wars among themselves, id., V, 1068; Lactantius, VI, 125.—Their favour is for sale, id., V, 1231.—They sell their grievances, id., V, 1226.—They accuse and clear persons of crimes. Arnobius, V, 963.—Their offices are diverse, id., V, 964, 968.—They manage farming, id., V, 968.—All gods are invoked for all temples of the gods. Lactantius, VII, 708, 792.—Whether gods are, as it were, virtues, members, or parts of Jupiter. St Augustine, XLI, 123.—Whatever natural philosophers referred to the world and its parts ought to be referred to the true God. St Augustine, XLI, 219.—Those who regard human works as gods are submerged more deeply than those who regard God’s works as gods, id., XXXIV, 70.—According to pagans, all gods are of one substance, although they have different offices, functions, and powers. St Augustine, XLII, 376.—They are not immortal by nature but immortal by God’s will, id., XLI, 794.—Gods made by the supreme God have immortal bodies, id., XLI, 388, 390.—For a god, a daemon serves as soul and an image as body, id., XLI, 254.—Gods are unclean spirits. St Augustine, XLI, 221.—When the gods of the nations first began to be named in Scripture, id., XXXIV, 572.—Some dead persons were placed among the gods by the empty superstition of the Greeks, id., XLI, 565.—In the times of the Caesars, no one was entered among the gods through error, but through flattery, id., XLI, 581.—Gods differ from human beings in place, eternity, and blessedness, id., XLI, 266.—Labeo’s classification of gods, id., XLI, 105.—Some gods are unmarried, others joined in marriage, XLI, 191.—Gods certain and uncertain, id., XLI, 87.—Three classes of gods, id., XLI, 133.—Three orders, id., XLI, 58.—Select gods, id., XLI, 130, 193, 194.—There is no rationale for the selection of gods, id., XLI, 195.—Why the select gods are so called, id., XLI, 196.—They maintain that the select gods are this world, id., XLI, 207.—Some thought that gods were both good and evil, id., XLI, 255.—Apuleius wished all gods to be believed good and blessed, id., XLI, 263.—The pagans passed over many things to which they might have assigned divine honours, id., XLI, 127.—The gods of pagans are dead gods, XLIII, 65.—Compared with barley bread, id., XXXIV, 802.—Golden gods and wooden gods differ in value, id., XXXVIII, 624.—Temples, idols, and sacred groves of false gods are to be converted to common uses or to the honour of the true God, id., XXXIII, 185.—It is futile for wholesome interpretations to be recited in temples concerning what was anciently written about the lives and morals of the gods. St Augustine, XXXIII, 315.—Various names of gods, id., XXXIII, 84.—What nonsense the pagans have uttered concerning Saturn and Jupiter, id., XXXIV, 1056.—Gods who are Jupiter’s parasites, id., XLI, [Col. 0373] 181.—The Manes gods, id., XLI, 253.—Only through the Christian religion could the deception of the gods be exposed. St Augustine, XLI, 221.—The gods of pagans are not to be compared with martyrs, id., XXXVIII, 1250.

Gods innumerable. Tertullian, I, 942.—Whence they made so many gods for themselves, id., I, 133.—They cannot be many. Lactantius, VII, 110.—On the names of gods. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1020.—Pagans believed that many gods must be won over to humankind. St Augustine, XLI, 645.—The method by which Varro arrived at their multitude, id., XLI, 189.—There ought not to be imagined as many gods as there are works of the true God in the world, id., XLI, 219.—At one time pagans make one God into several things, at another one thing into several gods, ibid., 207.—The Manichaeans worshipped a multitude of gods, id., XLII, 142, 307, 308, 321.—An immense throng of gods and goddesses is not required where virtue and happiness are present, id., XLI, 128, 129, 130.

Gods and daemons have one and the same quality of name. Tertullian, I, 413.—They are the same as daemons. Lactantius, VI, 534.—Most deceitful daemons. St Augustine, XLI, 111.—Those who fashioned gods for themselves were possessed by daemons, id., XLI, 251.—Gods are more rarely called by the name of daemons, id., XLI, 255.—Apuleius carefully distinguishes gods from daemons, id., XLI, 239.—It is absurd to maintain that gods are more willing to associate with daemons than with human beings, id., XLI, 315.—It is absurd that gods should need daemons as messengers and interpreters, id., XLI, 245.—Daemons pursue their own business, so that they may be considered and worshipped as gods, id., XLI, 42.

Antiquity erred concerning the worship of gods. Tertullian, I, 306.—They could not all be worshipped by everyone, so many and so great as they were, id., I, 573.—Their religion is empty. Lactantius, VI, 617.—The blindness of worship, id., VI, 625.—Mad worship. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 294, 312.—The worship of gods is an institution of daemons. St Augustine, XLI, 179, 187.—The worship of many gods is fornication. St Augustine, XXXIV, 70; XLI, 303.—It took varied forms, id., XXXIII, 373, 375.—It brought in every evil, Lactantius, VI, 573.—Why worshipping gods is wicked, id., XLI, 217.—It is shown that gods ought not to be worshipped because they were made, id., XLI, 251.—Gentiles feared the emperors less than the gods. Tertullian, I, 437.—Crowns and garlands were given to them. Arnobius, V, 1262.—On the sacred rites and mysteries of gods. Lactantius, V, 230.—The names of persons consecrated to them are changed, id., VI, 236.—Their images and insignia are carried on shoulders, id., VI, 241.—Who established their sacred rites in Italy, id., VI, 242.—Their custom of crowning images, id., VI, 256.—What method of fashioning images of gods was first devised, id., VI, 258.—The ridiculous form and figure of gods. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 309; Arnobius, V, 1131–1135.—The good gods, as the Platonists call them, do not wish to be worshipped in place of God. St Augustine, XLI, 281, 284.—False gods do not prohibit others from being worshipped with them, id., XXXIV, 1058.—A Christian ought not to use anything in honour of foreign gods, even if inwardly despising it, lest he encourage those who cannot see the mind to honour such things. Id., XXXIII, 185.—Varro vainly boasts that he gave the Romans knowledge for worshipping gods, id., XLI, 122.—Labeo judges that evil gods are placated by bloody victims and mournful supplications, good gods by games and cheerful services, id., XLI, 56, 237.—Appeasing gods by the obscenities of games is more harmful to human beings than their indignation would be, id., XLI, 76.—With what evil disposition the gods commanded theatrical games to be exhibited for them. St Augustine, XLI, 75.—Gods are worshipped unworthily by honourable people when they are appeased by shameful things.—From the prohibition of the worship of gods, pagans supposed that calamities were inflicted upon the human race, id., XLI, 29.—Porphyry admitted the worship of gods contrary to his own understanding, id., XLI, 303, 304.—Porphyry said that sacrifice must be offered to good and evil gods; Plato, to good gods alone, id., XLI, 237.

That the gods are false is shown. Tertullian, I, 349 ff.—By the testimony of the Gentiles’ conscience, id., I, 328.—Because they could receive divinity neither from themselves nor from others, id., I, 333.—By the public confession of daemons adjured by Christians, id., I, 413 ff., 417.—Their falsity is again demonstrated from their bodily forms—human, goat-like, bovine, leonine, avian, and those of other animals. Tertullian, I, 374, 574 ff., 577.—Profane gods. St Cyprian, IV, 253.—Those worshipped by the common people are not gods, id., IV, 125.—True gods do not desire sacrifices. Arnobius, V, 1219.—True gods are free from passions, id., V, 1163, 1222, 1223.—True gods do not become angry, id., V, 745, 1077, 1226.—False gods are angry with and hostile to Christians, id., V, 745–748, 750–751.—Why gods cannot be of different sexes. Lactantius, VI, 201.—No god can be called by the name of Father. Lactantius, VI, 453, 458.—Varro said that it was useful for gods falsely to claim that they were born as human beings are. St Augustine, XLI, 81.—Many gods are not necessary for governing the world. Lactantius, VI, 122.—They do no good unless they receive incense and salted grain. Arnobius, V, 970.—On the benefits they bestow upon human beings. Lactantius, VI, 209.—They are vainly adorned with costly gifts. Lactantius, VI, 270.—The Roman Empire did not grow through worship of gods. [Col. 0374] Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 315.—The gods took no care to prevent their worshippers from suffering moral evils. St Augustine, XLI, 49, 60, 74, 79.—They never gave their worshippers any precepts of moral goodness, id., XLI, 49, 51.—They never gave the Romans any precepts against luxury and greed. St Augustine, XLI, 64, 69.—The Romans vainly attribute the cause of their miseries to the destruction of the gods, id., XLI, 101.—Why gods cannot be said to have established, enlarged, or preserved the Roman Empire, id., XLI, 119, 135.—Nor to have supplied peace to the Roman Empire, id., XLI, 84, 85.—Gods are worshipped in vain for the advantages of this temporal life, id., XLI, 173, 174, 316; or for eternal life, id., XLI, 175, 183, 187, 193, 256.—Pagans are forced to admit this, id., XLI, 29.—And it is shown by examples, id., XLI, 29.—The variations of temporal affairs do not depend on the favour or displeasure of gods, id., XLI, 70.—It follows that gods are either worshipped superfluously or are unjust, id., XLI, 70.—They did not avert bodily evils from their worshippers, id., XLI, 79.—By deceiving and misleading their worshippers, they harmed them rather than helped them, id., XLI, 113.—Gods give no help to kingdoms in which they are worshipped, id., XLI, 117; nor to cities committed to their care, ibid.—It is absurd to ask one god for what belongs under another’s guardianship, id., XLI, 175, 176.—The temples of gods, as places of asylum, are poorly secure for those fleeing to them, id., XLI, 15, 17, 18.

The wretched condition of gods. Arnobius, V, 1112.—Their troubles. Lactantius, VI, 206.—Their sad ends, fates, and deaths. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 299.—Their servitudes, chains, battles, and wounds. Tertullian, I, 351, 575.—The gentiles destroyed the gods whom they feared and mocked those whom they defended, id., I, 344.—And did so in their temples, id., I, 363.—Gods ought rather to avenge their own injuries than reward flattery, id., I, 431.—They laughed when Roman emperors were made like themselves, id., I, 347.—Guardianship keeps gods shut up so that they do not perish. St Cyprian, IV, 221.—It is shameful to worship those whom one must oneself defend. St Cyprian, IV, 221.—They are afflicted by diseases. Arnobius, V, 964.—They accuse cruel fates, Arnobius, V, 1068, 1069.—They do not know what is imminent, id., V, 964.—They feel thirst, id., V, 1258.—They cannot defend themselves, id., V, 741.—They are enslaved to human beings, id., V, 1050, 1054.—They wash away filth with water. Arnobius, V, 1262.—They had their own veils and little cloaks. Lactantius, VI, 270.—They could do no harm even to those by whom they had been violated. Lactantius, VI, 273.—Temples of gods were destroyed and images broken at Carthage. St Augustine, XLI, 620.—Alexandria lost its gods, id., XXXVIII, 624.

Gods are not even decent human beings. Lactantius, VI, 216.—Their foulness is depicted by literary works and actors’ performances. Tertullian, I, 358.—Their crimes and most shameful deeds are represented in the auditorium, theatres, stage, comedies, and tragedies, id., I, 353 ff., 358 ff., 573 ff.—The whole artistry concerning gods is insulting and impious, id., I, 339.—They delight in mimes. Arnobius, V, 1265, 1266.—They have betrothed women and wives, id., V, 1040.—They indulge in shameful acts, id., V, 1265, 1266.—Their disgraceful intercourse with men and women, id., V, 1068.—They are lovers of boys. Arnobius, V, 1058, 1059.—On the immoral acts of those who worship them. Lactantius, VI, 575.—Why they cannot be good and just. Lactantius, VI, 583.—On their cruelty toward Christians, id., VI, 584.—They are rightly called beasts by the prophets, ibid.—On their ignorance and frenzies, id., VI, 611.—Narrative of the deeds of gods. Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1006.—Discord among the gods. St Augustine, XLI, 188.—Select gods are select by the nobility of their crimes, not by the dignity of their virtues, id., XLI, 221.—Select gods are more suited to insults than to honours, id., XLI, 197.—Select gods became better known by their disgraces than other gods, id., XLI, 217.—Hardly any of the select gods is not defamed, id., XLI, 198.—Gods are thereby convicted of obscenity, because they ordered obscene games to be performed for them, id., XLI, 53.—And for this reason ought to have appeared unworthy of divine honour to the Romans, id., XLI, 57, 58.—Fabulous crimes were enacted shamefully in the service of gods through games, id., XLI, 582.—The disgraceful deeds of gods are displayed to be watched even in theatres, id., XXXIII, 533.—False gods delight in the evil morals of their worshippers, id., XXXVIII, 1025.—Gods are thereby shown false because they delight in their crimes, whether true or false, id., XLI, 78, 111.—Laws for establishing good morals or correcting bad ones are not to be expected from gods who took care that immoral acts should be sown and increased. St Augustine, XLI, 59, 74.—It is shown that gods assisted the fulfilment of desires and did not preside over their restraint, id., XLI, 70.—Gods are spectators and supporters of crimes, id., XLI, 92.—They testify that they are authors of a wicked and impure life, id., XLI, 74.—Gods are authors and teachers of sins, not avengers, id., XLI, 81.—Gods are not to be approved because they punished crimes in some persons but did not avenge them in others, id., XLI, 82.—By demanding theatrical games, gods furnish, as it were, divine authority for committing crimes, id., XLI, 111.—It is proved even from the gentiles themselves that, through imitation of false gods, utterly wicked people become worse. [Col. 0375] Id., XXXIII, 315.—The examples of gods move people more than philosophers’ precepts, id., XLI, 52, 53.—The functions of gods accord more with the buffoonery of mime than with divine dignity, id., XLI, 187.

LOCAL GODS. The number of local gods is infinite. Tertullian, I, 645.—They were imagined to preside over marriages and the begetting of children. Tertullian, I, 600.—Every province and city had its own god, id., I, 418, 596.—How falsely they were called guardians and protectors of provinces and cities, id., I, 424 ff., 607.—They gave kingdoms to no one, id., I, 433 ff.; nor could they give them, ibid.; nor could they protect kingdoms, their own temples, or themselves, id., I, 438 ff.; nor could they confer safety on anyone, ibid.—They allowed their own homeland to be overthrown, id., I, 426.—Which were provincial gods. Lactantius, VI, 194, 195.—Which were gods of mountains, id., VII, 403 ff., 493 ff.

PUBLIC GODS: who they were. Tertullian, I, 598.—For sale under the spear and subject to the quaestor’s notation, id., I, 345 ff.—How the majesty of the gods was made a commercial commodity, id., I, 346.—Altars were prostituted among the Romans to incestuous gods, id., II, 255.—Private and household gods, id., I, 344.—Sold at each person’s discretion, id., I, 344, 347; and pawned or exchanged, ibid.—The more sacred and ancient they were, the more liable to tribute, id., I, 346.—Gods selected and expelled, id., I, 344, 596; adopted, id., I, 596.—Begging gods, id., I, 494.—For whom Christians were insufficient, ibid.—Some worshipped one god, others another, id., I, 344.—The dress and insignia in which gods were honoured, id., I, 347, 360 ff., 547.—With dishonoured head, id., I, 360.—Whom the heathen called a “long-suffering god,” id., I, 413.

ROMAN GENTILE GODS: who they were. Tertullian, I, 597.—They are rejected, ibid.—They were wrongly divided by Varro into certain, doubtful, and chosen gods, ibid.—They might somewhat better have been divided into common and proper gods, but this is refuted, ibid.—Their private gods, I, 419 ff., 606.—Foreign gods, I, 423 ff.—It is false that the Roman Empire was founded or enlarged through their worship, id., I, 422.—They gave their homeland to be ravaged by the Romans, id., I, 424 ff.—The Jews despised them, id., I, 432.—Native gods of the Romans. St Cyprian, IV, 226.—On the Romans’ proper gods. Lactantius, VI, 216.—Gods of the Romans. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 250.—For more than one hundred and seventy years, the Romans worshipped gods without images. St Augustine, XLI, 138.—Varro taught that Romans worshipped gods more chastely without images, id., XLI, 198.

UNKNOWN GODS. Altars were prostituted to unknown gods among the Athenians, Tertullian, II, 255; and to uncertain gods among the Romans, ibid.—Unknown gods. Arnobius, V, 929, 930.—Left-hand gods, id., V, 1011, 1246.—Great gods, id., V, 738, 739.—Lesser gods, id., V, 815.—The consenting and allied counsellors of Jupiter, id., V, 994–995.—Gods of Gain, id., V, 1018.—Gods who bring together, id., V, 1116, 1117.—Syrian gods. Arnobius, V, 758–763.—Popular gods. Lactantius, VI, 134.—Gods of the greater nations. Lactantius, VI, 199.—Above innumerable gods they established another, more exalted one. Tertullian, I, 332.—Human mediocrity knows more easily how to invent gods than to pursue the true God, id., II, 266.

DIOMEDES, made a god by the Greeks. St Augustine, XLI, 573, 576.—The birds of Diomedes treat Greeks kindly and pursue foreigners. Id., XLI, 576.—Transformation of the Diomedean birds, id., XLI, 576.—Diomedean island, id., XLI, 573.

DIONYSIA (mysteries). Tertullian, I, 474.—Instituted among the Greeks by Liber. Id., I, 643.

DIONYSES, five. Arnobius, V, 1031.

DIONYSIUS THE YOUNGER, mocker of images. Arnobius, V, 1205.—He stripped Aesculapius of his very large golden beard, ibid.

DIS, or Pluto, represented in the arena as conducting gladiators’ funeral rites. Tertullian, I, 576.—Dis is the same as Greek **Πλούτων**, “Plouton.” Lactantius, VI, 900.

DISCORD, goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 105.—She provoked the Trojan War, id., XLI, 105.—Gods of Discord. Arnobius, V, 972.

DISPATER: Pluto is so called. Lactantius, VI, 190, 900; St Augustine, XLI, 122, 207, 213, 218.

DIVINE STONES: which were so called. Lactantius, VII, 495.

DIVINITY, used in the sense of “god.” Lactantius, VII, 268, 431, 828, 829.

DODONAEAN Jupiter. Arnobius, V, 1209.

DOMIDUCA, goddess. Tertullian, I, 600.

DOMIDUCUS, god. St Augustine, XLI, 188.

DOMITIUS, god. St Augustine, XLI, 188.

DUSARES, or Diasares, Disares, god of the Arabs. Tertullian, I, 419, 596.

DUSII, certain daemons so called by the Gauls. St Augustine, XLI, 468.

## E

EDEA, goddess. Tertullian, I, 600.

EDUCA, or EDULICA, goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 122, 140.

[Col. 0376] EDULIA, goddess. See ELUDA.

EGERIA, goddess. Numa’s feigned meetings with her. Lactantius, VI, 243.—Whence she was named, ibid.—Egeria, a nymph. Arnobius, V, 1081.

ELAGABALUS, a god worshipped under the form of a mountain. Lactantius, VII, 404.—Whence he was named, ibid.—What his image was like, ibid.

ELEMENTS: physical superstition regards them as God. Tertullian, II, 477.

ELEUSINIAN RITES. Tertullian, II, 313, 539; St Augustine, XLI, 210.—It is forbidden to disclose them, id., I, 309.—The conception of Eleusinian Ceres. Arnobius, V, 1174.—Why the Eleusinian rites were so named and by what ritual they were celebrated. Lactantius, V, 237.—The Erythraean Sibyl, id., VI, 145.

ELUDA, goddess. Tertullian, I, 600.

ELYSIAN FIELDS. Tertullian, I, 520; II, 444.

ENDYMION, loved by the Moon. Arnobius, V, 1059.

EPONA, goddess. Tertullian, I, 365, 577.

BANQUETS OF GODDESSES. Arnobius, V, 1263.

ERICHTHONIUS, son of Minerva and Vulcan, a demonic portent—indeed the devil himself—not a serpent. Tertullian, II, 24.

ERIGONA, a false goddess. Tertullian, I, 666.—Depicted among the stars. Tertullian, II, 142.

EUDAEMONS. St Augustine, XLI, 256.—Eudaemons cannot be intermediaries between gods and human beings, id., XLI, 266.

EUPHORBUS, transformed into Pythagoras. Tertullian, II, 698, 708, 796.—The shield of Euphorbus was once consecrated at Delphi, id., II, 698.

EUROPA. Arnobius, V, 1265.—Violated by Jupiter, id., V, 1126.—Whether she was carried off by Jupiter transformed into a bull. Lactantius, VI, 170.

EVIUS (Bacchus). Arnobius, V, 1142.

## F

FABIUS, Jupiter’s chick. Arnobius, V, 1058.

FABLES OF ANTIQUITY concerning the gods. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 297.—The fables of Jupiter and Numa. Arnobius, V, 1081 ff.; 1084 ff.

FARMUS, god. Tertullian, I, 600.

FATUA, goddess. Arnobius, V, 751.—Faunus’ wife, called the Good Goddess, id., V, 759, 1116.—Beaten with rods for drinking unmixed wine, ibid.—Who Fatua Fauna was. Lactantius, VI, 245.—Why she was so called, ibid., and 909.—Her chastity, id., VI, 245.—The same as the Good Goddess, ibid.—A wine-amphora placed in her sacred rites, id., VI, 246.—No man was permitted to enter her temple, id., VI, 245, 415.—On her mysteries, ibid.

FATE: what it is. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 350; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 323.—Three Fates. St Cyprian, IV, 29.—Fates are unchangeable. Arnobius, V, 1231.—All things happen by fate, id., V, 1230, 1231.—Fate is more powerful than gods, id., V, 1230, 1231.—Fate is the same as the Parcae. Lactantius, VI, 168.—All gods obey it, ibid.—The word *fatum* is used in various senses, id., VI, 336.

FAUNA, goddess: where she was worshipped. Lactantius, VI, 218.—Whose prostitute she was, ibid.—She is not the same as Flora, ibid.

FAUNUS, god. Arnobius, V, 750, 751, 1082; St Isidore, LXXXII, 314, 323.—Who he was. Lactantius, V, 194, 244.—Faunus, son of Picus. Tertullian, I, 599.—Second king of the Laurentians. St Augustine, XLI, 573.—Admitted among the gods, id., XLI, 273.—When he lived. Lactantius, VI, 194, 247.—Where he was worshipped, id., VI, 194.—Founder in Latium of foolish religious observances, id., VI, 244.—Fauns as incubus spirits. St Augustine, XLI, 468.

FEVER, worshipped as though a goddess. Lactantius, VI, 222.—What fever is according to Galen, id., VI, 775.—Goddess of the Romans. St Augustine, XXXIII, 84; XXXVII, 1396; XLI, 59–88, 125.—The Romans made temples for Fever and Pallor, id., XXXIV, 1053; XLI, 105.

FEBRUTIS, goddess. Arnobius, V, 979.

CATS are worshipped by Egyptians. Lactantius, VI, 622.—How they were mourned when dead, id., VI, ibid.

FELICITY, goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 126.—Lucullus was the first to establish a temple for Felicity, id., XLI, 129.—If Felicity is a goddess, she alone ought to have been worshipped, id., XLI, 129, 131.—The Romans erred in worshipping Felicity as a goddess so late, id., XLI, 129, 130.—Felicity is superior to sovereignty, id., XLI, 120.—Felicity is not a goddess but a gift of God, id., XLI, 131, 140, 193.—Felicity is not to be worshipped, but God, id., XLI, 131.

FENONIA, goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 129.

FERETRIAN Jupiter. Romulus established games for Jupiter Feretrius. Tertullian, I, 637.

FIDES was believed to be a goddess and had a temple and altar. St Augustine, XLI, 127.

THE FLAMEN DIALIS. Arnobius, V, 786, 1072, 1277.

FLORA, a prostitute who sees that fields flower. Arnobius, V, [Col. 0377] 967, 968.—She was granted divine honours by the Romans. Lactantius, VI, 218.—Her worship among them was ancient, ibid.—On her various names, ibid.—Flora the mother. St Augustine, XXXIII, 1068.—The goddess presiding over crops in bloom, id., XLI, 118.—How obscene Flora’s theatrical games were, id., XXXIII, 315; XXXIV, 1068; XLI, 76.

FLORAL GAMES. Tertullian, I, 638.

FLORALIA. The occasion on which they were instituted. Lactantius, VI, 218.—The licentiousness with which they were celebrated, id., VI, 219, 905.—On what day and where they took place, ibid.—Whence they were named, id., VII, 218.—They were not the same as the festivals of Maiuma, id., VI, 219, 905.

FLUVIONA, goddess. Tertullian, I, 600.

FOCULUS, in gentile rites. Tertullian, I, 324.

FONTUS, god. Arnobius, V, 976.

FORCULUS, god of doors. Tertullian, I, 680; II, 97, 142.—Set over doors. St Augustine, XLI, 119, 184.

FORNAX, worshipped as a goddess. Lactantius, VI, 226.—The Fornacalia were named after her, ibid.

FORTUNA, bearded goddess. Tertullian, I, 601.—Bearded Fortuna, who clothes adults with a beard. St Augustine, XLI, 122.

FORTUNA (goddess), of women. A crown was placed on Fortuna Muliebris only by a woman married to one man. Tertullian, II, 952.—Virgin Fortuna. Arnobius, V, 920.—With a horn, apples, figs, and autumnal fruits, id., V, 1214.—The reciprocal variability of Fortune, id., V, 966 ff.—Equestrian Fortune. Lactantius, VI, 290.—She is worshipped as a goddess, id., VI, 437.—She is attacked with serious accusations, ibid.—She is nothing in herself, id., VI, 440.—Male and female Fortune worshipped, ibid.—Her difference from nature, id., VI, 441.—Her images, id., VI, 442.—The unjust declamations of the gentiles against her, id., VI, 442, 582.—Fortune the goddess receives her name from the chance occurrences over which she presides. St Augustine, XLI, 122, 126.—Fortune is not any divine power, id., XXXIV, 571.—She is undeservedly worshipped as a goddess, id., XLI, 126.—How she is thought a goddess when she can be evil, id., XLI, 126.—She was depicted blind, id., XXXII, 1273.—Why, id., XLII, 374.—Fortune distributes her gifts randomly to each person, id., XLI, 197.—The truest sages, who alone may properly be called happy, wished neither to fear nor desire Fortune’s goods, id., XXXIII, 65.—The image of Fortuna Muliebris spoke through the craft of daemons, id., XLI, 126.

FRUTESEA, goddess. St Augustine, XLI, 128.

FULGORA, goddess, a widow. St Augustine, XLI, 191.

THUNDERBOLT. On Jupiter’s own thunderbolt. Commodianus the African, V, 205.

FURIES, goddesses. Arnobius, V, 972; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 324.—Celebrated in poetry. Lactantius, VI, 704.

## G

GAULS appeased Hesus and Teutates with human blood. Lactantius, VI, 230.—When those rites were abolished, ibid.—They embraced the doctrine of metempsychosis, id., VI, 405.—The Galli, priests of Cybele, id., VI, 206.—Their rites, ibid.

GANYMEDE. Tertullian, I, 600, 606; Arnobius, V, 1265.—Carried off by Jupiter. Arnobius, V, 1158; Lactantius, VI, 170.—Authors to consult concerning his fable, id., VI, 896.—He is said to have been carried off because of the beauty of his soul, ibid.

GENIUS OF THE EMPEROR. Tertullian, I, 447.—Jovial Genius. Arnobius, V, 1002.—Genius of a place, id., V, 781.—Genius, a god so called from begetting. St Augustine, XLI, 205; Isidore, LXXXII, 323.

GENII worshipped by the heathen. Lactantius, VI, 333.—Whence they are named, ibid.—Unmixed wine was customarily poured out for them, id., VI, 333, 938.—Genii of cities. Arnobius, V, 781.—Genii of husbands invoked in weddings, id., V, 919.

GNIDIAN Venus. Arnobius, V, 1191, 1206.

GREEK PHILOSOPHERS’ GODS. Tertullian, II, 260.

GRUNDULES (Lares). Arnobius, V, 750.

## H
HAMMON, a god depicted with ram’s horns. Arnobius, V, 1188. HARMONIA, daughter of Venus. Lactantius, VI, 207. HARPOCRATES with his Cynocephalus. Tertullian, I, 305.—Expelled from the council of the gods; his altars and statues were overthrown and afterward restored, id., I, 305, 573. HARUSPICES. Brothers of the Magi. Arnobius, V, 1024.—Who were called haruspices. Lactantius, VII, 672.—They differed entirely from augurs, id., VII, 673. HASTA, the spear, worshipped by the Romans in place of Mars. Lactantius, VII, 499.—In former times spears were worshipped as gods, ibid. HECATE. Arnobius, V, 926.—Hecate praised Christ. Augustine, XLI, 652. HECTOR. Augustine, XLII, 585. HELEN of the Greeks. Lactantius, VI, 162; Augustine, XXXIII, 157, 237.—The wife of Menelaus, corrupted into adultery by Paris, [Col. 0378] id., XLI, 41.—Carried off at the instigation of the gods. Arnobius, V, 728.—Simon Magus rescued his own Tyrian Helen from a brothel. Tertullian, II, 708.—He said that she was the same woman as Helen, most destructive to Priam, ibid. HELEN, a certain prostitute whom Simon Magus wished to be believed to be Minerva. Augustine, XLII, 25. HERCULES. Commodianus the African, V, 212.—Augustine, XXXVIII, 164, 1249, 1250; XLI, 639.—When he lived. Lactantius, VI, 159; Augustine, XLI, 565.—Begotten through intercourse lasting nine nights. Arnobius, V, 1057.—His debaucheries and lusts. Lactantius, VI, 156.—In one night he dishonoured the fifty daughters of Thespius. Arnobius, V, 1057.—Laurentia, Hercules’ prostitute. Augustine, XLI, 145.—For a base love he serves under Omphale. Arnobius, V, 1051; Lactantius, VI, 159.—Hercules was prostituted in Omphale, and Omphale in Hercules. Tertullian, I, 605; II, 1041.—That he performed nothing miraculous. Lactantius, VI, 157.—When he captured Troy, id., VI, 159.—He did not deserve immortality by physical strength, id., VI, 210.—Hercules now wears a poplar upon his head, now a wild olive-tree, etc. Tertullian, II, 85.—He was said to have descended to the underworld, id., I, 605.—Because of a lost boy, he abandoned the Argonauts’ expedition, id., I, 605.—Why divine honours were conferred upon him. Augustine, XLI, 565.—Whence his chief distinction. Lactantius, VII, 45.—Labeo counts Hercules among the demigods. Augustine, XLI, 58, 59.—Called the god of strength, id., XXXVIII, 166.—Holy. Arnobius, V, 1057.—Great, id., V, 770.—Tamer of thieves, id., V, 764.—Philoctetes did not believe Hercules to be a god. Lactantius, VI, 160.—Deceived by the poisons of his wanton wife, he burned himself alive. Tertullian, I, 605; Arnobius, V, 779; Augustine, XLI, 569.—He is burned on Mount Oeta. Tertullian, I, 355; Cyprian, IV, 225; Arnobius, V, 761, 1054; Augustine, XLI, 569.—Rites of Hercules celebrated at Lindus. Lactantius, VI, 238.—An image of Hercules with its inscription. Augustine, XXXVIII, 164.—With a gilded beard at Carthage, where it was shaved off, id., XXXVIII, 166. Hercules removed at Rome, id., XXXVIII, 166.—The spirits of Juno and Hercules divided between themselves, id., XXXVIII, 447.—The Cynics’ Herculean aids, id., XXXII, 943.—Represented on stage burning alive. Tertullian, I, 576.—Mocked by Diogenes, id., I, 576.—History says that there were several Herculeses. Augustine, XLI, 569.—Three hungry Herculeses. Tertullian, I, 358.—Three mocked, ibid.—Three pairs [six], Arnobius, V, 1031.—Hercules Alexicacus, Lactantius, VI, 559, 560.—Oetaean, Arnobius, V, 1054.—Theban, id., V, 760, 1043.—The twelve mighty deeds of the Syrian or Tyrian Hercules. Augustine, XLI, 569.—The Tyrian was buried in Spain. Arnobius, V, 760, 761. HERCULEAN DESCENDANTS. Tertullian, II, 1035. HERMONIA, an oracle in Macedonia. Tertullian, II, 730. HEROES were worshipped as gods. Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 297, 299, 333.—Yet a god has neither beginning nor end, id., III, 309. HERTA. By this name the earth was worshipped by the Germans as a god. Lactantius, VI, 281. HESIOD’S Pandora. Tertullian, II, 84, 562. THE GOLDEN APPLES OF THE HESPERIDES. Arnobius, V, 1122. HESSUS, a god of the Gauls, is appeased by human blood. Lactantius, VI, 230.—He was the same as Mars, VI, 229. HIEROPHANTS. Tertullian, I, 313; II, 260. HIPPO, or Hippona and Epona, was worshipped by the heathen. Tertullian, I, 365, 577. THE CHILDREN OF HIPPOCOON wound Hercules. Arnobius, V, 1053. HIPPOCRATES. Cyprian, IV, 156. A GOAT worshipped by the Egyptians. Lactantius, VI, 787. HONOUR, a god. Augustine, XLI, 128.—Honour is called “mistress,” although grammatically masculine. Lactantius, VII, 572.—It is sometimes made into a goddess, ibid.—Honour and Virtue as gods. Arnobius, V, 1005. HORON, an Aeon of the Valentinians. Tertullian, II, 565, 577. VICTIMS: different victims for different gods. Arnobius, V, 1240, 1241. Those for the upper gods were white; those for the lower gods tawny, id., V, 1241, 1242. HOSTILINA, the goddess assigned to crops when they become level with their new ears. Augustine, XLI, 118. HOSTILIUS invented the god Fear. Tertullian, II, 266.—Fear and Pallor. Cyprian, IV, 226. THE HYDRA overcome by Hercules. Tertullian, II, 1042.—The use of its blood, ibid. HYMENAEUS. Augustine, XLII, 575.

## I

IBIS, an Egyptian goddess. Tertullian, II, 302; Lactantius, VI, 786. THE UNHEWN WOOD OF ICARIUS worshipped as Diana. Arnobius, V, 1186. ICARUS. The story of Icarus. Augustine, XLI, 571. IDAEA, mother of the gods. Cyprian, IV, 226. IDOLATRY, the mother of all games. Cyprian, IV, [Col. 0379] 340.—The origin of idolatry. Lactantius, VI, 155, 247.—What Lactantius thought about it, VI, 328.—How it spread among the nations. Lactantius, VI, 449.—Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 315. AN IDOL did not exist until some time afterward. Tertullian, I, 664.—The origin of the name “idol,” id., I, 665.—Idols—the names of dead persons—are nothing, just as their images themselves are nothing, id., I, 643.—God forbids both the making and the worshipping of an idol, id., I, 665.—Nothing is more unclean than an idol, id., II, 90. IDOLS ARE NOT GODS. Cyprian, IV, 262.—The idols which the Gentiles consider gods, IV, 121.—Demons of the dead dwell in idols. Tertullian, I, 645.—Satan and his angels had filled the whole world with idols, id., I, 640.—Why those who worship idols are like idols. Augustine, XXXVII, 1754.—A human being rightly falls away from him who made him when he sets above himself that which he himself has made, id., XLI, 249.—Who are called idolaters, id., XLII, 827.—The false natural philosophy of idolaters is rejected, id., XLI, 217.—The origin of idolatry, id., XLI, 685; XLII, 221, 224.—Idolatry from pride, id., XXXVIII, 1022; from vanity, id., XLIV, 212.—Idolatry, established in Egypt, was more manifold and far more disgraceful. Augustine, XLIII, 597.—None greater, none more superstitious, id., XXXVIII, 1022.—The world flooded with Egyptian inventions, id., XXXVIII, 1022.—Idolatry, a great evil, id., XXXIV, 743; XLII, 540.—The sins of idolatry are themselves also punishments, id., XXXVIII, 1022.—How mad the worshippers of idols are, id., XXXVII, 1757, 1957; XXXVIII, 777.—Idolaters are pressed hard, id., XXXIV, 1061.—The Apostles’ teaching against idolatry is defended from the prophets, id., XXXIV, 1066.—Idolatry cannot be defended, id., XLI, 221, 222.—They say in vain that they worship not images but that which is signified by images. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1023.—The excuses of idolaters are refuted, id., XXXVII, 1244, 1245, 1246; XLIII, 587.—Idolatry was either punished or restrained among the Jews, id., XLII, 290.—The worship of idols was forbidden and their temples shut by imperial laws, id., XXXVII, 1788, 1789.—The overthrow of idols did not thereby bring about the Romans’ ruin, id., XXXVIII, 623, 624.—Idolatry was destroyed by causes contrary to those by which it was established, id., XLI, 250. Various forms of idolatry, id., XXXIV, 152.—Idols of the heart, id., XL, 643.—If an artisan gave an idol a heart as well as a form, he would be worshipped by the idol itself, id., XXXVIII, 777.—The idolatry which the weakness of human thought attempts to establish in our heart from the habit of visible things, id., XXXIII, 798. ISIS first carried about ears of grain, discovered by her, upon her head. Tertullian, II, 86.—The linen garments of Isis, id., I, 612.—Isis expelled from the council of the gods and restored, id., I, 305, 573.—Dusky Isis mourns her lost son. **MERCURY.** Commodianus Africanus, V, 207; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 314.—Mercury was the first to explain letters. Tertullian, II, 87.—Inventor of letters, id., I, 616.—Originator of the first garment, id., II, 1038.—Winged upon his bald head, fiery upon his caduceus, id., I, 576.—Represented by actors as examining dead gladiators with a branding-iron, id., I, 382.—He flayed a little sheep, id., II, 1038.—Mercury called Cyllenian. Arnobius, V, 983.—Son of Maia, id., V, 1188.—Eloquent in speech, id., V, 1043.—Bald, id., V, 1188.—Wearing a petasos, ibid., V, 1188.—Bearer of serpents, id., V, 1043.—As though a certain *Medicurrius*, id., V, 983.—He is not a god, id., V, 983.—He is a thief, id., V, 1048.—Changer or broker of markets, merchandise, and commerce, id., V, 983.—He presides over boxing and wrestling. Arnobius, V, 969.—When Mercury, grandson of Atlas through his daughter Maia, lived. Arnobius, V, 965; St. Augustine, XLI, 565, 599.—Why he was enrolled among the gods, id., XLI, 565.—Mercury is called a messenger, id., XLI, 205.—Mercury as though “running in the middle” (*medius currens*), id., XLI, 205.—Mercury was mortal, id., XLI, 542.—Why he is painted winged, id., XLI, 205.—The offices of Mercury, id., XLI, 205.—Mercury is said to be the discoverer of letters, id., XXXVIII, 49.—He presided over eloquence, XLI, 128.—Over merchandise, id., 205.—Mercury’s burial in the city of Hermopolis, id., XLI, 254.—Mercury, grandfather of Trismegistus, id., XLI, 254, 599.

St. Augustine, XLI, 120, 566.—As though a certain *Meminerva*, id., V, 980.—Memory, id., V, 980.—They have said that Minerva is either the highest ether or the moon. St. Augustine, XLI, 207.—Varro wishes the Ideas to be understood as Minerva, id., 218.—When Minerva lived, why she was called Tritonia, and why enrolled among the gods, id., XLI, 566.—Minerva, goddess of arms and arts. Lactantius, VI, 208.—By what name she was called by the Egyptians, id., VI, 214.—Whether she is the same as Noema, daughter of Lanoch, ibid.—The judgment involving her and Juno. Lactantius, VI, 208.—Minerva’s bowl. Tertullian, I, 344.—Five Minervas. Arnobius, V, 1033; Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1018.—Their mutual contest over the dignity of the name. Arnobius, V, 1033, 1034.

## P

**PAGANS**, defenders, guardians, and worshippers of shameful gods. Arnobius, V, 1122.—They disgrace their gods by foul beliefs about them, id., V, 944, 1143–1147.—They did not think temples could exist without statues. Lactantius, VII, 317, 683.—They marked statues representing gods with the gods’ own names, id., VII, 473.—They worship gods through images. Arnobius, V, 1179–1181.—In their prayers they invoke gods and goddesses, id., V, 946–947.—They disparage divine works, id., V, 745–748.—Their hatred against Christ, id., V, 775–777.—It would have been better for them to be mute than to invent shameful stories concerning the gods. Arnobius, V, 1155.—They insulted Christians. Tertullian, II, 935.—They teach wickedness, id., V, 1145.—They expose their children to death, id., V, 932.—They think it preferable not to be defeated rather than to believe confessed truth, id., V, 1188.

**PALES**, god. Arnobius, V, 994.—He presides over flocks of cattle, id., V, 967.

**SATURN**, source of all, or of the greater or better-known, divinity among the pagans. Tertullian, I, 329, 601.—First and parent of all the gods, ibid.—What parents he had. Tertullian, I, 331, 601.—Saturn Quadratus, id., II, 266.—It is proved that he is not a god. Arnobius, V, 977.—He was not a god but a man who received kingdom and life from another man. Tertullian, I, 329, 602.—Lactantius, VI, 189.—He lived a mortal life, id., I, 330, 602 and following.—On his golden age. Lactantius, VI, 179.—While he reigned, justice flourished on earth. Ibid., 564.—Whence the story of this golden age was drawn, id., VI, 179.—He was not born from heaven. Lactantius, VI, 182.—Impious toward father and sons. # LVIII. INDEX OF THE OPINIONS OF ANCIENT PHILOSOPHERS MENTIONED IN THE *PATROLOGIA*, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECT

## Notice

In this index we list all the errors of ancient philosophers which the Fathers either mentioned or attacked in their writings; and, so as at once to provide the reader with an easier and more useful path, we arrange alphabetically the various matters or subjects concerning which the philosophers erred, indicating only the volume in Roman numerals and the columns in Arabic numerals.

**Air.**—Worship of air among the Assyrians and African peoples; refuted, XII, 989. Anaximenes believed air to be god, XXXII, 782; XXXIII, 443. He assigned the causes of things to infinite air, and imagined that gods arose from it, XLI, 226.

**Soul.**—Oenesidemus’s opinion concerning the substance of the soul, II, 660. Albinus’s doctrine concerning souls, II, 697; Anaxagoras’s, II, 666; Anaximenes’s, II, 660. According to many philosophers, the soul is divine and eternal, I, 610. According to Epicurus, the soul is mortal, ibid. Plato divides the soul in two, rational and irrational, II, 668, 672. Zeno divides it into three parts, or even six; Serenus into seven; Chrysippus into eight; Apollophanes into nine; and certain Stoics into ten, ibid. Every faculty of thought in the soul is flesh, II, 814. The soul is never without flesh so long as it is in flesh, II, 814. The soul has a bodily extension of its own, II, 182, 817. The soul is nothing if it is not a body, II, 657. If it had no body, the soul’s image could not receive the image of a body, II, 657. The soul has shape, limit, length, breadth, and height, II, 659. The soul is corporeal, possessing its own kind of solid substance, II, 816. Apelles’s error concerning souls, II, 686; he posited male and female souls prior to bodies, 712. Cleanthes’s opinion concerning the soul, II, 653, 693. Empedocles said that the soul consists of blood, II, 653; he located the cause of keen or dull intelligence in the quality of the blood, 683; placed it throughout the entire breastplate of the chest, 672; held it to be not divine but mortal, I, 610; II, 19. Erasistratus taught that the soul resides in membranes, II, 671. Heraclitus taught that the substance of the soul is air and that it consists of fire, II, 653, 660. Hermogenes rashly held that the soul’s sensation arose from the substrate of matter rather than from God’s breath, II, 646, 664. Seneca teaches that everything, including the soul, ends after death, II, 721, 795. Thales said that the soul consists of water, II, 653; Hipparchus, of fire, 663.

Arnobius sets forth and refutes the people’s various opinions concerning the excellence of the human soul, V, book II, *Against the Nations*, chapters 17–23 and 30, 34. Plato’s arguments about the soul and its immortality are presented and refuted, VI, 771, 772 ff., 961 ff. Aristoxenus’s doctrine on the nature of the soul, VI, 779. Cicero and others teach the immortality of souls, but without faith, VI, 410. Democritus does not believe that the soul subsists after the dissolution of the body, XXII, 591. Platonists believe souls fell from heaven; Stoics believe them to be from God’s own substance, XXII, 1085. The Manichaeans did not believe that the soul was made from nothing, but said it was of the same nature as God, XLII, 34. Their error concerning the soul, XLV, 1325.—They maintained that the soul is not God’s temple but a part or member of him, or his very substance, XXXIV, 361; XLII, 380, 381; likewise the Stoics and Priscillianists, XXXII, 1237, 1242; XL, 523; XLII, 27, 44, 668–670; XLIV, 477, 512. Plato and the Platonists maintained that souls existed before bodies, XLII, 1011; XLIV, 402. They held that the soul’s passions arise from the mortal members of the earthly body, XLI, 408, 711. Aristotle called the soul a fifth body; Plato, no body at all; Lucretius, [a thing] composed of atoms, XLI, 773; XLII, 72. Philosophers’ opinions concerning the substance of the soul, XLII, 978, 981, 982. Three degrees of soul according to Varro, XLI, 212. What philosophers thought about the state of souls after death: XXXV, 1132, 1135; XLI, 311,

[Col. 0394]

361, 375, 601, 776. Anaxagoras’s error concerning the succession of souls, CXCIX, 982. Epicureans teach that the soul perishes with the body, CXCIX, 977.

**Animals.**—The Platonists held that mortal animals were made by lesser gods or angels, XLI, 373, 375; Epicurus, that they arose from the chance concurrence of atoms, XXXIII, 444. Some said that rational animals alone are parts of God, XLI, 123. According to Plato, the gods are living creatures, XLI, 241.

**Antipodes.**—Lactantius’s error concerning the antipodes, VI, 425, 426. Augustine did not think the antipodes existed, XLI, 487.

**Water.**—Worship of water among the Egyptians; rejected, XII, 384. Thales held water to be the principle of things, XLI, 226, 230.

**Free Will.**—How freedom of choice is compatible with fate, CXCIX, 991.

**Atoms.**—Epicureans said that God arose from atoms, I, 517, 588. Epicurus’s atoms, II, 703; his void and empty space, II, 564. Epicurus’s error concerning atoms: VI, 401; 745; XLI, 181, 230, 320. Refuted by Cicero, XXXIII, 444, 445. Lucretius believes that souls consist of atoms, XLII, 72. Democritus is said to differ from Epicurus in these questions of nature because he thought that some animal and spiritual force inhered in the collision of atoms, XXXIII, 445.

**Highest Good.**—Calliphon and Dinomachus placed happiness in virtue joined with pleasure, VI, 364. See the entry **Happiness**.

**Flesh.**—The Stoics should be considered to live according to the flesh, XLI, 413.

**Certainty.**—Aristotle’s dialectic: a slippery artificer of constructing and destroying, harsh in conjectures, a workman of controversies in arguments, II, 20. Every opinion derives from the senses, II, 675. To sense and to understand are one and the same, II, 678. The Academics rather severely condemn trust in the five senses, II, 674. The Academics doubted even matters that are entirely evident, XLI, 625–627. The doctrines of the Academics were that knowledge cannot be attained by a human being, XXXII, 923. The wise person ought to assent to nothing, for one who assents to uncertain matters errs; but all things are uncertain, XXXII, 923.
