Suspension of assent is the great action of the wise person, XXXII, 924. Nothing is more shameful than to hold an opinion, XXXII, 923. Some Academics located the discovery of truth itself in bodily senses, XXXIII, 441. Epicureans and Stoics located the criterion for apprehending truth in the senses; Platonists in intellect alone, XXXIII, 441.

**Foods.**—What Epicurus teaches about foods, XXXIII, 630.

**Human Body.**—Apelles’s error concerning the human body, II, 811.

**Creation.**—Cicero’s opinion concerning the creation of the world, VI, 297. What Zeno conjectures concerning God and creatures, XXXIII, 497. Arguments by which the temporal creation of natures is attacked, and their refutation, XLI, 366.

**Demons.**—Gods and demons share one quality of name, I, 413. The Manichaeans’ error that some part of God’s nature had been mixed with the nature of demons, to be bound and polluted, XLII, 536, 537, 539, 544, 545, 565, 595. The Stoics hold that the conflicts of opposing pursuits are the work of demons, not gods, XLI, 262. Labeo, worshipper of demons, XLI, 372. Socrates’ demon, XLI, 239.

**God.**—Various errors concerning the one true God are enumerated here. Achamoth, Valentinus’s aeon, II, 68, 564, 571. Egyptians worshipped beasts, II, 596; consecrated sheep and oxen, I, 418; condemned to capital punishment those who killed one of them, ibid.; their gods were the ibis and crocodile, II, 302; bulls, etc., II, 928, 953. How undeservedly Aeneas was called pious and a god, I, 599. Aeons of the Valentinians, II, 47, 68; of the Ophites, II, 64. Anscharia, goddess of the Aesculani, I, 621. The Athenians worshipped Aesculapius and his mother, I, 605; Socrates ordered a cock to be offered to him, II, 648. Alburnus, a god, I, 290; discovered by Metellus, II, 266. All heavenly things and the air were called god, II, 260. Apelles makes a certain indeterminate god the creator of angels; he declares the god of the Law and Israel to be fire, II, 47, 686, 801. Apis, god of the Egyptians, II, 261. Argius, a god, I, 606. The pagans worshipped asses along with Epona and Isis, 577. Numentius, god of the Athenians, I, 596. Basilides denies that the God of the Jews is God and calls him an angel, II, 62. Cerdon introduced two first principles, that is, two gods, a good one and a cruel one, II, 70, 249. Human error worships everything except the Creator of all things himself, I, 666. God is a body, even if spirit, II, 102. The Platonists called God incorporeal; the Stoics, corporeal, I, 517. On God’s nature, and the diverse opinions concerning gods, I, 507. Some deny to God his own properties—simplicity and power, I, 1201. Plato and the Platonists affirm God’s providence; Epicurus and the Epicureans deny it, I, 517. The gods of paganism derive their origin from Saturn; according to Varro, from Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, I, 329, 601. Gods and demons share one quality of name, I, 413. Whence people made so many gods for themselves, I, 133, 328; II, 266. Antiquity erred in the worship of gods, I, 306, 418, 502, 587, 589, 594, 595, 598, 645. Gods for sale, private gods, and household gods, I, 344–347, 360, 413, 494, 547, 596. Gods of Roman paganism, I, 409, 423, 597, 606; II, 255. Marcion introduces two gods, as though two Symplegades [clashing rocks] of shipwreck, II, 248. Physical superstition regards the elements as god, II, 447. Philosophers have dared to declare nothing certain concerning God: Epicurus, II, 391, 726; Hermogenes, II, 198, 201, 202, 205; Marcion, II, 19, 248, 252, 264, 361, 432; Plato, I, 509; II, 260; Pythagoras, I, 517; Socrates, I, 354, 589; Stoics, I, 517, 518; II, 236; Varro, I, 387, 590, 601; Zeno, II, 260. On the vanity of idols in St Cyprian, IV, 563. On false gods in Arnobius, V, through almost the entire work; in Lactantius, VI, 134–281; in Firmicus Maternus, XII, 384, 987, 989, 992, 995 ff., 1085; in St Augustine, XXXII, 707, 782, 955, 1246, 1317, 1362; XXXIII, 442, 445, 619, 718, 724, 841, 861, 1033; XXXIV, 122, 123, 153, 164, 427, 436, 1056; XXXVI, 273, 1040; XXXVII, 1822, 1907, 1908; XXXVIII, 777, 986, 1134, 1138; XL, 297; XLI, 56, 81, 105, 123, 126, 138, 175, 181, 189, 199, 202, 208, 211, 218, 225, 226, 237, 241, 247, 250, 255, 262, 274, 277, 303–305, 336, 372, 373, 375, 388, 390, 601, 645, 650, 794; XLII, 46, 113, 214, 218, 222, 229, 248, 261, 333, 370, 376, 389, 390, 414, 466, 536, 545, 566, 595, 603; XLIII, 360; XLIV, 499, 572, 1126; XLV, 1325, 1328. Aristotle erred in many respects; he asserts that God can commit wrong, CXCIX, 932. Cicero doubts what he should think God to be, CXCIX, 991. Epicurus worships chance as god, CXCIX, 977. Socrates considers the human mind to be god, CXCIX, 982.

**Dialectic.**—Aristotle’s dialectic: a slippery artificer of constructing and destroying, constrained in propositions, harsh in conjectures, a workman of controversies in arguments, II, 20.

**Universal Doubt.**—Error of the Academics: what could be more foolish than to fluctuate about every individual matter, have certainty about nothing, and profess the name of philosopher? CXCIX, 638.—Arcesilaus, chief of the Academics, is pitiably torn apart, wavers uncertainly in everything, and does not know where he wishes to stand, CXCIX, 981.—The Platonists began to doubt about almost everything, CXCIX, 648.—On Zeno’s universal doubt, CXCIX, 981.

**Elements.**—Firmicus Maternus makes the elements the principles of things, XII, 983. That neither the whole world nor the elements are God, nor are animate, is demonstrated, VI, 281. See **Atoms**, **Creation**, **Origin of Things**.

**Error.**—On Epicurus’s errors and how he was led to deny Providence, VI, 399–401. His error concerning atoms, VI, 745. The Academics considered error a sin that cannot be avoided unless all assent is suspended, XL, 242.

**Evidence.**—The Academics held that knowledge cannot be attained by a human being; truth cannot be apprehended; the whole task of the wise person is located in the search for truth; the wise person should assent to nothing, since one who assents to uncertain matters errs; all things are uncertain; and nothing is more shameful than to hold an opinion, XXXII, 923. They said suspension of assent is the great action of the wise person, XXXII, 924. Some located the very discovery of truth in bodily senses, XXXIII, 441.

[Col. 0396]

They doubted even matters that are entirely manifest, XLI, 625–627. To the New Academics everything was uncertain, XLI, 646.

**Fate.**—How much Cicero attributed to Fortune, VI, 441. Democritus asserted that everything came to be by chance, VI, 119, 760. Some wicked persons think that everything is governed by chance, and that varying fortune plays in human affairs, XXXIII, 400. The foolish teaching of astrologers concerning fate is demonstrated from their own deeds, XXXIII, 1061. How freedom of choice is compatible with fate in Cicero, CXCIX, 991. Epicurus’s fate, CXCIX, 546. Epicurus worships chance as god, CXCIX, 977. Whoever posits fortune overturns and destroys the fates: “The fates,” says the Stoic, “govern human beings; fate lies in those parts which the folds conceal,” CXCIX, 546. The Stoic introduces a fated necessity, CXCIX, 976.

**Happiness; Blessed Life.**—The Peripatetics placed happiness in goods of soul, body, and fortune, VI, 364 ff.; XLI, 630. Aristippus, in bodily pleasure, VI, 364 ff.; XLI, 227, 601. Aristotle, in moral goodness and virtue, VI, 364 ff. Calliphon and Dinomachus, in moral goodness joined to pleasure, VI, 364 ff.; XLIV, 852. Diodorus, in freedom from pain, VI, 364 ff. Epicurus, in bodily pleasure, ibid., and XXXII, 942; XXXIII, 439; XXXVI, 944; XXXVIII, 809; XLII, 1019. Herillus, in knowledge, VI, 364 ff. Zeno, in life’s conformity with nature, ibid. Antisthenes, in virtue of soul, XLI, 776. Some held that the soul, even after attaining wisdom, passes from happiness into misery and conversely, XLI, 361. The Old Academics differed greatly from the New, placing happiness in this life, XLI, 630. Plato promises false blessednesses to the human soul, XLI, 776. Philosophers erred in locating blessedness in this life, XLI, 627, 628. They taught that people make a blessed life for themselves through the virtue of their own will, XXXIII, 830. By locating the highest good in the soul, the Stoics turned the soul away more from flesh than from body, XXXIII, 440. Stoic opinion concerning the blessed life, XXXVIII, 809, 812, 853, 854.

**Human End.**—Anaxagoras’s error in assigning an end to humanity, VI, 371 ff.: when asked for what purpose he had been born, he answered, “To behold heaven and the sun,” ibid.

**Grace.**—The Stoics’ doctrine that grace exists in God, VII, 89.

**Man.**—Plato’s [doctrine], XXXIII, 64.

**Ideas.**—Someone holds that “ideas” are certain invisible, incorporeal, supramundane, divine, and eternal substances, which he calls *ideas*, II, 678. What Democritus thought concerning ideas, XXXIII, 444, 445.

**Idolatry.**—The false natural philosophy of idolaters, XLI, 217; rejected, ibid.

**Fire.**—Heraclitus said that all things are born from fire, VI, 309; XLI, 181. Worship of fire among the Persians, XII, 992. Some imagined God to be a fiery body; others, the brightness of light, XXXIV, 464. Fire is the principle of things according to the Stoics, and is regarded by them as God, XLI, 230. Zeno said that God himself is fire, 955.

**Immortality.**—The immortality humans would have had if they had not sinned is wrongly denied by certain philosophers. See **Soul**, **Rewards of the Other Life**.

**Void.**—Epicurus’s void and empty space, II, 564.

**Oath.**—Why Socrates was accustomed to swear by any dog, stone, or whatever came in his way, XXXIV, 123.

**Children.**—In his *Republic* Plato wishes wives to be promiscuous and children consequently to be held in common, XXII, 656, 657.

**Brightness of Light.**—The Manichaeans imagined the brightness of immense light stretched everywhere through infinite spaces, yet divided on one side as though by a certain black wedge, teaching that there are two opposing kingdoms, XXXIV, 165.

**Evil.**—Pagans attributed evil to the stars or fate, I, 268. That is not evil which lacks the natural properties of evil, I, 269, 560. The Manichaeans’ doctrine concerning evil, XLV, 1529. Refuted, XLII, 588, 589. Their error concerning evil, XLIV, 1104, 1105. How they distinguished evil and good, XLII, 509. They held evil to be not an accident but a substance, XLV, 1330. Philosophers thought that evils befall people because of sins committed by souls in another life, XXXVIII, 1132. They asserted that the kingdom, or nation, of darkness is both eternal and the highest evil, XXXII, 1346. That earth is evil, XXXII, 716, 1351. They considered the nature of evil coeternal with God, XLIV, 1008. They mingle the unchangeable substance of evil nature with the nature of their God, XLIV, 1104, 1105. The Stoics’ error concerning the evils of this life, XLI, 629.

**Evil First Principle.**—The Manichaeans wish the evils of the human race to be assigned to some unknown first principle of evil, coeternal with God’s eternity, XLV, 1339. They asserted two gods, one good and the other

[Col. 0397]

evil, XXXII, 1317; or rather two natures or substances, and two mutually opposing principles, XXXII, 1346. Fiction concerning the battle of the God of light with the prince of darkness, XLIV, 1071. Other matters concerning the evil first principle, XXXII, 608, 1352, 1355, 1356; XXXIII, 722; XXXIV, 130.

**Matter.**—Hermogenes teaches that matter was necessary to God for the works of the world, II, 216. He introduces uncreated matter and equates it with the uncreated God, II, 46, 198; and holds matter to be evil, II, 208. The Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Plato himself held matter to be uncreated, II, 567, 667. Those are answered who try to establish the eternity of matter from the words of Scripture, XIV, 135. The Manichaeans asserted that evil is earth, or a black, immense, deep, and extended mass, and also mind, or a thin and subtle mass wandering through the earth, XXXII, 716, 1351. Some pagans join matter to God as coeternal with him, XLII, 380.

**Marriage.**—Plato rejects marriage in his *Republic*, XXII, 657. See **Marriage Rites**.

**Lying.**—Plato teaches lying, XXIII, 412.

**Metempsychosis.**—What metempsychosis is, II, 111. Thoroughly refuted, II, 697. Pythagoras’s and Empedocles’s doctrine concerning metempsychosis, I, 522, 613; II, 702. It is asserted not only by Pythagoras and Empedocles but also by Plato, XXII, 748; XXXIII, 484, 487.

**The Myth of a Thousand Years.**—Pythagoras is said to have been the first impiously to introduce the myth of a thousand years, CXCIX, 643.

**World.**—According to Varro, fire is the soul of the world, I, 589. Pythagoras called the world uncreated, I, 333. Other philosophers maintain that it is uncreated and unmade, II, 609. Plato taught that it was made by God, I, 333; II, 1033. It is demonstrated that neither the whole world nor the elements are God, nor are animate, VI, 281. Thales considered the world eternal, VI, 315, 735. Cicero’s opinion concerning the creation of the world, V, 297. Anaximander admitted innumerable worlds, XLI, 226. Epicurus says that worlds without number, living creatures, souls, and even gods themselves arise through the chance concurrence of atoms, XXXIII, 444; XLI, 320. Refuted by Cicero, XXXIII, 444, 445. Various and contradictory philosophical doctrines concerning the world’s unity, beginning, end, and governance, XLI, 601. Plato admitted two worlds, one intelligible and one sensible, XXXII, 588, 954. Plato and other philosophers held this world to be a living creature, XXXII, 602. Philosophers call the world a great living creature without bodily senses, whose soul is Jupiter or Hecate, XXXVIII, 1137. The Platonists teach that the world is the greatest living creature, XLI, 388, 390. A most blessed and everlasting living creature, XLI, 308. The structure of the body of the world, XLI, 212. Some held the world to be God’s body, XLI, 123. According to pagans, the body of the world is not God, but its soul is, XLI, 202. The soul of the world and its parts were believed to be true gods, XLI, 211; Varro held this view, VII, 198, 199, 202; it is refuted, XLI, 202; he believed the individual parts of the world to have distinct but divine souls, XLI, 199. Some pagans considered the universe the greatest of gods, XLII, 370. Varro judged the world to be god, XLI, 199; Plato, XLI, 390. The world is imagined to be eternal, XXXIX, 1137. The Platonists held the world to have been made and nevertheless to exist from eternity, XLI, 311, 319; they are refuted, 320, 321. Cicero agreed with the Platonists that the world would not perish, XLI, 759. Zeno said that there is nothing besides this sensible world and that nothing occurs in it without body, XXXII, 955.

**Nature.**—The Stoics divide nature into two parts: one which acts, and another which offers itself as malleable material for action, VI, 741. Leucippus’s opinion concerning the nature of things, VII, 101. The Manichaeans said that evil nature cannot in any way be changed, XXII, 1157. Ancient opinions concerning the nature of things, XXIII, 558; Zeno’s, XXXIII, 479. The Manichaeans admitted two gods—or rather two natures or substances, and two mutually opposing principles, XXXII, 1346; they held that evil nature had always existed without any beginning, XL, 363. Their madness concerning two natures warring with one another, XL, 360, 364. They admit that the good God made the world, although from an alien nature and matter, XLI, 603; that humanity was created from the mixture of two natures which have always existed, one good and the other evil, XLIV, 441. The Manichaeans’ error concerning nature, XLI, 336; XLV, 1325. The Manichaeans introduce a nature of evil endowed with its own principle, opposed to God, XXXIII, 722. They affirm that a bad nature is the cause of sin, XLIV, 612. They call vices natures and substances, XLIV, 1085. They condemn concupiscence not as an accidental vice but as a nature eternally evil, XLIV, 572. Scotus’s errors concerning the division of nature, CXXII, 355. “Nothing happens contrary to nature,” says Plato, who calls nature God’s will, CXCIX, 427.

**Numbers.**—Pythagoras believed gods to be constituted from numbers, XLI, 181.

[Col. 0398]

**Marriage Rites.**—Epicurus, defender of pleasure, discouraged marriage, XXIII, 280. Plato, despising marriage, feared the perverse opinion of his age so much that he sacrificed to nature, in order that it might be abolished as though it were a sin, XXXIV, 126; he rejects marriage, XXII, 657.

**Suicide.**—The Pythagoreans and Stoics, by asserting the immortality of souls, vainly recommend voluntary death, VI, 405.

**Origin of Our Cognitions.**—Epicureans and Stoics located the criterion for apprehending truth in the senses; Platonists, in intellect alone, XXXIII, 441. See **Perceptions**.

**Origin of Things.**—What Plato thought concerning the origin of things, XXIII, 479; the doctrines of ancient philosophers, XXIII, 558; of Anaxagoras, XLI, 226; of Anaximander, ibid. See **Atoms**, **Matter**, **World**.

**Pantheism.**—Thales considered the world eternal, VI, 315, 735. Much concerning the eternity of matter, VI, 303–306; refuted, XIV, 135. The Stoics hold the soul to be from God’s own substance, XXII, 1085. Stoics, Manichaeans, and Priscillianists said that the soul is from God’s own substance, XXXII, 1237, 1242; XXXIII, 718, 723; XL, 523; XLII, 44, 668–670; XLIII, 27; XLIV, 477, 512. The Manichaeans did not believe the soul made from nothing, but said it was of the same nature as God, XLII, 34; that the soul is not God’s temple but his part or member, XLII, 380, 381; that the soul is God’s very substance, XXXIV, 361; and other material on the same point, XXXII, 1362; XXXIII, 718, 841, 1033; XXXVII, 1822; XXXVIII, 986; XL, 297; XLI, 123; XLII, 380; XLIV, 572. The world’s soul and its parts were believed to be true gods, XLI, 202, 211; this was Varro’s view, VII, 198 ff.; XLI, 199; and also Plato’s, XLI, 390.

**Passions.**—What the Academics think concerning the extirpation of passions, XXII, 1148; the Stoics, XXIII, 529; Chrysippus and others, 542. The Stoics said that the wise person undergoes passions by necessity but does not yield to them, whereas the foolish person yields to them, XLI, 258–260. When Platonists and others speak of passions, they dispute over words rather than things, XLI, 259, 260. The Stoics are ridiculed because they neither fear nor grieve, XXXIX, 1528. What fear or passion of mind, according to Aulus Gellius and the Stoics, can affect the wise person, CXCIX, 651.

PECCATA.—The Stoics maintain that all sins are equal, XXIII, 511; XL, 539.

PERCEPTIONS.—Every opinion comes from the senses, II, 675; sensing and understanding are one and the same, 678; the Academics condemn more harshly the reliability of the five senses, 674. Zeno’s definition of the apprehension of truth, XXXII, 925; discussed at 943.

DISTURBANCES OF THE SOUL.—The Stoics are wrong to deny that disturbances can befall the wise person, XXXV, 1798.

PHILOSOPHY.—Seneca’s error concerning philosophy, which he calls the rule for living well. Here he plainly failed to consider the common name of philosophy: since it is dispersed among many schools and disciplines, has nothing certain, and indeed nothing whatever about which all agree with one mind and voice, what could be more false than to call philosophy the rule of life, when the diversity of its precepts obstructs and confuses the right path? VI, 391. Cicero errs in praising philosophy, VI, 385; his vain preoccupation with setting forth truth and assigning an origin to wisdom, VI, 351; likewise Lucretius and others, 386.

PHYSIOLOGY.—The false natural philosophy of idolaters is rejected, XLI, 217.

PUNISHMENTS AND REWARDS OF THE OTHER LIFE.—The Epicureans teach that nothing remains after death, II, 795; XXXII, 732; XXXVI, 944. They assert that death is the end of all evils, as do also those who judge the soul mortal, XXXIII, 389; XXXIX, 1528; CXCIX, 977.

FIRST PRINCIPLES OF THINGS.—What Thales declared to be the first principle of all things, I, 133, 309; XLI, 226, 230; what Firmicus Maternus declared, XII, 983; what Epicurus, XLI, 230; what Diogenes, 226; what Anaximander, ibid. The various opinions of philosophers, XLI, 225, 226, 230.

TWO ACCEPTED PRINCIPLES.—Cerdon introduced two first principles of things, that is, two gods, a good and a cruel one, II, 70, 249; likewise Marcion, II, 248, 252; likewise Hermogenes, 201; likewise the Manichaeans, XXXII, 1317, 1346; XXXIV, 130; XLII, 389, 390; XLIV, 1071.

THE PROBABLE.—The Academics introduced the probable, XXXII, 955. To follow what is probable without assent is harmless for the Academics, but wicked for Christians, 952, 953.

PROVIDENCE.—Epicurus and his followers denied God’s providence, I, 517, 588; VI, 303, 399–401; XLI, 601; XLII, 376; CXCIX, 977. Zeno and other pagan philosophers said that all things occur by fate, I, 268, 398, 560. The extent to which Cicero attributed things to fortune, VI, 441; likewise Democritus, VI, 119, 760. The opinion of certain philosophers who, from the course and constancy of the stars, suppose that there is providence in heavenly matters [Col. 0399], while earthly matters are disregarded, because nothing right or orderly takes place on earth, XXV, 82. Varro held God to be the soul governing the world by motion and reason, XLI, 138. The doctrine of the wicked—that God’s providence does not care for human affairs—is impious, XXXVIII, 924. Whence some derive the suspicion that the government of human affairs does not belong to God, XXXVIII, 318. The perverse in heart hold three opinions about God: either God does not exist, or God is unjust, or he does not govern human affairs, XXXVI, 273. Some deny providence, XXXII, 1272; others confess it in a thoroughly mistaken way, 1273.

REASONING.—Aristotle’s dialectic: a slippery artificer of construction and destruction, forced into dogmatic conclusions, harsh in conjectures, and a laborer in contentious arguments, II, 20. Matters that are clear ought not to be made doubtful by arguments, XXIII, 435.

RELIGION.—Cicero’s interpretation of the word *religion* is refuted, VI, 536. The dress of the Cynics creates no distinction in religion, XLI, 647.

REMINISCENCE.—The recollection of souls, according to Plato and Pythagoras, is disapproved and refuted, XXXII, 601; XLII, 1011, 1012.

RESURRECTION.—Philosophers most openly deny that the resurrection of the flesh can take place, XXXVI, 1134.

SACRED RITES OR SACRIFICES.—Plato and his disciples held that sacred rites ought to be performed for a great many gods, XLI, 237.

KNOWLEDGE.—The Academics abolished knowledge, VI, 355, 356; XXXII, 923. Arguing against the natural philosophers from obscure things, the Academics maintained that no knowledge exists; content with examples of a few incomprehensible matters, they embraced ignorance, as though they had abolished knowledge altogether because they had abolished it in part. The natural philosophers, on the other hand, inferred from things that are hidden [Col. 0400] that all things can be known; content with clear matters, they retained knowledge, as though they had defended it as a whole because they had defended it in part, VI, 369.

SENSATIONS.—The opinion of the Stoics and Peripatetics concerning affections, sensations, and pains, VI, 688 ff.

THE SUN.—Philosophers say that the sun is everlasting, XXXIII, 379.

THE EARTH.—The worship of the earth among the Phrygians, XII, 987; [the earth regarded as] one of the first principles of things, 983.

THEOLOGY.—According to Varro, three theologies: mythical, natural, and civil, XLI, 180, 192; mythical theology, shameful, 182, 183; theatrical theology proclaims the crimes of the gods, 223; it is unworthy of the gods, 182, 186.

TRUTH.—Arcesilaus removed truth from life, XXXIII, 431. The Academics held that truth cannot be apprehended, XXXII, 923; that the whole office of the wise person consists in the search for truth, 923; and that the wise person ought to assent to nothing, ibid. Philosophers did not know to what end the truths they knew ought to be directed, XLI, 602; why they held down truth in unrighteousness, XLII, 1034.

VIRTUE OF THE SOUL.—Where the Pythagoreans and Platonists placed true virtue of the soul, XLIV, 745. Antisthenes placed the highest good in virtue of the soul, XLI, 601. Calypho’s view of virtue, XLIV, 1083, 1084.

VICE.—The Manichaeans condemned concupiscence not as an accidental vice but as a nature evil from eternity, XLIV, 572. The Stoics class pity as a vice, XXXIII, 395, 396. Calliphus’ opinion on vice, XLIV, 1083, 1084.

PLEASURE.—Aristippus and Epicurus placed the highest good in pleasure, XXXVI, 944; XLI, 601.

[Col. 0399]

## LIX. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF ANCIENT PHILOSOPHERS WHOSE ERRORS THE FATHERS REFUTED IN THEIR WRITINGS

### NOTICE

In this Index, recalling in summary the various opinions of ancient philosophers in alphabetical order of their names, we indicate, by the numbers of both the volume of the *Patrologia* and the columns or pages, the places in which the Fathers refuted them in writing, and which the reader may thus easily find.

ACADEMICS.—These ancient philosophers condemned reliance on the senses; denied knowledge; and held that truth cannot be apprehended by man. Everything was uncertain to them, and they doubted even matters entirely manifest. They placed blessedness in this life and erred seriously concerning the eradication of passions: II, 674; VI, 355, 356, 360; XXII, 1148; XXIII, 479; XXVI, 597; XXXII, 923, 924, 955; XL, 242; XLI, 625–627, 630, 646; CXCIX, 638, 981.

EGYPTIANS.—The wise men of Egypt admitted the worship of water and worshipped beasts as gods—sheep, oxen, and so forth—I, 418; II, 261, 302, 596, 928, 953; XII, 384.

AENESIDEMUS.—His false opinion concerning the substance of the soul, II, 660.

ALBINUS.—What he thought concerning souls, II, 697.

ANAXAGORAS.—His confused opinion concerning souls and their succession, the end assigned to man, the sun, and God, II, 666; VI, 371 ff.; XXXIII, 442, 443; XLI, 226, 601; CXCIX, 982.

ANAXIMANDER.—He admitted innumerable worlds and believed the first principles of things to be infinite, XLI, 226.

ANAXIMENES.—His opinion concerning the substance of the soul and concerning God, whom he asserted to be air, II, 660; VI, 134; XXXII, 782; XXXIII, 443; XLI, 226.

APELLES.—He maintained that the creator of angels was some indeterminate god; he imagined the God of the Law and of Israel to be fiery; his errors concerning souls and the human body, II, 47, 686, 801, 811.

APOLLOPHANES.—He divided the soul into nine parts, II, 668.

ARCESILAUS, leader of the Academics.—He imagined three kinds of gods: physical, mythical, and national or popular [Col. 0400]. He removed truth from life and wavered uncertainly in all things, I, 587, 589; XXIII, 431; CXCIX, 981.

ARISTIPPUS, Socratic philosopher.—He placed the highest good in bodily pleasure, VI, 364; XLI, 227, 601.

ARISTOTLE.—His slippery dialectic; he placed the highest good in moral worth and virtue; his opinions on marriage and on the soul, which he asserted to be a fifth body; his errors concerning God and God’s providence. Empty glory, which he had attacked in words, overcame Aristotle, II, 20; VI, 135, 364; XXIII, 280, 479; XLI, 773; CXCIX, 648, 932, 983, 984.

ARISTOXENUS.—His opinion concerning the nature of the soul, VI, 779.

ATHENIANS.—They worshipped the god Numentinus and, like the Romans to uncertain gods, erected altars to unknown gods, I, 596; II, 255.

ATHEISTS.—Who the atheists were; their celebrated saying: “What is above us is nothing to us,” VI, 120, 416; VII, 99; XXXII, 1246; XXXIV, 153; XLIII, 360.

AULUS GELLIUS.—What fear or disturbance of the mind, according to Aulus Gellius and the Stoics, can befall the wise person, CXCIX, 641.

BASILIDES.—He denies the God of the Jews, whom he calls an angel, II, 62.

CALIPHO.—His opinion concerning virtue and vice, XLIV, 1083, 1084.

CALLIPHUS.—He placed happiness in moral worth joined with pleasure, VI, 364.

CERDON.—He introduced two origins or principles, that is, two gods, good and evil, II, 70, 249.

CHRYSIPPUS.—He divided the soul into seven parts and asserted that a human being can be completely without passions; his opinion concerning God, II, 668; VI, 134; XXII, 579; XXIII, 542.

CICERO.—His views concerning God, whom he thinks to be a body, though greater than a body; his opinion concerning the immortality of the soul, religion, philosophy, the origin of wisdom, the creation of the world, and the birth of man, VI, 135, 263, 297, 351, 386, 410, 441, 536; XXII, 1148; XXXIV, 1056; XLI, 759; CXCIX, 991.

CLEANTHES.—His opinion concerning the soul, II, 653, 693.

CYNICS.—These philosophers make no distinction in religion; their depravity and shamelessness, XXXII, 956; XLI, 428, 647.

THEODORE OF CYRENE.—He denied God, VII, 99.

DEMOCRITUS.—He asserted that all things came to be by chance and denied the immortality of the soul; what he thought of God, of the cause of our thoughts, and of atoms, to which he attributed a certain animate and spiritual force, II, 444, 445; VI, 119, 760; XXII, 591; XXIII, 445; XXIV, 390.

DIAGORAS.—He denied God, VII, 99; XLIII, 360.

DINOMACHUS.—He placed the highest good in moral worth joined with pleasure, VI, 364; XLIV, 852.

DIOGENES, distinct from the Cynic.—The first principles of things that he recognized, XLI, 226.

DIONYSIUS.—He imagined three kinds of gods: physical, mythical, and national or popular, I, 587, 589, 605.

EMPEDOCLES.—He asserted that the soul consists of blood and admitted transmigration of souls, I, 521, 613; II, 653, 702; XXXII, 748; XXXIII, 484, 487.

EPICURUS; EPICUREANS.—Epicurus and his disciples, denying God’s providence, attributed all things to fate; they denied the soul’s immortality and future life, and therefore placed the highest good in pleasure. Their various errors concerning atoms and innumerable cycles: I, 517, 587, 610; II, 391, 726; V, almost throughout; VI, 303, 364, 399–401, 745; XXIII, 280, 630, 644, 1019; XXIV, 390; XXXII, 732, 942; XXXIII, 63, 64, 389, 439, 441, 444, 445; XXXVI, 944; XXXVIII, 809, 811, 853; XXXIX, 1528; XLI, 181, 230, 320, 601; CXCIX, 546, 671, 844, 977.

ERASISTRATUS.—He taught that the soul is in the membranes, II, 671.

PAGANS.—The errors of the Gentiles concerning gods were almost innumerable; for they worshipped everything except God himself. They are refuted, I, 268, 269, 329, 409, 422, 423, 560, 577, 597, 601, 606; V, almost throughout, in which Arnobius demolishes the pagan gods and clearly shows that they are fictitious and therefore nonexistent.

HERACLITUS.—He teaches that the substance of the soul is fiery and consists of fire, as do all other things and the gods themselves, II, 653, 660; VI, 309; XLI, 181.

HERILLUS.—He placed the highest good in knowledge, VI, 364 ff.

HERMOGENES.—He makes God a liar and denies that God could have made anything out of himself, asserting that matter, which he calls ungenerated and evil, was necessary to God for his works; hence he infers two [principles]. He supposes that the soul consists of matter, II, 46, 198, 201, 202, 205, 208, 216, 646, 664.

HIPPARCHUS.—He asserted that the soul consists of fire, II, 663.

LABEO.—How this worshipper of demons distinguishes good gods from evil ones, XLI, 56, 372.

LACTANTIUS.—Lactantius’ error concerning the antipodes, VI, 425, 426.

LEUCIPPUS.—His opinion concerning the nature of things, VII, 101.

LUCRETIUS.—How Lucretius and others erred in establishing the origin of wisdom, VI, 386.

MANICHAEANS.—Errors of the Manichaeans concerning the soul, which they said is the very substance of God; they also asserted that souls—not only of human beings, but even of cattle—are of God’s substance. Concerning God: they admitted two mutually contrary principles, one good and the other evil, etc. Concerning concupiscence: they said that concupiscence is of an evil substance, coeternal with God; and they condemned it not as an accidental vice but as a nature evil from eternity. Concerning nature: they maintained that there is an evil nature which in no way can be changed, etc., etc. They are refuted, XXXII, 608, 716, 1157, 1237, 1242, 1317, 1346, 1351, 1352, 1355, 1356, 1362; XXXIII, 558, 718, 722–724, 841, 1033; XXXIV, 130, 165, 361, 436; XXXV, 1305, 1703, 1705; XXXVI, 108, 1040; XXXVII, 1822, 1907, 1908, 1922; XXXVIII, 106, 821, 847, 985, 986, 1132; XL, 297, 360, 363, 364, 523; XLI, 123, 336; XLII, 27, 34, 44, 113, 214, 218, 222, 229, 248, 261, 333, 380, 381, 389, 390, 414, 466, 509, 536, 537, 539, 544, 545, 565, 566, 588, 589, 595, 603, 668, 670; XLIV, 441, 477, 512, 572, 612, 1008, 1071, 1085, 1104, 1105, 1126; XLV, 1318, 1325, 1328, 1330, 1339, 1529.

MARCION.—Marcion advances two gods, as though two Symplegades, or shipwrecking rocks, and makes them unlike: one a fierce judge, mighty in war; the other mild, tranquil, supremely good and excellent, II, 19, 248, 252, 264, 361, 432.

FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—He maintained that the elements—earth, fire, air, and water—are the first principles of things, XII, 983.

ASTROLOGERS.—Their foolish doctrine of fate: they maintained that, in cases of wrongdoing, God, the author of the stars, ought rather to be accused than man, the author of crimes; they presumed to subject future events to their own judgment, XIV, 192; XXXIII, 1061; XXXIV, 278; CXCIX, 440, 455.

METELLUS.—He was the inventor of the god Alburnus, II, 266.

OPHITES.—The aeons of the Ophites, II, 64.

ORIGEN.—He thought souls had fallen from heaven, XXXIII, 718.

PERIPATETICS.—Their errors concerning pains and happiness, which they placed in goods of soul, body, and fortune, VI, 364 ff., 688 ff.; XLI, 630.

PHILOSOPHERS.—The varied and contradictory opinions of ancient philosophers concerning the unity, beginning, end, and government of the world; the first principles of things; the nature of God or gods; the substance of souls; the highest good or blessed life; their vanity, etc.: I, 268, 398, 516, 560, 610, 1231; V, almost throughout; XXII, 689, 964; XXIII, 431; XXIV, 47; XXV, 82; XXVI, 411, 503; XXXII, 707; XXXIII, 379, 830; XXXIV, 122, 123; XXXV, 1132, 1135; XXXVI, 1134; XXXVIII, 777, 1134, 1137; XLI, 225, 227, 232, 392, 601, 602, 627, 628; XLII, 978, 981, 982, 1134.

NATURAL PHILOSOPHERS.—The superstition of the natural philosophers treated the elements as gods, and they erred seriously concerning knowledge, I, 502, 589; II, 477; VI, 355, 336, 360.

PLATO; PLATONISTS.—The various errors of Plato and his followers concerning souls, which they maintained had fallen from heaven, admitting the transmigration of souls; concerning matter, which they asserted to be ungenerated; concerning the world, which they taught to be a most great, most blessed, and everlasting living being. They admitted two worlds, one intelligible and the other sensible. They said that the world had been made, yet that it exists from eternity and will not perish. Concerning God, they confessed him to be one and supreme, difficult to discover and impossible to describe; nevertheless, they said that he had created very many [gods] and worshipped them—males in heaven and females on earth—along with other errors that are refuted: I, 333, 509–511, 517; II, 260, 567, 668, 672, 1033; VI, 417, 961 ff.; XXII, 657, 748, 1085; XXIII, 276, 412, 479, 484, 487; XXXII, 587, 588, 601, 602, 954; XXXIII, 64, 441, 718; XXXIV, 126, 1056; XXXVIII, 1138; XLI, 126, 175, 218, 225, 237, 241, 259, 260, 277, 308, 310, 311, 319–321, 373, 375, 388, 390, 408, 711, 759, 773, 776, 794; XLII, 1011, 1012; XLIV, 402, 403, 745.

PORPHYRY.—He subjected the higher gods to disturbances; he said sacrifices ought to be offered to good and evil gods and admitted transmigration of souls, XLI, 237, 303–305, 310, 375.

POSIDONIUS.—He divided the soul into several parts, II, 668.

PRISCILLIAN.—He held that the soul is of God’s own substance, XXXIII, 1237, 1242; XL, 523; XLII, 27, 668–670; XLIV, 477.

PYTHAGORAS; PYTHAGOREANS.—Pythagoras imagined God to have arisen from numbers; he asserted matter to be ungenerated and the world uncreated; he admitted transmigration of souls and is said to have been the first to introduce the fable of a thousand years: I, 333, 517, 521, 613; II, 567, 702; VI, 405; XXII, 748; XXIII, 484, 487; XXXII, 589; XXXIII, 718; XLI, 181; XLII, 1011, 1012; XLIV, 745; CXCIX, 643.

ROMANS.—They erected altars to uncertain gods and worshipped both their own peculiar gods and foreign ones, I, 409, 422, 423, 597, 606; II, 255.

SCOTUS.—He erred concerning the division of nature, CXXII, 355.

SENECA.—He teaches that everything, including the soul, ends after death; he erred seriously concerning philosophy, which he calls the rule for living well, II, 721, 795.

SERANUS.—He divided the soul into seven parts, II, 668.

SOCRATES.—He denied that gods exist, yet thought the human mind to be a god; his celebrated error: “What is above us is nothing to us,” I, 354, 589; II, 648; VI, 416; XXXII, 1035; XXXIV, 123; XLI, 239; CXCIX, 982.

STOICS.—They asserted that God is corporeal and situated outside the world, and they held fire to be, as it were, the first principle of things. They said that men are governed by fate; that the soul, which they divided into ten parts, is of God’s own substance; that all sins are equal; that pity is a vice; and that the highest good is in the mind. They denied that passions could befall the wise person: I, 517, 518; II, 236, 567, 668; VI, 186, 204, 276, 405, 536 ff., 688 ff., 741; VII, 89; XXII, 780, 901, 1085; XXIII, 501, 529; XXXII, 1237, 1242; XXXIII, 394–396, 440, 441, 718, 723, 738; XXXIV, 1056; XXXV, [Col. 0403] 1798; XXXVIII, 809, 812, 853, 854; XXXIX, 1528; XL, 539; XLI, 230, 258, 259, 261, 262, 413, 601, 629; CXCIX, 546, 641.

TERTULLIAN.—He maintained that God is corporeal and that the soul likewise is corporeal, XLIV, 499.

THALES.—He asserted that water is the first principle of all things and that the soul comes from water, I, 133, 309; II, 653; XLI, 226, 230.

TRISMEGISTUS.—He said that some gods were made by the supreme God, others by human beings, XLI, 247.

VARRO.—He imagined three kinds of gods—physical, mythical, and national or popular; he called fire the soul of the world [Col. 0404]. His teaching on theology, which he established as threefold—mythical, natural, and civil—was not very consistent with itself: I, 329, 587, 589, 597; XLI, 138, 180, 182, 183, 186, 189, 192, 202, 208, 212, 218, 223, 625, 650.

XENOCRATES.—He imagined two kinds of gods, I, 587; XXIII, 304.

ZENO.—He asserted that air and fire are God, whom he called fate, and matter equal to him; he divided the mortal soul into three and even six parts; he placed happiness in the conformity of life with nature, etc.: I, 398; II, 19, 260, 398, 668; XXIII, 479, 497; XXXII, 943, 955; CXCIX, 981.

[Col. 0403]

## LX. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF COMMON AND SCHOLARLY OBJECTIONS BY WHICH PAGANS, PHILOSOPHERS, AND HERETICS ATTACKED THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION, AND WHICH THE HOLY FATHERS ENDEAVOURED TO DEFEAT IN WRITING

### NOTICE

In this Index we collect various objections of pagans, philosophers, and heretics against the religion of Christ. We recast them in syllogistic form, although they are otherwise presented in the *Patrologia*. We chose this method both for the brevity of the work and for the reader’s benefit; having set out the objection, we indicate only the answers, which may then be easily found.

### [INDEX OF OBJECTIONS]

ABRAHAM.

**OBJ.** Abraham seems to many deserving of blame and condemnation because he lied in saying that Sarah was his sister.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, I, 1319; St Ambrose, XIV, 462, 463; St Augustine, XXXIV, 565; XLII, 422, 423.

**OBJ.** Abraham, by receiving a son from a maidservant, committed adultery, since many reproach him for this.  
**RESP.** St Ambrose, XIV, 428, 429, 430; St Augustine, XLI, 503; XLIV, 656, 657, 658.

**OBJ.** The land of Canaan is promised to Abraham forever; this is false, since it was never fulfilled.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLI, 504; XXXIV, 557, 558, 559.

**OBJ.** Faustus maintains that Abraham sold his wife to two kings for sexual intercourse; this cannot be excused; therefore Abraham was guilty.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XL, 166; XLII, 420, 421.

**OBJ.** Abraham is falsely promised descendants like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven, since Judaea was very small and the Hebrew people was scanty and few in number.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 556; XLI, 500, 525.

ABSOLUTION.

**OBJ.** Absolution should never be delayed, since those doing penance are always in danger of death; yet it is very often delayed.  
**RESP.** Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 909, 910, 1098, 1099.

**OBJ.** General absolutions by bishops and priests—for example, at the consecration of churches, on Ash Wednesday, or on Thursday of Holy Week—are of no effect, because only private absolutions release from sins.  
**RESP.** Alan of Lille, CCX, 386, 387.

ABSTINENCE.

**OBJ.** Some maintain that monks’ abstinence was not as great as some authors claim, since it was too harsh and impossible.  
**RESP.** Rufinus, XXI, 449, 450.

**OBJ.** Abstinence from meat does not seem admissible because Scripture, far from commanding it, condemns it.  
**RESP.** Salvian, LIII, 193, 194.

RESPECT OF PERSONS.

**OBJ.** God shows partiality when he gives grace to one person and denies it to another; therefore partiality must be acknowledged in God, though it is condemned in many passages of Scripture.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLIV, 580, 581; XXXIII, 585, 386.

**OBJ.** God is a respecter of persons, since he saves one person and damns another.  
**RESP.** St Fulgentius, LXV, 448.

[Col. 0404] **OBJ.** It is granted that certain forms of partiality must be avoided; but it can lawfully and deservedly be maintained that it is permissible toward the rich and noble, as sometimes occurs in the Church.  
**RESP.** St Bernard, CLXXXII, 757, 758, 774, 775.

ACCIDENTS.

**OBJ.** It is absurd to say that the accidents of the Eucharist exist without a subject, because this is contrary to the essence of things.  
**RESP.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1247, 1248.

ACCUSERS.

**OBJ.** Accusers of pastors should always be received favourably, because the pastors’ wickedness must be exposed as soon as possible lest it harm others.  
**RESP.** Peter the Chanter, CCV, 475, 476.

ACTIONS.

**OBJ.** All our merit ought to be attributed to actions; contemplation, however, contains no action or work; therefore it is useless.  
**RESP.** St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1024, 1053, 1055.

**OBJ.** It cannot be said that all actions are good or evil by reason of their end or intention, because there are actions that possess intrinsic goodness or badness.  
**RESP.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1001.

ADAM.

**OBJ.** Adam is not guilty for the fault he committed in paradise, because it seems attributable to God alone, since God gave man free choice of will, foreseeing that he would use it badly.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 290, 291.

**OBJ.** One ought not to believe that Adam and Eve forfeited immortality through transgression of a divine command of the slightest importance, since so severe a punishment cannot justly be imposed for a slight fault.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 272, 599.

**OBJ.** Adam ought to have obtained from God forgiveness of his fault, since he frankly confessed his seduction.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 286.

**OBJ.** Adam was created mortal by constitution; therefore death was natural to him and is not a punishment for sin.  
**RESP.** Lactantius, VI, 323, 324, 931, 932.

**OBJ.** Catholics err concerning Adam’s fault when they maintain that through Christ they recover what they lost through Adam; for this cannot be understood.  
**RESP.** Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1037, 1038.

**OBJ.** Adam was not created good and upright; otherwise he would have remained such and would not have sinned.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLV, 1537; XL, 336; XXXVIII, 172; XLIV, 247, 248.

[Col. 0405] **OBJ.** Adam himself did not sin willingly and freely, since he was deceived by Eve.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 453, 454; XLI, 419.

**OBJ.** Adam’s sin was ineffable and necessary; therefore Adam is not to be blamed.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLI, 430, 431.

**OBJ.** It appears absurd and impossible that both guilt and punishment passed to Adam’s descendants, for this is altogether contrary to God’s justice and wisdom.  
**RESP.** St Prosper, LI, 194, 195, 237, 370, 371; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 505, 506, 507; St Leo the Great, LV, 140; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 525, 526; Gennadius, LVIII, 988, 989, 990, 1024, 1025.

**OBJ.** “Behold,” God says, “Adam has become as one of us.” Yet God said this after Adam’s transgression; therefore the transgression was not so great as to ruin him and all his descendants.  
**RESP.** Eugyppius, LXII, 654, 655; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 43, 44.

**OBJ.** Original sin is wrongly imputed to Adam alone, since Eve too shared in the sin and indeed was the first cause of sin.  
**RESP.** St Anselm, CLVIII, 441, 442; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 597, 598; CLXXVI, 290, 291; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1010, 1011.

HELP.

**OBJ.** God’s help is necessary for us to do good; therefore, if it is lacking, a person’s vice is excusable. But it is sometimes lacking; therefore people ought not to be blamed for their sins.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 771; XXXVIII, 108, 121, 375, 584, 856, 894.

ADORATION.

**OBJ.** God alone is not to be worshipped, because angels and saints were formerly worshipped, as is read in Holy Scripture.  
**RESP.** Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 9, 10, 11.

**OBJ.** Worship does not belong to God alone, since Blessed John wished to worship an angel.  
**RESP.** Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 338, 339, 340.

BUILDINGS.

**OBJ.** The superfluity of buildings is not blameworthy and should not be condemned, because it contributes both ornament and utility.  
**RESP.** Peter the Chanter, CCV, 255, 256, 281, 282.

EGYPTIANS.

**OBJ.** The Hebrews’ taking of Egyptian gold and silver was truly theft, because it cannot in any way be called payment for labour.  
**RESP.** Cassiodorus, LXX, 750, 751.

**OBJ.** It is falsely asserted that the Hebrews justly despoiled the Egyptians, because theft is never permitted.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 308, 309; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 920, 921.

AGE.

**OBJ.** It is falsely said that the path taken in youth will also be kept in old age, because one who is often worse as an adolescent becomes excellent when old, and vice versa.  
**RESP.** Alan of Lille, CCX, 592, 593.

AMBITION.

**OBJ.** Ambition is not evil because it makes men distinguished and illustrious.  
**RESP.** Peter the Chanter, CCV, 165, 166.

**OBJ.** Ambition is not to be blamed because absolutely everyone is captivated by it.  
**RESP.** Alan, CCX, 590, 591.

LOVE.

**OBJ.** Philosophers say that love for God is useless because God does not need it.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLI, 281; XXXIII, 556, 672, 674.

**OBJ.** Love for enemies ought not to be practised, because the former teaching was: “tooth for tooth, eye for eye.”  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXII, 615, 674, 675, 676.

ANANIAS.

**OBJ.** The death of Ananias and Sapphira seems lamentable and incomprehensible, and the punishment most severe, excessively rigorous, and almost unjust, because they sinned lightly and unknowingly, and because it was imposed for at least a most trivial sin.  
**RESP.** St Maximus, LVII, 475, 500, 501.

ANGELS.

**OBJ.** Forgiveness ought to have been available to evil angels, as it is available to human beings.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 777, 778; St Augustine, XXXV, 1925, 2123.

**OBJ.** Angels are not to be distinguished from God, since God himself is called in Scripture angel, angel of counsel, and angel of wisdom; therefore they are to be worshipped as God.  
**RESP.** St Hilary, X, 113, 116, 117, 118.

**OBJ.** It may be granted that angels have some knowledge of human beings, but it seems necessary to deny that they know their more hidden thoughts.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 473, 474.

[Col. 0406] **OBJ.** Nothing at all is certain concerning the creation of angels, because Scripture is silent about it, or at least speaks obscurely.  
**RESP.** Gennadius, LVIII, 1018, 119.

**OBJ.** Angels were worshipped under the old law; but Christ introduced no change in this matter; therefore [they are to be worshipped].  
**RESP.** Peter Lombard, CXCI, 248.

**OBJ.** The angel who guided Tobias lied, because he said that he was Ananias, son of the great Azariah.  
**RESP.** Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 865, 866.

**OBJ.** If each human being had a guardian angel of his own, there would be as many angels as human beings; and this is inadmissible.  
**RESP.** St Jerome, XXIV, 670, 406.

SOUL.

**OBJ.** The soul was not created, since, according to philosophers, it is divine and eternal.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, I, 610; II, 652.

**OBJ.** Souls are not each created individually for each individual, because a child’s soul is often like the souls of its parents.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 653, 693.

**OBJ.** The human soul cannot be called naturally Christian, as some would have it; for this seems absurd.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, I, 377, 378, 610.

**OBJ.** The soul was not created by God, as Catholics maintain, because according to philosophers it comes from seed or by propagation.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 712, 682, 665, 858, 683; St Cyprian, V, 84, 85, 86.

**OBJ.** Very many doubt the soul’s existence, because its seat is known to no one and cannot be known.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 651, 671.

**OBJ.** The soul is corporeal and mortal, because ancient and even modern philosophers regard it as such and rightly demonstrate that it should be so regarded; moreover, its origin is wholly uncertain and obscure.  
**RESP.** Arnobius, V, 851, 854, 833, 834, 892.

**OBJ.** We have only uncertain and obscure knowledge concerning the origin of souls, since Scripture scarcely reproves anything concerning them.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 355, 415; XLIV, 150, 506, 523, 525, 530, 532.

**OBJ.** The soul was not created by God, because it is either self-existent, or from nothing, or from God’s substance, or from fire, or from air, or from atoms.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XXXIV, 361, 366, 372, 412; XXXVIII, 853; XL, 11; XLI, 326; XLII, 72, 93, 99, 117, 666, 669.

**OBJ.** The soul is corporeal, since some philosophers said that it is blood, others fire, others earth, and finally some said that the souls of humans and animals have a common origin.  
**RESP.** St Ambrose, XIV, 403, 404, 560, 365.

**OBJ.** There are two souls in a human being, because human goodness and wickedness cannot otherwise be explained.  
**RESP.** Gennadius, LVIII, 984, 1021.

**OBJ.** There is not a single soul in a human being, because some think that there are three: the vital, sensitive, and rational.  
**RESP.** Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 370, 371.

**OBJ.** Souls were either created all at once, or they exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, as Origen holds; therefore they are not each created for individual bodies.  
**RESP.** St Isidore, LXXXIII, 1231, 1232.

**OBJ.** The soul is not immortal, because according to Scripture human beings and beasts have one destruction.  
**RESP.** St Gregory, LXXVII, 321, 324, 328.

**OBJ.** The suffering of the soul is not to be believed, because, being incorporeal, it cannot be tortured by material fire.  
**RESP.** St Julian, CXVI, 482, 483.

**OBJ.** The soul is a part of the Divinity, because according to Genesis it is his little breath (*spiriculum*).  
**RESP.** Ivo, CLXIV, 160, 161.

**OBJ.** It is rightly said that a soul passes from body to body, because the teaching of transmigration is altogether certain.  
**RESP.** Rupert, CLXVII, 536, 537.

**OBJ.** The soul comes by propagation, as does the body, because it cannot be said that God creates souls individually and thereby has a continual occupation in creating them.  
**RESP.** Hildebert, CLXXI, 1121, 1122.

ANTICHRIST.

**OBJ.** The coming of Antichrist may be called into doubt because for a long time it has been said that he is near, and yet he has not come.  
**RESP.** St Cyprian, III, 1015, 1032, 1033; IV, 350.

**OBJ.** The time of Antichrist’s coming must always and absolutely remain doubtful, because Christ himself wished to say nothing about it.  
**RESP.** Lactantius, VI, 788, 789.

**OBJ.** Antichrist’s existence itself must also be doubted, since some maintain that he will be the same as the devil, while others assert that he is someone else.  
**RESP.** Lactantius, VI, 1008, 1009.

**OBJ.** Antichrist’s coming may be doubted because the time of his persecution [Col. 0407] is uncertain and unknown to all.  
**RESP.** St Augustine, XLI, 616, 677, 678.

**OBJ.** It is said that the Jews will believe in Antichrist after refusing to believe in Christ; this is absurd, since his evil works make him evident.  
**RESP.** St Ambrose, XIV, 1100, 1101.

APOSTLES.

**OBJ.** The apostles are not to be believed because apostolic men taught a contrary doctrine.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 34, 45, 363.

**OBJ.** The apostles preached things contrary to one another; therefore they are not to be believed.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 37.

**OBJ.** The apostles’ teaching is suspect because they entrusted some things openly and to everyone, but others secretly and to a few.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 37, 38.

**OBJ.** The apostles are blameworthy because they took women with them.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, II, 490.

**OBJ.** It is doubtful whether the apostles were baptized, since Scripture is silent concerning their baptism; and yet this was necessary for their salvation, as for that of others.  
**RESP.** Tertullian, I, 1213.

APPARITIONS.

**OBJ.** Some maintain that there have never been any appearances of God himself, because, according to them, the reported appearances may be called into doubt.  
**RESP.** St Leo, LV, 1328, 1329.

OBJ. The appearance of God Himself to the Patriarchs in the Old Testament is not to be believed, since, according to some, only angels or saints appeared.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLII, 140, 853, 856.

## FREE WILL

OBJ. The existence of free will is much disputed; therefore, etc.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXVI, 401, 402.

OBJ. Freedom of choice has not been granted to man in both directions, because sometimes, as the Apostle says, a man cannot avoid the evil which he does not wish, nor do the good which he wishes.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 292, 916; St. Cyprian, IV, 507, 760; St. Jerome, XXX, 286, 575.

OBJ. If free will exists, the grace of God must be removed, because these two cannot be joined together.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXIV, 745, 796; XXVI, 401; St. Augustine, XL, 282; XLIV, 241, 342.

OBJ. It is falsely said that grace comes beforehand and free will follows, because free will would thereby be taken away.---RESP. St. Gregory, LXXVI, 298, 809.

OBJ. Either free will or grace must be eliminated, because they eliminate one another.---RESP. Rabanus, CVIII, 1204, 1205; CXI, 885.

OBJ. Free will does not exist, since it was entirely removed through Adam’s sin; but [it does].---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 133, 1268, 1275; XLI, 149; XLII, 451, 540; XLIV, 552, 564, 567.

OBJ. Free will must be wholly doubted, because some attribute more, others less, to it.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 85, 877, 1268; XLIV, 373, 374, 441, 570, 879, 880, 885; XLV, 1290, 1520.

OBJ. It is further objected that free will cannot be reconciled with grace, since those who preach grace take it away.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 677, 974, 987; XXXIV, 156; XXXV, 2071; XXXVI, 208; XXXVIII, 903; XLIV, 233, 265, 383; XLV, 1110, 1115, 1298.

OBJ. Free will is not present in everyone, since a man loses it when he has voluntarily given himself to the Spirit of God and to the devil [the source is grammatically irregular].---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 654, 655.

OBJ. No one can possess free will by himself, because its beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good unto the end are gifts of God.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 264.

OBJ. After grace, free will does not remain in nature; therefore, whoever has grace does not have free will.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 264, 265.

OBJ. After grace free will does not remain, since it is destroyed when everything is referred to God.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 983, 984.

OBJ. No one makes good use of free will without grace; therefore grace takes away free will.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 209, 210, 685, 686.

OBJ. Not every human being has freedom of choice, since it is clear that there are some persons who are driven into evil unwillingly and as though compelled.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLVIII, 490, 491, 493, 494, 496.

## ARIANS

OBJ. The doctrine of the Arians was once spread far and wide [Col. 0408], since, according to St. Jerome, the whole world was astonished to find itself Arian. Moreover, what once existed can exist now also; or this was the original faith and therefore ought to remain now as well; therefore the Arians are not heretics.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 542, 543.

OBJ. Arius asserts that Christ existed before the Blessed Mary and before the ages; but this appears to be Catholic doctrine; therefore, etc.---RESP. St. Hilary, X, 716, 204.

OBJ. The Arians would be heretics because they maintain that Christ was begotten and created, that He is not eternal, omnipotent, supremely good, wise, or cognizant of the day of judgment; but these points are established from the Scriptures; therefore, etc.---St. Ambrose, XVI, 562, 685, 840, 841, 941, 1045, 1046.

OBJ. The Arians teach that the Son and the Holy Spirit are less than the Father, being subject to Him and sent by Him; but this is established from Scripture; therefore, etc.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 369, 370, 814, 815.

OBJ. The Arians subscribed to the Council of Nicaea; therefore they are not heretics.---RESP. Cassiodorus, LXIX, 925, 926.

## ASS

OBJ. Christians were once reproached by pagans for worshipping the head and likeness of an ass; but this is ridiculous.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 364, 372, 579.

OBJ. Some mock when they read that the she-ass spoke against Balaam; therefore this speech is fabulous.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 664, 665.

## ATOMS

OBJ. The atomic system must be admitted: atoms are the principles of things, that is, from their collision—since Epicurus proves their origin exceedingly well—worlds without number, living beings, souls, etc., began to arise by chance.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 401; St. Augustine, XLI, 230; XXXIII, 444, 445.

## UNLEAVENED BREAD

OBJ. The Greeks rightly disapprove and reject unleavened bread in consecrating the Eucharist, because it is not properly and truly bread.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLVIII, 541, 542, 543.

## BAPTISM

OBJ. Tradition does not state when Christ instituted baptism; therefore we may doubt its existence.---RESP. Lactantius, VII, 616, 617.

OBJ. Baptism was formerly not administered to infants; therefore neither should it be administered today.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 1015, 1018; IV, 473.

OBJ. Little children are not to be baptized on account of original sin, nor for eternal life, but only for the kingdom of heaven, as the Pelagians say; a position nevertheless rejected by Catholics.---RESP. Augustine, XXXIII, 761, 763; XXXVIII, 1336; XLIV, 142, 146, 377, 385, 394, 395.

OBJ. Many people, even Christians, do not believe that infants who die without baptism are condemned, because, they say, this would be unjust. For they themselves are not so guilty as to deserve such a punishment.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLIV, 188, 189, 481, 505, 1330.

OBJ. Little children dying without baptism will not suffer condemnation, because, according to many, they will be in some intermediate place where they may live happily.---RESP. St. Leo, LVI, 486, 497, 498.

OBJ. Baptism and circumcision do not differ at all, since both remove original sin: baptism under the new law and circumcision under the old law. Therefore let a reason for the difference be given.---RESP. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 885, 886.

## BLESSEDNESS

OBJ. Philosophers place blessedness either in freedom from pain, pleasure, moral worth, or bodily goods; Catholics place it in God alone. Whom should one believe?---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 103, 104.

OBJ. Very many deny that blessedness is to be placed only in the other life, because, they say, it can be found in this world.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVII, 678, 679.

OBJ. Blessedness consists in pleasure according to Aristippus; in virtue of soul according to Antisthenes; in the goods of the appetite or of fortune according to others; therefore blessedness does not consist in God alone.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLI, 601; XLII, 101, 549, 551; XLIV, 852.

OBJ. It is wrongly said that we cannot be blessed in this world, because the powerful and wealthy are truly blessed.---RESP. Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 310, 311, 349, 450.

## BEASTS

OBJ. Beasts possess intelligence and foreknowledge of the future; yet man has nothing more, and some men do not even have these things [Col. 0409]; therefore beasts are not distinct from human beings.---RESP. Lactantius, VII, 94, 95.

OBJ. It cannot be said that beasts were created for the use and advantage of man, since many are harmful, injurious, and highly destructive to man.---RESP. Lactantius, VII, 117, 118.

OBJ. The opinion of those who attribute to beasts a soul like the human soul must be accepted, because beasts possess reason and knowledge, so that they surpass human perception: they know, feel, understand, remember, desire, etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 1018, 1063, 1066, 1067, 1368, 1370, 1371; XXXVI, 480; XXXVII, 1939; XLI, 240; XLII, 975, 999, 1057, 1061.

## WAR

OBJ. War cannot exist without sin, because it is always sinful for people to slaughter one another.---RESP. Regino, CXXXII, 295, 296.

OBJ. All wars must be condemned; indeed, they are altogether unjust, because they cannot justly be undertaken for any good end.---RESP. Ivo, CLXI, 721, 724, 725.

## BLASPHEMY

OBJ. Not all sins can be forgiven, since blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 448, 457, 458.

## CAIN

OBJ. God wrongly rejected Cain’s sacrifice, because it was offered with a good intention.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 611, 612.

OBJ. Scripture says that Cain built a city; but this is impossible, since at that time there were only three or four people on earth.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 548; XLI, 445, 446.

## FLESH

OBJ. The resurrection of the flesh is not to be believed, because it is difficult, impossible, and utterly repugnant to right reason.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 800, 810, 835, 868; St. Cyprian, III, 1113, 1114, 1115.

OBJ. The Archontics, the Gaiani, Carpocrates, Cerdon, etc., deny the resurrection of the flesh; therefore the resurrection of the flesh must be rejected.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLII, 27, 29, 39; XXXVI, 752; XXXVIII, 848; XLI, 783.

OBJ. Christ’s flesh was merely apparent and phantasmal; or, if real, it was assumed from a man and not from Mary alone, the Virgin, because a virgin does not know how to give birth.---RESP. St. Gennadius, LVIII, 984, 1007, 1008.

## CHASTITY

OBJ. Some censure chastity in ministers of the Church and maintain that it must be abolished, because, they say, it is not lawfully prescribed.---RESP. St. Leo, LV, 1331, 1332.

## CHANCE

OBJ. Great power belongs to chance, since everything happens by chance.---RESP. Boethius, LXIV, 513, 1153, 1154.

## CATHOLICS

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that Catholics alone possess what Christ instituted, because many others claim the same prerogative for themselves.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 23.

OBJ. Very many reject Catholic tradition because it does not seem safe and secure to them.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 931.

## CHARITY

OBJ. The mutual charity of Christians is wrongly praised, because pagans everywhere censure it.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 704.

OBJ. Charity has been completely destroyed in this world, since it is put into practice by few, while others turn it into hypocrisy or despise it.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 951, 952; X, 300, 301.

## CHRISTIANS

OBJ. The name “Christian” is hateful to the nations because Christians are wicked.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 277, 288, 566.

OBJ. Christians were formerly persecuted because of their evil deeds; therefore they were wicked.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 277, 278, 285.

OBJ. Not everyone who wishes can be a Christian, because one does not become a Christian but is born one.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 378.

OBJ. A Christian is not made but born, since the soul is naturally Christian.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 377.

OBJ. Christian morals were corrupt, because pagans reproached them with this.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 472, 473, 564.

OBJ. Christians were rightly accused of the crime of lèse-majesté against human authority, because they refused to obey the laws of the emperors.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 427, 436, 437, 450, 700.

[Col. 0410] OBJ. Christians were rightly called an unlawful and desperate faction, because they were guilty of every crime and enemies of the gods, emperors, laws, customs, and all nature.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 310, 311, 459, 464, 468, 699, 700.

OBJ. Christians are plainly evil, since they were accused of three dreadful crimes: infanticide, sexual immorality, adultery, and incest. The common cry against them was: “Christians to the beasts! Christians to the lions!” Moreover, if Christians had not been guilty, God would not have allowed them to suffer such great torments.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 306, 307, 341, 480, 488, 571, 580, 581, 651, 825.

OBJ. The world hates Christians because all consider them criminals.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 426, 537, 554, 665, 752.

OBJ. A Christian who is arrested and punished does not resist, because he feels and confesses himself guilty and worthy of every punishment.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 293, 557; III, 832, 833.

OBJ. Christians are the worst kind of people, since they are the cause of all the evils that disturb our mortal condition.---RESP. Arnobius, V, 719, 720, 723, 726, 727.

OBJ. Christians have been called by everyone dull, foolish, stupid, etc., and atheists as well, etc.---RESP. Arnobius, V, 703, 704, 750, 751, 816, 817, 829, 863, 958, 976.

## CHRIST

OBJ. Many refuse to believe in Christ’s coming because He was too humble, abject, and ignominious.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 352, 707, 708.

OBJ. Christ’s incarnation must be rejected because, unbelievers said, it is incongruous for God to put on our wretched and shapeless mortality.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 475, 517, 521, 524.

OBJ. Christ is not Mary’s son, since He existed before Mary.---RESP. St. Hilary, X, 513, 514.

OBJ. According to the Scriptures, Christ ought to be warlike and not peace-bringing.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 340, 351; 617, 618, 620.

OBJ. Christ has not yet come, because He is not shown to be such as He was proclaimed to be.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 331, 349, 609, 610.

OBJ. Christ is called the firstborn of every creature; therefore He was created.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 273, 274, 653, 654.

OBJ. Christ’s miracles do not prove His divinity, because they must be ascribed to magical powers.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 400; Lactantius, VI, 485, 491.

OBJ. It cannot be said that Christ died of His own accord, since He was killed by the executioner’s office.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 401.

OBJ. Christ ought not to have been distinguished from the gods of paganism, since Tiberius wished Him to be enrolled among the gods.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 290.

OBJ. Christ’s yoke is wrongly called light, because it is wholly intolerable to many.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 780, 781.

OBJ. After His resurrection Christ suddenly vanished from sight; therefore He was a phantom and a shadow.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXIII, 387, 388.

OBJ. If Christ had truly risen, He would have given certain and evident signs of His resurrection; but [He did not].---RESP. St. Jerome, XXIII, 310, 311, 387, 388.

OBJ. If Christ was free from actual sins, He cannot in the same way be said to have been free from original sin.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 733, 867; XXXV, 1696, 1847; XXXVI, 591; XXXVIII, 442, 823, 824, 928; XL, 255.

OBJ. Christ’s genealogy is false, because Matthew gave one genealogy and Luke another.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 530, 531; XL, 49; XLII, 214, 216.

OBJ. Among the Jews there is a report that Christ was taken from the tomb by His disciples; therefore He did not truly rise.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 261, 262.

OBJ. If Christ had risen, He ought to have risen in the sight of everyone, just as He suffered and died in the sight of everyone.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 833, 942, 943; XL, 188, 945; XLII, 41, 42.

OBJ. Christ is not coequal with the Father, because the contrary is read in Scripture.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 315, 316, 482.

OBJ. Christ was not begotten from Mary, because He was begotten before Lucifer.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 319, 320.

OBJ. Christ did not suffer or die for those to be condemned, since it profits them nothing.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 164, 165, 177, 178, 702, 703.

OBJ. No one comes to Christ unless drawn by God’s assistance; therefore not all who wish to come to Christ can do so.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 233, 234.

[Col. 0411] OBJ. Christ was merely an outstanding man, as philosophers maintain; or, as others prefer, a saint like Abraham, Moses, etc.; nor is He to be regarded as God.---RESP. St. Gregory, LXXV, 87, 88; LXXVI, 85; LXXIX, 66, 67.

OBJ. Christ is not the only son of the Blessed Virgin Mary, since He is called her firstborn.---RESP. St. Bruno, CLXV, 76, 77.

OBJ. Christ was not, from His conception, full of grace and truth, since according to Scripture He advanced in wisdom and age.---RESP. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 73, 74.

OBJ. Christ’s body ought to be consecrated in leavened bread, as is done among the Greeks; for this difference displeases everyone.---RESP. Algerus, CLXXX, 827.

OBJ. There is no reason why bread should be consecrated into the body and wine into the blood, since Christ is contained under either species.---RESP. Algerus, CLXXX, 825.

OBJ. Christ is not even equal to the angels, since according to Scripture He was made a little lower than they.---RESP. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 416, 417.

## CIRCUMCISION

OBJ. Circumcision ought always to have endured and never ceased, because it gave grace and salvation to the Jews.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 601, 602.

OBJ. Circumcision was wrongly abolished, since it was the same as baptism: that is, it cleansed original sin and delivered from eternal death.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 96, 309, 415; XXXVIII, 1548; XLI, 506; XLII, 309; XLIV, 450, 685, 720, 834; St. Gregory, LXXV, 634; Ivo, CLXI, 80; Alanus, CCX, 256; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1140, 1141.

## SUPPER

OBJ. We may be present at the Lord’s Supper without fasting, because the disciples did not receive Christ’s body and blood while fasting, and St. Augustine does not dare determine anything concerning this fast.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 202, 203.

## DOVE

OBJ. The Holy Spirit is said to have appeared in a dove; but such an appearance seems to deserve rejection.---RESP. St. Augustine, XL, 302; XXXIII, 747.

## COMMUNION

OBJ. Communion must be given under both species, because it was formerly done thus, and is still in use among the Greeks.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLIX, 255, 256.

OBJ. It is established that, in receiving Christ’s body at Mass, the priest receives Christ’s body alone in receiving the bread, and the blood alone in receiving the wine. Therefore, in the communion of the faithful under the species of bread alone, only Christ’s body is received; therefore the sacrament is defective.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLIX, 255.

## CONCUPISCENCE

OBJ. God ought to have taken concupiscence away from us, because we cannot resist concupiscence, as the Apostle says, who himself does what he does not wish.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 716; XLIV, 150, 433, 560, 679, 682, 815, 829, 855.

OBJ. Some cannot resist their desires, because God has given some over to their desires, according to Scripture.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 400, 829; XXXVIII, 391, 719, 816; XLIV, 793, 1343.

OBJ. Some are wholly unable to conquer their desires, since even the righteous cannot entirely uproot them.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 189, 815, 820, 892.

## CONFESSION

OBJ. Confession ought to be made publicly, because it would more strongly incite us to humility and edify others, as was customary among the first Christians.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 1222.

OBJ. Confession made to God is sufficient, rather than confession outwardly to a priest; therefore confession to God alone is to be retained.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLVIII, 866, 867, 877, 878, 1125, 1126; Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 168, 169, 175.

## CONFIRMATION

OBJ. Heretics do not admit the sacrament of confirmation because, according to them, it was not instituted by Christ.---RESP. Alanus, CCX, 369, 370.

OBJ. The minister of confirmation is not necessarily a bishop because, according to many, it was formerly entrusted to priests.---RESP. Alanus, CCL, 369, 370.

## MARRIAGE

OBJ. Married persons are permitted to divorce on account of fornication; therefore, after dismissing an adulterous wife, it ought to be lawful for the husband to marry another. This follows from its being lawful for him to dismiss a fornicating wife; nevertheless the Church forbids it.---RESP. [Col. 0412] St. Augustine, XL, 100, 451, 452; Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1546.

OBJ. There was no true marriage between the Virgin Mary and Blessed Joseph, since there was no bodily intercourse.---RESP. Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1256, 1257.

## CONSTANTINE THE GREAT

OBJ. It is falsely said that Constantine brought justice, wisdom, and peace to the world, since he made war on Maxentius unjustly, impiously, and cruelly.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 116; VII, 261, 367.

OBJ. In certain histories one reads that a cross was shown to Constantine in heaven, by which he would conquer; but this is a work of invention.---RESP. Lactantius, VII, 261, 262.

OBJ. Constantine is wrongly regarded by Christians as a saint, because much in his life is blameworthy.---RESP. St. Philastrius, XII, 1179, 1180.

## CONTINENCE

OBJ. Continence is not to be preferred to marriage, because a vow of chastity does not benefit society; indeed, it harms it.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 486, 487, 905, 925, 931.

OBJ. In ancient times, and before Christ’s coming, continence was unusual; therefore it was not always good.---RESP. St. Augustine, XL, 435; XLIV, 422, 423.

OBJ. For continence to be good, it is required that it be voluntary and proceed from free will; but this is not so, since no one can be continent unless God grants it, according to Scripture.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 729, 796; XL, 444, 445; XLIV, 297, 236, 886.

## CONVERSION

OBJ. Conversion is not to be sought, since it cannot be attained by human powers but proceeds from God’s gift alone, since Scripture says: “Convert us, O God,” etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 591; XXXVI, 48, 51, 137; XXXVII, 119, 1073; XLIV, 169, 888.

OBJ. Conversion is impossible, since the conversion of sinners is said to be more difficult than the resurrection of the dead.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 751; XXXVII, 1123.

## INSULT

OBJ. An insult must be returned for an insult, because [it is said], “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.”---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 136; XXXVII, 1185, 1434; XXXIX, 1584.

## BODY

OBJ. Eternal blessedness will not belong to bodies, since, according to many, it is not fitting that bodies should have the same happiness as souls.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 763, 944, 945.

OBJ. It is often said that the human body was made in the image of God; but this appears absurd.---RESP. St. Augustine, XL, 32; XLIV, 710.

OBJ. It does not appear admissible that the body would have been immortal and would have assumed an angelic form had Adam not sinned; for this is highly uncertain.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 283, 354; XL, 332; XLV, 200, 354, 355, 1599.

## TOMORROW

OBJ. The command not to think of tomorrow leads a person to idleness, lack of foresight, or neglect of the future; therefore it must be rejected.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1803; XL, 508, 509; XLII, 167.

## CREATURE

OBJ. The rational creature is most like God and entirely equal to Him, because everywhere one reads and says that man is another god and was made wholly in the image of God.---RESP. Constantine, VIII, 437, 440.

OBJ. What is said—that God made all things very good from nothing—seems false, because, according to the Manichaeans, many creatures are evil.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 743; XXXVII, 1878; XLII, 538, 580, 607, 743; XLV, 1537.

OBJ. All creatures cannot be called useful, because there are lowly animals that are useless and harmful.---RESP. Alanus, CCX, 311, 312.

## CROSS

OBJ. The sign of the cross upon the forehead is mere superstition, because it is prescribed by no law.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 514, 515, 715, 716.

OBJ. If there were some power in the sign of the cross, and if demons were, as has been said, driven away by it, this ought to be proved most plainly; moreover, etc. . . ; therefore, etc.---RESP. Lactantius, VII, 210, 216, 314, 671; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 293, 294; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 749, 750.

## CYPRIAN (ST.)

OBJ. St. Cyprian is censured because he had rather bitter disputes and controversies with Stephen.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 1133, 1134, 1116, 1117.

OBJ. St. Cyprian taught that heretics must be baptized again; but this is condemned by the Church; therefore St. Cyprian erred and consequently ought not to be called a saint.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 340, 341, 409; XLIII, 124, 131, 159, 340, 341, 409, 490, 606, 607.

OBJ. If he had not erred deliberately and had been, as is said, most devoted to the unity of the Church, he would immediately and of his own accord have given an example of submission; but he did not do this; therefore, etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 88, 89, 187, 188, 194, 198, 201, 203, 219, 226, 234, 244, 310, 340, 496, 497, 566.

## DEMONS

OBJ. Demons have something divine in them while they steal divinity.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 408.

OBJ. Demons possess divine knowledge when they recognize coming rains, accomplish things above the order of nature, lurk under the persons of the dead, etc.; but demons do these things; therefore, etc.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 409, 646, 700, 748, 1175; II, 748.

OBJ. It is absurd to say that almost no human being is without a demon, because this is contrary to God’s benevolence toward human beings; therefore this is untrue.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 748.

OBJ. It must not be believed that Christians have power over demons, so as to cast them out of those possessed.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 413, 434, 463, 534, 535, 677, 700, 703, 937.

OBJ. Demons at least possess great power, because they transform themselves into angels of light, are the authors and rulers of this world, accomplish many wonders, inflict diseases and death upon human beings, teach great arts, and tempt people against their will; therefore demons have something divine in them.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 748; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 383; XXXIV, 630; XXXV, 1854; XL, 292, 684, 586; XLI, 70, 251, 634, 717; XLII, 651, 663, 875, 876, 878.

OBJ. Demons certainly recognized the grace and mystery of the Lord’s coming, endowed as they were with such power of knowledge.---RESP. Philip of Harvengt, CCII, 305, 306, 721, 722.

## CONDEMNATION
