OBJ. Very many doubt condemnation on account of original sin because, they say, such condemnation is contrary to divine goodness.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 217; XLIV, 160, 250.

OBJ. There will be no eternal condemnation, because many, including Origen, think that the punishments of the condemned will not endure forever.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLI, 731, 733; XLIV, 523; Cassiodorus, LXX, 461, 548, 584, 657.

OBJ. Eternal punishments are not just, because an eternal penalty ought not to be imposed for a transitory fault.---RESP. St. Gregory, LXXV, 912, 913; St. Bruno, XCVI, 903, 904.

## DETRACTION

OBJ. Detraction is not always evil, because sometimes it concerns what is true.---RESP. Peter the Chanter, CCV, 56, 57.

OBJ. Detraction is sometimes extremely slight and almost nonexistent, because it is concealed and in no way manifest.---RESP. Peter the Chanter, CCV, 57, 58.

OBJ. If detraction is not to be committed, it is at least to be listened to, because hearing it can be useful.---RESP. Peter the Chanter, CCV, 57, 389, 390.

## GOD

OBJ. God’s patience ought not to be extolled as a perfection, because nothing of the kind appears in the punishments and torments of the condemned.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 813; I, 1252.

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that God could never have been unknown to anyone, because philosophers called God difficult to discover and describe.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 256, 265, 325, 285; I, 509.

OBJ. Temples are useless to God, because the whole world is God’s temple.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 576, 577, 578.

OBJ. God is not to be prayed to, because He does not need our prayer.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 241, 242.

OBJ. God shows partiality, since He grants earthly goods to one person while always giving evils to another.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 1016, 1017; Lactantius, VI, 120, 569, 626, 627.

OBJ. Very many deny God’s providence because, they say, care and concern for human affairs are unworthy of God.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 856, 857, 871, 872.

OBJ. God is bodily, because Scripture presents Him to us as walking, speaking, etc.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XV, 130, 308, 1120, 1121.

OBJ. God is not invisible and incorporeal, since [Col. 0414] He formerly appeared to many in bodily form.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 604, 605, 618; XXXIV, 448; XXXVIII, 59, 60, 477; XL, 662; XLI, 291.

OBJ. If God foreknows all things, then He takes away our free will.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 1276, 1277.

OBJ. Some maintain that God’s foreknowledge forces us by necessity to sin because, they say, foreknowledge on God’s part becomes compulsion upon us.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 297, 387, 619, 620.

OBJ. Some criticize God’s mercy because it is granted to some and, by God’s will, denied to others.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 129, 409, 410, 530, 531, 683, 684.

OBJ. According to some, God is the instigator of evils, since Scripture reads that He turned the heart of the Egyptians so that they hated His people.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 299, 300, 301; Alcuin, C, 919.

OBJ. Justice and clemency are not both to be admitted in God, because these two are mutually incompatible and opposed to each other.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 169, 170, 171.

OBJ. It cannot be said that God placed in all human beings a testimony to His recognition, because some are found who have no awareness of God.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 771, 772.

OBJ. God is said to have rested on the seventh day after creating the world; therefore He is subject to weariness.---RESP. Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 465, 466.

OBJ. Some accuse God because He wills some to be rich and others poor.---RESP. Peter Damian, CXLV, 210, 211.

## DEVIL

OBJ. It may be said hyperbolically, but not truly, that the devil was in the earthly paradise under the figure of the serpent, an animal.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XIV, 277, 278, 279.

OBJ. The devil is as powerful as God, since according to Scripture he surveys and circles the whole world in a single instant.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 507, 849, 850.

OBJ. It must not be believed that God speaks to the devil and the devil to God.---RESP. Ivo, CLXI, 988, 989.

OBJ. There must be no doubt about the devil’s divination, since it has very often been proved by the experience of many.---RESP. Ivo, CLXI, 766, 768.

OBJ. The devil is the maker of animals, thunder, and other calamities.---RESP. Isidore, CXXX, 564, 565, 894, 895.

OBJ. The devil sees the inward thoughts of human beings because he is ignorant of nothing in man.---RESP. Ivo, CLXI, 766, 767.

## DAYS

OBJ. It is not a correct way of speaking to say that creation was accomplished within six days, since it is impossible to count the first days of creation, when days and nights could not exist before the creation of the sun.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 183, 235, 258, 275, 314, 317, 319; XLI, 322; XLII, 295, 309, 314, 323, 338.

OBJ. Good and bad days are recognized by everyone; therefore some power belongs to days.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1204; XXXVIII, 123, 168, 245, 909, 1051, 1363.

OBJ. Very many despise the sanctification of the Lord’s Day because, according to them, such sanctification was neither instituted by the apostles nor founded in Scripture.---RESP. Rabanus, CVIII, 76, 355.

OBJ. The obligation to hear Mass on the Lord’s Day is denied because it is not founded on the Scriptures, etc.---RESP. Isidore, CXXX, 402, 403; Ivo, CLXI, 508.

## FLOOD

OBJ. Ancient writers are silent about the Flood; therefore it is not to be admitted.---RESP. St. Augustine, XL, 334; XLI, 569; XLII, 631.

OBJ. It is not wholly certain that the Flood existed, or at least covered the entire earth, because shells and conchs found in mountains do not prove it.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 481; II, 1033.

OBJ. The Flood was not universal, because there were cities older than the Flood.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 482.

## THE RICH

OBJ. The rich must be uprooted from human society, since all goods ought to be made common to all, just as the elements of the world are common to all.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XIV, 263, 264.

OBJ. The rich are always evil, since Christ despises them when He declares that they are admitted to the kingdom of heaven only with the greatest difficulty.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 494; XXXIV, 882; XXXVII, 1731; XXXVIII, 216, 521; St. Leo, LIV, 164, 165, 436, 437; LVII, 526, 731, 732.

## CHURCH

[Col. 0415]

OBJ. Ministers of the Church are always permitted to flee in time of persecution, because no one is bound to expose himself to danger.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 115, 144.

OBJ. The Church is falsely called holy, because there are many wicked people in it.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 1286.

OBJ. The Catholic Church is not true, because wheat is mixed and confused with tares in it.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 791, 792; IV, 344, 345.

OBJ. There are martyrs outside the Church; therefore salvation also can be had outside the Church.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 783, 1224; IV, 511, 512.

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that the Church will never perish, since, according to many, it is already dead or at least close to impending death.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 466, 476, 477, 807, 879, 880; St. Jerome, XXIII, 506.

OBJ. The Church may be despised and rejected without departing from God, since God and the Church are two different things and do not rest upon one and the same foundation.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1998; XXXVI, 175, 223, 508; XXXVII, 1103, 1297, 1684; XXXVIII, 448; XXXIX, 1615; XL, 668.

OBJ. Pelagians and Caelestians prove that the Church here ought to be without spot; therefore the wicked must be cast out from the bosom of the Church.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 336, 356, 998; XXXVIII, 981, 982, 1169.

OBJ. The Church is censured by many because it has recourse to secular powers to establish its dominion.---RESP. St. Leo, LIV, 873, 874, 1040.

OBJ. It is wrongly said that the Church of the Old and New Testaments is one, since their precepts are different, their faith and hope different, and their sacraments different.---RESP. Hincmar, CXXV, 454, 455, 458, 459.

## ECLIPSE

OBJ. Writers are silent concerning the famous eclipse seen at Christ’s death; therefore it is not to be admitted.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 401.

## THE ELECT

OBJ. The election of the good and reprobation of the rest must be rejected, because under a just God this is unintelligible.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1831, 1851; XXXVIII, 177; XL, 121, 122, 127, 275.

OBJ. Election does not presuppose merit but, on the contrary, precedes all merits; therefore it is unintelligible.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 821, 822, 827, 887; XXXV, 1851, 1852; XXXVII, 1744; XL, 620; XLIV, 582, 924; XLV, 1133, 1140, 1142.

OBJ. If election does not proceed from merits, then God is a respecter of persons, as is apparent from Esau and Jacob.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 887; XXXVIII, 587; XLIV, 580, 987.

## ALMSGIVING

OBJ. It is falsely said that a small alms receives a great reward from God, because there ought to be proportion between reward and gift.---RESP. St. Maximus, LVII, 818, 819.

OBJ. Almsgiving benefits those who give alms so that they may be able to sin with impunity, because alms redeem absolutely all sins.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 507, 508.

## EPICURUS
OBJ. Neither the whole world nor the human soul is a work of God, since, according to Epicurus, they arise from atoms.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 703, 564, 653.

OBJ. Epicurus’s atoms must be admitted, because they account excellently for the creation of things.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 64, 445.

**BISHOPS.**

OBJ. The elections of bishops ought to be made by the votes of the people, as formerly, according to the old maxim: “The people do not err.”---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 768, 769, 1025, 1026, 1027.

OBJ. Some contend that the episcopate is not higher than the presbyterate, because Scripture contains no distinction between the two.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 290, 780, 784.

OBJ. Bishops are not unlike presbyters, because they were formerly called presbyters.---RESP. Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 597, 598.

OBJ. Bishops are under no obligation toward kings, because the powers of each are very dissimilar.---RESP. Hincmar, CXXV, 739, 740.

**EUCHARIST.**

OBJ. The Eucharist seems inadmissible, because bread cannot and ought not to be Christ’s body, but only its figure and a memorial of the Passion; moreover, it is objectionable that Christ’s incorruptible body should be crushed by teeth and even gnawed by mice.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 348, 460, 461; Guibert, CLVI, 708, 709, 710; Anselm, CLVIII, 910, 911, 915, 922; CLIX, 253, 254, 255.

[Col. 0416] OBJ. Wine alone in the Eucharist, or bread alone, ought to be offered, because Christ’s body and blood would equally be present in wine alone and in bread alone.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 383, 384, 385.

OBJ. The Eucharist is not a sacrament more excellent than manna, since both were given from heaven as food for humankind.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 403, 404, 444.

OBJ. The Eucharist may be received by those who have not fasted, since the disciples first received it while not fasting.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 203, 204.

OBJ. The Eucharist was not instituted for human beings, since it is the bread of angels.---RESP. Peter Lombard, CXCI, 417, 418.

**EVANGELISTS, GOSPEL.**

OBJ. The divine inspiration of the Evangelists is disputed by many.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XV, 1531, 1554, 1555; XIV, 787.

OBJ. In many places the Evangelists do not agree with one another, as in setting forth Christ’s genealogy and in other matters; therefore they were not inspired.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XV, 1587, 1830, 1833; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1947; XXXVIII, 1117, 1130, 1135; XLII, 217, 515.

OBJ. Some reject the Gospel because it does not narrate everything that the prophecies foretold.---RESP. St. Leo, LIV, 312, 313, 314.

**BLINDING.**

OBJ. One ought not to believe what is read in Scripture, namely, that God blinded one person and enlightened another, because such a manner of acting would be unjust and wholly inequitable on God’s part.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1777; XXXVI, 116, 790, 794; XLII, 389, 394.

**EXORCISM.**

OBJ. Exorcism is of no use; therefore it must be rejected.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 203, 204, 555, 559; III, 1151.

**WOMEN.**

OBJ. With respect to women’s luxury, women who anoint their skin with cosmetics, stain their cheeks with rouge, and smear their eyes with soot do not sin.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 1325; St. Augustine, XLII, 438; XLV, 1551, 1552.

**FAITH.**

OBJ. Faith is not as effective as is asserted, since without works it is dead.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 960, 961, 977, 978, 1040, 1041.

OBJ. Faith in Christ cannot be called necessary, because it was not possessed in the Old Testament, and yet the righteous of old were saved by faith.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1396; XL, 287; XLIV, 249.

OBJ. Faith in Christ is not necessary, because a person can live justly without it, and because the works of the law are to be preferred to faith.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 257, 258, 261; XXXVIII, 236; XL, 204, 621.

OBJ. Faith cannot be called a gift of God; otherwise it would in no way depend upon free choice, and thus one who wished to believe could not believe—which is absurd.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 984, 987; XXXV, 1778; XXXVIII, 787; XLIV, 209, 235, 976.

OBJ. Some attribute the beginning of faith to the human being; therefore it is not from God alone.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 116, 117, 313, 314, 376, 377, 389, 390, 671, 672, 968.

OBJ. For salvation it is not necessary that faith be joined to works, since faith alone justifies, according to Scripture.---RESP. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 189, 190.

OBJ. Some do not admit faith, because it excludes inquiry and reason, and because it is therefore not rational to believe what we do not understand.---RESP. St. Guibert, CLVI, 24, 25, 353, 1153; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 255, 256, 262, 263, 264.

**THE SON.**

OBJ. The Son of God is not equal to the Father, since, according to Scripture, he came forth from the Father.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 161, 176, 183, 422, 802.

OBJ. The Son is not of the same eternity as the Father, because it is natural that a son should be later than his father.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 162, 176, 183, 422.

OBJ. Many are called sons of God; therefore he is not the only Son.---RESP. St. Hilary, X, 434, 435.

OBJ. The Son of God is improperly called both firstborn and only-begotten, because these two terms contradict one another.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 549, 550.

OBJ. It is impossible to understand how the Father begot the Son.---RESP. Rufinus, XXI, 341, 342.

OBJ. The Son of God is not like the Father, since he is only the image of the Father.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 159; XXXV, 1819; XLII, 688, 691, 701, 774, 777, 780, 788, 848, 931.

[Col. 0417] OBJ. The Son is not almighty, since Scripture reads that the Son can do nothing of himself, etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 701, 705, 746, 747, 860.

OBJ. The Son of God cannot be called consubstantial, coequal, and coeternal with the Father, because he was begotten by the Father.---RESP. St. Leo, LIV, 208, 233, 234, 769; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 366, 367, 750; Eugyppius, LXII, 904, 905, 910, 913.

OBJ. The Son of God must know the day of judgment, yet, according to Scripture, he does not know it.---RESP. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 436, 1437.

**SCOURGE.**

OBJ. God’s justice and providence must be accused because he scourges the good together with the wicked.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 255, 274; XXXVII, 1180, 1945; XXXVIII, 276; XL, 701.

**THEFT.**

OBJ. Theft is sometimes lawful, since the children of Israel despoiled the Egyptians by theft when fleeing from Pharaoh.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 608, 609; XXXVII, 1400.

OBJ. Neither one who commits theft by night nor one who commits it by day ought to be killed, because homicide is never lawful.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 627, 628.

**GENTILES.**

OBJ. Many among the Gentiles possess all virtues—namely mercy, sobriety, patience, charity, and so forth; therefore they are worth as much as Christians.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XIV, 943, 944.

OBJ. The nations sufficiently knew the true God, since they had the law written in their hearts and fulfilled it naturally.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 227, 228, 749, 750; XXXVI, 785, 786.

**GRACE.**

OBJ. Either grace or free choice must be removed, because they are opposed to one another.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 507, 653; Marius Mercator, LVIII, 671; St. Prosper, LI, 86, 87, 649, 650; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 521, 522, 527, 528.

OBJ. If grace is gratuitous, martyrs ought not to be praised, because their constancy amid torments must be attributed wholly to God’s grace.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 247, 291, 790, 802, 803.

OBJ. If grace is gratuitous, the old maxim no longer holds good: “Help yourself, and I will help you.”---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 528, 529, 536.

OBJ. Grace is not necessary; for if it were necessary, it would be denied to none who asks, or would be granted gratuitously to everyone; but neither is the case.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 409, 410, 569, 570, 685; X, 74, 75.

OBJ. Not all people are able to cooperate with grace, since many are drawn unwillingly toward evil, as the Apostle testifies when he does the evil that he does not wish.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 555, 557, 597, 598.

OBJ. Grace is the gift of one who bestows it; therefore we cannot obtain it at all.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 349, 350, 507, 508.

OBJ. Grace is not necessary for action, since it is given in abundance in order that action may be performed more easily.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 354, 775, 829; XXXVIII, 174, 856; XLIV, 264, 370, 584.

OBJ. Grace is given according to works, since we are sufficient in our own strength to avoid sins.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 771, 772; XXXIV, 416; XLIV, 259, 274, 281, 693.

OBJ. If a human being could not avoid sins by his own powers, the dominion of iniquity over humanity before grace would have to be admitted; but . . .---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 406; XXXVI, 233, 895, 898; XXXVII, 1224; XXXVIII, 108, 187, 855.

OBJ. God has mercy on whom he wills; therefore grace abolishes free choice.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 984, 985; XXXVIII, 179, 180; XL, 127, 128, 278; XLV, 1505.

OBJ. Not all receive grace; therefore God is unjust and shows partiality.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 882, 974; XXXVII, 1890.

OBJ. Finally, nothing certain can be said concerning grace and free choice, since the Apostle lost heart in these questions, crying out: “O man, who are you?” “O the depth!”---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 564, 565; XXXV, 2061; XXXVIII, 179, 905; XL, 278; XLIV, 241, 621; XLV, 1008, 1010.

**HERESIES, HERETICS.**

OBJ. Heresies ought not to be condemned, because Scripture says that they must exist.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 12, 13, 14, 17; Lactantius, VI, 540, 541.

OBJ. Heretics prove their doctrine from the sacred Scriptures; [Col. 0418] therefore they rely upon a legitimate principle.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXIII, 181, 182; St. Augustine, XXXII, 272; XXXIII, 459; XXXIV, 360; XLII, 400; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 289, 290, 552.

**HEROD.**

OBJ. Herod was not culpable in killing John the Baptist, because he had to keep his oath.---RESP. St. Ivo, CLXI, 795, 798.

**HUMAN BEING.**

OBJ. The human being was not created good, because some people are so wicked that they cannot in any way be recalled from wrongdoing.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 811, 812.

OBJ. The human being was not created by God, since, according to philosophers, he was formed either from atoms, by chance, or from earth.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 458, 459; X, 356.

OBJ. If the human being had been made in God’s image, he would either be God or possess some prerogative of divinity; but neither can be said; therefore, etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 626, 858; XXXIII, 26, 186, 244; XXXIV, 243, 292, 347, 366, 409; XXXVI, 218; XXXVIII, 362; XLII, 1001, 1003.

**HUMILITY.**

OBJ. Christians profess humility in vain, because it does not please God.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 1326; II, 911.

OBJ. Humility should be disregarded, because it is despised in this world and mocked by most people.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XV, 1236, 1237, 1776, 1777.

**IDOLATRY.**

OBJ. Quite a few defend idolatry because they say that they do not worship images themselves, but that which is signified by the images.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 801; XXXVII, 1244, 1245, 1788, 1789; XXXVIII, 1023; XLI, 221, 222; XLII, 290, 462.

OBJ. Idolatry was good, since the Roman disaster resulted from the overthrow of idols.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 623, 624; XLIII, 45.

**IGNORANCE.**

OBJ. Ignorance always excuses from sin, because it lacks will.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 261, 262; II, 27, 648.

OBJ. Sins arising from ignorance are not voluntary, because one who does not know cannot sin as one who knows does.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 883; XLI, 665; XLIV, 345, 884, 885; XLV, 1118, 1120.

OBJ. It is falsely said that ignorance is always sin, because ignorance is better than rash knowledge.---RESP. Peter Lombard, CXCI, 95, 96, 237.

**IMAGE.**

OBJ. Very many deny that the human being was created in God’s image because, they say, the human being resembles God neither in body nor in mind.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 640; XXXVI, 480, 564, 629; XL, 332, 628; XLII, 1038, 1040.

OBJ. The use of images must always be condemned, because it always savors and expresses idolatry.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 667; St. Ivo, CLXI, 206, 294, 298.

OBJ. Images must be prohibited because God formerly prohibited them to the Jews.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 430, 696; II, 310.

**IMPOSSIBILITY.**

OBJ. God commands impossible things, because many people are unable to fulfill his precepts.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1778, 1779; XLIV, 271, 288.

**INCARNATION.**

OBJ. The Incarnation must not be admitted because it is incomprehensible and incompatible with divine majesty and right reason.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 517, 518; St. Hilary, IX, 33, 34, 73, 74, 397, 398; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 368, 369.

OBJ. Many contend that the Incarnation was neither necessary nor wise because, they say, God could have employed another way of delivering human beings.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 134; XXXVI, 898; XXXVIII, 573, 710, 945, 951, 1006, 1016; XLI, 220, 222, 308; XLII, 1024; XLIV, 174.

OBJ. Christ’s Incarnation was not absolutely necessary, because the incarnation of a human being or an angel would have been sufficient to redeem the world.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 245, 246, 456, 457.

**HELL.**

OBJ. The eternity of hell is called into doubt by some.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXIV, 354.

OBJ. Many refuse to admit the existence of hell because, they say, no one has ever returned from the underworld to instruct us.---RESP. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 536, 537, 540, 541.

OBJ. The punishments of hell will be neither real nor eternal, since many assert that they will be merely temporary or phantasmal.---RESP. St. Gregory, LXXV, 911, 912; LXXVI, 737, 738.

**ENEMIES.**

OBJ. Enemies ought not to be loved, nor ought prayer to be offered for them, because this command is impossible, too harsh, and is not found in the old law.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 446, 698; St. Cyprian, IV, 759, 760; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 631, 447, 1274; XXXVII, 1518, 1524; XXXVIII, 120, 807, 1433, 1436.

OBJ. If enemies were to be loved, the killing of enemies would not have been lawful for the Jews, nor would holy and spiritual persons have carried out killings.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLII, 158, 159.

**INIQUITY.**

OBJ. God shares in some manner in the works of the wicked, since what the wicked person does wickedly, God has wickedly permitted.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 745; XXXVIII, 993; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 167, 168.

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that the brief life of the wicked is punished by eternity of torments, because a just God cannot impose an eternal punishment for a temporal and momentary fault.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 572, 573.

**DEATH / PERISHING.**

OBJ. A just human being is not to be distinguished from an unjust one, because humans and beasts have one and the same perishing.---RESP. Hugh, CLXXV, 197, 249, 250.

**ANGER.**

OBJ. Anger is not evil, since God himself becomes angry, according to Scripture.---RESP. Lactantius, IV, 693, 694; VII, 89, 92, 125, 126.

**ISAAC.**

OBJ. Very many refuse to hear that God commanded Isaac to be killed by his father because, they say, this command is cruel and unjust.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 244, 245; XXXVIII, 27, 133; XLI, 511.

OBJ. Isaac cannot be excused from lying because, according to Scripture, he affirmed that his wife was his sister.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 427, 428.

OBJ. Isaac was entirely deceived in blessing Jacob; therefore his blessing was ineffective.---RESP. Hugh, CLXXV, 630, 631.

**JACOB.**

OBJ. Jacob and Esau ought to have had the same lot from God, since they had the same lot from father, mother, conception, and birth, according to Scripture.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 887, 888.

OBJ. Jacob ought not to be preferred to Esau, since he received the blessing only by fraud and lying.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 567; XXXVIII, 41, 45, 46, 557; XLI, 515.

OBJ. Jacob cannot be excused from the fraud committed against Esau, because it was genuine fraud.---RESP. Alan, CCX, 342, 343.

**JOHN THE BAPTIST.**

OBJ. John the Baptist ought not to be praised, because, according to Scripture, he is scandalized on hearing of Christ’s miracles.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 402.

OBJ. John the Baptist was justly slain by Herod because he refused to render the reverence and obedience owed to authority and, according to Scripture, rebuked it.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 137, 402, 404, 623.

OBJ. We may doubt whether John the Baptist was sanctified in his mother’s womb.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 1201, 1202.

OBJ. John the Baptist ought not to have preached Christ, because he did not know him, since he sent disciples to him to ask who he was.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 921, 978, 980.

OBJ. John the Baptist’s abstinence is called into doubt by many because, they say, it is impossible.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 799, 800.

OBJ. John the Baptist is greater than Christ, since he is said to be greater than all those born of women.---RESP. St. Maximus, LVII, 389, 390.

**JOB.**

OBJ. God was cruel toward Job because he sent him excessively many trials.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVI, 354, 355, 1007, 1008, 1021.

OBJ. Job’s patience is undeservedly praised because he seems to have said something harsh against God and cannot be defended from blasphemy.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 1329; XXXVII, 1383, 1384; XL, 719; XLIV, 162.

**JONAH.**

OBJ. Jonah’s history must be rejected, because he could not have remained unharmed and uncorrupted for three days in the belly of a fish.---RESP. [Col. 0420] Tertullian, II, 840, 999; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 382, 383.

**JOSEPH.**

OBJ. Joseph cannot be called just, as Scripture calls him, because he refused to investigate his betrothed’s conception.---RESP. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 588, 589.

OBJ. Those who say that Joseph was merely Mary’s betrothed are mistaken, because many contend that he was Mary’s true husband.---RESP. St. Maximus, LVII, 638, 639, 640.

OBJ. Joseph knew Mary carnally because he is called Mary’s husband properly and without qualification.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 454, 455, 456.

**JUDAS.**

OBJ. Christ ought neither to have chosen Judas as an apostle nor endured him, because he knew and foresaw him long beforehand.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 626, 627; III, 1155, 1156; St. Ambrose, XIV, 1019, 1020, 1076, 1077; Rupert, CLXVII, 270.

OBJ. Some think that Judas did not receive the Eucharist with the other apostles because, they say, if he had received it, he would not have betrayed the Lord and Master.---RESP. St. Ivo, CLXI, 188, 189.

**JEWS.**

OBJ. Christ’s first coming was not sufficiently evident and manifest to the Jews, because the Jews could not recognize him.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 833; I, 381.

OBJ. The Jews would have been guilty only insofar as they had known Christ as Messiah; yet they did not know Christ as such.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 355, 356, 989, 990; X, 196, 197, 298, 299.

OBJ. The Jews are wrongly called blind, since they are called seeing in the Scriptures; moreover, according to Scripture, they expected a powerful king rather than one humbled, and hoped for temporal goods through Christ.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 546; XXXIV, 1858; XXXV, 1573, 1936; XXXVI, 522, 790, 862; XXXVIII, 260, 752; XL, 643, 664; XLII, 51.

OBJ. The Jews should be excused on grounds of ignorance or good faith, because in good faith they believed the Lord to be possessed by a demon.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1633, 1937; XXXVI, 765, 932.

**JUDGMENT.**

OBJ. The final judgment must be denied because, according to many, Scripture does not speak clearly of it.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 944, 945; XL, 305, 342, 346; XLI, 661, 663.

OBJ. The final judgment must be doubted because all the signs of judgment mentioned by the prophets have been fulfilled.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 576; XLIV, 326.

OBJ. The day of judgment is sometimes said to be about to come soon, but sometimes is affirmed to come only after the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world; therefore it must be doubted.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 900; XXXVIII, 76, 128, 228.

**OATH.**

OBJ. An oath is always lawful, because it is used by God and by the Apostle.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 972, 974, 977, 1406; XLI, 1660.

OBJ. Alternatively, no oath is lawful in any case, because an oath is always evil.---RESP. Peter Cantor, CCV, 321, 513, 240, 321.

**JUSTICE.**

OBJ. God has no justice, because evil and wicked people live joyful and tranquil lives, while good people are oppressed by every misery.---RESP. Zacchaeus, XX, 1104, 1106.

OBJ. God’s justice cannot be reconciled with his mercy, since God cannot be both just and merciful.---RESP. XXXVI, 1330, 1922.

OBJ. Human righteousness should not be located in God’s grace, as Christians wish, but rather, as Pelagians wish, in law, nature, or the will.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 760, 768; XXXVIII, 921, 926; XLIV, 249, 602, 603, 605, 616; XLV, 1210.

OBJ. Human righteousness must not be placed in God’s grace, since a person possesses it from himself, is born with it, and it arises from free choice.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 755; XXXVIII, 922; XLV, 1102, 1249, 1542; XLIV, 120, 204, 231, 245, 282, 605, 606.

OBJ. Catholics err when they assert that a person is made righteous by Christ’s grace and not by his own merits, because then free choice would have no force.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 1346; XXXIV, 380; XL, 331; XLIV, 242, 877.

OBJ. It cannot be said that a person is made righteous by Christ’s grace, because the righteous of old did not possess Christ’s grace, yet became righteous.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 858, 859; XL, 621; XLIV, 315, 399, 403, 450, 500.

**LAW.**

[Col. 0421]

OBJ. An unjust law, in the same manner as a just law, demands honor and obedience, because it proceeds from a ruler and consequently from competent authority.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 286, 287, 566; II, 290, 885.

OBJ. Divine law is not necessary for human beings, because before Moses there was no law.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 289, 599, 600.

OBJ. The Mosaic law must be disapproved because it is burdened with too many observances and had no signification.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 306, 374, 505.

OBJ. The yoke of the Gospel law is wrongly called light, because it appears intolerable to many and altogether beyond human powers.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 387, 388, 780, 781.

OBJ. It is useless to give the law to humanity, since it is already written in everyone’s hearts.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 673; XXXVII, 1574, 1575.

OBJ. Every law is neither useful nor good but evil, because it became the strength of sin; that is, once the law was given, a person who had formerly been an ignorant sinner and consequently not culpable became a transgressor.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 818, 831, 928; XL, 353; XLI, 380; XLIV, 557; XLV, 1605, 1606.

OBJ. If the law is good and not useless, it therefore justifies and saves the human being, as the Pelagians wish.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 769; XLIV, 219, 556, 826; XLV, 209, 214, 221, 364, 365, 904, 1227.

OBJ. Grace is not required for fulfilling the law, since human powers or fear suffice, as appeared under the old law, which was fulfilled only by threats and terrors.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 660; XXXVII, 851, 856; XLII, 71; XLIV, 219, 253, 617.

OBJ. The old law still binds, because it could not be changed without changing the plan of divine providence.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 526; XLII, 71, 154, 156, 345, 348, 359.

OBJ. The Jews ought not to be reproved for not having fulfilled the law, because the law was not fulfilled through no fault of their own.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 434, 435.

OBJ. The old law was not fulfilled through its own fault, because, according to Scripture, it was given so that transgression might abound.---RESP. St. Prosper, LI, 285, 286, 356, 357.

**MARY.**

OBJ. Blessed Mary was not a virgin, because she is everywhere compared with Eve.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 397; II, 897, 898.

OBJ. Mary’s virginity was not perpetual, since many deny this prerogative after childbirth because several brothers of the Lord born from Mary are enumerated.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 920, 921; St. Ambrose, XIV, 1150; XV, 1677; XVII, 873, 874; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 333, 334, 337; St. Paulinus, LXI, 415, 416.

OBJ. Blessed Mary was not perpetually a virgin, since she is repeatedly called spouse, woman, and wife.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XV, 1553, 1554; XVI, 1125; St. Jerome, XXVI, 372, 414, 415; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 343, 344.

OBJ. If Mary had been a virgin at conception, she would not have needed purification.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXIV, 697, 698; Alcuin, CI, 46, 1271, 1300.

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that Mary conceived through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, because, according to the Arians, the Holy Spirit came upon Mary only to purify and sanctify the child already conceived.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 422; XXXVIII, 442, 1069, 1074, 1114, 1319; XL, 399; XLII, 490, 736; XLIV, 175; XLV, 1553.

OBJ. Mary herself calls herself a handmaid, not the Mother of God; therefore, etc.---RESP. Alcuin, C, 749, 750; CI, 201, 202, 213.

**MARTYRS.**

OBJ. The constancy of martyrs ought not to be praised because it must more often be regarded as obstinacy or invincible pride, since many voluntarily and of their own accord offered themselves to tyrants.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 530, 535, 584, 704, 1270; II, 1027; St. Cyprian, IV, 246, 247, 268, 269, 795, 796.

OBJ. Martyrdom can be beneficial even outside the Church, because it may be endured for truth or in Christ’s name even outside the Church.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 793, 1120, 1197; IV, 509, 536.

OBJ. Children ought not to be numbered among martyrs, because they cannot sufficiently understand that death must be undergone for Christ.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 419, 427, 428.

OBJ. It is contended that the merits of martyrs are of no benefit to our advancement because, they say, Scripture makes no mention of this.---RESP. St. Ambrose, XVII, 716, 717.

**MARRIAGE.**

OBJ. Marriage is not good; therefore it must not be admitted.---RESP. [Col. 0422] Tertullian, II, 281, 695, 806, 903, 987; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 288; XL, 368; XLII, 597; XLIV, 416, 419.

**MEDIATOR.**

OBJ. The necessity of a mediator is scarcely understood by some and is therefore called into doubt by them.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 852, 1333, 1334.

OBJ. Our mediator is not at once God and human being, because his humanity was absorbed by divinity.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 238, 239, 273, 274.

OBJ. The mediator did not necessarily have to be God and human being, since an angel or a mere human being could have made satisfaction.---RESP. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 331, 332.

**MELCHIZEDEK.**

OBJ. Melchizedek was not a human being but an angel.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 567, 568.

OBJ. Melchizedek is either God himself, since he had no beginning, or Adam himself, since he was without father and without mother.---RESP. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 251, 252.

**LIE.**

OBJ. A lie is not always forbidden, because it is sometimes uttered for usefulness, recreation, and enjoyment.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 1158, 1159; IV, 777, 778; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 285; XXXVIII, 738; XL, 491, 508, 510, 513.

OBJ. It is lawful to lie lest an innocent person sought for death be betrayed; for temporal or eternal salvation; for the sake of chastity; to expose heretics; from humility; or under the appearance of repentance.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 497, 630, 654; XXXVIII, 981; XL, 244, 495, 496, 501, 503, 518, 544, 546; XLIV, 265.

OBJ. The authors of Scripture are shown not to be immune from lying: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the Egyptian midwives, Rahab, and so forth.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 112, 113, 155, 156; XXXVIII, 45, 740; XL, 492, 533, 539; Rupert, CLXVII, 573.

**MERITS.**

OBJ. It is falsely asserted that eternal glory is given for our merits, because such glory must be attributed solely to God’s mercy.---RESP. St. Hilary, IX, 770, 841; X, 412, 413.

OBJ. Grace does not precede merit, because merit begins through free choice.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 860; XXXVIII, 917, 1333; XXXIX, 1647, 1648; XL, 282; XLIV, 633, 889, 924, 968.

OBJ. If grace always precedes merit, then there is no merit of the righteous, nor demerit of the wicked.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 778; XXXIII, 820, 876, 970; XL, 282; XLIV, 341, 888.

OBJ. The merits of the saints suffice for us, since they may be applied to us to acquire eternal life, because they are most abundant and overflow even for the saints themselves.---RESP. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 481, 482.

**MINISTER.**

OBJ. An evil minister cannot validly administer the sacraments, because he cannot give grace which he does not possess.---RESP. St. Optatus, XI, 962, 963.

OBJ. Worldly people rightly and deservedly rebuke ministers of the Church because they sometimes seek and receive bodily support; they have been sufficiently provided for by the Church.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXII, 862; XXXIV, 1294; XXXVII, 1910.

**MIRACLES.**

OBJ. Miracles are never to be believed, because they can be performed by wicked people and even by demons.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 406, 409, 410; II, 738.

OBJ. The wise of the world are unwilling to believe any miracles because, they say, nearly all are false.---RESP. St. Cyprian, III, 1164; IV, 207, 511, 1189, 1192.

OBJ. All miracles performed in former times seem suspect or inadmissible because none at all are now performed.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 372, 519; XXXIV, 142, 1458, 1592; XXXVIII, 699, 725, 1139, 1157; XLII, 63, 64, 90, 871, 874.

OBJ. Miracles were formerly performed to awaken faith; therefore they ought still now to be performed to strengthen faith, since faith is failing in everyone.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLI, 760; XLIV, 182.

**DEATH.**

OBJ. Death follows the human being by nature, as is evident from his material or bodily constitution.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 738, 764, 942.

OBJ. Death is not to be feared, because it frees us from every evil.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 614, 615, 625, 1212, 1263.

OBJ. Death is wrongly presented to us as a punishment, because this is wholly denied: for if it were so, it would be because death arose from sin; but death does not arise from sin, since many contend that bodily death would have occurred in paradise even if no one had sinned.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLI, 387, 1585, 1586; XLV, 1112, 1181, 1222, 1596, 1603, 1604.

**MOSES.**

OBJ. Moses was not pleasing to God because he could not obtain from God what he requested.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 481, 482.

OBJ. Moses was a murderer, because his deed in killing the Egyptian cannot in any way be justified.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 597.

OBJ. It is falsely said that Moses saw God, since God spoke to him through an angel and not through himself.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 610, 611; XXXV, 1403, 1779; XXXVIII, 63, 64; XL, 622, 663; XLII, 811, 812.

OBJ. Many think that Moses was excluded from the eternal fellowship of the saints because, in their view, he sinned gravely by doubt, cruelty, and imprecation.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1267, 1802; XXXVIII, 553, 554; XXXIX, 1553; XLII, 325, 452.

OBJ. Moses’s truthfulness must be doubted because many things found in his books are suspect or highly doubtful.---RESP. St. Anselm, CLVIII, 635, 636, 652, 653, 654.

**WORLD.**

OBJ. Many refuse to believe that the world has existed only for six thousand years because, they say, the world is eternal, or at least its beginning is unknown.---RESP. Tertullian, I, 333; II, 609; St. Cyprian, IV, 653, 654, 668, 669; Arnobius, V, 898, 899.

OBJ. We may doubt the creation of the world and its qualities because philosophers’ opinions on these matters are innumerable.---RESP. Arnobius, V, 823, 824, 898, 899.

OBJ. The world was not created from nothing, since God established and adorned it from pre-existing matter.---RESP. Zeno, XI, 389, 390, 391.

OBJ. The eternity of the world must be admitted because many contend that it will never perish.---RESP. St. Jerome, XXV, 502, 503.

OBJ. If God had created the world, he would have made it more beautiful and excellent, so that the world might be more fitting to his majesty.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1892; XLII, 182, 291, 319, 376, 718.

OBJ. We cannot admit the beauty of the world because too many displeasing, indeed harmful, things are found in it.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 438, 498, 1134; XLI, 335.

OBJ. The world is not good, since the whole world lies in the evil one.---RESP. Hugh, CLXXV, 554, 555.

OBJ. The world was not created by the supremely good God because it is wholly evil and reprobate, according to Scripture.---RESP. Alanus, CCX, 311, 312, 545, 546.

**NECESSITY.**

OBJ. The human being is drawn to sin by necessity, since Paul says: “Not the good that I will,” etc.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLV, 118, 1299, 1393, 1398, 1490, 1492, 1500.

**NOTHING.**

OBJ. Some philosophers contend that God did not make things from nothing because, they say, he made everything from himself.---RESP. St. Augustine, XLV, 1470, 1471.

**NOAH.**

OBJ. Some refuse to believe that Noah alone was found just among all human beings because, they say, although the earth had become corrupt, its corruption had not yet advanced so far that only one just person could be found.---RESP. St. Cyprian, IV, 423, 424, 482; Philip, CCIII, 853, 854.

OBJ. It is wrongly said that Noah planted a vineyard, since Liberus sowed it with his own hand.---RESP. Lactantius, VI, 327.

**MIDWIVES.**

OBJ. God ought not to have rewarded the Egyptian midwives because, in lying to Pharaoh and refraining from the destruction of the Hebrews, they truly sinned; moreover, they lied boldly and knowingly.---RESP. Tertullian, II, 417; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 447.

**KILLING.**

OBJ. It is lawful to kill another person who wishes it, requests it, and no longer wishes to live, because then no wrong is done to him.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 940, 941.

OBJ. No one may in any case kill a human being, because human life is a good surpassing all other goods.---RESP. Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1150, 1151.

**WORKS.**

OBJ. If, as Catholics wish, God works in a human being both the willing and the working, then there is no human action; therefore there is no human free choice.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1775, 1778, 1783, 1784; XXXVIII, 850; XLIV, 918.

OBJ. It must not be believed that our works cannot be good without faith or grace, because some works possess intrinsic goodness.---RESP. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 853; XXXVIII, 32; XL, 111, 112, 204, 288, 323, 528; XLV, 1133, 1142.

### WORKS

**Objection.** Some perform good works from fear and not from love; therefore good works are possible without faith, grace, or charity. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 990; XXXVII, 1174; XXXVIII, 33, 792.

**Objection.** Grace is not absolutely required for good works, since the works of the law justify a person, according to Scripture. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 892; XXXV, 2117, 2118, 2137.

**Objection.** Unbelievers and the ungodly themselves perform certain good works; therefore grace is not required. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLIV, 230, 754.

### PRAYER

**Objection.** Prayer is neither necessary nor useful, since God knows our needs and wishes to provide for them without our prayer. — **Response.** St. Hilary, IX, 409, 538, 539, 568, 569, 785, 786.

**Objection.** God does not require frequent prayer from us, since He has never given us such a command. — **Response.** St. Ambrose, XIV, 351, 352; XV, 1473, 1474, 1720, 1721.

**Objection.** There is no necessity for prayer, because God knows what is necessary for us. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 500; XLIV, 151, 317, 318, 376, 380, 381; XXXVIII, 379, 494.

**Objection.** Prayer is not necessary, because by our own powers we can fulfil the law; and therefore it is foolish to pray that we may do what lies within our power. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 595, 761, 763, 775; XXXVIII, 895; XLIV, 256, 531.

**Objection.** Scripture commands what is impossible, namely, to pray without ceasing and never to fail. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 500, 501; XXXVI, 404.

### ORIGINAL SIN

**Objection.** Original sin does not exist, since individual souls are each created pure. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 725.

**Objection.** Original sin does not exist, because under the old law there was no remedy for its remission. — **Response.** St. Maximus, LVII, 655, 656.

**Objection.** It is falsely said that original sin passes from parents to offspring through the flesh, because sin is not in the flesh alone. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXV, 460, 461.

**Objection.** Original sin must be rejected, because it cannot be understood how and why it is imputed to descendants, or how it is removed in baptism. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXV, 460, 461; CLXXVI, 299, 300, 301.

**Objection.** Original sin is not from one’s own will; therefore it is not sin. — **Response.** Peter Lombard, CXCI, 162, 163.

### PARADISE

**Objection.** The paradise said to have been planted in Eden never existed, because the place in which it was has neither been designated nor can be designated. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIV, 378; XLIV, 398.

**Objection.** An earthly paradise does not exist, since what Scripture relates concerning it must be understood of spiritual paradise. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 394; XLV, 1089, 1310, 1328, 1332, 1408, 1599.

**Objection.** There is doubt concerning the paradise which Christ promised to the thief on the cross, because it cannot be conceived how, on the day of Christ’s death, the thief was with Him in paradise, since Christ remained in the tomb for three days. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 712, 833; XXXIV, 376, 377.

### PARENTS

**Objection.** Very many refuse to believe that children ought to be punished for the sins of their parents, because divine justice could thereby be called into question. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIV, 755; XXXVII, 1437; XLII, 137, 138; XLIII, 633.

**Objection.** Parents ought not to be honoured, because the Gospel and Christ Himself command that they be held in hatred. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 615; XXXIII, 1055, 1056; XXXIV, 1249; XLII, 136, 137, 138.

### INFANTS

**Objection.** Infants are not born with original sin, because otherwise they would already be evil by God’s act of creation and possessed by the devil; [Col. 0425] and this is improper to say. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 598; XXXIII, 871; XLIV, 188, 189, 441, 466, 838; XLV, 1154, 1212, 1216, 1240, 1241, 1402, 1404, 1557.

**Objection.** If infants were defiled by original sin, their souls themselves ought to renounce sin, and not do so through others; since it is impossible to believe through others—that is, it is impossible for one who is unbelieving to become believing through others. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 125, 127, 187, 505, 570, 951; XLIV, 132, 146, 505, 570; XLV, 1267, 1506.

**Objection.** It is wrongly said that infants who die without baptism are condemned on account of original sin, because they cannot perish through the fault of their parents. — **Response.** St. Prosper, LI, 706, 707.

**Objection.** Very many refuse to believe that infants are to be condemned, because this is contrary to the mercy and justice of God. — **Response.** St. Prosper, LI, 497, 498, 505, 506, 709, 710.

**Objection.** Infants are not born into the death of the soul, because no one ought to bear another’s iniquity. — **Response.** St. Fulgentius, XLV, 156, 157, 538, 539, 540.

**Objection.** God seems chargeable with injustice in that, of two infants guilty of the same sin, He condemns one and frees the other; brings one to grace and allows the other to be suffocated. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 177, 905; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 448, 617, 618.

### PASSION

**Objection.** In His Passion Christ did not suffer as much as is asserted, since, according to Scripture, the Passion was pleasant to Him. — **Response.** St. Hilary, IX, 805, 806.

**Objection.** Some maintain that Christ suffered not of His own will but through necessity, because, they say, His words show this: “Let it pass from me,” etc. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 333; XXXVII, 1104, 1105.

**Objection.** Christ’s Passion must be rejected in many respects, because it bears too much appearance of abasement. — **Response.** St. Maximus, LVII, 574, 575.

**Objection.** Christ’s Passion was not true and real, because it was merely phantasmal and apparent. — **Response.** Gennadius, LVIII, 1011, 1012.

**Objection.** The Father did not beget a Son equal to Himself, because the Father alone is wise, alone powerful, alone immortal, alone invisible, alone blessed, alone great, and alone good, as is read in Scripture. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 729, 730, 731, 733, 745, 761, 764, 766, 867, 925, 933, 935, 937.

**Objection.** The Son is not equal to the Father, since He is sent by the Father, carries out the Father’s commands, and is called the Father’s servant; whereas, on the other hand, the Father is called God and the Lord of the Son. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 821; XLII, 683, 733, 734, 838, 839.

**Objection.** The Father is greater than the Son, because, having been begotten by no one, He begot the Son. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 786, 787.

**Objection.** The Father is greater than the Son, because Christ says that the Father is greater than He. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXV, 1835, 1837.

**Objection.** The Father is greater than the Son, because the Son, sitting at the Father’s right hand, holds only a secondary place. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 692, 693.

**Objection.** The Father is older than the Son, since the Father existed before the Son’s generation. — **Response.** St. Fulgentius, LXV, 777, 778.

**Objection.** It cannot be said that the Father begets the Son daily, because this is contradictory. — **Response.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 896, 897.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit does not proceed jointly from the Father and the Son, since the Father and Son cannot be one principle of the Holy Spirit. — **Response.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 903, 904, 905.

### PATRIARCHS

**Objection.** The patriarchs ought to be censured, because they not only had several wives, but also mixed marriage with concubinage. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 1277; II, 921; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 345, 347; XL, 395; XLII, 403, 417, 440, 465.

**Objection.** It cannot be said that the patriarchs prefigured Christ, because very many of them were subject to many defects and vices. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, IV, 628.

### PAUL (ST.)

**Objection.** Not a few reject the rapture of St. Paul as a mental effort or an imaginative experience, as figurative; especially since Paul himself doubted whether he had been caught up into heaven in the body or outside the body. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, IV, 674, 675; St. Ambrose, XVIII, 329, 330; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 453, 458; St. Maximus, LVII, 395, 396; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 552, 553.

**Objection.** It seems wrongly said that Paul’s conversion should be attributed to God, because then Paul would not be praiseworthy in it, being in no way a participant. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 701; XXXVIII, 913, 914, 1465, 1466; XLIV, 207, 888, 889.

[Col. 0426] **Objection.** Paul does not seem excusable for lying, because at one time he observed the old sacraments with the Jews and at another time did not observe them; and he reproached Peter for what he himself had done. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 28, 113, 156, 257, 277, 289, 779; XL, 536; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 101, 102.

**Objection.** It is impossible to become all things to all people without lying; therefore Paul was a liar when he became all things to all people. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 288; XXXVII, 1182, 1183; XL, 493, 536, 558; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 413, 414.

**Objection.** Paul lied when he promised that he would come to the Corinthians, though he did not come. — **Response.** Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 544, 545.

### SINS

**Objection.** The punishments of sinners will not be eternal, because this is utterly contrary to God’s goodness. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXVI, 522, 523.

**Objection.** No distinction whatever should be made among sins, because Scripture makes no distinction between grave and light sins. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXIII, 328, 329; XXV, 91, 92, 755, 756; St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1132; XXXVIII, 1206, 1273, 1540; XL, 269, 539.

**Objection.** It is not just for God to punish the sins of fathers unto the third and fourth generation of their children; yet this is grounded in Scripture. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXV, 167, 168.

**Objection.** Human beings are not the cause of their actual sins, because sinners are accustomed to throw their sins back upon God, since He permits them. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 1271; XXXIV, 209; XXXVII, 1318; XXXVIII, 143, 587; XLII, 560; XLIV, 294, 731.

**Objection.** Free will is required in order to constitute any sin whatsoever; yet free will is not present in every sin, because human beings are compelled into sin, even unwillingly, by the necessity of their flesh. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 753, 759; XLII, 537, 538; XLIV, 286, 295; XLV, 1068, 1069, 1110.

**Objection.** Catholics falsely assert that a human being can be without sin in this life; yet according to Scripture whoever is born of God does not sin; therefore some can be without sin. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLIV, 164, 167, 168, 312, 370.

**Objection.** Certainly a person can be without sin, because God commands a person to be without sin. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLIV, 165, 295; XLV, 1212, 1213.

**Objection.** Certain unforgivable sins must be admitted, since the sin against the Holy Spirit is presented to us in the Gospel as unforgivable. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 814; XXXV, 2097, 2101, 2104; XXXVIII, 449, 455; XL, 272, 273.

**Objection.** By the term “sin against the Holy Spirit” is meant sin unto death; but Scripture gives sins unto death. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1229, 1230; XXXV, 1640, 1678, 1687, 1696, 1748.

**Objection.** Almsgiving and other good works redeem sins, according to Scripture; therefore Christ alone is not able to take away sins. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 659, 665, 675; XXVI, 810; XXXVIII, 88; XL, 265, 268, 636, 637; XLIII, 63; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 471, 472; Ivo, CLXI, 1015, 1016.

### PELAGIANS

**Objection.** The Pelagians rightly deny original sin, since, in their view, the flesh of every infant is equal to the flesh of Christ. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 723, 762, 773; XXXVIII, 992, 993.

**Objection.** The Pelagians teach that death comes not from sin, but from nature alone, and that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 598, 608; XLV, 436.

**Objection.** The Pelagians rightly praise free will, since human will, once the law has been given, can suffice to fulfil it. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 597, 763, 772; XXXVIII, 172, 409, 656, 1316; XLIV, 373.

**Objection.** The Pelagians teach that grace is given in abundance, or in order that action may be easier; therefore grace is not absolutely necessary. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 829.

### PUNISHMENTS

**Objection.** Punishments will not be eternal, because their eternity is contrary to the justice and goodness of God. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXV, 245, 246; St. Augustine, XL, 342; XLI, 732.

**Objection.** Punishments in hell are not diverse, because fire, which is hell’s greater punishment, cannot be more intense for one person and milder for another. — **Response.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1061, 1062.

### PENANCE

**Objection.** Penance appears useless and unfruitful, because God has not promised forgiveness for our offences through penance. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 785, 1001, 1233, 1240.

**Objection.** One should not believe that God repents, because divinity cannot admit repentance—that is, distress of mind. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1416, 1460, 1723; XXXVIII, 152; XL, 141; XLII, 539.

**Objection.** Present-day penance is of no value, because it is far less severe than ancient penance. — **Response.** Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1086, 1087, 1106, 1107; Alanus, CCX, 292, 293, 296, 297.

### REPENTANCE

**Objection.** Repentance is not necessary, since sins can be redeemed in many other ways, for example by prayers, good works, and the endurance of punishments. — **Response.** St. Ambrose, XVI, 375, 376, 508, 509, 519, 520, 1161, 1162.

### POWER

**Objection.** The power of the Roman Pontiff ought not to be both pontifical and royal, because these conflict with one another and have not always been united. — **Response.** St. Leo, LV, 625, 626, 627, 653, 654, 659, 666.

**Objection.** It is wrongly said that the devil’s power was diminished after Christ’s death, because the devil now has as much power as he had formerly. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXV, 457, 458.

**Objection.** Power should not be attributed to the entire Trinity, since it belongs to the Father alone, while wisdom is ascribed to the Son and goodness to the Holy Spirit. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXVI, 227, 228.

### PREDESTINATION

**Objection.** Predestination must be rejected, because it takes away free will and makes God unjust. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 639, 883; XLII, 614, 615; XLIV, 792, 975; XLV, 1132.

**Objection.** Predestination cannot be admitted, because it leads a person into despair. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLV, 1019, 1031, 1032.

**Objection.** Those who admit predestination must admit that God predestines people to do evil, since predestination to destruction is nothing other than predestination to do evil. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLV, 155, 156, 166, 172, 173.

**Objection.** A human being is not free with respect to good or evil, because God’s predestination and foreknowledge compel each person either to act well or to act badly. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLV, 375, 376.

### FOREKNOWLEDGE

**Objection.** God’s foreknowledge should not be admitted, because not a few deny it. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 290, 293.

**Objection.** God’s foreknowledge must be denied, because, according to some, it cannot be certain and fixed in God. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 1276; XXXVI, 655; XXXVIII, 350, 351; XLI, 472.

**Objection.** God’s foreknowledge must be abolished, because it makes God the cause of sins and unjust, and deprives human beings of freedom. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 1276, 1279; XXXV, 1776; XLI, 149, 152, 153; XLIV, 478.

**Objection.** God’s foreknowledge must be altogether denied, because it renders all laws, rebukes, prayers, exhortations, and so forth useless. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLI, 153; XLV, 1016.

**Objection.** God’s foreknowledge compels people to sin, since what God foreknew must necessarily come to pass. — **Response.** Peter Lombard, CXCI, 252, 253.

**Objection.** God ought not to create those whom He foreknows to be evil, because such creation can in no way be called good. — **Response.** Peter Lombard, CXCI, 240, 243.

### PROVIDENCE

**Objection.** All things happen by chance; therefore there is no divine providence. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 588; XXXVII, 1946; XXXVIII, 118; XL, 98; XLI, 153.

**Objection.** If divine providence cared for human affairs, no one ought to exercise personal diligence, because otherwise one would act against divine providence. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XL, 574, 575.

**Objection.** We may doubt whether God exercises His providence toward His servants, because many righteous persons seem wholly abandoned by God and given over to every misery. — **Response.** Peter Chrysologus, LII, 629, 630, 644, 645.

**Objection.** There is no providence in this world, because all things in it are governed either by chance or without reason. — **Response.** St. Anselm, CLVIII, 222, 223, 856, 837.

**Objection.** God’s providence can be mistaken, because a human being can act otherwise than he does. — **Response.** Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 712, 713.

**Objection.** Divine providence destroys the nature of things and consequently abolishes free will, since the sequence of things cannot be changed. — **Response.** John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 443.

**Objection.** Providence imposes necessity on things, because it is the same as knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, and predestination, [Col. 0428] which we certainly cannot oppose. — **Response.** John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 444.

### PURGATORY

**Objection.** Purgatory does not exist, because after death only two things remain: paradise and hell. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, III, 786, 787.

**Objection.** There is no intermediate place between heaven and hell; therefore neither is there purgatory. — **Response.** St. Gregory, LXXVII, 141, 398.

**Objection.** There cannot be fire in purgatory, because otherwise purgatory would be the same as hell. — **Response.** St. Gregory, LXXVII, 394; St. Julian, XCVI, 483, 484; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 773, 930, 931.

### THE PYTHONESS

**Objection.** The oracles of the Pythoness must be believed, because they are wholly true and certain. — **Response.** St. Philastrius, XII, 1135, 1136.

### REDEMPTION

**Objection.** Redemption could have been effected through either a human or an angelic person; therefore God’s own person was not necessarily required to accomplish redemption. — **Response.** St. Anselm, CLVIII, 365, 366, 377, 447, 448, 449.

**Objection.** Our redemption ought not to have been effected through Christ’s death, since it could have been accomplished by His word alone. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXV, 457.

**Objection.** Redemption could have been effected in a more fitting manner; therefore it was wrongly effected through Christ’s death. — **Response.** Hugh, CLXXV, 457, 458.

**Objection.** Christ is not to be praised very highly or uniquely for the resurrection, because He could have redeemed us through another. — **Response.** St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 733, 734.

**Objection.** Christ Himself ought not to have redeemed us, because He could have chosen another, more fitting method. — **Response.** Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 710, 711, 1022, 1023.

### RELIGION

**Objection.** Every religion must be abolished, because it is not necessary to human beings. — **Response.** Lactantius, VII, 97, 114, 115; VI, 376, 569, 536, 616, 617.

### RELICS

**Objection.** All relics must be rejected because they are always, or almost always, false. — **Response.** St. Gregory, LXXVII, 701, 702; Guibert, CLVI, 621, 622.

### REPROBATION

**Objection.** Whoever is reprobated can always complain of God’s injustice, because one must always ask God why one person is rejected while another is saved. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 822, 882, 860; XL, 120, 121, 122.

**Objection.** The reprobate can always complain of God’s inequity and cruelty, because surely God is unjust and cruel when He creates reprobates whom He foreknew would be condemned. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 824, 825, 833, 860, 884.

### RESURRECTION

**Objection.** The resurrection must be rejected because it seems wholly impossible; for it would require God to gather together and unite all, even the smallest, parts of the body from every region of the earth. — **Response.** St. Philastrius, XII, 1118, 1119, 1171, 1176; St. Hilary, IX, 402, 403, 672, 673, 948; Zacchaeus, XX, 1091, 1092; St. Jerome, XXIII, 378, 379; XXIV, 675, 676; XXV, 443, 444; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 786; XXXIX, 1622, 1623, 1631; XL, 193, 309; XLI, 780, 781; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 361, 362, 363, 364; St. Maximus, LVII, 623, 624; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVI, 393; St. Gregory, LXXI, 540, 865, 1149, 1151; LXXV, 738, 739; LXXVI, 1034, 1035.

**Objection.** The resurrection of bodies is not clearly demonstrated either in Scripture or in tradition; therefore it must be rejected. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXIII, 385, 386, 387.

**Objection.** A true and real resurrection must not be admitted, because it could take place by means of phantoms. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXIII, 310, 311.

**Objection.** It is wrongly asserted that Christ is our resurrection, because He could rise again even if others did not rise. — **Response.** Peter Chrysologus, LII, 226, 227, 312, 313, 314.

**Objection.** Not all will rise on the last day, because those living on the last day will be changed into incorruption and immortality without actual death. — **Response.** St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1230, 1231.

### ROME

**Objection.** The Roman Church has no more eminent dignity or authority than the other Churches of the world; yet the contrary is commonly believed. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 155; St. Cyprian, III, 766, 818, 819, 1043, 1114; IV, 226, 227, 309, 310; St. Ambrose, XVI, 945, 946; St. Augustine, XXXIII, [Col. 0429] 781, 782, 785; St. Leo, LIV, 882, 883, 1049, 1050; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 231, 232, 582, 586, 587, 656.

**Objection.** Although some grant that Peter is prince of the apostles, they nevertheless refuse to grant that his authority or primacy passed to his successors, because, they say, Scripture does not establish that transmission. — **Response.** St. Leo, LIV, 144, 146, 147, 154, 155, 1016, 1047.

**Objection.** The Church’s primacy is not a prerogative inherently belonging to the apostolic see, because the Roman pontiff has not always retained it. — **Response.** St. Leo, LIV, 367, 368, 458, 459, 505, 506, 561, 562, 643, 644, 761, 762.

### PRIESTS

**Objection.** Some deny that priests received from Christ the power to forgive sins, because forgiveness of sins is the work of God alone. — **Response.** St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 436, 437, 438.

**Objection.** Priestly celibacy is attacked by many as harmful to society and prescribed by no law. — **Response.** Cassiodorus, LXIX, 932, 933.

**Objection.** The people are persuaded that an evil priest does not consecrate the sacraments, because his wickedness is an impediment. — **Response.** Agobard, CIV, 142, 143.

**Objection.** It is wrongly said that priests ought to demand nothing for administering sacraments, because no labour ought to go without recompense. — **Response.** St. Ivo, CLXI, 83, 366.

**Objection.** It cannot be said that sacraments celebrated by a bad priest have equal efficacy with those celebrated by a good priest, because the minister’s goodness imparts at least some power to the sacrament. — **Response.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1073, 1074.

### SACRAMENTS

**Objection.** There is no difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, because both confer the same grace. — **Response.** St. Ambrose, XIV, 867, 868; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1146, 1147, 1227.

**Objection.** The righteous of old had no sacrament of regeneration, because Scripture is silent as to whether, before Abraham and after him, the righteous or their infants were marked by some bodily and visible sacrament. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 845; XLIV, 402, 403.

**Objection.** If the old sacraments existed, they ought still to remain, since Christ neither abolished the law nor its commandments. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 357, 359; XLIV, 179, 183.

**Objection.** It cannot be said that the wicked share in the sacraments and receive them really, because otherwise one would have to say that righteousness participates with wickedness. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1092; XLII, 355, 356; XLIII, 294.

### SACRIFICES

**Objection.** No sacrifices whatever ought to be offered to God, because God disapproved and wholly abolished the sacrifices of the Jews. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 1329; II, 310, 608, 806.

**Objection.** It is asserted without justification that the sacrifice of the altar is the same as the sacrifice of the cross, because Christ is not crucified on the altar. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, IV, 381, 382, 387, 388.

### SALVATION

**Objection.** God does not will all people to be saved, since not all are saved. — **Response.** Peter Lombard, CXCII, 337, 338.

**Objection.** All will have eternal salvation, because God, who is supremely just and merciful, cannot punish eternally that which is temporal with eternal punishment. — **Response.** Haymo, CVIII, 947, 948.

**Objection.** All will have eternal salvation, because after long periods the punishments of the damned will come to an end. — **Response.** Haymo, CXVIII, 947, 948, 950, 951; John Scotus, CXXII, 417, 418.

### SAVIOUR

**Objection.** It cannot be said that Christ is the Saviour of all people, since more are condemned than saved. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 985, 986; XXXVIII, 641, 1322; St. Prosper, LI, 84, 85, 627, 628, 685.

### SAINTS

**Objection.** It cannot be said that the saints are concerned for our salvation, because they take no care of us and cannot otherwise help us. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, IV, 601, 602; III, 874, 875, 876; St. Gregory, LXXI, 873, 910, 1181; St. Agobard, CIV, 153, 154; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 235, 236, 462, 463, 598, 599, 734, 735; Godefridus, CLXXIV, 922, 923.

**Objection.** The saints know absolutely nothing, since they do not know the day of judgment, nor our salvation and damnation. — **Response.** Alanus, CCX, 374, 375.

### SATISFACTION

**Objection.** Satisfactions are not necessary, because sins are not redeemed by satisfactions. [Col. 0430] — **Response.** St. Cyprian, III, 814, 815; IV, 241, 242, 243.

**Objection.** Some do not believe that satisfaction, or restoration of what has been taken away, is necessarily required for the remission of sins, because, they say, it suffices to perform other good works. — **Response.** St. Anselm, CLVIII, 375, 376, 391, 393, 394.

### SCRIPTURE

**Objection.** The study of the Scriptures alone makes a person saved, according to many passages of Scripture. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 489, 1299; II, 27, 510.

**Objection.** The Old Testament must be rejected because the New takes its place. — **Response.** St. Ambrose, XIV, 291, 292, 939, 940.

**Objection.** It is falsely said that a rule must be followed for the interpretation of Scripture, since Scripture itself teaches that it suffices for each person to follow his own sense without a rule. — **Response.** St. Jerome, XXVI, 187, 188; XXIII, 181, 182; XXV, 34, 35, 402, 403, 574, 575; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 222, 223; XL, 200; St. Gregory, LXXVII, 93, 400; LVIII, 289.

**Objection.** It is said without justification that sacred Scripture is superior to secular literature, because its reading is tedious and must be shunned on account of the harshness of its style. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 748, 809, 810; XXXIV, 65; XXXVIII, 30, 31.

**Objection.** Scripture is accessible to few, because it is obscure and, as it were, closed. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 542; XXXIV, 38, 65; XXXVI, 112, 159, 160, 413; XXXVII, 1189, 1360, 1803, 1917; XXXVIII, 849, 1237; XL, 36, 320, 539; XLI, 332; XLIII, 396; XLIV, 186.

**Objection.** The Scriptures must be rejected because they appear to contradict themselves and cannot be reconciled with one another. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 22, 53, 632, 799; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 164, 180, 213, 283, 332, 371, 510, 740, 791.

**Objection.** There are words of cursing, swearing, obscenity, and so forth in the Scriptures; therefore they must be rejected. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 88, 99, 100.

**Objection.** Some maintain that only the literal sense of Scripture should be accepted because, they say, other senses can never safely and without doubt lead us to truth. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 688; XXXIV, 68, 69, 257, 401, 430; XLIV, 257.

**Objection.** The Scriptures ought not to be searched, because one who searches the Scriptures searches the majesty of God and therefore will be crushed by it, according to Scripture. — **Response.** Rupert, CLXVIII, 174, 175, 573, 574, 1252, 1253.

### THE SERPENT

**Objection.** Moses seems deserving of censure for erecting an image of a serpent in the wilderness, because that image belongs to the category of idolatry. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 667, 668; II, 64, 347.

### THE SUN

**Objection.** Some deny the unusual eclipse of the sun at Christ’s death, because it cannot be precisely said what kind of eclipse it was, when it occurred, nor is it reported by contemporary historians. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 359, 401, 701; Lactantius, VI, 588, 610, 611.

### SPECTACLES

**Objection.** Christians may attend spectacles, because they cannot be defiled by them. — **Response.** Tertullian, I, 466, 630, 631, 655, 656; St. Cyprian, IV, 781, 782, 783; Lactantius, VI, 707, 712, 713; St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1918, 1919; XXXVIII, 85, 868; XLI, 44, 45; Cassiodorus, LXIX, 604, 605.

### THE HOLY SPIRIT

**Objection.** It does not seem credible that the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and upon Christ in the form of fire and a dove; for this appears to be a joke of the imagination and of little children. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, IV, 506, 507; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 747; XXXV, 1426, 2035; XL, 25, 302.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit is called gift, finger of God, charity, grace, and so forth; therefore He is not God. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXII, 1046, 1321; XXXIV, 111, 112, 616; XXXVIII, 447, 448, 1071; XL, 258, 634, 684; XLII, 30, 44; XLIII, 378; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 136, 137, 138.

**Objection.** If the Holy Spirit is God, at least He is not equal to the Father and Son, because it is proved that He is not of the same substance. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIV, 111, 112; XLII, 788, 797, 827, 828, 929.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit is not equal to the Father and Son, since He proceeds from them and is said to be sent by both. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 458; XL, 688; XLII, 686, 697, 755, 847, 908; XLIV, 531; XLV, 1032.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit is less than the Father because He is said to have worshipped the Father and to intercede with Him for us. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 756, 757; XLIV, 531; XLV, 1032.

[Col. 0431] **Objection.** The Holy Spirit does not proceed jointly from the Father and the Son, because He cannot proceed wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son. — **Response.** St. Fulgentius, LXV, 417, 418, 419, 574, 575, 780, 781.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit is nothing other than a breath, since He is everywhere compared to blowing. — **Response.** Vigilius, LXII, 382, 383.

**Objection.** Among the Hebrews, the Holy Spirit is of feminine gender; therefore. — **Response.** St. Agobard, CIV, 163, 164.

**Objection.** It is falsely said that sin against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable, because according to the Christian faith there is no sin for which we cannot obtain forgiveness. — **Response.** St. Leo, LIV, 206, 207, 403, 414.

**Objection.** It cannot be understood how the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters in the creation of the world. — **Response.** Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1382, 1383.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, since, according to the Greeks, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son. — **Response.** St. Anselm, CLVIII, 306, 307, 308, 310; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 914, 915.

### THE CREED

**Objection.** It is not sufficiently proved that the Creed was handed down to us by the apostles; therefore it does not appear to be admissible. — **Response.** St. Gregory, LXXVIII, 369, 370, 371.

**Objection.** The Nicene Creed is invalid because it does not state in it the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, nor does the name “Trinity” occur there. — **Response.** St. Anselm, CLXIII, 312, 313, 315, 318.

### TEMPTATION

**Objection.** Scripture contradicts itself concerning temptations, because at one time it says, “God tempted Abraham,” and at another, “God tempts no one.” — **Response.** Eugippius, LXII, 706, 707.

**Objection.** God truly and really leads us into sin, since in the Lord’s Prayer one reads, “And do not lead us into temptation,” that is, into sin. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIII, 773, 948; XXXIV, 562, 612, 1282.

**Objection.** In temptations God gave the devil too great a power to overcome us, for a person can scarcely resist them. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVI, 236, 743, 744; XXXVII, 1223, 1858; St. Anselm, CLVIII, 498, 499, 523, 524, 599, 600, 601.

### TRADITION

**Objection.** The tradition of Christians is invalid because it is not confirmed by constant custom. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 31, 33, 34, 40, 80, 81, 270, 745, 755.

**Objection.** No divine, ecclesiastical, or human tradition should be admitted, because such traditions are never secure. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, III, 1129, 1130, 1136, 1158, 1187; St. Augustine, XLIII, 265, 266, 288, 584; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 334, 340, 341, 342; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 233, 234, 235.

### TRANSUBSTANTIATION

**Objection.** Very many deny transubstantiation because, they say, the ancient creeds do not treat of it. — **Response.** Alanus, CCX, 358, 359, 360, 361.

**Objection.** The term “transubstantiation” must be rejected because it inadequately expresses eucharistic conversion. — **Response.** Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1246, 1247.

### THE TRINITY

**Objection.** The Trinity must be rejected because Scripture does not show its distinction with sufficient clarity. — **Response.** Tertullian, II, 158, 164, 165, 166; St. Ambrose, XV, 1557, 1566, 1567; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 206, 207, 646, 647.

**Objection.** The Trinity must be rejected because the Scriptures do not sufficiently prove it, especially Genesis, which treats of God. — **Response.** St. Ambrose, XVII, 511, 512, 515, 551, 552, 1004, 1005; St. Augustine, XLII, 941, 945, 947; Rupert, CLXVII, 206, 207, 246, 247, 400, 401, 616, 617, 757, 758, 854.

**Objection.** A threefold distinction of persons must not be admitted in the Trinity, because Scripture does not teach that there are three persons in the one God. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 941, 945, 947.

**Objection.** The Son in the Trinity should not be called equal to the Father, since the Father loves and the Son is loved; the Father bears witness and the Son receives it. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1740; XXXVIII, 775; XLII, 722, 754, 755.
