**Objection.** If the three persons were equal, the Son would not be called merely the power and wisdom of God the Father; but He is so called, etc. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XLII, 848, 923, 1066, 1080.

**Objection.** If the three persons of the Trinity were equal, the same works would be attributed to them; yet, moreover, the Son and Holy Spirit are said to be sent. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 357, 459, 463; XLII, 694, 761, 848, 869.

**Objection.** The Son of God is not consubstantial with the Father in the Trinity, [Col. 0432] because the Father is called greater than the Son. — **Response.** Cassiodorus, LXIX, 972, 1075.

**Objection.** The persons of the Trinity cannot be called equal because not all things are common to them: what belongs to the Father is not the same as what belongs to the Son, and what belongs to the Son is not the same as what belongs to the Holy Spirit. — **Response.** Boethius, LXIV, 1251, 1299, 1377, 1378.

**Objection.** The whole Trinity is not received in the Eucharist, because the faith teaches that Christ alone is in the sacrament of His love. — **Response.** St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 783, 784.

### UNITY

**Objection.** The Catholic Church has no unity, because it teaches one thing in one place and another elsewhere. — **Response.** St. Cyprian, III, 702, 711, 732, 768, 785, 790, 1046; IV, 345, 410, 411, 504.

### WIVES

**Objection.** They indeed try to prove that it is lawful for them, just as it was once lawful for the fathers to have several wives. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 347, 1064.

**Objection.** The saints of the old law are necessarily accused of lust because they had several wives. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXIV, 76; XXXVIII, 345, 347; XL, 395; XLII, 429; Guibert, XLVI, 517, 518.

### THE WORD

**Objection.** It must not be believed that the Word became flesh, because in the Incarnation He would have been changed and would have departed from God the Father. — **Response.** St. Augustine, XXXV, 1659, 1660; XXXVIII, 105, 671, 674, 680, 687, 995, 1001, 1002, 1097.

OBJ. The Word was changed in the Incarnation, since, by taking flesh from the Virgin Mary, it was changed into flesh. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIV, 1045; XLII, 541, 177, 178; XXXV, 1978, 1979; XL, 187.

OBJ. It is not clearly said that God bears all things by his Word, because these expressions have no real meaning. — RESPONSE: Hugh, CLXXV, 610.

OBJ. Irremissible sins must be admitted, since, according to Scripture, the word spoken against the Holy Spirit is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. — RESPONSE: St Fulgentius, LXV, 547, 548.

## VISION

OBJ. Those who hold that the Father is invisible but the Son and Holy Spirit visible do so because the Son and Holy Spirit have appeared to human beings many times, whereas the Father has not yet appeared. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 603, 605, 610, 619, 622, 633, 627.

OBJ. Those who rise to life will see God through the body, because God will grant this to them in reward for their merits. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 619, 623; XLI, 791.

OBJ. God must also be seen by the ungodly, because he has already been seen by the devil. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 602, 607; XXXVIII, 104, 105.

OBJ. The vision of God must not be admitted, because scriptural testimonies concerning the seeing of God contradict one another and cannot be reconciled. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 602, 603.

OBJ. God is to be seen through the body, because later we shall see him as he is, face to face. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 620, 625.

## LIFE

OBJ. It is falsely said that God made the days of this life shorter because of human sins, since more notorious sinners enjoy a longer life. — RESPONSE: St Ambrose, XIV, 1049, 1050.

## VICES

OBJ. Our vices do not concern God; otherwise he would punish them and would not grant prosperity to the wicked. — RESPONSE: St Jerome, XXV, 82, 83.

OBJ. Very many are persuaded that vices do not arise from the human will, because they cannot resist them. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 561, 571; XXXIV, 605; XL, 19; XLIV, 266.

OBJ. Perhaps it is falsely said that human life was shorter after the Flood because of human vices, since this is proved nowhere. — RESPONSE: Rupert, CLXVIII, 582, 583.

## CALLING

OBJ. Calling is not to be ascribed to God’s mercy, since those who worship God, and they alone, are most certainly called. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 863, 864; XLIV, 985, 986.

OBJ. If calling is to be ascribed to God’s mercy, then the participation of one’s own will is destroyed; therefore merit is removed. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXVII, 1308, 1309; XLIV, 240, 241.

OBJ. If calling is to be ascribed to God’s mercy, then [Col. 0433] we must despair of our calling, since we can never be more certain of God’s mercy. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1396.

## WILL

OBJ. Very many maintain that all their offences must be excused because, they say, nothing happens in us without God’s will. — RESPONSE: Tertullian, II, 915, 916.

OBJ. There is no human will, because it is wholly taken away through God’s grace. — RESPONSE: St Philastrius, XII, 1232, 1233.

OBJ. A person does not always have his will in his own power, since he is sometimes unable to change it, as the Apostle testifies when he says that he feels in his members a law, etc.; and St Augustine also acknowledges this. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXII, 753, 758; XLIV, 530, 531.

OBJ. God is the author of evil wills, since he himself prepares our wills. — RESPONSE: St Fulgentius, LXV, 157, 158, 171, 172.

OBJ. It is not God’s will that all should be saved, since many are damned. — RESPONSE: St Fulgentius, LXV, 657, 658; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 707.

## VOW

[Col. 0434]

OBJ. We are not bound to fulfil a vow to God, because it is always conditional. — RESPONSE: St Cyprian, IV, 752, 753; St Anselm, CLVIII, 394, 592, 688.

OBJ. Some maintain that a vow does not bind, because, according to them, it is considered to have been made only insofar as we are able to fulfil it. — RESPONSE: St Augustine, XXXIII, 486, 487, 1013; XXXIV, 744; XXXVII, 1058; XXXVIII, 799; XL, 468.

OBJ. A vow made in tribulation is never valid, because then it is not free. — RESPONSE: St Fulgentius, LXV, 306, 307.

OBJ. A vow is never valid, because it diminishes the grace of a good work. — RESPONSE: St Anselm, CLVIII, 401, 402, 403.

OBJ. Monastic vows are disapproved by many and rejected outright by them, because, they say, they take freedom away from a person and are opposed to the common good. — RESPONSE: St Anselm, CLVIII, 1162, 1163, 1171, 1172.

## THE COMMON PEOPLE

OBJ. It is false to say that the common people are foolish and credulous, because truth often, indeed almost always, resides among the people or the populace. — RESPONSE: St Cyprian, IV, 573, 574.

[Col. 0433]

## LXII. APOLOGETIC INDEX, OR SYNOPSIS OF APOLOGETIC WORKS AND TRACTS RECORDED IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY DOWN TO THE TWELFTH CENTURY

### NOTICE

In this Index we endeavour to bring together in a particular collection apologetic works and tracts, so that every reader may readily have at hand all that the Latin Fathers published for the defence and splendour of the Catholic religion, and may thus more easily assemble the most powerful arguments. We divide this Index into four sections: Section I, general, containing works concerning the defence of religion; Section II, apologetic-dogmatic, concerning some particular point or dogma of faith; Section III, apologetic-polemical, indicating demonstrations of truth directed against one error or another; Section IV, individual, setting forth the justification or apology of a particular person.

### I. General section, comprising works concerning the defence of religion

*Apologeticus against the nations, on behalf of Christians*, in which are treated: the defence and apology of Christians; their true doctrine; their outstanding morals, while pagans rush headlong into every vice. Christians are not guilty of injured divine or human majesty; they are neither the cause of disasters, nor conspirators, nor enemies of the state. The gods of the nations are false and absurd. How vain and shameful are the images, temples, and sacrifices of the gods: Tertullian, I, 258. — *Two Books to the Nations*, in which: hatred of the Christian religion proceeds from ignorance; those who know cease to hate; the charges by which Christians are persecuted are horrible and absurd. Their defence against the accusation of avarice, luxury, and wickedness. The pagans, however, are guilty of these offences; the origin, vanity, absurdity, and infamy of the pagan gods; why the Christian name is made into a crime: Tertullian, I, 559. — *Book to Scapula*, in which: Christians are innocent, whereas the pagans themselves truly offend in precisely that for which they falsely reproach Christians. They worship not fictitious and absurd gods, but the one God. They have never been found in seditions during that period; they sincerely honour the emperor; they patiently endure punishments. Nothing is more unjust than to order Christians, who devote themselves to every virtue, to be put to the sword and even burned. Whatever Scapula may do, the Christian sect will not fail; it grows precisely when it seems to be cut down. The religion that makes martyrs so steadfast amid every punishment is true and divine: Tertullian, I, 697. — *Book to Demetrianus*, in which: Christians are shown to have been condemned though neither defended nor heard. They are not the cause of public calamities. Those public disasters arise from the worship of false gods: St Cyprian, IV, 545. — *Book on the Vanity of Idols*, in which: the origin of idolatry; the absurdity of pagan gods: St Cyprian, IV, 563. — *Letter on the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, in which: idols are not gods; the crime of idolatry; God alone is to be worshipped: St Cyprian, IV, 651. — *Octavius, or the Apologetic Book*, in which: the absurdity of the worship of false gods, whose birthdays, unhappy ends, fates, shameful deeds, and deaths are known. Obscene, cruel, and ridiculous rites in their mysteries. How foolish and superstitious are omens and auguries. They ascribe false crimes to Christians. The accusation of sacrilege, debauchery, and incest must be kept far from Christians; they never sacrifice infants. Their banquets are sober and chaste. Their religion is true, and pagan superstitions must be rejected. The pagans are convicted of the foulest crimes: Minucius Felix, III, 231. — *Apocritica*, books by which the Christian religion is established and justified against a certain philosopher: Magnes the presbyter, V, 346. — *Books of Disputations against the Nations*, in which: the Christian religion must not be rejected as new; paganism, unlike the Christian religion, did not exist two thousand years ago; Christians worship nothing new; they are not the cause of calamities; the divinity of pagan gods is false. The pagans’ opinions concerning the gods are absurd; so are their vices; the shamefulness and falsity of each of their gods; their images, omens, and oracles are how vain and contemptible. The philosophers’ knowledge is slight; their disagreements and various opinions; a comparison of Christian and pagan opinions. From this it is evident that Christians are pious, but pagans guilty of frenzied impiety: Arnobius, V, 714. — *Book on False Religion*, in which: false gods; the origin of error; philosophers and false wisdom; philosophical precepts contribute little; true wisdom is found in religion: Lactantius, VI, 110. — *Book of the Divine Institutions*, in which: the divinity of pagan gods is false; the origin and shameful life of those gods; their utterly obscene festivals; all are quite recent; their images are ridiculous; their oracles and auguries arise from demonic deception. The philosophical schools differ from one another. Philosophy avoids the multitude, but heavenly teaching is easily found in the Christian religion. True wisdom is not in the worship of many gods but in true religion; nor is any justice possible among worshippers of false gods; it exists only in true religion: Lactantius, VI, 1019. — *Book on the Error of Profane Religions*, in which: the elements are not gods or the principles of things; from worshipping the elements pagans passed to other superstitions; the absurdity and shamefulness of each of those gods; the vanity of idols; signs and symbols in idolatrous worship are ridiculous and must be rejected. Emperors ought to proceed to the complete destruction of idolatrous rites; a command concerning their extirpation: Firmicus Maternus, XII, 981. — *Book on True Religion*, in which: true religion is found neither among pagans nor in any sect, except in the Catholic Church. God’s dispensation for human salvation; by a twofold way God provides for human salvation, by authority for believers and by reason for those who understand: St Augustine, XXXV, 918. — *Apology against the Pagans*, in which: not all things happen and are ordered by fate; idols are not gods, nor are the elements or the stars: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 781.

### III. Apologetic-polemical section, indicating a demonstration of truth against one error or another

**NOTE.** In this section, in order that what is sought may be found more easily, we present heresies and heretics in alphabetical order; thus against:

[Col. 0443]

LXIV. POLEMICAL INDEX, OR SYNOPSIS OF THE WORKS AND SHORTER WRITINGS WHICH TREAT OF POLEMICS IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY.

[Note: [Col. 0443] NOTE. We mention that index here only, and, lest repeated material be unwelcome, refer the reader to the INDEX ON HERESIES.]

SEVENTH SERIES.

[Col. 0443]

[PREFACE.]

Christ is the foundation of the whole Christian religion; the Holy Spirit sustains and illumines it; the Blessed Virgin Mary protects it and favors it. Therefore, before treating of this religion, we set forth in this seventh series indexes concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the Redemption of humankind: that is, we show Christ as promised and awaited, born, living, and suffering for the salvation of the world. Next we present the Holy Spirit with all His gifts; the Blessed Virgin Mary with her privileges, from the Immaculate Conception to the glorious Assumption. Thus the reader will find in this Series all the foundations of Religion.

[Col. 0445]

LXV. INDEX CONCERNING CHRIST’S INCARNATION, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER, AND SETTING BEFORE THE EYES WHATEVER THE FATHERS HAVE WRITTEN CONCERNING THIS MYSTERY.

NOTICE.

In this Index we treat in turn: I, the necessity and cause of the Incarnation; II, the fittingness of the Incarnation; III, the foreknowledge and prediction of the Incarnation; IV, whose work Christ’s Incarnation is; V, works treating specifically of the Incarnation.

I.—On the necessity and cause of the Incarnation.

Causes of the Incarnation. Tertullian, II, 773.—On the cause of Christ’s Incarnation. Lactantius, VI, 475.—It was necessary for us that God should be begotten as man. St Hilary, X, 723.—Christ’s Incarnation is not weakness but a sacrament; not necessity but mercy, ibid., 404, 405.—What was the cause of the Incarnation, save that the flesh which had sinned might be redeemed through itself? St Ambrose, XVI, 832.—Christ came into this world to blunt death’s sting, close up its devouring mouth, grant the living the eternity of grace, and bestow resurrection upon the dead, ibid., 890.—Christ became man in order to assume man into God, id., XVII, 309.—Because wickedness had increased, innocence had been abolished; the Lord came, to restore—indeed, to increase—the grace of nature, id., XVI, 1144.—His Incarnation was salvation for human beings on earth and for angels in heaven, id., XVII, 668.—What necessity had God to descend to the earth? Zacchaeus Christianus, XX, 1077.—On the cause of the Incarnation, ibid.—Christ redeemed us through love, not necessity. Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 697.—He endured the cross not by necessity but by will. St Jerome, XXIV, 507, 511.—For our salvation Christ assumed the flesh of human frailty, id., XXII, 794.—He became man for our sake, not for the sake of brute animals, ibid., 795.—The necessity of Christ’s Incarnation. St Augustine, XXXVIII, 573, 710, 998, 1006, 1099.—The chief cause of Christ’s coming was the commendation of love, id., XL, 314.—The cause of the Incarnation: sin, id., XXXVIII, 944, 951. Christ had no reason for coming except to save sinners: remove diseases, remove wounds, and there is no reason for medicine, ibid., 945.—Unless the Son of Man had come, man would have perished, ibid., 895.—Because Adam fell, Christ therefore descended, id., XXXVII, 1598.—Christ became a participant in our mortality, in order that we might become participants in His divinity, ibid., 1546.—Christ became man in order to make us gods, id., XXXVIII, 1012.—He assumed mortality in order to give immortality, ibid., 688.—Christ came for this purpose: that you might believe God, id., XXXII, 1898.—And that, after the life of faith, He might confer eternal life, id., XXXV, 1727.—The necessity and fruit of Christ’s Incarnation. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 346.—Christ’s Incarnation and Passion were for humankind, useful not to God but to humanity, ibid., 613.—What brought the Lord Christ into association with an earthly body? St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 594 and following.—Christ’s Incarnation necessary for human salvation. St Leo the Great, LIV, 191, 196, 201, 204, 211, 213, 216, 222, 257, 293, 313, 314, 412, 759, 792, 870, 1169, 1215.—If Adam had not sinned, the Word would not have been incarnate, id., LIV, 412.—The necessity of the Incarnation: that human errors and sins might be removed, ibid., 199.—Human beings attain salvation through the Incarnation of the Word alone, ibid., 313.—Why God provides for human salvation by this way, namely the Incarnation, ibid., 193, 195, 203, 222. He who is God from eternity is born in time as man from the immaculate Virgin, in order to free humanity from slavery to the devil. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 237.—The final causes of the Incarnation. Boethius, LXIV, 1336.—How Christ’s Incarnation was fitting for restoring human salvation. St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 468.—Man could not restore man, since he himself needed another’s help, ibid., 345.—Nor could an angel restore man, whose nature was bound by the mutability liable to fall, ibid.—Human flesh ought not to have been assumed by Christ if it were not to be saved, ibid., 232.—How many benefits came through Christ’s advent:

[Col. 0446]

through Him the power of the most holy Trinity was made known to human beings, death fell, and life rose again. Cassiodorus, LXX, 664.—Christ came to us so that we might return to Him, ibid., 494, 495.—The causes and fruits of the mystery of the Incarnation, id., LXXIII, 468, 571, 572.—Had the first man not sinned, the second man would by no means have come to the humiliations of the Passion. St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 612; LXXIX, 221.—The Lord appeared in the flesh in order to rouse human life by admonition, kindle it by supplying examples, redeem it by dying, and restore it by rising again, id., LXXVI, 196.—The final causes of the Incarnation. St Odilo of Cluny, CXLII, 392.—Why Christ assumed human nature. Lanfranc, CL, 381 and following.—Why He wished to become man though He was God. St Bruno of Cologne, CLIII, 500; St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 360 and following.—That humanity’s redemption could not be accomplished through any person other than a divine person, ibid., 365.—That God was conceived of a righteous Virgin, not by necessity, [lacuna], but because this was fitting, ibid., 451.—That He became man in order to perfect the heavenly city. Berengar of Tours, CLX, 1106.—He who, according to His divinity, was neither created nor made, according to His humanity created and made Himself. St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 700.—The necessity of the Incarnation of the Word for the offering of satisfaction. Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1122.—Why our redemption was accomplished through Christ’s death, although He could have accomplished it by a word alone; whether it could have been accomplished in a more fitting way. Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 457.—What was the necessity of the Incarnation of the Son of God. Hermann, CLXXX, 11.—Through the Incarnation satisfaction worthy of God is made, ibid., 20.—That Christ came into the world not only for our instruction, but also for our liberation. St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1071.—Why the Son assumed humanity. Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1071.—For four reasons the Word became flesh: to humble the proud, reconcile enemies, redeem slaves, and nourish friends. Innocent III, CCXVII, 453.

II.—On the fittingness of the Incarnation.

Why Christ was sent by God so late. Arnobius, V, 931, 932.—Why Christ came after so long a time. St Augustine, XLIV, 973, 974.—Why Christ did not come earlier, id., XXXV, 1638.—Why He did not come at the beginning of human sin, id., XL, 28.—Yet He came in the world’s youth and old age, id., XXXII, 626; XXXVIII, 504.—In the sixth age of humankind, id., XL, 55.—Why the Incarnation and Redemption were delayed. St Leo the Great, LIV, 202.—Why He came after the Law had been given, id., XXXVIII, 28.—It was more fitting for the Son to become incarnate than for the Father or the Holy Spirit. St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 272.—The time of Christ’s advent unknown to angels. St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1043.—Why Christ came when the world was growing old, id., CLXXXV, 41.

III.—On the foreknowledge and prediction of the Incarnation.

All the old and new Scriptures designate beforehand Christ, the Son of God. Tertullian, II, 186.—The prophets foretold Christ’s Passion, id., I, 401.—Everything which we see fulfilled in Christ was foretold. Lactantius, VI, 470.—The prophets foretold these things long beforehand, ibid.—Christ was not unknown even to philosophers, ibid., 469, 966.—That Christ’s advent was foretold by the prophets. Constantine the Great, VIII, 413.—The prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl concerning the coming of Jesus Christ,

[Col. 0447]

Lactantius, VIII, 452.—The very well-known verses of Virgil Maro, in which, obscurely celebrating the mystery of the Incarnation, he indicates a virgin birth, ibid., 456 and following.—Every spirit of prophecy, the hope of the patriarchs, the voices of angels, and the speech of divine utterance throughout the whole course of the age bore witness that He was the Redeemer. St Hilary, IX, 633.—Christ’s advent is contained in all the commands of the Law, ibid., 638.—The Psalmist hoped for Christ throughout his whole life, ibid., 723.—From nature itself God sent forth beforehand very many examples, by which He might demonstrate the beauty of the Incarnation He undertook and establish its truth. St Ambrose, XIV, 233.—The Incarnation was foreknown by Abraham. St Augustine, XLIV, 401.—Christ’s Incarnation is not improperly said to have been revealed to certain persons among the Gentiles, id., XLI, 609.—With what longing the ancient patriarchs desired to see the revelation of this mystery. Cassian, L, 132, 134.—The patriarchs hoped with certainty that Christ’s Incarnation would occur; the prophets announced it. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 627.—From the beginning of the world the mystery of the Incarnation was promised. St Leo the Great, LIV, 193, 204.—It had been foretold through so many ages by many signs, many voices, and many mysteries, ibid., 202, 359.—It was always believed by the ancient Fathers, ibid., 1169, 1170.—Christ’s conception from a Virgin foretold by Isaiah. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 255.—How great were the desires for the Incarnation of the Word among the righteous under the old Law. St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 881.—Christ’s eternal generation, divinity, Incarnation, birth, life, deeds, death, and all His mysteries foretold beforehand to the prophets. St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 451 and following, 498.—The Incarnation is announced by most clear testimonies. St Peter Damian, CXLV, 62.—Testimonies of the prophets concerning the future mission and Incarnation of Christ. Peter of Blois, CCVII, 835, 837, 842.—The passage of Jeremiah concerning the Virgin’s childbirth is examined, id., CCXIII, 763, 764. (See the table concerning Christ: “Christ prefigured and foretold.”)

IV.—On the reality of the mystery of the Incarnation.

In Christ are two substances, divine and human. Tertullian, II, 194.—Christ was seen, heard, and encountered, joining in Himself man and God: God in mighty acts, man in lowliness, id., 317.—Christ is man and God. St Cyprian, IV, 228.—In Christ God is joined with man, ibid.—On faith in the Lord’s Incarnation. St Eutychian, pope, V, 167.—On those who deny the Incarnation of the Word of God. Pope Caius, V, 185.—Arguments of unbelievers against Jesus’ Incarnation. Lactantius, V, 517.—That God the Word assumed a complete human being for our salvation. Athanasius, VIII, 1397.—The Son of God assumed a human being from the Virgin’s womb. St Hilary, IX, 793.—The Son of God remained such even when He became Son of Man, ibid., 267.—We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word and that the Son of Man consisted of soul and body, id., X, 388. Christ is at once God and man, and sometimes speaks what belongs to God and sometimes what belongs to man, id., IX, 317.—Though Christ was in the fullness of divinity, He emptied Himself and received the fullness of human nature and perfection. St Ambrose, XVI, 1147.—Christ became man; God was born, ibid., 155.—In Christ the divine and human natures entered into a sacred interchange, and what that interchange is, id., XVII, 526, 527.—According to His divinity Christ is in all respects equal to the Father; according to His humanity, He exists as a perfect man, ibid., 793, 794.—Christ was true God and true man. St Jerome, XXII, 776.—How wondrous is Christ’s Incarnation. St Augustine, XXXVI, 1011.—Christ so became man that He did not cease to be God, id., XXXV, 1621; XXXVIII, 999, 1203, 1205; XLV, 1137.—Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh, id., XXXV, 1836; XXXVI, 1084; XLII, 690.—As one man is soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man, id., XXXVIII, 940, 997.—Christ is at once God and man in unity of person, id., XL, 249.—In Christ are two substances, God and man, id., XXXVIII, 728, 999, 1205.—In Christ is a twofold form, or nature. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 316, 627.—At what time Christ’s Incarnation was completed, ibid., 701.—Christ, remaining God, becomes man, ibid., 627.—The mystery of the Incarnation, ibid., 436, 517.—The Transfiguration proved Christ’s true divinity and humanity. St Leo the Great, LIV, 309.—There are two generations in Christ: one eternal, by which God was born; the other temporal, by which man was born. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 239.—The Word became flesh, while the Word remained in His own substance and the man in his own nature. Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1006.—The Incarnation of the Word is folly to this world. St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 298.—Christ is true man and God. Boethius, LXIV, 1351.—Whence the truth of the Incarnation is demonstrated. St Fulgentius,

[Col. 0448]

LXV, 515, 516.—True faith is to believe that Christ is true God and true man, ibid., 463.—The mystery of the Incarnation explained. Cassiodorus, LXX, 78.—On Christ’s Incarnation. Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 776; Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 98, 139, 151, 164, 346, 349, 365.—Christ’s Incarnation is a mystery and sacrament of salvation. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1360.—The truth of the Incarnation. Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 835.—A declaration concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God, ibid., 199.—On faith in the Lord’s Incarnation. Othlo, CXLVI, 265.—Confession of the mystery of the Incarnation in the Ephesian Creed. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 61.—Our Lord is both God and man. St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 700.—On faith in the Incarnation. Hildebert of Tours, CLXXI, 1096.—How the Incarnation was accomplished. Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 432.—Faith in the Incarnation, or what must be believed concerning the Incarnation, CLXXVI, 70; Abaelard, CLXXVIII, 618.—On the Incarnation of the Word and related matters. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 757.—On the Incarnate Word. Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1071; Richard of Saint-Victor, CXCVI, 995; John of Cornwall, CXCIX, 1041; Ermengaud, CCIV, 1243.

V.—Whose work Christ’s Incarnation is.

Christ received from the Father the weaving together of flesh and soul. Tertullian, II, 843.—He is from Mary’s flesh, since He is of David’s seed, ibid., 350.—Mary did not give Christ’s body its origin. St Hilary, X, 355.—Christ’s flesh was not from the common stock of human origin, id., IX, 61.—Born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, He received an immaculate body. St Ambrose, XVI, 470.—The whole Trinity made Christ as man. St Augustine, XL, 251.—Christ’s Incarnation is the work of the whole Trinity, id., XXXVIII, 1096.—It is explained how the Holy Spirit joined human flesh to the Father’s Only-begotten Son. St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 636, 638.—He was born not from intercourse with a man but from the Holy Spirit. Gennadius, LVIII, 1007.—The Virgin conceived and bore God the Word according to the flesh. St Fulgentius, LXV, 457.—The Father and the Holy Spirit effected the Incarnation of the Word. St Peter Damian, CXLV, 35.—Christ’s Incarnation is the work of the whole Trinity. Geoffrey, CLVII, 244, 255.—Our Lord, according to His humanity, created and made Himself. St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 700.—How the Incarnation was accomplished. Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 432.—Why Scripture more frequently ascribes to the Holy Spirit the Incarnation, which is the work of the Trinity, and says that Christ was also conceived and born from Him. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 763.—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit effected the Incarnation of the Son. Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 438.

LXVI. INDEX CONCERNING CHRIST—NAMELY, HIS DIVINITY, HUMANITY, LIFE, MIRACLES, AND SO FORTH—SETTING OUT IN LOGICAL ORDER EVERYTHING THE FATHERS HAVE WRITTEN CONCERNING HIM.

NOTICE.

This Index treats: I. the name of Jesus Christ; II. prophecies and figures concerning Christ; III. Christ’s divinity; IV. Christ’s humanity; V. Christ’s body; VI. Christ’s soul; VII. sin in Christ; VIII. concupiscence in Christ; IX. hunger, thirst, fear, sorrow, and so forth in Christ; X. the two natures in Christ; XI. the wills in Christ; XII. knowledge in Christ; XIII. the communication of idioms, that is, the names and properties of each nature in Christ; XIV. Christ’s conception; XV. Christ’s birth, lineage, and infancy; XVI. Christ’s circumcision; XVII. Christ’s baptism, temptation, and fast; XVIII. Christ’s teaching, miracles, and powers; XIX. Christ’s Passion; XX. Christ’s death; XXI. Christ’s burial; XXII. Christ’s descent into hell; XXIII. Christ’s resurrection; XXIV. Christ’s ascension and His session at the Father’s right hand; XXV. Christ’s glory, power, various functions, and titles; XXVI. Christ’s satisfaction and merit; XXVII. various errors concerning Christ’s person; XXVIII. our duties toward Christ our Lord.

I.—On the name of Jesus Christ.

Jesus is the proper name of the Son of God, whereas Christ is an accidental designation. Tertullian, II, 193.—Why Jesus wished to be called Christ, ibid., 342.—Whether *Christ* is a name or an appellation, ibid., I, 192.—Christ is so called from *chrism* (*chrisma*), that is, an anointing, which supplied the Lord with His name, id., I, 1207.—Christ Jesus, in the sacrament of His very name, is the true and supreme priest of the Father, id., II, 330.—Since Christ’s name comes not from nature but from appointment, it becomes proper to Him through whom it is found to have been appointed, ibid., 341.—Why He is called Nazarene, ibid., 372.—The name of Christ must not be misused. St Cyprian, III, 1118, 1131. Jesus, the name of the Son of God among human beings. Lactantius, VI, 464.—The name Christ is not proper but a designation of kingship, ibid.—Altered by the Gentiles into “Christ,” ibid.—The meaning of this name, ibid.—Jesus is the name of our Lord from His body. St Hilary, IX, 936.—In the one name of Christ are expressed both divinity and Incarnation, as well as faith in the Passion. St Ambrose, XV, 1693.—Before His advent, Christ’s name was enclosed in the minds of the Jewish people as though in a vessel. St Ambrose of Milan, XVI, 727.—How it was afterward extended throughout all creation, ibid.—What the pouring forth of this name signifies, ibid.—If you say “Christ,” you have designated both God the Father, from whom the Son is united; the Son Himself, who is united; and the Holy Spirit, by whom He is anointed, XVI, 715.—In Christ’s name Paul bore witness to the sacrament of the Incarnation, ibid., 593.—Jesus is a Hebrew name, called *Savior* among us. Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 345.—Christ is called from *chrism*, that is, from anointing, ibid. Jesus in Hebrew, **Σωτήρ** (*Sōtēr*, “Savior”) in Greek, *Salvator* (“Savior”) in Latin. St Augustine, XLII, 1025; XXXVIII, 944, 1334, 1370.—Christ: *Messiah* in Hebrew, *Christos* in Greek, *anointed* in Latin, id., XXXVIII, 1370.—Christ named from *chrism*, XXXV, 1648; XLI, 549.—From anointing. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 482; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 358.—How the Greeks form the name of Christ. St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 544.—What Christ signifies. Alcuin, C, 728; CI, 1272.—Whence He is so called, id., CI, 1253.—Christ is the name of an office. Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 257.—Christ is called the Anointed One, not from visible oil but from the fullness of spiritual grace. Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1304.

II.—On prophecies and figures concerning Christ.

Christ is the seal of all the prophets. Tertullian, II, 615, 632.---The prophets foretold Christ’s Passion, id., 401.---Fulfilment of what had been announced concerning the marks of the Messiah—his origin, lineage, birth, and so forth. St. Cyprian, IV, 695 ff.---Everything which we see fulfilled in Christ was foretold. Lactantius, VI, 470.---The words of the prophets concerning his birth [Col. 0450], VI, 479, 483.---Concerning his priesthood, ibid., 488.---Concerning the Passion, ibid., 495, 506.---Christ’s miracles and works announced by the prophets and the Sibyl, ibid., 491 ff.---Oracles of the Erythraean Sibyl concerning the coming of Jesus Christ. Constantine the Great, VIII, 452.---The well-known verses of Virgil Maro concerning a virgin birth, ibid., 456 ff.---Christ, the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets. St. Hilary, IX, 481.---Some wish all the words of the Psalms to be referred to Christ, ibid., 408.---The coming of Christ is the work of the prophets, ibid., 236.---Prophecy of Christ’s death, ibid., 453.---Upon his coming hung the hopes of all the prophets. St. Jerome, XXIV, 26.---Christ himself teaches that Moses and the prophets prophesied everything concerning him, ibid., 115, 116.---Christ has not ceased to be proclaimed from the beginning of the human race. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 376; XLIV, 973.---The five divisions of time through which he has not ceased to be foretold, id., 314.---Christ foretold by many prophets, id., XXXIX, 1674.---The truth of the prophecies concerning Christ demonstrated from Jewish manuscripts, id., XXXIV, 1052.---Testimonies of the prophets concerning Christ, id., XXXV, 1658, 1660, 1661.---And their predictions concerning him, id., XLI, 584.---Job prophesied Christ, id., XLIV, 283.---Christ foretold in the second chapter of Genesis, id., XLII, 880.---In Isaiah’s prophecy, ibid., 282 ff., 643.---Miracles would not have announced Christ sufficiently without prophetic testimonies, ibid., 279.---The prophets, full of Christ, announced Christ, id., XXXVII, 1845.---They foretold him as God and man, id., XXXIII, 521.---The oracles proclaim Christ not as God but as man only, id., XLI, 652.---Many heralds preceded Christ as the great Judge, id., XXXVI, 1258.---The mystery of the Incarnation had been foretold through so many ages by many signs and many voices. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 202, 359.---Christ’s conception from a Virgin foretold by Isaiah. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 255.---Not only the writings of divine utterance but also the oracles of the Gentiles long beforehand foretold his birth and peace. Freculphus of Lisieux, CVI, 1117.---Prophecies concerning Christ’s birth fulfilled. St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 122, 128.---All Christ’s mysteries foretold by the prophets. St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 61, 62.---All the circumstances of Christ’s life and Passion foretold and now fulfilled, id., CXLIX, 343, 344.---Christ’s conception announced by the prophets long before. Peter Alphonsus, CLVII, 613 ff.---Christ’s having already come demonstrated from Daniel and others, ibid., 624, 625.---Prophecy fulfilled in Christ concerning the ruler to be born among the Jews, ibid., 627.---On the fulfilment of prophecies in Christ. Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 509 ff.---Daniel’s prophecy describes not only the year of Christ’s coming, but also that of his Passion and death, id., CXLIX, 564 ff.---Testimonies of the prophets concerning Christ’s future mission, Incarnation, birth, and so forth. Peter of Blois, CCVII, 835, 837, 842, 839, 844 ff.---Jeremiah’s passage concerning the Virgin’s childbirth examined [Col. 0451]. Peter of Blois, CCXIII, 763, 764.---Micah’s prophecy concerning the place of Christ’s birth, ibid., 764.---Amos’s prophecy concerning Christ’s coming, ibid., 765.---And David’s, ibid., 766.---The prophet Nahum, after describing Jerusalem’s overthrow, plainly declares that Christ’s Gospel is to be preached throughout the whole world, ibid., 767.---Habakkuk shows that Christ will come at the end of the age, ibid.---Zephaniah proclaims joy at Christ’s coming with an ineffable exultation of mind, ibid., 773.---The prophecy of Zechariah, who brought in the poor king upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass, ibid., 776.---Passages of Daniel announcing the time when Christ will come explained, ibid., 781 ff.

Abel.---How he prefigured Christ. St. Ambrose, XVII, 813.---Christ slain by his brother in Abel. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.---Abel, innocent and pleasing to God, slain by his brother Cain, bore the first figure of Christ. St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 172.---Abel, signifying Christ’s Passion, offered a lamb. Garnerius, CXCIII, 45.

Abraham.---Christ sojourned in Abraham. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.

Melchizedek.---Ibid.

Isaac.---Christ prefigured in Isaac. Tertullian, II, 346.---Isaac offered by his father is a figure of Christ. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1061; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1464; XXXVI, 245; XXXVIII, 133; XLI, 511; XLII, 852; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.

Jacob.---A figure of Christ. St. Ambrose, XIV, 624; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 610; CXI, 335.

Joseph.---A figure of Christ. Tertullian, II, 346, 626; St. Ambrose, XIV, 856; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1765; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 526, 527.

Moses.---Christ prefigured in the person of Moses. Tertullian, II, 316; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 758; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 359.

Joshua.---Christ prefigured in the person of Joshua. Tertullian, II, 342; St. Augustine, XLII, 328; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 137.

Job.---Job prefigured Christ not only by speaking but also by suffering. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 524, 533.

David.---A figure of Christ. St. Ambrose, XIV, 864; XV, 1461; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1819; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 250, 251.

Samson.---Christ prefigured in Samson. St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1640; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 263.---Samson is a figure of Christ, who in dying slew more enemies than while living. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 491.---Samson’s departure from Gaza by night, a figure of Christ rising and ascending into heaven, ibid., 1173.

Noah and the ark. St. Augustine, XXXV, 2022.

Elijah.---Christ prefigured in Elijah. St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1823; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 206, 207.

Elisha.---A figure of Christ. St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1827; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 894; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 225.

Enoch.---His translation, a type of Christ ascending. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1217.

Rod of Moses.---Christ designated in Moses’ rod. St. Ambrose, XV, 1231, 1232.

Pillar of cloud.---The pillar which went before the children of Israel signifies in mystery the Lord Jesus coming in a cloud. St. Ambrose, XV, 1251; St. Augustine, XLII, 269, 270.

Bronze serpent.---Christ prefigured by the serpent raised up by Moses. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1578; XLV, 1138; St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 492.

Tree of life.---The tree of life, a figure of Christ. St. Augustine, XLI, 701.

Rock in the wilderness.---A figure of Christ. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 270, 271.

Goat.---The sacrifice of the goat, a figure of Christ. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 499.

Sacrifices.---Those of the Old Law signified Christ’s Passion. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 451.

Various figures of Christ from the Old Testament enumerated. St. Augustine, XLII, 268, 269, 270, 271.---Christ prefigured by the four living creatures. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 625.---Figures of Christ. Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1594.---Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 328, 362, 363, 409, 447, 454, 455.---Godfrey, CLXXIV, 297, 616; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIV, 198, 275; CLXXXV, 177; Garnerius, CXCIII, 67, 68, 72, 83, 92, 101, 193, 387, 402.

It is demonstrated by induction that Christ was awaited in Adam and the other patriarchs. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1060.---The Jews thought that the Messiah would come through a woman, ibid., 1581.---Upon Christ’s coming hung all the hopes of the prophets. [Col. 0452] St. Jerome, XXIV, 26.---When Christ came, his coming was expected by the Jews, id., XXV, 1438, 1439.---Nor were there lacking those who believed in him. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 376.---Christ was sought with burning desires by the righteous of the Old Testament. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1039.---Job desires a mediator who may free us by his death, ibid., 881, 836.---The faith of the righteous in both Testaments is one faith in the mediator, id., LXXVI, 978, 985.---Judaea and the Gentile world desired Christ’s coming, id., LXXV, 770.---Many among the Gentiles awaited the Redeemer’s coming, ibid.---The saint of the Old Testament desired the bodily presence of his Creator, ibid., 978.

III.---On Christ’s divinity.

He possesses true divinity as a property proper to himself. Tertullian, I, 399.---By performing miracles he demonstrated himself to be the Logos, the Word or Reason, of God and true God, ibid., 1400.---Tiberius’s judgment concerning Christ, ibid., 290.---All the old and new Scriptures alike declare beforehand that Christ is the Son of God, id., II, 186.---That Christ is God. St. Cyprian, IV, 700.---On the consubstantiality of the Word. Pope Dionysius, V, 109.---Fragment concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity. Pope St. Eutychian, V, 155.---Holy Scripture teaches that he is the Son of God, God’s utterance, or also his Reason. Lactantius, VI, 467.---Christ proceeds from the Father and is joined and united with him. Constantine the Great, VIII, 405.---Plato had some, though imperfect, conception of the generation of the Son of God, ibid., 421.---By eternal birth Christ is the firstborn of creation; by temporal birth, the firstborn from the dead. St. Hilary, IX, 278.---Christ, the Son of God, ibid., 274, 275; X, 173, 174; XI, 41, 42.---The Son of God is proper, not adoptive, id., X, 82.---He was believed by the apostles to be Son by nature, not by adoption, ibid., 132, 183.---Arguments against Christ’s divinity, ibid., 42.---The Son is proved true God from his power of creating, ibid., 132.---If Christ is the true Son of God, he is also true God, ibid., 173 ff.---Paul everywhere proclaims Christ the true Son of God, ibid., 193.---Christ is true God even after assuming manhood, and how much more so before doing so, ibid., 270.---Many arguments for Christ’s divinity, ibid., 306.---His resurrection, an argument for Christ’s divinity, ibid., 209.---The Jews ought to have recognized his divinity from the magnificence of his works, ibid., 342.---Christ possesses in himself all that is true and complete in humanity, and all that is true and complete in Godhead, ibid., 357.---Christ’s divinity, id., IX, 467, 961; Faustinus the presbyter, XIII, 40.---Christ himself is he whom the Father begot before Lucifer as eternal; whom he begot from the womb as Son; whom he uttered from the heart as Word. St. Ambrose, XVI, 221.---We are sons by adoption; Christ is Son by the truth of his nature, ibid., 557.---Christ begotten of the Father before the ages, id., XIV, 689.---Christ fully expressed whatever divinity he received from the Father, id., XVI, 202.---It is established by many arguments that the Son of God is not a creature, ibid., 676 ff.---Christ is one with the Father by natural substance, not “one” according to Sabellian unbelief, ibid., 771, 772.---Christ the Son has all that belongs to the Father: eternity, majesty, and divinity, ibid., 567.---The Father remains in Christ as the true in the true, God in God, light in light, ibid., 795, 796.---Definition of faith of the Council of Nicaea against Arius’s errors, which destroy Christ’s divinity, ibid., 555, 556, 608.---Christ is the Father’s Son not by adoption of grace or by the religious status of a creature, but by the proper character of his kind and the truth of his nature. St. Chromatius, XX, 331.---The Father begot his Word, that is, Christ, from the womb of his heart. Evagrius, XX, 1169.---Christ is God by nature, not by advancement, as some think. St. Jerome, XXIV, 806.---Christ shows himself to be the giver of laws and true God, id., XXII, 775.---Signs of Christ’s divinity, id., XXVI, 488.---After Christ’s resurrection, Pilate sends Tiberius a report of his miracles; Tiberius asks the Senate that Christ be regarded as God. Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1066.---Christ’s divinity contrasted with Romulus’s divinity. St. Augustine, XLI, 757, 759.---Both the miracles and the prophecies fulfilled in him persuade us that Christ is God, ibid.---Christ proved to be God, id., XXXV, 1812; XLII, 1123, 1127; XXXIX, 2198, 1983, 1988, 2043, 1927; XXXV, 1749.---Christ equal to the Father, id., XXXIII, 751; XXXVIII, 990; XL, 32, 74, 191.---How the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, id., XXXIII, 846; XXXIV, 459.---What is prior in Christ is his divinity; what is subsequent, his humanity, XXXVII, 1609.---The steadfast confession of the martyrs persuades us that Christ is God, id., XLI, 676, 758, note.---The eternal generation of the Son of God is to be understood in the words, “Today I have begotten you,” id., XXXVI, 71.---Christ is God. Cassian, L, [reference incomplete].---Demons were compelled by many reasons to suppose that Christ [Col. 0453] is God, ibid., 224.---Christ, born of Mary, is proved to be God. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 590, 591.---Christ’s divinity received nothing by which it could grow. Cassiodorus, LXX, 928.---Christ is God not merely by appellation, but essentially. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 854, 959.---Outstanding testimonies of John the Baptist concerning Christ’s divinity, ibid., 1101.---Christ is true God and true Son of God, LXXVII, 1207.---Christ asserted to be God, id., LXXIX, 64.---Christ demonstrated himself to be God by incomparable miracles, ibid., 65, 66, 99.---On God the Father’s Son. Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 736.---Christ is the proper, not adoptive, Son of God: true God, not God merely by appellation. Alcuin, C, 333, 843; CI, 137, 173.---In assuming human nature, he did not cease to be God. St. Agobard, CIV, 160.---Whether Christ may rightly be called God. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1483.---Christ, Son of God, is Son by nature, not adoption. Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 742.---Christ’s divinity and humanity demonstrated. Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 1225.---We confess Christ as God and man. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 416.---Jesus Christ is true God and true man, ibid., 369.---Although no mortal can comprehend how great Christ’s divinity is, nevertheless the wonders, the holiness of his precepts, and his complete righteousness make it manifest. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 667.---Christ’s divinity is so joined to his humanity that it can never depart from him, id., CLXIV, 767.---Christ proved to be God. Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 310, 1310.---The divine generation of the Word is wholly ineffable because it is wholly incomprehensible. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1080.---How it is to be understood that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, ibid., 1151.---Christ’s miracles, the oracles of the prophets, and the Father’s voice prove his divinity. St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 933.---Christ was true God. Alanus of Lille, CCX, 335.

IV.---On Christ’s humanity.

Christ is man because of flesh, not because of soul. Tertullian, II, 874.---It is demonstrated that Christ is a true man, ibid., 14, 378.---Christ was seen, heard, and encountered, mingling in himself man and God: God in his powers, man in his weaknesses, ibid., 317.---Christ put on manhood. St. Cyprian, IV, 579.---Before becoming man, God, in taking up manhood, became man and God. St. Hilary, X, 360.---He was born a perfect man according to the condition of human conformity, ibid., 355.---He was a perfect man consisting of soul and body, ibid., 353.---Christ possesses in himself all that is true and complete in humanity, and all that is true and complete in Godhead, ibid., 357.---Whoever does not know Christ as both true God and true man does not know his own life, ibid., 282.---God and man are in Christ because they are united in power, id., IX, 472.---Christ, at once God and man, sometimes speaks what belongs to God, sometimes what belongs to man, ibid., 348.---Scripture itself speaks of Jesus as God and man, perfect in both. St. Ambrose, XV, 1625.---He was man according to the flesh, but beyond man according to his activity, id., XIV, 1126.---Though Christ was in the fullness of divinity, he emptied himself and received the fullness of human nature and perfection, id., XVI, 1147.---Christ’s humanity was not assumed by means of divinity, id., XVII, 824.---According to divinity he is in every respect equal to the Father; according to humanity he exists as perfect man, ibid., 794.---Christ became man in order to take man into God, ibid., 309.---He was truly God and man. St. Jerome, XXII, 776.---He became man for us, not for brute animals, ibid., 796.---Why Christ assumed human nature. St. Augustine, XXXIV, 170.---Christ became man in order to make us gods, id., XXXVIII, 1012.---Christ, God and man, id., XXXVI, 528; XXXVIII, 229, 196, 547, 573, 685, 1149, 1279.---As man, Christ is of the same nature as we are, id., XXXVIII, 941.---That Christ is truly man. Cassian, L, 55.---The Transfiguration demonstrated in Christ true divinity and humanity. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 309.---Christ, God and man, id., LV, 147.---Christ passes by according to humanity; he stands according to divinity. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1084.---The Word united man to himself in such a way that, as one man consists of body and rational soul, so one Jesus Christ consists of man and God. Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 247.---God and man meet together as one, so that, with the integrity of each nature preserved, the same one is man who is God. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 416.---Not one person and another, but the selfsame one, man and God, ibid., 425.---According to his humanity, he created and made himself. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 700.---The things proper to man are distinguished in Christ, ibid., 739.---According to humanity Christ is in heaven; according to divinity, everywhere. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 413.---Christ’s humanity is understood in silver, his divinity [Col. 0454] in gold. St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 49.---Christ’s head is divinity, his feet humanity, ibid., 708.---His humanity is signified by the cloud which shone by day, and his divinity by the fire which shone by night. Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 730.

V.---On Christ’s body.

Christ received from the Father the fabric of flesh and soul. Tertullian, II, 843.---Christ’s flesh is holy, ibid., 933, not sinful, ibid., 781.---Some say that Christ assumed Adam’s flesh and soul from the Virgin. St. Hilary, X, 357.---Christ’s flesh derived its origin from no other source than the Word, ibid., 356.---By himself he assumed for himself a body from the Virgin and a soul from himself, ibid., 359.---Christ assumed the body of our creation, id., IX, 927.---Christ is not the likeness of flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh, id., X, 596.---Whether Christ’s body possessed the nature of our suffering, ibid., 362.---By the power of his own body he took upon himself the sufferings of our body, ibid., 380.---He had a body capable of suffering, but not a nature capable of feeling pain, ibid., 363.---Christ’s flesh, as though surrounded by the wall-like brightness of divinity, possessed the heavenly protection of grace. St. Ambrose, XV, 1253.---When he assumed a body, he had to undergo everything that belongs to a body, ibid., 1734.---The flesh with which Christ clothed himself was clean from every fault, id., XIV, 876.---How Christ assumed in his flesh the likeness of sinful flesh and was made sin for us, ibid., 1005.---How many errors are authors of the view that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one substance, id., XVI, 831.---Born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, he assumed an immaculate body, ibid., 470.---The flesh he assumed was real; it was crucified, buried, and raised again, id., XVII, 524.---He did not have an ethereal and spiritual body. St. Jerome, XXII, 901.---Nothing imperfect was assumed by him, ibid., 798.---The Manichaeans’ error that Christ had no flesh. St. Augustine, XLV, 1586.---What Manichaeans and Pelagians thought concerning Christ’s flesh, and what Catholics believe against them, ibid., 1385.---The Manichaeans deny that Christ had a vulnerable and mortal body, id., XLII, 304.---Many have said that Christ had no flesh and did not rise in his body, id., XXXVI, 871.---Valentinus taught that Christ brought a spiritual body with him and assumed nothing from Mary, but passed through her as through a channel or pipe, id., XLII, 28.---Apelles taught that Christ did not bring down flesh from heaven but received it from the elements of the world, and returned it to the world when, rising without flesh, he ascended into heaven, ibid., 30.---What the Priscillianists thought concerning Christ’s flesh, ibid., 668.---Those who deny that Christ had a true body, saying that what was not was seen by the eyes, refuted, XXXVIII, 477.---Christ has true flesh, against the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, ibid., 1122, 1125.---Christ had a true body, id., XL, 14, 300.---Christ’s flesh signified by the psaltery and lyre, id., XXXVI, 672.---Christ alone had the likeness of sinful flesh which was not sinful flesh, id., LXV, 1384, 1385.---He did not bring flesh with him from heaven, but assumed it from the Virgin Mary. Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1007, 1012.---He had a true body, ibid., 1008.---Christ’s body was in the corruption of death, but not in the corruption of decay. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 496.---Christ’s flesh did not experience corruption in the tomb, nor did his soul experience punishment in hell, ibid., 294.---What Christ’s body was like before the Resurrection and what it is like now, according to Augustine, ibid., 496.---Not merely Jesus’ body, but Jesus himself, was in the tomb, because divinity never abandoned the body, ibid., 289.---Christ’s body was earthly, not heavenly, because he took hold not of angels but of Abraham’s seed, ibid., 299, 300.---The excellence of Christ’s flesh because of the union of the Word, ibid., 679.---Christ had true flesh and a true soul, ibid., 242.---Christ assumed immaculate flesh in order to remove the stain of flesh, ibid., 229.---Christ received his body from the earth; he did not bring it from heaven, ibid., 279.---The Lord’s body is a kind of garment of the Godhead. Cassiodorus, LXX, 323.---Christ’s body was incorruptible and tangible. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1198.---In Christ, human flesh shrank from the pain of death. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 373.---In Christ the flesh did not blossom, but blossomed again. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 559.---Christ assumed flesh in which he could suffer. St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 631.---Some held that his flesh was created from nothing in the Virgin, ibid., 392.

VI.---On Christ’s soul.

By himself he assumed for himself a body from the Virgin and a soul from himself. St. Hilary, X, 358.---He was a perfect man consisting of soul and body, ibid., 354.---We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word and that the Son of Man consisted of soul and body, ibid., 389.---How those who regard Christ’s soul as belonging to human nature and weakness are mistaken. St. Hilary, IX, 342.---How Christ’s soul was troubled by fear. St. Ambrose, XIV, 815.---Those who think that no soul was assumed by the Lord Jesus refuted, id., XVI, 834.---Those who separate the rational soul from the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation are struck down by divine judgment, ibid., 820.---Because Christ assumed a soul, he also assumed the passions of a soul, ibid., 571.---Christ laid down and took up his soul by the power of his divinity, ibid., 565.---He assumed the flesh and soul of human nature. St. Jerome, XXII, 427.---A question concerning his soul, ibid.---Arians and Apollinarians teach that Christ assumed flesh without a soul. St. Augustine, XLII, 39, 40, 686, 687, 689.---Some heretics believed that in Christ the Word was in the place of a soul; others, in the place of the human mind, id., XXXIII, 833.---The Apollinarians maintained that Christ did not assume a rational soul, id., XXXV, 1737; XLI, 404.---The Apollinarians thought that in Christ the Word stood in the place of a soul, id., XXXIV, 716; XLII, 40.---The Apollinarians said that Christ had a soul only, without a human mind, id., XXXVII, 217.---Some deriving from that heresy said that he lacked even the soul itself, ibid., 218, 1084.---It is rash to say that a rational soul came to Christ after he had already been born, id., XXXIII, 552.---Whence Christ received his soul, id., XXXIV, 422.---Christ’s soul is not transmitted by propagation, ibid.---The question concerning Christ’s soul is most difficult, id., XLII, 784.---Christ had a soul, id., XL, 302.---Whether his soul was propagated from Adam or created, id., XXXIII, 717.---Christ’s soul was not liable to original sin, ibid., 866.---Christ’s soul was real. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 287.---Christ showed that he had a soul when he declared that he had power to lay it down, ibid., 286.---How Christ’s soul differs from angels or holy men, ibid., 416.---Peter would not have spoken of laying down his soul for Christ if Christ had not had a soul, ibid., 288.---Christ would not provide aid for our soul if he did not have a soul in which he was tempted, ibid., 237.---The soul of the Church could not be saved if Christ lacked a soul, ibid., 235.---Christ’s soul, which is the soul of Truth itself, cannot have any deficiency of truth, ibid., 420.---Full knowledge of the entire Godhead is present in Christ’s soul, ibid., 417.---How Christ is known to his soul according to divinity, ibid., 420.---Christ’s soul is not therefore of the same nature as God because it knows his whole Godhead, ibid., 422.---The saying “in whom are all the treasures,” etc., pertains not only to Christ’s divinity but also to his soul, ibid., 418.---Christ had true flesh and a true soul with true understanding, ibid., 242.---Christ’s divinity could not be called his soul, ibid., 286.---Christ’s soul excepted from original sin. Cassiodorus, LXX, 1292.---Christ’s soul was drawn forth from the lower regions, ibid., 203.---When his soul was freed from necessities, ibid., 209.---Christ’s soul is the Father’s sword, ibid., 121.---He consists of three: soul, flesh, and Word. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 884.---Christ’s soul, joined to the Word, knew all things; the Word by nature, the soul by grace, ibid., 1100.---Whether Christ assumed a soul at the same time. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 72.---Whether his soul possessed the wisdom of all things, ibid., 74.

VII.---On sin in Christ.

Christ’s flesh was not sinful. Tertullian, II, 781.---Christ, himself ignorant of sin, did not refuse to become a participant in our sin. St. Hilary, IX, 796.---While dwelling in the world, Christ did not enter into the vices and sins of the world, ibid., 955.---He alone is outside sin, ibid., 815.---He alone is innocent of guilt, ibid., 376.---Christ is not a sinner but one who takes upon himself sins; not weak, but one who bears weaknesses, ibid., 794.---In Christ there could be no cause by which he could receive the wound of any sin. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1036.---Christ alone never turns aside, ibid., 458.---It was fitting that he who was not to have the sin of a bodily fall should feel no natural contagion of generation, ibid., 874.---Why, though he knows all things, he does not know sin, clearly demonstrated, ibid., 1026.---His taking upon himself sins belongs to mercy, not guilt, ibid., 1011.---Julian’s calumny against Catholics, that Christ was not free from sins. St. Augustine, XLIV, 561, 559.---Human nature in Christ was without sin because of the union, id., XLII, 668.---Christ suffered no contagion from human flesh, ibid., 720, 744.---Christ descended to earthly contagions in such a way as to have no sin, even according to the Arians’ confession, ibid., 761.---Christ was born without sin because conceived without lust, XXXVIII, 442, 785, 823, 832.---Christ had no sin, neither original sin nor personal wrongdoing, ibid., 824, 928.---Christ alone was without original sin, id., XXXVI, 591.---Christ alone was in the flesh without sin and ignorance, id., XL, 60.---Christ alone was without sin in this life, XXXIV, 733, 867; XXXV, 1696, 1697, 1847; XLIV, 184, 815.---Human nature in Christ incapable of sin, ibid., 934.---Because Christ [Col. 0456] was not born from the concupiscence of flesh, he did not have sinful flesh, id., XLV, 1590.---Christ transferred not sin into his flesh, but death, id., XLIV, 115.---Christ alone had the likeness of sinful flesh, which was not sinful flesh, id., XLV, 1384, 1385.---Christ was without sin but was nevertheless made sin, id., XL, 252.---In what sense, XXXVIII, 825, 845; XLIV, 599.---Christ was one who received sins, not one who committed them, id., XXXVI, 849.---In Christ there was integrity without sin, ibid., 463.---Christ alone was immune from every sin. Cassian, XLIX, 1231.---Christ assumed all human weaknesses except sin. St. Fulgentius, XLV, 280.---Christ had no sin. Cassiodorus, LXX, 70.---Christ’s humanity admitted no stain, ibid., 1087.---Christ alone without sin. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 545, 562, 592.---He was altogether without sin in and through himself. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 416, 417.---Neither original nor personal unrighteousness was in Christ, ibid., 452.---He could not sin. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1104; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 78.

VIII.---On concupiscence in Christ.

Julian tries to attribute lust to Christ. St. Augustine, XLV, 1371, 1375.---The reality of bodily members in Christ, not the desire of sins, ibid., 1370.---Christ did not have a desire for vices, ibid., 1366, 1369.---Christ did not have concupiscence; consequently, as he did not commit sin, so neither did he desire it, ibid., 1390.---Because Christ was not born through concupiscence, he desired no unlawful things, ibid., 1373, 1374.---Christ was not obliged to possess concupiscence merely because he offered himself for imitation, ibid., 1338, 1390.---The basis for his example is not removed even if he did not possess concupiscence common to us, id., XLIV, 815.---Had Christ possessed concupiscence of the flesh, he would not have healed it, ibid., 816.---Those who deny concupiscence in Christ do not thereby agree with the Apollinarians, ibid., 814.---Christ alone did not have concupiscence, ibid., 562.---The devil found no concupiscence in Christ, id., XLV, 1341, 1366, 1384, 1387.---Why concupiscence did not pass into Christ’s flesh, id., XLIV, 814.---Christ had bodily senses, not concupiscence, id., XLV, 1367.

IX.---On hunger, thirst, fear, sorrow, and so forth, in Christ.

Christ assumed the affections customary to human life in order to prove himself a true man. St. Hilary, IX, 594.---In him remained the capacity for weeping, thirsting, and hungering, id., X, 363.---Christ often subjected himself to sleep, weariness, thirst, and hunger, id., 474.---Taking upon himself our weaknesses and bearing sins, he spoke from the experience and habit of human fatigue, ibid., 473, 474.---By sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and tears he acted as man, id., X, 81.---In order to hunger Christ left his human nature to itself; no operation of his divinity intervened against hunger, id., IX, 928.---What kind of hunger Christ’s was, ibid.---In receiving food or drink he yielded to custom, not necessity, id., X, 364.---In the Gospels Christ’s soul is often sad and sorrowful, id., IX, 342.---Christ both wept and suffered pain, id., X, 388.---He truly wept, ibid., 387.---The Arians cannot account for the reason for his weeping, ibid.---The mystery of Christ’s tears, ibid.---Christ sometimes weeps, groans, and is sad; and this very fact is attributed to an example of weakness, id., IX, 477.---He did not weep, thirst, or hunger for himself, id., X, 364.---His tears were for us, id., IX, 360.---How Christ’s hunger, thirst, and so forth are to be understood, id., X, 522, 523.---Some attribute sorrow, fear, and so forth to Christ’s divinity and are refuted, id., IX, 1066.---Christ’s sorrow not according to human necessity, ibid., 479.---How Christ’s soul was troubled by fear. St. Ambrose, XIV, 816.---The Lord’s hunger is a pious stratagem, id., XV, 1617.---Blessed is his thirst, because he thirsted for us, id., XIV, 1172.---Why he wept for Lazarus. St. Jerome, XXII, 593.---He did not feign but plainly displayed all the affections of the human condition—not through necessity of condition, but by the will of his teaching office. St. Augustine, XLII, 484.---Christ hungered and thirsted because he deigned to do so, not because he was compelled, id., XXXVIII, 968.---Sleep, food, and human affections in Christ prove that human nature was assumed, not consumed, id., XXXIII, 519.---In Christ hunger, thirst, and so forth belong to human nature. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 495.---Unbelievers object that we do God an injury when we say that he was born of a woman and underwent hunger, thirst, the cross, and death. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 364.

X.---On the two natures in Christ.

In Christ there are two substances, divine and human: Tertullian, III, 194.---Not only do those two natures concur in him, as in one person, but there also exist in him properties corresponding to the two natures: Lactantius, VII, 972.---The two natures of Christ: St. Hilary, IX, 485, 486, 479, 348; X, 292.---In the Son of God we believe there to be two natures, one of divinity, the other of humanity: St. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 965.---In Christ there is a double substance, divine and human: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1836.---Two perfect and entire natures, ibid., XLIV, 1716, 1732.---The truth of the human and divine natures in one person, lest you either confuse or divide them, ibid., XL, 759.---The mystery of the twofold nature and the one person in Christ is demonstrated and explained: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 221.---The properties of each nature examined, ibid., LIV, 232, 233, 292, 367.---In Christ two natures, without confusion, united in one person: Peter the Deacon, LXII, 84.---Against Eutyches it is demonstrated that there are two natures [“sto” is uncertain/OCR]: Boethius, LXIV, 1347.---Catholics maintain that Christ subsists in both natures and from both natures, ibid., 1351, 1352.---In the one person of Christ, two natures are not confused but united: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 270, 273, 502.---In Christ, one person, two natures: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 89–90.---We confess one person in Christ in two natures: Charlemagne, XCVIII, 1113.---Those two natures are entire, not transfused or changed, ibid., 1114.---The two natures in Christ confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 301.---The two properties of Christ’s natures: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 601.---Christ assumed human nature, not a person: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 33.---On the manner of the hypostatic union: Werner, CLVII, 783.---Other testimonies concerning Christ’s two natures and one person: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 278, 294, 369, 423, 441 ff.---In Christ, two natures: Rupert, CLXVII, 1438, 1540.---On the hypostatic union in the Word: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 393 ff.---The divine nature was neither changed into the human nor the human into the divine, ibid., CLXXV, 432.---In Christ there is a double nature without confusion in one person: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 110, 111.

## XI.—On the wills in Christ

Christ’s two wills: St. Hilary, X, 372, 373.---Christ has a free will, not discordant with the Father’s will, ibid., 320.---Of his own will he fulfils the Father’s will, ibid., 80.---The human will in Christ shrinking from death: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1513.---Christ had two wills and operations: Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 104.---Christ had a natural and a spiritual will: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 489.---Christ had two wills, ibid., 1102.---On Christ’s wills according to the two natures: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 790.

## On the one person in Christ

Jesus Christ is one and the very same person, possessing true deity and true humanity: Caius, V, 187, 188.---Whether the term of that union, on the human side, was a simple or a composite person: Lactantius, VI, 973.---Christ is one person, one supposit, wholly God and wholly man: Pope St. Julius, VIII, 963.---Christ, perfect God and perfect man, in unity of person: St. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 965.---In the Son of God we believe there are two natures, yet not two persons, ibid.---One person in Christ: St. Jerome, XXIV, 777.---Christ, the same God, not by confusion of nature but by unity of person: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 999.---Christ received the visible form of man into the unity of his person, ibid., XLII, 756, 757.---Because of the unity of person, Christ both remained in heaven and walked upon earth, ibid., XLIV, 144.---There are not two persons but one, ibid., XXXIX, 2082; XL, 736, 771; XLII, 1195, 1206; XLV, 1716, 1732.---Cassian vehemently attacks the error of Nestorius, who proclaims two persons in Christ: Cassian, L, 97, 98, 89, 133 ff., 172 ff.---One hypostasis in Christ, ibid., 80.---The truth of both natures in Christ comes together in unity of person: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 221.---The errors of Nestorius, who asserts a double person in Christ, refuted, ibid., 451, 986.---In the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of the Word and the flesh: Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 138.---Against Nestorius he proves that there is one person in Christ: Boethius, LXIV, 1345 ff.---In the one person of Christ two natures are not confused: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 270, 273, 502.---Whoever admits a double person in Christ is not a worshipper of the Trinity but of a quaternity, ibid., 464, 465.---Just as the distinction of persons in the Trinity does not multiply substances, so the distinction of natures in Christ does not multiply persons, ibid., 275.---One person in Christ: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 89, 90.---In Christ the person of the assuming Word is not one thing and that of the assumed man another, ibid., LXXIX, 23.---In Christ there is one person, but the natures are neither exchanged nor confused: Alcuin, CI, 1058, 1068.---Christ is not one nature, although he is one person: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 920.---Testimonies concerning the one person in Christ, ibid., 278, 294, 369, 423, [Col. 0458] 441 ff.---There are not two persons in Christ: Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 258.---Whether a person assumed a person, or a nature a person, or a nature a nature: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 434.---In Christ there is a double nature without confusion in one person: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 110, 111.---Whether nature or person assumed person or nature: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 764.---On four wills in Christ: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 841.---On three wills in Christ, ibid., CLXXVII, 518.

## XII.—On knowledge in Christ

Christ’s knowledge according to his humanity does not surpass the Father’s knowledge: St. Hilary, X, 228.---Christ’s power with respect to knowledge: what that knowledge is, ibid., 213.---The teaching of the demonstration does not charge the only-begotten God with ignorance, ibid., 214.---Knowledge of the works which the Father willed to accomplish was innate in him, ibid., 215.---Christ’s ignorance is an economy or dispensation rather than ignorance, ibid., 331, 333.---That he does not know the day of judgment is a dispensation of silence, ibid., 341.---What he does not know belongs to the knowledge of his nature, ibid., 333.---Christ doubts through a human affection, ibid., XVI, 568.---As man he doubts; as man he is troubled, ibid., 571.---He feigns not to know in order to make believers know, ibid., 660.---How he is said to have been ignorant of the day of judgment, ibid., 695.---In Christ there was growth in age and growth in wisdom, but this belongs to his humanity, ibid., 837.---Those who think that Christ lacked knowledge for bearing witness judge not according to divinity but according to man, ibid., 675.---He was ignorant of the day and hour of the final consummation: St. Jerome, XXIII, 550.---Christ’s supreme wisdom: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 413.---He knew perfectly every good and was ignorant of no evil, ibid.---He had all knowledge, ibid.---People would not believe Christ if they knew him to be ignorant, ibid.---Whether his soul possessed wisdom concerning all things: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 74.---Christ’s experimental knowledge: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 946, 1047.---He did not know the day of judgment by experimental knowledge, ibid., 947.

## XIII.—On the communication of idioms, or of the names and properties of each nature in Christ

When in Christ you distinguish, according to time, the man from God, then distinguish the speech of God from that of man: St. Eutychianus, V, 170.---Christ is at once God and man; at times he speaks what belongs to God, at times what belongs to man: St. Hilary, IX, 348.---In both the Gospels and the prophecies he uses utterances suited to his twofold nature, ibid., 816.---How the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified: St. Ambrose, XVI, 571.---He calls God the Father whom he naturally has, because of the mystery of the body he assumed, ibid., 272.---As the Most High he gives; as man he prays, ibid.---In Christ, because of the unity of person, either nature imparts its designation to the other, the divine to the human and the human to the divine: St. Augustine, XLII, 257.---Christ is lesser than and equal to the Father, ibid., XL, 250.---How Christ is both Only-Begotten and Firstborn, ibid., XLII, 581, 583.---Because of the form of God Christ is called the beginning, first-born, and Lord of glory; because of the form of a servant, bridegroom and head of the body, the Church, ibid., 835.---“God was crucified” is rightly said of Christ, ibid., XXXIII, 746.---God is rightly said to have died, although his divinity does not die, ibid., XXXVI, 455.---The Son of God is truly said to have been born and to have suffered without alteration of his divinity, ibid., XL, 303.---The hypostatic union caused what belongs to the flesh in Christ to be attributed to God: Cassian, L, 184.---Although in Christ the man alone is handed over, because of the unity of person the whole Christ is said to have been handed over: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 291.---Sometimes “Christ” signifies the deity, sometimes the man alone, sometimes both together, or the body alone: Junilius, LXVIII, 22.---On the communication of idioms in Christ: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 89, 90.---The impassible may be said to suffer, the immortal to die, and the eternal, before the ages, to be temporal: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 565.---On the communication of idioms in Christ: St. Paulinus, XCIX, 388.---Since the natures are not parts of the person, it is thereby evident that one of them is predicated of the person: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 433.---The names of the natures are predicated of one another: God is man, and man is God, ibid.---The divine nature ought not to be said to have become flesh: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 766.---On these expressions, “God became man” and “God is man,” ibid., 768.---On the communication of idioms: Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1168, 1169.---Some have said that names fitting Christ according to humanity, when in the masculine gender, refer to the hypostasis, but when in the neuter to the essence of God, ibid., 1178.---On other expressions which can or cannot be predicated of Christ, ibid., 1177 ff., 1180.

## XIV.—On Christ’s conception

[Col. 0459]

It was not fitting that Christ should be born from human seed: Tertullian, II, 781 ff.---He descended into the Virgin, and in her womb was fashioned as flesh, ibid., I, 399.---He did not have a mother stained by unchastity, as Jupiter did, ibid., I, 396 ff.---How he was without father and without mother: Lactantius, VI, 483.---The dignity of Christ’s conception: St. Hilary, X, 67, 68.---Christ was born under the law of men, but not conceived under the law of men, ibid., 380.---On Christ’s conception, ibid., IX, 30.---St. Zeno, XI, 413, 416.---How Christ came into the world by a kind of leap: St. Ambrose, XIV, 513.---He knew no mother in his divine generation and no father in the Virgin’s childbirth, ibid., XVI, 1202.---Born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, he received an immaculate body, ibid., 470, 791.---Christ, made without a man by the Holy Spirit from a virgin, ibid., XVII, 142.---The possibility of Christ’s conception demonstrated: Rufinus, XXI, 349, 350.---Christ’s conception has no parallel: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 707.---Christ was conceived without concupiscence, ibid., 844; XXXIV, 422.---The mother conceived Christ not by concupiscence but by grace, ibid., XXXVIII, 823.---Christ’s flesh came from our mass, not from the knot of concupiscence between man and woman, ibid., 928.---Christ was made from a woman, with no intercourse intervening, ibid., XXXIV, 405.---Conceived by his mother’s faith, ibid., XL, 249.---The Virgin conceived Christ not by carnally desiring but by spiritually believing, ibid., XXXVI, 826.---Christ was conceived without sin in order to loose sin, ibid., XXXVIII, 817.---Born without sin because conceived without lust, ibid., 442, 785, 823, 832.---Christ was produced from Adam’s seed, though not by a seminal process, ibid., XLV, 1401.---How the eternal Son of God could be conceived, being born in time, ibid., XLII, 1166.---In Christ’s conception the husband is speech and the wife is the ear, ibid., XXXIX, 1991.---The arriving divinity fashioned flesh for itself in Mary’s womb from her own substance, ibid., 2199.---Christ was conceived not from the substance but from the power of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 2178.---God without a mother;
