man without a father: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 222.---Christ’s conception from a Virgin foretold by Isaiah: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 235.---In the womb of holy Mary, when the Holy Spirit comes upon her and the Most High overshadows her, Christ is begotten, ibid., 236.---Christ without mother as God, without father as man: St. Fulgentius, LXV, 251.---True God from the moment of conception in the womb: Alcuin, CI, 183.---In Christ’s conception neither body preceded soul nor soul body: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 886.---Christ’s conception was contrary to nature, and therefore ineffable, ibid., 884.---His conception renews ours: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 327.---The holiness of conception was reserved for him alone, ibid., CLXXXII, 335.---The manner of this conception was known only to God and the God-bearer, ibid., CLXXXIII, 82.

## XV.—On Christ’s nativity, lineage, and infancy

Christ is from Mary’s flesh, since he is from David’s seed: Tertullian, II, 350.---He was revealed in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, ibid., 264.---Whether he is the son of a carpenter or of a woman who earned wages, ibid., I, 662.---Whether Christ passed through every stage of infancy, ibid., II, 411.---The flesh, instructed by the Spirit, is nourished, grows, speaks, teaches, acts—and is Christ, ibid., I, 399.---On his twofold birth: Lactantius, VI, 465.---When Christ was born in the flesh: St. Hilary, IX, 1029.---He is from the stock of Judah, ibid., 463.---Christ’s birth from royal and priestly lineage, ibid., 917.---On the Nativity of the Lord: St. Zeno, XI, 407, 412, 415.---What is to be thought concerning the midwife said to have attended the Virgin in childbirth, ibid., 415.---Why Luke thought Christ’s genealogy should be traced back to God: St. Ambrose, XV, 1593.---Why Matthew thought Christ’s genealogy should be derived through Solomon, but Luke through Nathan, ibid., 1594.---How there can be more successions but fewer generations in Christ’s genealogy, ibid., 1608.---How Christ could be of true royal lineage if the Prophet foretold that none from Jeconiah’s seed would reign, ibid., 1607.---Why Matthew reckoned very many sinners among the ancestors of the Lord’s line, whereas Luke avoided this, ibid., 1604, 1610.---At his birth he is shown to be God by no ordinary signs, ibid., 1568.---How Christ could have a carpenter for a father on earth, ibid., 1589.---He honoured Joseph and Mary, not from a debt of nature but from the duty of filial devotion, ibid., XIV, 973; XV, 1575, 1788.---Why he was born in a time of peace, ibid., XVII, 608, 609.---Shepherds learned of his birth before rulers: simple rusticity before proud domination, ibid., 613.---How Christ’s father is called a carpenter, ibid., 616.---Whether it is unworthy that the majesty of God should pass forth through a woman’s genitals: Rufinus, XXI, 351.---Under which consuls Christ was born: Dexter, XXXI, 55, 56.---Christ’s generation and nativity are each twofold and wondrous: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 260, 773, 1007, 1015, 1017, 1019, 1073; XXXIX, 1655, 1659, 1661, 1675, 1676.---Christ’s birth from a Virgin, ibid., XL, 643.---Christ was born with his mother’s virginity unimpaired, ibid., XXXVIII, 999, 1004, 1005, 1011, 1068, 1075.---Her integrity remained uncorrupted, ibid., XL, 186, 249.---According to Ambrose, Christ’s bodily birth was free of fault because it did not result from the union of the two sexes, ibid., XLIV, 444, 1389.---Christ’s nativity was full of prodigies, ibid., XL, 663; XLI, 314.---Signs at Christ’s nativity, ibid., XL, 643.---At what time Christ was born, ibid., XLI, 109, 608.---The day and consulship in which he was born were known in Augustine’s time, ibid., XXXV, 1592.---How many years were counted from his birth, ibid., XXXIII, 911.---Christ was born when the days were already beginning to increase, ibid., XXXVII, 1735.---Christ was of royal and priestly stock, ibid., XXXIV, 809, 1072.---How Christ is son of Abraham and David, ibid., XXXVIII, 337; XLII, 468, 469; XXXV, 1742.---Christ is rightly called son of David, even if Mary derived no descent from David, ibid., XXXIV, 1072.---Why Matthew and Luke set out Christ’s genealogy differently, ibid., XL, 49; XLII, 214.---Why Matthew counts Christ’s generations in descending order and Luke in ascending order, ibid., XXXVIII, 351.---Why they are counted through Joseph rather than Mary, ibid., 342, 350; XLII, 470; XLIV, 810.---Why Christ did not wish to be born from the tribe of Levi, ibid., XL, 50.---Why the order of Christ’s genealogies differs in Matthew and Luke: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 234, 791.---Christ was born, in accordance with the prophecies, in Bethlehem, David’s city, and was wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed in a manger: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 238.---Why there was no place for him in the lodging, ibid., 246.---According to prophecy, Christ was born in the flesh from Jacob’s seed and David’s royal blood, ibid., 264, 265.---Various opinions of chronologists concerning the time of Christ’s birth, ibid., 481.---Why the Lord’s nativity is celebrated: Alcuin, CI, 1173.---Why he was born at night, ibid., 1175.---Born from priestly and royal stock; likewise the Virgin Mary: Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1176.---Why Christ wished to be born from Judah, passing over Judah’s three brothers: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 87.---Why Christ preferred to be born of a betrothed woman rather than an unmarried virgin, ibid., 104.---Why Christ was born when firm peace existed throughout the whole world, ibid., 122.---Errors in Germany concerning Christ’s nativity. The author gives reasons why Christ had to be born as others are: Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 83.---The author proves that Christ came forth through the vulva, ibid., 85 ff.---For Christ’s birthday: Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 835.---On the Nativity of the Lord and Saviour: St. Odilo of Cluny, CXLII, 991.---St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 846.---Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1696, 1707.---Goffridus, CLVII, 237 ff.---Ivo Carmel., CLXII, 568 ff.---The place of Christ’s nativity was revealed only to David and Micah: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 439.---On the Nativity of the Lord: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 381 ff.; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 946.---Christ’s nativity is wonderful: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 87.---Christ’s nativity is the day of new redemption, ancient restoration, and eternal blessedness, ibid., 91.---The place of his nativity considered, ibid., 112.---His birth at night teaches that ostentation should be avoided, ibid., 123.---Remedies brought by Christ’s nativity, ibid., 101.---On the Nativity of the Lord, ibid., 116; CLXXXIV, 827; CLXXXV, 29 ff.; Amadeus of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1319; Ernaldus, CLXXXIX, 1615; Aelred, CXCV, 220 ff.; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 200 ff.; Garnerius, CCV, 599 ff.; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 575; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 65 ff.; Innocent III, CCXVII, 451 ff.

## XVI.—On Christ’s circumcision

Christ, though not needing circumcision, was presented in the temple in order to be circumcised: St. Hilary, IX, 503.---Christ’s circumcision was performed on the eighth day, to signify his resurrection: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 680.---Why Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, was dedicated with the seal of circumcision: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 299.---It is demonstrated that the Church’s commemoration of Christ’s circumcision is older than the sixth century, ibid., 255.---Why Christ wished to be circumcised: Alcuin, CI, 1176.---At the feast of the Circumcision Christ accepted the observances of the law in order to free us from them: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 399.---Why Christ wished to be circumcised: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 153.---He was circumcised for the reason that he was born and suffered, ibid., 136.---As head, he underwent circumcision for his members, ibid., 138.---Christ’s circumcision proves the reality of the humanity he assumed, ibid., 133.---Christ’s humility in circumcision, ibid., 131.---What it teaches us, [Col. 0461] ibid., 674.---In it there is something to love, something to admire, and something to imitate, ibid., 137.

## XVII.—On Christ’s baptism, temptation, and fast

Christ’s baptism: St. Cyprian, III, 1124, 1168, 1176.---Heretics say that he was compelled by Mary to baptism, ibid., 1202.---In what year of his life he was baptized: Lactantius, VI, 977.---Christ’s humility in baptism: St. Hilary, IX, 795.---He had no need of the washing for himself, but for us, ibid., 927.---Christ sanctified humanity both by assumption and by washing, ibid.---Christ was baptized in the Jordan when he instituted the pattern of the saving washing: St. Ambrose, XIV, 816.---God is proved by no work more than by the mystery of his baptism, ibid., 1586.---There are chiefly three things in Christ that serve human salvation: namely, the sacrament of baptism, the wilderness, and fasting, ibid., XV, 1613.---Why he was baptized, ibid., XVI, 422.---How fitting it was that John should baptize him: St. Ambrose, XVII, 680.---Christ came to the washing in order to purify the streams of water for us, ibid., 623.---He was baptized in the thirtieth year of his age: St. Jerome, XXV, 414.---His baptism was on the fifth day of January, not his birthday, ibid., 18.---Why Christ wished to be baptized: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1411, 1415, 1418; XXXVIII, 1322; XL, 255; XLIII, 77, 182, 290.---Why he wished to be baptized though he had no stains, ibid., XXXVII, 1161.---He was baptized in order to be fitting to penitents, ibid., XLV, 1376.---In order to teach the way of humility, ibid., XXXVIII, 1321.---By wishing to be baptized, he commended his humility more fully, ibid., XXXIII, 843.---Why he was not baptized by John alone, ibid., XLIII, 238.---On Gospel authority, it is maintained that Christ was baptized at about thirty years of age, ibid., XXXIV, 55.---Why he underwent baptism: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 701.---Jesus came to the Jordan in the thirtieth year of his age to be baptized by John: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 290, 296, 654.---At Christ’s baptism the Holy Trinity was revealed, ibid., 298.---Christ did not need regeneration and baptism: Alcuin, C, 333, 158, 162.---Why he wished to be baptized, ibid., 785; CI, 49, 238, 1179.---Where, when, and by whom he was baptized, ibid., CI, 1179.---Christ wished to be baptized by the care/ministry of John in the water of the Jordan: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 167.---Christ baptized: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 630, 751.---Not that he might be cleansed by water, but that he might cleanse the waters, ibid., 751, 716.---By his baptism he opened heaven for us, ibid., 631.---And so that waters cleansed through his flesh might receive the power to purify sins, ibid., 716.---The Holy Spirit descended upon him in the appearance of a dove, ibid., 631.---Christ’s baptism, the Christian’s birth: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 415.---Christ was baptized on the same day on which he was adored by the Magi: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 145.---Christ was baptized when he had spent nearly thirty years in the flesh, ibid., 150.---The humility of Christ in wishing to be baptized, ibid., 146.

Christ’s temptation in the wilderness: St. Hilary, IX, 796.---He offered his manhood to the devil for temptation, ibid., 928.---So that the devil might be conquered in man, ibid., 929.---Even unto temptation, abstaining from human food, he was nourished by the Spirit of God, ibid.---His fast, hunger, and temptation are full of the effects of heavenly counsel, ibid., 927.---How Christ’s fast was made a reproach against him, ibid., 477.---Christ permits himself to be tempted by the devil so that in him we might all conquer: St. Ambrose, XV, 1613.---He deceived the devil and the prince of this world, ibid., 1554.---He exposed himself to so many temptations that he might pass over none of the contests of our temptation, ibid., XIV, 942.---He alone could be appointed our leader against the enticements of the world and the wiles of the devil, ibid., X, 1614.---There are chiefly three things in Christ that serve human salvation: namely, the sacrament of baptism, the wilderness, and fasting, ibid., XV, 1613.---Christ had to be tempted; he had to suffer with me, so that I might know how, when tempted, to conquer, and, having suffered, to escape, ibid., XVI, 579.---According to the flesh he is tempted; according to his dignity he is worshipped by angels, ibid., 596.---Why Christ permitted himself to be tempted by the devil: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 685.---When Christ wished to be tempted by Satan, he transfigured us into himself, ibid., XXXVII, 724.---Christ’s temptation is our instruction, ibid., 1149.---He was tempted in order to teach his own people to resist the tempter, ibid., XXXVIII, 685.---His temptation is threefold, because of the three kinds of vices: pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity, ibid., XXXVII, 116.---Why he admitted temptation: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 264.---The order of temptation explained, ibid., 278.---By what weapons it was overcome, ibid., 265.---Why he would not turn stones into bread, ibid., 269.---After fasting forty days and forty nights, Christ is tempted by the [Col. 0462] devil in the wilderness: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 303.---Tempted in three ways, he conquered the tempter with a threefold triumph, warning that one God is to be worshipped and served alone, ibid., 323.---Why Christ endured the devil’s temptation: Cassiodorus, LXX, 411.---Christ tempted by the devil in three vices: St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 196, 197.

His fast, hunger, and temptation are full of the effects of heavenly counsel: St. Hilary, IX, 928.---How Christ’s fast was made a reproach against him, ibid., 477.---There are chiefly three things in Christ that serve human salvation: namely, the sacrament of baptism, the wilderness, and fasting: St. Ambrose, XV, 1613.---Christ fasted so that his fast might be an example to us, ibid., XVI, 1195.---Why Christ fasted forty days: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1211.---He was hungry after fasting forty days: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 323.---When and with what fast he fasted: Cassiodorus, LXX, 246.---Christ’s fast, his victory over the devil, and the ministry of angels: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 717.---How Christ fasted: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 308.

## XVIII.—On Christ’s teaching, miracles, and powers

The perfection of Gospel teaching commended: Tertullian, II, 388 ff.---The promises of the old law are earthly, but Christ’s are heavenly, ibid., 389.---Christ teaches a new patience, ibid., 395.---Another excellence of the new law, ibid.---After Jesus Christ, we have no need of curiosity, nor of inquiry after the Gospel, ibid., 21.---Christ, illuminator and guide of humankind, ibid., I, 395.---Through Christ we have known God, ibid., 647.---He issued precepts of salvation for learned and unlearned alike, for every age and sex: St. Cyprian, IV, 538.---Christ is light and day, ibid., 645.---Christ taught what God is, how great, and of what kind: Arnobius, V, 764.---To instruct humanity, Jesus first had to do what he taught: Lactantius, VI, 521.---He taught that God is one and that he alone ought to be worshipped, ibid., 490.---He formed people in virtue and justice, ibid., 496.---Christ’s teaching compared with that of the philosophers: Constantine, VIII, 421, 428, 441.---Christ entirely forbids domination, ibid., 441.---But he exalts humility, ibid.---Knowledge of God handed down to us by Christ: St. Hilary, IX, 799.---It was Christ’s special office to offer knowledge of God, ibid., 1046, 1047, 806, 807; X, 90, 91.---Christ seems to teach not as a man, but rather as God: St. Ambrose of Milan, XVI, 577.---All truth is contained in his Gospel: St. Ambrose, XV, 1466.---In the New Testament we have learned precepts of new virtues and drawn new moral habits: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1059.---A wondrous beginning of heavenly teaching, which begins not from terror but from blessedness: St. Chromatius, XX, 325.---The sublimity of Gospel teaching, ibid., 324 ff.---The excellence of Christ’s teaching: St. Jerome, XXIV, 565, 566.---Christ commands us to forgive debts, ibid.---“Whoever gives a cup of cold water shall receive rewards,” ibid.---The efficacy of the teaching that penetrated the cities of the nations and the hardest hearts, XXVI, 416.---Why Christ spoke in parables, ibid., 85, 89, 91.---Christ commanded something more than what had been commanded in the Old Testament: St. Augustine, XLII, 129, 130.---Christ did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 135.---Christ brought truth as teacher, gentleness as liberator, justice as judge, ibid., XXXV, 1648, 1649.---Christ’s teaching is not hostile to the commonwealth, ibid., XXXIII, 532, 533.---Comparison of the Mosaic law and the new law, ibid., XLIV, 218.---Christ’s teaching commands humility: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 876; XL, 413.---It condemns moral corruption, ibid., XLI, 64, 74.---Gospel teaching is health-giving and life-giving: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, L, 428, 501.---Christ’s teaching rests in charity, ibid., 341.---By the anointing of the Holy Spirit Christ made sweet the teaching that had formerly seemed harsh and rigid, ibid., 327.---The Gospel books contain teaching full of every kind of perfection: St. Salvian, LIII, 58.---The difference between Gospel teaching and the ancient law, ibid., 193.---The excellence of Christ’s teaching and how greatly it surpasses the old law: St. Paulinus of Nola, XLI, 299.---Christ’s heavenly teaching forms the present life by good works and is full of divine promises: Boethius, LXIV, 1337.---The perfection of Christian teaching consists in love of God and neighbour: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 923.---On the perfection of Gospel teaching: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 793 ff.; CXI, 715, 718, 723.---The Gospel law delivers precepts far more perfect than the Mosaic law: St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 110, 111.---Christ’s teaching was wonderful: Rupert of Deutz, [Col. 0463] CLXVII, 1549 ff.---Its beauty is nothing other than the truth of its words, the gentleness of its morals, and the justice of its judgments: St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 204, 205.---Simple Christian teaching resolves all the arguments of dialecticians, ibid., CLXXXIV, 414.---Teaching full of every perfection: Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 25.---What else does Christ’s Gospel reveal to us but complete perfection in every respect? Adam the Scot, CXCVII, 510.

How many and how great Christ’s miracles were: Tertullian, I, 400.---By them he proved himself God, ibid.---With what shamelessness they were said to have been performed by magical powers, ibid., 400.---Christ wished to be acknowledged as the Son of God by human beings, not by unclean spirits, ibid., II, 373.---On Jesus’ life and miracles: Lactantius, VI, 490.---The source of Christ’s miracles: St. Hilary, X, 516.---Whether his body itself had power to perform them, ibid., 362.---Christ, like light, touched the man born blind and poured light into him: St. Ambrose, XVI, 1271.---In Lazarus’s resurrection are God’s power, life, light, and the resurrection of the dead, ibid., 1337.---His wonders are not buried in oblivion, but renewed through their powers, ibid., XVII, 622, 623.---Christ’s miracles: St. Jerome, XXV, 1090.---Why Christ could not perform signs in his own country, ibid., 865.---Christ’s miracles: St. Augustine, XLI, 608.---Some things are shared by him with others; but what is peculiar to him is to be born of a virgin, to rise from the dead, and to ascend into heaven, ibid., XXXIII, 522.---Unbelievers slander Christ by alleging that he performed what he did by magical arts, ibid., XXXVIII, 256, 447.---Christ’s deeds also signified something, like words, ibid., 486.---Something other than what they outwardly displayed, ibid., 592.---Why Christ performed miracles: Cassiodorus, LXX, 195.---He accomplished salvation better by preaching than by miracles, ibid., 330.---Seeing Christ’s miracles yet refusing to believe him God, the Jews wandered as though drunk: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 968.---How great Christ’s wonders were, ibid., 869.---Christ’s miracles signify two things for us, ibid., LXXVI, 1082.---Why, when performing a miracle, Christ wished silence, yet could not obtain it, ibid., LXXVII, 192.---With five loaves he feeds five thousand people, ibid., 309.---Christ proved himself God by incomparable miracles, ibid., LXXIX, 66, 67, 99.---Christ’s miracles: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1615.

## On the Humility of Christ

Christ’s humility in washing the disciples’ feet. St. Cyprian, IV, 233. — His humility is our nobility. St. Eutychian, V, 169. — Humility came into the world in order to bring aid to the humble and lowly and to show all the hope of salvation. Lactantius, VI, 529. — Jesus always showed himself humble, ibid., 498. — He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. St. Hilary, X, 419. — He supplied both the precept and the example of humility, id., IX, 592. — The reward of humility in Christ, ibid., 594. — Christ’s humility, our nobility, id., X, 67. — He showed himself the author of humility when he ministered to the disciples. St. Ambrose, XV, 1817. — He humbled himself so that you might learn what humility is, id., XIV, 1126. — Our Lord, the teacher of humility. St. Jerome, XXII, 345. — He humbly assumed the form of a servant, so that only then might the instruction in humility become more fitting. Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1042. — Christ’s humility commended in the Incarnation. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 302. — Christ’s humility, id., XXXV, 1390, 1681, 1787. — Christ is a worm because of the humility of his flesh, perhaps also because of the Virgin’s childbirth, id., XXXIII, 385. — Why Christ came to us in such great humility, id., XLI, 221; XXXVI, 163, 302; XXXVII, 1239. — Christ gave us a great example of humility, id., XXXV, 1631. — Christ showed the way of humility. Cassiodorus, LXX, 973. — By Christ’s humility the devil’s pride was conquered, ibid., 891. — Christ’s humility, the instrument of our redemption, id., LXXVII, 741. — On Christ’s humility in washing the disciples’ feet. Eligius of Noyon, LXXXVII, 607 ff. — His humility is to be imitated, 629. — His humility is highly commendable. Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 130, 131. — The degrees of humility in Christ are described. St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 211, 212. — Testimonies concerning Christ’s humility. Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 235. — Because of humility God gave him the name that is above every name. Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 115. — Christ wished to appear humble in every respect. Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 1320. — Christ’s example is the remedy for our pride. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 799. — His glorying is in humility alone. St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 821. — This humility confounds our vanity, ibid., 146, 147. — Christ especially loved and possessed humility. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 449. — Christ’s entire life is founded in humility. St. Peter the Chanter, CCV, 62, 63.

## Patience

How great Christ’s patience was. Tertullian, II, 348. — He wished to be filled with the delight of patience, ibid., I, 1254. — The Lord’s patience was wounded in Malchus, ibid. [Col. 0464] — Christ taught patience not only by words, but fulfilled it also by deeds. St. Cyprian, IV, 625, 626. — Christ showed the discipline of patience. Cassiodorus, LXX, 973. — Christ’s patience in his Passion, praying for his persecutors. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 846, 847. — By his example he taught us patience in injuries received, ibid., 1151. — A wonderful example of patience in Christ, ibid., 1152; LXXVII, 69; LXXIX, 576, 577. — Christ conquered the devil not by power, but by justice and patience. Wildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 600. — Christ’s patience. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 264 ff. — Richard of St. Victor, CXCVII, 380.

## Mercy

Christ’s love toward humankind. Tertullian, II, 772 ff. — Christ taught mercy not only by words, but fulfilled it also by deeds. St. Cyprian, IV, 625, 626. — How great his clemency and mercy toward us were in the mystery of the Incarnation. Constantine the Great, VIII, 432, 433, 434. — Where grace is to be bestowed, Christ is present. St. Ambrose, XIV, 440. — Christ’s mercy. St. Jerome, XXIV, 65. — Christ was of such clemency that on the cross he prayed for transgressors—indeed, for his persecutors. Id., XXV, 429. — Christ’s clemency: he prayed not only for the apostles before the Passion, but also on the cross for those crucifying him. St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 312, 313. — How greatly Christ loved the world. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 677, 678. — His kindness and compassion toward humankind. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 179. — How great Christ’s kindness toward his bride, the Church, is, id., LXXIX, 597, 598. — Christ’s kindness toward sinners and unbelievers gives us hope of obtaining pardon, ibid., 611. — Christ’s goodness received in the Incarnation. St. Boniface, LXXIX, 862, 863. — No knowledge is sufficient to comprehend how great Christ’s love is. St. Bruno of Cologne, CLIII, 333. — How much forbearance, mercy, and compassion Christ has had toward us. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 345. — Christ’s supreme love, by which he rendered good for evil. St. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 688. — How great Christ’s love for humankind was, ibid., 539. — Christ’s supreme mercy. Godefridus, CLXXIV, 1125. — How great Christ’s kindness and mercy are. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 142, 143, 144.

## Poverty

Christ wished to be born needy of the Virgin, for the sake of our salvation. St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 823. — He made himself poor so that we might become rich, ibid., 492. — Christ’s poverty and suffering. St. Ambrose, XIV, 954. — Rich in poverty, ibid., 1060, 1070. — Christ’s poverty is different; his hem heals; his hunger satisfies; his death gives life; his burial raises the dead, ibid., 686. — The Lord was so poor that he did not have the means to pay the tax for himself and the apostle. St. Jerome, XXVI, 128. — Christ’s utter poverty. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 844. — Christ wished to be born poor, id., XXXIV, 696. — Why Christ became needy, id., XXXVIII, 243, 916, 1120; XXXIX, 1591. — Christ wished to be in need for your sake, so that you might have where to sow the earthly things which he gave and reap eternal life, id., XXXVIII, 91. — Christ did not disdain to become poor. St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 315. — Christ enters the world poor. St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 397. — Christ’s poverty and nakedness at his birth, in his life, in death, and after death in the tomb. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 553, 554. — He gave us an example of enduring, for righteousness’ sake, incomparable contempt and poverty, ibid., 554. — He was so poor that, when he came into the world, he was born not in his own house but in another’s, ibid. — Christ’s poverty. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 289; CLXXXIV, 951. — Christ’s poverty appeared most fully on the cross. Peter the Chanter, CCV, 77.

## Obedience

He always subjected himself to the Father, both in the honor of the Son and in the condition of man. St. Hilary, X, 284. — The subjection of Christ, who is God, is an act of loving devotion, id., 518. — Christ, though God, was subject to the Father both in obedience and in name, ibid., 518. — He obeyed the Father’s will in all things, id., 340. — Christ was subject to Joseph and Mary as parents out of filial devotion, not out of weakness. St. Ambrose, XIV, 973; XV, 1575. — His subjection is not an appearance of weakness, but an exercise of power, ibid., 1169. — He was subject to his parents. St. Jerome, XXII, 954. — Christ’s wondrous obedience. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 866. — Christ, the tribunal of obedience, id., CLXXXIV, 857. — His obedience had humility in the heart, patience on the lips, and perseverance in action, ibid., 949, 950. — On Christ’s obedience. Baldwin of Canterbury, CCIV, 431. — Christ himself taught the order of obedience, perseverance, and glory, ibid., 431. — He descended from heaven in obedience, ibid.

## Meekness

What is severe in others is sweet in Christ—pleasant in Christ—because he himself is gracious. St. Ambrose, XV, 1266. — Christ joined meekness with the rigor of justice. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 534. — Christ corrected us by meekness rather than terror, ibid., 894. — He did not repay an injury received, but answered by bearing it meekly. [Col. 0465] LXXVI, 1151. — Christ ruled us by meekness, not severity, ibid., 894. — Christ’s meekness. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 880, 881. — Christ’s sweetness draws all people, ibid., 454.

Christ’s outstanding virtues. St. Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 49, 50, 51. — Christ has in himself all virtues. St. Guibert, CLVI, 503. — Christ is devout, humble, gentle, and kind, id., CLVII, 246. — By what virtues Christ redeemed us. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 391.

## XIX.—On Christ’s Passion

Christ and the prophets foretold Christ’s Passion. Tertullian, I, 401. — Christ’s Passion is described, ibid., 1252 ff. — Unless he were unrecognized, he could suffer nothing, id., II, 327. — In what year he suffered, ibid., 612 ff. — Christ had to suffer, not in order to experience death, but in order to conquer it, id., IV, 580. — Christ suffered in order to make us children of God, ibid., 354. — Christ’s Passion, ibid., 715, 802. — Pagans reproached Christians with Christ’s Passion. Lactantius, IV, 496. — Whatever he did or suffered has great figurative and symbolic meaning, ibid., 525. — In what year of his age he suffered, ibid., 967. — On what day he was thought to have suffered, Lactantius, ibid., 386, 437; VII, 194, 393, 608 ff.; St. Hilary, IX, 472, 473 ff. — Christ’s Passion was voluntary, not compelled, id., X, 381. — By his Passion Christ absorbed our weaknesses, id., IX, 956. — He suffered what human beings can suffer, id., X, 394. — He wept and grieved, ibid., 388. — At times he weeps, groans, and is sorrowful, id., IX, 477. — His tears were for us, ibid., 360. — Nothing concerning the sweat of blood and the coming of the angel occurs in most manuscripts. St. Hilary, X, 375. — Christ suffered because he delighted in doing good, not because he sought an increase of glory from his Passion. St. Ambrose, XIV, 849. — Christ’s Passion needed no assistance, id., XVI, 319. — The fullness of faith lies in the sacrament of the Passion, ibid., 806. — The Lord’s hands fastened to the cross, ibid., 296. — He mercifully prays for his persecutors, ibid., 1370. — He received vinegar in order to bring all temptations to an end, ibid., 1226. — He was wounded by the lance in order to heal us by the blood of the sacred wound, ibid., 201. — The mystery of the water and blood flowing from Christ’s side. Rufinus, XXI, 361. — In what year Christ was led before Pilate as an accused man. Dexter, XXXI, 69. — On what day he was crucified, ibid., 71. — As the hour of the Passion approached, Christ was troubled by power. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1797, 1799. — He was troubled because he willed it, ibid., 1755. — He was troubled so that we might not despair, id., XXXVIII, 1399. — In Christ our weakness is troubled, id., XXXV, 1799. — The human will in Christ shrinking from death, id., XXXIX, 1513. — What Christ’s sweating blood from his whole body signifies, id., XXXVII, 1817. — Christ was handed over both by Judas and by God, id., XXXVIII, 1383. — What Judas sold, the Jew bought, and the Christian acquired, ibid., 1474. — The author of the cup of his Passion is himself the one who drinks it, id., XXXV, 1932. — Why Christ did not offer the other cheek to one striking him, ibid., 1934, 1935. — Christ’s Passion, id., XLI, 585, 588, 591. — Whatever man suffered cannot be said not to have been suffered by God, id., XXXVII, 1711. — What Christ’s hands stretched out on the cross signify, id., XXXVI, 755. — Why Christ was silent in the Passion, ibid., 173, 407; XXXVII, 1339. — Christ did not wish to come down from the cross because he was teaching patience, id., XXXV, 1397, 1675; XXXVI, 462, 767, 882. — Christ suffered not by the desert of iniquity but by the office of his mercy, id., XLII, 543. — Christ’s Passion came not from need, but from mercy, ibid., 542, 547. — Hymn on the Lord’s Passion. Claudianus, LIII, 786. — Why Christ chose to suffer at the Paschal solemnity. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 331. — On the Lord’s Passion, id., LVI, 1133; LVII, 339 ff. — On the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion. St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 257 ff. — On the Lord’s Passion. Theodulf, CV, 375. — Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 1097 ff.; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 358, 392. — Why Christ suffered on Friday. St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 772; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 675, 761; CLIX, 271. — Why God suffered. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 562. — Christ’s Passion is described, in which he showed himself to be truly human. Ivo of Chartres, CLXIV, 746. — Book on Christ’s Passion and the sorrows of his mother. St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1134. — Sermons on the Lord’s Passion, CLXXXIII, 263 ff.; CLXXXIV, 741 ff., 953. — Christ’s Passion. Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 51 ff.; Ernaldus, CLXXXIX, 1656; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 761; Absalon, abbot, CCXI, 137, 148.

## XX.—On Christ’s Death

Christ died of his own accord. Tertullian, I, 401. — We say that he died not according to divine substance, but according to human substance, id., II, 194. — In Christ’s death, an extraordinary eclipse of the sun was foretold and described in secret records or archives, [Col. 0466] id., I, 401. — In what year he suffered, id., II, 612 ff. — Christ’s Passion was reported by Pilate to the emperor Tiberius, ibid., 403. — Christ willingly gave up his spirit. St. Cyprian, IV, 580. — At what hour he expired. Lactantius, VI, 940. — The cry of the dying Christ attests the separation of the departing divinity, IX, 1072. — He subjected himself to death, and why, ibid., 345. — The Word did not depart from the flesh in death, id., X, 286, 391, 392. — The effects of Christ’s death, ibid., 288. — He died for all, id., IX, 384. — Prophecy of Christ’s death, ibid., 473. — Christ tastes death in order to defeat death. St. Zeno, XI, 158. — Christ alone was chosen as worthy of such a death, by which he took away the sin of the world. St. Ambrose, XIV, 860. — Not even the saints believed that Christ would die, id., XV, 1662, 1663. — Christ could have avoided death, but did not will to do so, ibid., 1611. — Where the place of the cross was, ibid., 1832. — He was crucified for our faith; he was crucified for our desires, ibid., 1662. — Christ’s death resolves the enigmas of the prophets, ibid., 1115. — Christ’s death is the life of all; by his death we are sealed … his death is victory, id., XVI, 607, 1327. — He offered his own death for the death of all, ibid., 1115. — How Christ, the Son of God and life in himself, died. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 710, 1061. — Christ died when his flesh died, id., XXXV, 1817. — Death came to him by condescension, not by condition, id., XXXVIII, 1110. — Christ’s death killed death, id., XXXV, 1490; XXXVIII, 1114. — Christ died when he wished, id., XXXV, 1638, 1673, 1674 ff.; and because he wished, id., XXXIV, 304; XXXV, 1674, 1736; XXXVIII, 54. — Christ suffered and died by power and will, not necessity, id., XXXVII, 1104; XXXVIII, 1083; XLIV, 256. — Christ accepted death by the will of obedience, ibid., 180, 182. — Christ ought not to die except when it was fitting, id., XXXV, 1457. — The time of Christ’s death, id., XLI, 619. — The Evangelists are reconciled concerning the hour at which Christ was crucified, id., XXXVI, 763. — By Christ’s death, as by his trophy, the devil was conquered, id., XXXVIII, 1209. — Why Christ accepted death, id., XLV, 1181. — By Christ’s death his name was sown, id., XXXVI, 453. — Why one should not be ashamed of Christ’s death, id., XXXVIII, 1278, 1279. — Christ chose the hour of his birth and death. St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 490. — Christ died for all the ungodly, ibid., 702. — Christ suffered and died voluntarily, ibid., 294. — On the division of Christ’s garments after his crucifixion, and on the garment woven from the top, which was not divided, id., LVII, 331, 332. — Christ’s one death was salvation from our two deaths. Eugyppius, LXII, 590. — Who were especially responsible for Christ’s death, ibid., 829. — Through Christ’s death we were reconciled. St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 424. — How Christ tasted death without God, ibid., 284. — Christ died from the weakness of his humanity; from the power of his divinity he lives, ibid., 290. — Christ alone desired to die. Cassiodorus, LXX, 148. — Why Christ chose the death of the cross rather than another, id., 160. — The manner of Christ’s death was unique to him, id., 470, 471. — Why the inscription of the title in the Passion was not erased, ibid., 394. — The Lord’s death is described, ibid., 402. — The Savior’s death is called a sitting, ibid., 984, 985. — By Christ’s death we know what follows after death. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 490, 491. — Dying, Christ shattered the powers of hell, id., LXXIX, 23. — The command to die was imposed upon Christ by the Father, ibid., 29. — Dying on the cross, he raised up the Church, ibid., 541. — On Christ’s single death and our double death. Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 783. — When Christ’s death occurred. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1086. — Why he died at Passover, ibid., 332. — Christ and the Jews sought the same death for different ends, ibid., 380, 381. — Why Christ chose the death of the cross. St. Hildefonsus, XCVI, 131; Alcuin, CI, 1207. — Christ saved more by dying than by living, id., CVIII, 1197. — How Christ died for a time. Lanfranc, CL, 119. — For what purpose he died, ibid., 259. — He died in order to establish a testament, ibid., 396. — Outside the city, naked beneath the open sky, he is crucified naked. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 554. — Christ accepted death not in the nature of divinity, but in the nature of humanity, ibid., 920. — God the Father neither permitted Christ to be killed against his will nor compelled him to death, ibid., 369. — The Son, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, had ordained that he would reveal his omnipotence to the world only through death, ibid., 372. — In what sense the Father is said to have willed the death of the Son, ibid., 373. — Christ could have avoided death if he had wished, ibid., 375. — Christ voluntarily endured death, ibid., 370. — It was necessary by a consequent, not antecedent, necessity that God become man, suffer, die, and so forth, ibid., 423. — Christ, by his own will, could not fail to die, and by his own will he died—not from any necessity, but by his own power, ibid., 420. — Christ was born from the Jews and crucified by the Jews, [Col. 0467] ibid., 738. — At what hour Christ was crucified. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 511. — By his one death he brought a remedy for our twofold death. St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 933. — The remembrance of Christ’s death, more than that of his life, moves us to devotion, ibid., 932.

## XXI.—On Christ’s Burial

Christ’s body was placed in a tomb. Tertullian, I, 401. — In it nothing was found except wrappings, ibid., 402. — How Christ’s burial was removed from their midst, id., II, 629. — On his death, burial, and resurrection. Lactantius, VI, 510. — What his tomb was like, VI, 512. — How many days he remained in the tomb, VI, 535. — Christ’s body was subject to death, but not liable to corruption. St. Hilary, IX, 820. — Christ’s burial, ibid., 935. — How Christ was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, id., XIV, 802, 803, 1122, 1123. — A comparison of the burials of Christ and Moses, ibid., 320. — Christ’s tomb is not without miracle: by a certain new work, he himself dead opened the tombs of the dead, id., XVI, 828. — The conqueror of death had no tomb of his own, and why, ibid., 269, 270. — Why the New Testament is recalled in Christ’s burial. St. Augustine, XL, 187. — By resting from his works on the seventh day, God wished to foretell the day on which Christ would rest in burial, id., XXXIV, 305. — How Christ was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, ibid., 87. — At the same time Christ’s body was in the tomb and his soul in hell, etc., id., XXXIX, 2178. — Christ’s tomb, a womb, ibid., 2204. — Why he was placed in another’s tomb, ibid., 2205. — In the tomb he did not abandon his flesh by dying with it, id., XLII, 1169. — Christ in the tomb, in hell, and in heaven, id., 2083. — How Christ was three days and three nights in the tomb. Eugyppius, LXII, 764, 765. — The humanity of the Son of God was neither wholly in the tomb nor wholly in hell, but his divinity was wholly everywhere. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 299. — Christ’s body did not undergo corruption, not because of incorruptibility, but because of the swiftness of the resurrection, ibid., 495. — Christ lay in the tomb according to the flesh; he descended into hell according to the soul; he remained according to divinity, ibid., 525, 526. — Christ’s burial called into doubt in Spain. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 690. — The time of Christ’s burial shortened for the disciples’ sake, ibid., 387. — On Christ’s burial. St. Hildefonsus, XCVI, 132. — How Christ is said to have been three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Alcuin, CI, 1211. — He lay in the tomb according to the flesh alone; he descended into hell according to the soul alone, ibid., 47, 48. — Christ was in the tomb for forty hours, id., CIX, 1152. — How Christ’s body was in the tomb for three days and three nights. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 182.

## XXII.—On Christ’s Descent into Hell

By dying, Christ descended to the souls of the prophets and patriarchs. Tertullian, II, 657. — Christ was not to remain in hell. St. Cyprian, IV, 716. — Christ entered the infernal regions. St. Hilary, IX, 346, 473, 289, 572. — As man, he descended into hell, ibid., 803. — He penetrates hell in order to bring the dead thence back alive. St. Zeno, XI, 403. — Christ descended into hell so that those who were in hell might be released from everlasting chains. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1129. — Christ penetrated the infernal regions, but, incorrupt, escaped corruption, XVI, 300. — Although dead according to his humanity, he was nevertheless free among those very infernal regions, ibid., 1344. — How Christ preached to the dead, id., XVII, 143. — “He descended into hell” is absent from the creed of the Roman Church. Rufinus, XXI, 356. — Christ’s descent into hell demonstrated, ibid., 363, 364. — Christ descended into hell. St. Jerome, XXV, 936, 940, 1124. — Why he descended, id., XXVI, 498; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 710, 711, 715. — Why, id., XLI, 541. — Christ was in hell according to his soul, id., XXXIII, 833. — Whether Christ descended to the place of punishments, ibid., 834. — Christ descended even to those places where sinners are tormented, id., XXXIV, 481. — In hell he aided certain persons, id., XXXVIII, 436. — He released some from torments, ibid., 834; XXXIX, 481. — A certain heresy holds that, when Christ descended into hell, unbelievers believed and thereafter all were freed, id., XLII, 45. — Some think that Christ released from hell those who had not heard the Gospel, id., XXXIII, 714. — It is rash to define whom he released from hell, id., XXXV, 1697. — Christ, penetrating hell and ascending thence victorious over death, performed a great miracle for the dead, id., XXXVII, 1115. — Christ descended into hell, id., XXXIX, 2204; XLII, 1172; XXXIX, 2059, 2189. — There he bound the devil and freed those detained there, ibid., 2195; XL, 391, 1193, 1194. — He was in hell for thirty-six hours, ibid., 742. — The eternal night of hell experienced Christ descending as the liberator of those whom it already held. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 597. — He was free among the dead, because alone among mortals he had no cause for dying, ibid., 616. — On Christ’s descent into hell and what he did there. Gennadius of Marseille, LVIII, 1047, 1048. — “I still inquire whether he saved all the damned whom Christ found in hell, or some whom he judged worthy of that benefit,” says St. Augustine, LVIII, 1047. — Christ reached all the way to hell. Eugyppius, LXVII, 710. — Whether Christ truly descended into hell, and whether to every place of hell, even where the damned are tormented. Prudentius, LIX, 810. — The divinity abandoned neither Christ’s flesh in the tomb nor his soul in hell. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 287. — Christ’s soul did not suffer in hell, ibid., 295. — Christ’s descent was not local, ibid., 246. — Christ freed his own soul from hell. Cassiodorus, LXIX, 316. — Christ’s soul drawn forth from hell, id., LXX, 203. — In what sense Christ is said to have descended into corruption, ibid., 115. — When he descended into hell, whom Christ freed thence. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 869, 870. — Some have thought, along with Augustine, that Christ descending into hell also freed the damned from eternal punishments, ibid. — Christ descended into hell neither in his divinity nor in his flesh, but in his soul. St. Hildefonsus, XCVI, 132. — Christ led forth companies of souls from hell. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1212, 1213; CXII, 167. — When Christ descended into hell, whom he freed. Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 282. — Greeks and Latins believe that the Lord descended into hell. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 317. — The Nicene Creed does not say that the Lord descended into hell, ibid.

## XXIII.—On Christ’s Resurrection

Christ rose on the third day after his death. Tertullian, I, 401 ff. — Afterwards he appeared to his disciples, ibid., 402, 492. — Nothing is clearer than the reality of Christ’s body after his resurrection, id., II, 466. — On Christ’s journey to Galilee after the resurrection. Lactantius, VI, 514. — The risen Christ appeared to Mary Magdalene. Marius Victorinus, VIII, 1110. — Christ rose by his own power. St. Hilary, IX, 844, 361. — After the resurrection he was seen in the same body, ibid., 806. — Christ’s body passed through solid things, id., X, 362, 89. — Christ’s resurrection brought hope of overcoming death and admitted humanity to the rewards of immortality. St. Zeno, XI, 341. — Christ was born by his own authority, died by his own will, slept by his own power, and is himself the author of his resurrection. St. Ambrose, XIV, 680. — The first and greatest foundation of faith is belief in Christ’s resurrection. St. Ambrose, XIV, 670, 1134; XV, 1846. — Christ is Lord because he redeemed servants; he is God because he raised himself, id., 1096. — Christ was raised not by another’s aid and help, but raised himself, XIV, 1096. — Christ was raised not by another’s aid and help, but raised himself, id., XVI, 1274. — Why he is the firstborn from the dead, ibid., 1080. — From the resurrection Christ is known as Lord of all, id., XVII, 50. — All that the Savior taught he confirmed when he rose from the dead, ibid., 379. — After the resurrection he appeared to Peter alone, ibid., 261. — Christ took up his soul in the resurrection. St. Jerome, XXII, 797. — After the resurrection he had all his members, ibid., 901. — Christ’s resurrection, St. Augustine, XL, 187; XLI, 584, 587, 592. — The Manichaeans say that Christ’s resurrection was imaginary, id., XLII, 488, 459. — Christ’s resurrection ought not to have been delayed long, id., XXXIII, 548. — Nor was his flesh to be reserved for the final resurrection, ibid., 554. — Christ raised himself, and the Father raised him, ibid., 1399; XXXVI, 452, 666; XXXVII, 1442. — Christ died by power and rose by power, XXXVIII, 1399. — On the cross Christ showed patience; in the resurrection, power, id., XL, 665. — Christ’s body rose such as it had been placed in the tomb, ibid., 394. — Before Christ no one rose eternally, XXXVII, 1642, 1701. — How Christ is to be understood as now wholly God after the resurrection, id., XXXII, 622. — Faith believes both that Christ entered through closed doors after the resurrection and that, in being born, he came forth through his mother’s uncorrupted members, id., XXXVIII, 1010. — Among the Jews even today there is a report that Christ was taken out of the tomb by his disciples, ibid., 261. — Why his linen cloths and head-cloth were found in the tomb, id., XL, 60. — Why Christ’s resurrection was first announced by women to men, id., XXXVIII, 266, 1108. — Christ appears to Magdalene, ibid., 1148, 1154. — One should believe that the glory of Christ’s body when he rose was hidden from the disciples’ eyes rather than absent, id., XLI, 781. — Why he retained the scars of his body, id., XXXVIII, 539, 645, [Col. 0469] 658, 1140; XL, 647. — After the resurrection he showed scars, not wounds, to those who doubted, id., 372. — Those scars were not fictitious, ibid. — Why Christ suffered in the sight of all but did not rise in the sight of all, id., XXXIII, 548. — How after his resurrection he was recognized and not recognized, ibid., 643. — Christ may rightly be said to have feigned, id., XXXVIII, 556. — After the resurrection he associates with his disciples so that they may be confirmed in faith, ibid., 1212. — Why he spent forty days with the disciples after the resurrection, ibid., 1211, 1216. — After the resurrection he took food and drink, id., XLI, 395. — He ate by power and love, not necessity, id., XXXVIII, 659, 1360. — He had no need arising from hunger or thirst, id., XXXV, 1806. — Christ’s resurrection showed that nothing of human nature perishes, id., XXXIV, 135. — Christ’s birth and resurrection are his own proper and singular miracles, id., XLI, 314. — Christ’s resurrection: the glorification of Father and Son, id., XXXV, 1903. — Christ’s cross, burial, and resurrection are a figure of Christian life, id., XL, 257. — Christ’s resurrection is the hope of our resurrection, id., XXXVII, 1700. — By his Passion Christ showed what ought to be endured for truth; by his resurrection, what ought to be hoped for in eternity, id., XLI, 612. — We ought to place faith, hope, and love in Christ’s resurrection, id., XXXIV, 734. — Faith in Christ’s resurrection distinguishes Christians, id., XXXVIII, 1075, 1133. — Truly to wish to kill Christ is to extinguish the name of his resurrection, id., XXXVI, 694. — Why, in rising, he did not shine like the sun, id., XL, 738. — He always possesses the flesh in which he was born of the Virgin, ibid., 773. — He entered to the disciples while the doors were closed, id., XXXV, 2322. — By Christ’s resurrection all rise, id., XLVIII, 141. — The resurrection was accomplished on the evening of the Sabbath, as the Lord’s Day dawned with the moon, id., XVII, ibid.; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1086. — Demonstrated by many arguments, ibid., 387. — What change took place in Christ’s flesh through the resurrection, ibid., 388. — In Christ’s resurrection the pattern of the transformation of our flesh went before us, ibid. — Why the disciples’ hesitation concerning the Lord’s resurrection was permitted, ibid., 394. — We die with Christ and rise with him when we believe in God and renounce the devil, ibid., 330. — Why he retained the marks of the nails and lance, ibid., 396. — His resurrection was all the more certain and marvelous inasmuch as the Jews’ treachery was more vigilant in guarding the tomb. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 591. — Christ’s resurrection must be maintained among the articles of faith, ibid., 777. — He appeared to Mary Magdalene and rebuked her because she doubted his resurrection, ibid., 359. — He entered to the apostles through closed doors and showed himself alive again to them, ibid., 597, 620. — He invited Thomas to touch his wounds, ibid. — He wished to retain the marks of the nails after the resurrection, so that the memory of his Passion might not be erased from us, ibid., 622. — Christ’s body did not undergo corruption, not because of incorruptibility, but because of the swiftness of the resurrection. St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 496. — Christ’s flesh did not undergo corruption in the tomb, nor did his soul suffer punishment in hell, id., LVII, 294. — What Christ’s body was like before the resurrection and what it is like now, from Augustine, id., LXV, 496. — Christ began the work of grace when conceived in the womb and completed it when raised from the tomb, ibid., 729. — Christ died because he was human; because he was God, he raised himself, ibid., 464. — After the resurrection Christ demonstrated the solidity of true flesh by real scars and by eating fish and honey, ibid., 464. — Christ’s divinity is proved by the resurrection. Cassiodorus, LXX, 779. — Why he ascended above the west by rising from the dead, ibid., 463. — The Lord’s resurrection is compared with sleep, ibid., 298. — By the resurrection divine power was declared and believers’ hope strengthened, id., LXV, 617. — It is the hope of Christians, id., LXX, 204. — Christ progressively revealed his resurrection to the disciples. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 573. — In rising Christ overcame the tongues of the Jews and the sword of the Gentiles, ibid., 749. — And he made the hope of his own people firm, ibid. — Job openly foretells Christ’s resurrection, ibid., 1074. — By rising, Christ showed the life which we do not know, id., LXXVI, 491. — How greatly Christ’s resurrection differs from ours, ibid., 288. — Christ’s resurrection is the pattern of ours, ibid., 1030. — Why Christ foretold his death and resurrection, ibid., 1082. — Christ’s rising from the tomb was a greater miracle than his descending from the cross, ibid., 1173. — The resurrection was foreshadowed in the sign of Samson and afterwards made manifest in deed, ibid. — What Christ’s final meal after the resurrection signifies, ibid., 1187. — Christ’s body was incorruptible and tangible, ibid., 1198. — He rose on the third day. Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 247. — Christ was handed over after evening on Thursday, crucified on Friday, rested in the tomb on Saturday, and rose on the eighth day, ibid., 555. — Christ rose on the eighth day. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 604. — When Christ rose from the dead, the Jewish solemnities were fulfilled; the old things passed away and all things became new, ibid., 628. — After his resurrection Christ was incapable of suffering. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 632. — His resurrection requires us to pass to a better life, ibid., 281.

## XXIV.—On Christ’s Ascension and His Sitting at the Right Hand of the Father
Christ’s flesh: whether in heaven it is devoid of sensation. Tertullian, II, 792.—How he ascended into heaven. Lactantius, VI, 195.—Christ, in that he was bodily raised up, sits at the right hand of God. St. Hilary, IX, 806.—Christ carried back to heaven the substance of the body he assumed, united to his Spirit, ibid., 935.—He ascended to heaven, with the heavenly powers and the souls of the saints preceding him on his way, ibid., 462.—Ascending on high, he took away those held captive by the devil, ibid., 456.—Christ descended from heaven pure; he ascended into heaven incarnate. St. Zeno, XI, 404.—Having accomplished and brought to completion all mysteries, he opened the way to heaven for all who follow him, ibid., 433.—He ascended above all heavens to God’s throne, and how. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1048.—God descended; man ascended, id., XV, 1225.—Christ’s ascension is proclaimed. Rufinus, XXI, 367.—How Christ ascended above the heavens. St. Jerome, XXVI, 499.—Why Christ, after his resurrection, withdrew his presence from the world. St. Augustine, XLIV, 182.—Christ ascended lest the disciples remain in the flesh, id., XXXVIII, 1212.—Christ’s resurrection and ascension, ibid., 1070.—Christ’s two glorifications, ibid., 1222.—Christ’s glorification is recognized in the resurrection and the ascension into heaven, id., XXXIV, 595.—Christ’s ascent into heaven, id., XL, 187.—That Christ ascended bodily into heaven, id., XXXVIII, 1210.—How Christ alone ascended into heaven, id., XXXV, 1488; XXXVIII, 570, 789, 1341; XLIV, 144.—The credibility of Christ’s resurrection and bodily ascension into heaven is demonstrated, id., XLI, 755.—And what is already believed is shown, ibid., 756.—Many miracles bore witness to Christ’s ascension, ibid., 760.—Christ’s ascension: a great and salutary miracle, ibid.—Christ descended to us out of mercy; he ascended to the Father out of justice, id., XXXVIII, 789.—The ascension of Christ the Lord should be celebrated in such a way that we may ascend with him, ibid., 1202.—The Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven sustain our faith, id., XXXIV, 24.—Christ ascended into heaven so that, as head from the heights, he might assist the members labouring on earth, id., XXXVIII, 932.—Christ, by ascending, raises us up, to whom he descended when we had fallen, id., XXXVI, 203.—The Lord was on the cross in the evening, in the resurrection in the morning, and in the ascension at midday, ibid., 640.—How Christ goes to prepare dwelling-places that already existed in the Father’s house, id., XXXV, 1814.—How highly Christ’s last words when ascending into heaven ought to be valued, ibid., 2061.—Prophecy of Christ’s ascension, id., XXXVIII, 1208.—The footprints of Christ’s feet on the Mount of Olives, id., XXXV, 1735.—The Gentiles did not understand how an earthly body could be in heaven, id., XL, 188.—That Christ’s very body was raised into heaven, ibid., 304.—How Christ is now believed to be in heaven, id., XXXIII, 833.

Christ’s session at the right hand of the Father, XXXVIII, 1075.—As man he sits at the Father’s right hand; as God he is wholly present everywhere, id., XL, 658.—How Christ’s session at the Father’s right hand is to be understood, ibid., 188, 304.—Christ sits at God’s right hand while retaining the same nature of flesh in which he was born and suffered, id., XLV, 1717, 1732.—Christ ascended into heaven by his own power. Cassian, L, 244, 245.—Christ had to ascend in the form of a servant. Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 908, 1045.—Christ ascended into heaven according to his whole humanity. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 526.—Christ’s ascension is signified by the name of the eagle. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 625.—The difference between Christ’s ascent into heaven and Elijah’s being taken up, ibid., 1216.—Christ, in ascending into heaven, did not use the ministry of angels, ibid.—Christ reigning in heaven: how he can at once stand and sit, ibid., 1217.—What profit we derive from Christ’s ascension, ibid., 1218.—Whom Christ, ascending, led captive in captivity, ibid.—We ought to follow the Lord ascending into heaven, ibid., 1219.—How the Lord, ascending into heaven, went to the wedding, ibid., 1124.—On the ascension of Christ’s body. St. Hildf., XCVI, 133.—He ascended into heaven according to his whole humanity. Alcuin, C, 434. Sermon on Christ’s ascension. Otto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 845; Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 734, 740; Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1888, 1917, 1922; Peter Alphonsi, CLVII, 650; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 863, 1043; Hildebert of Le Mans, [Col. 0471] CLXXI, 580 ff.; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 309, 394, 1152.

## XXV.—On Christ’s glory, power, various offices, and titles

From his passion onward, Christ began to reign. Tertullian, II, 628.—Christ’s kingdom and name extend everywhere, ibid., 611.—He is believed everywhere; in every nation he reigns and is worshipped, ibid.—The glory of Christ’s body. St. Hilary, X, 423.—The glory of the Son of Man, id., X, 426.—Christ merited glory not because he created heaven, but because he was made in the form of a servant, ibid., 593, 594.—What his glory with the Father is, ibid., 310, 311.—The different degrees of Christ’s glory, ibid., 426, 427.—Christ’s authority. St. Augustine, XLI, 589, 593, 594, 595.—Christ was praised even by those who did not believe in him, id., XXXVII, 1370.—Pagans honour Christ as supremely wise, but deny that he is God, id., XXXII, 636.—Pagans did not dare to blaspheme Christ, id., XXXVII, 1243.—Christ’s first glory was to enter the tabernacle without stain. Cassiodorus, LXX, 109.—When Christ was crowned with glory and honour, ibid., 77.—Christ sits at the Father’s right hand, not because he is greater than the Father, but lest he be thought less than the Father. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 370.—He holds primacy over all things and is lord of the whole earth, ibid., 617.—Christ’s resurrection is glory. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 617.—Christ’s power is the glory of his resurrection, ibid., 624.—Before death Christ fled glory; after death he wished to be known, ibid., 384.—How he has been glorified and is to be glorified. Alcuin, C, 914, 915, 959.—The nature of the glorification of the Son of God. Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 910; CX, 228.—Christ crowned with glory and honour. St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 498, 499.—The humanity of Christ: brightness in heaven. St. Anselm, CLVIII, 605.—Jesus alone is in the Father’s glory, ibid., 611.—Christ’s glorying is in humility alone. St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 821.—Whether Christ in glory feeds among the lilies, id., CLXXXIII, 1129.—Christ is gentle and lovable in exile, just and terrible in judgment, glorious and wonderful in his kingdom, ibid., 148.—God gave the Son authority to judge as man, and why, ibid., 1136.—The whole world is Christ’s dominion by right of creation, by the merit of redemption, and by the Father’s gift, ibid., 758. Glorification at the Jordan, on Mount Tabor, and in heaven, ibid., 1152.—Christ as man is greater than the angels, ibid., 1138.—More people desire his glory than his cross, ibid., 873.

Christ’s proper office was to bring knowledge of God. St. Hilary, IX, 1046.—To preach the Father and fulfil his will, ibid., 806.—The greatest work was to reveal the Father to us as Father, not as his own Creator, id., X, 90.—How Christ intercedes for us. St. Ambrose, XVII, 129.—Christ prays for us as our priest; prays in us as our head; and is prayed to by us as our God. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1081.—Christ who intercedes for us with the Father. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 238.—Christ prays for the Church, LXXIX, 602.—The head prays for the members: Christ for the Church, ibid., 642.—How he intercedes. St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 76.—Christ the High Priest. Christ, High Priest of God the Father. Tertullian, II, 447.—God’s own and lawful high priest, ibid., 493.—High priest of eternal sacrifices, ibid., 609.—Christ Jesus, in the very sacrament of his name, the true and supreme priest of the Father, ibid., 330.—Christ, priest of the Most High God. St. Cyprian, IV, 376, 383.—On the priesthood of Jesus foretold by the prophets. Lactantius, VI, 487.—Christ, eternal king and priest, possesses, even in his carnal birth, the glory of both kinds. St. Hilary, IX, 919.—Christ, prince of priests. St. Ambrose, XVI, 671.—He is a new priest, ibid., 1141.—He did not demand but received the priesthood, ibid., 1202.—Melchizedek prefigured Christ’s priesthood. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 769.—Christ’s priesthood and kingdom foretold in Samuel and David, id., XLII, 271.—Christ, the priest through whom we propitiate God, id., XLI, 280.—Christ is, both in his humanity and according to the humanity he assumed, priest and sacrifice, ibid., 298, 313.—Christ alone is the high priest who had no need to offer sacrifice for his own sins, id., XLIV, 162.—Christ, our priest at the Father’s right hand, id., XLIII, 59.—Christ: priest and victim, propitiator and propitiation. St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 381.—Christ, at once victim and priest, instituted for the new people a new priesthood and a new sacrifice. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 595.—Christ is priest by right because he is encompassed by weakness, namely human nature. Eugyppius, LXV, 294.—Christ prays because he is priest, ibid., 759.—Christ’s new priesthood excluded the old. St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 105, 106.—Christ: prophet and priest. Alcuin, CI, 1128, [Col. 0472] 1129.—Christ is the true High Priest and Apostle of our confession. Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 298.—Christ’s priesthood remains for ever. St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 538.

Christ the King; Christ alone, the new king of new ages. Tertullian, II, 348.—Christ began to reign from his passion onward, ibid., 628.—Christ’s kingdom and name extend everywhere, ibid., 611.—Christ king for ever. St. Cyprian, IV, 720.—He is called Prince by the prophets. Lactantius, VI, 452. “To him was given kingdom and honour and dominion, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him,” ibid., 482.—On his earthly kingdom: Lactantius’s error, VI, 465, 808, 1013.—Christ the King. St. Hilary, IX, 311, 275, 276.—What Christ’s temporal kingdom is. St. Zeno, XI, 405.—What kingdom it is that Christ received from the Father and handed over to the Father. St. Ambrose, XVI, 677, 678.—The true king of peace, the true king of justice, ibid., 1202.—Christ, king of the city toward which we journey. St. Augustine, XL, 1101.—In Christ’s kingdom we shall reign with Christ; but we by adoption, he by power; we by grace, he by nature, XVI, 812, 813.—Christ’s eternal kingdom. Rufinus, XXI, 370.—Christ’s kingdom described in different senses. St. Augustine, XL, 76, 77, 78.—How Christ’s kingdom was spread among all nations, id., XXXVI, 389.—All creation is subject to Christ. Cassiodorus, LXX, 75.—King for ever, ibid., 437, 438.—Almighty King, ibid., 672.—King appointed by the Father, ibid., 38.—Why he is king, ibid., 530.—Christ entered this world especially as king, ibid., 471.—Christ reigning in heaven gathers his elect to himself. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 631.—How Christ reigning in heaven can at once stand and sit, LXXVI, 1216, 1217.—In what sense he is King of Israel. Alcuin, C, 910.—Christ the King: the character of his kingdom, id., C, 976.—Christ did not come to take away a kingdom, but to give one, ibid.—The character of the kingdoms of Christ and Solomon. Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 414, 480.—Christ’s kingdom was established when the synagogue, that is, Jewish dominion, fell. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 602, 688.—Christ the King in glory. St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 102, 103.—How Christ reigns in the house of Jacob for ever, id., CLXXXIII, 79.

Christ the mediator.—Christ, mediator between us and the Father. St. Cyprian, IV, 704.—How Christ had to come in order to be mediator of God and human beings. Lactantius, VI, 524.—The middle one between God and man, ibid., 972.—Christ: who the mediator is. St. Hilary, IX, 988; X, 248, 283, 414.—Christ, the one mediator of God and human beings. St. Augustine, XXXII, 601; XXXVI, 216; XXXVII, 1159, 1741; XXXVIII, 310, 503, 680, 1332.—What is required for this mediation, id., XLI, 268, 271.—Christ is mediator not because he is God, but because he is man, XXXV, 1842.—The grace of Christ the mediator is commended, ibid., 1843.—Christ’s mediation was necessary, id., XXXIV, 1070.—Christ, mediator of God and human beings, harmonizing us between divine and human things, etc. St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 202.—Christ, mediator for human beings with God. Vigilius of Thapsus, LXVII, 144, 145, 146.—How he is mediator of God and human beings, ibid., 594, 595.—Christ, mediator of human beings because of the union of the natures. St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 238.—Christ is mediator of God and human beings. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 613; LXXVI, 237.—The faith of the righteous in both Testaments is one faith in the Mediator, ibid., 977, 985.—Job desires a mediator, seeking freedom from sin, LXXV, 836, 880.—Christ the mediator. Venerable Bede, XCII, 885; XCIV, 121; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 683.—Christ is called mediator of God and human beings, id., CXXXIII, 329, 330; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 436, 437.—Christ was incarnate so that, as man, he might be mediator between God and human beings. Lanfranc, CL, 273.

Advocate.—Christ our advocate. St. Cyprian, IV, 213; St. Ambrose, XVI, 1141; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1062, 1370.—Christ is advocate only for those who believe in him, id., XL, 223.—Christ is advocate. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 853.

Physician.—Christ our physician. St. Augustine, XXXV, 1397, 2054; XXXVIII, 1370; the great physician, id., 945.—Christ, the Samaritan coming to the aid of the wounded man, id., 933.—Christ, the physician who first drinks the cup for the sick person, id., 542, 781.

Teacher.—Christ the true teacher. St. Augustine, XL, 678.—Christ is truly the good teacher because he is God, XXXII, 855.—The good teacher, teaching what it is useful to know, XXXVIII, 1221.—Christ’s entire life was moral instruction, by which we are taught what should be sought and what avoided, id., XXXIV, 135.

Bridegroom of the Church; head, etc.—Christ, bridegroom of the virgin Church. St. Jerome, XXIV, 697; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 820.—Head of the Church. St. Ambrose, XVI, 685.—Cornerstone. St. Jerome, XXVI, 476.—Christ [Col. 0473], truly the rock set in the midst of things. Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1064.—Head of the Church, of all the righteous, and of the angels. St. Augustine, XXXVI, 385, 749, 786.—Christ, the strength of the Church. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 734.—Christ is our head, id., LXXVI, 845; St. Agobard, CIV, 62, 64.—Bridegroom of the Church, ibid., 110, 189.—Whether Christ, according to his humanity, was head of the saints who preceded the Incarnation. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 582.

Other various titles.—Christ, enlightener of the human race. Tertullian, I, 395.—The one hope of the whole world, id., II, 760.—Christ is called an angel, id., III, 925.—The true sun. St. Cyprian, IV, 542.—The way and the truth, ibid., 750.—The bread of life, ibid., 731.—The house and temple of God, ibid., 686.—Christ the lamb, ibid., 708.—Redeemer. St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 726.—The sole Saviour, ibid., 1061.—The new Adam. St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 239.—Husbandman. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 722.—Fountain of life. St. Columbanus, LXXX, 254.—Mystical interpretation of the principal titles and names of Christ, ibid., 327 ff.—Moral explanation of the same names of Christ and their significance, ibid., 333 ff.—Christ is called a lion because he defeated the devil. Alcuin, C, 1121.—Prophet, id., C, 725.—Truth. St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 800.—Splendid epithets of Christ. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 631, 750, 949, 713, 588, 590.—The good shepherd. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 532.—The names of Christ described by Isaiah are explained. St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 829.

## XXVI.—Christ’s satisfaction and merit

Christ alone can grant pardon for sins committed by us. St. Cyprian, IV, 480.—He suffered for us and bore our sins; God delivered him up for our sins, ibid.—All things were purchased at the price of Christ’s blood. St. Hilary, IX, 396.—Christ, our propitiation, ibid., 415.—Our redemption, ibid., 1002.—There is no salvation without Christ, id., X, 37.—Because of the merit of obedience, Christ is advanced, by the force of judgment, to the salvation expressed in God’s name, so that God’s name and power may be in him, id., IX, 340.—To Christ as man are granted God’s name, kingdom, and honour; they are granted because of obedience, ibid., 795.—Christ merited glory not because he created heaven, but because he was made in the form of a servant, ibid., 594.—Christ himself was made sin for us, so that we might become in him God’s righteousness—we who were death’s captivity and the serpent’s prey. St. Ambrose, XIV, 1012.—By this “sin” (Christ), the eternal God absolved us: he did not spare his own Son, and made him to be sin for us, ibid.—He offered his death for the death of all, and shed his blood for the blood of all, XVI, 1115.—He is the Lamb, yet one of divine power, who not only cleansed the offences of all by his blood, but also bestowed divine power, ibid., 1224.—He paid blood; you owe blood; he paid it for you—pay it back for yourself, ibid., 299.—Christ came as remission of sins, redemption of captives, aid of the weary. St. Ambrose, XV, 1440.—Christ alone could redeem humanity, id., XIV, 1160.—As Christ is redemption, so he is mercy, ibid., 1152.—He accepted slavery to death in order to grant you the freedom of eternal life, ibid., 1467.—Christ’s blood is purple, which dyes the souls of the saints and makes them kings, ibid., 1447.—Christ bore the world’s offences in a crown of thorns. St. Jerome, XXII, 557.—By his wound he healed our wounds, id., XXIV, 507.—Christ alone had the likeness of sinful flesh without being sinful flesh. St. Augustine, XLV, 1384, 1385.—Christ, though without sin, was nevertheless made sin, id., XL, 252.—He made our offences his offences, in order to make our righteousness his righteousness, id., XXXVI, 172.—In Christ: wholeness without sin, repayment without debt, scourging without desert, ibid., 463.—Apart from the one mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, there is salvation for no one. St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 83, 84.—Crucified for the redemption of the whole world, ibid., 165.—Christ died for all. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 323.—Even for the unjust and ungodly, ibid., 312.—As all things were created through Christ and in Christ, so all things are reconciled through him and in him. St. Fulgentius, LXV, 492.—Christ is priest and victim, and through his death we have been reconciled, ibid., 424.—By suffering, Christ rebuked human guilt and appeased God’s wrath. St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 894.—Why Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s, ibid., 1029.—Christ is the propitiation for our sins, id., LXXIX, 636.—Whether Christ suffered for all who died before his coming. St. Remigius of Lyons, CXXI, 1122.—He died for all who believe and will believe, ibid., 1013. Through Christ’s blood we were delivered from the angel who devastates the world, that is, the devil. Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 555, [Col. 0474] 556.—Christ discharged both original and actual sin. Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 121.—Christ, the victim offered for sin, was called “sin.” St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 57.—Christ appeased the Father by himself, not by sacrifices. Guibert, CLVI, 522.—All hope is in Christ’s passion and merits. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 864.—After Adam’s sin no one is admitted to God’s kingdom except through Christ’s death, id., CLVIII, 457.—It is necessary that God-man should make that satisfaction, ibid., 404, 414.—Christ offered himself as sacrifice for us. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 71, 72.—By his blood Christ reconciled the whole human race to God the Father. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 250.—By his satisfaction Christ restored to us our original possession, ibid., 863. Christ paid more in punishment than guilt deserved. Rupert of Deutz, CLXII, 1612.—What Christ merited. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1104, 1105.—On the satisfaction to be offered to God for the injury caused by original sin. Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1131.—Whether Christ merited anything. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 578.—Peter Lombard, CXCII, 793 ff.—How reason infers that the mediator of God and human beings had to be true God and true man. Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1003, 1004.—For the fullness of satisfaction, the humiliation in expiation had to be as great as the presumption had been in transgression, ibid.—Christ did not merit the hypostatic union. Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 625, 626.—Christ’s single offering of himself was sufficient for the redemption of the whole human race. Peter Cantor, CCV, 102. All Christ’s works were equally meritorious. Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1190.

## XXVII.—Various errors concerning Christ’s person

Marcion dared to destroy Christ’s original documents. Tertullian, II, 755.—The Marcionites maintained that Christ was a phantom, ibid., II, 331.—Marcion said that the Christ who appeared under Tiberius was one person, while the Christ promised by the Creator was another, ibid., 264, 368.—The Jews deny to this day that Christ has come, ibid., 331.—Why, ibid.—Heretics say that Christ was compelled by Mary to undergo baptism. St. Cyprian, III, 1202.—The Jews regarded Christ as a magician, ibid., 580.—Error concerning Christ’s kingdom. Lactantius, VI, 465, 808, 1013.—The Jews say that he works miracles by demonic power, ibid., 485, 491.—The Arians do not dare openly to deny that Christ is God. St. Hilary, X, 238.—By what device the Arians insinuate that Christ is not true God, ibid., 131.—How the Arians prove Christ to be the Son of God against Sabellius, ibid., 203, 204. Those who say that Christ is not Wisdom itself but a work of wisdom are refuted, id., IX, 982 ff.—Some attribute sorrow, fear, and so forth to Christ’s divinity; they are refuted, ibid., 1066.—Those who say that the divinity and flesh of the Lord are one nature are authors of error. St. Ambrose, XVI, 831. Those who think that the Lord Jesus did not assume a soul are refuted, ibid., 834.—Those who say that Christ could not be born of the Virgin are refuted, ibid., 1124, 1128.—Christ did not, as some say, suffer in a phantom body, ibid., 830.—Pagans said that Christ was nothing other than a human being, though one of exceptional wisdom. St. Augustine, XXXII, 636; XXXIV, 1048, 1069, 1071.—Some dared to say that Christ learned his teachings from Plato’s books, ibid., 56.—The heretic Marcus asserted that Christ suffered not truly but only in appearance, id., XLII, 28.—Cerdon taught that Christ was neither born of a woman nor possessed flesh, ibid., 29.—The Cerinthians said that Christ was merely human, ibid., 27.—The Ophites hold Christ to be a serpent, ibid., 28, 29.—Some say that the Sabellians considered Christ to be Shem’s son, ibid., 29.—Errors of the Manichaeans, Photinians, and Apollinarians concerning Christ’s Incarnation, id., XLV, 1033, 1034.—The Photinians maintain that Christ is merely man, the Manichaeans merely God, id., XLIII, 229; XXXV, 1663.—The Manichaeans call Christ the serpent of paradise, id., XLII, 37, 38.—The Manichaeans said that Christ is not only fixed, bound, and concreted in heaven and the stars, but also on earth and in everything born upon it, id., XLII, 211, 212, 379.—They thought it unworthy to believe that Christ was born from a womb, ibid., 178, 213, 217.—They seek to assert that Christ had no mother, id., XXXVI, 129.—The Origenists introduce Christ as a creature, id., XLII, 33.—What the Arians thought concerning Christ, ibid., 680, 681, 686, 687.—The Noetians maintain that Christ himself is both Father and Son and Holy Spirit, ibid., 32.—The Proclianists deny that Christ came in the flesh, ibid., 41, 42.—And so do all heretics, [Col. 0475] id., XXXVIII, 989.—The error of some who deny that Christ’s body was formed from a woman, and think that it was made as was that body in which the Holy Spirit appeared as a dove, id., XL, 302.—The Arians and Apollinarians teach that Christ assumed flesh without a soul, XLII, 39, 40, 686 ff.—Some heretics believed that in Christ the Word was in place of the soul, others in place of the human mind, id., XXXIII, 833.—The Apollinarians dogmatized that Christ did not assume a rational soul, id., XXXV, 1737; XLI, 404.—It is rash to say that a rational soul came to Christ after he had already been born, XXXIII, 552. The Apollinarians teach that Christ’s flesh was not assumed from Mary’s flesh and that something of the Word was changed into flesh, id., XLII, 40.—Apelles taught that Christ did not lay aside flesh from heaven but received it from the elements of the world, ibid., 30.—The Ebionites say that Christ has not risen but will rise, ibid., 27.—Some have thought that in Christ the human form is to be changed into divine substance, ibid., 708.—After Valentinus and Marcion, Eutyches said that Christ’s flesh was assumed not from the Virgin but from heaven. Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 111.—Eutyches asserted that the divinity suffered, ibid., 106. The Priscillianists maintain that Christ is a liar, ibid., 846.—Some heretics called Christ a mere man. St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 88. Errors in Germany concerning Christ’s birth. Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 83 ff.—Faustus’s errors concerning Christ’s generation. Paschasius, CXX, 97, 98 ff.
