Prudentius and Gottschalk said that Christ did not suffer for all, CXXV, 312, 313, 370. Several patriarchs of Constantinople denied that there were two wills and operations in Christ. Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 738, 739.—Jewish errors concerning the Messiah. Blessed Odo of Cambrai, CLX, 1103.

## XXVIII.—On our duties toward Jesus Christ

Christ alone is to be heard. St. Cyprian, IV, 383.

Nothing is to be preferred to Christ, ibid., 529, 655, 660, 746.

To put on Christ, id., III, 1166; IV, 416, 504, 628.

Christ wishes always to be sought, and to be found more frequently. St. Ambrose, XV, 1366.

[Col. 0476] Christ loves to be sought long and often, id., XVI, 287, 354.

Where Christ is to be sought, id., XVI, 279, 353.—How he is to be sought, id., XVII, 671.

What it is to put on Christ, id., XVII, 166.

We follow him when we imitate him, ibid., 800.

We must love him more than father, ibid., 685.

Without invoking him, no one lives with God, ibid., 144.

Who would not praise Christ, by whose benefaction he lives? ibid., 70.

Let us imitate his manner of life, though we cannot imitate his birth. St. Jerome, XXIII, 221.

Follow naked the naked Christ, ibid., 548.

We should imitate Christ not in the power of miracles, but in endurance of sufferings. St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1149.

Why Christ’s death should not make us ashamed, id., XXXVIII, 1278, 1279.

Christ is to be loved, ibid., 727.—To be loved above all things, XXXVI, 222.

The godly love Christ freely; the ungodly hate him freely, id., XXXVII, 1432.

What it is to have Christ as foundation, id., XL, 155, 264.—To have Christ as foundation is to prefer nothing to him, id., XLI, 743.

What it is to come to Christ, id., XLIV, 888.—To come to Christ is to believe, ibid., 553.

All, even heretics, teach that Christ is to be believed, id., XLII, 86.

Christ is to be imitated. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 50, 269.

Some do not follow Christ but flee him; some do not follow but run ahead of him; some follow but do not overtake him, id., 688.

How shameful it is not to run after Christ, and by what motives we are stirred up to this running, ibid., 881.

One must live for Christ, id., CLXXXII, 300.—Whoever refuses to live for Christ is worthy of death, id., CLXXXIII, 867.

Christ is grasped not by reading, but by following him, id., CLXXXIII, 867.

One must cling to Christ the head, id., CLXXXIII, 168.

## LXIX. INDEX CONCERNING THE NAME JESUS, ITS EXCELLENCE AND POWER, AND MIRACLES WROUGHT BY INVOKING IT, ARRANGED ANALOGICALLY

### NOTICE

This index treats:

I. The origin of the name Jesus.  
II. The meaning of the name Jesus.  
III. The excellence and power of the name Jesus.  
IV. Miracles wrought through the power of this name.  
V. The use of this name and the honour rendered to it.  
VI. The necessity of invoking it.  
VII. Various short works treating of the name Jesus.

### Concerning the Name Jesus

[Col. 0483]

**1. The origin of the name Jesus.**—Before his own coming among the people of Israel, the name Jesus was, as it were, shut up in a vessel within the minds of the Jews: St Ambrose, XVI, 727.—Jesus was called by this name on the day of his circumcision; why this was so: Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 56.—God gave Jesus the name which is, etc.: Elipandus, XCVI, 877.—The name Jesus was announced beforehand by the angel to the Virgin: “and you shall call his name Jesus.” Alcuin, CI, 151.—But if anyone asks when his name was spoken by the angel before he was conceived in the womb, it was undoubtedly when the angel said to Mary: “Hail, etc.” Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 93.—Not only was this most holy name spoken by the angel before he was conceived in the womb, but it was also foretold long beforehand to the patriarchs and prophets that the Son of God, having become man, would be called by this name, ibid.—“His name endures before the sun”: St Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 332.—The designation Jesus, which it was not fitting that men should first utter into the world, but rather some loftier and more excellent nature: St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 852.—For all the prophets either did not know this name or kept wholly silent concerning it; and the dignity of this prerogative was reserved for the archangel Gabriel, who first disclosed it with holy mouth to the most holy Virgin, ibid.—The name by which he was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 133.—This has been his name from eternity, ibid., 136.—This name is innate to him, not conferred by a human or angelic creature, ibid.—It was not fitting that men should first utter it into the world, but rather some loftier nature. Id., CLXXXIV, 832.—The name was bestowed by the angel on the Son of God because, etc.: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1304.

[Col. 0484]

**II. The meaning of the name Jesus.**—The outpouring of this name signifies a certain abundant overflow of graces and a lavish bestowal of heavenly goods. St Ambrose, XVI, 727.—Jesus in Hebrew, **Σωτήρ** (“Saviour”) in Greek, *Salvator* (“Saviour”) in Latin: St Augustine, XLII, 1025.—Jesus is interpreted “Saviour,” or “Saving”: id., XXXVIII, 944, 1334, 1370; XLI, 553, 785; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 793, 866, 940, 1040, 1064, 1171, 1208.—The name Jesus, the name of triumph: St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 367.—Jesus is said in the Hebrew language; *Salvator* is said in Latin: ibid.; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1286; Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1165; Bede the Venerable, XCII, 1; XCIV, 34; St Beatus, XCVI, 911; Alcuin, CI, 177; Haymo, CXVIII, 33; St Paschasius, CXX, 112; Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII, 1133; St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 627, 639, 725; St Bruno, bishop, CLXIV, 777, 778; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 88; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1304; Garner, CXCIII, 230; Helinand, CCXII, 536; Innocent III, CCXVII, 577.

III. On the Excellence and Power of the Name of Jesus.—Apollo, struck by the name of Christ, is tormented and cannot endure the thunderbolts of the Word: Julius Firmicus Maternus, XII, 1015.—Nothing can be more excellent than the power of this name: St. Ambrose, XVI, 727.—The excellence of the name Jesus: St. Jerome, XXVI, 286.—Jesus died; his name will not perish: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 454.—The name of Jesus, which is for us the dearer and sweeter to pronounce: ibid., XLI, 591.—Through this name the Father’s splendor, honor, praise, wisdom, majesty, goodness, and mercy reign for ages: St. Prudentius, LIX, 831.—Jesus obtained from the Father the name above every name: ibid., 837.—In the mouth, Christ is nectar; on the tongue, honeycomb; in the throat, living ambrosia: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 741.—The name of Jesus can be as beneficial in grace as it was beneficial in the figure of the serpent: St. Caesarius of Arles, LXVII, 1047.—That which is above every name: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 233.—“In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, who gives me help, I shall overcome”: *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 290.—By the name of Christ we drive from possessed bodies the demons whom you worship and honor as gods: ibid., 404.—The name of my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, whom I have loved and love, is for me a most mighty wall: ibid., 289.—Even the unworthy and reprobate can work miracles in the name of Jesus: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 570.—The Father gave Jesus the name above every name: Bede the Venerable, XCIII, 1033, 1034.—Christ Jesus inherited the name above every name: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 408.—The name above every name belongs to the true God alone and to the true Son of God: ibid., 423.—The name of Jesus gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, running to the lame, speech to the mute, life to the dead; and the power of this name drove the entire power of the devil from possessed bodies: Alcuin, CI, 177.—The excellence of the name of Jesus: Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 37; CXII, 714, 728.—Whoever, without doubting in faith, persistently asks in the name of Jesus for those things which concern the salvation of his soul is undoubtedly heard: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 524.—Everyone who asks in the name of Jesus, etc., deserves to be heard: Servatus Lupus, CXIX, 698.—Saints Cosmas and Damian said: “We know no magic arts, and in the name of Jesus we despise the power of magic arts”: St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 367.—He drove away every disease through the power of the name of Jesus: St. Odo of Beauvais, CXXIV, 1117.—Uttering the name of Jesus Christ, he cast demons out of possessed bodies: ibid.—“He shall be given the name which is above every name”: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 712; Rupert, CLXVII, 1526, 1527.—Jesus wishes to be called by such a name because he knows that there is no other name in which the world can be saved: St. Odilo, abbot, CXLII, 994.—His holy and terrible name, which even that worthier nature scarcely dares to pronounce: St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 851.—Christ’s name gives light, nourishes, and anoints: ibid., 852.—Proclaimed, it gives light; pondered, it nourishes; invoked, it soothes and anoints: ibid.—The name Jesus, as Origen’s more noble tongue has defined it, is sweet and glorious, most worthy of every fragrance and honor: ibid.—The name of Jesus is honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, jubilation in the heart: ibid.—I know not in what way the son of Jesse murmurs something sweeter, and by the varied harmony of words and thoughts makes all those whom I had been accustomed to love ineloquent and mute: ibid., 853.—“If you ask anything of the Father in the name of Jesus Christ, the Father will without doubt give it to you”: Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1896, 1897.—If we wish what is asked to be given to us, let us ask something both of the Father and in the name of Jesus Christ: ibid., 1895.—Where is your glory, O Christian, except in the name of your crucified Lord Jesus Christ? St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 749.—In the name which is above every name, etc.: ibid.—“Glory in his holy name”: ibid.—Great indeed are those names; but where is the name that is above every name, the name of Jesus, at which every knee should bend? St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 136.—For this Jesus of mine, unlike the former ones, does not bear an empty or vain name: ibid., 133.—In him there is not the shadow of a great name, but its reality: ibid.—How the name Jesus is a health-giving medicine for faithful Christians in every adversity: ibid., 843 et seq.—In the light of this name God called us into his marvelous light: ibid., 846.—And he bore the name as a light: ibid.—Nor is the name of Jesus only light; it is also food—how this is so: ibid.—If one invokes the name of life, will he not immediately revive unto life? ibid., 847.—For one palpitating and trembling amid dangers, when has the invoked name of power not immediately given confidence and driven away fear? ibid.—Nothing restrains the onset of anger or calms the swelling of pride, etc., so much as the name of Jesus when invoked: ibid.—In the name of Jesus you have that by which you may correct your evil actions or bring less perfect ones to completion: ibid.—Likewise, you have that by which you may preserve your senses from corruption, or, if they have been corrupted, heal them: ibid.—The name of Jesus, lovable and consoling: ibid., 143, 144.—O holy and health-giving name, which is Jesus: Adam of Premontre, CXCVIII, 389.—This name alone, as it seems to me, is the unique token of our salvation: ibid.—A name of exultation and salvation, a name of gladness and sweetness, finally a name of delight and joy [Col. 0486]: ibid.—The name of Jesus tastes most sweetly: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 580.—All vain thoughts vanish most swiftly at the sign of the cross alone and the invocation of the Lord Jesus: Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 370.

IV. On Miracles Performed through the Power of the Name of Jesus.—Blessed Macarius, having invoked the name of Jesus over a certain dead man, raises him: Cassian, XLIX, 997, 999.—Having invoked Christ’s name, Abbot Abraham heals a certain man’s withered foot: ibid., 1001.—Men corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith both cast out demons in the name of the Lord and perform very great miracles: ibid., 1003.—When an Egyptian invoked the God of Martin, that is, Jesus, he escaped the danger of a storm: Amoenus, LXI, 1080.—Always having the name of Jesus upon his lips, Blessed Martin calms fevers, puts demons to flight, restores paralytic limbs, and by his prayer returns the bodies of three dead persons to their former life: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1009.—When the name of Jesus is invoked, a deaf and mute man is healed: ibid., 377.—When that same name is invoked, a blind man receives sight: ibid., 378.—An infant thirty days old, adjured in the name of Jesus, speaks and reveals what Bishop Bricius asks of him: ibid., 190.—When the name of Jesus is invoked, pagan sacred rites are disturbed and the gods put to flight: ibid., 741, 742.—Through invocation of Christ’s name Clovis deserved to obtain victory over the Alemanni: ibid., 225, 226.—A fever patient is healed when Christ’s name is invoked: St. Domnolus of Cenomanum, LXXII, 643.—And, having invoked Jesus, he restored the daughter unharmed: *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 148.—Satan was cast down at the naming of Jesus: ibid., 145.—Having been healed through Antony in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: ibid., 154.—And, when the name of Jesus was invoked, together with the expelled demons the vain wisdom of the philosophers then present was refuted: ibid., 161.—“In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk”; and, taking him by his right hand, he raised him up, and immediately his ankles and soles were strengthened, and he leaped up and walked: ibid., 400.—At the invocation of the name of the Lord Jesus, a foaming demon comes out of a woman: ibid., 638.—St. Eligius heals a lame man, uttering these words: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and stand upon your feet”: ibid., LXXXVII, 500.—Eligius frees a demoniac by Christ’s name: ibid., 520.—Eligius healed a servant through Christ’s name from *ficta* [uncertain reading]: ibid., 556.—Having invoked Christ’s name, he heals a certain sick man: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXXVIII, 461.—St. Leobinus extinguishes a fire by invoking Christ’s name: ibid., 553.—As St. Livina prays in the name of Jesus, a voice sent from God replies that she has been heard: St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 886.—Bishop Germanus, sailing to Britain with Lupus, suppresses raging waves by invoking the name of Jesus: Bede the Venerable, XCV, 46.—St. Gall freed a duke’s daughter from a demon through invocation of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 993.—St. Felix said to a tree: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to fall down by the roots and utterly shatter its temple and image, or altar”; and at his words this was done: St. Ado of Vienne, CXXXIII, 343.—St. Cornelius suddenly heals, in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, the paralyzed wife of the soldier Cerealis: ibid., 353.—King Clovis deserved to obtain victory over the Alemanni at the invocation of Christ’s name: Flodoard, CXXXV, 51.—Upon utterance of the name of Jesus Christ, an Arian heretic is converted: ibid., 58.—When the Lord’s name is invoked, one suffering from gout is suddenly healed: Richer, CXXXVIII, 257.—By the fearful invocation of Jesus’ name, he healed a leper: St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 404, 405.—In the name of Jesus Christ St. Godehard healed one afflicted with fever: ibid., CXLI, 1202.—In the name of Jesus Christ the same saint freed a demoniac woman: ibid., 1206.—A sick man abandoned by physicians is healed in the name of Jesus through the merits of St. Godehard: ibid., 1227.—In the name of Jesus, a man wholly ulcerated with horrible leprosy is suddenly healed: Lanfranc, CL, 759.—In the name of Christ a paralytic is healed: ibid., 758.

V. On the Use of the Name of Jesus and the Honor Rendered to It.—They pray in the name of Christ: VIII, 692, 694, 697, 707, 708.—This good name, which angels and archangels adore, which demons tremble at and cannot endure, which human beings take up for salvation: St. Hilary, IX, 324.—At the name of Jesus every knee should bend: St. Jerome, XXVI, 980.—The name of Jesus grows among all nations: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 454.—Every name that is in heaven or in hell confesses this name, trembling, kneeling, and bowing its head: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 370.—In this name the whole majesty of the Godhead is adored: ibid., 586.—All who dwell in heaven, all who inhabit the earth, and all who are held in the depths of hell prostrate themselves before this name and adore it: ibid.—The name of Jesus Most High, who reigns for ages of ages, must be sung in psalms: Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 340.—The Church confesses the wonderful name of the Lord Jesus throughout the whole earth: ibid., 335.—Blessed Peter speaks and heals the sick in the name of Jesus: ibid., 422; Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 173.—Oaths by the name of Jesus: St. Gregory the Great, LXXI, 788.—All the prayers and sacraments of the Church begin and end in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ the Savior [Col. 0487]: Pope Gelasius, LXXIV, 1055 et seq.—The name of Jesus is blessed: St. Eligius of Noyon, LXXXVII, 590.—All dwellers in heaven, those in the middle region, and those below hear the name of Jesus with bended knee: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 742.—In the name of Jesus the whole majesty of the Godhead is adored: Alcuin, LI, 177.—All who dwell in heaven, on earth, or are held in the depths of hell prostrate themselves before this name and adore it: ibid.—In the name of Jesus the apostles performed all their miracles: ibid., 178.—At the name of Jesus every knee bends in heaven, on earth, and in hell: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1483.—All cried aloud, “Blessed is the name of Jesus,” in which they saw innumerable miracles performed: Ademar, CXLI, 118.—Trials by water, red-hot plowshares, etc., through invocation of the most holy name of Jesus in order to make manifest God’s judgment: Richer, CXXXVIII, 1127 et seq.—What is asked must be asked in Jesus’ name, so that the petitioner’s joy may be full: Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1895.—“Let all God’s angels adore him, and at his name let every knee bend”: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 749.—The poured-out name of Jesus Christ, which not only flooded heaven and earth but also sprinkled hell, so that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend, etc.: St. Bernard, CLXXIII, 845.—Jesus speaks in his own name and heals the sick: Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1566, 1693, 1700.—All creation adores the name of Jesus with bended knees [Col. 0488]: John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 980.

VI. On the Necessity of Invoking the Name of Jesus.—Without invocation of the Lord Christ no one lives with God: St. Ambrose, XVII, 144.—On those who invoke the Lord’s name and are saved indeed in the name of Jesus Christ: St. Jerome, XXVI, 260.—There must be no doubt that, apart from the name of Jesus, there is no other name given to human beings under heaven in which we must be saved: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 234.—Whoever does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God has already been judged: Victor of Vita, LVIII, 223.—The name of Jesus is the profession of salvation: Cassiodorus, LXX, 180.—No one can be saved except through the power of Jesus’ name: Bishop Bruno, CLXIV, 1013.—The name of Jesus is poured out among all nations, and whoever invokes it shall be saved: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 845.—The Lord Jesus, rich toward all, bestows upon all who invoke his name: St. Gaudentius, CXCIII, 907.

VII. On Various Short Works Treating the Name of Jesus.—Poems on the name of Jesus: Pope St. Damasus, XIII, 377.—A poem on the name of Jesus: St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 741.—Verses on a storm stilled by invocation of Jesus’ name: Amoenus, LXI, 1079.—Sermon XV of St. Bernard: ibid., CLXXXIII, 843.—A rhythmic jubilation on the name of Jesus: St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1317 et seq.

[Col. 0487]

LXX. INDEX ON THE HOLY SPIRIT. CONCERNING HIS DIVINITY, ATTRIBUTES, GIFTS, AND OPERATIONS; SETTING FORTH, IN ANALOGICAL ORDER, VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE FATHERS ON THESE SUBJECTS.

NOTICE.

In this Index we treat successively: I, the divinity of the Holy Spirit; II, his procession and mission; III, his various attributes; IV, the names and figures under which he appeared; V, his diverse gifts and operations; VI, errors concerning the Holy Spirit; and VII, books treating of the Holy Spirit.

I.—On the Divinity of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0487]

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Most Holy Trinity: Tertullian, II, 163.—The third name of the Godhead and the third rank of majesty: ibid., 196.—He is of the same nature as the Father and the Son: ibid.—The Holy Spirit possesses one substance, power, divinity, majesty, and will with the Father and the Son: St. Zeno, XI, 428.—Those attacking the divinity of the Holy Spirit are refuted: ibid., 17, note 52.—The Spirit of God is such that he is of the same substance as the Father and the Son: Faustinus the Presbyter, XIII, 77.—Hence it is utterly clear that the Holy Spirit is not a creature: ibid., 78.—The Holy Spirit is proved to be God by this very fact by which he is shown not to be a creature: ibid., 79.—Where any divine operation, whether of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit, is designated, it is referred not only to the Holy Spirit but also to the Father and the Son: St. Ambrose, XVI, 712.—Who then would dare say that the substance of the Holy Spirit is created? ibid., 726.—Who therefore could doubt the divinity of the Holy Spirit, when, wherever the grace of the Spirit is present, the form of divinity appears? ibid., 738.—The Holy Spirit must not be separated from the Father’s divinity: ibid., 748.—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved from the fact that he has a temple: ibid., 798.—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved from his mission: ibid., 732.—The Holy Spirit is shown to possess all that God possesses, namely divinity, etc.: ibid., 810.—A heretical objection to the divinity of the Holy Spirit, drawn from the prophet Amos’s words about the blowing of the winds, is resolved: ibid., 753.—A heretical objection to the divinity of the Holy Spirit, taken from the Apostle’s words, “from whom are all things . . . through whom are all things,” is resolved: ibid., 761.—The Holy Spirit is proved to be God: ibid., XVII, 200, 201, 1010.—Page and time would fail me if I were to set down everything written to prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit: ibid., 1011.—Whether the Holy Spirit is God: Zacchaeus the Christian, [Col. 0488] XX, 1110.—Against the Sabellians, who deny that the Holy Spirit is God: ibid., 1133.—That the Spirit is of the same nature as the Son and the Father: St. Jerome, XXIII, 121.—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is maintained: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1046.—Peter showed that the Holy Spirit is God: ibid., XXXIV, 616.—The Holy Spirit is true God, equal to the Father and the Son: ibid., XLII, 788, 827, 828, 927.—The Holy Spirit is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son: ibid., XXXV, 1826; XLII, 928.—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 629, 631, 637.—The Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son: Victor of Vita, LVIII, 225.—The objection of Macedonius, who impiously asserts that the Holy Spirit is a more excellent creature: Paschasius the Deacon, LXII, 27.—The Holy Spirit is God: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 499.—The Holy Spirit is God: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 824.—“If you ask me what the Holy Spirit is, I shall say: God and Lord”: Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 588.—For the Holy Spirit is true God and truly and properly the Holy Spirit: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 293.—The Holy Spirit, although Paraclete—that is, advocate—is nevertheless God: ibid., 377.—The Holy Spirit exists as God in his nature: Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 243.—Let us hold that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are God by nature: ibid., 257.—Why the Holy Spirit is proclaimed God: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 23.—All divinely inspired Scripture of the Old and New Testament teaches that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God: ibid., 26.—Do you not know that the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Spirit is one God? Aeneas of Paris, CXXI, 691.—The Holy Spirit is God: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 289.—That the Holy Spirit is consubstantial God and Lord with the Father and the Son: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 1573.—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved: ibid., CCIII, 753.

II.—On the Procession of the Holy Spirit and His Mission.

[Col. 0489]

Let this be said by me also concerning the third rank: I consider that the Spirit is from no other source than from the Father through the Son: Tertullian, II, 159.—The procession of the Holy Spirit: St. Hilary, X, 250.—Whether receiving from the Son is the same thing as proceeding from the Father: ibid., 251.—The Lord did not leave uncertain from whom he is: ibid., 250.—Freedom is left to understanding as to whether he is from the Father or from the Son: ibid.—Though not by perception, yet by inward awareness we hold that the Spirit of God is from the Father through the Son: ibid., 470.—The Holy Spirit was not created: ibid., 468.—He was not begotten: ibid., 469.—The Holy Spirit did not take from created things: ibid., 340.—But from the things of the Father and the Son: ibid.—He receives from the Father and the Son: ibid., 656.—One rejoices in the other, shining with one original coeternity in the fullness of the Holy Spirit: St. Zeno, XI, 392.—The Son proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from him: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1170.—What the Son received from the Father through unity of nature, the Holy Spirit also received from him through the same unity: ibid., XVI, 771.—The Holy Spirit proceeds inseparably from the Father and the Son, not in time but from eternity: ibid., XVII, 675, 947, 1015.—The Holy Spirit, God proceeding from the Father: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1071; XL, 258, 634, 684; XLII, 697, 703, 722, 742, 752, 790; XLIII, 378.—The Holy Spirit was not made by the Father and the Son, but proceeds: ibid., XXXIII, 749.—Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son: ibid., XXXV, 1888, 1889.—Why the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son: ibid., XLII, 902.—Why the Holy Spirit is said to proceed but not to be born: ibid., 770.—The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is without time, nor may he be called the Son of both: ibid., 1094.—The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is equal to both: St. Augustine, XL, 648.—Why the Holy Spirit is not begotten and how he proceeds from the Father and the Son: ibid., XLII, 1092.—The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 696.—The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as he proceeds from the Father: ibid., 418.—It is proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the begetter and the begotten: ibid., 575.—The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: Cassiodorus, LXX, 23.—The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 541.—From the Father and the Son: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 534, 1198.—That the Holy Spirit is God proceeding from the Father and the Son: St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 134.—That the Holy Spirit is called neither begotten nor unbegotten, but only proceeding: ibid., 135.—What is the difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds? ibid.—The Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son: Alcuin, C, 844.—Many testimonies of the Holy Fathers concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit are cited: Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 239 et seq.—Whence the Holy Spirit proceeds: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 23.—Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 225, 247; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 636.—On the procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 285 et seq.—The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is affirmed: St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 359.—Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 14 et seq.—Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 590, 591, 1078.—The Holy Spirit’s twofold procession: St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 323.—The Greeks deny the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son and are refuted: St. Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 914.—The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son: ibid., CCXIII, 754.—The Holy Spirit is not unbegotten, since he was sent by the Son: St. Hilary, X, 519.—Why he is said to be sent by the Father when he is sent by the Son: ibid.—The Holy Spirit was sent to instruct, teach, and sanctify believers: ibid., 489.—The Spirit is given and sent, as the Son is; and in this they certainly possess unity of divinity: St. Ambrose, XVI, 778.—The Holy Spirit is sent by the Son because of the fellowship and unity of nature: ibid., XVII, 520.—The Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son: St. Augustine, XLII, 686, 697.—What it means for the Holy Spirit to be sent: ibid., 908.—How the mission of the Holy Spirit is to be understood: ibid., 850.—When the Holy Spirit was sent: ibid., 179.—The Holy Spirit was sent for fulfillment of the Law: ibid., XXXVIII, 1239, 1249.—As the Law was given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb, so the Holy Spirit came on the fiftieth day after Christ’s passion: ibid., XXXVII, 1167.—Why the Holy Spirit came on the tenth day after the Ascension: ibid., XXXVIII, 1239.—He is said to be sent by both, namely the Father and the Son: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 640; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 783.—Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 590, 591.—On the mission of the Holy Spirit, which occurs in two ways, visibly and invisibly: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 562, 564, 566.

III.—On the Various Attributes of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0490]

Holiness is the proper nature of the Holy Spirit: Tertullian, II, 933.—The Holy Spirit is proved to be eternal: St. Ambrose, XVI, 728.—The Holy Spirit is proved from Scripture to be omnipotent: ibid., 846.—Like the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit also is immaculate and omnipotent: ibid., 815.—Like the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is Creator of all things: ibid., 749, 755.—The Holy Spirit is good, the source and principle of goodness: ibid., 720 et seq.—The Holy Spirit is one, who blazed forth in the prophets, was breathed upon the apostles, etc.: ibid., 717, 718.—The Holy Spirit is true God, equal to the Father and the Son: St. Augustine, XLII, 788, 827, 828, 927.—The Holy Spirit is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son: ibid., XXXV, 1826; XLII, 928.—The Holy Spirit is Creator with the Father and the Son: ibid., XLII, 783.—The Holy Spirit is Creator: Cassiodorus, LXX, 739.—The Holy Spirit is immeasurable: St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 263, 786.

IV.—On the Various Names of the Holy Spirit and the Figures under Which He Appeared.

## VI.—Errors concerning the Holy Spirit

Those who attack the divinity of the Holy Spirit are refuted. St. Zeno, XI, 267, note 52.—Those who have denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit are either Jews among the Arians or Arians among the Jews. St. Ambrose, XVI, 820.—The objection of heretics against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, drawn from the words of the prophet Amos concerning the blast of winds, is resolved, ibid., 752 and following.—The objection of heretics against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, taken from the Apostle’s words, “from whom are all things, through whom are all things,” is resolved, ibid., 761.—Heretics blasphemously call the Holy Spirit created. St. Jerome, XXIII, 369.—Error concerning the Holy Spirit, the same author, XXVI, 375.—Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Photinians, and Jews sinned against the Holy Spirit. St. Augustine, XXXIII, 814.—Some heretics utterly deny the Holy Spirit; others maintain that He is a creature; who these are, the same author, XXXVIII, 448; XLII, 44.—How the Sabellians, Arians, Manicheans, Cataphrygians, and Donatists erred concerning the Holy Spirit. XXXV, 2099; XLII, 30.—The Sadducees denied the Holy Spirit, the same author, XXXVIII, 447.—The Macedonians refused to acknowledge the Holy Spirit as equal to the Father and the Son and of the same substance with them, the same author, XLII, 797.—What the Arians thought concerning the Holy Spirit, XLII, 680, 681, 736.—They said that the Holy Spirit was subject to Christ, ibid., 714, 716.—Errors of Arians, Eunomians, etc., concerning the Holy Spirit, the same author, XXXVIII, 448.—Certain heretics held that the Holy Spirit was the deity of the Father and the Son, XL, 191.—The Macedonian error concerning the Holy Spirit. St. Leo the Great, LIV, 206, 400.—The Arians and Macedonians blasphemously assert that He is lesser than the Father and the Son. Gennadius, LVIII, 1013.—Against the error of the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 633.—That the Greeks do not rightly say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, through whom are all things, etc. St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 307.—There were heretics, namely Macedonians, who believed in the Father and the Son but did not accept the Holy Spirit, denying that He was God; the Church condemned them at the Council of Constantinople. St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 238.—The Greeks deny the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son and are refuted. Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 914.

# LXXI. INDEX IN THE MARIANA OF THE FATHERS OF THE WESTERN CHURCH, OR A LIST OF WORKS AND SAYINGS CONCERNING THE HONOUR AND CULT OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY FOUND IN THE *PATROLOGY*, FROM THE EARLIEST BEGINNINGS OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION TO THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY

## Notice

Among the various indices of this volume, intended for the manifold and easier elucidation of the whole *Patrology*, you will find none—I speak from an ascetical standpoint—whose undertaking and excellence are so great, or from which so much benefit may be gained by preachers, pastors, and all readers.

Especially in our own times, it is of the greatest importance to compile a particular synopsis concerning the cult, praises, and privileges of the Blessed Mary, and to display, from the perpetual tradition of the Catholic Church, a most certain argument formed from deeds and sayings throughout all preceding centuries, as though in a chain: so that every doubt may be removed, and the devotion of the faithful toward the most holy Virgin may grow and be promoted still more ardently through innumerable testimonies.

Who, as is fitting, perhaps appreciates how great was the Christians’ confidence in the most august Mother of God from the first age of the religion; what honour was returned to her; and how fervent was the love displayed and poured forth in continual and most devout prayers, in most frequent sermons, and in reverential worship of many kinds?

This table or synopsis will clearly show everyone that our devotion toward the divine Mother Mary is not only most ancient, but is still inferior to the piety of the ancient Fathers.

Indeed, to pass over the holy Anselm and Bernard among the more recent Fathers, might one not ascend, as by a glorious and immovable ladder, even to Tertullian, through Innocent III, the Venerable Hildebert, Martin of León, Peter of Blois, Adam the Scot, St. Stephen the Cistercian, Peter Lombard, St. Amadeus of Lausanne, Hugh of St. Victor, St. Fulbert, the Venerable Guibert, St. Odilo, St. Paschasius Radbertus, Blessed Alcuin, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, the Venerable Bede, St. Ildefonsus, St. Isidore, St. Gregory the Great, St. Fulgentius, St. Augustine, St. Gaudentius, St. Peter Chrysologus, St. Ambrose, St. Hilary of Poitiers, Lactantius, and many others whom we have seen ardently follow the Greek Fathers step for step, and whom it would be too lengthy to enumerate all?

To bring forward yet one among the rest, who in his sermons and notes alone embraces the whole tradition: where, I ask, in our times is there a sermon or book that can equal Adam of Perseigne’s truly golden and Marian treatise in tenderest love, sweetest piety, and floriferous knowledge of Sacred Scripture and of the holy Doctors? Kindly read it, reader, not merely because of the holy and wonderful devotion of its pious author, but because of the almost innumerable testimonies gathered together in that precious book; then you will understand what remains for us to do if we are to equal and attain the devotion of our Fathers.

For the more ready use of preachers, or of every Christian who intends to find or say something concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, we divide this index into various sections. Thus, Section I, chronological, presents all authors who dealt with the Blessed Virgin from Tertullian to Innocent III; Section II, hagiographical, records whatever concerns the life of the Blessed Mary; Section III, dogmatic, enumerates the Fathers who asserted the motherhood and virginity of the Blessed Mary; Section IV provides a collection of matters relating to the Immaculate Conception; Section V, apologetic, sets forth whatever the Fathers said in defence of Mary; Section VI, paraenetic, gives sermons and homilies concerning the Blessed Virgin; Section VII, encomiastic, treats of Mary’s praises; Section VIII, liturgical, treats of feasts, hymns, and prayers in honour and glory of the Mother of God; Section IX, ascetical, shows the various virtues of the Blessed Virgin Mary; Section X, philological, presents all works and shorter writings concerning the Blessed Mary, in alphabetical order of the Fathers. Having said this:

## SECTION II. Hagiographical, in which are reported whatever things concern the life of the Blessed Mary

[Col. 0495]

The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, came forth from the loins of Abraham, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1245.—She came from a royal and free lineage, Blessed Alcuin, C, 450, 456.—From the seed of David, St. Paschasius Radbertus, XCIII, 94, 95; Alanus of Lille, CCX, 226.—She was born of father Joachim and Anna, according to a tradition widespread before St. Jerome and diffused throughout the world, St. Jerome, XXIII; Peter Lombard, CXCII, *passim*.—She first made a vow of virginity, St. Anselm, CLIX, 217; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 185; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 107.—Why Mary was betrothed to a man, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 740.—Reasons why she was betrothed to Joseph, a just man. St. Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 6 and following.—Joseph was the guardian and witness of Mary’s integrity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 764.—From the beginning she was commended to the angel Gabriel, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 636.—The angel greets and addresses Mary, Claudianus Mamertus, I, 279; St. Anselm, CLIX, 230.—Mary conceives God and man, St. Leo the Great, LV, 153.—She visits Elizabeth, St. Anselm, CLIX, 230.—The Virgin gave birth, St. Leo the Great, LV, 153.—She is purified, although not liable to purification, St. Bernard, CLXXIII, 764.—What Christ signified by not acknowledging His mother, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1086; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1136.—What Mary’s presence at the wedding morally signifies, and what her complaint to Jesus concerning the lack of wine signifies, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 209, 210.—Mary’s grief in the Passion of her Son, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 610; Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 71.—Mary was both martyr and virgin, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1031; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 60.—Mary’s threefold anguish: of fear, grief, and love, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1031.—The Blessed Mary is commended by Christ to John the disciple, [Col. 0496] St. Jerome, XX, 783; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 475; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 781.—Why Christ seems rather to have acknowledged His Mother on the cross. St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1035.—Why Mary did not come to anoint Christ’s body, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 429.—After Christ’s Ascension, the Blessed Mary presides over the college of apostles, and the apostles undertake nothing important without her counsel, Lucius Flavius Dexter, XXXI, 91.—Mary lived for many years after Christ’s death, Philip of Harveng, CIII, 151.—While she lived, she was visited by the faithful flocking to her from all sides, Lucius Flavius Dexter, XXXI, 91.—Mary’s rest after her labours, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1033.—Mary’s death, St. Amadeus of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1336.—The apostles gather at her death, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 724.—Mary dwelt and was buried in the valley of Jehoshaphat, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1031.—Her tomb was seen there, Godfrey, CLV, 1439.—The glory of Mary’s Assumption, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 764.—Her body is in heaven, Philip of Harveng, CIII, 151.—She is placed in paradise by Christ, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 475.—Mary is exalted at the right hand of her Son, St. Amadeus, CLXXXVIII, 1336.—Mary is read to have spoken only four times, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 730.—A history of the birth and praiseworthy life of the Blessed and untouched Mother of God, Hrotsvitha, CXXXVII, 1065.—Mary’s life was not only contemplative but active, Abbot Isaac, CXCIV, 1808.—She fulfilled the offices of Mary and Martha, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1036.—The illustrious life of the Blessed Mary illuminates all the Churches, St. Anselm, CLX, 1119.

## SECTION III. Dogmatic, in which are enumerated the Fathers who taught and affirmed both the motherhood and the virginity of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God

They affirm that the Blessed Mary was truly the Mother of God and at the same time remained an unviolated and immaculate virgin:

[Col. 0497]

Tertullian, I, 39; II, 19.—Lactantius, VI, 1050.—Victorinus the African, VIII, 80.—Emperor Constantine, VIII, 432.—St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, X, 118 and *passim*.—St. Eusebius of Vercelli, XII.—Julius Firmicus Maternus, XII.—St. Ambrose of Milan, XV, 729.—St. Gaudentius, XX, 281.—Zacchaeus the Christian, XX, 1078.—St. Jerome, XXI, XXII, *passim*.—Leporius the priest, XXXI, 1225.—St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1012, 1018; XXXVIII, 348.—Claudianus Mamertinus, L, verse 149.—St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 58.—St. Nicetas, LII, 864.—St. Leo the Great, pope, LV, 153.—St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 43.—Gennadius, LVIII, 37, 164.—Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 453.—Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 32.—Caelius Sedulius, LXIII, verse 11 and following.—St. Fulgentius, LXV, 508.—Facundus, LXVII, 527.—Taio, LXXX, 776.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1229.—Mozarabic Missal, LXXXV.—Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1162.—St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 207.—Haymo of Halberstadt, XCVIII, 378.—Blessed Alcuin, C, 731, 847.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 752.—St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 103, 104.—Ratramnus, CXXI, 189.—Hincmar, CXXV, 347.—Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 76.—Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 886.—Ratherius, CXXXVI, 769.—Abbot Gezo, CXXXVII, 381.—St. Odilo, CXLIII, 639.—St. Anselm, CLVIII, 455.—The Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 214.—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 321.—Abelard, CLXXXVIII, 1428.—St. Bernard, CLXXXII, *passim*.—Abbot Guerric, CLXXXV, 120.—Joslenus, CLXXXVI, 1484.—Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1143.—Abbot Ernald, CXCIX, 1617.—Peter of Blois, CCVII, 841.—Very many others also, whom one may see in the *Patrology*.

## SECTION IV. A collection of sayings and matters relating to the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary

Although in certain sections of this index we have noted various matters concerning the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Mary, we have judged that the following should also be included, for the honour of the holy Mother of God, the edification of the faithful, and the grave urgencies of this age; therefore:

**I. Sayings.**—The Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Mary was asserted by St. Ambrose, XV, 629, 827.—St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1830; XLIV, 420.—St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1229.—Gothic Breviary, LXXXVI, 282.—The Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 538.—Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 489.—St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 640, 731, 1032.—Master Bandinus, CXCII, 819.—Arnulf, CCI, 168.—Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 121.—St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 93.—Alanus of Lille, CCX, 146.—Adam of Perseigne, CCXI, 759.

**II. Matters.**—The feast of the Immaculate Conception was observed in the Eastern Church before the ninth century, as ecclesiastical monuments prove: from the Constitution of Emperor Manuel Comnenus of the year 1166; from the Menologion of Basil Porphyrogenitus; from manuscripts of the Gospels before the year 800; from St. Andrew of Crete; from the Typikon of Sabas; from John Damascene; from the Menaea; and from a Russian codex.

In the Western Church, the feast of the Immaculate Conception is older than the ninth century, as appears from the life of St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI; from hymns of the monastery of Monte Cassino before the ninth century; from Pope St. Leo IX, CXLIII; from St. Anselm, CLIX; and from Abbot Gauffrid in the *Chronicles*, CLXXXVIII.

From the cult of the Mother of God, the Virgin who was born, the cult of that same Virgin conceived is attested; thus: St. Ildefonsus, on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, XCVI; St. Fulbert, on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, CXLI; Blessed Alcuin, CI; St. Peter Damian, sermon on the Assumption, CXLV; Godfrey of Vendôme, on the Nativity, CLIII; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, on the Nativity, CLXXXIV; Odo of Morimond, on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, CLXXXVIII.

Nothing is more frequent than the commemoration together of the Nativity and the Conception of the Blessed Mary, as is evident from ancient monuments, from St. Paschasius Radbertus, *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, CXX; from St. Fulbert, *Sermons*, CXLI; and from Adam of Perseigne, CCXI. Nicetas, Photius, Emperor Leo, and St. John Damascene assert the same.

It is a most solemn feast, according to monuments which prove the cult of the Blessed Mary when first ensouled: St. Anselm, *Letter on the Immaculate Conception*, CLIX; Mozarabic Missal, LXXXIII; ancient hymns; Gothic Breviary, LXXXIV.

The Conception of the Blessed Mary is divine, holy, and most sacred, and is therefore to be venerated in worship: thus ecclesiastical monuments; George of Nicomedia; St. Andrew of Crete; St. John Damascene; St. Germanus of Constantinople, in the Menaea; in the Armenian and Gothic Breviaries; and in the Mozarabic and Gallican Missals, LXXXIII, LXXXIV.

[Col. 0498]

The Blessed Mary is the Mother of God; therefore God enriched her with an abundance of every kind of gift and grace, and the prerogative of the Immaculate Conception cannot be separated from this: thus St. Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, XVI; St. Peter Chrysologus, *Sermons*, LII; the Venerable Bede, XCIV; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI; Arnold of Chartres, CXXXIX; St. Anselm, *Hymns*, CLIX; Eadmer, *On the Excellence of the Blessed Mary*, CLIX; Abbot Rupert, CLXIX; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, *Homilies*, CLXXXIV; Peter of Celle, *Sermons*, CCII.

That the Blessed Mary was always set apart from sinners and preserved from every stain of sin was the common faith of the Church: St. Ambrose, Sermon XXII, XVI; St. Augustine, *On Marriage*, XXXIX; St. Peter Chrysologus, *Sermon on St. Anne*, LII; Paul the Deacon, on Isaiah, XCV; St. Ildefonsus, *Sermon on the Assumption*, XCVI; St. Anselm, on the Psalter, CLIX; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, *Sermon on the Assumption*, CLXXXIV; Adam of Perseigne, from St. Ephrem, St. John Damascene, Basil of Seleucia, and the Menaea, CCXI.

The Blessed Mary is distinguished from the first parents: thus Caelius Sedulius, XIX; St. Augustine, *On Marriage*, XXXIX; St. Maximus of Turin, *Sermons*, LVII; Prudentius, *Hymns*, LX; Arator, LXVIII; Hermannus Contractus, *On the Incarnation*, CXLIII; Adam of Perseigne, from John Chrysostom, St. Basil, St. Gregory Nazianzen, St. Justin, and the Menaea, CCXI.

The Blessed Mary is compared with God in what concerns purity and holiness: thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VI; St. Peter Damian, Sermon II, CXLV; St. Anselm, *On the Conception of the Blessed Mary*, CLIX; the Venerable Gerhoh, on Psalm XVIII, CXCIII.

The Blessed Mary is called divine, most divine, and exceedingly like God; consequently, she is immaculate: thus St. Paulinus of Nola, *Rhythmical Panegyric of Celsus*, LXI; St. Ildefonsus, *On the Assumption*, XCVI; St. Bernard, *Sermon on Advent*, CLXXXIV; Adam of Perseigne, from St. John Damascene, St. Cyril of Alexandria, and Theodotus of Ancyra, CCXI.

The Blessed Mary is the natural and moral mediatrix, and hence innocent. Thus St. Ildefonsus, *On Perpetual Virginity*, XCVI; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII; St. Peter Damian, *Sermons*, CXLV; Adam of Perseigne, from St. Ephrem, St. Germanus of Constantinople, St. Cyril of Alexandria, the *Triodion*, the *Paracletic*, etc., CCXI.

The Blessed Mary is wholly free from fault, wholly marked by purity: St. Columbanus, *Breviary on the Psalter*, LXXX; St. Paschasius Radbertus, *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, CXX; St. Anselm, *Hymns*, CLIX; Adam of Perseigne, from St. Andrew of Crete, St. Ephrem, Manuel Palaeologus, and Theophanes, CCXI.

The Blessed Mary knew no concupiscence, and therefore was preserved from original sin: St. Peter Chrysologus, *Sermons*, LII; Paul the Deacon, sermon on the Assumption, LXV; St. Leo the Great, Sermon XXII, LXV; Prudentius, fragment *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, LX; Ambrose Autpert, on St. Luke, LXXXIX; St. Ildefonsus, *On the Perpetual Virginity*, XCVI; Blessed Alcuin, sermon on the Purification, CI; St. Paschasius Radbertus, *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, CXX; St. Peter Damian, sermon on the Assumption, CXLV; St. Amadeus of Lausanne, *Homilies*, CLXXXVIII; Peter of Celle, *Letter*, CCII.

The Blessed Mary is believed always to have been a virgin in soul and body: St. Ambrose, *On Virgins*, XVI; Pope Innocent I, letter to Severianus, XX; St. Jerome, letter to Eustochium, XXII; St. Paulinus of Nola, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, LXV; St. Ildefonsus, *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Blessed Mary*, XCVI; St. Maximus of Turin, *Sermons*, LVII; St. Peter Damian, sermon on the Assumption, CXLV; St. Anselm, Meditation III, CLIX; St. Hildebert, sermon on the Advent of the Lord, CLXXI; St. Bernard, *Sermon on the Praises of the Blessed Mary*, CLXXXIV.

The Blessed Mary was without original sin; the holy Doctors explicitly affirm this, among them St. Maximus of Turin, sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, LVII; St. Ildefonsus, *On Perpetual Virginity*, XCVI; St. Paschasius Radbertus, *On the Holiness of the Blessed Mary*, CXX; St. Anselm, *On the Conception of the Blessed Mary*, CLIX; Alanus of Lille, in the *Anticlaudianus*, CCX.

Forms of speech concerning original stain absolutely exclude the Blessed Mary.

1. With respect to the efficient cause of original sin; hence such expressions as “to offend in Adam,” “to be subject to Adam’s guilt,” “to be wounded by Adam’s wound,” “to die in Adam,” and “to be stained by Eve’s guilt” never apply to the Blessed Virgin Mother of God: thus St. Cyprian, *Letter*, IV; St. Hilary of Poitiers, on Matthew, IX; St. Ambrose of Milan, *Apology of David*, XV; St. Jerome, on Hosea, XXV; St. Augustine, *On Sin and Merit*, XLI; Aurelius Prudentius, LIX; Adam of Perseigne, from St. Gregory Nazianzen and St. Irenaeus, CCXI.

2. To fall into death by the devil’s guile; to be wounded by his bite; to be subjected to the devil’s law; to forget the divine command: these never apply to the Blessed Mary. Thus Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, II; St. Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*, IV; St. Hilary of Poitiers, on Psalm CXXII, X; St. Ambrose,

[Col. 0499]

on Psalm XLVIII, XIV; St. Jerome, on the Books of Kings, XXIV; Adam of Perseigne, from St. Basil and St. Gregory Nazianzen, CCXI.

3. “Sin entered into this world” does not concern the Blessed Virgin Mary: thus Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women*, I; St. Optatus of Milevis, XI; in Adam of Perseigne, St. Irenaeus and St. Basil, CCXI.

4. Since original sin is ancient impiety, the vice of inborn infirmity, the filth of nature, etc., it does not pertain to the Blessed Virgin: thus Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, V; St. Hilary of Poitiers, on Psalm CXXII, X; St. Ambrose, in the *Apology of David*, XV; St. Jerome, on Ezekiel, XXV; Prosper, *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, LI; Aurelius Prudentius, in the *Apotheosis*, LX; Peter the Deacon, *On the Incarnation*, LXV; St. Ignatius, in Adam of Perseigne, CCXI.

5. The Blessed Mary can never be said to have been expelled from paradise, deprived of honour along with the first parents, consigned to death, slain by a deadly wound, ever divinely condemned, entangled in a curse, etc.: thus Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, II; St. Cyprian, letter to Fidus, IV; St. Ambrose, *Against Julian*, XVI; St. Jerome, on Hosea, XXV; Orosius, *Apology on Free Will*, XXXI; Prosper, *Poem on the Ungrateful*, LI; St. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, LXXVI; and in Adam of Perseigne, St. Athanasius, St. Basil, and St. Gregory Nazianzen, CCXI.

6. Infirmity, inward conflict, the contagion of earthly corruption, the root of error, the sickness of nature, and the incentive to sin are unfitting in relation to the Blessed Mary: thus St. Hilary of Poitiers, on Matthew, X; St. Ambrose, in the book *On Philosophy* cited by St. Augustine, XLII; St. Augustine, *City of God*, XLVI; Prosper, *Responses*, LI; Prudentius, in the *Apotheosis*, LX; and in Adam of Perseigne, St. Gregory Nazianzen and Abbot Macarius, CCXI.

Of the immaculate purity of Blessed Mary all the most distinguished Latin hymn-writers have sung, namely: Magnes, V; Victorinus Africanus, VIII; St. Hilary of Poitiers, X; St. Ambrose, XVII; Caelius Sedulius, XIX; Juvencus, XIX; Claudian Mamertus, LIII; Aurelius Prudentius, LX; Ennodius, LXIII; St. Paulinus of Nola and Paul the Deacon, LXV; St. Leander of Seville, LXXII; St. Eugenius of Toledo, LXXXVII; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII; St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCV; Conantius, John of Saragossa, and St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI; the Venerable Bede, XCV; Theodulf of Orléans, CV; Rabanus Maurus, CXII; Servatus Lupus, CXIX; St. Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII; St. Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI; St. Peter Damian, CXLV; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX; the Venerable Peter of Cluny, CLXXXIX; and, in Adam of Perseigne, the Greek hymn-writers, CCXI.

From this synoptic survey of testimonies and tradition, we can and ought once more to affirm—with the liturgies of St. Mark, of St. James in Allatius, and of Tesiphone; with St. Justin, St. Hippolytus, and St. Cyprian in the first two centuries; with St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, Origen, and St. Dionysius of Alexandria in the third century; with St. Athanasius, St. Ambrose, and St. Amphilochius in the fourth; with St. Jerome, St. Augustine, St. Maximus of Turin, and Theodoret in the fifth; with St. Fulgentius and St. Sabas in the sixth; with St. Ildefonsus, Sophronius, and the Sixth General Council of Constantinople in the seventh; with St. Paschasius Radbertus, St. John Damascene, Raymond Jordan, commonly called the Idiot, and the Second General Council of Nicaea in the eighth; with Theophanes and the Greek *Menaea* in the ninth; with St. Fulbert, St. Anselm, St. Peter Damian, and St. Bruno the Carthusian in the tenth; with St. Ivo of Chartres, St. Bernard, and innumerable others mentioned above in the eleventh; with St. Bonaventure, Innocent III, Albert the Great, and so many others that it would be lengthy to name them in the twelfth—that **BY A SINGULAR PROVIDENCE GOD EFFECTED THAT THE MOST BLESSED AND MOST HOLY VIRGIN, FROM THE VERY BEGINNING OF HER LIFE, SHOULD BE AS PURE AS IT WAS FITTING THAT SHE SHOULD BE WHO WAS TO BE WORTHY OF SO GREAT A GOOD, THAT IS, CHRIST.**

These are the words of the *Menaea*, that is, the book of prayers used by the Greeks, who have now long been separated from us by schism. Therefore there is no room for doubt concerning belief in the holy and Immaculate Conception of Blessed Mary, especially since Rome has spoken, and now the matter is settled for Catholics, to the greater glory of God and the honor of the Mother of God, blessed forever.

## SECTION V: APOLOGETIC

In which are reported all the things the Fathers said in defense and vindication of Blessed Mary.

Against those who deny that Blessed Mary remained a Virgin: St. Ambrose, XV, 289; St. Jerome, XXXIII, 183; St. Leo the Great, LVI, 260; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 429; [Col. 0500] Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 752; Hincmar, CXXV, 679; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 735.—Against Valentinian and others, that Christ did not assume a heavenly body, and that Blessed Mary was not a Mother merely by title but a true Mother: John Cassian, L, 111 and throughout; St. Vincent of Lérins, cited in vol. L, 910; Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 32; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 293; Facundus, LXVII, 529; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 366; Blessed Alcuin, C, 847; St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 729.—Against those who deny that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, it is asserted that this must be believed with unqualified faith: St. Augustine, XL, 186, 251; XLII, 1122; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 1240; Ratramnus, CXXI, 609; the Venerable Guibert, CLVI, 489.—On grumbling against Mary: Blessed Algrin, CLXXXVIII, 44.

Besides this, various testimonies of Sacred Scripture establish and prove the prerogatives of Blessed Mary, as follows:

1. The divine oracle of Genesis: “She herself shall crush your head,” etc.: Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, II; St. Cyprian, *On the Nativity*, IV; Lactantius, *On the Divine Institutions*, VI; St. Zeno, XI; St. Ambrose, XV; Caelius Sedulius, XIX; St. Augustine, *City of God*, XLVI; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII; St. Leo the Great, LIV; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII; Aurelius Prudentius, LX; Claudius Marius Victor, LXI; Bishop Primasius, LXVIII; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI; St. Ansbert, LXXX; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII; the Venerable Bede, XCIII; St. Agobard, CIV; Jonas of Orléans, CVI; Walafrid Strabo, CXIII; Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI; St. Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI; St. Odo of Cluny, CXLII; Hermannus Contractus, *Prayer to the Virgin Mary*, CXLIII; St. Peter Damian, CXLV; Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII; St. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI; Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII; Hermann of Tournai, CLXXX; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV; St. Amadeus of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII; Hugh of Rouen, CXCII; Peter of Celle, CCII; Peter of Blois, CCVII; Adam of Perseigne, from Gregory of Nyssa, St. Justin, Origen, Basil of Seleucia, St. Andrew of Crete, St. Chrysostom, St. Proclus, St. Germanus, and Emperor Leo, CCXI; Anonymous author of the twelfth century, CCXIII.

2. Isaiah’s prophecy, “A shoot shall rise from the root of Jesse,” etc., proves the purity of Blessed Mary, who was infected by no stain of sin, either original or actual: Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, II; Novatian, priest, III; St. Ambrose, *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, XVI; St. Jerome, *On Isaiah*, XXIV; St. Augustine, XL; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII; Paul the Deacon, LXV; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII; St. Ambrose Autpert, LXXXIX; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI; Etherius and Beatus, against Elipandus, XCVI; Rabanus Maurus, CIX; St. Peter Damian, CXLV; Radulfus Ardens, CLV; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV; St. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI; Honorius of Autun, *On the Seal*, CLXXII; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV; St. Amadeus of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII; Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI; Adam of Perseigne, *Letter*, and from St. Justin, Emperor Leo, and the *Menaea*, CCXI; Innocent III, *Encomium of Blessed Mary*, CCXVII.

3. On Esther, who was a type of Blessed Mary, and on Psalm CXVII, which is likewise typological of Christ’s Incarnation and of the Blessed Virgin Mary: St. Augustine, XXXVIII; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI; Cassiodorus, LXX; the Venerable Bede, XCIII; Abbot Rupert, *On the True Victory*, CLXIX; Adam of Perseigne, from Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and St. Chrysostom, CCXI.

4. Testimonies from the Gospel confirm the excellence of the Virgin Blessed Mary. Thus, concerning the angelic salutation: St. Ambrose, XV; the Venerable Bede, XCIII; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII; Abbot Aelred, CXCV; Adam of Perseigne, from Origen and John Geometres, CCXI; Innocent III, CCXVII.—On the first chapter of St. Luke and the comparison of Blessed Mary with Eve: St. Peter Chrysologus, LII; St. Fulgentius, LXV; Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII; Adam of Perseigne, from Gregory of Nyssa, Germanus of Constantinople, Gregory of Neocaesarea, and Theodore of Ancyra, CCXI.

5. The saying, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” was not known by the incorrupt body of Blessed Mary. This was the judgment of St. Augustine, *Sermon on the Assumption*, XXXVIII; the Gelasian Sacramentary, LIX; the Gregorian Sacramentary, LXXVIII; St. Autpert, bishop, LXXX; the Mozarabic Missal, LXXXV; the Gothic Breviary, LXXXVI; St. Ildefonsus, *On the Assumption*, XCVI; the Council of Mainz, in monuments of the tenth century; Pope Paschal I, CII; Pope Leo IV, CXV; Hincmar of Reims, *Dogmatic Poem*, CXXVI; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV; St. Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI; St. Odilo of Cluny, CXIII; St. Peter Damian, CXLV; St. Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI; [Col. 0501] St. Bernard, CLXXXIV; St. Amadeus of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII; Abbot Eckbert, CXCV; Peter of Blois, CCVII; Adam of Perseigne, from Modestus of Jerusalem, St. Germanus, St. John Damascene, St. Andrew of Crete, Emperor Manuel Palaeologus, and St. Epiphanius, CCXI; Sicardus, *Mitrale*, CCXIII.

Finally, very many Fathers maintain that no question should be raised concerning Blessed Mary when sins are under discussion: Caelius Sedulius, *Paschal Poem*, XIX; St. Augustine, XLII; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV; Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII; St. Bernard, CLXXXIV; Walter of St. Victor, against Abelard, etc., CXCIX; Innocent III, *Sermon*, CCXVII; and almost all the synods noted in the course of the *Patrology*.

## SECTION VII: ENCOMIASTIC

In which, alphabetically, are displayed the various names by which the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers called Blessed Mary.

### NOTICE

Although in truth the one and most glorious name of the Mother of God is **MARY**, nevertheless, since this name alone is insufficient for knowing her dignity, excellence, and sublimity, and for setting forth the variety and multiplicity of her perfections, it necessarily came about that the same Mother of God was called by the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers by so many varied and innumerable names. Therefore St. Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, wrote most truly: “Even if someone should utter innumerable encomia upon Mary, he would never attain the goal.” And St. Theodore: “Hail, Mary—as though you were saying *Myria*, ‘innumerable’ in Latin—because of the innumerable praise contained in your encomia.”

The names and praises of the Blessed Virgin, which we have gathered with no small labor, we have arranged in alphabetical order for the reader’s greater convenience. No name is given without indication of the source from which it has been drawn. Yet because the same words and appellations occur so frequently, we thought it enough merely to indicate the volume and works of each doctor, without page number; by consulting these works, the reader will readily find the words. Although, kind reader, you see that so many and such great names and praises of the Most Holy Virgin are brought forward in this Index, know nevertheless that they are a very small part of those which we could have produced had there been greater leisure of time and work. It remains our earnest wish that, by the same synopsis, not only the remaining tradition of the Latin Fathers from the thirteenth century onward may be faithfully recorded, but also that the innumerable and most illustrious [Col. 0503] roses may be gathered from the wondrous rose-garden of St. Caesarius. Having said this, we present the series of praises.

## SECTION VIII, LITURGICAL

Which treats feasts, hymns, and prayers in honour and glory of the Virgin Mother of God.

Here, lest things repeated twice prove displeasing, we mention only this section, which is found elsewhere. The reader should therefore consult the special Index on Feasts in General, in which everything pertaining to the feasts of Blessed Mary is listed. As regards hymns and prayers, let the reader also consult the Poetic Index and the Index on Prayer, and what is sought will be found.

[Col. 0527] Here we set an end to the Index, lest, through excessive prolixity, we should seem to draw it out at length. Material has not been lacking; it remains immense for all. Let the reader continually turn the pages of the *Patrology*, so that, gathering innumerable testimonies in honour of the Blessed Virgin, every doubt may be removed and vanish, and devotion toward Mary, Mother of God, may likewise be strengthened—Mary who is, as St. Bernard says:

THE ENTIRE GROUND OF OUR HOPE.

EIGHTH SERIES.

[Col. 0527]

[PREFACE.]

In this eighth series we deal with Christianity. Beginning from its cradle, that is, from the time when the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, were dispersed to evangelize the world, we trace its gradual advance through the diverse regions which it illuminates with its light. We present it as assailed from every quarter and yet, despite its enemies, extending its benefits even toward its persecutors. Accordingly, we here submit in turn to the reader historical, geographical, and bibliographical indexes concerning the preaching of the Gospel and the conversion of the nations; concerning the persecutions raised against the Christian Church by pagans, emperors, and others; concerning the benefits of Christianity toward peoples constituted in society, toward the family, and toward the individual person; and concerning the morals, customs, and other matters of Christians.

[Col. 0527]

LXXII. HISTORICAL INDEX OF THE PREACHING OF THE GOSPEL AND THE CONVERSION OF THE NATIONS; OR, AN ALPHABETICAL SYNOPSIS OF THE APOSTLES, EVANGELISTS, DISCIPLES OF THE LORD, AND ALL PREACHERS OF THE GOSPEL, WITH AN INDICATION AND DESIGNATION OF ALL PARTS OF THE WORLD, PROVINCES, REGIONS, NATIONS, PEOPLES, AND CITIES IN WHICH EACH OF THEM SCATTERED THE WORDS OF LIFE AND OF GOSPEL PREACHING, FROM THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD TO THE YEAR 1216.

[Col. 0527] A

**Abdias**, disciple of Simon Jude and first bishop of Babylonia, proclaims Christ in Persia (A.D. 60), Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 175.

**Abel**, bishop and companion of St. Boniface, preaches in Germany (A.D. 745), St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 757.

**Abhelinus**, bishop, was sent into Slavonia (A.D. 1026), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 532.

**Acca**, priest, one of the twelve companions of Willibrord, apostle of the Frisians, proclaims Christ in Frisia (noted under A.D. 692), Bede, XCV, 243.

**Acilinus**, with his companions, evangelizes Sweden (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, 617.

[Col. 0528] **Adalbert**, first bishop of Magdeburg, converts many to the faith in Slavonia (A.D. 968–981), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 608.

**Adalbert (St.)**, bishop of Prague, proclaims the Gospel in Prussia (Danzig) with St. Gaudentius (A.D. 990), St. Matilda the Queen, CLI, 1341; evangelizes Slavonia, Pannonia, and Poland (A.D. 980), Cosmas, dean of Prague, 92; Honorius of Autun, CLXXVII, 193; John Canaparius, CXXVII, 866; preaches to the Russians (A.D. 991), the same, ibid., 866, 888; Cosmas of Prague, CLXVI, 273.

**Adaldag (St.)**, bishop of Hamburg, evangelizes Slavonia (A.D. 936), St. Adalbert of Prague, CXXXVII, 501.

[Col. 0529] **Adalheri**, priest and companion of St. Boniface of Mainz, journeys throughout Germany with him in preaching (A.D. 730), St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 660.

**Adalward the Younger**, bishop in Gothia, sent to Sigtuna and Uppsala, preaches in Sweden (A.D. 1070), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 640; scatters the Gospel at Sictorrain and Birka, Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 145, 646.

**Adalwald (St.)**, the Elder, is ordained bishop of the Saxon nation (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 569; preaches in Gothia and Norway and converts many, id., ibid., 617, 640.

**Adelbert**, deacon, son of the king of the Deirans, one of Willibrord’s twelve companions, sows the faith with him in Frisia (A.D. 692), Bede, XCV, 243 (note).

**Adelbert (St.)**, also called Guilheth, bishop of Prague, proclaims Christ among the Bruttians and is crowned with martyrdom (A.D. 1015), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 201.

**Aedan, or Aidan**, bishop among the inhabitants of Hii on the island of Lindisfarne, a native of Scotland, spread the divine word in England (A.D. 615–640), Bede, XCV, 19–24; Bernold, abbot, CXLVIII, 1336; Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 120; William, CLXXIX, 1681; Henry, CXCV, 860; Helinand, CCXII, 772.

**Aeduin**, king of the Northumbrians, converted by St. Paulinus, brings Earpuald, king of the East Angles, together with his people, to the faith (A.D. 640), Bede, XCV, 107.

**Aegidius**, bishop of Tusculum, is sent by Pope John XIII to convert the Poles (A.D. 970), John XIII, pope, CXXXV, 949.

**Agathodorus**, bishop of Tarragona, preaches in Spain (A.D. 37), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 129.

**Agnellus**, bishop of Trent, evangelizes the Lombards (A.D. 583), Ekkehard, CLIV, 797.

**Agricius (St.)**, becomes bishop of Trier and brings the people from idolatry to Christ (A.D. 333–348), Anonymous, CLV, 1072, 1134.

**Alberic**, monk, evangelizes Wendilam, an island of Denmark (A.D. 1059), Adam of Bremen, 6, 6, 623.

**Alcfrid**, son of Oswi, king of the English, preaches the faith and converts Penda, king of the Middle Angles, together with his people, to the faith (A.D. 653), Bede, XCV, 150.

**Aldelm**, bishop of Sherborne, proclaims the Gospel in England and Saxony (A.D. 630), William, CLXXIX, 1533, 1619.

**Alexander I**, pope, converts the greater part of the Roman nobility to the faith (A.D. 111–113), Anastasius, CXXVII, 494.

**Alpinianus** preaches the faith at Toul and Limoges (A.D. 75), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 186; in Mauritania by the Garonne (A.D. 73), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 193.

**Amandus (St.)**, bishop of Trier and Tongeren, proclaims Christ at Ghent in Flanders (A.D. 628), Milo, monk of St. Amand, CXXI, 945; Heriger, CXXXIX, 1040; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1248; Helinand, CCXII, 785; at Tournai, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1251; in Brabant (A.D. 615), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1112; in Gascony, Milo the Monk, CXXI, 957; Helinand, CCXII, 787; among the Slavs, Milo the Monk, CXXI, 950; Helinand, CCXII, 786; with St. Landuald in Gaul (A.D. 614), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 115–120.

**Amantius (St.)**, deacon, evangelizes Gascony with St. Amandus (A.D. 650), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1113.

**Ananias**, to whom the Lord had directed Saul for instruction, baptizes at Caesarea (A.D. 34), Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 107.

**Anastasius (St.)**, monk and apostle among the Persians (A.D. 628), Bernold, CXLVIII, 1335.

**Andeolus (St.)** preaches in Gallaecia, Carpetania, and Spain (A.D. 208), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 358; while holding the episcopate at the city of Carpentras in Gaul (A.D. 200), John the Monk, CLXII, 756.

**Andochius (St.)** preaches the Gospel at the city of Sens (A.D. 195), St. Varnaharius, LXXX, 187, 190; John the Monk, CLXII, 757.

**Andrew**, apostle and brother of St. Peter, receives the Holy Spirit with the eleven on Pentecost and preaches the faith (A.D. 33), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 64; receives Scythia and Achaia as his field of evangelization (A.D. 33), Freculf, CVI, 1147; Haymo, CXVIII, 831; evangelizes Scythia, Achaia, Thrace, and Macedonia, Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 139, 142, 147.

**Anfred**, a priest and Dane by nation, proclaims Christ to the Swedes (A.D. 847), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 999.

**Angilbert**, a Gaul by nation, bishop of Dorchester and Winchester, preaches the faith in West Saxony (A.D. 634), Bede, XCV, 126; in England (A.D. 656), William, CLXXIX, 1523; Helinand, CCXII, 782.

**Two English priests**, whose names are unknown, preach among the Saxons.

[Col. 0530] (A.D. 604), Bernold, CXLVIII, 1339.

**Anianus**, bishop of Alexandria and successor of St. Mark the Evangelist, proclaims Christ at Alexandria (A.D. 68), Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 649.

**Ansgar**, also called Anschar, bishop of Hamburg and Bremen, sets out with King Harald to evangelize Denmark (A.D. 826), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 966; preaches through Saxony, Frisia, and Slavonia (A.D. 836), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 433; preaches to the Danes beyond the Elbe and to the Swedes (A.D. 840), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 476; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 190; converts Eric, king of the Danes, Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 480, 483; brings the Nordalbingians to the faith, ibid., 483; preaches at Birka in Sweden, ibid., 499.

**Antonius**, bishop of Meaux, preaches the faith with Sanctinus in Belgica among the Treveri (A.D. 70–97), Hugh, abbot, CLIV, 27–29.

**Apollinaris (St.)**, bishop of Hierapolis, preaches Christ at Hierapolis (A.D. 130), Freculf, CVI, 1166.

**Apollinaris (St.)**, bishop of Ravenna, evangelizes Ravenna (A.D. 70), Agnellus, abbot, CVI, 476.

**Apollos**, an Alexandrian by birth, preaches at Corinth, brings many to the faith, and refutes the Jews (A.D. 56), Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 175.

**The twelve apostles** are sent by Christ to preach the Gospel throughout the world (A.D. 33), Lactantius, VI, 1055 (appendix); preach to the Jews in the Temple at Jerusalem (A.D. 33), Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1631, 1634; cast lots for the lands in which to preach (A.D. 34; according to others, 38), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 87–88.

**Apuleius** teaches the faith at Alexandria (A.D. 72), Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 518.

**Aquila**, with Prisca and Paul, proclaims the faith through Asia (A.D. 50), Freculf, CVI, 1130; Haymo, CXVIII, 829; with Priscilla evangelizes the Corinthians, Anastasius, CXXVII, 462.

**Arcadius**, bishop of Juliobriga, proclaims the faith throughout Spain (A.D. 37), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 129, 130.

**Archippus**, with St. Timothy, proclaims Christ in Asia (A.D. 60–100), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 129.

**Ardgarius**, monk, preaches among the Swedes (A.D. 833), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 978.

**Arno**, bishop of Salzburg, preaches the faith among the Carantanians with St. Paulinus (A.D. 784), St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 70; Alcuin, C, 190, 192; labours for the conversion of the Huns and of Pannonia (A.D. 796), ibid., 76; Alcuin, C, 187–198.

**Arnulf (St.)**, bishop of Soissons, preaches in Flanders (A.D. 1056–1085), Harculf, abbot, CLXXIV, 1411–1464.

**Asgoth**, bishop, in Normandy, Sweden, and Norway (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 571, 617, 651.

**Athanasius (St.)**, first bishop of Saragossa, proclaims the Gospel in Celtiberia (A.D. 37), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 128, 167; with St. Theodore travels throughout all Carpetania (A.D. 52), ibid., 167.

**Athelm**, first bishop of Wells, preaches Christ to the West Saxons (A.D. 885), William, CLXXIX, 1543.

**Atrebanus**, cleric and companion of St. Willehad, preaches in Thiatmaresgau and is martyred by the Saxons (A.D. 780), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 1018.

**Attico**, bishop, evangelizes the Parthians and Persians and brings many to the faith (A.D. 379), Freculf, CVI, 1242.

**Audomar (St.)**, bishop of Thérouanne, preaches in Boulogne (A.D. 630), Folcard the Monk, CXLVII, 1182, 1190.

**Augustine (St.)**, apostle of the English, is sent by Pope St. Gregory the Great with forty companions to preach in England (A.D. 596), St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 835, 841; Bede, XCV, 52; Anastasius, CXXVIII, 645, 1370; Heriger, CXXXIX, 883; Bernold, CXLVIII, 1332; Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 112; Henry, CXCV, 841. With forty companions, among whom were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, Laurence, and Rufianus, he evangelizes England (A.D. 600), St. Augustine, Apostle of the English, LXXX, 79; Lanfranc, CL, 743, 764; William, CLXXIX, 968, 1441; converts King Ethelred to the faith (A.D. 604), St. Augustine, Apostle of the English, LXXX, 59; evangelizes the island of Thanet and baptizes the king in Kent, Bede, XCV, 55; Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 112; proclaims Christ in Scotland, St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 874.

**Austregisilus** evangelizes Bourges (A.D. 48), Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1493.

**Austriclianus** proclaims Christ in Gaul, at Toul and Limoges (A.D. 70), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 186; in Mauritania by the Garonne (A.D. 73), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 193.

**Autbert (St.)**, bishop of Corbie, sets out with St. Ansgar to preach in Denmark (A.D. 827), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 966.

[Col. 0531] **Avicianus (St.)**, bishop of Rouen and apostle of Normandy, preaches the faith in Gaul (A.D. 300), Orderic, CLXXXVII, 390.

**Avitus (St.)**, bishop of Vienne, journeys through Gaul in preaching (A.D. 490), Ekkehard, 778; establishes the faith against the Arians, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 93.

**Avoco**, bishop of Roskilde, proclaims the Gospel in Zealand (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 545, 624.

## B

**Barnabas (St.)**, with St. Paul the apostle, preaches at Antioch (A.D. 39), Freculf, CVI, 1125; Haymo, 826; Anastasius, CXXVII, 456, 458; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 114; is set apart with St. Paul for preaching the Gospel among the Gentiles, Hugh, abbot, CLIV, 24; goes up to Jerusalem, ibid., 24; and preaches there, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 17; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 640, 645; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 108; preaches at Athens, Haymo, CXXIII, 827; at Seleucia, Cyprus, and Salamis, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 114–116; in Seleucia, Lystra, Derbe, and Laodicea, ibid., 178; at Iconium, in Lycaonia, Lystra, and Pisidia, ibid., 115; having become bishop of Milan, he becomes a herald of the divine word in Italy, Landulf, cleric of Milan, CXLVII, 955.

**Bartholomew**, one of the twelve apostles and brother of St. Philip the apostle, receives India nearer at hand as his field of preaching (A.D. 33), Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 478; Haymo, CXVIII, 831; receives the Holy Spirit with the other apostles on Pentecost and preaches the faith (A.D. 33), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 64, 65; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1631; proclaims Christ in Lycaonia, India, Armenia, Assyria, and Albania (A.D. 34; according to others, 38), Freculf, CVI, 1147; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 165.

**Basil (St.)**, second bishop of Braga, preaches the faith in Spain (A.D. 37–65), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 199.

**Basil (St.)**, bishop of Carthago Spartaria, preaches in Spain (A.D. 37–60), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 128.

**Benignus (St.)**, priest, is sent into Gaul by St. Polycarp with St. Andochius and Thyrsus the deacon for the sake of preaching (A.D. 140), St. Warnaharius, LXXX, 187; John the Monk, CLXII, 756; arrives preaching at the fortress of Dijon, John the Monk, CLXII, 757; preaches at Langres, Warnaharius, LXXX, 188, 193.

**Benignus (St.)**, successor of St. Patrick, spreads the Gospel in Ireland (A.D. 460), William, CLXXIX, 1691.

**Benjamin (St.)**, companion of Willehad, is martyred by the Saxons while preaching at Cibhrinstri (A.D. 780), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 1018.

**Benno**, bishop, converts a multitude of Slavs (A.D. 1000), Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 535.

**Beregisus**, bishop and patron of the Ardennes, preaches in Gaul (year uncertain), Anonymous, CLIV, 1342.

**Bernard**, bishop, proclaims Christ in Normandy and Sweden (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 541, 651.

**Bernuinus**, priest, preaches the Gospel with Bishop Wilfrid on the Isle of Wight (A.D. 685), Bede, XCV, 196, 11, 197.

**Bertuin**, a Scot, preaches the faith in Gaul with Eton and Eloquius (A.D. 651), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 123.

**Betli**, together with Cedd and Diuma, natives of Scotland, proclaims the Gospel to the Middle Angles (A.D. 657), Bede, XCV, 150.

**Birinus (St.)**, apostle of the English and bishop of Winchester and Dorchester, proclaims the Gospel to the West Saxons and converts King Kinegistus and his people to Christ (A.D. 630), Bede, 126; William, CLXXIX, 1523; evangelizes the West Angles, Henry, CXCV, 861.
