ROUEN, a city of Gaul, was converted to the faith by Nicasius, bishop of Rouen, St Quirinus, and Scuviculus, sent into Gaul by St Dionysius (A.D. 70–100), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 386, 388.—Mello, archbishop of Rouen [Col. 0574] (A.D. 119), ibid., 386.—Mallonus and Avicianus of Rouen (A.D. 250–315), ibid., 390, 392. At RIBE, or Ripen, a city of Jutland, Christ was preached by Liasdagus, first bishop of Ribe (A.D. 948), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 503, 518, 821.—Odinkar the Younger, bishop of Ribe (A.D. 1000), ibid., 518, 526.—Wallus, bishop of Ribe (A.D. 1026), ibid., 552, 621.—Oddo (A.D. 1059), ibid., 616.

At ROFFIA or ROCHESTER, a city of England, the preachers of the divine word were St Justus, bishop of Rochester and companion of St Augustine (A.D. 600–630), Henry, CXCV, 853.—St Honorius the Roman and Paulinus, bishops of Rochester (A.D. 630–650), ibid., 857–859.

ROME. The apostle St Peter

> **[Note: [Col. 0573] At Rome Pilate, who had unjustly condemned Our Lord Jesus Christ to be scourged and crucified, reports His death, miracles, and resurrection to the emperor Tiberius and the senate (A.D. 38), Freculf, CVI, 1124; Haymo, CXVIII, 826; St Ado, bishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 75, 76; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 57; Bernold, CXLVIII, 1304; Ekkeard, [Col. 0574] CLIV, 663.—But Tiberius, Roman emperor, having received Pilate’s letter, announces the Lord’s miracles and resurrection to the senate and Roman people and attempts, though in vain, to enroll Him among the gods of the empire (A.D. 38), Haymo, CXVIII, 826.]**

came to Rome, founded the episcopal see there, and for twenty-five years preached and confirmed the Gospel of Christ by miracles (A.D. 45–69), Lactantius, VII, 621; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 553; Freculf, CVI, 1128; Haymo, CXVIII, 829; Anastas., CXXVII, 438; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 57; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 641; Ekkeard, CLIV, 667; Anonymous, ibid., 1116; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 122.—He ordained bishops and presbyters (A.D. 53), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 151; Anastas., CXXVII, 460; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 25, 26; Anonymous, ibid., 1117.—He wrote to the Dispersion, Anastas., CXXVII, 466.—Together with the apostle St Paul he preached at Rome, Sulpicius Severus, XXI, 144, 145; St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 173; Haymo, CXVIII, 830; St Ado, bishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 79; Anastas., CXXVII, 466, 468; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 58, 640; Bernold, CXLVIII, 1305; Ekkeard, CLIV, 667; Anonymous, ibid., 1116; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 128; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1715.—Peter and Paul confirmed their preaching at Rome by martyrdom (A.D. 69), Freculf, CVI, 1132; Heriger, CXXIX, 1008; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 132, 136.—Besides Saints Peter and Paul, the preachers of the divine word at Rome were Linus and Cletus (A.D. 50–69), Hugo, CLIV, 26; Ekkeard, ibid., 670.—St Mark, disciple of St Peter, who wrote his Gospel at Rome (A.D. 46), St Ado, bishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 77.—St Luke, who there wrote the Acts of the Apostles (A.D. 58), Freculf, CVI, 1148; Anastas., CXXVII, 468; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 101; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1643.—St Clement, pope (A.D. 69), Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 649; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 25, 26; Ekkeard, ibid., 670.—St Ignatius of Antioch was given over to beasts at Rome (A.D. 101), St Ado, archbishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 81.—Pope Alexander converted the greater part of the Roman nobility to the faith (A.D. 111–115), Anastas., CXXVII, 494.—A certain soldier Pontius converted the emperor Philip and his son Philip to Christ (A.D. 240), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 70.—Pope Sylvester baptized the emperor Constantine at Rome (A.D. 312), St Ado, archbishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 91; Anastas., CXXVII, 1511; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 44.

ROSCHALDIA, a city of Zealand, was evangelized by Avoco, bishop of Roschaldia (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 545, 624. The RUSSIANS were converted to the faith by Henry II, king and emperor of the Germans (A.D. 1002), Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 193.—St Adalbert, bishop of Prague (A.D. 990–1000), Adalbert, CXXXVII, 866, 888; Cosmas, dean of Prague, CLXXI, 273.

## S

At SALAMIS, Porto Costanza, a city on the island of Cyprus, the Gospel was proclaimed by St Paul the apostle (A.D. 48), Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 114; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1690.—St Barnabas, ibid. SALZBURG, Saltzbourg, a city of Bavaria, was evangelized by St John, bishop of Salzburg (A.D. 730), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 649, 741. At SAMARIA, a city of Palestine, the preachers of the divine word were Philip the deacon (A.D. 34–38), Freculf, CVI, 1123; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1490; Haymo, CXVIII, 825; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 106; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1668; Paul and Barnabas (A.D. 48–50), Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 115, 116; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1091.

SAMARITANIA, the region of Palestine, was evangelized by St Peter the apostle and St John the apostle, Anastas., CXXVII, 454, 462.—James the Greater, Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 113; [Col. 0575] Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1680.—The disciples scattered after the martyrdom of St Stephen, Haymo, CXVIII, 825; Anastas., CXXVII, 454; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 109.—Philip the deacon, from Azotus as far as Samaria, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 107. SAINTES, a city of Aquitania Secunda in Gaul, was evangelized by Eutropius (A.D. 80), Anonymous, CLIV, 1119. At SANIR, a city of Persia, Simeon the Canaanite and Judas of James proclaimed Christ (A.D. 38–53), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 176.

The SARACENS, peoples of Asia: Mavia, queen of the Saracens, having embraced the faith, requests for her people as bishop a certain Moses living in the desert (A.D. 374), Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 514.—Moses, made bishop, evangelized the Saracens, ibid. SARRONA, a city of Palestine, received the faith from St Peter the apostle, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1674. SAXONY in England was evangelized through St Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne (A.D. 630), William, CLXXIX, 1533, 1619.

SOUTH SAXONY in England was evangelized by St Wilfrid, bishop of York (A.D. 678), Bernold, CXLVIII, 1338; William, CLXXIX, 1553.—Pope Sergius, who baptized Ceadual, king of the South Saxons (A.D. 688), Bernold, CXLVIII, 1339.—Wilserius, king of the Mercians, by his exhortations brought Edelwalh, king of the South Saxons, to Christ (A.D. 700), William of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 1548. SAXONY in western England was instructed in the faith of Christ by St Birinus, apostle of the English and bishop of Winchester and Dorchester (A.D. 630), Henry, archdeacon, CXCV, 861.—Angilbert, a Gaul by nationality, bishop of Dorchester and Winchester (A.D. 634), Bede, XCV, 126.—Leutherius, bishop of Dorchester (A.D. 634–670), Bede, XCV, 126, 128.—Colman (A.D. 670), Anonymous, CLXIII, 581.

EAST SAXONY in England was brought to the faith by Finan, bishop on the island of Lindisfarne, Holy Island (A.D. 653), Henry, CXCV, 864.—Jarumarmus, bishop (A.D. 665), Bede, XCV, 170.—Cedd, bishop of London, ibid., 151. SAXONY, a region of Germany, was evangelized by two Englishmen of uncertain name (A.D. 694), Bernold, CXLVIII, 1339.—St Boniface, bishop of Mainz and apostle of the Germans (A.D. 716–745), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 622, 648.—Lobanus, bishop of Ahretata; Hadolfrid or Hadolf of Kundekar; and the monks Willilseri, Hamung, and Wintrung, presbyters, disciples and fellow-workers of St Boniface of Mainz (A.D. 755), LXXXIX, 660, 667, 805.—Charlemagne, king of the Franks, imposed baptism upon the Saxons (A.D. 777), Einhard, XCVII, 33; Ekkeard, CLIV, 857, 893; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 190.—Atrebanus, clerk; Benjamin; Count Emmingus; Foleward, priest; and Gerwalus, disciples and companions of St Willibrord, preached in Saxony (A.D. 780), St Ansgar, CXVIII, 1017.—St Ansgar, bishop of Hamburg and Bremen (A.D. 789–838), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 471.—Rimbert of Hamburg (A.D. 854), CXLVI, 486.—Athelm, first bishop of Wells (A.D. 885), William, CLXXIX, 1543; Heribert of Wiberg (A.D. 1059), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 616.

SCALDHOLGA, a city of Iceland, was evangelized through Islef, bishop of Scaldhoga (A.D. 1065), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 654. SCANIA or SCONIA, and the island of Scone, received the faith of Christ through the preaching of Haredo or Horit, bishop of Schleswig (A.D. 948), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 503.—Gotebald (A.D. 985), ibid., 529.—Eginon, bishop of Dalby (A.D. 1060), ibid., 617. SCARANA, a city of West Gothia in Scania, was converted to Christ by the preaching of Turgoth, first bishop of Scara or Sarana (A.D. 1013), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 541, 640.—Of Eginon, bishop of Dalby (A.D. 1060), ibid., 617. SCHIREBARGUM in East Saxony, England, was evangelized through St Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne (A.D. 640), William, CLXXIX, 1535, 1619.

SLAVONIA was evangelized by St Amandus, bishop of Trier (A.D. 628), Milo, monk, CXXI, 950; Helinand, CXII, 786.—St Ansgar, bishop of Hamburg (A.D. 836), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 433.—St Adaldag, bishop of Hamburg (A.D. 936), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 501.—Otto the Great, emperor of Germany, who imposed the faith upon the Slavs (A.D. 940), ibid., 503.—Adalbert, bishop of Magdeburg, and Bruno (A.D. 968–990), ibid., 503, 504, 508.—Adalbert of Prague (A.D. 980), Adalbert of Prague, CXXXVII, 866; Cosmas, dean of Prague, CLXVI, 92; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 193.—Foleward [Col. 0576], archbishop of Slavonia (A.D. 992), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 533.—Bishop Benno (A.D. 1000), ibid., 535.—Bishop Albhelinus (A.D. 1026), ibid., 1026, ibid., 552.—Ezzo of Aldenburg (A.D. 1065), ibid., 574, 617. SCONE: see SCONIA.

SCOTLAND was evangelized by Palladius, first bishop of the Scots, sent by Pope Celestine (A.D. 430), Bede, XCV, 121 (II); Henry, CXCV, 822.—St Columba the Irishman (A.D. 565), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 112.—St Augustine, apostle of the English (A.D. 630), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 874, 877.—Laurence, companion of St Augustine (A.D. 609), Bede, XCV, 86.—Menalchius, archbishop of the Scots (A.D. 630), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 874.—Livinus, Foilan, and Elias, disciple of Livinus (A.D. 648), ibid., 879. Among the SCRITEFINGI, peoples of Sweden, Simon, bishop of Hälsingland, proclaimed Christ (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 641.

SCYTHIA was converted to the faith by the apostle Andrew (A.D. 34–37), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 87; Freculf, CVI, 1147; Haymo, CXVIII, 831; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 139, 142.—St Philip the apostle, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 87, 88; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 156; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1698.—St John, bishop of Constantinople (A.D. 400), Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1167. In SEELAND, an island of Denmark, the Gospel was preached by Liasdagus, bishop of Ribe, and Haredus, bishop of Schleswig (A.D. 948), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 503, 518, 821.—Gerbrand, bishop of Roschaldia (A.D. 1050), ibid., 624.—William, bishop of an uncertain place (A.D. 1059), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 616, 623.—Avoco, bishop of Roschaldia (A.D. 1060), ibid., 545, 624.—John the Scot, bishop of Mecklenburg, ibid., 527, 595, 650.

SELEGIA, a city of the Mercians in England, was evangelized through St Wilfrid, bishop of Selegia (A.D. 680), William, CLXXIX, 1549. SELEUCIA, a region of Syria in Asia Minor, was evangelized by St Paul the apostle and Barnabas (A.D. 50–58), Anastas., CXXVII, 460; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 114. SENONES in Gaul, Sens, were converted to Christ by Potentianus (A.D. 50), Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1493.—St Andochius (A.D. 195), CLXII, 757; St Warnaharius, priest, LXXX, 187, 190.—Wulfram, bishop of Sens (A.D. 718), Helinand, CXII, 812. The SEQUANI, peoples of Gaul, embraced the faith through the preaching of St Marcellus, disciple of St Pothinus of Lyons (A.D. 180), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 1210.

SICILY: Roger, count of the Normans, established bishops throughout Sicily and extended the faith (A.D. 1080), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 486; Geoffrey, monk, CXLIX, 1188. SIETONA or SIETUNA, a city of Sweden, was converted by Adalwald the Younger (A.D. 1070), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 640, 645. SIDON, a city of Phoenicia, was evangelized by St Peter the apostle (A.D. 38–44), Anastas., CXXVII, 456; Heriger, CXXXIX, 1008; Hugo, CLIV, 25; Ekkeard, ibid.; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 116, 122; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1674, 1701. At SINOPE, a city of Paphlagonia in Asia Minor, St Andrew the apostle proclaimed Christ (A.D. 38–50), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 140.

SCHLESWIG, or Sliaskig, in Jutland, was evangelized by Bishop Haredus (A.D. 948), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 503.—Poppo, bishop of Schleswig (A.D. 1010–1015), ibid., 525, 526.—Odinkar, ibid., 535.—Ratolph (A.D. 1059), ibid., 616, 623, 668. SMYRNA, a city of Asia Minor, received the divine word from St Polycarp (A.D. 125), Freculf, CVI, 1164. At SONEGIUM, a monastery near Cambrai, St Vincent, abbot of Sonegius, instructed the people in the faith (A.D. 651), Sigebert, CLX, 123.

SWEDEN, a region of northern Europe, was evangelized by Gotebald, an Englishman by birth (A.D. 986), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 529.—Odinkar the Elder (A.D. 990–1000), ibid., 518, 526.—Olof, king of Sweden, who endeavoured to lead the peoples subject to him to the Catholic faith and at whose instigation Turgoth was ordained first bishop of Scara (A.D. 1013), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 541.—Turgoth, ibid.—John the Scot, bishop of Mecklenburg (A.D. 1023), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 527, 574, 540, 595, 617, 650.—Welfred, who converted many to the faith and destroyed idols (A.D. 1029), ibid., 543.—Tadicus (A.D. 1059), ibid., 617.—Sigofrid, monk of Glastonbury (A.D. 1060), ibid., 651.—Simeon, bishop of Hälsingland (A.D. 1060), ibid., 617, 641.—Thaolf, bishop of Trondheim, Seward, and Acilius (A.D. 1060), ibid., 617, 650.—Asgoth (A.D. 1060), ibid., 571, 617, 651.—Ezzo, bishop of Aldenburg (A.D. 1065), ibid., 574, 617.—Avito of Razzinburg and John of Bircac [Col. 0577] (A.D. 1065), ibid., 574, 617, 636.—Bishop Osmund (A.D. 1069), ibid., 568, 617.—Meinhard and Adalward (A.D. 1069), ibid., 617, 640, 653. SUELLO, a city of Celtiberia in Spain, received the faith (A.D. 86), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 251.

SUEONIA, a region of Slavonia, was evangelized by St Ansgar or Ansgarius, bishop of Hamburg and Bremen (A.D. 840), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 476; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 190.—Ebbo, bishop of Rheims; Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai; Gauzbert; Witmar, monk; Adgarius, monk; Gandbert, bishop; and Gislemar (A.D. 830–840), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 474–478; St Ansgar, CXVIII, 971.—Hartagarius, hermit (A.D. 845), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 480.—Anfrid and Erimbert, priests (A.D. 850), St Ansgar, CXVIII, 997–999; Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 481.—Rimbert, Danish priest, and Ragimbert (A.D. 860), St Ansgar, CXVIII, 999.—Unni, bishop of Hamburg, who converted many to Christ (A.D. 903–936), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 498, 499.—Liafdagus of Ribe (A.D. 948), ibid., 503, 518, 821.—Haredus of Schleswig (A.D. 948), ibid., 503.—Poppo of Schleswig (A.D. 1010–1015), ibid., 525, 526.—Rodulf of Schleswig (A.D. 1026), ibid., 541, 552, 662, 668.—Grimkil and Bernard (A.D. 1030–1060), ibid., 541, 650.

SOISSONS, a city in Gaul, was evangelized by St Memmius (A.D. 36–106), Flodoard, canon of Rheims, CXXXV, 32.—St Sixtus, first bishop of Rheims (A.D. 90), ibid., 32. SYRIA, a region of Asia, was traversed in evangelizing by St Paul the apostle, Silas, and Barnabas (A.D. 38–50), Freculf, CVI, 1130; Haymo, CXVIII, 831; Anastas., CXXVII, 464; Heriger, monk, CXXXIX, 1008; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 639; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 116; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1692, 1698.—Aquila, Prisca, and Priscilla, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1704.

## T

The island of THANET in England had as preacher of the divine word St Augustine with forty companions (A.D. 596), Bede, XCV, 55; Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 112. TARRAGONA, Tarragone, in Spain, was evangelized through St Agathodorus (A.D. 37–60), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 129. TARASCON in Gaul was converted to Christ by the preaching of St Martha, hostess of Christ and sister of St Mary Magdalene (A.D. 35–60), Rabanus, CXII, 1497. The TAXANDRIANS in Germany were converted to Christ by St Lambert, bishop of Trajectum (Utrecht) (A.D. 677), Sigebert, CLX, 769, 793. TÉROUANNE in Gaul was evangelized by St Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne (A.D. 630), Folcard, monk, CXLVII, 1182.

THESSALY, a region of Europe. See MYRMIDONS. THESSALONICA, a city of Macedonia, was evangelized by St Andrew the apostle (A.D. 37–60), Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 141, 147.—St Paul the apostle and his companions, namely Barnabas, Timothy, Silas, Luke, Prisca, Priscilla, and others (A.D. 38–58), Freculf, CVI, 1130; Haymo, CXVIII, 831; Anastas., CXXVII, 464; Heriger, CXXXIX, 1008; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 639; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1701.

THIATMARESGAO, a city of Frisia: Atrebanus, cleric and companion of St Willehad, proclaimed the Gospel in Thiatmaresgao and received the crown of martyrdom from the Saxons (A.D. 780), St Ansgar, CXVIII, 1018. Throughout THRACE preached St Andrew the apostle (A.D. 38–50), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 139.—Certain captive priests (A.D. 330), Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 939. THRET, a city of Frisia, was instructed in the faith of Christ by Eoban, fellow-worker of St Boniface and bishop of Ahretata (A.D. 755), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 660, 667, 805. THRIANTA, a city of Frisia, was converted to Christ by the preaching of St Willehad, first bishop of Bremen (A.D. 754), St Ansgar, CXVIII, 1015, 1016. THURINGIA, a region of Germany, was brought to the faith by St Boniface, bishop of Mainz and apostle of Germany (A.D. 717), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 466.—St Willibad, fellow-worker of St Boniface (A.D. 741), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 751, 806.

TILABURGA, a city of the East Saxons in England, received the faith of Christ from Cedd, bishop of London (A.D. 610), Bede, XCV, 151, 152, 154. At TOLEDO, a city of Spain, Christ was proclaimed by Elpidius, first bishop of Toledo (A.D. 37–60), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 129.—Eugenius Marcus Marcellus (A.D. 60), ibid., 273.—St Philip of Milan (A.D. 91), ibid., 261, 263. [Col. 0578] TOULOUSE, a city of Gaul, was evangelized by St Saturninus (A.D. 58), St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 175, 183; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1494; Martialis of Limoges (A.D. 58), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 169.

TOURNAI, a city of Belgium, was evangelized through St Amandus, bishop of Trier and Tongeren (A.D. 640), Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1251. TRAJECTUM, Utrecht, a city of Germany, was converted to Christ by St Willibrord, bishop of Trajectum (A.D. 690), Alcuin, CL, 698.—St Gregory, bishop of Trajectum (A.D. 736), St Boniface, LXXXIX, 646, 653.—St Amandus, bishop of Trier and Tongeren; St Landoald, archpriest; and St Amantius, deacon (A.D. 650), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1113.—St Lambert, bishop of Trajectum (A.D. 677), ibid., CXXXIX, 1113, 1114. TRANSALBIA, a province of Germany, embraced the faith while Willeric, bishop of Bremen, preached (A.D. 830), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 472.

At TRIER, a city of Belgica, the Gospel was proclaimed by St Valerius the confessor, who preached among the Treveri (A.D. 48), Rabanus, CXII, 1493.—St Sinicius, St Eucharius, first bishop of Trier, and St Maternus (A.D. 50; others say 250), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1010; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 25; Anonymous, CLIV, 1118.—St Anthony, bishop of Meaux, and St Sanctinus (A.D. 70–97), Hugo, abb., CLIV, 27, 29.—St Agricius became bishop of the Treveri and converted the people from idolatry to Christ (A.D. 333–368), Anonymous, CLIV, 1072–1134.—St Maximinus, bishop of Trier, succeeded St Agricius, apostle of the Treveri (A.D. 342–368), Anonymous, 1072, 1135.—St Amandus, bishop of Trier, preached the Gospel (A.D. 628), Milo, monk, CXXI, 945; Heriger, CXXXIX, 1040; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1248; Helinand, CCXII, 785.

At TRIPOLI, a city of Syria, St Peter the apostle preached the Gospel (A.D. 38–40), Anastas., CXXVII, 456; Heriger, XXXIX, 1008; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 25; Ekkeard, ibid., 667; Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 116, 122; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1674, 1701. TROAS, a region of Asia Minor, was converted to Christ through the preaching of Saints Paul, Luke, Timothy, and Barnabas (A.D. 38–60), Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1698, 1707.—Carpus, disciple of St Paul (A.D. 60–100), Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 129. TRONDHEIM, a city of Sweden, had as preachers of the divine word St Seward and Thoalf, who was bishop of Trondheim (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 650.

The TUNGRI were instructed in the faith of Christ by Saints Maternus, Eucharius, and Valerius (A.D. 50–80; others say 250), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1013; Hugo, abb., CLIV, 25; Anonymous, ibid., 1118, 1125.—St Amandus, bishop of Tongeren (A.D. 628), Milo, monk, CXXI, 945. TURGIA in Spain. See CASTRUM near Turgia. At TOURS, St Gratianus, bishop, preached Christ (A.D. 58), St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 155, 183. The TUTELENSES in Gaul were evangelized by St Martialis, bishop of Limoges (A.D. 58), Orderic, CLXXXVIII, 286.—Austriclianus and Alpinianus (A.D. 70), ibid., 186.—Mansuetus, Anonymous, CLIV, 1119, 1124. TYRE, a city of Syria in Asia Minor, was converted to Christ by St Peter the apostle (A.D. 38–40), Anastas., CXXVII, 456; Heriger, CXXXIX, 1008; Hugo, CLIV, 25; Ekkeard, CLIV, 667; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 125; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1692, 1698.

## U

At UPPSALA, a city of Sweden, Adalwald the Younger proclaimed Christ (A.D. 1070), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 640. URCI, a city of Spain, was evangelized through St Indalecius (A.D. 55), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 169.

## V

VALENCIA, a city of Spain, was evangelized by Eugenius Marcus Marcellus (A.D. 37–60), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 129.—St Philip of Milan (A.D. 91), ibid., 261, 263. VASCONIA was evangelized by St Amandus, bishop of Trier (A.D. 333), Milo, monk, CXXI, 957; Helinand, CXII, 787.—By Saints Landoald, Amantius, and Lambert (A.D. 650), Heriger, CXXXIX, 1113. The island of WIGHT in England had as preachers of the divine word St Bernuinus, priest, and Wilfrid, bishop (A.D. 685), Bede, XCV, 196, 197.—Hiddila, priest (A.D. 686), ibid., 196, 197.

[Col. 0579] The VENETI, inhabitants of western Gaul: St James called the Greater spread the divine word through the towns of the Veneti (A.D. 41), Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 135. VENTANA, a city of England, was evangelized through Unni, bishop of Ventana (A.D. 660), Bede, XCV, 127. VERDEN in Saxony was evangelized by St Willebad, first bishop of Bremen (A.D. 754), St Ansgar, CXXIII, 1017. VERGILIA, a city of Spain, received the faith of Christ from St Thesiphorus (A.D. 41), XXXI, 135. VERONA, a city of Italy, was converted to Christ by St Zeno, bishop of Verona (A.D. 368), St Zeno of Verona, XI, 150.

VIENNE, a city of Gaul, was evangelized by St Crescens, bishop of Vienne (A.D. 59), St Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 79.—St Avitus, bishop of Vienne (A.D. 490), Ekkeard, CLIV, 778. VIRDUNUM, Verdun, a city of Gaul, had as preachers of the divine word St Sanctinus, one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, bishop of Meaux and Verdun, together with St Dionysius (A.D. 70), Hugo, abb., CLIV, 27, 28.—St Antoninus or Antonius (A.D. 70–97), ibid., 27, 29. The city of the VIROMANDUI in Gaul embraced the faith through the preaching of St Quintinus, bishop of Amiens (A.D. 80; others say 280), St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1496.

## W
WAGRIA, a region of Germany, was converted to Christ by St. Egward, or Ewagrius, first bishop of Aldenburg (A.D. 980), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 508.—St. Vicelinus, apostle of Wagria (A.D. 1125), ibid., 455. WISIGOTHS. See ARIANS. The WAIGRI, peoples of Norway, were brought to the faith by two monks of uncertain name (A.D. 1065), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 573, 574. St. Willibard, sent by Pope John XIII with St. Procorius, preached Christ among the WANDALS, peoples of Germany (A.D. 970), Pope John XIII, CXXXV, 949. WARBARANA, or Barbarana (Warburg), had as heralds of the divine word Wittam, or Wisa, or Wetanus (A.D. 730–742), St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 749.—St. Winnibald (A.D. 740), Freculf, CVI, 646. The WARHABI, peoples of Slavonia, were converted to the faith by two monks coming from Bohemia (A.D. 1065), Adam of Bremen, 573, 574. WELLA, a city of West Saxony in Slavonia, was converted to Christ by Athelmus, bishop of Wells (A.D. 885), William, CLXXIX, 1543. WENDILA, an island of Norway, was evangelized by the monk Magnus (A.D. 1059), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 616.—The monk Albric, together with Magnus, ibid., 616, 623. The WERMIBANI, peoples of Slavonia, were converted to Christ by Simon, bishop of Hälsingland (A.D. 1060), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 617, 641. WESTERGOTHIA, a region of Sweden. Olaf, king of Sweden, brought the peoples subject to him to the faith and summoned Thurgot, first bishop of Skara, to preach the Gospel (A.D. 1013), Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 541. WEST SAXONY, a region of England, had as heralds of the divine word St. Birinus, apostle of the English together with St. Augustine, bishop of Winchester and Dorchester (A.D. 630), Bede, XCV, 126; William, CLXXIX, 1523.—Epelpine, or Edelwine (A.D. 651), ibid., 1605.—Pecthelm, apostle of the West Saxons and bishop of Candida Casa (A.D. 725), William, CLXXIX, 1517.—Edilfrid (A.D. 850), ibid., 1547.—Athelm, bishop of Wells (A.D. 885), ibid., 1543. WIBERT, a city of Denmark, received the faith from Heribert, bishop of Wiberg (A.D. 1059), Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 616. WIGMODIA was converted to Christ through the preaching of St. Willehad, first bishop of Bremen (A.D. 754), St. Ansgar, CXVIII, 1011; Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 466. WORCESTER, in the province of the Mercians in England, was evangelized by Bosel and Ostcar, its first bishops (A.D. 730–750), St. William, CLXXIX, 1587. WINCHESTER, or WITTONIA, a city of West Saxony in England, was enlightened by Birinus, apostle of the English together with St. Augustine (A.D. 630), Bede, XCV, 126; William, CLXXIX, 1523.—Angilbert, a Gaul by nationality and bishop of Winchester (A.D. 634), Bede, XCV, 126; Helinand, CCXII, 782. WÜRZBURG, a city of Germany, was converted to Christ through the preaching of St. Burchard, bishop of Würzburg (A.D. 730–751), St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 646; Bernold, CXLVIII, 1342.

## Y

YTHANCAESTIR, a city of the East Saxons in England. Cedd, bishop of London, proclaimed Christ in the city of Ythancaestir in East Saxony (A.D. 610), Bede, XCV, 151, 152, 154.

[Col. 0579]

# LXXIV. BIBLIOGRAPHICAL INDEX OF THE PREACHING OF THE GOSPEL AND THE CONVERSION OF PEOPLES, OR AN ALPHABETICAL SYNOPSIS OF THE HOLY FATHERS AND WRITERS WHO HAVE HANDED DOWN SOMETHING CONCERNING THE PREACHING OF THE GOSPEL AND THE CONVERSION OF PEOPLES FROM THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD TO THE YEAR 1216.

[Col. 0579]

## A

ADAM OF BREMEN, canon. *Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Hamburg* (A.D. 1076), CXLVI, 464. ADEMAR, monk of St. Cybard. Letter on the apostleship in Gaul of St. Martial, apostle of Limoges (A.D. 1028), CXLI, 87–112. ADO, saint, archbishop of Vienne. *Chronicle* (A.D. 875), CXXIII, 76. AIMOIN, monk of Fleury. *History of the Franks* (A.D. 1008), CXXXIX, 653. AGNELLUS, abbot of St. Mary at Blachernae. *Book of the Popes* (A.D. 842), CVI, 476. ALCUIN, Flaccus Albinus. Letter to Charlemagne, emperor (A.D. 790), C, 187.—Letter to Arno, C, 190, 192.—Letter to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, C, 198.—Lives of Saints Vedast, Richarius, and Willibrord, CI, 663, 686, 693.

[Col. 0580]

AMBROSE, saint, bishop of Milan. Exposition on the Apocalypse (A.D. 420), XVII, 867. ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN (chronology in the Prolegomena) (A.D. 888), CXXVII, 452–496, 528–1249. Life of St. Gregory the Great, pope, CXXVIII, 645; Life of St. Gregory II, pope, ibid., 975; Life of Pope John VII, ibid.; Life of Pope Nicholas I, ibid., 1370–1374; Life of Pope St. Sylvester I, ibid., 1511.—Translation of the chronology of Nicephorus, ibid.; by the same author, XXIX, 525. ANONYMOUS author of the eighth century, *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*, VIII, XCVIII, 1433. ANONYMOUS author (to Paulinus of Aquileia) (A.D. 804). *Life of St. Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia*, XCIX, 69. ANONYMOUS, eleventh century. *Chronicle of Aldenburg* (A.D. 1083), CLXXIV, 1461–1476. ANONYMOUS. *Deeds of Trier* (A.D. 1111), CLIV, 1116–1125. ANONYMOUS, twelfth century, *Chronicle of the Venerable Abbots of the Monastery of Saint Benignus of Dijon* (A.D. 1115), CLXII, 755–788. ANONYMOUS, twelfth century, *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz* (A.D. 1119), CLXIII, 579–581. ANONYMOUS, twelfth century. Historical notice on Pope Adrian IV, CLXXXVIII, 1349. St. ANSGAR, or Ansgarius, bishop of Hamburg and apostle of the Frisians. *Life of St. Willehad* (A.D. 865), CXVIII, 1015–1017. St. ANSELM, abbot. *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège* (A.D. 1008), CXXXIX, 1008–1040. St. ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury. Passion of the holy martyrs Guiner, Fingar, and their companions (A.D. 1109), CLIX, 325.—Ancient writers collected into one body. *Frankish Annals*, LXXI, 152.

## B

BALDRIC, archbishop of Dol. Acts of St. Valeria, martyr (A.D. 1080), CLXVI, 1209, 1210. VENERABLE BEDE, priest. *Ecclesiastical History* (A.D. 730), XCV, 30. BERENGOSUS, abbot of St. Maximinus at Trier. *On the Praises and Discovery of the Holy Cross* (A.D. 1112), CLX, 935. BERNOLD. *Chronicle* (appendix to the Gregorian monuments) (A.D. 1085), CXLVIII, 1304. BONIFACE, saint, bishop of Mainz, also called Winfrid, apostle of Germany. Various letters (A.D. 716–755), LXXXIX, 687–806.

## C

CASSIODORUS, Aurelius, senator and abbot of Vivarium. *Tripartite History* (A.D. 560), LXIX, 888, 1167. COSMAS, dean of Prague. *Chronicle* (A.D. 1125), CLXVI, 71–99.

## D

DUDO, dean of Saint-Quentin of Vermandois. *On the Deeds of the Dukes of Normandy* (A.D. 1029), CXLI, 651.

## E

EGINHARD, abbot, nephew of Emperor Charlemagne. *Life of Charlemagne* (A.D. 840), XCVII, 33. EKKEHARD, bishop of Uraug. *Universal Chronicle* (A.D. 1100), CLIV, 661–778.

## F

FLAVIUS LUCIUS DEXTER. *Chronicle* (A.D. 417), XXXI, 87–358. FLODOARD, canon of Rheims. *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims* (A.D. 956), CXXXV, 32–50. FOLCARD, monk of Sithiu. *Life of St. Omer, Bishop of Thérouanne* (A.D. 1080), CXLVI, 1183–1283. FRECULF, bishop of Lisieux. *Chronicle* (A.D. 850), CVI, 1121–1241. FREDEGAR THE SCHOLAR. *Chronicle* (A.D. 641), LXXI, 613.

## G

GAUFREDUS MALATERRA, monk. *Sicilian History* (A.D. 1000), CXLIX, 1187. GERARD, priest. *Compostellan History* (A.D. 1134), CLXX, 875. GOSCELIN, monk of Canterbury. *Life of St. Augustine, Apostle of the English* (A.D. 1100), LXXX, 41.—Historical eulogy of St. Laurence, CLV, 115–119. GREGORY, saint, the Great, pope. Letters (A.D. 595), LXXVII, 931. GREGORY, saint, bishop of Tours. Ten books of *Histories of the Franks* (A.D. 595), LXXI, 173–493.

## H

HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt. *Epitome of Sacred History*, CXVIII, 822–834. HARIULF, abbot of Aldenburg. *Chronicle of Centula* (A.D. 1142), CLXXIV, 1220. HELINAND, monk of Froidmont. *Chronicle* (A.D. 1212), CCXII, 772. HENRY, archdeacon of Huntingdon. *History of the English* (A.D. 1160), CXCV, 826. HERIC, bishop of Auxerre. *Life of St. Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre* (A.D. 881), CXXIV, 1164. HERIGER, abbot of Lobbes. *Deeds of the Bishops of Maastricht and Liège* (A.D. 1008), CXXXIX, 1008–1010. HERMANN THE LAME, monk. *Chronicle* (1054), CXLVII, 57–387.

[Col. 0582]

HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims. *Life of St. Remigius, Bishop of Rheims* (A.D. 882), CXXV, 1157. HONORIUS, saint, bishop of Autun. *Summary of All History* (A.D. 1136), CLXXII, 190. HUBERT, saint, monk of Andage. *Chronicle* (A.D. 1106), CLIV, 1342. HUGH, saint, abbot of Flavigny. *Chronicle* (A.D. 1100), CLIV, 24–110. HUGH OF ST. MARY, monk of Fleury. *History of the Kings of the Franks* (A.D. 1119), CLXIII, 913. HUGH, bishop of Porto. *Compostellan History* (A.D. 1134), CLXX, 875.

## I

Uncertain author. *Frankish Annals*, LXXI, 137–158. Uncertain author (in Mabillon). *Life of St. Augustine, Apostle of the English*, LXXX, 59. Uncertain author of the twelfth century. *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* (A.D. 1179), CXLIX, 26–28. Uncertain author (Prolegomena) on St. Patrick. *Life of St. Patrick, Apostle of Ireland* (A.D. 490), CLIII, 789–801.

## J

JOHN, saint, of Biclar. *Chronicle* (A.D. 599), LXXII, 869. JOHN CANAPARIUS, monk. Passion of St. Adalbert, bishop of Prague (A.D. 1000), CXXXVII, 866–888. JOHN THE VENETIAN, deacon. *Venetian Chronicle* (A.D. 1008), CXXXIX, 883. JORDAN, bishop of Limoges. Acts of the Council of Limoges (A.D. 1031), CXLII, 1353.

## L

LACTANTIUS FIRMILIANUS. *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, chapter 47 (fourth century), VI, 1055.—*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, VII, 621. LANDULF THE ELDER, cleric. Names of the Bishops of Milan (A.D. 1055), CXLVII, 955. LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury. *Life of St. Augustine, Apostle of the English* (A.D. 1089), CL, 743–764. LUPUS SERVATUS, abbot of Ferrières. *Life of St. Wigbert, Apostle of the Frisians* (A.D. 862), CXLX, 684.

## M

MARIANUS SCOTUS. *Chronicle* (A.D. 1080), CXLVII, 637, 761. MATHILDA, saint, queen. Letter to Mieszko, king of the Poles (A.D. 1027), CLI, 1334–1341. MILO, monk of Saint-Amand. *Life of St. Amandus, Preacher to the Slavs* (A.D. 872), CXXI, 945–957. MUNIO, bishop of Mondoñedo. *Compostellan History* (A.D. 1134), CLXX, 875.

## N

NICEPHORUS, saint (in St. Anastasius the Librarian). *Chronology* (A.D. 828), CXXIX, 525.

## O

ORDERIC VITALIS, monk of Saint-Evroult. *Ecclesiastical History* (A.D. 1147), CLXXXVIII, 64–390. OTHLOH, monk of Saint Emmeram. Fragment on the translation of St. Dionysius the Areopagite and apostle of Gaul (A.D. 1063), CXLVI, 387.—*Life of St. Wolfgang, Bishop of Regensburg* (A.D. 1063), CXLVI, 402.

## P

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, saint, abbot of Corbie. *On the Passion of the Saints Rufinus and Valerian* (A.D. 865), CXX, 1494–1496. # LXXV. INDEX OF THE PERSECUTIONS STIRRED UP AGAINST THE CATHOLIC CHURCH BY PAGAN EMPERORS AND HERETICS, ARRANGED IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER.

## I.—On persecution in general: its usefulness, causes, and so forth

[Col. 0583]

In time of persecution God is believed and feared more, Tertullian, II, 104. Faith is more vigilant and more disciplined, ibid. One is occupied solely with fear and hope, ibid. The blood of Christians is seed, the same author, I, 535. Persecution of the Christian name on account of public calamities, the same, III, 1163. Persecution comes because of sins, St. Cyprian, IV, 241. Persecutions occur so that we may be tested, ibid., 581, 656, 665. Persecution arose in order that God might raise up faith when it lay prostrate, ibid., 468. Persecution arose in order that it might become apparent which is the Church, the same author, III, 974. Fruits of persecutions, the same, IV, 351, 352. What good can you think of one whom persecution itself has not reformed? ibid., 483. How useful and necessary persecution is, St. Hilary, IX, 575. Persecution concerns not the denial of believers but their testing and their crown, St. Jerome, XXIV, 187. From Nero to Maximian, the Church of Christ suffered ten persecutions, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1130. The persecution of the Church is twofold: one consists in the violence of persecutors, the other in the ill will of those who devise evil, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 868. Various persecutions suffered by the Church, the same, XLI, 615. The final persecution of the Church, what it will be, ibid., 676. Persecutions are useful to the Church, ibid., 298, 299. Persecution is inflicted and endured both for righteousness and for unrighteousness, the same, XXXV, 1855. The usefulness of persecutions and tribulations, the same, XXXVII, 648, 653 ff., 1126, 1215, 1259. By divine dispensation, persecution is permitted to one person for punishment, to another for testing, and to another for a crown, ibid., 220. The persecutions inflicted by the wicked are effective like fire for gold, not like fire for hay, ibid., 1693. God delivers some from persecution bodily, that unbelievers may be confounded; others only spiritually, that examples may be offered to believers, ibid., 1166. Evils inflicted by persecutors should be avoided when possible, but endured when they cannot be avoided without impiety, the same, XXXIII, 1016. In persecution one may flee to another place, the same, XXXV, 1511. In the time of persecution, when sacred codices were sought for burning, Christian congregations used to assemble, martyrs were baptized in prison, and Christ’s sacraments were celebrated, the same, XLIII, 663. Benefit arising from persecutions, Cassiodorus, LXX, 669; Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1235. The memory of persecutors has perished, ibid., 1285. How persecutions are to be endured, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 229. The persecutions of the Church are signified by the sea, Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII,

[Col. 0584]

1471. God does not permit persecution to last long, ibid. In time of persecution flight is permitted, ibid., 1496. How all who desire to live piously in Christ will endure persecution, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 604. Four persecutions of the Church, ibid., 324. That persecution occurs for three reasons, the same, CLXXVII, 765. Persecution is never absent from the Christian, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXIII, 361. That in the second state of the Church, when the red horse went forth, the most grievous persecution of the saints blazed forth, Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1149. That in the sixth state of the Church, after a great earthquake, a most powerful persecution will occur in the time of Antichrist, ibid., 1158. What the persecution of Christians is, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 377. There are two kinds of persecutors, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 140. Threefold patience must be opposed to threefold persecution, ibid., 302. Three kinds of persecutors, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 315.

## II.—First persecution, under Nero

Nero was the first at Rome to make the rising faith bloody, Tertullian, I, 292. He was the first of the Caesars to draw the sword against Christians, the same, II, 151. Whether Nero was the first of all, after the Church had been established, to persecute Christians, Lactantius, VII, 196, 304, 473, 628 ff. On what occasion, and in what year, he began to rage against them, ibid., 438, 622. Nero persecutes Christians, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 145. Nero was the first at Rome to subject Christians to punishments and deaths, and he commanded that they be tortured with equal persecution throughout all the provinces, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1078. Nero was the first to persecute Christians, St. Augustine, XLIII, 323, 328. Nero set Rome on fire, wishing to see how Troy burned, the same, XXXVIII, 1356. The first persecution, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 554; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 173. The first persecution against the Church of God scattered throughout all Judaea and Samaria all the disciples except eleven, Freculf of Lisieux, CVI, 1123. Nero, after all the crimes he had attempted, was the first at Rome to subject Christians to punishments and deaths, and he commanded that they be tortured with equal persecution throughout all the provinces, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 78. Nero first stirred up persecution against Christians throughout his whole realm and, desiring to eradicate the very name, killed the chief apostles, Ekkehard of Uraug, CLIV, 673. Caesar Nero first raised persecution against Christians, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 214; Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 67; Sicard of Cremona, CCXIII, 451.

[Col. 0585]

Domitian gradually rose through every degree of crime, until he dared to assail the firmly established Church of Christ throughout the whole world by issuing everywhere edicts of most cruel persecution, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 1087. Therefore this persecution under Diocletian and the other rulers, like a small spark, set almost the entire Roman world aflame, especially Egypt, Africa, and Mauretania, Freculf of Lisieux, CVI, 1192. This persecution burned so cruelly and so frequently that within one month eighteen thousand martyrs are said to have suffered for Christ, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 90. Then a persecution so cruel, so fierce, and so frequent blazed that within one month seventeen thousand martyrs are said to have suffered for Christ, ibid., 700. In the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, while the Church of God was being extended and growing throughout the whole world by prosperous increases, suddenly the storm of persecution burst forth, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 253. In this tempest eighteen thousand martyrs suffered within Rome, ibid. In the nineteenth year, Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West commanded that churches be destroyed, Christians afflicted, and Christians killed, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 72. This persecution blazed so cruelly and so frequently that within one month eighteen thousand martyrs are said to have suffered for Christ, ibid., 72.

# LXXVI. INDEX OF THE BENEFITS OF CHRISTIANITY FOR THE PRIVATE OR INDIVIDUAL HUMAN BEING, ARRANGED IN A LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS AND A CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS.

## Notice

The benefits of Christianity for the human being may be considered under a threefold aspect: namely, that of the intellect, the heart, and the body. For the divine religion of Christ illumined the human intellect by imparting to it knowledge of truths most necessary: the nature and unity of God and His chief attributes; the Trinity; creation; original sin; the Incarnation; eternal life; the origin, dignity, duties, and end of the human soul; and so forth.

Under the aspect of the heart, Christianity was of the greatest benefit to the individual human being, for it purified the heart and raised it to a remarkable degree of perfection. It imbued it with the eminent virtues of humility, charity, and chastity, almost wholly unknown to pagans. Then all the other virtues flowed like streams from these three most abundant springs; and, through Christ’s grace, the human being is now not merely God’s most excellent work, but God’s son and heir, Christ’s brother and co-heir, a member of that Head, and a temple of the Holy Spirit; indeed, he has been made a sharer and participant in the divine nature.

Under the aspect of the body also, Christianity brought the greatest benefits to humankind, since it protected life and health in every way, either by prohibiting everything harmful or by commanding everything useful for their preservation.

Accordingly, this Index has three parts or sections. In each section we have observed both a logical order of subjects and a chronological order of authors. Their names, volumes, and columns are indicated, so that the reader may easily find what is sought.

[Col. 0587]

## § II.—The benefits of Christianity for the human person with respect to the heart

Christianity not only enlightened the human intellect, but also transformed the human heart and adorned it with every virtue, namely:

1. By inspiring faith. ## § III. The Benefits of Christianity for Humanity with Respect to the Body

The Christian religion has always protected human life and health in every way: both by forbidding what is harmful and by prescribing what contributes to their preservation.

1. By forbidding anyone to inflict death upon himself or another; by condemning private combats; by asserting the claims of captives and slaves to freedom; and so forth. On these matters, see the special indexes on Homicide, Duelling, etc., etc.

2. By prescribing labour, which is necessary to health and from which arise particular goods and private ownership, both of which contribute greatly to the safeguarding of health. Thus: St Ambrose, XV, 1298, 1397, 1531, 1665; XVII, 19, 179, 229, 318, 377, 444.---Rufinus, XXI, 320.---St Augustine, XL, 549, 551, 552.---Cassian, XLIX, 375, 377, 378, 383, 388, 396, 444, 451.---St Eucherius, L, 835.---St Benedict, LXVI, 703.---*Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 740, 767, 818, 896, 898, 900.---Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 193.---Halitgar, CV, 670.---Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 917.---Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 330.---Ratherius, CXXXVI, 149.---Blessed Odo, CLX, 1105.---Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 866.---Peter Cantor, CCV, 246.---St Martin of León, CCIX, 114.

[Col. 0601]

# LXXVII. INDEX OF THE BENEFITS OF CHRISTIANITY FOR HUMAN SOCIETY, OR FOR PERSONS ESTABLISHED IN SOCIETY, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS AND THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS

## Notice

Human society may be considered in two respects: namely, with regard to the family and with regard to civil life. Under both aspects the Christian religion has conferred the greatest benefits upon humankind. With regard to the family, it restored marriage to its former dignity; established the reciprocal duties of parents and children; and so forth. With regard to civil life, it instituted fairer laws; made the laws of war more humane; provided for every order of society; gave assistance and remedies to all who needed help; promoted letters and the various arts; and so forth. Hence this Index has two sections.

## § I. The Benefits of Christianity with Respect to the Family

[Col. 0601]

Christianity’s benefit for the family was outstanding and remarkable. Having abolished polygamy, which sullied marriage among pagans, it restored marriage to its original institution, whereby two are one flesh. It bestowed great sanctity upon it, establishing the bond of wedlock by the grace of a sacrament, so that the union of Christian spouses is an image of that most holy and most divine union of Christ with the Church.

Christianity restored woman to her proper dignity. For the Christian wife is no longer, as among the heathen, merely her husband’s servant and slave—indeed, a bondwoman whom he could dismiss at his pleasure and brutally deprive of life—but his dearest companion, inseparable in every circumstance of fortune, whether favourable or adverse: a gentle, sweet, and untiring companion until death. A husband, moreover, ought to cherish and love his wife as his own flesh, as Christ, that divine bridegroom, loved the Church.

The Christian religion provided no less admirably for children. It protected their life, as a sacred pledge granted by God, against both the neglect and even the inhumanity of parents. Parents no longer have the right either to abandon their children, expose them, sell them as any other thing, or—even more abominably—kill them, or, as often happened, sacrifice them to the images of false gods by a most cruel death. Parents, on the contrary, must love, nourish, and form their children in good conduct; and, as the Apostle excellently says, children must be taught whatever things are true, whatever holy, whatever chaste, whatever lovely.

Christianity also admirably defined the duties of children. It commanded children to venerate their parents as images of God. They ought to render all offices of dutiful affection to their parents, whether in illness or old age, with ready and willing hearts. After the final duties of burial have been performed, the grateful spirit of children continually commends their parents’ souls and their sweet memory before God by alms, good works, and devout prayers. Moreover, religion promises the greatest rewards to children who love their parents, and threatens the gravest punishments against those who despise them. The following held these views:

1. ## § II. The Benefits of Christianity with Respect to Civil Society

The Christian religion illuminated society as a whole, like an individual person, with the divine splendours of eternal truth and adorned it with outstanding virtues. Above all, it must be reckoned that Christianity overthrew the foolish worship of false gods, polluted by every crime. It also abolished the bloody contests of gladiators and the monstrous sacrifices of human victims. Now that truth has breathed abroad, from the rising of the sun to its setting, in every place a pure offering is sacrificed and offered to God, and God, who is spirit, is worshipped in spirit and truth.

Christianity also excelled in splendid virtues within every order of society. It taught kings justice and clemency; the rich, beneficence and compassion; the poor, patience; and all human beings, humility, chastity, and charity. It rendered laws in peace more equitable and the laws of war more humane. It opposed slavery and sought to remove it from the midst, preaching that God does not show partiality, but is the Creator, Father, and Judge of all, who will render to each according to his works.

Christianity shone in every age with benefits suited to what necessity required. It overcame and crushed persecutors through the constancy of its martyrs; spectators admired this constancy so greatly that they were converted to the faith, and the blood of the martyrs became the seed of Christians. When the persecutions had been quieted, and the plague of crimes grew powerful, while the former vigour of virtue weakened and charity cooled, almost countless Christians of both sexes and every rank, scorning worldly pleasures, withdrew into the desert. There they flourished in piety, manual labour, the study of letters, austere conduct, and all virtues, especially the most astonishing ones.

It converted and gentled the most distant nations, which Roman arms had been unable to subdue, to Christ. Grim leaders of the barbarians, stirred by a sudden and unfamiliar clemency and reverence, stood astonished before the majesty of defenceless Christians and bishops. Forgetting their former savagery, their swords—so often stained with blood—lay blunted.

After so many barbarian invasions, every law was thrown into confusion, and all rushed headlong through right and wrong alike. Yet in these so mournful times the religion of Christ did not fail in its most salutary work. By the memorable law called the Peace, or Truce, of God (*Trevia seu Treuga Domini*), it in some measure restrained the civil wars raging everywhere; it curbed the unrestrained passions of princes, kings, and emperors; and with salutary authority it checked the invading flood of every vice.

When heretics endeavour to obscure truth, the Holy Spirit raises up outstanding teachers. But if a tempest of crimes threatens, men and virgins, having trampled the enticements of pleasures beneath their feet, establish monasteries, where they shine with the splendour of every virtue and gladden the Church. The monks of the Middle Ages were distinguished not only for piety, but also for their energetic cultivation of letters, sciences, and every art. They preserved, transcribed, and disseminated almost throughout the whole world the books of ancient writers and of the holy Fathers. While everywhere the fields lay uncultivated because of discord among citizens, monks cultivated them diligently, constructed remarkable buildings, made agricultural implements, and thus rendered the greatest service to letters, sciences, liberal and necessary arts, the cultivation of the fields, and architecture.

How auspiciously, how graciously, how wonderfully, therefore, did Christianity shine upon the world! In it alone, as the prophet had once sung, mercy and truth met one another; justice and peace kissed. Whatever the condition either of times or of persons required, it furnished excellently and unfailingly; to every weakness it supplied its particular remedies. It opened hostels for the poor and sick; it commanded that Christ be fed in the needy; it took care that captives should be ransomed; it commended widows and orphans to protection; it piously and gently undertook to nourish and sustain in its bosom abandoned old people and children; like a wise and diligent mother, it distributed to every intellect food of doctrine suited to it, etc., etc., etc.—as nearly all the Fathers have maintained in their writings. Hence:

1.—To that law, “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself,” which is the first and natural rule for establishing peace among citizens, Christianity added the eminent summit of charity, and thus established true brotherhood. On these matters see the preceding Index, no. II, §3.

[Col. 0605]

## LXXVIII. PRAXEOLOGICAL INDEX, OR SYNOPSIS OF PRACTICAL LIFE, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY SUBJECTS, IN WHICH ARE SET FORTH THE VARIOUS WORKS, PRACTICES, AND CUSTOMS OF RELIGION, PIETY, AND DEVOTION THAT FLOURISHED AMONG CHRISTIANS IN THE WESTERN CHURCH AT DIFFERENT PERIODS.

## NOTICE

It may be permitted to preface a few remarks on the plan and usefulness of this Index. We warn the diligent reader that our purpose has been to gather together every indication of Christian life; to set forth the origins of the various customs of the Church which formerly flourished according to differences of locality; and to record the concerns and pursuits by which, in every age, the true Christian publicly professed his devotion and piety. Thus are presented the fraternity and concord of the disciples of the early Church; their care for the dead; reverence for the relics of the saints; the benefactions of wealthy persons and kings in building churches, feeding the poor, and founding monasteries; pilgrimages; holy wars; enacted laws; rules for monks; etc., etc., etc. We have also incidentally noted certain other matters, both useful and pleasing, arranging everything alphabetically.

**ABBOT**, that is, father, is derived from the Hebrew and Syriac word *abba*. By this title, from the earliest centuries of the Church, the heads of monasteries were designated both among Greeks and among Latins: Jerome, XXVI (451); Augustine, XXXVI, 1012; XXXVII, 1419.

**RENUNCIATION** of the pomps and works both of the world and of the devil was performed by Christians at baptism: Jerome, XXV, 1068; Augustine, XLV, 1241.

**ABSTINENCE** from the pleasures of life, especially in eating and drinking, was strictly observed from the Church’s infancy: Tertullian, I, 487. They abstained from every sort of spectacle, 466, 493; from the Saturnalia and the festival of Liber, 492; and from meat sacrificed to idols: Lactantius, VI, 541; Augustine, 385. The merit of abstinence: Ambrose, XVI, 1191. Abstinence is dangerous for the young before the years of vigorous adulthood: Jerome, XXII, 874. What it ought to be during Lent: Augustine, XXXVIII, 1043. It is most ancient in the Church: Maximus of Turin. It prepares the Lord’s way and lifts the mind to heavenly things: Leo the Great, LIV, 185. Abstinence from meat is praiseworthy: Gennadius, LVIII, 976; Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1234; Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 651. Three degrees of abstinence: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 548. In abstaining from food and drink, moderation must be observed: Augustine, XXXIII, 960; St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1085. The distinction between the abstinence of Catholics and that of heretics, ibid., 1096. It has always been practiced in the Church: Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1144. What selection of foods was formerly made in Lent, ibid., 1145. See below, **Fasting** and **Lent**.

**YOUNG PEOPLE.** The first weapons of demons are directed against youth: Jerome, XXII, 399. The path of youth is slippery, ibid., 310. It endures many conflicts of the body, ibid., 529. It is accustomed to be struck by the arrows of thoughts, ibid., 731. Association with young women must be avoided, ibid., 897, 1056. Moral precepts are handed down to young people: Augustine, XXXII, 1006. What vices are commonly abundant in youth: id., XLI, 556. Very few young people from the beginning commit nothing blameworthy, ibid., 730.

**ADOPTION.** On the adoption of infants exposed at the doors of a church: Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1107.

[Col. 0606]

**ADVERSITY** serves as a warning to the good and as chastisement to the wicked: Tertullian, I, 489. It often arises because God is not worshipped: Cyprian, IV, 548, 549, 759. It tests each person’s righteousness, ibid., 593. Patience is the greatest of virtues: Lactantius, VI, 700. In adversities the righteous person is not broken: Ambrose, XV, 1327. He is struck, but not overthrown, XIV, 460. Why adversities must be borne patiently, ibid., 863. Whoever hopes for better things is never broken by lesser ones: id., XV, 1282. When the mind is pressed by adversity, it then implores divine help, ibid., 1329. It is a great thing if you cleave to Christ when some storm disturbs you, ibid., 1292. In adversity and prosperity alike, God’s will should be praised: Jerome, XXII, 467. What can one say who glories in God’s mercy amid adversities? Ibid. God permits those whom he loves to be afflicted: Augustine, XXXIII, 424. Adversity is the gift of a God who admonishes, ibid., 957. Constancy must be employed in enduring adversities: id., XXXVIII, 623. Why adversity is common to righteous and unrighteous alike: id., XLI, 20, 21. Adversities are useful to some and ruinous to others: id., XLII, 451. Adversities either correct or test: Leo the Great, LIV, 169. Adversity is compared to night: Gregory the Great, LXXV, 563, 650. It tests friends, ibid., 780; it reveals enemies, ibid., 781. Adversity does not cast down one whom prosperity does not corrupt: id., LXXVI, 177. Adversities must be borne patiently: Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 437.

**THE SICK, THE INFIRM.** A sick person is made impatient by pain: St. Cyprian, IV, 477. Sick persons reject wholesome foods, ibid., 301, 306. Care for the infirm is commended, ibid., 326, 327. They must be assisted at their departure, ibid., 347. The infirm must be visited, ibid., 777. Let no one try or rashly press an invalid: Ambrose, XV, 1784. Who ought to attend a sick person: Jerome, XXII, 528. Gentleness and attentiveness toward the sick, ibid., 892. To be born here in a mortal body is to begin to be ill: Augustine, XXXVII, 132. He is more dangerously ill who thinks himself healthy: id., XXXVIII, 495. Two kinds of sick persons, ibid. A sick person is heard not according to his wish but according to his health, ibid., 1299. By observing the physician’s instructions, one becomes well only gradually, ibid., 1270. Unlawful remedies of the sick, ibid., 1439. Bodily health itself is a kind of illness: Gregory the Great, LXXV, 834.

[Col. 0607]

It is a natural concern to give joy to the sick: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 771. On visiting the infirm: Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 212. On visiting the sick: Guigo the Carthusian, CLIII, 655.

**AGE.** The forwardness of age must be restrained by the shame that is due: Tertullian, II, 203. God requires greater honor from greater age, ibid., 417. Every age is generous toward Christ: Ambrose, XV, 1565. The moments of our life are diminished by every individual action: Jerome, XXII, 602. To admonish a slippery age is an act of piety, ibid., 729. One should not easily believe everything said of advanced age, ibid., 1084. The heat of age is quenched by God’s mercy and by the rigor of fasts, ibid., 1116. The stages of life: Augustine, XXXIII, 966. As many stages of life, so many deaths of stages of life: ibid., XXXVIII, 1686. Though life may seem long, when it has arrived it is proved short because it comes to an end, ibid., 1613. Immature age: Gregory the Great, LXXV, 536. The third hour is adolescence, the sixth hour youth, the ninth hour old age, and the eleventh hour that age which is called decrepit or extremely old: Garner of St. Victor, CXCIII, 370.

**AGAPE**, a word interpreted as “love.” Thus was called the meal which Christians celebrated in common: Tertullian, I, 474. How they conducted themselves at this banquet, ibid., 477; see Zeno, XI, 366, note; Jerome, XXII, 418; Augustine, XLII, 383; Paulinus, LXI, 562. Agapes were religious banquets in churches in the early Church: Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1216.

**AGENDA.** Thus were called funeral rites in the time of Robert Pullen: CXXXVI, 799, 1106.

**AGNUS DEI**, that is, small wax images which were blessed, is mentioned in Prudentius, LIX, 808, and Amalarius, CV, 1038.

**DICE**, a game of most ancient origin, against which Church leaders protested vehemently: Tertullian, II, 1049; Ambrose, XIV, 772, 773; Innocent, XX, 478. The frenzy of gambling is described by Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 448, 449, 548. What dice are, and what their forms are: Isidore, LXXXII, 660, 661; John of Salisbury, CXCVIII, 398. The game of dice is called the seedbed of all evils: Peter of Blois, CCVII, 228.

**ALLELUIA**, a Hebrew word meaning “Praise God,” which more diligent Christians were accustomed also to append to their prayers: Tertullian, I, 1194. Likewise in the Psalms, ibid. From Easter to Pentecost fasts ceased and Alleluia was sung: Ambrose, XIV, 867. It was sometimes sung at funerals: Jerome, XXII, 697. See also Augustine, XXXVII, 1937, 1938. When Alleluia was sung at Rome: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1156. Why it is not sung from Septuagesima to Easter: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 582. One Alleluia is sung at Easter, but a double Alleluia on the following Saturday, from Alan of Lille, CCX, 210.

**ALTAR.** See **Altar**.

**AMEN**, that is, “Let it be,” according to the Hebrew interpretation. Why it is repeated more frequently in John’s Gospel: Ambrose, XIV, 1084. When a psalm is sung in church, “Amen” is said: id., XV, 1763; XVI, 625; Jerome, XXIV, 643; id., XXVI, 43, 317, 438. Amen is used to affirm something: Augustine, XXXIV, 649; id., XXXV, 1694. The faithful, on receiving the Eucharist, respond, “Amen”: id., XXXVIII, 1267; and likewise at the invocations of bishops, XL, 320.

**FRIENDSHIP.** To love friends belongs to everyone, but to love enemies belongs to Christians alone: Tertullian, I, 698. The laws of friendship: Ambrose, XVI, 179. It ought to be steadfast, ibid., 180. It cannot exist between unlike characters, ibid., 182. The friendships of the poor are for the most part better than those of the rich, ibid. Friendship is a virtue, not a means of gain, ibid. It is the guardian of piety and teacher of equality, ibid. Rebukes in friendship are welcome, ibid., 74. A friendship that can cease was never true: Jerome, XXII, 335. True friendship is that which is united not by the advantage of household affairs nor merely by bodily presence, but by the fear of God and devotion to the Scriptures, ibid., 540. True friendship ought not to conceal what it thinks, ibid., 735. Good and faithful friends are rare: id., XXIII, 548. In friends, one seeks not a thing but goodwill, ibid., 341. What friendship is: Augustine, XXXII, 941; id., XL, 22. No friendship is to be rejected: id., XL, 82. Friendship consists in mutual love, ibid., 173. Friendship is faithful nowhere except in Christ: id., XLIV, 550. Friendship must be treated seriously: Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 437. A kiss is a sign of friendship: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 755.

**ANCHORITES AND HERMITS.** The eremitic life is undertaken by innumerable Christians, whether to escape persecution or for the sake of perfection: Rufinus, XXI, 455 ff. The way of life of anchorites: Jerome, XXII, 420. What kinds of work should be chosen by solitaries: John Cassian, XLIX, 1288. Anchorites are those who, after the cenobitic life, seek deserts and live alone: Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 293. Anchorites imitate Elijah and John; cenobites, the apostles, ibid. They are also those called hermits, ibid.

[Col. 0608]

Anchorites are generally better than cenobites: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 796. The solitude of anchorites is more excellent than that of cenobites: Peter the Chanter, CCV, 213.

**ANATHEMA.** What an anathema is: Jerome, XXII, 998. Examples of anathema: Salvian, LIII, 107. What difference there is between anathema and excommunication: Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 591.

**ANNIVERSARY.** Anniversary days for the dead were customarily celebrated: Alcuin, CI, 1277.

**RING.** See **Staff**.

**ANTIPHON.** The ancient use of antiphons: Cassian, XLIX, 77. The origin of antiphons: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1171. The Greeks first composed antiphons, with two choirs singing alternately: Isidore, LXXX, 743. What an antiphon is and by whom it was invented: Alcuin, CI, 1247.

**APPEAL.** The practice of appeals to the Apostolic See: Leo the Great, LIV, 630. Appeals of bishops to the Roman pontiff: LVI, 65; Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 607, 608, 850, 948.

**WATER; HOLY WATER.** Praises of water: Tertullian, I, 1202 ff. Sprinklings of water customary among pagans, ibid., 1204. Water, a figure of baptism, ibid., 1203. Commendation of water: Ambrose, XIV, 172. Water in fountains at the doors of churches: Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 338, 850. Holy water at the tomb of St. Martin: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 376. The power of holy water, ibid., 958. Water from a saint’s fountain held in honor, ibid., 823. The use of holy water to drive away demons: Gregory the Great, LXXV, 237; LXXVII, 208. On sprinkling holy water: St. Remigius, CII, 1101. On water for sprinkling: Walafrid, CXIV, 963. Water should be blessed on the Lord’s Day: Hincmar, CXXV, 774. The people should be blessed with water sprinkled with salt: Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 94. Water mixed with salt and ashes, by which a cross is made through sprinkling at the dedication of a church: Remigius of Auxerre, CXXXI, 852. A new church is sprinkled with holy water: Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 194. Water should be blessed every Sunday: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 193; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 473.

**ALTAR.** Altars, commonly whitewashed and called tables because of their shape, were formerly erected over the graves of martyrs, and the sacred mysteries were celebrated upon them: Optatus, XI, 1008, 1009; see ibid., notes 77, 78. Altars of gods constructed by pagans, with inscriptions upon them: Tertullian, I, 347. The altars of gods are called altars of the devil: Cyprian, III, 781; IV, 478. Among Christians, *arae* as well as *altaria* are said to belong to God alone, even though they bear the names of martyrs: Augustine, XXXVIII, 1251, 1425, 1438. Hence the names of martyrs and saints were recited from them, ibid., 1251; XL, 423. An altar was sometimes wooden: Augustine, XLIII, 190. Altars and churches faced west: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 154. Women do not approach them: Leo IV, CXV, 677. They are covered with the cleanest linens: Regino, CXXXII, 203. Nothing is placed on them except the sacred offering, ibid., 402. Under St. Anselm, bare stones unattached anywhere were not consecrated: id., CXLIX, 194. Altars were sometimes of bronze: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVIII, 636. Relics of saints were placed beneath them: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 407. They were hollow or quadrangular: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 724.

**ARMS.** What the arms of Christians are: Tertullian, II, 517; Leo the Great, LIV, 266; Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 20; Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 206. The courage of God’s soldier, ready for battle: id., IV, 676. Christ watches over his soldier, ibid., 353. A soldier is tested in battle, ibid., 590. The duty of a good soldier, id.; III, 1115. He is crowned in persecution, id., IV, 676. What the heavenly arms are: Cyprian, III, 974. What a Christian soldier ought to be: Ambrose, XIV, 1056. What wars he must endure: id., XV, 1807. Worldly gains must not be sought in Christ’s soldiery: Jerome, XXIII, 264. Arms against the devil: Augustine, XL, 637, 638. The devil’s weapons against us, ibid. It is shameful for lust to conquer one whom a human being does not conquer: id., XXXIII, 856. Laymen may bear arms: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 614. Pope Urban II exhorts them to take up arms against unbelievers: CLI, 568, 570. How many lived holy lives in military service: Alan of Lille, CCX, 186. Alan rebukes the soldiers of his own day, ibid. Christianity did not forbid military service: Augustine, XXXIII, 531. Soldiers who, by God’s authority, wage wars are not murderers: id., XLI, 35, 39.

**CRAFTSMAN.** In former times craftsmen in the more famous cities formed separate associations according to their trades: Gregory the Great, LXXV, 436. Some paid dues when they sought to join such an order or association, ibid. The functions of diverse professions: Ratherius, CXXXVI, 144 ff.

**ASYLUM.** Those who flee to a church customarily remain there until their affairs are settled through a bishop’s intercession: Augustine, XXXIII, 430. The asylum of sacred places is defended: Alcuin, C, 40. Those who flee to a church must not be handed over: Regino, CXXXII, 372.

[Col. 0609]

No one is to be forcibly dragged out of a church, according to a decree of Pope Boniface: Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 116. Immunity for churches and for those who take refuge in them is affirmed: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 221. On those who take refuge in churches: Gratian, CXXXVIII, 1072; Innocent III, CCXV, 1255.

**STAFF; PASTORAL RING.** On staffs and rings wrongly bestowed through the hands of laymen: Humbert, CXLIII, 1148. What the pastoral staff signifies: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 110.

**BATHS.** The use of baths was not forbidden to Christians: Tertullian, I, 492. Mixed public baths of pagans were rejected by Christians because of their foulness: Cyprian, IV, 458. Formerly at Rome, adult sons did not attend baths with their parents: Ambrose, CXIV, 413. Young people ought to use them soberly, lest they foster lust: Jerome, XXII, 730, 876, 957, 1075. A bath is so called because it drives anxiety from the mind: Augustine, XXXII, 777. The use of baths once a month is allowed to nuns, XXXIII, 963. Whether it is permitted on the Lord’s Day: Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1254. To whom it is permitted: St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 206. It should be granted to the sick: St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1084, 1089, 1091. It should be allowed less readily to the healthy, ibid. Baths should be avoided by a monk: Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 787.

**BEARD.** The beard demonstrates the ordering of the whole body: Lactantius, VII, 33. A beard curled by handling: Tertullian, I, 410. Shaving the beard and head is a sign of mourning: Jerome, XXIV, 168. The beard is an adornment of manhood, not a defense: Augustine, XLI, 791. At the first cutting of a young man’s beard, a special prayer was once said: Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 233, 520. On the care of beard and hair among Christians: Ratramnus, CXXI, 322. It is unbecoming for a man to be without a beard: St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 349.

**BASILICA; CHURCH.** From the beginning, churches were called sacred strongholds and places of prayer; they were found very small and without architectural refinement: Zeno, 355, note. According to circumstances of time and place, because of pagan hostilities, sacred assemblies were held sometimes publicly, sometimes in secret: ibid.; Tertullian, 371, 468, 579. Approved elders presided, ibid., 469. Under Hilary of Poitiers they were called houses of God, IX, 695, 696. Christ’s true Church is not that which is confined to walls, roofs, and buildings: id., X, 616. There are many days on which one must come to church immediately at midday, sing hymns, and celebrate the offering: Ambrose, XV, 1314. Gold and gems in churches are condemned by St. Jerome, XXII, 535–536. Churches are distasteful to wealthy matrons puffed up with their own names: Tertullian, I, 1301. Women who come to church in proud dress are rebuked: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 205. The form of basilicas: id., XXXIV, 660. The construction of a church is a highly praiseworthy work: id., XXXIX, 1475. Churches were established for hearing God’s word: id., XLI, 52. There men sit apart from women, ibid., 76, 77. Why those set over others sit higher than the people: id., XXXVIII, 569. Churches are a secure refuge for those fearing death or punishments: id., XXXIII, 430, 647, 651; XLI, 14, 17. They were adorned with various gifts: Salvian, LIII, 127. Singing was frequent in churches: Leo the Great, LIV, 505. Certain basilicas were dedicated in the city of Rome under St. Leo, LIV, 218, 468. Christians were accustomed to kiss the thresholds of churches: Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 330, note; Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 513. Relics of saints were deposited there, 334. Water stood in fountains at the church doors, ibid., 338. Lamps were anciently used in churches, ibid., 611. Processions were once customarily held in basilicas: Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 542. It is not permitted to dine in churches: Criscus, LXXXVIII, 897. Very few are to be buried in a church: Theodulf of Orléans. Churches are not to be sold for a price: Hincmar, CXXVI, 264. Let no one presume to feast in churches: Regino, CXXXII, 202. On defenders of churches: Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 476; on founders, ibid., 491; on their administration, ibid., 496; on the generosity of King Sigismund toward churches, ibid., 663. On the construction, adornment, and honor of churches: Burchard, CXL, 673. On churches: Gerard, CXLII, 1284. On consecrating churches: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 77. Why churches are called basilicas, ibid., 215. An indecent song must be removed from church, ibid. The church must be honored, ibid., 216, 233. On the site of a church: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 586. Superfluous ornament in churches is condemned: St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 914. On the households, servants, and ministeriales of churches, which formerly had a condition far different from that of modern times: Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1228. On the ordering of church service: Guichard, CXCIX, 1093. On the establishment of a church: Sicard of Cremona, CCXIII, 13; on its foundation, ibid., 17; on the various parts of a church, ibid., 19; on its different names, ibid., 26; on its consecration, ibid., 28–36; on the consecration of a church, ibid., 37; on the church’s adornment, ibid., 40.

**WAR; MILITARY SERVICE; SOLDIER.** Whether military service is altogether fitting for a Christian: Tertullian, I, 690; II, 91. It is lawful up to the matter of the crown, id., II, 94.

[Col. 0610]

A soldier slain in battle is more beautiful than one saved in flight, ibid., 112. They were crowned with olive, ibid., 94. Christ’s soldiers are Christians, id., II, 927. A warrior’s courage is necessary in more difficult places: Ambrose, XIV, 364. In war justice and good faith must be preserved: id., XVI, 63. In martial courage there is no slight form of the honorable and becoming, ibid., 83. We have certain battles even in peace, and peace in war, ibid., 1091. Christian teaching does not condemn all wars: Augustine, XXXIII, 530. Wars must not be waged without mercy, ibid., 531. The acts committed under Gallienus were excessively cruel, ibid., 918. We have two kinds of war: id., XXXVI, 959. It is not lawful for everyone to wage war: id., XXXIV, 791. What just wars are, ibid. The calamity of civil war: id., XLI, 88. By wars God corrects human conduct, exercises virtue, and increases it, ibid., 15. Allied wars, ibid., 109. Necessity alone compels good people to wage war, ibid., 124. The end of those who wage war is peace, ibid., 440. The authority and counsel for undertaking war ought to belong to the ruler; the ministry of carrying it out, to soldiers: ibid., XLII, 447. A just man may rightly wage war under a sacrilegious man, ibid. There is also a certain war against oneself: id., XXXVI, 959. Sermons of Pope Urban II on waging war against unbelievers: CLI, 568, 570. What ought to be thought concerning war: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1159 ff. Knights Templar bound by vow to fight unbelievers: Guibert, CLVI, 702. See **Arms**, **Crusaders**.

**BLESSING** is the votive bestowal of sanctification and graces: Ambrose, XIV, 675. When the priest blesses, the people respond “Amen,” and why: ibid., 1084. Why God bestowed blessing only upon human beings, birds, and fish: Augustine, XXXII, 869. The bishops’ blessing over the people: id., XXXIII, 761, 775. Human beings wish to be blessed by God in many ways: id., XXXVI, 803. When God blesses, he does what he says: id., XXXVII, 1444. Prayers should first be made before that which is on the Lord’s table is blessed, and likewise when the people are blessed: id., XXXIII, 636. A priest’s blessing bestowed on a woman about to marry: Leo the Great, LIV, 249. The mysteries of priestly blessings, ibid., 626. Blessing of milk and honey, id., LV, 40; of the baptismal font, ibid., 156; of water: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 725, 958; Gregory the Great, LXXV, 237; id., LXXVII, 208; of garments: *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 254; of oil, ibid., 1117, 1118. Simeon Stylites bestows a blessing upon barbarians: id., LXXIV, 104. Blessing of salt and water, instituted by Pope Eutychian: LXXVIII, 232. Blessing of a sign, or bell, ibid., 427. Blessing of crops: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1442. Blessing of the paschal candle, instituted by Zosimus: id., CXXVIII, 174. The people should be blessed with water sprinkled with salt: Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 94. Blessing of candles: id., CXXXVIII, 1053; of ashes, ibid., 1055; of palms, ibid., 1058; of a queen, ibid., 1118; of weapons, ibid., 1122. Episcopal blessing at Mass, ibid., CXLVII, 154. A blessing should be sought before reading: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 87.

**LIBRARIES.** A library was assembled at Rome by Pope St. Gelasius: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 415. The pontifical library, ibid., 1366.

**ECCLESIASTICAL GOODS.** The alienation of Church goods is forbidden: Leo the Great, LIV, 704. Church goods must not be disposed of: LVI, 644, 646, 652, 657, 670, 676. What if necessity is present? Ibid., 644. Under what conditions they may be alienated, ibid., 661. The Church’s patrimony must not be diminished but rather increased: Gelasius I, LIX, 137. The estates of the Roman Church were distributed throughout the whole world: Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 444. The Church acquired very great wealth under King Dagobert: ibid., LXXX, 499 ff. Donations and wills, ibid., LXXXVIII, 1078. On administering and alienating the Church’s property: *Diurnus*, CV, 95. The goods of the Church are the vows of the faithful, the patrimony of the poor, the price of sins, and consist in Christ’s protection and defense: Hincmar of Reims, CXXVI, 128. A *massa*, a word meaning “land” in French, is very often found granted to the Church; hence mention is made in Roman territory of the estates of Garigliano, Muronica, Auriana, Sentiliana, Castis, Trapaea, etc.: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1516. The sale of these goods is forbidden under anathema: ibid., CXXVIII, 1059; Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 264. How many Church possessions at Reims passed into lay hands: Flodoard, CXXXV, 121. Restored by King Charles, ibid., 144. Possession of Church property must not be granted without rent: id., CXXXVI, 1303. See Abbo, CXXXIX, 489, 491, 496. King Æthelred of the English granted the Roman penny: id., CLI, 1166. Nothing is to be deducted from church revenues: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 202, 205, 209. Tithes must be paid to the Church, ibid., 237, 245. Laypersons must not dispose of ecclesiastical goods: Placidus, CLXIII, 627. What has once been given to the Church must never be taken away, ibid., 634. How wrong it is to take Church property, ibid., 635.

[Col. 0611]

**BRANDEUM** or *prandeum* was the name for cloths which the faithful applied to saints’ relics; they divided these among themselves and preserved them with honor: Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 702, 846.

**CLERICAL CELIBACY.** See below, **Cleric**.

**SHOE; FOOTWEAR.** Servants customarily untied and fastened the strap of shoes: Juvencus, XIX, 108. The use of shoes is most ancient, ibid. Footwear and its forms: Isidore of Seville, LXXXI, 704. Why sandals are so called, ibid. Kings and emperors wore shoes, ibid. What it signifies to be shod with sandals or with soles: Peter Lombard, CXCII, 220.

**BELL; NOLA; SIGN.** It was customarily rung for Matins: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 962. Ancient verses on the bell of a chapter, by a monk of St. Gall: LXXXVII, 66. The use of bells, and why it ceases during the three days before Easter: Alcuin, CI, 1202, 1203. Bells are treated by Rupert, CLXX, 19. On the significance of bells: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 544. The use and significance of bells: Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 473; CLXXVII, 875. How bells are to be rung in Lent: John Beleth, CCII, 35, 90.

**CANDLE; WAX TAPER.** The use of candles or wax tapers in churches: Prudentius, LIX, 663, 674. Candles customarily used at funerals, ibid., 880, note 45. Wax and small tapers at the tombs of saints: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 933, 941. St. Euphrasia offers wax tapers and incense in a convent of virgins: *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 627.
