The origin of candles at the feast of the Purification: Alcuin, CI, 1181. On the lighting of candles: Amalarius, CV, 1096. On blessing a candle: Walafrid, CXIV, 963. Pope Zosimus ordered candles to be blessed: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 74. Candles are not to be lit by day in cemeteries: Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 417. On the significance of candles: St. Anselm, CLVIII, 627; Hugh of St. Victor. What the two candles at the Gospel signify: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 551. The paschal candle: Amalarius, CV, 1038. Pope St. Zosimus instituted the blessing of the paschal candle in every parish: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 74. A candle must be blessed at the Easter vigil: Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 467. The aforementioned Zosimus was the first to order the paschal candle blessed: Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 76. Its blessing: Hugh of St. Victor. On the practice of consecrating or blessing the paschal candle: John Beleth, CCII, 112.

**ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS.** Ignorance of the canons is intolerable in a priest: Leo the Great, LIV, 612. Observance of the canons: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 550. See the various collections of canons.

**REGULAR CANONS.** A canon cannot be called one unless he is regular: Peter Damian, CXLV, 506. How frivolous is the excuse of canons, ibid., 484. The rule of canons: Guichard, CXCIX, 1092. On negligence in observing the order of the Church, ibid., 1093; on obedience, ibid.; on ordering church service, ibid.; on the penalties of those who neglect their offices, ibid., 1097; on silence in choir, ibid., 1099; on the care of boys, ibid., 1102; on not carrying *coyliis* [reading uncertain], ibid.; on blowing one’s nose, ibid., 1103; on the instruction of clerics, ibid., 1104; on keeping statutes, ibid.; on church servants, ibid., 1113. The canons of Blois: Stephen, abbot, CCXI, 357. The Grandmontines called “Good Men,” ibid., 361. Whether the Rule of St. Augustine comes from the apostles, ibid., 354. Public schools of the canons of St. Geneviève at Paris, 377, 378, 431.

**CANTHARUS.** Water in fountains at the entrance to churches: St. Paulinus, LXI, 338. The people washed themselves with water from them, ibid., 850. Wax-coated fountains: Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1514, 1515; Isidore, LXXXII, 717.

**SONG.** God is pleased by song not only to be praised but also to be reconciled: Ambrose, XIV, 923. The difference between a song and a psalm: Augustine, XXXVI, 78, 813. A new song belongs to the new person, the old song to the old person, ibid., 435, 807. What the song of rich and poor concerning the songs of Zion is like: id., XXXVII, 1768. The old song is sung by the desire of the flesh; the new song by the love of God, ibid., 1227. Why our song ought to correspond in conduct, as if by a dance, ibid., XXXVIII, 1416. Divine songs should be joined to the Lenten fast: Peter Chrysologus, LII, 215. A banquet song: Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 163. A song is the voice of one singing in joy, ibid., 252. A song of a psalm, ibid., 253. On the songs of the ancients: id., LXXXVIII, 741. Why the song of the Blessed Virgin is sung at evening: St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 226. What a virgin’s song is, ibid., 187. Who sings rightly: Wolbero, abbot, CXCV, 1245.

**DITTY; SONG.** The dangerous delight of frivolous songs: Augustine, XXXVIII, 79. Human beings are more inclined to listen to frivolous songs than to salutary admonitions, ibid. Profane songs and dances were expelled from the church in which St. Cyprian had been buried, ibid., 1415. Those singing indecent things are reproved: id., XXXVI, 157.

[Col. 0612]

The songs of sailors, farmers, and soldiers, intended to lighten labor: Peter Chrysologus, LII, 522. Diverse kinds of song customarily used among the ancients: Isidore of Seville, I, 273, 477. See “Lascivious songs” in the Index **On Unlawful Pleasures**.

**SINGING; SINGER.** What the singing of ancient Christians was: Tertullian, I, 273, 477. Church singing: Ambrose, XIV, 157. Singing by men, women, virgins, and boys, ibid., 165. Singing of Alleluia: Jerome, XXII, 876. The singing of Psalms famous throughout the world: Augustine, XXXIII, 766. Singing is beautiful sound: id., XXXII, 843. It was instituted at Milan by St. Ambrose, ibid., 768. Augustine was affected by it in a wonderful manner, ibid. The pleasure of the flesh must be guarded against even in sacred singing, ibid., 799. One sins when singing gives greater pleasure than the thing sung, ibid. It is useful for moving the mind devoutly: id., CXXXIII, 221. The time, usefulness, and sanctity of singing in church, ibid. The singing of psalms was instituted throughout the universal Church: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 145, 154, 505; Prudentius, LIX, 789. Gregory the Great established a school of singing: LXXV, 90. Why the Roman Church formerly did not sing the Creed at Mass: Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 592. What psalms are sung in church: Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 39. What must be sung daily by king and all the people: Æthelred, CLI, 1167. Pope Zosimus ordered psalms to be sung antiphonally: Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 78. On ecclesiastical singing: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 178. How a singer is to be appointed: ibid., 448; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 567. The effect and usefulness of singing: St. Bernard, 1274. On singing Alleluia: Peter Lombard. See **Psalmody**.

**CHAPEL.** The origin of chapels in churches: St. Paulinus, LXI, 336.

**CAPITULARY.** In the capitularies of Charlemagne, religion holds the foremost place: St. Paulinus, XCVII, 63 ff.

**FLESH.** See **Abstinence**.

**WAX; WAX TAPER.** See above, **Candle**.

**DANCES; DANCING.** The mysteries of the Resurrection revealed are incompatible with the disgraceful excesses of dancing: Ambrose, XV, 1670. The dancing of actors is shameful, ibid. Dances are forbidden in a place of burial: St. Cyprian, Augustine, XXXVIII, 1415; and at weddings: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 617. See “Dances” in the Index **On Unlawful Pleasures**.

**CHURCH CHOIR.** On the form of praying in choir: Guichard, CXCIX, 1099. On silence to be observed there, ibid. How one should enter choir, ibid., 1101. On avoiding laughter, ibid., 1111. The choir stalls: Stephen, CCXI, 475.

**CHRISTIANS.** The name Christian is derived from sweetness: Tertullian, I, 281. Pagans pronounced “Christian” incorrectly, ibid. The name of Christians was hateful to the nations, ibid., 277. For this reason worshippers of Christ were persecuted, ibid. No one was a Christian before Christ: id., II, 1001. True Christians are described: id., I, 269, 511, 624. Their knowledge, discipline, and learning are very different, ibid., 501. They lived among pagans, ibid., 490. They mingled their trades and work with theirs, ibid. How they conducted themselves at their banquets, ibid. They prayed before and after food, ibid., 477. The Christians’ meal was called *agape*, or love, ibid., 474. At public assemblies Christians rose by night to pour out prayers: Tertullian, I, 273. They prayed facing east, ibid., 370. On the Lord’s Day they gave themselves to joy, ibid., 371. They prayed bareheaded, ibid., 442. They abstained from spectacles, processions, public games, and theatrical performances, ibid., 466. They customarily assembled in one place to pray, to receive instruction from Scripture and offer petitions, to exercise moral discipline, regulate the assembly, and collect alms for burials, for supporting the needy, orphans, and elderly, and for relieving shipwrecked persons, exiles, or those cast into prison, ibid., 468. How they rejected pagan festivals of generosity, ibid., 492. They sometimes prayed with hands outstretched, imitating the Lord’s Passion, ibid., 1169. It is unlawful for Christians to attend the shameful pagan banquets of an association: Cyprian, IV, 400. They ought not to bring a case before a pagan judge, ibid., 758. Among Christians the practice prevailed of anointing and washing their dead: Lactantius, VI, 270. They abstained from food sacrificed to idols, ibid., 363. At first they met in private houses, ibid., 502, 791. They used light in their gatherings, ibid., 637. They frequently make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, ibid., 701. “I am a Christian” was a familiar expression among the faithful: Hilary of Poitiers. The fasts, solemn celebrations of mysteries, and prayers of Christians, ibid. They recited the Lord’s Prayer at the altar and privately: St. Optatus, XI, 975. They erected altars over martyrs’ tombs, ibid., 1008, note. They very frequently carried the Eucharist home: Zeno of Verona, XI, 309. With what great care they preserved it, ibid., 358, 359. In churches Christians stretched out their hands, bent their necks, prostrated themselves, and made confession, ibid., 334. There are many days on which the faithful come to church at midday, sing hymns, and celebrate the offering: Ambrose, XV, 1314. A Christian at every moment [Col. 0613] upon his own forehead, and in contempt of death, the cross
imprints the sign [of the cross], ibid., 1247. The assembly of Christians gathered in one place, Jerome, XXIII, 66, 78. It was the custom of Christians to contemplate heavenly things and always to pray to God, ibid., 629. Their concord and unity, idem, XXIV, 148. In comparison with Christians, the pagans are like women, ibid., 185. All days are alike for Christians, XXVI, 378. Christians were first so called at Antioch, Augustine, XXXII, 622. In Julian’s time Christians were forbidden to teach literature and rhetoric, ibid., 753. Christians may possess property, ibid., 1343. The life and morals of Christians living in a single city, ibid., 1337. As far as they can, Christians do not allow anything to be taken from a granary or winepress for sacrifices to demons, idem, XXXIII, 185. Banquets in churches are to be abolished, ibid., 115. A Christian is understood by the name of brother, idem, XXXV, 1266. He was not made in order to flourish in this world, idem, XXXVI, 190. Christians continually make the sign upon their foreheads whenever they are frightened for any reason, ibid., 585. It is an offence for Christians to litigate before judges, even ecclesiastical ones, ibid., 1045. The courage of Christians against the threats of tyrants, idem, XXXVIII, 1591. How much it benefited the first Christians to make their private possessions common, ibid., 1748. Seneca neither blames nor praises Christians, idem, XLI, 192. The dress and morals of Christians, ibid., 647. How great is the virtue of Christian warfare, Peter Chrysologus. By a certain voyage the Christian is brought to his homeland, ibid., 340. What Christian freedom is like, Leo the Great, LIV, 144. Among Christians, some are righteous, others penitents and catechumens, ibid., 288. The first Christians rejoiced to possess nothing of the world and to possess all things with Christ, ibid., 376. How unlike the primitive faithful are Christians of later times, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 483, 722. Christians offered prayers at sunrise and turned toward the east, Prudentius, LIX, 698. The white flock of Christians, ibid., 807. Christians did not hold all things in common, Arator, LXVIII, 114. They were commonly regarded as unlearned and ignorant of the arts, ibid., 116. How great is Christian nobility, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 161, 162. The three orders of Christians, ibid., 976. A rule of life for every Christian, St Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 870. Death is not to be feared by Christians, St Julian, XCVI, 467. What Christian life ought to be, Alcuin, C, 502. It is the custom of Christians to bless one another when they meet, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1330. A concise instruction in Christian life, Theodulf, CV, 196. On ordinary believers, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 93. By living badly Christians destroy in their deeds the force of their profession, Lupus of Ferrières. On the duties of Christians, Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 149. On laypersons of every condition, Burchard, CXL, 895. Every Christian is either good or bad, Lanfranc, CL, 127. Free person and slave, ibid., 177. What Christian freedom is like, ibid., 190. On not selling a Christian outside the kingdom, Cnut, CLI, 1177. Christians are the body and members of Christ, Anselm, CLVIII, 625. With what reverence they ought to preserve and use their own members, ibid., 963. Offerings to be made in church by Christians, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 168, 169. The Christian ought always to hang upon the cross, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 160. He must wage two wars: against demons and against himself, ibid., 218. Why Christians formerly rose three times during the night for the office, John Beleth, CCII, 31. Christian life ought to be a cross and martyrdom, Peter Cantor, CCV, 97. It does not become a Christian to swear, ibid., 210, 322.

## HAIR-SHIRT

Augustine gratefully received the hair-shirt sent to him from Cilicia, XXXII, 989, 991. A hair-shirt pertains to the signification of sin, idem, XXXIV, 1077; or to confession of sins, idem, XXXVIII, 518. The hair-shirt of a poor man, ibid., 1402. What a hair-shirt is useful for, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 214. Ashes and a hair-shirt are weapons of penitence, Peter Cantor, CCV, 348.

## ASHES OF PENITENCE

Penitents roll in ashes, declaring themselves to be like ashes, Augustine, XXXV, 1933. The custom of placing ashes on the foreheads of the faithful on the fourth weekday before Lent is very ancient, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 301. Blessing of ashes, Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1055. Why ashes are placed upon foreheads on the day which begins the fast, Rupert, CLXX, 98; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 880.

## CITY

All cities are later than the Flood, Tertullian, I, 639. The human race at one time existed without cities, ibid., 432. A city is a multitude of human beings brought together into a certain bond of concord, Augustine, XXXIII, 529. A city is truly to be said to flourish when it excels in chaste, honourable, and upright morals, ibid., 314. A city is a concordant multitude of human beings, ibid., 670. One city is of the righteous and the other [Col. 0614] of the wicked, idem, XXXIV, 436. The city of the devil, and the court, ministers, and people of this city, idem, XXXVI, 120. It is shown that citizens of a bad city sometimes administer the affairs of a good city, and conversely, ibid., 735. The city of God always endures the earth and hopes for heaven. It is called Jerusalem and Zion. It begins with Abel, as the evil city begins with Cain, idem, XXXVII, 1846. The spiritual city, where no one is born because no one dies, idem, XXXVIII, 42. Why God permits the city of the wicked to be more numerous, idem, XL, 337. In the city of God, God’s will is law, idem, XLI, 63, 284. Christ is the founder of the city of God, ibid., 64. It consists of angels and human beings, ibid., 349. One city is predestined to reign with God, the other to be tormented with the devil, ibid., 437. The origins of the two cities are two loves, ibid., 421, 436. In the earthly city two forms are found, ibid., 439. The victories of the earthly city are deadly, or at least mortal, ibid., 440. The war and peace of this city, ibid. The heavenly city is a pilgrim here, ibid., 438. The city of God is begotten from faith and lives by hope, ibid., 461. In what respect it has peace with the earthly city, and in what respect discord, ibid. It refers earthly peace to heavenly peace, ibid., 646. What desolated cities and the abandoned houses of a powerful wicked man signify, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1011. The image of a besieged city commends the guarding of the heart, idem, LXXVI, 118. The spiritual city is not built without a devout and just weighing, ibid., 944. The heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, ibid., 1252. What the city of God and the city of the devil are, idem, CXCV, 1057.

## KEYS OF THE CHURCH

That is, the power of the Church and of the successors of St Peter; whence the golden keys of St Peter’s tomb, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 729. Likewise, keys of gold and gems in the form of a cross in the Vatican basilica, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1261. Golden keys offered to the basilica of St Lawrence, ibid., 1351. What it means to wield the keys of the Church, Goffrid, CLVII, 99, 227.

## CLERIC

A bishop ought to write through clerics, St Cyprian, IV, 287. Who are called those nearest to the clergy, ibid. Cyprian consults the clergy in ordinations, ibid. Clerical ordination, ibid., 317. The Roman clergy deliberates with the bishops concerning the case of the lapsed, ibid., 316. Urban clerics, ibid., 333. Clerics ought to serve only the altar and sacrifices, ibid., 398. A cleric ought to demand works not only of office but also of virtue, Ambrose, XV, 1707. The clergy has often erred and changed its judgment, ibid., 1446. Those who approach the offices of the Church ought to despise human things, idem, XVI, 77. An ecclesiastic ought to abstain from every practice of trade, being content with the fruits of his little field, if he has one, and with the proceeds of his stipend, if he has none, ibid., 78. The priest should consider who is more suited to distinguish the reading, who more pleasing in psalmody, who more diligent in exorcising those troubled by an evil spirit, and who more suitable for the sacristy, ibid., 87. Public reputation ought to bear witness to the conduct of ministers of the altar, ibid., 96. It befits ecclesiastics, and especially ministers of the altar, to avoid the banquets of outsiders, ibid., 49, 120. Whoever you are in the clergy, the Lord’s portion and his possession, do not depart from the Lord’s possession, ibid., 1275. Interpretation of “cleric,” Jerome, XXII, 531. They are to be supported by the altar’s offering, ibid. Their duty in burying the dead, ibid., 330. They succeed to the apostolic rank, ibid., 352. Their dignity consists in consecrating the body of Christ and in forgiving sins, ibid. Clerics ought to visit the sick, ibid., 538. Let them keep their eyes and tongue chaste, ibid. On the life of clerics, ibid., 1076. Clerical office is a burden, not an honour, ibid. Praise of clerics, Augustine, XXXII, 1339. Even a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric, idem, XXIII, 228. Clerics are not to be received into a monastery, ibid., 233. Those who have withdrawn from, or been expelled from, a monastery are not to be made clerics, ibid. A cleric may not transfer from one Church to another, ibid., 231, 232. To whom the inheritance of clerics belongs, ibid., 293. How clerics ought to behave toward one another, ibid., 1018. Why they are called clerics, idem, XXXVI, 824. The life and morals of Augustine’s clerics in the monastery, idem, XXXIX, 1569. Augustine does not dare to depose clerics who depart from the purpose of common life, ibid., 1572. How great is the continence even of clerics elected unwillingly, idem, XL, 486. Exempt from every public duty, idem, XLIII, 777. They should be neither contractors nor agents, Leo the Great, LVI, 227, 640, unless necessity is present, ibid., 236. They are not to enter secular military service or rank, ibid., 229. They may not serve simultaneously the churches of two cities, ibid., 231. They are bound to dispense the word and teaching of God, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 272. They incur guilt from that from which others obtain pardon, ibid., 295. Secular business is prohibited to clerics, Maximus of Turin. How they ought to discharge their office, ibid., 520. The various grades of clerics, Cassiodorus, LXX, 340. On [Col. 0615] the celibacy of the clergy, Ratramnus, idem, CXXI, 324. Clerics are not to be shopkeepers or servants of the rich, Isidore of Nercy, CXXX, 309. They are not to wear lay clothing, ibid., 257. Clerics, rather than monks, ought to live from the altar, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 595. Clerics are tonsured, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 137. Hospitable, ibid., 221. Why Levites’ hair is to be shaved, ibid. Bishops, clerics, and poor persons have the same table, Gerhoh the provost, CXCIV, 1261. On the instruction of clerics, Guichard, CXCIX, 1104. On clerics who have no master, ibid., 1105. How much more dangerous the state of clerics is than that of monks, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 794. Prerogatives of the clerical order, ibid., 804. A cleric occupied in secular business differs in no respect from a usurer, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 62. Who are to be called regular clerics, Stephen, CCXI, 496. On the condition of clerics, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1143. On sacred persons, ibid., 775.

## CEMETERY

Tertullian makes mention of a cemetery, II, 738 and 796. The cemetery in which Pope Sixtus rested, St Cyprian, IV, 430. The Council of Elvira prohibits candles from being lit in cemeteries, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 347. A cemetery in which there is an altar or chapel is to be consecrated by a bishop, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 906. The cemetery of Tours, ibid., 563. That of Autun, ibid., 881. The various cemeteries of the city of Rome, Anastasius, CXXVII, 1203, 1317, 1323, 1482; CXXVIII, 10, 130, 186, 454, 515, 699, etc., etc. On cemeteries and the amount of space they ought to have, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 221. Nothing is to be demanded for a burial-place, ibid., 220. A monk is not buried in a sacred place because he has lapsed into the vice of private ownership, ibid., 993. On the cemetery, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 590.

## ASSEMBLIES, MEETINGS, AND GATHERINGS OF CHRISTIANS

See **Christians**.

## COLLECTION, IN THE SENSE OF ALMS

See **Almsgiving**.

## COMMENDATION, THING ENTRUSTED, DEPOSIT

They call *commendatio*, *commendatum*, and *depositum* that which we have entrusted to someone for safe keeping, Ambrose, XIV, 786. This is the rule of truth: do nothing for the sake of your own commendation by which another person is diminished, idem, XVI, 135. Commendation is also made to God’s mercy, Prudentius, LIX, 886; or to someone’s prayers, as Peter of Blois, writing to the Cistercian prior, idem, CCVI, 11. Letters of commendation from a bishop are necessary for clerics to be duly received elsewhere, Leo the Great, LVI, 233.

## ADVANTAGE

One who harms another for his own advantage violates nature, Ambrose, XVI, 151. We must seek not our own goods and advantages, but those of others, ibid., 148. It is natural for human beings to seek advantages and avoid disadvantages, Peter Cantor, CCV, 239.

## COMMUNION OR COMMUNICATION AMONG THE ORTHODOX

Ecclesiastical communion, Tertullian, II, 45. The exchange of peace, ibid., 32. The fellowship of communion ought to include no offence, Ambrose, XVI, 948. Gospel fellowship, Cyprian, IV, 304. Fellowship contrary to the Gospel, ibid. Communion rashly assumed, idem, III, 765. There is no communion outside the Church, idem, IV, 402. The order for attaining the right of communion, ibid., 252, 254, 255. How it is received, ibid., 252. Donatists say that good persons are defiled by communion with evil persons, Augustine, XXXII, 637. To communicate with the wicked is to consent to them, idem, XXXIII, 265. Even known evil persons do not harm the good in the Church if either the power to prohibit them from communion is lacking, or some consideration for preserving peace prevents it, ibid., 297. Emperors in our communion, idem, XXXVI, 684. Communion with heretics is to be avoided, Leo the Great, LVI, 342, 343. Heretics are to be avoided, following the example of vipers and a bad tree, Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII, 1074, 1075.

## COMMUNITY

From the beginning Christians, through charity, held everything in common except wives, Tertullian, I, 472. How Christians were brothers and equals among themselves, Lactantius, VI, 599. What belongs to all cannot be excepted for individuals, Ambrose, XVI, 1327. Things possessed in common do not generate lawsuits, enmities, and other evils that arise from possession of private property, idem, XXXVII, 1748. How it benefited the first Christians to make their private possessions common, ibid. The common life of nuns is praised, idem, XXXVI, 1050. Common life, idem, XL, 549. Christians did not hold all things in common, Arator, LXVIII, 114.

## COMEDY

See **Spectacles** in the Index of Illicit Pleasures.

## GRANT

See **Donation**.

## COUNCIL, SYNOD

After the persecution had been quieted, Cyprian attended a council, III, 767. After Easter bishops customarily assemble at Carthage, idem, IV, 348. Councils were frequently held at Carthage, idem, III, 811. Councils held before Cyprian, ibid., 399. Conference of councils with bishops, presbyters, and confessors who were deacons, while laypeople stood by, ibid., IV, 260, 262, 264. On the Council of Nicaea, Ambrose, XVI, 529. In the East the custom prevailed that there should be a council of Easterners, and in the West one of Westerners, ibid., 918. For the sake of one Auxentius, bishops ought not to be wearied by being made to come to a council, ibid., 1006. A synod had gathered because of the arrival of Gallic bishops, ibid., 1161. The most salutary authority of councils, Augustine, XXXIII, 200. A plenary council, ibid. A plenary council remains after the judgment of Rome, ibid., 169. A bishop does not have the council’s acts in his power when the primate objects, ibid., 164. African councils, idem, XXXII, 612; XXXIII, 577; XLIII, 114, 135, 141, 143, 145, 159, 214, 220, 225, 234, 495, 496, 523, 606, 612, 647, etc., etc. Ten councils held at Rome under Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 780, 821. The Council of Clermont convened by Pope Urban II to promote the holy war, Guibert, CLVI, 700. On councils, Gratian in the *Decretum*, CLXXXVII, 93. On the manner and time of holding a synod, Odo of Sully, CCXIII, 57.

## SERMON

How the voice ought to be modulated in sermons, Ambrose, XVI, 55. Prayer in the course of preaching, Augustine, XXXIII, 117. Who may preach, idem, XLI, 105, 106. Whether sayings of pagans should be used in sermons, Alan of Lille, CCX, 114.

## CONCORD

Commendation of concord, Cyprian, IV, 242. Concord of the priestly college, ibid., 315; III, 763. Indivisible concord, ibid., 787. Saving concord, idem, IV, 347. Concord, a bond, ibid., 1127. Concord is extremely difficult between two persons endowed with equal power, Lactantius, VII, 330. The concord and unity of Christians, Jerome, XXIV, 148. God is the author of concord and harmony, Augustine, XXXII, 1174. Precepts of concord are handed down in Christ’s churches, idem, XXXIII, 529. Worshippers of false gods did not possess such precepts, ibid. What harmony is in singing, concord is in a city, idem, XLI, 66. Concord cannot exist without justice, ibid. What concord between human being and God is required, idem, XXXVIII, 82. The concord of the members of the body recalls Christians to unity, idem, XL, 712. The highest concord of flesh and spirit will exist after the resurrection, ibid., 274. Concord with his people, idem, XII, 655. On concord in a church being consecrated, Odo of Canterbury, XXXIII, 949.

## CONFRATERNITY

On confraternities, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 777. On confraternities or associations, Regino, CXXXII, 347.

## CONGREGATION

An evil congregation cannot bear good fruit, Ambrose, XVI, 505. Singularity is to be avoided in a congregation, Peter Cantor, CCV, 205.

## MARRIED PERSONS, MARRIAGE

The continence of Christians, Tertullian, I, 326. They abstained from every excess after marriage, ibid. How great is the chastity of spouses, ibid., 472, 510. They did not exchange the female sex, ibid., 510. In mind they were blind to lust, ibid., 511. The two chief guardians of Christian holiness were monogamy and continence, idem, II, 939. Marriages with pagans are forbidden, Cyprian, IV, 470. A wife separating from her husband ought to remain unmarried, ibid., 774. Marriage is to be kept chastely, Lactantius, VI, 719. It is not the deflowering of virginity but the marital compact that makes marriage, Ambrose, XVI, 316. If a man uses a woman betrothed and given to him, he calls it marriage, ibid., 1183. Marriage is good, but nevertheless drawn from the yoke and from the yoke of the world, ibid., 274. Marriage itself is a bond, ibid., 312. On the good of marriage: a book against Jovinian, Augustine, XXXII, 639. On adulterous marriages, ibid., 653. Manichaeans condemn the use of marriage, ibid., 1344, 1372, 1373. Marriage is made not by carnal intercourse but by marital charity, idem, XXXVIII, 344. It is not dissolved because of barrenness, idem, XL, 385. It is dissolved by death alone, ibid., 473. Marriages between brothers and sisters were necessary in the beginning, idem, XLI, 458; why they were prohibited by religion, ibid. What the good of marriage is, idem, XLIV, 141. The threefold good of marriage, ibid., 404, 688, 810. What married persons seek when they seek the good of marriage, ibid., 738. Why marriages were instituted, idem, XLV, 1582. On the nuptial veil, Leo the Great, LVI, 248. The blessing which the priest places upon a woman about to marry, ibid., 249. What Christian marriages ought to be like, Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 633. No one is to join a spouse to himself from his own kindred, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 668. Which marriages are to be avoided, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46. For what purpose marriages were instituted, Peter Damian, CXLV, 662. On prohibited marriages, King Cnut, CLI, 1173. Marriages blessed and instituted by God, Ivo of Chartres in the *Decretum*, CLXI, 77. Dances at weddings are forbidden, ibid., 617. Christians ought to abstain from marriage celebrations on feast days, St Bruno, CLXIV, 279.

## COUNSEL

Counsel is given to the good; correction restrains those who go astray, Ambrose, XVI, 67. The use of counsels most greatly brings people together, and why, ibid., 114. Who can give useful counsel to another, ibid., 120. What the person who gives counsel to another ought to be like, ibid., 127. The difference between counsel and command, ibid., 256. A command is laid upon subjects; counsel is given to friends. Where there is command, there is law; [Col. 0617] where there is counsel, there is grace, ibid. Counsel invites the willing; command binds the unwilling, ibid., 1031. This is to have God’s counsel: diligently to examine all things, to recommend what is better, and to show what is safer, ibid., 1032. Persons should be encouraged toward counsels in such a way that a life governed by the rule of precepts is not condemned, Augustine, XXXIII, 691, 692. What the gift of counsel accomplishes, idem, XXXIV, 40. True counsel, from whatever soul it proceeds, is to be ascribed to God, ibid., 18, and is not to be despised, ibid., 619. Counsel is needed only in adversity, idem, XXXVI, 140. A rich person needs counsel: you give counsel and have bestowed alms, idem, XXXVII, 1665. Counsel has good and bad sides: there is a proverb concerning the person who lives and is governed by good and bad counsels, ibid., 1684. One who seeks counsel for salvation but does not willingly heed it, idem, XXXVIII, 524. No counsel is better than example, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 45.

## CUSTOM

Reason supports custom, Tertullian, II, 80. It makes no difference whether custom rests upon Scripture or reason, since reason also commends law, ibid., 81. It is to be observed, lest it prove not to be an interpreter of reason, ibid. Where law does not exist, tradition establishes custom, ibid. Even in civil matters custom is accepted in place of law when law is lacking, ibid. It confirms tradition, ibid. It is strengthened by succession into use, ibid., 889. What the force of custom is, ibid., 890. No one rejects a custom that he cannot condemn, ibid., 891. Custom without truth is the antiquity of error, Cyprian, III, 1134. One must not plead custom, but conquer by reason, idem, IV, 410. The various customs of churches, Lactantius, III, 1159. Because of varying customs, there has never been departure from the Church’s peace and unity, ibid. One should not readily depart from custom unless it opposes reason, Augustine, XXXII, 1108. Augustine’s answer concerning the use of custom, idem, XXXIII, 118. In matters concerning which divine Scripture establishes nothing certain, the custom of God’s people or the institutions of elders are to be held as law, ibid., 136, 209. Which customs in the Church are to be changed, ibid., 221. A change of custom, even one assisted by usefulness, disturbs by its novelty; thus a change which is not useful is harmful, ibid., 203. Custom must yield to truth, idem, XLIII, 143, 144, 220; and to reason, ibid. But when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be retained more firmly, ibid., 157. The customs of the elders are not to be despised, John Cassian, XLIX, 1185. What custom is, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 522. Which customs ought to be maintained and which abolished, ibid. Many things have been introduced into the Church which justice, prudence, or the canons now forbid to be exacted, ibid. Ecclesiastical custom is to be held as law, Regino, CXXXII, 372. The customs of churches do not harm the Catholic faith, Guibert, CLVI, 612. Church customs are to be regarded as laws, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 282, 309. Custom makes one love what is laborious, Rupert, CLXVIII, 163. Custom is vainly alleged in defence of abuses and vices, St Bernard, CXXXII, 774. Written customs of the community of Senlis, Stephen, CCXI, 512.

## BANQUETS

What a Christian banquet is like, Tertullian, I, 477. The public banquets of pagans: what they are and how abominable, ibid., 452. The Lord’s banquet, ibid., 1294. Let a sober banquet resound with psalms, Cyprian, IV, 222. Wanton banquets are to be avoided, ibid., 457. The feasts of detestable people are to be avoided, Ambrose, XVI, 228. Indulgence in food and drink belongs to such people, ibid., 881. Abundance of feasting weakens both body and soul, Jerome, XXIII, 302. Wars and the overthrow of cities are provoked by the delights of feasting, ibid., 300. Augustine worked to abolish the customary celebration of banquets in churches, XXXIII, 115, 116. Banquets formerly celebrated in the basilica of St Peter, ibid., 119. The Jews are not recorded to have celebrated luxurious banquets in the temple, ibid., 115. The feasts of this earth are daily remedies, idem, XXXVIII, 489. God’s feasts seek minds, not bellies, ibid., 581. Feasting and drinking bouts at martyrs’ tombs are censured, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 661. What Christian banquets are like, ibid., 634. Which banquets are praiseworthy, St Gregory the Great. Let reading, meditation, and prayer be our daily feast, Godefrid, CLXXXIV, 388, 394. See **Banquets** in the Index of Illicit Pleasures.

## CORRECTION, REBUKE

The good heed rebuke, Cyprian, IV, 776. Rebukes are often better than a silent friendship, Ambrose, XVI, 180. Rebuke is life-giving, Jerome, XXIII, 587. In rebuking, we are flatterers of the rich, ibid., 563. Straight things receive adornment; crooked things, correction, ibid., 1022. How fraternal correction is to be given and received, Augustine, XXXII, 1381. It is not to be neglected, though hateful, idem, XXXIII, 247, 957; XXXVIII, 111, 549; XLIII, 98; XLIV, 918. The good are corrected as sons; the evil are left as strangers, idem, XXXIV, 888. One who does not correct does not govern, ibid., 504. He who strikes is merciful; he who spares is cruel, idem, XXXVIII, 111. We must not neglect to correct those committed to our care, ibid., 549. To correct belongs to the true shepherd, ibid., 762. With what disposition rebuke ought to be given, ibid., 507, 549; XXXIX, 1698. Neglecting rebuke from desire or weakness is a sin, idem, XLI, 21. All are bound to give correction, ibid.; especially bishops and those set over others, ibid. Correction should not be given to insult, but to heal through shame, idem, XXXVIII, 779. What correction is lawful and to what extent, idem, XLIII, 432. How it is to be given, ibid., 83, 84. When it bears fruit, idem, XLIV, 920. Different correction according to difference of persons, ibid., 944. On those who refuse correction, ibid., 920. At one time it ought to be private, at another public, idem, XXXVIII, 510. Public sins are to be rebuked publicly, idem, XLIV, 946. There is a measure in correcting faults, St Anselm, CXLIX, 128, 131. Fraternal correction must be performed by an innocent person, idem, CLXXXIII, 395. Correction proceeding from charity pays no regard to persons, idem, CLXXXII, 367, 368. Rebuke is given for testing, idem, CLXXXIII, 1000. Rebuke and consolation are God’s twofold help, ibid., 877. What rebuke works in us, ibid., 560. Its harshness is to be softened by gentleness, ibid., 995. Let it be moderate, ibid., 286. It is unwelcome and hateful to the wicked, ibid., 1155, 1156. How unjust are those who bear it impatiently, ibid., 988. A corrector is a good adversary, ibid., 932. How Peter of Celle piously and moderately corrects a certain monk, idem, CCII, 523. He calls the fearless mouth of John the Baptist in rebuke a golden lip, ibid., 810. One’s neighbour is to be rebuked, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1197. Superiors themselves are to be rebuked with due reverence, ibid., 199. Fraternal correction is commended, Peter Cantor, CCV, 284, 285. See Peter of Blois, CCVII, 7, 16, 19, 39, 62, 169, 231, 285, 330, etc.

## CROSS, SIGN OF THE CROSS

Christians devoted to the cross, Tertullian, I, 365. We mark bed and little body with the cross, ibid., 1296. “At every entrance and exit, when dressing and putting on shoes, at baths, at table, when lights are lit, in bedroom and sitting-place—in every activity that occupies us—we rub our foreheads with the sign of the cross,” idem, II, 80. The bearing of the cross is necessary for those fighting against the devil, ibid., 347. The human body is in the form of a cross, ibid., 678. The sign of the cross is found in a person who prays with outstretched hands, ibid., 578. To whom, and how, Christ’s cross is folly, ibid., 481. By the power of the cross Christ now winnows the world through the cross; afterward he will winnow it through judgment, ibid., 346. The force and rationale of Christ’s cross, Lactantius, VI, 528, 531. Christians frequently sign themselves with the sign of the cross, ibid., 533. By this sign demons are put to flight by believers, idem, VII, 210, 314. On its power and efficacy, ibid., 216, 671. A heavenly and immortal sign, ibid., 261, 314. The cross shown to Constantine the Great, ibid., 261, 369, 428. On the sign of the cross in people’s garments and seen in the sky in Julian’s time, ibid., 427. The custom among ancient Christians of frequently applying the sign of the cross to their foreheads, ibid., 670. At every moment the Christian inscribes contempt for death upon his own forehead, since he knows that he cannot have salvation without the Lord’s cross, Ambrose, XVI, 1246. The sign of the cross, Augustine, XXXII, 668; XXXIII, 694. A dying young man began to make the sign upon his forehead, ibid. Christ’s cross is to be embraced, lest we be carried away and swallowed by the whirlpool of this world, idem, XXXIII, 335. A Christian ought to bear the cross in the present life, ibid., 215. Christ’s cross is the ship by which we cross the sea of this age, idem, XXXV, 1389, 1390. Christ’s tribunal, ibid., 1642. Unless the sign of the cross is employed, nothing is rightly accomplished in the celebration of the sacraments, ibid., 1950. It is a more precious sign upon kings’ foreheads than the jewel of the diadem, idem, XXXVI, 292, 934. The key by which things shut are opened, ibid., 514. We must be carried by the Lord’s cross in order to pass to our homeland, idem, XXXVIII, 475. The sign of the cross on the forehead, ibid., 181, 201, 876, 941. The sign of the cross appearing on the garments of those baptized, ibid., 136. The humility of the cross is the way to exaltation, ibid., 875. The school and chair of Christ, ibid., 1116. The tribunal of the Judge, ibid., 1293. The great exchange of the cross, idem, XXXIX, 1454. The sign by which the Church conquers its enemies, ibid., 1638. The sign by which catechumens are received, idem, XL, 659. By the power of the cross heresies are crushed, ibid., 696. Which cross must be taken up in following Christ, idem, XLII, 166. In time of persecution one must not depart from the wood of the cross, St Prosper, LI, 295. Crosses were formerly placed upon altars, St Paulinus, LXI, 548. Christians are granted a standard bearing the sign of the cross, Arator, LXVIII, 123. The worship of the cross among Christians, ibid., 124. On the finding of the Holy Cross, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 936. St Augustine, apostle of the English, and his companions enter England bearing a cross and an image of Christ, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 370. What it is to take up the cross, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 571. In how many ways the cross is taken up, ibid., 1101. On veneration of the Lord’s cross, Gerard, CXLII, 1304. On the image of the Saviour on the cross, ibid., 1306. [Col. 0619] Praises of the Holy Cross, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 715. On what grounds it is to be adored, ibid., 766. The benefits of the cross, ibid. The cross is fastened to the garments of Christian soldiers, Guibert, CLVI, 702. Christ commands one to carry the cross, not to seek burial, idem, CLVII, 54, 144. On the praise and finding of the Holy Cross, Berengosus, CLX, 936. How it was found by the Empress Helena, ibid., 937. At Pope Urban II’s urging, all Christians of the West put on the cross in order to redeem the Holy Land, Baldric, CLXVI, 1065. The cross puts demons to flight, Rupert, CLXIX, 323. The cross as a sealing sign, ibid., 389. The mystery of the cross, ibid., 786. How the cross is to be borne by us, ibid. God’s servants are marked with the sign of the cross, ibid., 959. Why a Christian is signed on the forehead, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1476. He ought always to hang upon the cross, idem, CXCII, 160. Adoration of the cross redounds to Christ, who is the Son of God, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1098. On the guardians of the Holy Cross and their obligations, Guichard, CXCIX, 1097. On the sign of the cross which those intending to go to Jerusalem impressed upon their clothing as a sign of their vow and forthcoming pilgrimage, William of Tyre, CCI, 231. Sermon on the Holy Cross, Martin of León, CCIX, 29. The custom of swearing upon the cross as upon the Gospels, Innocent III, CCXIV, XXIV.

## THOSE SIGNED WITH THE CROSS

Who they are, William, CCI, 223. The miseries of pilgrims, ibid., 226. Peter the Hermit, ibid., 227. Pope Urban II’s exhortations to arms, ibid., 231. Misfortunes of Christians, ibid., 248. Godfrey of Bouillon, ibid., 249. Soliman is put to flight, ibid., 288. The massacre at Tarsus, ibid., 295. Famine, ibid., 318. The capture of Antioch, ibid., 348. The Lord’s lance is discovered, ibid., 365. Tancred, ibid., 402. They enter Jerusalem, ibid., 421. The order of the Temple’s knighthood is established, ibid., 526. Assistance for the holy war, ibid., 659. Saladin, ibid., 928. Tithes are imposed, ibid., 1058. Innocent III vigorously urges and labours for aid and recovery of the Holy Land, CCXIV, LXXXIX. On the same subject, CXXXI ff.

## CRYPT

Underground crypts containing the bodies of the holy martyrs, Jerome, XXV, 375. Jerome had often entered them at Rome with companions of his own age, ibid. Description of the crypts in which martyrs’ bodies lay, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 539.

## ECCLESIASTICAL TITHE

Tithes and first-fruits are distinct, Ambrose, XVI, 1079. Tithes, Augustine, XXXVIII, 89. Whether it is sufficient for a Christian to give tithes of his possessions, ibid., 522. How unjust it is not to give tithes to God, idem, XXXIX, 2265. They are not ours, but assigned to the Church, ibid., 2336. They are the revenues of the needy, ibid., 2266. They are to be given from one’s patrimony, ibid., 1934. From all produce, ibid., 2195, 2217, 2267. The offering of tithes benefits us, ibid., 2666. An offering of tithes and first-fruits pleasing to God, John Cassian, XLIX, 1172. On payment of tithes, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 204; Walafrid, CXIV, 961. On tithes, Regino, CXXXII, 200 ff. On rendering tithes, Odo of Canterbury, CXXXIII, 949. On tithes and offerings, Burchard, CXL, 673. On giving the penny of Holy Church, Æthelred, CLI, 1166. On tithes, Cnut, CLI, 1174; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 237, 245. Tithes granted to the Knights Templar, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 871. A person is taught and instructed by God to offer tithes, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 344. Tithes are to be paid by laypeople to their own parish priests, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 918; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1042. They are distributed to priests according to the bishop’s direction, ibid., 1013. A fourth part goes to widows and the poor, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1309. A tithe is established as aid for the Holy Land, William of Tyre, CCI, 1058.

## DECRETAL LETTERS OF THE HOLY PONTIFFS

Stephen, abbot of St Geneviève, censures the excessive multitude of decretals, CCXI, 516.

## DEDICATION OF CHURCHES AND ALTARS

Dedication of a temple previously profane, Augustine, XXXVIII, 889. The foundation of the Church has already been dedicated; we too shall be dedicated when we rise again, ibid., 661. Relics for dedicating a new
things necessary for the church, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 334. Dedication of an altar with relics of saints, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 735. Dedication of a church, formerly called *Encaenia*, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 497. With what joy it was performed, ibid. At the dedication of a church, games and feasting forbidden, ibid., 498. Why, in dedicating a church, the threshold is struck three times and “Peace to this house” is said, Remigius, CXXXI, 547. What is signified by the priest or bishop writing the alphabet on the ground, ibid., 850. Why water mixed with salt and ashes is used in the consecration of a church, and a cross traced with it, ibid., 852. What is meant by the bishop making a cross with his finger at the four corners of the altar, ibid., 854. And pouring water into the base of the altar, ibid., 858. What the translation of relics and their deposition beneath the altar signifies, ibid., 862. Churches are not dedicated in honor of saints of the Old Testament, ibid., 968. Holy water is sprinkled over [Col. 0620] the new church, Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 194. Whether an altar transferred to another place must be consecrated again, ibid., 194. The altar is not made for the church, but the church for the altar, ibid. In St. Anselm’s time, bare stones not fixed anywhere were consecrated, ibid. When the principal altar has been violated, the whole church must be consecrated, ibid., 196. A double alphabet written on the pavement of a church during its consecration, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVIII, 385. Water, salt, and ashes in this consecration, ibid., 386. The dedication of a church is for souls, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 517. On the five sacraments of dedication, ibid. What the feast of dedication is like, ibid., 530. The five rites of dedication adapted to morals, ibid., 520. The day of a church’s dedication is a day of rejoicing, Garnier of Langres, CCV, 813. What the ceremonies of dedication are and what they signify, ibid., 816–817. Through dedication, a church becomes a house of prayer, refreshment, and rest, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 714.

**THE DEAD; PRAYERS FOR THE DEAD.** Christians made offerings and prayers for the dead on the anniversary day, II, 79, 942. Prayer must be made for the dead and refreshment requested for them, ibid. Public offerings for the dead, ibid., 737. Services are rendered to the dead so that they may live in memory and endure in affection, Ambrose, XVI, 1318. Some customarily observed the third and thirtieth day for the dead, others the seventh and fortieth, ibid., 1386. Christian dead are called sleepers, Jerome, XXII, 589. The Christian tradition concerning psalms and hymns recited over them, ibid., 697; XXIII, 27. Alleluia is sung, idem, XXII, 697. Prayer for the dead, Augustine, XXV, 1847. The whole Church is accustomed to offer supplication for the dead, idem, XL, 592. Solemn funeral rites; sacrifices of the altar, prayers, and alms for them, ibid., 609. Hymns are sung at funerals, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 879. The names of the dead are recited at the altar, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1181. On the offerings made for deceased believers, St. Julian, XCVI, 473; Regino, CXXXII, 355. On piety toward the dead, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 245. On the commemoration of all the dead after the feast of All Saints, Udalric, CXLIX, 688. Masses to be celebrated for the dead, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 212. On the care to be taken for the dead, ibid., 312. In how many ways the souls of the dead ought to be released, ibid., 887.

**DEPOSITION OF RELICS.** See *Relics*.

**DEVOTION.** Censure ought to yield to devotion, Ambrose, XIV, 1104. Blessed is one who dwells at the entrance of faith, in the lodging of the mind, in the dwelling-place of devotion, and in the practice of virtue, ibid., 1055. Peter labors in us when our devotion labors, ibid., 299. Wine offered for the sake of devotion, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 821. Who are companions in devotion, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1243. Devotion is twofold: that of grace and that of nature, Alan of Lille, CCX, 389.

**DEACON.** He publicly reads out the names of those making offerings, Jerome, XXV, 175. Some equated deacons with presbyters; they are answered, idem, XXII, 1193. What makes deacons honorable, ibid., 1194. Why deacons were instituted, ibid. They read the Gospel, ibid., 1200. How perilous is the office of deacon, Augustine, XXXIII, 88. By the deacon’s voice the common prayer is announced, ibid., 221. The office of a deacon is to minister the blood of Christ, ibid., 1385. *Diaconus* in Latin means “minister,” ibid., 1441. What sort of men deacons ought to be, Leo the Great, LVI, 459.

**THE LORD’S DAY.** On the Lord’s Day Christians indulge in joy, Tertullian, I, 371. The Lord’s Day is a feast day, ibid., 579; II, 79. On that day it is unlawful to fast or worship kneeling, ibid., 79. It was called the Day of the Sun, I, 371. Collections or assemblies were held on the Lord’s Day, Jerome, XXIII, 348. The elders decreed that on the Lord’s Day neither fasting nor bending the knee was permitted, John Cassian, XLIX, 110. The Lord’s Day, the day of our salvation and joy, Leo the Great, LIV, 279. Persons held in prison were treated better on the Lord’s Day, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 336. No manual work on the Lord’s Day, St. Benedict, CII, 1182. No fasting on Sundays, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 269. What may be done on the Lord’s Day, Regino, CXXXII, 264. On the Lord’s Day, King Canute, CLI, 1175. On not fasting on that day, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 265, 269, 274.

**FEAST DAYS.** How a feast should be celebrated, Jerome, XXII, 445. Feast of St. Peter the Apostle, ibid. For Christians every season is a feast, ibid., 1031. Festivals are not to be celebrated in wine, idem, XL, 549. How feasts should be observed, Augustine, XXXIII, 1404. The feast days of the Gentiles consist in an abundance of banquets and drunkenness, ibid., 118. Why, at the beginning of the Church, it was allowed for martyrs’ feasts to be celebrated with similar extravagance, ibid. Certain feasts celebrated joyfully by diners at public tables, idem, XXXVIII, 274. The carnal celebration of feasts is criticized, ibid., 1178. Martyrs’ feasts were instituted so that we might be reminded [Col. 0621] to imitate them, ibid., 52, 1293, 1352, 1364, 1414. To honor martyrs’ feasts without imitating them is nothing but to flatter them falsely, ibid., 1447. Christian feast days and pagan solemn days, idem, XL, 343. On feast days Christians ought to abstain from weddings, dances, and noisy hunts, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 279. To sanctify the Sabbath is not to cease from good works, ibid. The feasts of saints should be commemorated, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 510, 541. The festivals of saints are to be observed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 478. Why fasts precede the principal feasts of saints, ibid., 501. On the solemnity of festivals, John Beleth, CCII, 17. Clerics who desire feasts to be celebrated for the sake of payment are rebuked, Peter Cantor, CCV, 98.

**DIPLOMAS, PRIVILEGES, DONATIONS.** Charters of King Dagobert, LXXX, 499 ff. Of various persons, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 1078 ff.; of Charlemagne, XCVII, 68 ff.; of King Clovis, Flodoard, CXXXV, 53. On defenders of churches and monasteries, Abbo of Fleury, 476. On privileges, ibid., 479. On royal and imperial precepts, ibid., 480. On the difference between testaments and precarial grants, ibid., 480. On the generosity of Emperor Sigismund, Aimoin, CXXXIX, 663. On the donations of King Chlothar, ibid., 691. Likewise of King Dagobert, ibid., 788. Ecclesiastical charters of Emperor Henry II, CXL, 237; of Leo IX, 591. Likewise of Richard, duke of Normandy, William of Jumièges, CXLIX, 821. Charters of William the Conqueror, ibid., 1350, 1374; of Emperors Conrad II, CLI, 1043, 1079; Henry III, 1085; Henry IV, 1139. Of Æthelred, Canute, and Edward, 1165, 1171, 1195. Of Godfrey of Bouillon and Blessed Ida, CLV, 459. Of Fulk, duke of Anjou, ibid., 479. For the privileges of monasteries, see the special index of monasteries.

**DIPTYCHS, TABLETS.** A tablet on which clerics were inscribed, Augustine, XXXIII, 266, 269; XXXIX, 1580. On the tablet of the living faithful, ibid., 269. Marriage tablets, idem, XXXVI, 1045; idem, XXXVIII, 88, 225, 345. Tablets of slaves broken at their manumission, ibid., 145. Diptychs in which the names of the living were entered after baptism, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 187.

**DISCIPLINE.** The vain disciplines of the world, Tertullian, I, 1251. The testimonies of discipline contribute to proving truth, from which it benefits no one to depart, idem, II, 50. Doctrine is the index of discipline, ibid., 58. Nature is the first of all discipline, ibid., 82. Those who deny punishment despise discipline, ibid., 808. License is often the trial of discipline, ibid., 923. Ecclesiastical discipline, St. Cyprian, IV, 319, 334, 365. The teaching office of discipline, ibid., 324. Severity, ibid., 415. It is the guardian of hope, the restraint of faith, the guide of the saving path, the incentive and nourishment of a good disposition, the teacher of virtue; it is salutary to pursue it, ibid., 440–441. It is corrupted by a long peace, ibid., 468. The vigor of ecclesiastical discipline weakened, ibid., 781. Ecclesiastical discipline, Hilary of Poitiers, X, 674. With what zeal the discipline of wisdom must be embraced, idem, IX, 289. How discipline, wisdom, and understanding differ from one another, Ambrose, XIV, 1089. How great is the power of perfect discipline, ibid., 346. The whole sum of our discipline lies in mercy and compassion, idem, XVII, 473. *Disciplina* is derived from *discere*, “to learn,” Augustine, XXXII, 1223. Reason is the inventor of all disciplines, ibid., 1011. And of the knowledge of all things, ibid., 1021. Where discipline varies, what ought to be observed by a prudent Christian, idem, XXXIII, 151, 200. Disciplines are wrongly called liberal unless the pursuit of human piety is present, ibid., 368. What Christian discipline or instruction is, idem, XXXVII, 1204. There one learns to live well, so as to attain life everlasting, idem, XL, 669. Ecclesiastical discipline has its foundation in Christ’s words, ibid., 200. It especially combats pride, ibid., 413. How it is to be exercised, idem, XLIII, 84, 86. Threefold discipline, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 681. Discipline, the guardian of holiness, modesty, and honorableness, idem, CLXXXII, 786. A superior owes discipline and protection to an inferior, idem, CLXXXIII, 45. The necessity of discipline, ibid., 886.

**DISCIPLINE, AN INSTRUMENT OF PENANCE.** The use of scourges or rods in the sacrament of penance, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 915. The use of bodily discipline, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 181.

**DISPENSATION.** God can dispense with laws established by himself, Augustine, XXXIV, 803. What is done by inspiration contrary to a commandment is to be charged as transgression, ibid., 816. What is meant by “dispensatively,” idem, XXXIII, 228. How dispensation is made, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 535; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 862, 864, 865. Dispensations of the Church, Stephen, CCXI, 383.

**DISPUTATION.** It is no small progress in philosophy when, in the effort to discover what is right and true, victory is despised by the disputant, Augustine, XXXII, 910. The good life is not purified by the winding paths of disputations [Col. 0622], but by the easy authority of the sacred mysteries by which we are initiated, ibid., 1007. Certain conditions for disputing are laid down, idem, XXXIII, 276. What is more contentious than, when the matter is agreed, to contend over the name? ibid., 1040. It is dishonest to add anything to another’s words against which you dispute, idem, XLIII, 210. Things which may be common to both sides ought not be introduced into a disputation, ibid., 396. Nor things that are figurative or obscure, ibid., 398. What it is to dispute, ibid., 457. In disputations, contention must be avoided, ibid., 548. Human disputation and mutability afflict a person, not the variability of things, Hugh of St. Victor, 237. Human disputations about the world, ibid. The world has been handed over to human disputation, ibid. To dispute from cedar to hyssop, idem, CLXXVII, 689. God is not comprehended by disputation but by holiness, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 805. Further matters concerning disputation, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 867. Overly diffuse disputations have more noise and less usefulness, Peter Cantor, CCV, 30. In theological disputations one must not shout over trifles, ibid., and 374. The method of disputing requires that it be done without quarrel or contention, ibid., 34. In disputations, for the respondent to be too hasty is shameful and dangerous, ibid., 35. The early saints settled no question without prior deliberation, ibid.

**RICHES.** Contempt for riches is commended, Tertullian, I, 1260. The rejection of riches and injuries, ibid. The Lord is found in no riches, ibid. Riches offer no assistance toward the blessed life, Ambrose, XVI, 107. The beauty of riches lies not in the treasuries of the rich, but in the sustenance of the poor, ibid., 886. Riches are a burden if you do not know how to use them, if you do not scatter through them the fragrance of Christ, ibid., 1116. How riches should be used, Augustine, XXXII, 163. Riches are not to be loved, but only used, idem, XXXV, 1691. The safe place for riches is heaven, to which they are conveyed through the hands of the poor, idem, XXXVI, 423, 549. All who live badly leave their riches to strangers, ibid., 553. The richer you are, the more fearful you are, idem, XXXVII, 1762. They are thunderbolts that destroy those whom they raise up, ibid., 1769. They will perish and are full of dangers, XXXVIII, 114. They are not to be taken away from the dying here, ibid. Hope is not to be placed in riches, ibid., 958. What are the riches of Christians, idem, XLI, 23. Riches that cannot be taken away are to be sought, idem, XXXVII, 1645. On the unjust possession of riches, Innocent III, CCXVI, 722. The misery of rich and poor, ibid., 708. On the short and miserable life of magnates, ibid., 728.

**DOCTRINE.** Understanding, not memory, produces doctrine, Ambrose, XV, 1337. Every moral teaching is pleasant, ibid., 1197. A good life without doctrine has grace; doctrine without life lacks integrity, ibid., 1199. Why doctrine is called leaven, ibid., 1750. New doctrine must be suppressed, Jerome, XXII, 755. Foreign doctrine must not be received, ibid., 1120. False doctrine does everything for gain, idem, XXIV, 240. The bread of doctrine is not eaten unless we open the eyes of the mind, ibid., 536. The doctrine of teachers is to be considered more than their life, idem, XXV, 399. Through diversity of doctrine different gods are worshipped, ibid., 1056. Virtues perish if there is no doctrine in the churches, ibid., 1085. All doctrine concerns either things or signs, Augustine, XXXIV, 19. Many doctrines are either superfluous or harmful; one alone is useful and health-giving, idem, XXXIII, 1030. Secular doctrines are the husks on which swine feed, idem, XXXV, 1344. Saving doctrine consists partly of things to be believed and partly of things to be understood, idem, XL, 496. Christ’s doctrine commands humility, idem, XXXVIII, 876. It condemns corruption of morals, ibid., 64, 74. The aids of doctrine applied to the soul through a human being are beneficial only when God works to make them beneficial, ibid., 104. God placed the doctrine of truth in the chair of unity, idem, XXXIII, 403.

**CHRISTIAN DOCTRINE.** Christian doctrine must first be learned word for word, so that the mysteries may afterward be understood, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 355–356. Why Christ’s doctrine is made obscure by mysteries, ibid., 469 ff. It should vary its manner of teaching for the untrained, ibid., 495. Its order must be regulated so that one thing is not impeded by another, ibid., 512. Familiar doctrine handed down by Christ, ibid., 623. Catholic doctrine can have neither the stain of faithlessness nor the wrinkle of falsehood, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 361. It is not permissible to differ from evangelical doctrine by even one word, ibid., 918. On the instruction of men and women, Atto of Vercelli. The doctrine of the Spirit does not sharpen curiosity but kindles charity, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 812. Woods and solitude teach more than books, idem, CLXXXII, 242. Teaching should be by example rather than word, idem, CLXXXIII, 1063.

**LORD.** How many masters one has who has fled from the one Master, Ambrose, XVI, 1215. Masters, command your slaves not as persons subjected by condition, but remembering that they share the same nature as yourselves [Col. 0623], ibid., 1218. Men cannot be truly masters in any great degree, since they need slaves, Augustine, XXXVI, 872. Unjust and difficult masters must be endured, ibid., 736. What masters owe to slaves, idem, XXXII, 1329. An earthly master exacts anxious servitude, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 502. Let each person recognize himself here not as master but as steward, ibid., 545. Let the master withdraw the slave from sins, lest he himself also sin, ibid., 611. A slave’s peculium belongs to his master, ibid., 235. Carnal masters are customarily despised by their slaves, Salvian, LIII, 65. Whoever knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows, ibid., LXII, 233. The good servant of a good master, ibid., 62. How masters ought to conduct themselves toward slaves and subjects, Leo the Great, LIV, 271, 274, 201. Why God wills some to be subject to others, ibid., 305. The harshness of masters toward slaves is reproved, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 581. On masters and their duties, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 174.

**DONATION.** See above, *Diploma*.

**GIFT.** See *Offering*.

**DOUBT.** The credibility of history perishes if what has been established by authority and time is called into doubt, Augustine, XXXII, 1335. Whoever doubts whether truth exists has within himself a truth from which he does not doubt, idem, XXXIV, 155. It is better to doubt concerning hidden matters than to quarrel over uncertainties, ibid., 376. It is permissible to doubt concerning certain matters, idem, XII, 646. Doubts should, as far as possible, be made firm, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 503. In doubtful matters judgment must be avoided and the matter referred to God, ibid., 589. One who doubts divine promises is rebuked, ibid., 629. Doubts were frequently referred to Rome, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1191, 1200. Some matters are more suitably settled by conversation than by writing, ibid., 1202. What rule is to be observed in doubtful cases, ibid., 1419. They are determined either by Scripture or by the rules of the Fathers, ibid., 1191–1192. In doubtful matters the old custom must be adhered to, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 713. After the darkness of sin has entered the soul, the eye of reason becomes bleary, so that it sees uncertainly, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 329. Where doubt still exists, faith does not exist, ibid., 330. The Friend of the Bridegroom doubts and asks, ibid., 337. The Savior himself rebukes doubting disciples, ibid., 338. How one ought to act in doubtful cases, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 106–107. In doubtful matters the wise trust another’s judgment rather than their own, ibid., 202. Nothing concerning doubtful matters should be rashly pronounced, idem, CLXXXIII, 856. Doubt and falsehood are the two daughters of ignorance, ibid.

**DUEL.** Those who shed human blood destroy the work of God, Ambrose, XIV, 261. What punishment belongs to homicide, ibid., 405–406. God wills his disciples to bear injuries and not readily return them, still less strike, idem, XV, 1329. Injuries must be borne patiently, Augustine, XXXIV, 1257–1258. God vindicates those suffering injury by punishing the injurious, idem, XXXVII, 1894. What should one who has suffered injury do? idem, XXXVIII, 508. Cicero said that Caesar was accustomed to forget nothing but injuries, idem, XXXIII, 528. The devil is the presider over contests, idem, XXXVII, 1859. Duels are strongly opposed to Christian simplicity, St. Agobard, CIV, 119. Severely forbidden by canons and royal edicts, ibid., 258. On the combat of two men, which our people call “the field,” Regino, CXXXII, 300. St. Bernard calls for duels to be suppressed, CLXXXII, 581. Duels are criticized, ibid., 366. They are ascribed to madness, not virtue, ibid. The penalty for a duel: blinding, ibid., 147. Solemn fairs for duels, ibid., 581, note. On merciful forgiveness, Peter Cantor, CCV, 280.

**CHURCH.** See *Basilica*.

**ELECTION; ELECTED PERSON.** How Ambrose was elected bishop, whose humility shone forth, in his Life, idem, XIV, 28 ff. Election does not presuppose merit, Augustine, XXXV, 1851, 1853. It precedes all human merits, idem, XL, 620. The elect owe everything to God’s grace, idem, XXXVIII, 604. All good believers are deservedly called elect, idem, XLI, 194. How free ecclesiastical elections should be from flesh and blood, Leo the Great, LIV, 145. The marks of the apostles’ election, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 775 ff. The Lord’s two elections, ibid., 764. The election of a bishop is a great matter, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 370–371. It must be made after a fast, ibid. The king’s consent is required, ibid., 488. Louis VII, king of the Franks, obstructs episcopal elections, ibid., 388. A second election ought not to be made unless the first is shown invalid, ibid., 276. Bishops attend the election of an abbot, ibid., 297. Letters of King Louis VII and of the chapter of Chartres concerning the election of John of Salisbury as bishop, idem, CXCIX, 374, 375. A letter on an abbot’s election made by royal command, ibid., 24. Letter of John of Salisbury on the election of Pope Alexander III, ibid., 38. The method of electing, ibid., 63. An illegitimate election to dignities is like the altar of the idol Bel, Peter Cantor, CCV, 91, 124, 125. Canonical election is manifold in the Old Testament, ibid. The Church does not permit election to be made by the casting of lots, ibid., 227. Definition of election, ibid., 125. Three things impede the canonicity of an election, ibid., 122.

**ALMSGIVING.** Those who refuse to give alms, Tertullian, I, 1261 ff. Christians collect alms to relieve various [Col. 0624] necessities, ibid., 468. The command and merit of almsgiving, Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 641. The fruit of almsgiving, ibid., 974. The Lord does not wish wealth to be poured out all at once, but distributed, Ambrose, XVI, 67. The poor person asks for what you have, not for what you do not have, ibid., 203. No one gave more than the one who gave everything, ibid., 1043. Many give alms for the sake of vanity, Jerome, XXII, 418. Whatever you take from your own resources for expenditure, count as profit, ibid., 549. What must be considered in almsgiving, ibid., 556. Christ’s substance is not to be poured out imprudently, ibid., 584. One should give to individuals not for luxury but for necessity, ibid. How great are the powers and rewards of almsgiving, ibid., 642. The customary practice of almsgiving among Hebrews and Christians, ibid., 643. The Lord commands that alms be given, Augustine, XXXIII, 1092. We entrust to God what we bestow on the poor, ibid. Almsgiving is the beginning of charity, idem, XXXV, 2019. It is commended, ibid., 2023–2024. Gifts of alms are those in which the King is adored, idem, XXXVI, 511. God chose to be in need of you, and you withdraw your hand, idem, XXXVII, 1922. Let not a poor person first weep beneath you, so that a poor person may rejoice because of you, ibid., 1863. Christ is needy in the poor person, idem, XXXVIII, 240, 243. God receives and is fed in the poor person, ibid., 524. *Eleemosyna* is Greek for “mercy,” ibid., 1043. A pious loan to God, ibid., 239. The commerce of the almsgiver, ibid., 410. A person gives necessities so that another may live longer here, or live miserably, but does not give superfluities so that he may reign eternally with Christ, ibid., 1387. Many kinds of almsgiving, idem, XI, 265. Alms for the dead, ibid., 158. God considers not to whom a gift is given, but with what intention it is given, idem, XLI, 748. Those who live badly do not perform worthy alms, ibid. The merit and usefulness of almsgiving, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 157, 159, 160, 165, 176. It is a kind of baptism and another washing from sins, ibid., 159, 190. Sins are cleansed through almsgiving, ibid., 190, 303, 419. In it not wealth but disposition is weighed, ibid., 190, 442. It is a pious usury, ibid., 181. Gifts must be given to the needy before they ask, ibid., 491. It must be joined with fasting, ibid., 440. The efficacy of almsgiving, Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 121. What perfect almsgiving is, Cassiodorus, LXX, 265. How it should be given, ibid., 295. It should not be given grudgingly, ibid., 1094. Who should be exhorted to give alms generously, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 83. Let them not, through proud thought, exalt themselves over those to whom they give earthly goods, ibid. Let not pride lift them up, but fear press them down, ibid., 84. Almsgiving must not be made from theft, ibid., 88. By almsgiving a golden house is built for us, ibid., 388. The usefulness of alms on the last day, ibid., 1223. To give alms for the dead is good and salutary for them, Alcuin, C, 321. Alms are to be given to everyone who asks, St. Benedict, CIII, 1049. On the varieties of almsgiving, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 340. On almsgiving, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 188. Alms for the poor are established by Pope Zacharias, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1059. Alms for the poor are to be distributed from the patriarchate, ibid., 1060. The poor are visited by the pontiff much better through alms than through bodily presence, ibid., 1085. Adrian I assigns a daily alms to one hundred poor persons in the Lateran patriarchate, ibid., 1183. Christ’s poor, our brothers: their provisions in the same patriarchate, ibid., 454. Almsgiving is strong armor, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 256 ff. What is the reward of almsgiving, idem, CXLV, 212. Which almsgiving is greater, ibid., 214. An abundance of temporal goods often arises from almsgiving, ibid., 248. Almsgiving benefits the dead and is unwelcome to demons, ibid., 220. Praise of almsgiving, ibid., 222. On alms, Æthelred, king of the English, CLI, 1158. Almsgiving expiates many evils, Ivo of Chartres, ibid. Almsgiving is worth nothing unless one’s life is corrected, idem, 1015, 1016. How it should be bestowed, ibid., 1017. How acceptable to God almsgiving is, and what reward it receives, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 166. Almsgiving should be made from what is abundant, Venerable Rupert, CLXVIII, 814. Almsgiving is more useful to the giver than to the recipient, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 59. Praise of the alms of Cornelius the centurion before baptism, Garnier, CXCIII, 415. To whom, how, and when alms should be given, Peter Cantor, CCV, 148. Almsgiving is the daughter of mercy, ibid., 286. It must be given for the sake of God alone, ibid. Four kinds of almsgiving, ibid., 288. From what alms should be given, ibid., 289. On almsgiving, Alan of Lille, CCX, 175; Gunther, CCXII, 209. Pope Innocent III pours out very many alms to the poor, ibid., CCXIV, CXCVI. *Book on Almsgiving*, CCXVI, 747.

**BISHOPS.** In former times bishops were elected who were advanced in age and approved, Tertullian, I, 469. They assumed this honor not for a price but by testimony, ibid. They presided over Christian assemblies, ibid. A bishop is the high priest, ibid., 1218. The order and successions of bishops, idem, II, 44. They customarily appointed fasts for the whole people, ibid., 972. The Church is not the number [Col. 0625] of bishops, ibid., 1026. A bishop’s duty is to teach, Ambrose, XVI, 24. He ought to employ clerics as his members, and especially ministers, ibid., 139. Whomever he sees suited to each office, he should appoint thereto, ibid. His greatest necessity is to lend out to the minds of the people the words of God entrusted to him, ibid., 187. A bishop should be moderate through commendable poverty, ibid., 917. A bishop must above all avoid becoming like the common body of the Church through the admixture of Gentiles, ibid., 982. In seeking a bishop, malice must especially be absent in one in whom the life of all is shaped, ibid., 1201. All ought to agree in seeking him, ibid., 1189. Christians were ardently concerned that a prefect should not judge a bishop’s case, ibid., 1276. It is sedition against the primatial see when a bishop wishes to condemn persons whose case the primate wishes deferred, Augustine, XXXIII, 164. Bishops are to judge ecclesiastical cases, ibid., 169. The episcopate is not an art for conducting a deceitful life, ibid., 296. The bishop manages the care of the poor, ibid., 809. Bishops’ faults may be punished without prejudice to the honor of the episcopate, ibid., 954. Bishops are guardians and shepherds, but under Christ the Guardian and Shepherd, idem, XXXV, 1669. The bishops’ higher position is dangerous, ibid. The derivation of the term “bishop,” idem, XXXVIII, 580. The weight of the episcopal burden, ibid., 960, 1480. The name episcopate is one of work, not honor, idem, XLI, 647. A bishop’s private blessing, ibid., 762. A bishop must be examined before ordination, and how, Leo the Great, LVI, 653. What sort of bishop should be elected, ibid. He should take no concern for household property upon himself, but devote himself to reading, prayer, and preaching, ibid., 655. How bishops should be honored, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 223. On prelacies seized for the sake of shameful gain, Radulfus Glaber, CXLII, 635. On staffs and rings conferred by secular hands, Humbert, CXLIII, 1148. Episcopal blessing given at Mass on Holy Saturday, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 154. On those who say that spiritual matters belong to bishops but temporal matters do not, Placidus, CLXIII, 685. A bishop’s table ought to be the same as that of poor clerics, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1261. Whether bishops may engage in secular business, princes’ courts, and military pursuits; what the apostles thought on this; and how unworthy it is for bishops to grant ecclesiastical property to soldiers, ibid., 1209. The example of St. Martin, who loved not soldiers and nobles but the poor and monks, ibid., 1226. What the pastoral staff signifies, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 110. What the two horns of the mitre signify, Peter Cantor. It is wrong for bishops to take care of nephews rather than of the poor, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 178. The transfer of an episcopal see belongs to the pope alone, Innocent III, CCXIV, LXXXVI.

**EPITAPHS.** The use of epitaphs among Christians is very ancient, St. Julian of Toledo, XCVI, 813. Various epitaphs for buried bishops, Venantius Fortunatus, LXXXVIII, 151 ff. See the Epigraphic Index.

**DESERT; HERMIT.** See *Anchorite*.

**EULOGIAE, OR BLESSED BREAD.** A *eulogia* is said to be made when bread sent for the sake of unity is received, Augustine, XXXIII, 100. By being received it is blessed, ibid., 103. *Eulogia*: bread, XLIII, 357. *Eulogiae* were customarily sent to friends, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 28, 29, 31. A *eulogia* is the bread blessed in church on the Lord’s Day and customarily distributed to the people, ibid., 781. What *eulogiae* are, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1168. The various meanings of *eulogia*, St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1223. What the use of *eulogiae* is, ibid., 1224. St. Rigobert, archbishop of Rheims, frequently sends *eulogiae* to Pippin, mayor of the royal household, as a blessing, Flodoard, CXXXV, 114. The people of Strasbourg fortified with *eulogiae* of bread and wine, Aimoin, CXXXIX, 819. Blessed bread, also called the crown of the offering, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 994.

**GOSPEL.** The authority of the Gospel, Tertullian, II, 363. What authors the evangelical instrument has, ibid., 367. The Gospel, God’s trumpet, ibid., 828. In the Law, slavery; in the Gospel, freedom, Ambrose, XVI, 1089. Reading of the Gospel in church, ibid., 1009, 1013. We fear the laws of emperors and despise the Gospels, Jerome, XXII, 533. Praise of the Gospels, ibid., 548. The Gospels must never be put down from one’s hands, ibid., 876. In the Gospel all good things are doubled, idem, XXIV, 566. The concise and perfect evangelical word, ibid., 140. There is nothing in the Gospels that does not shine, idem, XXV, 28. The Gospel is placed at the head when one is in pain, Augustine, XXXV, 1443. Greater trust should be placed in Greek copies of the Gospels, ibid., 1259. The derivation of “Gospel,” idem, XXXVI, 1417. One confidently believes that there is no discord among the Gospels until one understands it, idem, XXXVIII, 336. *Evangelium* in Latin means “good news” or “good announcement,” ibid., 266, 710. “I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church moved me,” Augustine said, XLII, 176. The opening of John’s Gospel, ibid., 1013, 1015. A certain Platonist said that the beginning of the Gospel according to John ought to be written in letters of gold [Col. 0626], idem, XLI, 301. In former times Christians customarily wore the Gospel suspended around the neck for aid and protection, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 483, 1318. On the canon of the Gospels, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 124. The Gospel reading is to be given to catechumens and penitents, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 468. What the two candles at the Gospel reading signify, Honorius of Autun, CLXXI, 550. The Gospel, the mirror of truth, flatters no one and deceives no one, Bernard, CLXXXIII, 337. Why it is read, ibid. What the Gospel teaches and what the Law teaches, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 672.

**PARTICULAR EXAMINATION.** “Attend to yourself, O soul, what enters into you and what goes out from you,” Ambrose, XIV, 262. “Attend to yourself lest an iniquitous word become hidden in your heart; for it creeps like poison and brings deadly evils,” ibid., 268. Examination of conscience, Augustine, XXXVIII, 110. Daily self-examination is commended, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 213, 323, 494, 513, 542.

**EXCOMMUNICATION.** One separated from Christ’s body is handed over to Satan, Ambrose, XVI, 489. One who has fallen grievously must be excluded from the sacraments, ibid., 490. One who sells dignities and honors, or wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful, is cast out of the temple, ibid., 1013. A subdeacon excommunicated by his presbyter, Augustine, XXXIII, 419. The excommunication of a sinner, idem, XXXV, 1732. The incontinent are excommunicated, idem, XXXVIII, 1094. It is merciful truth, idem, XL, 199. It is a remedy against certain grave sins, ibid., 228. One must not communicate with those cast out from the unity of the Church, Leo the Great, LIV, 468. Excommunication must not be imposed for trivial matters, ibid., 635.
