Nor at the discretion of an angry person, ibid. What its effects are, ibid., 795. Threatened excommunication, ibid., 1009. To whom excommunication belongs, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 553. What difference there is between excommunication and anathema, ibid., 590. It must be imposed after a second and third warning, ibid., 598. An unjust excommunication does not bind, ibid., 624. Whether the excommunications prescribed by canons and those imposed by pontiffs are the same, Peter Damian, CXLV, 265. No association is to be kept with excommunicated persons, ibid., 284. Why the excommunication of Roman pontiffs is to be feared, ibid., 580. Whether excommunication is good, and whether one unjustly excommunicated may resist, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 521–522. What must be considered in excommunication, idem, CLXXVII, 394–395. Excommunicated persons are not to be heard unless they repent, Bernard, CLXXXII, 505. Excommunication by abbots, ibid., 104–105. Who are excommunicated and anathematized, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 482. A person excommunicated by an inferior prelate cannot be absolved by a superior unless the case has been investigated, Peter Cantor, CCV, 437, note. By the same bishop
must be absolved by the person by whom he was excommunicated, ibid. On the absolution of Raymond, Count of Toulouse, excommunicated as a heretic and defender of heretics, Innocent III, CCXIV, 844. Likewise, the absolution of the consuls of Toulouse, ibid., 846. Of the Count of Foix, the Count of Comminges, and Gaston of Béarn, ibid., 847–848.

EXAMPLE. One makes greater progress through examples than through words: why this is so, Ambrose, XVI, 207. Of those virtues whose praise we admire, let us strive to attain their practice, ibid., 1215. Those who lead in the Church ought to offer themselves as an example to their followers, Augustine, XXXVI, 436. An example is to be taken not from the many, but from the few who are righteous, ibid., 437. An excuse for sinning is not to be drawn from the falls of great men, ibid., 539. Examples of saints inflame some and cast down others, ibid., XXXVII, 1812. Examples are desolating coals, 1600. By examples we are urged to conversion, 1600–1601. Bad examples do not excuse us while good ones are available, id., XXXIX, 1547. Reason is to be preferred to examples, id., XLI, 36. Examples move more powerfully than precepts, ibid., 53. A good example is beneficial, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 298. Christ commends heavenly things through earthly examples, ibid., 309, 331. God’s affection is made known through examples, ibid., 352. We are strengthened by example, ibid., 500. Singularity admits of no example, ibid., 628. Examples reinforce precepts, ibid., 636. To provide a good example is to benefit oneself and others, Leo the Great, LIV, 252. The fruits of a good example and the harms of a bad one, ibid. Examples are more powerful than words, ibid., 435. Examples of remarkable penitence, Peter Damian, CXLV, 346. An example of a pious man devoted to the canonical hours, ibid., 229. Good examples of the Emperor Constantine, Placidus, CLXIII, 639; likewise of Charlemagne, ibid., 641. The examples of saints are to be imitated, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 932. No counsel is better than example, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 45. Example is a living and effective discourse, ibid., 287. Teaching should be by example rather than by word, ibid., 1063. Two charges are laid upon prelates: word and example, CLXXXII, 370. One who corrupts others by a bad example is a persecutor of Christ, ibid., 362. How the soul considers examples both of the perfect and of the imperfect, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 411. How examples of the good, once considered, humble and inflame, ibid., 414. Examples of the Fathers are wood, Garner of St Victor, CXCIII, 332. Examples of the good are sparks, ibid., 359. Examples are to be taken from good persons, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 105. As much as a good prelate benefits by example, so much does an unlearned one harm by silence, ibid., 40, 172. The efficacy of a good example, Alan of Lille, CCX, 553.

EXERCISE should never be undertaken except for useful and salutary purposes, Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 349. The necessity of exercise, ibid., 515–516. Human life is always in flux through exercises and passes from one thing to another, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 483. On the threefold exercise of the active and contemplative life, ibid. Christ possessed skill in practice from the beginning, but grew, with the passage of time, into experiential knowledge, Richard of St Victor, CXCII, 653–654.

EXORCISM. Demons are driven away by exorcisms, Tertullian, I, 657. Formula of exorcism, author attributed to St Ambrose, XVII, 1019. How exorcists may be called teachers, ibid., 387. What exorcism is, Augustine, XXXII, 968. Exorcism among the rites of baptism, ibid. It is a most ancient rite, id., XLIV, 467. Diabolical power is exorcized in baptism, ibid., 426. It is a most ancient tradition of the Church, ibid., 467. The use of exorcisms in the Church, Leo the Great, LIV, 439. Who exorcists are, and what exorcism is, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 121; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 138, 424, 456–457.

WOMAN, WIFE. See the Index under Unlawful Pleasures.

LITTLE WINDOW. In the tombs of saints there were little windows for prayer, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 857.

FEAST. See Festal Days.

SON, and DAUGHTER, AND THEIR EDUCATION.—With what care Constantine the Great wished his children to be brought up in the fear of God, VIII, 84. Letter of St Hilary of Poitiers to Abra, his daughter, id., X, 549. Letter of St Jerome to Laeta, id., XXII, 867. To Gaudentius on the upbringing of his daughter Pacatula, ibid., 1095. Children do not always answer to their stock, id., XXII, 551. Examples of persons who bore the death of their children with great steadfastness, ibid., 592. The steadfastness of a son redounds to his father, ibid., 654. It is no small merit before God to educate children well, ibid., 728. To love belongs to children; to fear, to servants, ibid., 533. Nothing is so godly as for a holy mother to preserve a holy son, ibid., 1076. Children consecrated to God are the first-born offered under the Law, ibid., 870. How children and heirs are a cause of sorrow to fathers, id., XXIII, 278. Nothing is more painful than to lose an only son, XXIV, 726. Many holy parents have wicked children, and conversely, id., XXV, 169. The begetting of children is a benefit of God, Augustine, XLI, 440. To have children is no longer happiness; happiness is to have good children, id., XXXVII, 1686. That children are born to parents belongs to fruitfulness; that they live, to happiness; that they are rightly trained, to will and power, XL, 441. Who truly loves children, ibid., 702. He who destroys his children’s pleasures offers such a sacrifice as Abraham offered to God, ibid. A father does not give a sword to a weeping son, id., XXXVIII, 498; nor does he lift him onto a horse, 147, 498. What you preserve badly for your children will harm both you and them, ibid., 529. Children’s devotion toward their parents should not be for sale, ibid., 264. If someone’s son dies, he mourns him; if he sins, he does not mourn him—and yet we are Christians, id., XXXVI, 409. You have children: count one more, and give something to Christ, ibid., 424. Sermons on the Prodigal Son by Peter Chrysologus, LII, 183, 187, 190, 194, 197. Children seem to be limbs of their parents, Salvian, LIII, 70. After God, children are to be loved before all else by parents, ibid., 178. Children are offered to God by their parents, ibid., 209. Children are not to be provoked to anger, ibid., 178. A multitude of children incites parents to avarice, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 530. Good parents with wicked children, and conversely, will not benefit one another at the final judgment, id., LXXVI, 1164. Who the children of fools are, ibid., 161. Who are the children upon whom God visits the iniquities of the fathers, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 67 ff. The Prodigal Son allegorically interpreted, ibid., 820 ff. The difference among sons, hired servants, and slaves, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 551. The advancement of children is not to be hindered, CLXXXII, 519. Parents do not lose children who become religious, ibid., 253. It belongs to children to keep watch, but to servants to sleep and be lazy, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 247–248. Carnal parental affection is to be avoided, 209.

FRINGES. Fringes which had touched the tombs of saints were kept with great reverence, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1045.

WEEPING, TEARS. Divine forgiveness dries up every shower of tears, Tertullian, II, 880. Present tears are the reward of future things, Ambrose, XVI, 226. Weeping, ready for the demands of the eyes, wins mercy, lessens toil, relieves pain, and preserves modesty, ibid., 245. Let us wash away sins of the body with tears of penitence, ibid., 226. In tears are the wages of charity and the offices of piety, ibid., 245. Tears bestowed upon the dead as redemptive tears are beneficial to the living, ibid. Tears are the safeguards of the priest, ibid., 1008. They are signs of piety, not of that grief, ibid., 1293. Sorrow alone does not have tears: joy too has its own tears; piety arouses weeping, and prayer moistens the couch, ibid. Tears often nourish, and weeping lifts the mind, refreshes the breast, and consoles the sorrowful affection, ibid., 1372. Tears to be condemned and full of unbelief, Jerome, XXII, 472. In what respect we all deserve tears and sorrow, ibid. The greatness of weeping is compared to the waters of the Flood, ibid., 1042. What is fulfilled in one who weeps, ibid. In calamities, while we are oppressed by the more powerful, tears alone are permitted to us, id., XXIII, 1044. Why weeping is sweet to the wretched, Augustine, XXXII, 697. The bread of tears is eaten day and night, id., XXXVI, 467. The pious tears of fellow-sufferers are the new wine of those who love, ibid., 1064. The tears of those who pray are sweeter than the pleasures of theatres, id., XXXVII, 1683. Babylonian weeping, ibid., 1763. Many weep with Babylonian weeping because they rejoice with Babylonian joy, ibid. They weep as though not weeping who are not broken by adversity, ibid., 1917. Tears are witnesses of pain, id., XXXIX, 1536. They are the blood of the penitent, ibid., 1542. The tears of saints in this life, id., XLI, 683. What it means to weep without weeping, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 102. What it means to draw down streams of water from the eyes, ibid., 107. The tears of one mourning sins which he does not abandon are filthy, ibid., 109. With what zeal the grace of tears is to be sought, ibid., 300. We must mourn in this life, Venerable Rupert, CLXIX, 43. Varieties of weeping, and what is to be mourned, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 503. Christ is recorded to have wept, never to have laughed, Bernard, CLXXXIII, 50. Tears are seeds of righteousness, 972. The tears of penitents are the wine of angels, ibid., 935. Tears and prayers were the weapons of St Bernard, CLXXXII, 258. How unlike the tears of the infant Christ were to the tears of other infants, ibid., 124. The cause of our weeping and what it ought to be, Richard of St Victor, 355. Tears are to be moderated, Alan of Lille, CCX, 137.

ANT. Source of the proverbial saying: “It is unbecoming for an ant to draw a wagon,” Geoffrey, CLVII, 157.

FORTITUDE. Men courageous under tortures were honored with statues, images, and inscriptions, Tertullian, I, 534. What fortitude is, Lactantius, VI, 379. The fortitude of Christians, ibid., 594. It conquers evils, ibid., 754. Fortitude without justice is the material of iniquity, Ambrose, XVI, 75. Fortitude is so called when each person conquers himself, ibid., 76. The fortitude of the Christian athlete, ibid. He ought to contend against every vice, ibid., 79. It belongs to a brave man to provide for future things, ibid. Fortitude is tested not only by prosperity but also by adversity, ibid., 82. It possesses a certain force of fierce virtue and contempt for death, ibid., 295. Examples of fortitude to be imitated, Jerome, XXII, 820. Let us raise up the mind when oppressed and fallen, through fortitude, ibid., 811. Fortitude always has rivals openly before it, id., XXIII, 935. Christian fortitude arises from hunger and thirst for righteousness, Augustine, XXXV, 1257. It is a vice when appropriated for pride, id., XXXVI, 427. All fortitude lies in humility, id., XXXVII, 1184. If it is human and not God’s, it is hardness, ibid., 1388. The source of our fortitude, ibid., 1797. The fortitude of Christ’s soldiers against the devil, id., XLI, 671. The fiercer the onset of war, the greater the glory of not yielding, ibid., 678. A brave man is not disturbed by evils, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 332. The brave soldier issues a challenge openly before all spectators, ibid., 472. Adversities do not cast down the brave, ibid., 541. The sweat of the strong is overcome by the tears of little children, ibid., 554. Fortitude is from God, St Prosper, LI, 679. In God are fortitude and praise, lest we fall, ibid., 334. True strength of spirit is shown in troubles, ibid., 435. The fortitude of the Gentiles is desire; that of Christians is charity, which is from God, 472. Bodily strength is to be disregarded, Salvian, LII, 34. Solid fortitude, which no disturbance arising from inequalities can shake, belongs to few, Leo the Great, LIV, 283. Who are truly called brave, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 673. Fortitude is shown in adversity, ibid., 697. What the fortitude of the righteous is, ibid., 778. Those who suffer with the weak become stronger, ibid., 775. In what the fortitude of the reprobate consists, ibid., 778. Fortitude needs the gift of counsel, id., LXXVI, 1017. What fortitude is, Alcuin, CI, 637, 944. What true fortitude is, ibid., 640. The fortitude of wisdom in every respect, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 189. Fortitude and its companions, CLXXVI, 1003. Fortitude without prudence is rashness, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 737. Fortitude is necessary to justice and temperance, ibid. It lies between pleasure and necessity, ibid. He is not a strong man whose courage does not grow through difficulty, ibid., 463. Examples of courageous spirit written in the Law, Wolbero, CXCV, 1052. What temptations are that exercise our fortitude, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 392. It belongs to fortitude patiently to endure adversities, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 316. What difference there is between fortitude and patience, ibid., 306. Magnanimity is the mother of fortitude, ibid., 316. Fortitude is the companion of penitence, ibid., 350.

FORTUNE. Worshipped by pagans as a goddess, Lactantius, VI, 437. Attacked by grave accusations, ibid. In itself it is nothing, ibid., 440. The difference between fortune and nature, ibid., 441. The unjust declamations of the Gentiles against her, ibid., 582. Those who maintain that everything came into existence by chance are refuted, Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 427. Those who teach that everything is governed by chance motions are refuted, ibid., 411. Some wrongly judge that everything happens by chance and that varying fortune plays in human affairs, Jerome, XXIII, 1083. What it means to prepare Fortune’s table, id., XXIV, 639. What fortune is, Augustine, XXXIV, 571. It is not any divine power, ibid. Why it was thought a goddess although it can be evil, id., XLI, 126. Fortune distributes her gifts indiscriminately to each person, ibid., 197. Why she is called blind, id., XLII, 374. Nothing is accidental; all things serve God’s laws, St Prosper, LI, 422. The inconstancy of fortune, Alcuin, CI, 807–808. God forbids the talent of fortune to be lent at interest, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 136. Pride arises from fortune’s gifts, ibid., 47. Fortune’s adversities are to be borne with equanimity, Alan of Lille, CCX, 138. One must yield to fortune, 584.

FORUM. The forum is to be shunned, and the streets likewise, Ambrose, XVI, 279.

BROTHER, BROTHERHOOD. Christians called one another brothers and loved one another sincerely, Tertullian, I, 471. Through charity they held all things in common except wives, ibid., 472. Brotherhood broken, Cyprian, IV, 333. Charity is the bond of brotherhood, 631. One must not defraud a brother, ibid., 773. Kings customarily call one another brothers, Lactantius, VII, 302, 484. How Christians were brothers and equals among themselves, id., VI, 599. All Christians are brothers, Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 1049. Where true fraternal unity is found, how good and delightful it is, ibid., 745. Even those who inflict the gravest wrongs upon churches are called brothers, id., X, 557. All those are brothers whom one spiritual birth has made, though their actions differ, Optatus, XI, 963. The name “brother” applies to schismatics, and why, ibid., 1029. Brothers are those whom one mother, the Church, has borne from the same womb, ibid. On this name among Christians, ibid., 1135. We are all brothers, born of one and the same mother, Ambrose, XIV, 405. By a certain right of kinship we are all joined together as brothers and ought to love one another as children of the same womb, ibid., 466. Among brothers, an inheritance ought to be divided not by a judge as intermediary but by piety as mediator, id., XV, 1730. Great is the increase of fraternal love, and not mean the lot of nature, which the growth of virtue enriches, id., XVI, 1316. Envy and boasting commonly empty in many persons the claims of fraternal devotion, ibid., 1268. Why they are called brothers, id., XVII, 54. Who are called brothers, ibid., 186. He insults who does not grieve with his brother, ibid., 280. Those who sow discord among brothers are poisoners, ibid., 940. In Scripture “brothers” is used in four senses, Jerome, XXIII, 197. We are all brothers in two ways, ibid., 198. Whoever does not forgive the sins of brothers is more righteous than is righteous, 1066. Every human being is a brother, Augustine, XXXIII, 95. What does the man who cannot bear his brother bear? ibid., 188. How we prove that we do not love brotherhood, id., XXXV, 1992. We are all brothers through the hope of a heavenly inheritance and neighbors through the condition of earthly birth, id., XXXVI, 189. All baptized persons are our brothers, ibid., 299. He who says to God, “Our Father,” says to Christ, “Our Brother,” ibid., 549. A brother is precisely the one whom, if a man does not redeem him, who will redeem him? ibid. His master does not disdain to have his slave as brother, since the Lord Christ chose to have him as brother, id., XXXVIII, 393. Under the heavenly Father, master and slave are brothers, ibid., 400. The persecution of false brothers is harsher than that of enemies, id., XXXVI, 638–639. False brothers within unity are to be tolerated, id., XLIII, 311. Sermon on fraternal concord, id., XXXVIII, 119. Brothers preserving concord while dividing a great paternal estate are praise of their father’s training, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 60. Fellowship of brotherhood begins from apostolic times, Agobard, CIV, 245. Fraternal meetings are reproved, ibid., 255. Bishops call one another brothers, ibid., 297. Brothers are named in Scripture in four ways, Alcuin, CI, 1335. Who is a fratricide, ibid., 1195. Religious call one another brothers, Hugh of St Victor, XVI, 1052 ff. Mutual love of brothers, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 878. We owe brothers counsel and assistance, ibid., 45. We are called brothers by charity, id., CLXXXII, 400. Brotherhoods among Cistercian monks, ibid., 150. Whom the Apostle calls brothers, Peter Lombard, CXI, 1321. Fraternal correction is a form of mercy, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 284. The fratricide’s words were: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” ibid.

FOREHEAD. Christians marked the cross upon their forehead, Tertullian, II, 80; Lactantius, VI, 670; St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 386. A wandering person is reproved by the contraction of the forehead and sadness of countenance, Jerome, XXII, 897. The forehead is the praise of our modesty, Augustine, XXXVII, 1839. Whoever has no forehead is shameless, ibid. There is a forehead on the face, and there is a forehead in the conscience, id., XXXVIII, 630. The forehead marked with the cross before battle, Prudentius, LX, 236. What a hardened forehead signifies, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 892.

TREASURY. The treasury is God’s chest, in which were collected things sent to relieve the need of God’s servants, Augustine, XXXVI, 765. Christ’s treasury is the hand of the poor person, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 210. What the treasury is, Alcuin, C, 860. Treasuries adjoin the Temple, ibid. Mystically, the treasury is called Christ, ibid.

GENUFLECTION. Christians were not permitted to bend the knee on the Lord’s Day or from Easter to Pentecost, Tertullian, II, 79. Some did not bend the knee on Sabbaths, id., I, 1191. He touches Christ and entreats Christ who extends his knees before the brethren, ibid., 1245. To bend the knee is a sign of earnest and most humble prayer, Jerome, XXII, 784. Concern of soul frequently prompts the bending of knees, ibid., 1119. The custom of praying with the knee placed on the ground, id., XXVI, 486. The elders decreed that one should not bend the knee on the Lord’s Day, Cassian, XLIX, 110. Why this is so, ibid. Why knees are not bent during Eastertide, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 371. A cenobite who, by bending his knees, hollowed out in his cell a stone slab more than four fingers deep, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV, 214. Penitents bent the knee daily, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIX, 46. Why genuflection is not made on Good Friday during the prayer for the Jews, Alcuin, CI, 1210.

HABIT is understood in many ways, Augustine, XI, 84. What it is, ibid., 396. The mode or manner of life in which anyone follows the faith does not pertain to the City of God, id., XLI, 647. Proper arrangement of one’s bearing, Alan of Lille, CCX, 552. Among medieval authors *habitus* is commonly used for clothing; see the Index under Unlawful Pleasures, “On Bodily Adornment.”

HERETIC. Heretics arose from the seed of philosophers, Tertullian, I, 519. The same matter is debated among both, id., II, 19. Etymology of “heresy,” ibid., 18. St Paul counts it among works of the flesh, ibid. Among heretics the passion for argument flourishes, ibid., 780. They provoke the pious to rhetoric and philosophy, ibid., 801. What is distinctive of heretics, ibid., 179. What their manner of life is, ibid., 56. How great an evil heresy is, Ambrose, XVI, 538, 821. Every sin concerns individuals, but that of heretics and schismatics concerns all, ibid., 503. Heresy is defended more ardently by heretics than it is attacked by Catholics, Jerome, XXII, 755. Heresy promises uncertain and great things, while taking away certain and moderate ones, ibid., 687. It easily deceives simple souls, id., XXIII, 166. Heretics belong not to Christ but to the devil, ibid., 169. Their cunning, ibid., 379; and their shamelessness, ibid., 1073. How heresies benefit the Church, Augustine, XXXII, 716. Who is to be judged a heretic, id., XXXIII, 160. It is exceedingly difficult to define what heresy is, ibid., 999. There would be no heretics if there were no pride, id., XXXIV, 142. They are compared to the serpent, ibid. Why they are excluded from Catholic communion, ibid., 127. They pursue contention rather than correction, ibid., 837. Gentleness is to be shown them, id., XXXIX, 1584. They do not belong to the Church, id., XL, 193. They may possess many gifts, but cannot possess charity, ibid., 137. Fasting is of no benefit to them, ibid., 711. How they are to be received into the Church if they return, id., XXXVIII, 1358; XLIII, 175. What warnings should be given to heretics, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 73. From precepts of peace they make discord, ibid. Their persecution and malice toward the Church, ibid., 559. They are to be restrained by priests through vigor and reason, ibid., 731. The cause of heretical depravity, Alcuin, CI, 129. Those wishing to gather a church without the Lord labor in vain, id., C, 628. They enter not by the door but from elsewhere, ibid., 884. The pride of heretics, ibid., 633; and their rashness in expounding Scripture, CI, 285. Heretics are to be avoided like vipers and a bad tree, Humbert, CXLIII, 1074–1075. How heretics open their mouths against the Church, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 302. The darkness of heretics, ibid., 339. Who should be called a heretic, ibid., 533. Bernard calls heresies absurdities, CLXXXII, 540. It belongs to the Supreme Pontiff to extinguish them, id., CLXXXIII, 1093. Heretics are crafty and hypocritical, ibid., 1091. Their obstinacy, ibid., 1100. They themselves are to be bound and cast into chains lest they infect others with poison, ibid., 1086–1087. The evil pastures of heretics, ibid., 935. Their society is to be avoided, id., CLXXXII, 363. Who is a heretic, Peter of Cluny, CXCI, 1037. They exercise the Church, ibid. How they benefit it, ibid. Their always restless boldness, ibid., 375. Saints Augustine and Hilary of Poitiers are called hammers of heretics, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 26.

HERBS. Little herbs plucked from the tombs of saints and kept with reverence, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1035.

JERUSALEM. In Augustine’s time Jerusalem was full of Christian praisers and had no Jew, Augustine, XXXVI, 759, 773. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” It is an image of the heavenly Church of Christ, id., 122; XXXVII, 1952. Why it is called the Holy City, id., XLI, 438. Christians make pilgrimage to it from every quarter, Alberic, CLXVI, 392; Baldric, CLXVI, 1065. Itinerary to Jerusalem, author attributed to William of Malmesbury, CLXXX, 1318. Charlemagne built lodging there for the benefit of pilgrims, ibid. How many pilgrims sought Jerusalem near the end of the twelfth century, William of Tyre, CCI, 226. The so-called Peter the Hermit, 227. What Pope Urban II did to free Palestine from the tyranny of the Turks, ibid., 231. Christians marked with the cross from the whole West, ibid. Peoples rush to arms under the leadership of Godfrey, id., 259. Description of the city of Jerusalem, ibid., 405. How the faithful were expelled thence by pagans, ibid., 401. It is besieged and captured by those marked with the cross, ibid.

CANONICAL HOURS. Days and nights are divided by intervals of hours, Cyprian, IV, 786. Under the Law, Daniel with the three youths, in the celebration of prayers, observed the third, sixth, and ninth hours according to the mystery of the Holy Trinity, ibid., 541. Worshippers of God, long ago spiritually determining the intervals of the hours, observed fixed and lawful times for prayer, ibid. No hour is excepted for Christians in which God ought not to be worshipped often and always, ibid., 542. We ought to have prayer-hours thus divided, so that, if we happen to be occupied with some work, the time itself may remind us of the office. No one is ignorant of the third, sixth, and ninth hour, dawn also and evening, Jerome, XXII, 421. The holy Doctor likewise wishes a consecrated woman, following her teacher’s example, to grow accustomed to rise at night for prayers and psalms; to sing hymns in the morning; at the third, sixth, and ninth hour to stand in battle-line as a warrior of Christ; and, when the lamp is lit, to offer the evening sacrifice, ibid., 875. In Jerome’s time no nun was permitted to sit after the Alleluia had been sung. But the one who arrived first, or among the first, urged them on to work. In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hour, in the evening, and at midnight, they sang the Psalter in order, ibid., 896. We pray with words at fixed intervals of time, Augustine, XXXIII, 506. What it is to sing psalms, id., XXXVI, 787. The singing of psalms in church, id., XXXII, 800; XXXIV, 45. Celebrated throughout the Christian world, id., XXXII, 766. Psalms were sung by the people standing, id., XXXVI, 384. When the singing of psalms was introduced at Milan, id., XXXII, 769. What it is to sing hymns, id., XXXVI, 320. The singing of hymns in churches, ibid., 914; XXXVII, 1947–1948. Assembly at the third, sixth, and ninth hour, id., XXXIX, 2019. Apocryphal: he who does not withdraw himself from the church gathering during the six hours gains profit, ibid., 2079. Apocryphal: the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours at which the householder sent laborers into his vineyard are interpreted allegorically, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1534–1535. Canonical hours recited before a sick person, id., LXXVII, 537 note. Varieties of canonical hours, ibid., 558. On the offices of the third, sixth, and ninth hours, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 757. On Vespers and Compline, ibid., 758. On Matins, ibid., 760. On Lauds, ibid., 750. On the antiquity of Vigils, ibid., 759. On choirs, canticles, and psalms, ibid., 741–742. On hymns, antiphons, responsories, and readings, ibid., 743–744. Mozarabic Breviary arranged, or at least enlarged, by Isidore, id., LXXXVI throughout. Offices of the third, sixth, and ninth hours, Alcuin, CI, 509, 1274. Evening hours and Compline, ibid., 1274. On Matins and their antiquity, ibid., 1275. Use of the canonical hours, St Bruno, CLII, 1310. On canonical hours, Venerable Rupert, CLXX, 13 ff.; Honorius of Autun, ibid. The offices of the canonical hours, their order and explanation, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 340 ff. Prime, ibid., 407–408. Terce, Sext, and None, ibid., 410, 873. Vespers, Matins, and Compline, ibid., 874. The divine office is called the work of God, Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1011. How one must attend the divine office, ibid. What ought to be read or sung in divine offices, id., CLXXXII, 609. Those who pursue gain and glory in performing the offices undermine the foundations of the commonwealth, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 95. A hireling is one who praises God for something other than God himself, ibid., 98. The double morning hymns on the feast of St Stephen move the spirits of clerics, ibid.

HOSPITAL. See the guesthouse (*xenodochium*).

HOSPITALITY. The token of hospitality among Christians, Tertullian, I, 1295; II, 31. It is a public form of humanity, Ambrose, XVI, 131. In duties of hospitality, humanity must indeed be shown to all, but more abundant honor is to be paid to the righteous, ibid., 132. The commandment of hospitality is to be observed, ibid., 235. Hospitality is to be loved, and why, ibid., 1217. Commendation and duties of hospitality, Jerome, XXIII, 469. What is to be feared in rejecting guests, ibid. Let us invite guests not with casual speech or merely with the lips, but receive them with the whole ardor of the mind, id., XXII, 1080. They offer themselves with our profit, ibid. In receiving unknown guests, it is far better to admit a bad person than, while guarding against receiving the bad, to exclude a good one, Augustine, ibid., 153. Among many there is a custom of washing guests’ feet, id., XXXV, 1794. At times the patriarchs unknowingly received angels, id., XXXVII, 615. Hospitality commended, ibid., 506, 642, 967, 1118, 1121, 1127. We are all guests here, ibid., 643. Duties of hospitality, John Cassian, XLIX, 1189, 1311. Hospitality is to be shown even to idle persons, ibid., 381. Christ himself is received in the guest, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 309 ff. Zacchaeus, having received Christ as guest, obtained salvation and the episcopate, ibid., 351. Chrysologus himself, once a guest and pilgrim, commended peace to his people, ibid., 572. How those who violate hospitality are to be punished, ibid., 333. The laws and properties of Christian hospitality set forth, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 483. Hospitality is commended by Abraham’s example, when he begged three men to turn aside to his tent, ibid., 725. In former times care for guests lay upon the faithful, especially bishops, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1085, 1145, 1184, 1313. A guest, upon arriving, asks a blessing from his host, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 214. How guests are to be received, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1215. How great a good hospitality is, Alcuin, C, 541. Guests are not to be avoided, ibid., 542. On the care of guests and pilgrims, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 776. On receiving guests, Guido, CL, 1278. On the same subject, Guigo the Carthusian, CLIII, 711. Those who receive guests are rewarded greatly, Rupert, abbot, CLXXVIII, 1504. What the reception of guests is, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 796. On hospitality to be cultivated by clerics, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 221. Hospitality is an outstanding grace among all virtues, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 324. On the practice of hospitality, Peter of Rheims, CCVI, 98; Alan of Lille, CCX, 181.

HYMN. A hymn is specially addressed to God, Ambrose, XVI, 89. They say that the people are deceived by the songs of my hymns; indeed, I do not deny even this, ibid., 1008. What a hymn is, Jerome, XXVI, 528. The singing of hymns at the altar instituted at Carthage, Augustine, XXXII, 634. It was attacked by Hilary and defended by Augustine, ibid. The singing of hymns flourishes in churches, id., XXXVI, 487. A hymn is a song containing the praise of God, ibid., 914. It must contain three things: praise, praise of God, and song, id., XXXVII, 1947–1948. A hymn is a song by which God is praised, St Prosper, LI, 423. All saints use this, ibid. Various hymns of Prudentius enumerated, LIX, 667 ff. Hymns at funerals, St Prudentius, id., 879–880. Hymns of martyrs at Vespers, ibid., 825. The hymnary of Thomasius, one part for the seasons (*de tempore*) and another for the saints (*de sanctis*), ibid., 578. What a *lucernarium* is, ibid., 678. It requires correction, ibid., 786 note. Hispanic hymnody corrected by Prudentius, ibid., 677–678, 747. *Hymnia*, *Hymnista*, *Hymnice*, ibid., 749; LX, 292 note. Exposition of hymns, id., LIX, 547. The very ancient custom of singing hymns, ibid., 773 note. Evening hymn of Ennodius, LXIII, 326. Various hymns by the same author in honor of saints, ibid., 927 ff. Hymns composed by St Gregory the Great, id., LXXVIII, 849 ff. On the hymns of the office of St Isidore of Seville, LXXXI, 87–88. Other hymns attributed to St Isidore, ibid., 573. Whether Sisebut was the author of the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”), ibid., 895–896. Decision of the Fourth Council of Toledo on the singing of hymns, id., LXXXIV, 370. What a hymn is, id., LXXXII, 253. On hymns, id., LXXXIII, 743. Hymns of the Mozarabic Breviary: see vol. CLXXXVI throughout. Preface of Jodocus Metzler to the sacred hymns of the Fathers of St Gall, id., LXXXVII, 27. In Greek, *hymnus* means “praise”; in Latin, “song,” Alcuin, C, 429. Why the hymn was omitted by the Apostles after supper, ibid. Fortunatus’s hymn, *Pange, lingua, [lacuna] praelium certaminis* (“Sing, O tongue, [lacuna] the battle of the contest”), on Christ’s birth and cross, id., CI, 562. The hymn of Blessed Sedulius, *A solis ortus cardine* (“From the quarter where the sun rises”), ibid., 609. The *Te Deum* (“We praise you, God”) hymn, ibid., 597. A most beautiful hymn on the work of the six days, C, 407. Praise of the hymn of the Three Children, id., CI, 485. Pope Gelasius composed many hymns, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 415. Various hymns composed by the most pious King Robert, CXLI, 939, 945. Hymns composed by holy men are to be sung in church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 468. On composers of hymns, Notker the Stammerer, CXXXI, 1000. Notker’s book of sequences, or hymns, ibid., 1005. Morning hymns, Regino, CXXXIII, 224. Four hymns of St Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 513. A hymn for the feast of All Saints, criticized by someone, is defended, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 262. Hymns of the office of Emperor St Henry, CXL, 181 ff. The angelic hymn *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) is sung because of the peace made by Christ, Blessed Rupert, CLXX, 27. Why this same hymn is sung at the chrism, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 565. It was composed by Hilary of Poitiers, 766–767. Pope Telesphorus instituted its singing at Mass, ibid. Why the priest sings it facing east, 767. The angelic hymn sung in Mass, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 420. Hymn and canticle teach us to praise God and rejoice in eternal things, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 213.

IDOL-SACRIFICES. Christians abstained from idol-sacrifices, that is, meats offered upon the altars of idols, Lactantius, VI, 363.

ILLUSION. On the deceptive character of certain signs, Agobard, CIV, 179. Whether garments should be washed because of a nocturnal pollution, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 891. Whether a deacon who has suffered it ought to celebrate, 1111.

SACRED IMAGES. The use of images was not condemned by Tertullian, I, 667. An image of the Good Shepherd depicted on a sacred chalice, id., II, 1000. Pagans vainly seek an image or likeness of God in the church at Nicomedia, Lactantius, VII, 317. The use of images was unknown to Christians from the beginning, ibid. A certain image hung in a church is torn down by Epiphanius, Jerome, XXII, 526. A painting representing Stephen’s stoning and Saul’s conversion, Augustine, XXXVII, 1434. Images in the church of St Felix of Nola, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 667. Origin of images upon altars, LX, 400 note. Image
carved image of the Galilean banquet, at the head of the church, ibid., 104. Images of the Lord and of certain saints are found at Rome, id., LIX, 667. Sacred vessels adorned with images, 860. Images of saints in ancient tombs, id., LX, 90. Image of Christ’s tomb on an ancient coin, ibid., 165. Ancient images of Christ, ibid. An image of the Blessed Virgin Mary holding Jesus, displayed in a church, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 715. An image of Christ to be treated with honor, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 517. An image of the Lord is honored in a certain monastery, ibid., 628. Saint Euphrasia kisses an image of Christ, ibid. An image of the Blessed Virgin Mary before the church of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the time of Mary of Egypt, ibid., 682. A candle lighted before an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary is miraculously diminished, ibid., 907. An image of the Blessed Mary and the infant Jesus venerated by John, id., LXXIV, 211. Saint Augustine the monk, travelling to England with his companions, carries as a standard an image of the Savior hanging upon the cross, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 370. What Saint Gregory’s view concerning the veneration of images was, ibid., 418. What veneration of images he rejected, ibid., 419. Legitimate use of images, id., LXXVII, 900, 901, 1027. Images of saints are neither to be broken nor worshipped, ibid., 1027, 1128. Various synods held concerning the veneration of images, ibid., 1027 note. The teaching of Saint Gregory concerning images defended, ibid., 1128, 1129. How even the emperors’ own portraits are received at Rome, ibid., 1850. The veneration of images, though attacked, defended, Pope Gregory II, LXXXIX, 476, 477 note. On sacred images, Agobard, CIV, 199. On the veneration of images, Jonas, CVI, 307, 343, 365. On images and paintings, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 927. Image of the Savior seated upon a chair, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1514. A silver image of the same, ibid., 1515. Golden images, id., CXXVIII, 226, 895, 1027, 1154, 1195, 1226, 1261, 1263. Silver images, 453, 1026, 1138, 1185, 1187, 1210, 1221, 1227, 1262, 1265, 1269, 1311. The veneration of images, impiously abolished by the emperor, defended by the orthodox, ibid., 979. Image of Blessed Peter, ibid., 226, 895, 1226. Images of the gracious Virgin Mary, ibid., 1027, 1267, 1285. The archetypal image of the Savior, ibid., 1087. Sacred images, ibid., 1138. Image of the Blessed Mary at the Martyrs, ibid., 1154. Images of angels, ibid., 1186. Image of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, ibid., 1195. Images of Saint Paul, ibid., 1211, 1219. Painting, or depiction, of the Greater Litany, ibid., 1220. Paintings in churches formerly prohibited for fear of idolatry, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 417. How images of Christ or the saints are to be venerated, Flodoard, CXXXV, 260. On the image of the Savior on the cross, Gerard, CXLII, 1306. The death of a certain Jew because of his dreadful profanation of an image of Christ, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 105. Veneration of sacred images, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 206, 294, 287. On the veneration of painted images of the Blessed Mary, Saint Bruno, CLXIV, 859. Veneration to be shown to images, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1590. Vain paintings to be banished from cloisters, Saint Bernard, CLXXXII, 913. Which image ought to be venerated, Peter Lombard, CXCIII, 263. How churches are customarily adorned with paintings, and what the purpose of these images is to be, Sicard, CCXIII, 40 ff.

IMITATION. What things we ought to praise and imitate, Saint Augustine, XXXIII, 201. He vainly praises the good deeds of others who does not imitate them, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 62. It is utterly shameful not to imitate what we are, 63. Among human beings, it is a fault, and before God a punishment, to refuse to imitate the good that pleases one, 800. See *Example*.

IMMUNITY. Immunity of clerics, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 520, 802, 1296. On the privilege and right of the priesthood, Saint Agobard of Lyons, LIV, 127. On the immunities of churches, Regino, CXXXII, 195. On the same subject, Saint Odo of Canterbury, CXXXIII, 947. Gregory VII received the Cluniac monks under Roman protection and immunity, CXLVIII, 665. The same pontiff confirms for the cloister of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon the liberty and immunity from every harassment granted by King Robert I, 686. See Ivo of Chartres, *On the Dignity of Bishops and Priests*, CLXI, 437. He who does not have the power to condemn an accused person, or cannot establish the charge, is exempt, CLXII, 143. The immunity of the cloister of Chartres is to be adjudicated against the clerics of the same church, ibid. On a certain presbyter whose imprudent act had caused the death of a boy, and who is therefore not to be judged exempt from trial, ibid., 205. The liberties and immunities of churches, from Saint Isidore, concern bishops, ibid., 208. A rebellious monk cannot claim for himself, against his superior, his own immunity or liberty, Saint Bernard, CLXXXII, 419. On the privileges and liberties of churches, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1326 ff. Ecclesiastical immunity, Alan of Lille, CCX, 397.

PRISONERS. Formerly treated better on Sunday, Paulinus of Nola, XCIX, 336.

INCENSE, FRANKINCENSE. Christians burned incense, but not in the same manner as pagans, Tertullian, II, 90. They used incense in tombs, id., 493. Sabaean frankincense more valuable than other kinds, ibid. Frankincense originates among the Sabaeans, Jerome, XXIII, 953. Frankincense as a symbol of spiritual incense, id., XXV, 1303. Prudentius calls the pagans the “incense-bearing flock,” LIX, 948. Martyrs reject incense and incense-burners belonging to idols, id., LX, 349, 350, 381. Golden and silver censers then found in Roman churches, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1209, 1231, 1236, 1237, 1265, etc. What frankincense is and whence it originates, Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 620. By frankincense the Magi signified that Jesus is God, id., LXXXIII, 117. What the censer signifies in the Mass, Alcuin, CI, 1214. On incense, Rupert, CLXX, 27. Form and ministry of the censer, Peter the Chanter, CCV. Censing among the offices, Sicard, CCXIII, 107, and passim.

INDULGENCE, or remission of punishment: the kind granted for one year by Alexander III to those who maintained the peace made between the monastery of Cluny and the Count of Forez, CC, 249. Whether indulgences granted by bishops are valid, Alan of Lille, CCX, 387. The use of indulgences in the Church, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1075.

SACRED VESTMENTS, SACRED CLOTHING. What priests’ vestments signify, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 31. Sacred vestments to be used only in church, Alcuin, CI, 1242. What they are, ibid. Worn-out sacred vestments are to be burned, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 174. On sacred vestments, Sicard, CCXIII, 72. On vesting the ministers, 84. How many and what are the sacred garments of the new priesthood, Hugh of Saint Victor, CLXXVI, 437 ff.

INFANT, CHILD. Christians were slanderously said by the pagans to be infanticides, Tertullian, I, 306. In Africa pagan parents sacrificed their children to Saturn when they displeased them, down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, ibid., 314. Parents even caressed them lest they be slaughtered weeping, ibid., 316. Pagans very often abandoned them to cold, hunger, and even dogs, ibid., 318, 326. An infant is a human being, and one who will become such, ibid., 320. Newly born children were handed over by King Psammetichus to a nurse whose tongue had been cut out, ibid., 570. Pagans sometimes devoured them when cooked beforehand, ibid., 580. Infancy is naturally spirited and affectionate, id., II, 682. Why infants weep upon entering life, ibid. The movements of the soul of an infant existing immediately from the mother’s womb are described, ibid. Infants killed in their mothers’ wombs in order to safeguard the mother’s life, ibid., 691. How they were extracted, ibid. Whether infants dream, ibid., 733. Obstacles to a child’s birth, ibid., 758. Sometimes overcome in the womb by their mothers, ibid., 909. Exposure of children, id., I, 325. Pagans sometimes sexually violated exposed children, ibid. Children’s lessons, ibid., 575. Children perceive and understand, id., II, 683. Infants are capable of baptism immediately from birth, Lactantius, VI, 754. If they are either killed or exposed, ibid., 578, 708. At the first moment of their birth infants do nothing but pray, Jerome, XXII, 485. Children should learn to read through play, ibid., 837. How they should learn to form letters, ibid. The salvation of older children is a greater gain, ibid., 873. Infancy does not know the difference between evil and good, ibid. A child with a tender hand strikes its laughing mother, ibid., 1096. Let him love what he is compelled to learn, so that it is not work but delight, ibid. Infancy itself is already liable to sins, Augustine, XXXII, 665, 666. Consecrations of infants, ibid., 1080. At what bodily size infants will rise again, id., XLI, 776. An infant of one day is not free from sin—not because of what it has committed, but because of what it has contracted—id., XXXVIII, 928. Infants themselves need a Redeemer and baptism, ibid., 1333. A newborn child cries because it enters into this life, id., XXXVII, 1664. By crying at birth, the child is a prophet of its own misery, id., XXXVIII, 909. Childhood is not yet capable of commandment, id., XLI, 730. Baptized infants dying in infancy itself enter the kingdom of heaven, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 349. Not all little children who can speak are saved, ibid. The entrance to that same heavenly kingdom is shut by parents against some little children if they are badly reared, ibid. Thus a five-year-old child accustomed to blaspheme, whose father did not correct him, is handed over to the devil, ibid., 349. Why infants formerly often died without baptism, ibid., 484. How infants are to be taught, ibid., 879. The words of those who nurse infants are milk if good, poison if bad, ibid. On the religious education of children, Jonas, CVI, 134. On the oppression of infants, punished by the Church, Regino, CXXXII, 297. On the adoption of infants abandoned at the door of a church, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1107. On little children, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 203. On children offered to a monastery, ibid., 400 note. When these children became adults, they confirmed their own offering, ibid. How children are to be offered to a monastery, Guido, CL, 1264. On children’s confession, ibid., 1271. How children ought to go to church, Guichard, CXCIX, 1102. On the correction of children, ibid., 1107. On avoiding their laughter in choir, ibid., 1111. See above, *Son*.

SICK PERSONS. See *Sick*.

INFULA. Honorary fillets, Cyprian, IV, 220. What it is, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, note 5. Difference between the *infula* and the *vitta*, LX, 269. An *infula* is a white band for a priestly head, in the form of a diadem and bound with fillets, Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 693.

INQUISITION. Here is asserted the Church’s right to investigate enemies who openly or secretly oppose her, corrupting both faith and morals; to overcome them; and, relying on divine and human laws, to compel them either to silence or to salutary return. For heretics everything is free and unrestrained, Tertullian, II, 58. They do not know respect for their leaders, ibid., 57. It is fitting that they be compelled to their duty, not merely persuaded, ibid., 125. In a disputation with heretics there is no victory, or only an uncertain one, ibid., 31. No evil deed is without fear, because none is without its own consciousness, id., II, 401. Wrongdoers are eager to hide; when discovered they tremble, when accused they deny, and they attribute their crime to the stars or to fate, id., I, 267. Christians are recognizable only from the amendment of their former vices, id., I, 701. What the conduct of heretics is, id., II, 56. Excommunication is separation from participation in prayer, assembly, and every holy communion, id., I, 469, 677, 1292. Dealings with the wicked forbidden, Cyprian, III, 829. The Catholic Church is one and true, ibid., 1037. In the Church there are wheat and tares, id., IV, 344. “I grieved intensely and was grievously distressed because I could not communicate with those whom I had once begun to love,” ibid. The obstinacy of the wicked must be restrained, id., III, 712. The agreement of all churches in condemning Novatian and deciding the case of the lapsed, ibid., 994, 1033. The venerable authority of all churches, ibid., 1184. All power and grace are established in the Church, ibid., 1161. Excessive indulgence is a kind of persecution, id., IV, 479. He compounds the offense who is angry with a priest healing a wound, ibid., 484. Firmness toward the wicked, gentleness toward repentant lapsed persons, id., III, 712. Heretics are not to be greeted with “Hail,” ibid., 1072. Heresy is a plague, ibid., 1134. Wolves separate sheep from the shepherd, id., IV, 338. “Let us be watchful in our guard; let us carefully fortify the entrance against the enemy’s snares. And if at any time error has led away a lost sheep from the flocks entrusted to us, let us strive with all our effort to bring it back to the Lord’s folds,” Pope Dionysius, V, 136. Pope Sixtus II decreed that, if anyone has a case against a bishop or officers of the Church, he should first approach them for the sake of reconciliation, id., V, 87. Vigilance especially rests upon those set over others, Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 1058. Heretics are men of blood, ibid., 814. By what great deceits they strive to overthrow faith, ibid., 411. Those rejected by the Church are handed over to the dominion of the devil, ibid., 607, 957. The Apostles and priests are the eyes of the Church, ibid., 810. The whole Church applauded and approved the zeal of the Emperor Constantine the Great when he used his power to root out the temples of idols, extinguish depraved morals, and reveal the way of faith, VIII, 63, 65 ff. How, after an inquiry among the heretics, as many impious books as were found were committed to the flames, ibid., 68. Hence very many heretics returned to the Church, ibid. He planted the sign of the cross among the Sarmatians and Scythians joined to his empire, [Col. 0636] ibid., 71. He gave his soldiers a form of prayer, ibid., 74. Everywhere he prohibited the worship of idols, and saw to it that martyrs were honored with feasts, ibid., 75. Most wicked words of a certain schismatic bishop, Optatus, XI, 911. The anger of a certain factional woman named Lucilla, ibid. Moved by the violence and bad faith of the schismatics, the emperor uttered these words: “O mad audacity of frenzy! In the manner of pagans, they lodge an appeal,” ibid., 934–935. The wretched condition of the schismatics, brought about by themselves, ibid., 956, 957. Their rage and cruelty, ibid., 968 ff. Innocent priests stripped of their rank by Donatists and subjected to penance; likewise matrons, children, and virgins undeservedly subjected to penance, ibid., 980, 984. Such things led the Church to establish a tribunal for herself and employ secular authority, ibid., 999, 1008 ff. See the laws of Emperor Honorius against the Donatists, ibid., 1204 ff. Athanasius, deposed from his see by heretics, wrote to Pope Felix II: “It is certain that the decrees of the Fathers, in honor of most blessed Peter, have assigned to your same holy see a special reverence for God, for investigating and determining matters which it is fitting that the apostolic head of bishops himself should examine carefully and justly,” id., XIII, 14. “It belongs to you to defend and free us,” ibid., 15. “To neglect, when you can, to cast down the perverse is nothing other than to foster them,” ibid., 16. See Pope Felix’s reply to the council, ibid., 18 ff. In the Church flourish the rod and priestly grace, Ambrose, XIV, 526. The voice must be exercised for Christ when wolves invade the Church’s sheepfold, ibid., 248. Heretics are compared with wolves, id., XV, 1273. When human beings are rebuked by priests, they aggravate their sin while wishing either to deny or defend it, id., XIV, 854. Heresies seek to wound us with parricidal swords, id., XVI, 821. Let the bishop cut away with sorrow what cannot be healed, ibid., 139. Heretics, schismatics, and the dissolute are cast out of the camp, id., XVII, 22. Bishop means “overseer,” ibid., 579. On priestly vigilance by which heresies and schisms are forestalled, Pope Innocent I, XX, 481. Hidden sins do not receive punishment, ibid., 499–500. When proof is lacking, the grounds for punishment cease, ibid., 500. Authority must be used against errors lest they spread more widely and contaminate many, ibid., 570. On separating or cutting off heretics if they remain obstinate, ibid., 588, 589. Innocent rebukes John, bishop of Jerusalem, for a failure of vigilance, and urges him to correct and suppress the evils arising from it, ibid., 601. He orders Bishop Lawrence to ensure the expulsion of heretics following the poisonous doctrines of Photinus, ibid., 607. It is permissible to accuse a murderer, ibid., 626. The name of an intruder is not to be entered in the registers, ibid., 631. Pope Zosimus complains that the truth is not investigated in the cases of Ursus and Tuentius, ibid., 662. He urges Patroclus to prevent Proculus’s audacity and unlawful ordinations, ibid., 673. Rebels must be resisted in every way, ibid., 679. On the improper contempt for rules of judgment, ibid., 682. The Church’s just judgments must not be destroyed by irrational clemency, Jerome, XXII, 828. A bishop is established in the Church to restrain the people from error, id., XXIII, 160. “We do not receive heretics,” ibid., 469. “What do you think of those who, though condemned, besiege palaces and, forming a wedge, persecute the faith?” ibid., 470. Heretics are to be rebuked only once and twice, ibid., XXVI. Heretics must by every means be brought back to the Church, Augustine, XL, 714. They are to be healed rather than destroyed, id., XXXVIII, 173. Augustine wishes heretics to be corrected so that they may be taught, id., XXXIII, 367; taught even through fear, ibid., 322. God mercifully admonishes heretics through human authorities, id., XLIII, 106, 108. Heretics, schismatics, and pagans may be restrained by severe laws on behalf of religion, ibid., 802; XLIII, 44. It is mercy to trouble them, id., XL, 715. Action against heretics and schismatics should not be called persecution, id., XXXVIII, 1482. Great mercy is shown toward heretics when they are involuntarily torn from their sect by imperial laws, id., XXXIII, 798. Imperial laws against them, id., XXXV, 685, 716. Law of Theodosius, XXXIII, 358, 804. Laws by which they are deprived of their basilicas, id., XXXV, 684, 685. Augustine wishes heretics to be corrected, not killed, id., XXXIII, 367. Emperor Constantius ordered a diligent inquiry against the Pelagians, as Theodosius had formerly done, he being the first to decree the appointment of investigators to seek out heretics, as was customary for heinous crimes, ibid., 405. Constitution of Honorius and Theodosius by which Pelagius, Celestius, and their followers are expelled from the City, ibid., 378. Edict of the urban prefects on the same matter, ibid., 392. Letter of Emperor Honorius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning subscription to the condemnation of Pelagius and Celestius, ibid., 394. Letter of Aurelius to the bishops of Byzacena concerning the same case, ibid., 100. [Col. 0637] Edict published by Volusianus, prefect of the City, concerning enforcement of the preceding measure. Constitution of Valentinian III entrusting to the bishop of Arles the cases of those found guilty of the same error, ibid., 409. On the constitutions of Theodosius the Younger for the Eastern Church, of which almost nothing survives, ibid., 413. Prosper likens heretics and schismatics struck in their faith to the Egyptians struck by the worst plague, LI, 584, and to idols, since they have lost every function of rational life, ibid., 386. “It is not so much the law that is opposed to you, O human being, as you who are opposed to the law … Indeed, it is for you, and you against it,” Salvian, LIII, 93. Pagans and heretics: two kinds of barbarians, ibid., 94. Heretics must be informed against, and the persons to whom they must be denounced, Leo the Great, LIV, 163; and this itself is great mercy toward them, ibid., 179. Heretics, ministers of the devil, ibid., 177. How they are to be avoided, ibid., 206. Not to be tolerated, ibid., 1016. How corrected heretics are to be cautiously received into communion, ibid., 393, 597, 653, 690. Names of heretics removed from the diptychs, id., LV, 248 note. Neither prayer nor psalmody with them, id., LVI, 887. Churches closed to them, ibid., 715. Scythian monks refusing to condemn their errors are to be expelled from Rome as heretics, Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 490. On receiving the lapsed, ibid., 515. Pope John II confirms King Athalaric’s decree against simoniacs, LXVI, 11. Memorandum against the Donatists, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 211. Brief statement of the grounds for their exclusion, ibid., 213. On officers of the Church and the establishment of advocates, ibid., 214. King Clovis, having professed the faith, subdued these very heretics with God’s help, Gregory of Tours, LXIII, 241. Alaric, however, denying the faith, was deprived of kingdom, people, and—what is greater—eternal life, ibid. Saint Martin was beaten with rods by heretics and expelled from Milan and Italy, ibid., 564. Nevertheless, he dissuaded Maximus from sending the sword into Spain to kill heretics, ibid. He secured only that they be separated from the churches and communion of Catholics, ibid. Secular authorities all too often strengthen heretics, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 763. Some rage with words, others with swords, ibid. How great are the evils the Church suffers from heretics, id., LXXV, 621. Ungodly and violent persons, id., CLXXVI, 48. They seek quarrels, not reasons, id., CLXXV, 803, 804. Persecutions of the Church by heretics, ibid., 801, 838; LXXVII, 528. They madly claim that the confession of the true faith is punished by the scourges of adversity, id., LXXV, 1001, 1125. The Church strives to call back those in error by arguments, ibid., 803, 1043. The law pursues their perversity, id., LXXVII, 708. They must always be restrained by Catholic priests with firmness and reason, ibid., 726. Under Emperor Maurice they were compelled to be silent, ibid., 1165. Inquiry concerning the baptism of heretics, ibid., 1205. As the holy Catholic Church patiently tolerates within herself those who live badly, so she drives away from herself those who believe badly, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 571. The heresy and faction of the Monothelites opposed by the holy pontiffs Theodore and Martin, LXXXIII, 75, 119. Saint Martin’s captivity and exile described by himself, ibid., 197, 199, 201, 203. Heretics, like pagans, are not to be admitted as accusers, from the Council of Carthage, title 3, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 828. Judgments assigning fitting punishments to various public sins and brought under ecclesiastical inquiry, Pope Saint Gregory III, LXXXIX, 589 ff. Decree of Pope Zachary confirming the order of Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, by which two perverse heretics usurping the sacred ministry had been committed to custody, ibid., 927. Capitularies of Carloman and Pippin concerning ecclesiastical persons, apparently adopted by the Church and put into effect under its authority, id., XCVI, 501 ff. Chapters of Charlemagne concerning ecclesiastical discipline, whose enforcement is entrusted to the emperor’s authority, id., XCVII, 509 ff. Capitular concerning the Saxon affair, ibid., 145 ff. Charlemagne compelled this people, repeatedly rebellious and always defeated, to accept evangelical teaching; this could not be done without the aid of a severe inquiry, Einhard, XCVIII, 33. How heresies troubled the Church in the time of Saint Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 153, 281. Heretics are not to be trusted, ibid., 552 note ff. See the penitential books of this period, ibid., 927, 1088. On the conversion of the Saxons brought about by Charlemagne, Alcuin, C, 442. Charles is said to be armed with two swords, ibid., 312. Everything done in the time of Louis the Pious makes royal and ecclesiastical power everywhere appear interconnected; this has given historians no small occasion for error, but under the bridle of inquiry heretical fury nevertheless seems to fall silent, CIV, 927 ff. Excommunication without cause is invalid and recoils upon its author, Pope Gregory IV in Agobard, CIV, 300. See Saint Agobard’s books against the law of Gundobad, a heretical man, ibid., 116 and passim. Leo IV himself submits both his person and his actions to examination by Emperor Louis, [Col. 0638] CXV, 674. At times, in a serious matter, the case of accused clerics was referred to the Apostolic See, Pope Benedict III, ibid., 691. Letter of Pope Nicholas I to Abbot Hucbert, brother of Queen Theutberga, concerning examination of his case, CXIX, 840. Decree of the same pope concerning the removal of Photius from the see of Constantinople and the restoration of Ignatius, ibid., 850. Letter to Emperor Michael sharply rebuking him over the deposition of Patriarch Ignatius, ibid., 926. On the judgment of priests by lay judges, ibid., 1194. How, at Hincmar of Rheims’s urging, the chapters of Gunthar, bishop of Cologne, against Pope Nicholas were deservedly condemned, CXXI, 379, 381. The chapters of Herard, bishop of Tours, should be consulted, ibid., 763 ff. Edict of Emperor Charles the Bald at Quierzy, establishing that perpetrators of certain crimes are to be punished by law, CXXIV, 862 ff. The book *On the Person of the King and the Royal Ministry* by Hincmar of Rheims should be consulted carefully, CXXV, 834 ff. The same Hincmar considers what a king ought to do in war both against unbelievers and among Christians, ibid., 964 ff. How Saint Ambrose admonished Maximus concerning the performance of penance, ibid., 978. The state of churches and monasteries is to be reported to the king, ibid., 1072, 1073. Royal power and the authority of the holy pontiffs are distinct, ibid., 1071. On the capitularies of kings and emperors, ibid., 1077 ff. On the amendment to be made through penance, ibid., 1081. What a bishop ought to carry out in safeguarding Church property, ibid., 1087. On criminal presbyters, ibid., 1093. From whom an accusation is to be accepted, ibid., 1099. On ecclesiastical interdict, ibid., 1102. Ecclesiastical rules and sacred laws have not been promulgated vainly and to no purpose, ibid., 1106. It is necessary that every year the ministers of bishops inquire what each church yields concerning the state of tithes, ibid., 1110. On the case of the presbyter Teutfrid, ibid., 1111. Pope John VIII urges King Charles the Bald to come to his aid against unbelievers and oppressors of the Church, CXXVI, 831. Innocent I banishes heretics to exile and monasteries, in Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 146. Pope Donus decreed the same, ibid., 798. Monothelites confined in monasteries under Leo II, ibid., 847. Investigation conducted by Pope Hadrian concerning those responsible for the murder of Pope Sergius, ibid., 1187. On matters falling under episcopal inquiry, Regino, CXXXII, 187 ff. What is to be required of a presbyter, ibid., 190. The bishop’s officials were those entrusted with the care of making inquiry throughout his parish, ibid., 195. Inquiry to be conducted by the bishop during visitation of the diocese, ibid., 404, 405. See the ecclesiastical laws of Anglo-Saxon kings: Alfred the Great, CXXXVIII, 447; Edward the Elder, 459; Æthelstan, 462; Hywel Dda, 471; Edmund, 479; Edgar, 485. Capitularies of Frankish kings: Lothair, 525; Charles II, 589; Louis II, 617; Carloman, 791; King Guy, 801. Louis of Arles concerning divine worship, Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII, 1164. So that unpunished license for foul lust may not roam abroad, Saint Peter Damian appeals to the severity of apostolic authority, CXLV, 160. Emperors as defenders of the Church, id., CXLIV, 438. A bishop must not pardon clerics’ outrages, ibid., 329. On public penance through which certain sinners are commanded to pass, id., CXLV, 166. Inquiry concerning the titles of candidates for ordination prescribed in the synodal statutes of John of Rouen, CXLVII, 238. How clerics dressed in secular clothing are to be treated, ibid., 246. Likewise those who attend heretics’ sermons, ibid., 249. Excommunication of Otto, bishop of Constance, for the offense of simony by Pope Gregory VII, id., CXLVIII, 656. Antipope Guibert and Emperor Henry, his supporter, excommunicated by the same Gregory VII in the year 1084, ibid., 821. An excommunicated adulteress expelled from the cemetery by order of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, CL, 545. Raynerius, legate of the Holy See, appointed judge by Urban II between the bishop of Barcelona and the abbot of Saint-Pons of Thomières, CLI, 314. Ecclesiastical laws of King Æthelred II, id., CLI, 1165; of Cnut, 1171; of Saint Edward III, 1189. Life of Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians, 1203. On the Holy War against unbelievers, in which God plainly spoke through his Church and, through the mouth of the holy pontiffs and all the prelates of that time, stirred princes to arms for the glorification of his name: see Godfrey of Bouillon, CLV, 370; *The Deeds of Tancred*, by Ralph, 490; Raymond of Aguilers’s *History of Jerusalem*, 591; likewise Fulcher of Chartres, 821; the heroic poem of Gilo of Paris, 932; the history of Albert of Aachen, CLXVI, 389. Excommunication of Bertrand, Count of Toulouse, by Paschal II, CLXIII, 207. On those communicating with excommunicated persons, and how heretics are to be received, ibid., 265. On extinguishing with the severity of the canons the countless evils occurring throughout Spain, ibid., 321. In a judgment four persons must always be present: appointed judges, suitable accusers, defenders, and lawful witnesses, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1199. What must be observed and considered in every judgment, ibid. What must be sought in a judgment, ibid., 1202. By how many witnesses each cleric must be convicted, ibid. In a judgment, questioning must be frequent lest anything be omitted, ibid., 1204. Bishops must be given a substantial period of delay lest anything appear to be done hastily, ibid., 1203. Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death, ibid., 1237. The laws of emperors may lawfully be enlisted in aid of the Church, ibid., 1118. Whoever does not obey the laws of emperors for God’s truth incurs a grave punishment, ibid. Decree of Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Holy See, concerning expulsion of the nuns of Saints Mary and John at Laon, with the consent and command of King Louis, CLXXIII, 1268. Whether it is good to excommunicate someone, and whether one unjustly excommunicated may lawfully resist, Hugh of Saint Victor, CLXXV, 521, 522. Whether one unjustly excommunicated remains bound, and what must be weighed in excommunication, id., CLXXVII, 394, 395. Canonical laws must sometimes be moderated in view of piety, necessity, and usefulness, ibid., 863, 864.

INSCRIPTION. Ancient inscriptions in the basilica of Saint Paul at Rome, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 365, notes 45 and 46. Inscription of Emperor Constantine in the church founded by him at Rome in honor of Blessed Peter, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1518.

ITINERARY. See *Pilgrimage*.

FASTING. What Christian fasts were and how rigorous they were, Tertullian, I, 487. Droughts of the earth dispelled by fasts, ibid., 703. Fasts prescribed before baptism, ibid., 1222. Interrupted by the necessity of joy and rejoicing for salvation, ibid., 1227. Christians nourished their prayers by fasting, ibid., 1244. No fasting on Sunday, II, 79; nor from Easter to Pentecost, ibid., 80. The powers of those fasting before God; heaven fights for such persons, ibid., 962. A fast, or station, until the ninth hour, ibid., 966; and until evening, ibid., 967. Fasting before councils, ibid., 972. Some did not fast on Saturday, ibid., 973. Christian fasts, Hilary of Poitiers, X, 557. The fast of Lent, Ambrose, XIV, 708. Fasting ceased during the time of Easter, ibid., 867. Those who attack the merit of fasting and abstinence refuted, id., XVI, 1191. Wednesday and Friday fast, Rufinus, XXI, 419. Cheerful countenance of one fasting, Jerome, XXII, 413. Those fasting sometimes worse than those not fasting, ibid., 421. Ecclesiastical tradition concerning the relaxation of fasting on certain days, ibid., 420. During fasting one must abstain from wine and meat, ibid., 820. The soft reins of fasting, ibid., 827. When fasts and prayers profit, ibid., 1079. Fasting is not a perfect virtue, but the foundation of the other virtues, ibid., 1116. Those fasting receive far more than they offer, ibid., 1143. With what intention fasting ought to be observed, Augustine, XXXV, 1287. What Christian fasting is, ibid., 1339. Fasts, prayers, and almsgiving belong to the clothing of sheep, ibid., 1306. Fasting, a great Christian work, id., XXXVI, 1108. Those who fast in order to dine more sumptuously conduct the business of the belly, not of religion, ibid. It is necessary for subduing the flesh, id., XL, 709. Frequent daily fasts in Catholic communion, id., XLII, 225. On not fasting on Sunday, John Cassian, XLIX, 110. The fast of the four seasons prescribed by the Church throughout the year, Leo the Great, LIV, 186. The Church’s fasts established by the author, the Holy Spirit, ibid., 418. Fasting accords with both Testaments, ibid., 447. The fasting of hypocrites reproved, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 303. The difference between Christ’s fast and Moses’ fast explained, ibid., 325. Why we do not fast for forty days after Easter, ibid., 371. One refreshed by God’s grace cannot be fasting, ibid. We ought to imitate Christ fasting. In how many ways fasting is sanctified, ibid., 307, 452. Bodily fasting fattens the soul, Saint Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 209. Fasting, by which we abstain from everything forbidden, is the garment of the soul, ibid., 313. It promotes chastity, ibid., 626. It is an aid, not the perfection of holiness, ibid., 761. What kind is praiseworthy, ibid. It must be strong in every virtue without exception, ibid., 762. The efficacy of fasting, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 107. Conditions of fasting, ibid., 232. Required for celebration, ibid., 783. What it is to sanctify a fast, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 82. What it is to fast not for God but for oneself, ibid., 82. Even very small children were customarily to observe fasting in Gregory’s time, ibid., 297. Fasting harmful to those suffering from vomiting blood, ibid., 1146, 1151. Homily in praise of fasting, Saint Eligius, LXXXVII, 498. What perfect fasting is and how beneficial, Alcuin, CI, 624. The fast of ordinands, or of the four seasons, ibid., 1227. When it was begun and ended by Christ, ibid., 1180. Fasts are necessary for our soul, like medicine for wounds, Smaragdus, CII, 120. On the Savior’s fasting, ibid., 124. On fasting, Benedictus Sedulius, CIII, 807. Relaxed for the sick, ibid., 1093. Formerly no fasting from Easter to Pentecost, ibid., 1137. Wednesday and
sixth weekday, ibid., 1138. On fasting, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 333. What difference there is between a fast and a station, ibid., 334. On fasting before Pentecost, ibid., 335. Before the Lord’s Nativity, ibid., 336. On other fasts, ibid., 337. On private fasts, ibid., 338. On true fasting, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 182. On the same subject, Anastasius the Librarian, CCXXVII, 1176. Pope Miltiades ordained that fasting should not take place on Sunday and Thursday, ibid., 1500. St Callistus commanded the observance of the Ember fasts, 1318. Lawful fasts are not to be relaxed except in the greatest necessity, Regino, CXXXII, 372. On fasts and almsgiving, St Odo of Canterbury, CXXXIII, 949. On the observance and benefit of fasting, Burchard, CXL, 583. On fasts and foods, Guigo, CLIII, 705. On the beginning of the fast, Goffrid, CLVII, 143. What rationale of fasting should be approved, ibid., 171. Appointed fasts must be observed, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 267, 270, 271. Almsgiving must be joined to fasting, ibid., 273. The usefulness of fasting, ibid., 275. Christ himself taught us fasting, St Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 91. On fasting in Advent, Rupert, CLXX, 62. How fasting prepares us for Christ’s coming, Godefrid, CLXXIV, 66. Fasting does not entail abstinence from every food, ibid., 106. The twofold fruit of fasting, labour, and prayer, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 553. Moderate fasts are commended, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1243. On fasts, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1859 ff. On the same, John Beleth, CCII, 20 ff. On the same, Alan of Lille, CCX, 176. Thirteen books on prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, Gunther, CCXII, 97, 207.

**JEW.** From the beginning, the Jewish people were distributed by tribes, clans, and households, Tertullian, II, 450. Because of their sins they came to be cast out from God, ibid., 21, 393. Hoping only for earthly things, they lose heavenly things, ibid., 833. They suffered dispersion because of Christ, ibid., 638. Jewish greeting, ibid., 480. Jews anoint and wash the dead, Lactantius, VI, 270. They await and hope for the Messiah in vain, ibid., 738. They were accustomed to be confused with Christians, ibid., VII, 473. How they behaved in time of persecution, ibid., 575. The Jews perished while they despise the depths of meaning and follow the bare words of Scripture, Ambrose, XVI, 597. Let us abandon Jewish rites; let us abandon the shadow, following the Sun, ibid., 1268. By killing the flesh of the Lord, the Jews became slaves of impiety, Jerome, XXII, 822. Although his virtues shine forth to all, they do not cease to blaspheme, ibid. The Jews believed neither Moses nor Christ, Augustine, XXXVIII, 250. They were excluded from their ancestral soil by order of the Roman emperor, ibid., 57. Why the Jewish sect was not wholly destroyed, Augustine, XL, 179. They are dispersed throughout the whole world because of the testimony of the Scriptures, ibid., XLI, 140. Their books support our faith, ibid., XL, 178. Jewish Sabbaths and sacraments censured by Seneca, ibid., XLI, 192. How the Jewish religion was weakened, ibid., 529. On avoiding association with Jews, Agobard, CIV, 107. On the four denarii to be paid by a Jew to the key-bearer of the monastery of Fleury, Richard, CXXXVI, 1308. Punishment of a certain Jew for the horrible maltreatment of an image of Christ, Sigebert, CLX, 105. Jews wander like Cain of old, Rupert, CLXIX, 949. The Jews’ twofold tribulation, ibid., 1104. They deserve to drink blood, ibid., 1118. The Jews’ life is detestable, ibid., 1174. How often, and at what times, Jews in Jerusalem wrote to brethren in Egypt, ibid., 1427. Though they are Jesus’ kinsfolk, the Jews do not believe in him, Godefrid, CLXXIV, 103. They are chastised according to the prophecies, ibid., 511. Yet at the end of the age they will be converted, ibid., 54, 56, 65, 104, 106, 143, 203, 268, 415.

**OATH.** The custom of swearing while touching the Gospels, Amuros. Why an oath upon the Gospels or relics of saints was introduced for canonical purgation, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 572. On parents’ oath when offering their sons in monasteries, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 400, note. It does not become a Christian to swear, Peter Cantor, CCV, 210, 322. When it is permissible to swear, ibid. The custom of swearing upon the Gospels, the cross, or relics of saints, ibid., CCXIV, XXIV.

**LAW / RIGHT.** Nature produced common law; usurpation made law private, Ambrose, XVI, 62. Ecclesiastical law, Augustine, XXXVI, 196. Right is that which is just, ibid., XXXVII, 1894. In former times there were no legal formulae; the judgment of the will was held as the norm of law, ibid., XXXVIII, 549. What one does not handle lawfully one does not lawfully possess, ibid., 327. Divine law and human law in the possession of earthly things, ibid., XXXIII, 345. How right and honour differ, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 454. Right and use are sometimes separated, ibid., 485. Each person’s rights must be preserved, ibid., 627. Right and force are opposed, ibid., 682. Customs and rights of the Church concerning the Rule, Richard, CXXXVI, 1303. What the laws of God are, Canute, CLI, 1174. Why the study of civil law does not suit clerics, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 91.

**JUSTICE.** It gives each person his own, Ambrose, XVI, 57. Justice’s first duty of devotion is toward God, its second toward one’s country, its third toward parents and likewise toward all persons, ibid., 60. It relates to the fellowship of humankind and to the common good, ibid., 61. Justice is the loftier virtue, ibid. Sparing of itself, it is wholly directed outward; and whatever it has, with a certain sternness toward itself, it pours out into its neighbours when it is carried away by common love, ibid., 1309. The many kinds of justice, ibid. Justice is maintained by labour, diligence, and God’s mercy, Jerome, XXIII, 569. Justice has rest; iniquity, toil, ibid., 1040. The great balance of justice is to give to whom, how much, how long, and of what kind—whether in a thing or in counsel, ibid., 1069. Justice is that by which what is his own is given to each person, Augustine, XXXII, 1235. Another definition of justice, ibid., 1189. Wherein justice consists, ibid., XXXV, 1337. The justice of God and the justice of man, ibid., XXXIII, 1607. What are the paths of justice, ibid., XXXIX, 1648. The justice of this life, ibid., CLIV, 1514. Let the judge display in his deeds the justice he bears in his mind, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 511. To cultivate justice is the highest good in kings, ibid., 1047. Jesus Christ, the true sun of justice, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 177. The wilderness of this world is illumined by the saving light of justice, ibid. What true justice is, Alcuin, CI, 640. What justice is, and what its parts are, ibid., 651, 944, 949. It is overturned in judgments in four ways: by fear, greed, hatred, and love, ibid., 629. One justice is God’s, another man’s, another the devil’s, Godefrid, CLXXIV, 350. The true kind is from God alone, ibid., 141.

**KYRIE ELEISON.** “Lord, have mercy” is said differently in the Roman Church and among the Greeks, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 956. Formerly it was chanted at Matins and Vespers, ibid., 936. Who ordered that *Kyrie eleison* be sung at Masses, Sigebert, CLX, 111.

**LABOUR.** Great is the labour, but great the reward, of being martyrs, Jerome, XXII, 422. Life has given mortals nothing without great labour, ibid., 586.
