The labour of the present age will receive its end, and everlasting joy will succeed it, ibid., 822. Egyptian monasteries admit no one without labour, and why, ibid., 1079. Labour must be joined with piety, ibid., 1119. It is more excellent to provide one’s own food and clothing by manual labour than to receive them from others, Augustine, XXXIII, 692. Labour exists where many things are sought and loved, though the will is not sufficient to acquire and retain them, ibid., 485. Labour cannot end unless each person loves that which cannot be taken away against his will, ibid., XXXVI, 107. Labour is the seed of iniquity; sin, the conception of pain, ibid. Nothing is more laborious than iniquity and impiety; pain follows this labour, ibid., 127. If you wish to endure labour, consider the reward, ibid., 372. How labour is commanded us, ibid., XXXVII, 1211. All labour for their children, not for themselves, ibid., 1159. Labour is brief and not lacking in consolation, ibid., 1212. Let a man labour to hold what he easily lost: what he has held after labour he will hold firmly, ibid., 1936. The labours of several conditions of life are enumerated, ibid., XXXVIII, 443. Whence this labour comes, ibid., 440. No human being is exempt from the penalty of labour, ibid., XLIV, 1578. Even the perfected must endure in this life the labours of old age, St Prosper, LI, 441. Why manual labour is necessary, St Benedict, CIII, 1184. Manual labour ought to be moderate, ibid. Manual work is commended to clerics and priests, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 486. Shadow signifies labour and day, reward, Wolbero, CXCV, 1156. On the labour of mortals, Innocent III, CCVI, 706.

**TEARS.** See *Weeping*.

**LAYPERSON.** What does not befit a layperson, Jerome, XXIII, 157. Laypersons of a lower calling—that is, persons other than monks—Augustine, XXXII, 639; laypersons, XXXVIII, 653, 758; XXXIX, 1440. The Church’s patrimony must not be entrusted to laypeople, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1002. The office of laypersons in the church, Alcuin, C. Laypersons ought not to eat with monks, Benedict Sedulius, CIII, 1255. Laypeople are neither to hold churches nor receive tithes, Regino, CXXXII, 237. On laypeople of every condition, Burchard, CXL, 895. Laypersons may not dispose of Church property, Goffrid, CLVII, 143. Laypersons may bear arms, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 614. Tithes are not to be possessed by laypeople, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1042.

**LAMP, LANTERN.** A lantern is nothing in comparison with a lamp, Jerome, XXII, 503. Lamps were formerly hung in churches, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 611. Description of a glass lamp suspended in a church, ibid. A golden lamp in the church of St John at Rome, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 347. On lamps, lanterns, and lights; carved lamps and cast lamps, ibid., CXXVII, 1519. Hymnic lamps, ibid., 1522. A golden lamp, ibid. Golden lamps, ibid., [Col. 0642] CXXVIII, 347. Silver ones, ibid., 350. Silver lamps, ibid., 1211, 1228, 1230. Lamps were established in churches for carrying out the sacred readings on Sundays and feast days, ibid., 1228, 1243. Lights were to be supplied from the Lateran palace in cemeteries every Sunday, ibid., 624. Lights before the altar of the Apostles, ibid., 811, 984. Lights were to be set in cemeteries around Rome on saints’ feast days, ibid., 1030. Before the altar of St Paul, ibid., 1227, and of St Mary at the Manger, ibid., 1269.

**WOOL, WOOL-WORKER.** See *Woman*.

**PRAISE.** People sometimes praise what they do not approve, Augustine, XXXIII, 421. Praise sparingly; blame more sparingly, Alan of Lille, CCX, 158.

**READING, READER.** Whoever reads much from the Scriptures and understands is filled; whoever has been filled waters others, Ambrose, XVI, 880. Readings are held in the new basilica, ibid., 997. Readings in church during the morning hours, ibid., 999, 1309. A young reader, ibid. A reader is demanded, ibid., 997. Sacred reading is commended, Jerome, XXII, 404. In it God speaks to us, ibid., 411. Negligence in reading, ibid., 478. Let sacred reading always be in one’s hand, ibid., 592. By continual reading and meditation let our breast become Christ’s library, ibid., 595. Reading should not be for drudgery, but for the soul’s delight and instruction, ibid., 1119. Let reading follow prayer and prayer reading, ibid., 875. At Christian gatherings, reading and psalm-singing were performed alternately, Augustine, XXXIII, 119. Those who had once performed the office of reader in one church could not be retained by another, ibid., 233. An ecclesiastical reader is not someone who reads a non-ecclesiastical writing, even if he reads it in church, ibid., 234. The reader first read the psalm that was to be expounded, ibid., XXXVII, 1784. Whoever cannot read should continually hear the word of God, ibid., 1159. The reader ascends; the expositor speaks, ibid., XXXVIII, 124. Sacred readings raise us against despair and frighten us against pride, ibid., 778. Readings and chants in church, ibid., 950. Reading is necessary for us here, not in our homeland, ibid., XXXVII, 1193. The errors of readers are threefold, ibid., XLII, 72. St Fulgentius urges Galla to read the Holy Scriptures, Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 323. By whom readings in church ought to be sung, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1335. In former times readers in church read the Gospel, ibid. Daily reading of the writings of the holy Fathers, St Eutropius, LXXX, 17. One must devote oneself to reading, Benedict Sedulius, CIII, 1176. How useful the reading of devout books is, ibid., 1177. Why two readings are read at Mass on Wednesday, only one on Friday, but four on the Ember Saturday, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 439. The twofold fruit of reading, ibid., 553.

**LAW.** The law of nature is presumed from customs, not from social conditions, Ambrose, XVI, 1088.—It is not written but inborn, ibid., 1251. The law of Moses took the place of natural law, ibid. Why the Mosaic law had to be borne, ibid., 1252. In the law is a portion; in the Gospel, perfection, ibid., 1256. Whoever binds lighter matters does not loosen but binds the weightier ones, ibid., 1195. The good of observing laws, Augustine, XXXII, 816. What the helm is to a governor, God’s law is to the mind, ibid., 825. It must be obeyed as the strongest leader, ibid., 817. Human decisions must not be preferred to God’s law, ibid., 827. Amid arms laws are silent, ibid., 682. In law one seeks not reason but authority, ibid., 924. Temporal law too is given by God, ibid., 689. This law may be changed through time, ibid., 1229. One law is eternal, another temporal, ibid. The concept of eternal law, ibid. Those who adhere to eternal law have no need of temporal law, ibid., 1238. For whose good law was given, ibid., XXXIII, 859. Law is not sufficient for free choice, ibid., 683. Natural law, ibid., 681. It is called the law of reason, ibid., 683. Human powers are insufficient for fulfilling the law, ibid., 393. The law would not command unless there were a will; nor would grace help if the will were sufficient, ibid., 766. God’s law is everlasting, ibid., XXXIV, 618. The weakness of the Mosaic law, ibid., XXXV, 1402. Why the law could not be fulfilled, ibid., 1401. God’s law: God’s will, ibid., XXXVI, 386. Natural law is shown to be present in all people, ibid., 673. The law knows how to command, not to help, ibid., XXXVIII, 822, 1171. It gives knowledge of the enemy, not victory over him, ibid., 794. Without grace it has no power, ibid., 1165. The law is fulfilled not through fear of punishment but through love of justice, ibid., 199, 1170, 1241. Whether a Christian is bound to keep the precepts of the old law, ibid., XLIV, 594. Why Christians now reject the observances of the law, ibid., 215. The law was given that grace might be sought; grace was given that the law might be fulfilled, ibid., 221. Ecclesiastical laws are cheapened by excessive dispensations or favours, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 641. Things done contrary to laws are not only useless but must be treated as null, ibid., 947. The laws of princes are sometimes rightly invoked to support the canons, ibid., 1297. They are commended by the authority of the canons themselves, ibid., 1299. Difference between law and custom, [Col. 0643] Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 482. Ecclesiastical laws of Æthelred, king of the English, ibid., CLI, 1165. Likewise of Canute, ibid., 1171. And of Edward, ibid., 1190.

**DOCUMENT; HOLDER OF A SACRIFICIAL CERTIFICATE.** What certificates given by martyrs were, and how St Cyprian censures them, St Cyprian, IV, 261, 285. The martyr Mappalicus granted a certificate to his mother alone, ibid., 283. Who the *libellatici* were, ibid., 311, 345.

**SACRED BOOKS.** See *Holy Scripture*.

**FREEDOM.** Freedom according to nature is older than slavery, Ambrose, XVI, 1264. Neither slavery diminishes nor freedom helps, ibid., 337. With Christ they are weighed in an equal balance, ibid. True spiritual freedom, ibid., 1090. How miserable it is that we are born in freedom and die in slavery, ibid., 1092. God alone is served in the highest freedom, Augustine, XXXII, 1170, 1320. True freedom is to serve Christ, ibid., XXXIII, 128. Free will will be freer insofar as it is healthier, and healthier insofar as it is subject to the grace and mercy of God, ibid., 676. The law of freedom is the law of charity, ibid., 740. Full freedom in eternity, ibid., XXXV, 1697, 1699. True and sound freedom consists in doing a good work not from fear but from love, ibid., XXXVI, 820. Freedom is twofold: immortality and perseverance, ibid., XLIV, 936. The freedom of the righteous is not as great in this life as it will be in the next, ibid., XLV, 1116. The question of freedom—whether a person is free or enslaved—requires weightier judges, Gregory the Great, XVI, 923. Christian, free and slave, Lanfranc, CL, 177. No one is to be sold outside his homeland, Æthelred, CLI, 1167. On not selling a Christian outside the kingdom, ibid., 1177.

**PERMITTED.** Some things are permitted which are not beneficial, Augustine, XL, 460, 463. At times one must abstain from permitted things, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 130. On three prohibited and three permitted things, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 838.

**THRESHOLDS.** Christians were accustomed to kiss the thresholds of churches; the thresholds of the Apostles at Rome, Aurelius Prudentius, IX, 330, note. The sick and wretched were very often brought to the thresholds of the saints, Dynamius, LXXX, 51. See *Pilgrimage*.

**LITANIES, ROGATION DAYS, PROCESSIONS.** Institution of Rogation observances, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 232. Standards carried in procession, ibid., 320. General processions and litanies in time of calamity were held at Rome under Gregory the Great, ibid., 528. Processions were formerly held in basilicas, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 542. A procession and the gathering of the people, ibid., 548. Whence the term “litany” derives, and how *litania* is improperly said, ibid., 1329. St Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted solemn litanies, ibid. In the greatest flooding of the Tiber, processions and litanies were held at Rome, Gregory II, LXXXIX, 465. On prayers to be made during the Major Litany before the Lord’s Ascension, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 168. On various litanies, Alcuin, CI, 522, 528, 649, 1219. On litanies, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 332. On conducting litanies, Walafrid, CXIV, 962. Processions on the four feasts of Blessed Mary under Pope Sergius, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 898. Litanies, ibid., 611, 917. A litany to the thresholds of St Peter, ibid., 700. Likewise to St Mary at the Martyrs, ibid., 1051. To St Mary at the Manger, with the image of the Saviour, ibid., 1087. A litany to three basilicas, ibid. Major litanies, ibid., 1214. Picture or narrative of the Major Litany, ibid., 1220. Three-day litanies before the Lord’s Ascension, ibid., 1223. Pope Leo III instituted litanies during the three days before the Lord’s Ascension, ibid. The frequent use of litanies and processions at Rome, ibid. On the Major Litany, Regino, CXXXII, 243. Processions on Rogation Days and St Mark’s Day, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 120, 121, 122. Procession on Ascension Day, ibid., 122. On the Sunday procession, Udalric, CXLIX, 653. On processions, Guido, CL, 1272. Rogations or litanies before the Lord’s Ascension are to be celebrated with fasting and abstention from servile work, Ivo of Chartres, 266, 272. Institution of Rogation observances, ibid., 272. Use of litanies with fasting, ibid., 854. The three principal rogations or processions, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 817. On processions, John Beleth, CCII, 20. Sermons on litanies, St Martin of León, CCVIII, 1009. On litanies, Sicard, CCXIII, 367. On processions, Innocent III, CCXVI, 805.

**LITIGATION; DISPUTE.** To escape the expense of litigation is no small gain, Ambrose, XVI, 130, 143. The cry of wicked litigants is that they have suffered wicked judges, Augustine, XXXIII, 169. No apostolic examples support recovering one’s goods by public judgment, ibid., 327. It is better to doubt hidden matters than to litigate doubtful ones, ibid., XXXIV, 376. Whether litigation is permissible, ibid., XXXVI, 1281. Even litigation before ecclesiastical judges is a fault for Christians, ibid., XXXVII, 1045. Litigants bring their cases before bishops, ibid., 1570. To yield something to a person bringing suit, so that you may devote yourself to God, is to redeem the time, ibid., XXXVIII, 910. Who is to be regarded as litigating, ibid., XXXIX, 1593. To have litigation concerning secular matters is forbidden by Christ, ibid., XL, 270. Christians must avoid lawsuits, Salvian, LIII, 61. Gregory the Great settles by his authority a suit between an abbot and a subdeacon, LXXVII, 966. St Gregory forbids litigation, ibid., 1152. Suits are to be ended by elected judges or arbitrators, ibid. He prefers leaving bequeathed goods rather than litigating, ibid., 1228.

**LETTERS DIMISSORY.** Letters dimissory were not formerly in use, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 461, 575, note. Formerly, without letters dimissory, laymen could be ordained by any bishop, ibid., 536. By privilege, the bishops of Constantinople and Carthage admitted clerics subject to another jurisdiction without dimissory letters, ibid. In current practice, dimissory letters are required only from the bishop of birth, ibid.

**SACRED PLACES.** See *Church*, *Holy Land*, *Jerusalem*.

**WASHING OF FEET.** To wash feet is a mystery of faith and a sign of humility, Ambrose, XVI, 280. Many did not wish to adopt the washing of feet on the day of the Supper as a custom, lest it seem to pertain to the sacrament of baptism, Augustine, XXXIII, 220. Some did not hesitate to abolish the custom; others transferred it to the third day of the octave or to the octave day itself, ibid. Washing of feet is performed at the Lord’s Supper, Alcuin, CI, 1202, 1203; St Benedict, CIII, 1201. On consecration of chrism and washing of feet at the Lord’s Supper, Rupert, CLXX, 143. Whether the feet of all guest should be washed, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 607.

**LANTERN.** See *Lamp*.

**GAME.** Wibold, bishop of Cambrai, instituted a clerical game to eradicate gambling with dice, CXXXIV, 1007, 1010, 1015. The order and rule of this game, ibid.

**LOINS.** What it means for a Christian to have his loins girded and a burning lamp in his hand, St Fulgentius, LXV, 725.

**LIGHT.** The use of lights in Christian assemblies, Lactantius, VI, 637, 994. Why that custom was retained, ibid. On the extinguishing of lights in Holy Week, Amalarius, CV, 1202. See *Candle*, *Lamp*.

**LUXURY.** Luxury is restrained by rustic food, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 210.

**MACHINE.** A war-engine invented by a certain craftsman, by means of which the crusaders captured the city of Nicaea, William of Tyre, CCI, 279.

**MOHAMMEDANISM.** The lamentable condition of humankind when Mohammedanism invaded, William of Tyre, CCI, 223.

**MAMERTUS (ST).** He instituted solemn rogations or supplications in the Church, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1329. See *Litanies*.

**MARY (THE BLESSED VIRGIN).** Etymology of the name Mary, Ambrose, XVI, 314. Beautiful things were prophesied of Mary in the figure of the Church, ibid., 326. Her virtues are described, ibid., 208. She was such that her life is a lesson for all, ibid., 210. “I read that Mary stood before the cross of her Son; I do not read that she wept,” ibid., 1371. Mary, a light cloud, ibid., 345. Whether St Mary was Joseph’s wife at the time of the Annunciation, Juvencus, XIX, 69, note. She is rebuked by Christ at Cana—or not, ibid., 159. She visits Elizabeth, ibid., 73. Her presentation in the Temple, ibid., 70. When her parents died, ibid., 71. Mary, Mother of God, virgin and fruitful at once, Jerome, XXII, 407. Her perpetual virginity, ibid., 509. Her purity is commended, ibid. Mary is entrusted by Christ to the disciple John, whom she had never left before the cross, ibid., 954. No midwife was present at her childbirth, ibid., XXIII, 91. She is not recorded as having married after childbirth, ibid., 202. Mary’s perfection is greater than Elizabeth’s, ibid., 510. Why Gabriel came to Mary, and not to Joseph as to Zechariah, Augustine, XXXVIII, 1317. Zechariah’s and Mary’s questions were alike; their dispositions unlike, ibid., 1314. Mary is freed from Joseph’s false suspicion, ibid., XXXIX, 1507. Mary’s modesty and humility should be imitated by women, ibid., XXXVIII, 343. Blessed among women, ibid., 1318. By grace she becomes Mother of the Son of God, ibid., 1319. With the love of faith burning, she conceived, ibid., 1069. A virgin believed, a virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, a virgin remained, ibid., 343. Through a woman, death; and through a woman, life, ibid., 1108. Mary was of the tribe of Judah and of priestly lineage, ibid., XL, 50. Mary had vowed virginity to God when she heard that Christ would be born from her, ibid., 308. Mary alone is mother and virgin both in spirit and body, ibid., 399. Out of honour for the Lord, Augustine wishes to entertain absolutely no question regarding the Blessed Virgin Mary when sins are discussed, ibid., XXXII, 746. The Virgin Mary conceived Christ first in her mind, then in her body, Leo the Great, LIV, 190. Her faith is confirmed by Elizabeth’s miracle, ibid., 192. She bore God and man, ibid., LV, 150. Mary, a fitting dwelling-place for Christ, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 225. She was betrothed to Joseph, who was just and young, ibid., 639. Mary, perpetual virgin, Gregory of Tours, CLXXI, 162, 170, 707, 712. Blessed Mary is entrusted to the disciple John, ibid., 524. At her death the Apostles gather, and Christ restores her bodily to paradise, ibid., 708, 713. [Col. 0645] A church of Blessed Mary is dedicated by Emperor Constantine, ibid., 713. Her feast in January, ibid., 714. An image of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus is displayed in a church, ibid., 715. Blessed Virgin, Mother of God, ibid., 1026, 1087. An image of the Blessed Virgin Mary before the church of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the time of Mary of Egypt, *Lives of the Fathers*. Before an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a lighted candle is miraculously not diminished, ibid., 917. Refreshment of mind was granted to Mary the Mother of God, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 54. The Virgin conceived the Son of God, ibid., 90. Thus Mary conceived and bore the Word of God, while remaining both virgin and Mother of God, ibid. How Mary is both handmaid and mother of the Lord, ibid., LXXVII, 1207. St Mary appears to the virgin Musa, who was shortly to die, ibid., 348. Nativity of Blessed Mary: 8 September, ibid., 137. Assumption of St Mary, ibid., 401, note. Dedication of the church of St Mary at the Martyrs, ibid., 384. Sermons on the praises and cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 239, 250, 254, 258, 259, 264, etc. On the name of Mary, Alcuin, C, 725, 728, 732. She must be believed and confessed to be Mother of God, ibid., 749. While virginity remained intact, she conceived and gave birth, CI, 38, 46, 1272. Honoured with three goods, ibid., 24. Verses on the Blessed Virgin Mary, ibid., 749, 758, 762. Why she was called “woman” by Christ, ibid., 766. She is mother of believers, ibid., 1300 (LXXXIX, 1291). How she subjected herself to the law of purification, ibid., 1300 (XCVI, 1178). Special praises of Blessed Mary, ibid., 1305. How effective her intercession is, ibid., 1306. Born of royal and free lineage, ibid., 1340. The history of the birth and praiseworthy life of the inviolate Mother of God: a poem, the virgin Hrotsvitha, CXXXVII, 1065 ff. Praise of Blessed Mary, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 847. Why Mary is called heaven, ibid., 861. Mary’s childbirth surpassed all miracles, ibid., 1020. The usefulness of the Hours of the Blessed Virgin Mary, ibid., CXLV, 230. The intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary is effective, Goffrid, CLVII, 211. Blessed Mary, perpetual virgin, ibid., 237, 244. Gate of the House of the Lord, ibid., 244. Purification of Blessed Mary, ibid., 262. Blessed Mary, mother of Christ and of Christians, ibid., 265. What St Anselm held concerning the conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, ibid., CLVIII, 416. She was among those cleansed of sins before Christ’s birth, ibid., 419. The Holy Spirit willed that he from whom it proceeded should be conceived and born of the Virgin Mary, ibid., 451. She was worthy to conceive by the Holy Spirit, ibid., 621. Humility of the Blessed Virgin, ibid., 645, 646. “If Mary is silent, none of the saints will pray, none will help; if she prays, all will pray, all will help,” ibid., 944. Mary’s services toward Christ, ibid., 646. Her presentation in the Temple, where she made a vow of virginity, ibid., 749. Nativity of Blessed Mary with its octave, ibid., CLIX, 84. Annunciation of Blessed Mary, ibid., CLVIII, 785, 963. Her purification, ibid., 621, 964. Assumption, glory, and blessedness of Blessed Mary, ibid., 965. Praises and cult of the most holy Virgin Mary, Rupert, CLXVIII, 311, 585, 839, 844, 846, 554, 875, 886, 909, 945. Blessed Mary, chosen by God to accomplish the work of redemption, Godefrid, CLXXIV, 37. How she is the Lord’s sister, ibid. She was immune from temptations, ibid., 40. Through her intercession humility is obtained, ibid., 88. And forgiveness of sins, ibid., 604. On the praise and cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 210, 334; CLXXXIII, 55 ff., 159, 396, 428 ff. The hymn *Salve Regina* was composed by saints, ibid., CLXXXIV, 1059. It was sung four times a year, ibid. On the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Thomas Cistercian, CCVI. Mary is a lentil, ibid., 39. Mary, the neck, ibid., 122. Our rising and ascent, ibid., 357. She offers Christ, ibid., 436. Miracle, ibid., 479. She is compared to the rainbow, ibid., 646. Mary: star, moon, dawn, ibid., 649. Mary’s fullness, ibid. Her privileges, ibid., 699 ff. Mary our mother, ibid., 763. Praises of the Virgin Mary, Alan of Lille, CCX, 53. Blessed Mary, God’s tabernacle, palace of the heavenly king, treasury of virtues, ibid. Why she is called black, ibid., 56. Mary’s outward and inward beauty, ibid., 60. She is compared with the Church and with the turtledove, ibid. Mary’s body was assumed into heaven, ibid., 64. She was beautiful in face, ibid., 70. No sin ever reigned in Mary, ibid., 80. She is called an enclosed garden and sealed fountain, ibid., 81, 82. Her mind is paradise, ibid., 82. A gate passable to God alone, ibid., 85. Mary full of grace and knowledge, ibid., 87. How she was wounded, ibid. She is the dove that laments, ibid., 93. Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, ibid., 94. Her steps are virtues, ibid., 97. On the praises and cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the book entitled *Mariale*, Abbot Adam, CCXI, 699.

**PHYSICIAN.** On the duties of physicians, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 186.

**MEDITATION.** One must often devote oneself to sacred meditations, St Leo the Great, LIV, 186. See *Prayer*.

**MEMORIAL; FUNERARY MONUMENT.** Memorial monuments for the dead, St Augustine, XXXII, 719. Marble memorials for wealthy dead persons, ibid., XXXVI, 322. Churches adorned with memorials of martyrs, ibid., XXXVII, 1590. The ancient custom of visiting the memorials of apostles and martyrs, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 118, 331, 333, 383. In the sense of prayer, commemoration of the dead was customarily placed at the altar, Augustine, XXXII, 778. At the point of death Monica asks that remembrance of her be made at the altar, ibid.

**BEGGAR.** Many wealthy persons, ruined by want amid their weights of gold and silver, came to a beggar’s end, Jerome, XXV, 71. Almsgiving is owed to a beggar, Augustine, XXXVII, 1367. A beggar often sings from door to door the commandment of God, ibid., XXXVIII, 205. We are all God’s beggars, ibid., 366, 380, 410, 515. Who our beggars here are, from whom and what they ask, ibid., 411. Your soul begs before you for the bread it needs, ibid., 627. On the beggar, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 186.

**MEASURE.** On maintaining equality and justice in different measures, Richard of Fleury, CXXXVI, 1308.

**MERCHANT.** What merchants’ duties are, Theodulf, CV, 202.

**SOLDIER; MILITARY SERVICE.** Christians sometimes abandoned military service, and why, Prudentius, LX, 281. The armour of the Christian soldier, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 20. Soldiers were formerly marked with badges, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 663. Six things necessary for a soldier, ibid. Soldiers’ conversion is for the most part sincere and complete, ibid. Emperor Maurice forbids his soldiers to become monks, ibid., 662 ff. Formerly soldiers were barred from the clergy, ibid., 650. Resurrection of a certain soldier after he had seen places of punishment and blessedness, ibid., 384. On restraining soldiers’ plundering: Hincmar’s address to Charles the Bald, CXXV, 953 ff. On soldiers’ duties, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 149. Pope Urban’s sermon to Christian soldiers at the Council of Clermont, exhorting them to liberate the Holy Land, Guibert, CLVI, 684. The cross is immediately attached to soldiers’ garments, ibid., 702. Leaders themselves exhort their soldiers, ibid., 724. Christian piety flourished in the camps, ibid., 746. Many attained the palm of martyrdom, ibid., 747. Rule of the Knights Templar, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 856 ff. The Christian soldier is figuratively described, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1174. Three contests of the faithful, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 681. How unworthy it is for bishops themselves to grant ecclesiastical goods to soldiers, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1209. The example of St Martin, ibid., 1221. A man who fears God is an excellent fighter, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI. Among Armenians Christians were not allowed to serve as soldiers, William of Tyre, CCI, 293. Sermon to soldiers: how many lived holy lives in military service, Alan of Lille, CCX, 186. Alan reproves the soldiers of his own time, ibid.

**MISERY.** On the various pursuits of human beings, Innocent III, CCXVI, 706, 707. On the misery of rich and poor, ibid., 708. On the misery of slaves and masters, ibid., 709. On the misery of good and evil persons, ibid., 711. On the enemies of humankind, ibid., 712. On the sale of justice; on the insatiable desire of the greedy, ibid., 719. On unjust possession of riches, ibid., 722. On the short and miserable life of magnates, ibid., 728.

**MASS.** This word is found rather rarely in Augustine, ibid. Mass for the dead, ibid., XXXIII, 694; XL, 284. The Mass of the catechumens takes place after the sermon, ibid., XXXVIII, 324. The sacrifice of the Mass, Victor of Vita, LVIII, 190, note a. To celebrate Masses, ibid., 203, 213. Public, morning, Lenten, and funeral Masses, ibid., 233, note e. Masses over martyrs’ graves and bones, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 356, note 212. The Mass of the catechumens, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 117. Completed before Communion, ibid., 130, 140. Duration of Gallican and Roman Masses, ibid., 131, 224. Sung daily by the bishop, ibid., 142. Several Masses celebrated on the same day at one altar, ibid. Mass was prescribed only on feast days, ibid., 143. Those present at Mass did not always communicate, ibid., 144. Three Masses were celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and Transfiguration, ibid., 174. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for the dead, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 417, 441. Origin of the thirty Masses customarily celebrated for the dead, ibid., 441. Mass for the living in distress
having been placed, ibid., 442. With what dispositions Mass is to be heard or celebrated, ibid., 425. Formerly the Roman and Gallican Churches had differing customs in the celebration of Mass, ibid., 1187. Mass is not to be celebrated except in consecrated places, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 668. A fasting priest must celebrate Mass, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 576. During the solemn rites of Mass the bishop bestowed a blessing on the people, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 154. Three Masses at the Nativity of the Lord are offered to God as Creator, Redeemer, and Rewarder, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 656. At what hours Mass should be celebrated, John Beleth, CCII, 56. The souls of the faithful are raised through the sacrifice of the Mass, Peter Cantor, CCV, 105. Whether it is permissible to celebrate Mass in the vernacular language, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1231. St Ambrose prohibited this at Milan, id., 1249. [Col. 0647] On the celebration of Mass, Sicard, CCXIII, 13.

MITRE. What the two horns of the mitre signify, Peter Cantor, CCV, 139.

MONK. In former times countless monks flourished in Egypt and Mesopotamia, Jerome, XXIV, 188. Of the monks at Carthage, some supported themselves by the work of their hands; others thought it right to live from the offerings of the faithful, Augustine, XXXII, 638. What they are accustomed to do and in what spirit they ought to act, id., XXXIII, 190. Many fast continually, except on Saturday and Sunday, ibid., 139. They are called servants of God, ibid., 993. The good pursuits of monks, id., XXXVII, 1278. Monks are called Fathers, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 341; and nuns, Mothers, ibid., note. He is not a monk who seeks a possession on earth, ibid., 245. They ought to devote themselves to sacred reading, ibid., 606. According to Gregory, monks are to be tested for two years, ibid., 1082. Clerics, rather than monks, ought to live from the altar, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 607. The frequency of guests among the monks of Clairvaux, ibid. On the new clothing of monks, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 636. The remarkable hospitality of the monks at Cluny, Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 370. Each person ought to retain the colour which he has chosen, ibid., 406. The reason and order for fulfilling a vow, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 593. What it signifies to be shod with sandals or shoes, id., CXCII, 220. Baths are to be avoided by a monk, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 787. The condition of clerics is more perilous than that of monks, ibid., 794. Whether monks may ride on horseback, ibid., 818. Singularity is to be most carefully avoided in a community, Peter Cantor, CCV, 205.

NUN. FEMALE MONK. The profession and dwelling of nuns, Augustine, XXXII, 1339. Their food and clothing are distributed to them by the prioress, id., XXXIII, 960. How they ought to regard one another, ibid., 961. The use of baths is permitted once a month, ibid., 963. They should obey the prioress as a mother, ibid., 964. In former times nuns were not veiled immediately after taking the vow of virginity, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 681. They devoted effort to copying sacred books, ibid., 172. Some were assigned possessions by their parents, ibid., 272. Gregory judges that Rome was preserved by their holiness, id., 881. Certain women were excommunicated because of unrestrained speech, id., LXVI, in the Life of St Benedict.

DYING PERSON. Prayers by which a dying person is commended to God, A. Prudentius, CLIX, 886.

DEATH. Not to be feared by Christians, St Julian, XCVI, 467. The death of those who live piously ought not to grieve us, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 717. For the miserable, death becomes deathlessness, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1063.

THE DEAD. See *Defuncti* [the deceased].

WOMAN. A woman effaces God’s image if she coats her face with material whiteness and covers it with an acquired blush, Ambrose, XIV, 260. Women who come to church in proud apparel are reproved, Augustine, XXXVIII, 205. What sort of hair becomes women, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 727. Among the ancients women spun wool; hence wool-working women were held in honour, Arator, LXVIII, 162, note 812. Women’s singing and choirs in church are to be forbidden, Leo IV, CXV, 681. Women must not touch sacred vessels or altar-cloths, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 30. On women, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 191; Guigo the Carthusian, CLIII, 681. The female sex is hostile to friends, Goffridus, CLVII, 67. It is accustomed to deceive, ibid., 126. A woman ought not approach the altar, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 169. Woman as a type of human frailty, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 152, 361.

WORLD. It is a battlefield with the devil and vices, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 231. In this world nothing is stable; all prosperity is thrown into confusion by adversity, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 647. Let the mind despise the pomps of the world, ibid., 1275. “World” denotes people deceived by love of the world, Alcuin, C, 747.

OFFICE. The offices of every ecclesiastical rank—provost, porter, weekly minister, doorkeeper, acolyte, exorcist, psalmist, reader, subdeacon, deacon, priest, bishop, archdeacon, primicerius, treasurer, and steward—St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 897.

MYSTERIES. This word is frequently used for the sacrifice of the Mass. Catechumens, possessed persons, and penitents do not attend the sacred mysteries, Gennadius, LVIII, 1027. On the sacred mysteries of the Church, John of Garland, fragment of a poem.

NATAL DAYS. Created potentially, Augustine, XXXIV, 326. The natal days of saints are to be celebrated soberly, id., XXXVII, 1141. The natal days of saints are called the days on which they passed out of this world, Alcuin, C, 956. Why they are celebrated joyfully, CI, 1211.

MERCHANT. His duties, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 159.

NEOPHYTE. Milk was formerly given to neophytes, St Zeno, XI, 478. In former times they were sometimes ordained bishops, St Jerome, XXII, 663; and XXIII, 516. On neophytes, Augustine, XXXIII, 220. The beginnings of neophytes, id., XL, 208. A neophyte formerly meant one newly planted in the faith; now it means one new in holy conduct, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 781. They are excluded from orders, ibid.

NEPHEWS. It is wicked for bishops to take more care of nephews than of the poor, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 178.

NICAEA. The privileges of this city, William of Tyre, CCI, 274. It is besieged by the crusaders and, with much toil and loss, taken by assault, 279, 282, 288.

NOBILITY. On the worthlessness of human nobility and the excellence of poverty, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 7.

ILLEGITIMATE CHILD. In Gaul illegitimate children are excluded from ecclesiastical dignities, Stephen, CCXI, 378.

ROMAN PENNY. A certain tribute payable to the supreme pontiff by the law of Cnut, king of the English, CLI, 1174.

MARRIAGE. See *Conjugium* [marriage].

OFFERING. How the offerings of the faithful are to be distributed, Gelasius I, LIX, 56. Votive offerings were formerly contributed for the relief of the poor, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 562. On offerings made for the departed faithful, St Julian, XCVI, 475. On the intercession of saints and the necessity of prayers and sacred offerings, Hincmar, CXXV, 900. Those who retain or defraud pious offerings for the dead are to be excommunicated, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 399. On revenues and the offerings of the Church, Regino, CXXXII, 232. On offerings for the dead, ibid., 355 ff. No one is to give or receive Church offerings except with the bishop’s permission, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 35. On Fulcher’s gifts offered to the church of St Andrew, Author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, CXLIX, 263. Blessed bread is also called the “crown of offering” (*corona oblationis*), Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 994. What has once been given to the Church must never be taken away from it, Placidus, CLXIII, 634. Various offerings made to the monastery of Monte Cassino, Leo of Marsi, CLXXIII, 534, 552, 564, 569, 588, 598, 611, 649, 660, 688, 694, 704, 731, 732, 740, 756, 769, 771, 775, 778, 781, 792, 794, 796, 822, 832, 848, 873, 882, 892. St Monica, wishing to offer offerings at Milan according to the custom of the African Church, was forbidden by St Ambrose, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 403.

OCTAVES. The third day of the octave, or even the eighth, was chosen by some for celebrating the washing of feet, Augustine, XXXIII, 220. Newly baptized persons who during their octave touched the ground with a bare foot are customarily severely punished, ibid., 221. The octave of the regenerate, id., XXXV, 1235. The octave of infants, XXXVIII, 1201. The holy day of the octave, XL, 581.

DIVINE OFFICE. St Gregory called the Divine Office the work of God, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 688. In the sixth century, Offices were performed by their own clergy or by neighbouring clergy wherever the relics of saints were kept, ibid. How the Divine Office should be heard, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 859. How many Lord’s Prayers should be recited if the Divine Office cannot be heard, ibid. On the Office of Tenebrae in Holy Week, John Beleth, CCII, 105. Why Christians formerly rose three times during the night for the Office, ibid., 31. On the Offices of Lent, ibid., 90. On the Office of the Dead, 159 ff. On the Offices of the Church, Sicard, CCXIII, 149, 159, 162 ff.

OIL. Why oil, rather than wax, was formerly burned in a church, Jerome, XXII, 1097. Blessed oil heals the bites of venomous animals, id., XXIII, 46. It is oil’s nature to sustain light and relieve the weariness of the fatigued, ibid., 1085. Oil blessed for administering the sacrament, Augustine, XLIII, 190. Visible oil is in the sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament, id., XXXVI, 505. Though Christ’s oil is administered through a sinner, it is not therefore the sinner’s oil, id., XXXVIII, 1225, 1229. Oil should be carried with one, ibid., 577. Whoever has oil with him does not seek a sinner’s oil, id., XXXVII, 1824. Why anointing with oil is frequently employed, Cassiodorus, LXX, 170. Christians venerate oil which has burned over the tombs of saints, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 459. Oil signifies the gentleness of piety, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 38. What it means to take oil in vessels with lamps, ibid., 1156. Blessing of oil, Anonymous, CXXXVIII, 1063. Innocent I decreed that not only priests but all Christians might use oil blessed by a bishop, Sigebert, CLX, 72. The three kinds of holy oil, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 577. The nature and properties of oil, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 523, 996.

VEGETABLE. Heretics rejected vegetables, Augustine, XLII, 235. Why vegetables ought to be eaten, Richard of St Victor, CXCVI, 499.

WORK. Although many are silent in speech, they speak by their deeds, Jerome, XXII, 418. The usefulness of labour and work, ibid. Work without faith is frail and unstable, ibid., 808. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied, ibid., 1078. Monks who live by the work of their hands, Augustine, XXXII, 638. Good works must be attributed to God, ibid., 1078. To God’s grace, not to one’s own powers, XXXIII, 688. What human work in Paradise was like, id., XXXIV, 204. [Col. 0649] Good works come not from us but from God, id., XXXV, 1843. Works together with faith are necessary, id., XXXVI, 259. The necessity of good works, ibid., 482. The highest work of a human being is to praise God, ibid., 500. Works of mercy ought to overcome our offences, id., XXXVIII, 1199. Against idle monks unwilling to work, id., XL, 566. Good works are weighed by God, Salvian, LIII, 181. We ought to be rich in good works, ibid. Christ is the rewarder of all works, ibid., 201. Everlasting goods follow upon good works, ibid., 220. After this life, fire will test each person’s work, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 309. Works of mercy are commended, ibid., 44. Good works lay forceful claim upon heaven, ibid., 346. They are necessary for salvation, ibid., 723. When the time for good works is anticipated, merit is lost, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 75. Christian life consists in the virtue of works, not in the display of signs, ibid., 213. Good works must be undertaken while there is time, ibid., 1094. What is learned through law and reading must be put into practice, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 798. The exercise of good works is in a human being like the very best age of life, ibid., 739. God must be glorified even in the smallest things, ibid., 774. Shadow signifies toil and day signifies reward, Wolbero, CXCV, 1156. See *Action*, *Labour*.

OPPRESS. What St Isidore of Seville thinks of oppressors of the poor, LXXXIII, 728. Hincmar of Rheims’s address to Charles the Bald, id., CXXV, 953 ff., and 1017. Why the just are oppressed by the wicked, St Bruno, CLIII, 415.

PRAYER. Christians formerly prayed facing east, Tertullian, I, 273; with heads uncovered, ibid., 442; in common, ibid., 1168; before and after food, ibid., 477; with hands spread out in the form of a cross, ibid., 1169; and frequently for the king, St Hilary of Poitiers. Prayers at the altar, St Optatus, XI, 975. Christians praying in churches stretched out their hands, St Zeno, XI, 334. The day is not enough for prayer: one must rise by night and at midnight, St Ambrose, XV, 1313. On most days one must come to church as soon as the noon hours arrive, sing hymns, and celebrate the offering, ibid., 1314. Prayer is especially to be made by night and morning, ibid., 1414. It was Christian custom always to pray to God, St Jerome. They prayed with the knee placed upon the ground, id., XXVI, 486. We accomplish more by common and responsive prayers than by solitary and private ones, Augustine, XXXIII, 788. In an oratory nothing else should be done except that for which it was made and from which it received its name, ibid., 960. Prayer for the dead, id., XXXV, 1847. Prayer before food, XLIV, 176. Morning prayer and commending oneself are to be performed by everyone, John Cassian, XLIX, 1201. Why knees are not bent in public prayer during Eastertide, ibid., 110. A brother is to be helped by prayer, fasting, and tears, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 210. A bishop should devote himself especially to prayer, St Leo the Great, 655. One must not pray or chant psalms with heretics, ibid., 665. He knows how to live rightly who knows how to pray, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 499. Prayer before and after food, Gennadius, LVIII, 1037. At sunrise, and turned toward the east, Christians poured out prayers, A. Prudentius, LIX, 790. Prayers are to be made morning, evening, and noon, ibid., 802. The power of the prayer of many, ibid., 829, note 139. The Christian custom of calling on God in every action, ibid., 860. Prayers over a dying person, ibid., 886. On prayer, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 671. On prayer at the time of the Greater Litany before Ascension Sunday, XCIV, 168. The praise and constancy of prayer, St Benedict, CIII, 803. Toward which regions of heaven Christians should turn in prayer, Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 922. On manners of praying and the interval between voices, ibid., 932. On the praise and usefulness of prayer, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 898. A domestic oratory, Isaac, CXXIV, 1106. Stephen VI, pope, fully explains why prayers performed in a church are more readily heard, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1400. The great efficacy of prayer, Peter Damian, CXLV, 230. On the prayer over the people in Lent, *Liturgical Monuments*, CXI, 1014. Silence must be observed while prayer is being made, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 870. The manner of praying, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 89, 90. Three kinds of prayer, ibid., 879 ff. Thirteen books on prayer, Gunther, CCII, 97. On the elements of prayer: namely, who asks, what is asked, from whom it is asked, for whom it is asked, why, and how it is asked, ibid., 115.

THE LORD’S PRAYER was recited at the altar, St Optatus, XI, 975; likewise Jerome, XXIII, 785. Explanation of it, ibid. Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, Augustine, XXXIII, 503. What might anyone ask for that is not found in the Lord’s Prayer? 504. Why it was handed down in words, ibid., XXXV, 1275. The preface to this prayer, ibid., 1276. In it three petitions concern eternal life and four temporal life, ibid., 1285. The Lord’s Prayer: a rule for petitioning given to the apostles by the heavenly Jurist, id., XXXVII, 1849. It is said daily at the altar, id., XXXVIII, 399. It is daily medicine, ibid., 127. Our daily cleansing, ibid., XLIV, 435. [Col. 0650] If said truthfully, it daily remits sins, id., XLV, 1232. The Lord’s Prayer is sung by all at Mass, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 955. The Lord’s Prayer is to be recited by one unable to attend the Divine Office, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 859. On the Lord’s Prayer, which is frequently used in every Office, ibid., CXCIV, 1549.

ORDINATION is signified by the laying on of hands, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1090. By whom, when, and how ordinations should be performed, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 431.

ORDER. Under the name of sacred order, both major and minor orders are sometimes understood, Gregory the Great. See vol. LXV, in the Life of St Benedict, and LXXVII, 695. Orders ought not to be repeated, ibid., 584. Why divine providence established diverse orders in the Church, ibid., 785, 786. What principal qualifications Gregory required in candidates for ordination, ibid., 575, 694. Those now to be examined, ibid., 695. Laymen should not be promoted immediately to sacred orders, ibid., 784, 785, 953.

EAST. Before sunrise, and turned toward the east, Christians poured out prayers, A. Prudentius, LIX, 790. Basilicas facing east, St Paulinus, LXI, 336.

KISS. The kiss of peace among the sacraments, Augustine, XXXVIII, 1025. When kisses were customary among Christians at church doors, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 518. The kiss of peace precedes reception of the Eucharist, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 304. The custom of kissing knees as a sign of reverence, St Benedict, CIII, 764. The most ancient custom of kissing the feet of the supreme pontiff, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1278, 1306, 1350. Emperor Charlemagne humbly kisses the steps of St Peter’s basilica in the Vatican, II, 78. Pope Innocent I decreed that the kiss of peace should be given at Masses, Sigebert, CLX, 72. A kiss is a sign of friendship, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 755.

SHEEP. Sick sheep abandon their shepherd and are devoured in the jaws of wolves, Jerome, XXII, 1122. Every part of a sheep was carried, ibid., 654. What it means for sheep to drink water muddied by the feet of shepherds, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 15. By the name of sheep are signified all who are simple and innocent, Garnerius, CXCIII, 105. How sheep ought to follow their shepherd, Peter Cantor, CCV, 121.

CHAFF. By chaff the wicked are to be understood, Garnerius, CXCIII, 442.

ALTAR-CLOTH. What altar-cloths were among the ancients, St Optatus, XI, 1077, note 87. Altar-cloths from the tombs of saints, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 886.

PALLIUM. How it differs from the Greek *homophorion*, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 481, note. Pallia are priestly and sacred vestments, which were also precious in monasteries, ibid., 524. Whether the material and form of the pallium were the same in East and West, ibid., 558, note. Which Roman pontiff first gave the pallium, ibid., 558. To whom it was granted, ibid., 481. Gregory did not grant it to everyone, ibid., 558. A bishop is reproved for using it proudly, ibid., 651. On the use of the pallium, *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, CV, 81–88. The pallium is granted rarely and with difficulty, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 657. On men’s pallia, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 573. On women’s pallia, 575.

PALM SUNDAY. The very ancient solemnity of Palm Sunday in the Church, at which a procession is held with blessed branches of trees, Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 310. Blessed palm branches, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 473.

BLESSED BREAD. Blessed bread, also called the crown of offering (*corona oblationis*), Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 994. See *Agape*.

CLOTH. Cloths laid upon saints’ tombs are regarded as relics, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 924.

POPE. See *Apostolic See*.

PREPARATION DAY. The Jews also call the Preparation Day the “pure supper,” Augustine, XXXVIII, 190. Veneration of the Holy Cross on the day of Preparation, Alcuin, CI, 1210. See *Cross*.

PARISH (*parochia*, *paroecia*). *Parochia* or *paroecia* and *dioecesis* are used interchangeably, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 548, 549, 812. In Gregory’s time there were several parishes in one city, ibid., 661. Each parish is to be governed under the bishop’s oversight, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 668. Establishment of parishes under Pope St Dionysius, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1418. On parishes, Regino, CXXXII, 195.

PARISH PRIEST. Tithes are to be paid by laypeople to their own parish priests, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 918. Travellers must first seek permission from their parish priest, ibid., 1088.

EASTER. The Lord’s Pascha is celebrated every year in springtime, Ambrose, XIV, 128. It must be celebrated by those who are chaste and sanctified, ibid., 281. Why it is called the Lord’s Pascha, ibid., 332. What the first day of Pascha was, Juvencus, XIX, 314. Pascha celebrated in spring, St Gaudentius, XX, 843, note. Sometimes in the second month, ibid., 845. The time for celebrating Pascha, ibid., 847. On Pascha, Jerome, XXII, 813. What is required for celebrating Pascha, ibid., 811. Bishops of Asia celebrate Pascha with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, XXIII, 657. Pascha is celebrated both in sacrament and in remembrance of the event that occurred, Augustine, XXXIII, 205. The passing-over, signified by the word *Pascha*, now takes place in us through faith, hope, and charity, ibid., 205, 206. Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Pascha according to calculations of sun and moon, ibid., 209. In the celebration of Pascha, the three days of the crucified, buried, and risen Lord must be observed, ibid., 215. During Eastertide Christians relax their fasts, pray standing, and sing Alleluia, the sign of redemption, ibid., 218. Christ’s immolation is the true Pascha, id., XXXV, 1785. The celebration of Pascha is annual, id., XXXVI, 171. Let us celebrate the Easter vigil outwardly and inwardly: so that God may speak to us in his readings, and we may speak to God in our prayers, id., XXXVIII, 1088. On this night the hostile world and the reconciled world keep vigil, ibid. The Paschal solemnity does not join old things to new, but weans the infancy of the new regeneration, and other matters, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 406. It is a harbour, life’s gain, and the joy of resurrection, ibid., 208. How the Lamb of God is sacrificed in it, ibid., 374. The question of Pascha was long and much debated, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 947. Announcement of Pascha was entrusted to the Roman pontiff, ibid., 948. This announcement was made on Epiphany, ibid. In Sardinia the announcement of Pascha belonged to the metropolitan, ibid., 947. The Churches of Gaul first adopted Anatolius’s Paschal Cycle, ibid., 1062. On the time when Pascha ought to be celebrated, Venerable Bede, XC, 599, and CXIV, 675. On arranging the Paschal feast-days, id., XC, 607. One Alleluia is sung at Easter, two on the following Saturday, Alan of Lille, CCX, 210.

SHEPHERD. The distress of sheep is the fault of shepherds and the vice of teachers, Jerome, XXVI, 60. Exhortation to the shepherds of the Church, ibid., 54. Who the good shepherd is and what his office is, ibid., 241. Whoever is a shepherd ought also to be a teacher, ibid., 500. False shepherds in the Church, ibid. Good shepherds are made from good sheep, Augustine, XXXVIII, 287. There is one good shepherd, because all good shepherds are one in him, ibid. The duties of shepherds and sheep, ibid., 796. How perilous an account shepherds must render, ibid. A shepherd is comforted in dangers because he is assisted by the prayers of his people, ibid., 915. An evil shepherd is such by his own wickedness; a good one only by God’s grace, id., XXXIX, 1484. Consult the *Pastoral Book* of Pope St Gregory, LXXVII, 13 ff.

HEAD OF A HOUSEHOLD. His care and discipline regarding his household, Augustine, XXXVI, 599. A father is pious when striking, and cruel when sparing, id., XXXVIII, 111. The householder provides for all his household, as for children, that they may worship and win God’s favour, id., XLII, 644. He ought to take precepts from the law of the state by which to govern his house, ibid., 645. Parents’ care and anxiety concerning their children, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 293. What a householder should do and what account he will render to God, ibid., 274. The title “father” is divine, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1108. A fatherly address always adds something to good minds, ibid., 1049. On father and mother, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 201.

PATIENCE. On the praise of patience, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 908. Adversities are to be endured patiently, Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 437. Patience is the queen of virtues, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 791.

PATRIMONY. The patrimony of the Church must not be diminished but rather increased, Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 137. Church estates were in various provinces, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 444.

GODPARENT. Godparents must teach the Lord’s Prayer to their godchildren, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 684. The godparents’ response for their godchildren, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 136. On the same subject, id., CLXXVII, 390. Why godparents are employed at baptism, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 844.

PATRON. Martyrs and saints are rightly called patrons, A. Prudentius, LX, 278, note. See *Saints*.

POOR PERSON; POVERTY. Care for the poor is the greatest work of ministry, St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 356. Christ feeds the poor when he invites assistance for their relief, ibid., 743. Exchange between poor and rich, ibid., 1060. Let the harshness of poverty not humble us, Jerome, XXII, 826. Whoever is poor with Christ is rich, ibid., 348. Give to the poor, not to the wealthy, not to the proud, ibid., 643. What use is it for walls to gleam with gems while Christ is in peril in the poor person? ibid., 584. Poverty chosen voluntarily brings glory; poverty imposed brings torment, ibid., 1077. The poor in spirit are understood to be the humble and those who fear God, Augustine, XXXV, 1232. The poor are the Lord’s feet, ibid., 1760. A poor person’s patrimony is health, XXXVI, 610, 971. Whoever is not puffed up amid abundance of resources is reckoned by God among the poor, ibid., 545, 1057. It benefits a poor person nothing if he lacks wealth and burns with greed, ibid., 609. He has given up much who has given up not only whatever he possessed, [Col. 0652] but also whatever he desired to possess, id., XXXVII, 1371. God’s poor person is poor in spirit, not merely in worldly circumstances, ibid., 1727, 1814. A poor person possessed by greed is worse than a rich one, id., XXXVIII, 114. A true poor person is scarcely found among a crowd of poor persons, ibid. The poor person is a citizen of the kingdom of heaven; by what we give him, he conveys us there, ibid., 240. Christ must be clothed and received in the poor person, ibid., 170. Poverty in itself is neither blessedness nor misery, ibid., 327. Care for the poor, ibid., 433. Friendship with the poor is to be acquired by alms, ibid., 250. Voluntary poverty belongs to Christian perfection, id., XLIII, 341. The poor person carries our goods to heaven and has God as surety for this, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 208. He preserves for us what the belly would have squandered, ibid., 210. The poor person is Abraham’s bosom, heaven’s treasure, Christ’s treasury, ibid., 210. Modest poverty is fearful, ibid., 213. For one thing given to a poor person, God gives you a hundred, ibid., 271. What a poor person should do, ibid., 275. A poor person who does not know how to lend at interest does not know how to be healed, ibid., 290. Poverty is kin to the virtues; its examples are the athlete, sailor, soldier, and philosopher, ibid., 278. Temporal poverty is scarcely bearable; how much more eternal poverty, ibid., 349. Poverty advances a person toward philosophy, ibid., 541. For whom poverty is burdensome, Salvian, LIII, 32. True poor persons delight in poverty, ibid., 31. God chose them in this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, ibid., 68. The poor are the Easter of the rich, ibid., 75. The plundering of the very poor is the greatest of all plunderings, ibid. As though placed amid storms, ibid., 101. Poverty has nothing that it can lose, ibid., 117. The crosses of the poor groaning to God, ibid., 144. Christ says that the evils of the poor are his own, ibid., 232. Formerly the Church supported the poor, Prudentius, LX, 306, note 159. Which poor persons should be admonished, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 52. Poor persons to be consoled, ibid. It often happens that a rich person is humble and a poor one proud, ibid., 574. Whether alms should be given to a poor sinner, ibid., 85. Alms are not to be made from the spoils of the poor, ibid., 89. The goods of the Church are the goods of the poor, 619. Poverty is the guardian of humility, ibid., 189. The security of poverty is to be preferred to riches, ibid., 245. What Isidore of Seville thinks of oppressors of the poor, LXXXIII, 728. The hand of the poor person is Christ’s treasury, Alcuin, C, 316. Poverty is tranquil if it is governed by the helm of humility, ibid., 455. Poverty is to be loved, id., 777. Ecclesiastical property consists of the vows of the faithful and is the patrimony of the poor, Hincmar, CXXVI, 128. The poor are visited much better through alms than by bodily presence, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1085. Christ’s poor are our brothers, ibid., 454, 1183. The poor and the aged are to be honoured, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 348. Defenders of the poor against the powerful must be established, ibid., 351. Evangelical poverty, St Anselm, CLVIII, 595. The benefits of poverty, ibid., 693. The causes of the poor, widows, and orphans must be heard and decided first, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 955. For the miserable, death becomes deathlessness, ibid., 1063. On the commandment concerning the poor, Rupert, CLXX, 146. Encomium of poverty, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 125. The Church’s goods belong not to the king but to the poor, Gerohus, CXCIV, 121. St Martin, lover of the poor, ibid., 1226. A fourth part of tithes is to be distributed to widows and the poor, ibid., 1309. A certain blessed poverty, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 23. The kingdom of God is bought with poverty, ibid., 411. On the worthlessness of human nobility and the excellence of poverty, Peter of Blois, CCVI, 7. On seeking out the poor, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1146. See *Almsgiving*.

PAVEMENT. On cleansing the pavement of a church, John Beleth, CCII, 108.

PEACE. Whoever does not take care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 89. What admonitions should be given to cultivators of peace, ibid., 90. Temporal peace is a trace of eternal peace, ibid. Peace should be maintained with everyone, if possible, ibid., 1121. Peace is to be maintained with all people, Alcuin, C, 1023. It is to be kept with the good, not with criminals, CI, 617. It is the mother of love, ibid. Why “Peace be with you” is sung at Mass, ibid., 1249. On God’s peace toward human beings, Bishop Rufinus, CL, 1597. On the peace of conscience possessed here by the good, ibid., 1607. On the condition of domestic peace, ibid., 1621. On the peace of Jerusalem, namely the Church, ibid., 1625. On the kiss of peace, ibid., 1634.

FURRIER. What furriers dependent upon the convent of Fleury are obliged to pay each year, Richard, CXXXVI, 1304.

PILGRIMAGE; PILGRIM. St Jerome’s pilgrimage to Egypt and the East, Pope St Damasus, id., XIII, 158. While we are pilgrims, the sure hope of our return consoles and exhorts us, Augustine, XXXVII, 1884. Pilgrimages from the various regions of the whole world to the thresholds of the apostles, Leo the Great, LIV, 513. Pilgrimages to St Sergius, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 435; likewise to the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul, ibid., 377; to the Holy Places, [Col. 0653] ibid., 435; to St James in Spain, ibid., 1115. Pilgrimage to Jerusalem, ibid. The pilgrimage of Basil and Eubulus to the holy places at Jerusalem, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 299. Likewise that of a certain Leontius to the tombs of the holy martyrs Cyrus and John in Alexandria, ibid., 361. Pilgrimage to the church of St Cyrus, ibid., 361; to St John the martyr, ibid., 366. The pilgrimage of Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, ibid., 415. Likewise that of Adolius to Jerusalem, 1192. Roman and Jerusalem pilgrimage, ibid., 1196. Talletaeus visits the holy places at Jerusalem, id., LXXIV, 165. Christopher travels toward Jerusalem to venerate the cross, ibid., 171. Pilgrimage of a certain Peter to Mount Sinai, ibid., 169. The same man’s pilgrimage to St Menas in Alexandria, ibid.; and to Christ’s tomb at Jerusalem, ibid. To Mount Sinai, ibid., 204. To the holy places, ibid., 238. John undertakes various pilgrimages, ibid., 211. Annual pilgrimages undertaken for religious reasons, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 264. On St Eligius’s pilgrimage to the Holy Places and his care for the needy, id., LXXXVII, 498. With what great kindness he cared for pilgrims, ibid., 508. St Ambrose, bishop of Cahors, having laid aside the episcopal office, makes a pilgrimage to Rome, to the thresholds of the holy apostles, id., LXXXIX, 1228. St Benedict, an English bishop, makes a pilgrimage to Rome, Venerable Bede, XCIV, 714. Roman pilgrimage, Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 335. Distinguished men from every region, including Saxon kings with many others, made religious pilgrimages to Rome, to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 951, 1355. Among these pilgrims were Theudo, duke of Bavaria, ibid., 175; and Charlemagne, emperor of the Franks, ibid., 1178. Concerning a certain pilgrim who was captured and delivered from chains through the assistance of St Faith, Bernard the Schoolmaster, CXLI, 151. On the gathering of people from the whole world at the Lord’s tomb in Jerusalem, Rodulfus Glaber, CXLII, 679. For whom pilgrimage is expedient, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 455. The pilgrim as an example of divine providence, ibid., 456, 484. How highly the pilgrimage to Monte Cassino should be valued, CXLV, 562. Our pilgrimage is twofold, St Bruno, CLII, 936. Itinerary of a certain Dermatius, an Irishman setting out for Jerusalem, id., CLV, 485. The Jerusalem journey of Peter Tudebode, priest of Civray, ibid., 667. Description of the holy places, ibid., 1084. Privileges granted to the Church of Jerusalem, ibid., 1111 ff. A vow of pilgrimage, St Anselm, CLIX, 57. Pilgrimage of a certain Fursy, an Irishman, Sigebert, CLX, 122. Seven thousand pilgrims seek Jerusalem in fulfilment of a vow of prayer, but are besieged by Arabs in a certain castle on Preparation Day and slain, so that scarcely two thousand return, ibid., 214. On Roman and Tours pilgrimages, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 877. On those who make pilgrimages under a pretext of religion, ibid. On administering a hospice in which pilgrims are received, ibid. On pilgrims who go to Rome, ibid., 896. Pilgrims and fugitives must be restrained, ibid., 959. Peter the Hermit makes a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Albert of Aachen, CLXVI, 390. There pilgrims are very often plundered and oppressed, ibid. Concerning a certain Walter going to Jerusalem—what he did and suffered, ibid., 392. Christians came to Jerusalem from the remotest parts of the whole world, Baldric, CLXVI, 1065. Pagans harassed Christians with many compulsory services, ibid. Hence zeal and ardour to fight the pagans, ibid., 1069, 1070. Whether holy pilgrimages are to be approved, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1152. Pilgrimage in a mystical sense, ibid., 205, 929. A certain monk Bernard, with two companions, made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem about the year 870, and an itinerary
described it, William, CLXXX, 1318. What peace Christians enjoyed in those places at this time, ibid. Charlemagne had established there a hospice for pilgrims, ibid. Those going on pilgrimage should first obtain permission from their own parish priest, Robert Pullen, 1088. On the pilgrimage of the king of the Franks to St. Thomas of Canterbury, and its cause, Herbert of Bosham, CXC, 1309. How the king entered Canterbury as a pilgrim, ibid., 1315. How the king, returning from his pilgrimage, departed from Canterbury, ibid., 1319. What it is to go on pilgrimage, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 39. We are pilgrims in the body, ibid. How, about 1190, crowds of the faithful hastened to the holy city of Jerusalem, and under what conditions they were treated both inside and outside it, William of Tyre, CCI, 226. Hence Peter the Hermit went on pilgrimage, ibid., 227. A poorly disciplined army of pilgrims perishes, ibid., 241. While still a young man, St. Martin of León undertook many pilgrimages to overcome the temptations of the flesh, id., CCVIII, 12. At one time to the threshold of St. James in Galicia, ibid., 13. At another, to Rome, to the Thresholds of the Apostles; thence to Constantinople, where he bought an exceptional chasuble, which he carried about everywhere, ibid.

**DANGER.** In all dangers, if faith remains in us, the defense of spiritual virtues is present, St. Hilary of Poitiers, [Col. 0654] IX, 787. Nothing is more burdensome to a person than awareness of danger, id., X, 200. Those who are advancing as members of Christ must pass through three dangers, Augustine, XXXIV, 820. Whoever does not guard against danger puts God to the test, id., XLI, 498. — What ought to be done in dangers, Guigo, CLIII, 737.

**PERSECUTION.** Flight during persecutions is permitted, St. Prosper, LI, 381. In a time of persecution one must not withdraw from the wood of the cross, ibid., 295. When persecution was imminent, baptism was formerly hastened, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 708. Martyrs approached battle with their foreheads marked by the cross, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 236.

**PERSEVERANCE.** What it is, Alcuin, CI, 945. It is commended in good works, ibid., 632. An exhortation to persevere in the good that has been begun, Bishop Placidus, CLXIII, 673.

**PIETY.** The beginning of piety is to think most rightly of God, Augustine, XXXII, 1224. True piety is the worship of the true God, id., XXXIII, 673. What the perfection of piety is, id., XXXIV, 132. What true piety is, id., XLI, 159, 160. Piety is the most sacred bond of the human race, id., XLII, 84. Piety is useful for all things, Salvian, LIII, 176. Examples of piety, ibid., 164. What exercises of piety ought to be, Alcuin, C, 472. Definition of piety, id., CI, 944.

**STREET.** Streets to be avoided, St. Ambrose, XVI, 279.

**CANONICAL PENALTIES**, inflicted for various offences, Richard, CXXXVI, 1309, 1310. On canonical penalties, Burchard, CXL, 777. See under *Penance*.

**PENANCE; PENITENT.** Who should be compelled to public penance, Augustine, XL, 18. Public penance was imposed for heinous sins, not for slight ones, ibid., 636. Haircloth, the garment of penitents, Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 438. Formula of absolution by which penitents were reconciled to the Church on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, ibid., 445. At what part of the Mass this absolution was given to penitents, ibid. On the praise and usefulness of penance, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 928. On penitents who die suddenly, Regino, CXXXII, 214. On giving penance, ibid., 246. On penitents, ibid., 252. On penance for various sins, ibid., 287, 289, 291, 293, 297, 300, 302, 303. Penitents bend the knee daily, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46. Dead penitents are to be buried, ibid. Penitents should abstain from secular business, ibid. Penance is to be imposed according to the nature of the sin, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 843. Treatise on penance, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1519. Ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penance, Peter Cantor, CCV, 348.

**PEOPLE.** Two peoples: the faithful and the unbelieving; the predestined and the reprobate, Augustine, XXXV, 1507. All those who bear God’s sacraments are now counted as the people of God, but not all belong to his mercy, id., XXXVI, 538. *Populus* and *turba* differ, id., XXXVIII, 614. A people is not every gathering of a multitude, but an association united by agreement in law and a sharing of common advantage, id., XLI, 67, 648. Where the people truly is, ibid., 655. One must speak popularly to peoples, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 320. The people washed their garments and bodies when about to hear God’s law, ibid., 362. They are invited to hear the Gospel, ibid., 495. Envy devastates peoples, ibid., 649. How a newly converted people should be taught and guided, Alcuin, C, 194.

**POSSESSION.** Christians may possess property, Augustine, XXXII, 1343. Possession of an earthly thing: what is lawful by divine law and what by human law, id., XXXIII, 345. All possessions are held by human law, id., XXXV, 1437. Possession of temporal things: how innocence is recognized from it, id., XXXVIII, 694. From possession of private property arise disputes and many evils, which are removed where things are possessed in common, id., XXXVII, 1748. Extensive possessions are to be avoided, Salvian, LIII, 202. Ecclesiastical possessions: see *Goods*.

**PRACTICE.** The origin of practical science and its division, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 745.

**PREBEND.** The grant of prebends may be transferred from one person to another, Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 483.

**ROYAL OR PONTIFICAL PRECEPTS.** Charlemagne’s enactments for the benefit of the Church, id., XCVII, 913 ff.; those of Louis I, CIV, 979–1308. On royal and imperial enactments, Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 475. Enactments of King Robert, CXLI, 945 ff.; of William, king of the English, id., CXLIX, 1350 ff.; of Emperors Conrad II, Henry III, and Henry IV, CLI, 1043–1164; of Godfrey of Bouillon in Jerusalem, CLV, 1111 ff.

**PRELATE.** See *Bishop*.

**REWARD.** God sets forth a reward so that we may do what he commands more by loving the good than by fearing evil, Augustine, XXXVIII, 123. Rewards suited to individual works, ibid., 367. There will be different degrees of reward in heaven, id., XLI, 802. A reward is appointed for those who must contend, in proportion to the greatness of the contest, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 259. A grateful mind leads to reward, ibid., 541. When a reward is received from the crown from which guilt had already been incurred, ibid., [Col. 0655] 564. Who may confidently demand a reward from Christ, ibid., 646. The reward of Christians, Salvian, LIII, 57. Fees must not be demanded either for baptism, penance, or burial of the dead, Leo IV, CXV, 678.

**PRESBYTER.** Formerly no one was ordained presbyter before the age of thirty, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 290. How presbyters ought to conduct themselves at feasts for the dead or at other gatherings, Hincmar, CXXV, 776. A certain presbyter in a church at Rome stole relics of St. Helena and carried them with him into Gaul, Flodoard, CXXXV, 109. Not little women are set before presbyters for imitation, but presbyters before them and the rest, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 753. See *Cleric*, *Priest*.

**FIRST FRUITS.** On payment to the Church of the first fruits of seed, according to the law of Cnut, king of the English, CLI, 1173.

**PRINCE; KING.** The title used by Gregory the Great in addressing kings and queens, LXXVII, 467, 673, 705. The kings of the Franks are rightly called “Most Christian,” ibid., 798. The Church is to be protected and defended by princes, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 520. When Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was deserted by nearly all the magnates, Heriveus, bishop of Reims, remained faithful and supported him piously, Flodoard, CXXXV, 293. On the zeal of holy kings for divine worship, and on the recompense, sin, and punishment of peoples, Humbert, CXLIII, 1164. The king of the Franks journeys as a pilgrim to Canterbury, to the tomb of St. Thomas, CXC, 1309. The property of the Church belongs not to the king but to the poor, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1215. The disease of princes is to believe and condemn quickly, Stephen, CCXI, 317. Book on the good government of a prince, Helinand, CCXII, 735 ff. On his diligence and wisdom, ibid., 736. On equity, ibid., 737. On public tax-collectors, 742. On the selection and office of soldiers, ibid., 743. On the mutual affection of prince and subjects, ibid., 744.

**ECCLESIASTICAL PRIVILEGES.** See *Diplomas*, *Precepts*.

**PROCESSION.** See *Litany*.

**PROCURATION.** The right of procurations, Stephen, CCXI, 318.

**BENEFITING.** One should strive to benefit everyone, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 229.

**MONASTIC PROFESSION.** Book on the various orders and professions that exist in the Church, Anonymous, CCXIII, 809 and throughout.

**GOD’S PROVIDENCE** extends to human beings and to all lower and even the least things, Augustine, XXXII, 978. Nothing happens without God’s providence, id., XXXVIII, 70. Through it all things are governed, id., XL, 17, 295. There would be no justice among human beings if God did not care for human affairs, ibid., 98. God’s providence is hidden, id., XLI, 224. Divine Providence concealed the awe of deity under the guise of humanity, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 204. God’s providence, ibid., 246. Blessed are those who trust in divine providence, ibid., 628. On God’s providence, and why the elect suffer in this world together with the reprobate, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1139.

**PSALM; PSALMODY; PSALTER.** In the time of St. Zeno, psalms were not only sung but also read in churches, id., XI, 362, note 3, and 467, note 3. Christian tradition concerning recitation of psalms over the dead, Jerome, XXII, 697. The custom of singing psalms at the altar was adopted at Carthage, Augustine, XXXII, 634. The singing of psalms is celebrated throughout the whole world, ibid., 766. They are sung at funerals of the dead, 776. A psalm was heard in part and sung in part by the people, id., XXXVI, 199. The canonical manner of psalm-singing, John Cassian, XLIX, 83, 88. Devotion of voice and gladness of mind ought to be joined in psalmody, Cassiodorus, LXX, 671. Psalmody performed by divided choirs, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 864. How psalmody was performed by the early Church, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 742. Psalmody should be performed with delight, Alcuin, C, 604. The custom of assigning a psalm, St. Benedict, CIII, 1168. On divine psalmody, Agobard, CIV, 325. St. Damasus ordered that all David’s psalms be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 74; and Celestine, id., 225; and Sigebert, CLX, 78. On the office of psalm-singing, Gerard, CXLII, 1303. To sing psalms is to pray, St. Bruno, CLIII, 199. What psalmody ought to be like, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1138, 1175. On the manner of singing psalms, Gratian, ibid. What it is to sing with spirit and mind, Wolbero, CXCV, 1272. Divine psalmody ought to be burdensome to no one, Adam, CXCVIII, 855.

**GIRL.** Whether girls ought to wear earrings, Ambrose, XIV, 453. Method of educating girls, Augustine, XXXII, 779. Cyprian, close to martyrdom, ordered that girls be guarded, XXXVIII, 1411. Girls consecrated to God, Salvian, LIII, 171. Sacred girls, ibid., 205. On suppressing the abduction of girls, widows, and nuns, Hincmar, CXXV, 1017.

**BOY; CHILDHOOD.** The vices of childhood pass on into succeeding ages, Augustine, XXXII, 674. They attain the kingdom of heaven by humility, not by age, ibid. Childhood is set forth both for imitation of humility and for avoidance of foolishness, [Col. 0656] id., XXXVI, 525, 526. How childhood should be joined with old age, XXXVII, 1472. Christian childhood is encouraged by light commands, so that youth may proceed to weightier ones, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 306. A child should receive nothing but good from his father, ibid., 353. One must not laugh with them, St. Benedict, Sedulius, CIII, 1041. They are to be habituated to discipline, ibid. How they should be treated, ibid., 1100. How they should be punished when they err in the oratory, ibid., 1165. They are to be treated more indulgently, ibid., 1197. To St. Benedict, *infans* and *puer* are the same, ibid. Boys must be guarded, 1365. Those offered by their parents were formerly compelled to remain permanently in the monastery even after reaching puberty, ibid., 1303, 1308. When they ought to make deeds of donation, ibid., 1308. Their lawful inheritance divided into three parts, ibid., 1312.

**WOMAN IN CHILDBED.** Her blessing for use among the Ethiopians, Anonymous Collection of Canons, CXXXVIII, 907.

**DUST.** Dust from the tombs of saints, collected and preserved with reverence, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 820.

**PUNIC CHRISTIANS** call baptism “salvation,” and the Eucharist “life,” Gennadius, LVIII, 1041.

**PUNISHMENT.** Punishment of a certain Jew for a dreadful profanation of an image of Christ, Sigebert, CLX, 105. On the punishment of Count Rudolf, who wished to plunder the monastery of Monte Cassino, Leo of Marsi, CLXXIII, 681.

**PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.** Origin of candles at the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Alcuin, CI, 1181. How the Mother of Christ subjected herself to this law, id., CI, 1300. Why we carry candles on the day of the Purification of Holy Mary, Rupert, CLXX, 87.

**LENT.** During Lent fasting is observed on every day except Saturday, Ambrose, XIV, 708. The Church’s custom concerning the Lenten fast, id., XXVI, 57. Lent, the principal observance of fasts, Augustine, XXXIV, 594. You who fast on other days, increase what you do on these days, id., XXXVIII, 1040. Abstinence from meat and wine, ibid., 1040, 1043. The days of Lent are most sacred throughout the world, ibid., 1046. What Lenten abstinence should be like, ibid., 1044. This observance is kept not superstitiously but by divine law, id., XLII, 492. During Lent almost everyone abstains not only from meats but also from certain fruits of the earth, ibid., 491, 493. What one entering the sea of Lent ought to do, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 208. Divine songs should be joined to the Lenten fast, ibid., 215. It is a time of spiritual wars, ibid., 222. The Lenten fast heals the ships of our bodies, ibid., 366. In Lent God must be served more diligently and life lived more holily, Leo the Great, LIV, 264. It arises from divine and apostolic institution, 275, 286. It is observed throughout the world, ibid., 269. It is a time of reconciliation and pardon, ibid., 274. It is the greatest and most sacred fast, ibid., 301. What pursuits should occupy one in Lent, ibid., 291. At that time the bishop shuts himself away, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 217. On Lent, ibid., 273, 278, 376. A summary of the Lenten abstinence from the authority of the Fathers, ibid., 1072. Birth celebrations or weddings must not take place in Lent, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 840. On the Lenten fast, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 335. The Lenten fast was instituted by Pope Gregory II, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 979. In Lent one should not eat before the evening hour, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 272. On Lent, Anonymous, CLI, 1013. In Lent the scrutiny of those to be baptized takes place, Hugh of St. Victor, CXXVII, 446. What the selection of foods in Lent was formerly like, id., CLXXXVI, 1145. On the observance of Lent and fasts, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1859 ff. How bells should be rung in Lent, John Beleth, CCII, 90. See *Fasting*.
