**REDEMPTION OF CAPTIVES.** Christians redeemed by St. Zachary, so that they might not be handed over to pagans for torture, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1058.

**REFECTION.** It is a vice to anticipate the hour of refreshment and sleep, John Cassian, XLIX, 550.

**RULE.** God’s will is an unchangeable rule, Augustine, XXXVII, 1206. The rule of life for every Christian, Boniface, LXXXIX, 870. Rule of the Knights Templar, John of Michelsberg, CLXVI, 859 ff. On the rule of regular canons, Guichard of Lyons, CXIX, 1093 ff. The Rule of St. Augustine is believed to derive from the apostles, Stephen, CCXI, 354.

**RELICS.** Everywhere the blood of blessed martyrs has been received as holy, and their venerable bones are daily testimonies, Hilary of Poitiers, X, 584. What Optatus handed down concerning the cult of relics, id., XI, 765. Honor is divinely joined to the relics of saints, Augustine, XXXVIII, 1255. Relics of saints are for the consolation of the faithful, ibid., 1257. At memorial shrines, prayers are made, not for the glory of martyrs, ibid. The relics of Stephen the martyr were transferred to Africa and became renowned everywhere for God’s benefits, ibid., 1435. They themselves were placed in a sacred place, ibid., 1437. The relics of saints must be honored most sincerely, [Col. 0657] but not worshipped, Gennadius, LVIII, 997. Vessels in which martyrs’ blood is preserved are a true sign of martyrdom, Aurelius Prudentius, LIX, 665; and LX, 428, note 53. Relics of saints are necessary for the dedication of a new church, St. Paulinus, LXI, 334. They were formerly displayed above altars for the veneration of the faithful, ibid., 534, note j. Discovery of the Lord’s cross and of the nails by which Christ was pierced, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 936. Martyrs’ relics marvelously discovered and placed above an altar, ibid., 923. The power of holy relics, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 780. Relics bought for a price and covered with a veil, ibid., 784, 785. Most holy relics, ibid., 823. Hung round the neck, ibid., 457. Placed above the altar, ibid., 484, 821. Various kinds of relics, or of things that touched saints’ bodies or tombs, ibid., 459–1123. Gregory scarcely dared to touch them, id., 382. How relics were formerly sent, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 54, 104. Their marvelous effects, ibid. How highly they ought to be valued, ibid., 54. Throughout the West it was regarded as sacrilege to touch relics, ibid., 272. St. Gregory’s reverence toward the relics of saints, ibid., 420. *Brandeum* or *prandeum* was the name for cloths applied to saints’ relics and distributed among the faithful, id., LXXVII, 702, 846. Under Gregory’s pontificate Latins scarcely dared to touch saints’ relics, but sent *brandea*, ibid., 702, 805. In some places relics were tested by applying fire, ibid. Relics of saints were customarily kept in baptisteries, ibid., 813. Altars were formerly erected above saints’ tombs and relics, ibid., 834. They are called sanctuaries, ibid., 1144, 1226. Translation of the body of St. Isidore, LXXXI, 39–50. The sale of saints’ relics is forbidden, id., CL, ibid.; Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 748. On depositing saints’ relics, Roman Diurnale, CV, 91, 93. Translation of St. Benedict’s relics, Adrevaldus, CXXIV, 901. Pope Eutychian laid down the rite by which martyrs’ bodies should be buried, Anastasius the Librarian, 1442. They are not to be buried without a dalmatic, ibid. Translation of the relics of St. Rigobert, Flodoard, CXXXV, 119, 120. On pledges of the saints revealed everywhere, id., CXLII, 655. On the translation of St. Adalard’s relics into Flanders, Gerald, CXLVII, 1073 ff. Halitgar brings back many pledges of the saints from Constantinople, id., CXLIX, 53. He sought and found the body of St. Vedast, ibid. On the relics of St. Symetrius, ibid., 313. The body of Bishop St. Ælfheah is found, Osbern, CXLIX, 389. How saints’ relics should be escorted or received, Udalric, CXLIX, 758. How they should be carried, Guido, CL, 1272. What was done concerning false relics, according to the testimony of Guibert himself, Guibert, CLVI, 621. The bodies of deceased saints should not be enclosed in gold or silver, ibid., 626. Guibert does not approve of bodies of saints being dug out of their tombs, ibid. Those who venerate the relics of one saint as those of another do not sin, ibid., 628. Whoever certainly believes someone to be a saint and venerates him, even though he is not such, receives from God the fruit of his prayer, ibid. On the veneration of holy relics, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 209, 215. Relics of saints honor the places where they are, ibid., 215. Relics placed beneath the altar, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1111. Relics of St. Ebrulf in the monastery of Saint-Evroult, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 488. Likewise those of St. Nicholas, bishop of Myra, ibid., 534. How much saints’ relics avail mortals, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1287. The custom of swearing upon saints’ relics, Life of Innocent III, CCXIV, XXIV, id.

**PAPAL RESCRIPT.** On rescripts and their interpretations, Innocent III, CCXV, 1221.

**RESIDENCE.** Governors of churches should reside, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 507.

**RESPONSORIES** were invented by Italians, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 744. Various hymns and responsories of King Robert, CXLI, 939–945.

**KING.** See *Prince*.

**RITES.** See volumes LXXXV and LXXXVI, containing the ancient Mozarabic liturgy.

**ROGATION DAYS.** See *Litany*.

**ROME.** It was devastated by the invasion of the Goths under King Alaric, Augustine, XXXII, 647 and XXXIII, 365. Paulinus goes to Rome every year, XXXIII, 355. The city is called venal, 532. Rome, the head of the nations, id., XXXVIII, 166. The devastation of the city was falsely attributed to the Christian religion or the extinction of idolatry, ibid., 505, 623, 624. The slaughter and destruction of Rome, id., XL, 718. It was captured and plundered by Alaric, id., XLI, 14, 15. The humanity of the barbarians toward most Romans, ibid., 45. Rome as a second Babylon, ibid., 561, 578.

**CHRISTIAN ROME. Roman Pontiff.** New pilgrims continually come to Rome, Augustine, XXXII, 119. There were daily bouts of drunkenness in the basilica of St. Peter, ibid. This basilica is removed from the bishop’s manner of life, ibid. The Roman people customarily fasted on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, ibid., 139. To Romans it did not seem necessary to fast on Thursday, ibid. In the Roman Church the primacy of the apostolic see has always flourished, ibid., 163. After Roman judgment, a plenary council remains, ibid., 170. Succession of Roman pontiffs from Peter to Anastasius, ibid., 196. The fathers of the Council of Carthage judged that their decree against the Pelagians should be communicated to Pope Innocent, ibid., 760. Authority of the Roman See, ibid., 781. Matters that may benefit all churches in common throughout the whole world are referred to the Apostolic See, ibid., 782. Innocent II treats inquiries with faithful and measured deliberation, ibid., 785. The care of all churches belongs to the Roman See, ibid., 786. The custom of consulting the Roman See concerning doubtful matters has always been observed by the whole world, ibid. Its authority in condemning heretics, ibid., 865, 869. The practice of appealing from judgments of African bishops to the Apostolic See, ibid., 955. When a difficulty arose, Augustine wished to discuss it in a council, or even to write concerning it to the Apostolic See, ibid., 1068. The Eastern Catholic Church never wrote to the bishop of Carthage while passing over the Roman bishop, id., XLIII, 516. The bishop of Rome is ordained by the bishop of Ostia, ibid., 642. Roman council concerning the case of Caecilian, ibid., 643. Rome glories in the special patronage of the blessed Peter and Paul, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 400. Rome, the See of St. Peter, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 686. Rome, pre-eminently the apostolic see, ibid., 728. Rome’s army was the avenger of Christ’s blood, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 219. The Romans, formerly persecutors, are now executors of the word of Christian faith, ibid., 255. The teaching of the faith belongs to the Roman See, ibid., 485. Ancient churches of the city of Rome: see *Basilica*. Ancient Roman cemeteries: see *Cemetery*. See *Apostolic See*.

**SABBATH.** It is both God’s rest and human leisure, St. Hilary, IX, 495. How God works on the Sabbath, ibid., 498. What the perfect Sabbath is like, and what must be prepared before it, ibid., 499. Christ gave rest on the Sabbath to wearied mortals. It is illuminated through Christ, not abolished, so that it may shine in the Church on the Lord’s Day, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 412. The primary Sabbath is Sunday; the secondary, Jewish Sabbath; and the purpose to which the latter is assigned, ibid., 418. With what care and religious devotion the Sabbath should be celebrated, Salvian, LIII, 45. Not to observe the Sabbath is an impiety, ibid., 119. Work must cease on the evening of the Sabbath, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 980, 987. To sanctify the Sabbath is not to cease from good works, St. Bruno, CLXV, 279.

**SAND.** Sand from the tombs of saints preserved with reverence, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1123.

**PRIEST.** On the reverence due to priests, from the law of Cnut, king of the English, id., CLI, 1172. Whether wicked priests at the end of life should be admonished and tolerated, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1134. Tithes are to be distributed to priests according to the bishop’s direction, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1013. On the unhappy end of a certain priest, named Godescalc, who had assembled an army against the Turks, William of Tyre, CCI, 246. See *Cleric*, *Presbyter*.

**SACRIFICE.** See *Mass*.

**DANCING; DANCE.** See *Dances*.

**SALVE REGINA.** Hymn composed by St. Bernard, Bernard, CLXXXIV. It was sung four times a year, ibid.

**SAINTS AND THEIR CULT.** Saints are called those cleansed from sins, Christ’s brothers, spiritual houses, and a royal race, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 310. They are the light of this world, ibid., 580. Judges, kings of the earth (*reges terrae*), ibid., 288, 547. The repose of saints lies in fellowship with Christ and the angels, ibid., 500. Saints take thought for us, ibid., 682. When we are not helped by the merits of saints, and when we are helped, ibid., 1060. You have saints near at hand to make supplication for you, St. Ambrose, XVII, 250. Angels and martyrs, who can pray for our sins, should be entreated, ibid. Christ alone walks among souls and moves in the mind of saints, ibid., 605. The vigilance of saints is necessary, ibid., 706. The life of saints is even and harmonized with itself, so that later things correspond to earlier ones, ibid., 813. Even the sleep of saints is active, ibid., 960. It is not unknown to us that saints struggle while they are being struck, ibid., 857. The life of saints is not here on earth but in heaven, ibid., 1373. No saint is crowned without contest, Jerome, XXII, 442. Sleep itself is prayer for saints, ibid., 621. In heaven saints favor those living and laboring on earth, ibid., 472. It is not lawful to form a rash judgment about holy men, id., XXIII, 203. Between saints and angels there is manifold and infinite diversity, ibid., 323. The prayers of saints benefit us, ibid., 344. No saint, as long as he is in this life, can possess all virtues, ibid., 512. Saints do not recognize children whom God does not love, ibid., 548. Saints are not debtors, but render to each person what is his own, id., XXV, 665. Many things appropriated from divine worship are used for honoring saints, Augustine, XLI, 281. The cult of saints, id., XLII, 602. Examples of saints are set before every race of humankind, id., XL, 699. The reward of saints is not in this world, [Col. 0659] id., XLI, 160. Saints now reign with Christ, ibid., 673. The intercession of saints at the Last Judgment, ibid., 732. Why saints humble themselves so greatly in this life, John Cassian, XLIX, 449, note, 1273. Why God permits them to be killed or afflicted by the ungodly, ibid., 647. Before Christ, saints longed for the Incarnation; after Christ, they desire his manifestation and judgment, St. Prosper, LI, 349. The death of saints is like sleep, because of the resurrection and glory that are to follow, ibid., 372. The exaltation of saints is eternal life, ibid., 360. The glory of all saints is that the whole world be subjected to God and to divine laws, ibid., 424. The intercession and benefit of saints, Leo the Great, LIV, 172, 179, 188, 421, 428. Their aid should be sought, ibid., 253. In them God has established for us both protection and example, ibid., 437. One should rejoice in the commemoration of saints, ibid., 427. Martyrs and saints are rightly called patrons, Prudentius, LX, 236. The lives of saints should be continually examined, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1074. Images of saints, ibid., 723. Performances must by no means be given on saints’ feast days, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 931. The merits of saints are gifts of God, ibid., 939. On the intercession of saints, Hincmar, CXXV, 900. Poem in fourteen books on the triumphs of Christ and the saints, Flodoard, CXXXV, 491 ff. On reverence toward saints, Bernard the Scholastic, CXLI, 62. On the Feast of All Saints, Udalric, CXLIX, 688. On saints and their pledges, Guibert, CLVI, 612. It is the duty of the Church’s prelates to ensure that the people give due attention to the cult of saints, ibid., 615. Just as true acts of saints turn to God’s honor, so false ones turn to dishonor, ibid., 620. Whoever certainly believes someone to be a saint and venerates him, though he is not such, receives from God the fruit of prayer, ibid. The prayers of saints are incense, Rupert, CLXIX, 974. Examples of saints are to be imitated, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 933 ff. Saints’ feasts are to be commemorated, id., CLXXCIII [sic], 540, 541. Saints’ solemnities are to be observed, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 478. Why fasts precede the principal feasts of saints, ibid., 501. The virtue of saints should always be imitated, not their actions, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 1244.

**SCHISMATIC.** On those who maintain their own opinion even to schism or heresy, Hincmar, CXXVI, 473.

**SCHOOL.** Where and how schools should be maintained, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 40. How each person should be taught, ibid., 48. On the instruction of men and women, ibid., 44. Public schools of St. Geneviève in Paris established, Stephen, CCXI, 377. They flourish under Stephen, ibid., 431.

**HOLY SCRIPTURE.** It is God’s writing, Tertullian, I, 377. Issued by men inspired by the divine Spirit, ibid., 378. The Old Testament translated from Hebrew into Greek, ibid. Deposited in the library of Philadelphus at the Serapeum, ibid., 380. The Jews recited them publicly, exempt from tribute, ibid., 381. Whoever studies them will be compelled to understand God and believe, ibid. The authority of the Old Testament cannot be doubted, ibid., 384. The majesty and authority of Holy Scripture, ibid., 386, 446, 468. Divine literature is more fruitful in proportion to the capacity of each subject, id., II, 53. Scripture divided into chapters, ibid., 127. They were read in the Christian assemblies, id., I, 477. They did not conceal them, nor could they, ibid., 446. Betrayers of the Holy Scriptures, Cyprian, IV, 433. The madness of those who turn the judgment of the heavenly Scriptures into a defense of crimes, ibid., 781. Holy Scripture is free from all artificial adornment, Lactantius, VI, 714. Many despise the Scriptures as fables of empty things, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 511. Many proclaim that there is nothing rational or perfect in them, ibid., 543. There is in them neither confusion nor poverty of words, ibid., 501. They contain nothing unworthy of their author, ibid., 768. Whatever is lofty, divine, rational, and perfect is in them, ibid. The many-sided teaching of the Scriptures, ibid. Those who think that everything must be understood literally are refuted, ibid., 770. Scripture is rich in meanings, ibid., 987. Whence the understanding of Scripture should be sought, id., X, 313. Scripture does not consist in reading but in understanding; nor in transgression but in charity, ibid., 570. Scripture, pregnant with mysteries, requires a skilled and devout reader, ibid., 549. Jews, when reading the sacred books, do not dare touch them with the hand, but place a linen cloth beneath them, ibid., 525. Scripture was scorned by pagans because of its humble and unpolished language, St. Zeno, XI, 285. It was attacked by certain pagans, ibid., 338. The authority of Scripture in settling controversies, annotation on St. Optatus, XI, 1157. The canon of the Holy Scriptures enlarged by various pontiffs according to the needs of the times, prologue to St. Damasus, XII, 241, 242. To adulterate is to seek to exclude the true sense of God’s word through a false one, Ambrose, XVII, 288. This is the priests’ vehement, abundant, and vindictive punishment: not to entrust the mysteries of the heavenly Scriptures to the unworthy, ibid., 713. Divine Scripture always speaks and cries out, ibid., 708. It is nourishment and life, ibid., 662. Some have learned it not for love of God but for love of the world, [Col. 0660] ibid., 766. The more it is chewed over in the heart, the more wholesome sweetness it offers the mind, ibid., 866. It is most sharp for cutting away vices, ibid., 926. The words of Scripture are divinely inspired, Jerome, XXII, 432. Scripture cannot be contrary to itself, ibid., 486. No one can sufficiently praise the mysteries and divine sense of Scripture, even though it uses simple words, ibid., 470. No one can enter the Holy Scriptures without a teacher, ibid., 546. The understanding of Scripture is difficult, ibid., 512. Everything we read in Scripture indeed shines and gleams in its outer bark, but is sweeter in its inner marrow, ibid., 585. The order of words in Scripture is a mystery, ibid., 732. A daily assigned portion of Scripture to be read, ibid., 875. The majesty of divine Scripture is to be admired, ibid., 909. Scripture has one and the same author, ibid., 1049. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh, ibid., 1078. In the Scriptures the penitent is lamented, the saint celebrated, the despairing person cursed, ibid., 1198. Those who weaken the meaning of Scripture with the rhetorical flourishes of declaimers are reproved, id., XXIII, 166. If we follow the letter of Scripture, we can manufacture a new dogma, ibid., 182. The usage of Scripture, ibid., 186, 188, 190. The standard of Scripture, ibid., 244. Knowledge of the Scriptures cannot be attained, ibid., 936. Knowledge of them is the riches of Christ, ibid. We cannot know the meaning of Scripture unless we learn it through its words, ibid., 1022. Praise and dignity of Holy Scripture, Augustine, XXXII, 854. Its authority, ibid., 723, 842, 852; XLI, 357. In it God himself speaks, id., XXXII, 864. It is discussed at length, ibid., 1335. What is to be said of its difficulties, id., XXXIII, 386. Study of Scripture requires humility, id., XXXIV, 64. Its understanding must be sought from God, id., XXXV, 1539. It is customarily read in church, id., XLIII, 330. How it should be read, id., XXXVIII, 354. Holy Scripture benefits learned and unlearned alike, Peter Chrysologus, LII, 253. It is better explained by God to faithful persons who pray for that purpose, ibid., 197. It should be expounded cautiously to opponents, securely to children, confidently to believers, steadfastly to unbelievers, ibid., 508. Since it is clear, one should rely upon it with complete simplicity, ibid., 592. Care must be taken that, through the hearer’s ignorance, it does not result in harm to souls, ibid., 611. The oracle of Holy Scripture is the mind of God, Salvian, LIII, 57. Heretics possess it interpolated and corrupted, ibid., 95. The authority of Holy Scripture is beyond doubt, Leo the Great, LIV, 314. Reading of Scripture in churches, ibid., 237. Canonical Scriptures are to be read in church, id., LVI, 428. Canon of the Holy Scriptures, ibid. Their author is God, ibid., 880. Reading the divine Scriptures is necessary, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 277. How Christians venerated the sacred books, Prudentius, XLIX, 972, note 613. St. Fulgentius exhorts Galla to the reading of Holy Scripture, id., LXV, 318. Understanding of Holy Scripture through
Humility is acquired by the assiduity of reading, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 633. We dig wells when we penetrate the depths of Holy Scripture, ibid., 1132. In former times Christians customarily wore the Gospel suspended from the neck and placed it upon the head, for protection and safeguarding, id., LXXVII, 483, 1318. The Gospel was placed in the middle in courts of judgment, ibid., 918, 979. Reading of Holy Scripture recommended, Alcuin, CI, 616. On the Holy Scriptures, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 103. On the canon of the Gospels, ibid., 124. Holy Scriptures to be read in church, St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 259. Holy Scripture should be read for the correction of morals, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 794 ff. What must be attended to concerning Holy Scripture, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 49 ff.

**SCRUTINY.** On the scrutiny of those to be baptized, Theodulf, CV, 228. When and why scrutinies are performed, Rupert, CLXIX, 113. Scrutiny conducive to knowledge, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 776 ff.

**APOSTOLIC SEE.** The supreme pontiff, or pope. It is best that the priests of the Lord from each and every province should report matters to the head—that is, to the See of the Apostle Peter—St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 639. In matters pertaining to religion, the entire supreme authority of judgment is due, according to the canons, solely to the Apostolic See, Leo the Great, LVI, 632. Prerogative of the Roman See, ibid., 761. The custom of consulting and referring matters to the Holy See, ibid., 458, 501. Authority of the Roman See, ibid., 643. An apostolic judgment is not to be annulled, ibid., 633. The Apostolic See and St Peter are used reciprocally as names for one another, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 491. All bishops are subject to the Apostolic See if any fault is found in them, ibid., 996. The Apostolic See is the head of all Churches, ibid., 1298. It belongs to the Roman pontiff to eradicate disputes arising in the Church, Leo IV, CXV, 658. The Roman See has never been accustomed to err, Goffrid, CLVII, 42. The custom of kissing the feet of the supreme Pontiff, ibid., 48. The pope riding on a white horse, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 776.

**OLD AGE.** It is held honorable among all nations, Ambrose, XVII, 474. Old age which trained its youth in honorable disciplines reaps the sweetest fruits, Jerome, XXII, [Col. 0661] 528. Disadvantages of old age, ibid., 557. Description of complete and sound old age, ibid., 343. Infirmities of old age, St Anselm, CLVIII, 694.

**TOMBS and graves of saints.** Tombs of martyrs adorned with flowers, Prudentius, LIX, 695, note 116. Whether tombs formerly existed within the City, id., LX, 134, note 190. Tombs of martyrs frequented, ibid., 277. Masses over martyrs’ tombs, ibid., 356, note. Crowds of people at martyrs’ tombs, ibid., 400. Banqueting and drinking-parties rebuked, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 661. Tombs of saints adorned with flowers, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 866. Dust from tombs treated with honor, ibid., 820. Cloths laid upon saints’ tombs are regarded as relics, ibid., 924. Tombs of saints to be venerated, ibid., 53, 1009. Gregory scarcely dared to touch them, ibid., 382. The faithful kiss them, ibid., 561. A little window there for prayer, ibid., 857. Strewn with laurel leaves, ibid., 892. Dust and little herbs taken away from there as protection, ibid., 916, 917. Bread and wine offered there by travellers, ibid., 999. A ribbon hung upon tombs, ibid., 1142. In former times altars were erected over saints’ tombs and relics, Gregory the Great, LXXVII. How to adorn the place of one’s paternal burial, Goffrid of Vendôme, CLVII, 207.

**SLAVE.** It is not an accidental condition that makes a person a slave, but disgraceful folly, Ambrose, XIV, 619. Many little slaves are freer than their very masters, ibid., 649. Under the heavenly Father, slave and master are brothers, Augustine, XXXVIII, 400. An enactment favoring the manumission of slaves and human freedom ought not to be revoked by the Church, Gregory the Great, LXXVII. Emperor Constantine permitted the manumission of slaves to take place in church, ibid., 547. Slaves who flee to the Church must not be handed over, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 372. On the duties of slaves, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 175. On the discipline of slaves, Peter Damian, CXLV, 342. On the ploughing slave, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 567.

**SIGN.** Signs of a healthy person and of a sick person, Wolbero, CXCV, 1223.

**SIMONIAC.** On the difference between merchants of the world and simoniacs, Humbert, CXLIII, 1084. Simoniacs worse than robbers, 1114.

**SINGULARITY** is especially to be avoided in a religious community, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 205.

**SOLITUDE:** one kind is of the body, another of the mind, Wolbero, CXCV, 1129. The solitude of anchorites is more excellent than that of cenobites, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 213.

**SOLEMNITY.** See *Festival Days*.

**SPECTACLES, THEATRES.** Christians abstained from spectacles, processions, public games, and theatrical performances, Tertullian, I, 466. On these and why it is unfitting for Christians to attend them, Lactantius, VI, 707. Let us withdraw our eyes from spectacles and the provocations of Egypt—from the arena, circus, theatres, and all things that contaminate the soul’s purity and enter the mind through the senses, Jerome, XXV, 189. NINTH SERIES.

[Col. 0665]

[PREFACE.]

In this ninth Series we diligently collect whatever pertains to the true Church of Christ. Here, therefore, we deal first with its origin, antiquity, and its four principal marks, namely unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity, by which it shines forth among others. We contemplate its wonderful Hierarchy, both of Order and of Jurisdiction, and accordingly in turn treat of the Supreme Pontiff, Metropolitans, Bishops, Priests, and other inferior Ministers, as well as their various offices and functions. Next we show the Church of God assailed by heresies, torn by schismatics, yet always immovable, like a rock amid storms. We further enumerate countless Saints and Martyrs, and the sacred interchange of suffrages, good works, and merits, by which all the members of the Church are gathered together through one spirit, bound by the bond of charity. Finally, since ecclesiastical Doctors and authors have always asserted Catholic doctrines in writing and defended them against heretics, we append special Indexes concerning these dogmatic writings.

[Col. 0665]

LXXIX. INDEX CONCERNING THE CHURCH, ARRANGED IN THE LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS, SETTING FORTH IN TWENTY-THREE CHAPTERS WHATEVER THE HOLY FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING IT.

NOTICE.

In this Index, providing at once for the usefulness and convenience of readers, we have established various chapters and present in each what has been collected from the Fathers. Thus we treat in turn: I. Of the definition of the Church with respect to its name. II. Of the definition of the Church with respect to the thing itself, that is, the Church considered in itself. III. Of the origin and antiquity of the Church. IV. Of the various names by which the Church is designated both in Sacred Scripture and in the tradition of the Fathers, listed in alphabetical order. V. Of the various types or figures by which the Church is foreshadowed in both the Old and New Testaments. VI. Of certain things to which the Church is likened or compared. VII. Of the parts of which the Church consists. VIII. Of those who do not belong to the Church. IX. Of the Church’s spiritual goods and how kindly she is toward her children. X. By what indication the Church is to be recognized. XI. Of the four principal marks by which the true Church of God is known. XII. Of unity. XIII. Of holiness. XIV. Of catholicity. XV. Of apostolicity. XVI. Of the doctrine and faith of the Church. XVII. Of the discipline and morals of the Church. XVIII. Of the perpetual duration, or indefectibility, of the Church. XIX. Of the authority and infallibility of the Church. XX. Of the power of the Church. XXI. Of the Roman Pontiff. XXII. Of bishops. XXIII. Of the reasons why one ought to enter the Church, and why, once having entered, one must never depart from it. Thus our Index offers the reader a true treatise on the Church drawn from the Holy Fathers.

I. Definition of the Church with respect to its name, and how it differs from the Synagogue.

[Col. 0665]

According to the force of the name ἐκκαλέω, “I call forth,” the Church is a calling forth, or an assembly of those called; for it received its name from calling: St. Augustine, XXXV, 2089; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 739, 740. The Synagogue, however, is so called from the word συνάγω, “I gather together,” ibid.---Hence there is a difference between Church and Synagogue from the meaning of their names: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1047, 1896.---Hence the Church is now more worthy than the Synagogue, which derives only from gathering together; for cattle are gathered together, whereas human beings are customarily only called together: St. Jerome, XXV, 1404; St. Augustine, XXXV, 2089.---The Church was indeed called after the Synagogue, but promised before it: Id., XXXIX, 2171; namely, to the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to the peoples who were their children through imitation of faith: id., XLIII, 822.---Already foretold in Genesis, chapter II: id., XLVII, 258.---Promised in Abraham’s blessing: id., [Col. 0667] XL, 174; for the Church is Abraham’s true seed: id., XXXIV, 789; announced and, as it were, revealed to this patriarch by the promise made to him: St. Ambrose, XV, 1591; it was prefigured in the Law: St. Jerome, XXII, 1554.---And foretold by the prophets: St. Augustine, XLI, 584; XLII, 289; especially by Isaiah, who prophesied concerning it more than the others: id., XLI, 585. Finally, in the promises themselves it was already then figured: id., XLII, 305.---The Church was foreshadowed by Rebecca, the Synagogue by Sarah: St. Jerome, XXIX, 1754.---The Synagogue is repudiated so that the Church may be introduced: id., XXIX, 1755.---The Synagogue is Christ’s heel; the Church, the beauty and glory of his countenance: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1159.---In this, as in many other respects, the Church differs from the Synagogue in gathering diverse peoples: id., XVII, 810; St. Augustine, XLI, 670; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 166; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 488; Venerable Bede, XCII, 68.---For the Church was built from both peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile: St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 618 ff.; whereas the latter belonged to one nation: Cassiodorus Senator, LXX, 501; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 139.---The Church and the Synagogue were foreshadowed by the two women grinding in the Gospel, one of whom is taken and the other left: St. Ambrose, XVII, 630.---Through the unbelief of the Synagogue, Christ lost one nation, though not that whole nation; through the faith of the Church he gained the whole world: St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1755.

II. Definition of the Church with respect to the thing itself, that is, the Church considered in itself.

The Church must be defined variously according to the various meanings of its name; for the name “Church” has multiple meanings: most extensive, more extensive, broad, strict and proper, improper and metaphorical.

The first meaning is so general that it extends to any assemblies of human beings. In that sense David says in Psalm 25: “I hated the assembly [Ecclesiam] of evildoers”: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 187.

The second is not so general, but is nevertheless broader; for it is used to designate the gathering of all the faithful, both those living on earth and those dead, whether they already enjoy bliss in heaven or are still detained in Purgatory. In this sense: the Apostle [lacuna]: “And he gave him [Christ] as head over the whole Church,” Eph. 1:22: St. Augustine, XXX, 826; XXXVI, 385.

The third, termed the broad meaning, is taken for the gathering of all the faithful from the beginning of the world to its end. In this sense Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1154, says that the Church begins with righteous Abel and extends to the last elect person. It therefore embraces the assembly of God’s people both before the Law and under the two Testaments.

The fourth, namely the strict and proper meaning, designates only the faithful from Christ’s advent until the day on which he will come to judge the world. It is so common and customary that, when uttered simply and without qualification, it is understood to mean that society which is united into one religious body through the profession of Christ’s doctrine and commandments under lawful pastors, and especially under the Roman Pontiff. In this sense Augustine says: “By the preaching of repentance the Church is called to Christ and assembled”: id., XXXVIII, 1963.

Finally, the fifth meaning, that is, the improper and metaphorical, is used for the place or consecrated buildings into which the faithful gather to pray. In this sense the Apostle says: “When you come together in church, I hear that there are divisions among you,” 1 Cor. 11:18: Firmianus Lactantius, VII, 213; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 430, 474, 477; XXXVII, 1590; XXXVIII, 205, 422, 569, 1165, 1174, 1212, 1475, 1600.

III. Origin and Antiquity of the Church.

If the Church of Christ is taken in its broad sense, that is, as the assembly of faithful persons believing in Christ, it preceded Christ’s birth in such a way that in the time of the law of nature and of the written Law there existed saints who were worshippers of the Christian religion: Abbot Godfrey, CLXXIV, 552, 1014.---It began with righteous Abel: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1164.---It was planted from the beginning with Abel: Bruno, Abbot of Asti, CLXIV, 163.---Even before Christ, it already existed in the Saints: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 38; for the Saints who preceded Christ were members of the Church: Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 313, 335.---If it is taken in the strict sense, as the assembly of faithful persons from Christ’s advent to the Day of Judgment, it took its beginning from Christ and its origin must be referred to his birth: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 736; St. Ambrose, XVII, 398; St. Augustine, XL, 645; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 213. Through Christ’s Passion and the death of his sleep, it was formed from his side: St. Ambrose, XVII, 530, 813; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 216; XXXV, 1513; XXXVIII, 55; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 355.---Judaea was its cradle: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 735; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 261; Venerable Bede, XCIV, 50; St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 139; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 23, [Col. 0668] 31.---God is the founder of the Church; he founded it forever: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1153.---It was not founded by human votes or resources: St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 610.---The prophets prepared, and the apostles laid, the foundations of the Church: St. Augustine, XXXVII, 380.---The primary and essential foundation of the Church is Christ, the rock on which it was built: Magnes the presbyter, V, 344; Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, XXI, 718; St. Augustine, XXXII, 618; XXXVIII, 479, 1238; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 290; Cassiodorus, Abbot of Vivarium, LXX, 336, 618, 729; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 939; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 259, 1005; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 930; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 868. For “no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ”: St. Ambrose, XVII, 199.---How it should be understood that the Church was founded upon Christ the Rock: Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 560 ff.---The secondary foundations of the Church are the prophets who prepared them and the other apostles who laid these foundations: id., XVII, 380; for all planted the Church, not by inflicting insults but by suffering and shedding their blood: St. Jerome, XXII, 741, 742; St. Leo the Great, LV, 51, 59.---It was first founded at Antioch by St. Peter: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 739.

IV. Various names under which the Church is designated both in Holy Scripture and in the Tradition of the Fathers, arranged alphabetically.

The Church is called the building up of Christ’s body: Abbot Florianus, LXXII, 925.---A field: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1150.---Why it is the blessed field of Christ: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 953.---The field of blood: why: Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1573.---Christ’s cultivation: St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 935.---The altar of God: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 492.---The ark: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 864.---The ark of the Lord, in which heavenly treasures are stored: Walafrid, CXIII, 487.---The ark of Christ’s sanctification: Cassiodorus, Abbot of Vivarium, LXX, 950.---The ark of Christ: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 127; XLIII, 355; Alcuin, Abbot, C, 635; in which there is now wheat not without chaff: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 119, 1174.---The ark must not be abandoned before the time of winnowing: id., XXXVI, 190.---The court: St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLII, 1147; the court of God’s house: Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 285.---The dawn: St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 648; LXXVI, 62; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 305 ff.---Christ’s flesh: St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1991; V. Various types or figures by which the Church is foreshadowed in both the Old and New Testaments.

Seven types or figures of the Church are found in the books of the Old Testament: four before the Mosaic Law, and three during the Law, namely:

1. Before the Law: the paradise of delight planted from the beginning: St. Augustine, XLIII, 153 ff.; XLIV, 798; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 479; Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 163.

2. Eve, for she was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, who figures Christ, from whose side, when he slept on the cross, flowed the sacraments of the Church: Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 802; St. Augustine, XXXIV, 216; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 355, 601, 883; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 327; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 163; St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 114; Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 1096; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 1077. For, as St. Augustine says, the formation of the woman mystically figured the formation of the Church: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 407 ff.

3. Noah’s ark was a notable type of the Church, not in the sense that all who were in it are saved, but that none among those who have not entered it is saved: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 874; St. Ambrose, XVII, 618, 814; St. Jerome, XXII, 1054; XXIII, 317; XXV, 134; St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1358; XXXIX, 2171; XLI, 472, 476; XLIII, 399; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 722, 883; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 401, 404 ff.; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 544; Cassiodorus, LXX, 23, 901, 950; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 164; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 982; LXXVIII, 322; Venerable Bede, XCII, 546; XCIV, 71; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 342; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 704; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 109, 456. How it figured the Church: St. Augustine, XLIII, 196. The diversity of its compartments prefigured the Church’s variety: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 236.

4. The fourth type of the Church before the Law was found in the wives of the ancient patriarchs, and especially in Sarah: St. Ambrose, XV, 434, 437; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 217; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 560; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 134, 135; Remigius the monk, CXXXI, 166; CXCI, 93.---In Rebecca: St. Ambrose, XIV, 618; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 39; XXXIX, 1754, 1755; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 771; Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 793; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1159; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 135 ff.---In Rachel, long barren and afterward fruitful: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 923; St. Jerome, XXV, 930; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 564; Venerable Bede, XCII, 14; XCIV, 52; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 156, 158.---And in Rachel weeping for her children: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1343.---In Leah: St. Augustine, XLIII, 123.

5. The fifth type of the Church, while the Mosaic Law stood, was the Jewish nation itself, which was indeed a great prophet of Christ and of the Christian kingdom: St. Augustine, XLII, 290.

6. The sixth type of the Church was the Temple of Jerusalem, which the Jews were obliged to visit in order to celebrate Passover and offer sacrifices to God: Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 587 ff.

7. The seventh type of the Church was that stone of which Daniel speaks, which was cut from the mountain without hands and became great and filled the earth: St. Augustine, XXXV, 1465.

In the books of the New Testament there are three principal types of the Church:

1. The two catches of fish made at Christ’s command in the Sea of Tiberias, one before and the other after his Passion, foreshadowed his present and future Church: St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1158, 1161, 1244.

2. Christ’s seamless tunic: Cassiodorus, LXX, 161, 728.---And its not being torn figures the unity of the Church: St. Cyprian, IV, 54.

3. That vessel descending from heaven which Peter is reported to have seen: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291.

Moreover, the Church is prefigured by many other things. For example, in the Old Testament the following are types of the Church: before the Law, Adam, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2171; Abel, XXXVII, 1589; Alcuin, C, 631; Jacob, Tichonius the African, XVIII, 32; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1015; Alcuin, C, 631, 634. Under the Law, Aaron, Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 327. Deborah, who in a remarkable manner prefigures the Church’s conflicts and triumphs, St. Ambrose, XVI, 247. Pharaoh’s daughter, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 52; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 188. Rahab, Cassiodorus, LXX, 619; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 9. A harlot in the type, the Church in the mystery, St. Ambrose, XV, 1598, 1776. The house of this harlot, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 544; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 825; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 1008. Jael, the foreign woman, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1140; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 678. Jephthah’s daughter, mourning sixty days for her virginity, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1189. Naomi, the wife of Elimelech, ibid., CVIII, 1201. Ruth, ibid., CVIII, 1214 ff. Zipporah circumcising her son, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 26. The widow of Zarephath, St. Ambrose, XVI, 239; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1828; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 262; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 808. David, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 691, 738; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 1227. Job, Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 123, 145, 151, 170, 185, 230, 235, 259, 328, 403. The Queen of Sheba, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 664; St. Jerome, XXIX, 2171; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 883, 885; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 163; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 678; St. Hildegard, CXCVIII, 136. The Church marvels at Christ, the true Solomon, in the doctrines given by him; at his wisdom in the making of the world, in the house which he built for himself through the Incarnation, and in the foods of his table, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2171. She comes with a great retinue, no longer, like the Synagogue, with one people, but with the nations of the whole world, ibid. When she beholds the glory of the Lord in the eternal Jerusalem, she will acknowledge it to be greater than what has been said, ibid.

In the New Testament, Peter prefigured the Church: St. Augustine, XXXII, 618; XXXIII, XL, 691, 196; XXXVII, 1432; XXXVIII, 478, 479, 480, 802, 1349; XXXIX, 1940; LXX, 786. Especially in the passage where it was said to him, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” ibid., XXXVIII, 802, 1339, 1350. John, Alcuin the abbot, C, 1091, 1095, 1100. All the Apostles bore the person of the Church when they received the Holy Spirit and the power to remit sins, St. Augustine, XLIII, 1550. Mary, virgin and mother, because the Church is immaculate yet married, St. Ambrose, XV, 1555; St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1989; XL, 659, 660; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 591 ff. The woman who appears in the Apocalypse clothed with the sun, Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 34. The woman spoken of in Proverbs, ibid., LXIX, 146. The angel who appeared to John together with the Apostle, Alcuin the abbot, C, 1091. The Canaanite woman whose daughter is tormented by a demon, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 487. The widow casting coins into the treasury, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1043. The woman suffering from an issue of blood, ibid., 476; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 416, 486; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 300; Venerable Bede, XCII, 411; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 382, 387. Mary Magdalene the sinner, St. Cyprian, IV, 1339; St. Ambrose, XVI, 110; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 171; XXXVIII, 53, 695; St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 469; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 278. The Church rightly received the appearance of a sinful woman: how this is so, St. Ambrose, XV, 1674. The mother of the Maccabees, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 1380. The mother of the sons of Zebedee, Godfrey of Admont, CLXXIV, 964.

We also have types of the Church in parables: the woman hiding leaven in flour, St. Ambrose, XV, 1749; XVI, 491; the woman who gives birth in sorrow, Alcuin the abbot, C, 955; CI, 1214, 1215; the household over which the master appointed a servant, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 921; the seven angels to whom seven trumpets were given—for they signify the Church in its preachers, who are heralds of eternal life—Alcuin the abbot, C, 1135; the pillar of fire, St. Ambrose, XVII, 863; Mount Zion—how this is so, Cassiodorus, LXX, 337; Alcuin the abbot, C, 637; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 480; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 462, 745, 1184; Mount Lebanon—why this is so, Wolbero, abbot of St. Pantaleon, CXCV, 1202. It is also prefigured by the islands of the nations, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 670; by the threshing floor of the Old Testament, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 579, 910. Not only the Church militant but also the triumphant and glorious Church is prefigured in the Ark of the Covenant, Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 308; by the first tabernacle, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 534; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 316; by the vine putting forth its clusters, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 499; by Solomon’s bed, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1140, 1141; by the mule on which Solomon sat, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 1146; by the house of Josiah, where Jesus son of Jozadak is crowned, ibid., CLXVIII, 670; by the house in which the lamb is eaten, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 756; by the city of Nazareth, Venerable Bede, XCII, 15; by Jerusalem, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 122; XLIII, 409; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 337; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 60; St. Hildegard, CXCVIII, 136; by Zion, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 122; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 134, 192, 641, 913, 1184; by Nineveh, a city of foreigners, St. Hilary of Poitiers, XI, 449; Tichonius the African, [Col. 0674] XVIII, 29. Above all, the beauty of the Church’s virtues is prefigured by this city, whose name is interpreted “beautiful,” Venerable Bede, XCII, 64. By the lodging or house into which the Magi entered and found the Child with Mary his mother, the beginnings of the Church are signified, ibid., 15. By the island of Patmos her persecutions are prefigured, Alcuin the abbot, C, 1095. By absolutely all the cities of Israel and provinces of the nations which Scripture addresses, or in which some event took place, Tichonius the African, XVIII, 38. By Cyprus: and not without reason is the Church said to be prefigured by Cyprus, abounding in wine, since, although shaken by the waves of the age, it overflows with abundance of graces, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 429. By the roe deer, ibid., CLXXXV, 181; by the field, Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 257; by the dove, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 607; Gerhoh, CXCIII, 73; by the sheepfold, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203; by the fold, ibid., CXI, 407; by the throne from which proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps, Alcuin the abbot, C, 1117; by the four living creatures, ibid., C, 1118 ff.; by the three measures from which ashes-baked loaves were made, Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 126; by the gathering of waters from every valley into one. The valley signifies the Gentile world, St. Ambrose, XIV, 155. Finally, the Church is fittingly prefigured by the turtledove, which knows no partnership other than Christ.

## VI.—Some things to which the Church is likened or compared

The Church is excellently compared to a ship, St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 957, 960, 993, 1007; St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 883; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 60; Pope Sergius III, CXXXI, 916; especially to Peter’s little boat, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 28; to a vessel tossed upon great waves, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 686; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LII, 253; to one battered by a storm, Tertullian, I, 1214; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 475; Venerable Bede, XCII, 665; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 598. The mast of this ship is Christ raised upon the cross; the Father sits in the stern; the Holy Spirit, the helmsman, guards the prow; the Apostles and Prophets are the rowers, St. Ambrose, XVI, 297; XVII, 697; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 694. A most beautiful description of the spiritual world—that is, of the Church floating above the waves—St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 275, 276.

It is frequently compared to a garden, St. Ambrose, XV, 1863; to a net cast into the sea, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 240; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 202, 203; to a threshing floor threshed with chaff, St. Augustine, XLIII, 587; to a pomegranate, Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 670, 738; to a flock of goats, St. Ambrose, XV, 432; to the ten virgins—why? Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 454; to Joseph’s many-coloured garment, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 902; to a winepress, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 121.

Why is it like a winepress? For the same reason that it is compared to a threshing floor: on the threshing floor the grain is separated from the chaff; in the winepress, the wine from the grape-skins; so in the Church the good are separated from the evil, not indeed by place but by disposition, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 66. The winepress particularly prefigures the afflictions of the Church’s saints, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 325. It is also aptly compared to the moon: for at one time the Church is bright amid prosperity, at another dark amid adversity, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 207, 208; XXXVI, 131, 132, 908; XXXVII, 1373; Pope Pelagius II, LXXII, 755 ff. It is still better compared to a tabernacle, because the present Church is neither a fixed house nor has a foundation, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 695, 705, 739, 743, 1312; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 158.

## VII.—The parts of which the Church consists

The Church is a great body, a living body, the great body of one great head, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 683. In the Church, as in the human body, three things may be considered: namely, the head, the body, and the members.

The head of the Church is Christ, St. Zeno of Verona, XI, 517; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 512; XXXV, 1991; XXXVI, 385, 749, 786, 613; XXXVIII, 265, 753; XLIII, 249, 320; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 525, 611; Alcuin, C, 622; CI, 1072; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 498; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 379; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1140; CXCII, 179, 213; Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1134, 1135, 1147. And he will be so from eternity, Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor, CCXI, 1215. Christ, who is the head of the Church, is also called its body, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1475; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 179, 197, 215, 262; Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1147.

Are Christ and the Church one flesh, one person, one Christ? Tichonius the African, XVIII, 55; St. Augustine, XXXVI, 161; XXXVIII, 55, 571; XXXIX, 1500; St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 602; Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 197; St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 111, 235. Thus Christ suffered in the Church, and the Church in Christ, [Col. 0675] St. Augustine, XXXIII, 545. Christ and the Church are one man, St. Augustine, XXXVI, 232, 250, 453, 629, 662, 693, 695, 723, 730, 761, 866, 948; XXXVII, 1082, 1156, 1679, 1784, 1785, 1817, 1819, 1846; XXXVIII, 571, 754; XXXIX, 1500; XLI, 532; XLII, 896; XLIV, 145; St. Agobard, CIV, 62 ff.; St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 111, 235; Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1134, 1135, 1147. The Church and Christ are one Christ, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1991; XXXVI, 161, 232, 250, 453, 629, 662, 693, 695, 723, 730, 761, 866. The Church and Christ are one flesh, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 215. Christ and the Church are one person, St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 62 ff.; St. Thomas, CXC, 111, 235. Therefore an injury done to the Church is an injury done to God, St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 236.

Under the name of the body of the Church, however, there is more often understood the external society which constitutes the Church taken in its third, that is, broad sense, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1154.

Without doubt the soul of the Church is the Holy Spirit, who gives life to the faithful through sanctifying grace, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 461, 1221, 1231, 1232; who contains and animates her, as the Master of the Sentences says, Lombard, CXCII, 197. More commonly, however, by the soul of the Church are signified the saints, and especially the elect, who by a living faith working through charity constitute the inner Church, Hildebert of Tours, CLXXI, 408.

The members of the Church are distributed according to their different condition into three parts. Those still militant belong to the first; those suffering in purgatory to the second; angels and the elect, already reigning in heaven, to the third, St. Augustine, XXX, 826; XXXVI, 385. Taken generally, the Church militant may be considered either as to body alone, as to soul alone, or as to both.

The members of the Church considered as to its body are all people bound and united by the profession of the true faith and the true use of the sacraments, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1963; St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 621, 623, 626, 661. The members of the Church considered as to its soul are the saints, and especially the elect, endowed with a living faith working through charity. Therefore the members of the Church are not only those who entered the Church in Christ’s time or after Christ, but also those who lived before Christ, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 39; XL, 313, 335. The members of the Church considered as to body and soul are all those united by the outward profession of Christian faith under the rule of pastors, whether they are good and holy, or evil and reprobate, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1484 ff.; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 345, 388; XXXV, 1431; XXXVI, 190; XXXVII, 1693; XXXVIII, 299, 307, 549, 1092, 1417; XXXIX, 1670; XL, 341; St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 128; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1221; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 198, 203.

Accordingly, here and now, and until the day of judgment, wheat and tares are in the Church, Pope St. Cornelius, III, 791; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 119, 1174; XLIII, 296, 297, 312, 444, 536 ff. So it will be until the end of the age, ibid., XXXVI, 735; XLI, 611; XLIII, 166, 249. The evil are to be separated from the good only at the end, XL, 333; XLIII, 162, 167, 192, 417, 420, 427; Eugyppius the abbot, LXII, 864; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 815, 826, 1119; LXXVI, 589, 1285 ff. This mingling of wheat and tares will endure until harvest-time, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 492. For the separation of false brethren, and consequently of the evil, before the time of harvest cannot occur without disturbance to the Church, ibid., XXXV, 1799. The mingling of the evil with the good, then, is not eternal but temporary, ibid., XLIII, 549. Although evil people are said to be in the Church, it must nevertheless be said of them that they are in it only bodily, while spiritually they are outside, ibid., XXXV, 1431, 1433; XLIII, 149, 150, 153, 156, 160, 189, 195, 199, 207. Accordingly, there are two kinds of people in the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 815, 1119. All churches established throughout the world are members of the Catholic and universal Church, Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 944. For no principle other than the single tradition of the same sacrament governs these churches, Tertullian, II, 1025.

## VIII.—Those who do not belong to the Church

Four classes of persons are outside the Church: namely, the damned, the excommunicated, schismatics, and heretics, Hermann the abbot, CLXXX, 93. Schismatics do not belong to the Church: they break the nets by breaking unity. For those who abandon Peter’s Chair, upon which the Church is founded, how can they trust that they are in the Church? Pope Alexander III, CC, 26. Yet in some respect they remain connected with the Church and possess something sound, St. Augustine, XLIII, 115. Schismatics must necessarily die eternally outside the Church, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 1596.

All heretics have been expelled from the Church’s unity and consequently do not belong to it, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 478. For far from being members of the Church, they do not acknowledge her—why this is so, Cassiodorus, 623. All heresies have gone out from the Church, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 707. They have gone out from the Church like useless branches cut from the vine, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 53, 55, 280. Heretics are alien children separated from the Church, Cassiodorus Senator, LXX, 1018. The Church detests them and does not acknowledge them as sons, Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 257 ff. No heresy is catholic; consequently no heretic is a member of the Church, St. Augustine, XLIII, 589. Heresies, insofar as they are daughters of the Church, have nothing in common with her, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 233. Heretics are strangers to the Church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 700. Heretics have fallen away from the Church by an open and bodily separation; evil persons do so only by a hidden and spiritual separation, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 442. Though these latter are bodily in the Church, spiritually they are outside, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1431, 1433; XLIII, 160, 189, 195, 149, 150, 153, 156, 199, 207. But one must not be said to be in the Church who is mixed with Christ’s sheep only by a bodily association, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 462. Neither Jews nor Gentiles are of the Church, St. Jerome, XXII, 664. Finally, outside the Church are all who dissent from Christ’s testimony either concerning the Head, Christ, or concerning his body, St. Augustine, XLIII, 395. Whatever is contrary to the Church, St. Ambrose, XVII, 200. Those who belong to a particular party cannot belong to the Catholic Church, St. Zeno of Verona, XI, 1005. Even a heretic whose life is good will nevertheless not possess life because of his heresy, Eugyppius the abbot, LXII, 882. So long as someone clings to the Church, his recovery is not hopeless; but this cannot be said of one who has been cut off, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 754.

## IX.—The Church’s spiritual goods, and how kindly she treats her children

She is a loving mother, who has the greatest care for her children, St. Augustine, XL, 692. She is always solicitous in nourishing and cherishing her own, Tertullian, III, 162. This mother has two breasts: namely, knowledge of truth and love of virtues; by the former she nourishes her children, by the latter she sanctifies them, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1163. She offers them her breasts in three ways: by deeds, by words—that is, by nourishing, warning, and stirring them up, ibid., CXCV, 1164. From her flow those things which benefit us, Mozarabic Liturgy, LXXXV, 257. She is full of gentleness toward those who were first deceived and afterwards corrected, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 337. Her zeal for our souls is constant and untiring, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 1202.

The Church’s prayers are offered for all by Apostolic tradition, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 209. She prays for unbelievers that they may believe, and for believers that they may persevere, St. Augustine, XLV, 1606. She even prays for her enemies, ibid., XXXVIII, 151; XLI, 737. The souls of the departed are aided by her prayers and by her saving sacrifice—and how this is so, St. Augustine, XXXVIII ff. Who can say how great is the power of her prayers? Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 612. Her groans and sighs, too, are heard in heaven, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 499. Through the Church’s prayers, we sinners are reconciled to God, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1011, 1012; St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 1215. She supplies her children with weapons by which hostile powers are conquered: faith and prayer, St. Ambrose, XVI, 249. She further assists them by the prayers of her saints, St. Augustine, XLIII, 149. She prays without ceasing for their welfare, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 662. She alone possesses true charity, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 302. She has oil with which she tends the wounds of her own, and with which she anointed martyrs and confessors, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1118. She is filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 629. She is the winepress of the eternal fountain, in which the fruit of the heavenly vine overflows, St. Ambrose, XVI, 703. She possesses the true and unique sacrifice of Christ’s flesh for sins, St. Augustine, XLIV, 600; the most true and singular sacrifice, ibid., 211; the daily sacrifice, ibid., XLI, 298; the true sacrifice owed to the one God, ibid., XXXVIII, 1101, 1356, 1413; XLII, 382, 386, 409. Through her eternal life is bestowed upon us, St. Ambrose, XVI, 311. She is rich in order to enrich her children; for, fruitful throughout the world in the harvest of righteousness and in the abundance of charisms, she has received from the fullness of her Joseph, Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 498. She raises and magnifies her own, for all her children are priests—why this is so, St. Ambrose, XV, 1645. Therefore the religion of the Church is to be embraced, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 128; and the Church is to be loved as a mother, ibid., XXXVII, 1140. How greatly she is to be loved is declared by the Council of Carthage, ibid., St. Augustine, XLIII, 211.

## X.—By what mark the Church is to be recognized

How the true Church of God is to be recognized, St. Augustine, XLIII, 289. Whence it must be demonstrated, ibid., 427, 429, 430. It must not [Col. 0677] be sought in any person’s own righteousness, but in the divine Scriptures, both of the Old and of the New Testament, ibid., XXXIII, 325. Where it is, must be sought only in the words of the Lord, ibid., XLIII, 392, 395, 396. It is recognized in the Scriptures, ibid., XXXIII, 401, 491; commended in them, ibid., XLIII, 466. It is first shown from the Law, ibid., 398, 415; from Genesis, ibid., 431, 44, 324; from the Psalms, ibid., 405, 431, 441; recognized from the Gospel of Luke, ibid., XXXVIII, 126; and from the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse, ibid., XLIII, 430. It is proved in the same Scriptures, ibid., 632; by innumerable testimonies, ibid., XXXVIII, 288, 294, 797.

It is signified in many ways and by almost innumerable types: St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 664; St. Zeno of Verona, XI, 449; St. Ambrose, XIV, 155, 434, 437, 463, 618; XV, 1339, 1749; XVI, 247, 476, 1043; XVII, 618, 658, 814, 863; Tichonius the African, XVIII, 32; Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 691; St. Jerome, XXV, 930; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1465; XXXVI, 1380; XXXVII, 1589; XXXVIII, 416, 486, 487, 1158, 1161; XXXIX, 1989, 2171; XLII, 290; XLIV, 798; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 921; Cassiodorus, LXX, 161, 337, 619, 728; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 756; LXXIX, 499; Venerable Bede, XCII, 15; Alcuin the abbot, C, 637, 955, 1127, 1135; Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 26, 1140, 1189, 1201, 1214 ff.; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 188, 327, 587 ff.; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 579, 910; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1398; Godfrey of Admont, CLXXIV, 964; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 203, 607; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 257, 316. Moreover, it is prefigured in certain parables, St. Ambrose, XV, 1749; St. Augustine, XXXII, 791; Alcuin the abbot, C, 637, 955.

The true Church is neither hidden nor invisible, St. Augustine, XLIII, 422. It cannot be concealed, ibid., 343. It is clear and visible to all, ibid., 493. It is hidden from no one, St. Augustine, XLIII, 284; nor can it be hidden, ibid., XXXVIII, 222. It is set in public view, ibid., XXXVI, 160, 161. It is most widely known throughout the world, and must not be sought in the desert or in a private room, ibid., XLIII, 443.

## XI.—The principal marks by which the true Church of God is recognized

Four are assigned: namely, unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity.

### I. Unity

How this unity is that in which alone the splendour of the Church’s virtues shines, Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 648. This unity is maintained, Tertullian, II, 891. In what words it is shown, Cassiodorus, CI, 1259. It is commended, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1432, 1433, 1489; XXXVI, 513, 538, 889; XXXVIII, 693, 1076, 1224, 1233; XXXIX, 1587, 1595. The Holy Spirit commended the Church’s unity, ibid., XXXVIII, 1231, 1234. The Church’s unity is, as it were, the peculiar work of the Holy Spirit—why this is so, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 463. For this reason he caused those upon whom he first came to speak in the languages of all peoples, thereby announcing that he would gather the languages of all nations into unity, ibid., XXVI, 161; XXXV, 1645. Whoever does not cling to this unity does not have the Holy Spirit, ibid., XXXVIII, 71, 73. The Church is unity, ibid., XXXVII, 1309. This unity is repeatedly commended by Christ glorified, ibid., XXXVIII, 1224. Testimonies concerning this unity from the royal Prophet, ibid., XXXIX, 1586. This is the unity which draws the world to faith, St. Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 258. Above all, it proceeds from divine steadfastness, Tertullian, III, 499 ff. It is prefigured by Christ’s tunic, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 235. It is not outside Christ’s Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 906. How pleasing this unity is to God, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 159. How great its power is, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 703. Christ suffered in order to establish this unity firmly in the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 512.

Therefore the true Church, or Christ’s Church, is one, St. Cyprian, IV, 36, 371; St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 941, 966; St. Augustine, XL, 1196; XLIII, 191; St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 542; Cassiodorus, LXX, 162; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 297; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1110; Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 224; Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 880; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 1029, 1771; Philip of Harveng, CCLII, 1201. It is one by the bonds of charity, one in confession, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXI, 254. It is one in faith, given life by one Spirit, Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1144, 1159. It is one although multiform and composed of diverse human persons, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 693, 757, 765, 1225, 1231, 1232, 1236; XL, 1196; XLIII, 635; Venerable Bede, XCII, 412, 417; Alcuin the abbot, C, 852. For there is one faith in them, one baptism, one God, one work; the Church is not one before the Law, another under the Law, and another under grace, but is established in one peace and one fear, Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 1159. From many people [Col. 0678] joined in the love of affection and fraternity, one Church is made, Bruno of Asti, CLXV, 895. The Church is one although among Jews and Gentiles, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 757; XL, 341. It is one, although it is proved to be governed and to subsist in three ways, Alcuin the abbot, CI, 1073. It is one although it has many orders, Pope St. Celestine I, L, 422 ff. It has three forms, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1485; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 297; St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 559; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 459. The Church of the Old and New Testaments is one, for hope and faith are the same, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 454, 455, although their sacraments differ, ibid., 458, 459. It is one though universal, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 555; and its law is one, though it is governed by several bishops and rulers, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 746. It is one although manifold and consisting of all churches, for all together make one Catholic Church, St. Cyprian, IV, 501; St. Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 301, 736; St. Ambrose, XVI, 255; Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 793; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 848; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 235; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 396; Peter Cantor, CCV, 314. In all churches it is one, and in each it is entire, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 235. It is one in heaven and on earth, though in part journeying and in part reigning, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1036. It is one throughout the whole world, though there are many pastors, St. Cyprian, IV, 343, 409, 500; St. Augustine, XL, 635; St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1153; Alcuin the abbot, CI, 130; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVII, 454 ff.

The holy Church is the congregation which rises into one body through unity of faith and charity, St. Ambrose, XVI, 150. The true Church alone is one, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 896, 900, 1479; because it alone is one, it refutes all heresies, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 202. Cyprian calls the Church “the dwelling-place of unanimity,” that is, of unity, IV, 506; and teaches, both through prophetic testimony and through the signification of the sacraments, that the Church consists of persons who are of one mind and in harmony, St. Augustine, XLIII, 240. God willed one Church, just as he himself is one, Hildebert of Tours, CLXXI, 793. To resist the Church’s unity with an impenitent heart is an unforgivable blasphemy, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 465. The true Church is so one that those alienated from her are alienated from eternal salvation, St. Cyprian, IV, 15, 16. Whoever does not preserve the Church’s unity does not preserve the faith and violates charity, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 550; Hincmar of Reims, CXXVI, 864. Such a person is an alien, is outside, Tertullian, III, 773, 790. Whoever separates himself from the Church’s unity does not remain in God, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1135. Separation from unity is destruction; outside this unity even gifts of the Holy Spirit are ineffective and offer no benefit for salvation, St. Augustine, XL, 137. Moreover, those who separate from unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit, ibid., XLIII, 491. Not even if they have been killed for Christ’s name are they to be admitted to the Church’s peace, Tertullian, III, 794, 835. For to be killed for Christ contributes nothing to salvation unless it occurs in the bosom of unity: a person may be killed, but cannot be crowned, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 410; XLIII, 16. Therefore one is mistaken who thinks that, without charity, one belongs to the Church’s unity, ibid., 464. How motherly charity grieves when unity is torn apart, ibid., XXXV, 1992. God has placed the teaching of truth in the Chair of unity, ibid., XXXIII, 403. Unity must never be forsaken, ibid., XXXVIII, 550; must in no way be violated, ibid., XLIII, 139; but must be loved above all things, ibid., XXXV, 1618. In order that the Church’s unity may be preserved, self-love must be despised, ibid., XXXVIII, 96. Heretics divide unity for the sake of their own honour, ibid. …, XXXV, 208. With Jews and pagans they made a unity against unity, ibid., XXXVIII, 423.

### II. The holiness of the Church

The true Church ought to be holy, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1485; and it is holy in fact, and therefore must be believed and confessed to be so, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVI, 437. The holiness of the Roman, that is, Catholic, Church is maintained, Tertullian, I, 1286. It is holy, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 941. The true Church alone is holy, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2191.

First, it is holy by reason of its Head, who is Christ himself, from whom comes all holiness, ibid., XXXVII, 1159; XXXVIII, 755; Mozarabic Liturgy, 110, 251, 462; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 162. Second, it is holy by reason of its sacraments, which are holy and confer holiness, St. Augustine, XXXV, 931, 983; XLIII, 156. These sacraments are holy even in criminal persons, ibid., XXXIII, 1172. They cannot lose their holiness because of the wickedness of their ministers, ibid., XLII, 73, 152, 153, 191, 293, 296, 298, 747; Alger of Liège, CLXXX, 834. Third, it is holy by reason of its sacrifice, which is holy, St. Augustine, XLIII, 57, 300, since it is the true sacrifice of Christ’s flesh, ibid., XXXIII, 115; XL, 1196; Ulrich of Cluny, CXLX [probably CXLIX], 488. Fourth, it is holy by reason of its members—not because all are holy, but because they are sanctified only through it; for it alone is the Church of saints, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1951.

With respect to holiness, the Church must be considered under two aspects: that of its present state in this life, and that of its future state in heaven. It is imperfect here and now; it will be perfect only in heaven, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1485. Therefore, when it is said not to have spot or wrinkle, Cassiodorus Senator, LXX, 1084, this must not be understood as though the Church already were such, but as what it will be, St. Augustine, XLIII, 107, 108. At present it has good and evil persons mixed together, Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1287. It will be without spot only after the resurrection, St. Jerome, XXV, 1050; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 810; XLIV, 310. For then it will have only good people, ibid., XXXVIII, 1175. Hence it is not yet without spot, ibid., 982. In the Church, wickedness oppressing and righteousness suffering have never been absent and never will be absent, Hildebert of Tours, CLXXI, 793. The present Church contains the city of God and the city of the devil, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1062. It must be understood in two ways: as not having spot or wrinkle and truly constituting Christ’s body; and as gathered merely in Christ’s name, but still lacking complete and perfect virtues, XXVI, 313.

Now, therefore, the Church is like a lily among thorns amid evil people, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1802. Although here it is not without sin and has certain wrinkles or spots, ibid., XXXII, 593, 617, 637; XXXIII, 842; XLIV, 336, 435, 621, yet its beauty is already wonderful, ibid., XXXVII, 1340, and it is holy. For the sins of her children do not pollute her holiness, ibid., XLIII, 177, 178, 179, 275, 270, 371. No evil persons whatsoever within it prejudice the Church’s holiness, ibid., 234, 616, 617; for the evils committed in the Church do not belong to her, ibid., 310, 312, 315. In the Church, evil people are tolerated by the good, and the latter are not polluted by the former, ibid., 344, 629. Therefore the Church is holy, although, besides the righteous, it is composed of impious, sinful, and foolish people, St. Peter Damian, 536, 753. Fifth, it is holy by reason of its doctrine, which is holy and health-giving, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1030. For it commands every virtue, ibid., XXXVIII, 876; XL, 413, and condemns moral corruption, ibid., XLI, 64, 74.

### III. The catholicity of the Church

The universal, or catholic, Church is known to exist in three ways: by the authority of Holy Scripture, universal tradition, and its distinctive institution, Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1211. Catholicity, or universality, being a mark of the true Church and its primary condition, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1749, promises were therefore made to it of extension among all nations, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 491; XXXVIII, 660; XL, 585, 586, 592, 593; St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 172. These promises have been fulfilled in large part, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 36; Peter the Deacon, LXII, 86, 862. The gift of languages granted to the Apostles foreshadowed the future Church among all nations, St. Augustine, XLIII, 476.

No one, certainly, will deny that Christ’s Church is catholic, St. Optatus of Milevis, XI, 946; St. Augustine, XXXIII, 95, 189, 196, 297, 330, 334, 339, 341, 343, 400, 403, 415, 491, 584, 794, 804; XL, 1196; XLIII, 655; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 740; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 472; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 942; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 555; Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 769. Even its enemies call it catholic, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 128. Therefore the true Church is catholic; and why is it catholic? Alcuin the abbot, CI, 1142, 1273. In what way is it catholic? In four ways.

1. On the ground of times. — For this Church, or assembly of those believing in Christ, so preceded his birth that, in the time of the Law of nature and of the written Law, there existed worshippers of the Christian religion; it was already present in the saints before Christ: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 38. — Since they are called saints, there is a Church on earth: ibid., XXXVII, 1689; ibid., XXXVIII, 38, 39; ibid., XL, 313, 335. — It existed from Abel: St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1164; Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 163. — Before Christ, the saints attained salvation only through faith in Christ: St Augustine, XXXIII, 845, 859. — It will endure until the day on which Christ comes to judge the world: St Ambrose, XVII, 398; ibid., XL, 645; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 625. — Indeed, it will not cease even then: Peter Lombard, CXCI, 660. — Rather, it will remain for eternity: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1484, 1485; St Ambrose, XV, 712; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 666.

2. On the ground of places. — It does not extend only to certain places or only to certain provinces: St Cyprian, IV, 502. Rather, it stretches its branches throughout the whole world: St Ambrose, XVII, 517. — Or it will stretch them; for the Scriptures affirm that it is to be spread through the whole world: St Augustine, XLIII, 32 ff. Hence it is called Catholic because it is spread throughout the entire world: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 834, 835, 839, 942 ff., 965, 1478; St Ambrose, XVI, 740, 771; ibid., XVII, 517; Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 795; St Augustine, XXXIII, 189, 194, 195, 198, 264, 331, 583, 794, 952; ibid., XXXIV, 127; ibid., XXXVI, 214, 513, 566, 640, 642, 669, 807; ibid., XXXVI, 244, 513, 566, [Col. 0680] 640, 642, 669, 807; ibid., XXXVII, 1159, 1630, 1924, 1925; ibid., XXXVIII, 163, 289, 659, 722, 723, 1701, 1126, 1221; ibid., XL, 53, 174, 306, 307, 1196; ibid., XLI, 609; ibid., XLII, 78; XLIII, 34, 35, 79, 144, 197, 252, 254, 256, 264, 265, 268, 269, 272, 283, 284, 306, 310, 318, 319, 330, 340, 346, 369, 370, 380, 400, 423, 427, 443, 444, 491, 492, 531, 542, 582, 587 ff., 603, 605, 628, 653, 718. — Ibid., XLVI, 892, 895, 897, 1226. — Cassiodorus Senator, LXX, 58; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 63; Alcuin, abbot, CI, 1072, 1257; Walafrid of Fulda, CXIII, 527; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 473, 476, 515. — St Lupus Servatus, CXIX, 615; Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 769, 1476, 1480; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 935; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 886; Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 868, 1085, 1295. — Therefore it is called Catholic, or spread throughout the world, because from the rising of the sun to its setting it is disseminated by the radiance of one faith: St Augustine, XXXIX, 2193; because it cries to God from the ends of the earth: ibid., XXXVII, 1602. — It is called from the four quarters of the world in the name of the Trinity: ibid., 1104. — Because throughout the whole earth it bears fruit and grows: ibid., XXXIX, 1586; XLIII, 616, 496, 587, 701. — The true Catholic Church is throughout the whole world, while each heresy exists only in its own part: ibid., XXXVIII, 280. — It is universal: Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 441; for the catholicity of the Church requires that it be among all nations, though not in such a way that all who are there believe: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 308. — It is certain by faith that the true Church is to be extended into all parts of the world: ibid., XLV, 1812. — The true Church of God is Catholic.

3.
