On the ground of the doctrine of faith, in which all have always and everywhere agreed. — Moreover, its doctrine is one and the same from the beginning until now: Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 942. — Faith and unity of minds make it Catholic: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 905; Alcuin, abbot, CI, 1073. — Hence Vincent of Lérins: “Greatest care must be taken in the Catholic Church itself that we hold what has always and everywhere been believed”: L, 640. — The Catholic Church is the true Church.

4. On the ground of the necessity of embracing it in order to attain eternal salvation; for outside it there is no salvation: St Cyprian, IV, 371; St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1477; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1076; ibid., XL, 776; St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 1082; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 501; for outside it God cannot be found: ibid.

## IV. The Apostolicity of the Church

The true Church is called apostolic in several senses:

1. Because it was founded by Christ through the apostles: Tertullian, II, 33, 50; St Cyprian, IV, 15, 16; St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 736; ibid., 202; St Augustine, XXXIII, 553; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 942; and founded especially upon the faith of Peter, prince of the apostles: St Zeno of Verona, XI, 351, 430; St Jerome, XXII, 475, who was established especially as the foundation of the Church; St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 218, 518, 587, 722. — Because all its doctrine comes from the apostles, who received it from Christ: St Zeno of Verona, XI, 49. — It still observes the apostolic custom: Eugyppius, abbot, LXII, 931; for whatever has been received by custom in the Church flows from apostolic tradition: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 418, 419. The apostles are fountains overflowing with the grace of preaching; the doctrine of Christ is learned only through their mouths and those of their disciples or successors: St Leo the Great, LIV, 319, 320. Hence they are called the light of the world: ibid., 820. — Though sent to establish all peoples, they are still called the salt of the earth: ibid., 470.

2. It is apostolic because it possesses a continuous succession of pastors and, consequently, of spiritual ministry: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1481, 1482; Bernard of Fontcaude, CCIV, 797; CCV, 174, 176.

3. Because its pastors may rightly and deservedly claim the mission which they hold from Peter, from whom come the episcopate and the whole authority of that title: St Augustine, XXXIII, 780, 784. Because the doctrine which it professes is one and the same from the beginning until now: Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 942.

## XII. On the doctrine and faith of the Church

The doctrine of the Church comes not from itself but from Christ the Lord: St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 164; to whom the mysteries formerly hidden were revealed by the Father: ibid., IX, 807, 808. — In the Church the doctrine is one and the same from the beginning until now: Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 942; one, even though the languages are diverse: St Augustine, XXXVI, 509. — It flowed forth from the beginnings of the Law: St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 463. — What sort the Church’s doctrine is: St Augustine, XXXII, 1336; XXXIV, 128, 129. What the Church thinks and teaches concerning God: St Augustine, XXXII, 1336. — What it teaches concerning grace: ibid., XXXIII, 767, 768, 817; ibid., XLIV, 332, 338, 378, 980. — Ibid., XLIV, 1033. — What it thinks concerning its temporal goods or revenues, and how it wishes to use them. — Their use ought to be proper: St Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 247. — They are to be used for supporting its preachers, maintaining the choirs of ministers [Col. 0681], the crowds of poor persons, and the multitude of pilgrims who come together: ibid., 245. — Its possession is expenditure for the needy; it possesses gold not in order to store it, but to distribute it and relieve necessities: St Ambrose, XVI, 140, 977. — The goods of the Church are unjustly possessed by laymen: St Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 229. — They are the property of the poor: ibid., 245. — Laymen cannot be their administrators: ibid., 241. — If they handle them and spend them for their own uses, they act against the prohibition and against the canons: ibid., 229. — One who takes away the Church’s goods is judged a thief, sacrilegious person, and murderer: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 172. — Church property must not be alienated: Flodoard of Reims, CXXXV, 103; Ademar, abbot, CXLI, 1101; St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 458. — This doctrine is confirmed by the authority of Leo the Great: Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIV, 1319. — What has once been given to the Church belongs to Christ in perpetuity and can in no way be alienated: Pope St Leo IX, CXLIII, 626. — One who seizes ecclesiastical property is to be excommunicated: ibid., 628. — Whatever has been received by custom in the Church flows from apostolic tradition and the doctrine of the Holy Spirit: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 418, 419. — Every doctrine agreeing with apostolic doctrine is to be reckoned the doctrine of the true Church and consequently counted as truth: Tertullian, II, 33. — Although great power has been conferred upon the Church, nevertheless in teaching it cannot depart from the Tradition of the Fathers: St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 672. — Therefore nothing is to be handed down in the Church except what Christ and the apostles committed to it: Tertullian, II, 18. — The Catholic Church teaches what it has believed, not what it has known: St Augustine, XXXIX, 1613; and in it it is not quickness of understanding that makes the common people most secure, but simplicity in believing: St Augustine, XLII, 175. — It commands faith of those coming to it; heretics promise reason: ibid., XLII, 19. — Wickedness does not grasp the power of heavenly doctrine: St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 575. — To whom the understanding of this doctrine is open: ibid., 616.

## XIII. On the discipline and morals of the Church

The Church’s discipline varies according to the variety of matters and times: St Augustine, XXXIII, 812. — Ecclesiastical rites must sometimes be changed: Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 445. — Whatever the Church has received into the custom of devotion flows from apostolic tradition and the doctrine of the Holy Spirit: Pope St Leo the Great, LIV, 418, 419. — On certain days, for definite reasons, the Church forbids us to fast: St Augustine, XXXIX, 1052. — Fasting is especially not observed on feast days: ibid., XXXIII, 145, 146. — During the Easter season it relaxes fasts for Christians and wills that they pray standing as a sign of the resurrection: ibid., XXXIII, 215; XXXVIII, 1048, 1052. — The Church celebrates three days of Litanies: ibid., XXXIX, 2076. — Moreover, it establishes and observes certain days which it calls medicinal, since they are healthful both for soul and body: ibid., XXXIX, 2019. — Ecclesiastical discipline ought to be vigilant in correcting the wicked not only with words, but also by excommunication and deposition: ibid., XLIII, 631. — Ecclesiastical correction is called bloodless discipline: ibid., St Augustine, XXXIII, 657. — It tolerates many things that it does not approve: ibid., XXXII, 222. — The Church does not prejudge communion with the wicked who are mingled with the good: ibid., XXXIII, 329, 492; for either it lacks the power to prohibit them from communion, or the consideration of peace prevents it: ibid., 207. — It tolerates the wicked but does not consent to their deeds: ibid., XXXVII, 1802; XXXVIII, 55, 56, 59. — Therefore it is not to be blamed for the evil morals of Christians: ibid., XXXII, 1342; XXXIII, 127. — Moreover, the wicked are so intermingled in the Church that they are not merely unknown while hidden, but, for the unity of peace, are often tolerated even when known: ibid., XLIII, 631. — Why the Church tolerates the wicked: ibid., XXXIII, 329, 403, 411; XXXVI, 190, 460, 635, 636, 637, 653, 654, 736; XXXVII, 1604, 1605; XXXVIII, 42, 49; XL, 228; XLII, 292; XLIII, 30, 32, 48, 51, 56, 69, 83, 104, 493, 742, 744. — Tolerance of the wicked has always been customary in the Church: ibid., XLIII, 825. — This tolerance is sometimes necessary: St Augustine, XLV, 1867, 1869; and it sometimes permits the wicked, even unwillingly, to make use of the sacraments, lest disturbance and schism occur: ibid., XXXVIII, 51. — At times it is useful: ibid., XL, 777, for the wicked serve the good: ibid., XXXIX, 1759. — They are like winepresses, by which the good, like grapes and olives, are pressed: ibid., 2249. — “The good in the Church tolerate the wicked for the good of unity,” says St Augustine, “and hate them for the good of equity”: XXXIII, 170, 179, 198, 335, 338. — The highest principle of the Church’s discipline lies in mercy and piety: St Ambrose, XVII, 474.

## XIV. On the perpetual duration, or indefectibility, of the Church

The Church is always stable, or indefectible: first, because its foundation is above in heaven: St Augustine, XXXVI, 223; [Col. 0682] XXXVII, 1103; XXXVIII, 479; St Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 322. — For God, who is the governor of the Church, St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 632, provides for it from eternity and will be with it until the consummation of the age: ibid., IX, 696, 697; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 317; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 153; St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 261. — And Christ is its primary and essential foundation: Remigius the Monk, CXXXI, 675; Rupert of Deutz, CLXIX, 1194. — How the assertion that the Church is founded upon Christ the rock is to be understood: Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 560 ff.; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 930. — Therefore the Church’s stability comes from Christ: Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVI, 255. — Secondly, the Church is stable because it is founded upon Peter and the other apostles as secondary foundations: St Ambrose, XVII, 380. — For all planted the Church, not by inflicting insults, but by suffering and shedding their blood: St Jerome, XXII, 741, 742; St Leo the Great, LV, 51, 59. — Therefore Peter is called the foundation of the Church: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 974. — Therefore the Church is said to have been built upon all the apostles: Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 560 ff. — Founded on apostolic firmness: St Leo the Great, LV, 51, 59. — Insofar as it has a foundation in the apostolic sees: St Augustine, XXXIII, 553; St Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 294; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 561. — And especially in Peter’s firmness: St Zeno of Verona, XI, 361, 430; St Jerome, XXII, 475; St Leo the Great, LIV, 145 ff. It is stable. — Thirdly, because it has another unshaken foundation in Holy Scripture: St Jerome, XXIX, 46. — The doctrine of pastors rests in faith: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 1150. — Therefore the kingdom of the Church will remain for eternity: St Ambrose, XV, 1722. — Because God is with it until the consummation of the age: St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 261. — Therefore the Church will endure perpetually, that is, eternally: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1451, 1485; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 666. — Because it will offer the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood until the consummation of the age: Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 356. — And it will never cease because Christ prayed for it: St Leo the Great, LIV, 394. — Because the unfailing protection of Christ and the Holy Spirit is promised to it: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 857. — Thus it is shaken neither by the rush of a river nor by any storm: St Augustine, XXXIII, 506. — For although it dwells amid diverse waves and storms, St Ambrose, XIV, 363, it is more ready to bring aid than liable to danger: ibid., 682. — It is struck by waves but not overthrown; battered but not weakened; it may be troubled by these waves, but cannot be submerged: St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 598. — Nor is it conquered by persecutions: St Ambrose, XIV, 1092; XVII, 697. — A most beautiful description of the spiritual world, that is, of the Church floating above the waves: St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 275, 276. — It is founded upon Peter with a stable mass: St Jerome, XXII, 475. — God, the faithful helmsman, will not allow the little ship of the Church, tossed by waves, to sink: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 855. — It may be attacked, but cannot be conquered: St Ambrose, XV, 707; St Agobard, CIV, 112, 296; Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVIII, 762; Pope Innocent III, CCXV, 273. — Nothing can prevail against the Church: St Leo the Great, LIV, 393. — The Donatists vainly say that it will perish: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 289. — As some depart and others come, it is founded so as to pass into eternity: ibid., XXXVI, 894, 901, 906, 1007; XXXVII, 1309. — It can neither perish nor be overthrown: ibid., 1353. — It is not conquered, uprooted, or yielded to any temptations until the end of the age comes: ibid., XXXVI, 726. — The Church’s foundation must prevail against all heresies: St Ambrose, XVI, 827. — Because it is built upon the rock, it stands like an impregnable wall: Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 51. — It may at times suffer eclipse, but never fail. — The Church has been planted in faith: ibid., CLXVIII, 958. — The firmness of Peter’s faith, that is, of the Church, is perpetual: St Leo the Great, LIV, 145, 146, 523. — For it is transmitted to his successors: ibid., 155. — Through Christ, steadfastness or firmness of faith was granted to Peter, but to the other apostles through Peter: ibid., 151, 152. — Finally, the Church is indefectible because God founded and propagated it for eternity: St Ambrose, XIV, 1152.

## XV. On the authority and infallibility of the Church

What sort of authority the Church possesses: St Augustine, XL, 319; XLII, 91, 216; XLIII, 466. — The Church’s authority is such that St Augustine would not believe even the Gospel except on its account: ibid., XLII, 176. — With regard to the number of books and the sense of Holy Scripture, even the canonical Scriptures lack authority when they have not always been received by the Church: St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 139; Alcuin, abbot, CI, 1679, 1080. — The authority of the Church is that sufficient ground by which, once known, it is understood that the testimony of the Church is truthful. — According as the Church’s testimony rests upon divine or human authority, it requires divine or human faith. — By “infallibility” is understood that special privilege granted by Christ the Lord to the Church, by which he promised his own assistance and that of the Holy Spirit, so that it may by no means fall into error while teaching. — Therefore, by the privilege granted it by God, the authority of the Church is infallible; for Christ, commanding the apostles to preach and teach what he had taught them, adds: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” Matthew 28:20. — The apostles themselves do not hesitate to assert that infallible authority was conferred upon them by Christ: 1 Timothy, chapter 1; 1 Corinthians, chapter 4; Acts of the Apostles, chapter 15. — The apostles require that faith be placed in them: 2 Thessalonians, chapter 3. — Furthermore, Christ willed his Church to remain and foretold that it would remain through every age as he himself had first instituted it, namely, endowed with infallible authority at least in those matters which concern faith and morals: Matthew 16:18; Luke 10:16. — And the Apostle gives truly weighty testimony to this infallible authority of the Church, writing to Timothy: “…that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth,” First Epistle to Timothy, III. — The Fathers also always recognized and handed down that this same infallible authority remains in the Church; as testimony I appeal to St Clement of Rome, *Epistle to the Corinthians*, I, 160, Latin edition of the Greek Fathers. — St Ignatius Martyr, *Epistle to the Magnesians*, ibid., III, 659. — St Irenaeus, ibid., V, 767; St Clement of Alexandria, VI, 908; St Cyprian, IV, 502; Lactantius, VI, 542; St Ambrose, XVI, 1004; St Augustine, XXXVI, 726. — But the Church’s authority is not to be regarded as infallible in all things. It is infallible only: first, in that doctrine and law which Christ himself revealed and delivered to the apostles, and which he willed to be continually preserved in their successors, whether assembled in a council or dispersed throughout the whole world; secondly, in defining doctrine concerning faith and morals; thirdly, in interpreting Holy Scripture and expounding the genuine sense of the word of God delivered by Christ and the apostles; fourthly, in expounding true divine traditions; fifthly, its judgment in controversies of faith and morals is infallible. — A different view, however, is to be taken of the Church’s judgment when it condemns persons as heretics; when it issues decrees concerning what are called dogmatic facts; when it judges laws, precepts, practices, and ceremonies that are merely ecclesiastical. — How the Lord fortified the authority of the Church: St Augustine, XXXIII, 448. — What the whole Church believes, even if it can be neither investigated by reason nor explained in speech, must be received: ibid., XLIV, 829. — Without the authority of the Church proposing the word of God there is no certainty of faith; but truth is held when that is done which has pleased the universal Church: ibid., XLIII, 466. — Christ referred to the Church the examination of matters pertaining to doctrine: ibid., XXXV, 1355. — Princes have accorded the Church such deference that whatever has been decided in it cannot be annulled: ibid., XXXVI, 196. — “Authority establishes the difference between the clergy and the people,” says Tertullian: II, 922.

## XVI. On the power of the Church

The Church possesses a twofold power: divine, because of the special assistance of the Holy Spirit promised to it and its infallibility in proposing the mysteries of faith, Matthew 28:20; and human, which it has when considered in itself, or as an assembly of persons professing by perpetual tradition one doctrine concerning divine things. — It rightly claims for itself the right and power to offer to God the one true sacrifice acceptable to him: St Augustine, XXXIII, 15; XLIII, 57, 300, 461; XLIV, 420; Udalric, monk, CXLIX, 488. — Likewise, it claims for itself the right of binding and loosing sins of every kind: St Ambrose, XVI, 468; St Augustine, XXXIV, 25; St Leo the Great, LVI, 622; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 563, 622. — There is no sin which is not forgiven through the Church to one who repents and seeks pardon: St Augustine, XXXV, 1336. — It has this power from Christ: St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 547; St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 63, 611. — It received it in the person of Peter: St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 690. — To him the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given: St Augustine, XXXIV, 25. — They were given indeed to Peter alone, as representing the unity of the Church: ibid., XXXVIII, 1349. — But in Peter they were given to the whole Church, whose person he bore: ibid., 802, 1349; XL, 308. — It alone exercises this power both lawfully and validly: Tertullian, II, 1025; St Augustine, XL, 263; St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 542. — Nor do those outside the Church possess it; it belongs only to those in whom faith and doctrine according to the apostolic rule are found: Rupert of Deutz, CLXX, 641. — This power of the Church is figured [Col. 0684] by the power which the Son had from the Father over the nations, not in his humanity but in his divinity: Alcuin, abbot, C, 1108. — By the power granted to it, it remits not only sins but also disgraceful crimes accounted most grave sins: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 867. — The office of loosing was given to the Church so that the bonds of those who have revived from sin may be loosed: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 434, 594; XXXIX, 1549, 1711. — Christ first raises sinners by his grace, and then the Church looses them: St Augustine, XXXVIII, 468. — In the Church of Christ there is a true power to establish and enact discipline; to institute rites and make laws. This is evident both from Holy Scripture and from constant tradition: Matthew 13; First Epistle to the Corinthians 5:11; 1 Corinthians 10:6 and 13:19; St Cyprian, IV, 301; St Augustine, XL, 199; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 609. — These laws of the Church bind in conscience, according to St Chrysostom explaining Christ’s words, “As the Father sent me,” etc., John 20:21. — It may hand over rebellious children to Satan: Bernard of Fontcaude, CCIV, 978. — Thus it uses the spiritual sword: Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 955. — Christ conferred legislative power upon the Church which he founded: Luke 10:16; Matthew 18:17. — The Church has the power and right to determine, judge, and decide controversies; the right and power to compel by deprivation of spiritual goods, as well as by censures and exclusion from its bosom, that is, by excommunication: Bernard of Fontcaude, CCIV, 798. — By no prescription can the Church be deprived of its own authority, derived from Christ. In spiritual matters it is supreme and does not depend upon temporal power; but in temporal matters it possesses no power by its institution or by divine right: St Bernard, CLXXXII ff.

## XVII. On the Roman Pontiff

The Roman Pontiff is Peter’s vicar, successor, and heir: Alcuin, abbot, C, 170; St Agobard of Lyons, CIV, 196. — For several centuries he alone has been called “Apostolic”: ibid., 298. — Whoever is not joined in communion with the Apostolic See is schismatic: ibid., 293. — He stands above the other bishops: St Augustine, XLIV, 541, 648; St Peter Damian, CXLV, 89. — Peter—and what is said of Peter is to be understood of his successors—was first and chief in the order of the apostles: St Augustine, XXXV, 480, 481, 797, 1353, 1368, 2269, 2384; XXXVIII, 479; XLIII, 127; XLIV, 648. — To Peter, and therefore to the Roman Pontiff, his successor, the pastoral care of the whole Church was entrusted: St Augustine, XXXIII, 786; XL, 858; XLV, 1763; Udalric, monk, CXLIX, 487, 491. — Peter was made by Christ prince of the whole Church: St Leo the Great, LIV, 430, 431, 432. — To Peter were entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 955; St Augustine, XXXIX, 1899. — Peter alone received them, to be communicated to the others: St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1087. — Power in the Church was conferred upon Peter by the Lord: St Augustine, XLV, 1771. — Equal power was given to those who merited the inheritance of his see: ibid., 1726. — The Roman Pontiff has authority over all others: ibid., XL, 1129. — To Peter was assigned power to judge; heavenly judgment was placed in his discretion, and governance of the universal Church entrusted to him: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 400. — The Roman Pontiff’s authority is so great that no one dares dispute his judgment: St Augustine, XLV, 1725. — The Roman Pontiff is judged by no one: Udalric, monk, CXLIX, 487. — He judges all: ibid., 488, 490, 492. — He alone convenes a general council and judges bishops: Lucifer of Cagliari, XIII, 971; St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1185. — Councils are neither held nor bishops condemned apart from his authority: Pope St Julius, VIII, 971. — No council is valid unless confirmed by apostolic authority: Geoffrey of Vendôme, CLVII, 196. — Still less is any valid that is contrary to that authority: ibid. — The Roman See has never been accustomed to err: ibid., 42. — It has never been contaminated by any heresies, but has always been Catholic: St Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1222. — The Church of Peter is the first of all Churches; from it all received faith and doctrine: Tertullian, II, 32, 1025. — The Apostolic See is the support of all bishops and the summit of all Churches: Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 32. — The various appeals to that see demonstrate the pre-eminence of the Roman See: St Leo the Great, LV, 576. — Appeal may be made to the Roman Church from any part of the world, but no one has ever been permitted to appeal from it: St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1184. — The custom of consulting the Roman See in doubtful matters has always been observed throughout the whole world: St Augustine, XXXIII, 796. — In the Roman Church the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished: St Cyprian, IV, 25, 26; St Augustine, XXXIII, 163. — Where the Roman Pontiff is, there is the Church: no death, but eternal life: St Ambrose, XIV, 1082. — The Roman Church is the Church of the whole world; it is the whole, while the others [Col. 0685] are, as it were, its parts: Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 625. — Not some synod, but Christ himself instituted the primacy of the Roman Church: St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1182 ff. — By a singular privilege entrusted to it alone, it opens or closes, for whom it will, the gates of heaven: ibid., 1186. — It was constituted by the Lord head and teacher of all Churches: Udalric, monk, CXLIX, 485; St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1128; Alger of Liège, CLXXX, 962. — God built the Church upon one, namely Peter: Udalric, monk, CXLIX, 487. — When Peter desired to die with Christ, the Lord himself told him that he could not then follow him, because he was being preserved for founding the Church: St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 347. — The enactments of the Apostolic See must be received as though confirmed by the voice of the divine command itself: St Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1107. — Andrew did not receive primacy among the apostles, even though he followed Jesus first; there is only one head of the Church on earth, namely the Roman See, and not two or more, as the Greeks maintain: Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1225. — Finally, the Apostolic See is set above all Churches and prelates: Alger of Liège, CLXXX, 962; St Bernard, CLXXXII, 751; Pope Innocent III, CCXVI, 1186. — Why the supreme pontiff is called Pope: Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 711.

## XVIII. On bishops: what they ought to be, and the fulfilment of their offices

As to the definition of the name, *episcopus* means “overseer”: St Ambrose, XVII, 579. — In fact, he sits upon a higher throne in the Church: ibid.; St Jerome, XXII, 1193. — Episcopal eminence cannot be equalled by any comparisons: St Ambrose, XVII, 569. — If you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, those will be far inferior, as if you compared lead ore with the brilliance of gold: ibid., 570. — Bishops hold the place of the apostles: St Jerome, XXII, 46. — They act in the stead of Peter and Paul: ibid., 353. — Therefore, possessing their honour, let them strive to possess their merit as well: ibid., 583. — Let them decrease in humility, not swell with eminence: ibid., 662. — The more elevated a bishop’s chair is, the more humble his conscience ought to be: ibid. — The sheep to be governed were entrusted by Christ to bishops: St Ambrose, XVII, 570. — In the person of the bishop the salvation of the whole people rests: ibid., 483. — Therefore they must feed them by the word; a bishop is bound by the necessity of command to preach the word of God: ibid., 568, 569. — Therefore he should possess knowledge so that he may teach others: St Jerome, XXV, 1407. — So that he may restrain from error the sheep entrusted to him: ibid., XXIII, 160. — It does not profit him to enjoy a conscience of virtues unless he can instruct the people entrusted to him: ibid., XXIII, 258. — Above all, he must feed by example; he ought to be an example to the Christian people. For what will the secular multitude do if, by illicit pleasures and forbidden acts, he has provoked the multitude of the people to a like gulf of crimes? St Ambrose, XVII, 578. — If a bishop falls, he obtains pardon with difficulty: St Jerome, XXIII, 159. — He must therefore feed by word and example; for if the bishop is the light of the Church in order to teach, he is also salt and seasoning, in order to preserve by virtues and examples the people entrusted to him from the contagion of vices: ibid., 158, 159. — The various endowments and virtues which bishops ought to possess are enumerated: St Ambrose, XVII, 572 ff. — For they must be known more by good work than by profession, more by merits than by name: ibid., 570. — Content with the stipends of his own Church alone, he should not seek what he knows to be superfluous, but should gladly share with the poor, out of his own poverty, the resources of his Church: ibid., 547. — The glory of a bishop is to provide for the want of the poor: St Jerome, XXII, 533.

## XIX. On the reasons why one ought to enter the Church and adhere to it, and why those who have once entered it should never depart from it
Once one has entered the Church, one must never depart from it. Why? Because salvation is found in it alone. St Cyprian, IV, 371; St Optatus of Milevis, XI, 1477; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1076; XL, 776; XLIII, 170; St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 420; St Leo the Great, [Col. 0686] LVI, 880; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 755; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 501.—For nothing defiled shall enter heaven; moreover, whoever stands outside the Church cannot possess purity. St Jerome, XXV, 71.—For salvation is from God alone, who cannot be found outside the Church. St Anselm, CLVIII, 628 and 629; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 501.—He does not have God as Father who does not have the Church as Mother. St Cyprian, IV, 503; St Augustine, XL, 668.—In the Church alone there is remission of sins, ibid., XXXV, 2062.—Nor is it possessed outside the Church, ibid., XXXVIII, 460, 463, 465, 1349; Rupert of Deutz, CLXVIII, 182.—In the Church all crimes whatsoever are forgiven. St Augustine, XL, 262.—The Holy Spirit forgives sins through the Church, ibid., XXXVIII, 600; XL, 263; XLIII, 146, 147, 150.—Outside the Church many are heard concerning many things, but not unto eternal life, ibid., XXXVI, 478; XXXVII, 1270, 1704, 1721.—Outside the Church the preaching of God, through which human beings are saved, is vain, ibid., XXXVI, 929.—The sacraments, through which salvation comes, may possess the visible form of godliness; but outside the Church they have no spiritual efficacy, ibid., XXXVIII, 463.—They do not profit toward life. St Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 546.—Indeed, outside the Church they are possessed unto destruction, ibid., XXXIII, 229; not because the sacraments lose their power of holiness when they pass to heretics, ibid., XLIII, 748; for the holiness of the sacrament may be there where holiness of life is absent, ibid., XLIII, 298; and wherever they are, they are themselves, ibid., 70; and the sacraments possessed among heretics and schismatics are not theirs but Christ’s, ibid., 154.—Baptism conferred anywhere in the name of the Most Holy Trinity is complete, but does not benefit if it is not given in the Catholic Church, ibid., XL, 1066.—Outside the Church no sacrifice, no abstinence, no mortification of the flesh profits toward salvation. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 338.—No sacrifice is true; even penance itself avails nothing, ibid., 1123.—Not even martyrdom itself profits. St Cyprian, IV, 495.—Indeed, outside the Church there are no martyrs, ibid., XXXIII, 410; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 58 ff.—Even if a heretic, schismatic, or any other person standing outside the Church were burned alive for Christ’s name, he shall be punished with eternal torment, ibid., XXXIII, 758.—Outside the Church no one, however holy his life, shall have eternal life, ibid., XXXIII, 579.—There is no share in God’s inheritance for those placed outside salvation, ibid., XXXVIII, 797.—Salvation is in and through the Church alone: not because all who belong to the Church are saved, but because all who are saved are saved in the Church. St Jerome, XXV, 980.—Outside the Church baptism itself does not profit for the remission of sins unless a person has been reconciled to unity, ibid., XLIII, 119, 121, 200.—Outside the Church charity is not possessed, ibid., XXXVIII, 1223; XLIII, 148, 149, 312.—The gift of blessed life can be obtained only within the Church, ibid., XLIII, 155.—Those cut off from the Church are exposed to every danger and to wolves, ibid., XXXIII, 723.—Those who are not in the Church are dead. St Cyprian, IV, 409.—Outside the Church the merits of virtues do not increase. St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 46.—Nor are the Holy Scriptures rightly understood; nor do good works possess merit for those who are outside, Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 639 ff.—Nor is a good work fruitfully performed, St Augustine, XXXV, 1500; XL, 1196.—The Catholic Church alone retains true worship, Lactantius, VI, 542.—And there is no place of worship except in the Catholic Church. St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 379.—Outside the Church no one praises or proclaims God, ibid., LXXIX, 623.—Whoever eats the Lamb outside the Church is profane. Ulrich of Cluny, CXLIX, 488.—Only the children of the Church may eat of the Lamb; it is forbidden to the rest. Bruno, Abbot of Asti, CLXIV, 261.—Christ is eaten in the Church alone. St Jerome, XXIV, 665.—Therefore one must enter the Church.—The gates of the Church stand continually open to those wishing to be saved, ibid., 594.—Moreover, one enters through faith in Christ. Remigius the Monk, CXXXI, 312.—Through the humility so often praised by him. St Augustine, XXXV, 1721.—For the door of the Church is Christ himself, ibid., 1721, 1726.—The Church is closed to no one: whoever promises to profess the Catholic faith is admitted, Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 507.—But once admitted, one must never depart from it. St Cyprian, IV, 371.

[Col. 0687]

## LXXX. INDEX CONCERNING THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY

There is a twofold hierarchy and a twofold power of clerics: namely, that of order and that of jurisdiction, or government. For when Christ established the Church, he gave laws to the society of human beings, whom he willed both to enjoy spiritual goods and to be governed in the best way, so that thereafter they might be participants in eternal blessedness. In order that people might enjoy spiritual goods, he created the power of order; in order that they might be governed in the best way, he established the power of jurisdiction. From this one may understand the force and rationale of each power and hierarchy.

But every power and hierarchy of jurisdiction is established for ruling and governing subjects; and jurisdiction, which consists wholly in this rule and government, cannot exist unless there are subjects to be ruled and governed. This hierarchy belongs to the best government of the Church; and, in order to be rightly constituted, it must have its magistrates, just as civil society has its own, to exercise authority over the multitude of persons of which the society consists, lest, if they obey no one, great disturbance and confusion of all affairs necessarily arise among them. For this reason bishops were created by Christ: not only that they might confer spiritual goods upon people, but also that they might be the chief magistrates of Christian society.

But among these magistrates there had to be one who presided over the rest and ruled and directed the whole society. This was required by the divine wisdom of the lawgiver, who would give this society a head and ruler; and by that unity both of faith, in which he willed all Christians to agree, and of charity, by which all members of the Church ought to be joined to one another in the same bond of peace and communion. For what would this unity be unless one person were set over the whole Church to protect and preserve it, and to join all together in one faith, one charity, and finally one Church? Therefore this primacy was given to Peter and to his successors, the supreme pontiffs, so that through one head the Church might be one.

Christ sent the apostles to proclaim the Gospel throughout the whole world, and did not divide it among individual provinces or cities. But afterward, when the number of believers had increased, they themselves instituted that division which they judged necessary in order that a proper system of government might stand. From this, then, must be traced the first origin of the division of dioceses, as also the origin of patriarchs and metropolitans. All these arrangements were sketched by the apostles and afterward completed and definitively established by the Church.

Therefore that mission to the whole world was proper and peculiar to the apostles, through whom Christ’s religion was to be proclaimed everywhere. But once it had been proclaimed and made known to peoples, definite boundaries were established within which each bishop should exercise jurisdiction. Hence several provinces and nations were assigned to patriarchs; one nation or kingdom to primates; one province to metropolitans; and one diocese to bishops. Each of these has authority in the tract of land over which he is set. Yet from all these one body must be formed, such as the Catholic Church is; and it cannot be formed unless all are joined into one, nor can they be joined unless all have one head and one common centre.

Therefore all bishops, who are set over their own Churches as members—while the one Catholic Church contains all those members gathered into one—must take care that the particular Churches which they govern flow together into one common centre and are subjected to one head. Thus the unity of the Church is brought about and preserved, when all members acknowledge one [Col. 0688] head and have one centre in which they are joined.

Christ established Peter as this common centre of unity and head of all. But since Peter was to die, whereas the Church was to endure until the consummation of the age, another had to be appointed after his death to govern the universal Church. For who would suppose that Christ gave a temporary shepherd to a flock intended to endure perpetually, such as he willed his Church to be? Therefore the office was transmitted and the authority transferred to Peter’s successors—namely, that which had been given by Christ to Peter. These are the Roman Pontiffs, who hold in the Church the very place which Peter held while living: that is, the place of the head, and of a head not idle but equipped and endowed with the authority which a head governing the Church ought to possess.

For Christ did not establish this head in order that it might bear an empty and vain title, but that it might preserve the unity of the whole Church. It follows that he gave it every power needed to fulfill its function; for it cannot be said that Christ gave someone an office and did not give the capacities without which the office itself cannot be exercised. Consequently, the primacy which Peter and his successors received from Christ must be a primacy not merely of honour and dignity but also of jurisdiction. Those are gravely mistaken who, although they cannot be ignorant that the reason for establishing the primacy was the unity of so many people and so many Churches from which the one Catholic Church is constituted, either suppose that there is no head through which that multitude of people and Churches is joined together, or imagine a head empty and inactive, without the force and authority by which it compels people to obey. It would be as though someone formed an army without a commander, or gave it a commander who bore a shadowy title, empty of the power and authority by which soldiers obey and are kept at their duty.

And since the supreme Pontiff must compel to unity all the dioceses, provinces, and nations comprised by the one Catholic Church, he must necessarily have power over all. Thus his authority, which embraces the whole Church, extends over all patriarchs, primates, metropolitans, and bishops; for if any one of them were not subject to this authority, he could with impunity break the unity from which the Catholic Church cannot be separated. And this is the ordering of the ecclesiastical hierarchy: all Christian bishops are subject to metropolitans; metropolitans to primates and patriarchs; and all, finally, to the Roman Pontiff. Bishops, metropolitans, primates, patriarchs, and the supreme Pontiff, prince of all, properly constitute the hierarchy called that of jurisdiction.

The remaining magistrates were created to assist bishops, and a part of the jurisdiction which belongs wholly to the bishop was delegated to them. Hence coadjutors, chorepiscopi, vicars, and parish priests were established to act in the bishop’s place, together with other magistrates to whom a definite authority over the people was given under the bishop. The ecclesiastical hierarchy truly and properly consists of all these.

But since in the following Indexes we deal separately with the supreme Pontiff, metropolitans, bishops, priests, and other subordinate ministers, we do not labour to add anything more here. In those sections the reader will find what is required concerning the hierarchy; moreover, let him consult the special Index concerning the sacrament of Order.

[Col. 0689]

## LXXXI. INDEX CONCERNING THE SUPREME PONTIFF, PRESENTING IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER THE CONSTANT TRADITION OF THE FATHERS CONCERNING HIS PRIMACY, POWER, AND INFALLIBILITY

### Notice

The supreme Pontiff, or Roman Pontiff, is by divine right the head of the Church and the centre of unity, Peter’s successor, Christ’s vicar, father and teacher of all Christians; and throughout the whole Church he possesses a primacy not only of dignity but also of jurisdiction. Hence he enjoys many rights beyond other bishops. For he is first among Christian bishops and exercises jurisdiction over all; he alone has the authority to rule and govern the universal Church; having undertaken the office of universal teacher, he cannot err in defining controversies of faith. But, lest we be drawn out at excessive length, we divide this Index into two sections. The first concerns the election, primacy, and authority of the supreme Pontiff; the second will treat his infallibility, presenting the Fathers’ constant tradition on these matters in chronological order, that is, by reporting or indicating their opinions from Tertullian to Innocent III.

### First Section. Concerning the election, primacy, and authority of the supreme Pontiff

The Church of Peter is first of all, from whom all received faith and doctrine, Tertullian, II, 32, 1025. The keys of heaven were given to Peter, and through him to the Church, ibid., 142.—Primacy is given to Peter in order that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown forth, St Cyprian, IV, 500. There is one head and one origin, ibid., 502. Peter did not say that he held the primacy when he was rebuked by Paul, ibid., 410. The Lord first gave Peter the power of binding and loosing, ibid., III, 1114.—The Church, founded upon Peter, is the source of unity, Council of Carthage, IV, 1043; St Cyprian, IV, 1114. Peter speaks in the name of the Church, ibid., 406, etc. To Peter alone Christ said, “Whatever you bind,” ibid., 1168. Peter alone speaks for all and answers in the Church’s voice, ibid., III, 806, 807. Christ entrusts his sheep to Peter, ibid., 449. In the Roman Church the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished, ibid., 25, 26.—The prerogative of Peter’s see: head, St Hilary, X, 639.—Among these sees it is first, St Optatus, XI, 946. Peter is head of all the apostles, ibid., 947. In that one chair unity was to be preserved by all, lest the other apostles should each claim individual chairs for himself, ibid., 947. To Peter were entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, ibid., 955.—Neither councils are celebrated nor bishops condemned apart from his authority, Pope St Julius, VIII, 971.—The Roman Pontiff hears bishops’ cases at first instance, as they say, throughout Italy and Gaul, Prolegomena to St Damasus, XIII, 228, 229.—Concerning not deciding bishops’ cases without the authority of the Roman Pontiff, Pope St Felix II, XIII, 22.—Outside the knowledge of the Apostolic See—that is, of the primate—let no one dare to ordain, St Siricius, XIII, 1157.—His supreme authority was often acknowledged by Easterners, Prolegomena to St Damasus, XIII, 144, 162, 163, 174, 181, 194, 255; confirmed by emperors, ibid., 194, 228, 236.—Peter is set over the Church, St Ambrose, XIV, 1109. Peter possessed the primacy of confession, not of honour; the primacy of faith, not of rank, ibid., XVI, 826. Those who do not possess Peter’s see do not possess Peter’s inheritance, ibid., 476. Peter was first among the apostles, ibid., XVII, 229. Andrew did not receive the primacy, but Peter did, ibid., 332. He was first among the apostles, to whom the Saviour had entrusted the care of the Churches, ibid., 334. Why Christ chose Peter’s boat, ibid., 677. What is Peter’s key? ibid., 671. What sheep and what flock did the blessed apostle Peter receive? ibid., 570.—Why the Apostolic See holds the primacy, St Boniface I, XX, 778.—The pre-eminence of the Roman episcopate, St Augustine, XLIV, 551. Peter is first and foremost in the order of apostles, ibid., XXXVIII, 479, 481, 797, 1353, 1365, 1368. The primacy of the apostles is pre-eminent in Peter, ibid., 480; XLIII, 127. Peter’s primacy of apostleship is to be preferred to every episcopate, ibid. The sheep were entrusted by Christ to Peter as signifying the unity of the Church, ibid., 1350. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter as representing the person of the Church, [Col. 0690] ibid., 1349. The authority of the Roman See, ibid., 781. In condemning heretics, ibid., XXXIII, 865, 869. In the Roman Church the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished, ibid., XXXIII, 163. The Roman Pontiff has authority over all others, ibid., XL, 1129. So great is the authority of the Roman Pontiff that no one dares dispute his judgment, ibid., XLV, 1725. The custom of consulting the Roman See in anxious matters has always been observed by the whole world, ibid., XXXIII, 796.—St Peter, first of all bishops, St Leo the Great, LIV, 147. Prince of the whole Church, ibid., 152, 395. Set by Christ over the calling of the nations, all the apostles, and all the Fathers of the Church, ibid., 149. First in apostolic dignity, ibid., 150. Prince of the apostolic order, ibid., 424. Having obtained the primacy of the apostolate, ibid., 513. Prince of the episcopal crown, ibid., 637. In Peter the episcopate was principally established, ibid., 629. Peter’s primacy, the reward of his faith, ibid., 615. The chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely entrusted to Peter in such a way that it is founded upon perpetual firmness, ibid., 507. The honour of power in Peter, ibid., 425. St Peter’s privileges, ibid., 145, 146. The right of this power passed to the apostles and other bishops, but Peter’s pattern was set over all, ibid., 151. What Peter’s privilege was in this respect, ibid. The Roman Pontiff is Peter’s heir, ibid., 147, 155. The Roman Pontiff acts in Peter’s stead, ibid., 147. In what sense, ibid., note. The same dignity which was in Peter is in the Roman Pontiff, ibid. Peter both lives and presides in his own see, ibid., 743. Peter is to be acknowledged and honoured in their person, ibid., 147. The Roman Pontiff’s primacy was divinely instituted, ibid., 507. Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, ibid., LVI, 392. How much the African Church deferred to the authority of the Roman Church, ibid., 1101. The prerogative of the Roman See, ibid., 268, 761. Reports were sent to the Roman See as to the head of the Churches, ibid., 506. Peter’s pre-eminence, ibid., LXXVI, 1002. The primacy of Peter and of the Roman Church, ibid., LXXVII, 746. The care of the Church entrusted to Peter, ibid., 745. Peter himself now sits in his chair in his successors, ibid., 899. Peter’s prerogatives, ibid., 1160. The Roman Pontiff is the ministerial head of the whole Church and the centre of ecclesiastical unity, ibid., 773, note. St Peter’s successor is by divine right set over the four patriarchs, ibid., 597, note. Boniface, a distinguished man of Africa, and several others are ordered to come to the threshold of blessed Peter to give account of their faith, ibid., 718. The Roman Pontiff anciently had the power to prohibit certain books, which even Easterners were bound to obey, ibid., 850. He ought to hear cases of primates according to the canons, ibid., 996. The Roman Pontiff’s authority in granting privileges, ibid., 1042.—St Peter received the primacy of judicial authority. Venerable Bede, XCIV, 223.—The Roman Pontiff is above the Church, not conversely, St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 181.—The Roman Pontiff is St Peter’s vicar and heir of his authority. Alcuin, C, 170.—Chosen by God, vicar of the apostles, prince of the Church, ibid., 178.—The Roman Pontiff, vicar of blessed Peter, St Agobard, CIV, 296, note. How he may be called “bishop of bishops”: alone he has for several centuries been called “apostolic,” ibid., 298, note. He is called “brother” by the other [Col. 0691] bishops, ibid., 297. Vicar of the Apostolic See, ibid., 295, note. His authority is not necessary in every ecclesiastical case of princes, ibid., 312, note. The letters of Roman pontiffs in a case of faith are examined by bishops gathered together, ibid., 241. The Apostolic Sees formerly possessed great authority, ibid., 293. Great reverence is owed by all to the Apostolic See, ibid.—Peter, prince of the apostles, who deserved to receive from the Lord’s mouth the primacy of the Churches, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 786.—Peter, who is set over all nations, all the apostles, and all Fathers of the Church, St Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 711. Most blessed Peter was established prince of the apostolic order, rock of the Church, and keeper of the keys of the kingdom, ibid., 712. This is entrusted to Peter uniquely because Peter’s pattern is set before all rulers of the Church, ibid.—Peter is present, and at his will the whole world is loosed and bound, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 646. O how powerful the dignity, how worthy the power: Peter judges, and the Almighty confirms Peter’s judgments, ibid. In Peter’s hand is the hand of the Most High, ibid. Concerning the power and primacy of the Apostolic See, St Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 555. That blessed Peter was granted by the Lord to preside over the other apostles, with their consent, ibid., 485. That, after the pattern of the apostles, a certain distinction was made among bishops, although the see of blessed Peter is pre-eminent over them, ibid., 486. That the Roman Church presides over all Churches, just as blessed Peter was granted pre-eminence over the other apostles, ibid. That no one may presume to judge or reconsider the judgment of the Apostolic See, ibid., 487. That more difficult cases and greater affairs, if an appeal has been made, be referred to the Apostolic See, ibid., 489. That primates investigate an accused bishop, but pronounce no sentence of condemnation without Apostolic authority, ibid., 490. That it was decreed that without the judgment of the Roman Pontiff neither councils be celebrated nor bishops condemned [lacuna]. Thus the Roman Church has the primacy over all Churches, ibid., 492. That special privileges were granted to the Apostolic See concerning the convening of councils, the trials and restorations of bishops, and the highest affairs of the Churches, ibid., 492. That in bishops’ cases the pope’s judgment should be awaited, ibid. As there was a distinction of authority among the apostles, such that one was pre-eminent over the others, so it was ordered among bishops that individual bishops preside over individual provinces; nevertheless, the Roman Church presides over all of them, ibid., 493.—A synod of bishops is not to be convened without the authority of the Roman See, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 316. Councils are not valid without Apostolic authority, ibid. Which is the first see, Ivo of Chartres, ibid., 321. That the Lord conferred primacy upon Peter among the disciples so that it might thus be diffused through the Church, ibid., 323. The Roman See judges concerning the whole Church, while itself passing under no one’s judgment, ibid., 325. A general synod is not to be summoned without a pope’s command, ibid., 326. That the election and consecration of the Roman Pontiff ought to be performed justly and canonically, ibid. That it is in the pope’s power to restore those unjustly condemned or excommunicated, ibid., 327. That imperial legates are not to be awaited in the election of the Roman Pontiff, ibid. That the judgment of the Apostolic See is not to be reconsidered by anyone, ibid., 328. Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, ibid., 329. That no mortal may presume to rebuke the Roman Pontiff even when he has gravely sinned, ibid., 329. Preface of the Council of Nicaea concerning the primacy of the Roman See, ibid., 330. That bishops’ judgments must be strengthened by Apostolic authority, ibid., 332. That doubtful matters are to be brought to the Roman See, ibid., 333. That decrees of the Roman See are to be received as rules of the canons, ibid. That no one may add anything to or subtract anything from the decrees of pontiffs, ibid., 335. That whoever violates the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs is anathema, ibid. That whoever refuses obedience to the Apostolic See incurs the crime of idolatry, ibid., 335. That the see of blessed Peter is head of all Churches and all must assent to its decrees, ibid., 336. That the Apostolic See has not departed from the way of apostolic preaching nor fallen into heretical novelties, ibid., 337. That councils are authorized by letters of the Roman Pontiff, ibid. That, as a whole door turns upon its hinge, so the welfare of the whole Church is ordered by Peter and his successors, ibid., 338. That the Roman Church holds first place among all, ibid., 340. As Peter was granted by the Lord to be pre-eminent over the other apostles, so was his see, ibid., 341. That the pope is to be called bishop of the first see, ibid., 346. That the authority to convene general councils has been entrusted, as a special power, to the Apostolic See, ibid., 375. That no bishop can be condemned without the authority of the Roman Pontiff, ibid., 412. That more difficult cases be referred to the summit of the Roman See for determination by Apostolic judgment, ibid., 413. That all bishops may appeal to the Roman See in necessities, [Col. 0692] ibid., 414. How and by what persons the election of the supreme Pontiff is to be made, ibid., 1127. Whose votes ought to prevail in the election of the supreme Pontiff, ibid., 1129. The authority of the Apostolic See cannot establish anything contrary to the statutes of the saints, ibid., 1130. The Roman Church received its primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord himself, ibid., 1182. No synod but Christ established the primacy of the Roman Church, ibid. The first see is subject to no one’s judgment, ibid., 1183. The first see judges the cases of others, ibid., 1184. No one is permitted to judge what the pope has decreed or to reconsider his sentence, ibid. The judgment of the Apostolic See is not to be reconsidered by anyone, ibid., 1185. It is not permitted for any persons to convene a synod without the Roman Pontiff’s authority, ibid., 1185. “O blessed gatekeeper of heaven, to whom not only the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted, but also the counsels of the heavenly mysteries!” ibid., CLXII, 596.—Concerning the primacy of Peter the apostle, Rupert, CLXVII, 1563.—Concerning the pope, Honorius of Autun, CLXII, 601.—His see has received primacy among all Churches, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 525.—A synod ought not to be convened without the authority of the Roman Pontiff, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 93, 94, 95. The Roman Church received primacy from Christ, ibid., 118, 119, 123. The emperor has the right of choosing the Pontiff, ibid., 335. The election of the Roman Pontiff belongs by right to the emperor, ibid. The Roman Pontiff should be ordained in the presence of the emperor’s legates, ibid., 338. Louis grants the election of Roman Pontiffs to the Romans, ibid., 339. The election and consecration of the Roman Pontiff should take place only justly and canonically, ibid., 340. No obstacle is to be raised by the emperor or his envoys against the election of the Roman Pontiff, ibid., 340. The Pontiff can in no way be loosed or bound by secular power, ibid., 457. The emperor ought not judge the acts of pontiffs, ibid. The sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power govern the helm of this world, ibid., 458. Emperors ought to be subject to pontiffs, not preside over them, ibid., 459.—Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1213. Peter’s principate is more excellent than all others, ibid., 1222.—Prerogatives of the supreme Pontiff, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 712.—Concerning the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, Innocent III, CCXVII, 778.

### Second Section. Concerning the infallibility of the supreme Pontiff

Christ promised that blessed Peter’s faith would not fail and directed him to strengthen his brethren; and it is known to all that the apostolic Pontiffs, predecessors of my lowliness, have always done this confidently, Pope Lucius, III, 982. The Church remains unblemished to the end, according to Christ’s promise in saying to Peter: “Peter, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you,” etc.; “but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned, strengthen your brethren,” Innocent III, CCXVII, 981, 982.

The one Church was founded by Christ the Lord upon Peter as the source and principle of unity, Council of Carthage, III, 1033.

To whom shall one who thirsts come: to heretics, where there is absolutely no spring or river of living water, or to the Church, which is one, founded by the Lord’s word upon the one who also received her keys? St Cyprian, III, 1116. They dare to sail and bear letters from schismatics and profane persons to Peter’s chair and to the principal Church, whence the unity of the priesthood arose; nor do they reflect that these are the Romans whose faith, as the Apostle preached, was praised, and to whom perfidy cannot gain access, ibid., 818, 821. Christ builds his Church upon that one, ibid., IV, 499. Does one who abandons Peter’s chair, upon which the Church is founded, trust that he is in the Church? ibid., 500, 501.

So that even the rock upon which the Church was to be built trembled. St Hilary, IX, 836. Blessed foundation of the Church, and rock worthy of her building, which would break the laws of hell, the gates of Tartarus, and every bar of death, ibid., 1010.

Accordingly, not without reason did he give Simon the name Peter, he upon whom he built the Church, St Zeno, XI, 351.

Where Peter is, there is the Church; where the Church is, there is no death but eternal life. And therefore he added: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it,” St Ambrose, XIV, 1082. For how could the ship be disturbed when he presided over it in whom the Church’s support is found? ibid., XV, 1633. For he was a wise and weighty man, in whom the Church’s support was found, ibid., XVI, 292. When he calls him rock, he indicated the Church’s support, ibid., 628. The Church of the Lord, as though built upon the apostolic rock, remains unmoved and persists upon an unshaken foundation against the assault of the raging sea, ibid., 879. Peter’s faith is the Church’s foundation, ibid., 827.

[Col. 0693] Peter is called steadfast, Peter strong, Juvencus, XIX, 237. That it may be understood that the Church is built upon Peter, ibid., note 371.

The Church is founded upon one person, St Gaudentius, XX, 995.

It is certain that the universal Church is founded upon him—Peter, Pope St Boniface I, XX, 781.

I know that the Church was built upon that Rock, St Jerome, XXII, 355. The prince of the apostles, upon whom the Church of the Lord is founded with stable mass, and whom neither the assault of a flood nor any storm shakes, ibid., XXIII, 506. Thus Christ founds the Church upon one of the mountains and says to him: “You are Peter,” etc., ibid., XXIV, 43, 44. But if one who asks this considers the matter, he will understand that the blessing and blessedness, the power, and the building of the Church upon Peter were promised for the future, not given in the present, ibid., XXVI, 120.—For two councils have already been sent concerning this matter to the Apostolic See; replies have also come from there. The case is finished; would that the error might someday be finished! St Augustine, XXXVIII, 734. Peter is called the foundation of the Church, ibid., XXXIX, 2100. Therefore the Church rightly venerates this foundation, upon which the height of the ecclesiastical building rises, ibid. Thus he who had previously been weak became a support to all; and he who had wavered under the trial of questioning might establish the rest in firmness of faith, ibid., 2102. For he is called rock because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations and, like an immovable stone, upholds the structure and mass of the entire Christian work, ibid.

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against you.” The gates of hell are the faith of heretics—or rather, their faithlessness—Cassian, L, 70.

Peter, the immovable foundation of salvation, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 498. Peter is guardian of the faith, the Church’s Rock, ibid. Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of faith to those who seek it, ibid., 71.

This faith of Peter has been fortified by God with such great firmness that neither heretical perversity has ever been able to corrupt it nor pagan unbelief to overcome it, St Leo the Great, LIV, 147. “Yet you too are Rock, because you are made firm by my strength, so that what belongs properly to me by power may be shared with you in participation,” ibid., 150, 430. “Upon this strength,” he says, “I shall build an eternal temple, and the height of my Church, which is to be raised to heaven, shall rise upon the firmness of this faith,” ibid., 150. In Peter the strength of all is fortified, ibid., 151, 152. For that firmness which he himself, having been made a rock, received from Christ the Rock, he also transmitted to his heirs, ibid., 155. The Lord undertakes a special care for Peter, and prayer is made specifically for Peter’s faith, because the condition of the rest would be more secure if the mind of the prince were not conquered, ibid., 431. Thus the chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely entrusted to him, so that it is founded upon perpetual firmness, ibid., 507. In Peter’s chair Christ utterly overthrew the wicked and established the good in everlasting stability, ibid. So that the building of the eternal temple might rest, by the wondrous gift of God’s grace, upon Peter’s firmness, strengthening his Church by this steadfastness, so that neither human rashness could attack it nor the gates of hell prevail against it, ibid., 629.—Christ asserted that the gates of hell would never prevail against the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, ibid., LVI, 633. Therefore we do not fear that the apostolic judgment will be annulled, supported as it is by Christ’s voice, the tradition of the elders, and the authority of the canons, so that it may always judge the whole Church instead, ibid.

Peter is called rock because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations and, like an immovable stone, supports the structure and mass of the whole Christian work, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 353. And he who had previously been weak became a support to all, and he who had wavered under the trial of questioning might establish the rest in firmness of faith, ibid. Peter is the Rock upon which the Church is built, ibid., 673. He upholds the foundation of faith in the Church, ibid.

In the Apostolic See religion has always been preserved unstained, Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 393. “You are Peter, and upon this rock,” etc. What was said is proved by the effects of events, because in the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been preserved free from stain, ibid., 460; Emperor Justinian, LXVI, 41.

Because Truth could not lie, nor can Peter’s faith be shaken or changed for ever. For when the devil demanded all the disciples in order to sift them, the Lord testifies that he prayed for Peter alone, and willed that the others be confirmed by him, upon whom he promised that he would build his Church; and he testified that the gates of hell would not prevail against it, Pope Pelagius II, LXXII, 707. Can one who abandons and resists the chair of Peter, upon which the Church is founded, be confident that he is in the Church? Ibid., 713.

The pontiff is above the council and the Church, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 181. That the building of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s solidity through the wonderful gift of God’s grace [Col. 0694], St. Agobard, CIV, 295; Hincmar of Laon, CXXIV, 10, 6. — Christ, establishing firmness upon the solid faith of the prince of the apostles (namely Peter), Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 773. Peter, from the firmness of the rock which is Christ, does not cease to fortify by his prayers the structure of the universal Church, unshaken and made firm by the strength of faith, so that he hastens to reform the madness of those who err by the rule of right faith, ibid. He deigned to establish his holy Church upon the solidity of faith, according to his truthful voice saying: “Amen, I say to you, you are Peter,” etc., ibid., 785.

Therefore it is no wonder if Peter is called from rock, because he was to be firm through the Holy Spirit in the firmness of faith, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 560. In him (Peter) there is one answer on behalf of all, upon which the Church is founded and against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, ibid., 561. For whether you say that they shall not prevail against this faith, or say that they shall not prevail against the Church, which is founded and made firm upon Christ by this faith, it is one and the same thing, since neither the foundation nor the faith is dissolved, ibid. It is asked: why shall the gates of hell not prevail against him, or against it? [lacuna] It must be believed without doubt that they shall prevail neither against the rock upon which the Church is built nor against the Church built upon such a rock, ibid.

When he calls him Rock, he indicated the foundation of the Church, Aeneas of Paris, CXXI, 687.

For you are, as the divine word declares, truly Peter, and upon your foundation the pillars of the Church—understood to be the bishops—have been strengthened, Hincmar of Laon, CXXIV, 1051. You know that the Apostolic See has been established as a foundation fixed and immovable by God, and as the most illustrious title of his priests, that is, of all bishops, and as the summit of the Churches, ibid. Because their foundation is immovable, unshaken, and incapable of being shaken, the building also remains incapable of overthrow and of dispute among those in whom there is one Spirit and one faith, one heart and one soul, ibid., 1052. That the building of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s solidity through the wonderful gift of God’s grace, ibid., 1066. — He himself founded his Church upon the foundation of the apostolic rock, which he entrusted to blessed Peter and, in him, to his vicars. Hincmar of Rheims, CXXVI, 33. The Church confirmed in the solidity of the prince of the apostles, ibid., 337.

What was said is proved by the effects of events: because in the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been preserved unstained and holy doctrine celebrated, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXIX, 36.

He who promised that blessed Peter’s faith would not fail, and instructed him to confirm his brothers—something which all know that the apostolic pontiffs, predecessors of my lowliness, have always confidently done—Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 199. Therefore this one immovable foundation, this one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth, ibid. That the building of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s solidity through the wonderful gift of God’s grace, strengthening his Church with this firmness so that neither human rashness could attack it nor the gates of hell prevail against it, ibid., 883; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 324.

It is necessary that, just as that rocky and apostolic foundation, firm in its holy angular joining, is eternal and immovable, so every ecclesiastical superstructure upon it may be established and stable, and inviolable against every human presumption, Pope Sergius III, CXXXI, 975.

“I am the foundation, [lacuna] yet you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power,” etc., St. Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 712. “Upon this strength,” he says, “I shall build an eternal temple, and the height of my Church, to be raised to heaven, shall rise from the firmness of this faith,” ibid. The gates of hell shall not hold this confession; the bonds of death shall not bind it, ibid. Therefore in Peter the strength of all is fortified, ibid., 713. Prayer is made properly for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others will be more secure if the mind of the prince has not been overcome, ibid.

Therefore the holy Church was built upon the rock in the solidity of apostolic faith, Atto of Vercelli, XXXIV, 53.

The Roman Pontiff occupies Peter’s See in order that he may not permit the gates of hell to prevail against the Church, Ratherius of Verona, XXXVI, 656.

In Peter’s faith, which hitherto has neither failed nor will fail until the end, Pope St. Leo IX, CXLIII, 748. “I have prayed for you, Peter, that you may not fail,” etc. By this saying he showed that the faith of the brethren would be endangered by various failures, but must be fixed, as by the help of a firm anchor, in Peter’s unshaken and unfailing faith, and confirmed in the foundation of the universal Church, ibid., 765. As a whole door is governed by its hinge, so the benefit of the whole Church is ordered through Peter and his successors, ibid. “But I have prayed for you,” etc. That venerable and effective prayer obtained that Peter’s faith has not failed hitherto, and is believed not to fail in his throne unto age upon age [Col. 0695]; rather, it will strengthen the hearts of brethren shaken by various perils to faith, as it has not ceased to strengthen them until now, ibid., 770.

Therefore this rock has seven eyes because the holy Church shines with the same number of gifts of the Holy Spirit, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 255. Christ prayed lest his faith (Peter’s), as the foundation of the whole Church, should ever fail, ibid., 577.

Peter is the foundation upon which the Church rests, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 222. The Lord gave him to be the foundation of the Church’s faith, saying: “You are Peter,” etc., ibid.

That the Lord built the Church upon one, namely Peter, St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 555.

When the Lord said to Peter, “You are Peter,” etc., he confirmed this also in Peter’s successors, Lanfranc, CL, 624.

Both firmness of his own faith and confirmation of another’s faith are granted to him by God himself, when he says to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter,” etc., Pope Urban II, CLI, 337. Therefore we, who, though unworthy, sit in Peter’s place, ought to correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and so order what must be ordered throughout the Church according to the judgment of the eternal Judge that judgment may go forth from his countenance and our eyes may see equity, ibid., 337, 341, 421.

The Church is founded upon Peter because he bears it by office, merit, preaching, example, care, and intercession, Radulphus Ardens, CLV, 1391. The gates of hell prevail not only not against Christ, but not even against Peter armed with Christ’s power, ibid.

It is greatly necessary that even now the faith of blessed Peter should flourish so greatly in his special See, which has never been accustomed to err, Goffridus, CLVII, 42. On earth he chose Peter in order to strengthen his Church by the vigor of Peter’s faith, ibid., 43. He made Peter the prince of the Catholic faith, ibid.

He who promised that Peter’s faith would not fail foretold that Peter himself would confirm his brethren, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 337. And the hearts of the brethren have been confirmed in Peter’s faith, which hitherto has neither failed nor will fail until the end, ibid., 338. That the judgment of the Apostolic See is not to be reconsidered by anyone, ibid., 328. The See of the Roman Church, built through Peter upon the rock, neither fails hitherto nor will fail for ages, Christ the Lord praying for it, as he himself testifies: “I have prayed for you, Peter,” etc., ibid., 339. By this saying he showed that the faith of the brethren would be imperiled by various failures, but must be guided, as by the help of a firm anchor, in Peter’s unshaken and unfailing faith and confirmed in the foundation of the universal Church, ibid. Can one who abandons Peter’s chair, upon which the Church is founded, be confident that he is in the Church? Ibid., 432. The Lord provided that his Church should be built upon this Rock, so that the confession of that faith, because of its solidity, was to be compared with a rock, id., CLXII, 596.

That the Son of God willed to establish and confirm his Church, redeemed by his precious blood, upon the singular, immovable stability of that faith, saying: “You are Peter,” etc., Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 39. Both firmness of his own faith and confirmation of another’s faith are ascribed to him by God himself, when it is said to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter,” etc., ibid., 194. They may despise the Apostolic See; they may raise the heel against us; they cannot set aside or take away the privilege given by God, by which it was said to Peter: “You are Peter,” etc., ibid., 429. Therefore we, who, though unworthy, seem to sit in Peter’s place, ought to correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and so order throughout the whole Church what must be ordered according to the judgment of the inward Judge, that our judgment may go forth from his countenance, ibid., 194; Pope Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1435; Anastasius IV, CLXXXIII, 1019.

“Upon this rock, which you have now laid as the foundation of faith, upon this faith which you have now taught, saying, ‘You are the Christ,’ etc.—upon this rock and upon this faith I shall build my Church,” St. Bruno, CLXV, 213. “And I say to you that you are Peter, strong in faith and steadfast in doctrine. For unless Christ had understood strength and steadfastness in this name, he would not immediately have added what follows, saying, ‘And upon this rock,’” etc., ibid. “Upon this faith of yours, by which you call me the Son of the living God, I shall build my Church,” id., CLXIV, 373.

“You are Peter, and upon this rock,” etc.: in these words, as it has most truly seemed to all holy teachers, a certain special prerogative to be preserved in the holy Church is laid upon blessed Peter, Placidus the Monk, CLXIII, 623.

He built his Church upon the rock of faith which Peter confessed, Abbot Rupert, CLXVIII, 1385.

Therefore, when we are endangered, he must at some time turn toward us and strengthen us. For the Lord prayed for him that his faith should not fail, Hildebert, LXXI, 795. — Peter upon whom the Lord built the Church, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 524. The Lord set Peter himself as, so to speak, the foundation of the Church, ibid. How great Peter’s firmness and constancy in faith were, so that he deservedly should from this be called rock, the Lord himself declares elsewhere, saying: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that you may not fail,” etc., ibid., 525. This is Peter, as has been said, the firm support and confirmation of the rest, as though he alone, ibid. Peter upon whom he placed and founded the Church, ibid., 1481. Peter upon whom the Church is founded, ibid. That the building of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s solidity through the wonderful gift of grace, ibid., 1482; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 109; Henry, CCIII, 317. — From this firmness of faith Peter himself is also instructed to confirm his brethren, Peter Abelard, CLXXXVIII, 525.

What has been decreed by him (the Roman pontiff) is observed without challenge, Pope Innocent II, CLXXIX, 226. Peter deserved to hear: “You are Peter,” etc., plainly designating the rock as firmness of faith and the solidity of Catholic unity, ibid., 516; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 360. Every danger and scandal arising in the kingdom of God, especially those concerning faith, ought to be referred to your apostolate. For I judge it fitting that injuries to faith be repaired especially there where faith cannot suffer failure; for this is the prerogative of that See, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1053. For to whom else was it ever said: “I have prayed for you, Peter,” etc.? Therefore what follows is required of Peter’s successor: “And when you have turned, strengthen your brethren.” This indeed is necessary now, ibid.

That he who had previously been weak in himself might become a support to all, and he who had himself wavered under the temptation of questioning might establish others in the stability of faith, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 281. He is called rock because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations and, like an immovable stone, holds together the framework and mass of the whole body of Christendom, ibid. For how could the ship be disturbed when it was governed by him in whom lies the Church’s support? Ibid., 1267. In the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been preserved free from stain, ibid., 1268.

Peter, who received this grace, that for those shipwrecked in faith you might always remain immovable and steadfast in faith: strengthen and correct others who are wavering, Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1215. He had received from the Lord, above all others, the privilege of preserving the integrity of faith, ibid. — The unchallengeable authority of this holy See itself ordained this, Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 138. From this Peter’s faith is the support of the present Church, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1310.

Here Peter, called from the rock, stands unconquered in conflict, Adam of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1494.

The Roman Pontiff does not cease to confirm throughout the world the children of the Church in the firmness of Christian faith, Alexander III, CC, 302. Christ willed this rock to be the foundation of the Church, and foretells that it will be shaken by no storms of winds and by no tempests, ibid., 1148. Peter upon whom the Church is founded, ibid. The eternal and immutable providence of the divine counsel established the most holy Roman Church as head, mother, and teacher of all churches and all the faithful, and raised it at its very birth upon the rock of Catholic and Christian faith, ibid., 1259. — From this power, which came to blessed Peter through the Lord’s institution, the most holy Roman Church obtained authority over all Churches, so that whatever its prudence decreed might everywhere be firm and binding, Lucius III, CCI, 1179.

The lofty counsel of heaven founded the most holy Roman Church with solidity upon the rock of faith, granting it that support in the strength of the apostolic confession against which neither the blast of a storm nor the force of a tempest can prevail, Urban III, CCII, 1351.

Peter is the rock and foundation of faith, and supports us firmly in its solidity so that we do not fall, Pope Clement III, CCIV, 1353. Peter is our support and house of strength, and we are planted and rooted in his faith, ibid.

He was to be called Peter, who would also make the people firm in the foundation of faith, Pope Celestine, CCVI, 1194.

Peter’s righteousness obtained such authority in judging that heavenly judgment depends upon his decision, and not even angels dare appeal from Peter’s sentence, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 644.
