So that what has been established by his authority as by the principal head may stand firm in him as in a stable foundation, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 625. “I have prayed for you, Peter,” etc. By this he plainly indicated that his successors would at no time depart from the Catholic faith, but would rather recall others and strengthen even those who wavered, ibid., 760. Therefore Peter’s faith shall not fail, nor shall the authority of the Apostolic See waver, id., CCXVI, 1691 [Col. 0697]. The Church is founded upon the rock, and therefore the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, id., CCXVII, 553. Therefore it belongs to Peter, as teacher, to confirm the others [Col. 0698], whose faith failed in no temptation, ibid., 778. For the faith of the Apostolic See is founded with stable solidity upon the firm rock, ibid.

[Col. 0697]

## LXXXII. INDEX CONCERNING METROPOLITANS

### NOTICE

The name *metropolitan* derives from *metropolis*, which is the chief city of a province. It is established that this dignity was in force before the Council of Nicaea, and many learned and weighty authorities trace its origin to the Apostles. A metropolitan presides over one province and has jurisdiction over all the bishops of that province, whom he calls suffragans. All metropolitans, besides the other pontifical ornaments, have the pallium. The pallium is a white woolen band about three fingers broad, woven in the shape of a circle, which encircles the shoulders and has on each side strips hanging down over breast and shoulders, with six woven silk black crosses; it is sewn and fastened with three golden pins. It is taken from the altar where the body of blessed Peter is deposited; therefore it is said to be taken from Peter’s own body, and through it the fuller authority of metropolitans is signified. Having said this, let the following be set down:

A metropolitan shall not hear the case of bishops without the bishops, III, 978. On primates and metropolitans, and on matters of bishops to be referred to them, St. Stephen I, III, 1004. — A metropolitan shall do nothing without a council of bishops, nor they without him, except insofar as concerns their own parishes, St. Julius I, VIII, 981. — On primates and metropolitans, Pope St. Felix II, XIII, 17, 18. On metropolitans who neglect to request the pallium, ibid., 1226. — A bishop shall be ordained by all bishops, or by three with the metropolitan’s consent, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 623. Without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, no bishop shall dare to ordain, ibid., 468. Without the metropolitan’s consent a bishop shall not be ordained, ibid., 627. That according to the constitutions of the emperors there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops, ibid., 547. — In every province no one shall be ordained bishop in disregard of the metropolitan, Pope St. Boniface I, XX, 772. — A bishop is to be ordained especially in the presence, or by the authority, of the metropolitan bishop; without him they wished the ordination to be invalid, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 473. — That every province ought to be content with its own metropolitan, Pope Celestine, L, 429. — Suffragan bishops shall be ordained by the metropolitan with the exarch’s knowledge; metropolitans, by the exarch himself, Pope St. Leo the Great, LIV, 617. Let metropolitans retain their rights, ibid., 667. As provincial bishops belong to metropolitans, so metropolitans belong to the exarch or vicar, ibid., 614. That they should ordain those who are metropolitans, ibid., 615. Suffragan bishops shall be ordained by the metropolitan with the exarch’s knowledge; metropolitans, by the exarch himself, ibid., 617. The ordination of a provincial bishop is reserved to the metropolitan, ibid., 628. Every bishop ought in doubtful matters to have recourse to the metropolitan, ibid., 1011. A bishop shall not be ordained without a synod and the metropolitan’s presence, id., LXVII, 66. Let metropolitans retain their rights, ibid., 293. — How a metropolitan ought to conduct himself in another province, Pope St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1183. — On the metropolitan, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 41. On primates of metropolitan bishops, ibid., 94. On metropolitan bishops, ibid., 124. That it is not permitted to ordain a bishop without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop, ibid., 127, 131, 188. A bishop shall not travel far without a credential from the metropolitan, ibid., 192. On not alienating Church property without consulting the metropolitan bishop, ibid., 209. No bishop shall be ordained without the metropolitan, ibid., 253. A bishop not ordained in the metropolitan city shall present himself to the metropolitan within two months, ibid., 311. A bishop who, warned by the metropolitan, has not come to the synod shall be excommunicated, ibid. On the primacy of the metropolitan, ibid., 575. — A province shall by no means be divided between two metropolitans, Cresconius Africanus, LXXXVIII, 903. No bishop shall be ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge, ibid., 913. — On the honor of metropolitans, Pope St. Zacharias, LXXXIX, 930. — A province shall by no means be divided between two metropolitans, Charlemagne, XCVII, 530. — No metropolitan shall hear the cases of any persons without the request of the suffragan bishops, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1104. — In what order a metropolitan and a diocesan bishop ought to be consecrated, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXVI, 186. On the right of metropolitans, when the primacy of Ansegisus was at issue, ibid., 189. On the ordination of archbishops, and on primates and patriarchs and their ministers, id., CXXX, 60, 73, 75. On primates of metropolitan bishops, ibid., 257. On metropolitan bishops, ibid., 281. That it is not permitted to ordain a bishop without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop, ibid., 283. A synod shall be convened at the metropolitan’s discretion, ibid., 380. On the primacy of the metropolitan, ibid., 579. — That one cannot be a bishop who has been consecrated without the metropolitan’s knowledge, Burchard, CXL, 554. On a metropolitan who postpones hearing a suffragan bishop in his own case, ibid., 564. No metropolitan shall hear the cases of any persons without the presence of all suffragan bishops, ibid., 565. No primate or metropolitan shall do anything concerning the Churches or parishes of suffragan bishops, or their cases, without the counsel of them all, ibid. Without the metropolitan’s letters bishops shall not travel into another province, id., CLVIII, 24. On not alienating Church property without consulting the metropolitan bishop, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 234. On the right of metropolitans, ibid., 322. — Until the next synod, one summoned by the metropolitan who has neglected, without grave necessity, to attend the synod shall abstain from communion, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 102. A bishop who, summoned by the metropolitan, scorns to come to the synod shall be deprived of communion, ibid., 103. Bishops shall be promoted by the examination of metropolitans and bishops; no bishop shall be ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge, ibid., 344. Without the metropolitan’s knowledge a bishop shall do nothing outside his own diocese, ibid., 794. Without the metropolitan’s knowledge or that of provincial bishops, bishops shall not go to the emperor, ibid., 1259.

[Col. 0699]

## LXXXIII. INDEX CONCERNING THE EPISCOPATE, OR CONCERNING THE AUTHORITY, DUTIES, OBLIGATIONS OF BISHOPS, ARRANGED IN A LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS

### NOTICE

*Bishop* is a Greek word, meaning in Latin “overseer,” and it denotes the office of a prelate: that he should preside over the people entrusted to him and observe their conduct. Hence the bishop must care for divine worship and defend the Christian religion; prescribe prayers; see that no wrong is committed in matters of faith, in the celebration of divine offices, or in the administration of the sacraments; take action against those who stir up disturbances in Christian affairs; investigate carefully books issued to the public, lest error creep into them; deliver sacred sermons in the church—an office so proper to the bishop that other clerics are forbidden to exercise it without his permission or consent; explain to the people the mysteries of faith and the meaning of Holy Scripture in accordance with the mind of the Church; and keep them in duty by writing and speech, etc., etc. But, to establish an order in this Index, we shall treat in turn: I, the institution of the episcopate; II, the qualifications required of one to be ordained bishop; III, the election of a bishop; IV, the duties of bishops; V, the virtues of a bishop; VI, authority; VII, episcopal administration; VIII, unworthy bishops; IX, the accusation of bishops; X, the deposition of a bishop; XI, the right of appeal; XII, the reverence due to bishops; and thus whatever is found in the *Patrologia* concerning bishops will be set before the reader’s eyes.

### I. Definition and institution of the episcopate

The order and successions of bishops, Tertullian, II, 44. Among heretics, one is bishop today, another tomorrow, ibid., 57. What form the apostles gave to the episcopate, ibid., 119. — God makes bishops, St. Cyprian, III, 711, 768, 803; IV, 396, 398, 401. Deacons ought to remember that the Lord chose the apostles, that is, bishops and rulers, id., IV, 396. God and his Christ made Cornelius bishop, id., III, 770, 771. — The multitude of episcopal sees in Africa, St. Optatus, XI, 832 ff. — Bishop is interpreted as overseer, St. Ambrose, XVII, 579. At first presbyters were called bishops, ibid., 388. — The individual bishops of the Churches, St. Jerome, XXII, 1080. Presbyters and bishops ordained by the apostles in the individual provinces, id., XXVI, 188. That one of the presbyters should be chosen and set above the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should belong, etc., ibid., 562. — The derivation of the term bishop, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 580; XLI, 647. How *episcopus* is interpreted in Latin, id., XXXVI, 1669. The name episcopate denotes work, not honor, id., XLI, 647. The unshaken succession of bishops from the very sees of the apostles, id., XLIII, 506. Before Christ ascended into heaven, he laid hands on the apostles and ordained them bishops, id., XXXV, 2296. In times of persecution, assistant bishops were appointed by the chief prelate even in towns and small places of his own diocese, id., LII, 973. That this was afterwards forbidden when peace was granted to the Church, ibid. Before the peace granted by Constantine, bishops had no cathedral church properly so called, nor a fixed place of residence, ibid., 986. Examples of bishops named after the region in which they exercised the episcopate, before and after the Church’s peace, ibid., 987. — The episcopate is the highest rank in the Church, Cassiodorus, LXX, 784. This name denotes not so much honor as labor, ibid. — Bishops now hold in the Church the place of the apostles’ mission, Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1200. A bishop is called the head of the faithful, id., LXXV, 1062. What the name bishop signifies, id., LXXVII, 600. What it is to bear the empty name of bishop, ibid., 822. — Bishop is the name of a work, not of an honor, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 782. — Evidence that episcopates were established in Germany, Pope St. Zacharias, LXXXIX, 917. — On the threefold order of bishops, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 300. Are you a bishop? Let the very name, I pray, remind you; let it teach you your duty, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 286. — After Christ, the priestly order began with Peter, St. Anselm, CXLIX, 486. — What is the episcopate to you but suffering? What is this honor but a burden? What is this height but a tempest that causes shipwreck? [Col. 0700] Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 29. — Ἐπίσκοπος (*episkopos*) is interpreted “superintendent,” so that he may understand that one is not a bishop who has loved to rule rather than to benefit others, Herveus, CLXXXI, 1421. — Paul also calls bishops presbyters, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 223. — It should be noted in what sense bishops are included under the name presbyters, Abbot Bernard, CCIV, 801.

### II. Qualifications required of one to be ordained bishop

If anyone deserves to be a bishop, let him first be a doorkeeper, then a reader, afterwards an exorcist, etc., Pope Caius, V, 190. — That laymen are not to be promoted to the episcopate, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1192. — If anyone desires to be promoted to the clergy, it is right that he should be a doorkeeper for one year, a reader for twenty years, an exorcist for twenty years, etc., Pope St. Sylvester, VIII, 826. — A bishop shall not be appointed before he has performed the ministry of reader, deacon, and presbyter, Hosius of Cordoba, VIII, 1324. — One who has had dissolute sons cannot become a bishop, St. Jerome, XXII, 873. Let us therefore consider what sort of presbyter or bishop ought to be ordained, id., XXVI, 563. Bishops are chosen either as virgins, or as widowers, or as chaste after entering the priesthood, id., XXII, 510. Let such a one become bishop as does not fear, because of his children’s vices, to rebuke strangers, id., XXVI, 565. — But it is now not enough that laymen are ordained, whom no order permits to be made [clerics]; even men whose crimes are known far and wide throughout nearly all provinces are ordained, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 578. — Let no layman, no bigamist, etc., but one irreproachable and such as the apostle chose, be made bishop, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 580. What sort of person ought one to be who is to be ordained bishop? Id., 879. — Bishops must be tested over a very long period, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 70. That one ought to ascend to the height of the episcopate through the successive grades, ibid., 180. — It has come to our attention that, when bishops die, certain laymen are tonsured and leap by a headlong bound to the episcopate, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 788. With what presumption does one dare approach the episcopate who is proved, by the testimony of his little daughter, still not to possess long continence over his body? Ibid., 1114. — On the sort of shepherds of souls who ought to be chosen in the Church, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 821. — Those still subject to vices are not to be promoted to the governance of the Church, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 706. — Whoever is chosen from the laity for the episcopate shall first spend a year in ecclesiastical ministry through all the grades, Fulgentius of Carthage, LXXXVIII, 817. No bishop, even if elected by the people, shall take possession of a vacant Church except by authority of a plenary council, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 819. One to be ordained bishop must first be examined as to what sort of man he is [Col. 0701], id., XCVI, 1282. On the ages at which one may be promoted to the episcopate, ibid. — No layman, no bigamist, etc., but irreproachable men shall be ordained bishops, Burchard, CXL, 551. Those to be ordained bishops must first be examined, ibid. One to be chosen bishop must not be a layman, novice, husband of a second wife, or husband of a widow, ibid. — A bishop is not to be chosen from another Church unless no worthy man is found in his own, St. Anselm, CXLIX, 486. That, according to the proper meaning of the name, one is not a bishop who has loved to rule rather than to benefit others, ibid. — No laymen, novices, bigamists, or husbands of widows, but irreproachable men shall be ordained bishops, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 346. Bishops are tested for a very long time both by the word of faith and by the example of upright conduct, ibid., 318. No one shall be elected bishop unless established in holy orders, ibid., 1130. That the clergy should choose their bishop not from another but from their own Church, ibid., 1131. One who has attained episcopal rank by royal appointment shall not be received by the suffragans, ibid. — One ought not be considered to desire the episcopate if he desires his own profit or honor, rather than the salvation of the people, Herveus, CLXXXI, 1421. What kind of man ought to be chosen as the future shepherd of the Church, ibid. He must not be drunken, but drink in such a way that it is unknown whether he has drunk, ibid., 1422. — He expresses the grave sorrow of his heart concerning Philip’s improper ambition for the episcopal office of the Church of Tours, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 310. — First, therefore, the bishop is commanded to be blameless, Gratian, CXCVII, 148. One who is to be ordained bishop must be monogamous after baptism, ibid., 149. We decree that everyone who is to be promoted to the rank of bishop must by all means know the Psalter, id., CLXXXVII, 209. — No one shall be chosen bishop unless found to be living devoutly in holy orders, ibid., 317. It is miserable for one who has never been a disciple to become a teacher, for one who has never served a priest in any rank to become chief priest, ibid., 318. No one is to be chosen for the episcopate except those whom a commendable life recommends, ibid., 320. According to the apostle, the man able to preside is the one who desires to work and benefit many, not to lord it arrogantly over them, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 34. The shepherds of Churches are to be appointed from among clerics who, etc., ibid., CXCII, 1248.

### III. On the election of a bishop by clergy and people
Episcopal elections: how they are to be conducted, St Cyprian, III, 1725, 1026.—They received this office not by payment but by testimony, Tertullian, I, 469.—The form of episcopal election, St Cyprian, III, 768.—Election of bishops by people and clergy, Hosius of Corduba, VIII, 1320.—A bishop is chosen by the vote of the whole people, St Optatus, XI, 919.—Election of St Ambrose; Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 522. Ecclesiastical proceedings drawn up by Blessed Augustine in designating Eraclius to succeed him in the episcopate, St Augustine, XXXIII, 968. “I was seized, made a presbyter, and through this rank came to the episcopate,” id., XXXIX, 1569.—“He who is to be set over all should be chosen by all,” St Leo the Great, LIV, 634. “Therefore, when the election of the chief priest is under consideration, let him be set over all whom the united agreement of clergy and people has jointly requested,” ibid., 673.—That mobs must not be permitted to make elections of those who are to be appointed to the priesthood, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 70, 166.—“The greater part of the peoples has chosen you: come, agree with us, and, giving our blessing, let us consecrate you to the episcopate,” St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 273. The king gave his approval to this assent, etc., ibid., 382. On the death of Egemon, Simplicius is elected by the people, ibid., 882. Then the clerics, choosing holy Nicetius, received him as bishop, ibid., 1031–1032. When he came, the bishop said to the king: “I ask that Nicetius the presbyter, my nephew, be appointed bishop for the Church of Lyons.” The king replied: “Let God’s will be done,” ibid., 1042. The king ordered him to be summoned to the episcopate; and, when the people’s consent had been given and the king’s decree issued, he was led away for ordination, ibid., 1079. On episcopal elections, ibid., 1176. He congratulates him on having been chosen by the unanimous consent of all, id., LXXVII, 558. Election of bishops by people and clergy, ibid., 620.—“They brought to us a presbyter who ought to be ordained bishop for them,” ibid., 901. It is neither novel nor blameworthy, in choosing a bishop, for the wishes of the people to divide into two parties, ibid., 1114. Signs are given by which bishops may know that they have been chosen by God, not by human beings, id., LXXIX, 280.—On the election of bishops, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 37.—For choosing a bishop, the decision of the mother church is sufficient, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 819.—On the calling of a lawful bishop, Angelramn, XCVI, 1056. No bishop is to appoint a successor during his lifetime; but after his death, let good men choose a good man, ibid., 1283.—Bishops are to be chosen from their own diocese by election of clergy and people according to the statutes of the canons, etc., Charlemagne, XCVII, 521.—Likewise, when a bishop dies, no one is to be appointed in his place except a native of that locality, whom the universal vote of the entire people has chosen and the will of the fellow-provincials has approved, Flodoard, CXXXV, 105.—While a bishop is being elected, if he has opponents, five bishops are to assemble, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 551. That the people are not permitted by themselves to elect priests, ibid., CXXXV, 552. No one is to be ordained bishop unless the clergy and parishioners have been summoned and are in unanimous agreement, id., CXL, 553.—Likewise, concerning the election of bishops: it is to be done with pure minds, and no payment is to intervene, St Anselm, CXLIX, 486. Every episcopal election made by princes is to be void, ibid.

## IV.—On the duties of bishops

Bishops must guard the camps divinely entrusted to them, St Cyprian, id., 1135. For a bishop ought not merely to teach, but also to learn, ibid. They must cherish all the sheep, ibid., 095. If any bishop attempts to introduce heresy and ravage the flock, the others must come to its aid and gather the sheep, ibid., 991. A bishop must provide for peace and tranquillity, id., IV, 335.—A bishop of the Church owes the ministry of preaching, St Hilary, X, 158.—The bishop’s office is to teach, St Ambrose, XVI, 24. What and how he ought to teach his people, ibid., 880. They are governors of crowds, devoted to peace, ibid., 1037. Each bishop ought to preside over a separate Church, id., XVII, 250. A bishop is bound by the necessity of the command to preach the word of God, ibid., 568–569.—Bishops should take the apostles as their example, St Jerome, XXII, 583. Let him honour priests and clerics, ibid., 533. He is established in the Church in order to restrain the people from error, id., XXIII, 160.—He must be able to refute opponents, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 961. The burden of the episcopate, well borne, wins greater glory, ibid., 1480. To preach, reprove, rebuke, build up, and labour for each individual: a great work, a great weight, a great toil—who would not shrink from this labour? ibid. The functions of the episcopal office, id., XXXVII, 1484. The episcopate is not a craft for conducting a deceitful life, id., XXXIII, 296. For this reason they are appointed in the Churches: that they may not spare sins in rebuking them, St Augustine, XLI, 23. The burden of preaching is heavy, but it must not be laid aside, id., XXXVIII, 1481. Even if one is not heard, ibid. On the grounds upon which a bishop is bound to refute those teaching what ought not to be taught, id., XXXIII, 133, 135. A bishop exists for the office of correction, id., XLI, 23. A bishop administers provision for the poor, id., XXXIII, 809. Bishops are guardians of orphans, id., XXXVIII, 950. Bishops are under an obligation to receive guests, id., XXXIX, 1570. It belongs to a bishop to dispense God’s goods and to receive the people, ibid., 2142. Prelates plead the cause of the human race before God, id., XL, 1759. It befits a bishop carefully to attend to sins and either correct sinners or cut them off from the Church, ibid., 1086. It belongs to bishops to restrain the impious acts of heretics where they are committed, id., XLV, 1710. What the office of bishops is like, id., LII, 1010, 102.

It belongs to bishops to watch lest the unity of the faith be violated, St Leo the Great, LIV, 1075. In time of war, bishops ought not to leave their Churches, ibid., 920. He who does not call another back from error shows himself to be in error, ibid., 688. What a bishop should be and what his duties are, id., LVI, 734.—“If we do not denounce their crimes, the guilt of those very crimes will involve us also,” St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 735.—When and in what cases bishops ought to go to the imperial court, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 178.—No bishop is to leave his own Church and move to another, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 17. There must not be two bishops in one Church, ibid.—“Remove thefts; separate from your people luxury, the devastator of the human race,” Cassiodorus, LXIX, 829. Let the bishop teach, ibid.—Bishops ought to preach, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 112. Duties of bishops, id., LXXVII, 559, 615, 626, 801, 847. Let them call back not only heretics to the Church, but also those within the Church to uprightness of life, ibid., 597. Let the bishop administer the ministry of the word diligently, ibid., 546, 587. Let him show priestly affection to the peoples, ibid., 832. Let him rescue those who have fallen into fault, ibid., 914. Let him show those in error the way back, ibid. Let the bishop seek the unity and concord of the peoples, ibid., 1027. Let him aid the afflicted, ibid., 492. Let him assist the people’s needs with pious compassion, ibid., 669. Bishops’ duties concerning the needy, widows, orphans, and oppressed, ibid., 459, 521. The administration of charitable resources was formerly entrusted to bishops’ care, id., 697. He has to administer not his own goods, but the goods of the poor, ibid., 1274. A bishop must bring help to the harassed and oppressed, [Col. 0703] ibid., 922, 1059, 1093. How bishops ought to defend the goods of the poor, ibid., 1085, 1274. Care of guests formerly lay upon bishops, ibid., 1145, 1184. Bishops’ duties toward the Church, ibid., 469, 817. Let him govern the Church according to the canons, ibid., 553. Let him be diligent in preserving and arranging the Church’s property, ibid., 575. A bishop summoned to a synod is bound to attend; if prevented by illness, he should send a presbyter and deacon, ibid., 787. Let him bring back to the Church those who stray from the truth of the faith, ibid., 659. Let a bishop keep his clerics to their duty, ibid., 1001–1002. Let him maintain discipline among them, ibid., 694. Correction of clerics belongs to the bishop, ibid., 653. Bishops’ duties toward monasteries, ibid., 1071, 1081, 1082. A bishop must watch over the conduct of monks, ibid., 936. He must provide protection for monasteries, ibid., 820, 935, 1081. He must settle the affairs of monasteries, ibid., 1000. He must preserve intact the privileges granted to monasteries, ibid., 1042. He must neither burden monasteries himself nor allow his clerics to burden them, ibid., 458, 820. He must not make an inventory of or administer monastery property, ibid., 578. Bishops’ duties concerning legal cases: the cases of clerics, monks, and religious persons belong to bishops, ibid., 653, 802, 803. In delivering judgments, a bishop must not be hasty, ibid., 568. He must not refuse to endure hatred for the truth, ibid., 916. He must show himself careful and strict between guilt and innocence, ibid., 930. The bishop who ought to correct faults and transgressions, ibid., 728, 916. A bishop is reproved if negligent in punishing crimes, ibid., 682. Let him correct vices promptly, ibid., 669. Let him correct some things gently and bear with equanimity some things that cannot be corrected, ibid., 1166. The bishop’s zeal during an impending or widespread pestilence, ibid., 483. Let the bishop be strict through zeal for discipline, ibid., 559. He must not keep silent but cry aloud, ibid., 187. Let him vigilantly watch over the souls entrusted to him, ibid., 576. Let him imitate earthly shepherds, ibid., 689, 390. Let him observe the sacred canons, ibid., 648–649. Let speech be on his tongue, and fervour of zeal in his heart, ibid., 848. Let his tongue be fiery, ibid. Bishops’ negligence is censured, ibid., 559, 912, 1044, 1279. What episcopal residence should be, ibid., 546 note. How it is to be maintained, ibid., 622 note. A bishop is compelled to reside; if he does not obey, he is to be confined in a monastery, ibid., 813. Bishops of Gaul are forbidden to travel farther without authority from their primate, ibid., 785–786. Bishops of Sardinia could not cross the sea without letters from their metropolitan, unless they were approaching the Apostolic See against that same metropolitan, ibid., 948. Bishops must not go to the imperial court but send deacons there, ibid., 525 note. They could not go to the court without letters from their primate, ibid., 995.—Bishops are to govern their dioceses, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 135. Bishops gathering annually in council are to be instructed by their primate concerning the paschal solemnity also, ibid., 194. A bishop appointed in a diocese is to retain only that people among whom he was ordained, ibid., 197. A bishop ought to devote himself solely to spiritual matters, ibid., 202. A sick bishop should send a representative to synod in his place, ibid. A bishop compels those at variance to be reconciled, ibid.—A bishop is to rebuke an offending cleric belonging to another bishop, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, LXXXIV, 261. A bishop who, having been warned by the metropolitan, does not come to synod is to be excommunicated, ibid., 311. Each year bishops are to visit the diocese and take no more than a third from the parishes, ibid., 312. By letters, the bishop should summon his diocesan presbyters and certain laymen to meet at synod, ibid., 313. Neighbouring bishops are annually to ask their primate about the holy paschal solemnity, ibid., 319. On his own behalf, a bishop should send to a council not a deacon, but either an archpresbyter or a presbyter, ibid. How a bishop, having received an admonition, should come to his metropolitan, ibid.—When and in what cases bishops ought to go to the court, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 891. Bishops are to attend synod without fail, ibid., 897. On bishops who do not attend councils, ibid., 932. If a bishop neglects his diocese, he is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 935. A bishop must not rashly deprive anyone of communion, ibid., 936.

Bishops should carefully examine presbyters throughout their parishes, their faith, etc., Charlemagne, XCVII, 238. On the care of bishops, ibid., 510. Bishops are to amend and correct incestuous persons, ibid., 740. All bishops are to make an annual circuit of their parishes, ibid., 816, 883. Matters which a bishop cannot correct in his diocese he should refer to other prelates, etc., ibid., 849. No bishop is to ravage another bishop’s property or invade his people, ibid., 850. On bishops and how they should thoroughly inspect their parishes, ibid., 881.—The episcopal office, Alcuin, C, 153, 159. “Your tongue is the key of the kingdom of heaven . . . let it never cease from admonitions,” ibid., 450. Let him chastise the proud and stubborn with stern rebukes, ibid. Let him refresh the humble and peaceable with pious exhortations, ibid. “See and consider very attentively how many souls, at the peril of your own soul, you have undertaken to govern,” ibid. “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel,” ibid. Let the tongue labour earnestly in preaching, the hand in almsgiving, and the foot in going about the flock of Christ, ibid., 451. Let the mind watch in prayers, be strengthened in psalmody, and rejoice in the praise of God, ibid.—What the bishop’s office is like, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831. “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season,” ibid., 842. “I will bring back the wandering; I will seek the lost,” etc., ibid. Whoever, though strong in virtues, refuses to feed God’s flock is shown not to love the supreme Shepherd, ibid., 851.—That bishops summoned to synod should not treat it with contempt, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 290. The bishop should exercise care of the needy through presbyters and deacons, ibid., 344. The bishop should hear cases in the presence of clerics, ibid., 339. A bishop compels those at variance to be reconciled, ibid., 340.—On bishops who rarely or never visit in person the peoples entrusted to them, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 193. Let the bishop travel through his diocese, ibid. Let him make the circuit of his parish with a few companions, ibid., 194. If a bishop cannot fulfil this, let him send his vicars in his place, ibid. Let bishops visit their diocese, ibid. How a bishop should excommunicate unbelievers, ibid., 358. How a bishop should reconcile or receive an excommunicated person, ibid., 362.—A bishop is to make an annual circuit of his parish, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 570. On bishops who rarely or never visit in person the peoples entrusted to them, ibid. Bishops should carefully examine their presbyters concerning their ministries, ibid. If a bishop cannot visit his parish, let him send in his place men of proven life, ibid., 571. During a bishop’s visitation, all who belong to the parish of each mother church, except the sick, must come to his synod, ibid., 572. Decretal constitution of Pope Eutychian: what bishops ought to inquire into at synod, ibid., 570. That a bishop ought without interruption to teach and love his Church, ibid., 580. A bishop compels those at variance to be reconciled, ibid., 581. A bishop ought to conduct himself as a guest, ibid. Bishops are to expel diviners and sorcerers from their parishes, ibid., 831.—Bishops are heralds and teachers of God’s laws, Carnutus, CLI, 1177.—A bishop should visit his diocese, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 383. He ought to preach the truth of our Saviour Jesus Christ, ibid., 385; St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 342.—Prelates of the Church are appointed not so much to preside and feed themselves as to benefit others, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 764.—He must not abandon his own wife, on grounds of religion, from his care, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 173. A bishop ought to correct the crime of his children, ibid., 650.—He must teach both by word and example, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 200.—“Feed the flock which is among you,” Gerolius, CXCIV, 1261.—Moreover, whenever anyone doubts concerning the divine law, he should immediately run to the priests and ask them, Abbot Bernard, CCIV, 799.—May the austerity of your countenance banish the wind of flattery and the poison of detraction, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1104.

## V.—On the virtues of a bishop

Why a bishop ought to be good, St Hilary, X, 158.—The Apostle describes what a bishop ought to be like, St Ambrose, XVII, 468.—What if a bishop has simple faith and holy conduct, St Chromatius, XX, 367.—Bishops and presbyters should take the apostles as their example, St Jerome, XXII, 583. The teaching of the apostles explains what gifts bishops ought to possess, id., XXIII, 515.—“Be a pattern of every goodness to all who see you,” Alcuin, C, 151. Let your meals be not in drunkenness but in sobriety, ibid. Let your hand be generous in almsgiving, ibid., 242.—A bishop must be blameless, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 791; St Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 440.—The care of sincere faith and unfeigned charity is especially necessary for a prelate, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 818.—As the wind scatters clouds, so may the austerity of your countenance banish the wind of flattery and the poison of detraction, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1104.—Many things are light for subjects which are heavy for prelates, Innocent III, CXVII, 649.

A bishop must show sincere love and affection to his ministers, Hosius of Corduba, VII, 1325.—The bishop’s glory is to provide for the need of the poor, St Jerome, XXII, 533.—It was decreed that bishops, according to ancient statutes, should abstain even from their wives, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 205.—First let him be examined: whether he is prudent by nature, teachable, chaste in life, sober, etc., St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1178.—Therefore love humility with all your strength, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 800. The pastoral office must be exercised from charity, [Col. 0705] ibid., 847.—On the humility of superiors, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 827.

Let the bishop acknowledge that he is the servant of the people, not their lord, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 711.—Let the bishop be blameless, St Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 383. “That, rooted and founded in charity, they may mutually possess true peace and complete concord,” ibid., 384.—A bishop must be the guardian of all moderation, St Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 440.—Let bishops shine forth in the splendour of virtues, St Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 313.—The chief and most worthy ornaments of prelates—chastity, charity, and humility—have indeed no colour, but are not without beauty, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 816.

Bishops are chosen either as virgins, or as widowers, or at least as perpetually chaste after entering the priesthood, St Jerome, XXII, 510.—Let a bishop be chosen who has had one wife, etc., id., XXIII, 257. But if laymen are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for the sake of prayer, what is to be thought concerning bishops? id., XXIV, 568.—No one should be considered worthy of episcopal eminence if he is found not yet to have restrained himself from marital pleasure, St Leo the Great, LIV, 672. Let a bishop possess humble furnishings, table, and fare, and seek the authority of his dignity by the merits of faith and life, id., LVI, 880. That bishops should abstain from wives, id., LXXXVIII, 819.—A bishop must be the husband of one wife, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 791.—The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1153.

## VI.—On episcopal authority

“Not, however, without the bishop’s authority, for the honour of the Church,” etc., Tertullian, I, 1218. Those whom bishops anathematized in their writings have likewise been anathematized, id., III, 104.—No bishop may retain, ordain, or judge a parishioner belonging to another bishop, Sixtus II, V, 86.—If a bishop from another parish wishes to appoint, to any rank, a minister belonging elsewhere without the consent of his own bishop, such an appointment is to be considered void, Hosius, VIII, 1328.—The welfare of the Church depends upon the dignity of the chief priest, St Jerome, XXIII, 165.—A bishop should not ordain clerics without the counsel of his fellow presbyters, St Leo the Great, LVI, 880. We decree that bishops have authority to oversee, direct, govern, and administer ecclesiastical property according to the authority of the canons, id., CXXXVIII, 581. No bishop ought to dare to pass from one province to another and ordain anyone in its Churches, id., 710. What should be done if a bishop without a see seizes a vacant Church, ibid. Bishops who are over a diocese should not approach Churches beyond their boundaries, ibid., 722.—Bishops must not invade other parishes, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 32, 78. Bishops are not to be ordained for villages and small towns, lest the name and authority of bishop be cheapened, ibid., 178. No bishop may usurp another people, id., LXXXVIII, 819.—A bishop who ordains clerics in another parish without their bishop’s knowledge is to be deposed along with those whom he ordained, Angelramn of Metz, XCVI, 1035. Whatever a bishop ordains uninvited in another parish is void, ibid., 1039. No bishop may dare to perform any ordinations or transact matters in another’s parish that do not concern him, id., XCVII, 156.—Chorepiscopi are to know their proper limits and do nothing without the permission of the bishop in whose parish they live, Charlemagne, XCVII, 509.

## VII.—On episcopal administration; temporal matters, etc.

Your pious concern has asked how the offerings and tithes of the faithful should be distributed, St Boniface, XX, 790.—A transgressor of canonical laws in ordinations, St Leo the Great, LIV, 711. A bishop must not be absent for more than three weeks, id., LVI, 409. Bishops are not to travel overseas unless they have first consulted the bishop holding the see of their respective province, ibid., 426. What should be done if a bishop refuses to go to the Church for which he was ordained, ibid., 711. A bishop must not transfer from one diocese to another, ibid., 712. The bishop has authority over ecclesiastical property, ibid., 713. A bishop must not undertake guardianship of wills, ibid., 880. A bishop must not litigate, even if provoked, over transitory possessions, ibid.—Therefore the holy synod decrees that henceforth no bishop is to involve himself in the administration of secular business, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 80. A bishop must by no means take on secular concerns; otherwise, he is to be deposed, ibid., 142. On synods which bishops ought to hold in their provinces at the appointed times, ibid., 163. That bishops ought not to lease others’ estates or transact [Col. 0706] secular business, ibid., 171.—To Bishop Maximian: after a bishop’s death, the Church’s property is to be inventoried without charge, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 679. No bishop may make strangers, or heretics even if relatives, his heirs, id., LXXXVIII, 820. Bishops or clerics may confer nothing by donation upon persons who are not Catholics, ibid. Bishops must not transfer to other places things belonging to the places where they were ordained unless they first give reasons, ibid. Without the bishop’s knowledge, no one may dare either give or receive the offerings due from the fruits of Church property, ibid.—All Church property is in the bishop’s power for the distribution to the poor, Angelramn of Metz, XCVI, 1036. Church property is to be administered by the bishop’s judgment, ibid., 1040. A bishop who has no children or grandchildren is to leave no heir but the Church, id., CXIX, 1034. The bishop is to have jurisdiction over all ecclesiastical business and administer it as in God’s sight, ibid. Bishops must not presume to alienate the Church’s possessions under any title or contract, ibid., 1031.—It was decreed that no bishop, while travelling through his diocese, should exact from Churches anything beyond the honour due his see, namely two solidi. Appendix to the ninth century, Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals collection, ch. II. A bishop must not presume either to sell servants or property belonging by right to the Church, or, after death, to alienate through any contracts the means by which the poor live, id., CXXXV, 103.

If a bishop has made a will bequeathing anything from property belonging to the Church, it is valid only to this extent, etc., Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 423. A bishop must not presume to alienate anything from the property of a widowed Church, ibid. A bishop has authority over ecclesiastical property for distribution among all in need, id., CLXIII, 631. The bishop must not badly manage what belongs to the Church from its lands, ibid. Transactions administered by bishops are to remain in perpetual stability, ibid., 685.—A bishop must not undertake guardianship of wills, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 418. A bishop must not take upon himself any care of household property, ibid. He should administer the oversight of widows, orphans, and strangers not personally but through the archdeacon, ibid. A bishop who neglects to visit the Church entrusted to him is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 432. A bishop may not appoint another as successor for himself, ibid., 773. While travelling through dioceses, a bishop must take nothing from Churches except two solidi, ibid., 813. On Church property placed under the bishop’s authority, ibid., 892. A bishop who has no heir is to appoint no heir for himself other than the Church, ibid., 910. A bishop’s sale or exchange of Church property is void without the concurrence and subscription of the clerics, ibid., 917. How ecclesiastical resources are to be distributed by bishops, id., CXCIV, 1220. It is contrary to the sacred canons for bishops permanently to alienate the tithes of Churches, ibid., 1314.

## VIII.—On unworthy bishops

Let no unworthy person be made bishop, St Siricius, XIII, 1164.—If a bishop does not have the fear of God before his eyes, accommodating himself rather to the times, God abandons him as an unbeliever and false prophet, St Ambrose, XVII, 469. Nothing is more pitiable than a bishop if, as bishop, he is endangered in respect of holy life, ibid., 571. If the bishop who seemed to provide light to the subject body is darkened by the blindness of wickedness, what will the other members do? etc., ibid., 578.—If the eye—that is, the bishop—becomes a scandal to the Church through perverse faith and shameful conduct, Christ commands that he be plucked out, that is, cast out from the body of the Church, St Chromatius of Aquileia, XX, 350.—Not all bishops are bishops, St Jerome, XXII, 353. Let your deeds not confound your word, ibid., 533. Since a bishop is established in the Church to restrain the people from error, how great will error among the people be when the very one who teaches is in error! id., XXIII, 160. “They devour my people as food, as bread,” id., XXV, 329. “They do not seek what has perished,” desiring not so much to save the lost as to devour those who are in the Churches, ibid. The Lord’s speech to evil shepherds, ibid., 330. Let bishops who educate their children in secular literature and make them read comedies read this, id., XXVI, 540.

Good peoples can exist where bishops are bad, St Augustine, XLIII, 55. We too know that there are false angels, false apostles, and false bishops, ibid., 271.—A bishop must not carry out ordinations for money, Dionysius Exiguus, CLXII, 171.—Those who expect a carnal person to preside over them repel divine grace from themselves, St Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 329.—One not instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines must by no means presume to aspire to the supreme priesthood of the Church, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 313.

## IX.—On accusations against bishops

[Col. 0707]

No bishop ought to be accused, nor may a charge be brought against him by anyone, before he has been restored in the fullest manner, Tertullian, III, 1003. No accusation is to be accepted in writing; it must be made in the accuser’s own voice, if the person of the accuser is lawful and qualified, in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse, ibid., 1004. No bishop can be accused, nor ought he answer his accusers, before he has been duly summoned by his own primate, ibid. A bishop ought not to be heard or judged except in the presence of all his fellow-provincials and by all the bishops of the province, ibid. A cleric who accuses his bishop is not to be received, because he has become infamous, ibid., 1005. Whether accusation of bishops is easy, ibid. How primates ought to judge a bishop, id., V, 146.—Letter concerning accused bishops, St Felix, Pope, V, 148.—A bishop is not to be accused before secular judges, Pope Caius, V, 183. On accusing a bishop before bishops, ibid.—That excommunicated persons cannot accuse bishops, St Cyprian, V, 88; St Julius, VIII, 992. Subject to the authority of the Apostolic Church, no bishop is to be summoned for judgment outside his province, ibid., 987. We exclude from accusing bishops slanderers who ought to be uprooted by divine authority and supporters of enemies, ibid., 989. What if a bishop, as though appealing, flees for refuge to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church? ibid., 1320.—No one is to accuse a bishop before secular arbiters, but before the highest primates, St Felix II, XIII, 19. If anyone has a case against a bishop, let him first state his complaint to him privately, ibid. If after this he chooses to accuse the bishop, let him bring his case before the highest primates of bishops, ibid. If the primates cannot privately reconcile the accusers of bishops with them, then let them summon them canonically to a synod, ibid. If accused bishops have been driven out through fear or despoiled of their goods, they cannot be canonically summoned to synod before they have been canonically restored, ibid., 20 ff.

A bishop can no more be judged by another than he can himself judge another, St Augustine, XLIII, 128, 141, 201.—The greater cases of bishops are to be brought to the Apostolic See at the very first hearing, St Leo the Great, XV, 518, 554, 578. What should be done if bishops differ in their judgment on an accusation against a bishop, id., LVI, 710.—If bishops judging a bishop disagree, the metropolitan bishop is to summon other judges from a neighbouring province to remove the dispute, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 64. On accusers of bishops, ibid., 175. No criminal person may accuse a bishop, ibid., 187. If a bishop is charged with a crime outside the time of synod, he is to be heard by twelve bishops, ibid., 188. If a bishop is accused, the case is to be referred to the primate of his province, ibid., 190.—If a bishop has a case, he is to be heard by twelve bishops, Fulgentius, LXVII, 952. If two bishops in one province have a dispute, they are not to call bishops from another province to judge it, ibid. A bishop against whom judgment has been given may, if he wishes, appeal to the Apostolic See, ibid. A deposed bishop must not bring his case before the emperor, ibid., 953. An accused bishop must not go to public courts, ibid.—On accused bishops, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 117 ff. On the kind of accusers of bishops who should be admitted to make an accusation, ibid., 170. If he appeals from the judges appointed by the primate, other judges in greater number are to be appointed; and if he appeals from them, the matter is to be deferred to the judgment of the council, id., LXXXVIII, 820. An accused bishop must not go to public courts, ibid., 822.

Bishops who have been expelled and despoiled must be restored before accusation, Angelramn of Metz, XCVI, 1059.—Bishops are to be heard by their metropolitans or fellow-provincials, Charlemagne, XCVII, 810. If a bishop has litigation with another bishop, he must seek judges not from another province but from his own, ibid., 758. Before a just determination, a bishop must in no way be deprived of his own authority, ibid., 809. On bishops not being accused except before the highest primates, ibid., 818–819.—On accusations against bishops, Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 59. On the kind of accusers of bishops who should be admitted to accuse, ibid., 308.—Bishops are to be judged by the Lord alone, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 588. A bishop is not to be reproved by his sheep unless he has erred in faith, ibid. If a bishop is charged with a crime and cannot assemble many persons, he is to be heard by twelve bishops, ibid., 593. How an accused bishop should be examined before patriarchs or primates, and by how many witnesses he should be convicted, ibid., 594. An accused bishop must not be deprived of communion unless he refuses to come on the appointed day, ibid., 593.—On bishops accused of crimes who refuse, when summoned, to go to synod, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 407.—Bishops [Col. 0708] may be condemned only by seventy-two witnesses, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 617. Whoever publicly complains against a bishop before approaching him privately is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 642. An accusation against bishops is not to be accepted readily, ibid., 643. Not all subjects, but only criminal persons, are prohibited from accusing prelates, ibid., 643.

## X.—On the deposition of a bishop
Let another be substituted in his place, and let the flock of Christ, which to this day is scattered and wounded and neglected by him, be gathered together, Tertullian, III, 994.---It is clear that a fallen bishop cannot claim for himself the priesthood which he has betrayed, as though, after the altars of the devil, it were lawful to approach the altar of God, St. Cyprian, IV, 389. Let him himself withdraw from the episcopate, and let them seek another for themselves, id., XI, 1199. What is to be ordered if an expelled bishop dares to enter the city from which he was expelled, id., XX, 790. The penalty of deposition and expulsion from their cities was established for bishops refusing to subscribe, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 437.---A bishop who seeks the administration of a more eminent see shall indeed be driven from another’s chair, but shall lose his own as well, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 674.---If a bishop deposed by a synod dares to perform any act of ministry, let him have no further hope of restoration in another synod, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 62. A bishop caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, ibid., 144. A bishop must not beat sinners, whether faithful or unbelieving, under penalty of deposition, ibid. If a bishop who has been justly deposed dares to lay hands upon the ministry formerly entrusted to him, he is to be cut off entirely from the Church, ibid. If any bishop obtains this dignity by money, both he and his ordainer are to be deposed, ibid. If any bishop, using secular authorities, obtains a church through them, he is to be deposed, ibid. A bishop is to be deposed if, in other bishops’ dioceses and without consulting them, he has performed ordinations, ibid., 145. If a bishop dismisses his own wife, let him be excommunicated, id., LXXXVIII, 840.

A bishop caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but not excommunicated, Angilramnus, XCVI, 1035. If a bishop has committed fornication, let him do penance for twenty-five years, id., XCIX, 960. If any bishop has taken a wife, he is to be deposed from office, id., CXXXVIII, 834. A bishop is to have no woman in his bed; if he does so, let him be deposed, id., CXI, 228.---A bishop caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, Burchard, CXI, 926.---If any bishop, using secular authorities, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 216. Let a bishop who takes a wife be deprived of office and benefice, id., CLXII, 1162.---Let a bishop who seeks to inspire fear by beatings be removed from office, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 236. Let a bishop who commits a capital crime fall from office, ibid., 257.

## XI.—On the Right of Appeal

Whenever necessary, bishops may freely appeal to the Apostolic See, Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 985. If anyone believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal Apostolic Church, ibid. It was decreed that, if an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, that is to be established which he himself shall judge justly, ibid., 986.---Those who evade the judgment of the Roman Pontiff throughout Italy and Gaul are ordered by the emperor to be sent to Rome, Pope St. Damasus, XIII, 228.---On appeals to the Bishop of Rome, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 402. Those who have cases should without doubt resort to the metropolitan city, ibid., 708. If necessity compels one to have recourse to the emperor, he must go with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan, etc., ibid., 709. A bishop who believes himself unjustly condemned is to turn not to the emperor but to a larger synod of bishops, ibid.---When one who has been deposed has appealed to the Roman pontiff, another bishop is not to be ordained in his place before the case has been concluded, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 177. If a provincial synod deposes a bishop, he may appeal to the Roman pontiff, ibid., 178. A bishop condemned by all the bishops of his province is not to have the opportunity of seeking a rehearing, id., LXXXVIII, 822. A deposed bishop is not to lay his case before the emperor, ibid. If any deposed bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, his case is to be determined by the judgment of the Bishop of Rome, id., XCVII, 810. If a bishop has been judged in another case and he himself wishes it, let the council be renewed, id., XCIX, 1037.---Let appeal be made by all to the Roman Church as to a mother, Pope Zephyrinus, CLXXXVII, 616.---On appeals, Clement III, CIV, 1481.

## XII.—On Reverence toward the Bishop. Immunities, Privileges, etc.

Bishops, therefore, are not lightly to be accused or disparaged, because injury done to them pertains to Christ, Tertullian, III, 977. Whatever is unjustly done concerning things consecrated to God and concerning bishops shall be reckoned sacrilege, ibid., 1002.---Let them be kept exempt from all public duties, Constantine the Great, VIII, 481.---In the bishop is the dignity of every order; for he is the head of the other members, St. Ambrose, XVII, 187. No bishop is to be brought before any judge, whether for a civil or a criminal cause, id., XX, 789.---Presbyters ought not to enter before the bishop and take their seats in the tribunals, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 720. In church, amid the assembly of presbyters, the bishop should sit in a higher place; within the house, however, he should recognize himself as their colleague, ibid., 880.---Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, plunder the property belonging to him, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 175. Those ordained later must not dare to prefer themselves to those ordained earlier, ibid., 208. The most signal judgment of the pious Emperor Constantine’s reverence toward religion, etc., [Col. 0710] Cassiodorus, LXIX, 896.---What matters are reserved to the bishop, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 895.---Let clerics, subject to bishops in every form of subjection, render them the obedience due to them, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 386. If abbots do anything contrary to the rule, let them be corrected by bishops, ibid., 387.---We command that no one should act lightly or harshly toward bishops, Charlemagne, XCVII, 741. It is not fitting that a man should judge gods, ibid.

“He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye,” Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 16 ff.---Revere bishops, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 223. Moses shows how great reverence is due even to negligent presbyters, ibid., 230.---That Christian princes ought to bow their heads to bishops, not judge concerning their heads, St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 509.---On the reverence to be shown to priests, King Canute, CLI, 1172.---Let everyone recognize how grave a matter it is not to obey a bishop, Gottfried of Viterbo, CLVII, 85.---How priests are to be honored, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 431.---On the honor that emperors have shown to priests, Placidus, CLXIII, 661.---The consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, the preparation of chrism, the laying on of hands, etc., belong especially to the bishop, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 430.---Brethren, let us revere their labors, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 832.

[Col. 0709]

# LXXXIV. INDEX ON THE PRIESTHOOD, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER, OR A COMPLETE SYNOPSIS OF WHAT THE HOLY FATHERS HAVE SAID CONCERNING THE DIGNITY, POWER, HOLINESS, VIRTUES, LEARNING, ETC., ETC., OF PRIESTS

## NOTICE

From bishops we proceed to priests. Noble is the office, and most noble the power, of the priests of the New Law: they sacrifice to God not calves or goats, but, under the law instituted by Christ, consecrate the very body and blood of the Lord and offer them in the sacrifice of the Mass. Priests are so called from performing sacred acts. They are also called presbyters—*seniores*, “elders,” in Latin—yet rather on account of wisdom than of age. All their power proceeds either from order or from jurisdiction.

From order is derived the anointing of the sick, the consecration of the divine body and blood, the preaching of the divine word, the power to baptize, and to bind and loose in the sacrament of penance. From jurisdiction is derived the very act and right of exercising this power; this is received from the bishop and, at the bishop’s discretion, is conferred, withdrawn, extended, or restricted, except at the point of death, when the Church gives presbyters free power to absolve the dying person from sins. Accordingly, the Roman Pontifical rightly describes their duties when it says: “A priest must offer, bless, preside, preach, and baptize.”

Yet not all these things may be done by every priest. For although at ordination a title is assigned to a priest—that is, a church in which he may serve—not all are assigned a people to govern and over whom they ought to preside in spiritual matters. The assignment of a title enables them there to offer the sacrifice of the Mass, distribute eucharistic bread to the people, and impart certain blessings. But with respect to the remaining duties mentioned in the Pontifical, ordination indeed makes the presbyter fit and qualified for them; nevertheless, since they concern a people and are signs of spiritual jurisdiction and authority over it, every presbyter who has no people subject to him uses the faculty of exercising those rights which he received in ordination partly unlawfully, contrary to the canons, and partly altogether vainly and without effect.

Having said this, let us set forth the method followed in this Index. We have established various articles, in which we treat successively: I, the dignity of the priest and his power; II, priestly holiness; III, the virtues appropriate to a priest, namely faith, charity, chastity, humility, gentleness, mortification, zeal; IV, the vices a priest must avoid, namely pride, avarice, drunkenness, incontinence, the vice of the tongue, envy, ambition; V, things forbidden to a priest, namely women, banquets, taverns, hunting, war, secular business, games, adornment; VI, the duties of priests, namely offering sacrifice, administering the sacraments, preaching, teaching, praying, applying themselves to study, residing in the parish, and caring for the church; VII, knowledge necessary for a priest; VIII, pastoral burden and reward; IX, counsels to be given to priests; X, finally, as an appendix, books treating of the priesthood. Under each article we present various sayings or opinions of the Fathers; and thus anyone who preaches, especially one who addresses priests, will have at hand, with the aid of this Index, whatever the *Patrology* offers on these matters.

## I.—On the Dignity of Priests and Their Power

[Col. 0711]

The heavenly priesthood, St. Siricius, XIII, 1166.---Priests in whom is the beauty of the Church, in whom its flower is more delightful, in whom its age is more perfect, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1360. A little book on priestly dignity, XVII, 568.---Priests, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in a sense pass judgment before the day of judgment, St. Jerome, XXII, 352. Great is the dignity of priests, but great is their fall if they sin, id., XXV, 443. The dignity of priests through the consecration of Christ’s body, id., XXII, 252.---The power of priests, St. Augustine, XL, 1122. Priests, protectors and rulers of the earth, ibid., 1299. Fellow citizens of angels and of paradise, ibid. Sons of prophets, kindred of patriarchs, successors of apostles, ibid., 1299.---By God’s grace priests become interpreters of the divine will, Pomerius, LIX, 445. Founders of Christ’s churches through the apostles, ibid. Leaders of the faithful people, ibid. Defenders of truth, enemies of corrupt doctrine, ibid. Fathers of those reborn in the Catholic faith, preachers of heavenly things, the foremost ranks in invisible battles, ibid.---They are the firmest columns, founded in Christ, on which rests the whole multitude of believers, Pomerius, LIX, 445. They are the gates of the eternal city, ibid. They are the gatekeepers to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given, and likewise the stewards of the royal household, ibid.---We are the stones of the sanctuary, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1147. “We serve as ambassadors for Christ,” etc., ibid., 1236. Priests can also cast out demons, ibid., 1215.

Clerics, because of the dignity of the heavenly priesthood, do not shed blood or bear the sword, St. Cyprian, IV, 861.---In Scripture priests are called angels and gods, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 766. “You are gods, established by the true God: Go, and settle your cases among yourselves, because it is not fitting that we should judge gods,” ibid. Since priestly dignity seems to surpass other dignities, ibid., 1043. Let the priest recognize his dignity and exercise the force of his dignity, because he has been anointed, id., LXXIX, 459. He is anointed in the midst of his brethren, that he may be humble and exalted: exalted in rank, humble in estimation, ibid.---It belongs to the presbyter to perform at the altar of the Lord the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, to say prayers, and to bless the people, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 895.---Priests are ministers of God and dispensers of his mysteries, Pope St. Zachary, LXXXIX, 924.---Let them recognize priestly power, strength, and dignity, Charlemagne, XCVII, 611. God has made you priests and has given you authority even to judge us, ibid. For you, given to us by God, are gods, and it is not fitting that a man should judge gods, ibid. They are the glory of the Church, in whom the Church shines more brightly, ibid., 612. By God’s grace they become interpreters of the divine will, fathers of Christians, columns of the Church, gatekeepers of heaven, etc., ibid. Those who are acknowledged to be vicars of Christ and key-bearers of the kingdom of heaven, ibid., 659. To whom so great a power has been conferred by Christ, ibid.---This is the dignity, praise, and honor of the priest, Blessed Alcuin, C, 254. Remember that, by priestly dignity, the tongue is the key of the heavenly empire and the most brilliant trumpet of Christ’s camp, ibid., 392. You are minister of the sacred altar, companion in the highest honor, vessel of wisdom, flower of youth: consider your dignity and be what you are called, ibid., 457. Priestly honor is no worldly sport, ibid. The excellence of the priesthood, ibid., 1064. *Presbyter* is a Greek word and in Latin means “elder,” not because of old age, but because of dignity, honor, and wisdom, id., CI, 1235.

Therefore, since so great a dignity of priesthood has been conferred upon priests, the people are commanded to obey them in all things, Agobard, CIV, 136, on the dignity of priests.---Theodulf, CV, 191.---For they preside over the Church of Christ and, in the consecration of the divine body and blood, share office with bishops, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 826.---They make Christ’s body by their sacred mouth, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 210. They possess the keys of the kingdom of heaven, ibid. In a sense they judge before the day of judgment, ibid. God has made you priests and given you power even to judge us, ibid. For you, given to us by God, are gods, ibid. “He who despises you despises me, and he who receives you receives me,” ibid., 211.---They are so called not because of age or decrepit old age, but because of honor and dignity, etc., Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 301.---The dignity of the priesthood, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 440.---How great is the dignity of the priestly order, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 187. That priestly dignity surpasses imperial dignity, ibid., 323. No secular dignity, not even the imperial, can equal priestly honor or dignity, ibid., 437. Gold is no more precious than lead than priestly authority is higher than royal power, ibid., 438. It belongs to the presbyter to perform at God’s altar the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, to say prayers, and to bless [Col. 0712] the gifts of God, ibid., 449. Therefore you must remember so great a dignity, remember your consecration, remember the sacred anointing which you have received upon your hands, so that you neither degenerate from that dignity, nor render your consecration void, nor defile by sinning hands anointed with sacred oil, ibid., 481. In this appears how great is the excellence of the priestly office, id., CLXII, 519.

On the dignity of priests, Hugh of St. Mary, CLXIII, 953.---For priests alone of the Church wash us from sins and offer sacrifices for us, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 388.---Priestly authority in the Church, Rupert, CLXIX, 1182. At the altar the priest bears the person and role of Christ, id., CLXX, 144.---Priestly dignity lies in election, Hildebert, CLXXI, 761. “He has placed you over the heads of men as stewards of his household,” ibid., 762. How great a thing it is that at the lifting of our hands the heads of kings are bowed, ibid. Four likenesses to Christ are in the priest’s hands, ibid., 774. “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” ibid., 781. On the excellence of the Christian priesthood, ibid., 786. O new and divine power, by whose ministry the bread of angels is daily prepared for mortals, ibid., 788. For in these ministers of his Church Christ judges before judgment, sifts before the final sifting, ibid. Not the tongues of emperors, but of priests, have been made the keys of heaven, ibid., 789. Priests alone, with Christ, open and no one shuts; they shut and no one opens, ibid. By the counsel of priests weak souls are aided, chains are broken, the way to the heavenly places is opened, earthly things are joined to heavenly, human beings to angels, the creature to the Creator. Great, therefore, is the honor of the priesthood, ibid. By the exercise, that is, of priestly ministry, they bring faithful souls into the heavenly treasury, ibid., 790.---They are called priests because they give what is sacred in consecrating the divine body, in baptism, and in the office of preaching, ibid., 927. On the dignity of the priesthood, ibid. There is also afterwards given by the Lord to priests a certain divine dominion, which belonged properly to God alone, ibid., 928. Whether in right and dignity the priesthood precedes kingship, or kingship the priesthood, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1258. As the soul is more worthy than the body, so the priesthood is more worthy than kingship, by which it is rightly ordered, ibid., 1263. Christ himself preferred priesthood to kingship, ibid., 1265. In both the Old and New Testaments priesthood has always preceded kingship, ibid., 1270.

Priests perform the role of mediator, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 428.---They themselves are mediators, Hildebert, CLXXVI, 429.---In this appears how great is the excellence of the priestly office, through which Christ’s Passion is celebrated daily at the altar and every guilty person who turns from sins is reconciled to God, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 429.---Ministries to be revered even by angelic spirits, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 853. Alas, chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, etc., ibid. On the dignity of priests, id., CLXXXIV, 784. Consider your dignity, priest of God Most High; behold with the eyes of the mind your eminence; reflect upon your prerogative; see your lot, ibid. Consider how greatly your God has exalted you, how greatly he has raised you above all creatures, ibid. At your spoken word the highest Father, at whose nod, etc., lays down his most sweet Son and places him in your hands, ibid. With what light do you think yourself surrounded, holy priest, in the presence of so great a Majesty, at so solemn an advent and assembly of the Trinity and of the entire heavenly host, ibid., 785. The power of priests is greater than angelic dignity, ibid. Therefore consider and always bear in mind, retain in continual remembrance, the grace singularly bestowed upon you by God, which he granted neither to angels nor to other human beings, ibid. All these holy orders of blessed spirits, although they enjoy blessedness so that nothing is lacking to their supreme happiness, nevertheless revere the glory of the priest, admire his dignity, yield to his privileges, honor his power, ibid., 786. O ecclesiastical race, royal priesthood, ibid. God chose you as his inheritance, ibid. What dignity God has conferred upon you! How great is the prerogative of your order! God has set you above kings and emperors; he has set your order above all; indeed, to speak more loftily, he has set you above angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, ibid., 1086. Thus he entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood not to angels but to men, and to priests alone, ibid. You who are vicars of Christ, who are shepherds of souls, ibid., 1091. The stones of the sanctuary—that is, priests—ibid. You are senators of the whole world, ibid., 1093.---On the dignity of clerics, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 668.---That the rank of priestly eminence does not deter, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 358. I know and openly profess that, at the time of the offering, in the very hour of incense, the heavens are opened at the priest’s voice and angels stand present, etc., ibid. Nor is there any doubt that priestly dignity surpasses the office of the ancient Fathers as greatly as the reality of hope surpasses a shadow, and the fulfillment of truth surpasses promises, ibid., 363.---That priesthood is greater than kingship, Innocent III, CCXVI, 1179. Kings are anointed by priests, not priests by kings, ibid. Hence God called priests gods, but called kings princes, ibid., 1180. Because of the dignity of his office, the priest is called an angel, ibid. Princes are given power on earth, but priests are granted power both in heaven. The former only over bodies, the latter also over souls. Therefore, as much as the soul is more worthy than the body, so much more worthy is priesthood than kingship, ibid. It precedes in antiquity, ibid. Priesthood is by divine ordination, but kingship by human usurpation, ibid.

## II.—On the Holiness of Priests

The holiness of priests is required in Exodus, Council of Carthage, III, 1022.---In ordinations of priests we ought to choose only blameless and upright bishops, ibid., 1023. Nor should the people associate themselves with the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest, ibid., 1025. For priests and ministers who serve the altar and sacrifices must be whole and unstained, ibid., 1049. How can they preside over integrity and continence if corruptions and the teachings of vices begin to proceed from themselves? St. Cyprian, IV, 369. In the divine Scriptures God forbids even priests guilty of a lighter crime to approach the sacrifice, ibid., 390.---Above all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be blameless, Pope Eutychian, V, 165.---How much more must a priest at every moment be ready, secure in the purity of cleanness, lest he either offer sacrifice or be compelled to baptize, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1160.---Here it is not nobility of birth but excellence of character, and the prerogative of virtues, that is chosen, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1202. Priestly virtue is by no means mediocre: one must beware not only of association with graver crimes, but even with the slightest, ibid., 1204. Let us avoid the path of a worn-out life, ibid., 1052.---That you may proceed to Christ’s altar as a virgin from the bridal chamber and have a good testimony from those outside, St. Jerome, XXII, 1082. What the holiness of a priest ought to be, id., XXVI, 566. He loses the authority to teach whose speech is destroyed by his conduct, id., XXII, 662. Therefore Christ’s pontiff should be such that those who disparage religion do not dare to disparage his life, ibid., 664.---By living wickedly and providing a bad example, evil shepherds kill their sheep, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 275. Let your charity consider what you ought to be, that you may worthily bear the vessels of the Lord, id., XL, 1299. In every respect he commands the presbyter, as the bishop, to be without fault—that is, blameless—ibid.---The election of priests is so excellent that those things which in other members of the Church are not called culpable are nevertheless held unlawful in them, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 672. A Catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought neither to be entangled in any error nor corrupted by any desire, ibid., 1001.---The necessity of holiness in a priest if he is to correct others, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 431. For, unless my judgment deceives me, the priest must live holily so that he does not render his words void by contradictory deeds, ibid., 434. A priest must live holily for the sake of example, ibid., 434. They are the glory of the Church, in whom the Church shines more brightly, ibid., 445. These are they who merited the priesthood not by ambition but by spiritual living, ibid.---Gold has indeed grown dim, because the life of priests, once bright through the glory of virtues, is now shown reprobate through base actions, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1147. The life of priests should correspond to their office and dignity, ibid., 1148. Let those still subject to vices not presume to govern others, ibid., 264. For the preacher whose conduct differs from his utterance sows while fasting what another may eat, ibid., 198. Preachers ought to surpass their hearers far in life, ibid., 1001. Let life not differ from speech, ibid., 549. As a ruler surpasses others in the honor of rank, so should he surpass them in virtue of conduct, id., LXXVII, 28. The ruin of the people comes chiefly from the fault of priests, ibid., 1295. The elect, purified by priests’ hands, enter the heavenly homeland, while priests themselves hasten by a reprobate life to the punishments of hell, ibid., 1148. Let the works of the priest themselves also cry out the way of life together with the sound of his tongue, id., LXXVII, 31, 473. It is shown how greatly a priest ought to shine in a diversity of virtues, id., LXXVII, 471. One who can show you the way of life not only by speaking but by living, id., LXXVII, 626. It befits the priest of the Lord to shine in conduct and life, so that in him as in a mirror of their own life the people entrusted to him may both choose what to follow and see what to correct, id., LXXVII, 935. “Let your priests [Col. 0714] be clothed with righteousness,” id., LXXVII, 473. Let the pastor’s life be an example for imitation, id., LXXVII, 559. Evil priests are the snare and ruin of my people, id., LXXVII, 16. Therefore, whoever after receiving sacred order has fallen into a sin of the flesh is to be deprived of sacred order, so that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar, id., LXXVII, 695. He ought to show himself an example for all to imitate, id., LXXVII, 1043. Let them live with good morals and, with God’s help, preserve heart, tongue, and body from all unlawful things, id., LXXVII, 1185. A pastor should possess holiness of life and learning of wisdom, id., LXXIX, 181. If a pastor retains eloquence of speech without holiness of life, even though he appears to be divinely endowed, he is by no means adorned with the honor of priesthood, ibid. He is commanded to scatter examples of virtue all around, id., LXXIX, 459. He who speaks and does not act is condemned by the sword of his own mouth, id., LXXIX, 450. “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place,” id., LXXIX, 115. The person of a teacher ought to be adorned with great splendors of virtues, id., LXXIX, 456.---Let them likewise shine with the splendor of life, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 822. As he surpasses others in the honor of rank, so let him surpass them in virtue of conduct, ibid., 824.---The ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine in doctrine as well as life, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 707. Every teacher must apply himself both to good conduct and good preaching, ibid. The tongue of teachers who teach well but live badly is a crooked bow, ibid., 708. It is necessary that a priest be holy in all things and held blameworthy in none, ibid., 785. He who rebukes another for sins ought himself to be free from sin, ibid.---Let them adorn their ministry with good morals, Charlemagne, XCVII, 176. Let them have good and commendable conduct, ibid., 517. Let priests, according to the Apostle’s word, be blameless and adorned with good character, ibid., 547. They are the glory of the Church, in whom the Church shines more brightly, ibid., 612.---Confirm all persons by the good examples of your life, Blessed Alcuin, C, 155. Be a model of salvation for all, ibid., 245. Let examples of holiness shine in your conduct, ibid., 244. Let holiness honor our ministry, ibid., 392. Show yourself blameless in all things, so that your life may be the people’s teaching and many may be edified by your good conduct, ibid., 458. Let a teacher’s wisdom shine in uprightness of conduct, ibid., 501.
