Live among your brethren as Lucifer among the stars, so that many may be exhorted by your good examples, ibid., 507.---A priest must be blameless in life and doctrine, St. Agobard, CIV, 145. Let your life be a rule for your children, *Book*, CV, 82.---Be for all a pattern, an ornament, order, and measure, Theodulf, CV, 338.---For if one established in the episcopate or presbyterate commits some mortal sin, he is removed, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 830. So holy is the priest’s name that it permits itself to be stained by no mark of vice, ibid., 850. He who strives to seek the governance of a priest should first examine himself, whether his life is fitting for the honor, ibid. He must live holily for the sake of example, ibid., 859. Let the priest’s good works themselves cry out together with the sound of his tongue, ibid., 858.---He who is about to proclaim God’s words to the people ought to have nothing in his conscience which he will rebuke in others, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 575.---Let your life and conduct be blameless, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 675.---For those who announce words of life to believers must not cease to cry out also by works of life, Haymo, CXVII, 1067. Preachers fly as clouds when, raised above earthly desires by the wings of virtues, etc., ibid., 1107.---Therefore every priest ought, with God’s help, to excel the people entrusted to him and all other subjects in life, morals, and good deeds, Riculf, CXXXI, 16. “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord,” ibid.---That a priest must flee even the slightest suspicion of crime, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 495. That no one sins more grievously than a bad presbyter, ibid., 500. It is fitting that the priest be adorned with the garments of piety and justice, ibid., 492. That the nobility of priests is a holy life, ibid., 494. Who is truly a priest, ibid., 501. Priests ought to surpass others in conduct and doctrine, id., CL, 593.---He who is called a priest and does not fulfill the priestly office by worthy deeds ought above all to fear because of the dignity of this office, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 914. The handling of so fearsome a ministry requires holiness in a priest, ibid., 910.---That sacrifice cannot rightly be offered except through a just and holy priest, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 189. That priests must approach sacrifice without stain, ibid., 190. For no one harms the Church more than one who acts perversely while bearing the name or order of holiness and priesthood, ibid., 422. That the more worthy priests are, the more readily they are heard, ibid., 454. In order that anyone may be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the sacrament but with justice as well, id., CLXII, 93. So that, as they excel in dignity of order, they may also excel in holiness of life, id., CLXII, 519.---Let your life be a rule for your children, Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 252.---Hear this, therefore, you who approach sacred orders . . . for if you are unstained, [Col. 0715] approach with confidence, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 445. Let priests be without stain, ibid., 447.---Set your conduct in order, so that all who see and hear you may receive from you an example of holiness and a model of good conduct, Hildebert, CLXXI, 760. His speech has no sweetness whose conscience reproaches him for a reprobate life, ibid. Take care that your works shine before the Lord, etc., ibid., 761. If the priest falls, how much more will the people perish, ibid., 777. Therefore priests ought, by living well, to guard themselves, lest by living badly they harm themselves and others, ibid. Without holiness God does not acknowledge a priest, ibid., 789. By these things it is shown how exalted priestly life ought to be, ibid., 790. A priest is called to the eminence of holiness, ibid., 789. Hence it is necessary that those who bear the vessels of the Lord become vessels of the Lord; not vessels of clay, but golden vessels, ibid., 790. What good is it to feed by the word those whom one kills by example? ibid., 821. God is not appeased by the offering of an evil priest, ibid., 753. Vicars of Christ ought to bear Christ’s likeness about them, ibid., 773. How necessary holiness and doctrine are to a priest, ibid., 789. How chaste the hands of a priest ought to be, ibid., 775.---If, then, one who approached the altar without garments would be detestable, how much more detestable, how much more dreadful, is one who presumes to approach with vices and without virtues? Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 927. The ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine in life as well as doctrine, ibid., 1070. Priests ought to have peace with God through eminence of holiness, id., CLXXVI, 429. Priests of Christ are to be admonished that, as they excel in dignity of order, so they may excel in holiness of life, id., CLXXVI, 430.---It is shown that every member of the clergy ought to be of uncorrupted life and faith, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1005.---Let nobility of conduct, not of rank or birth, distinguish priests, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 214. Priests are heard more readily in proportion as they are more worthy before God, id., CLXXXVII, 521.---Blessed Mark refuses the priesthood because of his own imperfection, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 363. Greater holiness is required of a priest, ibid. The hand of the priest who cares for the salvation of the soul must be clean, ibid., 366. As you excel in dignity, so it is fitting that you surpass others in holiness of works, ibid., 734. A wicked priest is the ruin of the people, ibid. Those who serve and minister to the Holy of Holies must be holy, ibid., 739.---The life of priests ought to injure no one, Alan of Lille, CCX, 385.---Observe that gold placed in the sun shines, flames, and sparkles: thus the ecclesiastical pastor, placed in the sun—that is, in public view—over the Church of God, ought to shine by the example of good conduct, Absalon, CCXI, 165.

## III.—On the Virtues of Priests
1. On faith.—That both integrity of faith and uprightness of conduct are required in a priest, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1212. “For we have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve a superstitious cult rather than purity of mind or faith,” id., LVI, 576.—“Be an example of the faithful in faith,” St. Benedict, LXVI, 973.—For a preacher ought to have such confidence in God that, although he does not provide for the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that these will not fail him, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1140; the Venerable Bede, XCII, 462. The power of the faith of preachers, ibid., 410.—“You have received the office of priesthood, and, seated at the stern of the Church, steer the ship against the waves. Hold fast the helm of faith, so that the heavy storms of this age may not be able to trouble you,” St. Ambrose, XVI, 879. In Christ preachers will be so firmly established that no force of persecutions can tear them away from faith in him, id., XVII, 927.—In priests, faith must be chosen together with life, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1039.—Priests therefore ought to have such confidence in God that they are in no way entangled in the cares of earthly business or in worldly desires, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1344.—Once integrity of faith has been preserved, strive all the more to adorn yourself, Paschal I, CII, 1088.—Before all else the faith of priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe, Hetto, CV, 763.—Pursue faith, Atto of Vercelli, CLXXXIV, 694.—Those who limp in faith are to be removed from the priesthood, Hildebert, CLXXI, 766.—St. Bernard shows that every member of the clergy is of incorrupt life and faith, CLXXXIII, 1005.

2. On charity.—All priests ought to love all Christians as their children, St. Jerome, XXIII, 340.—What Christ requires of Peter before entrusting the sheep to him, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 287. “For if you are such a one and love me, feed my sheep. You will not be a hireling but a shepherd,” ibid., 760.—“The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep,” St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 313.—“Be an example of the faithful in charity,” St. Benedict, [Col. 0716] LXVI, 973.—He who does not have charity toward another ought by no means to undertake the office of preaching, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1139. For preaching, the conscience of holy love builds up more than practice in speaking, ibid., 890. By words of charity, they transform either themselves into their hearers or their hearers into themselves, ibid., 309. The shepherd’s flame is the light of the flock, id., LXXVII, 935. Let the shepherd be near to each person through compassion, id., LXXVII, 32, 473. Let the shepherd pursue faults, but love persons, id., LXXVII, 488. “Do you love me? Feed my sheep,” id., LXXVII, 19. A preacher of truth ought to possess such great charity that, etc., id., LXXIX, 338.—Let charity not cease from doing good to all, Blessed Alcuin, C, 248. Let peace be in the mouth and charity in the heart, ibid., 451. Adorn yourself with love of God and neighbor, ibid., 453. Exercise yourself in charity, ibid., 459. May you live among the brethren in the sweetness of charity, ibid., 508. Remember this, that you may live happily in the charity of Christ, ibid., 508. Love God always, ibid., 509. Be mindful of the poor in almsgiving, ibid., 509.—Let the priest be hospitable, Sedulius Scotus, CIII, 244.—“Be an example of the faithful in charity,” St. Benedict, CIII, 784.—Preachers burn with love, loving those upon whom they bestow words, and even those from whom they suffer evils, Haymo, CXVII, 316. “I counsel you to buy from me gold tried and refined by fire”; by gold tried in fire we may also understand charity, ibid., 998.—Pursue charity, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 694.—That they may have compassion on their neighbors through charity, Rupert, CLXVII, 1083. Through the compassion of charity the priest’s breast ought to burn, ibid., 777.—He therefore who has charity along with other virtues is a priest, Hildebert, CLXXI, 928.—And he who has even other virtues without this is not a priest, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 928.

3. On chastity.—All priests and Levites are bound by an indissoluble law, that from the day of our ordination we dedicate both our hearts and bodies to sobriety and chastity, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1139. Any cleric, moreover, who takes a widow or certainly a second wife is immediately stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical rank, ibid., 1144. We urge what is worthy, modest, and honorable: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, ibid., 1160. Not only we, but Sacred Scripture also compels priests to be most chaste, and the Fathers likewise have commanded that bodily continence must be observed, ibid., 1184. For with what modesty would a bishop or priest dare to preach integrity or continence to a widow or virgin, or urge preservation of a chaste marriage-bed, if he himself exerted himself more for the world in begetting children than for God? ibid., 1185. That bishops, priests, and deacons are bound by the law of continence, ibid., 118.—These priests ought to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, St. Innocent I, XX, 497. If a priest or any cleric takes a widow as wife, or a repudiated woman, let him lose his office, ibid., 528.—If a priest must always pray, then he must always abstain from marriage, St. Jerome, XXIII, 257. Chastity is commended to those serving at the altar, id., XXV, 439. So too his own chastity and, so to speak, priestly modesty: that he abstain not only from an unclean act, but also from a wandering glance, etc., id., XXVI, 569. Either equally ignore or equally love all girls and virgins of Christ. Do not remain under the same roof; nor trust in past chastity, id., XXII, 538. Let priests preserve chaste eyes and tongue, id., XXI, 538. The celibacy of clerics, id., XXIII, 340.—The incontinent, placed in offices of this sort, were to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 501. How much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, id., LVI, 501.—Priests are compared to bees because of chastity, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 515.—“Be an example of the faithful in chastity,” St. Benedict, LXVI, 973.—That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with women, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 243. That deacons, like bishops and priests, ought to abstain from marital intercourse, ibid., 288.—That a cleric should not take a woman as wife, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 956.—Let a priest be chaste, Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 681.—The celibacy of priests under the new law, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 95.

Let them strive perpetually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, or at least be bound by the bond of one marriage, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087. Let chastity be guarded by Levites and priests, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 185. Concerning priests and Levites, that they abstain from their wives, ibid., 209. On the chastity of priests, ibid., 373.—Priests of God and deacons, and the other ministers of God who ought to serve in God’s temple, should always preserve their chastity, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 421.—If you have priests clean and chaste, free from every fornication and homicide, [Col. 0717] no nation will be able to stand before you; rather, all pagan peoples will fall before you, and you will be victors, Pope St. Zacharias, LXXXIX, 924.—Adorn yourself with chastity, Blessed Alcuin, C, 453.—Strive to preserve yourself in all chastity before the sight of the Lord God Most High, ibid., 507. Remember this, that you may live happily in chastity, ibid., 508.—“Be an example of the faithful in chastity,” St. Benedict, CIII, 784.—As priests ought always to minister, so they ought always to be continent, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 216.—Let him also have modesty, that he abstain not only from an unclean act, but also from errors of eye, mouth, and thought, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831. Let the priest be chaste, ibid. It should be your duty, dearest one, to preserve not only chaste eyes but also a chaste tongue, ibid., 886.—On the continence and chastity of clerics, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1419.—A bishop must be modest, that is, chaste from all uncleanness, Haymo, CXVII, 791. For those who ought to handle the sacred mysteries with their hands and minister them to others should be free from every unclean defilement, so that they may be chaste in mind and modest in body, id., CXVIII, 786.—A cleric who has lived chastely through ecclesiastical orders as far as the subdiaconate cannot take a wife, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 1193.

The celibacy of clerics is defended against the Greeks. The celibacy of clerics is maintained by ecclesiastical laws, Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 324.—Let bishops, priests, and deacons be continent, Aeneas of Paris, CXXI, 728. It has been decreed that bishops, priests, and deacons, in accordance with earlier statutes, should also abstain from their wives, ibid.—But if after ordination a minister happens to enter his own wife’s bed, let him not enter the thresholds of the sanctuary, let him not seek to offer sacrifice, nor touch the altar, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 39. Let chastity be guarded by Levites and priests, ibid., 325. By these enactments all priests and Levites are bound by an indissoluble law, that from the day of our ordination we dedicate both our hearts and bodies to sobriety and chastity, ibid., 681; St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 496.—Any cleric, moreover, who takes a widow or certainly a second wife is immediately stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical rank, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 682.—On priestly continence, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 208. Priests of the Lord and deacons, or whoever handle the sacraments, as guardians of modesty should abstain from their wives, ibid., 209. Priests and Levites should not have intercourse with women, ibid. It has been decreed that bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons abstain from wives, so that they do not beget children, ibid., 210.—Priestly modesty: that a priest abstain not only from an unclean act but also from the gaze of the eyes, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 706. That carnal marriage is forbidden to clerics, id., CXXXVIII, 411. Those who ought to teach God’s people the light of life should maintain chastity according to their rank, id., 482.—No priest, no deacon, no subdeacon, no one in the clergy, may admit a wife or concubine, St. Henry, CXL, 227.—Concerning a priest: if he has taken a wife, let him be deposed, Burchard, CXL, 645.

A priest who has taken a wife ought to be deposed from his order, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 454. It has been decreed that bishops, priests, and deacons who handle the sacraments, as guardians of modesty, abstain from their wives, ibid.; St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 361, 401.—It has been decreed that chastity be maintained in all things and by all who serve the altar, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 454. From the day he receives the honor of priesthood, let no priest enter into marriage, ibid., 455.—How much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, Humbert, CXLIII, 999.—What is to be done against priests, deacons, and subdeacons who do not preserve chastity, Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1315.—Let priests or deacons, ministers of the altar, be chosen for such offices of the Lord who left behind a wife before their ordination, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 361, 400. Why clerics ought to be chaste, id., CXLV, 387. It has been decreed that holy bishops and priests of God, as also Levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, be continent in all things, ibid., 400. It has been decreed—and confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, deacons and priests, and also bishops, according to their proper statutes, should abstain from their wives, ibid., 402. How great was the continence of ministering priests and Levites under the old law, ibid., 404.—Those established in the three sacred grades—priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate—who have not dismissed women and have not lived chastely are to be excluded from the dignity of those grades, Pope Alexander II, CXLVI, 1406. If henceforth any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman or retains one already taken, let him fall from his proper grade until satisfaction has been made, ibid., 1407.

The Church seeks a priest either holy from virginity or adorned by monogamy, Landulf, CXLVII, 934. Likewise, [Col. 0718] the Apostle commands above that bishops, priests, and deacons be modest, that is, continent, id., CXLVIII, 1125.—Priests and Levites should not mingle with their wives, because they are occupied in daily ministry, St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 519. Clerics who do not remain continent after a third admonition are to be excommunicated, ibid.—The marriages of priests condemned by the council under Lanfranc, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CL, 149.—An incontinent priest must not minister, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 465. On the chastity of priests or Levites, ibid., 467, 468. That a priest be chosen either monogamous or a virgin, ibid., 649. Those to be ordained deacons or priests promise that they will live chastely, ibid., 1135. Priests are commanded always to maintain chastity, ibid., 1151. A priest, who must always pray, must always abstain from marriage, ibid., 1152. Let no one approach sacred orders unless he is a virgin or of proven chastity, ibid., 1153. He who wishes to be a priest should clothe himself and fortify himself with chastity, id., 514.—Concerning married and concubinary priests, we decree that they be completely separated from ministry at the altar and deprived of ecclesiastical property, Paschal II, CLXIII, 469.—Let them strive perpetually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, Peter of Honestis, CLXIII, 708.—In the new priesthood it is not thus; rather, birth . . . but pure election is required, and marriage is renounced, Hildebert, CLXXI, 927.—Priests ought to abstain from their wives in accordance with the canons, Antipope Anacletus, CLXXIX, 715.—Would that those unable to remain continent were ashamed rashly to profess perfection or to enroll themselves for celibacy, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 854. Chastity is necessary for priests, id., CLXXXIV, 1085.—The celibacy of clerics, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 923, 1109.—Priests are commanded always to observe chastity, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 170. Ministers of the altar, together with bishops and priests, are under the same law of continence, ibid., 72.—On the continence of clerics, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 727.

4. On humility.—Priests ought to be humble, because both the Lord and his apostles were humble, St. Cyprian, IV, 402.—Whoever therefore desires to be accounted worthy before our God of the dignity of priesthood ought to be gentle and humble in heart, St. Boniface, XX, 781.—They do not enter through Christ because they are not humble, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 761.—Against pride, let priests shine with true humility, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 549. In every deed they do vigorously, let them preserve humility with their whole intention, ibid., 804. By bringing to mind the life of his hearers, the preacher humbles himself, ibid., 1001. In displaying their teaching, let preachers be humble, ibid., 548. The humility of the preacher who considers himself an unprofitable servant, ibid., 23. He endeavors both to speak of humility, the teacher and mother of all virtues, and to show it by living, ibid., 265. The rationale of humility in a preacher, ibid., 570, 925. In the Church’s peace, let preachers be humble; in persecution, strong and upright, ibid., 600. Let the words of the righteous come from the root of humility, that they may bear the fruit of piety, ibid. In whose mind both humility with rectitude and severity with piety shine, id., LXXVII, 626. When necessary, humility should not flee the approach to pastoral care, ibid., 13. Humility is necessary for shepherds, ibid., 858. Thus humility must be preserved in the heart and discipline in action, ibid., 36. Let humility not hinder pastoral zeal, nor pastoral zeal humility, ibid., 476. One who does not cease from pride when placed low cannot learn humility when raised high, ibid., 22. The virtue of humility must be so preserved that the rights of governance are not relaxed, ibid., 476. Let humility accompany preachers together with purity of life, id., LXXIX, 166.—On the humility of superiors, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 827; St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 711.—I desire you to possess gentleness and humility, lest because of the assault of wolves, that is, persecutors, you lose your patience and constancy, the Venerable Bede, XCII, 53.—May your character be distinguished by humanity and praiseworthy for humility, Blessed Alcuin, C, 153. Show yourself gentle and humble toward those better than yourself, ibid., 223. Let humility be in heart and body, ibid., 431. Let humility exalt you, ibid., 452. Adorn yourself with humility, ibid., 453. Be humble in ministering, ibid., 459.—The greater you are, the more you should humble yourself, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 842.—In him, the priest, let them see what they can imitate and follow by good works—namely chastity and humility, Riculf of Soissons, CXXXI, 19.—Let the priest’s humility be genuine, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 513.—Strive and labor that humility may be in you, Hildebert, CLXXI, 821.

5. On gentleness.—A priest ought not to be contentious, but gentle and teachable, St. Cyprian, III, 1135.—Let the priest maintain gentleness, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1204.—He ought to be gentle and humble in heart: why, St. Boniface, XX, 781.—The virtue of gentleness must always be preserved in the priestly breast along with the terror of severity, [Col. 0719] St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1145. In good shepherds kindness and authority, mercy and discipline, are joined, ibid., 143. “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves,” ibid., 1140. We are sent as lambs among wolves, so that, while preserving the disposition of innocence, we may not have the bite of malice, ibid., 1140. Let gentle shepherds possess zeal for justice, and angry ones add gentleness to zeal, id., LXXVII, 76. A shepherd must blend mildness with severity, ibid., 38. Gentleness must be maintained, so that even priestly indignation may be mingled with the virtue of sweetness, ibid., 669.—He will also possess gentleness according to the Apostle, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 786.—I desire you to possess gentleness and humility, the Venerable Bede, XCII, 53.—Show yourself gentle toward those better than yourself, Blessed Alcuin, 223. Let gentle words always be mixed with harsher ones, ibid., 451. Let mercy make you lovable, ibid., 452. Let the light of your goodness shine before all, ibid.—But he who is so prudent, gentle, and sweet that by seeing and hearing him people are turned and kindled toward love and praise of the Bridegroom is the Bridegroom’s friend, St. Agobard, CIV, 195.—Let the good find you kind, Liber papae, CV, 83. Let the sweetness of a good shepherd be in you, ibid.; Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 772; Pope Alexander II, CXLVI, 1324.—Be a lamb to the good, Theodulf, CV, 338. Let your heart be calm and your words sweet, ibid.—Toward the errors of subjects, let gentleness so temper zeal, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 854.—It is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in the heart, ibid., 868.—Let the ruler be calm and gentle, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1593.—Preserve kindness with your whole mind, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 23.—“The servant of the Lord must be gentle toward all,” Otto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 694.—Why the virtue of gentleness must be preserved in the priestly breast, Rupert the abbot, CLXVII, 1169. Let preachers be gentle in teaching, id., CLVIII, 495.—Christ’s mercy is to be imitated by shepherds, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 174.

6. On mortification.—A priest ought to be free from the enticements of various pleasures, St. Ambrose, XVI, 254.—A delicate teacher is one who disputes about fasting on a full stomach, St. Jerome, XXII, 533.—Let the priest be sober, Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 681.—“Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1233. “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps,” etc., ibid., 1234. What, indeed, did the perfect preacher do in order to furnish an example of abstinence? ibid.—An ecclesiastical man ought to be crucified to the world by mortification of his own flesh, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXX, 705; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 851.—Remember this, that you may live happily in every sobriety, Blessed Alcuin, C, 508.—He will also possess, according to the Apostle, sobriety and abstinence, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831. Let the priest be abstinent, ibid., 834.—For preachers ought to show in themselves the mortification of the flesh which they likewise proclaim should be practiced by others, Anselm of Laon, CLXI, 1212.—Let them chastise the body, Peter of Honestis, CLXIII, 709.—Let others see your fasts; let them see how, by sacrificially offering yourselves, you wear down and afflict your flesh, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 377.—Let the priest circumcise from his members every foreskin of his flesh, Hildebert, CLXXI, 775.

7. On zeal.—A priest who strives to preserve the Church’s chastity uncorrupted ought to have zeal, St. Ambrose, XV, 1456. “If the thorns of the woods tear me while I search, I shall press myself through every narrow way, shake every hedge . . . traverse all things; I shall call back the wanderer and seek the lost,” St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 278.—The zeal of a spiritual teacher, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 932. Against sluggishness, let priests glow with zeal, ibid., 549. The necessity of zeal in teachers, ibid., 355. “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” ibid., 932. Let us take up strong zeal, ibid., 933. The preacher inflamed with the zeal of charity, ibid., 263. Let the priest correct with great severity of zeal, id., 46.—On the zeal of the pastoral office toward subjects, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 829.—“Do you wish to stray? Do you wish to perish? I do not. I shall call back the wanderer; I shall seek the lost,” Amalarius of Metz, CV, 842. “I shall traverse all things; I shall call back the wanderer; I shall seek the lost. If you do not wish me to suffer, do not stray; do not perish,” ibid. Let zeal thus burn toward punishment, yet not by its burning exceed the limit of mercy, ibid., 854. On the zeal of a shepherd, ibid., 867.—Let us take up strong zeal, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 591. Let them desire to be cold with ardors of zeal, id., CX, 835.

IV. On vices to be avoided.

1. On pride.—I beseech you to amend your life, avoiding pride, St. Augustine, XL, 1301. We who are called shepherds should flee pride through humility and patience, ibid., 1316.—A priest must flee pride, St. Benedict, LXVI, 869. The ordained man ought most diligently to beware of self-exaltation or pride, ibid.—Let the priest [Col. 0720] not be proud, Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 680.—They exchange the place of humility for the self-exaltation of domination, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1140. How one who teaches others ought to fight against self-exaltation, ibid., 1001. Let the preacher beware lest he exalt himself through the vice of pride, ibid., 255, 263. Let preachers beware of serving Satan through self-exaltation, id., LXXVII, 95, 96. If our forefathers did not tolerate pride in kings, how much more must it not be tolerated in priests, ibid., 654.—On proud teachers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 710.—Let no priest dare to behave proudly against his bishop, Charlemagne, XCVII, 513, 827.—Let passing honors not exalt you, Blessed Alcuin, C, 245. Let the priest not be proud, ibid., 1014.—Priests must be admonished to give their subjects a holy example, far removed from every ostentation of pride, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 216.—Priests must not be proud, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 440.—Pride kills another, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 445.

2. On avarice.—Avarice is to be avoided in a priest, St. Jerome, XXII, 663.—I beseech you to amend your life, trampling down avarice, St. Augustine, XL, 1301. We who are called shepherds should drown avarice through almsgiving, ibid., 1316.—Let them flee love of money as the material of all crimes, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087.—Priests must take the greatest care to restrain themselves from the plague of avarice, which is the root of all evils and excludes its followers from Christ’s kingdom, Charlemagne, XCVII, 605.—Let not the deceptive appearance of gold withdraw you from confidence in diligent labor, Blessed Alcuin, C, 491.—Let the priest not be avaricious, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 836.—On avarice to be avoided among clerics, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1420. Above all, flee avarice, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 23.—The thirst of avarice also possesses the minds of priests, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 493. On the avarice of priests, Burchard, CXL, 713.—How detestable is clerical avarice, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 643. Priests shamelessly demand money even when it is refused, ibid.—Avarice kills another, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 445.—Priests ought to avoid avarice, Hildebert, CLXXI, 768.—There are those who give a little to the poor in order to receive more, St. Jerome, XXII, 535.

3. On drunkenness.—Both the Apostle condemns drunken priests and the old law forbids them, St. Jerome, XXII, 536. Those who serve the altar should not drink wine or strong drink, ibid. Priests are commanded not to drink wine or strong drink when about to minister in the temple, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, revelry, and the cares of this life, ibid., 609. Priests who minister in God’s temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, ibid., 662; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 835.—Let the priest not be a drunkard, Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 680.—“Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with revelry and drunkenness,” St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 39.—That no member of the priesthood nourish the vice of drunkenness or compel others by his command to become drunk, Charlemagne, XCVII, 219.—Flee drunkenness as the pit of destruction, Blessed Alcuin, C, 454. Let the priest not be a drunkard, ibid., 1014.—Not a drunkard, so that he may confidently rebuke drunkards, Sedulius Scotus, CIII, 234.—Not a drunkard: why, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 833. Flee everything that intoxicates and overturns the state of the mind, just as you flee wine, ibid., 885.—Let not impious cups of Bacchus weigh down hearts, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1600.—Priests must observe abstinence from drunkenness, Rodulf of Bourges, CXIX, 713.—That no priest presume to become drunk on an anniversary day or a thirty-third day, etc., Hincmar of Rheims, CXXXI, 776.—That drunkenness be avoided by clerics, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 404.—Above all, let drunkenness be avoided by clerics, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 41.—Let none of you be a drunkard, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 560. That drunkenness, the tinder and nurse of all vices, be avoided by clerics, id., CXXXVIII, 409.—Concerning parish priests, when they assemble, that they do not dare to make themselves drunk, Burchard, CXL, 654. No priest should through foolishness drink more than is fitting, nor provoke another to drink beyond what he desires, id., CXXXIX, 1474.—Priests should not be devoted to drunkenness, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 440. That priests, when they come to an assembly, presume in no way to make themselves drunk, ibid., 499. A priest devoted to drunkenness, unless he ceases, is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 1170.

4. On incontinence.—I beseech you to amend your life, despising lust, St. Augustine, XL, 1301. For fornication is forbidden to clerics, lest, since we are ministers of the Lord, we become members of a prostitute, ibid., 1303. If marriage is forbidden to priests, how much more will the crime of fornication be reckoned among us, ibid. We who are called shepherds should break lust through abstinence, ibid., 1316.—On the incontinence of priests [Col. 0721] or Levites, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 649.—If a priest has committed fornication or perpetrated adultery, he must be expelled and subjected to penance, Charlemagne, XCVII, 618.—Do not permit lustful pleasures to rule in yourself or in your brethren, Blessed Alcuin, C, 499. Avoid and flee youthful desires, that is, adultery, uncleanness, lust, and every wantonness, Haymo, CXVII, 805.—But if he has committed fornication or adultery, let him be cast out of the Church, Aeneas of Paris, CXXI, 727.—Therefore, if priests fall into the snare of fornication and the offense has been shown most plainly, they can no longer possess the honor of priesthood, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 210.—Resist lust and immodesty completely, Peter of Honestis, CLXIII, 708.—Lust destroys another, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 445.—Fornication and uncleanness must be removed from you, Hildebert, CLXXI, 770.—The incontinent who do not fear shamelessly to profane holy orders are rebuked, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 853.

5. On the vice of the tongue.—Beware lest you have itching tongue or itching ears, St. Jerome, XXII, 538; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 886. Refrain from the tongue’s slander, ibid. Let priests not go about with an unbridled tongue, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778. Let them utterly abhor obscenity in words as in deeds, ibid.; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 891.—Slandering no one, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 216.—Let them not serve idle talk, nor devote themselves to detractions, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 920.—A cleric should not speak buffoonish or jesting words that provoke laughter, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 220.—Let them restrain the tongue, which is in a certain manner mediator between God and us, from the frivolity of superfluous speech, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 499. Let no idle words flow from our lips, id., CXLIV, 258.

6. On envy.—Preachers must beware of envy, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 199.—Let priests flee envy, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087.—Far from every ostentation of pride and the biting of envy, let them give their subjects a holy example, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 216. Let them not be covetous, ibid.—St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 510.

7. On ambition.—We avoid the labor of our office and seek its dignity, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 435; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 865.—Let them restrain themselves from headlong ambition, if not through fear, at least through shame, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1031.—Let not worldly ambition restrain priestly severity, Blessed Alcuin, C, 458.—Many priests desire to preside more for their own advantage than for that of the flock, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 850.—For no one ought to become a cleric in order to gape after ambition, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 513. Nor should he seek anything other than to possess God as his inheritance, ibid.—St. Bernard censures the ambition of ecclesiastics, the promotion of younger men, and the plurality of benefices, CLXXXII, 825. He censures severely the ambitious who rashly and unworthily usurp the sacred functions of the Church, ibid., 852. People run everywhere toward sacred orders, ibid., 853. You may see wealthy men likewise flying toward ecclesiastical honors, id., CLXXXIII, 84, 85.

V. On things forbidden to priests.

1. On women.—“I do not wish you to have the company of matrons; I do not wish you to go to the houses of nobles,” St. Jerome, XXII, 403.—That foreign women should not live with any clerics whatsoever, but only mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, and sisters, etc., St. Leo the Great, LVI, 425.—The great synod altogether forbade that it be lawful for a bishop, priest, etc., to have a woman not of his household, except perhaps a mother, sister, paternal aunt, or only those persons who escape every suspicion, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 42.—That clerics should not live with foreign women, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 956.—Priests are forbidden to associate with women, except only a mother, sister, or wife, who must be governed chastely, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 515. Nor may other women live with priests, except those permitted, as stated above, by the sacred canons, ibid., 1033.—Let them neither converse with women nor retain them in their homes, St. Sonnatius, LXXX, 444.—Let them avoid very frequent visits to widows and virgins, and by no means seek cohabitation with foreign women, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778.—That priests should not have a foreign woman in their house, Charlemagne, XCVII, 237.—That, according to the venerable decree of the Council of Nicaea, no one permit introduced women to be kept in his own house or privately associate in cohabitation with them, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 297.—Women should not live with a priest, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 195.—It is not lawful for a bishop, priest, deacon, or any person at all in the clergy to have an introduced [Col. 0722] woman, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 874. Forbid virgins, even those of your own family, to live with you, ibid., 888. Let them avoid very frequent visits to widows and virgins, ibid., 891. Let them by no means seek cohabitation with foreign women, ibid.—That they abhor association with women, their access, and their management, Herard, CXXI, 765.—A cleric should not go alone to a woman’s dwelling without the command of a superior elder, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 40. Nor should a priest be alone with a woman alone, but, having brought two witnesses, should visit a sick woman, ibid. Nor should he alone engage in conversation with a woman alone, ibid.—That a cleric have no association with a woman after ordination, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 36. Those same priests must be commanded not to permit foreign women to live with them, id., CXXXVIII, 625. That priests should by no means dare to have introduced women with them, except perhaps their godmother or a close female relative, id., CXLVIII, 1120.—I see priests living with women, which it is wicked to say or hear, St. Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 462.—A cleric who frequents the homes of matrons is to be deposed, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 391.

2. On banquets.---I judge that, above all, those engaged in the offices of ministry should avoid the banquets of outsiders, St. Ambrose, XVI, 49.---You must avoid the banquets of secular persons, especially of those swollen with honors, St. Jerome, XXII, 536; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 885.---For it is not permitted to a cleric to arrange a luncheon or dinner, St. Augustine, XL, 1299.---A cleric who, though often invited to lunch, does not refuse, even when compelled by some necessity, is greatly despised, ibid., 1299. Therefore a cleric ought to take the utmost care not to dare eat outside his own house or that of the bishop, nor even there to dare prepare a meal for secular persons, ibid., 1299.---A priest ought not to be present at the banquet of a second marriage, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 444.---Let them avoid public banquets; let them attend private ones that are not merely decent but also sober, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087.---That clerics should avoid wedding banquets, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 269.---That a priest should not be present at a banquet of second marriages, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 823.---That clerics should avoid wedding banquets, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1088.---A cleric who is often invited to lunch and does not refuse is more readily despised, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 886. Flee crowds of people, official business, greetings, and banquets, as though they were chains of pleasures, ibid., 887.---That a priest ought not to attend the banquet of a secular wedding, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 267. Priests or clerics must not be permitted to watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets, ibid., 585. That clerics should avoid wedding banquets, ibid., 404.---That a priest should not dine at the wedding of a bigamist, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 38.---Priests ought not to attend wedding banquets, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 194. It is disgraceful for a priest to indulge in luxuries, feasts, and wantonness, ibid., 196. Clerics must avoid the banquets of heretics, ibid., 1308.

3. On taverns.---Let no one eat or drink in taverns, Eutychian, V, 165.---For one who has the care of souls ought not to enter taverns except when compelled by necessity, St. Augustine, XL, 1299.---That it is not fitting for priests, from presbyters to deacons, and thereafter for anyone of ecclesiastical rank down to ministers, readers, singers, etc., to enter a public inn, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 72. That no ecclesiastic ought to eat in taverns, ibid., 167. That clerics should not enter taverns except while travelling, ibid., 194.---That clerics should not enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking unless necessity of travel compels them, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 956.---That no priest should go to taverns for eating or drinking, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 382; Charlemagne, XCVII, 219.---That no priest should dare enter taverns to drink, nor mingle in such a gathering with secular people, where he may hear or utter shameful words, Charlemagne, XCVII, 295, 511.---That priests should abstain from drunkenness and taverns, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 195.---Nor should they go through taverns drinking or eating, Rodulf of Bourges, CXIX, 713.---Inquiry should be made whether priests keep themselves from taverns, as we have very often forbidden and do forbid, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 780.---We also admonish that this must be most carefully avoided: priests or clerics should not visit taverns for banqueting, Riculf, CXXXI, 20.---Do not drink in taverns, Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 560.---Clerics should not enter taverns without the necessity of travel, CXXXVIII, 409.---Let a cleric who wishes to own a tavern or workshop be deposed, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 229.

4. On hunting.---Bishops, priests, and deacons must not be permitted to keep dogs for hunting, or hawks, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 287.---That clerics should not hunt [Col. 0723] with birds or dogs, Charlemagne, XCVII, 816.---Nor should they keep dogs for hunting, or hawks, falcons, or sparrowhawks, Hetto of Basel, CV, 765; CXXXVIII, 625.---Avoid and flee hunting, Haymo, CXVII, 805.---That a bishop or cleric ought in no way to devote himself to hunting, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1126.---O wretched life of men, and especially of priests, who, while they ought to devote themselves to winning the faithful, busy themselves with hunting wild beasts; and when they ought to catch men, they catch birds and animals, ibid., 1126. That priests and Levites should not keep hunting dogs or hawks, id., CXXXVIII, 410. That a priest ought not to occupy himself with usury or hunting, ibid. We teach also that a priest must not be a hunter or a hawker, id., CXXXVIII, 503.---Concerning those of ecclesiastical rank who either hunt or play with hawks, Burchard, CXL, 661.---That bishops, priests, and Levites should not keep dogs for hunting or hawks, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 433.---Let them by no means devote themselves to dice or to any kinds of hunting, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 708.

5. On war.---That no priest whatsoever should bear arms among combatants, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 382; Charlemagne, XCVII, 219, 295, 723.---We prohibit altogether that priests should take up arms, Rodulf of Bourges, CXIX, 713.---That clerics should not bear arms, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 222.---Let none of you bear arms in a disturbance, because our weapons ought to be spiritual, Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 560.---That no one of the clergy should bear military arms, Burchard, CXL, 661; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 504. A priest must not bear arms, id., CXXXIX, 1475. Clerics who bear military arms should be punished by loss of their own rank, id., CLXI, 1169.---That clerics should not bear arms, Council of Clermont, CLXI, 717.

6. On secular business.---No one serving as a soldier for God binds himself to secular troubles, St. Cyprian, IV, 398. How much more ought those occupied with divine and spiritual matters not to be bound by secular troubles and snares, ibid.---From the fact that priests involve themselves in worldly business comes great danger, St. Hilary, IX, 810.---For one who has the care of souls ought not to engage in trade or dig with a hoe, St. Augustine, XL, 1299.---Priests are not permitted to work with their hands, dig with a hoe, forge iron, or do similar things, ibid., 1302.---Very many clerics devote themselves to dishonorable commerce and shameful profits, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 698. It is a crime of impiety for a priest, neglecting the study of God’s word, to undertake secular anxieties, ibid., 734.---That clerics should pursue no dishonorable commerce or shameful gain, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 306.---That clerics should not be permitted to undertake the administration or management of households, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 950.---Let them not be entangled with secular affairs, St. Sonnatius, LXXX, 444.---That priests and ministers of the altar should abstain from secular concerns, Criscus of Africa, LXXXVIII, 840.---Let them in no way serve shameful gains, Charlemagne, XCVII, 220. That a priest should not be a merchant, ibid., 296. That priests should in no way exercise secular offices—that is, that they should become neither judges nor headmen of villages, ibid., 723; Rodulf of Bourges, CXIX, 713.---On avoiding secular concerns, Watterius, CXIX, 735.---That clerics should not engage in buying cheap and selling dear, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 38. We teach also that no priest should be an unjust buyer or a greedy merchant, id., CXXXVIII, 500.---Concerning those priests who, against the statutes of the canons, become estate-managers and entangle themselves in other business not granted to them, Burchard, CXL, 649. A priest must not be a merchant, id., CXXXIX, 1475.---Concerning priests who, against the statutes of the canons, become estate-managers, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 492. A cleric is not permitted to engage in trade, ibid., 1286.---Let them by no means seek occupations involving shameful profit, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 708.

7. On games.---That a bishop, priest, or deacon should not be a gambler, Charlemagne, XCVII, 772.---Nor should they have leave for any game or spectacle, Hetto of Basel, CV, 765.---Let no one devote himself to games with dogs or birds, Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 560.---The game of tables is to be avoided, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1170.---A deacon, priest, or bishop who gives himself to dice must be deposed unless he stops, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 195.---Even if jokes are sometimes respectable, they must nevertheless be wholly proscribed among ecclesiastical men, St. Ambrose, XVI, 54.

8. On a priest’s dress and bearing.---Adornment and squalor alike must be avoided, St. Jerome, XXII, 535.---Priests are rightly forbidden both to shave the head and to grow their hair, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 856; Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 825.---Let them walk neither with roving eyes, nor an unbridled tongue, nor an insolent, puffed-up manner; rather, by simple dress and bearing let them show the modesty and reserve of their mind, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 778; St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1087.---Clerics ought not [Col. 0724] to grow their hair and minister thus, but should have shorn heads and uncovered ears, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 583.---It is decreed that clerics who grow their hair are to be tonsured by the archdeacon against their will, even if they refuse, St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 827.---That no cleric or monk should presume to let his hair grow long, on pain of anathema, Pope St. Stephen, LXXIX, 1028.---Forbid clerics to use gold or silken garments in the presence of the lord king; rather, let them proceed in humble dress, according to the custom of servants of God, Blessed Alcuin, C, 334. Let your dress be of moderate refinement, ibid., 452. Do not in any way permit vanity in dress, ibid., 499.---Both inwardly and outwardly, not only in dress and conduct but even in their very gait, let them be beyond reproach, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 920. Let the priest of Christ be cheerful of countenance, id., CXIX, 707.---That priests, as they are holier in rank, should likewise be more reverent in word, bearing, and deed, Herard, CXXI, 772.---Let a cleric demonstrate his profession in both dress and bearing, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 346. A cleric ought not to seek approval through the splendor of his garments, ibid. A cleric should neither grow his hair nor shave his beard, id., CXXX, 346; CXL, 1069.---That clerics should not put on lay clothing, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 257; Burchard, CXL, 661; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 31. Clerics should not seek elegance in clothing, id., CXXXVIII, 410.---How detestable is luxury of dress in clerics, Othlo, CXLVI, 357.---Let them not delight in possessing costly clothing, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 708.---That a cleric should not grow his hair, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 454.

VI.---On the duties of priests.

1. They must offer sacrifice.---We priests who daily celebrate the sacrifices of God, St. Cyprian, III, 857. Let them not depart from the altar and sacrifices, but serve heavenly and spiritual matters by day and night, id., IV, 399.---Pastors furnish the aid of prayer and sacrifices to subjects under temptation, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 209.---Just as for the people, so also for himself he must offer for sins, Blessed Alcuin, C, 1052. They are priests in offering to God, ibid., 1094. *Sacerdos* is Greek; in Latin it is called “one who gives what is sacred,” that is, one who offers holy sacrifice to God, id., CI, 1235.---Every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 853. For the ministry of a priest is to stand at the altar, ibid., 1044.---For them—that is, priests—prayer and sacrifice are a continual duty, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXI, 782.---What the duty of a priest about to offer sacrifice ought to be, Rupert, abbot, CLXIV, 430.

2. To administer the sacraments.---“Go, teach all nations, baptizing them,” etc., Council of Carthage, III, 1058, 1060.---See that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism, Eutychian, V, 165.---A priest is appointed to cleanse the sins of his subjects, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 181.---That no priest, whether in his own province or another, should presume to deny baptism to any sick person, Burchard, CXL, 736; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 117. That a priest should reconcile a penitent when commanded by his bishop, id., CLXI, 857, 866. By baptizing, they incorporate people into the unity of the Church and administer to God’s people all the sacraments up to the laying on of hands, id., CLXII, 518.---Their duty is to dispense the body of the Lord, baptize, absolve penitents, etc., Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 599.

3. To preach.---Woe will befall us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles preached, Pope St. Felix, V, 154.---Let each of you, according to his understanding, announce to his people from the Gospel, the Epistle, or some divine Scripture on Sundays and feast days, Pope Eutychian, V, 165.---That priests should invite the people entrusted to them to the heavenly homeland by words and at the same time by the merits of their lives, St. Ambrose, XVII, 760.---Priests are bound to preach, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2287, 2318. Raise your voice, so that the sound of your correction, rebuke, charity, and holiness may be heard throughout all the earth, id., XL, 1309.---The office of preaching belongs to priests alone, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1039.---The office of preaching ought not stubbornly to be declined when the divine will is recognized as calling one to undertake it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 20. Cry aloud; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, ibid., 472. “He who hides grain shall be cursed among the peoples”: to hide grain is to keep within oneself the words of holy preaching, ibid., 96.---A priest entering or leaving the tabernacle dies if a sound is not heard from him, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 829.---A priest must teach because of the duty of his office, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 434. The priest has been entrusted with the dispensation of the word, [Col. 0725] ibid.---The Lord requires his blood from the watchman’s hand, because the watchman himself killed him, since by keeping silent he delivered him over to death, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 909, 911, 1143.---“If you do not announce to the wicked man his wickedness, I will require his blood from your hand,” St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 650.---That on every feast and Sunday each priest should preach Christ’s Gospel to the people, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 381.---Always remember that your throat must be God’s trumpet and your tongue a herald of salvation to all, Blessed Alcuin, C, 151. The priest of God must be a preacher to the people of His will, ibid., 223. It is yours to preach the word of God to all, ibid., 492. Your mouth must be God’s trumpet, ibid.---“Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season,” Amalarius of Metz, CV, 842. A priest should always possess the voice of preaching, ibid., 857.---They must always devote themselves to preaching, Haymo, CXVII, 602. That priests themselves should preach to all by word and example, id., CXXXVIII, 626.---We command you that every one of you, every two or three weeks, on Sundays or saints’ feast days, should endeavor, after the Gospel has been read, to instruct in the church entrusted to him the people committed to him with salutary teachings drawn from Holy Scripture, Burchard, CXL, 666, 1069; CLXI, 503. “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel,” id., CXLVIII, 1136.---The priest’s duty is to preach, Hildebert, CLXXI, 767. Those whom they ought to draw back from sins by word and example, ibid., 930.---Their duty is to preach, etc., Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 599.---Good shepherds ought to feed their sheep by preaching, action, and prayer, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 323.---Go, therefore, preaching; do not go sinning, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 944.---Indeed, a priest ought to be diligent in preaching, etc., Peter of Blois, CCVII, 725.

4. To teach, rebuke, admonish, defend, recall, visit, gather, die, etc.---Certainly the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, Tertullian, II, 113. As Christ laid down his life for us, so it is fitting that we do the same for Him, and not only for Him but also for our brothers for His sake, ibid., 116.---To provide for the cherishing and preservation of the sheep, St. Cyprian, III, 996. To gather and restore Christ’s sheep, ibid. They ought to cherish the sheep entrusted to them, id., IV, 257. “You did not bring back what had strayed, nor seek what had perished,” id., III, 859. It is incumbent on us to guard the flock, id., IV, 225. Let him recall those at discord to concord and defend widows, Pope Eutychian, V, 165. Proclaim to all your people that the fast of the Four Seasons, Rogation Days, and the Greater Litany must be observed in every way, ibid., 165. Teach them to celebrate Sunday and other feasts, without servile work, from evening to evening, ibid., 166.---It properly belongs to priests not only to teach the law but also to do it; why this is so, St. Jerome, XXIV, 783. It belongs to a priest’s office to answer one who asks concerning the law, ibid., 1406. It is also the priest’s duty to teach the people, id., XXV, 441. That they should feed the Lord’s flock, id., XXII, 538.---Let pastors not neglect the weakness of the sheep, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 272. Let them provide the light of the word of truth for the enlightenment of people, ibid. “You did not strengthen what was weak,” etc., ibid. Pastors are bound to recall wandering sheep, ibid., 278. The shepherd himself everywhere seeks the wandering, strengthens the weak, heals the sick, and binds up the broken, ibid., 280. The shepherd’s office is to feed the sheep, ibid., 796. It is truly incumbent on us to help others, lest they descend into the deep like a stone, id., XL, 1310. That they should teach and admonish the people and announce the way of truth, ibid., 1347. Let us feed our sheep, ibid., 1317.---To teach and admonish subjects, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 50. Strive to rescue those fallen into sin, ibid., 914. Let pastors have compassion on subjects under temptation, id., LXXIX, 317.---Let the pastor care for his sheep; let him require it to attend the sacrifice of the Mass on solemn days and Sundays, St. Sonnatius, LXXX, 443.---A priest ought to rebuke the sinner, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 435. The Lord’s flock has been entrusted to priests to be fed and guarded, ibid.---They lie in wicked deeds, and we do not extend the hand of correction, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1146. He appointed priests for the correction of others, ibid. Let the pastor correct the faults of his subjects prudently and humbly, ibid., 318. That he may be able to refute those who contradict, id., LXXVII, 472. Let us keep watch lest anything perish, ibid., 590.---Those who do not receive a sinner but despise and reject him are severely rebuked, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 715.---Console the faint-hearted, strengthen the humble, lead the erring back into the way of truth, instruct the ignorant, Blessed Alcuin, C, 155. Let priestly authority be exercised in chastising the reprobate, ibid., 243. Let there be kindly concern in restoring the humble, ibid. Where is charity if you do not take care to correct one who errs? ibid., 248. Let him chastise the proud and obstinate with stern rebukes, ibid., 450. Let him restore the humble and peaceable with godly exhortations, [Col. 0726] ibid. Admonish the young men who are with you regarding the chastity of their bodies, confession of their sins, diligence in learning, sober conduct, etc., ibid., 459.---“They do not strengthen what is weak, nor heal what is sick,” St. Agobard, CIV, 197. That every pastor should feed, instruct, and correct his subjects in the discipline and fear of the Lord, not for himself but for the Lord, ibid.---Let your protection come to the aid of the oppressed, *Lib.* [uncertain abbreviated source], CV, 83.---Feed the hungry, clothe the naked, receive strangers, etc., Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831.---At three seasons of the year—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost—let him admonish all the faithful to approach communion of the Lord’s body and blood, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 189. Let him teach them to celebrate Sunday and other feasts, without servile work, from evening to evening, ibid., 190.---That they should bury penitents who have died, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46. Priests are condemned for the iniquity of their people if they neither instruct them when ignorant nor rebuke them when sinning, ibid., 83.---Visit the sick and reconcile them, etc., Rather of Verona, CXXXVI, 560. That priests should diligently instruct the young, id., CXXXVIII, 502.---That every priest on feast days should admonish the people what prayers they ought to pour out to God, Burchard, CXL, 638. That priests should announce to the people which days throughout the year are to be observed as holidays, ibid., 640. That, when priests announce feasts, they should not forget the vigils, ibid.---That priests should admonish the people to present their infants to the bishop for confirmation, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 120. Let them visit the sick and bury the dead, ibid., 410. What priests ought to admonish, ibid., 484.---Rebuke rebels publicly; observe the obedient; rebuke those less obedient, Hildebert, CLXXI, 917.---It belongs to good pastors to teach, St. Bernard, CLXXX, 855.

5. To pray.---A priest must always pray, St. Jerome, XXIII, 257.---After performing outward works, they always return to the bosom of contemplation, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 527.---For the sins of all, they beseech God unyieldingly as for their own, Charlemagne, XCVII, 612; XCIX, 963.---An intercessor with God for the people, as it were a mediator between God and men, Blessed Alcuin, C, 223. Persist in vigils and prayers, ibid., 453.---That one must devote oneself constantly to reading and prayer, Theodulf, CV, 193.---That they should by no means omit the canonical hours, whether nocturnal or diurnal, Hetto of Basel, CV, 768. To devote themselves to vigils, fasts, and prayers, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831. That they should perform the divine Office at the canonical hours with the utmost devotion, ibid., 920.---Priests of God ought to be constant in reading and assiduous in prayer; these are the weapons—namely, reading and prayer—by which the devil is overcome, Rodulf of Bourges, CXIX, 707. That they should observe the canonical hours by day and night, and chant the Psalms worthily according to the divisions of the verses, ibid.---If he rises every night at the nocturnal hours to perform matins, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 188. If at the appointed time he announces by the signal of the church Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, and sings the proper office, ibid. That every priest should solemnly perform the canonical hours, ibid., 229.---Rise every night for the nocturnal office, Rather of Verona, CXXXII, 559.---Let him discharge the task of his service by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, Burchard, CXL, 644. That priests should devote themselves to prayer at the proper time, before they offer sacrifice, ibid., 724.---Feed by prayer, so that you may intercede for those whose souls are entrusted to you, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 651.---Priests, by their prayers, blot out and consume the sins of the people, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 175. Let them celebrate the canonical hours not negligently but together with every devotion, ibid., 441.---Likewise, it is the priest’s task to appease God’s indignation by prayers, Hildebert, CLXXI, 774.---Let them offer the people’s prayers to God by interceding for sinners, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 429.---A priest ought to devote himself not to wars but to prayers, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 200. Clerics who absent themselves from morning or evening offices should be corrected, ibid., 427.---To pray for the people, Absalo, CCXI, 1113.

6. To study.---Let him diligently meditate daily upon the precepts of sacred discourse, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 48.---It is therefore necessary that those who keep watch for the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 822.---Let the reading of Holy Scripture often be found in your hands, so that from it you may be filled and may be able to feed others, Blessed Alcuin, C, 153. Do not in any way abandon the study of reading, but keep with you young men who are always learning, ibid., 244. At fitting times may sacred reading never leave your hands; let reading and prayer take their turns, ibid., 248. Devote yourself especially to Gospel readings and to the instruction of the canonical Holy Scriptures, for meditation on the divine law befits you, ibid., 451.---That one must devote oneself constantly to reading and prayer, Theodulf, CV, 193.---Whose special office above all others is to read the Scriptures and run through the canons, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 831. It is therefore necessary that those who keep watch for the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading, ibid., 845. You indeed should read the divine Scriptures often; rather, let sacred reading never be put down from your hands, ibid., 884. Learn what you are to teach, ibid. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh, ibid., 887.---Priests of God ought to be constant in reading and assiduous in prayer, Riculf of Bourges, CXIX, 707. And if one ever ceases from reading or prayer, work of the hands ought to follow, ibid.---That it is fitting for clerics diligently to pray and read and labor with their hands, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 39. Let the priest devote himself to his books, as befits his order, id., CXXXVIII, 503.---That priests ought to read constantly, Burchard, CXL, 643; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 486.---Let them devote themselves without interruption to reading and prayer, Peter de Honestis, CLXIII, 709.

7. To remain continually in the parish.---In a time of persecution, the leaders themselves—that is, deacons, priests, and bishops—ought not to flee, Tertullian, II, 113.---A priest must not leave his own church without the bishop’s knowledge, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 583. That clerics should by no means be allowed to move to another city, except those who have lost their own cities through persecution, ibid., 312. We teach also that no priest should voluntarily abandon the church to which he was consecrated, but should regard it as his lawful wife, CXXXVIII, 499.

8. To care for the church.---Forbid songs and dances of women, performances of entertainers, and songs from taking place in the church or its courtyard, Pope Eutychian, V.---It especially befits a priest to adorn God’s temple with fitting honor, so that by this service too the Lord’s hall may shine forth, St. Ambrose, XVI, 133.---That priests should admonish the people not to indulge in quarrels and wordy disputes in church, Charlemagne, XCVII, 816.---Forbid altogether women’s songs and dances in the churchyard, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 681.---If he admonishes the people not to sing at all in the churchyard or lead women’s dances, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 190.---That priests should admonish the people to prepare altar linens, Burchard, CXL, 695; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 216.

VII.---On the learning of a priest.

The priest should gather the waters by which he irrigates the minds of the people, St Ambrose, XVI, 880. “Fill the bosom of your mind,” ibid. “We priests are interpreters of the faith,” ibid., 1176. — It is the priest’s duty to know the law and to answer questions from the law, St Jerome, XXV, 1406. Priests should be able to teach what they have learned, and should increase knowledge rather than riches, ibid., 1407. Read the divine Scriptures often; indeed, never let sacred reading be put down from your hands, id., XXII, 533. I do not want you to be a declaimer, a pettifogging and irrational chatterer, but skilled in the mysteries and most learned in the sacraments of your God, ibid., 534. Priests ought especially to possess knowledge of the law and of doctrine, ibid., 609. That instruction is required from priests, ibid., 663. — “You are the light of the world,” St Augustine, XXXIV, 1237, 1681. Let the spiritual judge beware: just as he has not committed the crime of wickedness, so he must not lack the gift of knowledge, id., XL, 1129. He must know how to discern what he ought to judge, ibid. “You are the light of the world, a lighted lamp, a city set upon a mountain, the tree of knowledge placed in the midst of paradise,” ibid., 1299. “Be an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame,” ibid., 1301. — We are to be distinguished from the people or others by doctrine, not by dress, Pope St Celestine, I, 431. — For if ignorance seems scarcely tolerable in laypeople, how much more, in those who preside, is it worthy neither of excuse nor pardon, St Leo the Great, LIV, 867. — That no priest may be permitted to be ignorant of the canons, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 277. — “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge,” Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 51; St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1698. It is fitting that priests’ hearts be filled with the fullness of knowledge, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1145. Those who do not know the things of the Lord are not known by the Lord, id., LXXVII, 15. If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit, ibid. The Lord ascends into the exalted minds of his preachers and establishes there the height of his knowledge, id., LXXIX, 43. The teacher is beautiful in appearance because knowledge makes his face fair, ibid., 456. — The unlearned and unskilled are excluded from such an office, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 707. Unlearned priests are disapproved, ibid. An ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine both in doctrine and in life, ibid. What can he teach when he has not himself learned? ibid., 784, 785. Priests should have knowledge of the holy Scriptures and canons, id., LXXXIV, 374. — Always seek knowledge of the Scriptures, St Eligius, LXXXVII, 649. A priest who preserves knowledge [Col. 0728] and proclaims to the people the precepts of God’s law is an angel of the Lord of hosts, id., XCVI, 1484. — That no priest may be permitted to be ignorant of the ordinances of the holy canons, Charlemagne, XCVII, 238. If he is a priest, let him know the law of the Lord; if he does not know the law, he thereby proves himself not to be the Lord’s priest, ibid., 605. It is the priest’s duty to know the law and to answer questions from the law, ibid. That no priest be ignorant of the canons, ibid., 708. Let no one become a cleric unless he has a good testimony and is literate, ibid., 764. — Priests are the lamps of God’s holy Church, Blessed Alcuin, C, 154. — “Ask your presbyters, and they will tell you,” St Benedict, CIII, 487. — “Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, so that you may not exercise the priesthood for me,” St Agobard, CIV, 145. — Priests should know what the sacrament of baptism and confirmation is, and what the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is, Hetto, CV, 763. They should know the lawful times for baptism during the year, ibid. They should know the times for feast-days throughout the year, ibid., 764. — Knowledge of the Scriptures is also necessary for him, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 830. That instruction is sought from priests is both commanded by the old law and written more fully in the Epistle to Titus, ibid., 835. When those who preside lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are surely bent down to bear the burdens of sins, ibid., 848. The unlearned are excluded from the priestly office, ibid., 850. “They did not know: all are dumb dogs, unable to bark,” ibid. A priest ought to possess the grace of greater knowledge, ibid., 859. Through the prophet, the Lord complains against the contemptible knowledge of pastors, ibid., 860. — Discipline pertains to the priest, so that when questioned concerning the law he may answer, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 284. Why the teachers of holy Church are queens, ibid., 338. — Priests hold the keys of knowledge, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 984. — Presbyters should learn an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, etc., together with the Athanasian Creed, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXIV, 773. — Those who catechize—that is, who instruct beginners by the word—must first themselves be instructed; for the matter concerns human souls, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 24. Therefore he who teaches must himself be educated and learned, ibid. Christ taught that priests must be more learned than other people, ibid., 29. That no illiterate person be promoted to the clergy, ibid., 944. Everyone must learn before teaching, ibid., 1042. — Those ignorant of God’s law cannot announce and preach it to others, Riculf of Soissons, CXXXI, 16. — Let him keep written with him an exposition of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer according to the tradition of the orthodox Fathers, and understand it fully, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 191. Let him understand well the prayers of the Mass, also the Preface of the Canon and the Canon itself, and be able to recite them memorably and distinctly, ibid. Let him be able to read the Epistle and Gospel well, ibid. Let him know how to pronounce regularly from memory the words and divisions of the Psalms, together with the customary chants, ibid. Let him retain the Creed of St Athanasius by heart and understand its meaning, ibid. Let him know how to baptize, etc., ibid. — Let him retain by heart the exorcisms and the blessings of salt and water, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 191. Let him understand the lesser computus, that is, the epacts and the Paschal limits, ibid. — Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by God’s priests, who have undertaken the office of teaching among the people, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 29. Let priests therefore know the Scriptures and canons, ibid. Let all presbyters retain the Catholic faith by heart, ibid. “But if anyone does not know, he shall not be known,” id., CXXXIV, 81. — Let him understand well the prayers of the Mass and the canons; or, if not, at least be able to recite them memorably and distinctly, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 563. Let him be able to read the Epistle and Gospel well, ibid., 564. Let him know how to pronounce regularly from memory the words and divisions of the Psalms, together with the customary chants, ibid. Let no person ignorant of letters be promoted to the clergy, id., CXXXIX, 401. — What presbyters ought necessarily to learn and know, Burchard, CXL, 625. All the Lord’s priests must be taught, that they may instruct others and advance themselves, ibid., 651. Let an illiterate presbyter not dare to celebrate Mass, ibid., 759. — Let presbyters be taught the sacred prayers and ecclesiastical canons, St Abbo, CXXXIX, 451. — The necessity of knowledge in a priest, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 498. What results from the ignorance of pseudo-priests who do not know how to teach God’s people, ibid. That the unskilled are not to be promoted to the priesthood, ibid., 499. — That ignorance is intolerable in priests, St Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 515. That presbyters and deacons must know everything belonging to the Church, ibid., 517. — Concerning the presbyter who did not know grammar and yet baptized in the Trinity, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 116. Clerics should learn the canons from their bishops, ibid., 498. Each presbyter should know in order the eight principal vices, ibid., 885. Priests are reproved who, neglecting [Col. 0729] the Gospels, read comedies, ibid., 1114. Blessed Jerome is beaten by an angel because he was reading a book of Cicero, ibid. Secular clerics are not to be forbidden to read literature, ibid., 1115, 1116. Let him be enriched with the fullness of knowledge signified by the chasuble (*planeta*), id., CLXII, 526. — It is fitting that priests’ hearts be filled with the fullness of knowledge, Rupert, CLXVII, 1169. — The necessity of knowledge in a priest, Hildebert, CLXXI, 766. Others will seek knowledge from their mouth, ibid., 773. The law puts to death a priest without doctrine, ibid., 789. Study and work so that knowledge may be in you, ibid., 821. That he know letters, ibid., 927. He who ought to teach must possess the judgment that is fitting, ibid., 594. It is great rashness to receive the priesthood if one does not possess the gift of knowledge, ibid. He who wishes to govern the Lord’s people without knowledge is like a blind man leading a blind man, ibid., 595. — Knowledge is exceedingly necessary in churchmen, Venerable Godfrey, CLXXIV, 738. — In a preacher, perfection of knowledge is required, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 845. — The lips of priests ought to preserve knowledge, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 42. — A priest must possess knowledge of the law, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 200. Since voluntary ignorance is harmful to everyone, it is dangerous for priests, ibid., 207. What priests need to learn, ibid., 209. Let no one aspire to the high priesthood unless he has been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, ibid., 313. — On the knowledge of clerics, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 693.

## VIII.—On the Pastoral Burden and Its Reward

What account a pastor must render concerning his sheep, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 762. If each person will scarcely be able to render an account for himself on the day of judgment, what will become of priests, from whom the souls of all are to be required? id., XXXIX, 2283. The greater one’s dignity in honour beyond others, the greater the difficulty in rendering account, id., XL, 1310. — In what respects the burden of priests is so much heavier, St Leo the Great, LVI, 634; Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 42. — The priest renders an account to the Shepherd of all shepherds not only for himself, but also for the flock entrusted to him, Julianus Pomerius, LIX, 431. “I will require my flock from their hand,” ibid., 436; St Benedict, LXVI, 973. — Let us weigh the burden we have undertaken, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1149. They bear a burden laid upon them, as it were, according to the manner of beasts of burden, ibid., 1144, 1145. The ruin of the people arises chiefly from the fault of priests, ibid., 1295. The rulers of the Church will render account at judgment for the souls committed to them, ibid., 319. The burden of the pastor, id., LXXVII, 468. Priests deserve as many deaths as the examples of perdition that they transmit to their subjects, ibid., 54. The kingdom is weakened when pastors fall into certain faults, id., LXXIX, 395. — The more anyone is exalted in the dignity of secular honour, the more heavily he is burdened by the weight of cares, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 718. — Look and consider more attentively how many souls you have undertaken to govern at the peril of your own soul, Blessed Alcuin, C, 450. — “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves alone,” Amalarius of Metz, CV, 836. Whence we shall render account to God for our stewardship, ibid., 837. — For the care and solicitude of the people belong to you, and their salvation, welfare, and progress of souls depend upon you, Riculf of Soissons, CXXXI, 15. — On the burden of the presbyter, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 528. The government of souls is the art of arts, the burden of burdens, ibid., 45. — The sin of priests merits a greater judgment, Rupert, CLXVIII, 81. — Negligent priests will render eye for eye, Hildebert, CLXXI, 777. — Therefore let each consider his own burden, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 657.
