Let us not cast down the holy burden, ibid., 941. For we shall render account not only for ourselves but also for the souls committed to us, ibid. — Therefore the burden and the danger of this honour are grave, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 991. — Woe to those—may God avert it—who, having been at the head, fall back into the tail; though first, they become last, Hildebert, CLXXI, 762. — For many would not run to honours with such confidence and eagerness if they realized that they are also burdens, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 826.

It is a difficult and arduous thing to minister in the priesthood and govern souls, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 362. For you will render an account of the souls of the people on the day of dreadful judgment, [Col. 0730] ibid., 724. O how grave and dangerous is the office of administration, because on the day of dreadful judgment you are bound to answer not only for your own souls but for the souls committed to you, ibid., 727. The more worthy the eminence of priests, the graver their fall and the more dangerous their ruin, ibid., 733. Therefore let each one of you recognize the burden of his calling, ibid., 734.

There is Peter with converted Judaea. There is Paul leading, so to speak, the converted world, etc., St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1148. — As many as you recall in this exile from iniquity by your teachings and lead back onto the way of truth, without doubt you will receive as many rewards on that day, Blessed Alcuin, C, 248. Your reward with God will be very great if you have not neglected a brother’s salvation, ibid., 508. He who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way covers a multitude of his own sins, ibid.

## IX.—On Councils and Admonitions Given to Priests

Among clerics, pursue the better men. For in every condition and rank the worst are mingled with the best, St Jerome, XXII, 1082. If, because of your clerical office, you visit a widow or a virgin, never enter the house alone, ibid., 532. Do not sit alone with a woman alone, in secret and without an arbiter or witness, ibid. — Let the words of God be read at a priestly meal, Blessed Alcuin, C, 243; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1419; CXL, 1069. — Divine reading should always be mingled with priests’ meals, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 500; Gratian, CLXXVII, 232. — Wherever you go, let St Gregory’s book *Pastoral Rule* accompany you. Read and reread it often, Blessed Alcuin, C, 245. Amid the cups let the sound and speech of edification be heard, ibid., 248. Read diligently, I beseech you, the Gospel of Christ and also the other books of canonical authority, ibid., 458. — Either equally disregard all girls and virgins of Christ, or equally love them, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 883. Keep frequent vigils, and often sleep with an empty stomach, ibid., 887. Flee rumours, vain boasts, and flattering flatterers as enemies, ibid. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied, ibid. Remember that Christ’s apostles, although they had authority to live by the Gospel, laboured with their hands, ibid., 888. — Let every one of you endeavour to have a Missal, Lectionary, Martyrology, Antiphonary, etc., corrected and clearly arranged according to our books which we use in holy mother Church, Riculf of Soissons, CXXXI, 17. Have clean and suitably prepared places where, after receiving the sacred mysteries, you may wash your hands and mouths, ibid. Keep your houses neat and free from dirt and foul smells, ibid., 18. It is also fitting that you have one, two, or three clerics who celebrate Masses with you, ibid., 19. Teach your parishioners also that, when they assemble at church, they should strive to pray for themselves and others with groans and tears, and refrain from idle words, ibid., 23. — Let no presbyter receive another’s parishioner for Mass, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 203. Let every presbyter bring two ampullae to the city on the Lord’s Supper, ibid., 206. — Let no one travel without a stole, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 562. — A presbyter ought not to go among his people without chrism, Burchard, CXL, 740. — Let a presbyter always keep the Eucharist prepared for the sick, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 165. Let individual presbyters have authoritative chapters for assisting penitents, ibid., 885.

## X.—Books Treating of the Priesthood

*A Short Book on Priestly Dignity*, St Ambrose, XVII, 567. — *The Book of the Pastoral Rule*, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 14. — *A Short Work on the Celibacy of Priests*, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 380. *A Short Work against Intemperate Clerics*, ibid., 388. *A Short Work on Fleeing Ecclesiastical Dignities*, ibid., 456. *A Short Work against Court Clerics*, ibid., 464. *A Short Work against the Ignorance and Negligence of Clerics*, ibid., 498. *A Short Work on the Plain Dress of Ecclesiastics*, ibid., 518. *A Short Work on the Dignity of the Priesthood*, ibid., 492. — *Sermon on the Dignity of Priests*, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 981. — *Treatise on the Dignity of Clerics*, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 666.

[Col. 0731]

# LXXXV. INDEX ON CLERICS, SETTING OUT IN LOGICAL ORDER THE RIGHTS OF LOWER MINISTERS, THEIR VARIOUS OBLIGATIONS, AND THE OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING THEM

## I.—On Cases Involving Clerics

On the manner of receiving an accusation against clerics, Pope St Eutychian, V, 172. — No cleric may have his case examined in public, Pope St Sylvester, VIII, 835. Let no one examine a cleric in public, ibid., 839. Let no cleric, deacon, or presbyter enter a law court on account of his own case, ibid. — On accusations against clerics, Pope St Julius, VIII, 986, 988. — If he neglects to bring his case within a year, thereafter no one is to hear his claim, St Augustine, XXXIII, 234. — Cases of clerics, St Leo the Great, LVI, 867. — Clerics’ cases belong to the bishop, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 653, 1150 et seq., 1217. He summoned the more difficult cases of presbyters to himself, ibid., 653. Cases of presbyters are to be decided according to the rule of the canons, ibid., 707. Women are produced as witnesses against clerics, ibid., 633, 634. Ancient canons irrevocably depose ordained clerics who have fallen into sins of the flesh, ibid., 694, 695, 464, 724. Clerics were irrevocably deposed not only for public crimes but also for hidden ones, ibid., 988. A presbyter who has dared, after deposition, to approach the ministry is deprived of communion until death, ibid., 728, 729. Fornicating clerics are deposed and confined in a monastery to perform penance, ibid., 637. A presbyter fallen into idolatry and sodomy is to be imprisoned, ibid., 1069. He against whom no canonical sentence has been issued ought not to undergo canonical punishment, ibid., 612. Clerics are not to be summoned to court before laypersons, ibid., 802. — Clerics should not approach secular judges, Charlemagne, XCVII, 767. Clerics of any order are not to be accused before anyone other than bishops, ibid., 802. Accusers of clerics are not to be received without proof, ibid., 808. Clerics are to be heard by their metropolitans or fellow-provincials, ibid., 810. No cleric or abbot may presume to go to secular courts without the command of his own bishop, ibid., 817. Accusations against clerics are to be made within the province, ibid., 891. A cleric must not go to a secular judge without consulting the bishop, ibid., 908. — Clerics having a dispute with one another ought not to leave their own bishop and resort to secular courts, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 881; Isidore Mercator, LXXX, 307. Clerics are not to appeal to public courts, ibid., 329; Burchard, CXL, 655. Clerics are not to be compelled by foreign judges, ibid., 659. — No cleric may accuse another except in writing, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 497. On the deposition of an abusive cleric, ibid., 748. Let a cleric who lends at interest be deposed, ibid., 804. Clerics who bear military arms are to be punished by loss of their own rank, ibid., 1169. On clerics’ business and cases, ibid., 1189. No cleric is to be summoned before a secular judge except with the bishop’s permission, ibid. A case is to be heard only within the province and by fellow-provincials, ibid., 1190. How one wishing to accuse a priest ought to proceed, ibid. The people ought not to accuse or rebuke a priest, ibid., 1191, 1192. On accusations, ibid., 1194. Priests can be accused only by suitable and approved men, ibid., 1195. Neither clerics are to be accepted in accusations against laypeople nor laypeople in accusations against clerics, ibid. On witnesses to be admitted in accusations, ibid., 1199. On appeals, ibid., 1207. On clerics accused solely by ill repute without witnesses, ibid., 1211. — A flattering or treacherous cleric is to be degraded from office, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 243. An abusive cleric is to be removed from office, ibid. A cleric discovered to take usury is to be degraded, ibid., 246. Those fallen from holy orders cannot be restored, ibid., 258. An oath is not to be demanded from priests, ibid., 603. A priest accused by the people is to assert his innocence by oath, ibid., 604. A layperson is not to accuse a cleric, ibid., 638, 639, 640. A cleric is not to be accused before secular judges, [Col. 0732] ibid., 819, 820, 821. A presbyter must be judged only before the bishop, ibid., 832. Priests are to be honoured by kings, not judged by them, ibid., 833.

## II.—On What Is Commanded of Clerics

Clerics ought to devote themselves only to the altar and sacrifices, St Cyprian, IV, 399. — The office of clerics in burying bodies, St Jerome, XXII, 330. Let clerics preserve chaste eyes and tongue, id., XXVI, 538. Abstinence from wine is prescribed for them, id., XXII, 536. Let them flee women, ibid., 531. Let them not attend dinners, ibid., 536. Let sacred reading never be put down from a cleric’s hands, ibid., 533. Celibacy of clerics, id., XXIII, 340. — Clerics, however learned, should seek their livelihood by a craft, St Leo the Great, LVI, 886. They should provide themselves food and clothing by a small craft or agriculture, without detriment to their office, ibid., 883. Punishment of clerics unwilling to be promoted to a higher rank, id., CLVI, 873, 877. — Clerics ought to say the Lord’s Prayer daily, St Benedict, LXVI, 448, 450. — Clerics perform the office in church, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 864. — Travelling clerics are bound to recite the breviary, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 411. The obligation of clerics to recite the course, or Breviary, ibid., 409. — Clerics who abandon their own church, even in order to care for another, are to be restrained, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1000, 1001. The life and duties of clerics, id., LXXXIII, 1156. — Let a cleric remain in the church to which he was assigned, Charlemagne, XCVII, 708. Let all clerics be subject to their bishops, ibid., 711. — Let them seek their livelihood by a craft, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 341. On clerics who do not assemble for matins or vespers, ibid., 578. — Clerics should obey their bishops, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 37. — Let a cleric seek his livelihood by an honourable craft, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 486. Let clerics distribute their surplus to the poor, ibid., 888. — Clerics ought to make confession of their lighter faults to one another in chapter, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1082. — Clerics who absent themselves from the offices of matins or vespers are to be corrected, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 427. — On the knowledge of clerics, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 693. On the justice of clerics, ibid., 707. On the continence of clerics, ibid., 727. On the obedience of clerics, ibid., 840. Certain precepts proper to clerics, ibid., 715. — Let a cleric be rich in conscience but poor in money, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 74. — Clerics are to be compelled to personal residence at their churches, Innocent III, CCXIV, 93.

## III.—On What Is Forbidden to Clerics

A prohibition on appointing clerics as guardians or curators in one’s will, St Cyprian, IV, 399. — Clerics are to avoid the banquets of secular persons, St Jerome, XXVI, 538. A cleric does not arrange marriages, id., XXII, 539. A cleric who does not refuse to go to dinners when frequently invited is easily despised, ibid., 536. — Ecclesiastical discipline does not permit a cleric to transfer from one church to another, St Augustine, XXXIII, 231, 232. — Usury is forbidden to laypeople and clerics, St Leo the Great, LIV, 613. Clerics are not to attend spectacles, id., LVI, 720. They are not to be merchants, ibid., 698. They are not to enter military service or secular office, ibid., 540. They are not to transfer from church to church, ibid., 397. They are not to remain in a foreign city, ibid., 428. — Clerics are not to wear purple garments, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 147. — Clerics who have entered monastic life are forbidden to return to their own church unless summoned by their bishop, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 495, 496. Cohabitation with women is forbidden to ordained clerics, ibid., 1032. — Clerics should avoid wedding banquets, St Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1088. — Clerics are not to enter taverns for drinking. [Col. 0733] Charlemagne, XCVII, 196. On clerics: they are by no means to transfer from one church to another, ibid., 197. Let no cleric abandon his own bishop and go over to secular business, ibid., 803. If they do not avoid drunkenness, let them be excommunicated or beaten, ibid., 833. On clerics who have presumed to sing at a banquet, ibid., 898. On disobedient clerics and those late for office, ibid., 908. — That a cleric may not minister in the churches of two cities, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 877. That it is wholly unfitting for clerics to transfer elsewhere, ibid., 881. A cleric is not to practice usury either in his own name or another’s, ibid., 882. Clerics are not to pursue any dishonest trade or shameful profit, ibid. — On the prohibition against clerics attending spectacles, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 578. — Clerics are not to attend weddings, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 255. Clerics are not to be tenants of others’ property, ibid., 234. Clerics are not to wear lay clothing, ibid., 257. Weapons are forbidden to clerics, ibid., 222. — On clerics who abandon the places in which they were ordained, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 35. Clerics are not to walk through streets or markets, ibid., 37. Likewise, a buffoonish cleric is to be punished, ibid. A flattering and treacherous cleric is to be degraded, ibid. Clerics are not to engage in buying cheaply and selling dearly, ibid., 38. Clerics are not to seek secular protection against ecclesiastical discipline, ibid. — What is forbidden to clerics, Ratherius, 561 et seq. On ordained persons: they are not to be transferred from city to city contrary to the law of the canons, Burchard, CXL, 643. Clerics are not to begin banquets before the third hour, ibid., 653. A cleric is not to grow a beard, ibid., 654. — Against intemperate clerics, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 391, 398, 406, 416. Against the ignorance and negligence of clerics, ibid., 497. — Against clerics’ greed and rapacity, Othlo, CXLVI, 77. How detestable is luxury of dress in clerics, ibid., 357. Clerics’ negligence in divine matters, reproved and rebuked by God, ibid., 344. — No cleric may have familiarity with strange women, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 488. On disobedient clerics and those late for office, ibid., 522. Clerics are not to be enchanters, ibid., [Col. 0734] 747. — Vices of clerics, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 959. Ambition, ibid., 85, together with avarice, id., CLXXXII, 826. Incontinence, ibid., 853. Luxury, id., CLXXIII, 200. A cleric may not fight, id., CLXXXII, 371, nor urge others to fight, ibid., 294. — Let them practice no commerce in their ministry, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 930. — Clerics are forbidden to grow their hair, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 137, 139. — Clerics’ laziness must be rebuked before that of all others, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 249. Clerics are not to be notaries, Innocent III, CCXVI, 486.

## IV.—On the Rights of Clerics

Whether they may be deprived of patrimony, St Ambrose, XVI, 68. — Clerics are exempt from all public duties, St Augustine, XLIII, 777. Chilperic violates their immunities, id., LXXI, 345. Clerics may take refuge in monasteries for the sake of penance or reformation of morals, id., LXXVII, 496. Stipends are owed to clerics faithfully serving the Church, ibid., 834. — No churchman is to be compelled to give testimony, Charlemagne, XCVII, 809. — Clerics unjustly excommunicated may approach neighbouring bishops, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 273. — Clerics may become monks, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 384.

## V.—Books Treating of Clerics

*Treatise on the Distinctiveness of Clerics*, St Cyprian, V, 835. — *A Short Work against Intemperate Clerics*, St Peter Damian, CXLV, 388. *A Short Work against Court Clerics*, ibid., 464. *A Short Work against the Ignorance and Negligence of Clerics*, ibid., 498. — *A Short Work on the Dignity of Clerics*, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 666. *Treatise on the Knowledge of Clerics*, ibid., 694. *Treatise on the Justice of Clerics*, ibid., 708. *Treatise on the Continence of Clerics*, ibid., 728. On the obedience of clerics, ibid., 840. On the silence of clerics, ibid., 944.

[Col. 0733] Here we conclude the various indices concerning the ecclesiastical hierarchy. Whoever desires more on these matters should consult the special Index on the sacrament of Orders, where perhaps they will find what they seek.

[Col. 0733]

# LXXXVI. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF ALL HERESIES THAT AROSE IN THE CHURCH FROM THE FIRST BEGINNINGS OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION TO THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY

## NOTICE

To enable the reader more easily to find what is sought, we have arranged this Index alphabetically. After the name of each heresy or heretic, we cite the various authors who refuted them in writings or crushed them by censures, indicating volume and columns. After this we set before the reader a chronological survey of the chief sects, traced from the times of the apostles through each century down to the thirteenth century. But our present purpose is only to provide a concise account of those same sects here; therefore we do not mention the writers who attacked them. Should the reader wish to know them, let him return to the alphabetical Index, where under the heading of each heresy he will find them.

# CHRONOLOGICAL SURVEY OF THE PRINCIPAL HERESIES OR SECTS, TRACED FROM THE TIMES OF THE APOSTLES THROUGH EACH SUCCESSIVE CENTURY TO THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0743]

## Heresies arising in the first century

**SIMONIANS.**—The first to introduce into the world the pest of heresy was Simon Magus, a native of Samaria. When he had been baptized by Philip and saw that the Holy Spirit descended upon those upon whom the apostles laid their hands, [Col. 0744] he offered money and wished to buy from the apostles the power likewise to confer the Holy Spirit. By this act he first laid the foundation of the stain called after him Simoniacal. He maintained:

1. that he was the great power of God—indeed, God himself—who had appeared in Samaria as the Father, in Judaea as the Son, and among the Gentiles as the Holy Spirit;

2. that Christ had not truly [Col. 0745] come, nor truly suffered, but only appeared to do so;

3. that a certain wandering woman, Helena by name, with whom he secretly defiled himself with every kind of lust, was now the Holy Spirit, now Minerva, as he blasphemously asserted; and under the latter’s image he caused her to be worshipped by his disciples, just as he himself was worshipped under the image of Jupiter;

4. that the Law had been given not by God but by a certain inferior intelligence, and therefore he invented two gods;

5. that, having abolished all law and eliminated good works as entirely unnecessary, he opened for his adherents a broad way to commit every crime with impunity, especially permitting indiscriminate intercourse with women;

6. that, together with the Sadducees, he denied the resurrection of the flesh, while, with the Pythagoreans, he affirmed transmigration of souls.

After spreading these errors through various parts of the world and endeavouring to persuade many people by false signs wrought with the assistance of demons, he eventually came to Rome. There, when with their assistance he attempted to fly into heaven in order to prove himself the true God, he fell headlong through the prayers of St Peter; his bones were broken, and, exhaling his soul, he descended to the regions below. Simon’s disciples or successors were later Menander, from whom came the Menandrians; Saturninus, from whom the Saturnians; and Basilides, from whom the Basilidians. They propagated and enlarged the same madnesses.

**NICOLAITANS.**—They erred:

1. by teaching that the world was not made by God but by certain rulers, whom they designated by barbarous and frightful names in order to instil fear into their hearers;

2. by allowing indiscriminate intercourse with women;

3. by teaching that prostitution was permissible;

4. and by eating things sacrificed to idols.

**CERINTHIANS.**—So called from Cerinthus, who, having become a Christian from being a Jew, wished circumcision to be joined with baptism as necessary to salvation, and stirred up various disputes against Christ’s disciples. But his principal error consisted in distinguishing Jesus from Christ and saying that Jesus had been conceived and born not of a virgin but of a woman through marital intercourse; whereas Christ, or the Holy Spirit, descended upon him in the form of a dove and bestowed upon him holiness, the power to communicate it to others, and the power to work miracles. He added that, when Christ had returned to heaven, Jesus alone suffered and died.

**EBIONITES.**—The Ebionites, or Ebionaeans, so called from a certain Ebion, founder of that sect and contemporary of the apostles, taught:

1. that Christ was a mere human being, begotten in the intercourse of Joseph and Mary, after the manner of other human beings;

2. that circumcision and the other legal observances were still to be kept after Christ;

3. that they excluded virginity from their assemblies;

4. and that they permitted a plurality of wives.

## Heresies of the second century

**GNOSTICS.**—They were so called from the *gnōsis* (γνῶσις), or knowledge of all things, which they arrogantly claimed for themselves above others. Their chief author was one named Carpocrates, or Carpocras, from whom they were also called Carpocratians. They were especially deluded on the following points:

1. they admitted two gods;

2. they said that the world was made not by God but by angels;

3. they maintained that Christ was not born of Mary but manifested through her, and thus mocked the holy Mother of God; they also said that Christ himself possessed flesh only in appearance;

4. they invented two souls in a human being, one good and endowed with reason, the other evil and devoid of reason, and they wished the former, but not the latter, to be of God’s substance;

5. they admitted transmigration of souls and denied the resurrection and the future judgment;

6. they said that a Christian might deny Christ in order to avoid tortures;

7. and they rejected fasts and chastity.

**VALENTINIANS.**—So called from a certain Valentinus, who, inflamed by indignation and a spirit of revenge, attacked the Church with errors, the substance of which is set out under these principal heads:

1. He posited two first principles: Depth and Silence, or Chaos, as though they were the first two gods, calling one male and the other female. From these two, as from a marriage, he said that thirty Aeons had proceeded, whether immediately or mediately: fifteen male and as many female.

2. He invented three kinds of human beings: pneumatic, or spiritual; psychic, or animal; and hylic or choic, that is, material. To the first class, which all Valentinians believed themselves to belong to, he ascribed a soul naturally good and incapable of being contaminated by crimes, which they could commit with impunity. Accordingly, he said that a person of that class would someday rise again, but with another body, namely a spiritual one, and would certainly be saved. To the second class he ascribed a soul capable of good and evil, maintaining that it could be saved or condemned according to its manner of life. Finally, to the third class he said that a soul naturally evil was inherent and that it had been created for destruction, so that that class would perish, body and soul together. [Col. 0746]

3. He taught that Christ had been sent by the Father—that is, by Depth—for the sake of the people of the middle class, but had brought with him a spiritual or heavenly body. Thus he took nothing from the Virgin Mary, but passed through her as through a channel or pipe. Secundus was Valentinus’s chief disciple and successor; the Secundians take their name from him. He enlarged his teacher’s errors by devising a new series and nature of Aeons.

**MARCIONITES.**—The Marcionites, called after Marcion; the Apellites, after Apelles; and the Cerdonians, after a certain Cerdon, prepared the way for the Manichaeans by positing two principles of things and two gods, one good and the other evil: the former the Father of Christ, the latter the author of the Law and the prophets. The Tatians adopted this error. They were also called Encratites, or “the continent,” because they said that one must abstain from marriage and did not use meat or wine, which they said had flowed from the evil principle. Hence in the sacrifice of the Mass itself they used water only, without wine.

**MONTANISTS.**—They took their name from Montanus, who, having associated with himself two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, whom he advertised as prophetesses, taught:

1. that the Holy Spirit had descended upon himself and these women in a fuller measure than upon the apostles themselves; hence he called himself the Holy Spirit, indeed God the Father;

2. that in the Church there was no power to remit certain graver sins committed after baptism, and that God alone must therefore be prayed to for their remission;

3. that second marriages were unlawful and were fornications, while conversely saying that marriage could be dissolved;

4. that Christians might not flee in any persecution;

5. and that new fasts were prescribed by divine law.

**TERTULLIANISTS.**—So called from Tertullian, who, after vigorously fighting against the Montanists, was deceived by the false appearance of a stricter discipline which Montanus presented, and by the dreams of Priscilla and Maximilla. He adopted and augmented their errors. For he taught:

1. that angels are rarefied and subtle bodies; likewise, that our soul, although immortal, is nevertheless corporeal, and grows, matures, desires food, and agrees with the body in other respects. He therefore attributed to it, as to a body, length, breadth, height, shape, sex, disposition, and limit;

2. that, according to Augustine’s testimony, the souls of wicked persons are transformed after death into demons.

## Heresies of the third century

**NOVATIANS.**—They first acquired this name from Novatus, then also from Novatian; later they proudly called themselves Cathari, that is, the clean and pure. They spread the following errors:

1. They deprived those who had fallen away from the faith, or who after baptism had fallen into other crimes, at least graver ones such as adultery and homicide, of every hope of forgiveness—at least of forgiveness obtainable from the Church; and thus they denied that the Church had power to grant pardon for sins of that kind.

2. They baptized anew persons entering or returning to their sect, thinking that baptism conferred outside it was invalid. They entirely neglected, moreover, the sacrament of Confirmation.

3. They despised martyrs and their relics. Finally, with the Montanists, they condemned second marriages.

**SABELLIANS.**—[They took their name] from Sabellius, a native of Africa or Libya, who did not so much first devise a new heresy as propagate one received from Praxeas—at first an adherent of Montanus and afterward his deserter—and from a certain Noetus. He taught that there is in God only one person in reality, as there is one nature, though expressed under three names according to a threefold conception. Hence the Sabellians also said that the Father suffered in Christ, and for this reason they were called Patripassians. Sabellius’s heresy was afterward adopted both by Photinus, whence the Photinians, and by Paul of Samosata, whence the Paulians.

**ORIGENISTS.**—So called from Origen, who erred:

1. Concerning the creation and nature of souls. For he imagined that God first created all rational creatures equal; that those which, through free choice, had turned more or less toward God were promoted to different ranks of angels according to the diversity of their merits; and that those which turned away from God were bound to various bodies and became souls, enclosed as in a prison within a body more or less imperfect according to the diversity of their demerits. On this basis he also absurdly maintained that the soul even of Christ existed before it was united to a body; likewise, that the sun, moon, and stars are certain animate powers.

2. Concerning the resurrection of bodies, which he did indeed admit, but said that bodies would not rise upright as now, but would be spherical; nor would they have blood and limbs as they do now, since these would serve no purpose in that state, but would be [Col. 0747] subtle and aerial.

3. Concerning the state of souls after this life. Besides denying that the souls of the condemned suffer anything from corporeal fire, he also denied that their punishments—or those of the demons themselves—would endure eternally. He added that Christ must again be crucified for demons. Finally, he went so far in his madness that, just as he held that demons and the souls of the condemned would someday be delivered from punishment, so he held that angels and the souls of the blessed would someday fall from blessedness into the miseries of this life. Indeed, he held that the condemned would return again to this world and thereafter be called to blessedness, and that demons would be restored to their former state and rank.

**MANICHAEANS.**—They received this name from a certain slave, Persian by nationality, who was formerly called Cubricus and afterward wished to be called Manes. The Manichaeans:

1. Posited two opposed principles, eternal, immortal, and independent of one another: one good and the other evil. They made God corporeal, finite, and divisible. Moreover, they admitted Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but said that there was one God under a threefold name.

2. Said that flesh proceeded from the evil principle and was of its substance. Therefore they chiefly denied that Christ possessed true flesh, and consequently that he was truly born of the Virgin, lest he be defiled. Nor did they say that he truly suffered, was crucified, or died, but only seemingly and figuratively, and that he rose only in the same manner.

3. Invented two souls dwelling in one body: one good and rational, formed by the good principle; the other evil and animal, likewise made by the evil principle.

4. Affirmed transmigration of souls.

5. Denied that evils of guilt are attributable to human free choice, lest God, from whom it proceeds, should likewise be their author. They therefore attributed such evils to the soul, evil by its nature, which would compel a person toward them even unwillingly, etc., etc.

## Heresies of the fourth century

**DONATISTS or DONATIANS.**—They derived their name and errors from two Donatuses: the one, bishop of Casae Nigrae in Numidia, as their author; the other, bishop of Carthage, as their promoter. Their principal errors are as follows:

1. They maintained that the Church had perished throughout the whole world through communion with the wicked, and remained only among the Donatists in Africa. Yet, considering that the true Church could not exist without communion with the Roman Church, they secretly sent one of their own to Rome, who, as bishop, governed the members of their faction living there.

2. From that first error they drew another: that baptism was valid only when conferred among themselves. Accordingly, if any Catholics defected to them, they rebaptized them.

3. Many of them, under the pretext of martyrdom, voluntarily surrendered themselves to be killed by others; indeed, they frequently laid violent hands upon themselves and thus boasted that they were martyrs. Those seized with this insane frenzy were called Circumcellions.

**ARIANS.**—The Arian heresy had as its author Arius, a native of Libya and presbyter of Alexandria, who spread the following principal errors:

1. Although he professed to admit three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—he nevertheless maintained that the first alone was true, eternal, immutable God.

2. Hence he denied that the Son and Holy Spirit were of the same substance or nature as the Father. Indeed, he asserted that the Son’s nature was entirely different from that of the Father, and the Holy Spirit’s different from that of the Father and Son.

3. He said that the Son, just as the Holy Spirit, was made from nothing in time, and was therefore a creature and thus less than the Father. But he said that the Son was the first creature, made before all ages, the most perfect of all, and closest to God; that he was therefore called Son of God by excellence, and God by a certain participation, not by nature; and that God had made the ages and all other things through him as through a minister. He said that the Holy Spirit was the Son’s chief creature and therefore called him “the creature of a creature.” Thus, in place of the doxological verse customarily sung by the Catholic Church, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” he taught his followers to sing: “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.”

**SEMI-ARIANS.**—These partly agreed with the Arians and partly differed from them. For with the Arians they held exactly the same view of the Holy Spirit, and denied that the Son was consubstantial with the Father, or of the same nature as he. Yet, unlike the Arians, they said that the Son was like the Father in all respects, and therefore also in essence. Accordingly, they refused to call him *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος), “of the same substance,” but called him *homoiousios* (ὁμοιούσιος), “similar in substance.” The authors of Semi-Arianism were Basil of Ancyra and Gregory of Laodicea.

[Col. 0748]

**ACACIANS.**—So called from Acacius, bishop of Caesarea. As it were intermediate between Arians and Semi-Arians, they said neither, with Catholics, that the Son was consubstantial with the Father, nor, with Arians, that he was wholly unlike him, nor, with Semi-Arians, that he was similar in substance; but only similar in accidents and form, as a golden statue is similar to the prototype which it represents.

**MACEDONIANS.**—An offshoot of the Arians, they took their name and error from Macedonius, who taught that the Son was indeed God and in every respect similar to the Father; indeed, as St Augustine says, of one and the same substance or essence with him. But he taught that the Holy Spirit was a creature, lacking the same dignity as the Father and Son; indeed, he called him a servant and minister.

**AERIANS.**—They arose from a certain Aerius, a native of Pontus, who, when he had been excluded from the bishopric of Sebaste which he sought, began to rail against the episcopal dignity itself. Thus the first and chief point of Aerius’s errors was that bishops are not superior to presbyters and differ from them in no respect. He subsequently added other errors: namely, that prayers for the dead and good works undertaken for them are of no benefit to them and are therefore to be rejected; that fasts established by the Church and customarily observed by Christians are not to be kept; and finally, that Christians ought not to celebrate Easter.

**AETIANS AND EUNOMIANS.**—Named after Aetius and Eunomius, they too were offspring of the Arian heresy and enlarged it with new blasphemies. Their first error was to assert that the Son was wholly unlike the Father, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son; hence they were also called Anomoeans, that is, “the unlike.” Accordingly, they did not baptize with the words instituted by Christ, but by this formula: “In the name of the uncreated God, and in the name of the created Son, and in the name of the Holy Spirit, sanctifier, begotten by the Son.” Therefore they rebaptized Catholics who came over to them. Their second error was to assert that the divine Word had not assumed a soul, but that divinity supplied the soul’s function. Their third was to say that they knew God as perfectly as God knows himself, and thus blasphemously claimed likewise to comprehend him. Their fourth was that they despised the relics of saints and declared that miracles wrought by God at their invocation were delusive works of demons. Their fifth was to teach that an evil life joined to the faith which they preached did no harm: so that a person entangled in any sins whatsoever, even if he wished to persevere in them, might share eternal life provided he maintained his faith.

**APOLLINARIANS.**—This sect had Apollinaris as its author, who advanced the following errors:

1. That the Word had not assumed even a rational soul, or mind, but had supplied its function.

2. That Christ had not possessed true flesh.

3. That he also wandered in various ways concerning the Trinity.

To these errors he added the ridiculous fiction that, after the universal resurrection, we should return to the observance of the Mosaic Law.

**PRISCILLIANISTS.**—This heresy, propagated through Spain by Priscillian, received its name from him and borrowed its errors from nearly all the heretics who had existed before it. For:

1. With Sabellius they recognized only one person in God.

2. Sharing the Arians’ view of the Son, they imagined that certain powers began to proceed from God; but that the devil had never been good and that his nature was not the work of God, but had emerged from chaos and darkness; that he was the principle and substance of every evil, and consequently also of human bodies. Hence they also abstained from meats and denied that Christ had true flesh.

3. With the Manichaeans they imagined that the human soul was a particle of the divine substance.

4. With Origen they said that souls had first sinned in heaven and had been cast down into bodies as punishment.

5. With the Stoics they said that human beings sin not voluntarily and freely, but unwillingly, compelled by the fatal necessity of the stars.

6. Again with the Manichaeans, they condemned marriage and matrimony.

**AUDAEANS, or ANTHROPOMORPHITES.**—They received this name from their chief error, in which they held that God was corporeal and had limbs in the form of a human body.

**JOVINIANISTS.**—This heresy took its name from Jovinian, whose first error was to make marriage equal to virginity in merit. His second error was to teach that fasts and abstinence from certain foods are of no benefit to salvation. The third was that those reborn in baptism with full faith cannot be overcome by the devil or sin. The fourth was to teach with the Stoics that all sins are equal in gravity; likewise, that all merits are equal and therefore that all receive an equal degree of recompense in heaven. Finally, he added this fifth error: that although the Blessed Virgin was a virgin before childbirth and [Col. 0749] conceived Christ while her virginity remained untouched, and had no marital intercourse with Joseph either before or after the birth, nevertheless in giving birth itself she was corrupted, and her virginity corrupted.

## Heresies of the fifth century

**PELAGIANS.**—So called from Pelagius, British by nationality and a monk by profession. His principal errors are as follows:

1. He taught that the original state of the first human being was a state of nature, not a benefit of grace; and that Adam’s descendants are now born such as Adam was created—namely, he said, without virtue and vice, without grace and sin.

2. He denied that Adam’s descendants contract original sin from him, and accordingly said that Adam harmed only himself by sinning, not his descendants.

3. He maintained that by the powers of free will alone a human being could keep all divine commandments, overcome all temptations, entirely avoid all sins, and thus attain salvation by these same powers alone. Accordingly, he denied that God’s grace was necessary for any of these things, etc.

**COELESTIANS.**—They took their name from Coelestius, Pelagius’s disciple, who spread the same errors as Pelagius.

**SEMI-PELAGIANS.**—The Semi-Pelagians differed from the Pelagians:

1. In admitting that the primal stain of origin is transmitted to Adam’s descendants.

2. In maintaining the necessity of grace and baptism for its removal.

3. In likewise recognizing the weakness of our nature flowing from the same original fault.

4. They also confessed, at least most of them, the necessity of inward grace at least for carrying out and completing a good work; consequently, that a human being cannot attain salvation through natural powers alone.

But the Semi-Pelagians approached the Pelagians, and chiefly and especially erred, in saying that the beginning of faith, and hence of righteousness and salvation, comes from ourselves—that is, from the powers of nature left to themselves—and that no prevenient inward grace is necessary for such a beginning. They arranged their error thus:

1. They said: a person to whom the Gospel has been externally preached conceives, by natural powers alone, some initial faith, or a devout disposition of belief toward the Saviour, as one able and willing to deliver him from the misery contracted through sin.

2. From that initial faith follows a desire for spiritual health or salvation, aroused by it and merely natural.

3. There follows a feeble effort to rise, or to emerge from that misery, likewise by the powers of nature alone, which in fact are insufficient for rising.

4. The will has recourse to God by seeking and knocking through prayer and through imploring the aid necessary for this, likewise in a merely natural manner.

5. They said that God is moved by acts of this kind, merely natural and elicited without inward grace, to confer upon such a person inward grace, by which he may attain perfect faith and spiritual health, or justification; and that, when grace of this kind has been added, he may thereafter act well and savingly, keep God’s commandments, and finally obtain eternal salvation itself.

**PREDESTINATIANS (*Praedestinatiani*).**—Under this name, or the related designation “predestinarians,” come those who, from very badly understood books of St Augustine—especially those on Grace and Predestination—taught:

1. That among human beings some are destined by God’s antecedent, absolute, and efficacious will for glory, and others for eternal punishment.

2. That therefore those predestined for life can in no way be damned, nor those preordained for hell be saved in any manner.

3. Hence they inferred that, by the will of God predestining, human free will is utterly extinguished, or at least of no force: neither for obtaining salvation, if one is destined by God for damnation, nor for incurring damnation, if one has been preordained for salvation.

4. From this they further inferred that good works are of no benefit to the reprobate, nor evil works harmful to the predestined, and that neither group therefore ought to be concerned either to act rightly or not to act wrongly.

NESTORIANS.—Nestorius, a native of Syria, first a monk at Antioch and then patriarch of Constantinople, gave the Nestorians both their name and their errors. His first error was to posit two persons in Christ, as though dividing him into the Son of God and the Son of Man: the former begotten not of Mary but of God before the ages, the latter born of Mary in time. Hence, secondly, he would not have Mary called Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), that is, God-bearer, but Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*), that is, Christ-bearer. Thirdly, as a consequence, he denied that the Son of God suffered or died for us, thereby nullifying the mystery of our redemption.

EUTYCHIANS.—They derived their name from Eutyches, or Eutychetes. His chief error was that, while he attacked Nestorius more sharply for positing two persons in Christ, he himself asserted not only one person in him, but also [Col. 0750] one nature after the union. He maintained that Christ was indeed from two natures, but not in two natures; that is, that there had indeed been two natures before the union, but only one afterward. Thus, at the very point of the incarnation, one substance was formed from both the divine and human natures—whether Eutyches thought this occurred through confusion or mixture, as a composite nature arises from the four elements; through the conversion of one nature into another, as water at Cana in Galilee was changed into wine; through composition, as one human nature arises from body and soul; or whether he maintained that the human nature had been utterly absorbed by the divinity.

Heresies of the sixth and seventh centuries.

MONOTHELITES.—They took their name from two Greek words: *monos*, “one,” and *thelema*, “will,” as professors of one will; for they acknowledged in Christ only one will and operation. They believed that the human nature in Christ was never moved by a motion of its own, but only insofar as it was moved by the divinity of the Word.

Heresies of the eighth and ninth centuries.

ICONOCLASTS.—They were also called by the related name Iconomachians: contemners, assailants, and destroyers of the holy images.

SCHISM OF THE GREEKS.—Its principal author was Photius. There were five chief points upon which the Greeks differed from the Latins:

1. That the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father and the Son.
2. That the Eucharist may be celebrated not with unleavened bread, but only with leavened bread.
3. That there is no Purgatory.
4. That neither eternal blessedness is granted to the righteous nor eternal punishment inflicted upon the wicked before the day of judgment.
5. That the Roman pontiff is not the head of the whole Church and successor of Blessed Peter.

Heresies of the tenth and eleventh centuries.

In the tenth century scarcely any new heresy arose; but the sect of the Manichaeans revived in the West. In the eleventh century, however, there arose:

BERENGARIUS.—That famous father, or standard-bearer, of the Sacramentarians and chief disseminator of their heresy:

1. He overthrew infant baptism.
2. He abolished lawful marriages, shamelessly asserting that fornication with all persons was lawful.
3. He maintained that Christ did not enter to the disciples through closed doors.
4. He asserted that the Eucharist was not truly and substantially the body and blood of the Lord, but merely its shadow and figure.
5. Consequently, he held that bread and wine are not substantially changed, by the words of consecration, into the true body and blood of Christ.

Heresies of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

PETROBRUSIANS.—Those heretics took their name from Peter of Bruis, or Peter Brusius. To the foul errors of the Manichaeans they added these: that the sacrifice of the Mass is nothing; that baptism confers nothing upon infants apart from faith; and that the prayers of the faithful profit the dead in no respect—thus anticipating the innovators of the modern age.

ALBIGENSIANS.—The same sect, having established a permanent seat in the city of Albi near Toulouse, thereby gave its name to the Albigensian heretics, who in a short time corrupted almost the whole of France. They taught:

1. With the Manichaeans, that there are two principles of things.
2. With the Sadducees, they denied the resurrection of the flesh.
3. They rejected hell together with purgatory.
4. They repudiated the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist.

WALDENSIANS.—Their name came from Peter Waldo, a merchant of Lyons, a man without learning. They were also called the Poor Men of Lyons. Their principal errors were these:

1. That the Roman Church had fallen away from the time of Sylvester I, when it began to possess property. Hence they inferred that no one in it, however upright, could be saved; that its indulgences, blessings, consecrations, and ceremonies were to be despised; that tithes were not to be paid to the Church; and that no one ought to obey the supreme pontiff, bishops, or other prelates of the Church.
2. That all ministers of Christ’s Church who possess property sin against the Lord’s commandment: “Do not possess gold.”
3. That the ministry of the Eucharist and of the other sacraments belongs not to priests alone, but to all persons whatsoever, even laypeople.
4. That all authority, even civil authority, is lost by mortal sin alone; and consequently, that a priest living in mortal sin can neither consecrate nor absolve, while, conversely, a righteous layperson can duly do these things. The modern Jansenists adopted this error.
5. Finally, to omit more, that no prayer except the Lord’s Prayer ought to be offered.

[Col. 0751]

LXXXVII. INDEX OF SCHISMS, AND OF THEIR ORIGIN, CAUSES, AND HISTORY, FROM THE BEGINNINGS OF CHRISTIANITY TO THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY.

NOTICE.

Schism, according to the etymology and proper sense of the word, and according to common usage, is nothing other than the division or separation of a whole into two or more parts. In the present connection, however, it is a division or separation occurring in the moral body of human beings, or in the mystical body and society of those who profess the same faith, religion, and divine worship, although they live under differing laws and statutes of different kingdoms and commonwealths. It is, I say, their division with regard to faith or to the use and exercise of religion. In this Index, therefore, the origin and evils of schisms are treated without distinction, as are the baptism of schismatics and the various schisms which arose in the Church from the apostles to the thirteenth century.

Schism is unity among heretics, Tertullian, II, 57. Rivalry is the mother of schisms, same author, I, 1218.

Schisms arise from contempt for priests, St. Cyprian, IV, 396. Whence schisms arise, ibid., 403.

He is truly a schismatic who separates himself from communion with ecclesiastical unity, Tertullian, III, 1174. No offense can be greater than schism, ibid., 1049. Those who make schism are without hope, ibid., 1142. How great a sin schism is, ibid. The crime of schismatics is worse than that of the lapsed, same author, IV, 514. No agreement with anyone is possible for one who is not in agreement with the Church, ibid., 509. One cannot have God at peace with oneself when one has no peace with one’s brother, ibid. Schismatics are not united to the Lord’s bread, since they are not joined to Christ’s people, same author, III, 1142. Faith certainly cannot exist among schismatics, ibid., 1195. Souls that have divided themselves from God’s unity cannot be united, Tertullian, III, 1157. It is of no benefit to be near one another in body if minds disagree, ibid. One at discord with the brethren is not saved even by martyrdom, same author, IV, 536. Schismatics establish human churches, same author, III, 790. They inflate their number by falsehood, ibid., 811, 813. They are condemned by themselves, ibid., 728. Those deceived by leaders of schism perish, ibid., 1150. He who follows a leader of schism is liable to the same guilt, same author, IV, 514. The leaders of schism are guilty, as are those who follow them, same author, III, 1145. A lost faction will destroy those who agree with it, ibid., 726. Schisms ought not to disturb the faithful, because they were foretold, ibid., 805, 806. A confessor who defects into schism ought not to disturb them, same author, IV, 515. For a confessor who embraces schism, his deserts of punishment increase by that very fact, ibid., 516. The life of schismatics is abominable, same author, III, 823. Schismatics do not have the Holy Spirit, ibid., 1146. They make another prayer with unlawful utterances, same author, IV, 513. The Holy Spirit has departed from the breasts of schismatics, ibid., 401. Schism is adulterous, impious, and sacrilegious, ibid., 336. Whatever wicked persons attempt in order to destroy God’s ordering is done against God, ibid., 513. Certain schismatics cannot be received without scandal, same author, III, 823. Schismatic and heretical error, same author, IV, 344. The conflagration of schism, ibid., 728. Schismatics possess no authority, ibid., 1138. The baptism of schismatics, same author, IV, 408; III, 1040, 1046. Schism made in the city, same author, IV, 340. Schismatics are zealous in their beginnings, same author, III, 790. A schismatic cannot attain the rewards of the Church, same author, IV, 515. Schismatic and heretic, same author, III, 719, 727, 732. Schisms and heresies arise, ibid., 1134.

Separation from the root of Mother Church, St. Optatus, XI, 906. Its origin, ibid. The evils of schism, ibid., 890. Who are the authors of schism, ibid., 886. How grave an evil schism and division are, ibid., 925. Examples of punishments inflicted upon schismatics for the crime of schism, ibid., 924, 926. An outstanding description of the African schism, ibid., 1020. Who are schismatics, ibid., 905. Those who withdraw from their bishop and establish a new see are schismatics, ibid. How they differ from heretics, ibid., 906, 1047. They cause tears to God that cannot be comforted, ibid., 887. False prophets building a ruinous wall, ibid., 1021. Evils introduced by schismatics, ibid., 890. They may be called brethren even though they do not wish it, ibid. They are compared [Col. 0752] with severed branches and shoots, ibid., 962. They are compared with branches divided from a tree and with torn cloth, ibid., 1019, 1020. They possess the same sacraments, the same faith, and the same Lord’s Prayer as Catholics, ibid., 907, 1020. Why Catholics seek them for unity, ibid., 1083.

The schism of the Luciferians, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 501.—How schism differs from heresy, St. Jerome, VII, 758.

What schism is according to Faustus, St. Augustine, XLII, 369. Schisms: divisions, same author, XXXVIII, 1165, 1244. Schism: a recent dissension within an assembly, arising from some diversity of opinion, same author, XLIII, 471. Schism is seen in withdrawal; heresy in sacrilegious doctrine, ibid., 747. No cause of schism is lawful, ibid., 517. There is no just necessity for cutting off unity, ibid., 69. There is no bodily ground for separating the good from the bad, ibid., 59. Separation of heart, not of body, is commanded, ibid., 79, 80. One must not depart from Catholic bishops if they should happen to err by thinking something contrary to the canonical Scriptures of God, ibid., 410. Israel’s secession from Judah’s kingdom was not schismatic, ibid., 417. Hypocrisy must be opposed in such a way that the danger of schism is avoided, same author, XXXVIII, 94. Schisms are the Church’s dung, ibid., 53. Schisms are sacraments cut off, ibid., 53, 55. What follows from vain and rash separation, same author, XLIII, 105. Where charity is absent, justice cannot exist, same author, XXXIV, 1236. Charity grieves when unity is torn apart, same author, XXXV, 1992. The Lord’s threshing-floor could have endured those who made schisms as chaff until the time of the final winnowing, if they had not voluntarily separated themselves from us, same author, XXXIV, 127. We are certain that no one rightly separates himself from the communion of all nations, same author, XXXIII, 334.

Schism, by the Old Testament, is a crime graver than the burning of a prophetic book and the making of an idol, ibid., 192. It is a wound graver than idolatry or unbelief, XLIII, 115. The crime of schism is far more wicked than betrayal, ibid., 349; than homicide, ibid., 581. Schism is a most monstrous sacrilege, ibid., 333. Nothing is graver than the sacrilege of schism, ibid., 69, 132. Schism is a wound and death, ibid., 137, 138. Schism or heresy is a death more dreadful than bodily death, ibid., 43. Schism surpasses every crime, ibid., 38. Whether schism is a sin against the Holy Spirit, ibid., 554. God hates schisms, same author, XXXIII, 172. The punishment of Dathan and Abiram shows how highly schism is weighed in divine judgment, ibid., 298. Schisms are most justly punished by true unity alone, ibid., 55. Whence schisms are born, same author, XXXV, 1984. The origin of schisms is hatred of one’s brother, same author, XLIII, 118. Schisms are produced by the merely animal mind, ibid., 122. All schisms arise through carnal persons, same author, XXXVIII, 49. They could not make schism unless mad with the swelling of pride, deranged by the bitterness of envy, corrupted by worldly advantage, or perverted by carnal fear, same author, XLIII, 104. By wicked perseverance the Donatists made schism into heresy, same author, XXXIII, 298. Augustine charged the Donatists only with the crime of schism, ibid., 298. Communion with wicked persons does not stain anyone by participation in the sacraments, but by consent to their deeds, ibid., 579. The Donatists conceded this at the Conference of Carthage, ibid., 403, 409. Heresies and schisms are signified [Col. 0753] by the sons of Keturah, ibid., 2133. Exhortation to guard against schism, same author, XLIII, 350. How schismatics differ from heretics, same author, XXXV, 1367. Heretics and schismatics, born from the young mother and the aged father without the promise, ibid., 2134. Born of the free woman, but according to the flesh, ibid., 2133. Schismatics boast that they alone are Christians and condemn the rest, same author, XLIII, 588. All authors of schism adopt this one cause: that the righteous are stained by the sins of others when they share sacraments with them, same author, XXXIII, 339. How false this is, ibid. Some become schismatics while fearing defilement through fellowship with sinners, same author, 41. Tares and false brethren must be endured among the wheat until harvest time, same author, XXXV, 1799. Schismatics wish to show Christ in one part, though he purchased the whole, ibid., 1984. Schismatics are worse than Christ’s crucifiers, same author, XXXVI, 311. Schismatics must be reckoned among the dead and lost, same author, XXXII, 642. Those who have separated themselves from unity and kill souls by deceiving them shed blood spiritually, not carnally, same author, XXXVI, 645. Schismatics are murderers, same author, XLIII, 274. Spiritual life is lost through schism, same author, XXXVIII, 1231. Schismatics do not belong to the Church, same author, XL, 193. Schismatics break the nets, same author, XXXVI, 781. Schismatics are connected with the Church in some respect and have something sound, same author, XLIII, 115. But by the deadly wound of schism those sound things are drawn to death, ibid., 115. In whatever respect schismatics think with us, in that respect they are also with us, ibid., 110. Schismatics belong to God’s people, if not by the power, at least by the appearance, of godliness, same author, XXXVII, 1427. Though schismatics possess baptism, they do not possess the Holy Spirit, same author, XXXVIII, 462, 1235, 1236. Schismatics lack charity, same author, XLIII, 121. Schismatics cannot be good, same author, XXXIII, 952. He who does not know how to err ought to separate, ibid. Whatever good they may be able to do does not benefit schismatics, same author, XLIII, 116. Whether the patience of a schismatic who endures tortures in order not to deny Christ is praiseworthy, same author, XL, 623. Whether that endurance is a gift of God, ibid., 624. Whether it profits him, ibid. Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however praiseworthy he may suppose his life to be, shall not have life because of this crime alone, that he is severed from Christ’s unity, same author, XXXIII, 579. Schismatics have no share in God’s inheritance, same author, XXXVIII, 797. If you were outside the Church, you would be punished by eternal punishment even if you were burned alive for Christ’s name, same author, XXXIII, 756. Schismatics are not taken up by Christ, because he takes up unity, same author, XXXVI, 779. Schismatics are opposed, same author, XXXVII, 1254. Schismatics are to be recalled peacefully to peace, same author, XXXIX, 1583. Schismatics are rightly compelled to unity by emperors, [Col. 0754] same author, XXXVIII, 295. Augustine formerly did not approve of their forcible restoration to Catholic communion; but later, having experienced how much the diligent application of discipline could contribute to their improvement, he changed his opinion, same author, XXXII, 641. Penalties decreed against schismatics by the law of Theodosius, same author. For schismatics returning to the Catholic Church, the piety of unity must be added, but the sacrament of truth must not be denied, ibid., 603. It is lawful to deal with a heretic or schismatic concerning the matter of the soul, same author, XXXIII, 160.

What it means that schismatics “gnaw in solitude,” St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 149. No martyrs exist outside the unity of the Church, ibid., 58. There is no charity in schism, ibid., 59. How prudently Paul cured the Corinthian schism, ibid., 912. God is in unity, not in division of minds, ibid., 1176.—How schism differs from heresy, Alcuin, C, 1025.—Why they are called schismatics: because they do not assist the priests, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1102.—A schismatic is anyone who is not joined in communion to the Roman See, St. Agobard, CIV, 293; and anyone divided from the apostolic sees, ibid., 294.—How schism arises, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 94. What it was like under Abbot Ratgirius, same author, CXII, 1621.

On the schism raised in the Roman Church by Michael Cerularius, Pope St. Leo IX, CXLIII, 555.—Schism in the Church is to be avoided, Abbot Goffridus, CLVII, 220.—Those are called schismatics who hold separate assemblies apart from bishops communicating with us, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1198.—To avoid schism, many things, even if evil, must either be passed over or even endured, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXII, 236.—On the schism and reconciliation of Pope Calixtus and the abbot of Cluny, CLXX, 1151.—The schism of Anacletus II, CLXX, 1184.—On avoiding schism, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 708.—How schismatics differ from heretics, Algerus Scholasticus, CLXXX, 931. That schismatics are on our side in the holiness of the sacrament, but not in the wound of schism, ibid., 932. That the baptism of schismatics is indeed true, but does not profit them as long as they remain in schism, ibid., 932. That even ordained schismatics who convert are received, ibid., 935.—How great an evil schism is, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 382. The king’s counselors ought to repress schisms, ibid., 389. France, healer of schisms, ibid., 382. The schism of Peter Leonis for almost eight years, same author, CLXXXIII, 894. Bernard’s prayer for schismatics, same author, CLXXXII, 281.—On the Cluniac schism stirred up by Pons, formerly abbot, Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 922. On the schism of the Roman Church, and how manfully he defended the Catholic party, ibid., 928.

[Col. 0767]

# LXXXIX. INDEX ON THE RELATIONS OF ALL MEMBERS OF THE CHURCH MILITANT TO ONE ANOTHER, OR ON THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS IN THE STRICTER SENSE

## NOTICE

In this Index we deal only with the mutual relations among believers living in this life, by which the Church—commonly called the Church militant on earth—is united: first, we treat of the spiritual goods of the Church that believers hold in common; second, we show Christians, as St. Augustine says, becoming mutually sharers in labor and rest. As for the other aspects of the communion of saints, anyone wishing to pursue them should consult the special Index on the Cult of the Saints, which treats the relations between the Church militant and the Church triumphant in heaven. The Index on Purgatory will furnish the relations between the Church militant and the Church suffering.

## I.—On the spiritual goods of the Church held in common by believers

Holy Mother Church has the greatest possible care for her children, St. Augustine, XL, 692.—She is always solicitous in nourishing and fostering her own, Tertullian, III, 162.—This mother has two breasts: namely, knowledge of truth and love of the virtues; by the former she nourishes her children, by the latter she sanctifies them, Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 1163. She offers her breasts through deeds, words, and actions, nourishing, admonishing, and stirring them up, ibid., 1164.—The Church’s prayers are offered for all, by apostolic tradition, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 209.—She supplies her own with weapons by which hostile powers are overcome: faith and prayer, St. Ambrose, XVI, 249.—She alone possesses true charity, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 302.—She has oil with which she tends the wounds of her own, and with which she anoints martyrs and confessors, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1118.—She possesses the true and unique sacrifice of Christ’s flesh for sins, St. Augustine, XLIV, 600: the most true and singular sacrifice, ibid., 211; the daily sacrifice, id., XLI, 298.—She is rich, to enrich her children, Walafrid of Fulda, CXVI, 498, etc.

## II.—Christians become mutual sharers in labor and rest.

United in one body by a common religious consciousness, unity of discipline, and the covenant of hope, Tertullian, I, 468. How great was Christians’ mutual charity, ibid., 471. They called one another brothers, ibid. Through charity they held all things in common except wives, ibid., 472. “While there exists among them [the churches] a communion of peace, the designation of brotherhood, and the reciprocal token of hospitality: these rights are governed by no other principle than the single tradition of the same sacrament,” id., II, 32. — “For us the Church is one, and our mind is joined in indivisible concord,” St. Cyprian, III, 731–733, 830. The Apostles persevered unanimously in prayer, ibid., 524. The Church’s joy at the return of the confessors, ibid., IV, 465. “The one body of our union,” ibid., 360. Christ prayed that we might be one as the Father and the Son are one, id., III, 539. Peace is to be granted, when death is imminent, to the lapsed who have received certificates from martyrs and can be helped by their privilege before God, id., IV, 258, 261, 265. The martyrs requested that peace be granted to the lapsed, after Mother Church had first received peace from God, ibid., 252, 255. Offering sacrifice for the lapsed, ibid., 254. Peace granted by martyrs, ibid., 270–273, 281. The sacrament of unity, id., III, 799. Unanimity and concord, id., 341. Unanimity in faith and truth, id., III, 1156. The bond of unanimity, ibid., 1157. The unanimity of those praying, id., IV, 508. God urges unanimity in prayer upon the disciples, id., IV, 508. Unanimity existed under the Apostles, ibid., 518. The one and same Lord who dwells in us everywhere joins his own by the bond of unity, id., III, 1157. — Christians are brothers and equals among themselves, Lactantius, VI, 599. — The mark of communion in letters received and sent in turn, St. Hilary, X, 659, 660. Those who carelessly mingle in communion with persons condemned by anathema must suffer eternal punishments, ibid., 528. He commends himself to the holy prayers of the Gauls, ibid., 520. Liberius asks to be supported by the prayers of the confessors, ibid., 676. What constitutes the unity of the Church, id., IX, 434. All things must be obtained by the merit of unity, ibid., 659. — All believers are one in Christ, ibid., 477. The natural unity of believers through the nature of the one faith, id., X, 218. Through the nature of the sacraments, ibid., 218. The unity of believers with Christ and God the Father through participation in glory, ibid., 221.

St. Zeno on this text, “But all things were common to them,” XI, 287. The holy communion of the faithful, ibid., 438. — Communion with the whole world, St. Optatus, XI, 964. With the churches and the Apostles, ibid., 966, 1070. The one communion of the whole Church through the Roman Pontiff, ibid., 958–960. No defendant may be removed from communion unless accused and convicted, ibid., 1093, 1094. Communion is the union of churches, ibid., 1070, 1071. Kisses are signs of communion, ibid., 1034. — Those deprived of communion in sacred things with the Roman Pontiff are heretics, St. Damasus, XIII, 179. — “Therefore we are all one body and diverse members; but all are necessary to the body,” St. Ambrose, XVI, 150. “But if one is lacking in its function, the rest are hindered. If, for instance, someone tears out his eye, has he not denied himself the use of its work? … Now if the whole body is injured in one member, then in one person the communion of all humanity is dissolved. The nature of the human race is injured, as is the assembly of the holy Church, which rises into one connected and compact body through the unity of faith and charity,” ibid. For Christ is the faith of all; while the Church is, as it were, a form of justice, the common law of all: it prays in common, works in common, and is tempted in common, ibid., 65, 184. — Christians become mutual participants in labour and rest, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 187. What one person is less able to do, he does in the person who is able, if in the other he loves that which he himself does not do because he is unable, ibid., 507. The emperors of our communion—that is, of the Catholic Church—have enacted laws against heretics, id., XXXVI, 684. Those outside their communion call these men heretics, ibid. The affliction of others is shared by those whose trial, hope, love, and spirit are common, id., XXXIII, 365. Each person also possesses, when he loves it in another, what he himself does not possess, id., XXXV, 1812. All Christians have one commonwealth, id., XL, 573. All Christians are one human being, id., XXXVII, 1316, 1336, 1634, 1704. How a Christian, when another Christian works miracles, also performs them himself, id., XXXVII, 1707. In still carnal Christians who die, the Spirit completes whatever is lacking, because they have not departed from the unity of Christ’s body, id., XXXIII, 813. Cyprian taught that the Church consists of persons unanimous and concordant, both by prophetic testimony and by the signification of the sacraments, id., XLIII, 240. — The Church prays for all people, id., XLI, 737. — Since all the grace of God which deigns to work in any believer cannot be separated from any member of Christ’s body, and each makes his own the good that he rejoices to see accomplished through another, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 377, 378. A good and pleasant dwelling is that which produces unity among the children of adoption and, beyond bodily and local cohabitation, binds fraternal minds together in the peace of faith, ibid., 381. — Fraternal union assists brethren in danger to body and soul, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 253, 254. All are one, and one is all, when the one Spirit of God lives in all, ibid., 404. — How communion in good works is effected, St. Leo, LIV, 442, 443. How greatly it avails to perform works of piety together with the whole Church, ibid., 441–445. — The services and fruits of individuals become those of all through charity, St. Gregory, LXXVI, 462, 463. The various gifts of the Church’s members, ibid. The harmonious diversity of the Church’s members, ibid. The envious, however, who cannot possess the good things of others would, if they loved them, make them their own. For all who stand in the faith are like many members in one body: distinct indeed in their functions, but made one by the way in which they suit one another reciprocally. Thus the foot sees through the eye, and the eyes walk through the feet; hearing through the ears serves the mouth, and for its use the tongue of the mouth supports the ears; the stomach aids the hands, and the hands work for the stomach. Therefore, in the very arrangement of the body we receive what we should observe in action. Surely those whom we cannot imitate are ours when we love in them what they possess; and the things loved become ours in us who love them, id., LXXVII, 63. Through this charity, the unity of the universal Church—which is the cohesion of Christ’s body—rejoices in each individual in equality of mind, although it has inequality in the diversity of members. — Through this same charity, its members, afflicted in their own concerns, leap for joy at another’s joy; and, happy in their own concerns, waste away at another’s grief. For, as the Teacher of the Gentiles testifies, if one member suffers, the other members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it, ibid., 587. The effectiveness of brothers’ prayers when they pray together more earnestly for the salvation of a soul, ibid., 392. For while we are joined to you by the help of prayer, like persons walking over slippery ground we hold one another’s hand in turn; and, by the great providence of charity, it comes about that the charity of individuals is strengthened all the more firmly because each leans upon the other, ibid., 478. Many believers, while binding themselves together in charity and having one heart and one soul, make one body from many members, id., LXXXIX, 520. Some are helped by the good work of others, ibid., 393. — As many members in one body make one body, so the multitude of believers, joined by faith and love to their head, which is Christ, are one body with him, Haymo, CXVIII, 471. Each person ought, according to the grace divinely bestowed on him, to help others, so that they may be members of one another in spiritual as well as temporal matters—and in many other respects—ibid., 472–475. — The Church’s communion signified by Christ’s tunic, Hincmar, CXXV, 418, 419. — If someone cannot fast because of infirmity, let the fast which the Church observes generally benefit him; for we are all one body in Christ, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 567. — How effective the Church’s intercession is for sinners, Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXX, 423. — Through charity we share in the merits of others, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 903, 904. How dangerous it is to be deprived of the prayers of the Church, ibid., 971, 972. What individuality cannot achieve, community achieves; charity achieves, id., CLXXXIV, 259. — For all who everywhere hold to the unity of faith and love must rejoice, like members of a body, in mutual well-being; and what one has not yet merited to obtain in himself, when he sees it already in another he cannot but rejoice in it, Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 150. The prayers of the good benefit the wicked, ibid., 350.

XCI. DOGMATIC LIBRARY OF THE FATHERS, OR THE COMPLETE WORKS AND ALSO SHORTER WRITINGS OF THE ANCIENT LATIN FATHERS OF THE CHURCH CONCERNING CHRISTIAN DOGMAS, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY AUTHOR.

Book *On Images of the Saints*, against the superstition of those who think that the duty of worship ought to be rendered to paintings and images of saints, ibid., 200. Book *Against the Judgment of God*—or rather, against the damnable opinion of those who believe that the truth of divine judgment is disclosed by fire, water, or armed combat—ibid., 250.

Various letters concerning Christ’s person and two natures, ibid., Appendix, 1322.

Paulus Alvarus, abbot of Córdoba.—*Confession of Faith*, CXXI, 397.

Book, or dialogue, *On the Fall of the Devil*, also concerning good and evil will, ibid., 325. Two books *Why God Became Man*, showing that the Christian faith does not conflict with reason; that no human being can be saved without Christ; that human nature was established so that the whole human being—that is, in body and soul—might someday enjoy blessed immortality; and that it is necessary that that for which the human being was made should be brought about in the human being, but only through the God-Man, ibid., 361.
