Cyprian (Saint), bishop of Carthage.—Book *On the Vanity of Idols*, proving that God is one and that salvation has been given through Christ to believers, IV, 563. Three books *Against the Jews*: the first proves that the Jews withdrew from God and lost the Lord’s favor, and that Christians succeeded them in their place; the second contains the mystery of Christ, namely that the one foretold according to the Scriptures has come; the third contains certain commandments of the Lord and divine teachings, ibid., 675.

Drogo, cardinal and bishop of Ostia.—Book *On the Creation and Redemption of the First Human Being*, CLXVI, 1547. Short work *On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, ibid., 1553.

Dungal, monk.—Book *Against Claudius of Turin, or on the Veneration of Images*, CV, 465.

Durandus, abbot of Troarn.—Book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXLIX, 1375.

Elipandus, bishop of Toledo.—Letters I and IV, concerning the Trinity and Christ, XCVI, 859, 870.

Ernald, abbot of Bonneval.—*On the Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, CLXXXIX, 1589.

Ernulf, bishop of Rochester.—*On Incestuous Marriages*, CLXIII, 1457.

Facundus, bishop of Hermiane.—Twelve books *In Defense of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon*, concerning the Trinity and Christ’s two natures, LXVII, 527. Letter of Catholic Faith in defense of the Three Chapters, ibid., 867.

Faustinus, priest.—*On the Trinity, or on Faith against the Arians*, XIII, 37.

Faustus (Saint), bishop of Riez.—Two books *On God’s Grace and Free Will*, LVIII, 783.

Felix, bishop of Urgel.—*Confession of Faith*, XCVI, 881.

Ferrandus Fulgentius.—Letter III, concerning Christ’s two natures and that one of the Trinity may be called born and having suffered, LXVII, 889. Letter IV, concerning the essence of the Trinity and Christ’s two natures, ibid., 908. Letter V [Col. 0776], that our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity, ibid., 910.

Florus, deacon of Lyons.—Short work *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXIX, 71. Discourse *On Predestination*, ibid., 95. Book *On Predestination, Foreknowledge, and Free Will against John Scotus*, ibid., 101.

Franco, abbot of Affligem.—Twelve books *On God’s Grace*, CLXVI, 717.

Fulbert (Saint), bishop of Chartres.—Treatise *Against the Jews*, concerning the coming of the Messiah, CXLI, 305.

Fulgentius (Saint), bishop of Ruspe.—Three books *To Monimus*: 1. on God’s twofold predestination, one of the good to glory and the other of the wicked to punishment; 2. on the offering of sacrifice and the sending of the Holy Spirit; 3. an exposition of the Gospel words, “And the Word was with God,” LXV, 153. Three books *To King Trasamund of the Vandals*, concerning the mystery of Christ the mediator, who retains two natures in one person; the immensity of the divinity of God the Son; and the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, ibid., 224. Letter VIII, concerning orthodox faith and the various errors of heretics, ibid., 360. Letter XIV, concerning the Trinity and Christ, ibid., 394. Letter XV, concerning God’s grace and human choice, ibid., 435. Letters XVI and XVII, concerning the Incarnation and grace, ibid., 442. Letter XVIII: *Whether Christ’s Flesh Was Corruptible or Incorruptible*, ibid., 493. Book *On the Trinity*, ibid., 497. Book *On the Incarnation of the Son of God*, ibid., 573. Three books *On the Truth of Predestination and God’s Grace*, ibid., 603. Book *On Faith, or on the Rule of True Faith*, ibid., 671. Book *For the Catholic Faith*, ibid., 707. *Instruments of the Catholic Faith*, ibid., 750. Book *On Predestination and Grace*, ibid., 843, in the Appendix.

Gennadius, priest of Marseilles.—Book *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, LVIII, 979.

Gerbert, or Pope Sylvester II.—Short work *On the Lord’s Body and Blood*, CXXXIX, 177.

Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg.—*On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, CXCIV, 1073. Book *Against Two Heresies*, concerning Christ’s glory as equal to God’s glory, ibid., 1161. Treatise *Against Simoniacs*, ibid., 1335. *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist against Folmar*, ibid., 1481.

Gezo, abbot of Derton.—Book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXXXVII, 371.

Gislebert, abbot of Crispin.—*Disputation on the Christian Faith between a Jew and a Christian*, CLIX, 1007.

Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme.—Short work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord Jesus Christ*, CLVII, 211.

Gottschalk, monk of Orbais.—*Confession of Faith*, CXXI, 347.

Walter of Châtillon, master of Tournai.—Book *On the Trinity*, CCIX, 573.

Walter, prior of Saint-Victor.—Extracts from books *Against the Four Labyrinths*, concerning the proposition that Christ is some human being, CXCIX, 1129.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent.—Treatise *On the Incarnation against the Jews*, CLVI, 489. Letter *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body in the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, ibid., 527.

William, abbot of Saint-Thierry.—Book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, CLXXX, 341. Two books *On the Nature of Body and Soul*, ibid., 695.

William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons.—*On the Origin of the Soul*, CLXIII, 1043. Dialogue *On the Catholic Faith between a Christian and a Jew*, ibid., 1046.

Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa.—Short work *On the Lord’s Body and Blood*, CXLIX, 1427. *Confession concerning the Holy Trinity and Christ’s Humanity*, ibid., 1495.

Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt.—*On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXVIII, 815.

Hermann, abbot of Saint-Martin.—Treatise *On the Incarnation of Christ*, CLXXX, 9.

Heterius, bishop of Osma.—Letter to Elipandus, or two books *On Faith in Christ*, XCVI, 893.

Jerome (Saint), priest and Doctor of the Church.—Translation of Didymus’s books *On the Holy Spirit*, XXIII, 103. Dialogue *Against the Luciferians*, ibid., 155. Book *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Blessed Mary*, ibid., 183. Two books *Against Jovinian*, ibid., 211. Book *Against Vigilantius*, ibid., 339. Book *Against John of Jerusalem*, ibid., 355. *Apology against the Books of Rufinus*, ibid., 397. Dialogue *Against the Pelagians*, ibid., 495.

Hilary (Saint), bishop of Poitiers, Doctor of the Church.—Twelve books *On the Trinity*, vigorously defending the faith of the most holy Trinity against heretics, X, 25.

Hildebert the Venerable, archbishop of Tours.—Theological treatise in which various questions are resolved, CLXXI, 1067.

Ildefonsus (Saint), bishop of Toledo.—Book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary*, XCVI, 53. Book *On Knowledge of Baptism*, ibid., 112. Short work *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, ibid., [Col. 0777] 207, among doubtful works. Short work *On the Virgin’s Crown*, ibid., 284, among spurious works.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.—Book *On God’s Predestination and Free Will*, CXXV, 65. Collection *On the One and Not Threefold Deity*, ibid., 473. Short work *On the King’s Person and Royal Ministry*, ibid., 833. Short work *On the Diverse and Multiple Nature of the Soul*, ibid., 929. Short work *On Keeping Faith with the King*, ibid., 961. Short work *For the Defense of the Church’s Liberties*, ibid., 1035. Short work *On Criminal Priests*, ibid., 1093.

Honorius of Autun.—*Elucidarium*, or a dialogue on the sum of all Christian theology, CLXXII, 1109. Book *Of Twelve Questions*, in which the author treats various matters, especially asking whether the holy archangel Michael precedes the blessed Apostle Peter or Peter Michael, ibid., 1177. Short work *Of Eight Questions*, concerning angels and humankind, ibid., 1185. *The Inevitable*, or a dialogue *On Predestination and Free Will*, ibid., 1197. Short work *On Free Will*, ibid., 1223. *The Summit of Glory concerning the Apostle and the Emperor*, or *On the Preeminence of the Priesthood over Kingship*, ibid., 1257.

Hugh of Ribemont.—*Whether the Soul of the First Human Being Was Made from Nothing, and How Sin Is Contracted*, CLXVI, 1319.

Hugh of Saint-Victor.—*Institutions on the Decalogue of the Lord’s Law*, CLXXVI, 9. *On the Sacraments of the Natural and Written Law*, ibid., 17. *Summary of Sentences*, divided into seven treatises: 1. on the three theological virtues, the Trinity, and faith in the Incarnation of the Word; 2. on the creation and condition of angelic nature; 3. on the creation and condition of human nature; 4. on sacraments in general and the divine commandments; 5. on the sacrament of baptism; 6. on the sacrament of confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, and extreme unction; 7. on the sacrament of marriage, ibid., 41. Two books *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*: the first carries the narrative forward from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Word; the second proceeds in order from the Incarnation of the Word to the end and consummation of all things, ibid., 173. Short work *Whether God’s Power or Will Is Greater*, ibid., 839. Short work *On the Four Wills in Christ*, ibid., 842. *Whether the Wisdom of Christ’s Soul Was Equal to the Divine Wisdom*, ibid., 848. *On the Union of Body and Spirit*, CLXXVII, 285. Apology *On the Incarnate Word*, containing objections against those who say that Christ is not something insofar as he is human, ibid., 295.

Hugh Eterianus.—Book *On the Soul Already Stripped of the Body, or on the Return of Souls from Hell*, CCII, 167. Three books *On the Heresies of the Greeks*, or that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, namely Father and Son, ibid., 227.

Hugh, bishop of Langres.—Treatise *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXLII, 1325.

Hugh, archbishop of Rouen.—Seven books of *Dialogues*, especially concerning the highest good; evil and good; creation and the rational creature; freedom of choice and God’s ordinance; the grace of redemption and the sacraments, CXCII, 1141. Three books *Against the Heretics of His Time*, discussing the Church and its ministers, ibid., 1255. Treatise *On Memory*, comprising three books; this work is to be counted among dogmatic writings, for in it the author discusses God, the Trinity, the Incarnation, sin and its origin, and its remedy through redemption, ibid., 1300.

Humbert, cardinal and bishop of Silva Candida.—Three books *Against Simoniacs*, CXLIII, 1289.

Isaac, abbot of Stella.—Short work *On the Soul*, CXCIV, 1875.

Isidore (Saint), bishop of Seville.—Two books *On the Catholic Faith*, LXXXIII, 449. *On the Order of Created Things*, concerning faith in the Trinity, the spiritual creature, the devil and the nature of demons, purgatory, and so forth, ibid., 913. *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, ibid., 1227, in the Appendix.

Jesse, bishop of Amiens.—Book *On Baptism*, CV, 781.

John of Cornwall.—*Eulogy of the Incarnate Word*, proving that Christ is some human being, CXCIX, 1041.

John Scotus Eriugena.—Book *On Predestination*, CXXII, 347.

Jonas, bishop of Orléans.—Three books *On the Veneration of Images*, CVI, 305.

Lactantius Firmianus.—Seven books of *Divine Institutes*: 1. on the false religion of the gods; 2. on the origin of error; 3. on the false wisdom of philosophers; 4. on true wisdom and religion; 5. on justice; 6. on true worship; 7. on the blessed life, VI, 112. Book *On the Wrath of God*, resolving by various arguments the question, “Does God truly become angry?”, VII, 77.

Lanfranc (Blessed), archbishop of Canterbury.—*On the Lord’s Body and* [Col. 0778] *Blood*, CL, 407. Short work *On Keeping Confession Secret*, ibid., 625.

Licinianus, bishop of Carthage.—Letter II, showing that angels and rational souls are spirits, that is, entirely without body, LXXII, 691.

Lupus (Saint), abbot of Ferrières.—Book *On Three Questions*: namely, free will, predestination, and redemption, CXIX, 619. *Collection on Three Questions*, concerning the same matters, ibid., 647.

Mamertus Claudianus, bishop of Vienne.—Three books *On the Condition of the Soul*, LIII, 697.

Marius Mercator.—Scholia *On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*. This treatise is no more distinguished than it is useful, because it contains not only an explanation of three terms difficult to understand—*Christ*, *Emmanuel*, and *Jesus*—knowledge of which is necessary for treating the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, but also a resolution of the involved question how two natures, without confusion and change, came together in the unity of the divine person, XLVIII, 1005.

Marius Victorinus.—Book *To Justinus the Manichaean*, against the two Manichaean principles and concerning Christ’s true flesh, VIII, 999. Book *On the Generation of the Divine Word, to Candidus*, ibid., 1019. Four books *Against Arius*, setting forth the opinions of Arius and Eusebius concerning Jesus: wherein both agree with Catholics, wherein they differ, and wherein they themselves appear to conflict with themselves, ibid., 1039.

Maternus Firmicus.—*On the Error of Profane Religions*, explaining the various cults of nations and refuting their myths and shameful rites, XII, 981.

Maximus (Saint), bishop of Turin.—Three treatises *On Baptism*, LVII, 771. Treatise *Against Pagans and Jews*, ibid., 781.

Nicetas (Saint), bishop of Aquileia.—*On the Reason of Faith*, LII, 847. *On the Power of the Holy Spirit*, ibid., 853. *On the Various Names Applicable to Our Lord Jesus Christ*, ibid., 863.

Novatian, priest.—Book *On the Trinity*, setting forth what should be believed concerning God and his perfections, and what the Church’s faith is concerning the mystery of the most holy Trinity, the divinity of Jesus Christ, and his Incarnation, III, 885.

Odo (Saint), bishop of Cambrai.—Three books *On Original Sin*, CLX, 1071. Book *On the Coming of Christ against the Jews*, ibid., 1103. *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, ibid., 1112.

Paulus Orosius, priest.—Book *On the Freedom of Free Will against Pelagius*, XXXI, 1173.

Otto, priest and monk of Saint-Emmeram.—Dialogue *On Three Questions*: namely, recognition of divine mercy, the diversity of divine judgments, and the varying capacity for acting well, CXLVI, 60.

Paschasius, deacon.—Two books *On the Holy Spirit*, LXII, 9.

Paschasius Radbertus (Saint), abbot of Corbie.—Two books *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, CXX, 1365.

Paulinus (Saint), patriarch of Aquileia.—*Sacrosyllabus*, concerning Christ’s natures and person, XCIX, 152.

Peter of Blois, archdeacon.—Treatise *On the Lord’s Transfiguration*, CCVII, 777. *Instruction in the Catholic Faith Sent to the Sultan of Iconium*, ibid., 1069. *On Sacramental Confession and the Penance to Be Imposed by a Priest*, ibid., 1077.

Peter Chrysolanus, archbishop of Milan.—Discourse *On the Holy Spirit*, proving that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, CLXII, 1007.

Peter Damian (Saint), cardinal.—Short work *On the Catholic Faith*, CXLV, 20. Short work *Against the Jews*, proving the Trinity of persons in the divine essence, and that Christ was God and man and has already come into the world, ibid., 41. Short work *Against the Same Jews*, showing that the precepts of the Mosaic Law were mystical and foreshadowed future things, and therefore came to their end in Christ, ibid., 57. Book called *Gratissimus*, showing at length that those consecrated by simoniacal bishops ought not to be consecrated again, confirmed by many arguments and the authority of the holy Fathers, ibid., 100. Short work *On Degrees of Kinship*, namely on marriage between blood-relatives, ibid., 191. *On the Celibacy of Priests*, ibid., 380. *On Sacraments Administered by Wicked Persons*, ibid., 524. *On the Benefit of Intercessions and Various Miracles*, ibid., 560. *On Divine Omnipotence in the Restoration of Corrupted Nature*, ibid., 595. Short work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Error of the Greeks*, ibid., 633. Short work *On the Time for Celebrating Marriages*, ibid., 660. *On the Ruler’s Duty in Restraining Wrongdoers*, ibid., 819.

Peter the Deacon.—Book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, LXII, 83.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris.—Four books of *Sentences*, concerning the mystery of the Trinity, creation, the Incarnation of the Word, and the sacraments, CXCII, 519.

Peter of Poitiers, chancellor.—Five books of *Sentences*, containing a great many matters concerning the Trinity, the Incarnation, and so forth, CCXI, 783.

Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.—Treatise *Against the Jews*, concerning Christ, CLXXXIX, 507. Treatise *Against the Sect of the Saracens*, ibid., 659. Treatise *Against the Petrobrusian Heretics*, concerning infant baptism, churches, the veneration of the cross, the Eucharist, and sacrifices to be offered for the dead, ibid., 719.

Philip of Harveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance.—Response *On the Salvation of the First Human Being*, CCIII, 593.

Phoebadius (Saint), bishop of Agen.—Two short works *Against the Arians*, concerning the Son’s divinity and consubstantiality, XX, 13.

Prosper (Saint) of Aquitaine.—Letter to Rufinus, concerning grace and free will, LI, 77. Two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, concerning God’s grace and human will, ibid., 647.

Prudentius (Saint), bishop of Troyes.—Letter to Hincmar and Pardulus, concerning predestination, grace, and free will, CXV, 971. Book *On Predestination*, ibid., 1009.

Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda.—Letter and treatise *On Marriages of Blood-Relatives*, CX, 1083. Treatise *On Magical Arts*, ibid., 1095. Two short works resolving many questions, especially whether chorepiscopi may ordain with their bishop’s consent, ibid., 1187. The first five books *On the Universe*, in which many dogmatic and moral matters are found, CXI, 13. Letter III, *On the Lord’s Body and Blood*, CXII, 1510. Letters IV, V, and VI, concerning God’s foreknowledge and predestination, ibid., 1518, 1530, 1553.

Ratramnus, monk of Corbie.—Two books *On God’s Predestination*, CXXI, 13. *On the Nativity of God, or That Christ Was Born of a Virgin*, ibid., 81. Book *On the Lord’s Body and Blood*, ibid., 103. Four books *Against the Objections of the Greeks, Who Slander the Roman Church*, concerning the Holy Spirit and certain usages of the Roman Church, ibid., 223.

Remigius (Saint), bishop of Lyons.—Book *On Three Letters*, concerning God’s foreknowledge, predestination, redemption, grace, and free will, CXXI, 985. *On the Universal Condemnation of All through Adam and the Particular Deliverance through Christ of the Elect from That Same Condemnation*, ibid., 1067. Short work *On Firmly Maintaining the Truth of Scripture*, concerning free will and grace, ibid., 1083.

Remigius, monk.—Treatise *On the Dedication of a Church*, CXXXI, 845.

Richard of Saint-Victor, canon of Paris.—Two books *On Emmanuel*, refuting various Jewish objections concerning our Emmanuel, CXCVI, 601. Six books *On the Trinity*, ibid., 887. *On the Three Persons Appropriated in the Trinity*, ibid., 991. Book *On the Incarnate Word*, acutely showing that it was necessary for God to become incarnate, and that no person was more fitting than the Son, ibid., 995. *How the Holy Spirit Is the Love of Father and Son*, ibid., 1011. *On the Preeminent Baptism of Christ*, ibid., 1012. *On the Sending of the Holy Spirit*, ibid., 1017. *On the Power of Loosing and Binding*, ibid., 1159. Treatise *On the Spirit of Blasphemy*, ibid., 1185. *On the Difference between Mortal and Venial Sin*, ibid., 1191.

Robert Pullus, cardinal.—Eight books of *Sentences*, concerning God, God the Creator, the triune God, Christ, and many other matters, CLXXXVI, 673.

Rufinus, priest of Aquileia.—Commentary *On the Apostles’ Creed*, XXI, 335. Book *On Faith*, ibid., 1123.

Rupert, abbot of Deutz.—Forty-two books of the treatise *On the Trinity and Its Works*, CLXVII, 200. Seven books *On the Lord’s Incarnation in the Song of Songs*, CLXVIII, 839. Ten books *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man, on Matthew*, ibid., 1307. Nine books *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, CLXIX, 13. Thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word of God*, ibid., 217. One book *On the Will of God*, CLXX, 437. One book *On God’s Omnipotence*, ibid., 453. *Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew*, in which the Christian invites the Jew to the Catholic faith, while the Jew, as far as possible, counters the Christian from the letter of the Law and from his own understanding, ibid., 561.

Samuel Marochianus.—Book *On Christ’s Past Coming, against the Jews*, CXLIX, 433.

Tertullian, priest.—Book *On Baptism*, concerning baptism’s necessity and efficacy, I, 1197. Book *Against Praxeas*; in this treatise the Church’s faith concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and Incarnation is clearly explained, II, 153. Book *On the Soul*, concerning the state of the soul and other questions pertaining to it, ibid., 641. Book *On Christ’s Flesh*, proving that Christ’s flesh was both born from the Virgin and human, ibid., 751. Book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ibid., 791.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.—Book *On the Holy Spirit*, that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, CV, 240.

Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.—*Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, LXXXVIII, 585.

Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus.—Five books *Against Eutyches*, concerning Christ’s two natures and one person, LXII, 95. Twelve books *On the Trinity*, ibid., 237. Book *On the Unity of the Trinity*, ibid., 333. Three books *Against Marivadus*, concerning the Trinity of unity and the unity of the Trinity, ibid., 351. Treatise *On the Nicene Faith*, ibid., 466.

Vincent of Lérins.—*Commonitory*, or treatise for the antiquity and universality of the Catholic faith against the profane novelties of all heretics, L, 637.

Vivianus of Prémontré.—Treatise *On Free Will and Grace*, CLXVI, 1319.

Walafrid Strabo, monk of Fulda.—Book *On the Origins and Developments of Ecclesiastical Things*, CXIV, 919.

Zacchaeus the Christian.—Three books of *Consultations*, in which many doctrines of the Christian religion are affirmed, XX, 1071.

Zeno (Saint), bishop of Verona.—Second book of *Treatises*: throughout it the author devotes himself to defending the divinity of the eternal Word against the Arians, XI, 385.

### On the Incarnate and Redeeming Word of God
*Book Against Praxeas*; Tertullian, II, 153. *Book on the Flesh of Christ*; the same, II, 751. *Book on the Trinity*; Novatian, III, 885. *Book on the Vanity of Idols*; St Cyprian, IV, 563. # TENTH SERIES

[Col. 0797]

## PREFACE

The Church is the mother and teacher of all the faithful whom she bears for Christ; hence the sacraments and graces are given and received in her alone. Accordingly, this Tenth Series comprises everything that we have gathered concerning these matters.

First, we set forth the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning grace itself and its connection with human free choice: how it has been attacked by heretics and most vigorously defended by the orthodox. We treat of the sacraments in general, both under the Mosaic and under the Gospel law, and of their number, power, and efficacy. We then consider each one separately: baptism, namely, and its necessity, matter, and form; confirmation and its excellence and effects; the Eucharist, insofar as it is at once sacrifice and sacrament; the sacrifice of the Mass, the distinctive and highest act of the Catholic religion; penance, both as a virtue and as a sacrament, together with the parts required for it—contrition, confession, and satisfaction; canonical penance, formerly practised in the Church; extreme unction and its effects upon body and soul; orders, by which spiritual power is bestowed, and the conditions necessary for them; marriage, with the duties and obligations that arise from it; second marriages; polygamy. In short, in this series we bring together everything relating to the sacraments and to grace.

[Col. 0799]

# XCIV. INDEX OF GRACE, HUMAN FREE CHOICE, PREDESTINATION, AND REPROBATION

## NOTICE

In this index, in turn and in logical order, we set forth everything that the Fathers have said concerning the name *grace*, its essence, nature, necessity, and effects, and likewise concerning its harmony with human free choice. We also record the various errors concerning grace and the writers who have defended it more vigorously. But amid subjects so numerous and important, in order that the work may prove at once more suitable and more fruitful for the reader, we divide it into four parts. We present: first, general notions of the questions taken together; second, the dogmas and teachings of the Catholic faith concerning divine grace, human free choice, predestination, and reprobation; third, definitions and opinions regarding each matter considered separately; fourth, a treatment of Pelagianism and Semipelagianism. Under every article, we observe an alphabetical order of the Fathers, indicating volume and column.

# PART ONE

## SOLE SECTION. Survey, or General Notions of the Questions

This section notes the passages in which these questions—namely, God’s grace and foreknowledge, human free choice, predestination, and reprobation—are treated in connection and together, in their relation to one another as preceding or following. Since these matters are all exceedingly intricate, and no one of them can be raised without presupposing another bound up with it, we do not doubt that this general survey offers its own usefulness; and we have therefore determined that it should take first place.

# PART TWO. Dogmas and Teachings of the Catholic Faith concerning Divine Grace, Human Free Choice, Predestination, and Reprobation, according to the Method of Discussion and Catechesis

[Col. 0803]

## SECTION ONE. On Grace Freely Given

First, it must be said that, generally speaking, the name *grace*, whatever grace may be in question, signifies unmerited favour, mercy, undeserved generosity—something which we cannot earn for ourselves. For when God bestows grace upon a human being, he finds in that person nothing but sin, corruption, and misery.

Those graces, however, which are called “freely given” are external and belong to the order of nature.

Here, therefore, the treatment is: first, of merely natural gifts, such as bodily health and strength, maturity of judgment, ingenuity and keenness of intellect, prudence, temperance, and other gifts of this kind, which are common to unbelievers and Christians, good and evil alike; second, of God’s gifts situated outside ourselves, such as Christ’s incarnation and death, sacred preaching, counsels, miracles, and so forth; third, of the gifts of tongues, prophecy, miracles, the interpretation of Scripture, proclaiming the divine word, and so forth. These graces are given chiefly for the conversion of unbelievers and other sinners, for the instruction of the faithful, and, in a word, for the salvation of one’s neighbour.

## SECOND SECTION. On grace that makes pleasing.

These graces are interior and belong to the supernatural order; nor are they less freely given than the preceding ones, since every grace whatsoever proceeds from God’s sheer goodwill and generosity, without any natural merits. Yet, according to the customary theological manner of speaking, graces that make pleasing are those granted by God, in the order—as they call it—of our salvation: such as the devout affections infused into us by God, devout desires, virtues, and holy aspirations by which we are moved and drawn toward the things of God; for example, the gift of faith, hope, charity, and the moral virtues. Strictly speaking, however, if we attend to the force of the term, this name ought to be understood only of sanctifying grace, which reconciles us to God and makes us, from sinners, righteous; from enemies of God, his friends and children. Here, therefore, there is discussion of this habitual, or sanctifying, grace; further, of actual grace, which is illumination of the mind and a devout affection impressed by God upon our hearts, by which we are moved to flee evil and do good; of exciting, or sufficient and efficacious, grace, which not only prompts us toward good but causes us to do it; of inefficacious grace, which lacks the effect toward which it prompts; and finally of prevenient, subsequent, or accompanying grace, operative and cooperative grace, and the other graces usually treated by theologians.

## FOURTH SECTION. On human free will.

For a human being to merit or demerit before God, free will is necessary; nor are we ever determined by the grace of God of necessity, either toward good or toward evil.

## FIFTH SECTION. On the reconciliation of human free will with God’s grace.

The question is examined whether human free will was weakened in Adam’s descendants by Adam’s sin, but not extinguished; whether we are inclined toward evil and cannot will supernatural good unless our freedom is aided and awakened by God’s grace—that is, whether by our own powers we cannot live piously and holily, but for this purpose God’s grace is altogether necessary to us, with free will accompanying it, so that the principal cause of a good work, although the good work becomes ours, must be ascribed to grace itself. And unless this inward grace is present for each individual act, we can do absolutely nothing profitable for salvation: we cannot keep God’s commandments, rise from sin, pray to God, desire or possess a saving knowledge or love of virtue and truth, or do anything conducive to salvation; indeed, we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think anything good, but all our sufficiency is from God through Christ. But with the inward grace of Christ we can carry out and fulfil God’s commandments; for although we can do nothing of ourselves as though from ourselves, we can do all things in him who strengthens us. God does not command impossibilities, but by commanding he admonishes us both to do what we can and to ask for what we cannot do, and he helps us so that we can do it. This great necessity of God’s grace proceeds from God’s supreme dominion over creatures, by which creatures continually require the Creator’s influence in order to act; from the weakness which we have contracted through sin; and from the exceedingly great distance of natural power and means from supernatural ends and effects.

[Col. 0810]

Hence it is evident that external graces and graces belonging to the natural order are not sufficient for performing a good work profitable for salvation, since the grace of Christ—which inwardly affects, is received, and moves—is so necessary.

## SIXTH SECTION. On the predestination and reprobation of human beings.

1. It is certain that some persons are predestined and elected by God, and, conversely, that some are reprobated. . . . But what is God’s order in the mystery of predestination and reprobation? These questions are difficult to approach. Although it may be said a thousand times: “If the origin of all is equally corrupted, if all are born sinners and wrapped in the mass of original corruption, why then does God have mercy upon this one and not another?” the answer must always be: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” But if the guilt of all is one, there is no ground for anyone’s complaint. God owes nothing to anyone; he is Lord. Let it suffice that grace is never denied or withdrawn by God from any human being except as punishment for some preceding sin.

2. Besides God’s general will to save all, and although Christ died for all, there is in God a special and efficacious will to save some, and in Christ a will to communicate to some the benefit of his death and the merit of his passion. God does not give the gift of perseverance to all, but to whom he wills and in whatever manner he wills, according to the good pleasure of his will. And, Christ’s death remaining in force, although no human being is excluded from the right to receive the sacraments if he or she approaches them or is presented for them, it is certain that those who die without receiving remission of their sins are not saved—though they would have been saved if it had pleased God to deal mercifully with them. Thus, although in God there is a general but sincere will to save all, a will which theologians call antecedent—that is, a will which precedes foreknowledge of merits—there is also what is called a consequent will. By this latter will God wills to punish the guilty and sinful. Therefore, when God assigns some to eternal punishments, whether infants who die without having received baptism or adults who fall after baptism, he renders a just punishment to those who deserve it. Others he spares in mercy and, having drawn them by ineffable kindness from the mass of corruption, calls, justifies, and glorifies them with the gift of final perseverance; others, whom justice leaves in the corruption they have incurred, he permits to die in their sins and to be damned.

3. Human free will stands together with divine grace, predestination, and reprobation, since we can resist God’s grace and the merit of works is ours. Hence the whole merit of a human being consists in the right use of grace. For if anyone cooperates with God’s grace—which indeed is also from Christ—he or she obtains new grace; and through Christ one advances from grace to grace unto eternal life. At last the righteous Judge and merciful Father will render that life, heaping crowns upon his gifts; or, as the Church sings, “in crowning our merits, he crowns his own gifts.”

[Col. 0813] 4. Since the grace of justification is never withdrawn from a person unless mortal sin has first occurred, and since God abandons no one by withdrawing either actual or habitual grace unless He has first been abandoned by that person, one must provide for one’s own salvation with fear and trembling, put one’s trust in God alone, devote oneself constantly to prayer and good works, and keep the most vigilant watch lest negligence or any sin should creep in; finally, one must keep one’s spirit lowly and humbled beneath the mighty hand of God.

## PART THREE. Catholic dogmas and teachings concerning grace, etc., in the form of definitions and propositions.

## SECTION ONE.

### 1. Propositions concerning divine grace, drawn from Sacred Scripture.

To this category belong, first and directly, the Fathers’ commentaries, homilies, sermons, and treatises on the texts of Sacred Scripture which wholly remove our works—that is, works done from ourselves—from the business of our justification and salvation, and commend God’s grace alone. Such texts are:

### Propositions concerning divine grace collected from the Fathers.

These propositions are for the most part drawn word for word from the Fathers’ writings. They are principal propositions, as it were the hinges and axioms upon which the Catholic doctrine of the Catholic faith concerning divine grace is founded. We select only certain Fathers who have treated the present question in a special and, as it were, systematic manner.

### ADAM, Premonstratensian canon.

CXCVIII, 103. The same grace of the Saviour which preserved the angel raised fallen man. 116. Grace is both preservation from sins and their remission. 171. Gratitude for benefits received calls forth new benefits. 213, 214. In the absence of grace the soul is troubled, and in its presence it rests. 227, 331. Every good must be attributed to God’s grace. 248. The four marks of grace are signified by the four heads of the river of Paradise. 250. Grace is the seed of glory. 251, 351. Grace perfects intellect and will. 252. The grace of the Saviour appears to all; it instructs the elect alone unto salvation. 245, 264. Grace is creative in the Father, saving in the Son, confirming in the Holy Spirit; and the grace of glory belongs wholly to the Holy Trinity. 256. Reform of life is the work of special grace. 355, 426. How providential is the distribution of diverse graces among different persons.

### Saint AMBROSE, archbishop of Milan.

XIV, 88. Divine activity can infuse pursuits of piety into sacrilegious hearts. 329, 333, 346. SECOND SECTION.

Definitions and statements concerning free choice. From Holy Scripture.

Many statements about the free choice of man are found among the Fathers in commentaries on the following passages of Holy Scripture:

Genesis IV, 17, according to the Septuagint: “If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, sin will immediately be present at the doors; yet its desire will be subject to you, and you shall rule over it.” Deuteronomy XXX, 19: “I call heaven and earth as witnesses today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose therefore life.” Joshua XXIV, 15: “But if it seems evil to you to serve the Lord, the choice is given to you; choose therefore what pleases you.” Tobit XIII, 8: “Therefore turn back, you sinners, and do justice before God.” Psalm XXXI, 9: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.” Psalm LXXXIX, 3: “Turn back, O children of men.” Psalm CXVIII, 59: “Turn my feet toward your testimonies.” Ecclesiasticus XV, 14: “God established man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel; he added his commandments and precepts. If you are willing to keep the commandments, they will preserve you. He set before you water and fire; stretch forth your hand to whichever you will. Before man are life and death, good and evil; what pleases him shall be given to him.” Acts VII, 57: “You always resist the Holy Spirit.” I Corinthians VII, 37: “For he who has determined firmly in his heart, having no necessity, but possessing authority over his own will, and has judged this in his heart—to keep his virgin—does well.” II Corinthians VI, 1: “Do not receive the grace of God in vain.” Hebrews XII, 15: “Watching lest [Col. 0828] anyone fall short of the grace of God.” Revelation III, 20: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I shall enter to him.”

Statements collected from the holy Fathers.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux.

CLXXXII, 1002, 1005, 1018. What free choice is. 1002. Free choice cooperates with grace by consenting. 1006. From what kind of freedom free choice is so called. 1015. Free choice can fall by itself; it cannot rise again, either from evil to good or from good to better. 1024. Salvation belongs not to free choice, but to the Lord. 1027. The inseparable operation of free choice and grace.

CLXXXIV, 204. Free choice was not removed in the state of fallen nature. 206. It is one thing freely to will the good, another to will it affectionately. 361. Free choice is of no value without grace.

CYPRIAN (Saint), bishop of Carthage.

IV, 507, 760. What free choice is. 526. We ask that sanctification and quickening may be preserved in us through God’s protection. 530. We ask that we may be able to do what God wills. 537. God wills those reborn to persevere as he made us in the second birth. 536, 596. God permitted us to be tempted; everything occurs through divine condescension.

DRUTHMAR, Christian.

CVI, 1313. Whatever evil we have done is our own. 1353. Whatever good we have done, we shall receive a reward for it in the Lord’s name, either in this age or in the age to come. 1361. Each person is judged according to his will. 1466. God has left man in free choice, whether he wishes to keep the commandments or not. 1487. A person ought to guard against calling good evil or evil good.

FAUSTUS (Saint), bishop of Riez.

LVIII, 795. How the weakness of free choice should be understood. [Col. 0830] 796. On passages of Scripture that seem to remove every power of free choice. 799, 803, 804. Whether willing and not willing, as regards evil, so also as regards the good side, were entrusted to human choice.

FULGENTIUS (Saint), bishop of Ruspe.

LXV, 395, 436, 474. Free choice after sin: free indeed, but not good. 439. It is in no way made fit to fulfill the commandments unless it is helped by God. 505. The sinner has free choice for evil; for good he has it only when set free. 629. Both the good and the ungodly possess free choice: in the good it is upright, in the evil it is wholly turned away from God.

GREGORY THE GREAT I (Saint), pope.

LXXV, 174. What the free choice of the first man was capable of meriting in the state of innocence. 1026. We sin by free choice at the devil’s suggestion.

LXXIX, 277. Let no one follow his own free choice. 647. Since free choice was corrupted in the first parent, we cannot will the good unless helped by grace. 211. In victory over temptations, what belongs to the gift of grace and what to free choice.

GUIBERT OF NOGENT, abbot.

CLVI, 64. We sin by will, not by necessity. 74. The human will is fragile and changeable. 140. The effort of free choice prepares us to receive what grace pours in. 170. By our free choice we both plant and water; but what we do among ourselves is nothing unless God gives the increase through grace. 313. The earthliness of our affections is left to our own choice. 548. Faith consists in free choice, with grace going before.

JEROME (Saint), presbyter.

XXII, 815. An affirmation of free choice. 1154. Those who readily abuse it against the giver’s benefit destroy freedom of choice.

XXIII, 284. God created us with free choice; we are drawn by necessity neither to virtues nor to vices. 500. Free choice is preserved in our willing and running, but in the completion of willing and running all things are left to God’s power.

XXIV, 465. Man’s free choice is shown. 551. It lies in our choice to choose good or evil. 843. Why free choice is preserved for man.

ILDEFONSUS (Saint), bishop of Toledo.

XCVI, 145. Merit is acquired according to how each person has acted well in the body. 148. The pillar of fire and cloud, following and preceding the Hebrews, shows that free choice is governed by prevenient grace and God’s mercy.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims.

CXXV, 130. Man was created upright, without sin, and with free choice. 131. God willed that he should remain in righteousness, but he fell through free choice. 132. Fallen man became a mass of perdition for the whole human race. 182. Man did not lose free choice altogether, but weakened it. 183. We lost freedom of choice in the first man; we receive it through Christ. 184. We possess free choice for good when it is preceded and helped by grace; but for evil when grace abandons it.

PAUL THE DEACON (PAULUS WINFRIDUS).

XCV, 1206. By willing obedience a person will easily make God favorable, if, having turned, he has now changed his vice. 1214. The negligent and slothful servant will be condemned. 1216. A reward is due to the merits of free choice. 1217. Those who consume their lives in their wickedness, and are called accursed, prepare themselves for eternal curse. 1227. Every person, insofar as he is created by God, is good; and insofar as through free choice he has subjected himself to the devil by sinning, is evil. 1270. Free choice often makes the good planting of nature bad through an evil will. 1402. There are some who, converted by God’s grace from unbelief to faith, nevertheless persist ungratefully by good activity. 1402. A person is said to walk when he sets the step of a good work upon the way of God’s commandments.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint), archbishop of Ravenna.

LII, 390. When free choice obeys the Gospel, it is a benefit of the one who calls; and we need prayer so that it may be constrained by God. 512. How free choice was held captive by the devil. 458. Free choice, not necessity, causes sin. 479. To will and not to be able is the condition of free choice left to itself alone. 549. The will to sin is not taken away by fear of men.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz.

CVII, 215. Only the person is worthy of the fellowship of the elect who, helped by grace, fulfills according to his measure and capacity the decrees of the law understood spiritually. 232. Let no one claim the grace of his calling on the basis of preceding good works of his own. 318. To believe and purpose good things through God’s inspiration belongs to us. 336. Every work can be corrupted according to [Col. 0831] our will. 1133. If we do our own will rather than God’s, our praise will be obscured.

CIX, 659. Whoever does not wish to hear what the Lord commands cannot merit from the Lord what he asks. 675. God imposes upon no one the necessity of an evil word or wrongful deed. 713. Unless sustained by divine help, human weakness, failing in innumerable uses, will be reduced to nothing. 863. Free choice, blinded through itself, cannot illumine itself; it has been turned, not overthrown.

CX, 431. It belongs to us only to entrust our will jointly to God. 577. Discernment must not be neglected in a good work.

CXII, 170. Human beings have been left to their own choice; for they do not do good by necessity but by will, so that believers may receive a crown and unbelievers be consigned to punishment. 304. Human nature was capable of wounding itself by free choice; but once wounded and injured, it is not capable of healing itself by free choice. 1546. The will is always free in us, but not always good.

PROSPER (Saint), bishop of Aquitaine.

LI, 81. What free choice is like with or without God. 86. It is now not destroyed, but reborn. 123. After the fall it remains and is not wholly destroyed, but weakened for good and bound for evil; wherever it is carried, it falls and slips. 126. Free choice is not taken away when it is healed and liberated through grace. 127. Free choice cannot heal itself, but the grace of Christ can. 160. Before faith there is free choice, but it acts in darkness. 161. What free choice is like before grace and how grace heals it. 207. The harmony of free choice with divine help: no one uses free choice well without grace. 228. Free choice is not taken away by God’s grace, but is formed, governed, and ordered. 239. Free choice is evil through a defect of will, good only by the help of grace. 654. A person does not lose free choice when he is led by the Spirit of God, nor when he voluntarily gives himself to the devil.

SEDULIUS SCOTUS.

CIII, 62. A person has it in his own hand and within the power of his choice whether he is a servant of sin or of righteousness. 67. He has the will to act well, but like a captive he is compelled to do what he does not will. 78. We do not know what we ought to pray for or ask of God. 87. My very willing and running are not mine without God’s help. 88. A person cannot reach the prize of God’s heavenly calling unless he has run by will. 120. The freedom which we have in the Lord makes all things clean for us. 133. We have nothing of our own except the reward of our labor.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage.

II, 290. Man is said to have been made in God’s image in the power and freedom of free choice, not in bodily lineaments. 291. The power and freedom of choice, voluntarily exercised by man, makes good his own. 292. The power of choice was granted for either direction. 913. Even if we know what God wills and does not will, the will and choice to choose either belongs to us. 916. What has been placed in our choice must not be referred to God’s will; for every offense would be excused if we maintained that nothing happens in us through the choice of our own will.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.

CXIII, 176. God’s permission is just when he leaves the person who chooses the former things to his own free choice, so that he may fall.

CXIV, 101. The freedom of our choice must be joined through grace to God’s will, which is our sanctification. 503. In order to be moved to believe true things, the will is insufficient for itself unless God’s grace assists it. 951. Grace precedes all merits, so that our merits may follow God’s gifts; for grace does not arise from merit, but merit from grace, and works from grace, not grace from works. 672. Vices come to us not from God but from ourselves.

THIRD SECTION.

Definitions and statements concerning divine predestination.

From Holy Scripture.

The following texts are especially adduced for this question:

Romans IX, 16–26: “But it is not as though the word of God has failed: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’ ‘I shall have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I shall show mercy to whom I show mercy.’ Does not the potter have power from the same lump of clay to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? ‘I shall call not-my-people, my people; and her who had not received mercy, one who has received mercy.’” Romans XI, 1–32: “Has God rejected his people? But if some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive, have been grafted among them, do not boast. See therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who have fallen, but God’s goodness toward you. For just as you also once did not believe God, but now have received mercy because of their unbelief. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.”

From the holy Fathers.

ADAM THE SCOT, Premonstratensian abbot.

CXCVIII, 222, 283. The elect and the reprobate have one lot in being born, but diverse manners of living. 251, 252. Receiving God’s grace benefits the elect alone. 773, 830. The sins of the elect are, as it were, not present to eternity. 818. For the elect all things, even sins, cooperate for good. 829. Although God permits the elect to fall, he nevertheless mercifully turns them back to himself through his grace. 832. The elect never sin unto death in such a way as to be condemned after death.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo.

XXXII, 1270. It is necessary that the person concerning whom there is a predestination to sin should sin, although he is not compelled to sin. 1275. Predestination does not cause sin not to be committed by free will, or cause us to do anything else. 1277. By predestination it comes about that, just as God rightly punishes those whom he foresees will sin, so he justly rewards those whom he foresees will act rightly. 1278. God is good in creating a creature whom he foreknew would not sin and one whom he foreknew would sin.

XXXIII, 633, 639. Predestination is not from human merit but from grace. 639. Why some belong to predestination and others do not may have a hidden cause; it cannot have an unjust cause. 744. Not one of those for whom Christ died perishes. 879. Why one believes and another does not, though both hear the same thing, is the depth of God’s judgments. 883. Let whoever can investigate why God frees this person rather than that one, but let him beware of the precipice. 886. The number of the predestined is fixed, and the causes of predestination are inscrutable.

XXXIV, 887. Predestination is not from foreknowledge of good works. 982. To end one’s life in a consenting will belongs to the salutary teaching of the elect.

XXXV, 1725. The predestined sometimes err and are outside. 1742. Those who are predestined err for a time and do not perish eternally. 1743. The wolf and the thief destroy only those predestined for destruction. 1776. Predestination compels neither sinning nor devout living.

XXXVII, 1932. Those whom God predestined, he calls to repentance. 1962. Our predestination was not made in us, but secretly with God.

XXXVIII, 179. In God, who has mercy on whom he wills, there is no injustice. 304. He who predestined knows the sheep and the goats. 862. No one can harm the non-predestined. 1030. No one of the predestined will perish with the devil, and no one will remain under the devil’s power until death.

XL, 275. God’s judgments are hidden and inscrutable in the predestination of human beings. 277. Jacob was loved and Esau hated before any merits of their own; in the hatred of Esau a punitive judgment is imposed upon one worthy of it, while in the love of Jacob mercy is bestowed upon one unworthy of it.

XLI, 941. Mercy accompanies the predestined in whatever state they may be.

XLII, 614. The number of the predestined is great.

XLIII, 537, 582. How the predestined are few and many.

XLIV, 179. All are saved through the one mediator and through one and the same faith. 535. Predestination to eternal life and to eternal death. 620, 761. Why God makes some sheep and does not make others is an inscrutable question; nevertheless, there is no injustice with God. 940. No one is certain and secure concerning his own salvation and predestination.

XLV, 938. Those who fall and perish are not in the number of the predestined. 975. How predestination and grace differ. 985. The immovable truth of predestination. 1018. What is alleged against the preaching of predestination can likewise be said against grace. 1031. Predestination, preached as it ought to be, is not a cause of despair. 1136. From the same mass some are freed by God’s grace, while others are not freed by God’s judgment. 1200. In comparison with those who perish, those who are saved are few; but without comparison with those who perish, they too are many. 1523. The inscrutable depth of predestination and grace in the distinction between infants who reach baptism.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux.

CLXXXII, 203. The economy of predestination. 246. Predestination is preparation for justification.

[Col. 0833] CLXXXIII, 203. The means of predestination. 297. Signs of predestination. 302. Predestination is uncertain. 352. The beginning and end of predestination belong to grace alone; the work must also be attributed to us. 891. The happy state of the predestined, a heavenly generation.

CLXXXIV, 158. Divine predestination is ineffable. 158. The effect of predestination is human zeal or diligence. 553. Justification in the present is in some manner a certain signification of future predestination.

FAUSTUS (Saint), bishop of Riez.

LVIII, 811, 812. Predestination in no way impels people either toward good or toward evil. 814. Predestination did nothing directly in the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart. 817, 819. The one who perishes was able, as well as willing, to be saved.

FULGENTIUS (Saint), bishop of Ruspe.

LXV, 157. Knowledge of predestination is established. 157. God disposed, in his will, the future effect of renewing man. 158. XXII, 427. The subject matter of predestination.

XXIII, 343. Through foreknowledge and predestination, those things which are future have already been made. Predestination does not take away free choice, but indicates antecedent causes why each thing has occurred.

XXVI, 453. Concepts of predestination.

PROSPER (Saint), bishop of Aquitaine.

God’s predestination is neither uncertain, nor mutable counsel, nor ineffective will, nor a false promise.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter of Carthage.

II, 290. Predestination has as many witnesses as there have been prophets. 294. God, in disposing all things, foreknew them; and in foreknowing them, disposed them. 718. The children of believers are a certain kind of predestination. 915. It is not the mark of good and solid hope to refer everything so to God’s will that we do not understand that something exists in ourselves. 917. Not everything that God permits proceeds from his mere and entire will.

Since a heresy called Predestinatianism arose concerning predestination, certain matters seem to require addition here.

From Saint AUGUSTINE, LIII, 673–691: The beginnings of Predestinatianism in Africa among the monks of Hadrumetum.

They were detected by Saint Augustine and Evodius. When this heresy emerged among the Gauls, Saint Prosper and Saint Hilary appealed to Saint Augustine for assistance by letters; and, on their representations, the Predestinatians were censured by Pope Celestine in a letter to the bishops of Gaul. The author of the *Praedestinatus* was the first to attack the heresy of the Predestinatians; Gennadius of Marseille is refuted. The Predestinatians were condemned in the councils of Arles and Lyons. Faustus of Riez opposed the Predestinatian Lucidus. Possessor and John Maxentius appear, and the Council of Orange issued a decree condemning this heresy. Ennodius of Pavia [Col. 0834] is still one combatant against Predestinatianism . . . At last this heresy was renewed in Gaul through Gottschalk, and was crushed in two synods by Rabanus and Hincmar. An ecclesiastical sentence against Gottschalk was issued at the Synod of Quierzy, by twelve bishops. Whatever may be said, neither the Church of Lyons nor the Synod of Valence supports the errors of the Predestinatians in the case of Gottschalk.

See further LI, 1002; LIII, 673, 617, 620, 621, 624, 674, 685; CXXI, 347; CXXV, 50 and following; etc., where matters concerning predestination are reported in various places.

PART FOUR.

FIRST SECTION. On Pelagianism, Semi-Pelagianism, and Jansenism. The chief points of both heresies are almost the same.

Since these taught more or less the same things, or at least since the difference between their heresies can scarcely be distinguished without close attention, we have combined them in this Index, judging that those who wish to investigate it most carefully will note, in the inquiries indicated here, the slight points of difference.
