# XCV. INDEX CONCERNING THE SACRAMENTS IN GENERAL

In this index are treated in turn the nature of the sacraments, both of the Old and the New Law; their institution and number; their matter and form; their power, minister, and recipient; and so forth. Books dealing with the sacraments are also listed.

## I. The nature of a sacrament

Sacraments are so called because one thing is seen in them and another understood, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1247. Signs, when they pertain to divine realities, are called sacraments, ibid., XXXIII, 527. If sacraments had no likeness whatsoever to those things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all, ibid., 364. Bodily sacraments are, as it were, visible words, ibid., XLII, 356. A sacrament is a visible word, ibid., XXXV, 1840. Why sacraments are so called, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 309. What sacraments are, or why they are so called, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1275; Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 146. A sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, CLXXXVI, 102. What a sacrament is, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1089; Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, CXCII, 1211; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1227; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1145.

## II. The ancient sacraments

Certain Jewish believers maintained that those who believed in Christ could not be saved without the ancient sacraments, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 278, 279. The sacraments of the Old Law were commanded solely for signification, ibid., [Col. 0836] XLIV, 594. They were divinely given to signify future things, and so forth, ibid., XXXIII, 281. What the sacraments of the Old Testament signify, ibid., XXXVI, 954, 955. The ancient sacraments were a shadow of things to come, ibid., XLIV, 222. The sacraments of the Law foretold Christ who was to come, ibid., XLII, 355, 357, 359. The ancient sacraments were necessary before Christ, ibid., XXXIII, 156. The ancient sacraments were superfluous after Christ, ibid. The ancient sacraments were not harmful to the first Christians, but neither were they necessary, ibid., XLII, 357. The ancient sacraments are neither good nor bad, ibid., XXXII, 281. Those signs of the Old Testament were not condemned, but passed away when more fitting ones succeeded them, ibid., XXXIII, 96. The ancient sacraments were not to be imposed upon the Gentiles, ibid., XLII, 357. Why did the Apostle undertake to observe Jewish sacraments? Ibid., XXXIII, 278, 279, 282. The Apostle observed the ancient sacraments not by deceptive pretence but by prudent counsel, ibid., XLII, 357. Why sacraments were permitted to the Jews in the age of the apostles, ibid., XL, 536. How long the first Christians who believed from among the Jews were permitted to observe the ancient sacraments, ibid., XLII, 357, 358. Christ did not annul the ancient sacraments, but changed them, ibid., 53. The change made by Christ in the ancient sacraments, foretold in the Psalms, ibid., 53, 54, 55. On the difference between the ancient and new sacraments, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 840.

## III. Sacraments of the New Law: their excellence, difference, and so forth

[Col. 0837]

The sacraments of Christians are more divine and prior to those of the Jews, St. Ambrose, XVI, 420. The excellence of the sacraments of the New Law, St. Augustine, XXXII, 200. The distinction between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, ibid., XXXVI, 931; XLIII, 289. The new sacraments are greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in performance, and fewer in number than the ancient ones, ibid., XLII, 355. What difference exists between the sacraments of the Old Law and those of the New, Hervaeus of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXI, 1597. How the sacraments of the Old and New Law differ, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1091; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1229. That there are three kinds of sacraments, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 327.

## IV. Institution and number of the sacraments of the New Law, and so forth

Who is the author of the sacraments, St. Ambrose, XVI, 439. What is the cause of the institution of the sacraments, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1227. Four matters to be considered in the institution of the sacraments, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 317. Why sacraments were instituted, ibid., 319. Their institution is a dispensation with respect to God, and a necessity with respect to man, ibid., 323. There are three reasons for which sacraments were instituted, ibid., 117. Why sacraments were instituted, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1090; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXIV, 1145. The sacraments flowed from Christ’s side, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1513; XXXVI, 161, 668. Enumeration of the sacraments, Tertullian, II, 806; Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 519. Why sacraments were given to human beings, William, CLXXXIV, 406; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 839.

## V. On the matter and form of the sacraments of the New Law

The word is added to the element, and a sacrament comes into being, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1840. On the matter of the sacraments, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 326.

## VI. On the power of the sacraments

The new sacraments are greater in power and better in usefulness, St. Augustine, XLII, 355. The sacrament and the power of the sacrament are sometimes separate, ibid., XXXV, 2026. The sacrament is one thing, the power of the sacrament another, ibid., 1611. The power of the sacraments, namely grace, is not common to all, although the sacraments are common, ibid., XXXVI, 983. The minister sanctifies through visible sacraments; God does so through invisible grace, ibid., XXXIV, 712, 713. Divine power is present in the sacraments, either for the salvation of those who use them well or for the destruction of those who use them badly, ibid., XLIII, 144. The effect of visible sacraments is piety, ibid., XLII, 355. Temporal sacraments are medicinal bonds for our contrition, ibid., [Col. 0838] XXXVII, 1903, 1904. Whether the effect of the sacraments depends upon the goodness or perversity of ministers, ibid., XLIII, 67, 73. Sins are forgiven through the power of the sacraments, not through the merits of ministers, ibid., 156. Among schismatics, sacraments may possess the visible form of piety, but not its spiritual power, ibid., XXXVIII, 463. The same sacraments bring salvation to the righteous and condemnation to the wicked, ibid., XLIII, 293, 297, 298, 435. In those who love the world, sacraments remain for condemnation, not as an instrument for salvation, ibid., XXXV, 1994. Sacraments are the everlasting gates, Cassiodorus, LXX, 174. On the sacraments of the Church and their effect, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1168. Sacraments are vessels of grace, Alan of Lille, CCX, 204. Human wickedness does not profane the sacraments, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 498.

## VII. On the minister of the sacraments

God gives the sacraments of grace even through evil men, but grace itself only through himself or through his saints, St. Augustine, XLIII, 191. Sins are forgiven by the power of the sacraments, not by the merits of ministers, ibid., 156. Sacraments among heretics, ibid., XXXVIII, 463; XLIII, 179. On sacraments administered by unworthy persons, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 523; St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 521, 522. Which persons are ministers of which sacraments, St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 128. The merits of ministers contribute nothing to the validity of sacraments, Ralph Ardens, CLV, 1682. The wickedness of a minister does not obstruct the reality of the sacrament, Marbod of Rennes, CLXXI, 1472. Although evil persons administer sacraments, they do not confer forgiveness of sins, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 499. Every presbyter ought to know the sacraments of the Lord, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1150. He who is ignorant of the sacraments of the Church is unworthy to administer them, Gilbert, abbot of Saint Mary’s, CLVI, 901.

## VIII. On the recipient of the sacraments

Use of the sacraments by the unworthy is sometimes not forbidden out of necessity for the Church’s peace, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 51. Even if a righteous and a wicked person alike participate in the sacraments, one must not therefore say that righteousness participates with wickedness, ibid., XLIII, 294. The same sacraments bring salvation to the righteous and condemnation to the wicked, ibid., 293, 297, 298, 435.

## IX. Books dealing with the sacraments

Six books *On the Sacraments*, St. Ambrose, XVI, 417. A book *On the Divine Sacraments*, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1218. A short work *On the Sacraments*, Bonizo of Piacenza, CL, 857. *On the Diversity of the Sacraments*, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 548. *On the Sacraments of the Natural and Written Law*, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 17, 344, 351, 117. *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, ibid., 173. *On Ecclesiastical Sacraments*, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1090.

[Col. 0837]

# XCVI. INDEX CONCERNING BAPTISM, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ON THE NATURE, INSTITUTION, NECESSITY, AND SO FORTH OF THIS SACRAMENT

## Notice

Baptism, taken metaphysically, is correctly defined as: “the sacrament of regeneration through water, with an explicit invocation of the Holy Trinity.” It is the first of all sacraments, and no sacrament is received by one who is unbaptized. In this Index we discuss in turn the nature and figures of Baptism; the institution, matter, and form of this sacrament; its necessity and unity; the various kinds of baptisms; the baptism of Christ and that of John; the minister and recipient of Baptism; Baptism conferred by heretics, schismatics, and wicked ministers; the time at which it is to be conferred and received; the ceremonies and effects of Baptism; and the manner of conduct to be observed after Baptism. We also list various books that treat of Baptism.

## I. On the nature of baptism

The water of Baptism is a blessed sacrament, Tertullian, I, 1197. Baptism is the sealing of faith, ibid., 1239. The Holy Spirit rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself, ibid., [Col. 0838] 1204. Baptism is spiritual circumcision, St. Cyprian, III, 1018. The washing of saving water, ibid., IV, 198. Baptism is the sacrament of divine regeneration, St. Hilary, X, [Col. 0839] 39. It is the sign of death overcome, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2275. An image of the future resurrection, ibid., XXXIX, 2070. Baptism is God’s seal, a character, Victor of Vita, LVIII, 247. Baptism is the sacrament of reconciliation, Eugyppius, LXII, 871. The grace of divine baptism is, as it were, the root and sure foundation of the holy and undefiled faith of Christians, ibid., LXXIII, 470. Why it is called Baptism, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 256; Leidrad, XCIX, 861; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 309. Why the sacred font of Baptism is rightly called the fountain of life, Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 135. Three things in Baptism are visible—the priest, the body, and the water—and three invisible—the spirit, the soul, and faith, Hincmar, CXXVI, 105. Baptism is a figure of death and burial, ibid., CLVIII, 544. Baptism is the door through which one enters the temple of God, Rupert, CLXVII, 1151. In Baptism water is present visibly, Christ’s blood invisibly, ibid., 1651. Baptism is the doorway of God’s house, Godefrid, CLXXIV, 432. What the sacrament of Baptism is, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 129, 443. Baptism is like a gate for all those entering the courts of the Church, ibid., CLXXVII, 388. The outward washing in Baptism signifies the inward washing, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 479. In what sense it is called Baptism, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 843; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1092. The eastern gate is the sacrament of Baptism through which one enters the city, Henry, CCIV, 296. The second pool is Baptism, called the initiatory pool: how this is so, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 712. Baptism is washing with water sanctified through invocation of the Holy Trinity, signifying the washing away of sin, Alan of Lille, CCX, 613. Baptism is an outward washing of the body performed under the prescribed form of words, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1230.

## II. On the figures of Baptism

Figures of Baptism, Tertullian, I, 1209; St. Ambrose, XVI, 423. The Flood as a figure of Baptism, St. Optatus, XI, 894; St. Augustine, XLII, 263; St. Fulgentius, LXV, 543; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 321; St. Bruno the Carthusian, CLIII, 414; Rupert, CLXVII, 340; John Beleth, CCII, 115. Circumcision as a figure of Baptism, St. Optatus, XI, 895; St. Augustine, XLIV, 833. The Red Sea was a figure of Baptism, St. Ambrose, XIV, 867; Sedulius, XIX, 567; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1723; XXXVI, 917; XXXVII, 1037, 1411, 1420; XXXIX, 1551, 1555, 1562, 1635; St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 168; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1162; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 119; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 507; St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 1103; Rupert, CLXVII, 1659; Honorius, CLXXII, 672. The raven and dove sent out from Noah’s ark as a type of Baptism, St. Jerome, XXIII, 176. The turning back of the river Jordan as a sign of Baptism, St. Ambrose, XV, 1548.

## III. On the institution of Baptism and its author

When Baptism was instituted by Christ, Lactantius, VII, 616; St. Optatus, XI, 1055. For what reason Baptism was instituted, St. Augustine, XLV, 1120. The second birth was instituted because the first is condemned, ibid., XLIV, 857. When Christ says, “Go into the whole world; baptize,” and so forth, he clearly shows that not they, but undoubtedly he, was the author of Baptism, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 102. The question when the sacrament of Baptism was instituted, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 759. Baptism was instituted when Christ came to Baptism, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 128, 449. Why the sacrament of Baptism was instituted, ibid., 447; Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 840. By coming to John’s baptism, Christ conferred regenerative power on the waters, ibid., CLXXVII, 389. On the time of Baptism’s institution, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 844; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1092.

## IV. On the remote and proximate matter of Baptism

The matter and power of Baptism, Tertullian, I, 1203. At Baptism the head was immersed three times, St. Jerome, XXIII, 164. Triple immersion is on account of the mystery of the Trinity, St. Jerome, XXVI, 496. At Baptism triple immersion is performed according to the ancient custom of the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 343. Sometimes there is a single immersion, ibid. If someone, having no water, baptized an endangered infant in wine, no penalty is imposed upon him, St. Stephen, II, 1026. Triple immersion is to be performed in Baptism, Alcuin, C, 290, 342. Baptism is consecrated in water, so that it may be understood, and so forth, Haymo, CXVII, 411. No element is found more suited for burying us together than water; for by water the filth of bodies is cleansed, Paschasius, CXX, 170. The triple immersion of Baptism is indicated in the letter of Pope Gregory, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1103. Baptism is given through material water, [Col. 0840] Gerard, CXLII, 1274. Baptism takes place in water, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 543. In Baptism a triple immersion in water is made for three reasons, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1058. Baptism takes place under triple immersion, Rupert, CLXVII, 1632. Formerly Baptism was performed by immersion of the whole body, Hildebert, CLXXI, 1147. Baptism is uniformly performed in water, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 127. Why Baptism is performed more properly in water than in another liquid, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1739; Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 101. Baptism admits no liquid or element other than water, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 841. Baptism is celebrated only in water, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 844; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1092. According to the differing practice of Churches, the baptized person is immersed once or three times, ibid. Christ determined the matter in which Baptism should be administered when he showed that a human being must be regenerated in water, Ecbert, XCV, 53. It is not permitted to administer Baptism in anything other than pure water, John Beleth, CCII, 115.

## V. On the form of Baptism

Baptism is in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, St. Hilary, X, 39. Baptism is conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity, St. Jerome, XXII, 466. True Baptism is in the Holy Spirit and in the mystery of the Trinity, ibid., XXV, 935. The apostles baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ibid., 139. Baptism is given in the name of the Holy Trinity, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 803. One must baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 427. Baptism is given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Gennadius, LVIII, 993, 1026. How Baptism in the name of Jesus is valid, Vigilius of Thapsus, LXII, 324. Baptism is given in the name of the Trinity, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 300. Baptism conferred by any heretics whatsoever, provided it is in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is not to be repeated, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 692. On Baptism in the name of Jesus, Facundus, LXVII, 534. Invocation of the Holy Trinity is required in Baptism, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 227. The form of Baptism, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 343. The saving gifts of Baptism reside in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 821. If Baptism is given with any person of the Trinity omitted, clearly nothing is done in the solemnity of regeneration unless the whole Trinity is invoked, ibid. Penalty for one who has not baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, XCIX, 1023. That Baptism is given in the name of the Trinity, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 168. The mystery of Baptism can by no means be completed unless under invocation of the Holy Trinity, Theodulf, CV, 232. If any bishop or presbyter does not baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let him be deposed, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 20; Burchard, CXL, 732. Concerning a presbyter who did not know grammar and yet baptized in the Trinity, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 735. It is not permitted to baptize in the name of the Father alone, or in the name of the Son alone, or in the name of the Holy Spirit alone, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1059. Those baptized in the name of the Lord are to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, ibid. One baptized without invocation of the Trinity does not possess the sacrament of regeneration, ibid. The form of Baptism is the words “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” or their equivalents, Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 102. Invocation of the Trinity is called the word by which Baptism is consecrated, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 843. The form of this sacrament, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1095; Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 312, 313; Peter of Poitiers, ibid., 1230.

## VI. On the necessity of Baptism; infants who die without Baptism; and the time at which the law of Baptism began to bind

Without Baptism salvation belongs to no one, Tertullian, I, 1213. At what time the law of Baptism began to bind, ibid., 1215. Unless a catechumen has been baptized, he cannot receive remission of sins, St. Ambrose, XVI, 394. Baptism is necessary for all, St. Augustine, XL, 253; XLIV, 189, 190, 199. Baptism is necessary even for those living perfectly, ibid., XXXV, 1495. Pope Innocent affirms the necessity of Baptism, ibid., XLIV, 576. Christ’s Baptism is necessary for infants, ibid., XXXIV, 418. Baptism is necessary for infants because of original, not personal, sin, ibid., XLIV, 121. Whoever is carnally begotten needs to be spiritually regenerated, ibid. No one is freed from Adam’s condemnation unless reborn in Christ, ibid., XL, 256. Infants must be baptized in order that they may be freed from the devil’s power and from sin, ibid., XLIV, 1438. Through Baptism dying infants are drawn out of the power of darkness, ibid., XXXIII, 982; XLIV, 426. Infants cannot be freed from original sin [Col. 0841] except by Christ’s Baptism, ibid., XXXIII, 683. The Pelagians deny that infants are to be baptized for salvation, ibid., 761, 763, 773. Some Pelagians admit that remission of sins occurs in infants through Baptism: in what sense, ibid., XLIV, 146. The Pelagians concede that infants should be baptized, not for eternal life but for the kingdom of heaven, ibid., XXXVIII, 1336; XLIV, 142, 394. Without Baptism infants cannot have life in themselves, ibid., XLIV, 615. Unbaptized infants remain in darkness, ibid., 112, 129, 190, 131. Unbaptized infants are condemned, ibid., 188, 189. Infants dying without Baptism will not be in some intermediate place where they live blessedly, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 486, 487. Infants must be baptized so that what they contracted by generation may be cleansed in them by regeneration, Gennadius, LVIII, 989. This must especially be observed and maintained: the souls of infants at birth are bound by the bond of original sin, and the sacrament of holy Baptism is necessary for all, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 441. The Lord revealed to Nicodemus that no one would enter the kingdom without regeneration, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 620. Newly born infants suffer the pains of hell for the guilt of original sin alone if they have not been renewed by the laver, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 588. No one can obtain remission of sins or enter the kingdom of heaven without the laver of regeneration, Venerable Bede, XCII, 668. That only one reborn possesses eternal life, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 758. After death, the unbaptized are strangers to Christ’s kingdom, Alcuin, CI, 1224. The necessity of Baptism, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 234. Baptism is necessary in fact or in desire, Goffridus, CLIII, 256. No one will enter the land of the living who has not first passed through Baptism, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 533. Whoever departs this life without Baptism will lack the kingdom of God and will moreover pay eternal penalties for the original curse, Otto, CLXXIII, 1358. Whether salvation may be obtained without actually receiving the visible sacrament, or through martyrdom in its stead, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1031. When human beings began to be bound by the command to receive Baptism, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVII, 450, 452. The visible sacrament of water is necessary for washing the visible body, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1791. Anyone who despises the sacrament of Baptism and refuses to receive it can in no way merit or attain eternal life, Ermengaudus, CCIV, 1256. Baptism is necessary for infants and adults alike, Alan of Lille, CCX, 347. Baptism did not become obligatory from the time it was said to Nicodemus, “Unless one is reborn,” and so forth, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1031. The obligation of Baptism first began after its sufficient promulgation, ibid., 1034.

## VII. On the unity of Baptism, and that it is not to be repeated

Baptism is altogether one, both from the Lord’s Gospel and from the writings of the apostles, Tertullian, I, 1216. There is one Baptism in the Church, St. Cyprian, III, 407, 408, 412; St. Hilary, X, 399, 400. Baptism is not to be repeated, St. Optatus, XI, 1044, 1045, 1048; St. Ambrose, XV, 1789; St. Augustine, XXXV, 1484; XLIII, 54, 70, 72, 77, 158, 159, 162, 190, 192, 197, 199, 206, 219, 223, 226, 227, 232, 234, 237, 346, 515, 601, 602, 605, 804. The Lord’s Baptism is one washing for cleansing souls and bodies, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 647; Gennadius, LVIII, 993. Baptism is not to be repeated, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1193; Primasius, LXVIII, 445; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 160, 161; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 319, 678; St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 164; Rupert, CLXIX, 264; Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 629; ibid., CLXXVI, 458; Alan of Lille, CCX, 353.

## VIII. On the various kinds of Baptism

The second Baptism, or Baptism of blood through martyrdom, Tertullian, I, 1217. Very many kinds of baptism have been prefigured, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1248. Some are baptized with the Baptism of fire, others with the Baptism of the Holy Spirit, St. Jerome, XXV, 686. What the Baptism of blood is, St. Augustine, XLIII, 276. Martyrdom and, in a case of necessity, true conversion take the place of Baptism, ibid., 173. Baptism of blood, Prudentius, LX, 426. Scripture contains three kinds of baptism: of water, of spirit, and of fire; and of blood, by which martyrs are baptized, Primasius, LXVIII, 443. The Baptism of martyrdom is the most excellent of all, ibid., LXXIII, 488. The first Baptism is that of water, the second that of blood, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 160. There are three kinds of Baptism, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 820; Alcuin, CI, 1216. There are several kinds of baptism, which cleanse a person from sins and bestow progress in holiness, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 133, 134. There are four kinds of baptisms, Haymo, CXVII, [Col. 0842] 411. Those who have not been baptized are baptized if they die for Christ, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1068. The shedding of blood takes the place of Baptism, ibid. The shedding of blood takes the place of Baptism, and so does true contrition of heart when there is no time to receive it, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 843. Baptism is threefold, ibid., CLXXVII, 804; St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 273; Alan of Lille, CCX, 348.

## IX. On the Baptism of Christ and of John

Whether John’s Baptism was heavenly or earthly, Tertullian, I, 1210. John says that he baptizes unto repentance, St. Hilary, IX, 926. John’s Baptism differs from Christ’s Baptism, St. Optatus, XI, 1053, 1054. On John’s Baptism: when and why Christ’s Baptism was conferred after it, ibid. John’s Baptism is the eye of petitions; Christ’s Baptism, the eye of graces, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1010. John baptized with water; Christ with the Spirit, St. Ambrose, XV, 1840. Receiving the type of the Law, John baptized unto repentance; Christ baptized unto grace, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1043. John’s Baptism, Juvencus, XIX, 105. In what sense it was for remission of sins, ibid., 108. The Baptism of Christ and that of John, Chromatius, XX, 328, 329. The end of John’s Baptism, St. Augustine, XLIII, 182. Regeneration did not take place through John’s Baptism, ibid., 255. Christ received John’s Baptism, ibid., 256; XLIII, 174. He received it for the consecration of the sacrament itself, ibid., XXXVIII, 1335. John’s Baptism does not wipe away sins, ibid., XXXIX, 2010. Why it was received by Christ, ibid., XXXV, 2195, 2249, 2250. By Christ’s Baptism, waters were consecrated for our Baptism, ibid., XXXIX, 2010, 2012, 2015. On Christ’s Baptism, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 616; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 701; St. Maximus, LVII, 292, 294, 298; Prudentius, LIX, 679. Effects of the Baptism of St. John the Baptist, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 447. John’s and Christ’s Baptisms, St. Paschasius, LXII, 31. Why the Saviour received Baptism from John, Venerable Bede, XCII, 138. Christ’s Baptism was for the sanctification of water, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 173. John’s Baptism was not for remission of sins, but preparation for Christ’s Baptism, St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 116. Christ was baptized not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but so that his great humility might be commended, Alcuin, CI, 49. Christ’s Baptism was not in water alone like John’s, but in the Holy Spirit, ibid., 158, 238. John baptizes in the water of repentance, Christianus Druthmarus, CVI, 1293. For three reasons the Lord came to John’s Baptism, ibid., 1294. Christ wished to be baptized by John so that all believers might learn that no one is justified without Baptism, however innocently and righteously he may live, Gerard, CXLII, 1275. John’s Baptism is a figure of Christ’s Baptism, Lanfranc, CL, 670. The Lord wished to be baptized not because he needed remission of sin, but in order to fulfil the Law, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1050. John’s Baptism and Christ’s Baptism do not have the same power, ibid. John’s Baptism is the Baptism of a servant; Christ’s Baptism is the Baptism of the Lord, Rupert, CLXVII, 1643. John’s Baptism was preparation for Christ’s Baptism, Hildebert, CLXXI, 409. Christ’s Baptism is called the Baptism of remission, whereas John’s Baptism is called the Baptism of repentance, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 845. What difference there is between John’s Baptism and Christ’s, ibid., CLXXVI, 451. John’s Baptism washed bodies alone and did not cleanse from sins, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 842. On the form of John’s Baptism and those baptized by him, ibid. John baptized in water; Jesus in water and the Holy Spirit, Richard, CXCVI, 1016. Christ’s Baptism is worthier than John’s, Philip of Harveng, CCIII, 763. Why Christ came to the waters of the Jordan, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 591. Perfect Baptism began with Jesus Christ; for he was the first to baptize in the Holy Spirit, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 273. Christ was baptized not because he needed Baptism, but in order to confer regenerative power upon the waters, Alan of Lille, CCX, 350. The difference between John’s Baptism and Christ’s Baptism, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1237.

## X. On the recipient of Baptism and the dispositions required in adults
Baptism: at what age of life it should be conferred, Tertullian, I, 1220. Whether delaying baptism is more advantageous, ibid., 1221. Confession of all sins must precede baptism, ibid., 1222. As must repentance, ibid., 1229. The grace of baptism is to be denied much less to infants than to adults, St Cyprian, IV, 1018. Baptism is to be given to all, St Sylvester, VIII, 838. Children, adolescents, young people, and elderly persons of both sexes are baptized, St Zeno, XI, 493. Persons diverse in origin, age, sex, and condition are baptized into one, ibid., [Col. 0843] 491. Little children ought to be baptized, that they may be delivered from the devil’s power and from sin, St Augustine, XLV, 1438. Little children are baptized for the remission of sins, id., XXXVIII, 751. Parents ought to be concerned that infants are baptized, id., XLIV, 199. Even the children of believers are to be baptized, ibid., 175, 812, 847. The children of baptized persons are not baptized superfluously, ibid., 194, 195, 199. The dead are not to be baptized, St Leo the Great, LVI, 422. Pregnant women are to be baptized, same author, 444. In adults, neither confession without baptism nor baptism without confession, St Fulgentius, LXV, 388. Those to be baptized should learn the Creed, Ferrandus, LXVII, 959. When sick persons cannot themselves speak, baptism is not to be denied if others give testimony on their behalf, ibid. When it is unknown whether infants have been baptized, they should be baptized without any hesitation, id., LXVII, 959. Fasting preceded baptism, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1195. Fasting and prayer precede baptism, id., LXXII, 515. Peter taught that repentance must precede baptism, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 112. Whether baptism may be conferred on a pregnant woman, ibid., 1193. Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 828. Persons whose baptism is doubtful are to be baptized again, ibid. Baptism is not to be given to the dead, Angelrannus, XCVI, 1049. Those to be baptized should give their names and, after a long period of abstinence from wine and meat, receive baptism, Theodulf, XCIX, 1022. A person who suddenly becomes speechless may be baptized if there is sufficient evidence of a prior intention, ibid., 1023. The body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has received the truth of faith, Alcuin, C, 189. Those who are not proven to have been baptized should be baptized without scruple, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 353. The dead are not to be baptized, Burchard, CXL, 734. All who come to baptism ought, on Thursday of Holy Week, to profess their faith to the bishop or priest, id., CXL, 730. An adult intending to receive baptism ought first to repent of the old life, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1054. A person to be baptized must first be made a catechumen and instructed in the matters of faith, ibid. Before catechumens are washed with the element of water, they should vow to renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works, St Bruno, CLXIV, 471. Preparation of those to be baptized for baptism through fifteen days of fasting, Rupert, CLXX, 111. No one can be baptized in the maternal womb, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 853. Those who approach without faith or hypocritically receive the sacrament, not the reality, ibid., 846.

## XI.—On the Minister of Baptism

The chief priest, who is the bishop, has the right to administer baptism, Tertullian, I, 1218. Then priests and deacons, though not without the bishop’s authority. Laypersons also have the right, ibid. Concerning those baptized in the faith by schismatics or evil ministers, there should be no doubt that their baptism ought to be regarded as valid, St Optatus, XI, 765. Baptism is performed through Christ’s priests, St Ambrose, XV, 1227. A priest or deacon has no right to baptize without the bishop’s command, St Jerome, XXIII, 165. When necessity compels, laypersons may baptize, ibid. Baptism is conferred by a priest, St Augustine, XLI, 842. The right to administer baptism is received in ordination, id., XLIII, 71. In necessity, a layperson baptizes, ibid. Even laypersons are permitted to administer baptism in necessity, St Leo the Great, LVI, 695. Baptism is to be administered only by priests, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 822. A woman must not presume to baptize, Theodulf, XCIX, 1023. Only priests may administer baptism, apart from the necessity of danger, St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 159. Baptism is rightly conferred even by evil persons, St Agobard, CIV, 142. A deacon may baptize in the absence of bishop and priest, Regino, CXXXII, 142. The administration of baptism is entrusted to priests, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 232, 233. It is established that baptism has been entrusted to priests alone, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 82. A mother may baptize her child when danger of death is pressing, ibid., 1051. No one except a priest may presume to baptize unless necessity is present, ibid., 1052. A layperson is permitted to baptize in necessity, Honorius, CLXXII, 674; Alger, CLXXX, 838, 882; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1799; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1094. Who may baptize, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 852.

## XII.—On Baptism Conferred by Heretics and Schismatics, or Other Evil Ministers, or Received by Their Adherents

The baptism of heretics is not to be repeated, Stephen, I, 1009, 1010. Everything among heretics is empty and false, St Cyprian, III, 1043. Whoever approves their baptism shares in the heretics’ error, St Cyprian, III, 1122, 1126, 1130, 1173. Those baptized by heretics are to be baptized, ibid., 1162. Not even baptism of blood is beneficial in heresy, ibid., 1123. Those returning from heresy ought to be born through both sacraments, St Cyprian, III, 1046, 1081, 1117. On those who have been admitted from heresy into the Church without baptism, ibid., [Col. 0844] 1122, 1171. Stephen’s judgment concerning the baptism of heretics, III, 1128. He prohibited baptism for anyone coming from any heresy, ibid., 1129. Heretics do not properly baptize those who come to them, ibid. The baptism of heretics had long been rejected in Africa, St Cyprian, III, 1038, 1110. The Montanists baptize the dead, St Philastrius, XII, 1166. Baptism administered by heretics is good, just as baptism administered by evil persons is, St Augustine, XLIII, 190, 191. The baptism of evil persons is invalid if that of heretics is invalid, ibid., 193, 203, 204, 205, 206, 207, 209, 211, 212. It was defined at the Council of Nicaea that baptism can be administered by heretics and schismatics, ibid., 72. Whatever Cyprian and his colleague said at the Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics can be said of the baptism of the unrighteous, ibid., 239. Baptism, wherever it is conferred, is to be revered, id., XXXIII, 301. Baptism administered among heretics is valid and is not to be repeated, ibid., 362; XXXVII, 462, 797. One must not baptize after heretics if one does not baptize after drunkards, the licentious, and so forth, id., XLIII, 218, 437. Those baptized in heresy or schism are not to be rebaptized, ibid., 219, 220, 491. Baptism given by heretics or evil persons is whole and unimpaired, ibid., 207, 244. But it does not avail for salvation, ibid., 110, 144, 170, 235, 236, 239, 257, 437, 756. Heretics and evil persons can possess baptism, but they do not possess remission of sins, ibid., 227, 228, 238, 244. Whether baptism received from evil persons effects remission of sins, ibid., 165, 166. Heretics and perverse persons can give baptism; they cannot give remission of sins, ibid., 192. Those baptized by heretics or unrighteous persons, if they are not converted with a false heart, are baptized by Christ, ibid., 219. Whether those baptized among heretics should be rebaptized, Gennadius, LVIII, 1026, 1028. Ferrandus, LXVII, 958. Baptism administered even by heretics in the name of the Trinity is deemed valid, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 828. The baptism of heretics is given not for remission of sins but as testimony to punishment, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 588. Those baptized among heretics who come to us are to be received as baptized persons, Burchard, CXL, 734. Whether a heretic may baptize, Ivo of Chartres, 1052. Heretics and sinners administering baptism beget children for the Church, St Bruno, CLXIV, 210. Whether the baptism of heretics should be repeated when performed in the name of the Holy Trinity, Rupert, CLXVII, 813. Baptism given by a good person or an evil person, to a good person or an evil person, is equally holy, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 850.

## XIII.—On the Time for Conferring or Receiving Baptism

The time for conferring baptism, Tertullian, I, 1222; St Siricius, XIII, 1134. Within how many days infants should be baptized, St Cyprian, III, 1015, 1017, 1018. Baptism is conferred at Easter and Pentecost, St Jerome, XXV, 1528. Baptism was solemnly celebrated in Sicily on Epiphany, St Leo the Great, LIV, 696. It should be celebrated at Easter, ibid., 698. And at Pentecost, ibid. According to apostolic example baptism is to be celebrated at Pentecost, ibid., 700. Baptism was conferred on the Easter night, ibid., 609. Leo prohibits its celebration on Epiphany, ibid., 698. In a case of necessity, baptism is to be administered at every time, ibid., 700. At what seasons of the year baptism was customarily conferred among the Greeks, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 925. At what seasons among the Latins, ibid. That after the second week of Lent no one should be admitted to baptism, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 828. Little children should not be presented for baptism except at the two prescribed seasons, Charlemagne, XCVII, 770. On the time and place of baptizing, St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 157. Baptisms should take place at the fixed times of Easter and Pentecost, except in case of illness, Herard, CXXI, 766; Burchard, CXL, 729; St Anselm, CXLIX, 521; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 79. Solemn baptism ought to take place on Easter Day, not on Epiphany, Rupert, CLXX, 84. Baptism is canonically celebrated only twice a year, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 673. Unless necessity compels, no one may presume to baptize between Easter and Pentecost, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1799. In baptizing the elect, two seasons must be observed, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 854.

## XIV.—On the Effects of Baptism

In baptism there is regeneration, Tertullian, II, 280, 862. And remission of sins, ibid., I, 1238; II, 280. Through baptism stains are washed away, but through martyrdom blemishes are made white, ibid., II, 147. The Spirit is physically spread over the waters, and the flesh is spiritually cleansed in those same waters, ibid., I, 1204. We are baptized not in order that we may cease sinning, but because we have ceased, since we have already been washed in heart, ibid., I, 1239. By baptism every wickedness is abolished, Lactantius, VI, 433. [Col. 0845] In baptism remission of sins is given, St Hilary, IX, 412. It is the sacrament of divine birth, ibid., X, 39. Through the sacrament of baptism souls receive brightness, ibid., IX, 1060. By the laver of baptism, through the power of the Word, we are renewed in soul and body, ibid., 976. Baptism obtains life for the soul, St Zeno, XI, 341. It cuts away the vices of the soul and original sin, ibid., 353. It washes away absolutely all sins, St Zeno, XI, 470, 519. One reborn in baptism becomes a child of the Church, ibid., 437. Where the Trinity agrees with faith, one born to the world is spiritually reborn to God, St Optatus, XI, 963. In baptism all righteousness is fulfilled, St Ambrose, XIV, 867. Sin is washed away, ibid., 345, 727. In baptism the Holy Spirit descends, ibid., 428. Through the laver of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit we receive hope of eternal life, ibid., 791. The Lord takes away sins through baptism, ibid., 1240. Through baptism we die to sin but live together with Christ, St Chromatius, XX, 329. Baptism makes the new human being and creates wholly anew, St Jerome, XXII, 655. The old Adam wholly dies in the laver, and the new is raised with Christ in baptism, id., XXIII, 424. Baptism forgives only past sins, ibid., 569. The power of baptism, St Augustine, XLII, 572; XLIII, 165. Its effects, XLIV, 570, 847. Christ’s baptism erases all sins, XXXVIII, 53, 382, 383, 390, 401, 752, 1064; XL, 262, 288, 659; XLI, 40; XLIV, 430, 600, 688. Baptism grants forgiveness of all sins and removes crimes; it does not merely shave them down, ibid., 562, 563. Through baptism, those who die before the use of reason are delivered from condemnation, St Augustine, XXXIII, 364. By the laver of baptism not only sins but even the sinful desires themselves are cleansed, id., XLIV, 407. The baptized are released from liability for the evils that remain after baptism, ibid., 853. The body also is sanctified by baptism, id., XL, 694. The effects of baptism are remission of sins and the bestowal of grace, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 285; St Leo the Great, LIV, 193. The sacrament of baptism is useful and necessary, because in it remission of sins is bestowed, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 538. The water of baptism, called Christ’s water, both erases sins and confers the grace of justification, ibid., 481. Its benefits are set forth, ibid., 338, 709. The effect of baptism in remitting sins proceeds from God’s grace and power; for the Holy Spirit works in that water, ibid., 775. So great is the power of holy baptism that it washes away all sins it finds, even those added to original sin, St Fulgentius, LXV, 387. Not only the original debt, but also actual sin, is erased through baptism, Primasius of Hadrumetum, LXVIII, 442. Christ daily accomplishes the cleansing of sins through baptism, St Germanus, LXXII, 856. Baptism utterly removes sins, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1162. While the body is immersed, the soul is washed from all sins, id., LXXIX, 510, 515. Baptism is that by which all sins are most truly forgiven and the heavenly kingdom is opened to believers, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1291. By baptism a human being changes from a child of wrath into a child of adoption, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 112, 173; Heterius, XCVI, 729. Baptism removes both original and actual sin, St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 158. When we are baptized in Christ, through him we are reborn so that, cleansed, we may be made alive, Leiraldus, XCIX, 862. That water not only washes away stains but also frees the soul from sins, ibid. Through baptism sins, both original and actual, are forgiven, Alcuin, CI, 1073. Baptism renews the inner human being, St Agobard, CIV, 177. O glorious and wonderful sacrament, which makes children of God from children of wrath, new persons from old, beautiful persons from foul, in which we are both regenerated and cleansed, and so forth, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 232. In baptism the old human being is put off and the new put on, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 126. Baptized infants, if they die, are saved, St Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 608. Reception and fruit of baptism, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 373, 374. Against Gottschalk: those redeemed by baptism can perish, ibid., 380, 301. Through the sacrament of baptism all sins are erased, even if no repentance has preceded, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 442. Through baptism a human being is regenerated and renewed when the Holy Spirit comes upon him, through whom remission of sins occurs, Lanfranc, CL, 371. In baptism we die, not in the flesh but to sin, ibid., 388. In baptism a human being is spiritually created and is called a Christian from Christ, Geoffrey of Vendôme, CLVII, 214. Why the baptized and martyrs do not immediately become incorruptible, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 531. Through the washing of baptism we are added among the children of adoption, ibid., 885. All sins are erased in baptism, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 970. Life is born from the waters, Franco, CLXVI, 765. Baptism makes us the throne and temple of God, Hildebert, CLXXI, 788. What is forgiven in baptism, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 390. Baptism erases all sins, both original and personal, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1501. We are washed in baptism [Col. 0846] because the written bond of our condemnation is erased, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 272. Through faith and baptism we are justified from sins, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1794. How baptism benefits those who approach with faith, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 849. Whoever has been baptized in the name of God obtains remission of all sins so completely that, if immediately after baptism that person departs this life, the gate of the heavenly kingdom stands open, Eckbert, CXCV, 46. Through baptism we become members of Christ, a temple of the Holy Spirit, and children of God, Richard, CXCVI, 1014. As water washes dirt from the body and clothing, so baptism cleanses and wipes away the stains of the soul and the impurities within, Henry, CCIV, 300. In baptism not only original sin, but also other sins, even venial sins, are forgiven, Alan of Lille, CCX, 350.

## XV.—On the Ceremonies of Baptism

The rite of baptism, Tertullian, II, 806. In baptism we renounce with our mouth the devil, his pomp, and his angels, id., I, 635; II, 79. On emerging from baptism they were anointed, id., I, 1206. Hands were laid upon them, ibid., 1207. They were refreshed with milk and honey, id., II, 79, 262. Baptismal promises were made, St Zeno, XI, 470. At the conferral of baptism a solemn hymn was sung, ibid., 478. Among the baptismal ceremonies in Zeno’s time a denarius was handed over, ibid., 481. A double anointing in baptism, ibid. Washing of feet before or after baptism, ibid. The baptized person renounces the devil and his works, St Ambrose, XIV, 129. He also renounces the world, id., XV, 1802. Triple immersion at the conferral of baptism, id., XVI, 429. In baptism the priest consecrates the waters, ibid., 391. No one can be cleansed except by triple confession, ibid., 765. The solemn questioning in baptism, St Jerome, XXIII, 166. Why those emerging from the baptismal font are anointed on the head, and why the feet are also washed after baptism, ibid., 398. The form or rite of baptism, St Augustine, XXXIII, 97; XLIV, 145. Children to be baptized are brought to church, ibid., 1333. The person to be baptized was asked whether he or she was turning to God and believed in him, id., XLIII, 352. Whether he or she renounced the world, ibid., 190. Why another person ought not answer for one who can answer, ibid., 175. The Creed was delivered to those to be baptized and required to be recited back, id., XI, 206. We are baptized while confessing the rule of faith, id., XXXIX, 1614. At Rome, those to be baptized customarily made from memory a profession of faith from a more elevated place before the faithful, id., XXXII, 751. The baptized person was anointed with oil, id., XL, 693. A hand is laid upon him or her, id., XXXVIII, 1445. In baptism a kiss was given to infants, id., XLIV, 625. The newly baptized were clothed in white garments, id., XXXVIII, 678, 1092. Those to be baptized receive chrism and the oil of blessing, id., XXXIX, 1828. Those to be baptized are questioned concerning faith in the Trinity, XL, 1209. Once baptism is completed, chrism is poured upon the head, id., XL, 1211. The newly baptized receive a white garment, id., XXXIX, 2070. Their feet are washed, id., XL, 1211. What preparation for baptism formerly took place, St Leo the Great, LIV, 702. The covenant, profession, and renunciation in baptism, ibid., 366. On the various rites pertaining to baptism, John the Deacon, LIX, 399. Scrutiny and exorcisms before baptism, Fulgentius, LXV, 378. Recitation of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer, ibid. The baptized were anointed with oil, and their foreheads were marked with the cross, Arator, LXVIII, 90. The rite of baptism, St Germanus, LXXII, 362; Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1084. Among the Latins the candidate for baptism is anointed on the breast, shoulders, and so forth, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 322. The names of the candidates for baptism were entered, ibid., 342. On renunciation in baptism, St Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 870. On sacred anointing, Leidrad of Lyons, XCIX, 863. On white garments, ibid., 865. On the meanings of holy baptism, Leidrad of Lyons, XCIX, 855. On the touching of the nostrils and ears: why, according to ecclesiastical tradition, it is performed by all Catholic priests of Christ, Leidrad of Lyons, XCIX, 857. What it signifies that an infant is immersed in water, St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 159. On the renunciation of Satan, and what his works and pomps are, ibid., 858. Letter on the ceremonies of baptism, Amalarius of Trier, XCIX, 893. Various ceremonies of baptism and their meanings, Alcuin, C, 292. Alcuin’s letter to the priest Oduinus on the ceremonies of baptism, id., CI, 612. Explanation of baptismal ceremonies, Magnus of Sens, CII, 981; Theodulf, CV, 224; Jesse, CV, 781. Collections concerning ancient baptismal rites, Maxentius, CVI, 54. On baptismal immersion and anointing with chrism, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1176. How the sacraments of baptism ought to be celebrated, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 32. That, if necessary, there may be one godfather in baptism, Burchard of Worms, CXL, [Col. 0847] 732. That priests should ask godparents whether they know the Creed, ibid. The devil is to be renounced in baptism, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 84. The Creed of faith is to be believed, ibid., 84, 85. Why triple immersion ought to take place in baptism, id., CLXI, 1058. Various baptismal ceremonies are enumerated, ibid. and following; Honorius, CLXXII, 672, 673; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 391 and following, 456; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1821. Why godparents are necessary for a child in baptism, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 844; John Beleth, CCII, 113, 114; Odo of Sully, CCXII, 59.

## XVI.—On the Manner of Life to Be Maintained after Baptism

Baptism is a new birth, Tertullian, I. From faith through baptism one must live in newness, id., II, 862. Temptations after baptism must be restrained, id., I, 1223. Those reborn through baptism should remember that they no longer possess their own flesh but Christ’s, so that they may enter into fellowship with Christ’s flesh; they should afflict the flesh with its vices and desires, St Hilary, IX, 499. The garment with which the Lord clothed us as we emerged from the sacred font must be preserved, St Ambrose, XV, 1642. “You have been washed once by saving baptism: do not return from the font to the mire; preserve the cleanliness granted you,” St Gaudentius, XX, 904. Baptism is given so that we may both die and live again, St Augustine, XL, 253. Since all past sins have been erased, the time after baptism is a time to guard against every future sin, id., XLI, 40. The newly baptized are exhorted to display innocence of conduct, id., XXXIX, 1560. Whoever does not put off the old human being does not make worthy use of baptism and therefore will be condemned, id., XLV, 1781. “You who rejoice in receiving baptism, live in the holiness of the new human being,” St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 478. Those renewed through baptism ought to be admitted to the Lord’s table, Leidrad, XCIX, 866. If anyone returns to what he or she renounced, and likewise, after receiving such great faith, lapses into apostasy, and so forth, that person is without doubt a transgressor of both covenants, Jonas, CVI, 128. If all sins have been forgiven us in baptism, why do we obey the vices and promptings [Col. 0848] of the flesh? Haymo, CXVII, 410. After baptism one must abstain from carnal sins, ibid. Having died to sin through baptism, we ought not live for it again, Hervaeus, CLXXXVII, 670. Those baptized in Christ ought to die and be buried to the world in deed, word, and affection, Henry, CCIV, 301. The covenant made in baptism may under no circumstance be transgressed, Garnerius, CCV, 787.

## XVII.—Sermons, Letters, and Books Treating Baptism

Book on Baptism against Quintilla, Tertullian, I, 1197. Letter of St Cyprian on baptizing heretics, St Cyprian, III, 1103. Letter of St Cyprian to Pompey against Stephen’s letter on baptizing heretics, ibid., 1127. Letter of St Cyprian to Magnus on baptizing Novatians and on those who receive grace while in bed, ibid., 1137. Anonymous book on rebaptism, ibid., 1184. Sermon on baptism, St Pacian, XIII, 1089. Seven books on Baptism against the Donatists, St Augustine, XLIII, 107. Three books on the baptism of little children, id., XLIV, 109. Treatise on baptism, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 772. Book on Understanding Baptism, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 112. Book on the Sacrament of Baptism, Leidrad, XCIX, 853. Letter on the ceremonies of baptism, Amalarius of Trier, XCIX, 892. Short work on the mystery of baptism, Magnus of Sens, CII, 981. On the Order of Baptism, addressed to Magnus of Sens, Theodulf, CV, 223. Jesse’s letter on baptism, id., CV, 781. Collections concerning ancient baptismal rites, Maxentius of Aquileia, CVI, 54. On the Sacrament of Baptism, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 309. Treatise on the order of holy baptism, id., CXII, 1173. On the Sacrament of Baptism, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1046. Treatise on baptism, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1031. On the Sacrament of Baptism, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 441; CLXXVII, 388. On the Increase and Immersion of Baptism, and the Reasons for Baptizing, Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 957. On Baptism, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 843.

[Col. 0847]

## XCVII. INDEX ON CONFIRMATION, SETTING FORTH THE EXCELLENCE AND NECESSITY OF THIS SACRAMENT, THE DISPOSITIONS REQUIRED TO RECEIVE IT, ITS EFFECTS, AND WORKS TREATING IT

### Whether Confirmation Is a Sacrament

Confirmation is a sacrament, Tertullian, II, 54. The sacrament of confirmation, St Cyprian, III, 1114. The sacrament of chrism belongs to the class of visible sacred signs and is most holy, just as baptism itself is, St Augustine, XLIII, 342; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 351. Chrism is a sacrament, Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 146. What confirmation is, Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, CLVII, 226; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1740; Robert Pullen, CLXXVI, 846; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 855; Alan of Lille, CCX, 369.

### On Its Excellence and Necessity

Whether the sacrament of laying on of hands is greater than baptism, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1069; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1856; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 462; Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1241. How great are the dignity, usefulness, and necessity of this sacrament, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 378. On confirmation, which the people should diligently seek from bishops, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1106. This sacrament is necessary for those who are to live, that they may be fortified by the strengthening of the Holy Spirit, St Otto of Bamberg, CLXXIII, 1358.

### On Its Effects and Whether It Can Be Repeated

Confirmation clothes with the Holy Spirit, Tertullian, II, 50. In that laying on of hands the flesh is overshadowed, so that the soul may be illumined by the Spirit, ibid., 806. The Holy Spirit is now received through laying on of hands, St Augustine, XXXV, 2025; St Isidore of Seville, LXXIII, 824. In the laying on of hands gifts of virtues are conferred, Leidrad of Lyons, XCIX, 865. Why the sacrament of confirmation is bestowed upon a baptized person, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1070. Through the sacrament of confirmation we are incorporated into the body of the faithful, Hildebert, CLXXI, 595. Inquiry concerning the efficacy of this sacrament, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 137. The opinion of heretics who say that confirmation has no efficacy, Alan of Lille, CCX, 369. No one is to be confirmed a second or third time, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1072. It is not repeated, St Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 1102; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 161; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1745; Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 846; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 855.

### On the Minister of This Sacrament

Confirmation is given by bishops alone, Tertullian, III, 1197. Those baptized are presented to the Church’s rulers, that they may be perfected by the Lord’s seal, ibid., 1115. Formerly, confirmation was given by the bishop immediately after baptism, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 385. The bishop is the minister of this sacrament, ibid., 349. Whether priests may anoint baptized persons with chrism, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 235. The Greeks maintain that the sacrament of confirmation can be conferred by priests; they are refuted, Ratramnus of Corbie, CXXI, 332. With respect to the sealing of infants, it is plainly unlawful for it to be done by anyone other than a bishop, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 695. The bishop alone performs so great a mystery, St [Col. 0849] Peter Damian, CXLIV, 808. Baptized infants should be presented to bishops for confirmation, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 120. The sacrament of laying on of hands can be performed by none other than bishops, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1857; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1069; Sicard of Cremona, CCXIII, 333; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 459.

### On Dispositions for Receiving It

That persons of full age should come fasting to confirmation, Herard of Tours, CXXI, 769; Burchard, CXL, 739; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 121, 1071. Preparation for receiving this sacrament; confession required before confirmation, Odo of Sully of Paris, CCXII, 59.

### On the Matter, Form, and Rites of This Sacrament

The faithful are anointed with chrism, Tertullian, I, 1206; III, 1040. The sacrament of chrism, St Augustine, XLIII, 342. The anointing of divine chrism, St Salvian, LIII, 42. The sacrament of confirmation is given through anointing with chrism, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 711, 717. The apostles used anointing with chrism and laying on of hands to confirm the baptized, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 350. It is called the sacrament of chrism, St Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 1102. Anointing with chrism is done on the forehead, ibid.; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 673. On chrism and its use, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 459. What oil and balsam signify, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1102. What the form of this sacrament is, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 352. What this form is among the Greeks, ibid. The form is explicit: namely, the words spoken by the bishop, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 855. After baptism, neophytes received laying on of hands, Tertullian, I, 1207. The rite of giving confirmation, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 318. The twofold rite of this sacrament: laying on of hands and anointing of the forehead with chrism, ibid., 350, 494, 495. Order of confirmation, id., CXXXVIII, 957. On the eighth day the baptized lay aside their mitres and are marked on the forehead by the bishop with chrism, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 673. When little children ought to be confirmed, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 847.

### Books Treating Confirmation

On laying on of hands, or confirmation, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 824. On the sacrament of confirmation, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1070; St Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 1102; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 673; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 137, 459; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 855.

[Col. 0849]

## XCVIII. INDEX ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST

### Notice

The Eucharist may be considered in a twofold respect: either as a sacrament or as a sacrifice. We have therefore established two indexes concerning it. In this first one we present the Eucharist insofar as it is a sacrament of the new law, instituted by Christ the Lord for the heavenly nourishment of our souls, in which the body and blood of Christ are truly, really, and substantially contained under apparent species. We treat: I. of the nature and institution of this sacrament; II. of the real presence and transubstantiation; III. of the excellence and necessity of the Eucharist; IV. of its recipients and use among ancient Christians; V. of its effects; VI. and we list the various treatises on the Eucharist found in the *Patrology*.

### I.—On the Nature and Institution of the Eucharist

The sacrament of the Eucharist, Tertullian, II, 79. Institution of the Eucharist, St Cyprian, IV, 376. The most august sacrament of the Eucharist, Lactantius, VI, 635, 993. What is the Eucharist? St Optatus, XI, 90. The mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated during supper, was not a supper, St Ambrose, XVII, 242. Institution of the sacrament of the Eucharist, ibid.; Juvencus, XIX, 317. On the sacrament of the Eucharist, St Jerome, XXII, 570; St Augustine, XXXIV, 723; XLII, 382, 658, 881; XLIII, 202; XXXIII, 200; XXXV, 1348. The sacrament of our price of redemption, id., XXXII, 338. It is called the sacrament of the altar, XXXVIII, 401. Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood at the time when the plan for his death was being formed, St Leo the Great, LIV, 332. The sacrament of the Eucharist, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 600; St Avitus, LIX, 321; St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1195; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 498, 264, 94; St Eligius, LXXXVII, 623. The mystery of the Eucharist is not to be investigated by reason, Alcuin, CI, 412. What the sacrament of the Eucharist is, St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 625; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 316; Florus, CXIX, 16. The institution of the Eucharist: when and why, ibid., 22 and following; Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1280. The sacrament of the Eucharist, Rodulfus, CXIX, 706; Ratramnus, CXXI, 132; Gezo, CXXXVII, 377; Hugh, CXLII, 1327; St Bruno, CLII, 66; Geoffrey, CLVII, 269; St Anselm, CLVIII, 453. The Eucharistic mystery, great and unsearchable, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 143, 145. Institution of the Eucharist, St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 429; Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 961; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1640; Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1618; Garnerius, CCV, 673; Innocent III, CCXVII, 874. (See the Table of the Sacrifice of the Mass: “On the Institution of the Sacrifice of the Mass.”)

### II.—On the Real Presence in the Eucharist and on Transubstantiation: Including Miracles

[Col. 0850]

Bread he calls his body, Tertullian, II, 348. In the Eucharist the substance of Christ’s body and blood is present, ibid., 461, 462. The Eucharist is a figure of Christ’s body, in what sense, note, ibid., 460. His body is reckoned as being in the bread, in what sense, note, id., I, 1160. The Eucharist is the Lord’s holy body, St. Cyprian, IV, 376. We receive Christ’s flesh assumed from the Virgin, St. Hilary, X, 355. We truly receive, under the mystery, the flesh of his body, ibid., 246, 247. The Eucharist given by the Donatists to dogs, which, maddened with rage, tore their own masters to pieces, St. Optatus, XI, 972. The altar is the seat of Christ’s body and blood, ibid., 1065. Chalices, bearers of Christ’s blood, ibid., 1068. You pluck the rose—that is, the blood of the Lord’s body, St. Ambrose, XV, 1390. Once consecration has taken place, bread becomes Christ’s flesh, id., XVI, 440. To offer upon altars the body which is to be transfigured, ibid., 824. Christ’s body is on the altar, ibid., 437. As the Son of God is true, so true is his flesh which we receive, and true is his drink, ibid., 453. The Lord himself testifies to us that we receive his body and blood, ibid., 444. In the Eucharist Christ’s flesh is truly received, and his blood is truly drunk, id., XVII, 753. In the sacrament of the Eucharist the truth and reality of Christ’s body and blood are established, St. Jerome, XXVI, 195. Christ’s body in the Eucharist is true and substantial, ibid., 569. The Eucharist is Christ’s body, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 401. The bread is Christ’s body; the cup is Christ’s blood, ibid., 1246. The Eucharist is called communion in the Lord’s body, id., XXXII, 720. The Eucharist is called the great table, from which we receive Christ’s body and blood, id., XXXVIII, 193. From the Lord’s table [Col. 0851] we taste beforehand not cheap foods or ignoble drinks, but the flesh and blood of Christ himself who was slain, id., XXXIX, 1662. Not every bread, but that which receives Christ’s blessing, becomes Christ’s body, id., XXXVIII, 1116. Christ bore his own body in his hands when he said, “This is my body,” id., XXXVI, 306, 308. Even the ungodly receive Christ’s true body and blood in the sacrament, id., XLIII, 181. The Eucharist is participation in Christ’s body and blood, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 357. In it is the truth of Christ’s body and blood, ibid., 452. The Eucharist contains Christ’s body and blood, id., LV, 67, 74, 76. Christ’s true body is contained in the Eucharist, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 690. The Church daily adores the Lord’s body and blood among the sacraments of the supreme mystery, Cassiodorus, LXX, 980. A highly memorable miracle concerning a Jewish boy, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 714. The healing of a blind man, ibid., 946. A paralytic healed, ibid., 952. A cripple whom an ox was dragging, ibid., 962, 963. Sick persons healed, ibid., 1116. The Eucharistic sacrifice contains the real presence of Christ’s body, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 228. Christ’s flesh and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist, ibid., 1127, 1178. Christ’s body is received in the Eucharist, and his blood is drunk, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 193. The truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 625; St. Ildephonsus, XCVI, 168. Revealed in ancient times to certain persons, Alcuin, CI, 1013. The truth of that presence is shown by a miracle, ibid., 1015. Christ is truly eaten and drunk, ibid., 504.

To doubt that the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ’s body and blood is most abominable madness, Haymo, CXVIII, 815. The Eucharist displays not a shadow or figure of Christ’s body, but his very body, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1367. It contains Christ’s very flesh, ibid., 1357. Whether Eucharistic bread is in reality Christ’s body, Ratramnus, CXXI, 129. The Redeemer’s flesh is in the Eucharist, Ratbertus, CXXXVI, 230, 402. An explanation of the conversion of wine into true blood and of bread into Christ’s flesh, ibid., 645. Firm faith in the real presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, Gezo, CXXXVII, 387. Various miracles concerning Christ’s ineffable presence in the Eucharist explained, ibid., 392, 393 and following. On the reality of Christ’s body in the host and of his blood in the cup, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 312. The judgment of the doctors concerning the truth of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist, ibid., 109, 145. The reality of Christ’s body and blood, St. Anselm, CXLIX, 520. The truth of the Eucharist maintained, Durandus, CXLIX, 1380. Various examples of Christ’s real and visible presence in the sacrament of the altar, ibid., 1417 and following. On the truth of Christ’s body and blood, Guitmund, CXLIX, 1427. Faith in Christ’s presence in the Eucharist is the faith of the whole world, ibid., 1489 and following. In the Eucharist Christ’s body is present in name, reality, and effect, Rupert, CLXVII, 1659. Bread truly becomes Christ’s flesh and wine his blood, Hildebert, CLXXI, 601. The real change of bread into Christ’s flesh is affirmed, ibid., 600; Stephen of Balgiac, CLXXII, 1293; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 468; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1518; St. Alger, CLXXX, 756; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 904; CLXXXIII, 493; Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 508, 504; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1777; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 861 and following. Faith in Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1209. Christ’s true body is eaten on the altar, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1117. Christ is truly received in the Eucharist, ibid. Supreme and living faith in Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, Peter of Celle, CCII, 769. The reality of Christ’s presence in the Eucharist, Baldwin, CCIV, 407; Ermengaud, ibid., 1252 and following; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1138, 1141. III.—On the excellence and necessity of the Eucharist.

The sacrament of the Eucharist commanded by the Lord for all, [Col. 0852] Tertullian, II, 79. It must be feared and prayed against, lest, while someone is kept apart from Christ’s body, he remain far from salvation, St. Cyprian, IV, 532. “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc., St. Hilary, X, 357. For otherwise one cannot attain the kingdom of heaven, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1107. The Eucharist is a sacrament older and more excellent than manna, id., XVI, 405; and than the other sacraments and mysteries of the Jews, ibid., 438. We eat Christ’s body in order that we may be partakers of eternal life, id., XV, 1816. Nor can those who have not eaten have life, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 785, 826, 984. Apart from baptism and participation in the Eucharist, no human being can attain not only the kingdom of God, but even salvation and eternal life, id., XLIV, 128, 129. This saying, “Unless you eat my flesh,” etc., binds everyone, including infants, ibid., 123, note 124. Participation in the Eucharist is necessary for little children to attain eternal life, ibid., 576, 648. Whoever neglects to eat Eucharistic food cannot have life in himself, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 330. The command to eat Christ’s body, ibid., 138. The excellence of the Eucharist, St. Avitus, LIX, 321. Whether the Eucharist is necessary for everyone’s salvation, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 861. The usefulness of the Eucharist, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 159. Its dignity makes the devout tremble, ibid., 161. The excellence of the Eucharist, St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 625. He who does not eat the bread of the Eucharist or drink the blood does not have eternal life, Bede the Venerable, XCII, 718. The consecration of Christ’s body and blood is the chief sacrament of our salvation, Alcuin, C, 428. Sacred honor and reverence are owed to the sacrament of the Eucharist, Jonas, CVI, 208. The Eucharist should be received daily, Regino, CXXXII, 428. Communion should be made at least on every Sunday, ibid., 225. Communion should be made three times a year, ibid., 189, 227. The Eucharist should be received four times a year, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562. An exposition on the dignity of the Eucharist, Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 179. Laypersons ought to communicate at least three times a year, Burchard, CXL, 756. The Eucharist is the Church’s chief sacrament, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 109. Whether the Eucharist is necessary for salvation, Lanfranc, CL, 611. Whether infants are obliged to receive it, ibid., 532. A Christian should prepare to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at least three times a year, id., CLI, 1176. When receiving the Eucharist is necessary, Guibert, CLVI, 329. It is necessary for salvation, Rupert, CLXVII, 1661. A magnificent encomium of the Eucharist, Hildebert, CLXXI, 516. For whom it is necessary, Otto, CLXXIII, 1358. We must eat Christ’s flesh if we wish to have abiding life in ourselves, William, CLXXX, 349. The excellence of the Eucharist, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1092. The Eucharist is the chief sacrament, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 257. No Christian may lawfully abstain from participation in so great a sacrament, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1271. Great and inestimable is the dignity of the sacrament of the Eucharist, Baldwin, CCIV, 403. No one is saved unless he has eaten, Bonacursus, CCIV, 782. No one can have eternal life unless he has eaten Christ’s flesh and drunk his blood, ibid., 1252.

IV.—On the recipient and use of the Eucharist, and on dispositions for receiving it.

We anxiously suffer if even some small part of our cup or bread falls to the ground, Tertullian, II, 80. Before every food they tasted Eucharistic bread, id., I, 1296. We receive the sacrament of the Eucharist even in gatherings before dawn, and not from anyone’s hand except that of the presiding ministers, ibid., 79. The ancient use of the Eucharist among the early Christians, ibid., 80. They received it in their hands, ibid., 669. From the hand of the priest, id., II, 79. An actor is not to be admitted to communion, St. Cyprian, IV, 362. The Eucharist carried in the hand, ibid., 486, 631, 784. The Lord’s holy thing is stored in a chest for domestic communions, ibid., 486. The unbaptized ought not to touch the Lord’s body and blood, ibid., 1172. The Eucharist is received daily, ibid., 90, 209. Unworthy communions punished by miracles, ibid., 485. On dispositions for communion, ibid., 254. To give the Eucharist to the unworthy is to profane the Lord’s holy body, ibid. One must not receive the Lord’s body with defiled hands, or drink the Lord’s blood with a polluted mouth, ibid., 484. They approach the Lord’s holy thing with hands foul and infected with stench, ibid., 478. What fault unworthy communion is, ibid., 479. One must not receive the Eucharist before sins have been expiated, before public confession of one’s crime has been made, before conscience has been cleansed, ibid. Violence is inflicted upon his body and blood, ibid., 486, 631, 784. How cautiously those who carry Christ’s body with them ought to proceed, ibid., 784. The Eucharist must be received with fear and honor, ibid., 774. Daily communion, St. Hilary, X, 970. Judas was not worthy of communion, id., [Col. 0853] IX, 1066. The old man does not receive this food, ibid., 1963. The Eucharist could not be seen by catechumens, St. Zeno, XI, 60. Women formerly received it in linen cloths, men in bare hands, ibid., 113. Christians carried it home, ibid., 60. Eucharistic communion after baptism, ibid., 241. How impious it is to cast away the Eucharist, St. Optatus, XI, 976. The sacrament of the Eucharist is not disclosed to those to whom it is unsuitable, ibid., 340. Let us cleanse our hearts and bodies, so that at the Lord’s altar we may be satisfied with his body and blood, id., XVII, 654. One must approach communion with a devout mind and with fear, ibid., 243. He who approaches the Lord’s table heedlessly differs in no respect from an unbeliever, ibid., 244. We are commanded to ask for this bread daily, so that, through the Lord’s mercy, we may be worthy daily to receive the bread of the Lord’s body, St. Chromatius, XX, 361. How it must be eaten, ibid., 857. Communion is received before food, Rufinus, XXI, 418, 419. Preparation is required for receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 419. Daily communion is recommended, ibid. Daily reception of the Eucharist, St. Jerome, XXII, 672. Delayed communion in Christ’s body does not make one holier, ibid., 506. Whether intercourse prevents communion, ibid., 505. “I know that this is the custom at Rome: the faithful always receive Christ’s body; I neither censure nor approve it,” ibid., 506. What the Roman Church and the churches of Spain observe concerning the Eucharist, and whether it should be received daily, ibid., 672. The Eucharist was administered to the people from an elevated place, id., XXIII, 157. The pure ought to receive Christ’s body, ibid., 238. The Lord’s Eucharist must be received cautiously, ibid., 529. Whoever approaches the Lord’s cup unworthily shall be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood, id., XXII, 352. Abstinence from fornications, id., XXXVIII, 85; XL, 1204. Chastity, id., XXXVIII, 735. The Eucharist should be received while fasting, ibid., 203. Whoever is to receive the Eucharist must be free from every hatred, ibid., 1974. The Eucharist was formerly given to the newly baptized, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 196; it is still offered to infants in the Eastern Church, ibid. Holy communion is not hindered by venial sins, Cassian, L, 1277. No one ought to judge himself worthy of it, ibid., 1215, 1230. It is not denied to the possessed, id., XLIX, 709. Aurel., LIX, 125. It was formerly given to newly baptized children under the form of wine, St. Paulinus, LXI, 861, 862. It was also kept in churches in ancient times, ibid., 877. On the altar beneath the cross, ibid., 877, 884. In a golden or silver tower, ibid., 878. In a dove-shaped vessel, ibid., 882, 884. The Eucharist received by disciples who were not fasting, St. Eugyppius, LXII, 762. Frequent communion for preserving chastity, St. Benedict, LXVI, 335. Daily communion, ibid., 578. On feast days, ibid., 577. On Sunday [Col. 0854] and Saturday, ibid., 578. Once a month, ibid., 579. Those who have suffered a nocturnal emission abstain from communion, ibid., 419. Food should not be taken immediately after communion, St. Benedict, LXVI, 613. Communion is given to penitents at the point of death, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 46. Those to whom it must be denied, ibid. The Eucharist must not be given to dead bodies, Fulgentius, LXVII, 960. The Eucharist was formerly given to laypersons in their hands, Cassiodorus, LIX, 345. Communion under one kind, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 17. The use of the Lord’s body in the Church is most ancient, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 159. Christ’s blood is drunk not only by the mouth of the body, but by the mouth of the heart, Taio, LXXX, 795. Preparation for communion, St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 625. Separation at times from receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 626. Communion should be granted to the sick person before completion of penance, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 385. Viaticum must be carefully administered to the sick, ibid., 382. The Eucharist must not be dispensed to the dead, St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 822. Christ’s body is eaten by all Christians, Heterius, XCVI, 933. Daily communion, ibid., 941. Preparation for communion, ibid., 942. Religious devotion and humility in receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 941 and following. It is always received while fasting, ibid. The Eucharist must always be ready for communicating the sick, Charlemagne, 326. A priest should always have the Eucharist prepared, lest anyone die without communion, ibid., 532. Disposition for receiving the Eucharist, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 230. Confession and penance must precede communion, ibid., 231. Neglect of the Eucharist strongly rebuked, Theodorus, XCIX, 946. When communion should be made, ibid., 955, 1028. The Eucharist must not be withheld at the last extremity, Alcuin, CI, 1276. Those who can or cannot communicate daily, ibid., 1263. How one should approach this sacrament, ibid., 1090. Reception of the Eucharist, St. Benedict of Aniane, CII, 1097. Communion should be frequent, Theodulf, CV, 205; Jonas, CVI, 201. The greatest discernment and sufficient preparation must be joined to it, ibid., 292. How Christ’s body should be received, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 316. The grave crime of those who approach unworthily, ibid., 318. Sinners must be barred from the Lord’s sacrament, Walafrid Strabo, CXIV, 938. When communion takes place, ibid., 941, 943. How the Eucharist should be received, ibid., 539. It should not be administered except to those fasting, ibid., 939, 940. One must approach that sacrament trembling, Haymo, CXVII, 574. Why the Eucharist is now received fasting, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1330. On reception of the Eucharist, Isaac, CXXIV, 1077. Sick penitents should not be suspended from communion, ibid., 1079. Communion granted to penitents at the point of death, ibid., 1078. Dispositions for communion, ibid., 1077. Unworthy communion, St. Adrevold, CXXIV, 951. Heavenly bread must be eaten spiritually, ibid., 950. Communion must not be denied to penitents at the last extremity, Hincmar, CXXVI, 413. Viaticum must be carefully administered to the dying, ibid.
