The Eucharist must not be administered to dead bodies, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 328. Whoever, having received the Eucharist, does not consume it is to be regarded as sacrilegious, ibid., 435. After reconciliation, priests should provide sick persons with the sacred viaticum, Riculf, CXXXI, 18. The Eucharist given to children, Regino, CXXXII, 205. The sacrament of the Eucharist must be handled with reverence and fear, Odo, CXXXIII, 575. Whoever handles the Lord’s body unworthily declares himself Judas’s companion, ibid. How the Eucharist should be received, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 402 and following. On those communicating unworthily, ibid., 504, 558. Whether it is preferable to receive the Eucharist frequently or rarely, ibid., 646. Sinners must be excluded from communion, Gezo, CXXXVIII, 389. Disposition for receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 391. A pure mind in all things, ibid., 388. Devotion, ibid., 400. The Eucharist must not be given to the dead, Burchard, CXL, 758. Those at the point of death must be refreshed with the sacred viaticum, ibid., 939. What daily reception of the Eucharist is, ibid., 755. [Col. 0855] One must not use marriage on the day of communion, for three or five days, ibid., 757. Communion must not be administered except to those fasting, except in a case of grave illness, ibid., 759. When one should abstain from receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 1075, 1076. The proper course concerning nocturnal emissions in relation to receiving the Eucharist, ibid., 762. In former times it was lawful to communicate under both kinds, John of Avranches, CXLVII, 37, 50, 52. To whom communion may be permitted on every Sunday, St. Anselm, CXLIX, 520. Penitents should abstain from the Eucharist, Lanfranc, CL, 424. In ancient times the Eucharist was offered to baptized infants, ibid., 609. We must receive the Eucharist fasting, ibid., 193. What unworthy profanation of the Eucharist is, and how great a crime it is, Radulfus Ardens, CLV, 1837. The sacrament of the Eucharist requires a state of grace and dispositions of devotion, ibid., 1552. Worthy preparation is required for holy communion, ibid., 1834. Infants formerly received Christ’s blood, Guibert, CLVI, 514. Now they communicate under the form of bread, ibid. The offering of an Eucharist moistened with blood is prohibited, ibid., 564. What equality of merits accomplishes in receiving Christ, ibid., 631. Christ’s body is eaten daily, and his blood drunk daily by priests, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 265. Communion under both kinds and under one only, id., CLIX, 255. Those who eat Christ’s body must be clean from all leaven of malice, id., CLVIII, 541, 912. The Eucharist was formerly given to little children, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 94. It must not be communicated to actors and magicians who persist in their vice, ibid. Augustine neither praises nor censures receiving the Eucharist daily, ibid. How one approaching the Eucharist can be secure and fearless, ibid., 94. People ought to approach communion fasting, ibid., 170. Evil Christians are forbidden to receive Christ’s body and blood, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 298. Whoever approaches to receive Christ’s flesh and blood should be fragrant with moral integrity and the sweetness of virtues, ibid., 436. Faith and purity of soul, ibid., 169. Dispositions for communion, St. Stephen, CLXVI, 1432. Who they are that eat Christ’s body unworthily, Rupert, CLXIX, 201. The Eucharist must be denied to those convicted of a crime, id., CLXVIII, 1545. Let one polluted by his own guilt not receive the Eucharist, id., CLXVII, 941. Faith, id., 39. Humility, id., CLXIX, 1238. Mutual charity is especially necessary for worthy reception of the Eucharist, Hildebert, CLXXI, 562, 572; and penance, ibid., 565. Whoever is about to approach the Eucharist should judge himself, lest he be judged by Christ, ibid., 663. Whoever receives the Eucharist is bound to cleanse his thoughts, ibid., 601. Whoever communicates unworthily is guilty of Christ’s death, ibid., 803. Those who handle the Eucharist worthily shall be rewarded, Honorius, CLXXII, 1129. Those who do so unworthily are at once betrayers and crucifiers of the Lord, ibid. The Eucharist is food for the soul and must be received devoutly, Otto of Bamberg, CLXXIII, 1358. Spiritual communion, ibid. A twofold manner of receiving the Eucharist mentally and spiritually, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 143. The Eucharist dipped in wine is forbidden, ibid. Bodily eating of Christ’s body, William, CLXXX, 354; spiritual eating, ibid., 351. How Christ’s body may truly and beneficially be received, St. Alger, CLXXX, 803. No unworthy person should presume to approach the Eucharist, Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 936. Easter communion, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 281. Threefold communion, id., CLXXXII, 908. The difference between good and unworthy communion, id., CLXXXIII, 218. How great purity is required for communicating, id., CLXXXII, 601. To whom the Eucharist should be given or denied, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 373. Whoever continually sins should continually receive the medicine of the heavenly sacrament, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1838. We ought to receive the sacrament of Christ’s body only while fasting, ibid., 1757. Before holy communion each person should abstain from his own wife, ibid., 1739. Both good and evil persons receive Christ’s body and blood, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 858. Whoever does not examine himself receives death, ibid., 1646. Whether the Eucharist should be received daily, ibid., 1647. Worthy and unworthy persons partake of the sacrament of the altar, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1181. Whoever is to approach the table should first wash his hands, Isaac of Stella, CXCIV, 1840. Worthy and unworthy communion, Richard, CXCV, 263. How the Lord’s lamb should be eaten, id., CXCVI, 262. Chastity, holiness, piety, justice, and devotion for communicating, Peter of Celle, CCII, 763. When a second communion is permitted, ibid., 763, 1132. Faith and holiness, Ermengaud, CCIV, 1254. Receiving the Eucharist belongs to all Christians, Peter Cantor, CCV, 101. How great purity of conscience is required for receiving Christ’s body and blood, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1149.

V.—On the effects of the Eucharist.

The flesh feeds on Christ’s body and blood so that the soul too may be nourished by God, Tertullian, II, 806. We receive the Eucharist daily as food of salvation, St. Cyprian, IV, 531. We cannot shed our blood for Christ if we blush to drink Christ’s blood, ibid., IV, 386. The Lord’s cup so intoxicates those who drink it that it makes them sober, and brings their minds back to spiritual wisdom, etc., ibid., 382. After Christ’s blood has been drunk, the memory of the old man is set forth, ibid., 383. The faithful drink Christ’s blood daily as they shed their blood for Christ, ibid., 350. Mouths sanctified by heavenly foods, ibid., 466. Christ is the bread of those who touch his body, ibid., 531. The Eucharist is life-giving food, St. Hilary, IX, 505. The power of this Eucharistic bread is that, being itself living, it gives life also to those who receive him, ibid., 709. As Christ lives through the Father, so we live through his flesh, id., X, 248. The natural unity of the faithful in God is bestowed through the incarnation of the Word and the sacrament of the Eucharist, id., IX, 245. The Eucharist is a pledge of eternal salvation, a safeguard of faith, and hope of resurrection, St. Optatus, XI, 1065. It has been proved that our Lord is food, a feast, or nourishment for those who eat, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1107. It is food of refreshment, etc., id., XV, 1780. The affection of the faithful is intoxicated, but the body does not stagger; rather, it rises again, ibid., 1420. It is forgiveness of sins, id., XIV, 686. This food supplies the substance of eternal life, id., XVI, 404. Whoever eats this body receives forgiveness of sins and shall not die eternally, ibid., 444. You who receive his flesh partake of his divine substance in that food, ibid., 455. The protection and effect of the Eucharist, ibid., 1306. Whenever you drink Eucharistic wine, you receive forgiveness of sins and are intoxicated in the Spirit, ibid., 449. The Eucharist supplies the substance of eternal life, ibid., 404. “I ought always to receive that blood, so that my sins may always be forgiven,” ibid., 446. When we eat Christ’s body, we partake of divinity and humanity, id., XVII, 20. We receive the mystical cup of blood for the protection of our body and soul, ibid., 243. Christ becomes our refreshment in the Eucharist, St. Gaudentius, XX, 855. The Eucharist alone nourishes, Rufinus, XXI, 432. The effects of unworthy communion: it does not help the defiled, St. Jerome, XXX, XXVI, 352, 575. The effects of the sacrament of the Eucharist, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 145, 649. It gives life to the good and brings death to the evil, id., XXXV, 16[lacuna]3. In the Eucharist the faithful person has that by which to live, and that from which to live, ibid., 1612. “Eat life; drink life; you shall have life, and life is whole,” ibid., 729. Christ willed to be our salvation in his body and blood, id., XXXVI, 303. The Eucharistic cup intoxicates martyrs for undertaking heavenly things, id., XLIII, 298. The Eucharist is the sacrament of piety, the sign of unity, id., XXXV, 1612. The Jews were darkened by the crucified Christ; we are enlightened by eating and drinking the Crucified One, id., XXXVI, 313. The Eucharist is the mystery of peace and unity, id., XXXVIII, 1100, 1103. Harmony and union are effects of the sacrament of Christ’s body, id., XXXV, 1613, 1614. The power understood in the Eucharist is unity itself: so that, gathered into Christ’s body and made his members, we may be what we receive, id., XXXVIII, 589. In the Eucharist, how many eat and drink judgment upon themselves, ibid., 645. Receiving the Eucharist greatly helps against demonic illusions and nocturnal emissions, Cassian, XLIX, 1225. The Eucharist is strength for body and mind, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 401. It is viaticum and a banquet, and is given for salvation, ibid., 623. Taken unworthily, it inflicts a wound, ibid., 395. It makes us sharers in the divine nature, St. Leo the Great, LV, 74. It benefits mind and body, ibid., 79. The Eucharist should be received not for judgment but for protection, ibid. For those who receive it unworthily, it turns into an increase of condemnation, ibid., 25. Christ’s body cleanses from sins and defends from dangers, ibid., 67. Effects of the Eucharist, St. Avitus, LIX, 321. The power and grace of the Eucharist, St. Paulinus, LXI, 905. The Eucharist is a remedy against temptations of the flesh, St. Benedict, LXVI, 335. Effects of the Eucharist, Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 534. Christ refreshes us through participation in his body, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1038. Wine gladdens the heart when it has been consecrated into Christ’s blood, ibid., 733. Christ nourishes the faithful with his body and blood, ibid., 973. How the Lord’s blood intoxicates, ibid., 170. Christ is manna in communion, ibid., 562. The Eucharist is the fountain of the thirsty soul, Lives of the Fathers, LXXIII, 638. It is light to worthy recipients, and then a consuming fire, ibid., 648, 869, 887, 720. It effects forgiveness of sins, ibid., 1161. Through reception of Christ’s life-giving body and blood, the Church is fed and given drink, washed and sanctified, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 640. We are fed and given life, nourished and filled, by Christ’s body and blood, ibid., 654. The effects and fruit of the Eucharist, St. Isidore, LXXXV, 103, 191, 314; LXXXVI, 491; St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 626. Those who eat Christ shall live [Col. 0857] eternally, Bede the Venerable, XCII, 119. The soul is nourished by Christ’s body and blood, Angelomus, CXV, 560. The effects of worthy reception of Christ’s body, Gezo, CXXXVII, 382. Whoever receives the Eucharist frequently is terrible to demons, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 734. The deeper the humility of those approaching the Holy Eucharist, the greater will be their acquisition of grace, St. Bruno, CLXV, 139. Whoever eats Christ’s body and drinks his blood becomes one with him, ibid., 582. The effects and fruit of the Eucharist, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 274; CLXXXIV, 984, 985. Wicked persons who do not cease communicating are defiled, not cleansed, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1741. This common bread, changed into flesh and blood, procures life and growth for bodies, St. Anselm, CLXXXVIII, 1643. It is life for the soul and health for the mind, ibid., 1644. By this sacrament paradise is opened to humankind and the devil is overcome, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1147. The Lord’s body is salutary to some, deadly to others, Alan of Lille, CCX, 284.

VI.—Books treating of the Eucharist.

Books on the Body and Blood of the Lord, St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1267. *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* [Col. 0858], Ratramnus, CXXI, 104. *On the Body and Blood of the Lord against the Absurdities of John Scotus*, Adrevaidus, CXXIV, 948. *Book on the Body and Blood of Christ*, Gezo, abbot of Derton, CXXXVII, 372. *Short Treatise on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 177. Adelmann’s letter to Berengar on the sacrament of the Eucharist, Adelmannus, CXLIII, 1290. Profession of faith concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, Maurilius, CXLIII, 1390. *Book on the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar and His Followers*, Durandus, abbot of Troarn, CXLIX, 1376. Three books on the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, Guitmundus, archbishop of Aversa, CXLIX, 1428. *Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar of Tours*, Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 407. *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, Bonizo of Piacenza, CL, 858. *Short Work on the Sacrament of the Altar*, Blessed Wolphelmus, CLIV, 434. *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 135, 1071. *Book on the Holy Eucharist*, Hildebertus, CLXXI, 1196. *Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, William of Saint-Thierry, CLXXX, 346; Algerus Scholasticus, CLXXX, 744; Baldwin, CCIV, 641.

**NOTE.** Questions concerning the matter, form, minister, and so forth, of the Eucharist are treated in the index of the sacrifice of the Mass.

[Col. 0857]

## XCIX. INDEX ON SACRIFICE IN GENERAL

### NOTICE

Sacrifice, taken in its broader sense, is, as it were, a sacred act: a work proper to religion and to be offered to God alone. In this Index we treat in turn: I. Sacrifice in general; II. Spiritual sacrifice; III. Ancient sacrifices among the Patriarchs, Gentiles, and Hebrews; IV. Offerings and firstfruits; V. Tithes; VI. The new sacrifice.

### I.—On Sacrifice in General

The rational institution of sacrifices, Tertullian, II, 310. For the honour of God, ibid. On sacrifice and a gift worthy of God, Lactantius, VI, 728. External sacrifice is indeed always owed to God, even by natural reason, ibid., note 913. Yet we maintain that both inward sacrifice, by which the mind is offered to God, and outward sacrifice also are owed by us to him, ibid. On the true and perfect sacrifice, St Augustine, XLI, 283. Four things to be considered in every sacrifice, idem, XLII, 901. Sacrifice is an ancient institution, idem, XXXIII, 377. The antiquity of worshipping God through sacrifice, idem, XLI, 281. The first parents in Paradise offered themselves to God as most pure victims, ibid., 701. Sacrifice is due to the one God, idem, XXXII, 377, 378; XXXVIII, 1249; XXXIX, 1667; XLI, 255, 256, 281, 654; XLII, 382. The miracles performed through the ark of the testimony attest this, idem, XLI, 296, 297. Visible sacrifice is to be offered to no other than him to whom invisible sacrifice is due, ibid., 297. Why demons demanded sacrifice, ibid., 460. Demons demand it be rendered to them because they know it is due to the true God, ibid., 298. They delight not in the smoke of any bodily thing, but in the mind of the suppliant, ibid., 298. Sacrifice shows clearly to whom it is due, not only when the true God justly commands it, but also when a false god arrogantly demands it, idem, XLII, 409. Demons would not have sought sacrifice, priesthood, and temple for themselves unless they knew these were due to the one God, idem, XXXIII, 377. Pagans are not to be blamed for sacrifices, but because they offer them to idols, ibid. Sacrifice must not be offered to a bodily creature, nor to a spiritual creature, however just, and still less to one that is wicked, ibid., 378. Not to good gods nor to evil ones, idem, XLI, 650. Not to angels or to the powers of God, ibid., 654. Not to martyrs, ibid., 255, 256, 772. Angels and holy human beings rejected sacrifice or divine honours, ibid., 298. Very few persons are recorded as having desired sacrifices for themselves or wished through them to be regarded as gods, idem, XLII, 624. Why a demon demands sacrifices, ibid. Why God wished sacrifices to be offered to himself, idem, XLI, 296. God has no need of sacrifices; but in accepting, rejecting, or receiving them, he provides only for human beings, idem, XXXIII, 377; XLI, [Col. 0858] 281, 295, 296, 654. To offer sacrifice and praises is beneficial to us, not to God, ibid., 527; XLII, 624. Why God commanded sacrifices to be offered to himself, although he did not need them, idem, XLII, 231, 321. God desires sacrifice not as something by which he may increase, but as something beneficial to humanity, idem, XXXIX, 2252. Sacrifice is rightly offered when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered, Eugyppius, LXII, 671. What sacrifice is, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 254. The ancient distinction between *sacrificium* (“sacrifice”) and *hostia* (“victim”), idem, LXXXIII, 62. What sacrifice is, Alcuin, CI, 1134. Whence *immolatio* (“immolation”) takes its name, ibid., 1135. What a libation is, ibid. Whence victims are called *hostiae*, ibid. What *victimae* are and why they are so called, ibid. Whence a holocaust takes its name, ibid. In every sacrifice four things must be considered: to whom, by whom, what, and for whom it is offered, idem, C, 434. The distinction between sacrifice and holocaust, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 946; Hildebertus, CLXXI, 142. On sacrifice, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 553, 576. The question is resolved why God commanded sacrifices to be offered although they did not please him, Haymo, CXVII, 890. The example of Abraham’s sacrifice expresses the qualities by which an offering becomes pleasing to God: namely, promptness, perseverance, and faith, St Ambrose, XIV, 331. By indicating the twofold fault in Cain’s sacrifice, he shows that three vices may insinuate themselves into our offerings, ibid., 329. The firstfruits of the soul are especially to be offered, and what they are, ibid., 336. Firstfruits are to be evaluated not by time but by holiness, ibid., 342. Good works must be joined with faith, which is above all necessary, for a true sacrifice, ibid. What is fitting for those who offer sacrifices from plunder and the stripping of the poor, St Jerome, XXIV, 726, 727. He rebukes them because they sacrifice victims not from reverence for God but from desire for feasts, ibid., 733. God does not accept the sacrifice of those who sacrifice for a perverse end, St Augustine, XLI, 444. What sacrifices we ought now to offer, idem, XXXVI, 659. What sorts of sacrifices God loves and crowns, idem, XXXIV, 811. What kind of sacrifice is acceptable to God, idem, XXXVII, 1318. Whoever wishes to offer God a holocaust should be wholly inflamed with the fire of divine love, ibid., 1775. The mind that wishes to offer a gift to God must first be cleansed, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 915. What is given is received from the heart of the giver, ibid. Outward gifts are seasoned by the inward purity of the heart, ibid. The Lord does not wish to receive sacrifice from persons at discord, ibid., 916. The sacrifices of the impious are abominable, ibid. Those who sacrifice victims not from reverence for God but from desire for feasts are rebuked, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 863. These virtues are pleasing to the Lord in God’s sacrifice, and without them no sacrifice is acceptable, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 904. In order that these our sacrifices may please God, they must be rich and full of marrow, ibid. Sacrifice is seasoned with wisdom, St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 385. “Put your hand upon the head of your victim”: that is, restrain the pride of your flesh, ibid., 387. Let us gather wood to kindle this offering: that is, let us follow the examples of the righteous, ibid. Whoever departs from the Church derives no benefit from sacrifice, ibid., 388. One offers the Lord an unblemished lamb who keeps himself unharmed by every wickedness of sins, St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 395. Nothing but what is holy can be offered to God, ibid., 453. Let no one stained by vices offer sacrifice to God, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 251.

### II.—On Spiritual Sacrifice

That God must be propitiated not with earthly sacrifices but with spiritual ones, Tertullian, II, 608. Spiritual sacrifices of praise are indicated, ibid. Spiritual sacrifices are proclaimed acceptable, ibid. Celebrate this sacrifice without interruption by day and night, St Cyprian, IV, 417. On the true worship and sacrifice of God, Lactantius, VI, 1066. An incorporeal sacrifice is necessary for the incorporeal God, ibid., 1067. This is true sacrifice: not that which is brought forth from a chest, but that which proceeds from the heart; not that which is offered by hand, but that which is offered by mind, ibid. The sacrifice of praise, St Hilary, IX, 405. Let it proceed from holiness of works, ibid. What the evening sacrifice is, ibid., 826. “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise,” St Zeno, XI, 000; St Jerome, XXIV, 542. The altar and tabernacle upon which spiritual victims were offered to God, ibid. One offers God the victim of one’s conscience and humility, ibid., 821. We ourselves are sacrifice to God, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 317. No sacrifice of the righteous is more acceptable to God than that they offer themselves to God, idem, XLI, 700. We ourselves are the most splendid and best sacrifice, ibid., 772. A human being himself is God’s invisible sacrifice in his own heart, ibid., 297. We always have a sacrifice to offer God, idem, XXXVI, 659. Within us we have a sacrifice by which to move God, ibid., 475, 598. The sacrifice of righteousness through repentance, ibid., 81. The sacrifice of a contrite heart, idem, XXXVIII, 133; XLI, 282. One offers sacrifice to God who punishes oneself, idem, XXXVII, 1824. Humility of heart is sacrifice, ibid., 1705. In the New Testament the sacrifice of praise succeeds the bloody victims of the Old Testament, idem, XXXIII, 558. The sacrifice of praise, a gratuitous sacrifice, idem, XXXVI, 578; XXXVII, 1220, 1568. The holier sacrifice of praise is thanksgiving, idem, XLII, 624. The sacrifice of righteousness, idem, XXXII, 1195. Of thought and speech, ibid., 809. The sacrifices which we offer must be kindled by charity, idem, XXXVI, 629. Christ, priest and victim, fulfilled the sacrifice of praise, idem, XLII, 57. God requires a twofold sacrifice from us, idem, XXXIX, 2169. No sacrifice is so just as when we offer ourselves to God, idem, XXXV, 3339. A sacrifice of the heart offered to God remains whole for us, idem, XXXIX, 1955. No wicked person offers the sacrifice of praise, ibid., 1847. You were seeking what you might offer God for yourself: offer yourself; there is nothing better in all earthly creation, idem, XXXVIII, 317. God seeks you more than your gift, ibid., 50. On the wonderful sacrifice whereby a human being is both victim and priest to God, and how this is so, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 500. On the victim of body and soul rationally to be offered to God, ibid., 501. Human sacrifice derives from the pattern of Christ’s sacrifice, ibid., 502. How the victim of fasting is to be offered, ibid., 227. What victim we ought to offer God, one which also remains ours, ibid., 322. To strive after goodness and mercy is an acceptable sacrifice, St Valerian, LII, 702. The prophet David did not believe himself to be expiated by the sacrifices performed at that time, but rather by the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart, Cassiodorus, LXX, 351. One voluntarily sacrifices to the Lord who, from zeal for compassion, intercedes for even the least of his own, ibid., 383. We ought to sacrifice ourselves to God; what the sacrifice of righteousness is, ibid., 50. To offer oneself to the Lord is the sacrifice most acceptable to him, ibid., 198. What the voluntary sacrifices of the mouth are, ibid., 873. Who sacrifices the sacrifice of praise to God, ibid., 351. The sacrifice of praise honours the Lord when it has been offered in purity of faith and integrity of conduct, ibid., 357. Sacrifice should be voluntarily offered to the Lord, not at anyone’s coercive command, idem, LXIX, 815. The holocaust of prayer, to cleanse each virtue, must be offered, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 548. One does not offer it who does not restrain inward impulses, ibid., 549. Since in this life we daily offend in many things, we must offer God a sacrifice of a contrite heart and crushed spirit, idem, LXXIX, 599. The saints will offer the sacrifice of righteousness to God in eternal life, ibid., 600. What sacrifices God requires, Alcuin, CI, 586. Through Christ we ought to offer to God the Father the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving for every good received from him, Haymo, CXVII, 934. There are three chief and perfect sacrifices which we are bound to render to the Lord, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 904. The sacrifice of devout contrition, the sacrifice of righteous action, and the sacrifice of praise and rejoicing, ibid. The first sacrifice propitiates God, the second delights him, and the third honours him, ibid. The sacrifice of devout contrition requires the butter of humility, which consists in three things, ibid. The sacrifice of righteous action requires the oil of discretion, ibid. The sacrifice of praise requires the balm of devotion, ibid. Opposed to the sacrifice of contrition is the wormwood of indignation, ibid., 905. Opposed to the sacrifice of righteous action is the vinegar of confusion, ibid. Opposed to the sacrifice of praise is the poison of flattery or detraction, ibid. How we offer the Lord morning and evening sacrifice, ibid., 332. Sacrifices of praise, St Bruno of Cologne, CLII, 857. On the sacrifice of the heart, Goffridus, CLVII, 167. How we ought to immolate and offer ourselves to the Lord, St Bruno of Segni, CLXI, 381. A sacrifice acceptable to God, idem, CLXIV, 387. The altar is the human heart, ibid., 398. On the sacrifice of angels, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 556. Threefold sacrifice, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1152.

### III.—On Ancient Sacrifices

**On the sacrifices of the patriarchs.**—The first parents in Paradise offered themselves to God as most pure victims, St Augustine, XLI, 701. God accepted Abel’s sacrifices, Tertullian, II, 601. Why, ibid. He prefigured the Christian people, ibid., 607. Why God rejected Cain’s sacrifice, ibid., 601. On the sacrifices of Cain and Abel, and what they prefigure, ibid., 607. Abraham’s sacrifice, a model for ours, St Ambrose, XIV, 331. What Cain’s sacrifice shows must be avoided in ours, ibid., 329, 336. On Abel’s sacrifice, ibid., 336. Cain offered the Lord a victim from the fruits of the earth; Abel, from the firstlings of his sheep, idem, XVI, 819. Where was the crime? Where the fault? Not in the offering of the gift, but in the disposition of the offering, ibid. Abraham divided the sacrifice which he was offering, ibid. Why Abel’s sacrifice pleased God more, idem, XIV, 956. He offered God not second things but first things, not scanty things but fat ones, ibid., 337. St Augustine, XXXV, 2017. Abel’s sacrifice: the faith of the New Testament, idem, XLII, 258. What the sacrifice offered by Abraham signifies, idem, XXXVII, 1362; XLI, 501. Abraham’s sacrifice as a figure of Christ’s immolation, idem, XXXVIII, 133. Sacrifices performed before the Flood, idem, XLI, 459. What the sacrifice of Abraham narrated in Genesis 15 signifies, ibid., 1361, 1362. The flame produced from heaven in Abraham’s sacrifice was not a miracle: why, idem, XXXII, 648. Abraham’s sacrifice on the mountain, idem, XXXVIII, 31. Cain’s sacrifice represents the earthly possessions of the Old Testament, idem, XLII, 258. The Patriarchs’ sacrifices correspond to ours because they were made to the whole Trinity, St Fulgentius, LXV, 342. How the sacrifices of Cain and Abel were received, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 164. Job offering sacrifice on the eighth day, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 532. Job does not cease to offer sacrifice on every day, ibid., 542. Since Cain and Abel offered gifts with unequal dispositions, the vows of the two were not accepted equally, Venerable Bede, XCI, 63. On the sacrifice of Abraham and Isaac, ibid., 244. Saul offers a holocaust and is rebuked by Samuel for his foolish action, ibid., 577. On Samuel’s sacrifice, idem, XCIII, 433. On Noah’s sacrifice, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 520. On Abraham’s sacrifice, ibid., 540. On the holocaust which Gideon offered God through the ministry of the angel sent to him, idem, CVIII, 1156. The question is asked why Gideon dared to offer sacrifice to God apart from the place where God had commanded it, ibid., 1157. The significance of the same sacrifice, ibid., 1158. How fittingly Noah offered sacrifice from all the creatures that had been preserved, as a figure of ours, Rupertus, CLXVII, 352. Job’s sacrifice, idem, CLXVIII, 964. On Abraham’s sacrifice, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXV, 645. How Abraham’s sacrifice differs from David’s sacrifice, Richard of Saint-Victor, CXCVI, 1037.

**On pagan sacrifices.**—Arnobius proves, whether by authority or reasoning, that no sacrifices should be made to the gods, Arnobius, V, 1219, 1220. For victims are not slaughtered for the gods’ pleasure, ibid., 1222. Arnobius also overturns the common opinion that the anger of the gods is appeased by sacrifices, ibid., 1217, 1226, 1227. Nor can anyone plausibly contend that victims are immolated to the gods in order that they may grant prosperity and remove adversity, ibid., 1229, 1230. Next it is said: It is absurd that gods should sell their benefits at the price of sacrifices, ibid., 1231. Nor is it more reasonably asserted that sacrifices are made to the gods as honour and to increase their power, ibid., 1232, 1233, 1234, 1236, 1239. Nor does it help to reply that, by antiquity and long custom, different victims are slaughtered for different gods, ibid., 1244, 1245. What Arnobius answers those pagans who object that sacrifices must be made to good gods so that they may benefit us, and to evil gods so that they may not harm us, ibid., 1246. On the sacred rites of the Roman gods, Lactantius, VI, 1028. On the rites introduced by Faunus and Numa, ibid., 1029. On the gods and rites of barbarians, ibid., 1030. Human sacrifices, ibid. On the origin of sacred rites and religions, ibid., 1031. The rites of Cybele were celebrated by Gallic priests, ibid., 206. Among the Cypriots, Teucer sacrificed a human victim to Jupiter, ibid., 230. There was a law among the Taurians that strangers be sacrificed to Diana, ibid. The Gauls propitiated Hesus and Teutates with human blood, ibid. Yet this rite of sacrificing human beings is evidently ancient, ibid., 231. On infants sacrificed to Saturn because of Jupiter’s hatred, ibid., 232. The sacrifice of the Gentiles is detestable, St Zeno, XI, 363. Pagan sacrifices are not to be thought good because God did not prevent them from being performed, St Augustine, XL, 583. The Gentiles performed sacrifices in wine-presses, idem, XXXV, 2085. The difference between Hebrew and pagan sacrifices, idem, XLII, 386. Among the Gentiles sacrifice availed for adults to remove original sin, and faith alone for infants, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 636.

**On Jewish sacrifices.**—The Jews were required to sacrifice in only one place, Tertullian, II, 607. The sacrifices of the Law were necessary, not voluntary, St Hilary, IX, 345, 596. Jewish sacrifice reproved, St Zeno, XI, 363, 364. It could be performed only in the Temple at Jerusalem, ibid., 515, note 2. Temporal sacrifices, neither perpetual nor true nor salutary, were prescribed for the Jews, St Philastrius, XII, 1231. Why Moses, after offering sacrifice, put half the blood into bowls and poured the other half upon the altar, St Ambrose, XV, 1220. He rejects the sacrifices of victims and teaches that Gospel obedience is above sacrifice, St Jerome, XXIV, 34. Victims, therefore, and the immolation of victims were not principally sought by God, but rather so that they should not be made to idols, ibid., 34. Let the Jews hear that God seeks not sacrifices but the disposition of those offering them, ibid., 654. “I do not want flesh; I abhor victims”: the sacrifices of the Jews, ibid. Jewish sacrifice in animal victims, St Augustine, XXXVI, 302, 303. Why formerly only unblemished animals were offered, idem, XLII, 624. Animal sacrifices did not delight God, idem, XXXIV, 810. Why the children of Israel visibly sacrificed animal victims, idem, XL, 31. Ancient sacrifices were imposed as suited to a perverse people rather than offered because God desired them, idem, XLII, 346. Carnal sacrifices were given to the Jews lest they lapse into idolatry, idem, XXXV, 1468. Whether sacrifice outside the Temple at Jerusalem was permitted, idem, XXXIV, 702, 863, 804. What sacrifices were offered for the people, the ruler, and the priest, ibid., 686, 687. Sacrifices for sins, called “sins,” idem, XL, 253; XLII, 744; XLIV, 403. Different sacrifices for sins, idem, XXXIX, 1541. The difference between Hebrew and pagan sacrifices, idem, XLII, 386. What the sacrifices of Hebrews, Gentiles, and Christians are in relation to the true sacrifice, ibid., 382, 409. The ancient sacrifices of the saints were figures of Christ’s true sacrifice, idem, XLI, 293. All these sacrifices signified in many and various ways the one sacrifice whose memorial is now celebrated, idem, XLIII, 231, 386, 406, 624, 625, 626, 661. All the sacrifices of the Law and Prophets were shadows of Christ’s sacrifice, idem, XL, 249. Abolition of the old sacrifice, idem, XXXIX, 2066. What animals were to be used for the sin-offering, holocaust, and so forth, idem, XXXIV, 686, 698. The sin-offering was not offered except together with a holocaust, ibid., 675, 676. The old sacrifices signified grace; they did not effect it, idem, XXXIII, 633. By the sacrifices of the Old Testament, sinners were convicted rather than cleansed, idem, XLIV, 139. The sacrifice commanded by God was suitable in the earliest times, but is not so now, idem, XXXIII, 527. The old sacrifices, like words of promise, were removed when the sacrifice of Christ’s body was given, idem, XXXVI, 441, 442. Though sacrifices are no longer performed, they remain authoritative in their signification, idem, XLII, 231. Everything pertaining to the old sacrifices was a figure of ours, ibid., 320. No one ate from the holocaust, idem, XXXIV, 823. Why God formerly commanded sacrifices although they did not please him, idem, XXXV, 2390. The abolition of the ancient sacrifices revealed, idem, XXXIX, 1816. The sacrifices of the old Law explained allegorically, St Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 194. The sacrifices of the ancient Law prefigured the sacrifice in which Christ offered himself to the Father, St Fulgentius, LXV, 182, 342. Why sacrifices ended at Christ’s coming, [Col. 0862] Cassiodorus, LXX, 288. The sacrifices of Aaron’s order perished, but those of Melchizedek remained, ibid., 796, 797. What the sacrifices of the old Law signified, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 73. The sacrifices of the old Law receive their dignity from the Eucharistic sacrifice of the new Law, idem, LXXXIII, 179, 432. Reprobation of ancient sacrifices from the testimony of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Joel, and Malachi, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 526. On the various Jewish sacrifices, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 256, 260 and following. To what those sacrifices commanded to be offered under the ritual of legal ceremonies refer, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 607. On the rejection of Jewish sacrifice and the election of the Christian sacrament, Samuel Marochitanus, CXLIX, 358, 359. The peace-offering, St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 386. The law of the sin-offering, ibid., 401, 402. The sin-offering, ibid., 433. The sacrifices of the old Law had their appointed time until Christ, ibid., 837. Ancient sacrifices were accepted by God not because of the shedding of blood, but because of their signification, ibid., 375. Among the Jews, a sacrifice for the dead was called the bread of mourners, Rupertus, CLXVIII, 138. The carnal sacrifices of the Law were not commanded but permitted, idem, CLXX, 583. On the various Jewish sacrifices, idem, CLXVII, 747 and following. The purpose of legal sacrifices, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1151. On holocausts and the manner of offering them, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1195. On peace-offerings and salutary offerings, ibid., 1196. On the offering of inanimate things, ibid., 1197. On victims for sin, ibid., 1198. For the sin of a priest, ibid. For the sin of the synagogue, ibid., 1199. On the victim for the sin of a ruler, ibid. On the victim for the sin of a soul, ibid., 1200. The three kinds of sacrifices in the old Law, and what they signify, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 554.

### IV.—On Offerings and Firstfruits

Firstfruits are to be valued not by time but by holiness, St Ambrose, XIV, 342. On the offering of firstfruits, Cassian, XLIX, 1172. An offering of firstfruits pleasing to God, ibid., 1171. Firstfruits must be offered to God, Maximus of Turin, LVII, 901, 904. In former times the faithful, clergy and laity alike, who were to communicate in the Mass offered their own offering at the altar for their communion, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 179, 432, 497, 549. Offerings were of two kinds: some to be consecrated into the Lord’s body; others to be blessed for the use of the poor, ibid., 550. On gifts or offerings to be offered to God, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 915. The four kinds of offerings, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 323. On offerings of fruits bestowed upon ministers of the Church, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 885. Offerings ought not to be made in Lent, ibid., 899. An offering ought not to be made in houses, ibid., 900. On the four kinds of principal offerings, Venerable Bede, XCIII, 387, 408. The children of Israel are commanded to offer the Lord firstfruits and to make a sanctuary, idem, XCI, 399. On firstfruits to be offered, idem, XCIII, 376. On firstfruits, Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 953. On what the Lord said to Moses concerning the offering of firstfruits, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 139. Where he grants all the offerings and firstfruits of the children of Israel to the priests and Levites, ibid., 695. On the firstborn to be sacrificed to the Lord, ibid., 393. On firstfruits of crops to be offered, ibid., 946. What was offered among the Jews was applied to the uses of priests, Haymo, CXVII, 33. What kinds are offered at the altar but not for sacrifice, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 204. That things which cannot be offered in churches are to be brought by the faithful to the priest’s house, ibid. On the offerings, that they are to be renewed from Sabbath to Sabbath, ibid., 306. On Church offerings, ibid., 232. To whom the offerings of parishioners ought to belong, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 699. That from the revenues and offerings in every Church four portions ought to be made, ibid., 701. On those who deny or reluctantly render offerings for the dead, ibid. Why salt is prescribed for all offerings, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 897. On firstfruits of seeds, Cnut, CLI, 1174. Into how many portions the offerings of the faithful are divided, and what falls to each person, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1084. On the firstfruits which the Lord commanded to be collected for constructing the tabernacle, Abbot Rupertus, CLXVII, 699.

### V.—On Tithes

On the offering of tithes, Cassian, XLIX, 1172. The offering of tithes pleasing to God, ibid., 1171. Tithes must be offered to God, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 901, 904. On dividing tithes, St Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1089. On offering tithes, Venerable Bede, XCIII, 376. On tithes, Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 953. On the tithes of the faithful, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 204. How tithes of land, crops, and fruits may be redeemed [Col. 0863], Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 583. On tithes to be given for the use of Levites, ibid., 701. On the payment of tithes, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 961. On tithes to be given by the faithful, Rodulfus of Bourges, CXIX, 714; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 200, 201. That four portions be made from tithes, ibid., 258. On a holding and tithes, ibid., 393. On rendering tithes, St Odo of Canterbury, CXXXIII, 950. That tithes must in no way be neglected, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 699. On those who refuse to give tithes, ibid. That tithes ought to be demanded as a debt from all Christians, ibid. On those who refuse to give a tithe unless they redeem it for a price, ibid., 700. That a tithe be called God’s tribute, ibid. That all churches and tithes be subject to the authority of bishops, ibid., 702. On rendering tithes, Cnut, CLI, 1174. On rendering Church tithes from sheep and piglets, Edward III of England, CLI, 1192. On bees and many other small tithes, ibid. That tithes which God has ordained to be given must be paid to God, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1093. Abbots and bishops are not to pay tithes from their own estates, ibid. That tithes ought to be given by the authority of the old Law, ibid., 1094. Three portions should be made from tithes: two for the clergy and a third for the bishop, ibid., 1095. Tithes are not to be redeemed by the people, ibid. A person taught and instructed by God offers tithes, Hugh of Saint-Victor, CLXXVI, 1344. Tithes are not to be possessed by laypersons, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1042 and following. One faithfully gives tithes who pays a tenth of all one possesses, ibid., 1044. Those who refuse to give tithes to priests are to be excommunicated, ibid. Tithes are to be paid following the example of the ancients, ibid., 1045. But tithes are not to be redeemed by the people if they refuse to give them otherwise, ibid. Because tithes are not rendered to God, the fiscal levy has been imposed, ibid. A fourth part of tithes is to be distributed to widows and the poor, Gerhohus, CXCIV, 1309. It is shown by the authority of councils that a fourth part of tithes must be bestowed upon the poor, ibid., 1313. It is contrary to the sacred canons for bishops permanently to alienate the tithes of churches, ibid., 1314. The objections of monks who claim for themselves a fourth part of tithes, though unwilling to assume the care of souls, are answered, ibid., 1320. Gregory VII’s decree concerning the tithes of monks and Regular canons is explained, ibid., 1325. On tithes, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1216.

### VI.—On the New Sacrifice

[Col. 0864]

Whether a priest of new sacrifices is expected must be investigated, Tertullian, II, 609. Whether he has already come or not, ibid. That the old sacrifice was to be annulled and a new one celebrated, St Cyprian, IV, 687. How much Christ’s sacrifice surpasses those sacrifices, St Hilary, IX, 345. The sacrifice of grace and praise is preferred to the sacrifices of the Law, ibid., 486. The sacrifices of the new Law are performed by the praises of living and intelligent victims, ibid., 405. The pure sacrifice of the Christian people, St Zeno, XI, 363, 364. The sacrifice of our God has abounded, and the sacrifices of the gods have been prohibited, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1356. All sacrifices have yielded place to our sacrifice, idem, 655. Christ’s sacrifice was signified by the sacrifices offered for sins, idem, XXXIV, 704. Christ’s sacrifice foretold by many figures, idem, XXXIX, 1667; XLIII, 154. The sacrifice of Christ’s flesh: the true and sole sacrifice for sins, idem, XLIV, 600. The sacrifice of the cross, idem, XXXIX, 1501. Christ offered himself as sacrifice in place of all sacrifices, idem, XXXVI, 71. Christ found in human beings nothing clean that he could offer for human beings; he offered himself as a clean victim, idem, XXXVII, 1953. The sacrifice of the New Testament, idem, XLII, 626. The sacrifice of Christians, ibid., 382. The truest and unique sacrifice, idem, XLIV, 211. Sacrifice to God in the Church, idem, XXXVIII, 1101, 1356, 1413. The figures, truth, and memorial of the sacrifice owed to God, idem, XLII, 386. The faithful know the sacrifice Christ offered, idem, XXXVI, 178. There is no place for the true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, St Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 430. Christ’s sacrifice confirmed by an oath, St Leo the Great, LIV, 154. How Christ’s sacrifice is not multiple but one, Alcuin, C, 1077. On the sacrifices of the New Testament and why sacrifices were changed through Christ, Rabanus Maurus, CXIV, 936. The passion of Jesus Christ is the truest sacrifice of righteousness, St Bruno, CXLII, 208. What is prefigured by the sacrifice offered in the ark of the cross, St Peter Damian, CXLIV, 607. On the new and true sacrifice, Abbot Rupertus, CLXX, 34. The dignity and difference of the sacrifice of the new Law and the old, St Bernard, CLXXXIV, 784. On the continual sacrifice, Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1242. On the three sacrifices of the Church, Innocent III, CCXVII, 842. (See *Sacrifice of the Mass*.)

[Col. 0863]

## C. INDEX OF THE SACRIFICE OF THE MASS, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER, AND SETTING FORTH THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING IT

### NOTICE

The Mass is the sole sacrifice of the new Law. It is *latreutic*, or honorary; Eucharistic, in thanksgiving for every benefit bestowed and to be bestowed; propitiatory and satisfactory for sins and punishments due; and impetratory of every good thing, first spiritual and secondarily temporal. In this Index we treat in turn: I. The figures and prophecies concerning the sacrifice of the Mass; II. Its institution; III. Its nature and excellence; IV. Its form; V. Its matter; VI. The power of this sacrifice; VII. To whom it is offered; VIII. For whom it may or may not be offered; IX. The minister of sacrifice; X. The manner of offering; XI. The language, time, and places in which Mass ought to be celebrated; XII. Defects occurring in celebration; XIII. The manner of hearing Mass; XIV. Attendance at Mass; XV. The celebration of Mass, historically and liturgically; XVI. The ordering of Mass; XVII. Various statutes concerning Mass; XVIII. Theological questions; XIX. Various Masses; XX. The various parts of Mass; XXI. Books treating of Mass found in the *Patrologia*.

### I.—On the Figures and Prophecies of the Sacrifice of the Mass
Figures.—In the priest Melchizedek we see prefigured the sacrament of the Lord’s sacrifice, St. Cyprian, IV, 375. In Solomon there is a type of the Lord’s sacrifice: mention is made of the victim offered and of bread and wine, ibid., 377. The same is signified in Judah’s blessing, ibid., 378; and also in Isaiah, ibid. — In Melchizedek’s sacrifice the sacrifice of the Mass was expressed, St. Ambrose, XVI, 403, 445. — In Melchizedek’s offering first appeared the sacrifice [Col. 0864] now offered to God by Christians throughout the whole world, St. Augustine, XLI, 500. By the sacrifices offered for sins was signified the sacrifice of the Mass, in which true remission of sins takes place, id., XXXIV, 704. The ancient sacrifices of the saints were manifold and diverse signs of the sacrifice of the Mass, id., XLI, 298. All those sacrifices signified, in many and various ways, the one sacrifice whose memorial is now celebrated, id., XLII, 231, 386. The promissory figures of this sacrifice had to be celebrated in animal victims, ibid., 409. By these sacrifices was signified the unique [Col. 0865] sacrifice now offered, ibid., 626. Melchizedek signified the Lord’s future sacrament and expressed the mystery of the body and blood by a sacrifice of bread and wine, id., XXIII, 1102. — Christ’s sacrifice and its figures, St. Leo the Great, LV, 147. Melchizedek’s sacrifice, a figure of the sacrifice of the Mass, id., LIV, 154. The offering of Christ’s body and blood now stands in place of all sacrifices of the Old Law, ibid., 341. — The saving sacrifice was prefigured by Melchizedek, who, in the type of the Lord’s body and blood, made an offering, St. Gregory, notes, LXXVIII, 365. — The figure of this most sacred offering came beforehand in Melchizedek, who used to offer wine and bread to God Most High, Letters of Alcuin, C, 289. — Likewise, in the priest Melchizedek we see prefigured this mystery of the Lord’s sacrament, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 321. — Melchizedek’s sacrifice was bread and wine, in which Christ’s body and blood were signified, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 1127. — Noah’s sacrifice was a figure of the sacrifice which Christ does not cease to offer to God the Father, both through himself and through the hands of his priests, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 352. — The Paschal lamb, a figure of Christ immolated in the sacrifice of the Mass, Peter Damian, CXLV, 879. — Isaac’s sacrifice, a figure of Christ’s sacrifice in the Mass: how this is so, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 430–431. The blood of Christ offered in the sacrifice of the Mass was prefigured in the blood of calves, ibid. The Paschal lamb was a figure of Christ, the Lamb of the new sacrifice, in which he himself first immolated himself to God the Father with his own hands, taking bread and wine, etc., ibid., 613. — The figure of this sacrament likewise preceded it in the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 139. The Paschal lamb, whose flesh was eaten by the people, preceded it as a figure of the sacrament of Christ’s body, ibid., 465. The bread and wine which Christ had earlier offered figuratively through Melchizedek, he consecrated into his body and blood at the supper, id., CLXXVII, 426–427. — The Mass figured by the sacrifice of the red heifer, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 705. — The lamb immolated in the Law and eaten by the Israelite people was a type of Christ offered on the altar, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1140. So was it prefigured in Melchizedek, who, in the type of our Savior, is read to have offered bread and wine together as a libation, ibid., 1143.

Prophecies.—Malachi’s prophecy concerning the sacrifice of the Mass: “For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great,” etc., “and in every place sacrifice shall be made and a clean offering shall be offered to my name,” St. Augustine, XLI, 594. We now see this sacrifice offered in every place through Christ’s priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, ibid. The same prophecy of Malachi concerning the sacrifice of the Mass, id., XLII, 61–62. Open your eyes and see: from sunrise to sunset the Christians’ sacrifice is offered not in one place but in every place, ibid., 627. — The same prophecy of Malachi, in Florus the Deacon, CXIX, 19.

## II.—On the institution of the sacrifice of the Mass

Having taken the bread and distributed it to the disciples, Christ made it his body, saying, etc., Tertullian, II, 460. Christ consecrated his blood in wine, ibid., 462. — Christ offered his own body and blood, St. Cyprian, IV, 376. He was the first to offer himself as a sacrifice to the Father, ibid., 385. Christ, author and teacher of our sacrifice, ibid., 373. Why Christ offered in the evening, ibid., 387. Christ offered the same thing as Melchizedek, ibid., 375. Account of the institution of the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 381. — “Desiring to offer that wonderful and heavenly sacrifice which you, O Lord my God, immaculate priest, instituted and commanded to be offered in commemoration of your death and passion,” St. Augustine, Appendix, XL, 956. On the day of the supper Christ consecrated the saving mysteries of consolation, id., XXXIX, 2035. — The sacrifice offered to God by Christians was first instituted by Christ our Lord and Master, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 754. Christ offered the sacrifice not in the morning but after supper, in the evening, ibid. — Christ gave humankind his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 316 ff. Account of the institution of our sacrifice, ibid., 318. Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ first instituted this rite of sacrifice when he entrusted his body and blood to his apostles, ibid., 322. With blessing and thanksgiving the Lord first dedicated the sacraments of his body and blood and delivered them to the apostles, ibid. — Institution of the sacrifice of the Mass, Florus the Deacon, CXIX, 22–23. The Lord offered the chalice after supper, because—ibid., 24. — Christ our Lord and Master first instituted the Christians’ sacrifice, Rodulfus of Bourges, CXIX, 717. — The Lord handed on the mystery of sacred communion to the apostles after supper, Gezo, CXXXVII, 374. — Christ made material bread his body [Col. 0866] on the very night on which he was voluntarily about to hand over his body to death for us through the mystery of his passion, Gerard of Cambrai, CXLII, 1278–1279. — Christ instituted the sacrifice of the Mass on the day before he suffered, Adelmann, CXLIII, 1292. — Christ instituted bread and wine as the sacrifice of his body and blood, Peter Damian, CXLV, 881. Christ took bread and the chalice into his holy and venerable hands, ibid. On the aforesaid night—namely, at evening on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month—in order to fulfill the figures of the Law, Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood after the typical Passover, ibid., 879. It can indeed be said that Christ, by divine power, made the body with the expressed formula by which those after him would bless it, ibid., 881. Christ gave this sacrament after supper so that the testator’s final command might be more firmly commended to memory, ibid., 883. The Lord himself commanded that we do this in remembrance of him, ibid., 884. — Christ offered the chalice as a sacrifice after supper and in the evening, Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 553. — Why Christ chose bread and wine for making the Eucharist, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 535. — Why, after the sacrament of the typical lamb, the Lord gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 530. — Our Lord Jesus Christ handed this sacrament to the disciples at supper, where the institution of this sacrament was first made, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 139. Our Lord and Savior Jesus instituted the celebration of the Mass when—id., CLXXVII, 416. The bread and wine which he had earlier offered figuratively through Melchizedek, he consecrated into his body and blood at supper, and commanded the same to be done in the Church, ibid., 426–427. When the sacrifice of the Mass was instituted, id., CLXXVI, 461. After the supper of the old Passover, he changed bread and wine into his body and blood by divine power, ibid., 461. Why Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine, ibid., 467. — On the day before he suffered, Christ prescribed to his disciples the form of this sacrament and displayed its efficacy—that is, he commanded that it be done, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 983. Returning to the table, Christ orders the sacrifice of his body and blood, handing over bread separately and wine separately, ibid., 984. Concerning the bread he says: “Take and eat; this is my body,” ibid. Concerning the wine likewise: “Drink of this, all of you. This is my blood, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins,” ibid., 984. By these words Christ commanded the sacrifice of the Mass to be celebrated, ibid. — Institution of the sacrifice of the Mass: “Do this in commemoration of me,” Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 687; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 856; Baldwin of Canterbury, CCIV, 651. — Explanation of the words by which Christ changed bread into body and wine into blood, Baldwin, CCIV, 654 ff. — How Christ consecrated, and under what form, Innocent III, CCVII, 859. On the hour of the institution, id., CCXVII, 874. On the various reasons for instituting the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 884; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 867.

## III.—On the nature of the sacrifice of the Mass and its excellence

Nature.—Having taken bread and distributed it to the disciples, Christ made it his body, etc., Tertullian, II, 460. Christ consecrated his blood in wine, ibid., 462. In the Eucharist the substance of Christ’s body and blood is present, ibid., 461. — Christ united the nature of his flesh to the nature of the flesh to be communicated under the sacrament unto eternity, St. Hilary, X, 246. Christ, about to suffer, consecrated the blood of his body which was to be poured out for the remission of sins, id., IX, 1068. — Before Christ’s words, the chalice is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have taken effect, there is Christ’s blood, St. Ambrose, XVI, 444. — The mystery of the Christian Church lies not in the immolation of irrational victims, but in the offering of bread and wine—that is, of the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, St. Jerome, XXIII, 961. — That bread which you see on the altar, sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s body, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1099. That chalice—indeed, what the chalice contains—sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s blood, ibid. Christ bore his body in his hands when he said, “This is my body,” id., XXXVI, 306. — The offering of Christ’s body and blood now stands in place of all sacrifices of the Old Law, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 341.

In the Eucharist Christ’s true body is contained, and its true offering takes place in the Mass, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 689. The Lord’s body and Christ’s blood are poured out in the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid. — The bread which we break is Christ’s body; the wine, moreover, is his blood, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 755. — In the sacrifice of the Mass the truth of the body and blood of Jesus Christ is affirmed, Alcuin, CI, 1087. — Christ gave humankind his body and blood under the appearances of bread [Col. 0867] and wine, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 316 ff. This is the very flesh—and therefore Christ’s flesh—which is still offered today for the life of the world, id., CXII, 1513. The Lord’s body, which is daily consecrated by the Holy Spirit from the substance of bread and wine for the life of the world, is another thing, ibid., 1514. Christ’s passion is renewed whenever Mass is celebrated, ibid., 1517. — On the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrifice of the Mass, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1277 ff. — Christ is daily immolated for us on the altar, Hincmar, CXXV, 915. And in the appearance of bread Christ’s flesh is true flesh, ibid., 920. — In the Mass Christ’s body and blood are made, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 714. — Christ is both sacrifice and priest on the altar, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 922. In the Mass Christ’s body and blood are sacrificed, ibid., 553. — That bread and chalice become Christ’s body not by any consecration whatever but by a definite consecration, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 135. That the bread which the Lord broke and gave to his disciples is the body of the Lord Savior, and that the chalice which he handed them is his blood, ibid., 140. The Church’s sacrifice is made of, and consists of, two things: the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ. In Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 152. Our Lord Jesus Christ gave his disciples to eat the body which he was shortly to hand over for us, and gave them to drink the blood which he was to shed for us, id., CLXII, 588. — For he is the true Lamb, immolated for us on the cross; his sacrifice is mystically renewed in the Mass and is substantially and spiritually given under the appearances of bread and wine, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 253. — After the supper of the old Passover, Christ changed bread and wine into his body and blood by divine power, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 461. — Before consecration that bread is bread, and likewise wine is wine; after consecration, the bread is Christ’s body and the wine his blood, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1741.

Let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to the disciples is the body of the Lord Savior, Alger of Liège, CLXXX, 777. — Why Christ’s immolation on the altar is not said to mean that he is killed again, but that his true immolation is represented and that what he then accomplished on the cross he now accomplishes on the altar, Alger the Scholastic, CLXXX, 786.

That what is offered and consecrated by the priest is called sacrifice and oblation because it is a memorial and representation of the true sacrifice and holy immolation made on the altar of the cross, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 866. — That the flesh now consecrated from bread on the altar is truly one and the same flesh as that believed to have been born of the Virgin and to have suffered on the cross, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1138. That the priest, in consecrating, commemorating the sacrifice and uniting Christ’s passion with tears, is Christ and crucified, both sacrificing and sacrificed, ibid., 1141.

Excellence.—“That divine and heavenly sacrifice, in which your flesh is truly received, in which your blood is truly drunk,” St. Ambrose, XVII, 753. “Where the presence of the holy angels is at hand; where you are established, wondrously and ineffably, as priest and sacrifice,” ibid. “Grant me, a sinner, to celebrate this heavenly sacrifice with fear and trembling, with purity of heart,” etc., ibid. “May that invisible form of your Holy Spirit descend, who may teach me, your unworthy priest, to handle so great a mystery,” ibid., 754. “That most holy mystery itself of your body and blood, by which we are daily washed and sanctified in your Church,” etc., ibid. — That sacrament of the heavenly table which feeds faithful and devout souls with flesh and gives them blood to drink, St. Augustine, Appendix, XL, 977. “This sacrament of yours surpasses all things,” ibid. The sacrifice of our ransom, ibid., 777. — The offering of Christ’s body and blood now stands in place of all sacrifices of the Old Law, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 341. — What believer can doubt that, in that mystery of Jesus Christ, choirs of angels are present, the highest are joined to the lowest, and earth is united to heaven, etc., Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1087? Therefore, although it is offered by a human being, this sacrament is nevertheless a divine reality, ibid. I do not doubt that the citizens above take part in this mystery, ibid. At the very hour of immolation Christ, together with the heavenly ministers standing by him, must be believed present in order to consecrate the things set before him, ibid., 1088. Who can comprehend the profound mysteries of this sacrifice, which continually imitates the passion of the only-begotten Son for our absolution? ibid., 1089. This ineffable sacrament is instituted, by whose sanctification we might be expiated without interruption, ibid., 1091. — Nothing can be greater among sacrifices than Christ’s body and blood, nor is any offering more powerful than this; rather, this surpasses them all, Remigius of Auxerre, CII, 1101.

Do not doubt that, at the hour of the sacrifice of your Redeemer’s body and blood, angels are present with their Creator, St. Anselm [Col. 0868] of Canterbury, CLVIII, 918. “That divine and heavenly sacrifice in which your flesh is truly received, in which your blood is truly drunk,” ibid., 922, from St. Ambrose. “Where the presence of holy angels is at hand, where you are sacrifice and priest, wondrously and ineffably,” ibid. Teach me through your Holy Spirit to handle so great a mystery with the reverence and honor, devotion and fear, which are fitting and proper, ibid., 921. By your grace make me always believe, understand, perceive, firmly hold, say, and think concerning so great a mystery what pleases you and what is beneficial to my soul, ibid. For I am unworthy to approach so great a mystery because of my excessive sins and innumerable negligences, ibid., 922. — The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is one of those things in which salvation principally consists, and is unique among all things, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 461. — The whole heavenly court is present with our Savior whenever Mass is celebrated, Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris, CCXII, 60. — Angels are always present at the sacrifice, Innocent III, CCXVII, 891.

## IV.—On the form of the sacrifice of the Mass

By the Lord’s own words his body and blood are consecrated and truly made, St. Ambrose, XVI, 443. Christ’s word is efficacious, so that things which were may be, and may be changed into something else, ibid., 440. In the Eucharist, before the blessing of the heavenly words another appearance is named; after consecration, the body is signified, ibid., 407. — That bread which you see on the altar, sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s body, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1099. That chalice—indeed, what the chalice contains—sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s blood, ibid. By the cross and the insertion of the Lord’s words the sacraments of the altar are made, id., XXXIX, 2204. — It is always consecrated, and will be consecrated, by Christ’s power and words, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1087. By Christ’s power and words that bread was consecrated from the beginning, ibid. This body and this blood are not gathered from ears of grain and vines, but are mystically made for us by a definite consecration, ibid., 1088. — At those words of the Lord, “This is my body,” the Lord’s body comes to be, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1514. — When the priest pronounces those words of Christ, “This is my body,” bread and wine are changed into flesh and blood, Peter Damian, CXLV, 881. — Almighty God, through the faith and solemn words of the priest, even if he is a sinner, changes the substance of bread and wine into the true substance of the flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, John, Archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 235. — Oath of Berengar, priest of Tours, by which he confesses that the bread and wine placed on the altar are, through the mystery of the sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, substantially changed into the true and proper flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 811. — The priest’s words uttered for consecration are words of power, Hildebert, CLXXI, 536. — The visible priest, by his word and secret power, changes visible creatures into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1525. Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is Christ’s body, ibid., 1521. This bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, bread becomes Christ’s flesh, ibid., 1520. — We believe without doubt that those words, spoken by the priest in that order and with that intention, change bread and wine into Christ’s true body and true blood, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 141. Before Christ’s words the chalice contains wine and water; when Christ’s words have taken effect, blood is made, ibid., 142. — When these words are uttered, “This is my body,” etc., bread and wine are changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 856.

## V.—On the matter of the sacrifice of the Mass

Christ made bread his body, Tertullian, I, 1260. Christ calls bread his body, id., II, 461. He represents his body by bread, ibid., 262. — The Lord offered bread and a chalice mixed with wine, St. Cyprian, IV, 377. Christ’s blood is not offered if wine is lacking in the chalice, ibid., 381. Water alone cannot be offered, nor wine alone, ibid., 382, 384. — What is put into the chalice? Wine. And what else? Water, St. Ambrose, XVI, 446. — The mystery of the Christian Church lies not in the immolation of irrational victims, but in the offering of bread and wine, St. Jerome, XXIII, 961. — In the Eucharist water alone should not be offered, but wine mixed with water, St. Augustine, XLII, 1220. — As water cannot be consecrated without wine, so wine cannot be transubstantiated without water, Gennadius, LVIII, 1045. The Aquarian heretics offer water alone [Col. 0869] in the cup of the sacrament, ibid., 1044. — That no one should offer in sacrifice without bread and wine, Council of Carthage, LXVII, 960. — The offering to be consecrated on the altar must be whole bread, bright and carefully prepared, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 550. — In consecrating the Lord’s chalice, water alone cannot be offered, nor wine alone, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 755. The Lord’s chalice is offered mixed with wine and water, because, etc., ibid. — That in the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood nothing more be offered than what the Lord himself handed on: namely, bread and wine mixed with water, Third Council of Carthage, LXXXIV, 192. — Some priests take from breads prepared for their own use a small round piece, and offer it on the altar with wine and water as a sacred libation, Sixteenth Council of Toledo, LXXXIV, 540. It is decreed that bread to be sanctified on the Lord’s altar by priestly blessing be set forth in no other form than whole and bright bread carefully prepared, ibid., 510. — Nothing other than bread, wine, and water ought to be offered in the sanctuary, Second Council of Braga, LXXXIV, 582. — Priests of God should always take care diligently that the bread, wine, and water without which Masses are celebrated are pure and clean, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 590. — That water always be mixed in the chalice in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, Charlemagne, XCVII, 296. — There are three things to be offered in the sacrifice of this testimony: bread, water, and wine, Blessed Alcuin, C, 289. The bread consecrated into Christ’s body must be most pure, without the leaven of any other contamination, ibid. The water must be utterly pure and without every impurity; the wine thoroughly cleansed of every mixture of another liquid, except water, ibid. The bread consecrated into Christ’s body is made from water and flour, ibid. In the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing more is offered than what the Lord himself handed on: bread and wine mixed with water, ibid. Jesus Christ offered the same thing that Melchizedek had offered, namely bread and wine—his body and blood, that is, ibid., 435. — When water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united with Christ, Amalarius, CV, 1131. The Lord’s chalice is neither water alone nor wine alone, unless both are mixed together. Nor can the Lord’s body be flour alone or water alone, unless both have been united and combined. The people offer wine; the singers, water, ibid. The singers should seek water at the spring, keep it covered until the time of sacrifice, and then offer it clean, ibid. — Why Christ gave humankind his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 316 ff. Unleavened bread and wine mixed with water must be sanctified for the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, ibid., 318. Wine mixed with water must be offered in the sacrament: why this is so, ibid., 320. Neither wine without water nor water without wine, ibid. The mystical rationale of this mixture, ibid. Nor may anyone offer a grain of wheat alone without the addition and preparation of water into bread, ibid. — The nature of bread and wine is substantially changed into another substance, namely flesh and blood, Haymo, CXVIII, 815–816. — Why this mystery is celebrated in bread and wine, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1303. — As we have received from the Fathers and reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone should be offered in the Lord’s chalice, but both mixed together, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 93. Milk is not to be offered in the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 589. Bread, wine, and water are the matter of the sacrament of the altar, ibid., 93, 333, 585. — Why Christ instituted bread and wine as the sacrifice of his body and blood, Peter Damian, CXLV, 881. Leavened bread should not be offered for sacrifice, both on account of the historical fact and on account of the mystery, ibid. The Greeks consecrate with leaven, ibid. — Without prejudice to the truth of the sacrament, unleavened or leavened bread may be used, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 541. It is more fitting for the sacrament to be made with unleavened than with leavened bread, ibid., 542. Latins who consecrate with unleavened bread are not Judaizing, ibid., 543. — Why the sacrifice of the Mass is made from bread, wine, and water, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1256. — Why water is put with wine in the Lord’s chalice, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 531. The bread and wine which he had earlier offered figuratively through Melchizedek, he consecrated into his body and blood at supper and commanded the same to be done in the Church, id., CLXXVII, 426. Whether the sacrifice would be invalid if water were omitted through forgetfulness or negligence, id., CLXXVI, 145. — Why Christ’s body and blood are consecrated in bread, wine, and water rather than in other bodily appearances, Alger, CLXXX, 822. Why Christ’s body is more fittingly consecrated in white rather than black bread, or bread of any other color, ibid., 827. — Why Christ’s body is more fittingly consecrated in unleavened than in leavened bread, ibid. — The Church customarily offers unleavened, not leavened, bread, Baldwin, CCIV, 651. [Col. 0870] The Roman Church has chosen to offer unleavened bread, following Christ’s example, ibid. Yet the Greeks are said to offer leavened rather than unleavened bread, lest they seem to Judaize, ibid. — Whether bread without wine, or wine without bread, can validly be consecrated, Innocent III, CCXVII, 872. Whether, under compulsion of necessity or in an intervening accident, the matter of bread alone may be consecrated into the Eucharist, ibid., 873.

## VI.—On the power of the sacrifice of the Mass

The conscience of the fallen is cleansed by sacrifice and the hand of the priest, St. Cyprian, IV, 479. — “The sacrifice which you instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of you for our salvation,” St. Ambrose, XVII, 753. The sacrifice is for the salvation of all, living as well as dead, ibid., 754. “May the enemies of all good things depart confounded through the power of so great a mystery,” ibid., 752. — The sacrifice of the Mass, in which true remission of sins takes place, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 704. Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are aided by the piety of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them, id., XL, 158. Therefore, when sacrifices—whether those of the altar or almsdeeds of whatever kind—are offered for all the baptized: for the very good they are thanksgivings; for those not very bad, propitiations; for the very bad, although they provide no help to the dead, they are consolations of some kind to the living. But for those whom they benefit, they benefit either by bringing full remission or at least by making condemnation itself more tolerable, ibid. In this sacrifice is the great sacrament by which we give thanks to the Lord our God, id., XXXIII, 558. Evil spirits are driven away by the sacrifice of Christ’s body, id., XLI, 764. — Frequent celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass benefits us, St. Leo the Great, LV, 125. It appeases God, ibid., 83. It both brings the removal of sin and sanctification, ibid., 80. The sacrifice makes satisfaction for the dead, ibid., 135. The sacrifice is offered so that the souls of the dead may ever rejoice gloriously in their heavenly dwelling, ibid., 137; so that eternal light may possess their souls, ibid., 136. By celebrating Mass, the work of our redemption is carried out, ibid., 29. — The sacrifice of the Mass is propitiatory for sinners, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 690. — How great is the sacrifice of the Mass’s efficacy before God, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1279. What the sacred sacrifice of the Mass accomplishes for the release from sin, ibid. If sins are not beyond remission after death, the sacred offering of the saving victim is often accustomed to help souls even after death, id., LXXVII, 416. How great is the power of the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 417. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for the dead frees them from punishments, ibid. The sacrifice of the Mass effectively offered for the living who are in distress, ibid., 424. The bonds of a captive in prison were loosed when sacrifice was offered for him, ibid. A sailor is divinely rescued from shipwreck through the power of the sacrifice offered for him, ibid. — To offer sacrifice for the rest of departed believers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 757. Unless the Catholic Church believed that sins are forgiven to departed believers, it would not offer sacrifice to God, ibid. But for those whom the sacrifices benefit, they benefit either by bringing full remission or at least by making condemnation itself more tolerable, ibid., 757; St. Ildefonsus, XCVI, 145; from St. Augustine. — This is the true offering in which the Son is offered and the Father is reconciled, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1088. This is the true and eternal victim, because its power is true and eternal; through it true and eternal salvation is accomplished, ibid. For faithful hearts had to be cleansed by a rational offering in order to become heavenly, ibid. For this victim uniquely frees the soul from eternal destruction, since through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten, ibid. So great is the power of this sacrifice that Christ’s body and blood are for the righteous alone ([not] for sinners), ibid., 1091. — Crimes and sins are forgiven through these sacrifices offered to the Lord, Remigius of Auxerre, CII, 1101. By such victims the Lord will be appeased and will forgive grievous sins, ibid. — The power of the sacrifice of the Mass for the very good, the not very bad, and the very bad, Amalarius of Metz, from St. Augustine, CV, 1163. — It has often been shown by example or disclosed in a vision that sacrifices offered for departed souls are greatly beneficial to them, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357. The power of the sacrifice of the Mass for the dead, ibid., from St. Augustine, CVII, 358. This is the very flesh—and therefore Christ’s flesh—which is still offered today for the life of the world, id., CXII, 1513. The Lord’s body, which is daily consecrated by the Holy Spirit from the substance of bread and wine for the life of the world, is another thing, ibid., 1514. — The sacrifice of the Mass is celebrated for the sins of believers, both living and dead, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 447. — How greatly the immolation of the sacred offering benefits the spirits of the dead, Abbot Gezo, CXXXVII, 399. For this victim uniquely frees souls from eternal destruction, since through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten, ibid., 400. Therefore let us consider what kind of sacrifice [Col. 0871] this is for us, by which we continually imitate the passion of the only-begotten Son for our absolution, ibid. — As often as we offer him the victim of his passion, so often for our absolution we restore to ourselves his passion, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 505. A man held captive was loosed as often as the saving victim was offered for him, ibid., 506. — Every crime and sin is blotted out by sacrifices offered to God, Burchard, CXL, 751. — Whenever sacrifice is offered, the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, and the remission of sins are signified, St. Gregory VII, CLVIII, 327.
