The sacrifice of the Mass continually imitates the passion of the only-begotten Son for our absolution, ibid. — The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood is remission of all sins for the living and the dead, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 919. Christ is daily immolated because we sin daily, id., CLIX, 257. All the saints behold the price of their redemption celebrated upon earth, id., CLVIII, 920. A sacrifice for the release from my sins and distresses and for the everlasting salvation of my soul, ibid., 936. — Every crime is expiated by sacrifices offered to God, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 162. Crimes and sins are blotted out through these sacrifices offered to the Lord, ibid., 164. — The Eucharistic sacrifice contains within itself the truth of Christ’s body and blood and the whole grace of the Incarnate Word, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 760. The sacrifice of the altar contains not animal but spiritual life, id., CLXX, 41. — What is the power of this sacrament, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 532. On the efficacy of the Mass for the dead, id., CLXXVII, 456. — The repeated offering of the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass is a singular antidote against concupiscences and sin, and a support of our hope and confidence, Adam of Prémontré, CXCVIII, 356.

## VII.—To whom the sacrifice of the Mass is offered
Christ first offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, St. Cyprian, IV, 385. He commanded that, in remembrance of himself, he himself should be offered to the Father, ibid. Then a true and full sacrifice is offered in the Church to God the Father, ibid., 386.---Sacrifice is offered to God, St. Optatus, XI, 1013.---If they are already participants in it, they see such a sacrifice now being offered to God throughout the whole world, St. Augustine, XLII, 627.---The holy Catholic Church sacrifices not to the Father alone, but at the same time to the holy Trinity, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 808. We humbly immolate one sacrifice to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ibid., 812. In the truth of faith, hope, and charity, the holy Church is accustomed to offer one sacrifice to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ibid. Whoever denies the Son and the Holy Spirit the sacrifice offered to the Father should recognize himself as alien to the members of Christ, ibid. The sacrifices of the patriarchs correspond to ours, because they were made to the whole Trinity, ibid., 182. Another testimony from the prophets, that sacrifice is offered also to the Son, ibid., 183. The hardening of heretics who do not sacrifice to the Son, ibid. Catholics offer to the whole Trinity, even if they expressly name the Father alone, ibid. To him—the Son—together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he possesses one divinity, the holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world does not cease to offer the sacrifice of bread and wine in faith and charity, ibid., 699.---Those established in heavenly abodes do not wish us to sacrifice to them, but to God alone, whose creatures both they and we are, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1088.---To the equally indivisible Trinity, the sacrifice of praise is offered alike to the Father, to the Son, and to the Spirit of both, Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 847.

## VIII.—For whom the sacrifice of the Mass is offered—and for whom it is not

Christians offered and prayed for the dead on the anniversaries of their deaths, Tertullian, II, 79, 942.---A sacrifice for one’s falling asleep (death), St. Cyprian, IV, 399.---We make offerings for the dead on the annual day of their birth-anniversaries, Arnobius, V, 495. Commendation of the dead at the altar, ibid., 496.---The sacrifice offered for the souls of the dead, St. Zeno, XI, 378, note 35.---In the celebration of the mysteries, an offering is said to be made for the one Church spread everywhere, St. Optatus, XI, 965.---The offering of sacrifice for the people, St. Ambrose, XIV, 1052. The sacrifice is for the salvation of all, both living and dead, ibid., 753.---A Mass for a deceased person whose soul is uncertain, St. Augustine, XI, 284. Sacrifices for the dead: prayers and alms at the altar, ibid., 609. The whole Church is accustomed to pray for the dead in the prayers of the priest which are poured out to God at his altar, ibid., 593. The sacrifice of our price is customarily offered for the dead, with the corpse placed beside the tomb, id., XXXII, 777.

After the Masses had been celebrated, they buried the blessed body with the highest honor and joy, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1067. [Col. 0872] The sacrifice of the Mass offered for the dead, ibid., 875, 876.---From this day onward, endeavor to offer the sacrifice for him continuously for thirty days, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 69; LXXVII, 421. Origin of the thirty Masses for the dead, id., LXXV, 69, note. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for a prisoner, id., LXXVI, 1279. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for a soul detained in purgatory, id., LXXVII, 417. It should be observed from Ambrose that some formerly observed the third and thirtieth day for the dead, others the seventh and fortieth, ibid., 417, note. We ought to offer for good persons, but by no means for evil ones, id., LXXVIII, 456.---We believe that offering the sacrifice for the repose of deceased believers has been handed down by the apostles themselves, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 757. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for the dead, ibid.---For a deceased monk, Mass is to be sung immediately on the third day and according to the abbot’s direction, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 410. For a devout layperson, Mass is to be sung on the third day or about the seventh day, ibid. For a penitent person, Mass is to be celebrated about the thirtieth or about the seventh day, ibid. Among the Romans it is customary for the body of a deceased man and husband to be buried in the church, and Mass to be celebrated over him, ibid. Mass is to be sung for that person on the first, third, ninth, and thirtieth days, and thereafter as each person wishes, ibid.---Sacrifices of the altar offered for the dead, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 145. Concerning those for whom the sacrifice of the Mass ought to be offered, ibid., 1286.---We ought to offer sacred rites for good kings, but by no means for evil ones, St. Ildefonsus of Seville, XCVI, 1316.

According to the Roman Church, the custom is to carry deceased monks or religious persons into the church and celebrate Masses there for them, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 929. Mass is to be said for them on the first, third, ninth, and thirtieth days, ibid., 730. Three Masses for deceased secular persons in the year: on the third, ninth, and thirtieth days, ibid.---In some places Mass is celebrated daily for the dead, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1278. Concerning the third, seventh, and thirtieth day for the dead, ibid., 1280.---The sacrifice for the repose of deceased believers is offered, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357. We believe that it was handed down by the apostles themselves, ibid.---The sacrifice of the Mass celebrated for the sins of believers, living as well as dead, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 447.---That it is permissible to celebrate Masses every day for each of the faithful departed, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 686. That the Mass of the dead is to be sung for all Christians, ibid., 687.---On the seventh day after someone’s death, we offer sacrifice for that person, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 767.---Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 593.

For whom the sacrifice of the Mass is not offered. The sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood cannot be offered for the unbaptized, St. Augustine, XLIV, 480. For who would offer Christ’s body except for those who are Christ’s members? ibid. Nor has anyone offered, or will offer, sacrifice for them—that is, unbaptized infants—ibid., 508. Christ’s body is not to be offered for infants who die without Christian baptism, because they are not known in Christ’s Church, ibid.---Before a deceased excommunicate person is reconciled, sacrifice ought not, according to canonical authority, to be offered for that person, St. Benedict, LXVI, 511.---Many say that it is not permissible to celebrate Masses for children before seven years of age, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 930. Whether it is permissible to offer Masses for an evil person, ibid. It is not lawful for a priest or deacon to celebrate Mass if he is not permitted, or unwilling, to receive communion, ibid. No commemoration is to be made in the offering for those who inflict violent death upon themselves, whether by a sword, poison, a fall, hanging, or any other means, ibid., 1143. Whether it is permissible to celebrate Masses for one who has killed himself deliberately, ibid. Whether it is permissible to celebrate Masses for one who, in a sudden temptation, loses his reason, or kills himself through insanity, ibid.---Likewise, no commemoration in the offering is to be made for catechumens who have died without the redemption of baptism, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 570.---That sacrifice is not to be made for murderers and robbers, Gezo, abbot of Derton, CXXXVII, 402.

## IX.—On the minister of the sacrifice of the Mass

That priest truly acts in Christ’s place who imitates what Christ did; then he offers in the Church to God the Father a true and full sacrifice, St. Cyprian, IV, 356. We celebrate divine sacrifices with God’s priest, ibid., 522.---The work of sacrifice cannot exist without a presbyter, St. Hilary, X, 643. A sacrifice performed by holy and upright priests, ibid., 665.---Today he gives us him whom he himself, as priest, consecrates daily by his words, [Col. 0873] St. Ambrose, XIV, 686. At the banquet of the Church Christ both ministers and is ministered, ibid., 326. Deacons have never been permitted, in the absence of priests, to consecrate the Eucharist, id., XVI, 85, note. In the sacrifice of the Mass Christ is constituted, wonderfully and ineffably, both priest and sacrifice, id., XVII, 753.---At whose prayers—the presbyters’, that is, the bishops’—Christ’s body and blood are consecrated, St. Jerome, XXII, 1193.---What disposition the person who offers that sacrifice ought to have, St. Augustine, XL, 956. Where Christ is both victim and priest, id., XXXIX, 2154. We see this sacrifice offered in every place, from the rising of the sun to its setting, through Christ’s priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, id., XLI, 594. By this he is both priest and offerer, and himself also the offering, ibid., 298. For then the bishops, like advocates, offer those whom they have received, through the laying on of hands, to the most merciful power, id., XXXIII, 637. Not everyone is permitted to make sacrifice and offer to God, id., XXXVIII, 759.---Ministers ought not to give the bread or bless the cup, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 717.---In the sacrifice of the Mass Christ is victim and priest, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 690.---Presbyters who have offered sacrifice and then recoiled are not permitted to offer, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 48.---None other than priests consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses or offer sacrifices upon the altar, Pope Felix IV, LXV, 21.---How a woman celebrating the solemn rites of Mass daily did so, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 875.---A priest ought to consecrate fasting and with an unstained mind, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 145.---Pope Gregory orders a priest conscious of sin with a concubine to abstain from the celebration of Masses for two months, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 640. None except bishops and presbyters ought to offer sacrifice, id., LXXVIII, 609, note.---He surely is priest—Christ—and he is sacrifice, etc., Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1087. Priests perform the office, but Christ acts by the majesty of divine power, ibid. For he is that true Melchizedek who fulfills, by the offering of his body and blood, the holy mysteries which Melchizedek then foreshadowed in mystery, ibid.---None except bishops and presbyters ought to offer, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 247.---Nor is it consecrated by anyone other than Christ himself, St. Odo of Cluny, CXXXIII, 575. Indeed, the visible priest stands by, through whose hands it seems to be consecrated and bestowed; but it is Christ who consecrates and bestows it, ibid.---Christ on the altar is sacrifice and priest, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 922.---That an illiterate presbyter should not celebrate Mass, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 170. That it cannot rightly be offered except through a just and holy priest, ibid., 189. That priests ought to approach sacrifice without blemish, ibid., 190.---For although bishops and priests have hands extended and raised over Christ’s body and blood, there is nevertheless one high priest, Jesus, who sanctifies and blesses, etc., St. Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 407.---Whether wicked priests can consecrate the sacrifice of the Mass, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 532. We believe without doubt that, when those words are uttered by a priest in that order and with that intention, they change bread and wine into Christ’s true body and true blood, id., CLXXVI, 141. Whether those outside the Church, such as excommunicates and manifest heretics, consecrate Christ’s body, ibid., 146; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 867, 1097.---Priests alone are ministers of the sacrifice of the Mass, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 790.---By whom the sacrifice of the Mass is to be consecrated, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 968.---That God alone is the sacrificer and administrator of the sacrifice, while the presbyter is merely minister, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1142.

## X.—On the manner of offering the sacrifice of the Mass

In consecrating the Lord’s cup and ministering it to the people, they do not do what Jesus Christ did and taught, St. Cyprian, IV, 373. In sacrifice one must do what Christ did and what he commanded to be done, ibid., 383.---The powerful compel the presbyter to shorten Mass and sing it according to their pleasure, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2275. How the Ophites consecrate the Eucharist, id., XLII, 28; the Cataphrygians, ibid., 30; the Pepuzians, ibid., 31; the Manichaeans, ibid., 35. At Masses one must stand for the space of one or two hours, id., XXXIX, 2277, 2278.---The sacrifice of the Mass is to be celebrated by fasting persons, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 427, except on the anniversary day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, ibid.

A priest may not celebrate Mass without an *orarium*—commonly called a stole—hanging from both shoulders, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 490.---A priest ought to consecrate fasting and with an unstained mind, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 145.---With what disposition of heart Mass ought to be celebrated, [Col. 0874] St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 425. When nocturnal pollution prevents the celebration of Mass and communion, ibid., 1198.---That Masses be celebrated by all in the same order, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 566, First Council of Braga. It is decreed that a presbyter must not dare, after food, to consecrate upon the altar an offering for the dead, ibid., 573, Second Council of Braga. Mass is to be celebrated by fasting persons, ibid., 192, Third Council of Carthage.---Priests of God should always take careful care that bread, wine, and water—without which Masses are in no way celebrated—are pure and clean, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 390. It is decreed that no presbyter presume to celebrate Mass alone, ibid., 1089.---Every presbyter should have a cleric to read the epistle or lesson and respond to him at Mass, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 1376.---It has been heard that some presbyters celebrate Mass and do not communicate: whether this is lawful, Charlemagne, XCVII, 154. That no presbyter presume to sell the sacred office for any price, ibid., 219. Whether a presbyter can celebrate Mass alone, ibid., 618, 721. Every presbyter is to celebrate Mass according to the Roman order and wearing sandals, ibid., 750. It has been decreed that whenever one sacrificing immolates upon the altar the body and blood of Christ Jesus our Lord, he should at the same time make himself a participant in receiving Christ’s body and blood, ibid., 764.---Certainly, as many offerings should be made upon the altar as ought to suffice for the people, Remigius of Courcelles, CII, 1093.---Whether one ought to celebrate Mass after the emission that commonly occurs in sleep, or not, St. Benedict Sedulius, CIII, 626.---The priest himself, as often as he performs Masses in a day, does not omit to communicate, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 950. If he does not do so, he is to be punished by canonical judgment, ibid. In earliest times they celebrated Mass clothed in ordinary dress, ibid., 952.---No one may sing unless fasting; no one may sing who does not communicate, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 675.---No one may sing Mass without amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble, ibid. No one may dare celebrate Mass in a wooden or glass chalice, ibid., 677.---With what vestments Mass ought to be celebrated, Isidore Mercator, CXXXII, 207. That no presbyter presume to sing Mass without priestly vestments, ibid.---That nothing is to be placed upon the altar except the most holy offering, Gezo of Derton, CXXXVII, 375.---That Mass ought to be completed not by another, but by the one who began it, Ancient Collection of Canons, CXXXVIII, 413. No one may presume to enter to celebrate Mass carrying a staff, or stand at the altar with covered head, ibid. That a priest should never at all celebrate Mass except upon a consecrated altar, Ecclesiastical Laws of the Anglo-Saxon Kings, ibid., 501. That a priest should never celebrate Mass without a book, with the canon placed before his eyes, ibid. That every priest should have a corporal cloth when he celebrates Mass, an under-tunic beneath his alb, and all the Mass vestments properly made, ibid. That a priest should never presume to celebrate Mass unless he has everything pertaining to the Holy Eucharist, namely pure wine, etc., ibid.---Priests should devote themselves to prayers for a time before they sacrifice, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 724.---If the sacraments were celebrated in one manner throughout the whole Church, it would be good and praiseworthy, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 552.---That presbyters communicate whenever they have celebrated Masses, from the Council of Rouen, CLXI, 196.---That a bishop or presbyter, after beginning Mass and saying the prayer, must not leave God’s altar in any way before completing the ministry, unless some emergency intervenes, Pope Zacharias, CLXI, 260.---Unless two persons are present, a presbyter should not presume to celebrate Mass, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1082.---Mass is not to be celebrated while one’s mind is stirred against another, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 891. Some, after such a meal, did not fear to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, id., CLXXXIV, 717.---To celebrate Mass for the prospect of temporal gain is forbidden, Robert Pullus, CLXXVI, 1121, note.---Not to double, triple, or multiply the sacrifice of the Mass under the appearance and pretext of sale, Peter Cantor, CCV, 103.---No one may dare to celebrate Mass twice in one day, or with a double Introit, except in great necessity, Odo of Sully, Bishop of Paris, CCXII, 60. No one may presume, before saying the canonical Matins and Prime, to celebrate Mass without some necessity, ibid., 60.

## XI.—On the language, time, and places in which the sacrifice of the Mass ought to be celebrated

Language.—Pope John VIII forbids Masses to be celebrated in the Slavonic language, CXXVI, 850. Mass ought to be sung in Latin or Greek, ibid.---Why Mass is celebrated in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 418.---On the languages in which [Col. 0875] Mass may be celebrated, Beleth, theologian of Paris, CCII, 44.---Whether it is permissible to celebrate Masses in the vernacular, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1231, 1232.

Time.—Sacrifice at evening hours in Africa, St. Cyprian, IV, 386, 387. The Lord’s rite is not celebrated after supper, ibid., 386. We celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning, ibid.---Mass solemnly celebrated on Sunday at about the seventh hour, St. Augustine, XLI, 829.---That the celebration of Masses begin in God’s name at the third hour, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 282.---That all priests ring the signals of their churches at the appropriate hours of day and night, and then celebrate the sacred offices to God, Charlemagne, CXVII, 219.---Pope Telesphorus decreed that at no time should anyone presume to celebrate Mass before the third hour, id., CXXXI, 1030; CXXXII, 188, 224.---At no time except Christmas is Mass to be celebrated at night, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 175. Celebrations of Mass before the third hour of the day are in no way to take place, because, etc., ibid., 1090, from the letter of Pope Telesphorus. Mass is not to be celebrated after noon except in a time of fasting, id., CXLVII, 110.

Places.—Masses are to be held only in God’s house, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2277.---Formerly Mass was celebrated in cemeteries in memory of martyrs buried there, St. Leo the Great, LV, 21, note.---In what places the sacrifice of the Mass is to be performed, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 899.---That the celebration of Masses ought not to occur anywhere other than places dedicated to God, unless great necessity compels it, Pope Felix IV, LXV, 15.---Private Masses in private houses, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 395. Public Masses are not to be celebrated in oratories lest the rights of others be impeded, id., LXXVII, 547, 548; nor in monasteries, lest an occasion for assemblies be provided or a new entrance for women be made, ibid., 1342. Why bishops were sometimes forbidden to celebrate public Masses in monasteries, ibid., 832.---No one may sing Mass outside a church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCV, 1376.---That no priest dare to celebrate Masses in houses or other places except dedicated churches, unless necessity compels, Charlemagne, XCVII, 219. That no presbyter presume to sing Mass in another’s parish unless he is traveling, ibid., 325. It has seemed necessary to us to reiterate and announce most emphatically to the people that celebrations of Mass must never take place in unsuitable locations, ibid., 619. It is therefore better for Mass not to be heard than for it to be celebrated or heard where it is neither lawful nor fitting, ibid. That no presbyter presume to perform the sacred mysteries except in places consecrated by a bishop, ibid., 772. That celebrations of Masses not take place in unconsecrated and unsuitable places, ibid., 773.---It is decreed that Masses be celebrated over a body, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357.---That no one celebrate Mass on an unconsecrated altar, or without a portable altar consecrated by a bishop, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 791. Masses are not to be held in a house without the bishop’s permission, ibid., 802.---It is not permitted to sacrifice and celebrate Masses in other places except those in which the proper bishop has commanded, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 50. Concerning the fact that it is not permitted to hold Masses over the monuments of the dead, ibid., 578. Except in necessity, Masses should not be celebrated except in consecrated places, ibid., 1057. Laypeople have Masses celebrated in their houses, ibid., 218.---No one may sing Mass in another parish without the permission of that parish’s priest, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 561. No one may sing Mass outside a church, or in houses or unconsecrated places, ibid., 559. We teach that a priest may celebrate Mass in no house except in consecrated churches, save because of someone’s extreme illness, id., CXXXVIII, 501; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 177, 1089.

## XII.—On defects occurring in the celebration of Mass

Defects of Mass, or accidents concerning the Eucharist, and the canonical penalties by which they are punished, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 456. If, while priests are consecrating the sacred mysteries at the time of Mass, some event of illness occurs so that the ministry of consecration begun cannot be completed: what is to be done? Sixth Council of Toledo, id., LXXXIV, 406.---Whoever spills the chalice during his Mass must fast thirty days, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 428.---If through negligence something drips from the chalice onto the ground: what must be done? Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 950. If the chalice drips upon the altar, the minister is to consume the drop and do penance for three days, ibid. Whoever vomits the sacrament and it is consumed by dogs must do penance for one year; otherwise, he must do penance for forty days, ibid. If he vomits the sacrament because of illness, he must do penance for seven days, [Col. 0876] ibid. Whoever spills the chalice while the solemnity of Mass is being celebrated must do penance for forty days, ibid., 951.---If, at the time of Mass, some occurrence of illness arises: what must be done? From the Seventh Council of Toledo, id., CLXI, 194.---How severely defects of Mass were formerly expiated, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 181. What is to be done when, through negligence, the chalice is not consecrated at Mass, ibid.

## XIII.—On the manner of hearing Mass

During the mystery refrain from groaning, spitting, coughing, and laughing, St. Ambrose, XIV, 223.---The celebration of holy Masses must be awaited in silence, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2275. Whenever Masses are held either on Sunday or on other major feasts, no one may leave the church until the divine mysteries are completed, ibid., 2276. The fault of those who chatter in church while the divine mysteries are celebrated, ibid., 2287. Those who leave church before the mysteries are completed are reproved, ibid., 2077.---It was not permissible to eat before Mass on Sundays, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 256, note.---With what disposition of heart we ought to hear Mass, St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVII, 425.---No layperson may depart from Mass before the Lord’s Prayer is said; and if a bishop is present, his blessing must be awaited, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 285, Second Council of Orléans. No one may attend the morning or evening sacrifices of Mass with weapons suitable for warfare, ibid. Mass must be heard in its entirety, ibid.

That the people should not presume to depart before Mass is completed and the blessing received, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 897.---At that time it was not lawful not only for a presbyter to celebrate Masses, but also for other believers to be present at the divine mysteries, unless they wished to receive communion, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 1136.---The Council of Orléans decreed that the people should not leave Mass before the priest’s blessing, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 951.---Mass is to be heard by Christians in their own church, Isidore Mercator, CXXXII, 420, 482. It is to be heard in full, ibid., 225, 226, 287.---Each believer ought to approach that Mass with as much devout compassion as he ought to behold him crucified for himself, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 687.---What dispositions those attending the sacrifice of Mass ought to possess, Guerric, abbot, CLXXXV, 87.

## XIV.—When Mass is to be heard and celebrated, and by whom it is to be heard

When.—All Christians ought to offer and communicate every Sunday, St. Ambrose, XVII, 656. I urge that whoever lives near a church and can come should hear Mass daily, ibid.---In some places no day is omitted on which sacrifice is not offered; elsewhere it is offered only on Saturday and Sunday; elsewhere only on Sunday, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 200. Sacrifice is offered twice, morning and evening, on Thursday of the last week of Lent, ibid. Let everyone attend the celebration of Mass on Sunday, id., XXXIX, 2275. On Sunday no one should separate himself from the sacred celebration of Masses, ibid. Whenever Masses are held on Sunday or on other major feasts, no one may leave the church until the divine mysteries are completed, ibid., 2276.---We also wish this to be observed: whenever a more solemn feast calls together a larger assembly of people, and such a multitude of faithful gathers that a single basilica cannot receive them all at once, the offering of sacrifice is without doubt to be repeated, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 627. The sacrifice of Mass was not celebrated during the two days before Easter, ibid., 516.---Mass is prescribed only on feast days, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 143.---One Mass in one day is sufficient for a priest to celebrate, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 386.---That the Mass of the holy Mother of God be solemnly celebrated four times a year, Charlemagne, XCVII, 208.---That on Sundays the people not be drawn away from public Masses by special Masses, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 205.---Let everyone have his swineherds and other servants come to Mass on Sundays and feast days, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 683.---Mass is to be heard on Sunday, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 405.---Masses are to be attended frequently on Sundays and other feast days, Riculf, CXXXI, 16.---Make your swineherds and other shepherds come to Mass even on Sunday, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 563.---That the altar offering be made on every Sunday, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 757, from the decrees of Pope Fabian.---Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 168.---That presbyters should admonish their congregations to permit oxherds and swineherds to come to Mass on the principal feasts, from the Council of Rouen, CLXI, [Col. 0877] 194.---Let them celebrate Masses on the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1540.

By whom it is to be heard.—All Christians ought to offer and communicate every Sunday, St. Ambrose, XVII, 656.---Let everyone attend the celebration of Mass on Sunday, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2275.---Those who are known not yet to have been regenerated cannot participate in the sacraments of the altar, Gennadius, LVIII, 1027.---Excommunicated persons are expelled from the church at the time of Mass, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1080.---No one may receive another person’s parishioner at Mass, except while traveling or if it pleases him, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 1377. Do not sing Mass for excommunicated persons, and strictly forbid the people entrusted to you to do so, ibid., 1378.---At that time it was not lawful not only for a presbyter to celebrate Masses, but also for other believers to be present at the divine mysteries unless they wished to receive communion, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 1136.

## XV.—On the celebration of Mass: the historical and liturgical part of Mass

To bless their Eucharist, the Ophites introduced a serpent, Tertullian, II, 64. They received Christ’s body in their hands, id., I, 669. From the hand of the presiding ministers, id., II, 79. Even in gatherings before dawn, ibid.---In consecrating the Lord’s cup and ministering it to the people, they do not do what Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, did and taught, St. Cyprian, IV, 373. We celebrate divine sacrifices with God’s priest, ibid., 522. Sacrifices are offered without interruption both in peace and persecution, ibid., 406, 407. Certain rich persons come to the Lord’s rite without a sacrifice, ibid., 613. They take a portion of the sacrifice which the poor person offered, ibid. The deacon pours from the sacrament of the cup into an infant’s mouth, ibid., 485.

We now offer the unbloody, ineffable sacrifice instituted by Christ the Lord, Lactantius, VI, 913, note.

We have heard that some, held by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine orders and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; Pope Julius, VIII, 969. Others also present to the people Eucharist dipped in the cup as the completion of communion, ibid. Some likewise offer pressed wine in the sacrament of the Lord’s cup, ibid.

Formerly women received the Eucharist in linen cloths, men in bare hands, St. Zeno, XI, 358.

Prayers preparing for Mass, St. Ambrose, XVII, 1010. In almost all Eastern churches and some Western ones, at the offerings of sacrifices the people sing with the priest: “Holy, holy, holy,” etc., ibid.

After the consecration, “Amen” is said, id., XVI, 407. What the priest says after the Lord’s Prayer, ibid., 460.

Christ’s body is offered daily upon the altar, and his blood is poured out for sinners, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2154. In the celebration of the mysteries, readings from the prophets, apostles, and Gospels are recited, ibid., 2276. When “Lift up your hearts” is said, you answer, “We have them to the Lord,” id., XXXVIII, 1100. Then the bishop or presbyter offering says, “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God”; the people answer, “It is fitting and just,” ibid. When the sanctification has been accomplished, we say the Lord’s Prayer, ibid., 1101. After the Lord’s Prayer, “Peace be with you” is said, and Christians kiss one another with the holy kiss, ibid. At the words “Forgive us,” etc., we approach the altar with washed face and communicate in the Lord’s body and blood, ibid., 127. Men who are about to receive the Eucharist wash their hands; women provide clean linen cloths on which to receive Christ’s body, id., XXXIX, 2168.

In the same basilica Mass is to be repeated as often as a new body of people arrives, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 627. The names of those making offerings are to be recited within the mysteries, id., LVI, 515. The names of those making offerings are not to be recited before the offerings are commended, ibid. Peace is to be given not before but after the mysteries have been completed, ibid. Those receiving the Eucharist answered, “Amen,” id., LIV, 452. Manichaeans avoided communion in the blood, ibid., 280. The sacrifice of Mass was not celebrated during the two days before Easter, id., LVI, 516.

The sacrifice of Mass is celebrated daily, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 690.---Several Masses celebrated by the same priest on the same feast day, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 568. The sacrifice of Mass over the graves and bones of martyrs, ibid., 356, note 212. The chief deacon in sacred offices carried the cross and read the Gospel, ibid., 336, note 563. When the bishop has completed the prayers and Eucharist, all the people present cry out in favorable approval: “Amen,” id., LIX, 816, note 72.

Mass was not celebrated on weekdays in Lent, St. Benedict, LXVI, 710.---Two Masses celebrated by one presbyter in a single day, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 864.---The archdeacon, clothed in an alb, invited the bishop to the altar to [Col. 0878] celebrate the sacrifice of Mass, ibid., 306. Greetings were received by the bishop near the church, and matters were commended to him before the celebration of Mass, ibid., 217, note. Clerics celebrating sang the Masses, ibid., 1033. Prophetic readings were recited on Sunday, and the reader stood before the altar, ibid., 918. The Gospel was sung in church by a deacon, ibid., 451. All the people answered, “Glory to God Almighty,” ibid. The Lord’s Prayer is sung by all at Mass, ibid., 955. Peace in Mass: the kiss of peace, ibid., 1182.

Masses in the Gallican rite: a specimen, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 86, 87. The rite according to which Mass was celebrated in Gaul in the time of Charlemagne, ibid., 103. Various rites elsewhere used for celebrating Mass, ibid. The order of the Ambrosian, or Milanese, liturgy, ibid., 114, 115. The order of the Mozarabic liturgy to be followed in the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 116 ff. The order of the African liturgy in the offering of the most holy sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 118 ff. How the Roman Order proceeds in celebrating Mass, ibid., 114. Roman chant introduced by Pippin into the Gallican churches, ibid., 119. Charlemagne decreed that every priest should celebrate Mass according to the Roman Order, ibid., 120. Four indications that Mass was celebrated in the Gallican manner before Charlemagne, ibid., 121, 122. Mass sung daily by the bishop, ibid., 142. Formerly, only one Mass on the Nativity of the Lord in the Gallican Order, ibid., 170. The three Masses of the Nativity of the Lord were formerly celebrated at Rome not in the same church, ibid., 174; nor by the same priest, ibid. Three Masses on the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and the Transfiguration, ibid. *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) at the offering in Mass, ibid., 211; recited by all in Mass, ibid., 131. The Gospel read by the deacon from the ambo, ibid., 132. The Gallican Canon of the Mass varied for feasts, ibid., 137; recited silently, ibid., 403. What is altered in the formula of consecration according to the Ambrosian Order, ibid., 125. The formula for consecration of Christ’s body in the Mozarabic rite, ibid. The Lord’s Prayer recited in Mass by all the people among Greeks and Gauls, ibid., 139. Among Romans, the Lord’s Prayer is said by the priest as far as the words, “But deliver us from evil,” ibid., 140. It is said in part among the Mozarabs, ibid.

Formerly the Roman and Gallican Churches differed in their custom of celebrating Mass, St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1187. In ancient times there was not one and the same practice for beginning Mass, id., LXXVIII, 267. Some sang psalms before Mass; others read the Scriptures, especially the Apostle Paul and the Gospels, ibid., 266 ff., note. Both at the Apostolic See and throughout all the eastern provinces and those of Italy, the custom has been introduced that *Kyrie eleison* be said with great devotion and contrition, ibid., 267, note. The manner of singing *Kyrie eleison* is not the same among Greeks and Latins, ibid. By whom and when the angelic hymn, “Glory in the highest,” was to be said in the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., 268, note. One prayer, or Collect, is used in the first part of Mass before the Gospel; two are rare in the codex of St Eligius, as in the codices of Rodrad and Ratold and in the Roman Order, ibid. In the Rheims codex two are found, and only one rarely, ibid. From apostolic times the recitation of three prayers in this first part of Mass has not been customary, except on double feasts, with the same number over the offerings and after Communion, ibid. Formerly among the Greeks five prayers were performed before the giving of peace, which was followed by the offering of the mysteries, ibid. Formerly the Epistle was not read, just as the Gospel is not now read, except at the direction of the bishop or the celebrating priest, ibid., 547. Formerly the Epistle was read by readers, ibid., 479; likewise the Gospel, ibid. The Nicene Creed was not sung in the Roman Church at Mass before the year 1014, ibid., 548, note. Emperor Henry II persuaded Pope Benedict VIII to order the Creed to be sung at Mass in the Roman Church, ibid. The ancient Greek Churches had the contrary practice, ibid. The Spaniards began to sing it during the reign of Reccared, at the Third Council of Toledo, ibid., 560.

In Africa, in the time of St Augustine, a psalm was sung before the Offertory, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 548. Only nine prefaces, which the Roman Church now uses, were received by Pope Pelagius II, ibid., 285. Two were added to Pelagius’s nine prefaces, ibid., 286. What the formula for consecrating the chalice is in St Ambrose, ibid., 279. By ancient and apostolic custom, the Lord’s Prayer is recited over Christ’s body, ibid., 281. The formula for giving Communion, ibid., 52. Formerly Communion was not received in churches outside the solemnities of Mass, ibid., 333. Faithful people, both clerics and laity, intending to communicate at Mass each offered bread and wine for his own Communion, ibid., 432. Formerly a psalm was sung at the time of Communion, ibid., 556. The bishop gives the body of the Lord into the hands of priests and deacons who are to communicate, according to the ancient custom of the Church [Col. 0879], ibid., 563. In the ancient times of the Church all the faithful brought the body of Christ, received in the hand, to the mouth, ibid. The pontiff, being about to communicate immediately, gives the kiss of peace, according to the rite of the Roman Church, ibid., 553. The Greeks give the kiss of peace, after the hands have been washed, before the Preface, the mystical prayers, and the consecration, ibid. Daily attendance at Mass was not customary in the seventh century, id., LXXVII, 660. Yet some persons are praised for having celebrated Mass daily at that time, ibid.

He celebrated the solemnities of Mass every day with great conscientious care, having proper Masses assigned to each day of the week, Blessed Alcuin, C, 104. The Apostle Peter is said to have been the first of all to celebrate Mass at Antioch, id., CI, 1246. Latins pronounce *Kyrie eleison* in Greek, and Greeks in Latin, ibid., 1248. Why the Gospel is carried to the lectern with candles preceding it, ibid., 1250. Why, at the salutation “The Lord be with you,” spoken before the Gospel, the people make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, ibid., 1251. Why, when the Gospel has been completed, the people hasten again to fortify themselves with the sign of the cross, ibid. The custom arose in the Church that this entreaty and consecration be sung silently by the priest, lest words so sacred become cheapened, ibid., 1256. Three Masses in the night of the Nativity of the Lord, ibid., 1175. Likewise three on the feast of St John the Baptist, ibid., 1230.

Pope Leo frequently celebrated the solemnities of Mass seven or nine times in one day, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 943. Archbishop and martyr Boniface is said to have celebrated Mass only once per day, ibid., 943.

Mass was celebrated daily by some, rarely by others, Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 645.

Prayers before Mass, ibid., 447. *Eulogiae*—blessed bread or gifts—to be distributed after Mass on feast days, ibid., 562.

How the celebration of Mass was conducted in the early times of the apostles, Berno, CXLII, 1055. How Mass was celebrated in the time of the apostles and shortly afterwards, id., CXLVII, 199, 212.

## XVI.—Who arranged the Mass

Pope Gelasius is said to have arranged prayers of the Mass composed both by himself and by others, LXXIV, 1055 ff.; Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 946. Many among Greeks and Latins established the order of Mass as seemed good to them, ibid., 944. The Romans received their observance from Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, ibid. In their respective times, each added what was judged suitable, ibid. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, arranged the ordering of Mass in his own Church, ibid., 944. St Alexander, in the year of Christ 121, incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated, id., CXIII, 949; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1147; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 212.—And he instituted the practice of blessing and sprinkling water, John of Rouen, ibid. St Telesphorus, in the year of Christ 142, ordained that the angelic hymn—namely, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be said before the sacrifice, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1245; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1175; CXXIX, 1163; CXXXVIII, 1174; CXXXIX, 537.

St Celestine, in the year of Christ 423, ordained that the 150 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice; previously this was not done, but only the Epistles, etc., were recited, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1244; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 200; CXXXI, 1063; CXXXIX, 543.—Who is considered the author of the Canon of the Mass beginning with the prayer *Te igitur* (“Therefore, you”), etc., and continuing to the Lord’s Prayer: St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 273; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 430.—St Symmachus, in the year of Christ 498, ordained that on every Sunday or anniversary of martyrs the angelic hymn—that is, *Gloria in excelsis*—should be said, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1245; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 454.—St Gregory, in the year of Christ 590, added to the prayer of the Canon: “And order our days in your peace,” etc., Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 949; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 646; CXXIX, 1230; CXXXI, 1054; CXXXIX, 554.—Sergius, in the year of Christ 687, decreed that at the breaking of the Lord’s body, “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us” should be sung by clergy and people, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1246; Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 950; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 898; CXXXI, 1149; CXXXIX, 565. Pope Sixtus VIII was the first to institute the hymn “Holy, holy, holy,” id., CXLVII, 662. Damasus, the thirty-fifth pope, instituted the singing on solemn days of “I believe in one God,” by decree of the holy ecumenical synod held at Constantinople by 150 bishops, id., CXLVII, 212. Pope Leo, the forty-third, added to the Canon of the Mass, “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate Victim,” ibid.

## XVII.—Various enactments concerning Mass

[Col. 0880]

It is ordained that the hymn of the three youths be sung at all solemn celebrations of Mass, St Isidore of Seville, Fourth Council of Toledo, LXXXIV, 371. It is decreed that Masses be celebrated by all in the same order, ibid., 566. It is decreed that bishops and priests greet the people in one manner, saying, “The Lord be with you,” and that the people reply, “And with your spirit,” ibid., 566. In all churches the Creed is to be recited on Sunday, ibid., 351.—Every Sunday before Mass bless water, with which the people and the places of the faithful are to be sprinkled, St Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 1377.—Every priest is to celebrate Mass according to the Roman Order, Charlemagne, XCVII, 750.—Pope Anastasius ordained that, whenever the Gospel is read, priests should not sit but stand around, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1245.—The celebration of Masses over the memorials of martyrs is ordained: by whom, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 357.—Pope Telesphorus ordained that at no time should anyone presume to celebrate Mass before the completion of the third hour, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 951. Zephyrinus, twenty-sixth Roman pontiff, ordained that Masses be celebrated with glass patens, ibid.; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1315.—Pope Sylvester ordained that the sacrifice of the altar be celebrated not upon silk or dyed cloth, but only upon linen produced from the earth, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 951; Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 1513.—Stephen the twenty-fourth pope ordained that priests and levites should not use sacred vestments in ordinary daily life, but only in church, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 952.—No woman is to approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice, Pope Leo IV, CXV, 677.—St Innocent, in the year of Christ 402, commanded that peace be given after the mysteries have been completed, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXIX, 1193. He likewise ordered that the offerings first be commended in Mass and then the names of those whose offerings they are be recited, ibid. St Leo I, in the year of Christ 440, commanded that at solemnities, as often as the basilica to which one goes has been filled by the presence of a new congregation, so often a further sacrifice should be offered, ibid., 1208. Pelagius II, in the year of Christ 576, records that only nine prefaces are to be received in the sacred catalogue, ibid., 1229. No priest is permitted to celebrate Mass on the same day at an altar where a bishop celebrates Mass, id., CXXXVIII, 413.

Every priest is to bless water in his own church every Sunday before the solemnities of Mass, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 634. Innocent decreed that the kiss of peace be given, and it is given to all, id., CXXIX, 1195; CXL, 892. It is decreed that henceforth individual parish priests, or their vicars, shall on Sundays in the porch of parish Masses pronounce aloud and intelligibly, and distinctly say, the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father,” and both Creeds, id., CXLVII, 239.—Blessed Alexander, successor of Evaristus, instituted the offering of unleavened bread only, Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 861.—The altar-offering is to be made every Sunday, from the decrees of Pope Fabian, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 168. All priests are to admonish the people, on feast days after the sermon during the solemnities of Mass, what prayers they ought to offer, from the Council of Orléans, ibid., 193. Prayers and prefaces not approved in a council are not to be celebrated, from an African council, ibid., 213.

## XVIII.—Theological questions concerning the Mass.—The mystical rationale of certain rites of Mass

The mystical explanation of water, grains of wheat from which bread is made, wine, and the mixing of wine with water, Blessed Alcuin, C, 289. Why the Gospel is carried to the lectern with candles preceding, id., CI, 1250. Why, at the salutation “The Lord be with you” spoken before the Gospel, the people make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, ibid., 1251.

After the Gospel has been read, why the people hasten again to fortify themselves with the sign of the cross, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 1251.—The mystical meaning of water mixed with wine, St Cyprian, IV, 384; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 755; Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 1131; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 320. Why the four sides of the chalice are touched, ibid., 325. What is shown by a particle of the offering placed into the chalice, ibid., 326. What is suggested by that left upon the altar, ibid.—Why the Lord offered the chalice after supper, Florus of Lyons, CXIX, 24. Why in the sacrifice of Christ’s body we begin with thanksgiving, ibid., 30.—Why this mystery was handed over to the disciples before the Passion, St Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 1325.—Why this mystery is celebrated in bread and wine, Abbot Gezo, CXXXVII, 374; CXLV, 881.

Why three parts are made from Christ’s body, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1076.—Why Christ chose bread and wine for making the Eucharist, Hildebert, CLXXI, 535.—Whether Christ handed to the disciples at supper his mortal or his immortal body, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXXVI, 462.—Why seventy-two crosses are made in the Canon over the offering and chalice, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 791. Why “The Lord be with you” is said seven times in Mass, ibid. Why the sacrifice of the Mass is made from bread, wine, and water, ibid., 1256.—Why, after the sacrament of the typical lamb, the Lord gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 530. Why he gave this sacrament under another species rather than under its own, ibid. Why Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood under the species of bread and wine, id., CLXXVI, 467; Innocent III, CCXVII, 854.—Why he chose the species of bread rather than another food, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1741. Why he preferred also to give his blood in wine rather than in another drink, ibid.; Alger, CLXXX, 822. Why Christ’s body is consecrated more fittingly in white bread than in black bread, or bread of any other colour, ibid., 827.—Whether the consecration of one species without the other is valid, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 181; Innocent III, CCXVII, 872. Whether, under compelling necessity or upon an intervening accident, the matter of bread alone can be consecrated into the Eucharist, ibid., 873.

## XIX.—Various Masses

Masses for the cycle of the year, from the first book of the Sacramentaries of the Roman Church, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1056 ff.; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 25 ff.—Masses for saints’ feast-days (collects and prayers), from the second book of the Sacramentaries of the Roman Church, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1156 ff.; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 25 ff.

Masses for Sundays (collects and prayers with the Canon), from the third book of the Sacramentary, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1189 ff.; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 25 ff.

Mass for requesting rain, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1209; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 209; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 837.—Mass for requesting fair weather, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1210; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 210; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 837.—Mass for peace, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1217; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 205; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 834.—Mass in time of war, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 218; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 204; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 833.—Extracts from the Avellana Codex, CLI, 904.—Mass for travellers, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1201; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 211; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 831; Old Sacramentary, CLI, 858.—Extracts from the first Avellana Codex, CLI, 905.—Mass for sins, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 203; Blessed Alcuin, CI, 448.—Extracts from the first Avellana Codex, CLI, 902.—Mass for the request of tears, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 448.—Extracts from the first Avellana Codex, CLI, 903.—Mass for requesting angelic assistance, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 449.—Mass for the health of the living, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1242; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 237; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 830.—Mass in time of pestilence, Gelasian Sacramentary, LXXIV, 1207; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 1207.—Mass for requesting the grace of the Holy Spirit, Blessed Alcuin, CI, 446. Extracts from the first Avellana Codex, CLI, 900, etc., etc. For the rest, see Gelasian Sacramentary [Col. 0882], LXXIV, 1056 ff.; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 25 ff.; Blessed Alcuin, CI, 445 ff.; Grimald of St Gall, CXXI, 814 ff.; Old Sacramentary, CLI, 836 ff. Extracts from the first Avellana Codex, CLI, 888 ff. Extracts from the second, ibid., 910 ff.

## XX.—On the various parts of the Mass

On the Introit of Mass: what it is and why it is repeated, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 265; *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, CLI, 979; Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 808.—On *Kyrie eleison*: the manner of singing it among Greeks and Latins, why it is sung nine times, and why *Kyrie eleison* is said six times and *Christe eleison* (“Christ, have mercy”) three times, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 265; Amalarius, priest, CV, 1113; Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 809.—On *Gloria in excelsis*, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 267; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1115; Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 810.—On the prayer or Collect in the first part of Mass, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 267; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1115; Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 814.—On the Epistle: by whom it was formerly read, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 269; *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, CLI, 982; Innocent III, CCXVII, 816.—On the Gospel, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 479; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1126; *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, CLI, 982; Innocent III, CCXVII, 820, 824.—On the Offertory, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 269; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1132; Innocent III, CCXVII, 850.—On the Preface, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 269; Innocent III, CCXVII, 835.—On the Canon, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 562; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1135; *Micrologus*, CLI, 984; Innocent III, CCXVII, 848.—On the Consecration, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 562; Innocent III, 858, 859.—On the Lord’s Prayer, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 281; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1148.—On the *Agnus Dei*, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1153.—On the final Blessing, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 288; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1155.

[Col. 0883]

## CI. INDEX OF PENANCE TAKEN IN A BROADER SENSE, OR OF THE VIRTUE OF PENANCE, SETTING FORTH IN LOGICAL ORDER VARIOUS SAYINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ON ITS NATURE, NECESSITY, ETC.

### NOTICE

Penance, as a virtue, may be defined as follows: an infused moral virtue, or supernatural habit, inclining the mind to detest sin and grieve for it insofar as it is an offence against God, together with the purpose of amendment and satisfaction, and hope for and petition for pardon; or, more briefly: it is the grace or virtue by which we mourn and hate evils committed. In this Index we discuss in turn: I. the nature of penance; II. its necessity; III. its conditions; IV. the fruits of this virtue; V. we present outstanding examples of penitents.

## I.—On the nature of penance

Every penance is a confession of wrongdoing, Tertullian, II, 769. The name *poenitentia* derives not from confession of wrongdoing but from a change of mind, ibid., 314.—Penance is self-correction, Lactantius, VI, 1081. To do penance is nothing other than to profess that one will sin no more, ibid., 684.—Penance is to mourn past evils and not commit again what must be mourned, St Ambrose, XVII, 655. It is condemnation of one’s former life and promised correction in the future, ibid., 969. This is true penance: now to cease from wrongdoing, ibid., 289. Doing penance is of no benefit unless it is done in the beneficial way, id., XIV, 1009. A full definition of penance: the recalling of offences, ibid. One who does penance should not be disturbed if someone reproaches him with the charge of his sin, ibid., 1014.—To repent is to undergo punishment, St Augustine, XL, 1128. Penance is the house of God, XLV, 1630; XL, 271, 421. Penance is threefold, id., XXXIX, 1537, 1550. The first is that before baptism, ibid. The second belongs to everyone here and is perpetual, ibid., 1556. The third is more severe, for deadly sins, ibid., 1542, 1558.—Definition of penance, Cassian, XLIX, 1154.—Penance is a change in a person’s will, St Fulgentius, LXV, 472. It is a gift of God, ibid. No one can do penance in this life unless God has converted him, ibid., 702.—Perfect penance is to avoid future sins and mourn past ones, Cassiodorus, LXX, 361. Penance is an inestimable remedy, ibid., 222.—It is a kind of judicial proceeding, ibid., 65.—To do penance is nothing other than to recognize oneself as dust and ashes, Taio of Zaragoza, LXXX, 904.—Penance is called, as it were, *punientia* (“self-punishment”), because by repenting a person punishes in himself what he has wrongly committed, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 258.—Penance takes its name from punishment, because the soul is tormented and the flesh mortified, Defensor, LXXXIII, 622. Penance is medicine for a wound and hope of salvation, by which God is moved to mercy, ibid.—Penance is said to derive from repenting, because a person repents in heart and blushes before God that he has sinned, St Gregory III, LXXXIX, 587.—Penance is medicine for a wound, hope of salvation, through which sinners are saved; it is measured not by time but by the depth of mourning and tears, Alcuin, CI, 1282.—Penance is called, as it were, *punientia*, because the person punishes in himself by repenting what he has wrongly done, Rabanus, CXI, 137.—To do penance is to punish in oneself the errors of one’s former life; then, by the promises of the kingdom of heaven, to raise minds in hope to things above and urge them towards the pursuits of a better life, St Paschasius, CXX, 150. Penance is rightly believed to be named from punishing, because each person punishes what he knows he has unlawfully committed; no one can do this worthily unless, enlightened by wisdom, he has begun to distinguish good from evil, ibid., 751.—Penance received its name from punishment, so that a sinful person may have punishment in the body, Abbo, CXXXII, 767.—Penance is humble satisfaction for past sins, prudent concern to avoid future ones, the end and hatred of evil, and a certain beginning and love of good, Goffridus, CLVII, 241.—Penance is a meal acceptable to the soul, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 997.—One penance is inward and another outward, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 555. Penance is to undergo punishment, so that one continually punishes, avenging in oneself what one committed by sinning, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 346. Penance is vengeance continually punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed, ibid.—The origin of penance, Alanus of Lille, CCX, 173. Penance is twofold: passing and persevering, ibid. Various senses of penance, 294. Interior and exterior penance, ibid. Civil, private, and ecclesiastical penance, ibid., 295.

## II.—On the necessity of penance

To the extent that you have not spared yourself, to that extent God will spare you, Tertullian, I, 1244.—Penance is necessary for the fallen, St Cyprian, III, 812.—Whenever we have perhaps fallen in deed or word, let us at once recover our senses and confess that we have done wrong, Lactantius, VI, 1081. Whoever removes penance cuts off from himself the way of life, because no one can be so righteous that penance is never necessary for him, ibid.—Repentance is necessary for the fallen as medicines are necessary for the wounded, St Ambrose, XVI, 376. We ought to repent daily of sin, ibid., 520. If I do not have water, I have tears, with which, while I wash Christ’s feet, may I wash myself, ibid., 513. Penance must not be delayed, ibid., 520. Greater crimes are washed away by greater weeping, ibid., 469. Grief must be stronger where sin has been stronger, ibid., 379. Whoever does penance ought not only to wash away his sin with tears, but also by more amended deeds to cover and conceal his former offences, ibid., 506. Faith that mourns former sins is accustomed to avoid new ones, ibid., 116. I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who did penance fittingly, ibid., 525.—Penance is necessary for all, St Augustine, XXXIX, 2033, 2220. It is continually necessary for those continually sinning, id., XL, 1119. Without voluntary penance there is no return to the former state, id., XXXIX, 2202. It must be done as long as we live, ibid., 2020, 2221, 2223. Penance must not be put off under hope of God’s mercy, ibid., 1802, 1969, 2208, 2218, 2226. The remedies of penance should be applied while the wounds of sins are still warm, ibid., 1803, 1974, 2219; XL, 1177. How dangerous, foolish, unjust, and hateful to God it is to reserve penance for old age, id., XXXIX, 2046, 2220.—Penance must be performed, St Peter Chrysologus, LII, 545. Penance must be done when the kingdom of heaven draws near, ibid., 637.—Conversion from wickedness and impiety is commanded, St Fulgentius, LXV, 540. Paul would not mourn many who sinned and did not do penance if he believed remission were conferred without conversion of heart, ibid., 538. In Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews not only is conversion signified as necessary, but perseverance to the end is also commanded to be retained, ibid., 559. One who has not been changed in this world by conversion will not be changed into incorruption, ibid., 560. Penance is supremely necessary for those who fall after baptism, ibid., 702; necessary even for the righteous in this life, ibid.—Penance must forestall the wrath of God, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 528.—What penance is, and how necessary it is to sinners, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1085.—Everyone must hasten to God by repenting while he can, lest, if he has refused while he can, when he later wishes too late he may be wholly unable, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 616. Whoever wishes to be certain at death of pardon should repent while sound in health and, while sound, mourn the crimes he has committed, ibid. Let the fallen consider their past deeds and avoid those impending, ibid., 1187.—The rottenness of flesh needs iron and cautery, Defensor, LXXXVIII, 620. A wicked person who has amassed perishable riches by wrongdoing, if he is ever converted and wishes to escape eternal punishments, must act so that he may equal the multitude of his sins by an abundance of virtues, ibid. It is necessary for one who wishes in every way to be cleansed from sin first to cut off the very faults, ibid., 621.—The building-up of a person through penance and tears, St Ildefonsus, XCVI, 170. If the swallow knows how to restore its young’s sight with the juice of celandine, and wounded she-goats seek dittany, why do we not know that a remedy has been set before sinners? Jonas, CVI, 136. We must raise ourselves after a fall, ibid.—Let us do penance with tears, prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and other good works, for our sins and crimes, lest we be tormented without end in everlasting punishments, Haymo, CXVIII, 929. Let each person flee swiftly to the harbour of penance, seize it safely, and hold it fast, Lupus, CXIX, 640.—One must first sit down through penance, so as afterwards rightly to rise through pardon; for whoever does not now voluntarily humble himself by penance is not at all exalted by the glory that follows, Hincmar, CXXV, 633.—Let us not defer penance, but quickly be converted, Radulphus, CLV, 1669.—Since we are images of God, we ought to offer ourselves to God, washing away the stains of sin, St Bruno, CLXV, 449. Whoever has sinned and repented must live innocently, so that his penance may be acceptable and fruitful to God, ibid., 467. Let him who was not ashamed to sin not be ashamed to repent, ibid., 471.—Penance is necessary for salvation, Rupert, CLXX, 465. Penance must be done because we sin, id., CLXVIII, 196.

## III.—On the conditions of penance
Where there is no amendment of life, repentance is necessarily vain, Tertullian, I, 1228.---Let repentance not be less than the offense, St. Cyprian, IV, 492.---True repentance is measured not by years, but by contrition of heart, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2216. It is true when it admits no further things requiring repentance and bewails those already committed, ibid., XLII, 1218. Or when one so turns that one does not return to sin, ibid., XXXIX, 1977. Nothing makes repentance certain except hatred of sin and love of God, ibid. Repentance that proceeds neither from faith nor charity remains barren and does not wash away crimes, ibid., XL, 1122. Repentance must grieve over absolutely all sins, ibid., 1121, 1128. A more humble repentance, ibid., 220. How necessary is the humility of repentance, ibid., XXXIX, 1535. One approaches God by the humbling of repentance, ibid., XXXVI, 374. Repentance is a certain anger against oneself, ibid., XXXVIII, 133. Do you wish to flee from God? Flee to Him. Do you wish to flee from one who is angry? Flee to one who is appeased, ibid., XXXVII, 1913. Let the soul, punishing itself, pierce itself with remorse, lest, condemned in God’s judgment, it be tormented, ibid., XXXVI, 80. One who, acting in God’s mercy, henceforth guards against sin so that he begs pardon for his other sins, propitiates God, ibid., XXXV, 1917.---Conversion in a person is true when impiety and iniquity are driven from the heart, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 540. The promise of salvation depends entirely on the condition of conversion, ibid., 536. Forgiveness of sins is granted only to those truly converted, established in the bosom of the Church, and still living in this present age, ibid., 532. Forgiveness of sins takes effect only in conversion of heart, ibid., 537. True conversion can exist only where there are also true faith and a good life, ibid., 551. Groaning without conversion is a wound without medicine, ibid., 566. Repentance without a fitting opportunity of time is barren, ibid., 551. Repentance is in vain if pardon is despaired of, ibid., 355.---Repentance rejects avarice, shudders at fury, flees lust, strengthens love, tramples pride, restrains the tongue, orders conduct, hates evils, excludes vices, and so forth, St. Caesarius, LXVII, 1082. In its heart is contrition, in its mouth confession, and in all its work humility: this is perfect and fruitful repentance, ibid. How true repentance is to be performed, ibid., LXXIII, 486.---By what admonitions those who do not lament the sins they abandon are to be stirred up, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 110. To the extent that a person does not cease to look back upon his sins, those sins are the less looked upon by God, ibid. No one should be secure from sins until the time for lamenting them has passed, ibid., 878. To do true repentance is to bewail what has been committed and to avoid what must be bewailed, [Col. 0886] ibid., 1163.---The bitterness of repentance makes the mind both examine its deeds more closely and recall with weeping the gifts of God which it has despised, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 615. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: because he did not do what he ought to have done, and did what he ought not to have done, ibid.---The Lord requires not length of time, but weighs the sincerity of the penitent’s disposition, Defensor, LXXXVIII, 620. Sackcloth and fasting are the weapons of repentance and remedies for sins, ibid. We do not make satisfaction for offenses if we do not cease from iniquity, ibid. Repentance must be performed not in word but in deed, ibid., 621. One who laments what he has done but does not abandon it, and after tears repeats what he had bewailed, is washed yet not clean, ibid. The medicine must be applied according to the disease; remedies must be applied according to the wound, ibid.---He who bewails sin and commits it again is like one washing an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes, Smaragdus, CII, 612. He performs repentance worthily who bewails his guilt by lawful satisfaction, condemning and lamenting what he has done, weeping for it all the more deeply insofar as he was more prone to sin, ibid.---Perfect repentance is to lament past sins and admit no future ones, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 138. True repentance, ibid., CXII, 1304. How repentance should be performed, ibid., 1327.---If sins separate God and man, let them be removed from between them by repentance, Haymo, CXVIII, 925. What are fruits worthy of repentance except that you do things contrary to sin? ibid.---Repentance must be undertaken with all humility and purity of heart, without anger, Abbo, CXXXII, 769.---A change of outward dress does penitents no good unless conversion of heart is present, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 714. Repentance does not benefit those who do not abandon the sin they bewail, ibid., 520.---Let us so mourn past sins that we commit none thereafter which must be mourned, Goffridus, CLVII, 242.---True repentance is to weep over what has been committed and not commit things that must be wept over, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 429. The penitent must wash his sins in living waters, namely spiritual works, almsgiving, fasting, and so forth, ibid., 435. If anyone undergoes harsh repentance, it does not profit him toward salvation unless he abstains altogether from all grave sins, ibid., 828.---Worthy repentance is recompensed not so much by mortification of the flesh or length of time as by contrition of heart, CLXV, 178.---What true repentance is, Rupertus, CLXVIII, 978.---It is not worthy repentance to repent of past sins unless one ceases from the others, Hildebert, CLXXI, 442.---Tears in repentance are of greater value than fasts of long duration accompanied by joy and laughter, ibid. Repentance does no good unless it is whole, ibid., 875.---Repentance must be undertaken with discernment, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 1138. By distinguishing sin from sin, ibid., 1069. Just desires ought to accompany it, ibid., 826; and humility, ibid., 865; and works, ibid., 1071.---If what you have done displeases you, you repent; if you pursue and punish what you have done, you produce the fruit of repentance, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 555.---On fruitful repentance, Abelard, CLXXVIII, 663.---Signs of true repentance, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 967.---He produces fruits worthy of repentance who presents his members to serve righteousness and sanctification, Aelred, CXCV, 293.---That is true repentance by which past sins are regarded in such a way that future sins are feared, Wolbero, CXCV, 1232.---True repentance is abhorrence of sin together with the resolve to avoid it, confess it, and make satisfaction for it, Richard, CXCVI, 1163. Humility ought to precede the labor of repentance, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 348. In order that repentance may be fruitfully undertaken, its labors must be embraced, ibid. Repent while you live, worthily and fruitfully; this will be so if you despise the allurements of all seductive pleasure, weep more abundantly, support the poor more generously, burn more ardently in charity, and so forth, ibid., 349. On the caution required in repentance, ibid., 350, 331. There are many reasons to hasten repentance: the habit of sinning, a fall from sin into sin, sudden, untimely, and uncertain death, difficulty in repenting, and so forth, 357.---What true repentance is, and what are fruits worthy of repentance, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 496.---True and false repentance, Absalo, CCXI, 105. What sort of repentance, and how great it ought to be, CCXIII, 879.

IV.---On the fruits of repentance.

By repentance God is softened, Tertullian, I, 1243. By affliction of flesh and spirit we make satisfaction for former sins, ibid., 1223. The fruit of repentance is pardon, ibid., II, 1001. God has promised pardon for all offenses through repentance, ibid., I, 1233. As often as one sins, so often is one forgiven, ibid., 1240. From repentance the fruit of amendment ripens, ibid., II, 1001. Repentance recalls us to the Lord’s grace, ibid., I, 1231.---The fruits of repentance, St. Cyprian, [Col. 0887] IV, 561. Repentance strengthens one to return to the contest, ibid., 494. The true penitent is made stronger for battle through sorrow, ibid. True repentance not only merits pardon but also a crown, ibid.---Great is repentance’s help, great its consolation, Lactantius, VI, 1081. It is the healing of wounds and sins; it is hope; it is the harbor of salvation, ibid.---Repentance is a remedy for sin, St. Ambrose, XVI, 518. It is undertaken because of hope, ibid., 499. God, who requires repentance, promises pardon, ibid., 481. He awaits our groans, but temporal ones, that He may remit eternal ones; He awaits our tears, that He may pour out His mercy, ibid., 473. Repentance comes first, grace follows; neither is there repentance without grace nor grace without repentance, ibid., 1044. If repentance is from a true mind, it immediately bears fruit, ibid., XVII, 282. Through mercy God regenerates and reforms penitents again, so that there is not only pardon but restoration of their former state, ibid., 276. To practice repentance is true medicine, ibid., XIV, 1011. The water of tears, the water of repentance, is the second cup by which you restore the first, ibid., 1014. God is readily reconciled when earnestly entreated, ibid., XV, 1759. Sweet are judgments to one practicing repentance, ibid., 1266.---Repentance is the second plank after shipwreck for the wretched, St. Jerome, XXII, 1115. For one who sins seventy times seven, if he turns to repentance, sins are forgiven, ibid., 1044.---Effects of repentance, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2229; XL, 1123. Sins are quickly forgiven to one who practices true repentance, ibid., 1323. Before repentance no sin can remain, ibid., 1114, 1116. Repentance recalls those who have fallen away to perfection, ibid., XLV, 1631. Repentance both merits pardon and brings restoration, ibid., XXXV, 2304, 2305. To the penitent God not only remits faults but also promises rewards, ibid., XL, 1350.---The diverse fruits of repentance, Cassian, XLIX, 1160.---Repentance is the resurrection of the soul, Eugyppius, LXII, 589.---Through conversion of heart we are reconciled to God, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 536. Repentance is fruitful only in this life, ibid., 688. Repentance is never late with God, ibid., 354.---Repentance mitigates every adversity and heals everything broken, St. Caesarius, LXVII, 1081. More ruddy than gold, brighter than the sun, it raises the fallen, restores the despairing, and through it Christ signifies that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to us, ibid., 1082.---God protects penitents, Cassiodorus, LXX, 590. The shame of penitents removes everlasting reproach, ibid., 627. Sins make people foul, but the washings of repentance make them beautiful, ibid., 679.---The fruits of repentance, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 528.---Through repentance the first robe is recovered, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 990.---The fruits of repentance in the righteous, ibid., 1138. Through repentance God rescues us from corruption and then from the sword of divine judgment, ibid., LXXVI, 278. Repentance repairs lost innocence, ibid., LXXV, 990.---As a loving mother gives milk from her breast to an infant, so loving repentance offers tears from the compunction of the heart to the penitent, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1300. A mother nurses an infant that it may grow; repentance sheds tears over the penitent that he may revive, and so forth; repentance does so for the penitent that he may in no way grow old, ibid. A mother does not wish life for all; repentance wishes salvation for all, ibid. Repentance revives the guilty, raises the fallen, calls back fugitives, strengthens the broken, cleanses the sick, and so forth, ibid.---God is ready to assist penitents, St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 637. Repentance, however slight, is not despised by God the just Judge, Defensor, LXXXVIII, 619. Repentance changes manners, ibid., 620. Every sin receives healing of its wound through repentance, ibid., 622. Divine clemency comes to the aid of penitents, and pardon is given through repentance, ibid. To one who does not spare himself for his sins, God will quickly grant pardon, ibid., 623.---Sins are blotted out by the compunction of repentance, Alcuin, CI, 1283. However sinful and impious anyone may be, if he turns to repentance, let him not doubt that by God’s mercy he can obtain pardon, ibid., 623. God heals without labor and provides the medicines of pardon without delay, if repentance, devotedly written with tears, is read in the ears of His mercy, ibid., 652.---One must approach repentance with every confidence and believe firmly, from faith, that sins can be abolished by repentance, Halitgarius, CV, 635.---Repentance is salvation of the soul, restoration of virtues, dispersal of vices, conqueror of demons, shutting-up of hell, and so forth, Haymo, CXVIII, 926. In God’s mercy, repentance forgives sins, opens paradise, heals the contrite, and so forth, ibid., 929. Through repentance David, after his crime, received the Holy Spirit again. Through it Manasseh, after bloody deeds, deserved to be received. Through it Peter, and so forth, ibid. For those who abandon guilt and tearfully request pardon, God readily grants forgiveness, [Col. 0888] Lupus, CXIX, 640.---Repentance is so efficacious and powerful for abolishing sins that, even if someone repents of offenses committed in the last breath of life, he does not lose the fruit and hope of saving pardon, Gerard, CXLII, 1298.---The moisture of tears purifies the soul from every stain and makes the fields of our heart fruitful for bringing forth the shoots of virtues, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 308.---Repentance opens, whenever it wills, for sinners the gate of paradise that had been shut, Goffridus, CLVII, 241.---There is no sin so grave that it cannot be blotted out through repentance, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 737. God has mercy on all who cleanse their wickedness through repentance and good works, ibid., 872. Sinners should be certain that they will obtain pardon if they endeavor to leave their sins and perform repentance, ibid., 738.---Every sin is forgiven through repentance, Blessed Odo, CLX, 1114.---Through repentance the sinner recovers from sickness, St. Bruno of Asti, CLXIV, 713.---Repentance bends God’s will to the human will, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 177. It covers sins, ibid., 122. It always obtains pardon for all sinners, ibid., 199. It brings joy to the soul, ibid., 438. It exalts the humble in glory, ibid., 593. It is a banquet in which God delights, ibid., 417. It beneficially troubles a person, ibid., 1099. It kills vices, ibid., 1128.---Repentance is the refuge of sinners, aid of the wretched, hope of exiles, fuel for the weak, light of the blind, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 349.---Hannah, Samuel’s mother, deserved through compunction and tears to have a son, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 1216. David obtained pardon for the murder and adultery he had perpetrated; Tobias deserved to receive healing from blindness and consolation in poverty, ibid., 1216, 1217. Mary Magdalene received forgiveness of sins, ibid.
