Where tears are found, there the spiritual fire is kindled which illuminates the secrets of the mind, ibid.---The fruits of repentance, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 900, 901.---The benefits of repentance, Thomas, CCVI, 767.

V.---Examples of repentance.

Works of repentance performed by Christians in a time of public calamity, Tertullian, I, 486; and by pagans, ibid., 487.---I have known some who in repentance furrowed their faces with tears, scored their cheeks with continual weeping, and, always fasting and with pale mouths, bore in their bodies the appearance of death, St. Ambrose, XVI, 494. The repentance of the Ninevites is set before penitents, ibid., XVII, 977; likewise David’s twofold repentance, ibid., 979; that of the publican, ibid., 990; that of the sinful woman and of the prodigal son, ibid.; and that of King Manasseh and Ahab, ibid., 988 ff.---The public repentance of Fabiola, who, clothed in sackcloth and while all Rome looked on, stood in the rank of penitents and lowered her dishevelled hair, pallid face, unwashed hands, and filthy neck, St. Jerome, XXII, 692. Peter blotted out his threefold denial by a threefold confession; David made amends for murder and adultery by seven days’ fasting, ibid.---The repentance of Theodosius, Rufinus, XXI, 525.---The repentance of Peter, St. Maximus, LVII, 349; of the Ninevites, ibid., 459.---David’s repentance, to be imitated by sinners, St. Paulinus, LXI, 685.---David effectively obtained mercy from God because, wholly converted, he groaned, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 537. The conversion of the noble young man Theodore, ibid., LXXIII, 249. The repentance of Arsenius, who wept continually, ibid., 793; of Fabiola, ibid., 695; of Symeon Stylites, who bound his whole body with a rope, ibid., 325. A bishop who had fallen into sin performs repentance for forty-nine years, ibid., 1010.---After his offense David sang a psalm, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1300. Manasseh wept before the Lord, Mary shed tears, Peter wept bitterly, ibid.---David was not ashamed to flee penitently to the Lord’s mercy, Alcuin, CI, 1282. Peter washed his threefold denial with most bitter tears, as did the sinful woman. The publican went away from the Temple justified by repentance, and so forth, ibid.---Examples of penitents, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1310, 1312. On David’s repentance, ibid., 1323; that of the Ninevites, ibid., 1324.---Examples of repentance in Blessed Peter, in the prodigal son, and in the Ephesian youth, Gerard, CXLII, 1297, 1298.---The repentance of King Ahab, Rupertus, CLXIX, 884.---The repentance of St. John the Baptist, Aelred, CXCV, 293; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 348, 349.---Job first set forth an example for penitents, when he took up lamentations of repentance in ashes and sackcloth, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 329. David provided instruction in repentance when, having fallen into grievous fault, he immediately repented, ibid., 330.---The repentance of the Ninevites, Absalo, CCXI, 106, 107.---The example of David, truly repentant, ibid., CCXIII, 881.---Of the adulterous woman, ibid., 889.

[Col. 0889]

CII. INDEX ON THE SACRAMENT OF REPENTANCE AND ITS CONSTITUTIVE PARTS, NAMELY CONTRITION, CONFESSION, AND SATISFACTION.

NOTICE.

[Col. 0889] Catholics commonly define repentance as: a sacrament instituted by Christ the Lord, by which, through the juridical absolution of the priest, sins committed after baptism are forgiven to a person who is contrite, has confessed, and promises satisfaction. Hence in this Index we treat: I. the existence and efficacy of this sacrament; II. contrition, confession, and satisfaction; III. the qualifications and office of the confessor; IV. various books treating repentance.

I.---On the existence and efficacy of the sacrament of repentance.

The act of repentance is exomologesis, by which we confess offenses to the Lord: by confession satisfaction is arranged; from confession repentance is born; by repentance God is softened, Tertullian, I, 1243. God has placed at the threshold a second repentance, which opens to those who knock, ibid., 1241. Since you know that, against Gehenna, after those first defenses of the Lord’s washing, exomologesis is still a second aid, why do you abandon your salvation? ibid., 1248. Satisfaction and remission performed through priests are pleasing before the Lord, ibid., IV, 1243.---Repentance does what baptism does, St. Jerome, XXV, 928. Through repentance sins of every kind can be forgiven, ibid., 1551, 1558. The same ground applies to those reconciled as to baptism. One who is bound after baptism must flee to the keys of the Church, ibid.---One must certainly believe that repentance abolishes sins, Gennadius, LVIII, 998.---On the sacrament of confession, Eugyppius, LXII, 583.---Repentance is a second baptism, Jonas, CVI, 135.---If anyone jeopardizes the cleanness received in baptism, he can rise again and escape through repentance, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 393. For repentance to be useful, three things are necessary: compunction of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction, ibid., 536.---Through the medicine of repentance, hope of eternal life is restored, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1535.---On the institution of the sacrament of repentance, Ernaldus, CLXXXIX, 1650 ff.---Repentance is the second plank after shipwreck because, if anyone has defiled the garment of innocence received in baptism, he can restore it by the remedy of repentance, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 868. Repentance is the second plank by which we rise after a fall, while the returned oldness is driven away and lost newness is resumed, ibid. It is proved that repentance forgives sins not only once, but frequently, ibid., 871, 872.---In the sacrament of repentance, certain persons think and preach that priests have no power of binding and loosing, but only of showing persons to be loosed or bound, Richard, CXCVI, 1168.---Repentance is the second plank after shipwreck, Peter of Celle, CCII, 680. As in baptism everything of guilt that preceded was blotted out, so through repentance the liability remaining from sin is blotted out, ibid. The sacrament of repentance is the true pool, ibid., 691.---Repentance is baptism because it effects the burial of crimes, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 591.---The sacrament of repentance, Alan of Lille, CCX, 205. It requires three things: contrition, confession, and satisfaction, ibid., 275. Heretics think that after forgiveness of sins which occurs in baptism, repentance has no place, ibid., 352. They are refuted, ibid., 353. Other heretics reject repentance altogether, ibid., 356. They are refuted, ibid.

II.---On the constituent parts of the sacrament of repentance.

1. On contrition.---Priests do not take away the sin of one who presents himself deceitfully and still intends to sin, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1230.---Confession of sins and groaning over them, if they are without conversion, anger God rather than propitiate Him, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 536. Two kinds of contrition, ibid., LXXVI, 1070. Contrition is the sorrow of a soul trusting in God’s mercy, ibid., LXXIX, 552. Causes of contrition, ibid., 553.---Compunction of heart is humility of mind with tears, arising from recollection of sin and fear of judgment, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 613.---In the act of repentance, not so much the time of repentance as the sorrow of the soul is to be weighed, Ildefonsus, XCVI, 141.---There are four qualities by which the souls of righteous men are strongly affected in compunction, Smaragdus, CII, 614.---Compunction of heart arises from the virtue of humility, Rabanus, CX, 101. It is humility of mind with tears, remembrance of sins, and fear of judgment, ibid. Tears usually flow from a double fountain of compunction: either when the mind carefully considers the evils of its works, or when it sighs in desire for eternal life, ibid.---This is true compunction of heart for a baptized person: to do great things and speak humbly; to act justly and fear on account of sinners, Haymo, CXVIII, 922. As fire removes every vice of the soul, so compunction of heart frightens away and utterly destroys whatever evils it finds, however great, ibid. On the two kinds of compunction, ibid., 923.---How great is the power of compunction is evident: through it sins are blotted out and virtues acquired, Adalgerus, CXXXIV, 927. By it many have pleased the Lord; by it the devil is overcome; by it vices are conquered, ibid.---One confessing his sins ought to grieve because he has offended his Creator, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 832. Let there arise also a sharper grief that he has offended his Creator and Father, ibid. Let there be added the most acute grief that he has despised so great a benefactor, ibid.---Contrition is sorrow of heart arising from recollection of sin and fear of judgment, Radulphus, CLV, 1810. Three things form contrition: shame, fear, and sorrow, ibid.---Contrition of heart is fruitful when someone grieves and is troubled over the sin by which he has offended God, because iniquity displeases him through love of righteousness, Wernerus, CLVII, 1205.---Compunction of heart represses temptations of the heart, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 94. It purifies us, ibid., 148; consoles us, ibid., 184.---Compunction consists in contrition of heart, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 146. Its necessity, ibid., 147.---How contrition ought to be had in confession, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 649.---On contrition, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 877.---Threefold compunction, Richard, CXCVIII, 315. Its necessity, ibid., 375.---Contrition is compunction of heart, born from recollection of past evils, Ermengaaldus, CCII, 1259. Its necessity in repentance is proved, ibid.---For the sufficiency of repentance, contrition of heart is required, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 339. How great it ought to be, ibid., 340.---What compunction is, Alan of Lille, CCX, 170. Its nature and power, ibid. Its efficacy, ibid., 171. The cause of compunction is twofold: fear and hope, ibid., 274. Description of contrition, ibid., 358. Contrition must be aroused before confession, ibid., 286. Interior contrition is necessary, ibid., 300. It is also required for venial sins, ibid., 302. The practice of stirring up contrition, ibid., 292. Through contrition sin is not forgiven without the purpose or vow of confession, ibid., 358.---The efficacy of compunction, Adam, CCXI, 674. The threefold effect of sorrow of mind in the soul of sinners, ibid. How effective are tears of compunction, ibid., 675. The power of contrition, ibid.---Whether greater contrition is required for the blotting out of mortal rather than venial sin, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1051. Whether there is an obligation to be more contrite for a greater sin than for a lesser one, ibid., 1056.

2. On confession, its nature and necessity.---Exomologesis is that by which we confess our offense to the Lord, Tertullian, I, 1243.---Exomologesis, St. Cyprian, IV, 263 ff.---Confession of sin consists in this: that, through recognition of sin, you confess that what has been done by you is sin, St. Hilary, IX, 785. Old offenses must be confessed without interruption, ibid., 620. Confession must not be interrupted even by those justified, ibid., 770. The offense must be confessed, ibid., 526.---Confession of sins before baptism, St. Zeno, XI, 486. Confession of hidden crimes, ibid., 493.---God awaits the voice of your confession, St. Ambrose, XIV, 972. No one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed the sin, ibid., 310. Confession of sin is a shortening of punishments, ibid., 354.---Confession of guilt is the second plank after shipwreck, St. Jerome, XXII, 748. Confession of sins, ibid., XXV, 641. Confession of offenses in conversion, ibid., 941.---Confession of sins, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 635; XXXVIII, 153; XL, 358. The medicine of confession, ibid., XXXVIII, 139, 982. Confession is a sacrifice to God, ibid., XXXVII, 1233. Confession of sins belongs to the righteous; defense of merits, to the proud, ibid., XXXVIII, 1382. Necessary for salvation, ibid., XXXIV, 138, 186, 756. The medicine of confession and repentance is necessary for the sinner, ibid., XLII, 419. On the necessity of confession, ibid., XXXVI, 108, 253, 959; ibid., XXXVII, 1080, 1219, 1232, 1318, 1761, 1827, 1853, 1861, 1883; ibid., XXXIX, 1851; ibid., XL, 1288. When confession is lost, there will be no place for mercy, ibid., XXXVI, 854. God questioned Adam in order to compel him to confession of sin, ibid., XXXIV, 207. God commanded confession so that the devil may hear us repent and may no longer accuse us on that account, ibid., 1288. Confession is not to be deferred to the last day of Lent or of one’s life, ibid., 1289. Offenses must be washed away promptly by confession and repentance, ibid., 1049.---We recognize from Christ’s word that confession of sins is always necessary, St. Prosper, LI, 402.---Confession, and accusation within it, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 215.---Sacramental confession in the Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 695.---Confession is necessary for putting off the old man, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 623.---Exomologesis is a Greek word, interpreted in Latin as *confessio*, “confession,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 259.---The sinner who did not hasten to embrace confession, by which pardon is born, cannot be excused, St. Eligius, LXXXVII, 635. Pardon cannot be bestowed unless God’s wrath can be appeased by confession, ibid.---Since we have committed many things contrary to God’s will and commandment, it is necessary that we cleanse ourselves through confession while repenting, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1071.---When we must receive Christ, let us hasten quickly to wash away our sins by confession and true repentance, St. Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 231. If anyone is wounded through frailty of the flesh or negligent lack of watchfulness, let him quickly have recourse to the medicine of confession, ibid., 340. Wounds must be opened in confession so that the medicines of salvation may be able to work, ibid., CI, 655.---Sinners ought to make confession of their sins, Jonas, CVI, 151.---Let the living sinner confess what he has done, for confession in hell is not fruitful, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 102, 103. How can a physician heal a wound which the sick person is ashamed to show? ibid.---On confession of sin, Haymo, CXVIII, 924.---No one can repent rightly unless he first confesses his sin and condemns the errors of his former life, St. Paschasius, CXX, 154.---Confession of sins, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 715. Necessity of confession, ibid., 595. You will not attain salvation unless you confess that you have sinned, ibid.---Confession of sins is like a wound, Lanfranc, CL, 634.---Confession is a sorrowful recounting of one’s own sins, Radulphus, CLV, 1899.---One must confess one’s sins while bodily health remains and while each has the use of his own faculties, Goffridus, CLVII, 225.---Confession of sins, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 872, 875, 887, 927; Rupertus, CLXVIII, 1010.---The institution of confession, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 552 ff.; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 668, 670.---The confession of the sinner is life; that of the righteous, glory, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 258. It is the only remedy after sin, ibid., 931. No sin is forgiven unless it is first confessed, ibid., CLXXXIV, 539. Without it there is no justification, ibid., 509.---Confession necessary for salvation, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 896.---Without oral confession sin is not forgiven, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1541.---It is necessary that we speak our iniquities, so that afterward we may be justified, ibid. Various examples showing that no pardon can be merited without confession, ibid., 1544.---On confession, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 877 ff.; [Col. 0892] Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1816.---External confession is necessary for salvation, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 168.---The necessity of confession is demonstrated, Ermengaaldus, CCIV, 1259, 1260.---On sacramental confession, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1078 ff.---Confession of sins, Alan, CCX, 172, 272. Its necessity, ibid., 300.---Confession is a voluntary and truthful accusation of the soul and an orderly disclosure of sins in the presence of a priest, Adam, CCXI, 676. The necessity of oral confession is shown, ibid., 681, 682. Three kinds of persons making confession, ibid., 676.---The commandment of confession, Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 1070. What confession is and its various kinds, ibid., CCXIII, 871. As often as we fall into sins, hope of pardon is always available to those who rise again, ibid., 873 ff.

### 3. On the qualities of confession

In danger of illness, confession (*exomologesis*) is to be made to whatever priest is present, St. Cyprian, IV, 258. — Confession must be complete, St. Hilary, IX, 786. This is the true confession of a righteous man, which commends present righteousness through awareness and confession of past sins, ibid., 326. How one is to confess to no one other than God, ibid. — Sins are to be confessed to God and to the priest, St. Ambrose, XVII, 654, 655. A confession that is not faithless holds the place of pardon, ibid., 979. “You will be condemned in silence, though by confessing you could be set free,” id., XXXVI, 808. What disposition the penitent ought to have, id., XL, 1289. Let the penitent beware of putting forward excuses for sins, ibid., 1126. Confession of sins is to be made humbly, id., 1056, 945. One must confess with one’s own mouth, not through a messenger or in writing, ibid., 1122. To whom all sins are to be confessed, with all the circumstances surrounding them, ibid., 1124. If any are kept silent, or if those stated are cunningly disguised, they murder the soul, ibid., 1156. The person confessing sins without sorrow seems to mock the judge, id., XXXV, 2336, 2339. Confession of sin is good if healing follows it, id., XLV, 1867. — Through humble confession, a human being reveals himself to God who knows him; and God reveals him to a human being who does not know him, St. Prosper, LI, 296. — Confession of sins is to be made at Christ’s feet, as it were, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 466. — Unless confession is true, it does not obtain the abolition of sin, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 931. It is made only to priests, and secretly, ibid., 1374. — Not everyone who confesses sin receives remission, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 536. Confession benefits only if the person who has confessed what he did wrongly does it no longer, ibid., 567. — Confession of sins with tears and groaning, St. Benedict, LXVI, 331. Humble confession commended in the ancient rules, ibid., 389. — It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling, and, once it has been committed, not to disclose it by confessing, but to defend it by denying it, and, when convicted, to multiply it by defending it, Smaragdus, CII, 613. Signs of true confession are these: when anyone calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same of him, ibid. — What does confession profit unless abandonment of the things confessed follows? Ratherius, CXXXVI, 401. — Confession must be made purely, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 832. One part of one’s sins must not be told and the other retained; nor are light sins to be confessed and grave ones concealed; nor is another to be accused while one excuses oneself, ibid. One must confess humbly, so that what is in the heart is the same as what will sound from the mouth, etc., ibid. — We ought to confess with compunction of heart, humility of countenance, beating of the breast, bodily supplication, and a mournful voice, Radulfus, CLV, 1900. Confession must be made with tears; for unless the sinner groans, weeps, and sighs when admitting that he has sinned, he proclaims his sin rather than confesses it, ibid., 1810. It must be true and open, complete and undivided, ibid. — Every uncleanness of the heart must be vomited out through confession, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 580. He does not pour out his heart before God who opens his mouth in confession but does not remove evil desire from his heart, nor does the person who does not humble himself, ibid. — Confession must be made by the tongue, the heart, and action, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 1130. Self-examination must precede it, ibid., 1057. As it is, such will be the remission of sins, ibid., 152. — Those who, while confessing their sins, fear to pour out some of them retain, as it were, dregs of thick liquid in the vessel of the heart, Hugh, CLXXV, 312. But the person who by pure confession reveals the secrets of his heart, retaining nothing through attachment or concealing anything through silence, pours out his heart like waters before the Lord, ibid. — What confession ought to be, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 650, 651. Its conditions, id., CLXXXIV, 1176. — Confession must be complete, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 899. We must also confess noteworthy circumstances, ibid., 900, 901. — Completeness of confession, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1098. It must not be divided among different priests, ibid., 1099. — Let confession be humble, pure, and faithful, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 772. — On true confession, Peter of Celle, CCII, 1128. — How great and what kind confession ought to be, Peter Cantor, CCV, 343, 345, 346. — Confession must be pure, complete, open, and faithful in three respects, Thomas, CCVI, 37, 38. — Three things are required for confession, Alanus, CCX, 300. Preparation is necessary for the penitent before confession, ibid. It must be made orally, not in writing, ibid., 386. It must be universal, ibid., 273, 301. The circumstances of sins must be confessed, ibid., 273, 290. Doubtful matters must be confessed as doubtful, ibid., 302. If the penitent omits even one mortal sin, the confession is invalid, ibid., 587. Confession must be humble, simple, true, complete, and firm, ibid. Its completeness requires three things, ibid., 173. Heretics say that it is enough to confess to God alone, ibid., 356.

### 4. On the effects of confession

Once crimes have been confessed, the inquiry proceeds no further, Tertullian, I, 276. From confession repentance is born, and satisfaction is ordered, id., 1243. — Fruits of confession, St. Hilary, IX, 648. In confession consists the whole reward of our hope, ibid. In the confession of sins is the greatest remedy for the diseases of deadly vices, ibid., 785. Confession of sins ensures that, although we deserve rebuke, we are nevertheless not rebuked, ibid., 526. Where there is confession of sin, there also is justification from God, ibid., 690. — Confession of error is a remedy, St. Ambrose, XVI, 312. The modest confession of sins loosens the bonds of crimes, ibid., 507. A crime is lighter when a person voluntarily confesses his sin, ibid., 378. How useful confession of sin is to the sinner, id., XVII, 969. “Then you will be rid of all your iniquities, when you stand against yourself as witness and accuser,” ibid., 971. Your penitential confession is a remedy, ibid. In confession is pardon, and in condemnation of one’s own sin is righteousness, ibid., 1053. — Confession is a plank after shipwreck, St. Augustine, XXXIX, 2226; the beginning of health, ibid., 2214. Confession of a hidden sin heals the sick person in two ways, id., XLI, 847. Usefulness and fruit of confession, id., XXXIX, 2050, 2215; XL, 1289; XLV, 1879. As God hates one who defends his sins, so he raises up one who confesses them, id., 1491, 2006. Reformation begins with confession and is completed through good works, ibid., 1281, 1338, 1908. The sinner who confesses proceeds from darkness to light, ibid., 1578. — Confession of sin is good if healing follows, St. Prosper, LI, 441. Before the mercy of God, the confession of the penitent has great power: by confessing, the sinner makes God propitious; by denying, he does not make Him ignorant, ibid., 461. — The person confessing his sins gives glory to God, Cassiodorus, LXX, 397. It is a greater glory to God to spare one who confesses than to grant favor to one who lives without confession, ibid., 754. He obtains divine gifts, ibid., 669. To reveal one’s fault to God is a remedy; to confess it is security, ibid., 523. Confession of offenses makes the judge favorable to oneself, ibid., 576. — The medicine of confession, Alcuin, CI, 620. Through confession sins are washed away, id., C, 576. The sinner is freed from a threefold death, ibid., 339. In confession consists every hope of pardon, id., C, 622. Confession justifies and grants pardon for sins, ibid. — Usefulness of confession, St. Benedict, CIII, 853. — Fruits of confession, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 101, 102. — Dead sinners rise again through confession, repentance, and God’s mercy, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 715. Confession is the common way to God, a spring mighty for righteous persons and sinners alike, which cleanses an abundance of crimes with a more abundant stream, ibid., 901. It restores the first robe of innocence and brings the runaway son back to his father’s embrace, ibid. — Power of sacramental confession, Lanfranc, CL, 55. Sins revealed to the confessor will by no means be judged, ibid., 49. Confession makes light, ibid., 301. — Through confession we cleanse ourselves, Radulfus, CLV, 1899. — The necessity of confession restrains from sin, Guibert of Nogent, CLVI, 258. Confession of sin is the best remedy, ibid., 603. — Through confession every burden of sin is lightened, St. Anselm, CLVIII, 738. In true confession every stain of offense is cleansed, ibid. — Remission of sins is effected through their secret confession, St. Bruno, CLXIV, 405. Confession raises those who have fallen, binds and heals wounds; God himself places the lost and found sheep upon his shoulders and restores it to pasture, ibid., 919. — Confession cleanses leprosy, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 577. It also restores the strength of the soul, ibid., 1459, and leads to the joys of heaven, ibid., 46. — Oh, how exalted is that confession through which the thief, condemned and crucified, ascended from the gallows to the kingdom, from earth to heaven, from the cross to paradise! St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 648. Glorious is the confession that freed the Apostle Peter from the crime of threefold denial, ibid. — Whether sin is forgiven without confession, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 880, 881. — In confession all things are washed, conscience is cleansed, bitterness is removed, the sea is driven away, tranquility returns, hope revives, and the spirit is made glad, Richard, CXCVI, 1075. — David, confessing, is admitted to pardon, Adam of Scotland, CXCVIII, 171. The usefulness of sacramental confession, ibid., 204 ff. — On the efficacy of true confession, Peter of Celle, CCII, 1128. — How great is the effect of confession, Peter Cantor, [Col. 0894] CCV, 345. Through confession the stains of all sins are erased, ibid., 361.

## III. On satisfaction

A great crime has a great necessary satisfaction, St. Ambrose, XVI, 378. — Indication of perfect satisfaction, Cassian, XLIX, 1156 ff. — Satisfaction in repentance consists in cutting off the causes of sins and allowing no entrance to their inducements, Gennadius, LVIII, 994. — Those whose sins are public ought to undergo public repentance; those whose sins are hidden ought to undergo hidden repentance, Radulfus, CXIX, 724. — What certain repentance is, Regino, CXXXII, 255. — Satisfaction is the fitting performance of an imposed work, Radulfus, CLV, 1810. No one can be released from sin unless he repays what he seized by sinning, ibid., 391. Remission of sin does not occur unless the debt has been repaid and full satisfaction made according to the magnitude of the sin, ibid., 398. Every sin must necessarily be followed either by satisfaction or by punishment, ibid., 381. After sin, a human being cannot be saved without satisfaction for sin, ibid., 389. The satisfaction every sinner must make, ibid., 392. For complete satisfaction the sinner must either give something on behalf of it from what is his own, which is not owed to God and cannot be required of him by God, ibid., 375. It is not enough to restore what was taken; because of the insult inflicted, the sinner must restore more than he took, ibid. Satisfaction must correspond to the measure of the sin, ibid., 392. The necessity of satisfaction in repentance, id., CLXXI, 423. Satisfaction consists in three things: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer, ibid., 447. — Satisfaction ought to follow repentance, Godefridus, CLXXIV, 421. Satisfaction for sins should not be made sadly or under compulsion, ibid., 665. It perfects repentance, ibid., 1106. It breaks sinful inclinations, ibid., 1128. — It is not enough to improve one’s conduct and withdraw from evils, unless satisfaction for guilt is made through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 554. — On satisfaction, Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 665. — What penances are to be imposed and how, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 902. — Penitential satisfaction is to be given to those confessing, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1535. Without satisfaction in deed, sin is not forgiven, ibid., 1541. — On satisfaction, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 877 ff. — The necessity of satisfaction demonstrated, Ermengaald, CCIV, 1260, 1264. — Satisfaction is the completing performance of an imposed penance, or fitting correction for sins, Alan of Lille, CCX, 275. Satisfaction confirms contrition, corrects evils, and restores health, ibid., 274. It must be proportionate to guilt, ibid., 290. Diversity of penances for the same sin, ibid., 276.

## IV. On the qualities and practice of the confessor, and his office

The sacrament of repentance is to be administered to the dying, St. Cyprian, IV, 231. — It is the Lord’s command that even persons guilty of the gravest crime, if they repent from their whole heart and with open confession of sin, should receive again the grace of the heavenly sacrament, St. Ambrose, XVI, 501. — If a priest refuses repentance to the dying, he will be guilty of souls, Julius, VIII, 864. — It is for the priest to judge the weight to be assigned to offenses, St. Innocent I, XX, 559. If anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, ibid. — What manner of person one receiving confessions should be, St. Augustine, XL, 1129. The power of binding and loosing does not belong to those who possess something as private property, ibid., 1215. How the confessor ought to conduct himself, ibid., 1289. — Reconciliation is not to be denied to the dying, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 396, 397. — Before hearing a penitent’s confession, the priest should begin with prayer, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 451. There is danger that one receiving confession of sins may be inflamed by the obscene matters he hears, id., LXXIX, 419. — Final repentance must not be refused, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 914. — Let all priests, with the utmost vigilance, prescribe to all who confess to them a fitting penance for their crimes, St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 382. — If someone asks for repentance in illness and, by chance, when the priest comes to him is struck dumb by illness, those who heard him should bear witness and he shall receive repentance, St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 823. — The confessor should ask the penitent whether evil works are present in him which separate a person from the kingdom of God, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1072. After he has confessed his sins, if he wishes to abandon them, give him penance; but if he does not wish to do so, do not give it, because he cannot receive it, ibid., 1073. Care must be taken that persons persisting in grave sins and those committing lighter offenses are not judged alike; rather, the remedy must be applied according to the disease, ibid. [Col. 0895] — Those who, at a time of necessity and under pressing danger, seek the aid of repentance and immediate reconciliation are neither to be refused satisfaction nor denied reconciliation, Charlemagne, XCVII, 716. In dispensing God’s gifts we ought not to be harsh, nor disregard the groans and tears of those accusing themselves, ibid. No priest is to absolve the penitent of another parish, ibid., 807. The priest should ask in what way the sin was first committed, whether it was repeated or frequently performed, whether voluntarily, under compulsion, or through drunkenness, ibid., 845. — The confessor should admonish the penitent concerning the principal vices and the virtues through which those vices can be overcome, Theodore, XCIX, 940, 941. The confessor’s manner of acting toward the sick, healthy, rich, children, elderly, etc., ibid., 1087. — What a confessor must observe in relation to the various states of penitents, Alcuin, CI, 1196. How he ought to question the penitent, ibid. He must judge according to the canons, ibid. Prayers of the confessor, ibid., 1199. — Times of penance must be determined according to the nature of the sin, Halitgar, CV, 677. On the manner of receiving, judging, or reconciling penitents, ibid., 217. — When someone comes to confession, diligent inquiry must be made as to how or on what occasion he committed the sin he confesses to having done; and penance must be prescribed to him in proportion to the deed, Rodulfus, CXIX, 719. He must be persuaded to confess his perverse thoughts and the eight principal vices, ibid. The manner of penance for those confessing their sins must be imposed either by the ordinance of ancient canons, by the authority of Holy Scripture, or by ecclesiastical custom, ibid., 720. Above all, care must be taken that repentance and reconciliation are not denied to a penitent at the end of life, ibid., 724. — Every priest should carefully discern the sex, age, condition, status, person, and very heart of the penitent, and according to these judge each matter as seems proper to him, Herveus, CXXXII, 673, 674. — The sacraments are to be administered, even at the end, to one showing signs of repentance, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 347. If danger of death threatens one doing penance, he is to be reconciled at once, ibid., 545. — The method of priests’ conduct toward penitents, Atto, CXXXIV, 45. How the confessor should question and judge the penitent, id., CXXXVIII, 504, and impose penance, ibid., 505. — On confession, repentance, and reconciliation of those confessing their sins, and on the order for giving them penance, Burchard, CXL, 949. What should be the priest’s procedure toward persons unable to fulfill what is written in the penitential, ibid., 981. Toward penitents generally when their faults differ; toward those hastening to fulfill the penance imposed upon them, ibid., 986. Toward the fallen, ibid., 988. One who receives confessions must be learned, so that he may know what to impose, whom to spare, and when he ought to spare, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 853. He must be religious, so that he may raise pure hands to God and confidently intercede for sinners, ibid. The confessor should ensure that a fitting penance is administered to his penitent, ibid., 901. — Priests must carefully examine the sins of those confessing, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 885. They must also understand how to receive confessions and prescribe penance, ibid. What persons approaching confession must be questioned about, ibid., 892. Confession must not be revealed, ibid., 433. Penance must be imposed according to the nature of the sin, ibid., 843. What penance should be imposed upon those who have communicated without fasting, ibid., 166. What is to be done with those who return to their former sins, ibid., 879. — What is to be done for penitents at the final stage of life, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1535, 1536. — What is to be done for those who repent at the end, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 892. Those who do not complete their penance, ibid., 893. Satisfaction is not to be imposed on the dying, but made known to them, ibid., 894. In necessity, repentance or reconciliation is not to be denied, ibid. What kind of person an ecclesiastical judge ought to be, ibid., 891. — Priests can and ought to forgive the sins and absolve from the debt of damnation those who truly repent and undertake due satisfaction; the rest, however, they should dismiss without absolution, Richard, CXCVI, 1166. — The confessor should have for penitents the wine and oil of the Samaritan, Peter Cantor, CCV, 199. He should impose three things especially upon the penitent, ibid. He may impose an arbitrary penalty, ibid., 245. Let him be prudent and discerning, mild, gentle, sweet, kind, merciful, and approachable, ibid., 345. — A penitential priest—that is, a priest—should possess goodness, knowledge, and discipline, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1093. What penance and satisfaction he should impose, ibid., 1293. — One who sought a confessor only by gestures is to be absolved, Alan of Lille, CCX, 295. How the confessor should stir the penitent to contrition, ibid., 290. He ought to pray for the penitent, ibid., 299. Confessors ought to be prudent in imposing satisfactions, ibid., 288. What penances should be imposed on the sick, ibid., 276. The penitent’s wishes are to be accepted in imposing penance, ibid., 274. — What is the priest’s duty toward those who truly repent, Adam of Perseigne, CXI, 678. Mercy must take precedence in all judgments, ibid. A spiritual judge ought to hear attentively, examine prudently, and act with discernment, ibid. — What priests should observe in hearing confessions, Odo of Sully, CCXII, 60.

## V. Books treating of repentance

*Book on Repentance*, Tertullian, I, 1224.

*Parænesis, or a Little Exhortatory Book on Repentance*, St. Pacian, XIII, 1082.

*Two Books on Repentance*, St. Ambrose, XVI, 465.

*One Book on Repentance*, St. Ambrose, XVII, 971.

*On True and False Repentance*, St. Augustine, XL, 1113.

*On the Remission of Sins*, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 527.

*Short Work on the Confession of Sins*, Alcuin, CI, 649.

*On Repentance*, Abbot Smaragdus, CII, 611; Halitgar of Cambrai, CV, 677 ff.

*Penitential*, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 468.

*Book of Penitents*, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1397.

*On Repentance*, Haymo, CXVIII, 925.

*Little Book on Concealing Confession*, Lanfranc, CL, 625.

By what commutation penance may be mitigated, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 857.

*On the Power of Binding and Loosing*, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1160.

[Col. 0895]

# CIII. INDEX ON PUBLIC PENANCE, RECORDING EVERYTHING THAT WAS ONCE IN USE CONCERNING IT IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH, AND THE VARIOUS COLLECTIONS OF PENITENTIAL CANONS PROVIDED BY THE *PATROLOGIAE CURSUS*

## I. The existence of public penance established

[Col. 0895]

In the time of persecution, penance was not imposed upon fallen bishops, St. Optatus, XI, 983. — The stations of public penance, St. Ambrose, XVI, 510; its works, ibid., 520; and its exercises, ibid., 376. How harsh the labors once were, ibid., 1041. Public penitents were required to abstain from marital intercourse, ibid., 520. Public penance of a fallen virgin and her seducer, ibid., 493, 495. — In the ancient centuries of the Church, sacramental and public confession was not required before the faithful’s daily communion, except from those who felt themselves bound by some grave sin, St. Chromatius, XX, 279. — In the age of St. Nicetas, it was the common practice of the Church for a sin brought to light by investigation to be punished with a graver penance than if the sinner had confessed it voluntarily, St. Nicetas, LII, 1105. What length of penance was imposed on a fallen virgin, ibid., 1108. The authority of St. Cyprian considered concerning public penance for fallen virgins, ibid. St. Nicetas calls the penitential course the “contest of repentance,” ibid., 1109. By what outward acts a fallen virgin of the monastery had to perform public penance, ibid., 1110. In imposing ancient public penances, consideration was given both to sex and to physical strength, ibid. — One oppressed by mortal sins committed after baptism made satisfaction through public penance, Gennadius, LVIII, 994. It was imposed on persons for the most grievous sins, ibid. — The manner of public penance among the ancients, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1151. — What penance was and how great a penance was imposed upon catechumens seeking admission, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 360. Among the Greeks it lasted forty days, ibid., 371. There was another penance for catechumens if, during their catechumenate, they happened to commit a capital crime, ibid., 372. The rationale for undertaking public penance, ibid., 437. The four celebrated grades of penance: weeping, hearing, prostration, and standing with the faithful, ibid., 440. — An old custom granted penance to those who deferred it to the end of life but denied them absolution, id., LXXVII, 723. — In many places, performing penance according to the ancient institution of the canons has fallen out of use; neither the ancient order of excommunication nor that of reconciliation is observed, Rodulfus, CXIX, 720. Those who sinned publicly were punished by public penance, and, according to canonical order and their desert, were excommunicated and reconciled, ibid. — All incestuous persons, according to the degree of their guilt and without exception of rank, were judged by priests; and at an appropriate time public crimes were brought to the bishop’s attention, Herardus, CXXI, 765. — On public penance, Regino, CXXXII, 245. — Parish priests imposed penance according to the quality of the offense, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 562. It belonged to the bishop alone to reconcile public penitents, ibid. — Formerly, confession preceded the Lenten fast, Hildebert, CLXXI, 426. The use of public penance in Hildebert’s time, ibid., 611. Reconciliation of penitents took place on the Lord’s Supper, ibid., 509. — On penitents, Honorius, CLXXII, 663. — Solemn penance is called that which takes place publicly outside the Church, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 150. Concerning that penance in ancient times, ibid. — There was formerly one general confession of penitents, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 1085, and another made by parish priests in church, ibid. Public confession of sins was formerly not conducted in a single rite, ibid., 1082. The sacrament of repentance was denied even to sinners who sought it only in the final danger of life, ibid., 1071. — On solemn penance, Alan of Lille, CCX, 295. Penance was formerly imposed much more rigorously than now, ibid., 294.

## II. On penitential canons

[Col. 0898]

Whoever murmurs blasphemous words against the good Prince through hatred or envy shall do penance on bread and water for seven days, St. Patrick, LIII, 823. — If anyone sins in thought—that is, desires to kill a person, commit fornication, steal, or become drunk—he shall do penance on bread and water: for greater sins, half a year; for lesser ones, forty days, St. Columbanus, LXXX, 225. If anyone has stolen, he shall do penance for a year, ibid. If anyone has defiled himself, he shall do penance for a year, ibid., 226. — The measure of penances for gluttony and drunkenness, fornications, and other unclean pollutions, St. Cummian, LXXXVII, 981. — Let one who has committed adultery do penance, Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 826. Let women who kill infants do penance, ibid. — A penitential concerning an adulterous bishop and priest; concerning a priest who defiles himself by impure speech or other vices, etc., Egbert, LXXXIX, 379. — On the sacrilegious person, St. Gregory III, LXXXIX, 589; on the murderer, adulterer, fornicator, etc., ibid. — Let a priest or deacon committing fornication do penance; likewise a monk who steals a garment or another thing, one who unknowingly eats carrion, etc., Abedoc, XCVI, 1315 ff. — Let those do penance who strike someone in anger; who rise to strike another person; who bathe with women in a bathhouse, etc., Theodore, XCIX, 945. — *Penitential Book*, Halitgar, CV, 697. — On various penitents, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1077. Penitents doing penance for graver sins are to remain among the hearers for three years, if they have truly performed penance, ibid., 1080. Those doing public penance are to be among the hearers in haircloth for one year, ibid. — Statutes concerning penitents, Hincmar, CXXV, 793. — Public penitents are not to be ordained clergy, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 347. During the time of penance, penitents ought not to contract marriage, ibid., 380. After penance, they ought not to enter secular military service, ibid., 890. Those who have undertaken penance, forgotten their profession, and returned to the world are to be received by no one, ibid., 410. — Holy oil is not to be poured upon sick penitents, Atto, CXXXIV, 45. Penitents are to bend the knee daily, ibid., 46; bury the dead, ibid.; and abstain from secular business, ibid. — Ancient collection of canons: On the judgment of penitents, id., CXXXVIII, 437 ff. Ecclesiastical laws of the Anglo-Saxons: *Book of Penances*, ibid., 586 ff. Liturgical monuments: *Judgment of a Penitent*, id., CXL, 963. — *Penitential Book*, Burchard, CXL, 951. — Canonical penances, St. Fulbert, CXLI, 339, 340. — Collection of penances, St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 526. — Penances, Innocent III, CCXVII, 1145 ff.

[Col. 0897]

# CIV. INDEX ON EXTREME UNCTION, PROVIDING THE FEW BUT ALL ITEMS FOUND IN THE *PATROLOGIA* CONCERNING THE EXCELLENCE AND EFFECTS OF THAT SACRAMENT

The flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated, Tertullian, II, 806. — On the blessing of the sick by priests, St. Ambrose, XVI, 477. This blessing and pouring on of oil is now called extreme unction, note, ibid. — On the Epistle of St. James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick is commanded, St. Innocent I, XX, 551. — On attendance upon the sick at the point of death, St. Jerome, XXIV, 258. — The sacrament of unction; invisible anointing, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2004. On sacraments to be received by the sick person, id., XL, 1154. — The holy oil with which the sick are anointed is a kind of sacrament, St. Leo the Great, CLVI, 518. Priests are ministers of the anointing with oil, ibid. — The nature of extreme unction, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 235, 236. The form of this sacrament was formerly indicated by the term “oil,” ibid., 534. One priest alone is sufficient for administering this sacrament, [Col. 0898] ibid. — On extreme unction, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 270. — On diligently providing the sick with viaticum and blessed oil, St. Egbert of York, LXXXIX, 382. On anointing at the end of life, ibid., 416. — Prayer for the sick and anointing them are commanded, St. Chrodegang of Metz, LXXXIX, 1088. — When anyone falls ill, he is to summon the priests of the Church, and they are to pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord’s name, Charlemagne, XCVII, 326. — On the Epistle of St. James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick and anointing with oil are commanded, Halitgar of Cambrai, CV, 680. — On visiting the sick and anointing them with holy oil, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 258. — On visitation and anointing of the sick, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 815, 1031. — On the order and rite for administering the sacrament of unction, St. Prudentius of Troyes, CXV, 1440. — On the order of reconciling and anointing the sick, [Col. 0899] Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 773. — On anointing the sick with holy oil after confession and reconciliation, Riculfus of Soissons, CXXXI, 18; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 214. On the administration of extreme unction and instruction concerning this sacrament, id., CXXXVIII, 560. On the diligence priests must exercise lest the sick be deprived of this sacrament, ibid. — On anointing a sick brother, St. William of Hirsau, CL, 1132. — On the effects of the sacred anointing of the sick and the manner of administering this sacrament, Goffridus of Vendôme, CLVII, 298. — What the anointing with oil avails for the sick, [Col. 0900] Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1155. — When and by whom the anointing of the sick was instituted, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 577. Whether this sacrament may be repeated, ibid., 578. On anointing of the sick, id., CLXXVII, 596; Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1744; St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 681; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 899; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1102; John Beleth, CCII, 96; Garnerius of Langres, CCV, 677. — The opinion of those who say that extreme unction is not a sacrament, Alan of Lille, CCX, 370.

[Col. 0899]

# CV. INDEX ON THE SACRAMENT OF ORDER, IN WHICH THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING SACRED ORDINATION ARE SET OUT LOGICALLY

## Notice

Order, or sacred ordination, is defined as: a sacred rite or sacrament of the new law instituted by Christ, by which spiritual power is conferred for consecrating and administering the sacraments and lawfully performing the other ecclesiastical offices. Insofar as Order is called a sacred rite, it includes absolutely all grades or orders; insofar as it is called a sacrament, it applies only to those grades in which the true nature of a sacrament is recognized. Accordingly, in this Index we treat in turn: I. the existence of the sacrament of Order; II. its effects; III. its minister; IV. the subject of this sacrament; V. the conditions for lawfully receiving orders; VI. the various orders.

## I. The existence of the sacrament of Order

The sacrament of ordination, St. Augustine, XLIII, 109. — Ordination is a sacrament, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 648. — Sacred Order is the sacrament by which a person is marked out so that he may thereby benefit others through honor, Alan of Lille, CCX, 681. The opinion of those who say that order is not a sacrament, ibid., 369. They are refuted, ibid., 370. The sacrament of Order was instituted by God, ibid. The Apostles ordained priests and bishops, ibid.

## II. The effects of the sacrament of Order

That crimes or vices ought not to be thought removed by ordinations, St. Innocent I, XX, 530. — The sacrament of ordination may not be repeated, St. Augustine, XLIII, 70, 71, 72. It is not lost, ibid., 109. The sacrament of ordination remains in those ordained, id., XL, 394, even in one removed from office because of some fault, ibid. Grace is infused into those ordained through the laying-on, id., XXXV, 228. — The power of the sacrament is the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 299. Great is the burden of order; great is the weakness of the flesh, ibid., 460. — One ordained by a prohibited bishop must not exercise the orders received, nor should he be reordained by any bishop, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 52. — A bishop ordained simoniacally gave gold and lost his soul; the ordaining bishop received money and gave leprosy, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 355. Crimes are not removed in ordinations, ibid., 457. Reordinations ought not to occur, ibid., 463. — Those who returned to the Church from the Novatians are to be ordained again, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 572. Ordinations performed by excommunicated persons without simony are tolerated out of mercy, ibid., 787. — The sacrament of Order cannot be repeated, Alan of Lille, CCX, 353.

## III. On the minister of the sacrament of Order
A heretic may neither ordain nor impose hands, Firmilian, III, 1161.---The ordination of heretics is rejected, Council of Carthage, III, 1048, 1049.---The ordination of a cleric ordained by a pseudo-bishop is valid, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1203. Let no presbyter presume to ordain a deacon or presbyter; id., LXXXIV, 595.---That perverse ordainers should take part in no further ordinations, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 387. A presbyter shall not ordain a deacon or presbyter, id., CXXXVIII, 403.---One ordained by a prohibited bishop ought not to exercise the orders received, nor ought he to be reordained by any bishop, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 52.---That those who ordain unworthy persons ought to lose the right of consecrating, [Col. 0900] Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 360. Let no presbyter ordain a deacon or presbyter, ibid., 443.---Without consultation with his clerics, a bishop shall not ordain clerics, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 142. Priests may be ordained by one bishop, ibid., 351. On presbyters ordained by persons known not to have been bishops, ibid. A bishop who presumes to ordain an unwilling person shall be subject to suspension for one year, ibid., 361.

IV.---On the Subject of the Sacrament of Orders: Those Who Must Not Be Ordained.

Those who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical ranks, Stephen, III, 999, 1000.---A twice-married man shall not be ordained priest or deacon, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1141.---That after the remission of sins, one who has chosen to wear the military belt may not be admitted to the clergy, St. Innocent I, XX, 472. Those who cannot be received into the clergy, ibid., 477. That if a layman has married a widow, he shall not become a cleric, ibid., 379. Those who must be excluded from orders, ibid., 491, 492. That if a catechumen has had a wife and, after her death, has taken another after baptism, he shall not be a cleric, ibid., 528. That twice-married men cannot be admitted to the clergy, ibid., 604.---By the canons, bishops may not ordain someone belonging to another jurisdiction, St. Augustine, XLV, 1771. Those wounded by penance cannot be ordained, id., XLIII, 804. Whether it is permissible to ordain those who were baptized as children by Donatists, ibid., 807, 808.---The untrained and neophytes ought not to be ordained, St. Leo the Great, LV, 651. The discipline of the Roman Church admitted to orders only those who, either from childhood or, if adults, immediately after baptism, had devoted themselves to the clergy, id., LIV, 649, 650. An illiterate person, or one deprived of some bodily member, is not to be ordained, id., LVI, 699. Nor a slave without his owners’ consent, ibid., 697. Nor one who has been rebaptized, ibid., 872. Nor a municipal councillor, ibid., 525. A seditious person, usurer, or avenger of injuries is not to be ordained, ibid., 885. Those who are not to be promoted, ibid., 694.---A man cannot be a cleric if he has had in marriage a concubine, widow, divorced woman, or prostitute, Gennadius, LVIII, 1039. Nor can one who has mutilated his own genitals, ibid., 1040. Nor one convicted of having taken usury or performed on the stage, ibid. Nor one who has undergone public penance, ibid. Nor one who has become insane or has been tormented by demonic affliction, ibid. Nor one who offers money, ibid.---Gregory the Great excludes from orders those involved in public administration, LXXVII, 662. Advocates, soldiers, officials, actors, and persons liable for public accounts were barred from the clerical state, [Col. 0901] ibid. Who are irregular for receiving orders, ibid., 575, 696. Twice-married men, or those who have not obtained a virgin as wife, must be excluded from orders, ibid., 601, 602, 696, 1261. Those impaired in body, ibid., 575. The ignorant, ibid. Penitents, ibid. The rebaptized, ibid. Boys, ibid., 643. That demoniacs are not to be promoted to the clergy, id., LXXXIV, 257. On slaves not to be ordained, ibid., 284. That the priesthood is not to be given to persons unknown, ibid., 640. That advocates, municipal councillors, or persons devoted to secular military service are not to be admitted to the clergy, ibid., 671.---They are not to be ordained unless all those associated with them are believers, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 329.---One who has cut off part of his finger ought not to be a cleric, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 272, 278. That one who has made himself a eunuch shall not become a cleric, id., CXXXVIII, 401. That no cleric shall be made from among municipal councillors, ibid., 402. Twice-married men cannot be admitted to the clergy, ibid. The rebaptized are not to be promoted to any grade of the clerical state, ibid.---That one lacking an eye cannot obtain the office of the priesthood, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 472. That a cleric who has killed a pagan cannot be promoted, ibid., 474. That penitents or twice-married men are not to be promoted, ibid., 478.---Usurers ought not to be promoted to sacred orders, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 246. One who after baptism has been implicated in homicide by act, command, or counsel shall not be ordained a cleric, ibid., 257. One who kills accidentally may, by dispensation, remain in his order, ibid., 275. One shut up in a monastery to perform penance shall not be ordained presbyter, ibid., 282. Apostates are not to be admitted to the clerical office, ibid., 286. Those who have served as soldiers after baptism, or contended in court, are prohibited from sacred orders, ibid. No one of servile condition may attain sacred orders, ibid., 291. Penitents or illiterate persons are not to be ordained, ibid., 302. Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy, ibid., 304. Nor is one barred from the clergy who has accidentally cut off his finger, ibid. Sons of presbyters are not to be admitted to sacred offices, ibid., 305. If the sons of priests are found to be religious, they are to be ordained, ibid., 311. A monk is not to be ordained a cleric unless he has been presented to the bishop with the abbot’s consent, ibid., 313.

V.---On the Conditions for Lawfully Receiving Orders.

Ordination by stages.---Pope Caius, V, 190.---That monks or laymen ought not to reach the highest priesthood except through ecclesiastical grades, St. Innocent I, XX, 670.---What ordination is just and lawful, Council of Carthage, III, 1022, 1023, 1026.---Candidates for ordination must be tested, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 618, 649. No one is to be ordained by leaping over grades, ibid., 620. No layman or monk is to be ordained bishop unless he has been tested through the grades of lower orders, id., LVI, 571, 578. The periods to be observed in each grade, ibid., 572.---Fixed intervals between grades of orders must be kept, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 643. Because the canonical intervals between orders had not been observed, Pope Constantine was deposed from his rank, ibid., 585, note. On the periods to be spent in clerical orders, id., LXXXIV, 654.---The orders to be conferred with what intervals of time, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 682.---That one ought to attain the office of the episcopate through ecclesiastical grades, Burchard, CXL, 554.---Let no one approach the priestly office unless tested in each individual grade, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 313. No one may aspire to the priesthood except through distinct grades, ibid., 374. What intervals of time are to be observed in each grade, ibid., 375. At what intervals one chosen from monks for the clerical state is to be ordained, ibid., 377.

Ordination must not be for sale.---Let ambition, favour, or money have no power, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 618. Clerics ordained for a price are to be deposed from office, id., LVI, 702.---Giving or receiving anything for receiving orders is forbidden, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 131, 133. Let there be no sale in ordination, id., LXXVII, 644. Clerics are to be ordained without charge, ibid., 697. They must not permit clerics to be ordained or promoted through a reward given, favour, or anyone’s petition, ibid., 792, 951. Ordination is not to take place through favour or sale, ibid., 643, 644, 794, 801.---Let bishops not be ordained for a reward, St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 38. That bishops or any among the clergy ought not to be ordained through money, ibid., 166; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 309. Ordination is not to be obtained by gifts, ibid., 574. Orders are not to be conferred for a price, ibid., 545. That sacred ordination must by no means be sold, id., CXXXVIII, 400.---That a bishop ordained simoniacally gave gold and lost his soul, while the ordainer received money and gave leprosy, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 355. That nothing be received for ordination, the pallium, or documents, ibid., 361. On one who gave or received the laying on of hands for money, [Col. 0902] ibid., 364. By what sentence those are to be struck who are elected to the episcopate simoniacally, or who, when elected, are ordained simoniacally, ibid., 366. Let no bishop ordain anyone for money, ibid., 367. A bishop is not to be made by reward or the patronage of persons, ibid. He who ordains or is ordained for money is excluded from the priesthood, ibid., 1155. A bishop who performs an ordination for money is condemned, ibid. Those who do not exercise freely the grace they receive from God are sellers of doves, ibid., 1157. On one ordained by a person whom he knows to be a simoniac, ibid., 1158.---No one can be ordained or promoted in the Church of God through money, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 482. On those ordained by simoniacs, though not simoniacally, ibid., 533. Whoever approaches sacred orders by any gift will find eternal condemnation, ibid., 535. Let no one approach sacred orders for price, prayer, favour, or petition, ibid., 536. Let no one be promoted to sacred orders by favour or sale, ibid., 537. Nothing ought to be demanded from one being ordained, but neither ought voluntarily offered gifts to be refused, ibid., 543. On those who dispense sacred orders by receiving gifts, ibid., 546. Just as ordination, so election or consent must be offered without sale, ibid., 564.---On those knowingly ordained by simoniacs, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 907.

Where, when, and how ordination is to be performed.---Priestly ordinations ought to take place only with the awareness of the people who are present, Council of Carthage, III, 1026. What was done for the proper celebration of ordinations, ibid., 1027.---“In the ordinations of clerics, we customarily consult you beforehand,” St. Cyprian, IV, 318.---The Nicene rules are to be observed in ordinations, St. Innocent I, XX, 491, 492.---The fast of both ordainer and candidate must precede, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 625. Observance of the canons is especially commended in ordinations, ibid., 617. He rebukes ordinations performed amid tumult, ibid., 645. Certain unlawful ordinations among the Africans are censured, ibid., 646. Clerics are not to be ordained in the presence of catechumens, id., LVI, 715. The most ancient formulas or rubrics for ordinations, ibid., 887, 888.---Order for blessing sacred orders, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 208. The ministers of the Church who are ordained among Latins, Greeks, Maronites, etc., ibid. The Roman Order now extant is ancient, ibid., 446. The rite for ordaining a pope, ibid., 505. Two loaves are given to the ordinand, by which he is taught to weep for sins, both his own and those of others, id., LXXIX, 287. In former times many were ordained by bishops other than their own without letters dimissory, id., LXXVII, 536. Today, in order to receive any order, only letters dimissory from one’s bishop and letters of birth are required, ibid. The major grades were formerly conferred before the Gospel and the minor after Communion, ibid. Today the minor are conferred first and the major afterward, ibid., 475. Sacred ordination is to be conferred on fasting persons by fasting persons, id., LXXVIII, 475. The rite of conferring orders according to the Greeks, ibid., 508.---A bishop ought not to ordain apart from the metropolitan’s authority, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 697, 924. No one ought to be ordained by another’s bishop, ibid., 260. The ordained ought to obtain from the bishop letters of their ordination, ibid., 372. An ordination performed by someone other than one’s own bishop is void, ibid., 579.---How a bishop ought to confer an order. From the Council of Nantes, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 278. Ordinations ought not to be performed by the judgment of the multitude, id., CXXXVIII, 399.---That ordinations ought not to be celebrated under the gaze of hearers, Burchard, CXL, 626.0. That every ordained person receive letters from his own ordainer, ibid., 634.---Orders are to be conferred on fasting persons by fasting persons, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 59.---That whoever has been ordained contrary to the forms of the canons be deposed together with his ordainers, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 458. That every presbyter, when ordained, receive letters from his ordainer, ibid., 480. No one is to be ordained without a title, ibid., 1136.---When and how ordinations are to be performed, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 431.---Without consultation with his clerics, a bishop shall not ordain clerics, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 142. The ordination of one ordained without the bishop’s consent is void, ibid., 357. No cleric is to be ordained in another church without letters dimissory, ibid., 1112.

Presbyters and deacons, as well as priests, are to be consecrated only on Sundays, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 617, 624. On what day priestly or Levitical blessing ought to be celebrated, ibid., 625. Sunday as the day of ordination, ibid., 620, 634, 1021. By apostolic tradition, ibid., 1021. On the ordination of a presbyter or deacon being celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, Sunday, id., LXXXIV, 783.---The minor grades could formerly be conferred on Sundays, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 475. The major grades on the Saturdays of the Four Seasons [Ember Saturdays], ibid. Also on Sunday morning, after the Saturday fast had been continued, ibid. The present practice by which major and minor orders are conferred together [Col. 0903] on Ember Saturdays is ancient, ibid., 476.---Orders are not to be celebrated indiscriminately or at every time, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 779. When the ordinations of presbyters ought to take place, ibid., 940. On the time of ordination, id., CXXXVIII, 399. That the ordinations of presbyters be performed at fixed times, ibid., 403.---The ordination of a bishop is to be celebrated on Sunday, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 59.---That ordination may take place on Sunday morning after continuing the Saturday fast, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 460. That priestly and Levitical ordination take place on the day of the Resurrection, ibid. Ordinations are not to be performed except in the Ember fast, ibid., 461. At what hour episcopal ordinations ought to be performed, ibid., 1132. Why priestly ordinations are celebrated on Sunday, ibid., 1133. On the times of ordination, ibid., 1136.---Why orders are conferred in the Ember seasons, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 686. On the time for conferring sacred orders, ibid., 757.---At what hour the ordinations of presbyters or Levites ought to be performed, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 367. Why on Sunday, ibid. After the hour of baptism on Holy Saturday, a bishop may be ordained, ibid., 374.

The places in which bishops ought to be ordained, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 654. Where bishops are to be ordained, id., XCIX, 1002. That a bishop is not to be ordained in a diocese that has never had a bishop, id., CXXXVIII, 399.---That a cleric of one diocese is under no circumstances to be ordained in another parish, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 379. That ordinations ought to take place only in a fixed and sacred place, ibid., 451.---The places in which primates or patriarchs ought to be ordained, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 383. By apostolic permission, a cleric of one church may be ordained in another, ibid., 357.

On title, examination, age, and qualifications of candidates for ordination. No cleric is to be ordained unless to the title of some church, city, village, or martyr-shrine, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 540.---That none are to be ordained unless assigned to a title somewhere, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 451.---Formerly no clerics were ordained unless attached to some title, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 461. They were not ordained without a title, id., LXXVIII, 484.---That priests are not to be ordained without a fixed title, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 431.---An ordination performed without a title is void, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 355.---It is not permissible to ordain without a title, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1107. “In the ordinations of clerics, we customarily weigh the character and merits of each person by common counsel,” St. Cyprian, IV, 318. The ages, conditions, and merits of individuals are distinguished, ibid., 330. Human testimonies need not be awaited when divine support has preceded, ibid.---In what respects candidates for ordination are to be tested, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 618, 649. With thorough examination, ibid., 708. Ordination without examination is reproved, id., LVI, 395.---Clerics must be carefully examined before being ordained, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 694. What chief qualifications Gregory required in candidates, ibid., 575, 696. What councils formerly required, ibid. What they are now to be examined about, ibid., 696. The character of candidates was formerly examined carefully, id., LXXVIII, 484. The matters on which those to be placed in sacred order are to be examined, id., LXXVII, 532, 644, 696.---On examination before ordination, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 267. How a bishop-elect is to be examined, ibid., 279.---On examining one who approaches the clerical office, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 230, 450.---On presbyters promoted without examination, Burchard, CXL, 627.---That those to be ordained bishops ought first to be examined, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 347, 348.---Those to be ordained shall assemble on Wednesday for examination, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 140. On those ordained without examination who afterward confess their sins, ibid., 142. Ecclesiastical order does not receive one who is ordained without examination or who confesses afterward, ibid., 387.

The age of candidates for ordination, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1142.---At what age a presbyter is to be ordained, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 445. Clerics are not to be ordained before twenty-five years of age, ibid., 693. At what age clerics are to be ordained, ibid., 420, 560, 868.---None are to be admitted to sacred orders except persons of mature age, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 644.---No one is to be ordained cleric before the thirtieth year of age, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 280.---They are not to be ordained before twenty-five years, Council of Arles, LXXXIV, 243. On the age of deacons, ibid., 33.---A presbyter under thirty years is by no means to be ordained, Council of Neocaesarea, LXXXIV, 110. A deacon before twenty-five years and a priest before thirty years are not to be ordained, ibid., 243. At what age deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 266. At what age bishops or presbyters, ibid. On the number of years at which priests and Levites are to be ordained, ibid., 273. On the lawful age for ordaining a presbyter, ibid., 577.---A deacon is not to be ordained before twenty-five years and a priest before thirty years, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 381. At what age deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 402. At what age bishops [Col. 0904] or presbyters are to be ordained, ibid., 268, 581.---A deacon is not to be ordained before twenty-five years and a priest before thirty, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 377. At what age bishops or presbyters are to be consecrated, ibid., 378.---A layman is not to become bishop before thirty years, Burchard, CXL, 553. That it is not permissible to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years, ibid., 627. On presbyters ordained before twenty-five years, ibid. That deacons are not to be ordained before twenty-five years, ibid.---At what age deacons ought to be consecrated, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 433, 452. On the age of candidates for ordination, ibid., 1135 and following; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 432.---When necessity requires it, presbyters of twenty-five years may be ordained, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 380.---Pope Nicholas decreed thus concerning the age of candidates for ordination, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 908.

That unworthy persons are sometimes ordained, not according to God’s will but according to human presumption, Council of Carthage, III, 1027.---The ages, conditions, and merits of individuals are distinguished, so that the worthy may be promoted to ecclesiastical grades, St. Cyprian, IV, 330.---Candidates for ordination must be without crime, St. Augustine, XLIV, 563.---Blameless men are to be ordained bishops, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 672.---None are to be admitted to sacred orders except persons of mature age and of spotless conduct, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 644. Nor those whose life can be censured, ibid., 678. That no cleric be ordained unless his life has been approved, id., LXXXIV, 192. That criminals are not to be promoted to the clergy, ibid., 803. What kind of men, and in what manner, should approach sacred orders, id., XCIX, 1002.---A deacon is not to be promoted unless he professes chastity, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 584. Married deacons may be ordained priests provided they live chastely, ibid., 433. Married deacons ought not to be promoted to the priesthood, ibid., 393. Whether deacons who declare that they cannot remain continent ought to be promoted to the priesthood, ibid., 264. What adornment of character a candidate for ordination ought to possess, ibid., 1042. What sort of men, or how learned, bishops ought to be ordained, id., CXXXVIII, 399. That no one ignorant of letters be promoted to the clergy, ibid., 401. That criminal clerics cannot be promoted, ibid.---Nor illiterate persons, Burchard, CXL, 628.---That one worthy in life and morals be chosen for sacred orders, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 351. That one being ordained to the diaconate renounce marriage, ibid., 524. Those to be ordained deacons or presbyters are to promise that they will live chastely, ibid., 1135. On the qualifications of candidates for ordination, ibid., 1139 and following. Which laymen ought to be ordained, ibid., 1151. On the continence of candidates for ordination, ibid., 1149 and following. A subdeacon must observe continence, ibid., 1132. Let no one approach sacred orders unless he is a virgin or of proven chastity, ibid., 1153. Those constituted in the three grades must also abstain from their wives, ibid. Ministers of the altar, together with bishops and presbyters, are under the same law of continence, ibid. Those in minor orders may marry unless forbidden by a vow or religious habit. Let readers either marry or profess continence, ibid., 1154.---What sort of men are to be chosen for sacred orders, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 432.---Let none be ordained unless called, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 922.---A deacon is not to be ordained unless he has professed chastity, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 142. Let no one become a subdeacon who has not promised to live chastely, ibid., 155. Those about to enter the subdiaconate are to profess continence, ibid., 157. (See the article “On the Subject of the Sacrament of Orders.”)

VI.---On the Various Orders.

On persons to be ordained.---Pope St. Caius, V, 181. On ecclesiastical orders, ibid., 190; Collection of Canons, LXXXIV, 32 and following; Alcuin, CI, 1234.---On ecclesiastical grades, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 299. On sacred orders, id., CXII, 1193.---The various ranks of clerics, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 608.---On sacred orders, Burchard, CXL, 681; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 443 and following; CLXII, 514 and following; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 598; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 421 and following; CLXXVII, 399 and following; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 136 and following; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 900 and following; Sicard of Cremona, CCXIII, 61.---On the six orders of clerics, Innocent III, CCXVII, 775.

On clerical tonsure.---Clerical tonsure, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 852.---The first mention of the clerical crown, St. Gregory the Great, LXXI, 1078. Clerical dignity is conferred by cutting the hair, according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church, id., LXXVIII, 212, 436. This is done before receiving any order whatsoever, ibid., 436. Among the Greeks, clerical tonsure is given at the ordination of a reader, ibid. St. Peter the Apostle was the author of ecclesiastical tonsure, ibid. What clerical tonsure signifies, ibid. This is not a double but a single tonsure, id., LXXVIII, 437. The ancient crown of St. Peter and the early clerics represents Christ’s crown of thorns, ibid.---On the tonsure of clerics, [Col. 0905] St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 779; Alcuin, CI, 1233; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 821, 1081, 1234; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 298; CXII, 1167; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 340; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 392; John of Rouen, CXLVII, 28, 65; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 442; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 602, 603; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 422; Anselm of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1101.---Tonsure proceeded from apostolic teaching, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 28.---Tonsure or religious dress assumed in childhood by one’s parents may be annulled, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1103.---What the crown signifies, Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1269; Peter Cantor, CCV, 485.

On doorkeepers.---The office of doorkeeper was the first clerical grade in the time of Paulinus, St. Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 535, 536. Their ancient ministry in the Church was to sleep there at night and keep watch, ibid., 537, 538.---A doorkeeper ought to be an old man in age and character, St. Benedict, LXVI, 901.---At what point in the Mass doorkeepers are ordained, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 475. The rite for ordaining doorkeepers, ibid., 218. Mention of doorkeepers in the ancient Fathers, ibid., 476. The duties of doorkeepers, ibid., 477.---On doorkeepers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 794; LXXXII, 293. How doorkeepers are made, id., LXXXIV, 201.---Why he is called a doorkeeper, Alcuin, CI, 1132. The office of doorkeepers in the Old Law, ibid. In the New Law, ibid., 1132, 1234.---On doorkeepers, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 822, 1083; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 305.---How doorkeepers are ordained, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 339.---What sort of man a doorkeeper should be, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 313.---The origin and office of doorkeepers, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 207; Lanfranc, CL, 629; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 514; Stephen of Autun, CLXXII, 1276.---On the ordination of doorkeepers, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 448; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 136.---Whence the doorkeeper is so called, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1103.---Where Christ exercised the office of doorkeeper, ibid.; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 514.---When they are ordained, the keys of the Church are handed to them by the bishop, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 514.

On readers.---On the office of reader, St. Cyprian, IV, 319. Let readers read the Gospel, ibid.---No reader may touch the sacred vessels, St. Sylvester, VIII, 835.---Readers may marry and beget children, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1204; LVI, 543. When they have reached puberty, they are to be compelled either to marry or to profess continence, id., LVI, 868.---Arrogance is a vice characteristic of readers, St. Benedict, LVI, 605.---A reader read through the psalm that was to be explained to the people, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1784. A reader recites the Gospel, id., XXXVIII, 433, 1117. Boys in the rank of readers, id., XXXIV, 1049; XXXIX, 1550.---On the reader, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 963, 918, 273, 763.---Formerly the Epistle in Mass was read by readers, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXVIII, 479. The Gospel was read in Mass by readers, ibid. Readers have a place among the clerical grades, ibid., 314. Readers are granted liberty to marry, ibid. Readers are forbidden to devote themselves to gambling and drunkenness, ibid. Readers who do not fast during Lent, on Wednesday, or on Good Friday are to be deposed, ibid. Among the Greeks, the readerate alone of the minor orders is conferred, ibid., 436. The ordination of readers among the Greeks, ibid. At what point in the Mass the ordination of readers is performed, ibid., 475. Ancient mention of readers in the Church, ibid., 478. In the early times of the Church readers read the Gospel and Epistle in Mass, ibid., 479, 547. The duty of readers was to guard the sacred books, ibid.---How readers are ordained among the Greeks, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 511.---On readers, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 791. How readers are made, id., LXXXIV, 201. Their duty, Alcuin, CI, 1234.
