Their duty in the Old Law, ibid., 1232.---On readers, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 823, 1084; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 305; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 285; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 443; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 598; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 424; CLXXVII, 100; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 901.---On the ordination of readers, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 448, 1138; Stephen of Autun, CLXXII, 1276; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 136.---What kind of cleric a reader ought to be, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 313.---The origin and office of readers, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 208; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 514; Stephen of Autun, CLXXII, 1276.---Readers should either marry or profess continence, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1154; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 181.

On acolytes.---Blessing of the acolyte, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 318.---On acolytes, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 293; LXXXIII, 793. How acolytes are made, id., LXXXIV, 200.---Whence the acolyte is so called, or what ministry he has, Alcuin, CI, 1132. The office of acolytes in the Old Law, ibid., 1232.---On acolytes, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 824, 1085; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 304.---How acolytes are ordained, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 359.---On the ordination of acolytes, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 447, [Col. 0906] 1137. The order of acolytes, id., CLXII, 515.---On acolytes, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 598; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 425; CLXXVII, 400; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 912; Innocent III, CCXVII, 775.---The acolytes are the fourth order, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1104.---When Christ performed this office, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 515; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1104.---Why acolytes hold lighted candles during the chanting of the Gospel, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 709.---What their ministry is, Innocent III, CCXVII, 775.

On exorcists.---Exorcists cast demons out of the bodies of the possessed, Tertullian, I, 413.---Let exorcists lay hands on demoniacs, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 885. Exorcism is forbidden to those not ordained by a bishop, ibid., 717.---Ordination of an exorcist, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 317, 319. Blessing of an exorcist, ibid., 319. Exorcists are recorded as existing in the Acts of the Apostles, id., LXXVIII, 355. The Holy Church also includes the ministry of exorcists among ecclesiastical grades, ibid. Exorcists assail the devil with many rebukes, ibid., 368. At what point in the Mass the ordination of exorcists is performed, ibid., 475, 480. Mention of exorcists in the Church among the ancient Fathers, ibid. Also among the pagans, ibid.---On exorcists, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 792. How exorcists are made, id., LXXXIV, 200.---Their office in the Old Law, Alcuin, CI, 1232. In the Church, ibid., 1234.---On exorcists, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1084; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 304; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 285; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 444; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 598; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 424; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 912.---The origin and office of exorcists, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 208.---On the ordination of exorcists, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 448, 1138; Stephen of Autun, CLXXII, 1276; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 136.---Exorcists are the third order, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1103.---When Christ exercised the office of exorcist, ibid.; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 515.

On subdeacons.---Continence is imposed also upon subdeacons, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 871.---The office of subdeacon, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 273. The subdeacon offered wine to be consecrated at the altar, ibid., 875.---Chastity is commended to the subdeacon at his ordination, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 319. Blessing of the subdeacon, ibid. Address to the subdeacon to be ordained, ibid.---No subdeacon is to be ordained unless he promises chastity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 307. In the Roman Church subdeacons observed celibacy, ibid. Subdeacons already ordained in Sicily are not to be compelled to continence, but those to be ordained in the future must promise and observe it, id., LXXVII, 503, 504. In Gregory’s age the subdiaconate was not counted among sacred orders, ibid., 506. Subdeacons of the Roman Church observed continence, ibid. The contrary custom prevailed in Sicily, ibid. Pelagius’s constitution decreed that they should abstain either from their wives or from their ministry, ibid., 710. Gregory moderates this constitution of Pelagius, ibid., 506. Yet he forbids any subdeacon henceforth to be ordained in Sicily who does not promise continence, ibid. Let subdeacons chant in church and themselves read what is to be read, ibid., 1335. Formerly the book of Epistles was not handed to the subdeacon at his ordination, id., LXXVIII, 484. Nor did reading the Epistle at Mass belong to his office, ibid. At what point in the Mass subdeacons are ordained, ibid., 475. The subdiaconate was not a sacred order, ibid., 482. Subdeacons were forbidden to touch the sacred vessels, ibid. A subdeacon is not ordained by the laying on of hands, ibid., 220, 493. He is ordained by the presentation of an empty chalice and empty paten, ibid. Formerly the book of Epistles was not handed to the subdeacon at his ordination, ibid., 484. Among the Greeks subdeacons are ordained by the laying on of hands according to the Apostolic Constitutions, ibid., 508, 510. How subdeacons are appointed, id., LXXXIV, 200.---Subdeacons and their office in the Old Law, Alcuin, CI, 1232. In the New Law, or Church, ibid., 1132, 1134.---That subdeacons ought not to bless, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 881.---On subdeacons, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 303.---On the ministry of subdeacons, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 285. Subdeacons ought not to have permission to enter the sacristy and touch the Lord’s vessels, ibid., 288.---What kind of man a subdeacon ought to be, Ratherius, CXXXVI, 313.---On subdeacons not living chastely, Pope Alexander II, CXLVI, 1405.---The origin and office of subdeacons, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 200. Let the subdeacon place the codex of the Gospels above the right-hand corner of the altar, ibid., 32. With his chasuble removed, let him read the Epistle, ibid., 34, 75. Formerly he remained in the choir except during the time of his ministry, ibid., 33, 75. The subdeacon’s vestments, ibid., 32.---On subdeacons, St. William, CL, 1020; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 221.---On the ordination of subdeacons, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 447, 1137.---On the office, ordination, and continence of subdeacons, Stephen of Autun, CLXXII, 277.---From what time the order of subdeacons is regarded as sacred, Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1109.---The subdeacons are the fifth order, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1104.---Where Christ performed this office, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 515; Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1104.---The subdiaconate has recently been inserted among the sacred orders, Peter Cantor, CCV, 158.

### On Deacons

—How deacons’ ordinations are to be performed, Third Council of Carthage, 1026.  
—The apostles appointed deacons for themselves as ministers of their episcopal office and of the Church, St Cyprian, IV, 396. When the solemn rites have been completed, the deacon offers the chalice to those present, ibid., 485. Confession before a deacon, ibid., 259.  
—Deacons are called simply ministers, Lactantius, VII, 503, 695; likewise ministers of God, ibid.  
—On the deacons of parishes and the cardinal deacons of the city of Rome, St Sylvester, VIII, 835.  
—The consecration of the Lord’s blood entrusted to the deacon, St Ambrose, XVI, 84. They were bound to continence, ibid., 342.  
—Deacons read the Gospel, St Jerome, XXII, 1200. The deacon publicly recited the names of those making offerings, id., XXV, 175.  
—The office of deacon, St Augustine, XXXVIII, 1395; St Leo the Great, LIV, 436. The ordination of deacons, id., LV, 114, 620. What deacons ought to be like, and their duties, id., LVI, 736. Their continence, ibid., 438. On the number of deacons, ibid., 757.  
—The deacon calls for silence during Mass, St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 421. He offers the chalice at the altar, ibid., 748.  
—Prayer for ordaining a deacon, St Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 320.  
—Formerly only seven deacons were ordained in the Roman Church, St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 242, 265. They were called regional deacons, ibid.; cardinal deacons, ibid., 266. Let deacons devote themselves to preaching and almsgiving, id., LXXVII, 1335. When deacons began to chant the Gospel during the solemnities of Mass, ibid. At what point in the Mass a deacon is ordained, id., LXXVIII, 475. Why, when a deacon is ordained, the bishop alone lays hands upon him, ibid., 221, 485, 487. The laying on of hands alone is the essential matter of the diaconate, ibid., 492. The ordination of a deacon according to the Greeks, ibid., 509. Formerly the Book of the Gospels was not presented to a deacon at his ordination, ibid., 487. By ancient custom deacons read the Gospel at Mass, ibid., 488. Formerly in Gaul a custom had arisen whereby deacons’ hands were anointed with chrism at ordination, ibid., 489. Formula for ordaining a deacon, ibid., 221. Deacons distributed Holy Communion to the faithful, ibid., 555. It belongs to the deacon to admonish the people to bow down, ibid., 563. How deacons are to be appointed, id., LXXXIV, 200.  
—Let deacons live soberly, chastely, and with modesty, Charlemagne, XCVII, 207.  
—Deacons are forbidden to sing anything in church other than the Gospel, St Agobard, CIV, 336.  
—Why the deacon, when in the ambo, faces south, Amalarius of Metz, CV, 1322.  
—A deacon devoted to gambling or drunkenness must either desist or certainly be condemned, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 19. On deacons not giving Christ’s body to presbyters or receiving Communion before presbyters, ibid., 256. A deacon ought not to give the bread or bless the chalice, ibid., 289. At what age deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 377.  
—That a deacon, if necessary, receive confession, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 247. That a deacon not be ordained before the age of twenty-five, ibid., 377.  
—How deacons are to be ordained, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 447.  
—If a deacon is found guilty of fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide, he is to be suspended from office, Burchard, CXL, 657. That deacons not sit in the presence of presbyters, ibid., 662.  
—The origin and office of deacons, John of Rouen, CXVII, 200.  
—The various duties of deacons, Lanfranc, CL, 629.  
—Deacons must not dare to exchange or sell property of the Church entrusted to them, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 235. How deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 447. How deacons who have fallen into crime ought to be reconciled, ibid., 459. The law of continence imposed on deacons, ibid. A deacon is not to be ordained unless he has professed chastity, ibid., 1152.  
—Why a blessing is given to a deacon about to read the Gospel, Rupert, CLXX, 31.  
—Why a deacon about to read the Gospel proceeds from the south toward the north, Rupert, CLXX, 83.  
—Deacons are not to be ordained before their twenty-fifth year, St Bernard, CLXXXII, 1077. A deacon who has experienced a nocturnal emission ought not to minister on that day, ibid., 1111.  
—Among them confession was also made in the absence of priests, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 1083.  
—Without apostolic permission, non-deacons may not use dalmatics, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 134. Nor may non-deacons anoint their hands with chrism at consecration, ibid.  
—The office of deacons, Master Bandinus, CXCII, 1104. Where Christ performed the office of deacon, ibid.  
—Deacons ought to be perfect in learning and conduct, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 183. The deacon’s office is not to preach by authority, ibid., 184. What the status of deacons ought to be, ibid., 183.  
—On the blessing which a deacon requests and receives, Innocent III, CCXVII, 821.

### On the Ordination of a Presbyter

—On what day a priest is to be ordained, St Leo the Great, LIV, 620. At what age, id., LVI, [Col. 0908] 445. What is to be done concerning a presbyter who committed a carnal sin before ordination, ibid.  
—The laying on of hands alone is the essential matter of the priesthood, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 492. Ordination by the laying on of hands is customarily performed by bishops, ibid., 495. How presbyters are to be ordained, id., LXXXIV, 199.  
—On the ordination of presbyters, Charlemagne, XCVII, 531; XCIX, 949; Burchard, CXL, 625.  
—How presbyters ought to be ordained, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 447, 450. That Abraham was the first to be called presbyter, and why he is called presbyter, ibid., 451. How a presbyter is ordained, ibid., 1137. The order of presbyters took its beginning from the sons of Aaron, id., CLXII, 518. On the ordination of priests, ibid., 519. When the Lord exercised the office of priest, ibid.  
—On presbyters, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 598; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 428; CLXXVII, 401.  
—How a presbyter is ordained, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 133. Neither presbyters nor deacons may anoint their hands with chrism at consecration, ibid., 134. Candidates for ordination as presbyters promise to live chastely, ibid., 156. At what hour ordinations of presbyters or levites ought to take place, ibid., 367. Why priests are ordained on Sunday, ibid.  
—On presbyters, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 904.  
—The apostles ordained priests and bishops, Alan of Lille, CCX, 370. (See the article, “On the conditions for lawfully receiving orders.”)

### On the Ordination of Bishops

—In ancient times bishops were chosen when advanced in age and proven, Tertullian, I, 469.  
—No single bishop is to presume to ordain a bishop, St Siricius, III, 1157.  
—How a bishop’s ordination was performed, and who was chosen, St Jerome, XXII, 1193.  
—Suffragan bishops are to be ordained by the metropolitan with the exarch’s knowledge; metropolitans by the exarch himself, St Leo the Great, LIV, 618, 619. On what day bishops are to be ordained, ibid., 620. A bishop’s ordination is to be reserved to the provincial metropolitan, ibid., 633. On the ordination of bishops, ibid., 636. In what places bishops ought to be ordained, ibid., 654. That no one be ordained bishop without the people’s consent, ibid., 666. That no one be ordained bishop unwillingly, ibid., 673. The anointing of bishops, ibid., 341. Let suffragan bishops consecrate them with the metropolitan’s judgment, ibid., 1203. The consecration of bishops, id., LV, 113. The day of their consecration was called their birthday, ibid., 116, 119. A bishop is to be examined before ordination, and how, id., LVI, 879. Bishops are not to be ordained from among laymen, ibid., 408, 581. No one is to be ordained bishop without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, that is, of the primate, ibid., 727; or of the metropolitan, ibid., 520, 575, 711, 716. Bishops’ ordinations are not to be delayed, but are to occur within three months unless necessity compels postponement, ibid., 547. At the ordination, the ordinators are to make known to the bishop the decrees of the council, ibid., 869. By whom and how bishops are to be ordained, ibid., 590, 711, 716, 867. No single bishop is to presume to ordain a bishop, ibid., 521. He is to be ordained by no fewer than three bishops, ibid., 432. When a bishop in another province ought to be ordained by neighboring bishops, ibid., 403. No layman is to be ordained bishop unless he has been tested through the grades of lower orders, ibid., 571, 578. When a bishop is to be taken from another Church, ibid., 579. The examination of bishops-elect was sometimes entrusted to other bishops before ordination, id., LXXVII, 874, 875; sometimes entrusted jointly to the subdeacon who managed ecclesiastical property and to a bishop, ibid., 1079. Laymen, whatever their merit, are to be excluded from the episcopate, ibid., 576, 577, 717, 784, 788, 812, 871, 1010. The ordination of a bishop, ibid., 1191. How many bishops must be present as witnesses at a bishop’s ordination, ibid. That ordination is lawful which has been examined by the vote of all, ibid., 543, note. Penalty for bishops ordained contrary to the canons, ibid., 1294, 1295. Penalties for those ordaining bishops contrary to the canons, ibid. Newly ordained bishops sent letters of communion to other bishops, ibid., 510, note. Formerly the anniversary of a bishop’s ordination was solemnly celebrated, ibid., 733, note. In Gregory’s time the bishops of Sicily and of other provinces of Italy were consecrated by the Roman pontiff, ibid., 443, note; 560, 576. Gregory forbids the ordination of a bishop for Salona without his consent, ibid., 678. Formerly bishops were customarily ordained by three bishops, id., LXXVIII, 495. The laying on of hands alone is the essential matter of the episcopate, ibid., 492. From what persons bishops are not to be ordained, id., LXXXIV, 36. Bishops are not to be ordained for payment, ibid., 38; nor through canvassing, ibid.; nor without the metropolitan, ibid.; nor by two bishops, ibid., 39. Bishops are to be ordained at the people’s request, ibid. On bishops ordained but not received by the people, ibid. On bishops’ ordination not being delayed, ibid., 40, 171. On ordaining bishops with the council of metropolitan and neighboring bishops, ibid., 130. Bishops ought not to be ordained in hamlets and villages, ibid., 134. What kind of men ought to be ordained bishops, ibid., 199. How they are consecrated, [Col. 0909] ibid., 200. When a bishop is ordained, three bishops are to ordain him with the metropolitan’s consent, ibid., 241, 251, 253, 257. On bishops to be ordained, ibid., 291, 372, 574. No layman is to be ordained bishop before a year has elapsed, ibid., 297. No one is to be ordained bishop unwillingly, ibid. On annulling an ordination performed in the metropolitan’s absence, ibid., 574. That no unworthy person become bishop, ibid., 637. That no one become bishop contrary to the order of the canons, ibid., 658. That no one ought to be ordained bishop against the wishes of the clergy or people, ibid., 689. That bishops ought not to be ordained from laymen while the clergy of the churches are disregarded, ibid. That those are not to be accounted bishops whom neither clergy elected, nor people sought, nor provincial bishops consecrated, ibid. Blameless men are to be ordained bishops, ibid., 771. On removing bishops who were unlawfully ordained, and on not having two bishops in one Church, ibid., 790. A king’s directive to the metropolitan that he ordain the designated bishop with his suffragans, id., LXXXVII, 901, 902. Decree of the clergy and people of the Church of Laon concerning the election of Bishop Hedenulf, addressed to Hincmar, metropolitan, and the bishops of the province, that they ordain him, ibid., 909. Letter of the clergy and of a vacant Church to the metropolitan, asking that he deign to consecrate as bishop the man elected by them, ibid., 912. Examination of Willebert of Châlons, to be ordained bishop, by Hincmar the metropolitan, with bishops of the province of Reims and other provinces present, ibid., 913. Profession of Adalbert, future bishop of Thérouanne, submitted to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, before ordination, ibid., 916. A second, general profession of a bishop-elect, ibid., 917. The letter of authorization of Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, sent through a representative to the ordination of Aeneas of Paris, ibid., 918. Document concerning the ordination of Electramnus, bishop of Rennes, ibid., 919. Canonical letters issued by the ordinators to Hedenulf, bishop of Laon, for the clergy and people of the Church of Laon, ibid. Election, consecration, and enthronement of Gauzbert, bishop of Cahors, ibid., 924. Election, consecration, and enthronement of Berellius, bishop of Rodez, ibid., 926. On the ordination of a bishop, XCIX, 1005, 1006, 1007.  
—How a bishop is ordained in the Roman Church, Alcuin, CI, 1236. On the ordination of bishops, CII, 1097, 1105. On the ordination of a suburban bishop by the supreme pontiff, CV, 59. Decree concerning the bishop-elect, to be read by the regional notary, ibid., 61. Summonses, ibid. Decretal read by the deacon to the designated bishop, ibid., 62. The bishop’s profession of faith, ibid., 64. The bishop’s pledge, ibid., 68. The bishop’s certificate, ibid., 72. The synodal document received by the bishop, ibid., 74.  
—On the ordination of archbishops and other bishops, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 67. How bishops ought to be ordained, ibid., 15, 68, 257, 281, 288, 333, 343, 377, 378, 379, 577, 578, 1123.  
—On the ordination of a bishop, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 378; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 68; CXXXVI, 358; CXXXVIII, 398. That no one ought to be ordained bishop against the wishes of clergy or people, CXXXVIII, 398. That ordinations ought not to be made by the judgment of a crowd, ibid., 399. That bishops being ordained receive letters from their ordinators, ibid. What sort of men, or how learned, bishops ought to be when ordained, ibid. How they are consecrated, ibid. That they recognize the canons before ordination, ibid. On not rashly making laymen bishops, ibid., 399. Ancient statutes are to be observed in a bishop’s ordination, ibid. No bishop is to be ordained apart from the metropolitan’s decision, ibid. That a bishop not be ordained in a diocese [Col. 0910] which has never had a bishop, except with the consent of the bishop to whom that diocese belongs, ibid. A successor may be ordained for a sick bishop, ibid., 400. On the ordination of patriarchs, ibid.  
—Those who are to be ordained bishops must first be examined, Burchard, CXL, 551. They must be tested with the utmost care before ordination, ibid., 552. No one ought to be ordained bishop except by agreement, ibid., 553. That bishops’ ordinations ought to be performed by all the bishops of the province under apostolic authority, ibid. A layman is not to be made bishop before the age of thirty or before a year has elapsed, ibid. That one ought to arrive at the episcopal office through the ecclesiastical grades, ibid., 554. That a bishop be ordained by no fewer than three, and, if possible, that an archbishop be ordained by all his suffragans, ibid., 556. On the deposition of one whom two bishops have presumed to ordain, ibid., 557. On not ordaining bishops in villages and small cities, ibid. On Wamba, king of the Gauls, who contrary to the canons created a bishopric in a small village, and how it was annulled, ibid., 558. On those bishops who are not received by those for whom they are ordained or designated, ibid., 560. On the rank of bishops: those ordained later must not dare to set themselves before those ordained earlier, ibid., 563.  
—A bishop’s ordination is to be celebrated on Sunday, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 59. Its ceremonies and prayers, ibid., 142.  
—Treatise on the ordination of bishops, Godfrey of Viterbo, CLVII, 281.  
—If a bishop is consecrated by one bishop alone, both the one ordained and the ordainer are to be deposed, St Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 179.  
—On the ordination of bishops, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 347 and following, 363, 365, 367, 369, 370, 371, 374, 375, 427, 452, 1133, 1134, 1135.  
—What is to be observed in a bishop’s ordination, Placidus, CLXIII, 686.  
—On bishops, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 600; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 430; CLXXVII, 401.  
—Only persons recommended by a proven life are to be chosen for the episcopate, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 320. No one is to be consecrated bishop unless canonically elected, ibid., 326. Bishops are to be consecrated by their metropolitan, and he by them, ibid., 344. If, while the others consent to bishops’ ordination, two or three object, the decision of the majority is to prevail, ibid., 343. Without the primate’s consent a metropolitan is not to ordain a bishop, ibid., 347. An archbishop is to be ordained by all his suffragans, ibid., 349. At what hour bishops’ ordinations ought to take place, ibid., 365. A bishop’s ordination is not to be delayed beyond three months, ibid., 366.

### On the Ordination of the Supreme Pontiff

—The rite for ordaining popes, St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 505.  
—On the ordination of the supreme pontiff, *Liber diurnus*, CV, 27 and following. Notice to the exarch concerning the death of the pontiff, ibid. Decree concerning the election of a pontiff, ibid., 28. Report of the election of a pontiff to the prince, ibid., 31. Rite for ordaining a pontiff, ibid., 38. Certificate of the pontiff, or papal profession, ibid., 39. Second profession of faith, ibid., 44. Third profession of faith after ordination, ibid., 54.  
—That two bishops must not presume to ordain a pontiff, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 335.  
—That the election and consecration of the Roman pontiff ought to be performed justly and canonically, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 327. That if a Roman pontiff has been intruded simoniacally and without the consent of the cardinals, he is to be excommunicated by them and even expelled from the see by human judgment, ibid., 352.  
—On the supreme pontiff, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 430; CLXXVII, 402.  
—The will of the prince is required in the pontiff’s ordination, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 129.

[Col. 0911]

## CVI. INDEX ON MARRIAGE, PRESENTING IN LOGICAL ORDER THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING THIS SACRAMENT

### Notice

Marriage considered in itself must be considered either insofar as it is an office of nature, or insofar as it is a sacrament—that is, insofar as that office has been sanctified by Christ. Insofar as it is a sacrament, it is customarily defined as: “A sacrament of the new law by which the union of Christ with the Church is signified, and grace is bestowed for sanctifying the lawful union of man and woman, for binding more closely the minds of spouses, and for training their offspring piously and holily in the duties of virtue and in the Christian faith.”

In this Index we discuss:

1. Marriage as a sacrament.
2. Its matter and form.
3. Its dignity, honorableness, and virtue.
4. Its unity and indissolubility.
5. Second marriages and polygamy.
6. Impediments to marriage.
7. Obligations of marriage.
8. Its benefits and disadvantages.
9. Books treating marriage.

### I. Whether It Is a Sacrament; Its Blessing

—The happiness of marriage, which the Church brings about and confirms, whose offering and sealing the angels announce, and which the Father ratifies, Tertullian, I, 1302. God the Creator blessed marriage, id., II, 281. The Apostle commands marriage “in the Lord,” id., I, 1290.  
—First marriages are solemnly celebrated under God’s blessing, St Ambrose, XVII, 225. Marriage ought to be sanctified by the priestly veil and blessing, id., XVI, 985. Marriage is blessed once only, id., XVII, 476. Marriage is not valid without devotion to God, ibid., 219.  
—Marriage was instituted and blessed by God, St Gaudentius, XX, 888.  
—The Lord came to a wedding in order that the sacrament of marriage might be manifested, St Augustine, XXXV, 1459. Neither separation nor adultery removes the sacrament of marriage, id., XLIV, 420, 424. The sacrament of marriage is great in Christ and the Church, but very small in husband and wife, ibid., 427. The handing over in marriage remained in the Synagogue and is now celebrated in the Church, so that God’s creature may be joined under God’s blessing, id., XXXV, 2379. God is the author of marriage, id., XLV, 1733.  
—The venerable sacrament of marriage, Salvian, LIII, 76.  
—The sacrament of marriage, Pope St Leo, LIV, 1204. Marriage was instituted by God as author, id., LV, 131.  
—Marriage, instituted by God, is sanctified by Christ’s presence, St Maximus of Turin, LVII, 274.  
—In marriage the holiness of the sacrament is of more value than fertility of the womb, Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 1042.  
—Matrimony derives from God’s institution, not from a polluted mingling, St Fulgentius, LXV, 314, 608, 704.  
—Marriage is a sacrament, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 549.  
—Marriages are blessed by a priest, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 808. Marriages are not to be contracted without a priest’s presence, Paulinus, XCIX, 298, 319; Hincmar, CXXV, 649.  
—Marriage was confirmed and instituted by God, Jonas, CVI, 167.  
—Marriage is a sacrament because it is a sign of a sacred reality, Radulf Ardens, CLV, 1743.  
—The sacrament of marriage is the union of a man and a woman, whom God the supreme Creator gave to Adam as a companion for the propagation of the human race, St Bruno of Segni, CLXIV, 164. On the reason why the Apostle calls marriage a great sacrament in Christ and the Church, ibid., 165.  
—The sixth sacrament is marriage, that is, the marital union, Otto, CLXXIII, 1359; Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 132.  
—A marriage without devotion to God is not valid, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1592, 1593. What marriage is, id., CXCII, 910. Marriage is one of the Church’s sacraments, bearing the image of Christ and the Church, ibid., 1586.  
—The nature of the sacrament of marriage is the union between lawful persons. Its matter is the consent of the parties, expressed in words of the present tense, Bandinus, CXCII, 1105.  
—Christ consecrated marriage at the wedding feast, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1289. Marriage was instituted by God, id., CCIV, 780, 781.  
—The sacrament of marriage was instituted by the Lord before sin, St Martin of León, CCVIII, 483. Marriage was established in the first human beings by God and praised and confirmed by Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, ibid., 490.

[Col. 0912]

**Matter and form.** Its matter is the consent of the parties, expressed in words of the present tense, Bandinus, CXCII, 1105, 1106.  
—According to some, there is no marriage before carnal intercourse, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 911.  
—The efficient cause of marriage is material consent expressed in words of the present tense, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 524; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 910.

### II. On Its Dignity, Honorableness, and Virtue

—How great is the dignity of marriage, in which spouses pray together in God’s Church, are together at God’s banquet, and so forth, Tertullian, I, 1302, 1303.  
—The dignity of marriage, Salvian, LIII, 132.  
—Especially in marriage shines forth the power which Christ leaves to the Church, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 952, 953.  
—The dignity and virtue of the sacrament of marriage, Alan of Lille, CCX, 193.

—Marcion abolished marriage, Tertullian, II, 247, regarding it as an evil and an affair of indecency, ibid., 282.  
—The marital union is not to be avoided as though it were a fault, but set aside as though it were a burden of necessity, St Ambrose, XVI, 259. Marriages are not to be condemned but approved, ibid., 273.  
—We approve marriages granted by God their author, Bachiarius, XX, 1033.  
—Honorable marriages do not displease God, Zacchaeus the Christian, XX, 1149.  
—We do not deny that marriage is honorable and the bed undefiled, St Jerome, XXII, 495. The Church does not condemn marriages but subjects them: whether you wish it or not, the husband is subject to virginity, ibid., 501. Heretics condemned marriage, id., XXIII, 269; they are refuted by many arguments, ibid., 270.  
—Although marriages can no longer exist without the evil of concupiscence, they are not for that reason evil, St Augustine, XLIV, 730. Marriage is not evil, ibid., 404; it is not sin, id., XL, 381. Marriages are good, id., XLIV, 725, 406, 758, 687, 418. The law of marriage is honorable and useful, id., XLV, 1459. Marriage by its nature and institution is not a cause of sin, id., XLIV, 460. Marriage is good; virginity is better, id., XLII, 494. The good of marriage is manifold, St Augustine, XL, 375. The good of marriage among Christians is threefold, ibid., 394. The goods of marriage, id., XLIV, 424. Which heretics condemn marriage, id., XXXII, 1344, 1372; XLII, 31, 30; XLV, 1462; St Leo the Great, LIV, 683.  
—That marriage is a good thing is proved from the fact that the Lord is read to have instituted it between the first parents, Gennadius of Marseilles, LVIII, 1037. Marriage is not forbidden, St Paulinus, LXI, 734.  
—Marriage is not sin but God’s gift, St Fulgentius, LXV, 320.  
—St Gregory the Great rebuts those who disparage marriage in most eloquent language, LXXV, 1125. Marital intercourse is not sin, id., LXXIX, 586.  
—Marriage is good because in it appears the image of the most holy union between Christ and the Church, Sonnatius, LXXX, 444.  
—The honorableness and goodness of marriage, Taio, LXXX, 857.  
—The goodness of marriage defended against Tatian, Marcion, and the other heretics, the Venerable Bede, XCIV, 68.  
—Lawful marriages are not to be condemned, Alcuin, CI, 1226.  
—Marriage is permitted to laypeople as a good, Aeneas, CXXI, 721.  
—Marriage ought not to be condemned, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 461.  
—Marriages are to be praised, not [Col. 0913] rejected, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 897, 270.  
—The threefold good of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 587.  
—Marriage is a good thing, and marital intercourse occurs without sin, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 155, 156.  
—That marriage is good is demonstrated by many arguments, Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1566.  
—That marriages are good, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 909.  
—Marriage is good and honorable, Martin of León, CCVIII, 483; approved in many passages of Scripture, ibid., 484.  
—The virtue of the sacrament of marriage, Alan of Lille, CCX, 193. “O how great is the power of this sacrament, by which one who might otherwise fall into the precipice of lust or incontinence is received into the honorableness of marriage,” ibid.

### III. On the Unity and Indissolubility of Marriage

—To marry while the first marriage remains is adultery, Tertullian, II, 442. Marriage, instituted by God, is one, id., I, 1277. Monogamy is not burdensome, id., II, 932. Its discipline is neither new nor foreign, but ancient and proper to Christians, ibid., 933. It is held in the highest honor among pagans, ibid., 928. It is recognized even among animals, ibid., 935. The monogamy of Adam and Eve continued to the end; Lamech was the first to violate it, ibid., 934. Second marriages undertaken for the sake of children are not expedient, id., I, 1282; they are not to be entered into, ibid., 915, 983.  
—There is room for repudiation between husband and wife upon established and proven grounds, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 354; but not on trivial grounds, ibid.  
—Marriage can be dissolved on account of one spouse’s fornication, St Hilary, IX, 940.  
—The divine law forbids dismissing one’s wife, St Ambrose, XV, 1766, 1767. The indissolubility of the marital union, id., XVI, 273. Marriage is a bond, ibid., 242. A husband may marry if he has put away a sinful wife, but not conversely a wife, id., XVII, 217, 218.  
—The chaste union of marriage is to be maintained by an indissoluble law, St Chromatius, XX, 351. Christ abolished the permission of a writ of divorce, ibid.  
—God joins one woman to one man, St Gaudentius, XX, 888.  
—Those who, after divorce intervenes, join themselves in other marriages are shown to be adulterers, St Innocent, XX, 500, 602.  
—Marriage cannot be dissolved because of sterility, St Augustine, XL, 385. A mutual vow of chastity does not dissolve marriage, id., XLIV, 420. The marriage covenant is not invalidated by the spouses’ separation, id., XL, 378. It is wicked for one departing by repudiation to marry another while her husband lives, ibid., 394. Continence by mutual consent does not dissolve marriage, id., XLIV, 422.  
—Whether a spouse who wishes to remain unmarried may depart without a cause of fornication, id., XL, 451. A spouse may not depart except for the cause of fornication, ibid., 452. The marital bond is dissolved by death, not by fornication or by separation of spouses, ibid., 473. A man unwilling to be reconciled to his adulterous wife cannot marry another, ibid., 476.  
—The indissoluble bond of marriage, Pope St Leo, LIV, 683, 1136; St Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 851, 1161, 1162; LXXVIII, 457.  
—The marriage bond is established by God, Sonnatius, LXXX, 444.  
—It has been decreed that, according to evangelical teaching, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband is to be joined to another, St Zacharias, LXXXIX, 934.  
—Husbands or wives who dismiss one another are not to marry, Benedict, XCVII, 758.  
—Marriages can be dissolved because of fornication, St Lupus, CXIX, 483.  
—Formerly there were more grounds for dismissing a wife, Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 252.  
—Marriage is bound by an indissoluble bond, St Prudentius of Troyes, CXV, 1434, 1435.  
—No one may presume to separate a marriage entered into under divine authority, Hincmar, CXXX, 652, 653, 654. The grounds for dissolving a marriage are more difficult than those for abrogating an episcopate, ibid., 642, 643.  
—On the indissolubility of marriage while the other spouse lives, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 319; Ratherius, CXXXVI, 191.  
—One who has dismissed his wife and married another is to be excommunicated, Jordanus, CXLII, 1398.  
—Marriage is not to be dissolved on grounds of religion, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 271.  
—The marriage bond remains between separated spouses, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 654.  
—Marriage is not dissolved by one spouse’s fornication, Anselm of Laon, CLXII, 1412.  
—Married persons cannot enter religious life without mutual consent, Rupert, CLXVII, 282, 283. Grounds upon which a wife may be dismissed, id., CLXVIII, 1414, 1415.  
—On the stability of marriage, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 166, 167.  
—The unity of marriage defended, Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 875.  
—Its indissolubility, ibid., 877; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1496.  
—The unity of marriage, Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 945. The dissolubility of marriages with unbelievers, ibid., 947. Separation can take place on account of a vow or fornication, ibid., 949, 950.  
—The indissoluble marriage bond on both sides, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1592, 1593; Martin [Col. 0914] of León, CCVIII, 487.  
—Divorce condemned by the pontiff, Innocent III, CCXIV, 884, 885.

### IV. On Second Marriages and Polygamy

—Second marriages undertaken for the sake of children are not expedient, Tertullian, I, 1282. “We know one marriage, as one God,” id., II, 931. Second marriages are less pleasing to God, id., I, 1287. A second marriage ought to be called nothing other than a kind of fornication, id., II, 924. Second marriages are not to be entered into, ibid., 915, 983.  
—A widow may enter a second marriage without the crime of adultery, St Hilary of Poitiers, IX, 446.  
—Second and further marriages are discouraged, St Zeno, XI, 379. Among the ancient Fathers, second and further marriages were poorly regarded, ibid., 129. Yet they did not regard them as intrinsically evil and unlawful, ibid., 131. They reproved them on account of immoderate lust, ibid., 132. How detested they were also among the pagans, ibid., 133.  
—Apostolic precepts do not condemn second marriages, St Ambrose, XVI, 238. Ambrose does not forbid second marriages, but does not approve of their frequent repetition, ibid., 254.  
—“Let my detractors open their ears and see that I have allowed second and third marriages in the Lord,” St Jerome, XXII, 497. “I do not condemn those twice married—indeed, not even those thrice married, or, if such a word may be used, eight-times married,” ibid., 499.  
—Some heretics condemned second marriages, St Augustine, XLI, 513; XLII, 657. The Cataphrygians condemned second marriages as fornications, id., XLII, 30.  
—Second marriages are not blameworthy, St Fulgentius, LXV, 693.  
—Second marriages are not sin, St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 808.  
—That a presbyter ought not to pray at the wedding of a bigamist, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 884.  
—We do not condemn second marriages; indeed, we receive them: Hincmar of Reims, CXXX, 649; Peter Damian, CXLV, 240, 241; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVI, 172; Hervaeus, CLXXXI, 1435; St Bernard, CLXXXIII, 1496; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1598, 1599, 1600.

—The common use of wives among some, St Jerome, XXII, 657, 658. The use of many wives and concubines among the patriarchs, ibid., 1054.  
—Formerly it was not forbidden to take several wives, St Augustine, XLI, 517. It was not sin in the time of the Old Testament, because it was neither contrary to nature, nor contrary to custom, nor contrary to command, id., XL, 395. It is not permitted to keep concubines, id., XXXIX, 1710.  
—He teaches that several wives are not to be had, Haymo, CXVII, 929.  
—God permits several wives in the Old Testament, Guibert, CLVI, 518.  
—Simultaneous polygamy is declared forbidden, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1147; Otto of Bamberg, CLXXIII, 1359; Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 131 and following.  
—Jacob took several wives in order to beget offspring for God’s worship and to multiply the people of one faith, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 119.

### V. On Impediments to Marriage

**The impediment of religion.**  
—Marriage with a pagan is forbidden, Tertullian, I, 1290.  
—Marriage with unbelievers is censured, St Zeno, XI, 134, 137, 306. “Why do you marry a profane person when you can marry a Christian?” ibid.  
—A Jew is forbidden to marry a Christian woman, and a Christian man a Jewish woman, Theodosius, XIII, 526.  
—Christians ought not to be joined in marriage with pagans, Jews, or heretics, St Ambrose, XIV, 451.  
—Cyprian maintains that it is unlawful to marry unbelievers, St Augustine, XL, 221, 469; St Fulgentius, LXVII, 959.  
—Daughters of Christians are not to be joined to pagans, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 412.  
—Marriages between Jews and Christians are forbidden, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 311.  
—Marriage ought to be between persons of the same religion, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1265 and following.  
—In the Law of Moses marriages were forbidden whenever there was a difference of religion between the contracting parties, St Bruno, CLXIV, 164, 165.  
—Difference of worship, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 934.

**Error.**  
—How error dissolves marriage, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 595, 596, 619; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 910.  
—The impediment of error concerning the person or qualities, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1434; Peter Lombard, CXCI, 916, 1371, 1375 and following.

### Condition

Women who join themselves to their own slaves are punished, Eusebius Pamphilus, VIII, 312.—If one spouse is of servile condition, the marriage must be dissolved, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 404.—Marriages of free persons with slave women not known to be such are null, Pippin, XCVI, 1507.—A union of slaves without their masters’ consent shall not be valid, Ahyto of Basel, CXV, 15.—On the impediment of servile condition, Burchard, CXL, 818.

### Vow

A bishop shall not bless a consecrated virgin for marital union, St. Sylvester, VIII, 885.—A virgin consecrated by profession cannot marry, St. Ambrose, XVI, 373.—Those who have made a vow of virginity, if they marry, are to be separated, St. Innocent I, XX, 478; St. Patrick, LIII, 825.—For those who have vowed continence, seeking marriage is blameworthy, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 704.—No one ought to marry a woman bound by the bond of a vow, Pippin, XCVI, 1506.—Those who have made a vow are to be excluded from marriage, Herard, CXXI, 773. Union with a nun is condemned, same author, CXXXVIII, 483.—Those consecrated to God may not enter into matrimonial rights, Burchard, CXL, 797, 801.—Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 707.—The marriage of one who has undertaken a vow is invalid, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 888; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1648.—Those who have solemnly professed chastity in the Church are to be barred from marriage, Hugh of Rouen, CXCII, 1291; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 932.

### Orders

Holy orders become an obstacle to marriage, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 1339.—Holy orders dissolve marriage, Stephen, CCXI, 571.

### Clandestinity

Secret unions—that is, those not previously declared before the Church—are evil, Tertullian, II, 987.—Clandestine marriages are forbidden, Pope St. Leo, LIV, 1205; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 298, 299, 319.—A wife must be taken publicly, not secretly, Hervaeus, CXXXII, 697; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 616, 1249; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1447.

### Consanguinity

Because of nearness of his own blood or that of his wife, no one may take a wife up to the seventh degree, St. Julius, VIII, 969.—It is not lawful to take one’s wife’s sister as wife, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1189.—Marriage between father and daughter is forbidden by natural law, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1185. Marriage in the fourth degree is forbidden by divine law, ibid., 1184.—Marriages with relatives are forbidden not by divine but by human law, St. Augustine, XLI, 459. Marriage between siblings was already unlawful in Abraham’s time, same author, XLII, 422.—Marriage in the fourth and third degrees of consanguinity is permitted to the English, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 101, 102, 388, 459. Marriage is forbidden in the second degree of consanguinity, same author, LXXVII, 1189. Within which degrees marriage may be contracted, ibid., 1188, 1189.—Marriages in the third degree of kinship are forbidden, St. Cummian, LXXXVII, 986.—Persons may marry in the fifth degree of consanguinity; in the fourth, if this has occurred, they are not to be separated; in the third, they are to be separated, Egbert, LXXXIX, 408.—The various degrees of consanguinity and affinity in which marriage is not to be contracted are enumerated, St. Boniface, LXXIX, 819.—Marriages are forbidden through the seventh degree of consanguinity, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 298; Herard, CXXI, 767.—Marriages are forbidden through the fourth generation, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1122.—That no one may take a wife from his own kindred, Burchard, CXL, 779, 783, 784.—Consanguinity ends at six degrees, Peter Damian, CXLV, 192, 193.—Marriages between blood relatives within the seventh generation are forbidden, John of Rouen, CXLVIII, 270.—The fourth and sixth degrees of consanguinity are forbidden, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 243. In Ireland marriages between relatives openly and with impunity took place, ibid., 174. Christian religion forbids marriages through the sixth degree of consanguinity, ibid., 559, 560.—No marriage exists between blood relatives and relatives by affinity, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1275, 1276.—Relatives cannot contract marriage until after the seventh degree, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 165, 510, 511.—Carnal kinship, St. Peter Lombard, CXCII, 937.

### Legal Kinship

There is no marriage between adopter and adopted person, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 975.

### Spiritual Kinship

It is not lawful for a son to marry the woman whom his father received from the sacred font of baptism, St. Zacharias, LXXXIX, 957.—There is no marriage between baptismal sponsors and those sponsored, nor in the direct line without limit, Pope Nicholas, CXIX, 979.—No one may contract marriage with a spiritual blood-relative, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 91. Spiritual relatives are not to be joined to one another, ibid., 164, 516, 517, 518.—On spiritual kinship, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 940; Innocent III, CCXIV, 360.

### Affinity

Marriage is forbidden in other degrees of affinity, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 457.—Marriages even between relatives by affinity are forbidden, Pippin, XCVI, 1508. Such marriage is forbidden in the second degree of affinity, 1513.—The degrees of spiritual affinity explained, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 89, 90; Benedict the Deacon, XCVII, 759.—The impediment of spiritual affinity dissolves marriage, Theodore, XCIX, 1060.—Union with spiritual relatives by affinity is forbidden, Herard, CXXI, 769; Burchard, CXL, 781.—Marriage with spiritual relatives by affinity is prohibited, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 1146, 1147; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1667; Bandinus, CXCII, 1109.—Marriage in the third degree of affinity is forbidden, Peter Cantor, CCV, 93.—Dispensation for contracting marriage in the third and second degrees of affinity, Innocent III, CCXIV, 1231.

### Existing Bond

No one may take another’s betrothed as wife, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1136.—It is not lawful to admit another’s betrothed to the rights of marriage, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 233; Halitgar, CV, 683.—The impediment of an existing bond, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1638, 1639.

### Violence

Whether a marriage contracted through violence is valid, Tertullian, II, 443.—In marriage the will must be free, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 682.—A woman must not take a husband against her will, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 353.—No one should be compelled unwillingly to contract marriage, Urban II, CLI, 67.

### Insanity

On the impediment of insanity, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 309.—Those who contracted marriage while sane are not to be separated because one has become insane or mad, Nicholas, CXIX, 1198.—If one spouse becomes insane, the marriage is not dissolved, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 619.

### Impotence

On a woman who cannot have intercourse with her husband, Benedict, XCVII, 757; or on an impotent husband, ibid., 760.—Spouses unable to render the conjugal debt may proceed to other marriages, Theodore, XCIX, 949.—A marriage must be dissolved if one spouse cannot render the marital due, St. Agobard, CIV, 308.—On the impediment of impotence, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 330; Burchard, CXL, 821, 822; St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 524, 566.—The sexually impotent must not enter marriage, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXV, 166.

### Crime

An adulterer cannot marry the adulteress after her husband’s death, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1281.—There can be no marriage with a woman with whom adultery is committed, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 165.—That no one may take as wife the woman with whom he has fornicated, Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1563.

### Consent of Parents

Children cannot properly and lawfully marry without parental consent, Tertullian, I, 1302.—It is not the modesty of a virgin to choose a husband; she ought to await her parents’ judgment, St. Ambrose, XIV, 453.—While parents are living, marriages between children under paternal authority are not lawfully contracted without their consent; yet unions already made are not dissolved, Marculf, LXXXVII, 785.—Marriage is not to be contracted without the parents’ knowledge, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 298, 299, 319.

### Abduction

On abductors and abducted persons, Fulgentius, LXVII, 957.—On those who abduct girls, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 906; CXXXVIII, 429.

### Time

No one may be joined to a wife before the octave of Easter, St. Ambrose, XVIII, 224.—Marriages are not to be celebrated in Lent, Pope St. Leo, LIV, 720; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 76, 170; Fulgentius, LXVII, 960; Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 210; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 290; Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46.—Times forbidden for marriage, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 612.

### Age

A suitable age is required for contracting marriage, Pope St. Leo, LIV, 131.—A girl of fourteen may have control over her own body; a youth of fifteen enjoys the same right, Egbert, LXXXIX, 408.—On marriage forbidden before the age of puberty, Charlemagne, XCVII, 216, 217; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 298.—A boy of fifteen has control over his own body, Theodore, XCIX, 935.—Boys under fourteen and girls under twelve cannot enter into marriage, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 166.

### Betrothal

No one may take as wife a woman betrothed to another, Pope St. Leo, LIV, 557.—On betrothed girls, Fulgentius, LXVII, 958.—On the obligation of betrothal, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 547, 548.—Betrothed girls cannot enter marriage with others, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 95.—Betrothal dissolves a subsequent marriage, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1412, 1462, 1466; Innocent III, CCXIV, 44.

Impediments to marriage enumerated, Zacharias, CLXXXVI, 132; Robert Pullus, CLXXXVI, 949 and following; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1434; Peter Lombard, CXCII, 916, 1371 and following, 929 and following; Bandinus, CXCII, 1107 and following.

Let those who conceal the various impediments to marriage be excommunicated, Odo of Sully, CCXII, 62.

## VI.—On the Obligations of Marriage

The duties of married persons explained, St. Paulinus, LXI, 604.—How spouses ought to conduct themselves before God, Egbert, LXXXIX, 419.

### Love

Let both spouses love one another, Victorinus, VIII, 1288, 1289. Let husband and wife be joined to each other in spirit and soul, ibid.—Excessive love for one’s wife is condemned, St. Jerome, XXIII, 281. A husband ought rather to love his wife by judgment than by affection, ibid.

### Chastity

Excess in marriage is immodest, [Col. 0917] Tertullian, II, 695.—In marriage chastity is to be maintained with the highest reverence, Lactantius, VI, 717.—Chastity is prescribed to one who has a wife, St. Jerome, XXII, 1097. The acts of marriage commend chastity, ibid., 522.—The chastity of marriage is especially to be commended, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 616.—Conjugal modesty and continence are God’s gift, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 314.—“Marriage is honourable and the bed undefiled”; those who transgress marital chastity are guilty of eternal punishments, St. Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 416.—Those wishing to find chaste wives should strive to approach them chastely and incorruptibly, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 170, 171, 172. Let husbands love their wives in chastity, ibid., 177.—Married persons should preserve chastity, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 649.—For marriage has its own chastity, Ralph, CLV, 1743.—Christ has introduced into marriage a norm of modesty and progress in holiness, Peter of Harvengt, CCIII, 748.

### The Conjugal Debt

On sacred fast-days married persons should abstain from their spouses, Pope Liberius, VIII, 1408.—Times have been prescribed for marriage and for begetting children, St. Ambrose, XV, 1550, 1551.—Wife and husband do not have authority over their own bodies, nor do they possess freedom with respect to chastity, St. Jerome, XXII, 1048, 1049. One who renders the conjugal debt cannot pray, ibid., 409.—What ought to be the intention of believers in the use of marriage, St. Augustine, CLIV, 416, 419.—When the use of marriage is a venial sin, same author, XXXII, 345, 1272; XL, 269. The procreation of children is the sole lawful reason for sexual union, ibid., 368. There is no marriage where effort is taken to prevent a wife from becoming a mother, same author, XXXII, 1373. Intercourse contrary to nature is more abominable with a wife than with a prostitute, same author, XL, 382. Use of a wife is to be made only for the sake of procreation, same author, XXVIII, 345. And unless it is done for the purpose of begetting children, it is sin, ibid., 88; XXXIX, 1541. In the use of one’s spouse: what is without fault, what with venial sin, and what with mortal sin, same author, XLIV, 423. The sin of spouses who hinder the generation of offspring, same author, XL, 423. Sins committed in rendering the conjugal debt, ibid., 304 and following. On the times in which married persons ought to be continent, same author, XCVI, 1303.—Married persons should abstain from sexual intercourse for several days in order to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist, Charlemagne, XCVII, 220, 221. That believers should abstain from intercourse with pregnant women, ibid., 775.—The act of marriage is not lawful on certain feast days, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 300, 301.—On the days in which married persons ought to be continent, Theodore, XCIX, 946, 966; Halitgar, CV, 685.—On the conjugal debt, Haymo, CXVII, 543, 544.—Use of one’s wife is forbidden for a time for the sake of prayer, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 189, 457.—The times of intercourse must be distinguished: when spouses should unite and when they should abstain, Gerard, CXLII, 1300.—The first night of marriage should be spent in prayers, Ralph, CLV, 1744.—Spouses should refrain from carnal intercourse on feast and procession days, and during conception and childbirth, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1247. Rendering the marital due is not a sin, but demanding it beyond the need of generation is a venial fault, ibid., [Col. 0918] 1248.—The rendering of the carnal due, Peter Lombard, CXCII, 922. When one must abstain from intercourse, ibid., 923.—Intercourse for pleasure alone, not for the procreation of offspring, is evil, Martin of León, CCVIII, 488.

### Union

That husband and wife may be joined to each other in spirit and soul, Victorinus, VIII, 1288, 1289.—Unions of minds are taught to be more religious than unions of bodies, St. Ambrose, XV, 1677, 1678.—There ought to be a holy union between husband and wife, St. Jerome, XXVI, 531.—Spouses ought to be one not only in flesh, but in spirit and mind, St. Prosper, LI, 772.—The holiness of marriage consists in one spirit and one faith, Rupert, CLXVIII, 1319.

### Fidelity

Fidelity is to be maintained between spouses, St. Ambrose, XVII, 216; Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 174 and following. Married persons ought mutually to give one another faithfulness, and even the service of accepting one another’s weakness, in order to avoid illicit intercourse, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 1248.

### Duties of a Wife toward Her Husband

A wife becomes the servant of a man, St. Jerome, XXII, 1053. A wife’s concern for her husband’s salvation, ibid., 1045, 1046.—A good wife both calls her husband lord and feels him to be so in her heart, St. Augustine, XXVIII, 225.—A wife must be subject to her husband, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 330.

### Common Duties

Married persons ought to exercise pastoral ministry in educating their children, Jonas of Orléans, CVI, 197, 198.—They should rise together at night to pray, St. Ambrose, XIV, 451.

# ELEVENTH SERIES

[Col. 0917]

## [PREFACE]

Since the Church is the pillar, foundation, and guardian of truth, and that fountain to which Christ entrusted the supreme authority of teaching, and since her authority is the only means suited to producing in Christian minds a firm and secure faith, she had to teach all believers what they should believe, what they should do, and what they should avoid, lest they stray from salvation. Accordingly, she took care that the primary and principal points of faith should be briefly gathered together, and thus established various creeds, which are a summary of the articles proposed for the belief of all. Therefore our Eleventh Series presents to the reader these creeds and the various professions of the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0919]

# CVII. INDEX CONCERNING CREEDS IN GENERAL AND EACH CREED IN PARTICULAR, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER, REPORTING OR INDICATING EVERYTHING WRITTEN ABOUT THEM BY THE HOLY FATHERS

## NOTICE

*Symbolum* in Greek is called in Latin both “token” (*indicium*) and “contribution” (*collatio*). It is a token because it indicates in whom we must believe—namely, in the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; it is called a contribution because many persons contribute to one whole. Among Catholics, *symbolum* denotes the rule of faith, that is, the summary of the articles of faith proposed for the belief of all. In this Index we establish two sections. The first treats of creeds in general and each particular creed—namely, the Apostles’, Nicene, Athanasian, and so forth—as well as the various professions of Catholic faith which the Church has either received or set forth. The latter presents separately each article of the Apostles’ Creed, reporting or indicating the various opinions of the Holy Fathers.

## SECTION I.—ON CREEDS

### I.—On the Creed in General

The creed is called *symbolum* in Greek, but *collatio* (“contribution”) in Latin, St. Ambrose, XVII, 1155.—Whence it is called *symbolum*, Rufinus, XXI, 337; St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 1058, 1072. Why it was instituted, ibid., 1065. The creed of faith is called a confession, same author, XL, 276. The creed is a rule of faith, same author, XXXII, 631; XXXVIII, 400, 1060; XL, 627. The creed is the foundation of the Catholic faith, same author, XL, 651.—The creed is a covenant of life, an ordinance of salvation, St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 361.—*Symbolum* in Greek may be called a token or sign, or a contribution, St. Martin of León, CCVIII, 1344.—On the name of the creed and what a creed is, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 126.

### II.—On the Apostles’ Creed

The holy apostles, coming together, made a compendium of faith, so that we might briefly comprehend the entire sequence of faith, St. Ambrose, XVII, 1155. In what manner there are twelve apostles and twelve propositions, ibid., 1158. Holy faith was conceived in the creed of the twelve apostles, who, like skilled craftsmen assembling together, forged by their counsel a key, ibid., 671.—As the apostles were about to depart, filled with the Holy Spirit, they compose the creed of faith: why they did so, Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 59, 337.—The creed of faith handed down by the apostles, St. Jerome, XXIII, 380. It is not written on paper and in ink, ibid. How it is concluded at the end, ibid.—The holy apostles handed down a definite rule of faith, which, comprehended in twelve propositions according to the apostolic number, they called the creed, St. Augustine, XL, 1189. The creed must be held in memory, same author, XXXVIII, 399. Why the creed of faith was instituted, ibid., 1065. What each apostle composed in it, same author, XXXIX, 2190. The words of the creed are the Lord’s heavenly mysteries, which preserve grace uncorrupted in us, ibid. The creed must be held in memory, same author, XXXVIII, 399, 1066.—The creed of faith has divine and human authority, St. Cassian, L, 149.—Some expositions of the Apostles’ Creed were domestic and private, others public and solemn, St. Nicetas, LII, 1010.—The creed was instituted by the apostles, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 466. It was marked with as many propositions as there were twelve apostles, ibid., 794. An antidote against every heresy, ibid., 757, 794. Its recitation in baptism, ibid., 1068.—The creed handed down by the apostles: why, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 433.—The creed of the Christian faith was ordained by the apostles, St. Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 823. What the creed is and why it was instituted, ibid. All articles of the creed enumerated, ibid., 826. The Apostles’ Creed had not one author but many, same author, LXXII, 350.—How the creed is constituted, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, XCVI, 126. The beginning of the creed and what belief is, ibid., 127. The creed of faith explained, ibid.; Leidrad of Lyon, XCIX, 859; Amalarius of Trier, ibid., 896.—The creed was composed by the apostles, Alanus, CI, 1138. How, ibid., 1139 and following.—What is the interpretation of *symbolum* according to the Latins, Theodulf of Orléans, CV, 226.—When and to what end the creed was composed by the apostles, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 368. Its complete explanation, same author, CX, 27; CXII, 1224.—The creed is to be impressed upon Christian believers, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 189, 190, 242; Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 562, 563. The creed, that is, the contribution of the apostles, as it is found in corrected psalters, ibid., 555.—The Apostles’ Creed and its explanation, St. Bruno of Würzburg, CXLII, 559. ## TWELFTH SERIES

[Col. 0927]

### [PREFACE.]

Religion, as we have already said, is, in the broader sense, nothing other than the fellowship between God and human beings; it embraces their mutual relations and consequently the rights of God and the duties of humankind. Moreover, a human being consists at once of body and soul and, under this twofold substance, is bound to render his whole self subject and devoted to God. Therefore, in order that religion might provide human beings with a means of rendering to God what is due through the body, it established outward signs, which are called **worship** (*cultus*).

Accordingly, in this Twelfth Series we treat of external worship and its various kinds: the worship of saints, relics, and images, and the benefits flowing from this veneration. Afterwards, since the liturgy is the rule of worship and the Calendar orders the times and days of festivals, we set out here, in two Indexes, everything concerning these matters contained in the *Patrology*.

[Col. 0927]

## CVIII. INDEX CONCERNING WORSHIP IN GENERAL, PRESENTING IN LOGICAL ORDER THE VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS CONCERNING ITS NECESSITY AND BENEFITS, ESPECIALLY FOR HUMAN SOCIETY, WHOSE SAVAGE AND DEPRAVED MORALS IT HAS SOFTENED AND REFORMED.

### NOTICE.

Under this designation is indicated humanity’s service toward God, or *latria*: that is, the commandment, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” This commandment, implanted by nature in human beings in relation to the divinity, just as this one is implanted in relation to one’s neighbour—“What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another”—is found even before the written Law among the ancient patriarchs, and thereafter among the nations, although most shamefully corrupted.

Therefore, this Index must state:

[Col. 0929]

1. What the worship of divine *latria* is, or wherein it consists, and what it was like under the unwritten law;

2. What it was like by the precept of the Old Law;

3. What it is now by the precept of the New Law, together with the worship of *dulia* and *hyperdulia* received in the Catholic Church, and concerning prayer for the dead;

4. The favours and persecutions, on the human side, that befell worship under each written Law;

5. The lack, excess, or abuse of worship—that is, heresy and schism, and paganism—and, in these final series, the evils, misfortunes, miseries, shameful acts, and so forth which will appear. By contrast, from the happiness, peace, and good morals noted in the other four series, it will become entirely clear to everyone how greatly the worship of the true God has always contributed to human prosperity, gladness, and the like.

In accordance with custom, this Index is arranged alphabetically by the Fathers, with an indication of volume and column, and with the question to be discussed in each series stated beforehand.

## FIRST SERIES. On worship under the unwritten law.

The one true divinity alone claims for itself the worship of *latria*, which consists especially in the disposition of the mind, the devout presentation of the body, and sacrifices, offerings, and gifts of every kind, practices customary even among the first patriarchs. For since all of us are his temple, and each individual one a temple, whenever the human heart is lifted up to God above, it has been his altar. We worship God manifestly when we adore him with the most fragrant incense and burn in his sight with devout and holy love; when we vow and render ourselves to him; when on solemnities and appointed days we consecrate an enduring remembrance of his benefits; when we sacrifice to him on the altar of the heart the offering of humility and praise with the fire of fervent charity; and when we acknowledge him as the fountain of our blessedness and the end of all our desire. Since these things existed and are found among the earliest inhabitants of the world, it follows that worship flourished among them; this is most clearly demonstrated by the materials indicated below.

Cain offered God gifts from the fruits of the earth because he was envious of his brother, XVII, 813. ## SECOND SERIES. What kind of worship was prescribed in the Old Law

This series treats of the Old Law, properly begun on Mount Sinai under Moses, leader of the Hebrews, and continued through the prophets until Christ’s coming. This law had ordinances of worship, as Saint Paul says in Hebrews 9, and an earthly sanctuary: a tabernacle, lampstands, a table, the bread of presentation, a veil, the Holy Place, the Holy of Holies, a golden censer, the ark of the covenant, Aaron’s rod, the mercy seat, cherubim, diverse washings, and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation. All these, like the elementary principles of God’s utterances, possessed only a shadow of good things to come, the way into the holy places not yet having been revealed. For Moses, like the other prophets and holy men chosen by God, was faithful only in all God’s house, as a servant, for a testimony to those things which were to be spoken. Therefore we must now discuss these shadows and all the furnishings of this house, even in their smallest details, especially those concerning the legal ordinances.

## THIRD SERIES. What worship is now prescribed by the new law; and concerning *dulia* (veneration) and *hyperdulia* (higher veneration), and prayer for the dead

Since Christ was deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses, as Paul says in Hebrews III, he who built the house has greater honour than the house; he is as a son in his own house, and we are that house. Through him the preceding commandment was set aside because of its weakness and uselessness; dead works and teachings concerning baptisms gave way to the new law. Christ, therefore, is the author of the new law.

In this paragraph we shall understand “worship” in its broadest sense within the Church, as when in French, in civil administration, one says: “Ministry of Catholic Worship” (*Ministère du Culte Catholique*). Worship therefore includes the doctrines of faith, sacraments, pious practices, ceremonies, persons, objects, places, churches, chants, hymns, and countless other things of this sort, which serve to preserve, spread, and defend this new law by means judged suitable for this work by the governors of the Church. Moreover, it will treat of the honour due to the saints and their relics, and likewise to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of their miracles; and finally, of prayers for the dead, piously offered to God from the most ancient tradition for their deliverance from the punishments of purgatory. This entire part of the index concerning worship belongs to the history of the Catholic Church and, together with the two following series, might properly be designated by that name and said to constitute Catholic tradition.

## SECTION FOUR

On the favors and persecutions that befall the worship prescribed in both Laws, on the part of men, especially rulers.

There have always been innumerable adherents and opponents of religious causes; each has always had his own judgment as to whether the matters proposed to him for belief stood well or ill. . . . . . The Spirit of God blows where it wills. . . . It is therefore no wonder that the Old Law, like the New now, had more vehement defenders and assailants. Each was believed and defended by holy men, just as each was denied, harassed, and attacked by false prophets, false brethren, and the powerful of this world. The question considered in this sequence now concerns these connected matters taken together.

Let the reader pardon a certain confusion presented here, since friends and enemies of worship are placed on an equal footing in our index. This will seem scarcely any inconvenience or stumbling-block to a man learned in sacred and ecclesiastical Scripture, who frequently observes in his daily study and constant reading the material of protection and persecution as indiscriminately interwoven with the Synagogue and the Church. This aim seemed to us especially natural, lest the ordering of the Index by divisions become too extensive and bring most troublesome weariness to the reader.

[Col. 0955] **ADAM OF SCOTLAND.**—The kings of England are called “Most Christian,” and concerning their reverence toward the Apostolic See, CXCVIII, 715, 722, 723.

**ADO (St.), of Vienne.**—Josiah, son of Amon, after casting the filth of idolatry out of the renewed Temple, celebrated a most solemn Passover to the Lord, CXXIII, 46. Nebuchadnezzar forbids the worship of the true God to be celebrated and carries part of the Temple vessels to Babylon, CXXIII, 46. Under Cyrus, the Jews, freed from captivity, began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord, CXXIII, 51. Cambyses, Cyrus’s son, having conquered Egypt, abhorred all its worship and overthrew its rites and temples, CXXIII, 31. Gaius Caesar scorned to worship in God’s Temple, and Caesar Augustus praised him for this deed, CXXIII, 75. Tiberius referred to the Roman Senate the proposal that Christ should be regarded as God; the Senate refused and decreed by edict that Christians should be driven from the city, CXXIII, 76. Caligula, most hostile to the Jews, ordered Jupiter and himself to be worshipped as gods in God’s Temple, CXXIII, 77. Nero, the first persecutor, attacked and sought to exterminate Christian worship, CXXIII, 78, 79. Domitian ordered that he be worshipped as God; he persecutes Christ’s worship and tries to overthrow the Church, CXXIII, 80, 81. Trajan persecutes Christian worship, CXXIII, 81. Lucius, king of the Britons, embraces Christ’s worship, CXXIII, 83. The Emperor Antoninus acknowledges in his letters that beneficial rain and victory had been granted, through Christian soldiers, because Christ had been invoked, CXXIII, 84. Decius issued deadly edicts against Christians, CXXIII, 87. A great pestilence spread through all provinces of the Roman Empire, in vengeance for violated worship of Christ, CXXIII, 87. Valerian fiercely harasses Christian worship and, on this account, dies most miserably and ignominiously as a slave among the Persians, CXXIII, 87, 88. Aurelian decrees persecution against Christians and, suddenly struck by lightning, is killed shortly afterward, CXXIII, 88. Constantine, an emperor transformed from a persecutor into a Christian, granted Christians leave freely to assemble in Christ’s honor and to build churches, CXXIII, 91. Arian impiety, supported by the Emperor Constantius, persecutes the defenders of Catholic worship, CXXIII, 92. Julian, made emperor after having been a cleric, turns to the worship of idols and tries by crafty devices to overthrow Christ’s worship, CXXIII, 93. King Clovis, victorious over the Alamanni through invocation of Christ’s name, embraces Christ’s worship, CXXIII, 102. Phocas the emperor ordered the shrine called the Pantheon, after removal of the filth of idolatry, to be dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and all martyrs, CXXIII, 112.

**AGOBARD (St.).**—Agobard suffers persecution from the Jews, CIV, 70. Charlemagne is called bishop of bishops, CIV, 197. Charlemagne brings the Saxons and other peoples to Christ’s worship, CIV, 103. Jewish ravings concerning Christ, CIV, 87. The Jews pretend that the worship of *latria* rendered to Christ was offered only under Pilate’s law, CIV, 88. The Jews assert that Christians worship idols and that the miracles they perform are wrought by the devil, CIV, 88. Constantine the Great is called universal bishop, CIV, 198. Constantine the Great’s devotion toward images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of others, CIV, 217. The bronze serpent, which the wandering Hebrew people worshipped, is destroyed by Hezekiah, CIV, 218. Administration of the Gallican Church divided between kings and bishops, CIV, 76. The wives and offspring of emperors and consuls are converted to Christ, CIV, 175. The Emperor Nero persecutes Christians, CIV, 177. Nero’s household servants and court officials are converted to Christ, CIV, 176. King Uzziah is struck with leprosy for contempt of the priests and usurpation of the sacred ministry, CIV, 135, 181. Uzzah, who presumed to support the ark of the Lord, is punished, CIV, 134, 181. Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, is converted to Christ, CIV, 124.

**AIMOIN.**—Clovis invokes Christ, the God of Clotilda, and promises that he will become a Christian if he gains victory; and he becomes victor over the Alemanni, CXXXIX, 653. Clovis declares that he yields himself to Christ and, by edict, deters his subjects from the worship of gods as useless, so that they may be converted to Christ, CXXXIX, 654. Although not yet initiated, Clovis becomes the apostle of his people, and many of the people are baptized, CXXXIX, 655. On the persecution of Catholics in Spain, CXXXIX, 718. On the conversion of the Angles or Britons, CXXXIX, 748. On Dagobert’s generosity toward churches, CXXXIX, 788.

**ALAN OF LILLE.**—The Albigensians and Waldensians revive ancient heresies, CCX, 305. The Waldensians are arrogant and disobedient to prelates, CCX, 389.

**ALCUIN.**—King Charles, pious and just, is defender of Catholic worship and of the Roman Church, C, 207. King Charles cleanses Christ’s churches of the doctrines of the faithless, C, 322. King Charles summons Alcuin to him to spread God’s worship, CI, 232, 233. King Charles is Catholic in faith,

[Col. 0956] a pontiff in preaching, a judge in equity, illustrious in conduct, and pre-eminent in every virtue, CI, 251. Willibrord won many thousands of Frisians for Christ, CI, 833.

**ALEXANDER III, pope.**—On the murder of Blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, CC, 37. On the great slaughter of Christians by pagans in the East, CC, 48. On the return of schismatics to the unity of the Church, CC, 54.

**AMBROSE (St.).**—The king of the Egyptians ordered the burdens of the Jews to be increased, so that they might not know God and devote themselves to His worship, XIV, 1144. Jeroboam’s hand withered when he poured libations to idols upon the holy altar of the true God, XVI, 217. Jeroboam, turning to the Lord, asked forgiveness, and immediately his hand, which had withered through sacrilege, was healed through religion, XVI, 217. What triumphs the faith of Theodosius won, XVI, 1389.

**ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN.**—Herod Antipas goes up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifice to God, CXXVII, 1036. Nero is the first to proscribe Christ’s worship, CXXVII, 1039. Simon Magus seeks to prove himself God by magical arts; supported as he flew by two demons, he fell to earth and, before the watching people, burst asunder, CXXVII, 1043.

**ANSELM OF HAVELBERG.**—That the Greeks, contrary to universal tradition, separate themselves from the rite of the Roman Church and sacrifice with leavened bread, CLXXXVIII, 1211, 1228.

**AUGUSTINE (St.), bishop of Hippo.**—The law of Theodosius against heretics and schismatics, XLIII, 48. Constantine and Licinius, the Caesars, favor Christian worship, XLIII, 784.

**AUGUSTINE (St.), apostle of the English.**—King Æthelbert, having become Christian, pursues idol worship at the instigation of St. Gregory the Great and endeavors everywhere to overthrow its temples, LXXX, 73.

**BALDWIN.**—On the splendid exploits of the crusading army, CCIX, 927.

**BEDE THE VENERABLE.**—The Philistines return the ark with reverence and offer sacrifices to God, XCI, 532. Saul offers a burnt offering and is rebuked by Samuel for his foolish act, XCI, 577. Saul seeks through a sorceress the oracle of Samuel raised up, and learns what adversities are to come upon himself and his people, XCI, 698. On Solomon’s Temple, XCI, 735. Ezra, hearing that the people of Israel had been defiled by foreign wives, assumes the garb of mourning and prays to the Lord for pardon of their guilt, XCI, 873, 875. Nehemiah cleanses the storehouses of vessels belonging to the Gentiles, XCI, 920. Nehemiah zealously ensures that the Sabbath rest is not violated by Gentile trade, XCI, 921. Nehemiah cleanses the Jews of foreign wives, establishes the orders of priests and Levites, and commends himself to God’s remembrance for good, XCI, 923. Because Constantine had spared their sons, mothers prayed to God for the salvation of the leprous Constantine, and the prayer of these women was heard, XCIV, 495. As Peter prayed, Simon Magus fell from on high to the ground and burst in the middle, XCIV, 497. The Emperor Nero, to avenge the death of Simon Magus, ordered Peter to be crucified and Paul beheaded, XCIV, 497. Lucius, king of the Britons, sent letters to the pope requesting to become Christian, XCV, 30. Diocletian persecutes Christian worship, XCV, 31. Germanus, by prayer, extinguished fires in houses, XCV, 92. What counsel Edwin took with his chief men concerning adoption of Christian worship, and how his priest profaned the sacred altars, XCV, 103, 104. How the province of the East Angles adopted Christ’s worship, XCV, 107. Edwin’s first successors betrayed Christian worship and the kingdom; King Oswald, however, restored both, XCV, 115.
