King Oswald raised the wood of the cross, worked miracles, and fought the barbarians, XCV, 117, 118. How the people of the Picts adopted Christ’s worship, XCV, 121. The king of the Kentish people ordered idols destroyed, XCV, 128. How the East Saxons, under King Sigeberht, received Christian worship which they had long since rejected, XCV, 151. The East Saxons, having returned to idolatry, were soon corrected from their error through Jaruman’s insistence, XCV, 170.

**BOETHIUS.**—The Emperor Justin, protecting Catholics, persecutes Arians, Manichees, and all other heretics, together with pagans, LXIV, 1487, 1488, 1489. Justin, when many calamities raged, prayed to God in sackcloth and ashes with all the people of Constantinople, LXIV, 1490.

**BRUNO (St.), of Asti.**—Constantine, the first of emperors publicly to profess Christian worship, granted the imperial insignia to St. Sylvester and his successors, CLXIV, 221.

**BRUNO (St.) THE CARTHUSIAN.**—The Apostle Paul was a great persecutor of Christians and later Christ’s greatest preacher, CLII, 284, 285.

[Col. 0957] **CHARLEMAGNE.**—Charlemagne, perpetual defender of Catholic worship and the Church, XCVIII, 152, 153. Charlemagne brings the conquered Saxons to Catholic worship, XCVIII, 388. Pippin, by the authority of Zacharias, Roman pontiff, king of the Franks, is called a new Moses, a new David, etc., XCVIII, 101, 102. Pippin, defender of sacred images, XCVIII, 194, 195. Pippin made a donation to Peter and his vicars for the reward of his soul, XCVIII, 163, 165, 214, 251, 285. The Sultan, tyrant of Egypt, was a most hostile enemy and destroyer of Catholic worship, XCVIII, 820, 821. Charlemagne gains the empire not by arms but by defense of the Holy See and Christian worship, XCVIII, 511, 512. Charlemagne was defender of Catholic worship and of the Roman Church before and after gaining the empire, XCVIII, 487, 488, 524, 529. Charles V, at his coronation, performs the office of deacon contrary to the custom of his forefathers, XCVIII, 684. The Normans despise baptism, XCVIII, 1408.

**CASSIODORUS.**—Constantine, knowing that the gods worshipped by Diocletian were of no benefit, and rejecting pagan worship, considered how he might worship the true God and have Him as helper against his enemies, LXIX, 888, 889. On the laws Constantine established for Catholic worship, the alteration of pagan rites, and the advancement of Christians, LXIX, 891. Under the Emperor Jovian, orthodox worship flourished and heretical worship was suppressed, LXIX, 1069, 1070. The emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian decreed that the worship promulgated at the Council of Nicaea alone was Catholic and was to be offered to God and Christ alone, LXIX, 1074. Julian removed Christ’s wonder-working image and placed his own statue there, LXIX, 2057. Pagans dragged down and smashed Christ’s statue, LXIX, 1058. Julian imposed a heavy fine on those unwilling to sacrifice to idols, LXIX, 1056, 1057. Through favor with Julian, pagans severely oppressed Christians, LXIX, 1057. Julian tried by various arts to incline soldiers toward idol worship, LXIX, 1050. Julian organized idol worship after the model of Christian worship, LXIX, 1048. How Julian favored Cyzicus because of its pagan worship, LXIX, 1047. Julian sought to wash away his Christian baptism by sacrifices and invocations which pagans call expiations, LXIX, 1032. How Julian armed the Jews against Christians, LXIX, 1058, 1059. Christian feast days, and Socrates’ opinion concerning them, LXIX, 1153, 1154. How Theodosius endeavored to destroy pagan worship in order to restore Catholic worship, LXIX, 1141, 1142. Which emperors, after Christianity had been preached, forbade or permitted idol worship, LXIX, 1149. On the laws Julian enacted against Christian worship, LXIX, 1040. Julian’s letter to Arsacius the high priest for establishing pagan worship, LXIX, 1048, 1049. The Emperor Valens granted pagans, Jews, and heretics power to observe their own festivals, and everywhere forbade this to the orthodox, LXIX, 1111, 1112.

**CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, emperor.**—Constantine, pretending to worship idols, expelled from his palace those ready to sacrifice, while retaining in the palace those who preferred to profess themselves Christians, VIII, 17. Constantine, considering the destruction of those who had worshipped idols, chose Christianity instead, VIII, 21. God showed Constantine, while praying, a vision—namely, a shining cross, with an inscription urging him to conquer by it, VIII, 22. The impiety and magical arts of Maxentius, his flight and destruction at the bridge of the Tiber, VIII, 25. Licinius dismissed from military service those unwilling to sacrifice and ordered that those imprisoned be fed, VIII, 33, 34. Constantine prepared for war by prayers to God, Licinius by divinations, VIII, 37. Wherever the sign of the cross was present in battles, victory was won, VIII, 38. Licinius’s magical arts and his flight, VIII, 39. Constantine, praying in the tent, gained victory, VIII, 40, 41, 42. Constantine’s law concerning piety toward God and Christian worship, VIII, 44. Constantine promoted Christians to govern provinces and forbade pagans to sacrifice, VIII, 44. On laws by which sacrifices were forbidden and churches ordered to be built, VIII, 44, 45. Comparison of Constantine’s piety with the impiety of persecutors, VIII, 47. The Empress Helena, journeying to Bethlehem to pray, built very many churches, VIII, 60, 61. Constantine built martyr-shrines at Constantinople and abolished all worship of idols, VIII, 62. On the destruction of pagan temples, VIII, 63, 64, 65, 66. Constantine endeavors to root out heresies, VIII, 67, 68. The subjugation of the Scythians, conquered through the sign of the cross, VIII, 71. Constantine’s letter to Sapor, king of the Persians, confessing God and Christ with the highest piety, VIII, 72.

[Col. 0958] How peace was granted to Christians through Constantine’s continual prayers, VIII, 73. On Constantine’s religious devotion in many acts, VIII, 73, 74, 75. How Constantine, setting out for war against Persia, prepared a tent in the form of a church, VIII, 86. How Constantine praised God after baptism, VIII, 88. Mass celebrated in the martyr-shrine of the Apostles at Constantine’s funeral, VIII, 91. Edict for religious liberty, VIII, 105. Constantine’s pious words concerning God and his diligent exhortation to worship Him, VIII, 259, 269. On Diocletian and Maximian, persecutors of the Church, VIII, 271. Constantine’s decree against heretics, VIII, 279, 281. Constantine’s enactments against Jews disturbing Christian worship, VIII, 384, 385. That the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied certainly concerning Jesus Christ and His worship, VIII, 449, 453, 457, 463. On the disastrous end of emperors who destroyed Christ’s worship, VIII, 469, 470, 471. Heads of churches are declared exempt from public obligations, VIII, 481. Money is granted to churches for the fitting celebration of worship, VIII, 481. Constantine’s letter on building and restoring churches and on worthily celebrating the worship of God and Christ, VIII, 491. Constantine’s letter on agreement in celebrating the feast of Easter and against the Jews, VIII, 501. Constantine’s letter to Sapor, king of the Persians, against images and on the glorification of God, asking him benevolently to embrace Christian worship, VIII, 545.

**CYPRIAN (St.).**—Daniel, devoted to God, would not worship Bel, III, 354, 667, 973. Cyprian serves God and Christ, III, 406, 1503. On Decius the tyrant and his hatred of Christians, III, 774. On Demetrian’s false accusations against Christians, III, 546.

**DAMASUS (St.), pope.**—The Emperor Constans orders altars and idols destroyed, XIII, 188. The Emperor Gratian permits free worship, but later withdraws that permission, XIII, 189. Theodosius the Great restrains the Apollinarians by laws, XIII, 257.

**DEXTER.**—Theodosius the Great restores Christ’s worship, especially in the eastern regions, XXXI, 507, 508. The Emperor Gratian zealously defends and spreads Christ’s worship, XXXI, 507, 508.

**ECKEHARD.**—Attila, terrified by God’s prompting, would not speak to Pope Leo except as Leo himself chose, CLIV, 745. When Attila was asked by his men why, contrary to his usual manner, he had shown such reverence to the Roman pontiff, he replied that he had seen another man, venerable for his gray hair, threatening him with death by a drawn sword unless he fulfilled all that the pope demanded, CLIV, 745. Valens, an Arian emperor, led the Visigoths into Arianism, CLIV, 739. Alaric, king of the Goths, after Rome had been taken, ravaged, and burned, ordered that anyone fleeing to holy places should suffer no harm, CLIV, 741.

**FLODOARD.**—Clovis, king of the Franks, embraces Christ’s worship, CXXXV, 51, 52. The Franks are converted to Catholic worship, CXXXV, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52. Persecution by the Vandals in Gaul, CXXXV, 36, 37, 40. The terrified Vandals flee from the city of Rheims, CXXXV, 40. On Christ’s triumphs in Italy, CXXXV, 854.

**FRECHULF.**—On Justin the philosopher and how greatly he labored in defense of Christianity, CVI, 1164. On Decius, persecutor of Christians, CVI, 1178. How Constantine suppressed emperors who persecuted Christ’s worship, CVI, 1193, 1199. At what time the peoples of Iberia and Armenia were converted to Christ’s worship, CVI, 1198. How Julian turned from Christianity to idolatry, CVI, 1210, 1211, 1212. On the evil deeds of the Emperor Valens against Catholics, CVI, 1217. On the Empress Justina, who, while ordering St. Ambrose to be carried into exile, herself underwent exile, CVI, 1223. Julian vowed the blood of Christians to his gods, openly declaring that he would persecute the churches if he gained victory, CVI, 1211. The Emperor Jovian favored Catholic worship as strongly as possible, CVI, 1213, 1214. How the Bessi desired to be killed for worship, CVI, 1218, 1219. On persecution of Catholics by the Vandal kings, CVI, 1252.

**GENNADIUS.**—Photius the patriarch refused to admit Basil the emperor, a murderer, to Holy Communion, LVIII, 1032.

**GERHOH.**—An exhortation that the duke of Saxony and Bavaria should defend the Church, following the example of holy kings and dukes, CXCIII, 604. Henry V usurps priestly prerogatives, CXCIV, 1465. Pope Paschal is taken captive by King Henry, CXCIV, 1466.

**DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF CAMBRAI.**—Because of a favorable outcome in battle, Clovis, king, compelled toward Christ’s worship, is led to St. Remigius for baptism, CXLIX, 28. The cruelty of pagans toward Christians, CXLIX, 26.

[Col. 0959] **GODFREY OF BOUILLON.**—On victories won over the Turks by the Christian army, CLV, 390. *Cartulary of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem*, CLV, 1105. Knights of the hospital are instituted to repel pagans and defend Christian worship, CLV, 1099, 1100.

**GODFREY OF VITERBO.**—Julian the Apostate is slain by a divine weapon, CXCVIII, 880. On Pope Boniface, who obtained from the Emperor Phocas the primacy of all churches, CXCVIII, 911. On the temple of the Pantheon granted to Pope Boniface for worship, CXCVIII, 912. On the younger Heraclius and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, CXCVIII, 913. On the Goths and Lombards, from whom Pippin freed the Roman Church, CXCVIII, 925. How Charlemagne was called into Italy to aid the Roman Church, CXCVIII, 929. On Charlemagne’s coronation, CXCVIII, 940. Charlemagne travels as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, CXCVIII, 943. Henry V makes Pope Paschal captive, CXVIII, 988; for this he is excommunicated, CXCVIII, 985. On Conrad’s journey overseas with an army of crusaders, CXCVIII, 989.

**GOFFRIDUS OF VENDÔME.**—The two swords in the Church, kingship and priesthood: neither ought to be blunted by the other, CLVII, 220. Henry, the German king, is sacrilegious toward Catholic worship and Pope Paschal, CLVII, 42, 45, 46.

**GOSCELIN OF CANTERBURY.**—On the great solemnity of the translation of St. Augustine, CLV, 18. Wulfric is punished for demolishing a church, CLV, 33. King Æthelbert is numbered among the saints, CLV, 42.

**GRATIAN.**—The Roman emperors, and especially Constantine, the first openly to embrace Christian worship, gave all subjects leave to pursue divine worship, build churches, etc., CLXXXVII, 889.

**GREGORY THE GREAT.**—The Roman Pantheon is converted into the church of St. Mary and All Martyrs, LXXVIII, 384. Christian emperors and kings desired to be crowned in church by the supreme pontiffs, LXXVII, 568.

**GREGORY (St.) OF TOURS.**—Clovis, king of the Franks, invokes Christ, conquers and subjugates the Alemanni, LXXI, 225. Queen Clotilda continually urged Christian worship upon the king, LXXI, 586. Chlothar, king of the Franks, purged the laws of paganism and destroyed the most ancient customs of the heathen, LXXI, 1163. Reccared, king of the Goths, embraces Christian worship and orders all Arian books burned, LXXI, 613. Nero, infamous for many crimes, is the first to undertake persecution against Christ’s worship, LXXI, 173. The Gauls, or Franks, followed pagan worship before Clovis embraced Catholic worship, LXXI, 18.

**WILLIAM OF TYRE.**—Chosroes, king of Persia, marries a wife for whose sake he favors and embraces Christian worship, CCI, 214. Chosroes, having taken Jerusalem, spares Christians and orders a church built, CCI, 215. The caliph utterly destroys the church of the Lord’s Resurrection, and why, CCI, 217. Saladin endeavors through a sorceress to enchant the Christian army, CCI, 912. How well Saladin treated Christians, CCI, 928. The count of Tripoli refuses to receive Christians, CCI, 928. The Saracens’ kindness toward Christians, CCI, 929. Saladin has the Temple washed with rosewater, CCI, 930. Saladin refuses to restore the holy cross, CCI, 943. Emperor Henry prepares a fleet for a holy expedition, CCI, 952. Many barons of France take the cross, CCI, 962; all are captured by Saladin, CCI, 965. St. Louis, king of the Franks, takes the cross, CCI, 1037, 1039.

**HAYMO.**—Gaius Caligula hates the Jews because they made neither altars, temples, nor images for him, CXVIII, 826. In his madness, Caligula wished to be called God, CXVIII, 826. Christ is rejected as God by the Senate, CXVIII, 826. Simon Magus is decreed to be God, CXVIII, 828.

**HERBERT.**—The king of the Franks offered wine and gold at the tomb of St. Thomas of Canterbury, for the perpetual annual celebration, in joy, of the martyr’s birthday, CXC, 1318. Henry, king of England, the unwilling author of St. Thomas’s murder, pursued by his son, invokes the aid of the same martyr against his enemies, CXC, 1315.

**JEROME (St.).**—King Nebuchadnezzar worshipped Daniel because of the greatness of the miracle—or rather worshipped the true God working miracles in Daniel’s person, XXV, 504, 505. Judah and Benjamin set up a statue of Baal in the Lord’s Temple and there worshipped idols and the Lord together, XXV, 1343. Judas Maccabaeus cleansed the Temple of images of idols, XXVII, 505, 506. Antiochus compels the Jews to idolatry and kills those unwilling, carries off the Temple vessels, etc., XXVII, 505, 506. Hadrian enrolls among the gods Antinous, who had died in Egypt, XXVII, 617, 618.

[Col. 0960] **HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.**—Domitian is the second emperor to attempt the destruction of Christian worship, CLIV, 28. Domitian builds the Pantheon in order to demonstrate his sacrilegious devotion toward the gods, CLIV, 28. Domitian orders himself to be called God and Lord, CLIV, 28. Geris, devoted to demon worship and wholly ignorant of the truth, is converted to Christian worship by the prayers of Blessed Sanctinus, CLIV, 31. Philip was the first of all emperors to be Christian, CLIV, 41. Valerian persecutes Christ’s worship and is suddenly punished, CLIV, 42. The Emperor Diocletian orders himself to be worshipped as a god, CLIV, 43. The Emperor Constantine gains victory through the banner of the holy cross shown to him from heaven, CLIV, 44. Helena, Constantine’s mother, finds Christ’s cross and gives it to peoples for worship, CLIV, 44, 45. Constantine, baptized and cured of leprosy by baptism, declares that there is no other God except the Trinity worshipped by Christians, CLIV, 48. Constantine declares that all the gods he had formerly worshipped were demons, made by human hands, CLIV, 48. Constantine grants the Roman Church imperial power and primacy over all God’s churches throughout the world, CLIV, 48, 49. Julian, a gentle persecutor of Christian worship, CLIV, 54. Valentinian embraces Arian worship and gives the churches to the Arians, CLIV, 55.

**HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.**—Domitian built the Temple of the Pantheon, now consecrated in honor of All Saints, CLXXVII, 248. Valerian, the eighth from Nero, ordered Christians to be driven to idolatry through tortures, CLXXVII, 251. Because of this persecution of Christians, Valerian was subjected to an unheard-of punishment by Sapor, king of Persia, CLXXVII, 251. Gallienus, acting more mildly toward Christians, made God favorable to himself and prospered, CLXXVII, 251. Under Diocletian, while Christian worship was spreading and increasing throughout the whole world, a severe persecution suddenly raged, and eighteen thousand martyrs suffered within Rome, CLXXVII, 253. Constantine the Great, leprous, could not be healed by the priests of the Capitol; he was baptized by St. Pope Sylvester and cured of leprosy, CLXXVII, 254, 255. Constantine the Great publicly ordered throughout the Roman Empire, by edict, that temples of idols should be closed and churches built, CLXXVII, 255. The Emperor Constantius, embracing Arian worship, proscribed Catholic worship, CLXXVII, 256. Julian the Apostate reopened the temples of the Gentiles and, by public edict, ordered soldiers either to sacrifice to idols or leave military service, CLXXVII, 256, 257. Justina the Arian persecutes St. Ambrose and incites the people against him; but the people preferred death to losing their bishop, CLXXVII, 258. Theodosius the Great gave the sign of the cross in battle and won victory, CLXXVII, 261. Theodosius the Great, by a law, ordered idol temples to be razed to the ground, and commanded all sacrifices, libations, and sacred fires to be extirpated root and branch, CLXXVII, 261. After a mortality at Byzantium, the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary began to be celebrated, and that mortality ceased, CLXXVII, 267. The Emperor Phocas decreed that the Roman See was head of all churches, CLXXVII, 269. Clovis, king of the Franks, invokes the Lord Jesus, whom his wife Clotilda worships, immediately gains victory, and is baptized with his people, CLXXVII, 277. Charlemagne avenges Pope Leo and is crowned by him at Rome, being invested with the imperial robe, CLXXVII, 282. The Roman people acclaim that Charles, crowned by Pope Leo, has been crowned emperor by God, CLXXVII, 282. Rollo is baptized, and thereafter the people of the Northmen embrace Christian worship, CLXXVII, The Theban Legion suffers for Catholic worship, CLXXVII, 252, 253.

**HUMBERT, cardinal.**—On the excommunication of Michael and his followers, CXLIII, 1001. What are the signs and miracles of Catholics, CXLIII, 1125. On holy kings’ zeal for divine worship, CXLIII, 1164.

**INNOCENT II, pope.**—On Abelard and Arnold of Brescia, condemned for anti-Catholic teaching, to be confined in monasteries and their books burned, CLXXIX, 515. The antipope Anacletus is excommunicated, and Louis the Younger is crowned king of the Franks by Innocent, CLXXIX, 675.

**INNOCENT III, pope.**—That sacrilegious persons and plunderers of Church goods should be restrained, CCXIV, 267. That the emperor of Constantinople should strongly resist the Saracens and compel the Greek Church to return to the Latin Church as to its mother, CCXIV, 325. On restraining the tyrant who miserably tortured Christians in Norway, CCXIV, 362, 363. That the king of Hungary should proscribe heretics, their goods having been confiscated, CCXIV, 871. The king of Bulgaria and Wallachia subjects his empire to the Roman Church, CCXIV, 287. That the king of England should restore the archbishop of Dublin to favor

[Col. 0961] and restore to him all that had been taken, under penalty of interdict wherever he might remain, CCXIV, 484. That the king of the Franks should restrain the insolence of Jews living in his kingdom and rise against heretics, CCXV, 501, 526. He rejoices at the return of the Church of Constantinople to obedience to the Apostolic See and, declaring void the election of a patriarch made by the clergy of Constantinople, elects that same man by apostolic authority, CCXV, 512. A sentence passed against the Templars is annulled, CCXV, 1425. The king of the Franks is induced to attack the Provençal heretics, CCXV, 1545. On Durand of Huesca and his brethren reconciled to the unity of the Church, CCXVI, 73, 74. On free power to make wills in favor of churches, CCXVI, 296, 302. On the Prussians newly converted to Christian worship, CCXVI, 315. That the count of Toulouse should expel heretics from his lands, CCXVI, 356. On the sentence pronounced against the count of Toulouse, CCXVI, 410, 411. On free preaching of the word in Prussia, CCXVI, 668–670. On the war against the Saracens in Spain, CCXVI, 699. That the king of Cyprus should desist from attacking Christians, CCXVI, 736. On the absolution of the king of England, CCXVI, 926. On relaxing the interdict of England, CCXVI, 955. That Grimald and his companions, who had taken the cross, should fulfill their vow, CCXVI, 962. The oath of Otto, king elected emperor of the Romans, CCXVI, 1082, 1169. That the priesthood, CCXVI, 1179. That all faithful Christians established in the kingdom of Saxony and Westphalia should manfully arm themselves for Christ’s worship, CCXVII, 54. That the king of England should attend to the relief of the Holy Land, CCXVII, 213. On various appearances of the cross while the legate preached the cross in the province of Cologne, and on the multitude of crusaders in that province, CCXVII, 238.

**ISIDORE MERCATOR.**—Arians oppress Catholics, CXXX, 650. Carloman, king of the Franks, restorer of Christ’s worship, CXXX, 1161, 1162. Charles, king of the Franks, recalled all Germany to Christ’s worship, CXXX, 1162. Constantine, emperor of the Romans, was the first powerfully to profess Christ’s worship, CXXX, 243. He raises the body of clergy of the city of Rome to senatorial rank, CXXX, 250. Constantine granted Pope Sylvester and his successors a golden diadem, CXXX, 250. Edict against the worship, Sabbaths, and feast days of the Jews, CXXX, 558, 559. On receiving the diadem, a prince must swear that he will not be a supporter of heretics, CXXX, 488. A Christian prince must root out every superstition and therefore not permit to live in his kingdom anyone who is not Catholic, CXXX, 488.

**IVO OF CHARTRES.**—Constantine the Great, upon becoming emperor, granted Christians power to build churches, CLXI, 201. In the last days, Israelites will be converted to the worship of Christians through the Church’s preaching, CLXI, 1011. Jews, pagans, and all heretics outside the Catholic Church are not saved, CLXI, 76. Catholics may seek defense from established authorities against heretics, CLXI, 1311. He who dies in defense of Christians receives the heavenly kingdom from God, CLXI, 1311. King Philip is crowned by the archbishop of Tours contrary to the pope’s interdict, CLXII, 83, 87. Pope Zacharias anoints Pippin king of France and is freed by his aid from Lombard oppression, CLXII, 614. Clovis, the first of the kings of the Franks, is baptized with his people by Blessed Remigius, CLXII, 611.

**JOHN II, pope.**—The Emperor Justinian is praised because he supports Catholic worship and pursues it with great piety, LXVI, 17. John asks Augustus to recall with all zeal those whom he knows to have strayed from Catholic worship, LXVI, 17.

**JOHN V, pope.**—The command of Augustus Justinian for confirming and establishing Catholic worship, LXVI, 20.

**JOHN VIII, pope.**—He congratulates Methodius on his observance of the orthodox faith, CXXVI, 928. He informs the Emperor Charles that he and Catholic worship are afflicted by the Saracens, requests aid from him, and sends him a palm branch with a blessing, CXXVI, 914, 929. He excommunicates all who engage in moneylending with Saracens, CXXVI, 930. He rebukes Prefect Pulcher because he neither broke the treaty made with pagans nor defended St. Peter’s dominion, CXXVI, 878. He absolves Athanasius, bishop of Naples, from excommunication, provided that he break the pact made with the Saracens, CXXVI, 946.

**JOHN IX, pope.**—On the Northmen recently converted to Christian worship, CXXXI, 28.

**JOHN, deacon.**—That Helena the mother carried to her son all things found in the Temple after its destruction, CXCIV, 1547. On the ark and the Holy of Holies, which are in the basilica of the Savior, CXCIV, 1547. Temple vessels and utensils transported to Rome and deposited in the Temple of Peace, CXCIV, 1548, 1549. On the church of St. Mary Major and its sanctuary, CXCIV, 1155.

[Col. 0962] **LANDULPH THE YOUNGER.**—Trial by fire in the presence of Pope Paschal against simony, CLXXIII, 1466. Emperor Henry took Pope Paschal and the curia captive and, on the following day, was solemnly crowned by him, CLXXIII, 1478.

**LOTHAIR, king.**—To avoid excommunication because of association with
Waldrada having made threats, he promises assistance against the Saracens, should it be needed, CXXI, 374.

LUCIFER OF CALARIS.—Constantius, as a promoter of Arian worship, is called Antichrist, XIII, 789. Constantius differed from Jehoshaphat, who restored the worship of the Lord in the kingdom of Judah, XIII, 846, 847; he persecutes Athanasius on account of his faith, XIII, 849, 850, 854, 860. George the Cappadocian, imposed by Constantius upon the Church of Alexandria, is killed by the Alexandrians in a sedition, XIII, 829, 830, 831.

LUCIUS, pope.—King Alfonso of Portugal makes his kingdom tributary to the Roman Church, CLXXIX, 844.

LUPUS (St.).—The Truce of God was sworn by the Northmen, CLV, 141. Raymond, by divine inspiration, and likewise other counts, making for themselves the sign of the cross upon cloth on their right shoulders, proceed to fight the pagans at the Lord’s Sepulchre, CLV, 142. When battle had been joined with the Turks, Christ granted victory to his own, CLV, 142.

MAXIMUS (St.) OF TURIN.—King Antiochus raged against the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother because they refused to violate the holy law by eating forbidden meats, LVII, 693, 694. The outstanding courage of women is celebrated: stronger than men who had grown faint, they overcame tortures for the worship of Christ, LVII, 714, 715. Through the Magi, all nations were called to the worship and recognition of the true God, LVII, 259, 260. The most unconquerable Maccabean brothers endured the most atrocious tortures in order to preserve the laws of their fathers, LVII, 288, 289.

ODO OF PARIS.—King Philip exempts Bishop Odo from the burdens of war, CCXII, 59, 60.

ORDERICUS VITALIS.—Clovis, king of the Franks, is converted to Christ, and with him his entire army and nearly all the people of the kingdom, CLXXXIII, 79. The opinion of the Roman Senate concerning Christ and his worship, CLXXXVIII, 110. The emperor Tiberius prevented any action being undertaken against the worship of Christ, CLXXXVIII, 110. Constitutions of Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory VII concerning investitures, CLXXXVIII, 516. Melaz [reading uncertain] becomes Christian and is joined in marriage to Roger, a Christian prince, CLXXXVIII, 782.

PASCHAL II, pope.—That King Philip and his concubine may be absolved from the bond of excommunication, CLXIII, 128. Supporters of investitures in England are excommunicated, CLXIII, 154. King Henry is to be regarded as Catholic if he renders to Pope Paschal and his successors the obedience which his predecessors, whether kings or emperors, rendered, CLXIII, 283.

PAULINUS (St.) OF NOLA.—Constantine’s care in venerating the bones of the apostles, LXI, 531. Constantine and other pious emperors enacted laws against pagans, LXI, 527.

PAUL OF CHARTRES.—Ebrard, viscount of the Chartrains, grants an estate to St. Peter of Chartres and to the monks serving there, CLV, 300. Landric, abbot of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, prays for those who support the monks by their donations, CLV, 302. Odo gives certain possessions to St. Peter of Chartres, CLV, 303.

PETER COMESTOR.—Concerning the stoning of Achor, CXCVIII, 1264. Gideon destroyed the altar of Baal and offered the bull as a burnt offering to the Lord upon the altar which he built upon the rock, CXXVIII, 1278. Gideon made an altar besides that which was at Shiloh; having become a priest, he offered victims upon it to the Lord, for which reason the Lord, offended, almost destroyed his entire house, CXCVIII, 1280. Saul consulted the Pythoness, who raised Samuel; he worshipped the Samuel thus raised and questioned him concerning his lot, CXCVIII, 1320, 1321. David danced and played the psaltery before the Ark of the Covenant, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, CXCVIII, 1330. After committing adultery and murder, David entreated the Lord, weeping and fasting for the health of the child who was dying; but when he had died, David became cheerful and neither wept nor worshipped the Lord in order that the child might live, CXCVIII, 1333, 1334. Concerning the priests of Baal whom Elijah killed, CXCVIII, 1479. Concerning Naboth’s vineyard, CXCVIII, 1383. Concerning Ahaz offering burnt offerings and peace offerings upon the new altar, CXCVIII, 1405, 1406. Concerning Hezekiah’s illness and the sun’s retreat, while he was praying, CXCVIII, 1411.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).—The piety of Emperor Constantine; his edict concerning the Roman pontiff, CXLV, 70, 71. Such was the piety of Constantine, newly converted to Christian worship, that he wished to confer all the imperial insignia upon the Roman pontiff, CXLV, 87, 88. Robert, [Col. 0963] king of the French, excommunicated, was abandoned by all his subjects and household, and was made so detestable that the only two servants who remained offered to the flames as loathsome fuel all the vessels from which the king ate or drank, CXVI, 580.

PETER, deacon.—Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, becomes a monk for the worship of God and the salvation of his soul, and in the monastery becomes a shepherd of sheep, CLXXIII, 1080.

RABANUS MAURUS.—The Israelites are taken captive and sold by their enemies; everywhere divine vengeance follows them because of idolatry, CVIII, 1123. While the Egyptians deservedly suffered for idolatry, the Hebrews received food from God, CVIII, 745. Antiochus erected an abominable idol, CIX, 1138. How Antiochus ordered the feast of Liber to be celebrated, CIX, 1123. Antiochus compelled Eleazar, advanced in age, to eat swine’s flesh, CIX, 1125. Josiah, renowned for piety, destroyed various images of the gentiles and abolished idolatry, CIX, 266, 267. Judith did not sin in doing obeisance to Holofernes, CIX, 567, 624. Judith, praying to God with tears, cuts off the head of Holofernes, who had been stupefied with wine, CIX, 572. Judith sings a song to God for the victory won, CIX, 581. The day of Judith’s victory over Holofernes is perpetually celebrated among the Jews among the number of holy days, CIX, 590, 634. King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded Holofernes to exterminate all the gods of the earth, so that he alone might be called god, CIX, 604. The mother of the Maccabees exhorts them to suffer for their law and for the worship of God, CIX, 1236, 1237. Whether Manoah wished to offer sacrifice to the angel or rather to God, CIX, 1191.

REGINO.—The king of the Persians and his wife, with all their retinue, embrace the worship of Christ, CXXXII, 34. Paul, successor of Pyrrhus, persecutes Christian worship, CXXXII, 34. King Dagobert, at the emperor’s instigation, commanded that all the Jews and Saracens of his kingdom should embrace the worship of Christ or be expelled from the kingdom: the reason why, CXXXII, 37. Nomenoe, king of the Bretons, dies, struck by St. Maurilio at the divine prompting because he was ravaging the churches of God, CXXXII, 82.

REINERUS.—The devotion of the people toward a small portion of the Lord’s Cross, CCIV, 107. Concerning holy wars against the Saracens, CCIV, 249. Concerning lamentation for Jerusalem captured by the unbelievers, CCIV, 350.

ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS.—King Robert was a most zealous defender of the Catholic faith, CXLI, 898. King Robert absolves three men condemned to death for conspiracy against him, because they received the sacrament of the Eucharist, CXLI, 898.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ.—Darius built the house of God which Cyrus had decreed should be built, CLXIX, 1378. The contest between Jews and Samaritans, CLXIX, 358, 359. The zeal of Phinehas and Elijah, CLXIX, 881.

SICARDUS OF CREMONA.—The Jews chose death rather than profane the laws of their fathers, CCXIII, 449. Concerning a feast in honour of Octavian, CCXIII, 445. When that feast had been suppressed, the feast of Blessed Peter in Chains succeeded it, CCXIII, 446. Domitian ordered himself to be worshipped as a god, and golden and silver statues of himself to be erected on the Capitol, CCXIII, 458. Pliny, procurator of a certain province, wrote to Trajan that he found nothing evil in Christians except their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice, CCXIII, 459. The impiety of the count of Toulouse toward God and the Church, CCXIII, 551. The count of Toulouse deceitfully assumes the cross, the badge of holy warfare, CCXIII, 564, 565. Sacrileges violently perpetrated by the count of Foix, CCXIII, 602, 603.

STEPHEN OF TOURNAY.—The count of Flanders is excommunicated, CCXI, 503, 504. The whole land of the count of Flanders is placed under interdict, CCXI, 501. Jews rarely embrace and observe the worship of God, CCXI, 333.

TERTULLIAN, presbyter.—The worship of Christ is built up when it is afflicted, I, 704. No one is ashamed of or regrets having embraced the worship of Christ; all rejoice and glory in it, I, 269. Why the festivals of the Caesars were not observed by Christians, I, 452. To moderate or remove calamities, Christians entreated God day and night, I, 486. Christians believed that emperors were chosen by God, I, 448, 470. The kingdom of the Jews flourished so long as they obeyed the divine commandments, I, 393.

URBAN II, pope.—In a dangerous time the Church rejoiced at the conversion of many, while it did not cease to grieve at the falling away of the excommunicated, CLI, 88. The liberty of the clergy of Flanders vindicated, CLI, 92. Christians prevail in Spain, CLI, 116. King Philip is excommunicated, CLI, 141. Holy expeditions, CLI, 141. Concerning the redemption of altars; disturbances arise on that occasion, CLI, 171, 174. King Philip is absolved, CLI, 228. Urban resides at Rome while the antipope Guibert flees, CLI, 232. King Philip is again placed under interdict, CLI, 246. Constitutions of the emperors of Germany [Col. 0964] and kings of the Franks concerning ecclesiastical affairs, CLI, 1021, 1164. Laws of the kings of England concerning ecclesiastical affairs, CLI, 1165.

WALAFRID STRABO.—The Egyptians persecuted Israelite worship; the Romans persecuted Christian worship, CXIII, 213. Ahaz, who shut the doors of the Temple, worshipped the Baals, and consecrated his son to an idol, was justly abandoned by the Lord and handed over to his enemies, CXIII, 1245. When Cyrus and Darius devastated Babylon, its idols too were broken, and the temple of Bel was overthrown and burned with fire, CXIII, 1263.

VALERIAN (St.).—The mother of the Maccabees is praised, and their struggle for divine worship is described, LII, 746, 747. That mother proves that she loves her children who has delivered the fruit of her womb as an offering to God, and has willingly offered herself and her own, intending daily to sacrifice them to the Lord, LII, 749.

VICTOR OF VITA.—The confession of faith offered by the Catholic bishops to King Huneric, LVIII, 219.—Huneric’s cruelty toward the Catholic bishops, LVIII, 233. The edict of King Huneric against Christians, LVIII, 235. A general persecution against all Catholics, LVIII, 241.

WILLIAM CALCULUS.—Rollo yielded, not to the Burgundians, but to divine power, which was present in the tunic of the holy Mother of God, CXLIX, 1559. King Charles gave Rollo his daughter in marriage, together with the coastal land and Brittany, on the condition that Rollo himself should embrace Christian worship, CXLIX, 800. Rollo is baptized with his entire army, CXLIX, 801. Rollo builds churches that had been destroyed and restores Catholic worship, CXLIX, 801.—Duke William restores the monastery of Jumièges and the Christian worship formerly destroyed there by pagans, CXLIX, 807. Concerning the conversion of pagans brought about at the exhortation of Duke Richard, CXLIX, 820. Duke Richard built a church in honour of the Holy Trinity, adorned it with various ornaments, and restored very many abbeys, CXLIX, 821. How devoutly the pious Empress Matilda, while ill, distributed her treasures among various churches and the poor, CXLIX, 896. Concerning the churches which pious Matilda built, and the other pious acts for propagating Catholic worship which King Henry performed, CXLIX, 900.

WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY.—Alfred the Great defeats the Danes in battle and compels the survivors either to embrace Christian worship or to withdraw from the kingdom, CLXXXIX, 1078. King Æthelberht embraces Christian worship and establishes many laws for the propagation of Christianity, CLXXIX, 968, 969. Erconberht destroys all the shrines of the gods, so that no trace of sacrilege may remain for posterity, CLXXIX, 970. Erconberht orders the solemn fast of forty days to be observed throughout the kingdom, CLXXIX, 970. The conversion of the English to Christian worship during the reign of King Ælla, CLXXIX, 1000. Theobald, count of Blois, is declared by the supreme pontiff, upon the denunciation of Louis VI, to be a rebel against God, CLXXIX, 1361. An image of the crucified Christ is said to have spoken, CLXXIX, 1129, 1130. The origin of the holy war for liberating the Holy Land, CLXXIX, 1293. The universal ardour of Christian lands when that war is proclaimed by the supreme pontiff, CLXXIX, 1290. Christians observe a fast of three days, chant litanies, and send Peter the Hermit in order to obtain peace, CLXXIX, 1315. The Turks are put to flight while martyrs fight for the Christian army, CLXXIX, 1316. The disputes of Pope Paschal with Henry V concerning sacred investitures, CLXXIX, 1371. Their reconciliation by oath and Henry’s coronation, and through the Eucharist administered to Henry by Paschal, CLXXIX, 1376, 1377. King Edwin, converted to Catholic worship, CLXXIX, 1003, 1004. King Sæberht becomes a Christian, CLXXIX, 1049. Constantine brings the bodies of saints from Rome to Constantinople, CLXXIX, 1308. Concerning the excommunication of King Philip of the Franks and his followers, CLXXIX, 1295.

### FIFTH SERIES

On the deficiency, excess, and abuse of worship; or on heresy, schism, and paganism, and on their misfortunes, miseries, and evils; and, conversely, on the good morals and public prosperity always and everywhere found in the worship of the true God.

We shall cite only the argument of St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, addressed to Demetrianus, in order briefly to establish the foregoing propositions in summary. For St. Cyprian said to Demetrianus: “It is not, as your false complaint and your ignorance, unaware of the truth, boasts and cries, that barrenness and famine increase anxiety, diseases rage, health is broken down [Col. 0965], and the human race is devastated by the ravages of pestilence, because your gods are not worshipped by us; but because God is not worshipped by you. For since He Himself is Lord and ruler of the world, and all things are governed by His will and nod, and nothing can happen except what He has either done or Himself permitted to be done, surely, when those things occur which reveal the wrath of an angered God, they do not occur on account of us, by whom God is worshipped; rather, they are inflicted because of your offences and deserts, by whom God is not sought at all, nor feared; nor, after vain superstitions have been abandoned, is true religion recognized, so that the one God, who is one for all, may be worshipped and entreated by all.”

ADO (St.) of Vienne.—Nimrod the giant taught the Persians to worship fire, and thereafter certain rulers of nations were worshipped as gods, CXXII, 28. The Egyptians worshipped Isis, CXXIII, 33. Serapis, son of Jupiter, is enrolled among the gods, CXXIII, 35. Cecrops, sacrificing an ox, first commanded Jupiter to be worshipped in sacrifice, CXXIII, 35. Mercury, grandson of Atlas, is enrolled among the gods, CXXIII, 35. Numa Pompilius first established the Vestal Virgins, CXXIII, 45. The Senonian and Viennese Gauls established a temple of Mars and Victory, CXXIII, 52. Domitian ordered himself to be worshipped as God, CXXIII, 80.

AGOBARD (St.).—On the bronze serpent which the wandering people worshipped, CIV, 218. For a long age the Romans worshipped gods without images; those who first made images set them up in order to remove fear from the peoples and add error, CIV, 219. Paul and Barnabas refuse sacrifices of victims offered to themselves, CIV, 203. The Rising Sun (Sol oriens) is worshipped, CVI, 221.

ALAN OF LILLE.—The Albigensians and Waldensians revived ancient heresies, CCX, 305. The worship of Bacchus is described, CCX, 462.—Certain forms of idolatry, CCX, 203. What poets wrote about the gods of the nations are fictions, CCX, 451–452.

ALCUIN.—The Chaldeans regarded fire as God and worshipped it, C, 534. Terah, with his sons, was cast into the fire by the Chaldeans because he refused to worship fire, C, 534.

AMBROSE (St.) of Milan.—The Arians deny to Christ the worship due to the living God, yet will not deny it to Antichrist, XV, 1809. Dionysius the tyrant mocked Jupiter in his temple, and Aesculapius and the other gods holding golden bowls; he stripped them, so that neither Jupiter could defend his garment, nor Aesculapius his beard, nor could all those called gods withdraw the bowls they held, XVI, 217. Jeroboam’s hand withered when he poured libations to idols upon the holy altar of the living God, XVI, 217. The idols worshipped by Jeroboam could not heal him, XVI, 217. The Gentiles worship precious and grand things and adore images, XVI, 972. In pagan worship their eyes are veiled, lest, seeing what they call sacred rites, they perceive themselves mocked by manifold varieties, XVII, 257.

ARNOBIUS.—The Arabs worship a stone as God, V, 1185. Arnobius, while remaining a pagan, worshipped stones, V, 767–768. Attalus, king of Phrygia, sent to Rome a stone which was received as the Great Mother, V, 1284. According to the pagans, this stone drove the mighty enemy Hannibal from Italy, V, 1284. The stone gave strength to some and weakness to others, V, 1284. The charge of atheism is turned back against the pagans, V, 720. Gods are not appeased by gold, V, 1167. The Bacchanalia: monstrous sacred rites, V, 1118–1119. On the mysteries or initiations of certain gods, and especially of Fauna or Fatua, called the goddess Boica, which no one can explain without defilement, V, 1122. On Jupiter’s sacred initiations, V, 1122. The intercourse of the gods and their shamefulness, V, 1115–1116. Foul pagan mysteries, V, 1122. The ridiculous divinities of the Gentiles, V, 1185. Sacrifices by which pagans thought to appease the souls of their fathers, V, 1288. The Romans often altered their ancient rites, V, 914. The Romans worshipped a spear as Mars, IV, 1186. Pagans pour out incense and wine to the gods, V, 1164. Temples were built by nations for gods so that they might address their gods at close hand, V, 1169. The sun is worshipped as a god by pagans, V, 754. The moon is worshipped as a goddess by pagans, V, 754.

AUGUSTINE (St.), Bishop of Hippo.—The Manichaeans worshipped the sun, XXXII, 1351; XXXIV, 199, 216. Manichaean hearers, together with the elect, worship and pray to the sun and moon, and fast on the Lord’s Day, XXXIII, 1032. Pagans become worse by imitating their gods, XXXIII, 414. Pagans do not excuse their sacrilegious rites and images by elegantly interpreting what each signifies, XXXIII, 378. Pagans are not blameworthy because of sacrifices, but because they offer them to idols, XXXIII, 377. The rites of Liber are disgraceful and full of frenzy, XXXV, 2344. Worshippers of the moon, XXXV, 2278. The goddess Caelestis was held in the highest honor among Africans and Carthaginians, XXXV, 752; XXXVII, 1270. Pagans worship the sun, XXXVI, 189. The sun is worshipped by pagans and Manichaeans, XXXVI, 189. The Manichaeans said that the sun is Christ, XXXVII, 36, 105. The kind of worship pagans render to demons, XXXVII, 1220. Servitude to demons is more dangerous than servitude to idols, XXXVII, 1245. In Neptune’s image [Col. 0966] the Gentiles worshipped the sea, XXXVII, 1487. In pagan temples nothing is worshipped but evil spirits, XXXVII, 1245. Temples of gods under imperial laws, XXXVII, 1788. To consult astrologers, haruspices, or sorcerers is to commit fornication with demons, XXXVII, 76. Pagans regard dead human beings as gods, XXXVII, 1249. The harmony of pagan litigants in the worship of gods, XI, 712. Pagan sacrifices are not to be judged good because God did not prevent them from being performed, XI, 583. Superstitious observances concerning the moon, XL, 1172. The Romans celebrated annual rites for the goose, XLI, 70. The Bacchanalia: sacred rites instituted for Father Liber, XLI, 571. The disgraceful rites of the goddess Caelestis, XLI, 75. Codrus was regarded as a god by the Athenians, XLI, 576. Demons pursue their own business, namely, that they may be regarded and worshipped as gods, XLI, 72. The worship of demons was introduced by leaders of cities, XLI, 139. How many absurdities and contradictions there are in worshipping and invoking demons, XLI, 288. Demons must not be worshipped, neither because of what is now in them nor even if they possessed virtue and wisdom, XLI, 241. Mucius Scaevola, a pontiff, was killed at the altar of Vesta, XLI, 108–109. Pagan games and sacred rites are most shameful and cruel, XLI, 50, 52. Plato and his disciples thought sacred rites should be performed for very many gods, XLI, 237. Porphyry is to be blamed for having sacrificed to gods, XLI, 651. The Romans preferred Romulus to many gods and themselves instituted a Flamen for him, XLI, 60, 757–758. The earth is called and worshipped as the mother of the gods, XLI, 120. Christians did not convert the sacrifices of the nations into love-feasts, XLII, 383. Arians refuse to worship the Son of God as true God, XLII, 930. Manichaeans are worse than pagans in worshipping many gods, XLII, 369, 374. Why a demon demands sacrifices for itself, XLII, 624. Why the Manichaeans worship the sun and moon, XLII, 369.

BEDE THE VENERABLE.—In the Capitol were images of gods with little bells on their necks, to warn what nation had rebelled against the Romans, XC, 961. The madness and folly of human beings is rebuked for rendering the worship of latria due to God alone to lowly animals—ram, dog, and bull—by worshipping Jupiter, Ammon, Apis, and the rest, XCIII, 369. On the calf burned by fire, and on the three thousand men slain because worship had been rendered to the calf, XCIII, 377. Augustine, bishop of the English, is instructed what he is to do concerning shrines, solemnities, and idol sacrifices among the English, XCV, 70–71. The East Saxons reverted to idolatry during a time of plague, but were soon corrected from their error, XCV, 170.

BRUNO (St.) OF ASTI.—Aaron set up a golden calf, to which the mad people sacrificed, making themselves rebels against the true God, CLXIV, 366. The sacrilegious worshippers of the golden calf, about twenty-three thousand, were struck with the sword and destroyed by those who had not worshipped the idol, CLXIV, 369. The Israelites worshipped Beelphegor; and, by the Lord’s command, each man killed his brother or son initiated into this worship, CLXIV, 496. Gentile philosophers erred in all matters pertaining to the worship of God, CLXIV, 733. Before Christ, not only Gentiles but sometimes Jews worshipped idols and adored demons, CLXIV, 732. The Jews will receive Antichrist and worship him for a time as though he were God, CLXV, 492.

BRUNO (St.) THE CARTHUSIAN.—Obstinate heretics must be excommunicated, CLII, 1417–1418. To proceed against heretics is more dangerous than to proceed against blasphemers, CLII, 1315–1316. The worship of idols must be avoided, CLIII, 175. To observe the Law now is almost to worship idols, CLIII, 302–303.

BRUNO (St.) OF WÜRZBURG.—The malice of Antichrist, CXLII, 208–209. At the end of the world the nations will cleave to Antichrist, the Jews to Christ, CXLII, 227. Heretics and Jews reject Christ, CXLII, 235. The prayer of heretics is turned into sin, CXLII, 402.

CASSIODORUS.—Hercules, twice a murderer, obtained purification in the rites of Ceres, LXIX, 890. Arian worship rises against Catholic worship even unto killing, LXIX, 1171. Cleomedes the athlete is deified by pagans, LXIX, 1067. Pagans deify not persons formed in good morals, nor the just or chaste, but rather the lustful, unjust, and drunken, LXIX, 1066. Arian worship, the fruit of unbelief, was overthrown at Nicaea, LXIX, 1068–1069. The festival of Daphnis was celebrated for seven days, LXIX, 1072. Pagans dragged away and shattered a statue of Christ, LXIX, 1057–1058. Pagans, owing to Julian’s favor, grievously oppressed Christians, LXIX, 1059. Julian attempted by various devices to incline soldiers to idol worship, LXIX, 1050. Julian arranged pagan worship in imitation of Christian worship, LXIX, 1048.

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT.—Shrines and images everywhere destroyed, VIII, 63. The destruction of the shrine at Aphaca in Phoenicia and the suppression of immorality, VIII, 64. The destruction of the temple of Aesculapius, VIII, 65.

CYPRIAN (St.).—It is forbidden for Christians to attend the shameful Gentile [Col. 0967] banquets of a guild, III, 1030. All heretics and schismatics, without exception, are adversaries of Christ; all are Antichrists, worse than pagans, IV, 1138. Idols are not gods, IV, 654. Idols which Gentiles think to be gods, IV, 764. Idols are renounced and scourged by Christians, IV, 555. Infant girls were brought to sacrifices, IV, 485. Bread mixed with unmixed wine, left over from the sacrifice, was given to infants at the idol, IV, 486. Parents who bring infants to sacrifices are parricides, IV, 473. Heretics have no authority either to offer sacrifice, baptize, or administer other sacraments, IV, 1040, 1043, 1161, 1187. Heretics cannot administer Christ’s sacraments and therefore cannot give Christ’s grace, IV, 41. Evils do not occur because the gods of the pagans are not worshipped by Christians; rather, good things occur so that God, if not understood through benefits, may immediately be understood through punishments, IV, 561. Among pagans impatience is always noisy and complaining; among Christians, strong and devout patience is calm and always grateful toward God, IV, 558. The gods worshipped by the common people among pagans are not gods, and why, IV, 564–565. The gods adored by Gentiles are renounced and tortured by Christians, IV, 555. It is disgraceful to worship those whom one must oneself defend, IV, 555.

DAMASUS (St.), Pope.—The emperor Constans ordered altars and idols destroyed, XIII, 188. On Mithraic rites in which crimes and orgies were committed, XIII, 188. The emperor Constantius ordered the doctrines of Arian worship to be promulgated and accepted, XIII, 294. The Donatists are called sacrilegious par excellence, XIII, 204. Gracchus destroyed Mithras’ cave, XIII, 187–188. The emperor Gratian permitted free worship to sects—the Eunomians, Manichaeans, and others, XIII, 189. Manichaean worship was prohibited and suppressed by a law issued by the emperor Valentinian, XIII, 155–156.

DRACONTIUS.—The apotheosis of the Gentiles, LX, 663. The impious commonly do not reach old age, LX, 829.

ECKEHARD.—The emperor Valens, infected by Arian unbelief, brought the Visigoths over to his sect, CLIV, 739. Attila consults his diviners, who, after inspecting the entrails of cattle, predict disasters; they are mistaken concerning the death of Aetius, who escaped safely from battle, CLIV, 743–744.

EUGYPPIUS (St.).—The names of Gentile gods assigned to days, CLXII, 686–687. The nations believe gods to have been created by God, LXII, 786. The Manichaeans worshipped the sun and moon, LXII, 686. The nations sacrifice to demons and not to God, LXII, 702. Idolaters must be treated with severity, LXII, 699. Books of haruspices and augurs, LXII, 949–950. Two institutions originated with pagans: first, everything pertaining to making and worshipping idols; second, everything pertaining to worshipping a creature as God, LXII, 949. Various superstitions of pagan worship, LXII, 949–951.

FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—On the false and superstitious worship of profane religions, XII, 981. On water worship among the Egyptians, XII, 984. On water worship among the Phrygians, XII, 987. On air worship among the Assyrians and Africans, XII, 992. On fire worship among the Persians, XII, 992. On various superstitions and their secrets, XII, 995. On the Bacchanalia, XII, 995. On Proserpina, XII, 999. On Liber worshipped as the sun, XII, 999. On the worship of Adonis, XII, 1004. Abominations in the worship of Paphian Venus, XII, 1005. The abominations of Sabazian Jupiter, XII, 1005. On the foul rites of the Corybantes, XII, 1006. On Serapis and his rites, XII, 1011. On the Penates and Vesta, XII, 1015. On the five Minervas, XII, 1018. Explanation of the symbols and signs of the worship of gods, XII, 1020, 1022, 1026. On dragon worship, XII, 1036. On uprooting idolaters so that the empire may prosper, XII, 1048.

FRECULPH.—An image at Sirmium was publicly preserved, lest in later times pagans should deny that they had worshipped such gods, CVI, 1230.

GAUDENTIUS (St.).—The parts of idolatry are sorcery, augury, divination by lots, and so forth, XX, 870. For the sake of their own gluttony, pagans began preparing meals for the dead which they themselves ate; then they dared to celebrate sacrilegious sacrifices for them, XX, 870.

GENNADIUS.—The Anthropomorphites worship and adore a corporeal god, LVIII, 1013. Pagans worship many gods, LVIII, 1000.

GREGORY THE GREAT (St.).—Temples of idols are consecrated as churches by a Christian rite, LXXV, 100–101. When pagans offered sacrifices to their idols, they feasted upon slaughtered oxen, LXXV, 388. Gregory bought pagan boys in order to make them Christians, LXXV, 107–108. The sacrifices of heretics are useless, LXXV, 523. How those returning from idolatry are to be received into the Church, LXXVII, 903. Arian processions, LXXVIII, 405. The emperor Hadrian ordered the common temple of all gods, namely the Pantheon, to be built, LXXVIII, 393. At the Feralia, the spirits of the dead were appeased [Col. 0968] by food placed on their tombs for them to eat, LXXVIII, 303. A festival which pagans called the Terminalia was formerly celebrated by certain Christians, LXXVIII, 303. In February the Romans purified the City in honor of the god Februus with burning candles, LXXVIII, 298.

GREGORY (St.) OF TOURS.—The Arians teach religious toleration, LXXI, 360. The Gauls, or Franks, followed pagan worship or Arianism before Clovis embraced Catholic worship, LXXI, 18.

GUIBERT.—The Jews worshipped the fiery serpent, CLVI, 525. The Jews adored Beelphegor, that is, Priapus, CLVI, 525.

HAYMO.—He who now sacrifices an ox to God would please God as much as one who kills a man, CXVI, 1976. The nations think Christians have no God; or, if they have one, they think him powerless, CXVI, 590. Those who make images of gods are so foolish that they worship them as though they were their creator, CXVI, 590. The impotence of images described, CXVI, 590. Idols are nothing; and with respect to worship, they are nothing, CXVI, 921. The material from which idols were made was something, but the worship itself was nothing, CXVI, 961. Gaius Caligula hated the Jews because they made neither altars, temples, nor images for him, CXVIII, 826. In his madness Caligula wished to be called God, CXVIII, 826.

HELINAND.—The priests of Jupiter in Crete always abstained from certain foods, CCXII, 698. Those once called priests of the devil, that is, priests of idols, are now bishops of heretics or their elect, CCXII, 697. Once the ancient priests of Egypt had devoted themselves to the worship of false gods, they always abstained from wine, meat, women, eggs, and cheese, CCXII, 698.

JEROME (St.).—The ancient priests of Egypt never had intercourse with women from the time they began serving divine worship, XXIII, 302. The doctrines and worship of the Magi among the Persians, XXIII, 303. Individual Egyptian cities worshipped individual animals, XXIII, 294. The doctrines and worship of the Indians, XXIII, 304. The doctrines and worship of Antichrist, XXIII, 315–316. The doctrines and worship of Arians concerning Christ, XXIII, 166. Paganism worshipped fauns and satyrs near Alexandria, XXIII, 25. Idols are said to have first been manufactured in the time of Enos, XXIII, 946. Eunuchs were the chief priests and pontiffs of Heliopolis, XXIII, 998. The city of the Athenians was devoted to idolatry, XXIV, 569. There were many Chaldean augurs, XXIV, 457. Many customarily worship demons lest they harm them, and entreat others to grant benefits, XXIV, 747. Description of the idols worshipped by the nations, XXIV, 747. The Egyptians have divinities drawn from animals, XXIV, 450. Bel fell and was shattered; such was the religious devotion paid to him by the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims—captives and lowborn mortals—but even their own children, XXIV, 450. Images of beasts and brute animals were especially consecrated to divine worship in Egypt, XXIV, 450. Nabo and Dagon, made mute and shattered by the truth of the Gospel, XXIV, 450. Idols are images of the dead, XXIV, 385–386. Moloch, idol of the Ammonites, XXIV, 552. Nisroch, god of the Ninevites, XXIV, 389. Pharaoh, triumphing and worshipping his idol, is mocked in the temple of a false deity, XXIV, 389. The prophets of Samaria prophesied in the idol Baal, XXIV, 822–823. The prophets of the nations pretend, by a divine spirit, to foretell future events, XXIV, 851. Baal, idol of the Sidonians, XXV, 1343. Ninus enrolled Bel, his father, among the gods, XXV, 838. It is not lawful to worship statues and images of kings, XXV, 511. The religion of the nations worships every kind of beast, XXV, 80. The error of the Gentiles, who regard everything above themselves as gods, XXV, 514. At Memphis is the temple of Apis, where consulted oracles give responses, XXV, 289. Heretics have many altars: indeed, they have as many altars as schisms, XXV, 1022. Worshippers of Baal in Judah and Jerusalem, XXV, 1343. Judah and Benjamin set up a statue of Baal in the Temple of the Lord and worshipped idols and the Lord in the same sanctuary, XXV, 1343. What Beelphegor, an idol, is, XXV, 896. Those who serve gluttony and lust worship the idol Beelphegor, XXV, 896. Lachish, a city devoted to idols, was the beginning of idolatry in Judah, XXV, 1160. Melcham, idol of the Ammonites, XXV, 1002. Baal, an idol near Jerusalem, XXVI, 66. In their madness the people of Israel sacrificed victims to an idol, and burned or initiated their children to demons, XXVI, 66. Inscription on the Athenians’ altars: “To unknown and foreign gods,” XXVI, 572–573. Demons are worshipped through vices, XXVI, 415. Judas Maccabaeus cleansed the Temple of images of idols, XXVI, 505–506. Antiochus compelled the Jews to idolatry, killed those unwilling, and placed an image in the Temple of Olympian Jupiter, XXVII, 505–506. Hadrian enrolled Antinous, who died in Egypt, among the gods, XXVII, 617–618.

HILARY (St.).—The vain fear of idolaters, IX, [Col. 0969] 632. Idolaters seek honor for the gods they have made for themselves through the value of metals, IX, 766. Cows worshipped in Samaria, IX, 387, 465. Arians do not adore and worship Christ as true God, IX, 141. Worshippers of the creature are likewise reproved, IX, 256. Arians are not bishops of Christ but of Antichrist, IX, 609.

HINCMAR.—Idolatry, mother of heresy, CXXV, 479. Magical arts arise from evil angels, CXXV, 718. Diviners utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols and offer deadly sacrifices, CXXV, 718. Magi or sorcerers disturb the elements and, without poison, kill men merely by the force of incantation, CXXV, 718. Sortilegers who divine through the lots of saints, CXXV, 718. Various kinds of magical arts, CXXV, 718–719.

HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.—Simon Magus, worshipped by Nero as God, alone opposing the truth, died when cast down into the depths of the pit of the abyss, CLIV, 25–26. Domitian built the Pantheon to demonstrate his sacrilegious devotion toward the gods, CLIV, 28. Domitian ordered himself to be called both god and lord, CLIV, 28, 43.

ISIDORE (St.) OF SEVILLE.—Arian worship is proved hateful to God by a miracle performed by St. Isidore, LXXXII, 43. On Christian heresies, LXXXII, 298. The Ophites worship a serpent, LXXXII, 299. The Adamites pray naked and men and women meet together naked, LXXXII, 299. The Cainites worship Cain, LXXXII, 299. The Angelics worship angels, LXXXII, 299. The Marcionites worship one good and another evil god, LXXXII, 300. The Artotyrites offer bread and cheese, saying that the first human beings offered to God an offering from the fruits of the earth and the fruits of sheep, LXXXII, 300. The Aquarians offer water alone in the sacramental cup, LXXXII, 300. The Hermogenians worship matter, coeternal with God, as a goddess, LXXXII, 300. The Manichaeans worshipped two substances, good and evil, namely two gods, LXXXII, 300. Poets and seers enriched the worship of their gods with varied ornaments of speech, LXXXII, 308. The theological poets composed poems about gods, LXXXII, 309. The Sibyls spoke in poems of the worship of God and of Christ who was to come, LXXXII, 310. The sacrifice which the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus, by which whoever partook of it was transformed into the forms of beasts, LXXXII, 311. Magi use blood and victims and often touch dead bodies, LXXXII, 312. Diviners utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols and offer deadly sacrifices, LXXXII, 312. Haruspices inspect the entrails of cattle, LXXXII, 312. Augurs attend to the flights and cries of birds, LXXXII, 312–313. Pagans set up sacred groves and idols in country districts, and from this received their name, LXXXII, 314. Apostates are Christians who turn to idol worship and the contaminations of sacrifices, LXXXII, 314. On the gods of the nations and the worship of gods in various places, LXXXII, 314. Cecrops was the first of all to name Jupiter, invent images, establish altars, and sacrifice victims, LXXXII, 315. Those who fashion Janus with four faces make a monster, not a god, LXXXII, 318. Beelphegor is interpreted “image of shame”; it is the same as Baal upon Mount Phegor, whom the Latins call Priapus, god of gardens, and whom the Greeks dedicated and worshipped in gardens because of his fertility in generation, LXXXII, 316–317. Apis among the Egyptians was the bull consecrated to Serapis, and was thus named after him; Egypt worshipped it as a deity because it gave clear signs concerning future events, LXXXII, 322. The Gentiles called all the gods they worshipped at home Penates, LXXXII, 325. They call the gods of the dead Manes and worship them that they may be mild, LXXXII, 325. On worshippers of idols, LXXXIV, 537. On Arians not to be baptized by Catholics, LXXXIV, 631. On apostates to be separated from the Church, LXXXII, 632.

ISIDORE MERCATOR.—Catholics must not enter the cemeteries or basilicas of heretics, CXXX, 285. Catholics must not contract marriages with heretics, CXXX, 285. Catholics must not observe the Sabbath, CXXX, 285. Catholics must not pray with heretics or schismatics, CXXX, 286. Catholics may not celebrate festivals with pagans, CXXX, 286. Arians oppress Catholics, CXXX, 650. The sacrilegious priests of pagans wished infants to be slaughtered and a fountain filled with their blood so that Constantine might cleanse his leprosy in it, CXXX, 246. Worshippers of idols are to be sought out and punished as sacrilegious persons, CXXX, 560. Christians must not observe Gentile rites, CXXX, 586. The superstition of the Kalends of January among the Gauls, CXXX, 1176.

JOHN OF SALISBURY.—Who the Magi are and whence they are called so, CXCIX, 407. On the kinds of magic, CXCIX, 407. Who incantators, diviners, sortilegers, and augurs are, CXCIX, 407. On haruspices, palm-readers, and pythonesses, CXCIX, 461. Israel, apostate from its Savior, sacrificed its sons and daughters to demons, CXCIX, 725–726. Epicurus worships chance as a [Col. 0970] god, CXCIX, 977. The fear of God produces contempt for the world and deifies human beings, CXCIX, 980. Aristotle was called the son of Apollo, CXCIX, 983. Socrates regards the human mind as a god, CXCIX, 982.

LACTANTIUS.—The Egyptians were the first to begin observing and worshipping the stars, VI, 328. On their worship of animals among the same Egyptians, VI, 620, 786. The Egyptians worshipped the sun under the name of Jupiter, VI, 621. Apollonius of Tyana was worshipped by the Ephesians, VI, 559. Before the worship of gods had been established, the true God was worshipped, namely while Saturn reigned, VI, 565. Through the example of Jupiter, the people, made almost parricidal, ceased to worship the true God, VI, 566. When people began, whether from fear or by their own choice, to regard a king as a god, they violated piety; justice and all virtues left the earth, VI, 556. Jupiter persecuted justice and removed it; when God’s worship was removed, the bond of the covenant of human society was broken, VI, 567. Favor and Pallor began to be worshipped by Romans as goddesses, VI, 220. Unjust and impious worship of gods brought in all the evils by which the human race destroys itself mutually, VI, 575. Enumeration of the crimes committed by those who worship gods, VI, 575. Worshippers of gods cannot be good and just, VI, 580, 583. The stars must not be worshipped, VI, 277. Who the atheists were, VI, 120. On the worship of Apis and the hawk among the Egyptians, VI, 786–787. Orpheus brought the rites of Liber into Greece, VI, 247. Why the Orphic rites and Bacchic orgies are so called, VI, 247. Julius Caesar was the first of the Caesars enrolled among the gods, VI, 193, 197. Dogs worshipped by Egyptians, VI, 621. On eagle worship among the Egyptians, VI, 787. Idolatry originated with the Greeks, VI, 196. On the wickedness of Greeks in consecrating images of Cupid and Love, VI, 221. Juba was enrolled among the gods and worshipped by the Moors, VI, 194. Laurentia, Romulus’ nurse, was worshipped by Romans as a goddess, VI, 216–217. The false religion found in worship of gods, VI, 1048. The Arabs worshipped a stone as god, VII, 494. The emperor Aurelian appropriated the title “lord and god,” VII, 397. Aurelian held the sun in great reverence, VII, 506. Altars were treacherously set up by pagans in many places, VII, 408.

LANFRANC.—Not all Israelites remained under God’s worship; some passed over to Gentile rites and idol worship, CL, 135–136. Debate between Jew and Gentile, CL, 103–104. How a Gentile is excused or accused before God on account of idolatry, CL, 103–104.

LEO THE GREAT (St.), Pope.—The rites used by Manichaeans in bloody sacrifices, LV, 974, 803. The Priscillianist heresy abolished Catholic rites, LV, 1033. On Persian supplications celebrated with superstitious worship, LV, 840. On the abominable mysteries of Mithras among the Persians, LV, 841. Persian sacrifices of bread and water, LV, 841. The Manichaeans customarily invoked demons in their abominable rites, LV, 794. Neither prayer nor psalmody with heretics, LVI, 887. The false martyrs of heretics must not be worshipped, LVI, 718. Law against the Manichaeans, LVI, 683.

NICETAS (St.).—Belenus, a famous divinity at Aquileia still worshipped in the sixth century, LII, 1006. Nestorian worship was declining in the time of St. Nicetas, LII, 931. In the region of Ravenna, pagans followed the old worship of idols, LII, 1006.

OPTATUS (St.).—On the false and hypocritical worship of the Donatists, who scrape and break Catholic altars and commit innumerable other sacrileges, XI, 1065. New disturbances stirred up by the Donatists, XI, 818.

OROSIUS.—The deceit and malice of Egyptian priests in removing worship of the true God in favor of idol worship, XXXI, 807.

PAULINUS (St.) OF NOLA.—Constantine and other pious emperors enacted laws against pagans, LXI, 527. Bel fell, along with all the demons worshipped in temples as divinities, LXI, 527. At Christ’s birth the Delphic demon was struck dumb, LXI, 516. St. John imposed silence on Diana, LXI, 517. The belly-god, also Dagon, worshipped among the Philistines, LXI, 525. Paulinus shows that Fate and Fortune, to which certain philosophers entrusted the governance of some human affairs, are nothing, LXI, 228. The emperor Hadrian set up idols at the sites of Christ’s nativity and passion, LXI, 326, 321. Neglect of God because of idolatry, LXI, 237, 524. The excess of idolatry, LXI, 523. Abominable rites prevailed both in Isiac observances and in orgies, LXI, 525.

PETER COMESTOR.—On the bronze serpent against fiery serpents and the superstitious worship which the people rendered to it, CXCVIII, 1234. Balaam falsely claimed to be the Lord’s prophet, although he consulted demons while sacrificing, CXCVIII, 1237. On Balaam, CXCVIII, 1238–1239. The Israelites sacrificed with the daughters of Midian, ate things sacrificed to idols, and worshipped gods, especially the idol Beelphegor, whom Greece called Priapus, CXCVIII, 1239. Moses, by the Lord’s command, hanged on the gallows the authors of this idolatry and all initiated into Beelphegor [Col. 0971], CXCVIII, 1239. On Moses, buried by God in an unknown place lest the Hebrews worship him as a god, CXCVIII, 1260. On the repentance of the children of Israel for idolatry, CXCVIII, 1283. On the idol Bel and the dragon, CXCVIII, 1468.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (St.).—Fools suppose created things themselves to be gods, LII, 450. Gentiles made the sun, moon, stars, gold, stones, and wood into gods for themselves, LII, 450. Astrologers serve as many gods in heaven as there are stars, LII, 612–613. The Gentile people, obedient to peoples of gods and monsters of gods, ignorant of reason, does not attain the service of the one true God, LII, 502.

PHILASTRIUS (St.).—On the Sethians, who worship Abel and Seth, XII, 1116. The abominable worship of the Chaldeans and Sidonians, XII, 1128. Abraham was justified when he broke idols, XII, 1128. Gideon likewise earned great merit when he broke idols, XII, 1128. On those worshipping the fly in the city of Accaron, XII, 1125. In Africa the inhabitants worship heavenly Fortune, XII, 1127. On worshippers of Baal, XII, 1127, 1133. On certain Christians reveling like pagans in Bacchic fashion, XII, 1187. Manichaeans worshipping demons, adoring the elements like pagans, and serving abominable depravity, XII, 1176. The Ophites, or Serpentines, venerate a serpent, XII, 1114. The Manichaeans asserted two gods, one good and one evil, XII, 1175. Epicurean madness, XII, 1119. On worshippers of Fortune, XII, 1126. Worshippers of idols, XII, 1128. Destructive pagan impiety, XII, 1127. The Jews worshipped Astar and Astaroth, images of men and women, XII, 1137. The blood of infants in Montanist mysteries, XII, 1166. Worshippers of the bronze serpent, XII, 1131. On those worshipping the sun, XII, 1169. On worshippers of mice, XII, 1124.

PRUDENTIUS AURELIUS.—The apotheosis of the pagans, LIX, 968. Bald priests of Isis, LIX, 172. Phoebus’ frenzies and other ridiculous solemnities of gods and goddesses, LIX, 172. Calamities happening to Christians were charged against them by pagans because they worshipped Christ and despised the gods, LX, 233–234. Worship of gods, LX, 23. Saturnian rites smoking with the slaughter of children, and altars resounding with their cries, LX, 202. Rome, called a goddess and worshipped by some, LX, 136. Roman nobility remained devoted to idol worship until the reign of Theodosius, LX, 325. Idolatry was extinguished at Rome, though some nobles retained paganism for a long time, LX, 170. The Romans worshipped all gods, and why nevertheless they persecuted Christians, LX, 133. Origin of the gods in Italy, LX, 122. Human victims, LX, 292.

RABANUS MAURUS.—Aaron falls into idolatry, CVIII, 211. Why Aaron, author of idolatry, was not punished with the people at the same time, CVIII, 226. Association with Gentiles and idolaters is sternly forbidden to Israelites, CVIII, 236–237. The pomp and garments of idolatry, CVIII, 1151. Israelites are captured by their enemies, sold, and everywhere pursued by divine vengeance because of idolatry, CVIII, 1123. After Gideon’s death, the Jews worship Baal, CVIII, 1177, 1179. While the Egyptians suffered deserved punishment because of idolatry, the Hebrews received food from God, CIX, 745. Antiochus erected an abominable idol, CIX, 1138. Why Antiochus ordered the feast of Father Liber to be celebrated, CIX, 1125. Antiochus compelled the aged Eleazar to eat pork, CIX, 1125. Baalim, an idol worshipped by the Jews, CIX, 33. The Gentiles looked for more silver and ornament in their idols than they worshipped divinity, CIX, 733. Gentiles worshipped not only gold but also earthenware vessels, CIX, 743. Various idols observed by pagans, CIX, 731, 740. Why idols are called “weeping idols,” CIX, 83, 343. The idolatry of King Amaziah, CIX, 508. Jehu is sent to kill the priests of Baal, CIX, 238, 498. The idolatry of the Israelites, CIX, 1121. Joash was worshipped as a god by the leaders of Judah and therefore incurred God’s displeasure, CIX, 504. Josiah, renowned for piety, destroyed various images of superstitious nations and abolished idolatry, CIX, 266–267. King Nebuchadnezzar ordered all gods to be destroyed, so that he alone might be called god, CIX, 604. Uzziah, intending to sacrifice contrary to the Law of Moses, was struck with leprosy, CIX, 246. How pagans together with heretics oppose righteousness, CIX, 855. Various kinds and rites of Gentiles, CIX, 740. God is not pleased by the multitude of Gentile rites, CIX, 1040. How great was Egyptian idolatry, CXI, 816. Auguries by the flight of birds, CXI, 242. Dathan and Abiram, with their companions, are a type of heretics, CXI, 53. The usefulness of idols, CXI, 877. Whence pagans derive their name, and who they are, CXI, 426. Enumeration and origin of the Sibyls, CXI, 420. Heavenly signs are forbidden to be venerated, CXI, 877. The victims of the impious are displeasing to God. Why superstitious paganism sacrificed victims at the heads of springs and in groves, CXI, 864. What idols the Israelites worshipped, CXII, 1141.

ROBERT PULLUS.—On the elect and ministers of Antichrist, CLXXXVI, 981. The blindness of idolatry concerning a plurality of gods, CLXXXVI, 675.

[Col. 0972]

RODULFUS GLABER.—On the plagues of the pagans, CXLII, 623. On the mad heretic Leutard, CXLII, 643. On heresy found at Orléans, CXLII, 659. On heresy discovered in Italy, CXLII, 671. On battles of Saracens against Christians in regions of Africa, CXLII, 682.

RUFINUS.—Egypt, a workshop of idols, XXI, 413. Julian’s public madness in devotion to the worship of idols, XXI, 501. Julian, forbidding Christians to attend the studies of pagan authors, decreed that schools of letters should be open only to those who venerated gods and goddesses, XXI, 501–502. Magicians, philosophers, haruspices, and augurs alleged that Athanasius was an obstacle to their arts, XXI, 502. A statue of Venus was placed at the site of the Cross, so that, if any Christian wished to worship Christ in that place, he might seem to be worshipping Venus, XXI, 476.

RUPERT OF DEUTZ.—Gold is the god of the Jews, CLXVIII, 365. Jezebel brought the idol Baal from Sidon, and Israel worshipped it, CLXVIII, 126–127. Baalim is the name given to all idols whatsoever, CLXVIII, 43–44. Beelphegor is the same as Priapus, god of the Romans, CLXVIII, 145. Galgala was a place of idols, CLXVIII, 78. The Jews worshipped idols in Egypt, CLXVIII, 21. Alexander the Great wished to be worshipped as the son of Jupiter Ammon, CLXIX, 1408.

SALVIANUS, Saint.—Aaron made the calf, for the worship of which God struck the Hebrews, LIII, 44. The sons of Aaron, offering strange fire to the Lord, were consumed by heavenly fire, LIII, 45–46. The impious opinion of the Epicureans concerning God, LIII, 30–31. An idol of the Africans, LIII, 154. Gods or idols worshipped in the various public games, LIII, 113–114. Neptune was worshipped in circuses, Minerva in gymnasia, Venus in theatres, Mars in arenas, Mercury in wrestling-schools, LIII, 120.

SICARDUS OF CREMONA.—Domitian ordered himself to be worshipped as a god and golden and silver statues of himself to be erected on the Capitol, CCXIII, 458. Pliny, governor of a certain province, wrote to Trajan that he had found nothing evil in Christians apart from their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice, CCXIII, 459. On the heretical perversity of the Waldensians, CCXIII, 554–555.

SIDONIUS.—The procession of Venus, LVIII, 525. Hecatombeon, LVIII, 699–700. The gods of the Persians: water and fire, LVIII, 644–645.

TERTULLIAN.—Why the festivals of the Caesars were not observed by Christians, I, 452. Human error worships everything except the very Creator of all things, I, 666. Above innumerable gods the pagans set another, more exalted one, I, 332. Antiquity erred concerning the worship of gods, I, 306. So many and such great gods could not be worshipped by everyone, I, 573, 645. The pagans destroyed the gods whom they feared, mocked those whom they defended, and feared gods less than emperors, I, 344, 363, 437. The gods ought rather to avenge their injuries than reward flattery, I, 431. It is false that the Roman Empire was founded or extended through the worship of gods, I, 422. The gods handed over their own country to be ravaged by the Romans, I, 424. The Jews despised the gods, I, 432. In public disasters the pagans performed certain acts of public penitence, by which they tried to bend the gods, and what these were, I, 487. Pagans, having eaten every day and about to dine again immediately, offered rain-making rites (aqualicia) to Jupiter in baths, taverns, and brothels, I, 487. Astrologers, augurs, haruspices, magicians, I, 459. How falsely pagans made vows and sacrifices for the emperor’s welfare, while swearing by their genii and celebrating solemn rites, I, 458, 700. Pagans exposed or slaughtered their own children, I, 315. In time of tribulation the pagans invoked the God of Christians, I, 703. They invented gods for themselves to worship, I, 486. They despised them, I, 699. The pagans were impious, sacrilegious, and irreligious toward their own gods, and how, I, 344. Pagans were permitted to worship whichever god they wished, I, 344, 417. Pagans had assigned Saturn’s day to idleness and eating, I, 371. Romulus instituted games for Jupiter Feretrius, I, 637. The Gauls sacrificed to Mercury, I, 316. On the worship of Cybele, I, 415.
