Pagans paid their emperors, both dead and living, the same honor as to gods, I, 347. They called them gods, I, 483. Pagans swore by the genius of emperors, I, 447. Children were sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, I, 314. How initiation into the worship of any god or goddess took place, I, 309, 313. The January festivals, I, 581. The Isthmian rites of Neptune were instituted, I, 644. In the public mysteries of Liber, pagans reclined at table, I, 492. Father Liber, or Bacchus, was made a god because of the discovery of wine, I, 334. Certain pagans worshipped a rough piece of wood, I, 366. How oracles were delivered among pagans, I, 413. Oracles were produced by the deceptions of demons, I, 408. The Persians believed that he was a god and worshipped him, I, 369. In public games the Romans drenched Jupiter Latiaris with human blood, I, 136, 317. It was forbidden to disclose the Samothracian mysteries, I, 309. In Africa pagans sacrificed children to Saturn in order to propitiate him, and for how long they did so, I, 595. [Col. 0973] The Scythians made a covenant after drinking blood and ate the flesh of dead human beings, I, 321. The priests of the Egyptian bull-god observed continence, II, 928. The Kalends of February were celebrated among pagans for the dead, II, 494. Having abandoned God, the Jews served idols, II, 598. On the superstitious worship of Serapis, III, 235, 628. On the sacred rites and mysteries of Isis, III, 631. On the Eleusinian mysteries, III, 635. On the Luperci, III, 638. The image of any god was consecrated by various ceremonies and thus became a god, III, 626. With what great madness pagans repeatedly worshipped and adored the images and statues of often criminal human beings, or of wholly fictitious gods, as though they were true gods, III, 626.

URBAN II, Pope.—Furious schismatics rage against Catholics and kill several bishops, CLI, 50. A new kind of religion in Germany, CLI, 87. On witches, diviners, and so forth, CLI, 1178. On abolishing pagan superstitions, CLI, 1178.

WALAFRID STRABO.—The Egyptians abominate sheep [Col. 0974] and worship them because of Jupiter Ammon, who is depicted with a ram’s head, CXIII, 209. The Egyptians worship the bull consecrated to Apis, just as the cow is consecrated to Isis, CXIII, 209. Apis was the greatest divinity of the Egyptians and appeared to their priests once a year at a fixed time, CXIII, 209. The priests of Apis, accompanying him with hymns and praises, prophesied like persons possessed by frenzy, CXIII, 209.

WICBODUS.—The Manichaeans worship the sun and, together with it, all animals, even the smallest, which they regard as particles of the sun, XCVI, 1111. The philosophical worship of the gentiles admits the transmigration of the souls of beasts into human beings, or of human beings into beasts, XCVI, 1141–1142. Manichaean worship maintains that the soul of a plant or a little worm is the very substance of God, XCVI, 1142.

ZENO, Saint.—On the priests of Cybele, XI, 345–346. On the sacrifices of the gentiles, XI, 363. On the worship of the gentiles, XI, 451. Unchastity as a goddess among idols, XI, 295. Unchastity gave birth to the gods of the gentiles, XI, 294–295.

[Col. 0973]

CIX. INDEX OF THE CULT OF THE SAINTS, AND OF THE VENERATION OF HOLY RELICS AND IMAGES, COMPILED ACCORDING TO THE CHRONOLOGICAL TRADITION OF THE HOLY FATHERS OF THE WESTERN CHURCH.

NOTICE.

Since in our own times there are no lack of enemies of the Catholic Church—namely heretics and pseudo-philosophers—who, shamefully following Vigilantius and other supporters of ancient errors, now endeavor also to defile by words and contempt the honors rendered to the host of Saints, this sequence of our universal and constant tradition, which we here set before the eyes, will abundantly demonstrate and most invincibly establish the enduring doctrine of the Catholic faith concerning the invocation and cult of the Saints, as well as the veneration of holy Relics and Images. For from the earliest ages of the Church down to our own time, the understanding of believers in this matter has been the same; the custom of veneration and honors, or the rites directed toward the heroes of religion, have been the same. Thus those whom eternal glory joins together in heaven are celebrated on earth by the annual recurrence of feasts and praises. Look, kindly reader, and listen not only to the voice of Catholic faith but also to that of sound reason and conscience; and you will hold it as most certain that no avenue of escape remains by which adherents of any heresies may defend themselves. We divide this index into three parts: in the first, we discuss the invocation and cult of the Saints; in the second, the cult and veneration of holy Relics; in the third, the veneration of Images.

PART I.—On the Invocation and Cult of the Saints.

[Col. 0973]

## CX. INDEX OF BENEFITS GRANTED BY GOD TO HUMANKIND THROUGH THE MERITS AND INTERCESSION OF THE SAINTS, COMPILED ACCORDING TO THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS

## NOTICE

In the preceding Index we set forth whatever the Fathers wrote concerning the invocation of Saints, the honour due to sacred Relics, and the veneration of Images. We now deal with benefits obtained through the intercession of those same Saints. When Saints are invoked, all trust must be placed in God alone. Nor should the faithful suppose that the cure of particular diseases has been assigned so peculiarly to particular Saints that, in obtaining their cure or relief, others can contribute nothing by their prayers before God; this will be clear from what follows. In this Index we observe no order except the chronological one, collecting under the name of each author the various miracles he records.

[Col. 0985] **TERTULLIAN.**—By the power and merits of St. Stephen, bishop of Rome, the daughter of Nemesius the tribune, blind from birth, receives sight, III, 1293. An idol and shrine of Mars, struck from heaven, collapse for the most part, 1294. **ST. CYPRIAN.**—By the power and merits of St. John the Baptist, a notable victory is won; twenty dead persons are raised, IV, 935–937. **LACTANTIUS.**—By the power and merits of St. Peter, many are converted to Christ and righteousness, VII, 196.

[Col. 0986] **CONSTANTINE THE GREAT.**—By the power and merits of St. Sylvester, pope, Constantine is baptized and cleansed of leprosy, VIII, 572. Idols and their temples are destroyed, 576. Churches are built and adorned everywhere, 576, 797. By the power and merits of St. Felix, bishop of Tubyzaca, many sick and languishing persons are healed, 683. **ST. HILARY, BISHOP OF POITIERS.**—By the power and merits of the martyrs, various illnesses are expelled; demons are driven away and demoniacs are delivered, X, 584, 585. By the power and merits of

[Col. 0987] St. Hilary, the dying Probianus is healed, IX, 195. Two lepers are cleansed, 196; a contracted hand is healed, 196. A blind man receives sight, 196. Victory is granted to Clovis, 197. A reader grievously afflicted by headache is healed, 611. Gold is found in the saint’s bones, 615. By the power and merits of St Mansuetus, a boy drowned in a river is found alive after three days and restored to his father, 625, 627. A woman blind for seven years receives sight, 634, 635. A possessed girl is delivered, 635. A man suffering elephantiasis is cured, 631, 636. A cleric grievously afflicted by fevers and many other fever sufferers are healed, 636. In a great drought abundant rain is obtained, 639. A count with a contracted hand is healed, 639. A crippled boy is cured, 640. The people are delivered from bubonic plague or cholera, 641, 642. A bishop suffering grave illness is healed, 642, 643. By the power and merits of St Basolus the confessor, a spring rises on the summit of a mountain, 654. A boy blind from birth
Restored to sight, 655. A boar is protected against hunters, 656. A man hanging on the gallows is preserved unharmed, 657. A monstrous man is healed, 661. A forty-year-old girl blind from birth is restored to sight, 661. Another woman, blind for a long time, receives her sight, 661–662. Many are freed from a tyrant’s torments, 662. Vandals are put to flight, 662–663. A thief is punished for his crime, 664. Robbers are rendered motionless as a correction, then, when repentant, are released, 665. A rector, for contempt of St Basolus, becomes rabid, but is later healed when repentant, 665–666. An unchaste cupbearer is torn by a demon, but, when repentant, is healed, 666. A certain man, for his crime, becomes like a naked corpse, but is later healed when repentant, 666–667. By the power of St Bercharius, abbot, oil springs forth for healing the sick, 686. By the power and merits of St Waldebert, abbot of Luxeuil, the monastery is preserved against fires set by pagans [Col. 1014], 693. Invaders of the church are afflicted with plagues but, when repentant, are healed, 696, 698. Berneric, crippled in his feet, is raised up and healed, 699–700.

**ST MAIOLUS, ABBOT OF CLUNY.**—By the power and merits of St Maiolus, abbot, seven solidi are found to relieve the poor, CXXXVII, 749–750. A monk seriously afflicted with fevers is healed, 752. Many are freed from demons, 759. Many sick persons are healed, 759. Many who are mentally dead are restored to life, 759. A blind man is restored to sight, 759–760. Another blind man receives sight, 760–761. A monk seized by a severe fever is healed, 761. A bishop suffering from a grave illness is healed, 761–762. A naked poor man is clothed, 763. A matron afflicted with a grave illness is healed, 772. A moneyer seriously afflicted by sickness is healed, 772–773. A servant is freed from his master’s insolence, 773–774. A book of St Dionysius is saved from fire, 775. Sailors are saved from shipwreck, 775–776.

**LETALD, MONK OF MICY.**—By the power and merits of St Julian, bishop of Le Mans, the people of Le Mans are converted to Christ, CXXXVII, 785. Three dead persons are raised, 787–788. A girl tormented by a demon is freed, 790. A most savage dragon is put to flight and loses its power to harm, 791. A boy is freed from a serpent, 792. Two demoniacs are freed, 792. The doors of a prison are opened, and chained prisoners are freed from prison and bonds, 793. An infant is saved from fire, 795–796. By the power and merits of St Maximin, abbot, the blind sister of St Theodemir is restored to sight, 801. A savage dragon is destroyed, 799. A sick man named Agilis is healed, 799. The church and monastery of St Maximin are saved from fire, 804–805. By the power and merits of St Avitus, abbot of Dun, a monk is raised from the dead, 800–801. By St Maximin’s power, two brothers are saved from death, 810. A robber becomes demoniac because of his crime, but is later freed when repentant, 811. A charioteer is safely preserved amid the waves of the Loire, 811–812. A certain man drowned and lifeless in a river is recalled to life, 812–813. A cleric who falls from a church roof is preserved unharmed, 813. A man whose hands are contracted and stuck to a digging-tool is healed, 813. Two monks are saved from death, 814–815. Workmen buried alive underground are preserved alive, 817. A blind poor man drowned in a river is saved from death, 817. A poor man living beneath a rock with his wife and six children is saved from death, 818. Persons burning in a devouring fire are delivered and recover full health, 820, 822. Bernerius, delirious, is healed, 822. By the power and merits of St Junian, fever patients are healed, 826. A woman suffering from elephantiasis is healed, 826.

**ST ADALBERT, BISHOP OF PRAGUE.**—By the power of holy Mary, the dying Adalbert is restored to health, CXXXVII, 865. By the power and merits of St Adalbert, certain people become mute as a correction but, later repentant, recover speech, 890–891. A pagan, for contempt of the saint, becomes mute and contracted in the mouth, but after conversion and repentance receives speech and full health, 894. Emperor Otto, suffering from a grave illness and abandoned as hopeless by physicians, is suddenly healed, 894–895.

**HROTSVITHA, NUN OF GANDERSHEIM.**—By the power and merits of Saints John and Paul, a boy possessed and violently tormented by a demon is freed and healed, CXXXVII, 994. By the power of St John the Apostle, Drusiana and Callimachus are raised from the dead, 1001, 1010–1011.

**ANONYMOUS WORKS** (*opera adespotika*, Greek “unattributed works”).—By the power and merits of St Clodoald, confessor, demons are expelled from possessed bodies; the mouths of the mute are opened; sight is restored to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame; and health is granted to all sick persons who ask in faith, CXXXVIII, 203.

**ABBO, ABBOT OF FLEURY.**—By the power and merits of St Sylvester, pope, Emperor Constantine the Great, suffering from a most foul leprosy, is healed, CXXXIX, 540–541. By the power and merits of St Liberius, pope and confessor, many sick people are saved, 551.

**AIMOIN, MONK OF FLEURY.**—By the power and merits of St Benedict, the basilica of St Peter is saved from fire, CXXXIX, 814–815. The table for poor people and pilgrims is preserved from a general fire, 815–816. An architect is unharmed in a serious fall, 816. A woman is freed from a demon, 816–817. A cripple is raised up, 817. Twelve poor people are fed, 817. The people of Argentomagus are supplied with blessed bread and wine, 819. A small boat is provided from heaven, 821. A sick man is healed, 822, 824. A fire is extinguished, 826. A cripple is raised up, 826–827. An ungrateful man becomes crippled again but, when repentant, is healed once more, 827–828. Otherius, suffering since youth from paralysis of hands and feet, is healed, 828–829. Ademarus, an invader of the monastery, is defeated by divine will and captured with his companions, 830 and following. A horse is brought out of a well, 834. Soldiers are not injured in battle, 836–837. Armentarius is rescued from the waters, 839. Felix is twice saved from shipwreck, 842–843. A plundering advocate of the poor is punished as a correction, 843–844. A monk, abandoned by everyone, is aided, 844–845. Two women suffering from four diseases are healed, 840–841. Adelais, mute and [Col. 1015] lame, speaks and walks properly, 847. A woman unable to use her feet is healed twice, 847–848. A fire is extinguished, 848–849. A girl with contracted legs is raised up and healed, 850–851. Two blind people receive light, 851. Placidus, drowned in water, is recalled to life, 853–854. A spring rises from a rock, 854. Thirteen solidi are found so that a poor debtor may be freed from another’s debt, 854.

**HERIGER, ABBOT OF LOBBES.**—By the power and merits of holy Berlendis, virgin, many persons afflicted by every sort of disease are healed, CXXXIX, 1107. A fish is changed into flesh, 1107. Water is changed into wine, 1107–1108. Many blind people are restored to sight, many lame persons are raised up; deaf and mute persons receive hearing and speech; demons are expelled, 1108. An unbelieving woman becomes demoniac, but, when repentant, is freed, 1108. By the power and merits of St Laudoald and his companions, a blind woman is restored to sight, 1117. A noblewoman suffering from dropsy is healed, 1117–1118. A cripple is raised up, 1119–1120. A possessed woman cruelly tormented by a demon is freed and healed, 1120. Another, blind for four years, receives sight, 1120. Another, suffering severely from dropsy for six years, is healed, 1120. A stolen horse is restored, 1120. A woman long infirm is healed, 1121–1122. A shipmaster is punished for his guilt but, when repentant, is healed, 1122. A woman blind for many years receives light, 1123. A blind girl is restored to sight, 1123. Another woman, weak and unable to use her feet, is healed, 1123. Another, wholly disabled and despaired of by doctors, is healed, 1123. Adalger, blind and hunchbacked, is restored to sight and healed, 1123. A girl suffering for many years from an inflammation of the eyes is healed, 1123–1124. A poor blind woman recovers sight, 1124. Another blind woman receives sight, 1124. Theodore, crippled for many years, is raised up and healed, 1124. A blind woman receives light, 1124. Another woman, suffering severely from pain in her kidneys, is healed, 1124.

**NOTGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE.**—By the power and merits of St Hadelin, confessor, an abundant spring rises to assuage the thirst of labouring harvesters, CXXXIX, 1145. A mute woman recovers speech, 1145. A matron is restored to life so that she may make a gift, 1146. The broken door of a poor woman’s house is restored, 1146.

**ST HENRY, EMPEROR.**—By the power and merits of St Cunegund, empress and virgin, a possessed man is freed, CXL, 214–215. Three cripples are raised up, 215. A paralysed woman and another woman who is lame receive full health; a lame man walks properly, 215. A weak and crippled boy, and another wasted by grievous emaciation, are healed, 215. A girl with sciatica, a crippled boy, a girl crippled in foot and knee, and another with a withered hand, are raised up and healed, 215. A man hanged on the gallows for a stolen horse is saved from death, 215. Another, hanged and strangled on the gallows, is recalled to life, 215. Two others are freed from chains and death, 215. A boy is raised from the dead, 215–216. A suffocated boy is recalled to life, 216. A girl drowned in a spring is raised from the dead, 216. A person mute from birth speaks properly, 216–217. A wolf becomes gentle, nurses a little boy, and returns him unharmed to his mother, 217. A servant seriously afflicted by headache is healed, 217–218. Blind persons receive sight, lame persons walking, mute persons speech, deaf persons hearing, and the other sick receive full health, 222. Dust is changed into grain, 222.

**THANGMAR, PRIEST.**—By the power and merits of St Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim, a crippled girl is raised up, CXL, 435. A little girl suffering from a grave illness is healed, 436. A girl suffering from pain in the eyes is healed, 436. A certain man severely tormented by acute eye pain is healed, 436–437. Dodo, seriously afflicted in hands and feet, is healed, 437. A possessed woman, severely tormented by a demon, is freed and healed, 437. A young man violently possessed and horribly tormented is freed, 437. Merchants are saved from shipwreck, 438. A boy suffering for five years from a fistula is healed, 438–439. An abbot suffering from a wound in the shin is healed, 440. A crippled woman is raised up, 439. A man with a withered hand is healed, 439–440. A peasant afflicted by a grave illness is healed, 440. A girl with a contracted hand is healed, 440. A woman suffering from a severe swelling of the eyes and nose is healed, 440. A girl crippled for five years is healed, 410, 441. Adelward, paralysed, is healed, 441. An infant nearly lifeless is restored to life and health, 442. A knight wasted by a long illness is healed, 442. A matron suffering from a grave illness is suddenly healed, 442. A knight afflicted by a severe fever is healed, 442. A peasant, seriously afflicted by fevers for a long time, is healed, 442.

**ANONYMOUS AUTHOR.**—By the power and merits of St Henry, emperor, a paralysed man is healed, CXL, 131. A blind man is restored to sight, 132. A sick man, disabled in all his limbs, is healed, 132. A cripple is raised up, 132. Weak persons are healed, blind persons restored to sight, demons expelled, and many afflicted by diverse diseases healed, 132. John, a cardinal and detractor of the holy emperor, becomes blind but, when later repentant, recovers his sight, [Col. 1016] 133. Another man, doubting the miracles performed through the saint, likewise becomes blind, but when repentant is restored to sight, 133. A youth wholly crippled is raised up and healed, 134–135. A demoniac and two possessed women are freed, 135. A blind woman is restored to sight, 135. A deformed woman unable to use her limbs is healed, 135. A matron worn out by severe toothache is healed, 135–136. A detractor of the saint is deprived of the use of his five senses but, when repentant, is healed, 136. A man pretending to be crippled becomes crippled in his foot, 137. A blind man is restored to sight, 137–138. A peasant with a withered foot is healed, 138. A woman deaf and mute from birth hears and speaks properly, 138. A possessed woman is unwillingly freed, 139. Many fever patients are healed, 140.

**ADELBOLD, BISHOP OF UTRECHT.**—By the power and merits of St Walpurgis, a dying girl is healed, CXL, 1093. A maidservant suffering from illness and gluttony is healed, 1095. An epileptic boy is healed, 1097. An abbess suffering from gout is healed, 1097–1098. A poor man crippled and monstrous from birth is raised up and healed, 1098. A weak woman unable to use her feet receives full health, 1098. A sick and dying man is restored to health, 1099. A murderer involuntarily adheres inseparably to his victim so that his crime may be punished, 1099–1101.

**BERNARD, SCHOLASTICUS OF ANGERS.**—By the power and merits of St Faith, virgin, Wilbert, whose eyes have been torn out, receives sight, CXL, 131, 133. For a knight’s consolation, a dead mule is recalled to life, 137–138. A sterile woman becomes fertile and bears two sons, 139–140. A woman suffers from a grave swelling for having usurped a ring, but is healed when repentant, 140. A merchant is seen amid flames for having stolen a candle, but is saved from the fire when repentant, 140–141. A boy blind, lame, deaf, and mute from birth sees, walks properly, hears, and speaks, 141–142. Another blind and lame person is restored to sight and walks properly, 142. An innocent man hanged on the gallows is freed from the gallows and death, 142, 144. Another is released from chains and prison, 144–145. Another man, chained in prison, is freed from prison; still chained, he is carried by a heavenly ass and, finally, when the chains are broken, is saved from every danger, 145–148. Raimundus, shipwrecked, is saved from death, 148, 151. Bodias, a pilgrim, is freed from chains and prison, 151–152. A youth laid in a bier is recalled to life, 152–153. The knight Helias obtains children from his formerly sterile wife; they pass through flames unharmed, 153–154. A horse’s eye, torn out by the roots, is restored, 154. A youth is raised from the dead, 155–156. Raimundus, tormented by epilepsy, is healed, 157. The same man is freed from fetters and chain, 157, 157. A dead mule is recalled to life, 160–161. A knight seriously afflicted by an internal disease is healed, 161–162.

**ARNOLD, MONK OF ST EMMERAM.**—By the power and merits of St Emmeram, bishop, an adulterous woman is driven away from the saint’s church, CXL, 999. A man captured by robbers and sold twice is saved from death, 1000–1001. A girl, fasting for a whole year and abhorring all food, is restored to her former health, 1001–1002. A monk is saved from shipwreck, 1007. An apostate monk seized by a demon is repeatedly freed, 1007–1008. A demoniac possessed by a legion is freed and healed, 1008–1009. Twelve men swearing contrary to law are most severely punished, 1010, 1041. A woman becomes paralysed for having stolen a chalice but, when repentant, is healed, 1011–1013. A paralysed man is healed, 1014–1015. A blind man is restored to sight, 1044. A crippled woman is healed, 1044–1045. A weak poor man is healed, 1045. A possessed man cruelly tormented by a demon is freed, 1057–1058. A blind woman is restored to sight, 1058–1059. Two possessed women are healed, 1059. A woman with a contracted hand is healed, 1060. A man suffering in his eye is healed, 1063–1064. Water is changed into wine, 1065. A fever patient is healed, 1065. A crippled poor man is raised up, 1066. A robber is converted to Christ because of the miracles performed, 1066. The mouth of St Emmeram’s accuser is divinely closed, 1068.

**WOLFER, CANON.**—By the power and merits of St Godehard, bishop, a man afflicted by weakness of the foot is healed, CXLI, 1198–1199. A woman blind for many years receives sight, 1199. A peasant suffering from a long illness is healed, 1199. A girl lifeless for two days is recalled to life, 1199. A paralysed boy is healed, 1200. Desiderius, blind and infirm, is restored to sight and healed, 1200. A man suffering from fevers for a long time is healed, 1201. A monk afflicted by a most acute fever is healed, 1201–1202. A young woman seriously afflicted by fevers is healed, 1202. A fever patient is healed, 1202–1203. A youth drowned in a river is recalled to life, 1203. A woman in labour is freed from the pains and danger of childbirth, 1204. A companion of the saint, suffering on the road from a broken leg, is suddenly healed, 1204–1205. A blind woman is restored to sight, 1205. Another possessed woman is freed, 1205–1206. A very dull boy becomes teachable and a learned bishop, 1206. Excommunicated dead rise [Col. 1017] from their graves in order to be absolved, 1206–1208. A man immersed in a river for a long time is recalled to life, 1214. A mute mother speaks and her blind son is restored to sight, 1214. A lame and crippled man walks properly and is raised up, 1214. A shepherd weak in his hand is healed, 1214–1215. A man mute for a long time suddenly speaks, 1215. A man lame and disabled in all his limbs walks properly and is healed, 215. A hunchbacked and greatly bent girl is raised up and healed, 1215. A hunchbacked and bent man is freed from every illness, 1215. A matron afflicted by many illnesses is healed, 1215. A man hanging on the gallows is saved from death, 1216. Two women suffering from grave illness are healed, 1216–1217. A possessed man violently tormented by a demon is freed and healed, 1217. A lame and weak man walks properly and is healed, 1217. An anxious woman in her misery finds nine coins in a little cloth, 1218. A lame and horribly crippled boy walks properly and is raised up, 1218. A man suffering from a fistula is healed, 1218. A paralysed matron is healed, 1218–1219. A girl suffering severely because a bone is lodged in her throat is suddenly freed and healed, 1219. A man unjustly taken captive and imprisoned is freed, 1219–1220. A pagan is freed from fetters and obtains his favour, 1220. A boy suffocated beneath a mass of earth is recalled to life, 1220–1221. A man suffering from dropsy is healed, 1221. Unarmed pilgrims defeat armed robbers, 1221. A boy is saved from shipwreck, 1221–1222. A very weak girl is healed, 1222. A blind man is restored to sight, 1222. A possessed man violently agitated by a demon is freed and healed, 1222–1223. A merchant is saved from shipwreck, 1223. Many are saved from an inundation of the sea, 1223. A servant drowned in the sea is saved from death, 1223. The dying son of a count is restored to health, 1224. A boy drowned in a river is recalled to life, 1225. A merchant is freed from captivity, 1225–1226. A man whose hand has been cut off is restored to its former condition, 1226–1227. Theodoricus, suffering from phthisis, is healed, 1227–1228. John, afflicted with a grave illness, is healed, 1228. The city of Poitiers is freed from siege, 1227–1228. An abbot exhausted by a flow of blood is healed, 1228. A matron suffering from dropsy and gout is healed, 1229. Many afflicted by every kind of disease are healed, 1229. A poor woman finds two coins, 1229. An evildoer suffers from swelling of the throat but, when repentant, is saved from the jaws of death, 1230. A woman bearing twins, in very great danger, is happily delivered, 1230.

**ANGELRANNUS, ABBOT OF CENTULA.**—By the power and merits of St Richarius, abbot, a cripple is raised up, CXLI, 1432. Prisoners are released from chains, 1432. A monk is saved from plague, 1432. A spring rises in a waterless place, 1433. A sick woman is healed, 1433. A prostitute becomes crippled as a correction but, when repentant, is raised up, 1433. A woman with contracted hands is healed, 1433. A girl blind from birth is restored to sight, 1434. A sick and dropsical person is healed, 1434. A weak boy is healed; a blind and crippled person is restored to sight and raised up, 1434. A blind woman receives sight; a prisoner in jail is released from chains; two crippled girls are raised up, 1434. A crippled girl is raised up; a blind person is restored to sight; a cripple is raised up; a person suffering from the eyes is healed, 1433. A man horribly crippled, and five male or female cripples, are raised up and healed; a person mute from birth speaks; a boy crippled in the cradle is raised up, 1434. A husband and wife who fall into a well are saved from injury and death, 1436. A man suffering from a fish bone is freed, 1436. A smith falling from a high roof is saved from death, 1437. An insane girl climbing on a roof is preserved safe, 1437. Servants are released from chains, 1438. The saint’s brother is healed; on that saint’s feast day rain ceases, 1438.

**ST BRUNO, BISHOP OF WÜRZBURG.**—By the power and merits of St Bruno, a woman crippled for eight years is raised up, CXLII, 35. Another woman suffering from poison is healed; a lame virgin walks properly; another blind woman is restored to sight; another crippled woman is raised up; a crippled boy and a crippled girl are raised up and healed, 35. A deaf, mute, and crippled woman hears, speaks, and is raised up; another hunchbacked woman is healed; a crippled boy is raised up; a mute virgin tormented by a demon speaks and is freed; another woman with a contracted hand is healed; a blind man receives sight; a crippled boy and crippled girl are raised up, 35. Two crippled girls are raised up, 35–36. Another woman crippled for five years, and a servant crippled from childhood, are raised up, 36. Agnes, crippled in her feet for five years and crawling on her hands, is raised up and healed, 36. Another woman with a contracted and withered leg is healed, 36. A boy badly injured by a wolf and almost lifeless is restored to life and health, 36. A woman deaf and mute from birth hears and speaks, 36. A possessed woman is freed, 36. A blind woman receives sight, 36. A boy dead in water is raised, 36. A possessed girl is freed, 36. A boy captured by thieves is released from chains and freed from captivity, 36. An innocent man hanging on the gallows is freed from death, 6. A possessed woman is healed, 36. A certain possessed mother [Col. 1018] of eleven children, tormented by a demon in each of their births and insane in the last, is freed and healed, 36. A cripple is raised up; a merchant is freed from fetters; a boy crawling on the ground walks properly; a boy dead in a well is recalled to life; a blind virgin is restored to sight; a boy suffering from stone disease is healed; a paralysed man is healed; an innocent man hanging on the gallows is saved from death; a boy weak in the knees and a woman bound with three chains are freed, 36. A boy with a contracted left hand is healed, 36–37. A lame woman with a contracted leg and her son suffering from stone disease receive full health, 37. A woman with a contracted foot who crawls upon her knees is healed, 37. A cripple and two crippled women are raised up, 37–38. Albert, a canon suffering from dropsy, is healed, 38.

**RODULFUS GLABER, MONK OF CLUNY.**—By the power and merits of St William, a man put to death is restored to life, CXLII, 717.

**ODORANNUS, MONK OF ST PETER-VIF OF SENS.**—By the power and merits of Saints Savinian, Potentian, and others, a blind man is restored to sight, 785. In a great drought, abundant rain is obtained, 786. A poor woman crippled in her feet is raised up and healed, 787. The oratory of St Serotinus is saved from fire, 788. Mainardus, blind for three years, is restored to sight, CXLII, 798.

**ST ODILO, ABBOT OF CLUNY.**—By the power and merits of St Odilo, he himself, as a boy, is divinely delivered from grave illness, CXLII, 915. A blind man is restored to sight, 916–917. Water is changed into wine, 917. Thefts are detected, 917–918. A deep river is crossed without a boat, 919–920. A fish of enormous and unusual size is caught in the River Seine, 922. Very many are fed from a few little fish, 922–923. Wine increases and becomes abundant on the Aventine Hill, 923–924. A fever patient is healed, 924. Wineskins emptied for the use of the poor are again divinely filled with wine, 924. A broken glass vessel is mended, 924–925. A monk suffering from a throat ailment is healed, 929. Another suffering from a grave illness is healed, 930. A man suffering severely in an eye is healed, 931–932. A cleric suffering from a wound in his arm is healed, 932. A demoniac is freed, 932–933. A mute person recovers speech, 933. Wine is multiplied, 933–934. An insane, deaf, and mute girl receives full health, 935. A deaf and mute person hears and speaks, 933. A mute and paralysed person speaks and is healed, 933. A mute priest recovers speech, 936–937. A blind man is restored to sight, 937. A blind man and blind woman receive light, 937. An insane person is restored to reason, 937. Rainaldus, paralysed, is healed, 938. A young man with dropsy and an old man with dropsy are healed, 938. A crippled young woman is raised up, 938–939. Another woman, crippled in her legs and infirm, is healed, 939. Another, weak throughout her body, is healed, 939–940. A captive is freed from chains, 94. A mentally deranged person is healed, 940. By the power and merits of St Maiolus, Christians are freed from Saracens, 960. The country is freed from an infestation of wolves, 960–962. By the power and merits of St Adelaide, queen, a lame man walks properly, 985. A blind man is restored to sight, 986. King Henry, afflicted by grave illness, is healed, 987. A rash knight becomes disabled in mind and body but, when later repentant, is healed, 987. A nun limping in both feet walks properly, 987. An innocent man accused of theft and blinded recovers sight, 988. A blind man whose eyes are torn out by the roots recovers his eyes and sight, 988. A blind woman is restored to sight, 988–989. The mute son of a countess speaks, 989. A man lame, bent, and crippled from birth receives full health, 989–990. Burchardus, unjustly despoiled of his property, recovers it, 990–991.

**BERNO, ABBOT OF REICHENAU.**—By the power and merits of St Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, a certain gardener loses his reason together with sight and hearing as a correction, but, when repentant, recovers all these things, CXLII, 1196–1197. Many sick persons, especially epileptics, are freed and healed, 1197. He himself, suffering from a grave illness, is healed by oil consecrated by himself, 1197–1198. A nun becomes lame and weak because of disobedience but, when repentant, walks properly and is healed, 1199.

**LEO, BISHOP OF ATINA.**—By the power and merits of St Mark, bishop and martyr, a priest suffering from a grave illness and despaired of by doctors is healed, CXLIII, 1419. Abundant rain is obtained, 1420–1421. A young man with a withered hand is healed, 1421. A possessed girl is freed, 1421–1422. A monk afflicted by severe headache is healed, 1422.

**SAINTS ARIALDUS AND HERLEMBALD, MARTYRS.**—By the power and merits of St Arialdus, deacon, a paralysed peasant is healed, CXLIII, 1486. A man afflicted by grave illness is healed, 1486. Another, for contempt of the saint, suffers severe internal pain but, when repentant, is healed, 1486.

**ST ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE.**—By the power and merits of St Anno, a wrongly conceived foetus of a nun vanished, CXLIII, 1528. The saint himself, seized by severe fever, is suddenly healed, 1536. A fire is extinguished, 1540. Andrew is raised [Col. 1019] from the dead, 1540. A monk suffering from grave illness is healed, 1544–1545. A blind man is restored to sight, 1545. Another blind man receives sight, 1546. A needy blind woman is restored to sight and helped in her need, 1547. A youth with dropsy is healed, 1547. A woman wholly weak is healed, 1547–1548. By the power and merits of St Bardo, a cripple is raised up, 1551. By the power of St Anno, two innocent young men are freed from hanging, 1553. A demon is expelled, 1572. CXI. LITURGICAL INDEX, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED BY SUBJECT, REFERRING TO EVERYTHING THAT CONCERNS THE RITES, PRAYERS, AND CEREMONIES OF CATHOLIC WORSHIP, AND WITH WHICH THE *Patrology* DEALS.

NOTICE.

A ceremony is an external religious act instituted either by Christ, by the apostles, or by the Church, both in order that the sacrifice may be celebrated more fittingly and solemnly, and that the sacraments may be administered more sacredly and with greater pomp.

A rite is a customary practice that gives solemnity to the performance of an act; thus, wherever usage regulates the solemnity of an act, it may be called a rite or observance. Accordingly, that solemnity of an act which is exercised in sacred matters—such as sacrifice, the sacraments, sacramentals, prayers, or the divine offices—is called a rite; and this seems to be the common ecclesiastical use of the word.

In this Index, therefore, we deal with the various ceremonies and rites used in the Catholic Church. But, lest we be carried too far afield, we have adopted alphabetical order, placing under each word whatever the Fathers have said concerning its nature, origin, usefulness, or necessity, and indicating the various passages by numbers.

[Col. 1041]

**CXII. INDEX OF ECCLESIASTICAL COMPUTATION, OR OF THE VARIOUS CALENDARS, THE PASCHAL CYCLE, AND THE VARIOUS CALCULATIONS OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL YEAR, arranged in alphabetical order of subjects.**
Aequinoctium [Equinox].—The equinox falls on 25 March, according to the Romans, or, as others think, on 28 March: St. Ambrose, XIV, 389. The day of the equinox is 21 March: ibid., XVI, 1032.—On the day of the equinox and solstice: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 506.—On the equinox: the Venerable Bede, XC, 283, 426, 724.—Why equinoxes are so called and when they occur: Alcuin, CI, 1118; Helpericus the monk, CXXXVII, 23.

Annus [Year].—The year of the Hebrews: St. Cyprian, IV, 948. The year of the Romans: ibid.—What the year was like among the Egyptians: Lactantius, VI, 325, 934. On its diversity among the peoples: ibid., 325, 647.—What is the solar year? St. Ambrose, XIV, 200. What is the lunar year according to the Hebrews [Col. 1042] and Romans? ibid. In what month does it begin? St. Ambrose, XIV, 389, 395. The new year is on the Kalends of January: ibid., XVII, 861. Why the year is so called: St. Jerome, XXV, 23. The Jewish Jubilee year: ibid., XXIV, 60. The true Jubilee year: ibid., 565. Years were counted differently among different peoples: ibid., XLI, 451. Egyptian years were formerly ended at intervals of four months: ibid., 358.—What Hebrew years were like: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 607.—What they were among the Alexandrians: ibid., LIV, 601.—Some reckoned the beginning of the year from the day of the Lord’s Nativity: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 537. How many days the lunar year has: Anonymous, LIX, 548.—When the four seasons of the year begin: St. Benedict, LXVI, 407.—Common years: Dionysius Exiguus, [Col. 1043] LXVII, 23. Embolismic years: ibid., 24. Solar years: ibid. On the years of Christ: ibid., 497.—From what month the year begins: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 821. The beginning of the ecclesiastical year formerly in Gaul: ibid., 773, note. A year begun from the Nativity of the Lord: St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 347. From Easter: ibid., 404.—A year is lunar, solstitial, or great: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXII, 222. The common year: ibid., 249. The embolismic year: ibid. The leap year: ibid.—On years: St. Isidore, LXXXI, 971; the Venerable Bede, XC, 284.—On natural years: ibid., 462. On the unequal years of the ancients: ibid., 464. On the years of the Lord’s Incarnation: ibid., 491. Why the year is so named: ibid., 589. In how many senses are years spoken of? ibid. How do you define the solar year? ibid.—What is a year? Alcuin, CI, 1119. Lunar, solar, and great year: ibid. From what month a proper year should begin: ibid., C, 266, 267.—The common year: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 127. The embolismic year: ibid. The leap year: ibid. There is a lunar and a solar year: ibid., 304.—How the solar year is constituted and the rationale of the leap year: Hilpericus the monk, CXXXVII, 27. How years from the Incarnation of the Lord may be found: ibid., 37.—The year is called from renewal (*innovando*), or from a ring (*annulus*), because, like a circle, it turns back repeatedly upon itself: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 154. Lunar year: ibid., 155. Common year: ibid. Embolismic year: ibid. Leap year: ibid. What the civil year was among the ancients: ibid. How the solar year is found: ibid., CLXXII, 161.

Assis.—What an *assis* is: Anonymous, LIX, 546, 554, 555.

Atomi [Atoms].—The Venerable Bede, XC, 316.—On the indivisible atom: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 677.—On atoms in the first instant: Anonymous, CXXIX, 1316.—How time is divided into atoms, instants, moments, and so forth: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 147.

Bissextus [Leap Year].—The leap day comes after four years: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 275; XLII, 893.—How the leap year is marked: Anonymous, LIX, 547, 548.—The leap day: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 502.—When a year is a leap year: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1250.—A year is called leap-year through the addition of one day, which occurs every fourth year: St. Isidore, LXXXII, 249. Why it is called *bissextus*: ibid.—How a leap year is found: the Venerable Bede, XC, 725. Hours are omitted for three years, and on the fourth one day is added; then the year is called leap-year, having 366 days: ibid., 463. On the rationale of the leap year: ibid., 466 ff. On the measure of the increase and the leap year: ibid., 469.—On the leap year in the courses of sun and moon: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 698. A rule for finding the leap year: ibid., 699.—On moments for the leap year: Anonymous, CXXIX, 1293. How to find the leap year through the twelve signs: ibid., 1294. On the rationale of the leap year: ibid., 1296. On displaying the leap year through the solar cycle: ibid., 1314.—The leap year, inserted in the fourth year, ends one day longer than the preceding year: ibid.; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 155. On finding the leap year: ibid., 162.

Circulus [Cycle].—The Paschal cycle: Hilarianus, XIII, 1105.—The cycle of the lunar year: St. Jerome, XXII, 822.—The number of the lunar cycle is indicated: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 494. What is needed to find the year of the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 501.—Which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1249.—How Eusebius of Caesarea first introduced the order of the nineteen-year cycle: the Venerable Bede, XC, 483. That lunar nineteen-year cycle is divided into embolismic and common years: ibid., 485, 488. On the division of the nineteen-year cycle into an octaeteris and a hendecaeteris: ibid., 488, 489. How to know what the moon is in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 394. In every nineteen-year cycle one day is omitted, called the leap of the moon: ibid., 473, 474. The sequence of lunar dates in each year of the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 505, note and following.—How the year of the nineteen-year cycle is found: ibid., 508.—A book on the cycles of Cyril, Dionysius Exiguus, and the Venerable Bede: St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 574. That the solar cycle is completed in 28 years, but the lunar cycle in 19: ibid., 574, 575.

Concurrentes [Concurrent Days].—On displaying the concurrents: Anonymous, CXXIX, 1315, 1321.—What is needed to find the concurrents of each year: Hilpericus, CXXXVII, 58. A table in which concurrents are marked and compared together: ibid., 1287; Honorius, CLXXII, 159. From what point concurrents take their beginning: ibid., 160. How concurrents are found: ibid., 162.

Computus [Computation].—A book on Paschal computation: Anonymous, LIX, 545.—Paschal computation: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1249.—On the method of computation: the Venerable Bede, XC, 579. Dialogue on computation: ibid., 647. The common computation called the *Ephemeris*: ibid., 727. Computation concerning the method of embolisms [Col. 1044]: ibid.—A book on computation: Helpericus, CXXXVII, 21.

Cyclus [Cycle].—The Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle: St. Leo the Great, CIV, 601 note, 607. Its division into the octaeteris and hendecaeteris: ibid. The Latin eighty-four-year cycle, beginning with the consulship of Antoninus and Siagrius: ibid., note.—The nineteen-year cycle continually returns upon itself through the octaeteris and hendecaeteris: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 23. On the Dionysian cycle and its origin: ibid., 453, 454. How, after various cycles had successively been tried, the nineteen-year cycle was finally established as the limit by Heto, in year 428 of the Julian Period, 321 from the foundation of the City, and 433 before the Incarnation: ibid., 455, 456, 457. Who first among Eastern Christians employed this cycle for the Paschal question: ibid., 458. The Council of Nicaea subsequently approved it: ibid. Eusebius of Caesarea and Anastasius wrote about this cycle: ibid., 460. At the beginning of the Dionysian cycle, A.D. 532, in solar cycle 19, dominical letter C, golden number 1, Easter Sunday is marked as 11 April, the twentieth moon: ibid., 487, note. When the cycle of ninety-five years had elapsed, namely in A.D. 627, Easter in the cycle of Isidore is marked as the day before the Ides, or 12 April, the twenty-first moon: ibid. Dionysius appears to have so arranged the ninety-five-year cycle that it would represent in rotation weekdays, Easter Sundays, and lunar dates: ibid., 488, note. The Dionysian cycle, in which the fourteenth Paschal moons are found without error at every time: ibid., 493 ff. What is needed for finding the lunar cycle: ibid. What is needed for determining on which weekday the fourteenth moon falls in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 505. Likewise in the second year, with annotation: ibid.—On the Paschal cycle: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, 245. On the cycle of St. Hippolytus: ibid. On St. Cyril’s ninety-five-year cycle: ibid., 245. The nineteen-year cycle consists partly of common and partly of embolismic years: ibid.—On the lunar cycle: the Venerable Bede, XC, 506; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 711. A rule for the lunar cycle: ibid., 712.—A marble table representing the statue and Paschal cycle of St. Hippolytus the bishop: Anastasius, CXXVII, 1293. Sequence of the nineteen-year periods of each cycle: ibid., CXXIX, 1286 ff. On the interruption of the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 1298. On displaying the leap year through the solar cycle: ibid., 1314. On demonstrating the solar and lunar cycles by the fingers: ibid., 1322. Rules concerning the great nineteen-year and lunar cycles, and on demonstrating the great cycle through years from the creation of the world: ibid. On the number of cycles, leap days, and lunar leaps from the creation of the world: ibid., 1331. On the nineteen-year cycle: ibid.—How the solar cycle is found through the zodiac: Helpericus, CXXXVII, 59. On the three years of the nineteen-year cycle in which the moon does not keep the order of the epacts, and how the Paschal moon is to be observed: ibid., 46.—Commentary on the cycle of Victorius: CXXXIX, 570.—The great Paschal year of 532 years is repeated; it contains twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles and nineteen solar cycles: St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 574, 575.—A table in which concurrents are marked and compared together. The epacts of the nineteen-year cycle: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 1287.—On the leap-year cycle: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 156. Why it is called the nineteen-year cycle: ibid., 157. That it is divided into an octaeteris and a hendecaeteris: ibid. On finding the lunar cycle: ibid., 162.

Dies [Day].—The Romans never attached days to those following the Kalends: Lactantius, VII, 384.—Lunar days begin in the evening and end on the following evening: Hilarianus, XIII, 1109.—Day and night follow one another in fixed spans of hours: St. Jerome, XXII, 821.—How the names “day” and “night” are to be understood: St. Augustine, XXXIV, 230, 295. How day and night could have existed before the creation of the sun: ibid., XLI, 231, 273. A day is made by the revolution of the fixed stars: ibid., XXXIV, 236. “Day” is now called the sun’s stay over the earth, now the duration of its whole circuit from east to west: ibid., XXXII, 821; XXXIII, 911. In earlier times the day was twenty-four hours, as it is now: ibid., XLI, 455. A winter day has as many hours as a summer day, although shorter ones: ibid., XXXIV, 159. Weekday: ibid., XXXVIII, 1201. Intercalary days: ibid., XLI, 451. Sunday is called the first of the Sabbath, second of the Sabbath, or second feria: ibid., XXXVII, 1192, 1960. Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Easter by calculation of sun and moon: ibid., XXXIII, 209.—Intercalary days: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 21. Leap day: ibid., 502.—Which day of the week it is: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1250.—On the names of days among Romans and Jews: St. Isidore, LXXXII, 216. On days: ibid., LXXXI, 963. A day is the sun’s presence above the earth and, properly so called, is completed in twenty-four hours: the Venerable Bede, XC, 279. A day is air illuminated by the sun and takes its name from separating and dividing darkness from light: ibid., 308, 580. A day properly speaking is completed by the circuit [Col. 1045] of the sun illuminating the whole world, which occurs in twenty-four hours: ibid., 309, 580. On the days of creation: ibid., 309, note and following. Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Persians reckon the course of the day from morning to morning: ibid., 513, 581. Egyptians, from sunset to sunset: ibid. Romans, from midnight to midnight; Umbrians and Athenians customarily reckon their days from noon to noon: ibid., 313, 581. Christ in the Gospel commanded the day’s time to begin from evening, that is, from sunset: ibid., 314, 581. The question is asked why the Hebrew people celebrated all their feasts from the preceding evening, the Lawgiver saying: “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your sabbaths”: ibid., 316. The pagans distinguished days by the names of their gods: ibid., 328, 583. The German names of days are derived in the pagan fashion: *Sontag* means “day of the sun”; *Montag*, “day of the moon”; *Donnerstag*, “day of Jupiter,” and so forth: ibid., 332, note. On the inequality of days: ibid., 431.—A legal day consists of twenty-four hours: Alcuin, CI, 1114. Among Egyptians the day begins at sunset; among Persians, at sunrise; according to the Athenians, at the sixth hour of the day; and among the Romans, at midnight: ibid. Why the day is named from gods: ibid. Roman names of the days: ibid. What they were called among the Hebrews: ibid. How the day is divided: ibid. On the day and its parts: ibid., 679. Where the day begins and where it ends: ibid. On the days of the year: ibid., CXXIX, 1295. What a day is: ibid., 1307.—Why days are now shorter and now longer: Honorius, CLXXII, 147. On the beginning and end of days among various peoples: ibid., 150.

Embolismus [Embolism].—The embolisms, or differences, arising from the five remaining days at the end of the year, produce one month after a certain lapse of time: Hilarianus, XIII, 1112. What the effects of embolisms are: ibid.—The embolismic year: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 601 and 607. In the octaeteris there are five common years and three embolisms: ibid., LXVII, 24. Calculations of common and embolismic years by days: ibid.—An embolismic year is one that contains thirteen lunar months, or 384 days; *embolismus* in Greek means “addition”: St. Isidore, LXXXII, 249. How embolisms and common years are found: ibid.—The embolismic lunar year is called that which, beginning from the Paschal moon, includes thirteen months and 384 days: the Venerable Bede, XC, 463.—On common years and embolisms: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 700. On the common year and embolism: ibid., CXXIX, 1285. When Easter ought to be celebrated in an embolismic year: ibid., 1285. On the greater embolism: ibid.—Why we call a year now common, now embolismic: Hispericus, CXXXVI, 31. On the controversy over embolisms: Pope St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 1289.—The embolismic year, or increase, is made up of thirteen months: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 154. On embolism: ibid., 164.

Epactae [Epacts].—The epacts, as the Greeks call them, are annual lunar additions of eleven days, which return to themselves after thirty days: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 20. In twelve lunar months 354 days are counted, to which eleven epact days must be added so that the lunar year may equal the solar: ibid., 21. In the first year of the following cycle, not eleven but twelve lunar epacts are added: ibid., 25. What is needed to find the epacts: ibid., 499, 500.—How many epacts there are: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1249.—Epacts, or intercalary days, are annual lunar additions: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 245. No more than twenty-nine epacts are to be counted; beyond that one must return and pronounce eleven: ibid., 250.—Epacts, so called from Greek, are additions of eleven days made in every year: the Venerable Bede, XC, 497. To understand these additions that must be made yearly, it is necessary to note that the lunar date advances and increases by eleven days every year: ibid. Once the nineteen-year cycle is completed, the epacts return to themselves: ibid. Solar epacts: ibid., 503. Hence the solar epact is called the addition occurring in every leap year, every fourth year: ibid. How the epacts of the solar cycle are found: ibid., 504. On the return and finger-reckoning computation of the epacts of the nineteen-year lunar cycle and of the solar epacts: ibid.—On lunar epacts: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 706. Rule concerning the epacts to be received: ibid. On solar epacts: ibid., 708. Rule concerning solar epacts: ibid. On the return and finger-reckoning computation of both epacts, solar and lunar: ibid., 711. On epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months: ibid., CXXIX, 1289. On epacts on 22 March: ibid. Rule for solar epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months: ibid., 1323.—Why epacts are so called: Helpericus, CXXXVII, 1323. What use epacts have: ibid. How epacts are found: ibid., 58. On the three years of the nineteen-year cycle in which the moon does not keep the order of epacts, and how the Paschal moon is to be observed: ibid., 46. On epacts: ibid., 160, 161.

Feriae [Weekdays].—Why *feriae* are so called: Alcuin, CI, 1115. On weekdays, and who taught them: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 682.

Hebdomada [Week].—On the week: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, [Col. 1046] 218.—*Hebdomada* is a Greek word and means the number seven: the Venerable Bede, XC, 326, 582. What the distinction is between *hebdomada* and *heptomada*: ibid., note. Marcus Varro, a man of the keenest intellect, wrote a book *On Weeks*: ibid. Among the Jews a week was counted from the Sabbath: ibid., 327, 583. The Hebrews sometimes had weeks of years, as is found in Daniel: ibid., 333 ff. Daniel’s weeks are calculated: ibid. What a week is and why it is so called: Alcuin, CI, 1117. On the week and the kinds of weeks: ibid., 681. On Daniel’s weeks: ibid. On the week: ibid., CXXIX, 1300. On the week among the ancients: Honorius, CLXXII, 151.

Idus [Ides].—According to Roman custom, the month is divided into Nones, Ides, and Kalends: Dionysius Filocalus, XIII, 354.—The Ides are derived from *iduare*, an Etruscan word meaning “to divide”; hence a widow is called “divided.” Some derive *Ides* from εἰδέα, “form,” because on that day the moon displays her full form: the Venerable Bede, XC, 354.—What Kalends, Nones, and Ides are: Alcuin, CI, 1118. On the Ides: ibid., 686.—The Ides derive from *iduo*, that is, “divide,” or from *idea*, “form,” because the moon shows herself full: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 153.

Indictio [Indiction].—Roman indictions begin in September: St. Ambrose, XIV, 390.—The indication of the indiction, and how variously it is marked on inscriptions: St. Nicetas of Aquileia, LII, 944 ff.—Indictions are revolutions of fifteen years: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 20. The years of the Roman indiction: ibid., 493. What is needed to find the indiction: ibid., 499. Which indiction it is: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1249.—On Roman indictions: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 705. Rule for finding indictions: ibid., 706. On the Roman indiction: ibid., CXXIX, 1364, 1365. The origin of indictions and how they are found each year: ibid. Indictions are called from *indicendo* (“proclaiming”), because after fifteen years the census returned: ibid.—On finding the indiction: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 161.

Jubilaeus [Jubilee].—What the Jubilee is: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, 222; Alcuin, CI, 1120.

Kalendarium [Calendar].—In a decree of the year 414, the word *kalendarium* is used for the public treasury, or rather for what is now called in French a *budget*: Constantine the Great, VIII, 110, 111.—Certain calendars are cited in the Dissertation on the death of St. Zeno: St. Zeno of Verona, XI, 154. The ancient calendar of Polemius Silvius: ibid., XIII, 676, note. St. Isidore’s book on the calendar: LXXXI, 963. Mozarabic calendar: ibid., LXXXV, 95 ff. Mention of an ancient Neapolitan calendar written on marble: ibid., 934. Fragment of a very ancient calendar published by Francisco de Pisa: ibid., 1050. Gothic calendar, indicating the days of the month, more ancient than the rest: ibid., LXXXVI, 37. That knowledge of the calendar has been of no little use among more recent writers, etc.: ibid., CXXIX, 1275. A calendar revolving through the twelve months of the year: ibid., 1337.

Kalendae [Kalends].—Polemius Silvius, XIII, 676.—The Kalends are marked: St. Prothadius of Besançon, LXXX, 411.—The Kalends are named from Greek χαλῶ, “I call,” because on that day the people were summoned to the sacred buildings.—The Venerable Bede, XC, 353, 585. The Greeks and Egyptians do not have Kalends as the Romans do: ibid., 354. On the Kalends: Alcuin, ibid., 1118.—Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 686. On finding the weekday of the Kalends of any month: CXXIX, 1288.—Whence arise the regulars for finding the weekday of the Kalends: Hilpericus, CXXXVII, 27.—How to find the weekday on which the Kalends fall, through the days of the month or year: ibid.—Kalends are called in Greek χαλέω, “I summon”: why this is so: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 153.

Luna [Moon].—The first moon is to be sought from 5 March to 2 April, or from 18 March to 15 April: ibid.—How the moon, increasing from the first day to the fourteenth, comes to its fullness, and from the fifteenth to the thirtieth decreases back to its earlier state: ibid., 2109.—This day of the full moon is the first of the month and year according to Moses: ibid., 1109.—Lunar days begin in the evening and end on the following evening: ibid., 1109.—By completing its course twelve times in 300 days, with a few days added, the moon completes the year according to the Hebrews: St. Ambrose, XIV, 200.—According to the Romans, after one day has been added in the leap year once within five years, the moon completes its course: ibid.—When the moon is said to be in the third cycle: St. Ambrose, XVI, 329.—The cycle of the lunar year: St. Jerome, XXII, 822. What the moon’s poverty and wealth are: ibid.—What the moon was like when created: St. Augustine, XXIV, 275. In what sense it is always full: ibid., 216. Whence it has its light: ibid., XXXVI, 131. Whence its waxing and waning arise: ibid., XXXIII, 207.—Which is the fourteenth Paschal moon: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 488. What is needed to find the lunar cycle: ibid., 501. What is needed to determine on which weekday [Col. 1047] the fourteenth moon falls in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle: St. Augustine, 505.—What is needed to find the lunar cycle: Cassiodorus, LXXIX, 1250. What lunar date Easter Day falls upon: ibid.—On the moon: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, 174. On the interval between moons and the course of the moon: ibid., 176. The moon completes the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months, traversing each sign in two days, six hours, and a *bisse*, that is, eight ounces of one hour: the Venerable Bede, XC, 370, note; 391. Calculation for finding in what sign the moon is: ibid., 382. In each month—that is, in twenty-nine days and twelve hours—the moon circles the twelve signs and one additional sign: ibid. Every day, by four points, if waxing, the moon departs from the sun; if waning, it returns to the sun: ibid., 381. How one who does not know the signs can nevertheless know the course of the moon: ibid., 388.—That the moon remains in each sign two days, six hours, and a *bisse*, that is, two thirds of an hour: the Venerable Bede, XC, 391.—What lunar date falls on each Kalends: ibid., 394. How one unable or unwilling to compute may know the moon’s age: ibid., 398. For how many hours it shines: ibid. Or by how many points it shines: ibid., 399. A rule concerning any lunar date or weekday: ibid., 396. When or why the moon appears prone, supine, or upright: ibid., 403. Why the moon, although lower in position, sometimes appears above the sun: ibid., 409. On the leap of the moon: ibid., 472. The lunar year properly so called consists of twelve like months and is completed in 354 days: ibid., XC, 463, 586. The lunar nineteen-year cycle is divided into embolismic and common years, which follow one another in this order: XC, 485, 486. The sequence of lunar dates in every year of the nineteen-year cycle, where common and embolismic years are marked according to Dionysius: ibid., 505, note and following. Rule for finding the moon: ibid., 14, 510, 514. On the moon of the present day: ibid., 513. Rules for finding the moon: ibid., 828. Rule for investigating the moon’s course: ibid., 592. Rule for finding how many hours the moon shines: ibid., 398. On the lunar leap: ibid., 472. On lunar regulars: ibid., 701. Rule concerning the course of sun and moon through the days of the year: ibid., 703. On the return and finger-reckoning computation of both epacts, solar and lunar: ibid., 504. On the lunar cycle: ibid., 506. Rule for the lunar cycle: ibid., 508.—Rule for finding what lunar date falls on the Kalends of January: ibid. On the fourteenth Paschal moon: ibid. Rule concerning the same fourteenth moon: ibid., 713. Another rule: ibid., 714.—On the rationale of the lunar leap: Alcuin, C, 234, 266; ibid., CI, 979. On seeking the moon’s birth: ibid., CXXIX, 1284. On the four differences of the moon: ibid., 1287. On the rule for the moon: ibid., 1288. On the leap of the moon: ibid., 1297. On the course of the moon: ibid., 1298. On the Paschal moon: ibid., 1299. On the month and inquiry concerning the moon; on the points of the moon: ibid., 1305. On the kindling of the moon: ibid. On the fourteenth moon: ibid., 1308. On the Paschal moon: ibid., 1309.—On the moon on the Kalends of January and 22 March: ibid., 1311. On displaying the first moon of the first month: ibid., 1314. In what sign the sun runs, and in what sign the moon: ibid., 1325. On the speed of the moon’s course: ibid., 1320. Rules concerning the great nineteen-year and lunar cycles: ibid., 1330. What one ought to do if ignorant of the moon’s course: ibid., 1334. On the moon’s course through the twelve signs in the year: ibid., 1337. How the night decreases through the lunar leap over nineteen years: ibid., 1349.—How the lunar date is pronounced each day: Hilpericus, CXXXVII, 30. Why now the thirtieth and now the twenty-ninth moon is pronounced: ibid. Whence lunar leaps are made, or where they are more properly omitted: ibid., CXXXVII, 32. How many hours the moon shines on each night: ibid., 34. In what sign the moon is on each day: ibid., 35. At what hour the moon is kindled, or at what hour in its kindling it changes its age: ibid., 36.—On the usefulness of lunar regulars: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 1289. On the leap of the moon: ibid.—How the moon’s course is calculated on the joints of the fingers: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 157. On the leap of the moon and its origin: ibid., 159. How many hours the moon shines: ibid., 161. By how many parts the moon is distant from the sun: ibid. In what sign the moon is: ibid. On finding the lunar cycle: ibid., 162.

Mensis [Month].—How months are distinguished into groups of three by capital letters: Dionysius Filocalus, XIII, 675. According to Roman custom, the month is divided into Nones, Ides, and Kalends: ibid.—A book on the exposition of the month and day of Easter: Hilarianus, XIII, 1105. Correspondences of each Hebrew month with Roman months: ibid., 1110.—The Greek *mēn* [μήν, “month”] is derived from *mene*, “moon”: St. Ambrose, XIV, 1033. The ancients customarily observed months from the beginning of the moon: ibid., 1100; XVI, 1033. The moon makes months; the sun makes the day: ibid., XVII, 360. The Egyptian months Phamenoth and Pharmuthi, in which the days of Lent and the Passion occur: ibid., 828.—The month Quintilis is called July by decree of Antony, because Julius Caesar was born in it: LI, 548.—How greatly those err who count twelve lunar months as consisting only of thirty days, even if they add five intercalary [Col. 1048] days in seeming to compute the solar year: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 21. In twelve lunar months 354 days are counted, to which eleven epact days must be added so that the lunar year may equal the solar year: ibid.—A month is called from measure, but is better derived from the Greek μήνη, a word meaning “moon”: the Venerable Bede, XC, 341, 584. In Hebrew a month is called *fur*, which also signifies the moon: ibid., 341. The ancients customarily counted their months not from the course of the sun but from that of the moon: ibid. A lunar month is rightly defined as “the circuit and renewal of the moon’s light, from new moon to new moon”: ibid., 343. A solar month is the sun’s passage through a twelfth part of the zodiac, completed in thirty days and ten half-hours: ibid., 344. By nature the solar month has thirty days, ten hours, and a half; by convention it has only thirty days: ibid., note. Likewise by nature the lunar month has twenty-nine days and twelve hours, but by convention it has twenty-nine or even thirty days: ibid., note. The first month of the Hebrews, whose middle—that is, its fourteenth moon—is the first after the vernal equinox, is called Nisan: ibid., 348. Only Roman and Egyptian months are fixed: that is, the first day of every month—for example, January—always comes twenty days after the winter solstice: ibid. A table diligently collected by Bede from good authorities, giving the names of Roman, Egyptian, Hebrew, Greek, and British months according to the temporal order in which they fall: ibid., XC, 347. Another table comparing the months of Athenians, Achaeans, Macedonians, Bithynians, and Cypriots with Roman months, taken from Theodorus Gaza: ibid. Among Greek writers, the reckoning of months is not always consistent; for example, Anthesterion corresponds to November according to Gaza, to April according to Macrobius, and to March according to others, etc.: ibid. A table of German, Indian, Chaldean, and Alexandrian months in barbarian times: ibid. The etymology of the Roman months: ibid., 349, 585. At first March was the first month and April the second: ibid., 349. Romulus established a year of only ten months, namely 304 days: ibid., 351. Numa made two other months from the remaining fifty-six days and added them to the beginning of the year: ibid. Why the Romans divided the month into Kalends, Nones, and Ides: ibid., 353, 585. The Greeks distinguish the month by decades, and the first day of every month is called *Neomenia* (“new moon”): ibid. The etymologies of English months: ibid., 356. How in an embolismic year they had thirteen months and added a fourth month to summer: ibid. Each month has its own signs in the circle of the zodiac: ibid., 358.—Why the month is so called: Alcuin, CI, 1117. How and why months are named: ibid. On months—what they are and whence *mensis* is derived: ibid., 682. What a lunar and a solar month are: ibid., 683. On the names of months among Romans: ibid. On Hebrew months: ibid., 683. On Egyptian months: ibid., 684. On Greek months: ibid. Which months the Romans had, and the derivation of each name: ibid., 684, 685. On months: ibid., CXXIX, 1298, 1301, 1302, 1303. On the correspondence of months: ibid., 1333. On the names of months among Romans, Hebrews, Macedonians, and Egyptians: ibid., 1363. A table of correspondence among Roman, Hebrew, Egyptian, Greek, English, and Armenian months: ibid., 1291, 1292.—What a month is: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 151. A lunar month consists of twenty-nine days and twelve hours: ibid. A solar month is made up of thirty days and ten half-hours: ibid. On names of months among the ancients and various peoples, and their etymologies: ibid. Whence months receive their names: ibid., 153.

Nonae [Nones].—According to Roman custom, the month is divided into Nones, Ides, and Kalends: Dionysius Filocalus, XIII, 675. Why the Nones are so called: ibid., 676.—The Nones are so called because nine days are always counted from them to the Ides: the Venerable Bede, XC, 353, 555.—On the Nones: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 686.—They are called Nones because the populace then assembled in the city over nine days: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 153.

Olympiades [Olympiads].—What Olympiads are: St. Isidore of Spain, LXXXII, 222.—An Olympiad is a period of four years: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 156.

Pascha [Easter].—We celebrate Easter in an annual cycle, in the first month: Tertullian, II, 973. Blastus, a Judaizing heretic, says that Easter must be observed only according to the Law of Moses, on the fourteenth day of the month: ibid., 72.—Computation concerning Easter: St. Cyprian, IV, 940 ff.—Easter was sometimes celebrated in the second month: St. Gaudentius, XX, 845. The time for celebrating Easter: ibid., 816.—The bishops of Asia celebrate Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon: St. Jerome, XXIII, 883.—Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Easter by calculation of sun and moon: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 209. They observe that the Sabbath should occur, which [Col. 1049] the Jews do not observe: ibid., 211.—Easter is to be celebrated on 23 April: St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 600. Easter was celebrated on 24 April by Leo, out of concern for peace, owing to the obstinate insistence of the Alexandrian bishop and the Easterners: ibid., 606. The question concerning Easter Day arises: ibid., 565, 566.—Leo, concerned to determine Easter Day, writes concerning Easter of 444 to St. Cyril and Paschasinus, from whom a reply was received: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 606. What the controversy over Easter in that year concerned: ibid., 601. Concerning Easter of 445, he writes to Paschasinus, Marcian, and Julian: ibid., 929, 1055, 1058, 1072, 1082. The reply of Proterius: ibid., 1084. Easter Day appointed for all Westerners by the Roman pontiff: ibid., 1111. Formal letters indicating Easter: ibid., 945, 1081, 1101. What Easter Day was in the year 452: ibid., 945. What it was in 453 and 454: ibid., 1058. Controversy concerning Easter of 444: ibid., LV, 429, note. Another concerning Easter of 454: ibid., 299. Responsibility for the Paschal computation entrusted to the Alexandrian bishop: ibid. On Paschal computation: ibid., LIX, 545.—On what day Easter should be celebrated: St. Benedict, LXVI, 410.—A book on Easter: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 485. Dionysius’s letter on the method of Easter: ibid., 513. Two letters on the method of Easter: ibid., 20.—At what time Westerners celebrated the Paschal feast: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1116, 1153. How it may be known on what lunar date it falls: ibid., 1250.—The question of Easter long and extensively debated: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 947. In Sardinia, the announcement of Easter belonged to the metropolitan: St. Gregory, LXXVII, 947. In assigning Easter Day, the Scots dissented from the Church: ibid., 1061, 1063.—On the Paschal controversy: St. Commianus, LXXXVII, 969.—On Easter Sunday: the Venerable Bede, XC, 511. A book on the celebration of Easter: ibid., [Col. 1050] 599.—On Easter: Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 951.—On what day Easter is celebrated: Remigius of Chur, CII, 1104.—On the Paschal cycle: Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 125.—What the Paschal limit is, or when it is to be observed: Helpericus, CXXXVII, 40. A restatement concerning the Paschal limit, and why the feast itself is celebrated only on Sunday: ibid., 43. How that limit is found in each year: ibid., 44. How through
the others are found under “Paschal limit,” ibid., 45.---It is not to be celebrated at the same time by all, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 403. **Regulars.**---Regulars for finding the weekday; lunar regulars of the ancients; lunar regulars of the Egyptians; lunar regulars of the Romans, CXLVIII, 1287. On lunar regulars, ibid., 1289. On the regulars of the Fathers, ibid. On the usefulness of lunar regulars, ibid., 1290.---On the regulars of weekdays, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 159. **Solstitial.**---A solstitial year is one in which the sun, having completed its circuit through all the signs, returns to that from which it began its course, St. Ambrose, XIV, 200. **Zodiac.**---Each sign of the Zodiac has ten points, or two hours, Bede the Venerable, XC, 381.---On the twelve signs of the Zodiac, Alcuin, CI, 690. Demonstration of the signs by the sun’s course, ibid., 691. On the twelve signs of the Zodiac, the same author, CXXIX, 1223. On the reasons why the twelve signs received their names, ibid. In which sign the sun runs, and in which the moon, ibid., 1325. Computations concerning the sun’s course through the twelve signs, ibid., 1327. On the sun’s course through the twelve signs of the Zodiac, ibid., 1343 ff.---How the lunar cycle is found through the Zodiac, Helpericus, CXXXVIII, 39.---On the twelve signs of the Zodiac, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 142. On the signs of the Zodiac and the sun’s parallels, ibid., 148.

SERIES THIRTEENTH.

[Col. 1049]

[PREFACE.]

The Church, which is the society of those who truly worship God, was established and ordered by Christ the lawgiver, who conferred upon it legislative power. Hence the Church has a twofold power, namely human and divine; hence ecclesiastical laws require due submission and inward assent, and bind in conscience. Accordingly, in this series we present Indexes concerning Canon Law; concerning the legislation and laws of the Church; concerning Councils; concerning the decrees of the supreme Pontiffs; concerning ecclesiastical and monastic discipline; concerning censures, excommunications, and irregularities, etc.; concerning civil legislation insofar as it touches religion; and concerning the immunities and privileges of the Church of God granted by secular power.

[Col. 1049]

CXIII. INDEX CONCERNING CANON LAW, SETTING FORTH THE POWER OF THE CHURCH WITH RESPECT TO MAKING LAWS, AND THE VARIOUS COLLECTIONS OF DECREES AND CANONS NOTICED IN THE PATROLOGY.

NOTICE.

In this Index we have established two parts. The former sets forth various opinions and statements of the Holy Fathers concerning the authority and power of the Catholic Church to impose laws which Christians must obey; the latter records all the various Collections of Decretals and Canons found in our course of Patrology. But since we have already treated the authority and power of the Church with respect to laws in Index LXXIX, let the kindly reader consult that Index; here, therefore, they are only listed.

Various collections of decrees and canons.

[Col. 1049] Decrees attributed to St. Lucius, III, 975. Decrees of Pope Lucius drawn from Gratian, III, 981. Decretal letters attributed to St. Stephen, III, 997. Councils of Carthage concerning the baptism of infants, III, 1012. [Col. 1050] Four doubtful letters of St. Felix I, pope and martyr, V, 145. Decrees of Pope Eutychian, V, 177. Decrees and constitutions: Constantine the Great, VIII, 93. [Col. 1051] Decrees of Pope Julius I, according to Gratian and Ivo, VIII, 968. Rescript of Julius I against the Easterners, VIII, 980. Rescript to the bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod: St. Felix, pope, II, 17. Selected decrees of Theodosius concerning religion, XIII, 521. Letters and decrees of St. Siricius, pope, XIII, 1131. Letters and decrees of St. Innocent I, pope, XX, 463. Letters and decrees of St. Zosimus, pope, XX, 669 ff. Letters and decrees of St. Boniface I, pope, XX, 749. Letters and decrees of St. Celestine I, pope, L, 429. Letters of St. Leo the Great, pope, LIV, 593, 597, 610, 614, 616, 624, 628, 636, 645, 663, 666, 695, 709, 1199, 1209. Code of ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the holy Apostolic See: St. Leo the Great, LVI, 359. Ancient Latin edition of the canons, LVI, 748. Old Latin translation of the Nicene, Sardican, and Carthaginian canons, LVI, 824. Documents of ancient canon law, LVI, 863. Letters and decrees of Pope Felix III, LVIII, 924. Letters and decrees of Pope Gelasius, LIX, 47. Canons attributed to Gelasius, LIX, 142. Letters and decrees of Pope Symmachus, LXII, 49 ff., 54. Letters and decrees of Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 423, 525. Code of the canons of the universal Church: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 40. Ancient code of canons of the Roman Church, LXVII, 136. Collection of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs: Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 229. Abridgment of the canons: Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 949. Letters and decrees of Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 16. Canons of St. Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre, LXXII, 761. Abridgment of the canons by Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, LXXXVIII, 817. [Col. 1052] Canonical compendium of Crisconius, African bishop, LXXXVIII, 830. Rule for canons according to D’Achery’s recension: St. Chrodegang of Metz, LXXXIX, 1057. Chapters selected from an ancient collection of canons compiled in Ireland about the eighth century, XCVI, 1281. Irish canons to be added to the published editions of the *Spicilegium*, XCVI, 1131. Canons selected from the most ancient collection of canons in the Herovallian manuscript, XCIX, 989. Canons for his own diocese: Remigius of Curvensis, CII, 1093. Code of monastic and canonical rules: St. Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 393. Canons issued at the Council of Vern: St. Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 612. Decrees or rescripts collected from Gratian, CXIX, 1184. On ecclesiastical disciplines: Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 185. Capitulary of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 28. Two parts on contempt for the canons: Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 485. Ancient collection of canons, CXXXVIII, 397. Ecclesiastical laws of Anglo-Saxon kings who flourished in the tenth century, CXXXVIII, 447. Collection of canons: St. Abbo, abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 471. African canons, CXXXIX, 1469. Twenty books of Decrees: Burchard of Worms, CXL, 537. Statutes of the canons concerning priests’ duties, CXL, 1067. Canonical collection divided into thirteen books: St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 485. *Decretum*, seventeen books: Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 60. *Panormia*, eight books, CLXI, 1045. *Concord of Discordant Canons*: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 29.

[Col. 1051]

CXIV. INDEX CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL AND MONASTIC LEGISLATION, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGING ALL LAWS, DECREES, AND DECISIONS RELATING TO RELIGION AND TO ECCLESIASTICAL LIFE.

[Col. 1051] **Absentees.**—That judges are not to pronounce sentence against an absent person, and that an informer is not to be heard, Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 988.—That a sentence of bishops against an absent person is void, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 345.—Absent persons can neither be accused nor judged, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 699.

**Accusation.**—On the manner of receiving an accusation against clerics, St. Eutychian, V, 172.
