Those who are not to be admitted to accuse religious persons, ibid.—Pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians, Pope Caius, V, 183. On bishops, priests, or deacons, or other clerics, being accused before bishops, ibid.—That no one is to accuse a bishop before secular arbiters, Pope Felix II, XIII, 19. On accusations against bishops and the restoration of property taken from them, ibid., 20. Those not permitted to accuse or bear witness, ibid., 21. On the persons of accusers, ibid. On judges and accusers, what sort they ought to be, ibid., 22.—On accused bishops, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 504. How the accusers of priests are to be examined, ibid., 502.—On the accusers and witnesses of bishops, Burchard, CXL, 600. On accusers of clerics, ibid., 659. How many witnesses ordained persons, if accused, must use to clear themselves, ibid., 660.—That laypersons ought not to accuse clerics, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 510. What accusations ought not to be received, ibid., 512. On the order of accusation, ibid., 513. Those not to be admitted to accusation, ibid. On the manner of accusing, ibid., 516. How accused priests ought to clear themselves, ibid., 535.—Laypersons ought not to accuse clerics, Gratian,

[Col. 1052] CLXXXVII, 639. Why laypersons are not heard in accusations against bishops, ibid., 641. Accusations against bishops are not to be received without two or three witnesses, ibid., 643. An accusation must always be made in writing, ibid., 663. Those not to be received in an accusation, ibid., 675. Persons recently enemies cannot be accusers or witnesses, ibid., 677. Intimates, suspects, and persons proceeding from the household are not to be received in an accusation, ibid., 680. A person persisting in excommunication is not admitted to accuse, ibid., 705. An accused bishop is to be heard by twelve [bishops], ibid., 720. Persons voluntarily confessing the crimes of others are not to be admitted to accuse, ibid., 722. No one may be accused by criminals, ibid., 727. Before making satisfaction, excommunicated persons are not to be admitted to accuse, ibid., 728. Subjects ought not to accuse their prelates, ibid., 731. Priests are not to be accused before a civil judge, ibid., 223.

**Plaintiffs.**—On plaintiffs, whether they ought to be ordained, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 478.

**Adulterers.**—On receiving an adulteress after penance, St. Patrick, LIII, 823.—Whoever has committed adultery is to do penance for seven years, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 441. On those who have adulterous wives and themselves commit adultery, ibid., 753; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 155; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 882.—That husbands are not to cohabit with adulterous wives, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 247.—On excommunicating every adulterer, Abedoc, XCVI, 1304. On receiving an adulteress after penance, ibid. He who renders the marital due to an adulteress is to do penance for three years, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 978.—On adulterers, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 266. The husband of an adulterous wife ought not to become a cleric, ibid., 268. That he whose wife has committed adultery is not to take another [wife], ibid., 375. On adulterers, if they have taken refuge in the Church, ibid., 497. On women who commit adultery with other men until death, ibid., 420.—On an adulterous husband, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 304. That a woman accused of adultery, if she is to undergo legal trial with her husband, must temporarily be restored to his authority, ibid., 307. Why husbands do not communicate with adulterous wives, ibid., 310. That adulteries are not to be committed in the houses of the faithful, ibid., 335.—On a woman who has left an adulterer and taken an adulterer [as husband], Burchard, CXL, 825. On a man without a wife who commits adultery with another man’s wife, ibid., 827. Why husbands communicating [in the Eucharist] are not to cohabit with adulterous wives, ibid., 828.—That a wife is not to be killed for adultery according to divine laws, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 610. Why adulterous husbands receive communion while communion is withheld from adulterous wives, ibid., 628.—Adulteries are not to be committed even with the intention of begetting children, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1482. In both sexes adultery is punished on equal grounds, ibid., 1492.

**Apostates.**—On separating apostates from the Church, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1136.—Christian apostates are to be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 556.—On apostates, Dionysius, LXVII, 233.—That penance is not to be denied to apostates, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 334. On separating apostates from the Church, ibid., 677.—On apostates, if they do not return, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 859.—Apostates are not to be admitted to the clerical office, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 286.

**Appeals.**—On appeals of bishops to the priest of the Roman Church, Pope St. Zosimus, XX, 680; Pope St. Boniface I, XX, 752.—On appeals, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 872. On appeals to the Roman Church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 115.—That bishops charged with crimes may freely appeal to the Apostolic See, Burchard, CXL, 691; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 403.—Within how many days an appeal must be made, ibid., 410. That all bishops may appeal to the Roman See in cases of necessity, ibid., 444.—In more serious cases, those prosecuted are to appeal to the Apostolic See, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 618. All are to appeal to the Roman Church as to a mother, ibid., 619. No one except the person to whom appeal is made may take cognizance of the cause of appeal, ibid., 620. He who is oppressed by his own metropolitan is to appeal to the primate or to the see of the universal Church, ibid., 622. It is permissible to withdraw by appeal before conclusion of the case, ibid., 623. Within what period each person ought to appeal after a sentence has been pronounced, ibid., 624. The remedy of appeal is granted within ten days, ibid., 625. When one must appeal for the first or second time, ibid., 628. On receiving or refusing appeals, ibid., 630.

**Baptism.**—That baptism is not to be celebrated apart from Easter and Pentecost, except in necessity, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1131; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 232; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 906.—Outside Easter, priests may confer baptism, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1188.—On those to be baptized, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 694.—That baptism is not to be conferred outside Easter except upon those dying, St. Aunarius, LXXII, 764.—Those for whom it is uncertain whether they have received baptism must be born again, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 870. On those compelled unwillingly to repeat baptism, ibid. On those who receive baptism during sickness, ibid., 871. And no fees are to be required for baptizing and signing faithful persons, ibid., 922.—That baptism is to be celebrated for Catholics at Eastertime, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1106.—And baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 678.—Whether payment may be required for baptisms, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 215.—How the sacrament of baptism ought to be celebrated, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 32. That priests are not to celebrate baptism without deacons, ibid.—That baptism is not to be performed apart from Easter and Pentecost except for those in danger of death, Burchard, CXL, 729. At what time baptism is to be celebrated, ibid. And baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated, ibid., 734. On priests who demand payment for baptism, ibid., 740.

**Basilicas.**—All basilicas belong to the bishop in whose territory they are situated, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1047.

**Ecclesiastical benefices.**—That no one is to give or receive a benefice contrary to the canons for money or any other agreement, Council of Tours, CXLIII, 1410. That no bishop is to sell or grant away a benefice, or alienate what belongs to the Church, ibid., 1411. And that a cleric engaged in military service loses his benefice, ibid., 1412.—He who has bought ecclesiastical benefices is proved also to have bought churches, Gratian,

[Col. 1054] CLXXXVII, 548.

**Bigamists.**—That bigamists are not admitted to the clergy, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 143. On bigamists, ibid., 165; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 285. And bigamists are not to advance to ecclesiastical ranks, ibid., 921. On bigamists and other persons who are in no way admitted to the ministry of the clerical office, ibid., 938.

**Chalice.**—That a chalice is to be made of gold or silver, Burchard, CXL, 692. That no one may presume to pledge a chalice to a tavernkeeper, ibid., 694. That no one may presume to use a chalice for other purposes, ibid.—Of what material a chalice together with its paten ought to be made, Gratian, CXXXVII, 1720.

**Catechumens.**—That, if a catechumen has had a wife and, after her death, has acquired another after baptism, he is not to be a cleric, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 528; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 918.—On fallen catechumens, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 763, 821; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 46. On catechumens who sin, ibid., 155; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 267. On a pregnant female catechumen, ibid., 156. If a catechumen has had a wife and, after her death, has taken another after baptism, he cannot be a cleric, ibid., 258.—That catechumens are not to approach baptisteries, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 393. That catechumens are not to receive the blessing together with the faithful, ibid., 393.

**Canons.**—Regular canons ought not to become monks, Gratian, LXXXVII, 1094. With their father’s permission, regular canons may become monks, ibid., 1095.

**Chorepiscopi.**—That those called chorepiscopi may not ordain anyone without a bishop, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 752. On those called chorepiscopi, ibid., 796.—That chorepiscopi may not ordain priests or deacons, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 52. That chorepiscopi ought not to ordain clerics except in rural districts and small villages, ibid., 154. On those called chorepiscopi, ibid., 164.—On a chorepiscopus, matters pertaining to his office, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 878.

**Clerics.**—On the conduct of clerics, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1142. On clerics who enter second marriages, ibid., 1131. What women ought to live with clerics, ibid. That clerics rejected by their bishop are not to be received or promoted by others, ibid., 1193.—That, after the remission of sins, one who has chosen to wear a soldier’s belt is not to be admitted to the clergy, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 468. That one who has taken a second wife ought not to be ordained a cleric, even if he entered such a marriage before baptism, ibid., 474. Which laypersons ought not to be promoted to the clergy, ibid., 604.—A person who has worn the belt of secular military service ought not to be admitted to clerical status, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 521. That he who has taken a second wife is not to become a cleric, ibid., 522. If a cleric has a case against a cleric, he is not to forsake his own bishop, ibid., 547. Traveling clerics and readers may never minister in another city without synodal letters from their bishop, ibid., 543. Clerics serving in the Church may not serve in the Church of another city, ibid., 546. Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, plunder things that may belong to him, ibid. What women may live in clerics’ houses, ibid., 561. On the business dealings of clerics, ibid., 698. That no one may presume to ordain a cleric from another Church, ibid., 728. On clerics, that they are not to move from one city to another, ibid., 763. On not receiving clerics of another Church, ibid., 764. That no cleric is to lend at interest, ibid. On clerics excommunicated by others, who are by no means to be received, ibid., 782. On not ordaining clerics belonging to another [bishop] without their bishop’s consent, ibid., 784. If a cleric has a case against the clergy, he is to approach his bishop, ibid., 858. That a cleric may not serve simultaneously in the Churches of two cities, ibid. Traveling clerics may nowhere minister in another city without letters of recommendation from their bishop, ibid., 859. That clerics are not to be contractors, ibid., 868. A cleric is not to grow either hair or beard, ibid., 883.—That one who has married a non-virgin wife is not to aspire to holy orders, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 13.—If a cleric has a dispute with a cleric, he is not to abandon his own bishop, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 88. A cleric may not be enrolled in the Churches of two cities simultaneously, ibid., 88. Traveling and unknown clerics may nowhere and in no way minister in another city without letters of recommendation from their own bishop, ibid., 90. That clerics are not to leave their own Churches, ibid., 143. That one who has made himself a eunuch is not to become a cleric, ibid., 144. Which clerics ought to be joined to wives, ibid. That clerics who have business against one another ought not to leave their own bishop, ibid., 173. That a cleric may not marry a wife of another sect, ibid., 174. That clerics ought by no means to migrate, ibid., 175. On not ordaining clerics belonging to another [bishop] without the consent of their own bishop,

[Col. 1055] ibid., 182. Clerics or continent persons are not to approach virgins or widows, ibid., 194. Which clerics ought to abstain from their wives, ibid., 205. On clerics, what sort ought to be promoted, ibid., 235. That he who has taken a second wife is not to be a cleric, ibid., 243. That clerics are to pursue no dishonest trades or shameful profits, ibid., 306.—That a cleric is not to drag a cleric before a secular court, St. Aunarius, LXXII, 766.—By how many witnesses clerics ought to be convicted, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 947.—No cleric ought to travel without his bishop’s authorization, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 290. That clerics are not to enter taverns, ibid., 330.—That clerics are not to wear secular clothing, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 31.—That it is not lawful for a cleric to lease another’s possessions, Burchard, CXL, 649. That clerics are not to be compelled by outside judges, ibid., 659. That none of the clergy is to carry military weapons, ibid., 661. On clerics freed by their masters, ibid., 665.—A cleric having a case against a cleric is not to resort to secular courts, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 494, 521. That clerics are not to conduct secular business, ibid., 529.—By how many witnesses each cleric ought to be convicted, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 616. The clergy are not to be heard by a secular judge, ibid., 822. Clerics who conspire, having lost their rank, are to be confined in prison, ibid., 826. He who has a lawsuit with a cleric is to approach that cleric’s bishop, ibid., 835. A cleric is to possess nothing secular, ibid., 883. Clerics are to possess nothing as their own, ibid., 885. All things ought to be held in common by clerics, ibid., 886. Clerics may bear witness for their own church, ibid., 956. Clerics are to abstain from profits of trade, ibid., 958. Whoever strikes a cleric is to be excommunicated and absolved only by the Roman Pontiff, ibid., 1070.—That clerics are to be compelled to personal residence at their own Churches, Innocent III, CCXIV, 95.

**Councils.**—That councils are to be held twice yearly, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 869; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 145, 175, 294; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 857; St. Paulinus, XCIX, 283.—That councils are to be held annually, from such provinces as can [attend], Pope Hilary, LVIII, 24, 27.—On holding a council every year, Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 423.—A general council need not be convened except from necessity, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 932.—That a council is to be held annually, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 331, 336, 1043.—That councils of bishops ought to be held once a year, not twice, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 435.—Provincial councils lack authority without the presence of the Roman Pontiff, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 95. Councils ought not to be held contrary to the decision of the Roman Pontiff, ibid., 685.

**Communion.**—That faithful laypersons entering a church ought to communicate, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 142; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 841.—On those who withdraw themselves from receiving holy communion, and those who communicate with excommunicated persons through gifts, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 159.—That a woman is not to receive communion without the Lord’s bread, St. Aunarius, LXXII, 766.—Communion is to be received in the basilicas of martyrs, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 272.—On communion, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 356, 396; St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 497.—That the faithful are to communicate on every Sunday in Lent, Burchard, CXL, 756. When each person ought to abstain from his wife before holy communion, ibid., 757.—That the faithful are to communicate on every Sunday in Lent, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 167. Nothing is to be demanded for communicating the faithful, ibid., 182.

**Concubine.**—That no one is permitted to have a concubine, Burchard, CXL, 817; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 617. On those who had concubines before marriage, ibid.—No one may have several concubines at the same time, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 933.

**Corporal.**—That the corporal cloth is to be of the purest linen and of one material, Burchard, CXL, 693.

**Curiales.**—Municipal councillors are not to be admitted to the clergy, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 494.—Municipal councillors are not to be admitted to clerical office, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 287. Why it has been established that municipal councillors are not to be ordained, ibid., 289.

**Deans.**—On sending deans through parishes, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 356.

**Tithes.**—Holy communion is to be denied to those who have not paid tithes, and they are forbidden entrance to the Church, Pope St. Damasus I, XIII, 1203.—On tithes, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 200 ff. That laypersons are not to receive tithes, ibid., 237. That tithes are to be divided into four portions, ibid., 258.—That tithes are to be demanded as a due from all Christians, Burchard, CXL, 699. That four portions ought to be made from tithes, ibid., 702.—On tithes unjustly withheld by laypersons, Council of Rome, CXLVIII, 801.—On tithes of the Church, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 237. That tithes are never to be neglected, ibid., 245. How many portions ought to be made from tithes,

[Col. 1056] ibid., 246.—Tithes ought to be given to baptismal churches, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1008. Tithes are to be distributed according to the bishop’s disposition, ibid., 1013. Anathema be upon him who wishes to administer tithes and offerings without the bishop’s knowledge, ibid., 1014. He who has not paid tithes to priests is held guilty before God, ibid., 1019. Tithes are possessed by laypersons, ibid., 1042. He gives tithes faithfully who pays tithes on all that is his, ibid., 1044. Tithes are not to be redeemed by the people, ibid., 1045.—On tithes, Pope Celestine III, CCVI, 1023.—That merchants seek to pay the Church’s tithes, Innocent III, CCXIV, 189. That tithes are to be paid by all, ibid., 802.

**Deacons.**—Deacons are bound by the law of continence, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1184.—On trying the cases of deacons before neighbouring [bishops], Pope St. Zosimus, XX, 680.—That deacons are not to be lessees or agents of private persons, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 425. That deacons who have sacrificed [to idols] and afterwards returned are to cease from sacred ministry, ibid., 435. There ought to be seven deacons, ibid., 446, 757. On deacons, ibid., 695. On deacons who have sacrificed, ibid., 750. That deacons are not to rank above priests, ibid., 764, 820. On sending deacons to the imperial court, ibid., 778; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 892. On accused deacons, ibid., 870. On deacons who at the time of ordination gave testimony concerning marriage, ibid., 877.—On the ordination of seven deacons, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 81. On deacons: that they are not to administer Christ’s body to priests, or communicate before priests, ibid., 259. How deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 343.—At what age deacons are to be ordained, ibid., 401; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 377. That a deacon is not to be ordained before twenty-five years of age, ibid.; Burchard, CLX, 662. That deacons are to keep their proper measure, ibid., 738. That deacons ought to abstain from marital intercourse, ibid., 645.—That deacons are not to have wives, Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1360.—At what age deacons are to be consecrated, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 433. That deacons are under the same law of continence as bishops and priests, ibid., 459.

**Digamists.**—That digamists cannot be admitted to the clergy, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 603; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 250; Bishop Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 846; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 706; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 377.—Deacons who do not profess chastity are not to be ordained, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 158.

**Diocese.**—That dioceses are not to receive a bishop except with the consent of their own bishop, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 197.—On dioceses, how bishops are to divide them among themselves, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 934.—That dioceses are to be visited every year, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 34.

**The Lord’s Day.**—On observance of the Lord’s Day, St. Aunarius, LXXII, 764.—On Sunday, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 264. That there is to be no market on Sunday, ibid.—That no cleric may presume to pursue any secular business on Sunday, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 37. That trade is not to be conducted on Sunday, the same author, CXXXVIII, 468.—That judicial decisions in matters are not to be made on Sunday, Burchard, CXL, 581. How Sunday is to be venerated, ibid., 640. That secular court sessions are not to be held on Sundays, principal feast days, and fast days, ibid., 888.—That markets are not to be held on Sundays, Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1360.—On observing Sunday, and that neither market nor court session is to be held on it, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 207. That secular court sessions are not to be held on Sundays and other principal festivals, ibid., 274.

**Church.**—When a church once consecrated to God is to be consecrated again, Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 969.—On churches, Theodosius, XIII, 531.—Meals ought not to be held in churches, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 167, 194.—On what is to be observed in restoring church buildings or in their dedication, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1077.—On the immunity of churches, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 195. On the freedom of churches, ibid., 197. From what sources churches ought to be restored and obedience rendered to the bishop, ibid., 198. On restoring the churches of God, ibid., 199. That more than one priest is not to be appointed in one church, ibid., 237. That laypersons are not to hold churches, ibid.—That feasts and reclining at table are not to take place in a church, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 33. That burials are not to take place in churches, ibid., 33.—That images ought not to be made in a church, Burchard, CXL, 678 ff. That individual priests are each to have a single church, ibid., 680. That every priest is to be content with one church, ibid., 681. That each church is to have one full hide of land free from service, ibid., 682. That no one is to feast in a church, ibid., 690.—A church once consecrated ought not to be consecrated again,

[Col. 1057] Gratian, CLXXXVII, 352. Nothing is to be demanded for dedicating churches, ibid., 541. Founders of churches, if they begin to be poor, are to receive support from those same churches, ibid., 1053. Founders of churches are to present to the bishop candidates to be ordained in them, ibid., 1054. No one may remove a person from a church, ibid., 1063. The consecration of churches ought not to take place without Mass, ibid., 1706. A new church is not to be dedicated without a command of the Apostolic See, ibid. A new church is not to be dedicated without the authority of the supreme pontiff, ibid., 1707. A church ought not to be established without the consent of the Apostolic See, ibid., 1708. A new church is not to be dedicated without the dignity of the bishop of the place, ibid.

**Ecclesiastical property.**—When immovable property is forbidden to churches, and when it is not, Lactantius, VII, 566.—Holy communion is to be denied to all sacrilegious persons who have seized ecclesiastical property, Pope Damasus, XIII, 1203.—On the income of the Church, St. Leo the Great, LVI, 704.—That Church property is not to be alienated, Pope Symmachus, LXII, 54.—That the bishop alone is to have care of ecclesiastical property, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 858, 859.—That no one is to take ecclesiastical estates and apply them to personal use, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1104.—That Church property is not to be alienated without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 350. On the Church’s own or acquired property, ibid., 405. On Church property not to be alienated by anyone, and on freed persons, ibid.—That priests are not to sell Church property in the place where they are appointed, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 259. On ecclesiastical goods, ibid., 393.—On Church property not being plundered upon a bishop’s death, Council of Trosly, CXXXII, 675.—On possessions of the Church, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 489. On plundering Church property, ibid., 496.—On immovable Church property, Burchard, CXL, 706. On exchanges of ecclesiastical property, ibid., 707. That priests are not to presume to sell Church property, ibid., 708. On Church property sold by priests after the bishop’s death, ibid., 713. That the disposal of ecclesiastical property does not pertain to laypersons, ibid., 807. How ecclesiastical property ought to be restored, ibid., 865.—On those who seize ecclesiastical property, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 240. That priests are not to presume to sell Church property, ibid., 254.—Laypersons retain no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical property, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 452. Why estates were sold in the primitive Church, ibid., 889. Why the estates of the faithful are not today alienated by the Church, ibid., 890. He who seizes ecclesiastical estates is subject to excommunication, ibid., 896. What penance is to be imposed on invaders of ecclesiastical property, ibid., 901. A bishop is not to presume to appropriate or alienate Church property, ibid., 902. Nothing belonging to the Church is to be alienated, ibid., 905. Church property taken away during a bishop’s absence is to be restored to ecclesiastical right, ibid., 913. How alienation of Church property can be valid, ibid., 918. For what reasons sacred property ought to be alienated, ibid., 925. How priests may make a testament concerning Church property, ibid., 931. A fourth part of Church revenues is to be distributed to clerics, ibid., 1018.—That the property and goods of the Church, especially those from the bishop’s table, are not to be alienated, Innocent III, CCXIV, 93.

**Energumens.**—On baptized energumens, Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 557; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 913.—That energumens are not to be promoted to the clergy, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 393.—That energumens are not to receive communion, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 42.

**Bishops.**—And no bishop is to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner, Pope Sixtus II, V, 86; Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 980.—That accused bishops are to appeal to the Apostolic See, Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 980. On bishops stripped of their property or driven from their sees, ibid., 986, 991. On the unjust condemnation of bishops, ibid., 988. Whether a bishop may be restored by a smaller number of bishops than had condemned him, ibid.—On bishops’ cases not being concluded without the authority of the Roman Pontiff, Pope Felix II, XIII, 22.—Bishops are bound by the law of continence, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1184. That laypersons are not to be promoted to the episcopate, ibid., 1192.—That the office of bishop must be attained through ecclesiastical grades, Pope St. Celestine I, L, 429. That bishops ought not to be ordained from laypersons while the clerics of churches are disregarded, ibid., 436.—On bishops being ordained by their fellow-provincials, Pope St. Leo, LVI, 390. That bishops are not to travel overseas without consulting the bishop of the first see of their respective province, ibid., 426. If a bishop wishes to usurp another’s church or stir up sedition, ibid., 440. A bishop ought not to be ordained in hamlets and villages, ibid., 720. On bishops rashly seeking another’s see, ibid., 775. When bishops may be ordained in another province,

[Col. 1058] ibid., 776. When bishops ought to go to the imperial court, ibid., 777. How long a bishop may sojourn in another city, except in grave necessity, ibid., 781. That a bishop may not be absent for several weeks, ibid., 782. No bishop is to transfer from his own Church, ibid., 799. That no bishop is to choose his own successor, ibid. On bishops being ordained by fellow-provincials, ibid., 818. On bishops who leave their Churches and transfer to others, ibid., 824. That bishops are not to travel overseas, ibid., 871. That a bishop may not seize property of the titular church, ibid. That a bishop is not to have a lodging far from his church, ibid., 880. That a bishop is not to take upon himself any care of family property, ibid., 881. That a bishop is not to undertake the protection of wills, ibid. That a bishop is not to hear any case without the presence of his clerics, ibid.—That no bishop is to leave his own Church and transfer to another, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 18. That two bishops are not to be held in one Church, ibid.—A bishop, if rebaptized, is to receive lay communion at death, Pope Felix III, LVIII, 924.—That no payment is to be received for a bishopric, Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 423.—That a bishop may not keep an unrelated woman, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 42. A bishop is not to be ordained without a synod and the presence of the metropolitan of the province, ibid., 66. A bishop is to have authority over Church property, ibid., 68. If any bishop performs an ordination for money, he is to risk losing his rank, ibid., 86. That a bishop who receives clerics of another [bishop] is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 143. That a bishop may not ordain clerics in another province, ibid., 145. That the bishop alone is to have care of ecclesiastical property, ibid., 146. That a bishop has authority over ecclesiastical property for the administration of the poor, ibid. That bishops ought not to lease estates belonging to others, ibid., 171. On not ordaining bishops in hamlets and small cities, ibid., 178. How long a bishop may remain in another city, ibid., 180. That a bishop may not be absent from his own Church for more than three weeks, ibid. That no bishop is to be a contractor, ibid., 189. That bishops ordained in dioceses are not to claim any diocese for themselves, ibid., 199.—On not ordaining bishops in hamlets and small cities, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 891. That, if a bishop neglects his diocese, he is to be deprived of communion, ibid., 935.—That bishops’ cases ought not to be decided without consulting the Roman Pontiff, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1106. How many witnesses bishops ought to have, and that no absent person is to be judged, ibid.—A bishop is not to transfer from province to province unless invited, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 273. Uninvited bishops ought not to go beyond their own diocese, ibid., 291.—That bishops, for the sake of their own comfort, are not to neglect the people entrusted to them, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 193. That a bishop is to make the circuit of his parish with a small retinue, ibid., 194. On bishops who, without visiting parishes, require the price of servitude, ibid. That a bishop is not to keep hunting dogs, ibid., 222.—That no one is to choose a bishop as his successor, St. Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 497.—That, when a bishop is being elected, if he has opponents, five bishops are to assemble, Burchard of Worms, CXL, 551. That episcopal ordinations ought to be performed by all provincial bishops with apostolic authority, ibid., 553. That bishops are not to obtain a place of government through the simoniacal heresy, ibid., 555. That a bishop is not to be consecrated without three bishops, ibid., 556. That a bishop may in no way transfer from one parish to another, ibid., 570. How traveling bishops are to be received, ibid., 585. That it is not lawful to ordain a bishop before the age of thirty, ibid., 627. That no bishop is to receive another’s cleric without letters from his bishop, ibid., 633.—That bishops are not to live at all with women, Pope Zacharias, CXLVIII, 1120.—How bishops ought to be ordained, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 363. How long a bishop ought to remain in another city, ibid., 389. By how many bishops a bishop is to be heard, ibid., 404. That bishops ought to be judges of accused bishops, ibid., 405. How an elderly bishop is to be corrected, ibid., 420. How accused bishops ought to be summoned to a council, ibid., 425. That a bishop ought by no means to devote himself to hunting, ibid., 430. That no bishop is to be compelled to appear before a secular court, ibid., 434.—A bishop may not ordain another’s clerics or consecrate altars [outside his jurisdiction], Gratian, CLXXXVII, 757. Transfers of bishops may occur for reasons of necessity or utility, ibid., 759. Bishops are not to demand dues from parishioners except with charity, ibid., 816. A bishop is not to presume to receive more than two solidi from parish churches, ibid. A bishop ought not to take cognizance of secular business, ibid., 828. Bishops’ cases are not to be examined before princes, ibid., 1120.—The transfer

[Col. 1059] of bishops belongs by right to the Roman Pontiff alone, Innocent III, CCXIV, 486.

**Eulogiae.**—On *eulogiae*—blessed bread—to be given to the people by a priest, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 256; Burchard, CXL, 757; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 168.—That one ought not to receive *eulogiae* from heretics, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 258.

**Eunuchs.**—On eunuchs and those who have castrated themselves, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 147.

**Excommunicated persons.**—That excommunicated persons cannot accuse bishops, Pope Sixtus II, V, 86; Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 992.—That laypersons by their own bishop …

…excommunicated persons be promoted to the clergy by another [bishop], St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1194.

**Excommunicated Persons.**—On rejecting an excommunicated person, St Patrick of Ireland, LIII, 819.—On those who are excommunicated by their bishops, St Leo the Great, LVI, 391. On hearing cases of excommunicated persons before neighbouring bishops, ibid., 783. On clerics or laypersons who are excommunicated, ibid., 795. On those who have been excommunicated by their bishops, ibid., 818. On those excommunicated by their own bishop, ibid., 826. That one must not pray with an excommunicated person, the same author, LXVII, 142. On excommunicated clerics and laypersons, ibid., 160. On hearing cases of excommunicated persons before neighbouring bishops, ibid., 181.—That no one should communicate with an excommunicated person, St Aunarius, LXXII, 766. That one who communicates with an excommunicated person is subject to a like sentence, ibid.—That one must not pray with excommunicated persons, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 841.—On the rule that no one should be quick to excommunicate, Abedoc, XCVI, 1297. That the alms of an excommunicated person must not be received, ibid. That an excommunicated person ought neither to offer nor to baptize, but only to pray, ibid.—One must not communicate with excommunicated persons, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1108.—On excommunicated clerics or laypersons, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 255. On excommunicated persons departing this life, ibid., 259. That excommunicated persons may not communicate, ibid., 277. On excommunicated persons, ibid., 361; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 350. On an excommunicated person who has presumed to communicate, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 358. On those unjustly excommunicated, St Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 494.—On excommunication, Burchard, CXL, 856. That the names of excommunicated persons be recorded and posted upon the doors of the church, ibid., 868.—That no one be excommunicated before the cause of his excommunication has been proved, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 435.—No one ought to be excommunicated before the cause has been proved, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 588. A person excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another, ibid., 838. Bishops who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be deposed, ibid., 842. The names of excommunicated persons are to be announced openly and publicly to all neighbouring [bishops], ibid., 846. It is not lawful to eat with an excommunicated person, ibid., 849. Let one who obtains churches through laypersons be excommunicated, ibid., 1049. A bishop may not excommunicate anyone for a personal injury, ibid., 1190. An excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another, ibid., 1264. Those excommunicated by heretics are not regarded as excommunicated, ibid., 1283. Excommunicated persons are not to be admitted to pass judgment, ibid., 1284. Whoever is excommunicated by heretics because of discipline is not to be received by Catholics, ibid., 1285.—Excommunicated persons can neither elect nor be elected, Innocent III, CCXIV, 802.

**Heretics.**—The manner of receiving heretics into the Church, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1133.—That Catholics ought not to enter into matrimonial unions with heretics, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 861. That *eulogiae* [blessed bread] ought not to be received from heretics, ibid., 862. That baptisms performed by heretics ought not to be approved, ibid., 862. That persons ordained by heretics are not to be admitted to the clergy, ibid., 886.—On one ordained by heretics, Collection of Canons, XCIX, 1001.—Heretics persisting in heresy ought not to enter a church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 287. On avoiding marriages with heretics, ibid., 289. One ought not to pray with heretics or schismatics, ibid.—A heretic may accuse and bear witness against a heretic, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 645.

**Actors.**—On whether actors ought to receive communion with the other faithful, Burchard, CXL, 756; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 167.

**Those Sacrificing [to Idols].**—On priests who sacrificed during persecution, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 151. On deacons who sacrificed, ibid. On those who repeatedly sacrificed to idols, ibid., 153; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 263.

**The Sick.**—On visiting the sick, Burchard, CXL, 963. On sick persons in danger of death, ibid., 941.

**Investitures.**—That no cleric shall receive investiture of a bishopric, abbey, or church from the hand of an emperor, [Col. 1060] king, or any layperson, male or female, Council of Rome, CXLVIII, 800.

**Metropolitan.**—That a metropolitan should do nothing without the council of bishops, nor they without his [counsel], St Julius I, pope, VII, 988.—On metropolitans, St Felix II, pope, XIII, 21.—That, according to imperial enactments, there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops, St Innocent I, pope, XX, 548.—That in every province no one, disregarding the metropolitan, be ordained bishop, St Boniface I, pope, XX, 772.—That no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, St Leo the Great, LVI, 520. On the metropolitans of each province, ibid., 795.—That bishops should not proceed into another province without letters from the metropolitan, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 24.—On the metropolitans of individual provinces, Dionysius Exiguus, LVII, 161. That a bishop should not be ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge, ibid., 242. That metropolitans’ rights be preserved to them, ibid., 293.—A metropolitan is to be ordained, if possible, with all the bishops of his province present, Collection of Canons, XCIX, 1004.—On metropolitans: that none should hear anyone’s cases without the request of the bishops of the province, Remigius of Chur, CII, 1104.—On metropolitan bishops, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 281. That a synod be convened at the metropolitan’s discretion, ibid., 380. That bishops are not to be ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge, ibid., 699. That no one be ordained bishop without the consent of the metropolitan bishop, ibid., 924.—What sort of letters a metropolitan should send to his brethren, Burchard, CXL, 562. On a metropolitan who delays hearing a bishop of his province in his case, ibid., 564.—That every metropolitan must, within three months of his consecration, send to Rome or go there for the pallium, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 431.—There ought not to be two metropolitans in one and the same province, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 478. A metropolitan is to be ordained by the will of the clergy and citizens, ibid., 334. Without the primate’s consent, a metropolitan may not ordain a bishop, ibid., 347. A newly made bishop is to present himself to the metropolitan, ibid., 348. The metropolitan shall appoint stewards whom a bishop has neglected to have, ibid., 794. Without the metropolitan’s knowledge, a bishop is to do nothing outside his own diocese, ibid. A metropolitan may not hear cases without the consent of the bishops or the presence of one of them, ibid., 795.

**Mass.**—See the table concerning the sacrifice of the Mass.

**Monks.**—On the goods of monks, Theodosius, XIII, 525. On monks, ibid., 532.—On monks who do not keep their profession, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1138. On the promotion of monks, ibid., 1144.—That, if a monk wishes to strive for clerical rank, he ought not to depart from the former profession which he undertook as a monk, St Innocent I, pope, XX, 477.—That monks ought not to attain the highest priesthood except through the ecclesiastical grades, St Zosimus, pope, XX, 669.—A monk and a virgin, one from one place and the other from elsewhere, are not to lodge together in one dwelling, St Patrick of Ireland, LIII, 824.—On monks desiring to enter the ecclesiastical grades, St Leo, pope, LVI, 571. On monks who, after long residence in monasteries, later seek to attain clerical rank: they ought not to depart from their former profession, ibid., 524. We decree that those once made monks shall come neither to military service nor to secular office, ibid., 540. If monks are found to have conspired, they shall lose their own rank, ibid., 545. Monks under thirty years of age are to be promoted through the minor orders, one grade at a time, as time advances, ibid., 561. On the order of monks, ibid., 893. Monks may not enter into marriage, ibid., 859.—Monks may not be joined in marriage, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 90. That monks ought not to lease other people’s estates, ibid., 171. No monk shall attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs, ibid., 172. On monks who do not remain in their profession, ibid., 173. A monk may not contract marital rights, ibid., 174. On monks who come to the imperial city contrary to their bishop’s will, ibid., 176. On the promotion of monks, ibid., 236. That monks ought not to attain the highest priesthood except through the grades of the Church, ibid., 261. That if anyone abandons the profession of a monk, he must be purified through the satisfaction of public penance, ibid., 290. That, if any monks [act] when no necessity compels, the ancient enactments concerning them must be observed, ibid., 309.—A monk may not go to a wedding, St Aunarius, LXXII, 764. A monk may not have children from baptism [i.e. godchildren], ibid., 765.—On monks who do not preserve their profession, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 880. That monks ought not to lease others’ estates, ibid., 900.—That one ought not to become a monk without an abbot, Abedoc, XCVI, [Col. 1061] 1296. That a monk ought not to possess private property, ibid. On fugitive monks, whether they are to be received or not received, ibid. That he must give to the abbot what he has acquired, ibid. That both are to be excommunicated—the fugitive monk and the one who receives him, ibid. On excommunicating a wandering monk, ibid., 1297. That monks ought not to withdraw from the community, ibid. That monks ought not to build a cell without the abbot’s permission, ibid.—A monk may not make a vow without the abbot’s consent; otherwise it must be broken, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 985.—That monks in each province or city are subject to the bishop, Collection of Canons, CXIX, 1052. We both desire and decree that monks commended by gravity of character and holy life be added to clerical duties, ibid., 1054. Monks who attain clerical rank ought not to depart from their former profession, ibid.—No monk shall attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 30. If a monk takes a wife, ibid., 411. That a monk should not build cells without permission of the bishop or abbot, ibid. That a monk who has become a cleric must preserve his profession, ibid., 701.—On the election of an abbot, St Abbo of Fleury, CXXXIX, 484. On a monk’s priesthood, ibid., 487. On a monk summoned to court, ibid., 496.—No monk who is not a priest, nor any layman, may preach, Burchard, CXL, 651. On monks’ churches, ibid., 724. That a monk’s voluntary profession may not be changed, ibid., 793. On monks and nuns who have mingled in sacrilegious intercourse, ibid., 797. Monks are not to attend secular courts, ibid., 809.—That a deserter from monastic religion be excommunicated, Council of Tours, CXLIII, 1409.—That monks neither lease possessions nor involve themselves in secular business, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 491. That monks in each city be subject to bishops, ibid., 541. On fugitive monks not to be promoted to the clergy, ibid., 545. That no unknown person be quickly admitted into a monks’ monastery, ibid., 554. That monks and nuns must not be permitted to live together in the same monastery, ibid., 564. That communities of monks not be formed without the bishop’s consent, ibid., 566. What is to be done concerning monks who take wives, ibid., 572. On prohibiting monks’ wandering, ibid., 582.—Monks cannot accuse priests or bear witness against them, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 661. Monks are not to be heard in an accusation, ibid. Monks who conspire are to be deprived of their own honour, ibid., 826. Monks promoted to clerical rank ought not to depart from their former profession, ibid., 991. Without bishops’ consent, monks must not usurp episcopal rights, ibid., 993. Monks residing within cloisters are not to perform clerical offices outside, ibid. Monks who are in cities must be subject to the bishop, ibid., 994. Monks who wander without the bishop’s permission are to be compelled to return to their own places, ibid., 995. No monk, except priests of the Lord, may dare to preach, ibid., 996. A monk ought not to be an advocate, ibid., 997. A monk who is a priest may freely enjoy ecclesiastical benefices, ibid. Monks may be promoted to clerical rank, ibid., 999. Deserters from monasteries are not to be chosen for the service of the clergy, ibid., 1002. All monks ought to possess immunity of protection, ibid., 1005. Without the bishops’ permission, monks are not to receive tithes or churches from laypersons, ibid., 1056. No one is to be received into a monastery before a three-year probation, ibid., 1061. Abbots and other offices ought to be instituted by bishops, ibid., 1079. The monastery’s community, not the bishop or any outsider, is to appoint the abbot, ibid. On the liberty of monks, ibid., 1080. With the bishop’s permission, an abbot may leave his place, ibid., 1082. Monks may not lawfully expel abbots at their own discretion or ordain others, ibid., 1083. Without the will of the bishop or abbot, no monk may presume to build a cell, ibid., 1085. Abbots are to remain under the authority of bishops, ibid. Monks may neither make women their spiritual co-mothers nor approach women, ibid., 1087. Monks may not live with nuns, ibid. Monks and nuns may in no place live together, ibid., 1088. Monasteries of girls are to be built at a greater distance from monasteries of monks, ibid. Whoever seeks the monastic profession is to be received even against the bishop’s will, ibid., 1093. After entering a monastery, no one retains permission to make a will, ibid., 1097. Those given by their parents are to remain in the monastery permanently, ibid., 1100. Persons shut up in monasteries against their own will are not to be retained, ibid., 1101. No one is to be subjected unwillingly to monastic disciplines, ibid., 1106. No one may receive or ordain a monk without his abbot’s permission, ibid., 1109. One abbot cannot preside over two monasteries, ibid., 1111. [Col. 1062] If a monk marries, let him be excommunicated, ibid., 1378. A monk taking a wife is never to obtain the office of a sacred grade, ibid., 1385. Monks associated with wives are to be confined in a monastery, ibid., 1387. A monk may not have spiritual co-mothers, ibid., 1832.—That monks should not reside alone in towns, Pope Clement III, CCIV, 1379.—That monks expelled from a monastery be restored to their former condition, Innocent III, CCXIV, 208. That monks may not transfer to another order without the abbot’s permission, ibid., 545.

**Monasteries.**—That regular monasteries may neither be sold nor exchanged, Burchard, CXL, 677.—A prescription of forty years is granted to religious houses, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1038. A bishop may not take away a monastery’s possessions because of an abbot’s sin, ibid., 1041. On no title can the property of a monastery be separated from its right, ibid., 1076. Bishops are not to celebrate public Masses in a monastery, ibid., 1081. A baptistery may not be established in a monastery, ibid., 1082. Without the bishop’s permission no one may presume to begin or found a monastery, ibid., 1084. The revenues of a monastery must be administered by its own bishop, ibid., 1086. Monasteries must not become dwellings for clerics or laypersons, ibid., 1090. Those established in sacred order are to have no authority over monasteries, ibid. A bishop may visit a monastery for the purpose of visitation and exhortation, ibid., 1091. Bishops should frequently visit monasteries and correct what needs correction, ibid., 1091. A bishop ought not to demand anything from a monastery beyond the terms established at the time of its dedication, ibid., 1091. Monasteries are to render the customary services to the bishop, ibid., 1092. A person whom his father or mother caused to be ordained during his childhood may not leave the monastery, ibid., 1099.

**Neophytes.**—That neophytes are not to be made priests, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1161.—On neophytes who, after baptism, apply themselves to the clergy, St Leo the Great, LVI, 760. That neither bishops nor priests are to be ordained from neophytes, ibid., 817. On whether neophytes may be admitted to the clergy, ibid., 826. A neophyte is not to be ordained bishop, ibid., 250.

**Marriage.**—That women who married others while their husbands were captive ought, when their former husbands return from captivity, to be reunited with those former husbands, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 296.—What marriages are to be avoided, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46.—At what time marriages are to be celebrated, Burchard, CXL, 816. That dancing not take place at Christian weddings, ibid., 817. On those who celebrate marriage for the third time, ibid., 818.

**Offerings.**—Church offerings of produce are not to be received or given outside the church, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 58. What kinds [of offerings] should be presented at the altar not for sacrifice but for a simple blessing, ibid., 141. That things which cannot be offered in churches be brought by the faithful to the houses of priests, ibid.—On offerings of produce bestowed upon ministers of the Church, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 885.—On the offering of the faithful, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 137. On fruits to be given in church and nowhere else, ibid., 271. Holy offerings must not be sent to other parishes as *eulogiae* [blessed bread], ibid., 288. On the offerings of the faithful: that they should be divided into four portions, ibid., 946.—To whom the offerings of parishioners belong, Burchard, CXL, 700. That in every church four portions should be made, both from revenues and from offerings, ibid. Offerings are to be renewed from Saturday to Saturday, ibid., 755. That offerings be made by everyone equally at the greater feasts, ibid., 758.—Laypersons may not usurp the offerings of the Church, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 805.

**Ordinations.**—That it is not lawful to conduct ordinations in another’s territory, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1193.—Certain ordinations contrary to the canons, St Innocent I, pope, XX, 490. The Nicene rules are to be observed in ordinations, ibid., 492. That crimes or faults are not rightly believed to be removed by ordination, ibid., 531.—Hasty ordinations and ordinations by leaps are forbidden, St Zosimus, pope, XX, 669.—That one must abstain from unlawful ordinations, St Celestine I, pope, L, 434.—Abstain from unlawful ordinations, St Leo the Great, LVI, 580. On those ordained for money, ibid., 702. On those who obtain orders through reward, ibid., 803.—That whoever has been ordained contrary to the forms of the canons be deposed together with his ordainers, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 458. Ordinations are not to be performed except during the fast of the Ember Days, ibid., 461.—Those who are to be ordained should assemble for examination on Wednesday, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 140.

**Parish.**—That it is not lawful to invade another parish or, without consulting its bishop, do anything in it, St Innocent I, pope, XX, 605.—That no one usurp another parish, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 238. That a bishop not perform an ordination in another bishop’s parish, ibid., 240; that no priest receive another’s parishioner, ibid., 239.—That a bishop in another parish not under any circumstances ordain clerics of another diocese, Burchard, CXL, 567; persons who have oratories outside parishes are to be compelled on these days to return to their parishes, ibid., 1716.

**Easter.**—At what time Easter is to be celebrated, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 742; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 840; Remigius of Chur, XCIX, 1104.—That Easter be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 111. It is not lawful to celebrate Easter at a different time, nor to celebrate it with Jews, ibid., 277. Easter is to be celebrated throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, ibid., 1789.

**Patriarchs.**—On patriarchs, Burchard, CXL, 594.—That patriarchs ought not to judge their subjects at first instance, Innocent III, CCXIV, 475.

**Penitents.**—On penitents, St Innocent I, pope, XX, 559; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 195.—That final penance must be denied to no one, St Celestine I, pope, L, 429; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 275; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 914. How penitents ought to be received in church, ibid., 872.—On penitents, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 940.—Penitents are to abstain from secular business, Otto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 46.—Penitents are forbidden to contract marriages, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1516.

**Priest.**—A priest who refuses penance to the dying is guilty of souls [i.e. accountable for their loss], St Julius I, pope, VIII, 968.—Priests are bound by the law of continence, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1184. Those who have begotten children while in the priesthood ought to be removed from office, the same author, XX, 605. On cases of priests to be handled before neighbouring bishops, St Zosimus I, pope, XX, 680.—If a priest takes a wife, he is to be degraded, St Leo the Great, LVI, 442. If a priest committed a carnal sin before his ordination and afterwards confessed it, he is to be deprived of the office of the altar, ibid., 445. On fallen priests, ibid., 755. On those promoted to the priesthood without examination, ibid., 827. At what age they ought to be promoted to orders, ibid., 757. On accused priests, ibid., 870. On fallen priests, ibid., 872. A priest may not sell the property of his benefice, ibid., 873.—If a priest takes a wife, he is to be removed from his order, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 54. A priest is not to feast at the wedding of persons married for a second time, ibid., 56. A priest is not to be ordained before thirty years of age, ibid. A priest who abandons his own parish and goes to another is to minister no more, ibid., 60. On a priest deposed by his own bishop who dares to trouble the emperor’s ears, ibid., 64. On priests who have taken wives or committed fornication, ibid., 155. On those who withdraw themselves from ecclesiastical ministry and assemble separately, ibid., 160. That priests ought not to eat in taverns, ibid., 167. No priest is to be a contractor, ibid., 189.—A priest is not to sing or dance amid banquets, St Aunarius, LXXII, 766.—On priests who, despising their bishops, attempt to gather separate assemblies, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 854.—On priests fallen during persecution, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 261.—On priests invited by the faithful to dinner, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 231. On priests’ banquets, ibid. That every priest teach his parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, ibid., 242. That no priest presume to live or associate with women, CXXXVIII, 443.—On priests ordained before thirty years of age, Burchard, CXL, 627. On priests who have fled the parishes in which they were placed, ibid., 665. That priests ought to read continually, ibid., 543. On a priest: if he takes a wife, let him be deposed, ibid., 645. On priests degraded because of their negligence, ibid., 657.—On priests with wives not to be rejected by the people, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 178. By how many bishops a priest is to be heard, ibid., 404. That priests not leave the places committed to them and move elsewhere, ibid., 485. That priests lodge beside the church, ibid., 487. That priests give the bishop an account of their ministry every year, ibid., 498. Priests ought not to attend wedding banquets, ibid., 194.—A priest caught in adultery cannot be restored, Gratian, CLXXXVI, 270. Sons of priests are prohibited from sacred offices, ibid., 306. A priest ought to be judged only before his bishop, ibid., 832. A priest deposed by his bishop is not to appeal to the emperor, ibid., 1119.

**Primates.**—On primates, St Felix II, pope, XIII, 21.—On the primates of metropolitan bishops, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 257.—On primates, Burchard, CXL, 594. What sort of man a primate ought to be, or what he ought to do, ibid., 595. Who are primates, ibid., 597.—In what order primates or other judges are to be approached, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 397.—In [Col. 1064] what places primates ought to be ordained, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 383.—That primates ought not to judge the subjects of archbishops and bishops at first instance, Innocent III, CCXIV, 445.

**Province.**—The permission to accuse is not to extend beyond the bounds of a province, St Julius, pope, VIII, 991.—That every province ought to be content with its own metropolitan, St Celestine, pope, L, 434; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 276. That a province is by no means to be divided between two metropolitans, ibid., 174. Every province, because of distance, is to have its own primate, ibid., 189.—That it is not lawful for a bishop to ordain clerics in another province, Crisconius, CXXXVIII, 903.

**Lent.**—During Lent bread ought not to be offered except on Saturday and Sunday alone, St Leo the Great, LVI, 720. During Lent one ought not to celebrate the feasts of martyrs, ibid. During Lent one ought not to celebrate either marriages or any festivals, ibid.; Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 76.—Offerings ought not to be made during Lent, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 899.—That saints’ feast days ought not to be celebrated during Lent, Burchard, CXL, 886.

**Rogation Days.**—On the fast of the Rogation Days, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 243.

**Sacrilegious Persons.**—On sacrilegious persons and their condemnation, Council of Trosly, 675.—That those who have sexual relations with consecrated women are to be judged sacrilegious, Burchard, CXL, 803.

**Nuns.**—On those who abduct nuns, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 314. What nuns ought to do, ibid., 316. On precautions concerning nuns, ibid. On corrupted nuns, ibid. Nuns are not to go to the palace or public gatherings, ibid., 317.—On nuns who depart from their sacred profession, Burchard, CXL, 794. On nuns who presume to veil others, ibid., 795. On those who take nuns in marriage, ibid., 797.—That nuns not presume to eat or drink in their houses with any males, Burchard, CXL, 811.—That nuns not leave without the abbess’s permission, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 563.—Nuns may not have private lodgings or residences, Gratian, CLXXXVIII, 1089.

**Burials.**—That no one demand anything whatsoever for burial, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 215.—That burials not take place in churches, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 33. That burials not be sold, ibid.—Which dead persons are to be buried in a church, Burchard, CXL, 723. Where the faithful ought to be buried, ibid., 723.—That absolutely no price be demanded in any way for a place of burial, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 220. That no one be buried in a church unless, by living piously and justly, he has acquired such a place for himself in death, ibid., 249. That nothing be demanded for a place of burial, ibid., 349, 252.—Wherever a person has paid tithes, there he ought to choose burial, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 941. Even when compelled, we ought not to receive payment for burial, ibid., 944. Who are buried in a church, ibid., 946. Why the dead are buried beside a church, ibid., 947.—That arsonists and excommunicated persons not be buried in a church, Innocent III, CCXIV, 546.

**Slaves.**—Slaves are permitted to contract marriages, St Julius I, pope, VIII, 969.—On slaves not to be admitted without their masters’ consent, St Leo the Great, LVI, 967. On slaves who despise their masters, ibid., 788. That slaves ought not to accuse [anyone], ibid., 222. On slaves who cast off the yoke of service under pretext of Christianity, Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 885.—On an ordained slave, Collection of Canons, XCIX, 1007.—That a bishop may lawfully sell fugitive slaves of the Church, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 405. On slaves who flee to a church, ibid., 497. That slaves not be admitted to the clergy or to a monastery under pretext of religion, ibid., 943.—That fugitive slaves of the Church are threatened with sale, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 260. That no one presume to ordain another’s slave, ibid., 267. On ordaining slaves, ibid., 268. On slaves of churches, ibid., 269. Form of manumission for one’s own slave, ibid., 270; Burchard, CXL, 640. If a freeborn woman has intercourse with her own slave, ibid., 342. On one who made himself a slave, ibid., 324. On slaves who flee to a church, ibid., 372.—That a slave ought not to be ordained without his master’s knowledge, Burchard, CXL, 629. That a slave not be received into a monastery without his master’s knowledge, ibid., 797. On lawful marriages of slaves, ibid., 819. On a slave who has fled his master, ibid., 870.—On a slave who flees to a church with an abducted woman, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 222. On slaves not to be admitted to the clergy, ibid., 469. How slaves to be ordained ought to be made freeborn, ibid., 476. On the ordination of slaves, ibid., 477. On slaves of churches, ibid., 478. On slaves ordained without their masters’ consent, ibid., 518. That no cleric dare remove his slave or disciple from a church, [Col. 1065] ibid., 523.—On a slave who fled his master, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 813. On criminal slaves, 924. If a slave secretly intrudes into the priesthood, let him be fined by the loss of his property, 293.—Neither for a profession of religious life nor for clerical office are slaves to be admitted without their masters’ consent, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 295. Slaves who pass from unbelief to faith are to be vindicated into freedom, ibid., 298. It is not lawful for an abbot or monk to free a slave belonging to a monastery, ibid., 299. A slave cannot make a will, ibid., 940. After security has been given, slaves who flee to a church are to be restored, ibid., 1072. A slave is permitted to contract marriage, ibid., 1433.

**Subdeacons.**—That carnal marriage is forbidden to subdeacons, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 293.—Subdeacons are to be ordained, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 399.—No cleric, not even a subdeacon, is permitted carnal marriage, Burchard, CXL, 650.—Subdeacons are not to have wives, Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1360.—That a married subdeacon or one living with a concubine lose both office and benefice, Council of Reims, CLXXIX, 680. Let no one become a subdeacon who has not promised to live chastely, ibid., 155.—Those approaching the subdiaconate are to profess continence, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 157.

**Synod.**—On a provincial synod to be reconsidered by the pope, St Julius I, pope, VIII, 987.—That synods be held twice yearly in every province, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 42; Ancient Collection of Canons, XCIX, 995.—That two episcopal assemblies be held every year, Burchard, CXL, 561. On synods, at what time they should be held, ibid.—A synod ought not to be convened without the authority of the Roman pontiff, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 93.

**Vessels.**—That sacred vessels ought not to be handled by any except sacred persons, Burchard, CXL, 714, 715. If they have been worn out by age, what is to be done with them, ibid. On the vessels in which the sacred mysteries are performed, Burchard, CXL, CXL, 721; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 262.—That priests have a clean vessel in which the body of the Lord may be stored with care, Burchard, CXL, 754.—Sacred vessels are not to be handled by any except persons consecrated to the Lord, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 175.—Unconsecrated ministers may not touch the Lord’s vessels, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 138. Sacred vessels are not to be alienated except for the redemption of captives, ibid., 899. Vessels worn out by age are to be burned, ibid., 1717. Sacred vessels are to be handled only by consecrated persons, ibid., 1718.

**Widows.**—On widows, St Leo the Great, LVI, 697, 700.—That widows who have professed continence not marry, Pope Symmachus, LXII, 54; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 380.—That widows not be veiled, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 306; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 923; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 379.—On true widows, Abedoc, XCVI, 1303.—How widows or nuns are to be ordered for the baptistery, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 344.—On secular widows, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 316. On veiled widows, ibid., 381. On widows who violate their professed continence, ibid., 395.—That widows ought not to put on a veil without consulting their bishop, Burchard, CXL, 797. That widows are to be veiled under no blessing, ibid., 798. On widows who once receive the veil of sacred life, ibid. On widows abandoning their profession, ibid., 801. On veiled widows accused of serving the pleasures of the flesh, ibid., 803.—That widows not put on a veil without consulting their bishop, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 556. That no one attempt to veil widows, ibid., 557. That widows departing from the profession of widowhood be excommunicated, ibid., 559.

**Virgins.**—On a veiled virgin who has changed her profession: what is to be judged, St Siricius, pope, XIII, 1182.—On sacred virgins, St Leo the Great, LVI, 697, 700.—That virgins who have professed continence not marry, Pope Symmachus, LXII, 54.—On virgins, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 174, 234. On veiled virgins if they have gone astray, ibid., 244; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 880. On unveiled virgins if they have gone astray, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 245. That sacred virgins be veiled on appointed days, ibid., 306; Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 923.—That virgins not be consecrated before twenty-five years of age, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 334. On the guardianship of sacred virgins, ibid. How virgins who are nuns are to be ordered, ibid., 339. On virgins veiled before twenty-five years of age because necessity compels, ibid., 374. On virgins consecrated to God if they have committed adultery, ibid., 415. On secular virgins if they have committed adultery, ibid. On sacred virgins, if they have fallen, or
have married publicly, ibid., 701. Concerning unveiled virgins, if they have gone astray, ibid. Concerning when consecrated virgins are to be veiled, ibid., 943. That virgins who have professed continence are thereafter not to marry, ibid., 993. — Concerning unveiled virgins, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 394. — At what time the sacred veil ought to be imposed upon consecrated virgins, Burchard, CXL, 795. Concerning virgins: at what age they ought to be veiled, ibid., 793. In what dress virgins ought to come for consecration, ibid., 796. — Concerning consecrated virgins, if they have fallen, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 549. At what time the veil ought to be imposed upon consecrated virgins, ibid., 553. Concerning consecrated virgins who have resolved to transfer to another monastery for the sake of a stricter life, ibid., 154. — Virgins are not to be consecrated before their sixtieth year, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1102.

[Col. 1065]

CXV. INDEX OF THE COUNCILS MENTIONED IN THE *PATROLOGY*, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED, GIVING THEIR HISTORY, THEIR VARIOUS PROCEEDINGS, AND THEIR CHRONOLOGICAL SEQUENCE.

NOTICE.

A council or synod is generally defined as: an assembly of the prelates of the Church in one place, for the examination and determination of matters pertaining either to faith, to morals, or also to discipline. Four kinds are distinguished: general, national, provincial, and diocesan. Since very many councils are either mentioned or cited in the course of our *Patrology*, we have resolved briefly to set forth their history in this Index; and, in order that the reader might more easily find what is sought, we have arranged them alphabetically, indicating the year, volume, and columns. We have moreover added a chronological sequence of the same councils.

[Col. 1065] **African Council (A.D. 249).**—Saint Cyprian presided over this council. It decreed that clerics were not to undertake testamentary guardianship, lest, being entangled in secular affairs, they should be drawn away from sacred duties; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 178.

**African Council (A.D. 251).**—Saint Cyprian again presided, [Col. 1066] in the case of Felicissimus and the five priests who had embraced his party. There they were condemned and excommunicated. Novatus was convicted of heresy and treachery. The lapsed were also discussed. Seventy bishops were present; St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 178.

**African Council (A.D. 369).**—Chronopus was here deposed from [Col. 1067] the episcopate. Having been condemned, he appealed to the secular magistrate contrary to the provisions of the laws, and Emperor Valentinian condemned him to pay a sum of money for the poor; St Isidore of Seville, LXXX, 178.

**Universal African Synod (A.D. 425 or 426).**—Convened by Aurelius concerning the Pelagians and the monk Leporius, converted from error to the right faith; Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 363.

**African Council (A.D. 646).**—The three primates—Columbus of Numidia, Reparatus of Mauretania, and Stephen of Byzacena—sent a synodal letter to Saint Pope Theodore regarding the promulgation of the *Ecthesis* in support of the Monothelites. They sent another to Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, asking him to reject this novelty; and a third to the emperor, asking him to command that the scandal of the new teaching be removed and to compel Paul to conform himself to the faith of the whole Church. They also condemned the teaching of the Monothelites; Isidore of Seville, LXXX, 178.

**Council of Agde (A.D. 506).**—Alaric, king of the Visigoths, though an Arian, permitted the Catholic bishops to be summoned to a council. About thirty-five bishops then assembled in the city of Agatha (Agde) and enacted forty-seven disciplinary canons; ibid., LXXXIV, 256.

**Council of Alexandria (A.D. 326).**—Five months after the Council of Nicaea had been held, Saint Alexander, near death, chose Saint Athanasius as his successor in the Church of Alexandria, by God’s command. Athanasius was absent. “Athanasius,” Alexander then cried, “you are trying to flee, but you shall not escape”; Cassiodorus, LXIX, 288.

**Council of Alexandria (A.D. 339).**—When Eusebius of Nicomedia and his adherents had substituted an Arian priest for Athanasius in the episcopal see, Athanasius summoned this council lest the Arian doctrine should grow in Alexandria. About one hundred bishops sat in it; ibid.

**Council of Alexandria (A.D. 362).**—Held under the emperor Julian, after the killing of George, who had been imposed by the pagans. From a manuscript found in the Church of Vercelli, Saint Eusebius is said to have presided with the authority of legate of Pope Liberius, who had entrusted the same mission to his fellow-exile in the Thebaid, Lucifer of Cagliari. Lucifer, however, sent in his own place two deacons, Heremius and Agapetus, while he himself went to Antioch, where he ordained Paulinus, leader of the Eustathian party. Rufinus of Aquileia, XXI, 498.

**Synod of Anazarbus (A.D. 423).**—Held by Maximian against Julian; Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 359.

**Council of Ancyra (A.D. 314).**—Vitalis of Antioch presided. It was convened to deliberate and determine matters concerning those who, during the persecution raging under Emperor Maximinus Daia, had denied the faith; these matters are explained in twenty-five canons; Tertullian, III, 314.

**Conventicle of Ancyra (A.D. 358).**—This pseudo-council was held by twelve Semi-Arian bishops, with Basil of Ancyra presiding. They produced an exposition of the faith of the Fathers containing eighteen anathemas. All these enactments must be rejected; and the false charge that Pope Liberius subscribed to an Arian or Semi-Arian formula must likewise be dismissed; Saint Hilary of Poitiers, X, 489.

**Conventicle of Ancyra (A.D. 375).**—Demosthenes, praetorian prefect in Pontus and Cappadocia, convened it. He ordered Hypsius, bishop of Ancyra, to be deposed and Cedic(i)us to be substituted in his place. At the same council, a certain low fellow named Philocharis accused Saint Gregory of Nyssa. The council mentioned above is regarded as spurious and must be rejected; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 264 and following), against Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch.**—The first of these councils was presided over, as is thought, by Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Since the Fathers could not convict him on that occasion, they held another there, in which, as noted, Firmilian absolutely condemned and rejected the new doctrines of Paul of Samosata. But since this heresiarch promised to correct his errors, the Fathers deferred their sentence; Pope Saint Damasus, Prolegomena, XIII, 303; Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 1129.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 270), against the same Paul of Samosata.**—The disputed case of Paul of Samosata was not ended by either the first or the second council. Rufinus, following Eusebius, records that the bishops met against him again and again at different times, and at each meeting conferred with him, to induce him to acknowledge his errors and return to the faith. This was the third council concerning him. When Firmilian had died while travelling to Tarsus, Helenus, bishop of that city, presided. In it the Fathers deposed Paul and pronounced sentence of excommunication. After this sentence, they chose Domnus, son of Demetrianus, bishop of Antioch. One hundred and eighty Fathers sat there; ibid., 1139.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 332).**—Bishops of the patriarchate of Antioch sat there in order to elect a new patriarch in place of Saint Eustathius, who had died in exile. At this council the twenty-five canons commonly ascribed to the Dedication were enacted, concerning confirmation of the Nicene decree, the celebration of Easter, and so forth; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 341).**—The occasion of this council was that Constantine the Great ordered the basilica he had built at Antioch to be dedicated to God, and summoned a great many bishops to that city for the dedication. One hundred and thirty-seven Fathers sat there: ninety bishops of orthodox faith, and forty who professed Arian doctrines covertly. Pretending to adhere to the right faith, they set forth a formula of faith for this purpose. The twenty-five canons mentioned above were adopted by the Fathers, who sent them to the bishops of all provinces with a synodal letter asking them to subscribe in confirmation of them, affirming that they had made and decreed nothing except by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 348), against Stephen, intruded into Antioch.**—The occasion was that Emperor Constans, wishing to execute the judgment of the Council of Sardica and restore bishops unjustly deposed, sent Vincent of Capua and Euphratas of Cologne, with the prefect Salianus, to his brother Constantius, to deliver a letter in which he stated firmly that, if necessary, he would establish them in their episcopal sees by force of arms. Stephen, intruded into Antioch and deposed by the Council of Sardica, then devised a plot against Constans’s two envoys. He was therefore charged and excommunicated; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 361).**—The occasion was this: when Emperor Constantius, returning from war, was staying at Antioch, he convened a council there to promote the Arian cause, for he greatly favoured that party. The emperor intended that the Fathers should reject consubstantiality and the distinction of substance. They, however, declaring above all that, the see being vacant, they must proceed to elect a bishop, gave their votes from the various sides to Saint Meletius. Within thirty days he expelled the Arians and cured the city of every error; this caused his expulsion. He was succeeded by the Arian Euzoius; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 379).**—Saint Gregory of Nyssa tells us that the orthodox bishops of the East, after being recalled from exile and restored to their sees, held a council at Antioch. Its principal and unquestionable purpose was the peace of the Church of Antioch and the confirmation of Saint Meletius in episcopal rank; for he holds first place in the subscriptions, surely because he presided. It is well known that the Fathers accepted the synodal letter, or exposition of faith, of the council held at Rome under Saint Damasus, which confirmed the Church’s faith concerning the Trinity and specifically concerning the Holy Spirit, and rejected the errors of Apollinaris; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 383 or 390).**—Held by Flavian, bishop of Antioch, with three other bishops and thirty priests or deacons. (It was against the Messalians.) It denied penance to Adelphius, who maintained associations with them. The Messalians were condemned in this council and in the councils of Side, of the East, and the ecumenical Council of Ephesus; ibid.

**Council of Antioch (A.D. 388 or 389).**—Its occasion was the violent death of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Apamea. While he was engaged in destroying a pagan temple in the village commonly called Aulon, in the territory of Apamea, he was seized by pagans and thrown into the fire. The people of Apamea burned to avenge the death of their bishop. But the Fathers sitting in this council pronounced a sentence of pardon in favour of the accused; ibid.

**Synod at Antioch (A.D. 417).**—Held by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, against Pelagius, in October; Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 344.

**Council of Aquileia (A.D. 381).**—This council was held against Palladius, suspected of favouring the party of Arius; Saint Hilary of Poitiers, X, 685.

**Council of the Province of Aquileia (A.D. 440–450).**—Convened by Saint Leo against the Pelagians; Saint Leo, LIV, 593.

**Council of Aquileia (A.D. 557).**—Held by Paulinus, archbishop of Aquileia, but disapproved. It condemned the latest ecumenical council of Constantinople, and those sitting rejected communion with those who supported it, not excepting communion with the pope; Saint Hilary of Poitiers, X, 685.
