[Col. 1069] **Council of Aquileia (A.D. 698).**—Those sitting there unanimously renounced the schism binding the bishops of Istria from the time when Pelagius I obtained the apostolic see; ibid.

**Council of Aquileia (A.D. 1181).**—Valdericus, or Ulric, convened it in order that his canons might adopt the common life; ibid.

**Council of Aquileia (A.D. 1184).**—Convened against arsonists and sacrilegious persons; ibid.

**Council of Aachen (A.D. 789).**—There survives a collection of thirty-seven capitularies concerning ecclesiastical discipline, issued by Charlemagne. The Synod of Soissons calls these synodal capitularies, as relating to the present council; Caelius Sedulius, Prolegomena, XIX, 518.

**Arabian Council (A.D. 246 or 249).**—In the fourth year of Philip’s reign and the eleventh of Fabian’s pontificate, a council was held in Arabia, at which very many bishops sat, against certain Arabian heretics whose doctrine was that the human soul dies with the body and will one day rise again with it; Cassiodorus, LXIX, 289.

**First Council of Orange (A.D. 441).**—Held under Valentinian III, in the pontificate of Saint Leo I, and in the church of Justianiana. Saint Hilary of Arles presided. The seventeen Fathers sitting there enacted thirty canons; Saint Augustine, XLI, 1785.

**Second Council of Orange (A.D. 529).**—Held under Saint Caesarius, who presided, in the pontificate of Pope Felix IV and the reign of Athalaric, king of Italy. Grace and free will were discussed according to the Catholic faith. Twenty-five articles were enacted concerning this faith; Saint Prosper, LI, 612 ff.

**Council of Orange (A.D. 1229).**—Albigensians and persons suspected of this heresy, whom the inquisition at Toulouse had discovered, were admitted to penance; Saint Caesarius, LXVII, 1142.

**First Council of Arles (A.D. 314).**—It decreed, against his Donatist accusers, the innocence of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, and more besides. It enacted Canon 8: “Concerning Africans who are accustomed to employ rebaptism according to their own law: if anyone comes from heresy to the Church, question him on the Creed. And if they ascertain that he has been baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, let hands only be laid upon him, that he may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, he does not answer this Trinity, let him be baptized.” Several authors, such as Abbot Cuminus and Ado, count six hundred bishops present; Baronius counts two hundred, of whom thirty-six are recorded in the subscriptions. Tertullian; Thomassin, *Dissertation on Synods, on the Baptism of Heretics*, III, 1223.

**Council of Arles (A.D. 353–354).**—This conventicle, in which several Arian bishops sat, was convened by Constantius. It condemned the holy doctor Athanasius, Photinus, and Marcellus of Ancyra, as Sulpicius Severus affirms; Albaspinaeus, *Observations on Saint Optatus*, XI, 1176.

**Council of Arles, held in an uncertain year.**—Some maintain that it was held in 443 or 444; others, in 451 or 452. The Fathers sitting there are not named. At this council Quelidonius, or Celidonius, was deposed from the episcopate; ibid.

**Third Council of Arles (A.D. 445 or 461).**—Held under Bishop Ravennius. It reconciled Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, and the abbot of Lérins, who were disputing concerning jurisdiction; ibid.

**Council of Arles (A.D. 475).**—Convened by Leontius, bishop of that city. There the priest Lucidus renounced his errors concerning predestination and grace. About thirty bishops sat there; ibid.

**Council of Arles, commonly called the Fourth (A.D. 524).**—Saint Caesarius, bishop of the city, presided. It was convened on the occasion of the dedication of the Church of the Holy Virgin, on 6 June in the first year of the pontificate of John I. Many matters were enacted, especially concerning the ordination of deacons, promotion to the episcopate, and so forth; ibid.

**Fifth Council of Arles (A.D. 554), convened under Sapaudus, bishop of that city.**—Among other matters, it made certain decrees concerning liturgy and ecclesiastical discipline; ibid.

**Council of Arles (A.D. 813).**—At this council, the convocation of which, together with four others, was initiated by Charlemagne, the Fathers enacted several articles concerning reform; ibid.

**Council of Arles (A.D. 1059), held under the legates of Pope Nicholas II.**—At this council Berengar, viscount of Narbonne, made a petition [Col. 1070] for revocation of the excommunication imposed upon him by Guifred, archbishop of that city; ibid.

**Council of Arles (A.D. 1205).**—Held by the legate Peter of Castelnau, where he issued several constitutions for the Church of Arles; ibid.

**Council of Rimini (A.D. 359), a general council, probably presided over by Restitutus, bishop of Cardi. [unexpanded in source].**—At this council ten anathemas were pronounced against the various errors of Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius; moreover, those who advocated them were unanimously condemned and deposed, among them Ursacius, Valens, Caius, and Germinius. All the bishops said: “We desire these heretics to be condemned, so that the Catholic faith may remain firm and there may be peace in the Church.” Four hundred bishops sat there from different provinces of the West, Illyria, Italy, Africa, Spain, Gaul, and so forth. After a long time, the envoys to the emperor, wearied out, annulled what the Fathers at Rimini had determined so solemnly and yielded to the Arians; Saint Hilary of Poitiers, X, 699.

**Council of Auvergne.**—Held in A.D. 525; see its notice in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 519; Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 406.

**Council of Auvergne, Clermont (A.D. 535), the first under the pontificate of Agapetus.**—Honoratus, archbishop of Bourges, and fourteen other bishops of Gaul sat in council in the city of Clermont with the consent of King Theudebert. They began by kneeling and offering prayer for the prosperity of the king and kingdom; then, after the old statutes had been read, they renewed several of them and added sixteen others; ibid.

**Council of Auvergne, Clermont (A.D. 549).**—Hesychius, archbishop of Vienne, presided. It was held shortly after the Fifth Council of Orléans, whose sixteen canons it renewed in their entirety. Ten prelates sat there; ibid.

**Council of Auvergne, Clermont (A.D. 587).**—Saint Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, presided and, in unanimous agreement with the other prelates sitting there, ended the dispute between Innocentius, bishop of Rodez, and Urcinus, bishop of Cahors. The dispute had arisen concerning jurisdiction over several parishes assigned to the former; ibid.

**Council of Auvergne, Clermont (A.D. 1077).**—Held by the legate Hugh of Die, who presided. Simoniacal bishops were deposed there; ibid.

**Council of Astorga (A.D. 445 or 446).**—When the acts composed by Saint Leo against the Manichaeans reached Spain, the bishops of that region sought to discover adherents of that doctrine wherever they might be concealed. Idacius and Turibius, having found several Manichaeans in Astorga, sent writings concerning them to Antoninus of Mérida. Antoninus then ordered Pascentius, already apprehended, to be expelled from Lusitania. Hence, as is thought, the council here mentioned was held in that city; Saint Leo, LV, 1034.

**Council of Arras (A.D. 1025).**—Gerard, bishop, presided. The Manichaean heresy was spreading in the diocese of Arras. The bishop perceived the poison of perverse doctrines; he searched out the sectarians, compelled them to attend the synod, and urgently demanded an explanation from them, pressing and insisting that they abandon and abjure their evil doctrine. To confirm the attestation of their faith, he required each one to write a certain [+] character in the form of a cross; Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, CXLII, 1269.

**Council of Arras (A.D. 1097).**—Held by Bishop Lambert, with his archdeacon and five abbots sitting. The bishop confirmed for the abbot and monks of Saint Eligius’s Mount the privileges granted by his predecessors; he also exempted another monastery, of the Arroasians, from every other jurisdiction, including his own, granting the monks the right to elect an abbot and the abbot the right to reconcile defiled places; Pope Saint Urban II, CLVI, 1174.

**Assembly of Augsburg (A.D. 952).**—There were discussed, with united diligence of both holy clergy and people, the advancement of the Church’s stability and the interests of all Christendom. The venerable Frithuric, archbishop of the see of Mainz, presided. Several archbishops and about twenty bishops were present. There the most pious King Otto pledged himself to be a supporter of ecclesiastical affairs. On hearing this royal promise, the presiding archbishop, with the common assent of the others, ordered the chapters to be entered under titles; *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 833.

**Council of Autun (A.D. 590), convened by Guntram concerning Tetradia.**—Tetradia was the wife of Eulalius, count of Auvergne; she had left her husband in order to attach herself to a count named Didier. The council, however, condemned her to restore to Count Eulalius her own paraphernal goods twice over, or up to four times their value, and what had been removed from his house; and it imposed the stigma of infamy upon the adulterine children whom she had borne to the adulterous count, declaring them illegitimate; Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 520.

**Council of Autun (A.D. 670).**—Saint Leodegarius, bishop of that city, convened another council and presided over it. Several of its statutes survive, while others are lacking; for in the order of transcription there is a transition from the first to the fifth, from the sixth to the eighth, from the eighth to the tenth, and from the tenth to the fourteenth and fifteenth, according to the most ancient collections, in which the preceding material is wholly and entirely absent; ibid.

**Council of Orange (A.D. 408).**—In the time of the consuls Theodosius Junior and Cyrus, on 8 November, in the church of Justianiana; Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 391.

**Council of Orléans (A.D. 511).**—King Clovis convened it on the advice of Saint Remigius of Reims. Five metropolitans sat there—of Bordeaux, Bourges, Tours, Auch, and Rouen—who, with other bishops, enacted thirty-one canons; Saint Leo, LVI, 312.

**Council of Orléans (A.D. 538), under Pope Silverius.**—Saint Lupus, archbishop of Lyons, presided, together with nineteen other bishops, who subscribed to thirty-three canons enacted to renew the ancient canons concerning discipline; ibid.

**Council of Orléans (A.D. 549), in the reign of Childebert.**—Sacerdos, archbishop of Lyons, presided. It was assembled in order that the case of Marcus, bishop of Orléans, might be heard. It was composed of bishops from all the provinces of the three kingdoms of Gaul. Marcus was restored to his episcopal see, and four canons were enacted; ibid.

**Council of Orléans (A.D. 634).**—Convened against the Monothelite heresy which threatened to spread through Gaul. This council was held through the efforts of Saint Eligius, who was still a layman; ibid.

**Council of Orléans (A.D. 1129).**—Held by Umbald, archbishop and legate of the Apostolic See. The reason for this council is unknown; Pope Saint Urban II, CLVII, 70.

**Conventicle of Bagaia (A.D. 394), irregularly convened by Primian, Donatist and bishop of Carthage, with indispensable formalities omitted.**—Three hundred and ten bishops sat there. What it decreed against Maximian, bishop of Carthage, was of no authority; Saint Optatus, Prolegomena, XI, 846.

**Council of Bagoria (A.D. 740).**—Held in an uncertain place by Saint Boniface, on the recommendation of Pope Gregory III. Eight Fathers sat there; Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 805.

**Council of Bagoria (A.D. 903).**—The matter of this council was a certain donation made by Emperor Louis III to the monastery of Saint Emmeram, with the approval of the archbishop of Salzburg and five other bishops; ibid.

**Council of Bagoria (A.D. 906).**—It confirmed the privilege by which the Frisian Church enjoyed the right to elect its own bishop. Six prelates took part in this solemn proceeding; ibid.

**Synod of Bayeux (A.D. 1518), under the Reverend Lord Louis de Canossa, bishop of that city.**—Various constitutions were issued and published at this synod; John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 235.

**Synod of Beauvais (A.D. 795).**—Charles de Villers, bishop of Beauvais, held this synod with his priests. There he promulgated synodal constitutions, some concerning confraternities, others concerning the sacraments, clerical life, wills, burials, and collections; Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 392.

**Synod of Beauvais under Charles II (A.D. 845).**—This synod was held at the city of Beauvais in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Charles. Venilo, Erchanradus, Ymmo, Rothadus, Simeo, Lupus, Ragenarius, Helias, Erpoinus, Aio, Hincmar, priests, and summoned archbishops sat there and made chapters which the same glorious prince promised, God being witness, under the pledge of his faith, to observe toward all the churches and bishops of his kingdom; *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 543.

**Council of Beauvais (A.D. 1114).**—Held by Cono, cardinal and legate, with three bishops of the provinces sitting. Emperor Henry V was excommunicated there. Several decrees of recent popes concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical property and other matters of ecclesiastical discipline were renewed; Pope Saint Urban II, CLVI, 1199.

**Council of Barcelona (A.D. 599).**—This council seems to have been held at the direction of Pope Gregory in order to uproot the vice of [Col. 1072] simony in those provinces. Asiaticus, archbishop of Tarragona, presided, and eleven bishops sat there and enacted four canons; Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 607.

**Council of Barcelona (A.D. 1064).**—Convened by Cardinal Hugh Le Blanc, legate of Alexander II. The command of clerical continence was recalled to mind; the same council also dealt with abandoning the Gothic rite and adopting the Roman rite. Alexander II was unanimously acknowledged as the legitimate supreme pontiff, and Cadalous was condemned as antipope; ibid.

**Council of Bari (A.D. 1097).**—Held by Pope Urban II, with 183 bishops present. Its purpose was the common reunion of Greeks and Latins; Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 242.

**Councils of Basel and Sens (A.D. 1198).**—These councils were convened concerning the wearing of almutias on the head; Robert Pullen, CLXXXVI, 1118.

**Councils of Basel—or, more accurately, the Council of Basel divided into forty-five sessions (A.D. 1431).**—A long account would be required of the dissensions between the Fathers of Basel and Eugenius IV, and there is a question whether it was ecumenical or not. This assembly caused great disturbance throughout the whole Church. By votes of those sitting, the supreme pontiff was deposed and the antipope Felix V proclaimed; Saint Leo the Great, LVI, 312.

**Council of Benevento (A.D. 1087).**—Held by Pope Victor III. There he excommunicated Guibert, his rival, and pronounced the same sentence against Hugh of Lyons and Richard, abbot of Marseille, both supporters of the antipope. Finally, with the consent of the whole council, he condemned investitures under penalty of excommunication; Pope Victor III, CXLIX, 965.

**Council of Benevento (A.D. 1091).**—Pope Urban II convened this council. There he renewed the sentences of condemnation issued against Guibert the antipope and enacted four canons; ibid.

**Council of Benevento (A.D. 1108).**—Held by Pope Paschal II concerning investitures and the luxury of clerical clothing. He declared excommunicated both the cleric who obtained an ecclesiastical benefice from a layman and the layman himself; ibid.

**Council of Benevento (A.D. 1091).**—Held by Pope Urban II, who confirmed by synodal judgment the sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch and all his accomplices; Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 81.

**Council of Bonogisilus (A.D. 618).**—Held at Bonogisilus, or Bonogel, three leagues from Paris. It forbade a layman to be ordained archpriest; likewise it forbade laypersons to celebrate sacred rites for the dead, administer baptism, or bury laypeople in monasteries except with the ordinary’s permission; Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 634.

**Council of Bonogisilus (A.D. 855).**—The occasion of this council was the dispute between the bishop of Le Mans and the abbey of Anisole, or Saint Calais. Maurice, archbishop of Tours; Venilo of Sens; Hincmar of Reims; Paul of Rouen; and twenty-three bishops sat there with thirteen abbots; ibid.

**Synods of Braga and Tarragona (A.D. 464, 465).**—When Bishop Sylvanus of Calahorra had ordained bishops without the knowledge of Ascanio, the metropolitan, the latter held this synod of his province in order to write concerning the matter to Saint Hilary, supreme pontiff. After examining the matter in a council held at Rome, he sent a synodal letter to the metropolitan of Tarragona, declaring that, in view of several letters of the grandees and magistrates of certain Spanish cities sent to him in Sylvanus’s favour, he granted Sylvanus pardon for the past, provided that in the future he no longer disregarded the canons; Saint Leo, LV, 471.

**Council of Braga (A.D. 560, 563).**—Held by Archbishop Lucretius. In it were read Saint Leo’s letter to Turibius and another synodal letter of the Council of Celenes to Baleonius against the Priscillianists. The decrees against these heretics were confirmed, and abuses that had crept into clerical ministry or the service of God were further reformed; ibid.

**Council of Braga (A.D. 572).**—This is the first council in which the formula “Christ reigning” was used, although it had long been found in other documents. The archbishop of Braga presided, and twelve bishops sat there, six from each province, who enacted ten canons concerning discipline; Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 561.

**Council of Braga (A.D. 675).**—Leodecisius presided and eight bishops sat there; it enacted nine canons; ibid., 585.

**Council of Brenne (A.D. 580).**—The occasion was the accusation brought against Saint Gregory by Leudastes, count of Tours. He charged him with having intended to surrender the city of Tours to Childebert, king of Austrasia, and with having insulted Queen Fredegund by accusing her of an illicit liaison with Bertram, bishop of Bordeaux. The charge was a fabrication by the count, from whom the government of Tours had been taken away. A sentence of excommunication was pronounced there against Leudastes; Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 367.

**Council of Bordeaux (A.D. 1097).**—Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, held this council with the archbishop of Auch and several other bishops and abbots. The church of Saint Peter of Néris was adjudged to the abbot of Saint John of Angély against the abbot of Saint-Maixent; Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 244.

**Synod of the Province of Byzacena (A.D. 507).**—The occasion was that King Thrasamund forbade successors to be appointed when Catholic bishops of Byzacena died. The bishops, however, assembled in council and decreed against the prince’s prohibition. Hence arose a new persecution; Saint Leo, LVI, 120.

**Synod of the Province of Byzacena (A.D. 541).**—Various measures concerning discipline were enacted, and a rescript of Emperor Justinian was approved; ibid.

**Synod of the Province of Byzacena (A.D. 602).**—Held by order of Saint Gregory the Great, supreme pontiff, in order to examine the case of Clementius, primate of that province, accused of grave crimes; ibid.

**Synod of the Province of Byzacena (A.D. 646).**—Stephen, primate of the province, convened this synod. Striking the false teaching of the Monothelites of Constantinople with an anathema, he solemnly confessed two wills and two operations in Christ; ibid.

**Conventicle of Cabarsussa (A.D. 393).**—It definitively condemned Primian, Donatist and bishop of Carthage. One hundred bishops of the Maximianist sect sat there; Saint Optatus, Prolegomena, XI, 861.

**Council of Chalon-sur-Saône (A.D. 470).**—After the death of Paul, bishop of Chalon, a great dispute arose in that Church among the factions of three candidates. Saint Patiens, archbishop of Lyons, whose duty it was to arrange the ordination of a successor, went to Chalon with Saint Euphronius. Other bishops of the province came there, and the lot of election fell upon a holy priest named John, who, in such high matters, silently sought nothing. This pious and holy archdeacon had given everyone a good opinion of himself from the time of his election; the election was confirmed by that bishop; Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 345.

**Council of Chalon-sur-Saône (A.D. 579).**—Salonius, bishop of Embrun, and Sagittarius, bishop of Gap, had been deposed at the Council of Lyons in A.D. 567. They obtained permission from King Guntram to go to Rome; Pope John III, deceived, spared them and restored their episcopal sees. But when they relapsed again, the king held a council at Chalon, at which they were again deposed from the episcopate; ibid.

**Council of Zaragoza (A.D. 380).**—Held against the Priscillianist heretics, whose sect’s first author was Marcus, born at Memphis in Egypt, very skilled in magic and a follower of the doctrine fabricated by Mani; Saint Leo, LV, 996.

**Council of Zaragoza (A.D. 418).**—Held in the form of a conference, attended by Emeritus, one of the Donatist bishops. Saint Augustine in turn exhorted both the people and the Donatists, to bring the latter to unity of faith. But Emeritus maintained profound silence; Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 317.

**Council of Capua (A.D. 389–391).**—Held in order to end the Antiochene schism; the canons of the African Church regard it as plenary. The absence of Flavian, bishop of Antioch, prevented the matter from being concluded. Nevertheless, to establish peace, it was decreed that communion should be granted to all bishops of the East, whatever party they belonged to, provided that they confessed the Catholic faith. The teaching of Bishop Bonosus was also discussed—namely, his denial that the Mother of the Saviour remained a virgin after childbirth. This innovator (*novator*) was referred to the archbishop of Thessalonica and his suffragans, who, assembled in council, condemned him; Pope Saint Damasus, Prolegomena, XVI, 339.

**Council of Quierzy (A.D. 838).**—These are the words of the learned Mansi concerning this council: “In the same year also, that is, 838, the monks of Anisole were again heard at the Synod of Quierzy and again rejected; they were punished by deposition from every priestly rank. At the same council, Florus, a priest of the Church of Lyons, better known under the name Deacon Florus, gave notice and opened the way for the condemnation of the liturgical works of Amalarius, chorepiscopus of Lyons”; Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, CXXV, 85.

**Council of Quierzy (A.D. 842).**—This council was convened for the marriage of Charles the Bald with Ermentrude; ibid.

**Council of Quierzy (A.D. 849).**—By Hincmar’s order, the monk Gottschalk was summoned before this assembly held by King Charles at Quierzy. Twelve bishops sat there. When Gottschalk was questioned concerning his doctrine, he was judged a heretic and incorrigible, and was deposed from the priestly order which he had received from Rigbold, chorepiscopus, without the consent of Rothad, bishop of Soissons; ibid.

**Synod of Quierzy (A.D. 855).**—This synod was held under Benedict III; Flodoard.

Canon of Rheims, CXXXV, 231.

**Council of Carpentras (A.D. 527).**—Saint Caesarius of Arles presided, during the pontificate of Felix IV and the reign of Athalaric, king of Italy. The Fathers punished Agraecius, bishop of Antibes, with suspension from sacred functions for one year, because he had not come to the council and had performed irregular ordinations. Sixteen bishops sat there and subscribed to a canon concerning the administration of parish property, Saint Caesarius, LXVII, 1287.

**Synod of Carrouges [Carrofensis] (A.D. 989).**—Gumbald, archbishop of Bordeaux, held this synod with six other bishops of Aquitaine at the monastery of Carrouges, in the diocese of Poitiers. The Fathers there composed three canons, Letaldus, monk of Micy, CXXXVII, 824.

**Synod of Carrouges (A.D. 1027).**—This was held against the errors of the Manicheans, who were spreading through Gaul, and for the confirmation of peace, ibid.

**Synod of Carrouges (A.D. 1080).**—At this synod the abbot of Saint-Maixent lodged a complaint before the legate Amatus, bishop of Oloron, against the abbot of Mustien-le-Neuf, to whom Count Guy had given property which he had taken from the abbot of Saint-Maixent, ibid.

**First Council of Carthage (A.D. 254).**—This council decreed excommunication against Felicissimus, the unhappy author of the African schism, and against those five Carthaginian presbyters—deserters from the faith and schismatic adherents—who had already twice been excommunicated. It further decreed that the lapsed who were doing penance should be received into the communion of the Church, but not, except in pressing necessity, before the appointed period of satisfaction had been fulfilled, Tertullian, III, 849.

**Second Council of Carthage (A.D. 255).**—This council determined that those among the lapsed who sought return to the Church should be granted it after completing the penance imposed upon them, ibid., 851.

**Third Council of Carthage (A.D. 256).**—This council decreed:

1. That the deacon whom Rogatianus had denounced for insolence and for injuries proved against him should be deposed altogether, unless he refrained [from such conduct].
2. It confirmed a decree of an earlier council against Germinius Victor Christianus, prohibiting his name from being mentioned at the altar in the offering of the sacrifice.
3. It appears to have answered that, in a case of necessity, the baptism of infants ought to be hastened before the eighth day, Tertullian, III, 1013.

**Fourth Council of Carthage (A.D. 258).**—This council decreed concerning Basilides and Martialis, bishops of Spain and holders of certificates of sacrifice (*libellatici*), that they could indeed be admitted to perform penance, but were rightly excluded from clerical ordination and priestly dignity, having also rightly been deprived of their episcopal dignity, ibid., 1019.

**Fifth Council of Carthage (A.D. 258).**—Because of uncertainty, some holding one view and some another in the question of rebaptism, it was finally determined that, since there is one baptism in the holy Church, no one can be baptized outside the Church. It was added that those who, having been rightly baptized by Catholics, had gone over to heretics were to be received, should they strive to return to the Church, not by baptism but by the laying on of hands alone, ibid., 1035.

**Sixth Council of Carthage (A.D. 258).**—This council decreed:

1. That those baptized among heretics or schismatics should, upon returning to the Church, be baptized.
2. That those ordained presbyters or deacons in the Church who had fallen into schism, or had been advanced by heretics, should, upon returning, communicate as laypersons—while preserving nevertheless the bond of concord with bishops who held otherwise, ibid., 1444.

**Seventh Council of Carthage (A.D. 258).**—Held under Bishop Agrippinus, it pronounced unanimously against baptism conferred by heretics. The acts of this council have been lost, ibid., 7051.

**Eighth Council of Carthage (A.D. 258).**—“Whether this council be genuine or spurious,” says Baluzius, “it is placed in this collection, just as certain councils are reported [Col. 1075] in the published editions of councils although it is not established that they were ever held,” ibid., 1101.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 311).**—In this little council Botrus and Celeusius, or rather seventy schismatic bishops, condemned Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, Saint Optatus, XI, 777.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 349), held under Bishop Gratus.**—It is called the first not because no council had been held there previously, but because it was the most ancient, orthodox, and approved among those convened there. At this council thanks are given to God for unity restored, ibid., 803.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 390).**—Genethlius, or Genedius, bishop of Carthage, presided. This council was called the Second Council of Carthage. It decreed concerning the continence of bishops, presbyters, and deacons, ibid., 1195.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 401).**—This council was convened by Aurelius in the secretarium of the Basilica of Restituta. It deals with children baptized among the Donatists, ibid.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 412).**—Convened by Aurelius against Caelestius, in the tenth consulship of Honorius and sixth of Theodosius, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 321.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 416).**—Convened by Aurelius against the absent Pelagius and Caelestius, in the seventh consulship of the Emperor Theodosius and fourth of Junius Palladius, ibid., 331.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 416).**—Held against Pelagius and Caelestius, Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 101.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 418).**—Convened by Aurelius, in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and eighth of Theodosius, Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 347.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 418).**—Gathered by Aurelius from all the provinces of Africa, in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and eighth of Theodosius, ibid., 350.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 418).**—Held there, ibid., 353.

**Synod of Carthage (A.D. 418).**—Gathered by Aurelius from the whole diocese of Africa, ibid., 358.

**Universal Council of Carthage (A.D. 418).**—This council was proclaimed for 1 May at Carthage, Saint Optatus, XI, 821.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 419), held under Aurelius.**—It was agreed at this council to enter in the acts of the Council of Carthage thirty-three canons decreed in preceding councils concerning clerical continence, usury, consecration of holy chrism, public reconciliation of penitents, and so forth, ibid., 862.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 419).**—This council condemned Pelagius and Caelestius as previously, in A.D. 419, Saint Optatus, XI, 1502.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 525).**—This council, convened by Bishop Boniface, was held in the secretarium of the Church of Saint Agilaeus the Martyr. It confirmed the privileges of the Church of Carthage, ibid., 847.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 534), held under Reparatus.**—It decreed that Arian bishops who had returned to the right faith should be barred from ecclesiastical dignities. There the canons of earlier councils were read, and many decrees were issued for restoring ecclesiastical discipline, ibid., 843.

**Council of Carthage (A.D. 550).**—This council was not approved. The bishops sitting there dared to excommunicate Pope Vigilius, because the supreme pontiff had condemned the Three Chapters; and they wrote to the Emperor Justinian, whom they were attempting to draw to their side. Justinian, however, promulgated a rescript in which, refuting the African bishops, he showed himself the defender of Pope Vigilius, Saint Isidore of Spain, LXXXIV, 226.

**Council of Causey [Causeiense] (A.D. 995).**—Held under Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Boniface in Rome and legate of Pope John. At it Arnulf, disturber of the peace of the Church, was condemned and stripped himself of the priesthood, Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 347.

**Council of Chalcedon (A.D. 451), at which Paschasinus presided with the legates of Pope Saint Leo.**—It was assembled as an effective remedy for the storms then agitating the holy Church. The bishops deposed at the Ephesian “council” had urgently petitioned Emperor Marcian for it. There, against Eutyches and Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, the three legates of the supreme pontiff—Paschasinus, Lucentius, and Boniface—pronounced sentence in these words:

> The impious acts committed by Dioscorus are known. He received into his communion Eutyches, condemned by his own bishop; this he denied at Ephesus, and he continues to maintain it, far from seeking pardon. Nor did he permit Leo’s letter to Flavian to be read; moreover, he excommunicated the supreme pontiff. Much inquiry has been made concerning him. Summoned three times, he did not come at the command. Therefore Leo, most holy archbishop of Rome, through us and through this council, together with the apostle Saint Peter, who is the rock, the base, and foundation of the Catholic Church, has deprived him of episcopal dignity and of every priestly ministry.

There were also received there the synodal letters of Saint Cyril, addressed both to Nestorius and to the Orientals, as suitable for rejecting Nestorius’s doctrine and for canonically defining the symbol of the true faith. At this council many other matters were handled in various sessions. Six hundred Fathers sat at it, Pope Saint Damasus, XIII, 364.

**Council of Cirta (A.D. 305).**—There bishops who, during the raging persecution, had handed over sacred books to pagans, and with whom communion had been forbidden by the African proconsular council, were reconciled and received pardon, Saint Augustine, XXXIII, 161, 580.

**Council of Cirta (A.D. 412).**—Bishop Sylvanus, primate of Numidia, presided. This council was convened against the Donatists, Saint Optatus, Appendix to the History of the Carthaginian Conference, XI, 1451.

**Council of Clermont (A.D. 1095), where a decree was made for communion under both kinds.**—This was convened by Saint Robert Pullen [as stated in the source], Pope Urban II, CLXXXVI, 1036.

**Council of Clarendon (A.D. 1164).**—An assembly of the whole realm of England. There were established enactments conforming to the king’s wishes but contrary to the liberties of the Church. Saint Thomas subscribed to those articles called the royal rights. For he was pressured by the other bishops and the magnates of the kingdom. But afterward he was so overcome by grief that he did not dare to celebrate until he had been absolved by the supreme pontiff, Saint Thomas of Canterbury, CLXXXVIII, 131.

**Council of Compiègne (A.D. 823).**—This council dealt with sacred objects unlawfully used; and at the same council penance was again imposed upon Louis the Debonair for certain faults, whose amendment he promised, Saint Agobard, CIV, 230.

**Council of Constance (A.D. 1094).**—Hebehard, bishop of Constance and legate of Pope Urban II in Germany, presided. The incontinence of clerics and the violence of simoniacs were condemned there. The case of Queen Praxedis was also handled: she had secretly left Emperor Henry and fled to Matilda, Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 126.

**Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople (A.D. 381).**—Among many other decisions, this council decreed that heretics joining the right faith, including Arians, Macedonians, Sabbatians, and Novatians, should be received by anointing with chrism; but Eunomians, Montanists or Phrygians, Sabellians, and many others who are baptized by a single immersion should be baptized, Tertullian, III, 1243.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 382).**—This council was assembled under Emperor Theodosius and at his command to resolve various matters, among them the affair concerning Flavian. Gregory Nazianzen was twice invited by delegates sent to him from the council; he excused himself on the ground that he was burdened by illnesses and near death, and could now do nothing, Saint Leo, LIV, 955.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 383).**—The reason for this council was that Emperor Theodosius, to whom nothing was more important than peace in the Empire and the Church, ordered that the bishops of all the separate sects should hold a council, so that from their discussions the fruit of unity and a single judgment might be gathered, ibid.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 448).**—Held by Saint Flavian against Eutyches. After being summoned three times, Eutyches at last came to the council; when the patrician Florentius asked him whether he confessed two natures in Christ after the Incarnation, he replied: “I confess that Christ had two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one alone.” He was therefore anathematized, idem, LV, 1098.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 449).**—Eutyches, condemned in the preceding council, appealed to Pope Saint Leo. At this council, after an examination of the acts of the recently held council, he was ordered by the emperor to set forth his confession of faith, ibid.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 450).**—After Theodosius’s death, his successor gladly received the legates of Saint Leo. Anatolius, whose appointment as replacement for Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, Theodosius had asked Saint Leo to approve, soon assembled this council of bishops then present in the city, abbots, presbyters, and deacons. Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian was read, and Anatolius subscribed to it, saying: “Anathema to Nestorius, Eutyches, and their doctrines,” ibid., 1214.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 519).**—This was held because Timothy had usurped the episcopal and patriarchal see of Alexandria; and while he raged against the orthodox, many Catholic bishops sent a petition to Emperor Leo, requesting Timothy’s deposition and the canonical election of a patriarch. This was the reason for the council, ibid., 1219.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 532).**—At the emperor’s command, for three continuous days six orthodox bishops engaged in prayers and disputations with six bishops favorable to the party of Severus, the Eutychian patriarch of Antioch. But truth triumphed over error, and one of the heterodox was converted to the faith with many clerics and monks, ibid., 975.

**Council of Constantinople (A.D. 543).**—This council was convened by Mennas, patriarch of Constantinople, in the matter of Origen and the Origenists, Liberatus, LXVIII, 1059.

**Council of Córdoba (A.D. 349).**—Hosius presided; it was held against the followers of Arius, Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, *Letter to Constantius*, VIII, 1327.

**Spurious Council of Córdoba (A.D. 852).**—Convened at the order of King Abd al-Rahman, a follower of Muhammad’s sect. It decreed a prohibition against offering oneself for martyrdom and condemned the veneration of such martyrs. Saint Eulogius, priest of Córdoba, attacks and rejects it as false in his work entitled *Memorial of the Saints*, ibid.

**Council on the Bank of the Danube (A.D. 741).**—This council was held by Saint Boniface and a legate of the Apostolic See. The council ordered that the case of any cleric or layperson who had incorrigibly departed from the law of the Lord should be referred to the pope, Pope Saint Gregory III, LXXXIX, 584.

**Council of Diospolis (A.D. 415).**—Held against Pelagius. He was indeed acquitted there, while his doctrine was condemned, since he was compelled to anathematize it in order to avoid his own condemnation. Pelagius’s errors had been gathered into a dossier by Bishops Heros and Lazarus so that they might be read before the Fathers sitting in this council. But when the errors were heard, Pelagius knew how to deceive them, confessing with his mouth the true faith which he denied in his heart, Saint Augustine, XXXIII, 776, 827.

**Synod of Évreux (A.D. 1576).**—At this summer synod there was discussion of restoring ecclesiastical discipline, which had collapsed through the iniquity of the times. It was held under Claude, bishop of Évreux, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 239.

**Council of Egara (A.D. 615).**—Egara was a city of Spain, today Tarraca or Tetrassa. This council was held in that city concerning the celibacy of presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 614.

**Council of Elne (A.D. 1027).**—This was held by Oliba, bishop of Vic, on behalf of Berengar, bishop of Elne. There was discussion of peace and certain matters of discipline. It was decreed that the divine office should be performed for three months on behalf of the excommunicated, that their conversion might be obtained, Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 742.

**Council of Elvira, or Illiberis, the First Held in Spain (A.D. 303 or 309).**—The Fathers who sat there composed eighty-one canons concerning ecclesiastical discipline, Saint Leo, LV, 1019.

**Council of Epaone (A.D. 517).**—This council was held in the first year of the reign of Sigismund, whom Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, had converted to the faith. That bishop presided. Twenty-five bishops of Burgundy sat there and composed forty canons, Saint Dionysius Exiguus, LXVII, 994.

**Council of Ephesus (A.D. 245).**—It was held either at Ephesus or in some other place of proconsular Asia. It was convened against the heretic Noetus and Paul of Samosata. At this council a certain exposition of faith concerning the word *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance”)—which that heresiarch rejected—was read, Pope Saint Damasus, Prolegomena, XIII, 303.

**Council of Ephesus (A.D. 401).**—Held against Nestorius, it condemns him with many Pelagians, Saint Prosper, LI, 594.

**Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431).**—Held against the Messalians and Euchites, and also in the case of Eustathius. Two hundred bishops sat at this same council against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who maintained that a mere man was born of the Holy Virgin Mary, so as to make one person belong to the flesh and another to the Godhead; he did not understand Christ as one in the Word of God and flesh, but preached separately and disjoinedly one Son of God and another son of man, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 151.

**Ephesian “little council” (A.D. 434).**—Assembled in an inn by those bishops who favored Nestorius’s party. Saint Cyril and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus, were deposed there, Saint Prosper, LI, 594.

**Council of Ephesus (A.D. 444).**—Convened in the case of Eutyches, Saint Prosper, LI, 601.

**Council of Ephesus (A.D. 449).**—It became a “Robber Council,” because, with every principle overthrown, Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum were condemned by Dioscorus, Saint Leo, LIV, 966.

**Council of Exolun [Exolunidense] (A.D. 1081).**—Held by the legates Hugh of Die and Amatus of Oloron. The clerics of Exolun were excommunicated because they had not received one of the two legates in procession, Saint Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 182.

**Council of Friuli (A.D. 796).**—This council was convened by Saint Paulinus in the matter of the most holy Trinity and the Incarnation of the divine Word, under Pope Leo III, Saint Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, XCIX, 283.

**Council of Fleury (A.D. 1110).**—Held by the legate Richard, bishop of Albano. Those who made themselves guilty by harassing the Church of Mauri were excommunicated, Saint Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 219.

**Council of Frankfurt (A.D. 794).**—Held by command of Emperor Charlemagne against Elipandus and Felix, bishop of Urgell. Their errors concerning adoption, which they ascribed to the Son of God, were condemned there. Three hundred Fathers sat in this council, Caelius Sedulius, Prolegomena, XIX, 517.

**Council of Frankfurt (A.D. 1006).**—This council decreed the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg. The occasion of this foundation was Saint Emperor Henry II’s desire to honor his birthplace. Although the bishop of Würzburg had vainly demanded the establishment of this new see while retaining his own see with the title of archbishop, he opposed—yet again in vain—the emperor’s petition, Saint Henry, Emperor, CXL, 384.

**Council of Fuscello [Fussellense] (A.D. 1104).**—This council was convened to settle the boundaries of the dioceses of Burgos and Osma. Several other decrees were made there as well, Pope Saint Urban II, CLII, 32.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 197).**—Montanus was condemned there, Saint Leo, LVI, 53.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 355).**—Saint Hilary of Poitiers convened several councils in Gaul against the Arians. At this one the Fathers renounced communion with Saturninus, Valens, and Ursacius, ibid.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 362).**—At this council the Fathers decreed that those who renounced the Arian doctrine should be admitted, provided that they professed the Nicene faith, ibid.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 371).**—At this council faith in the Holy Trinity was confirmed, and the Fathers appealed to the pope against any who denied that faith, ibid.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 429).**—Held when the Pelagian heresy was troubling the region of Britain, now England. In this danger to the true faith, the Catholics of England sought the help of the bishops of Gaul against the error. This was the reason for the council, in which Saint Germanus of Auxerre and Saint Lupus of Troyes sat as defenders of the grace of Jesus Christ, ibid.

**Gallican Synod (A.D. 451).**—Forty-four bishops sat there and approved Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, patriarch of Antioch. Ravennius of Arles presided. The aforesaid letter had been written against Eutyches, ibid., 1236.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 516).**—At this council, when a certain admirer of the Arian doctrine was unable to answer Saint Remigius’s objections, he was converted to the true faith, ibid.

**Gallican Council (A.D. 796).**—This council seems to have been held at Tours, by Charlemagne’s command, in the case of Joseph, bishop of Le Mans, who had been accused by the diocesan clergy of harsh and barbarous tortures. Being on the very point of condemnation, he fled in military dress, yet did not escape deposition, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 178.

**Council of Gangra (uncertain date, A.D. 364).**—This council was held in the metropolis of Paphlagonia against the Eustathians and Manicheans. According to Baronius, Hosius of Córdoba presided as legate of Pope Sylvester. Twenty canons were composed at this assembly, and fifteen bishops sat there, Saint Leo, LV, 979.

**German Council (A.D. 744).**—Saint Boniface, legate of the Holy See, presided. The Fathers composed a capitulary divided into twenty-eight articles; many of these concern civil society more particularly, though at that time they no less concerned ecclesiastical affairs, Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 807.

**German Council (A.D. 759), in an uncertain place, perhaps at Constance.**—According to the *Collection of the Councils of Germany*, Warinus and Ruithard, serfs of the fisc, threw Otmar, abbot of Saint Gall, into prison as though guilty of wicked and lascivious conduct. The abbot’s offence consisted in his having complained, and in wishing still to complain, of their exactions, ibid.

**German Council (A.D. 850), in an uncertain place.**—There was discussion [Col. 1079] whether the dioceses of Bremen and Hamburg should be united into one, ibid., 830.

**Council of Gerona (A.D. 517).**—The metropolitan of Tarragona presided there with six other bishops, and they composed ten canons concerning liturgy and discipline, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 314.

**Council of Gerona (A.D. 1019).**—At this council Peter, bishop of that city, established canonical life with the support of several bishops present in the city, ibid.

**Council of Gerona (A.D. 1097).**—The archbishop of Tarragona held this council with three bishops. It decreed the confirmation of ecclesiastical liberties, Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 230.

**Irish Councils (A.D. 450 or 466).**—Two under the name of Saint Patrick, of which a very ancient manuscript copy is preserved in the library of the Benedictines at Cambridge, Saint Leo, LVI, 302.

**Irish Council (A.D. 795).**—Almost unknown, except that it is cited by a certain author (see Duguet, Dissertation 17, on the first and second canons of the Council of Ancyra), who says that an Irish council was held in A.D. 795, at the beginning of the pontificate of Leo III; from these two canons he infers that a presbyter admitted to public penance caused scandal among the people, ibid.

**Council of Hippo (A.D. 393), a general council of all Africa, convened and presided over by Aurelius.**—Among the other enactments made by the Fathers concerning ecclesiastical discipline, this council decreed that the celebration of Easter should be declared each year in the council customarily held. Ancient monuments, Saint Optatus, XI, 1185.

**Council of Hippo (A.D. 397), a general council of Africa.**—Convened by Aurelius at Hippo, concerning Donatists, the bishops of Carthage, and Donatist clerics to be received among the laity, ibid.

**Council of Hippo (A.D. 422).**—At this council the Fathers condemned Anthony, bishop of Fussala, and deprived him of episcopal governance, though they did not depose him from the episcopate, ibid.

**Synod of Hippo (A.D. 426).**—Convened by Saint Augustine in his old age. At it he chose the presbyter Heraclius as his successor in the episcopate, ibid.

**First Council of Seville, or Hispalis (A.D. 590).**—Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, held this council with seven suffragans, in the fifth year of King Reccared, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 593.

**Second Council of Seville, or Hispalis (A.D. 591).**—This council was held in the sanctuary of the church called Jerusalem, under King Sisebut and Pope Boniface V. Saint Isidore of Seville presided; seven other presbyters sat there, along with two laymen of illustrious rank, including Pisisellus, governor of the province of Baetica, ibid., 595.

**Spanish Council (A.D. 362).**—The bishops assembled in this council decreed that all who returned to the true faith should be admitted, provided they accepted the Nicene faith and anathematized the impious doctrine of Euzoius and Eudoxius, Saint Leo, LVI, 218.

**Spanish Council (A.D. 793).**—This was held by Spanish bishops. They adopted the unfortunate error of Elipandus and Felix of Urgell, attempting to support it with several corrupted passages from the Holy Fathers, ibid.

**Council of Iconium (A.D. 258).**—This council established and decreed against the Cataphrygians and all other heretics that nothing done by heretics—ordinations, baptism, the laying on of hands, or anything sacred administered by heretics—was to be accepted by the Catholic Church, but was invalid. As regards this council, Pope Stephen excommunicated the Eastern bishops who enacted these measures and deprived them of communion with the Apostolic See; he rejected the synod itself as wandering and as confirming an erroneous doctrine contrary to the tradition of the apostles, Tertullian, III, 1152.

**Council of Lleida [Ilerda] (A.D. 524).**—According to Cardinal d’Aguirre, this council was held in the fifteenth year of Theodoric’s reign in Spain. Eight bishops—or rather nine, as the acts testify—sat there and produced sixteen canons, Dracontius, LX, 796.

**Council of Lleida [Ilerda] (A.D. 1229).**—John, cardinal legate and bishop of Sabina, held this council. The Fathers sitting there established enactments concerning ecclesiastical discipline, notably the conduct of clerics, and one special ordinance for the good administration of the Church of Barcelona, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIX, 321.

**Council of Lleida (A.D. 1237).**—At it the task of seeking out heretics was entrusted to the religious of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic, ibid.

**Illyrian, or Illyrican, Council (A.D. 368, 370, or 375), assembled by Emperor Valentinian’s command.**—The reason for its convocation was that the Fathers might put an end to disputes still being debated in Asia and Phrygia concerning doctrine, and to certain abuses committed in electing bishops and ministers of lower rank. The debates especially concerned the nature of the Holy Spirit, which the heterodox had separated from the nature of the Father and the Son; this revived the heresy of Macedonius. The council’s decree was sent to the bishops of Asia and Phrygia with a synodal letter, Pope Saint Damasus, Prolegomena, XIII, 136.

**Illyrian Council (A.D. 415).**—This council was held for Perigenes, a priest of Corinth who had been ordained bishop of the city—commonly Patras—in Thessaly, in the diocese of Eastern Illyricum, by Alexander, bishop of Corinth. Since the inhabitants of the city refused to receive him as bishop, the council was convened to prepare letters of testimonial before the pope concerning Perigenes’s piety and good character. But Rome proved unable to overcome the stubborn resistance of those opposing him, and the matter was delayed for a long time; Alexander, bishop of Corinth, then died, and Perigenes succeeded him, ibid.

**Illyrian Council (A.D. 516).**—Held by John, bishop of Nicopolis, metropolitan see of Old Epirus. Seven bishops sat there and composed a declaration against the Eutychians and in favor of communion with Pope Hormisdas, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 950.

**Illyrian Council (A.D. 550).**—At this council the Illyrian bishops, supporters of the Three Chapters, boldly rose against Pope Vigilius’s *Judicatum* and condemned Benenatus, who had opposed the Three Chapters, ibid.

**Italian Council (A.D. 251 or 255).**—This council was assembled under Pope Cornelius in the case of the heretic Novatian. Such a designation was unusual and foreign to the received ecclesiastical custom by which all councils held up to that time, and thereafter as well, took their name from a particular and determinate place. It would scarcely be possible to produce any council of this period called “Italian” rather than “Roman,” Pope Damasus, Prolegomena, XIII, 329.

**Italian Council (A.D. 381).**—Saint Ambrose presided over this council, perhaps held at Milan, of which he was bishop. The Fathers were deceived by the machinations of Maximus the Cynic. Having been expelled from Constantinople, where he had usurped the episcopal see during the time of Saint Gregory Nazianzen, he approached the council, which proclaimed him patriarch of Constantinople and regarded Nectarius as an intruder. The Fathers also condemned the Apollinarians and wrote two letters to Emperor Theodosius the Great, ibid.; Saint Ambrose, XVI, 951.

**Council of Lillebonne [Juliobona] (A.D. 1080).**—William, king of the English, celebrated it with the bishops and nobles of Normandy at Lillebonne, in the eighth year of Pope Gregory VII and the twentieth of Philip, king of the Franks. It decreed concerning the Peace of God, incestuous marriages, and many matters pertaining to discipline, William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 1323.

**Council of Lampsacus (A.D. 364).**—At this council all decrees issued at the Council of Constantinople by Eudoxius and Acacius were repealed, whereas the decrees of the Council of Seleucia were confirmed. When Emperor Valens heard the Fathers’ enactments, he repealed them all, condemned every participant to exile, and ordered all churches to be handed over to the supporters of Eudoxius, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1075.

**Council of Langres (A.D. 1278).**—This council was held by John of Montsoreau, archbishop of Tours. His suffragans sat there and made sixteen statutes, Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 564.

**Council of Laodicea (A.D. 364).**—This was famous in ancient times, and its sixty canons have always possessed great authority, Saint Leo, LVI, 714.

**Lateran Council (A.D. 649).**—This council was held against Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, and Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, together with Pyrrhus and Paul, who admitted in Jesus Christ only one operation and one will. In twenty canons it established the Church’s faith concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, and anathematized those same heretics, Saint Optatus, XI, 844.

**Lateran Council (A.D. 1179).**—Pope Alexander III, reconciled with Emperor Frederick, convened this eleventh general council for three weighty reasons: first, to abolish the remaining effects of the schism; second, to condemn the heresy of the Waldensians; and third, to restore ecclesiastical discipline, which had been torn apart by so long a schism, Saint Bernard, CLXXXII, 202.

**Lateran Council (A.D. 1215).**—This Fourth Lateran Council, the twelfth ecumenical council, was convened by Pope Innocent III. Its purpose was the recovery of the Holy Land, reform of the discipline of the universal Church, the extinction of wars and heresies, the strengthening of the faith, and restoration of peace. Four hundred and twelve bishops sat there; more than eight hundred abbots and priors; and a great number of representatives for absentees. The pope himself presented to the council seventy decrees or canons, beginning with an exposition of faith, Peter of Vallis, monk of Ceruaius, CCXIII, 702.

**Council of León (A.D. 1088).**—It was decreed there that ecclesiastical offices in Spain should be celebrated according to the rule of Saint Isidore, and that writers should afterward use Gallic script in place of Gothic script, Pope Saint Urban II, CLI, 85.

**Second Council of Limoges (A.D. 1028 and 1031).**—This council deals with Saint Martial’s apostleship and many matters pertaining to discipline. Jordan, bishop of that city, presided, Jordan, bishop of Limoges, CXLII, 1353.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (Toul; A.D. 916).**—Drogo, bishop of Toul, restored to the abbey of Saint Aper, at the request of its abbot, tithes claimed from it by a neighboring church, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 65.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 971).**—Saint Gerard, bishop of Toul, there made a donation of several *villarum* [rural estates] to the Church of Saint Michael, ibid.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 982).**—At this synod Saint Gerard, bishop of Toul, confirmed the property and privileges of the abbey of Saint Mansuetus, ibid.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 983).**—At this synod a new donation was made to the Church of Saint Michael, ibid.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 1050).**—Pope Saint Leo, with others present, at this time canonized Saint Gerard by translating his body from the place where it had been laid to the church of the abbey of Saint Mansuetus, ibid.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 1072).**—At this synod Bishop Pibo issued a confirmation of donations made by his predecessors and by himself, ibid.

**Synod at the City of the Leuci (A.D. 1076).**—At this …

At the synod, the same bishop’s mandate was issued in favour of the church commonly called Notre-Dame, founded by Countess Sophia and consecrated by the bishop himself, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1090).—In this synod Bishop Pibo adjudged the church of Bar to the abbess of Épinal, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1091).—In this synod an endowment was made for the abbey of St Leo at Toul by Luctulf, dean of the cathedral, and confirmed by the bishop, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1105).—In this synod Pibo confirmed donations made to the church of St Gengulph at Toul, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1111).—In this synod Riquin, administrator of the church of Toul, pronounced a judicial sentence in favour of the Abbey of Cluny, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1116).—Riquin, having become bishop, made a new donation to the Abbey of St Aper, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1122).—There Bishop Riquin confirmed a donation of the priory of St Dodon made to the Abbey of St Mansuetus, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1136).—Confirmation by Bishop Henry of a donation made to the Abbey of St Mansuetus, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1192).—Odo, bishop of Toul, there promulgated several statutes against usurpers of ecclesiastical property, and another against the Waldensian heretics, whom he ordered to be brought before him in chains, so that he might inflict upon them the punishment they deserved, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1359).—In this synod Bertrand de la Tour promulgated most lucid statutes. He ordered abbesses to attend the episcopal synod, ibid.

Synod of the Leuci at the city (1658).—André Saussé, bishop of Toul, held this diocesan synod, in which he renewed many old statutes, reformed others, and added others. In his pastoral letter the prelate, full of zeal, maintains that a diocesan synod is an exceedingly useful means for the reformation and correction of morals, ibid.

Council of Lisieux (1055).—Bishop Hermenfrid, papal legate, presided over this council. Mauger, archbishop of Rouen, was accused there of having despoiled his church, squandered its possessions through prodigality, lived in incontinence, and failed to revere the Apostolic See. When these charges had been proved, he was deposed by the unanimous voice of the bishops assembled there [Col. 1082], and Maurilius was appointed in his place. Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 42.

Council of Langres (830).—Alberic, bishop of Langres, procured confirmation of the donations which he had made to the monastery of St Peter, commonly called Bèze. St Leo, LVI, 312.

Synod of Langres (1017).—In this synod the monastery of St Benignus at Fruttuaria was exempted from the jurisdiction of the ordinary, ibid.

Council of Langres (1116).—This was held by the archbishop of Vienne, commonly called Guy, in open country between Luz and Til-Châtel, in the diocese of Langres, now Dijon. Several particular matters were dealt with there, ibid.

Council of Liptines (743).—In it the decrees of the preceding German synod were approved and new enactments made. It was celebrated under Carloman, mayor of the royal household. There abbots and monks received the Rule of the holy father Benedict in order to restore the norm of regular life. It was also decreed that, by way of *precarium* and rent, some part of ecclesiastical revenue should be retained to assist the army; that adulteries and incestuous marriages, which are unlawful, should be prohibited and corrected by episcopal judgment; and that Christian slaves should not be handed over to pagans. St Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 809.

Council of London (971).—St Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, presided. Edgar, king of England, confirmed the privileges enjoyed from that time by the monastery of Glastonbury, while reserving for himself and his successors the right of placing the abbatial staff in the hands of the abbot elected by the monks. Pope John XIV, *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVII, 518.

Council of London (1075).—This was convened by Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. Thomas of York, archbishop of York, was present, and several abbots sat there. Regulations concerning discipline were enacted, and several constitutions made. Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 41.

Council of London (1078).—Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, presided. It was decreed that several episcopal sees situated in villages should be transferred to cities. Blessed Lanfranc, ibid., 42.

Councils of London (1085).—Two were held in this year by Archbishop Lanfranc, so that the assembled Fathers might reform and regulate discipline, ibid.

Council of Lyons (475).—The heresy of the Predestinarians was again proscribed. Faustus teaches us this in the preface to his treatise *On Grace and Free Will*. Jacques Sirmond, LIII, 681.

Council of Lyons (490).—At this council the Fathers heard the retraction by Lucilius the presbyter of his errors, which he rejected and which had been denounced in the Council of Arles. After the reading of this retraction, those assembled approved it. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 311.

Council of Lyons (575).—Several magnates of the kingdom attended this council. There the brother of Gregory of Tours, accused of murder by his enemies, pleaded his case and cleared himself of the charge by oath, ibid.

Council of Lyons (581 or 586).—This, commonly called the Third Council of Lyons, was held in the twenty-second year of Guntram’s reign. The bishop of that city presided, together with seven other bishops. With twelve delegates of other absent bishops also present, the Fathers enacted six canons, ibid.

Council of Lyons (814).—At this council Agobard was ordained archbishop of Lyons in succession to Leidrad, who had withdrawn to a monastery near the city of Soissons. St Agobard, CIV, 76.

Council of Lyons (829).—It is one of the four councils held by command of Emperor Louis the Debonair. Only the synodal letter of Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, Bernard, archbishop of Vienne, and Eaofou Fove, bishop of Chalon, to the emperor survives; they complained of the protection granted to the Jews and of the harms thereby befalling Christians, ibid.

Council of Lyons (848).—Amolo convened this council concerning a certain presbyter named Godelcarius, whom Usuard, abbot and archdeacon, ordered to be arrested, ibid.

Council of Lyons (1055).—Hildebrand, legate of the Holy See and later Pope Gregory VII, held this council against simoniacs. St Peter Damian reports that, by a miracle, a simoniacal bishop sitting in the council was compelled to confess his crime when ordered to say aloud, “Glory be to the Father.” The bishop could not utter the words, “and to the Holy Spirit.” William, bishop of Tyre, CCI, 1054; St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 311.

Council of Macrianum (934 or 935).—This council [Col. 1083] had the purpose of restraining plunderers of the goods of the Church and despoilers of holy places. Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 328.

Council of Marazanum (418).—Baluze preserved three canons of this council, ibid., 322.

Council of Mâcon (582).—King Guntram ordered this council to be held in the twenty-first year of his reign and the fifth year of the pontificate of Pelagius. Twenty-one bishops sat there. Why it was held is not stated; but it is reported that the bishops, gathered for the needs of the poor, caused the old canons to be renewed rather than new ones enacted. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 455.

Second Council of Mâcon (582).—This council was held by command of King Guntram, ibid.

Council of Mâcon (585).—St Priscus, patriarch of Lyons, presided. According to the king’s counsel, the case was heard of bishops favouring the party of Gundobad; Faustianus, ordained bishop of the city of Aix, was deposed; Bertram of Vaison (Vazarensis), Orestes, and Palladius of Saintes, who had ordained him and were obliged under the law of Bordeaux to provide his necessities of life, were condemned by sentence. Moreover, the Fathers enacted twenty canons, ibid.

Council of Milan (346–349).—This was held against Photinus, already condemned at a Council of Milan, who would not submit. There Ursacius and Valens asked for and obtained pardon, and pronounced anathema upon Arius and his followers. St Leo, LIV, 945.

Council of Milan (355).—Held at the command of Emperor Constantius, after hearing the petition of Pope Liberius. St Athanasius was condemned there; and anyone who refused to subscribe to the sentence of condemnation was, by Constantius’s order, driven into exile. More than three hundred Western bishops sat there, but fewer from the East. St Hilary of Poitiers, X, 562.

Council of Milan (451).—The occasion of this council was as follows. After Eusebius, bishop of Milan, had received a letter from the supreme pontiff, he convened it so that, after this letter had been read, another letter of Pope Leo to Flavian might be read. Both were approved by all and found consonant with the teaching of the Gospel and the Fathers. St Leo, LIV, 945.

Council of Meaux (1082).—In the common collections of councils it is read that one council was held in which Arnold was ordained bishop of Soissons, and another in which Robert was ordained bishop of Meaux. But Mansi proves them to be one and the same. To the acts of this council should be added the charter by which Count Guarin gives the church of St Margaret to the Abbey of Cluny. St Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 101.

Council of Melfi (1059).—This council was held by Pope Nicholas, who presided and pronounced the deposition of the bishop of Trani, canonically convicted of crimes. Most probably, at this council the pope granted the Normans absolution from all censures which they had incurred, on condition that they restore the estates of the Apostolic See which they had usurped. Blessed Urban II, pope, CLI, 56.

Council of Melfi (1089).—Pope Urban ordered this council to be celebrated; Duke Roger was present with many bishops and counts of Apulia, Calabria, and all other provinces. There they enacted sixteen canons, ibid., 57.

Council of Melfi (1100).—Pope Paschal II held this council in October, and there excommunicated the city of Benevento because it had withdrawn itself from obedience to the Apostolic See. He also issued two bulls in the same council, ibid.

Council of Metz (550).—Those assembled there proceeded to the election of a successor to St Gall in the episcopal see of Clermont. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 551.

Council of Metz (590).—There Giles, archbishop of Reims, was deposed. At the same assembly Chrodieldis and Basina, nuns of St Radegund’s at Poitiers, who had been excommunicated in the preceding year, were reconciled to the Church. Basina was restored to her monastery, whereas Chrodieldis withdrew to the estate which the king had granted her, ibid.

Council of Metz (815).—King Charles ordered this council to be held in the church of St Stephen at Metz. The metropolitans Venilo of Sens, Hincmar of Reims, and Rodolphus of Bourges sat there with their suffragans and enacted eighty canons. Adventius, bishop of Metz, CXXI, 1149.

Council of Metz (1204).—Convened by Abbot Cosemarius, legate of the Holy See, in order to reconcile the kings of France and England, who were divided over the county of Poitou, which the king of England said Philip Augustus, king of France, had usurped from him, ibid.

[Col. 1084]

General Council of Milevis (402).—Held under the fifth consulship of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. Aurelius of Carthage presided. The Fathers there enacted several canons. St Leo, LVI, 116.

Second Council of Milevis (416).—Convened against Pelagius. Sixty-one Fathers sat there and sent a letter to Pope Innocent, requesting his condemnation of Pelagius’s errors. St Optatus, XI, 1502.

Synod of Mainz (636).—The object of this assembly, held by King Dagobert, was to make a donation of the city and territory of Ladenburg to the basilica of St Peter at Worms. St Agobard, CIV, 31.

Council of Mainz (813).—This was convened in the sanctuary of the church of St Alban the martyr. Thirty bishops, twenty-five abbots, and many lay counts and judges sat there. The assembly was divided into three groups or orders: first, the order of bishops; second, that of abbots and monks; third, that of counts and judges. They enacted fifty-six canons, ibid.

Council of Montpellier (1195).—Michael, legate of the Holy See, presided; peace was restored there in the province of Narbonne. Heretics and pirates who supplied aid to the Saracens were struck with sentence of excommunication. Several statutes were made, one of them in favour of those fighting the unbelievers in Spain. Five archbishops and bishops attended. Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, monk, CCXIII, 693.

Council at Montil (date uncertain).—Milo, with his colleague Theodosius, summoned very many archbishops and bishops to a certain castle called Montil; and a day was appointed for their appearance before Milo, count of Toulouse, at Valence. Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, monk, CCXIII, 563.

Council of Mouzon (995).—The legate of Lord Pope John, Leo, abbot of the monastery of St Boniface in the city of Rome, presided. Abbots and many laymen attended this council, and before them Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, gave an account regarding his ordination. Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 343.

Council of Nantes (658), a national council assembled at the command of Pope Vitalian.—Flodoard reports one act of this council relevant to his history of Reims: namely, that the Fathers assembled permitted St Nivard, bishop of Reims, to rebuild the monastery of Hautvilliers. Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXXV, 167.

Council of Nantes (1227).—Hildebert, archbishop of Tours and metropolitan in Brittany, convened this council. Conon attended with the bishops of the province. It enacted provisions concerning incestuous marriages. Venerable Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 253.

Council of Narbonne (237 or 260).—There two deacons, accusers of the bishop of Narbonne, confessed both their own guilt and the innocence of St Paul, whom they had accused. St Leo, LVI, 576.

Council of Narbonne (589).—Migetius, bishop of that city, and seven other bishops assembled there and enacted fifteen canons, ibid.

Council of Narbonne (788).—Twenty-six bishops and a certain royal commissioner sat there. They at least discussed, expressly and solemnly, the Felician heresy first condemned in the Council of Regensburg, but defined nothing. They then put an end to disputes among the bishops of Narbonne, Elne, and Bourges concerning the delimitation of the boundaries of three dioceses. St Paulinus of Aquileia, XCIX, 567.

Council of Narbonne (879).—On the borders of the provinces of Arles and Narbonne, two metropolitans met one another in order to judge the dispute between Walfred, bishop of Nîmes, and Rotfred of Avignon, whom the former accused of usurping one church of his diocese. I do not know the outcome of that lawsuit, ibid.

Council of Narbonne (1054).—Guifred convened this council. Ten bishops sat there with the archbishop of Narbonne, together with a large number of abbots, clerics, and nobles. They enacted twenty-four canons. St Urban II, pope, CLI, 746.

Council of Neocaesarea (314–315).—Vitalis of Antioch seems to have presided. It dealt with the case of the lapsed. The twenty-three bishops assembled there enacted fourteen canons. St Leo, LVI, 24.

Council of Neocaesarea (358), against Eustathius, in which he, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, was deposed, ibid.

Council of Nicaea, First Ecumenical (325).—This council defined several prerogatives of the Son of God and confessed against the Arians that he was consubstantial with the Father, using the Greek word ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance.” Nor did it condemn rebaptism, which had been the particular law of the Africans. The Nicene synod likewise judged that, in undertaking to settle the whole baptismal controversy, it should do so not by a creed or confession of faith but by a single canon, decreeing only that henceforth Paulianists should be baptized. The canons of that council comprise only rules of discipline; the definition of faith in ancient councils was generally promulgated separately. Three hundred and eighteen bishops sat there. Tertullian, III, 1236; St Ambrose, XVI, 528; St Prosper, LI, 570.

Second Council of Nicaea (787).—Held under the reign of Irene and her son Constantine. Patriarch Tarasius presided. In the seventh session a decree concerning sacred images was made, and an anathema was pronounced upon the Council of Constantinople in which they had been restored. Three hundred and five bishops assembled there subscribed to this decree. St Leo, LV, 967.

Council—or rather conventicle—of Nicomedia (328).—St Eustathius of Antioch was condemned there to exile. According to others, it was convened at Antioch. Cassiodorus, LXIX, 264.

Council of Noyon (814).—The cause of this council was as follows: Windelmar, bishop of Noyon, and Rotald, bishop of Soissons, disputed with one another concerning certain parishes, each claiming them as his own. Vulfarius, archbishop of Reims and their common metropolitan, wishing to settle the controversy, convened this council, at which a decision was made concerning those parishes. St Agobard, CIV, 311.

Council of Noyon (814).—This was convened so that the Fathers assembled might adopt measures and form a league of the suffragans of the archbishop of Reims against lay incursions upon the liberties of the Church, ibid.

Synod of Noyon (1233).—Henry de Braine, archbishop of Reims, convened this synod against lay incursions upon the liberties of the Church. Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXV, 126.

Council of Huesca (598).—Huesca, formerly Saturnia or Osea, of the Ilergetes, is an episcopal city of Spain in the province of Tarragona under the metropolitan see of Saragossa. This council was held there, and two canons were enacted: one concerning the celibacy of presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons; the other concerning synods to be held annually. St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 982.

Council of Ostia (1077).—Hugh of Die, legate, presided. By order of the pope Manasses of Reims, accused of simony and usurpation, was struck with sentence of suspension there. The legate placed under interdict the archbishops of Tours, Sens, and Besançon, and the bishop of Chartres, because they had not attended this council. In the following year Gregory VII released the submissive prelates from the interdict. Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 334.

Council of Ostia or Autun (1094).—This council was convened by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, with archbishops and abbots of various provinces. King Philip was excommunicated there. Likewise the heresy of simony and the incontinence of priests were condemned under excommunication. St Urban II, CLI, 133.

Council of Palestine (765).—This council was convened at Jerusalem, at the request of John, bishop of Gothia, conveyed by his deacon Longinus, in order to send him a definition of the true faith. Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 204.

Assembly of Pavia (971).—At it a capitulary of Otto the Great, emperor of the Romans, was issued. *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 851.

Synod of Pavia (977).—Ratherius, bishop of Verona, who had been expelled from his see and had withdrawn to Pavia, invoked a council so that he might be restored. Ratherius of Verona, CLXXXVI, 91.

Council of Paris (362).—St Hilary of Poitiers, after returning from the Gauls, ordered various councils to be held so that the Nicene faith might be strengthened and the perfidy of Rimini condemned. Among these councils the Council of Paris is mentioned first. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 426.

Council of Paris (552).—Saffaracus, bishop of Paris, was deposed there, found guilty of violating the canons of Orléans to which he had subscribed. Some say he was guilty of incontinence; others, of simony. In any case, he confessed the crime and was confined in a monastery, ibid.

Council of Paris (615).—This council was held about the third year of Pelagius I and the forty-sixth year of Childebert. Fifteen bishops sat there and enacted ten canons, ibid.

Council of Paris (638).—King Dagobert attended; magnates and bishops sat there. The privileges of the church of St Denis were confirmed there. Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXXV, 102.

[Col. 1086]

Council of Paris (649).—When King Chlothar II had gained possession of the boundaries of the entire Frankish empire and wished to establish administration throughout all its parts, he convened this council in the city of Paris. It is counted as the fifth there, and down to that epoch was held with the greatest number of participants. Eighty-one bishops, together with many magnates and vassals of the prince, sat in the church of St Peter, now St Geneviève, under Bishop Deusdedit. They enacted fifteen canons. St Boniface IV, LXXX, 449.

Council of Paris (649).—When Martin I resolved to convene a large council in order more solemnly to condemn Monothelitism, he sent representatives to Chlothar, asking him to summon the most learned prelates of his realm to this assembly. It was decreed there that the two most eminent men, St Audoenus and St Eligius, should go to Rome as legates to sit in the council. Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXXV, 102.

Council of Paris (1072).—This was held by Gerald, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, so that judgment might be given concerning the dispute between the monks of St Albinus of Angers and the monks of Vendôme over the church of Notre-Dame of Cerdon. St Urban II, pope, CLI, 97.
