Council of Poitiers (590).—This council was held at the time when Chrodieldis and Basina, nuns of the Abbey of Holy Cross at Poitiers, rebelled against their abbess, named Leubvera. For this rebellion they were struck with the penalty of excommunication. St Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 545.

Council of Poitiers (937).—Or rather a diocesan synod. In this synod Bishop Albuin ordered the restoration to the monastery of St Cyprian of a certain right to tithes which had been usurped from it, ibid.

Council of Poitiers (1106).—This council was held before Bohemond, prince of Antioch [the printed “Austriae” is likely an OCR error]. The holy war was proclaimed there, and measures enacted concerning various ecclesiastical matters. St Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 113.

Synod of Pîtres of Charles II (862).—In this synod King Charles summoned several bishops in order to deliberate with them concerning political affairs. *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 683.

Council of Piacenza (1091).—This was held by Pope Urban II, who presided. The crowd of those present was so great that it was held in the open plain. Queen Praxedis received absolution there concerning the marital debaucheries to which she had been compelled by her husband, the emperor. St Urban II, pope, CLI, 141.

Synod of Pontion of Charles II (876).—Part of its acts survives: namely, the petition of Archbishop Hincmar against King Louis; confirmation of the assembly of Pavia, together with the formula of the oath rendered by all the nobles; and so forth. *Monumenta diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 767.

Council of Regensburg (792), against Felix of Urgel.—Alcuin reports that, before Felix of Urgel crossed into Gaul, his case had already been considered at Regensburg before Charlemagne in council, and that his heresy had there been condemned by the assembled Fathers. Coelius Sedulius, *Prolegomena*, XIX, 516.

Council of Ravenna (874).—Pope John VIII presided with seventy bishops assembled there. They put an end to the dispute between Ursus, duke of Venice, and Peter, patriarch of Grado. Authors of uncertain date, CXXIX, 1098.

Council of Ravenna (874).—This council was held concerning Formosus and his ordination, ibid.

Council of Ravenna (874).—This was held by Pope John VIII for the restoration of the discipline and immunities of the Church. To this end nineteen canons were enacted, ibid.

Council of Ravenna (882).—John VIII presided. Charles the Fat attended and issued a diploma in favour of the Abbey of Brum; another declaring that he placed the church of Reggio with its possessions under his protection; and a third in favour of the immunities of churches, particularly the church of Arezzo, ibid.

Council of Reggio (477).—At this council, held under the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, it was decreed that the man whom only two bishops had rashly presumed to ordain should be removed, and it was forbidden that anyone be ordained bishop without the metropolitan. Thirteen Fathers sat there. St Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 249.

Synod of Reims (625).—Sonnatius, bishop of Reims, celebrated it. Bertold, St Arnulf, and many other bishops attended. Many useful enactments were read there concerning the proper administration of Church affairs. *Gesta pontificum Cameracensium*, CXLIX, 34.

Council of Reims (900).—This council was held on the sixth day of July. The murderers of Archbishop Foulques were excommunicated there. Hervaeus presided. Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, CXXXII, 673.

[Col. 1087]

Synod of Reims (991).—Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, presided. Since all the bishops of Gaul could not meet there because of certain affairs of the realm, those chiefly assembled who were fellow-provincials. Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 289.

Council of Reims (993).—Gerbert, archbishop of Reims and later pope under the name Sylvester II, presided over this council of his province. Despoilers of the church of Reims and persecutors of clerics were summoned to do penance and make satisfaction. Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVII, 92.

Council of Reims (1074).—This council was held by Renaud de Martigné, archbishop of Reims, who prevented Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders, from thereafter usurping the succession to the property of deceased clerics. St Urban II, pope, CLI, 97.

Council of Reims (1092).—The presbyterate of Arras had sought from the archbishop of Reims the ordination of Lambert, whom they had chosen bishop of their church. But the archbishop, foreseeing that the presbyterate of Cambrai would obstruct this consecration, did not wish to act on his own authority; for this reason he held the council mentioned here, to which he summoned the presbyterate of Arras, ibid., 110.

Council of Reims (1119).—This council was held by Pope Calixtus II. Four hundred and twenty-seven bishops, abbots, and lay magnates sat there. Those assembled enacted five canons in this council. Guibert, *On His Own Life*, CLVI, 990.

Council of Reims (1141).—There Samson Deprets confirmed the privileges and the possessions of the canons of St Peter of Castet (or Cassel), in the diocese of Thérouanne. St Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 394.

Council of Reims (1148), under the presidency of Eugenius III.—A great number of bishops and abbots from Gaul, and a multitude of foreigners, sat there; only four were English. The Fathers enacted eighteen canons. St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 1169.

Council of Rome (251).—This council decreed separation from the Church of Novatus and those favouring his party. About sixteen bishops sat there. St Cyprian, IV, 135.

Council of Rome (220, 300), convened by Leo so that the Fathers assembled might examine and condemn Manichaean doctrine, as well as the Manichaeans themselves and very many adherents and teachers of Manichaean impiety. St Leo, LIV, 620.

Council of Rome (313).—At it Caecilianus, bishop of Carthage, accused by the Donatists, was acquitted. Nineteen bishops sat there. St Optatus, XI, 932.

Council of Rome (325).—This council was convened by St Pope Sylvester in the presence of Constantine Augustus. In it: first, everything done at Nicaea was confirmed; second, instructions were given concerning the solemn observance of Easter; third, concerning councils to be celebrated three times annually, and so forth; fourth, no cleric was permitted to have a case examined in public; fifth, concerning appointments and advancement through orders; sixth, concerning ordinations and the prohibition upon ordaining neophytes. This synod was held in the city of Rome within the Baths of Domitian, and 275 bishops sat there. St Pope Sylvester, VIII, 825.

Council of Rome (325).—At the same time a council was held at Rome in Constantine’s presence; it again condemned Callistus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. Two hundred and sixty-seven bishops sat there, ibid., 827.

Council of Rome (337).—Convened by Pope Julius in support of the Nicene faith and St Athanasius. One hundred and sixteen Catholic bishops sat there. St Pope Julius, VIII, 857.

Council of Rome (367).—The cause of this council was that Pope St Damasus had been falsely accused of adultery by schismatics. The forty-four bishops assembled there, once the calumny had been exposed, attested the pontiff’s innocence. The same Fathers are thought to have condemned at this council the Paterniani or Venustiani, who rejected marriage. St Pope Damasus, XIII, 129.

Council of Rome (369).—The city of Milan had an Arian bishop named Auxentius. This council was held because St Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt had asked Pope St Damasus for Auxentius’s deposition. Accordingly he was deposed there by ninety Fathers, and they sent a synodal letter concerning his deposition to the bishops of Illyricum, whom he had largely deceived. The schismatic Ursinus was also deposed at the same council. St Pope Damasus, XIII, 129.

Council of Rome (374).—Lucius the Arian, who had usurped the episcopal see of Alexandria, was condemned there; Florens, a bishop favouring the antipope Ursinus, was likewise deposed there. St Pope Damasus, XIII, 129.

[Col. 1088]

Council of Rome (377).—This council was assembled against Eustathius of Sebaste, because he had returned to the heresy of the Macedonians, and against Apollinaris, who had begun to generate a new sect. He was struck both in doctrine and person, and the Fathers deposed him together with his disciple Timothy, who caused himself to be called bishop of Alexandria. This sentence was later confirmed at the Council of Antioch, ibid.

Council of Rome (378).—This later council was held near the end of 378. Its causes were the calumny brought against Pope Damasus by a Jew named Isaac, who favoured the party of the antipope Ursinus, and the audacity of several bishops who, though deposed in councils, still retained episcopal dignity by force. A letter of the Fathers to Gratian and Valentinian survives concerning these evils, inviting them to provide a remedy, ibid.

Council of Rome (379).—The creed of this council survives, together with anathemas against the Macedonians, Eunomians, and errors of the Apollinarians. This confession of faith is contained in the letter which Pope Damasus wrote in 379 to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch. St Pope Damasus, XIII, 164; Coelius Sedulius, appendix, XIX, 787.

Council of Rome (382).—Emperor Gratian strongly favoured the calling of this council. It was numerous, for besides Damasus, the supreme pontiff, and five Western metropolitans, two Easterners also sat there: St Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in the East, and Paulinus of Antioch, with St Jerome. It is thought that communion with Paulinus was confirmed in it, and that it was decreed no longer to communicate with Flavian. There was also disputation with the Apollinarians and discussion of how they were to be received into the Church when they returned to it. St Pope Damasus, XIII, 177.

Council of Rome (386).—This was held under St Pope Siricius and was large in the number of bishops assembled there. The reason for convening it was to renew several old regulations that had fallen into disuse, ibid.

Council of Rome (390).—Convened under Pope Siricius against Jovinian, who, having been denounced by the renowned Pammachius, was condemned and excommunicated there by the Fathers together with his supporters, ibid., 231.

Council of Rome (445).—St Leo convened this council in order to settle the question between Quaelidonius and Hilary of Arles, who had deposed him. Both were heard. Excessive pride—or at least arrogance—was found in St Hilary’s reply; afterwards accused by others of arrogating to himself alone the authority to govern all the churches of Gaul, he incurred the supreme pontiff’s displeasure. Pope Leo declared him separated from communion with the Holy See; nevertheless, he sought to show him favour by allowing him to retain his church and not deposing him. St Leo, LIV, 630.

Council of Rome (447).—At this council St Leo provided a remedy for the stripping of church property in Sicily, committed by certain bishops through alienations or donations made without the consent of the entire clergy and without benefit, ibid., 703.

Council of Rome (449), held by St Leo against the “Robber Council” of Ephesus, which condemned Flavian, ibid., 826.

Council of Rome (454),
held under Pope St. Leo in the affair of the Manichaeans, ibid., LV, 947. **Roman Council (A.D. 487).**—This council was held under Felix II and dealt with the reception of the lapsed, ibid., LVIII, 487. **Roman Council (A.D. 494).**—It was celebrated under Pope Gelasius. In this council he composed the catalogue of the books of the Old and New Testaments which the holy Roman Church holds in veneration. Seventy bishops sat there, Coelius Sedulius, XIX, 329. **Roman Council (A.D. 495).**—It was held under Pope Gelasius. The petition of Misenus was read there, and the Fathers acclaimed pardon in his favour. This Misenus was one of the bishops sent as legates who, in 483, had fallen away from the Church at Constantinople in order to join the party of Eutyches, Dioscorus, and their followers. For that reason, and in hope of obtaining pardon, he rejected, condemned, and anathematized the doctrine of those heretics in this council, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 499).**—Under Pope Symmachus, it was held in the Basilica of St. Peter on account of disturbances raised among the people at the election of the supreme pontiff. Accordingly, three canons were enacted on this matter, with the threat of deposition and excommunication against any presbyter, [Col. 1089] deacon, or cleric who, while the pope was living, should be proved to have given or promised a vote for someone to be chosen to the chair of St. Peter. Sixty-two bishops, seventy-seven presbyters, and more than five deacons sat there, St. Leo, LVI, 124. **Roman Council (A.D. 500).**—This is also called the Palmarian Synod, provided that the various sessions of the same council are distinguished; for this is its only difference. One and the same matter was dealt with there: namely, the vindication of Pope Symmachus, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 501).**—In this council they decreed Pope Symmachus’s acquittal and the restoration to the Roman Church of all temporal goods belonging to it which the schismatics had usurped; likewise, they decreed the condemnation of Laurentius, claimant to the Apostolic See, and of Peter of Altino. One hundred and sixteen bishops sat and subscribed there, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 610).**—Bede reports that Boniface IV convened this council in order to make a decree concerning the life and tranquillity of monks. This testimony removes every doubt that this council was held, St. Boniface IV, LXXX, 103. **Roman Council (A.D. 680).**—It was assembled by Agatho, in order that the Fathers might expound certain verses of Holy Scripture. Hence came the faith of the Catholic Church concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, against the teaching of the Monothelites. One hundred and twenty bishops sat there, St. Leo, LV, 1089. **Roman Council (A.D. 792).**—When Felix, bishop of Urgel, had been brought to Rome by Angilbert, he confessed his error there before the Fathers of the council occasioned by his case, and resigned his bishopric before the supreme pontiff, Coelius Sedulius, XIX, 518. **Roman Council (A.D. 794).**—This was held shortly after the Council of Frankfurt. When Felix of Urgel had relapsed into error, he was again condemned there by Pope Adrian, who presided over it, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 799).**—Felix of Urgel had abjured his heresy, but only with his lips, whether at Rome before Pope Adrian or at Regensburg before Charlemagne and the Fathers sitting there, while retaining something different in his heart. This was thus the occasion of this council, at which he was condemned by Pope Leo III, who presided over it, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 826).**—Eugenius II presided over it, and with him were present seventy-two bishops of Italy, eighteen priests, six deacons, and many other clerics. Thirty-eight canons were promulgated there, almost all for the reform of ecclesiastical discipline, Charles, XCVII, 685. **Roman Council (A.D. 868).**—It was held by Adrian II. In it the pope three times struck Photius with a sentence of anathema, because he had dared to depose Nicholas I in a conventicle at Constantinople, Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1387. **First Roman Council (A.D. 1074).**—Celebrated by Gregory VII against simoniacal and incontinent clerics, St. Gregory, CXLVIII, 785. **Second Roman Council (A.D. 1075).**—A multitude of archbishops, bishops, and abbots attended there, together with a great number of clerics of various ranks, for the reform of ecclesiastical discipline, ibid., 788. **Third Roman Council (A.D. 1077).**—At this council Henry, king of Germany, Siegfried of Mainz, William of Utrecht, and Robert of Bamberg, bishops, were excommunicated, ibid., 790. **Fourth Roman Council (A.D. 1078).**—There Gilbert of Ravenna, Theobald of Milan, and several bishops were excommunicated, ibid., 795. **Fifth Roman Council (A.D. 1078).**—This council was celebrated in the Church of the Holy Saviour for the restoration of the holy Church, ibid., 800. **Sixth Roman Council (A.D. 1079).**—In it Berengar, often called to repentance and more often relapsing, again abjured his heresy and professed the Catholic faith, ibid., 810. **Roman Synod (A.D. 1079).**—It was held by Pope St. Gregory. One hundred and fifty bishops attended. In this synod Berengar professed the true faith concerning the Eucharist, and, after returning to Gaul, wrote against this doctrine, ibid., 733. **Roman Synod (A.D. 1079).**—It was celebrated by the same pontiff. Among other matters, the emperor of Constantinople was excommunicated. The envoys of Henry and Rudolf also swore in the same synod, each for his own lord, that they would obstruct by no stratagem the meeting of the legates of the Apostolic See [Col. 1090] to be held in the German kingdom. Many other matters likewise were decreed there, ibid., 133. **Roman Synod (A.D. 1080).**—It was held by the same Pope Gregory, after the battle won by Rudolf over Henry, who had been deposed. Rudolf was proclaimed lawful king there. The prohibition against receiving or conferring investitures was renewed; and excommunications were again promulgated against Theobald of Milan, Guibert of Ravenna, and certain other bishops, and against the Normans who were despoiling the dominions of the Church in Italy, ibid., 136. **Seventh Roman Council (A.D. 1080).**—At this council the kingdom of Germany was taken from Henry and conferred upon Rudolf, with the added ordinance that thereafter investitures of benefices should neither be conferred by laymen nor received from them, ibid., 874. **Roman Synod (A.D. 1081).**—It was celebrated by the same pope, and there he again pronounced the sentence of excommunication against Henry and his supporters, and confirmed the deposition pronounced by his legates against the archbishops of Narbonne and Arles, ibid., 136. **Roman Synod (A.D. 1083).**—Pope St. Gregory held this against all those preventing King Henry from making his way to Rome, ibid. **Ninth Roman Council (A.D. 1083).**—It was celebrated in the Lateran Basilica, and at it the apostolic lord discoursed on the form of faith, ibid., 822. **Tenth Roman Council (A.D. 1084).**—At this council Guibert, antipope and heresiarch, and Henry, pseudo-emperor, together with all their supporters, were excommunicated, ibid. **Roman Council (A.D. 1104).**—This was held by Pope Paschal II. He severely rebuked Bruno, archbishop of Trier, because he had received investiture from Emperor Henry, Geoffrey the Abbot, CLVII, 69. **Roman Council (A.D. 1121).**—This council was held in order to determine the order to be observed in councils by the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan. The archbishop of Pisa also claimed the exercise of metropolitan rights over the bishops of a certain island. The council rejected the claim, ibid.

**Council of Rouen (A.D. 1072).**—This was held by John, archbishop of Rouen, who presided over it. His suffragans attended, while William, king of the English, governed Normandy, in the eleventh year of Pope Alexander II and the thirteenth of Philip I, king of the Franks. The Fathers sitting there enacted several canons, John, archbishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 267. **Council of Rouen (A.D. 1096).**—This was held by William, archbishop of Rouen, with his suffragans in his metropolitan church. There they unanimously confirmed the chapters of the synod held at Clermont; they added eight canons, Pope St. Urban II, CLI, 197. **Council of Rouen (A.D. 1118).**—King Henry of England there made peace in the kingdom with the lords and with Ralph of Canterbury, while Geoffrey of Rouen arranged ecclesiastical matters with four suffragans and several abbots. Conrad, the pope’s legate, complained there about the emperor and the antipope Bourdin, asking the bishops of Normandy to assist with prayers and money, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 855. **Synod of Rouen (A.D. 1119).**—Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, held this synod in order to make the canons known to the priests of his diocese, and especially the canon prohibiting women or concubines, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 889. **Council of Rouen (A.D. 1189).**—This was held by Archbishop Walter, all the suffragans being present, along with very many abbots and many discerning and prudent men. The chapters subscribed below were enacted in it, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1180.

**Council of Seligenstadt (A.D. 1023).**—Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, presided. It was held so that the manifold disagreement in divine offices and synodal laws might be settled, and the diversity of individual customs reduced to unity, Burchard, bishop of Worms, CXL, 1058. **Council of Salzburg (A.D. 741).**—This council, or rather this second synod, was convoked at Salzburg on the Franconian Saale. Several bishops attended, among them Edda or Etto of Strasbourg and Reginfrid of Cologne. **Council of Salzburg (A.D. 807).**—Arno, the first archbishop of Salzburg, presided. It was decreed there that tithes should be divided into four parts: the first belonging to the bishop, the second to the clergy, [Col. 1091] the third to the poor, and the fourth to the fabric of the church, St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 805. Bishoprics were then to be founded in New Francia, or Franconia, and in Hesse. Boniface therefore divided the whole province into three dioceses, and established Würzburg, celebrated by the martyrdom of St. Kilian, Büraburg in Hesse, and Eichstätt on the borders of Bavaria as episcopal sees, St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 805.

**Council of Saintes (A.D. 579).**—This council commended Count Nantinus to the mercy of Bishop Heraclius, who had struck him with the penalty of excommunication. The count was urgently requesting absolution, which the bishop granted him, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 352. **Council of Saintes (A.D. 1089).**—Amatus, bishop of Oloron, was named archbishop of Bordeaux there, Pope St. Urban, CLI, 63. **Council of Saintes (A.D. 1097).**—Pope Urban II convoked this council, in which a decree was made concerning fasts on the vigils of apostles’ feasts, St. Urban II, ibid., 224. **Council of Saintes (A.D. 563).**—Leontius, archbishop of Bordeaux, convoked it and deposed the bishop of Saintes there. The deposition appears just: for this bishop had been ordained without the votes of clergy and people, and had obtained an edict from King Chlothar that he be ordained without the consent of the absent metropolitan. These two acts were contrary to the regulations of ecclesiastical discipline established in the last Council of Paris, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 352.

**Council of Sardica (A.D. 347).**—The legates of Julius presided there; among the Westerners the chief places were held by Protogenes, bishop of Sardica, and the illustrious Hosius. It was held to confirm sound faith and doctrine and to settle controversies between Catholics and Eusebians, St. Hilary of Poitiers, X, 575. **Conventicle of Sardica (A.D. 347).**—It was assembled at Philippopolis. The Eusebians attended it, having fled Sardica, where the Catholics had convoked the council mentioned above. There the Eusebians established a suspect creed from which they removed the word “consubstantial,” St. Hilary of Poitiers, ibid., 507. **Council of Sauriciacum (A.D. 590).**—At this council Droctegisilus, bishop of Soissons, was permitted to be restored to his episcopal city, from which he had been compelled to live in exile four years earlier by order of the bishops of his province because of a habit of intemperance, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 514.

**Council of Seleucia (A.D. 399).**—At it Cajumas, bishop of that see, resigned his episcopal see voluntarily before the bishops who had been summoned, and with such humility that he moved the Fathers present to tears, Cassiodorus, LIX, 274. **Council of Seleucia (A.D. 410).**—It was held during the reign of Theodosius the Younger, son of Emperor Arcadius. The forty Fathers sitting there enacted twenty-seven canons, ibid. **Council of Seleucia (A.D. 485).**—This was held by Babucius, bishop of Seleucia. The decision of Barsumas and of his false council was condemned there, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 34 gr.–82 gr. **Conventicle of Seleucia (A.D. 495).**—At it Barsumas, a bishop devoted to Nestorian doctrine, confirmed what had previously been decreed concerning the marriages of presbyters and monks, ibid. **Council of Septimunicia (A.D. 418).**—The bishops who sat there enacted six canons, which Baluzius reports in the collection of Ferrandus the deacon, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 315.

**Councils of Sirmium against Photinus (A.D. 351).**—First the Fathers sitting there deposed him. Then they proposed that Photinus, though deposed, should subscribe the formulary of faith which they had drawn up, promising to restore him to his bishopric. But he did not so much as consent; rather, he provoked the Fathers to contentious litigation, Pope St. Damasus, Prolegomena, XIII, 288. **Conventicle of Sirmium (A.D. 357).**—It was assembled by the Arians while Emperor Constantius was wintering at Sirmium. The Fathers sitting there, together with all the Westerners, composed a formula of faith which Hosius himself was forced to subscribe. This formula was not orthodox, ibid. **Conventicle of Sirmium (A.D. 359).**—At this council Valens and the Anomoeans who favoured his party prepared a third exposition of faith, to which they compelled Basil of Ancyra and several other bishops present to subscribe, ibid.

**Council of Étampes (A.D. 1072).**—There the case of Ivo of Chartres was discussed. Richerius, archbishop of Sens, wished to depose him in order to restore Godfrey to this see, but acted unsuccessfully because the lawful bishop of Chartres appealed to the supreme pontiff, Pope St. Urban II, CLI, 97. **Council of Étampes (A.D. 1130).**—King Louis the Fat convoked this council so that they might take sides between the elected popes Innocent and Anacletus. St. Bernard was invited to it; after fasting and prayers had been observed, it was agreed that the assembly should report the matter to him, Pope St. Urban II, CLVI, 403.

**Council of Soissons (A.D. 745).**—Pippin, prince and duke of the Franks, convoked this council for the part of Francia subject to him. Twenty-three bishops sat there with priests and clerics; Pippin himself was present there with other nobles. Boniface of Mainz is said to have presided. About ten decrees, almost the same as those of the German and Estinnes councils, were made there, St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 824. **Council of Soissons, place uncertain (c. A.D. 845).**—This capitulary, of uncertain year, was issued in a synod attended by Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, LXXXIX, 826. **Council of Soissons, place uncertain (c. A.D. 745).**—Held in the province of the Franks, or rather the sixth synod celebrated by St. Boniface. Eight bishops, all Englishmen, attended. In this synod Aldebert and Clement were condemned, as is clear from the Acts of the Roman Council. Gewilib, bishop of Mainz, had already also been deprived of episcopal rank, ibid. **Synod of Soissons (A.D. 1078).**—In this synod Ratbold, bishop of Noyon, ceded an altar to the abbey of St. Theodoric at Emmes, Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 388. **Council of Soissons (A.D. 1092).**—Renald, archbishop of Reims, presided over this council assembled against the errors of Roscelin, a cleric of Compiègne. He abjured them before the bishops, but out of fear; afterwards he taught the same errors, Pope St. Urban II, CLI, 97. **Council of Soissons (A.D. 1122).**—At this council the legate Cono, bishop of Palestrina, compelled Abelard with his own hand to burn his book *On the Trinity* and to make a new profession of faith. He was ordered to read the Creed of St. Athanasius; he read it, though with difficulty and many sighs. Then he was sent to the monastery of St. Medard, whence shortly afterward he was transferred to the monastery of St. Denis, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 1049.

**Council of Suffetula (A.D. 418).**—At this council it was forbidden that a layman be promoted to the episcopate unless he had passed through every grade of clerical ministry, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 144. **Council of Suffetula (A.D. 524).**—St. Fulgentius attended this council. By the consent of the other bishops who had been compelled, he yielded the honour of presidency to Bishop Quodvultdeus, which had been granted to himself at the preceding Council of Junca; so great was his humility and his ardent desire to preserve peace, St. Leo, LVIII, 278.

**Council of Synada (A.D. 256–258).**—It was held against the Montanists. In it it was decreed that baptism administered by heretics must be repeated. St. Dionysius of Alexandria testifies to this, adding that the council had been assembled long before the African councils concerning the same rebaptism. Bishops of Phrygia, Galatia, and Cilicia sat there, St. Augustine, XL, 495.

**Council of Tarragona (A.D. 516).**—John of Tarragona presided before ten bishops sitting there, who enacted thirteen canons to confirm the ancient discipline, St. Leo, LVI, 268. **Council of Turin (A.D. 401).**—It was held in the church at Turin so that the Fathers might resolve the various difficulties by which peace in Gaul was disturbed. See there what that council assigned to the bishop of Arles concerning primacy, ibid. **Council of Tauritania (A.D. 1089).**—This was held by the archbishop of Pisa, legate of the Holy See. There Torquitor, lord of Sardinia, who had rebelled against the pope, was excommunicated. According to Mansi, this lord was, by the customary title of the region, a judge; perhaps he was a supporter of King Henry and Guibert the antipope, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 247. **Council of Tauritania (A.D. 1156).**—It was held by Atho, archbishop of that city, ibid. **Council of Tauritania (A.D. 1625).**—It is also, and more correctly, called the Synod of Turritana; it was held by James Passamaro, archbishop of that city. He promulgated there statutes concerning the administration of the sacraments, concerning confraternities, etc., etc., ibid.

**Council of Tegernsee, Tegernscense, or Zeren (A.D. 804).**—This council was held in the monastery of that name, situated in the diocese of Freising. Its occasion was this: Bishop Atto of the city complained that religious men were claiming as their own parish churches belonging to him. Since at this council the monks produced no document to prove their entitlement, they were compelled to restore them to Atto, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 178. **Council of Tela or Thelepte (A.D. 418).**—It was held in the Church of the Apostles. Donatianus presided; in the acts he is called bishop of the first see and of the city of Thelepte. Two letters of Pope Siricius and several decrees were read there, ibid., 724. **Council of Theveste (A.D. 362).**—It was held in Numidia because the Donatists had used violence against the Catholics. Those schismatics, wishing to be recalled from exile, sent a supplicatory letter to Julian the Apostate, asking to be restored to their churches, which Emperor Constantine had taken from them. Julian assented to their petition. Yet it was an affront to the Donatists that, among emperors, only he who was openly hostile to the unity, peace, and faith of the Church assented to them, ibid., 307. **Council of Thenis (A.D. 362), in Byzacena.**—Baluzius cites three canons enacted at this council, ibid., 319.

**Council at the royal estate of Thionville (A.D. 835).**—It was convoked by Emperor Louis the Pious for his own restoration, because he had been deposed in the conventicle of Compiègne through the machinations of his son Lothair. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, the chief instigator, deposed himself there in this manner: “This profession of Ebbo was made and confirmed by his own handwritten subscription; before all he confessed himself unworthy of the episcopal ministry and that he ought to withdraw from it, and that, by undertaking penance, he wished to make the Lord propitious to himself,” Hincmar of Reims, CXXV, 325. **Synod at the royal estate of Thionville (A.D. 844).**—It was held at a place called in Latin *Judicium* and commonly Sulz. Emperor Lothair and his two royal brothers, Louis and Charles, attended there. Drogo, bishop of Metz, presided, and the Fathers sitting there enacted six canons, Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXXV, 151.

**Council of Thessalonica (A.D. 390).**—There the heresy of Bonosus was condemned, by which he maintained that the Mother of God had ceased to be a virgin after childbirth, St. Leo, LVI, 190. **Council of Thessalonica (A.D. 455).**—At this council Eutyches, Dioscorus, and Timothy were anathematized. The Fathers sitting there confirmed the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. Emperor Leo had convoked this council, ibid. **Council of Thessalonica (A.D. 518).**—It was assembled at the will of Hormisdas, supreme pontiff, in order that the decrees established at Chalcedon might be confirmed. At night the schismatics burned the place of the council, ibid. **Council of Thessalonica (A.D. 650).**—Paul, bishop of that city, presided. He held two councils in favour of the Monothelite heresy with which he was infected. In the first he set forth an exposition of his teaching, which he sent to St. Martin, sitting in the chair of Peter, together with a synodal letter in its defence. The pope replied to him and sent two legates, through whom he ordered him to subscribe the profession of Catholic faith, ibid.

**Second Assembly of Emperor Louis II at Pavia (A.D. 855).**—Chapters which the glorious Emperor Louis commanded his bishops to consider concerning the condition of his kingdom, *Monumenta Diplomatica*, CXXXVIII, 609. **Third Assembly of Emperor Louis II at Pavia (A.D. 855).**—Chapters promulgated by the emperor at the request of the people, ibid., 617.

**Council of Tigisilanum (A.D. 418).**—In Mauretania Caesariensis. Some writers believe that the council at which the legates of Pope Zosimus presided was held not at Carthage but in Mauretania Caesariensis, namely at Caesarea or perhaps at the above-mentioned Tigisdanum. The purpose of this council was to discuss and resolve certain affairs of the churches, St. Augustine, XL, 443–639. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 400).**—It was held under the pontificate of Anastasius, while Honorius and Arcadius were emperors, so that discipline might be restored and the churches divided by the Priscillianists reunited. Twenty canons were enacted there. Dictinius and Symposius abjured their errors there, St. Leo, LX, 1007. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 447).**—It was convened by St. Leo, who entrusted Turibius, bishop of Astorga, with opposing the errors of the Priscillianists then spreading through Spain. He issued a written refutation, which he sent to Idatius and Ceponius, ibid. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 527).**—It was held by Montanus, bishop of Toledo; seven bishops of Spain sat there and enacted five canons, ibid., 280. [Col. 1094] **Council of Toledo (A.D. 559).**—This council was convened in Spain by Reccared, son and heir of Leovigild, king of the Visigoths, and recently converted from Arianism, in order to strengthen the conversion of his subjects, who after his example and at his urging had abandoned the heretical doctrine, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 585. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 587).**—This council took place between Catholic and Arian bishops. There the Arians were put to confusion. The mark of holiness, proved by miracles and incompatible with the Arian sect, was particularly powerful in these circumstances. King Reccared, convinced, was converted and baptized, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 613. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 610).**—In the first year of King Gundemar’s reign, when some disputed the primacy of the church of Toledo, this council was held, which adjudged that primacy to this church and threatened anathema against anyone denying it, ibid., 506. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 683).**—It took place in the fourth year of King Erwig. Forty-eight bishops sat there, twenty-seven by deputies, five abbots, the archpriest, archdeacon, and primicerius of the church of Toledo, and twenty-six magnates. They made twelve decrees upon the prince’s requests, ibid., 486. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 688).**—It was held in the first year of King Egica. Sixty-one bishops sat there with nine abbots, the archdeacon and primicerius of Toledo, five presbyters, of whom two were delegates for abbots, and three of the twenty counts. First, the doctrine was discussed; second, the two oaths of the king, one of which appeared contrary to the other, ibid., 510. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 693).**—This was the sixteenth. Fifty-nine bishops sat there with five abbots and three deputies for absent bishops. King Egica himself was present with sixteen counts. First, after its presentation to the bishops, a memorandum containing the matters to be considered in the assembly was read; second, they enacted thirteen canons, ibid., 527. **Council of Toledo (A.D. 694).**—This was the seventeenth. It was held in the Church of St. Leocadia, in the suburban district of the city. King Egica attended with many bishops, who enacted eight canons, ibid., 551.

**Council of Toulouse (A.D. 1090).**—This council was held by legates, with bishops of different provinces in attendance, notably Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, returning from Rome to Spain. Various abuses were abolished there, and a legation was sent to Toledo so that religion might be restored there, Pope St. Urban II, CLI, 70. **Synod of Trier (A.D. 566).**—St. Goar, accused of intemperance, testified to his innocence in this synod and revealed his crimes to Bishop Rusticus, Flodoard, canon of Reims, CXXXV, 139. **Synod of Trier (A.D. 664).**—Numerianus, bishop of Trier, confirmed there before several bishops and clerics the donations made to the monastery of Saint-Dié, ibid., 311.

**Council of Trebur (A.D. 1036).**—Emperor Conrad convoked this council at Trebur near Mainz so that the Fathers sitting there might confer together concerning matters of public advantage and religion, Chronicle of St. Andrew’s Castle, Cambrai, CXLIX, 250. **Council of Trebur (A.D. 1076).**—This council was held by papal legates with certain magnates and bishops of Germany, who again tried to depose Henry. These repeated attempts finally moved him to go to Italy in order to receive absolution from the pope, Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 732.

**Council of Trent (A.D. 1545).**—Convened by a bull of Pope Paul III for the Kalends of November in the year 1542 from the Incarnation of the Lord, this council did not begin until the thirteenth day of December in the year 1845 [clearly an OCR error for 1545]; it was the last ecumenical council. Three papal legates presided: Cardinals Del Monte, bishop of Palestrina; Marcello Cervini, priest; and Reginald Pole, deacon. At the first session sat four archbishops, twenty-two bishops, five generals of orders, several theologians, and certain delegates of princes. The council was concluded in five sessions, Bracontius, LX, 821. **Synod of Trent (A.D. 1593).**—It was held under Cardinal Ludovico Madruzzo, bishop of Trent. In it he promulgated statutes concerning minor matters of ecclesiastical discipline. He strictly ordered married persons to live together, and threatened ecclesiastical penalties against those who lodged them so that they might live apart. He threatened excommunication against any beneficiaries who converted arable land into meadows in order to exempt themselves from tithes, [Col. 1095]

**Council of Troyes, or Trecense, or Tricassinum (A.D. 429).**—When the bishops of Britain had sought assistance from the bishops of Gaul in combating the Pelagians, whose errors were spreading through Great Britain, they assembled a numerous council to deliberate on this matter, Pope Urban II, CLI, 60. **Council of Troyes (A.D. 1093).**—It was held by Pope Urban II. Nearly seventy-five bishops and twelve abbots sat there. Two canons of this council survive, ibid., 107. **Council of Troyes (A.D. 1107).**—Pope Paschal II, who had gone to Gaul at the beginning of that year, held this council around the time of the Ascension; the holy war and the Truce of God were deliberated there, ibid. **Council of Troyes (A.D. 1128).**—It was held by Matthew, cardinal legate in Gaul. The Fathers sitting there resolved to draw up a new rule for the Knights Templar, to be approved by Pope Honorius, ibid.

**Council of Trosly (A.D. 909).**—Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, presided. This council was assembled against fornications, adulteries, homicides, pillaging, and violence of every kind. Twelve bishops sat there and enacted fifteen canons, Hervaeus of Reims, CXXXII, 675. **Council of Trosly (A.D. 921).**—Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, held this council, where, at the king’s request, he annulled the excommunication which he had imposed shortly before on Count Erdebald. But the count had been killed in the meantime. Thus he was absolved only after his death, ibid. **Council of Trosly (A.D. 924).**—Sculfus, archbishop of Reims, presided. At it Stephen, bishop of Cambrai, accepted the excuse of Count Isaac, who had burned one of his castles. The bishop absolved the count, provided that one hundred pounds of silver were paid as compensation, ibid. **Council of Trosly (A.D. 927).**—At this council Herluin, count of Ponthieu, who had been excommunicated because, while his wife was living, he had contracted a second marriage, performed penance. Six bishops sat there, and Count Herbert, who had convened the council, was present, ibid., CXXXII, 676.

**Council in Trullo (A.D. 692).**—Held in the palace at Constantinople called the Trullus. Among many approved matters, this council, together with the other most authoritative synods, approves some things and rejects others; it also approves the synod held under Cyprian, archbishop of the Africans and martyr, and the canon issued by it, which was observed only in the places of the aforesaid prelates and according to the custom handed down to them, Tertullian, III, 1243.

**Council of Toul (A.D. 550).**—St. Nicetius, archbishop of Trier, who had sat in the fifth Council of Orléans and the second Council of Clermont, convoked this council at Toul with the consent of King Theobald. Its convocation seems to have resulted from the insults which the Franks had inflicted upon St. Nicetius after he had struck them with excommunication for the crime of incest in contracting marriages, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1165. **Council of Toul (A.D. 833), or more properly the Synod of Toul.**—At this council Frotharius, bishop of Toul, confirmed the rights of the Abbey of St. Aprus, situated in the parish of Saint-Maximin (Mesmin), ibid. **Council of Toul (A.D. 860).**—More properly, a diocesan synod, in which Drogo, bishop of Toul, at the complaint of the abbot, whose right of possession a neighbouring church disputed, ordered the tithes to be restored to the Abbey of St. Aprus, ibid.

**Council of Tours (A.D. 375).**—This council was held for the ordination of St. Martin as bishop, St. Leo, LVI, 312. **Council of Tours (A.D. 461).**—Its occasion was the feast of St. Martin; nine bishops sitting there enacted thirteen decrees, ibid. **Council of Tours (A.D. 567).**—St. Euphronius of Tours presided. St. Radegund wrote to the Fathers of this council to obtain confirmation of the monastery which she had founded at Poitiers and of its rule. The Fathers sitting there enacted twenty-seven canons, ibid. **Council of Tours (A.D. 858).**—Herard or Gerard, archbishop of Tours, held this council of his province on the sixteenth day of May. Several extracts from canons were collected there, Victor II, CL, 36. **Council of Tours (A.D. 1055).**—It was decreed there that the feast of the Relics of St. Martin should be celebrated annually, ibid. **Council of Tours (A.D. 1122).**—It was held by Pope Urban. There the decrees of the Council of Clermont were confirmed. Although part of the bishops demanded it, the supreme pontiff refused to absolve King Philip, Pope St. Urban II, CLI, 199. **Council of Tours (A.D. 1223).**—This council was held by Juhel de Mayenne or de Matheflon. The Fathers sitting there enacted fourteen canons, ibid. **Council of Tours (A.D. 1163).**—This council was convoked by Pope Alexander III. Seventeen cardinals, one hundred and twenty bishops, and four hundred and fourteen abbots attended, together with a great multitude of others, both ecclesiastical and lay, from every province subject to the kings of France and England, St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 389.

**Council of Tyana (A.D. 365).**—The assembled Macedonians sat at this council, and there they brought letters of communion from the supreme pontiff and from other bishops of the West. The Eastern Catholics
They went there, unanimous with the Macedonians. They issued a summons for the Council of Tarsus, so that the Nicene faith might be confirmed; the Arians opposed it, supported by the authority of the emperor Valens, who by edict forbade the bishops to assemble, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1090.

Tyrian Council (A.D. 335).—At this council Saint Athanasius, struck by the rod of calumny, was unjustly deposed by the Eusebians hostile to him, ibid.

Tyrian Council (A.D. 518).—This council was held on the sixteenth day of September. Only four bishops sat there with the metropolitan of Tyre. It adopted whatever had been decided at the Councils of Constantinople and Jerusalem, which had previously been held. Hence these three councils were partly received and partly rejected by the Roman Church: received insofar as they themselves receive the Council of Chalcedon and condemn the Severians and Eutychians; rejected insofar as they restore to the diptychs Euphemius, Macedonius, and Acacius, whom the holy pontiff Hormisdas had removed, ibid.

Council of Urgell (A.D. 799).—This was convened so that the assembled Fathers might summon Felix of Urgell to approach the emperor, in order that he might withdraw from error, Saint Agobard, CIV, 107.

Council of Urgell (A.D. 887).—At this council the deposition of two intruded bishops was confirmed; and Frodoin, bishop of Barcelona, clothed only in a tunic, sought pardon from the Fathers there because he had ordained one of those two men, ibid.

Council of Urgell (A.D. 991).—This council was held by the bishop of Urgell and two of his colleagues. There he assembled the canons, priests, and monks of his diocese, and struck the entire regions of Cardona and Baraquerra with an interdict, because the churches of this see had been usurped by evil men who afterwards denied the bishop the rights vested in them. The bishops thought fit to spare Countess Ermengard and her sons, although the plundering had been committed in their name; they were content to excommunicate their officials, ibid.

Council of Valence (A.D. 374).—Under the emperor Gratian. It was convened because of certain disputes then prevailing in the churches of Gaul, which were settled there. Twenty-two bishops sat there, Saint Leo, LV, 1000.

Council of Valence (A.D. 419).—Those sitting at this council examined certain accusations brought by the province of Orange against the bishop of Valence, Saint Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 611.

Council of Valence (A.D. 530).—The acts of this council have been lost. From a fragment reported in the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles* by Cyprian the deacon, we know that questions concerning grace were discussed there, ibid.

Council of Valence (A.D. 584).—At this council Sapandus, bishop of Arles, presided, and sixteen other bishops sat with him. They confirmed gifts made to sacred places consecrated to God by King Guntram, by his late wife Queen Austrechilde, and by their sons, ibid.

Diocesan Synod of Valence (A.D. 1255).—It was held by Andrew d’Albalat. This prelate there promulgated constitutions concerning the administration of the sacraments and the residence of parish priests. He prohibited gambling, dancing, spectacles, and taverns. [He prohibited] disorderly conduct in churches and cemeteries on the occasion of vigils, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 391.

Synod of Valence (A.D. 1548).—It was held by Saint Thomas of Villanova, archbishop of that city. The holy pontiff there enacted several statutes concerning discipline to be observed in choir. He forbade priests to carry the bodies of the dead, except those of deceased fellow-brothers, ibid., 67.

Synod of Valence (A.D. 1590).—It was held under Martin Ayala, archbishop of Valence, and had two sessions. In the first it grants permission to celebrate Mass a second time on Sundays and feast days in parishes to which a church is annexed. [Col. 1097] It also orders the Roman Breviary to be recited there and the missal of the same liturgy to be used, in accordance with the prescription of Pius V’s bull, ibid.

Synod of Valence (A.D. 1590).—At this synod three new statutes were made concerning Mass stipends, the burial of the poor, and the ceremonies of Mass, ibid.

Council of Valladolid (A.D. 1137).—This council was celebrated at the request of King Alfonso VII, and Guy, cardinal and legate of the Holy See, presided over it. It concerned methods of reconciling Alfonso with the king of Portugal, Saint Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 325.

Council of Valladolid (A.D. 1155).—It was held during the reign of Alfonso VIII, and Cardinal Hyacinth, legate of the Holy See, presided. There was confirmed the privilege granted by Lady Queen Sancha, sister of King Alfonso, to the monastery of Saint Peter of Eslonza near the city of León, ibid.

Council of Vaison (A.D. 442).—It was held under Auspicius, the Catholic bishop of that city. Ado, bishop of Vienne, who speaks of this council near the end of the year 457, relates that Nectarius, one of Auspicius’s predecessors, presided over it and publicly proclaimed that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit possess one nature, one power, one divinity, and one virtue. Ten canons were enacted there, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 81, 105.

Council of Vaison (A.D. 529).—Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, presided over it, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Felix and of the reign of Athalaric, king of Italy. All assembled in this council gave thanks to God because they had not violated the ancient canons, and then enacted five further canons, concerning both liturgy and discipline, ibid., 261.

Council of Vercelli (A.D. 1050).—It was held by Pope Saint Leo IX. Various bishops attended. Berengar was summoned but did not come. His error was condemned there, as was Scotus’s book on the Eucharist, Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, CL, 32.

Council of Vercelli (A.D. 1570).—It was held under John Francis Bonhomme. We possess the statutes of several synods held under him as bishop, ibid.

Council of Verona (A.D. 967).—This council was held against clerics living with concubines, Saint Leo, LVI, 153.

Council of Verona (A.D. 994).—Its occasion was this. There was a dispute between John, patriarch of Aquileia, and Otbert or Othelbert, bishop of Verona, concerning certain churches situated in the same city, whose incumbents refused to obey the ordinary. Those refusing claimed that they were bound to obey the patriarch; but the council ruled against them and restored jurisdiction to the bishop of Verona, ibid., 1286.

Council of Vienne (A.D. 177).—This council would more properly be called an assembly of the faithful, at which the history of the martyrs of Lyons was compiled and sent to the churches of Asia along with letters of the martyrs against the heresy of Montanus. To the same churches the Fathers of the Council of Lyons sent their judgment pronounced against this impostor, ibid., 576.

Council of Vienne, held concerning the election of Ravennius, successor of Saint Hilary in the see of Arles, ibid.

[Col. 1098]

Council of Vienne (A.D. 474).—It was convened by Saint Mamertus, bishop of that city, on account of fires, earthquakes, and other calamities ravaging Gaul and the city during Saint Mamertus’s episcopate. At this council he instituted the public Rogation prayers, with fasting and processions, ibid., 576.

Council of Vienne (A.D. 1141).—This council was held by Stephen, archbishop of Vienne, who, concerning the episcopal see of Valence—John I, abbot of Bonneval of the Cistercian Order, in place of Eustace, deposed by the pope—[sentence incomplete in the source], Saint Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 496.

Council of Verdun (A.D. 947).—Robert, archbishop of Trier, presided. Artald and Odolric, archbishop of Aachen, were deputed as the two bishops to go to Hugh and bring him to the council; when he refused to come there, Artald was maintained in possession of the episcopal see of Rheims. Another council was appointed for the thirteenth day of January in the following year: this was the Council of Mouzon, Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 551.

Council of Verdun (A.D. 967).—At this council the chapel of Saint Martin was adjudged to the church named after Saint Cyriacus, ibid.

Synod of Verdun (A.D. 1080).—The fellow-bishops of Henry, bishop of Liège, whom Count Arnold had seized by ambush together with his property, assembled at this synod by order of Saint Gregory VII. They threatened the count with excommunication unless he restored everything he had taken from Henry and turned to penance, Flodoard, canon of Rheims, CXXXV, 308.

Synod of Verdun (A.D. 1135).—At this synod Bishop Albero installed [someone; the object is omitted in the supplied text] in possession of the monastery of Saint Paul, ibid.

Synod of Verdun (A.D. 1574).—There it was decreed that the faithful of each parish should provide, according to their means, all things necessary for divine worship, ibid.

Council of Winchester (A.D. 1070).—This council was held by King William, and Emenfred, bishop of Sion, the legate, presided over it. Elgeric, bishop of Selsey, was deposed there with several abbots, Saint Lanfranc, CL, 35.

Council of Windsor (A.D. 1101).—There the charter of the foundation of the church of Northuensis was confirmed; the instrument of this charter was subscribed by the king and queen, by the two archbishops of Canterbury and York, by the bishops present, and also by the magnates, Orderic Vitalis, CLXXXVIII, 322.

Council of Worms (A.D. 700).—At this council twelve canons were enacted. The first provides that the Eucharist is not to be granted, even at the point of death, to those unable to prove an accusation made against a bishop, priest, or deacon; the eleventh and twelfth declare null any sentences issued by bishops against foreign clerics, Saint Leo, LVI, 320.

Council of Worms (A.D. 772).—At this council war against the Saxons was decreed, a war that burned for thirty-three years. At the same place Charlemagne held a council with the bishops assembled there concerning the means of bringing the peoples of Saxony to the Christian faith, ibid.

[Col. 1213]

CXVII. INDEX OF BULLS, LETTERS, DECREES, STATUTES, DECISIONS, RULES, AND OTHER WRITINGS CONCERNING THE GOVERNMENT OF THE CHURCH, ISSUED BY THE SUPREME PONTIFFS, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY AUTHOR, AND GIVING A BRIEF ANALYSIS OF EACH BULL OR WRITING.

> [Note: [Col. 1213] NOTE. Volumes LXVII, CXXX, and CLXXXVII, containing (I) the collection of canons of Dionysius Exiguus, (II) the decrees of Gratian, and (III) the decretals of Isidore Mercator concerning the supreme pontiffs, cannot here, because of the nature of this index, their number, the intermingling of their subjects, and other reasons, be brought into analysis and specific notice. The reader should therefore have recourse to the aforesaid volumes. Nevertheless, he should know that very often what he finds in them he will find also in each Father under his own volume entitled *On the Same Matter*. There remain, moreover, the *Abridgment of the Canons* of Fulgentius Ferrandus and the *Canonical Compendium* of Crisconius, African bishop: LXXXVIII, 818 and 831.]

**ADRIAN I, pope.** Letter to King Charles, that he grant certain bishops permission to return to their own sees, XCVIII, 280.---Concerning the usurped government of certain cities of Emilia, that it be restored to him, XCVIII, 283.---Concerning a donation promised to him by the king, to be handed over as soon as possible, XCVIII, 286.---Concerning the jubilation over the triumphs of God’s holy Church, XCVIII, 288, 291.---That a certain duke, invader of the dominions of the Holy See, be expelled, XCVIII, 295.---That the plunderers of the duchy of Spoleto be cast out and restrained, XCVIII, 297.---He reports the conspiracy of ill-disposed persons against Rome and Italy, XCVIII, 300.---That the king himself hasten, as promised, to the threshold of Saint Peter, XCVIII, 302.---He promises that he will receive from the sacred font of baptism a newly born son [as godfather], XCVIII, 304.---Concerning the conduct of certain persons by which the law of nations is violated, XCVIII, 311.---That Roman priests are falsely accused of incontinence, XCVIII, 317.---Prayers are prescribed for the safety of the king waging war upon the Saracens, XCVIII, 315.---He rebukes the sale of enslaved persons by the Lombards to the Saracen people, XCVIII, 317.---Concerning Bishop Maurice, whose eyes the Istrians had torn out, XCVIII, 320.---That the Neapolitans with the Greeks had invaded the city of Terracina, XCVIII, 321.---He requests that timber be brought to Rome as quickly as possible to repair the roof of the Basilica of Saint Peter, XCVIII, 325.---Concerning the Sabine territory: as the king had promised Saint Peter, he should order it to be delivered intact, XCVII, 328.

[Col. 1214] Letter to Bishop Egila in Spain, concerning the fast of the sixth day and Saturday, XCVIII, 333.---Concerning the Paschal feast, the predestination of a human being either to good or to evil, defilement in food and drink, and other errors; concerning freedom of the will and other points contrary to the Catholic faith that had arisen, XCVIII, 336.

Letter to King Charles, commending the Sabine patrimony, whose ancient right belongs to the Holy See, and asking that the Holy See be put in possession of it, XCVIII, 346.---To the same, concerning the consecration of Bishop Peter and the Sabine territory, XCVIII, 348.---Concerning the recovery of the Sabine territory, insofar as it had been delivered intact to Saint Peter, XCVIII, 352.---To the king he offers thanks in grateful recognition for his benevolent messages concerning the Church’s protection, XCVIII, 354.---It contains an assurance that the faith or love which he had promised toward blessed Peter should remain unshaken and indissoluble, and that no crafty guile may be able to separate his mind from apostolic love, XCVIII, 356.---That a certain innocent abbot, falsely accused, be received by him mercifully, XCVIII, 359.---That, by the king’s own permission, he had heard the case concerning the dispute of certain abbots and found guilty the very persons bringing accusation and commencing litigation, XCVIII, 361.

Letter to bishops or priests, that they should not put on military service but spiritual warfare; that is, that they should devote themselves to fasts and prayers; and concerning the prohibition of other things committed by wicked persons, XCVIII, 365.

[Col. 1215] Letter to King Charles, that he not permit the monastery of Saint Hilary and others situated in the Alps, intended to receive pilgrims as guests, to be invaded or harassed by anyone, XCVII, 369.---He grants him the marble he had requested, to be extracted at Ravenna, XCVIII, 371.

Letter to the Spanish bishops, concerning the heresy or blasphemy that calls the Son of God adoptive; concerning the Paschal feast; concerning the blood of animals, pork, and the blood of strangled animals, matters concerning which there had been disorderly error; concerning predestination, free will, monogamy, and many other matters for which wicked persons who preached such things are reproved from the traditions of the holy Fathers, XCVIII, 373.

Letter to King Charles, concerning Venice or the Venetians, that they should be expelled from Ravenna and the Pentapolis; and concerning the duke who had violently invaded the possessions of the Church of Ravenna, XCVIII, 386.---Concerning the Saxons happily converted through his efforts, and concerning litanies, fasts, and prayers established for giving thanks to God for such great benefits, XCVIII, 307.---That Saxons who had returned to paganism, if they converted, should be admitted and that penance should be enjoined upon them according to the bishop’s prudence, XCVIII, 390.---He asks him to order the territories of Populonia and Roselle, delivered entire to the Holy See, and the cities of the duchy of Benevento, in accordance with his very recent donation, to be handed over to him, XCVIII, 396.---He asks that he forbid his envoys to return before the cities of Campania have been delivered entire, and likewise the entire territories of Populonia and Roselle. For just as the Holy See possessed Suana and the other cities of Tuscany with their territories, so it was equitable that it possess the cities of Campania entire with their territories, XCVIII, 398.---Concerning commerce in temporal matters belonging to the pontifical dominion, XCVIII, 402, 406.---He gives thanks because the king had ordered the cities of Campania and the territories of Populonia and Roselle to be delivered to the Apostolic See; but only bishoprics, monasteries, and public estates, with the keys of cities but without their inhabitants, had been delivered to him, XCVIII, 412.---It contains the case of Constantine and Paul, dukes of the pope, who had been maliciously accused without cause before the aforesaid king by wicked men; he asks that the king deign kindly to receive one of them, namely Paul, whom he had sent to be presented to him, XCVIII, 418.---He praises the king for scorning the fabricated story—namely, that Offa, king of the English, had urged Charles himself, once Adrian was deposed, to create another pope from his own nation; then he says that he was set over the whole Christian world not by men but by Christ Jesus, and therefore proclaims to kings and peoples the word of life and truth, XCVIII, 420.---It contains matters concerning the dioceses and parishes of bishops in regions of Italy and Tuscany, variously invaded and possessed by the bishops themselves, and concerning the correction of various episcopal abuses, XCVIII, 424.---Concerning the bishops’ parishes, their consecration, the honour of the lord king’s patriciate, and other articles, XCVIII, 427.

**ADRIAN III, pope.** Letter to Sigibod, Archbishop of Narbonne: he commands him to warn Gibert, Bishop of Nîmes, not to inflict any harassment upon the monastery of Saint Giles, which is under the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, CXXVI, 973.

**ADRIAN IV, pope.** He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Aniane, CLXXXVIII, 1361.

He confirms the ordinance made concerning the churches of Saint Geneviève, saving the rights and reasonable customs which the Bishop of Paris has in them, CXXXVIII, 1302.---Concerning the dispute between the abbot of Saint Remigius of Rheims and the master of the schools of Saint Remigius of Rheims, CLXXXVIII, 1363.

He commends to Wibald, Abbot of Corvey, the affairs of the Roman Church before the emperor and his legates who are to negotiate with him, CLXXXVIII, 1371.

He commands the clergy and laity of the church of Blessed Peter of the Mount firmly to observe, in surplices and black copes, the Order of Blessed Augustine instituted in their church from ancient times, CLXXXVIII, 1372.

He commands Bernard, Bishop of Paderborn, to examine and determine the case of the bearer of this letter, CLXXXVIII, 1275.

He confirms the election of Hugh among the Piacentines and absolves their city from interdict, CLXXXVIII, 1381.

He informs the Archbishop of Zara of the arrangements he had made for the Patriarch of Grado to acknowledge his primacy, CLXXXVIII, 1388.

He commands the bishops of Scotland to obey Roger of York, CLXXXVIII, 1391.

He commends to the prelates of the diocese of Piacenza Bishop Hugh, consecrated by himself, CLXXXVIII, 1362.

He commends Bishop Hugh to the clergy and people of Piacenza, CLXXXVIII, 1392.

He commands the monks of Saint Sylvester of Monte Suavi to obey the Camaldolese prior, CLXXXVIII, 1398.

He entrusts to the Church of Saint Mary of Reno the administration of the church of Saint Pontianus, CLXXXVIII, 1399.

He commends to Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, the Camaldolese communities of Berading and Saint Peter of Rota, CLXXXVIII, 1400.

He commands Eraclius, Archbishop of Lyons, and Humbert, Archbishop of Besançon, not to allow the monastery of Tournus to suffer wrongs from Count Girard of Mâcon, CLXXXVIII, 1401.

He commands the canons of Chalon to restore a certain church to the monastery of Tournus, CLXXXVIII, 1402.

Concerning the investiture of certain personal benefices, CLXXXVIII, 1406.

Concerning certain personal benefices and their investiture, CLXXXVIII, 1407.

To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, that certain prebends be restored to the Knights Templar, CLXXXVIII, 1410.

He commends two canons of Orléans to Louis, King of the Franks, CLXXXVIII, 1417.

To the Archbishop of Tours: he invites him to an amicable settlement with the Bishop of Dol, or to come to the Apostolic See, CLXXXVIII, 1421.

To the archbishop, archdeacon, and dean of the Church of Rouen, that they cause the possessions of the Church of Dol in Normandy to be restored, CLLXXVIII [sic], 1423.

He commands the bishops of Langres, Autun, Nevers, and Auxerre to excommunicate the Count of Nevers unless within thirty days he repairs the damage done to the monastery of Vézelay, CLXXXVII, 1423.

He commands the bishops of Gaul to excommunicate and impose various penalties upon the burgesses of Vézelay unless they make satisfaction to the monastery for the injuries inflicted, CLXXXVIII, 1424.

He exhorts Louis, King of the Franks, to pursue the burgesses of Vézelay by armed force, so that they may be subjected to the abbot as lord, CLXXXVIII, 1425.

He commends the monasteries of Saint Antimus and Farfa to the neighbouring archbishops and bishops, CLXXXVIII, 1427.

To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, concerning money to be restored to a certain person, CLXXXVIII, 1430.

He entrusts to Wichmann, Archbishop of Magdeburg, for final determination the case concerning tithes between the Bishop of Osnabrück and Abbot Wibald, CLXXXVIII, 1432.

He subjects the monastery of Werden to Wibald, Abbot of Corvey, and his successors, CLXXXVIII, 1434.

He commands Arnold, Archbishop of Mainz, to protect the monastery of Werden from the injuries of Count Bobbo, CLXXXVIII, 1434.

He grants Brinerius, Bishop of Siena, an estate on Mount Bonizi for building a church, subject to an annual rent, CLXXXVIII, 1436.

He declares that Hillin, Archbishop of Trier, has been appointed legate of the Apostolic See throughout the whole German kingdom, CLXXXVIII, 1438.

To the Archbishop of Tours, that he make an amicable settlement with the Bishop of Dol, LLXXXVIII [sic], 1439.

To all clergy and laity established throughout the province of Dol: he confirms the sentence issued by Archbishop Hugh against evildoers and occupiers of ecclesiastical property, 1439.

He commands Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, to order both the money and the ship taken by his men from the citizens of Genoa to be restored, CLXXXVIII, 1440.

To the monks of Corbigny, concerning the reform of the monastery, CLXXXVIII, 1442.

He commands Silvester, Abbot of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, to make his profession to Archbishop Theobald, CLXXXVIII, 1440.

To the Archbishop of Braga, that he obey the Primate of Toledo, CLXXXVIII, 1441.

He praises the Church of Paris because it has granted the revenue of a prebend to Hugh the chancellor, CLXXXVIII, 1445.

He commands John, Archbishop of Toledo, to investigate the crimes of the Bishop of Pamplona, CLXXXVIII, 1451.

To the rectors of the Roman fraternity, that chaplains promise obedience to the rectors of the titular churches, CLXXXVIII, 1452.

For the Church of Ferrara and concerning certain peasants, CLXXXVIII, 1453.

Concerning confirmation of the judgments which King Louis pronounced against Duke Odo of Burgundy, CLXXXVIII, 1446.

He commends his chaplain R. to the canons of the Church of Pisa, concerning the cutting of stones used by the canons of Saint Rufus for building a monastery, CLXXXVIII, 1461.

To the clergy of Augsburg: he declares Bishop Conrad of Augsburg innocent and condemns his accusers to a severe penalty, CLXXXVIII, 1466.

He confirms Pope Eugenius III’s judgment concerning the controversy between the canons of Saints Alexander and Vincent of Bergamo, CLXXXVIII, 1468.

He confirms the peace made with William, King of Sicily, through legates, CLXXXVIII, 1470.

He commands the bishops of certain churches constituted as suffragans of the Church of Palermo to obey Archbishop Hugh, CLXXXVIII, 1471.

At the request of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, he commands the Archbishops of Vienne and Lyons not to allow the monastery of Celsiniac to be harassed by Eustace, CLXXXVIII, 1477.

Bull for the Church of Nîmes, confirming its possessions, CLXXXVIII, 1483.

Confirmation of the privileges and possessions of the churches of Saint Denis, the monastery of Saint Bavo, and Saint Peter, CLXXXVIII, 1485–1487.

He confirms the election of Archbishop Berengar, CLXXVIII, 1489.

He secures for the hospital house at Canterbury the church of Northbourne, granted by Silvester, Abbot of Saint Augustine’s, for the relief of pilgrims and the poor, CLXXXVIII, 1490.

He confirms the agreement concluded between Stephen, Bishop of Paris, and Theobald, archdeacon, CLXXXVIII, 1490.

He commands Silvester, Abbot of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, to render obedience to Archbishop Theobald within thirty days, CLXXXVIII, 1491.

He grants the nunnery of Saint Mary of Caramagna to Anselm, Bishop of Asti, CLXXXVIII, 1491.

To Wilbald, Abbot of Stavelot, that he urge the emperor to continue in reverence for the Apostolic See, CLXXXVIII, 1492.

He secures for the Church of Geneva the property granted by Emperor Frederick, CLXXXVIII, 1507.

To Henry, Patriarch of Grado: he confirms his patriarchal dignity and his primacy over the archbishopric of Zara, CLXXXVIII, 1516.

He commends Henry, Patriarch of Grado, to the bishops, duke, and people of Venice, CLXXXVIII, 1520.

He secures for Rudolph, Camaldolese prior, and his successors the monastery of Pratalia, donated by Jerome, Bishop of Arezzo, CLXXXVIII, 1521.

He reproaches Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, because, notwithstanding his admonitions, he had still left unpunished the sacrilegious seizure of Eskil, Archbishop of Lund; he recalls that the imperial crown had been conferred upon him by the pope, etc., CLXXXVIII, 1525.

He confirms to the Milanese monastery of Saint Denis all its rights and property, CLXXXVIII, 1527.

To the archbishops and bishops of Germany he complains of the injuries inflicted by Emperor Frederick upon his legates; he commands them to exert themselves so that the emperor may compel Chancellor Reinald to make satisfaction, CLXXXVIII, 1531.

He forbids the canons of Calvimont to alienate ecclesiastical goods; for it had long ago been decreed that brothers of the monastery of Saint Denis should be installed in their church, CLXXXVIII, 1533.

He exhorts Raymond, Bishop of Maguelone, not to dispose at his own discretion of Church property assigned to the common use of the clergy, and to restore the tithe to the canons of Montpellier, CLXXXVIII, 1534.

He commands Godescalc, Bishop of Arras, to restore to Chancellor Hugh the altar of Asines which had been taken from him, CLXXXVIII, 1535.

He exhorts Theobald, Bishop of Paris, to grant Chancellor Hugh the first personal benefice or dignity that falls vacant in the Church of Paris, CLXXXVIII, 1336.

He prescribes to the nobleman William and to all the people of Montpellier that, at the end of five years, they return the altar of Saint Saviour and its offerings into the hands of the prior of the Church of Blessed Mary, CLXXXVIII, 1536.

For the Church of Jerusalem and for the Knights Templar, CLXXXVIII, 1537.

He commands the abbots of the diocese of Béziers to obey the Bishop of Béziers, CLXXXVIII, 1538.

To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, that without any hesitation he continue to perform the episcopal office, CLXXXVIII, 1539.

Concerning not seizing the goods of deceased bishops, CLXXXVIII, 1542.

He confirms the agreement made between the Bishop of Béziers and the prior of Cassian, CLXXXVIII, 1543.

He commands archbishops and bishops to compel the serfs of the monastery of Saint Denis to render the services due from them, CLXXXVIII, 1544.

[Col. 1218] He commands Hugh, chancellor of the King of the Franks, to reconcile the Abbot of Compiègne to the king’s favour, CLXXXVIII, 1545.

Admonitory letter to the abbot and convent of Saint Vedast, CLXXXVIII, 1545.

He informs Bishop Peter and the canons of Marseille that he has commanded Pons, Archbishop of Aix, to render judgment between them and the monks of Saint Victor, CLXXXVIII, 1546.

Concerning confirmation of the donation of the first year’s revenue of prebends of the cathedral church of Auxerre, CLXXXVIII, 1547.

For the liberty and customs of the Church of Soissons, CLXXXVIII, 1547.

He commands the provost and all the clergy of the Church of Piacenza to return to canonical discipline and obey Bishop Hugh, CLXXXVIII, 1553.

He addresses Emperor Frederick in sufficiently mild terms, excuses passages in a certain earlier aforesaid letter, and commends his legates sent to admonish Henry, Duke of Bavaria and Saxony, CLXXXVIII, 1556.

He confirms the possessions and rights designated for the support of the canons of the Church of Blessed Peter, [including] the churches of Saints John and Paul, etc., CLXXXVIII, 1557.

He confirms the goods of the Church of Saint John of Selbod, CLXXXVIII, 1568.

After settling the controversy between the canons and the Bishop of Sutri concerning the Church of Saint Sylvester, he renders the agreement perpetual by a charter, CLXXXVIII, 1573.

He secures for Master Adam the mastership of the schools of the Church of Meaux, granted by Bishop Manasses of blessed memory, CLXXXVIII, 1574.

To Hugh, chancellor of the King of the Franks: he congratulates him on having rendered useful service toward securing peace between the kings of the Franks and the English, CLXXXVIII, 1575.

He exhorts Prior Gregory and the whole Camaldolese chapter to virtue and peace, CLXXXVIII, 1576.

He does not comply with Emperor Frederick’s request that Guy, subdeacon of the Roman Church, be placed over the Church of Ravenna, CLXXXVIII, 1579.

He writes to the Archbishop of Thessalonica concerning the reconciliation of the Greek Church with the Roman Church, CLXXXVIII, 1580.

He exhorts the consuls and all the people of Castrum Grassa to defend the Lérins monks against Saracens and other enemies, CLXXXVIII, 1581.

To Louis, King of the Franks: he commends the king’s especially ready love for religious men, which he asks that the Premonstratensian brothers may experience for reverence both for Saint Peter and for the king himself, CLXXXVIII, 1582.

To the Archbishop of Narbonne, etc., against Count Gaufred of Roussillon, CLXXXVIII, 1582.

To Walter, Bishop of Laon, that he preserve the benefices granted by his predecessors to the Church of Prémontré, and neither inflict nor permit any harassment concerning those benefices, CLXXXVIII, 1583.

To the monks of Pontida, that they pay the tithes of a certain place, CLXXXVIII, 1586.

He commands Stephen, Bishop of Metz, and N., Bishop of Verdun, to declare Duke Matthew of Lorraine excommunicated, CLXXXVIII, 1587.

He thanks Louis, King of the Franks, for protecting the Abbot of Vézelay; he advises him to continue defending the monastery against the Count of Nevers and to order the stone houses of the burgesses of Vézelay to be demolished, CLXXXVIII, 1592.

He exhorts Abbot Odo and the monks of Saint Denis to follow in Saint Benedict’s footsteps, CLXXXVIII, 1593.

He confirms the Archdeacon of Arras, the privileges of the monastery of Saint Denis granted by Kings Robert and Dagobert, and certain goods of the Church of Saint Ursus, CLXXXVIII, 1593–1596.

For the cantor of the Church of Péronne, for Master Nicholas, and for others, CLXXXVIII, 1595–1598.

He asks Albert, Abbot of Nonantola, to grant anew a certain precarial grant to the noblemen Lot and Turcl., CLXXXVIII, 1598.

He confirms the transaction and subjection of the monastery of Vallemagna to Bonneval, CLXXXVIII, 1599.

To the Bishops of Saint-Brieuc and Tréguier, that they prevent their priests, against the will of the Archbishop of Dol, from celebrating divine offices, CLXXXVIII, 1600.

He commands Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, and Hartwic, Bishop of Regensburg, to restore to Abbot Conrad of Rieburg the monastery which he had abandoned because of injuries inflicted by the brethren, and to punish the monks, CLXXXVIII, 1601.

He commands the monks of Biburg to obey Abbot Conrad, CLXXXVIII, 1601.

[Col. 1219] He commands Henry, Bishop of Autun, to grant the Abbot of Tournus the investiture of the Church of Petraficta within twenty days, CLXXXVIII, 1602.

To the Archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans, that they defend pilgrims journeying to Jerusalem from assaults by the wicked, under threat of a sentence of excommunication, CLXXXVIII, 1603.

To the canons of Holy Cross, Orléans: he rebukes them because, during Chancellor Hugh’s absence, they had not granted him the full prebend. He orders them henceforth to do so and to restore what has been withheld, CLXXXVIII, 1603.

To Hugh, chancellor of France: he absolves him from the oath and unlawful condition by which the Bishop of Arras had bound him when granting him the archdeaconry, CLXXXVIII, 1604.

To Samson, Archbishop of Rheims, that he restore to Chancellor Hugh the altar which he had taken from him, CLXXXVIII, 1605, 1606.

He commands the dean, cantor, and whole chapter of Paris to confer upon Chancellor Hugh the provostship that becomes vacant in the Church of Paris, CLXXXVIII, 1606.

To the clergy and people of Murmiral, that they obey Hugh, Archbishop of Dol, CLXXXVIII, 1607.

He praises the plan of Louis, King of the Franks, who was considering hastening into Spain with Henry, King of the English, to defeat the barbarism of the pagans; yet he fears that the enterprise may be undertaken rashly, proposes delays, and gives instructions so that its outcome may be favourable, CLXXXVIII, 1615.

To William, Bishop of Le Mans, and to the monks of Roche-Boviscurt: concerning the settlement of a long-disputed controversy between the Cluniac monks and the canons of Périgueux, CLXXXVIII, 1619.

Concerning confirmation of the property of the monastery of Saint Magloire in Paris, and of the monasteries of the Valley of Saint Mary, Saint Clement, Mure, Prüfening, Saint John of Blanburen, and Saint Opportuna, CLXXXVIII, 1621–1631.

He confirms the agreement made between Hugh, Abbot of Prémontré, and Walter, Bishop of Laon, CLXXXVIII, 1632.

To Emperor Frederick, concerning the twofold injury inflicted by him upon the Apostolic See, CLXXXVIII, 1635.
