**AGAPETUS I, pope.** Letter to Emperor Justinian: he confirms Justinian’s statement of faith insofar as it conforms to the sacred canons, LXVI, 37.---He thanks him for congratulating him upon his election to the pontificate; praises his faith and exhorts him to defend the Catholic faith; he replies that fallen bishops cannot be received back with their honours, LXVI, 38.

Letter to the African bishops: he congratulates them on having escaped unhurt from the hands of heretics, and answers the matters about which they had consulted his predecessor Pope John, LXVI, 43.

Letter to Reparatus, Bishop of Carthage: he thanks him for conveying by letter his congratulations upon the pope’s election; he exhorts him to ensure publication of what he had written for the Catholic faith, LXVI, 45.

Letter to Caesarius, Bishop of Arles, that estates belonging by right to the Church must not be alienated under any title, LXVI, 45.---Concerning Bishop Contumeliosus, when he had appealed to the Apostolic See, LXVI, 46.

Letter to Bishop Anthimus: he shows that there are in Christ two perfect natures, condemning Anthimus for asserting the contrary, LXVI, 77.

**AGAPETUS II, pope.** He exhorts Atenulf, Prince of Benevento, to restore the monastery of Saint Sophia to the Cassinese monks, CXXXIII, 892.

Against Leo and Benedict, intruded into the churches of Trivento and Termoli, CXXXIII, 894.

To Gerard, Archbishop of Lorch: he announces that he has settled the disagreement between the Churches of Lorch and Salzburg, CXXXIII, 898.---That robbers be kept away from the monastery of Celsiniac, CXXXIII, 912.

Letter to Landulf, Prince of Capua: he warns him not to violate the liberty of the monastery of Capua, CXXXIII, 913.

**AGATHO, Saint, pope.** Letter to Emperor Constantine the Great and to the emperors Heraclius and Tiberius Augustus: he congratulates them on the protection they afford the See of the Roman pontiffs; exhorts them never to depart from such a course; he expounds the Church’s faith regarding the mysteries to be believed, especially concerning the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word, and the consequences of these mysteries—namely Christ’s death, the nature, persons, and attributes of each person of the Holy Trinity, LXXXVII, 1161–1212.

Decretal letter to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, etc., in which he appoints Abbot Meda as Roman legate over all England and decrees that his monastery shall serve, in the manner of the thresholds of the Apostles, for the discharge of vows undertaken to make a pilgrimage to Rome, LXXVII, 1213.

Instruction for the legates sent to celebrate the Sixth Synod, LXXXVII, 1215.

**ALEXANDER III, pope.** Concerning his election, CC, 69–75.

That Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, having rejected the perversity of Octavian, steadfastly persist in his devotion; concerning Octavian’s intrusion; concerning the schism and Octavian’s excommunication; against Victor and Octavian, antipopes, CC, 80–82.

Concerning clerics who, being below the rank of subdeacon, take wives; concerning a prebend conferred on a certain priest; concerning releasing from vows a boy not yet fifteen years old; concerning Roger, a canon, appealing in a certain case; concerning a woman who had killed her son, that she should enter a monastery; that the canons of the Church of Rheims, rejecting the simoniacal wickedness of the schismatic Octavian, should remain steadfast in the faith, CC, 83–85.

He announces the excommunication of Emperor Frederick and the antipope Octavian: that the Archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans should stand for the Church against Emperor Frederick and the antipope Victor; that the Bishop of Beauvais should persevere in devotion to the Roman Church; that the people of Thérouanne should kindly receive Bishop Milo, CC, 88–98.

To Louis VII, king of the Franks: he commends his piety toward the Apostolic See; he urges Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, to remain steadfastly faithful to the Church and to try to bring back the emperor; that Robert de Valognes should restore to the monks of St. Alban the wood of Northaga; concerning the canonization of Saint Edward, king of England, CC, 100–106.

He asks Bishop Hugh of Soissons for some financial assistance; he beseeches Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, to help the Church afflicted by Emperor Frederick; he praises Master Nicholas for his zeal toward the Apostolic See; he congratulates Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, on measures taken for the Apostolic See against heretics; concerning the deposition of Hugh, Abbot of Cluny, CC, 107–113.

Concerning a dispute over the inheritance of William de Saccavilla; concerning his joyful reception in the city of Rome; he urges the bishops of the March to be steadfast against the schismatics; that Hugh, Bishop of Soissons, should preserve intact the rights of the monastery of St. Martin of Épernay, CC, 114–122.

That the bishop-elect of Dol should receive consecration from the Archbishop of Tours; that Peter, Archbishop of Salona, should excommunicate certain bishops of churches. Concerning the business of the Church of Flavigny; concerning accusations, civil and criminal, against the Abbot of Flavigny; concerning the controversy between Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, and the Abbot of Ferrières, CC, 122–129.

He congratulates the Abbot and brethren of Prémontré on their constancy for the Apostolic See, and warns them to recall schismatics of their order to the bosom of the Church under penalty of excommunication; that the Archbishop of Salzburg should win over the emperor’s mind; he warns King Louis concerning the condition of the Church and the affair of the Church of Flavigny, CC, 130–152.

That the Archbishop of York should not presume to have the cross carried before him in the province of Canterbury; he complains that the Bishop of Orléans unjustly harasses certain canons; that Hugh, Bishop of Soissons, should bring it about that the king of the Franks abstain from the conference which he had planned to hold with Emperor Frederick, CC, 161–164.

Concerning the affair of the Church of Châlons; concerning the constancy of Louis, king of the Franks, at his conference with King Frederick; he confirms the excommunication pronounced by Bishop Uldaric against invaders of the Church of Kattemborn; a bull for the monastery of Compiègne concerning the receipt of property; he admonishes Louis, king of the Franks, concerning the holding of a council; concerning the Count of Boulogne, who had taken a nun as wife and expelled two abbots from regular churches, CC, 165–184.

To Louis VII, king of the Franks: that a knight wishing to go to Jerusalem may sell his possessions without his wife’s consent; concerning the heretics of Barges and their corrupted faith; concerning those accused of heresy in the parts of Flanders; for the cause of the Church of Saint-Remi of Joinville, CC, 186–195.

That in the German kingdom he has appointed a legate in order to suppress the schism; he sends a golden rose to King Louis VII; that an interdict imposed by the Archbishop of Rheims should be relaxed by that archbishop himself; he gives thanks to Henry, king of the English, because he is sending all archbishops and bishops to the council, CC, 197–204.

That Gilbert should undertake the governance of the Church of London; against the devastators of the Church of Brioude; on behalf of the Count of Namur, that his wife should return to him; he dedicates the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris; for the case pending between the Church of Saint-Remi and that of Derve concerning a certain tithe, CC, 205–224.

Concerning the canonization of St. Anselm of Canterbury; concerning the Count of Avignon, whom he absolves; against Joscelin, Abbot of Rebais, who had performed sacred rites against the bishop’s interdict; he rebukes those who harass the monastery of Grasse with unjust exactions; he reports that the monks of St. Maximin were dispersed among monasteries and others substituted in their places, CC, 237–248 [lacuna].

The whole aforesaid volume CC contains similar materials: various exhortatory, threatening, reproachful, and other documents, for various persons and circumstances, CC, 248–1466. Since in the table of contents appended at the end of the volume the subject matter, cause, and rationale of each affair are explained specifically and clearly, it should be consulted.

Apostolic letters to the Gallican Church concerning Blessed Bernard’s enrolment among the saints, and the solemn celebration thereafter of his feast in the Church, CLXXXV, 622.

Letter to the king of France, to all abbots of the Cistercian order, and to the brethren of Clairvaux, on the same matter, CLXXXV, 623–624.

ANACLETUS, antipope.—He announces his elevation to the papacy to churches and kings, CLXXIX, 690–695.

To certain bishops he commends Gregory, cardinal-deacon, sent by him into Aquitaine; and he prescribes that a council be held, CLXXIX, 699.

To Philip, son of Louis, king of the Franks, he commends his legate Otto, lest Philip lend his ears to his enemies’ lies, CLXXIX, 701–704.

These and similar matters of little importance concern Pope Innocent II, for whose benefit these actions were undertaken; see CLXXIX, 704–731.

ANASTASIUS I, Saint, pope.—Letter in which he replies that Rufinus should be condemned if, of his own mind and while praising and approving them, he translated Origen’s condemned works from Greek into Latin; otherwise, if he did so while accusing their author. He states that he is troubled not by groundless fear, but that he will take care lest the churches throughout the world be corrupted from this source, XX, 68.

Letter to Simplician: he praises the zeal and vigilance of Theophilus; having been approached by Theophilus’s letters, he informs Simplician, bishop of Milan, that he too had pronounced an anathema upon the Origenist heresy, XX, 74.

Letter to all bishops of Germany and Burgundy: that all should hear the holy Gospel not seated but standing; concerning Manichees discovered in the city of Rome, XX, 75.

ANASTASIUS IV, pope.—Letter to Peter, Archbishop of Bourges, that he should restore to the Abbot of Saint-Denis the church of Casa Major and other goods, as he had already been warned, CLXXXVIII, 1003.

Letter against the Count of Nevers and the townsmen of Vézelay, CLXXXVIII, 1008–1011.

Letter to Eugebald, Archbishop of Tours: he directs him to summon the Bishop of Tréguier and investigate his case, CLXXXVIII, 1017.—Letter to the regular canons of the Lateran: he confirms their statutes, CLXXXVIII, 1019.

He confirms the property, possessions, and immunities of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, CLXXXVIII, 1030.

He commands the Archbishop of Braga to render to the Bishop of Toledo, within thirty days, the obedience due to him as primate, CLXXXVIII, 1053.

He confirms the judgment pronounced by Eugenius III in the dispute of the canons of Saints Alexander and Vincent at Bergamo, CLXXXVIII, 1058.

He informs the bishops of Sweden that he has received with joy the news that the people have made progress in apostolic teaching, CLXXXVIII, 1084.

He exhorts King Werker and the magnates of Sweden to continue following the commands of Nicholas, legate of the Apostolic See, CLXXXVIII, 1086.

BENEDICT I, pope.—Concerning the impediment of consanguinity, LXXII, 683.

He proves from the sacred Scriptures that the supreme Trinity is unity, LXXII, 685.

BENEDICT II, pope.—Letter to Peter, notary: he warns him to ensure that the synodal acts of the Sixth Council of the bishops of Spain are authenticated by subscription, XCVI, 423.

Letter to King Ervig: he informs him that he is sending him the definition of the Sixth Synod, together with the edict of Emperor Constantine and the acclamatory document of the same synod, XCVI, 424.

BENEDICT III, pope.—Letter to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims: he confirms the Synod of Soissons, II, CXV, 689.

Letter to bishops, against Hubert, a cleric: that he should come to Rome to answer the charges of which he was accused, CXV, 691.

BENEDICT IV, pope.—He restores Algrin, Bishop of Langres, to all the rights of his church, CXXXI, 40–42.

He commends Bishop Malacen and his companions, who had been badly treated by the Saracens, CXXXI, 43.

BENEDICT VI, pope.—Letter to Frederick, Bishop of Salzburg: he grants to him and his successors apostolic vicariate authority in Noricum and Pannonia, CXXXV, 1081.

Confirmation of donations in the third region of Rome, CXXXV, 1084.

BENEDICT VII, pope.—Letter to the Gauls and Germans: he decrees that the Church of Padua is metropolitan; he determines the boundaries of it and of Salzburg; he delegates apostolic vicariate authority to Silgrin, Archbishop of Lorch, CXXXVII, 315.

Bull by which he grants to Theodoric, Archbishop of Trier, and his successors the cell of the Four Crowned Saints, CXXXVII, 318.

The monks of St. Benedict are reintroduced into the monastery of St. Martin at Trier, CXXXVII, 319.

At the request of Count Teudald, he confirms the foundation of the Church of Saint Apollonius and the establishment of twelve canons there in the castle of Canossa, CXXXVII, 325.

He holds a Roman council against simoniacs, CXXXVII, 336.

He compels Abbot Leo to restore many things to the monastery of Subiaco, CXXXVII, 346.

BENEDICT VIII.—Letter to the bishops of Burgundy and Aquitaine: he orders that invaders of Cluniac property be excommunicated unless they make satisfaction, CXXXIX, 1601.

Establishment of the Church of Bisuldun as a bishopric, CXXXIX, 1604–1606.

Bull by which he grants the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the county of Macri to the abbey of Farfa, CXXXIX, 1616.

Bull by which he grants that in the church of the monastery of Ripoll the “Alleluia and Glory in the Highest” (*Alleluia et Gloria in excelsis*) may be sung on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, even if it falls after Septuagesima, CXXXIX, 1630.

Blessed Simeon, monk of the monastery of Padolirone, is enrolled in the canon of holy confessors, CXXXIX, 1633.

Bull which testifies that Henry’s health was restored by Saint Benedict, and maintains that Emperor Henry conveyed property to the monastery of Monte Cassino, CXXXIX, 1636.

BONIFACE I, pope.—Letter that the case of Maximus, bishop of the city of Valence, accused of various crimes, should be examined in the synod of that province, XX, 756.

Letter that the Corinthians should receive Gerigenes as the bishop whom they request, XX, 760.

Letter in which the vigilance of Rufus in fulfilling the office of vicar of the Apostolic See is praised. The office itself is explained. Boniface recalls that several bishops had approved his own letters, conveyed to them through Rufus’s agency; and on that occasion he launches into praise of Perigenes, XX, 761.

Letter to Hilary, Archbishop of Narbonne: that in every province no one should be ordained bishop in contempt of the metropolitan, XX, 772.

Letter to Bishop Rufus: he reminds him of the dignity and office of vicar of Blessed Peter granted to him; communicates with him; and states what he has written to the Thessalians concerning the various affairs being conducted in those regions, and what remains for Rufus himself to do, XX, 774.

Letter to the bishops of Thessaly: he confirms the authority granted to Bishop Rufus, which some had disregarded, and asserts the pre-eminent authority of the Apostolic See, XX, 777.

Letter to the bishops of Macedonia, Achaia, and elsewhere: he declares that the Illyrian bishops have no right to investigate or reconsider the case of Perigenes, whom he had made bishop for the Corinthians without failing to consult them; and that if any undertake this, they will not remain in his communion. He repeatedly explains Rufus’s authority in the same provinces, more explicitly at the end, XX, 779.

Decrees: that a man should not be ordained priest before thirty years of age; that affairs which a metropolitan cannot settle should be referred to the primate; that whatever is consecrated to the Lord belongs by right to the priest; concerning bishops who desire to harm their brethren; what should be done if a deposed bishop dares to enter a city, XX, 789.

BONIFACE II, pope.—Letter to Caesarius, Bishop of Arles: he confirms what had been defined at the Synod of Orange, LXV, 31.

Letter to Eulalius, Bishop of Alexandria, concerning the reconciliation of the Church of Carthage, CXV, 43.

BONIFACE IV, pope.—He holds a Roman council, where the case of the English Church is addressed, together with the manner in which monks may serve anywhere while exercising priestly office, LXXX, 103, 106.

BONIFACE V, pope.—Letter to Justus, bishop, praising him for having brought King Eadbald to the faith, LXXX, 435.

Letter to Edwin, king of the English: he exhorts him to the Christian faith, LXXX, 436.

Letter to Queen Æthelburg: he congratulates her on receiving the faith, and warns her to bestow this benefit upon her king through her own merit, LXXX, 438.

CALIXTUS II, pope.—Letter to Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, concerning his elevation to the papacy, CLXIII, 1093.

Consecration of the church of Saint Anthony, CLXIII, 1093.

Letter to Bernard, Archbishop of Auch: he grants that henceforth the bodies of the dead may freely be buried at the Church of Saint Mary of Auch, CLXIII, 1094.

That a council should be held at Rheims for the happy condition of the Church, CLXIII, 1093.

He commands the clergy and people of Lucca not to permit the brethren of Saint Frigdianus to be harassed, CLXIII, 1096.

Apostolic bull by which the chapter of Brioude is declared immediately subject to the Roman Church, CLXIII, 1099.

He confirms the possessions of the monasteries of Saint Blaise, Blessed Mary of Elne, and Saint Giles, CLXIII, 1100–1105.

He releases the disputing canons of Saint John and Saint Stephen from their oaths, CLXIII, 1106.

Synodal letter, issued after the Council of Toulouse had been held, by which the cell of Saint Mary of Gordian is adjudged to the monastery of Aniane, CLXIII, 1110.

To Berengar, abbot of the monastery of Grasse, and his successors, he grants the church of Saint Peter of Valeriis for an annual payment of two gold pieces, CLXIII, 1114.

Letter to Henry, king of the English, to settle the controversy concerning the primacy of the Church of York, CLXIII, 1117.

Letter to Hervé, abbot of the monastery of Redon: he is to restore to the people of Quimperlé the money taken from Belle-Île, or come to the Council of Rheims to render an account, CLXIII, 1117.

The various possessions of churches and monasteries are confirmed, CLXIII, 1121–1136.

He confirms the decree issued by Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, against simony, CLXIII, 1137.

That the Abbot of Redon should be compelled by canonical coercion to pay the money owed to the Abbot of Quimperlé, CLXIII, 1138.

Letters addressed to the kings of Norway concerning the admission of Ralph, bishop of Orkney, CLXIII, 1142.

He appoints Josceran, Bishop of Langres, judge of the dispute between the Abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif of Sens and the Abbot of Molesme, CLXIII, 1146.

He commands the monks of Saint Viventius of Verzeio, under penalty of interdict, to receive a prior from the monastery of Cluny, CLXIII, 1146.

That Ulrich, Bishop of Constance, should restore to the people of Schaffhausen an estate taken by force, CLXIII, 1149.

Letter to the Bishops of Mâcon and Chalon, informing them that he has consecrated the altars of the monastery of Tournus and blessed its cemetery, CLXIII, 1155.

Letter to Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, concerning the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the abbot and monastery of Saint-Melaine, CLXIII, 1157.

He grants to the Church of Compostela the metropolitan dignity of the Church of Mérida, CLXIII, 1168.

He commands the bishops of Coimbra and Salamanca to obey their metropolitan, Diego, CLXIII, 1170.

He grants to Oberto, Bishop of Cremona, and his successors the right to consecrate the abbots of the monastery of Saint Peter, CLXIII, 1177.

He commands that the Church of Aversa remain a suffragan of the Roman Church, CLXIII, 1183.

He commands the bishops of Upper Dalmatia to obey their metropolitan, the Archbishop of Ragusa, CLXIII, 1184.

He appoints Gerard, Bishop of Angoulême, apostolic legate, CLXIII, 1186.

He removes from the archbishops of Pisa the right to consecrate Corsican bishops, CLXIII, 1192.

Bull concerning the establishment or restoration of a bishopric at Tres Tabernae in Calabria, CLXIII, 1195.

He assigns the Church of Bornhem to the monastery of Affligem, CLXIII, 1199.

He approves the institute of the regular canons of Bergtestaden, CLXIII, 1206.

Letter to Diego, Archbishop of Compostela, concerning bishops suspended because they did not attend the council, CLXIII, 1210.

He writes to the Archbishop of Compostela that the marriage of Gerald, who had married a kinswoman of his former wife, must be dissolved, CLXIII, 1211.

Letter to the Bishop of Uzès: that he should excommunicate Count Ildefonsus unless he restores what he has taken from the monastery of Saint Giles, CLXIII, 1212.

[Col. 1224] He threatens certain nobles that he will excommunicate them as counsellors and helpers of Count Ildefonsus unless, within forty days, they cease harassing the monastery of Saint Giles, CLXIII, 1213.

He absolves the burgesses of the monastery of Saint Giles from the oath of fealty rendered to Count Ildefonsus, who had compelled them to perjury, CLXIII, 1213.

He commands Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse, under penalty of excommunication, to repair the losses inflicted upon the monastery of Saint Giles, CLXIII, 1214.

Concerning confirmation of the regular canons of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem and of their possessions, CLXIII, 1215.

Letter to the Archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans: that they should warn Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse to allow the Abbot of Saint Giles, whom he had expelled, to return to the monastery; otherwise they should punish him with excommunication and interdict, CLXIII, 1218, 1219.

Letter to bishops, abbots, and others in Spain: that they should obey Bernard, Primate of Toledo, as apostolic legate, CLXIII, 1224.

At the request of Louis, king of the Franks, he confirms the union of the bishoprics of Noyon and Tournai, CLXIII, 1225.

Letters to King Alexander and to the bishops of Scotland, that they should obey their metropolitan, the Archbishop of York, CLXIII, 1229.

Letter to Ralph, Archbishop of Rheims: concerning avoidance of simony in the prebends of Saint Timothy; concerning recalling Robert, prior of Saint-Oricle; and concerning retaining monks in the church of Reitestein, CLXIII, 1247.

He commands Count Raynulf, under penalty of excommunication, to restore within twenty days the church of Cingla to the monastery of Monte Cassino, CLXIII, 1249.

He informs the Archbishop of Dol and his suffragans of a general council to be held in the city, CLXIII, 1249.

He informs Archbishop Otto and all the people of Capua that an interdict has been imposed upon the Church of Cingla and the monastery of Saint Mary, and that Abbess Alpherada has been excommunicated, CLXIII, 1249.

He commands Theresa, queen of Portugal, to release from custody, in accordance with his letters, Pelagius, Archbishop of Braga, whom she has captured; otherwise, from that time onward, he pronounces a sentence of excommunication against her and her supporters, CLXIII, 1255.

To the Cluniacs, he approves Peter, abbot-elect, CLXIII, 1256.

To the regular canons of Berne: he approves their institute, CLXIII, 1257.

He congratulates Emperor Henry because he has at last returned to the bosom of the Church, CLXIII, 1260.

He decrees, against the claim of the monks of Nonantola, that the estate of Wilzaccara, with the church of Saint Caesarius in the territory of Modena, belongs to the regular canons, CLXIII, 1266.

At a general council he enrols Conrad, formerly Bishop of Constance, among the ranks of the saints, CLXIII, 1273.

To Gilbert, Bishop of Paris: that all clerics and abbots of the diocese should obey him, CLXIII, 1274.

He assigns the church of Saint Macarius to the monastery of the Holy Cross at Bordeaux, CLXIII, 1276.

Letter to the canons of Besançon: he settles the controversy between the churches of Saint John and Saint Stephen, and orders that the privilege granted to the Church of Saint Stephen by Pope Paschal be restored, CLXIII, 1286.

He grants to Amadeus, Bishop of Maurienne, the provostship of the Church of Saint Mary of Susa and parochial jurisdiction in the city of Susa itself, CLXIII, 1293.

Letter to Louis, king of the Franks: he commends Peter, cardinal and apostolic legate, CLXIII, 1297.

He declares the judgment rendered by him in favor of the mother church of Saint John, CLXIII, 1298.

Letter to the Spanish bishops and others: that they should obey Diego, Archbishop of Compostela, his vicar, CLXIII, 1299.

He forbids Berard, Bishop of Mâcon, to exercise episcopal office until he desists from wrongs against the monastery of Cluny, CLXIII, 1304.

Letter to all kings, counts, and princes: he exhorts them to assist the afflicted churches of Spain, granting indulgences to those who help, CLXIII, 1305.

That aid should be given to the monks of Saint Giles against Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse and his supporters, whom he declares excommunicated by himself, CLXIII, 1306.

He commands the Bishop of Roussillon to cease harassing the monastery of Albaron, CLXIII, 1307.

He informs Louis, king of the Franks, that Robert, Bishop of Arras, having been summoned to court at the general council by Burchard, Bishop of Cambrai, came to him with the latter’s letters, CLXIII, 1312.

He rebukes the Bishop of Roussillon because, contrary to his command, he continues to inflict injuries upon the monastery of Albaron, CLXIII, 1313.

Bull confirming property belonging to the Church of Saint Mary, CLXIII, 1314.

He settles the discord between Oberto, Bishop of Cremona, and his canons, CLXIII, 1316.

Letter to Diego, Archbishop of Compostela: he grants that the city of Mérida should remain perpetually subject to the city of Compostela, CLXIII, 1521.

That an interdict imposed on account of an unlawful marriage should be observed, CLXIII, 1323.

He exhorts Jordan, prince of Capua, not to devastate the land of the monastery of Carduense, CLXIII, 1335.

CLEMENT III, antipope, or WIBERT.—Letter to Vratislaus, first duke of Bohemia: he exhorts him to pay the offering due to the Roman See and to promote a certain person to a bishopric, CXLVIII, 831.

Synodal letter to the entire clergy, CXLVIII, 832.

Letter to the Bishop of Ostia concerning measures established by him in the Roman synod; he rebukes him because, having been summoned to the synod, he did not come, CXLVIII, 836.

Letter to Ruithard, Archbishop of Mainz: he appoints a day for him to attend the synod to be held at Vercelli, CXLVIII, 841.

Letter to Robert, Bishop of Bamberg: he warns him to come to the synod as accuser of Ruithard, Archbishop of Mainz, CXLVIII, 841.

CLEMENT III, pope.—He confirms the possessions of churches and monasteries, CCIV, 1273–1286.

To the bishops of Scotland: he announces that Hugh, Bishop of St. Andrews, summoned by Urban, had obstinately refused to appear and was deposed from the episcopate; he recommends that John be elected, CCIV, 1287.

He commands Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, not to delay demolishing whatever the monks of Canterbury had done in the work of the chapel after the prohibition of Urban VII, his predecessor, CCIV, 1294.

He commands archbishops and bishops not to allow possessions of churches to be alienated and conferred on laymen by priors of Cluniac brethren without the consent of the abbot and convent, CCIV, 1301.

He assigns the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre to Abbot Hugh and the convent of Cluny, CCIV, 1312.

He commands the Prior of Faversham and Master Firmin to declare excommunicated the invaders of the goods of the Church of Canterbury if, after warning, they do not repair the losses, CCIV, 1327.

He commands William, Bishop of Worcester, and the Abbot of the Holy Sepulchre of Warwick to judge between the canons of Kenilworth and the clerics of Gnosall, CCIV, 1327.

He permits Lanfranc, Bishop of Bergamo, to recover possessions of the Church alienated against the will of the chapter, CCIV, 1335.

He grants the same Lanfranc authority to punish disobedient clerics, CCIV, 1336.

He informs the consuls and people of Pisa that cardinals have been sent to settle their dispute with the Genoese concerning Sardinia, CCIV, 1346.

He exhorts Abbot Joachim to complete the *Exposition of the Apocalypse* and the work *Concordia*, and diligently to endeavor to revise them, CCIV, 1357.

He commands the Abbot of Saint Geneviève at Paris to compel the Bishop of Troyes to take regular canons from the church of Saint Lupus at Troyes, in order to establish them in the Church of Marigny, CCIV, 1367.

He commands Abbot Silvecanus to protect the monks of Saint Victor at Marseille from the injuries of canons, CCIV, 1378.

He commands the bishops of Regensburg and Freising to defend the monastery of Aldersbach from the wrongs of Albert of Kam, CCIV, 1378.

Letter to Henry, Archbishop of Bourges: monks and regular canons are not to stay alone in towns, CCIV, 1379.

He assigns the bishopric of Vexhull to Hartwig, Archbishop of Hamburg, CCIV, 1381.

He commands Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, to restore to the monks of Canterbury, within eleven days, what he had taken from them, CCIV, 1401.

He forbids all clerics established throughout Norway to presume to go on campaign, unless perhaps to administer penance and ecclesiastical sacraments to the dying, CCIV, 1418.

He announces that he has given orders that it should be made known that Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont, has been enrolled among the saints, CCIV, 1426.

[Col. 1226] He commands Pistor, Bishop of Vicenza, to investigate whether the sisters of Saint Christina, their church having been destroyed, are building another within the city of Treviso against the bishop’s wishes; he is to restrain the nuns, CCIV, 1430.

He commands certain bishops diligently to investigate the life and miracles of Otto I, Bishop of Bamberg, and, unless they find impediments, to declare him enrolled among the saints, CCIV, 1438.

He absolves the whole chapter of Trier and all persons within the archbishopric from obedience to Archbishop Fulmar in spiritual and temporal matters, CCIV, 1442.

He commands all bishops, whenever requested by the brethren of the Church of Saint Nicholas at Stendal, to administer the sacraments without delay and without appeal, CCIV, 1446.

He informs the Church of York that the Archbishop of York has been acknowledged by him, CCIV, 1454.

He commands Melon, Archbishop of Milan, that he has directed the Bishop of Piacenza to punish the consuls of Piacenza severely unless they desist from wrongs against churches, CCIV, 1455.

Bull for the canonization of Blessed Malachy, CCIV, 1466.

At the request of Alfonso, king of Castile, he establishes an episcopal see in the city of Plasencia and confirms the diocese founded by the king, CCIV, 1476.

Decree to the abbot and archpriest of Montolano: that they should restore to a certain acolyte a benefice taken from him, CCIV, 1477.

Decree concerning a certain marriage which is not to be dissolved, CCIV, 1478.

Decree concerning priests who have incurred the guilt of adultery, perjury, or false testimony, CCIV, 1479.

Decree concerning the absolution of those who, when summoned to judgment, scorn to appear and are bound by the bond of anathema for their contumacy, CCIV, 1480.

Decree concerning the consecration of an oratory, CCIV, 1480.

What has been decreed by the greater and sounder part of a council should always prevail, CCIV, 1481.

Concerning Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith, CCIV, 1482.

Concerning those who have contracted clandestine marriages contrary to prohibition, CCIV, 1483.

Concerning two men who have taken two sisters as wives, CCIV, 1484.

Concerning the oath of fidelity to be rendered by a king’s heirs to the Roman pontiffs, CCIV, 1486.

Concerning the penance to be imposed on a certain priest through whose fault it is uncertain whether a servant died, CCIV, 1486.

Concerning a certain girl, not yet eleven years old, who had been given in marriage to a certain man, although unwilling, CCIV, 1487.

Concerning the absolution of the excommunicated, CCIV, 1489.

Against clerics who bear arms, CCIV, 1492.

Concerning conventual churches, CCIV, 1493.

Concerning one who had intercourse with his wife’s kinswoman, CCIV, 1495.

Concerning a deacon who had unwillingly killed a boy, CCIV, 1496.

To the Bishop of Livonia and his companions: that they should use foods set before them by unbelievers, CCIV, 1497.

He prescribes that assailants of clerics and arsonists are to be absolved only by the Roman pontiff, CCIV, 1497.

Decree concerning judicial combat, CCIV, 1501.

Letter to a canon learned in medical science: he urges him not to ascend to the higher sacred orders, because he has administered medicines to several persons who thereby incurred danger of death, CCIV, 1505.

CELESTINE II, pope.—He informs the Cluniacs of his election and requests their prayers, CLXXIX, 766.

He calls to himself the case of a certain marriage, CLXXIX, 767.

He commands archbishops and bishops not to hinder the annual assemblies of Premonstratensian abbots, CLXXIX, 782.

To Arnaud, Archbishop of Narbonne, and his suffragans: that their parishioners should not furnish refuge to Aimon and other rebels, otherwise they are to be excommunicated, CLXXIX, 782.

To Hugh, Archbishop of Tours: that he should come to the Apostolic See to answer the Bishop of Dol, who complained that he had been deprived of the bishopric of Arles, CLXXIX, 783.

To Peter, Abbot of Saint Giles: he commands him, in the pope’s name, to lay the first stone in the foundation of a certain chapel, CLXXIX, 783.

He settles the controversy between the monks of Vivens and of Camaldoli, CLXXIX, 806.

Letter to the Archbishop of Toledo: that he should restore several parishes to Bishop N., CLXXIX, 811.

[Col. 1227] CELESTINE III, pope.—He announces to all that Peter, formerly Archbishop of Tarentaise, has been enrolled among the saints, CCVI, 869.

He promises Geoffrey, Archbishop-elect of York, that Hugh, Bishop of Durham, will be made subject to him after he has received consecration, CCVI, 872.

He commands Bishop Reginald and others to restore what Archbishop Baldwin took from the monks of Canterbury, CCVI, 874.

He grants Humbert, Archbishop of Arles, authority to restrain by ecclesiastical censures disorders that have arisen in Provence, CCVI, 897.

Concerning the perpetual establishment of the Order of Saint Benedict in specified places, CCVI, 898.

He commands Stenar, Bishop of Växjö, not to invade the possessions of Kol, Bishop of Linköping, CCVI, 906.

He informs Sven, Bishop of Aarhus, that he has permitted Absalon, Archbishop of Lund, to grant him leave to resign his bishopric, CCVI, 908.

He commands certain bishops to release from a vow of continence, undertaken on account of illness, the wife of Canute, king of the Swedes, CCVI, 909.

That Cluniac monks may excommunicate and place under interdict wrongdoers who harass them, CCVI, 916.

Letter to the bishop and clergy of Gubbio concerning the canonization of Saint Ubald, CCVI, 918.

He commands the Archbishop of Vienne and his suffragans not to allow their parishioners to be prevented from giving goods to the Carthusian Order, CCVI, 924.

He grants the dean and chapter of Rouen permission to celebrate divine offices without solemnity during an interdict, CCVI, 930.

He confirms the possessions of certain churches, CLVI, 931–938.

He commands the abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal, freely to perform the duty of his office concerning the correction of monks and lay brothers, CCVI, 942.

He assigns to the Abbot and convent of Cîteaux the church of Schardeburg, donated by Richard, king of the English, CCVI, 961.

He grants Conrad, Bishop of Regensburg, authority to absolve those who, fighting for the Church of Regensburg, committed arson, CCVI, 965.

He approves the foundation of the Church of Saint Peter at Marchial, CCVI, 966.

Bull for the canonization of Saint Bernward, Bishop of Hildesheim, CCVI, 970.

He writes to the archbishops and bishops established throughout England that the army sent to the East had failed, because of dissensions, to fulfil expectations; he wishes the princes to be warned that, once discord is quieted, they should bring aid to the Holy Land, CCVI, 970.

He commands the Abbot and convent of Fécamp that they may remove from their benefices those who do not personally serve their churches, CCVI, 977.

Bull forbidding churches subject to the monastery of Fécamp to be placed under interdict, CCVI, 985.

He grants John, dean, and the chapter of Rouen that, when there is a general interdict of the land, they may celebrate offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice, CCVI, 996.

He grants the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury that no one may presume to burden its abbot or monks with any sentence unless sent from the side of the Roman pontiff, CCVI, 1025.

He forbids Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to demand obedience from the abbot and monks of Saint Augustine, CCVI, 1225.

Bull for the reform of the monastery of Saint Caesarius at Arles, CCVI, 1032.

He commands the Bishop of Lincoln to investigate the excesses of the Archbishop of York, CCVI, 1037.

He commands the chapter of Tarragona to declare anathematized William, who cruelly murdered the archbishop in the city of Girona, and to place his land under interdict, CCVI, 1045.

The possessions and goods of every kind of various monasteries and churches are confirmed, CCVI, 1054 and passim.

He commands the Bishops of Münster and Osnabrück to anathematize certain ministeriales of the Church of Bremen if they do not restore property unjustly taken from that church, CCVI, 1067.

Letter to Humbert, Archbishop of Canterbury: he entrusts him with the legation of the Apostolic See, CCVI, 1074, 1075.

He commands Anselm, Bishop of Foligno, to recall the Abbot of Saint Silvester of Ospedale to obedience to the Camaldolese order, CCVI, 1076.

[Col. 1228] Concerning the dissolution of a certain marriage, CCVI, 1080.

He informs Philip, king of the Franks, that his sentence of divorce is invalid and annulled; and urges him to take back his wife and treat her with marital affection, CCVI, 1098.

Confirms the sentences of excommunication and interdict pronounced by the authority of Walter, archbishop, against the citizens of Rouen, CCVI, 1098.

Commands the archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans to exhort men to provide aid for the land of Jerusalem, CCVI, 1107.

Letter to certain bishops, concerning the sedition stirred up by the citizens of Rouen against the canons, and concerning the satisfaction to be made to them, CCVI, 1116.

Announces that in a certain island, hitherto schismatic, he has appointed legates who, notwithstanding the obstacle of an appeal, should regulate whatever pertained to providing the Church’s endowments, CCVI, 1147.

Exhorts the count of Toulouse to repair the damages inflicted upon the monastery of Saint Giles; otherwise he declares that the count will be excommunicated by the neighboring bishops, CCVI, 1156.

Appoints the bishop of Vercelli and the abbot of Locedio to make peace between Archbishop Boniface and the Genoese canons, CCVI, 1178.

Commands Abbot Hugh of Cluny, in the abbeys belonging to the monastery of Cluny, to correct whatever he shall see needs correction according to God . . . , CCVI, 1179.

Commands archbishops, bishops, etc., to excommunicate lay plunderers and persecutors of the brethren of Cluny, and to remove the others from offices, CCVI, 1181.

Commands the archbishop of Ravenna and his suffragans, under penalty of excommunication, to admonish the citizens of Modena to restore what they had taken from the monastery of Nonantola, CCVI, 1184.

Grants Gerard, bishop of Cahors, permission to receive from the church of Saint Amator the expenses necessary for a journey to the apostolic see and for other matters belonging to his church, CCVI, 1201.

Grants the sisters of Saint Mary of Soissons that, notwithstanding an oath formerly made, they may, with the consent of the abbesses or female superiors, receive any suitable nuns, CCVI, 1203.

Permits the monks of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest to sing on certain feast days: “Glory to God in the highest,” etc., CCVI, 1207.

Grants forty days’ remission from the penances imposed for their offenses to all the faithful established in the kingdom of Denmark who give money toward building the church of Aarhus with a stone wall, CCVI, 1210.

Permits Gerard, bishop of Bologna, to excommunicate those who seize the property of the Church, CCVI, 1212.

Appoints the bishop of Laon judge between the bishop of Pavia and the canons of Piacenza, CCVI, 1234.

CONSTANTINE, pope.—Letter concerning Egwin’s vision, the holding of a council, and the founding of a monastery, LXXXIX, 335.

Confirms the possession of the lands in which the Blessed Virgin Mary is said to have appeared to Bishop Egwin, together with many other properties bestowed upon the monastery of Evesham in the Lateran church, LXXXIX, 336.

Receives under the protection of the holy see the monastery founded by Egwin, LXXXIX, 338.

DAMASUS, Saint, pope.—Letter to the Catholic bishops established throughout the East, on firmly maintaining the Nicene faith, XIII, 347.

Statement of faith issued in the Roman synod and sent to the East, XIII, 350.

Persons unwilling to subscribe to the exposition of the Nicene faith are not to be admitted into the Church, XIII, 356.

Confession of the Catholic faith which he sent to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, XIII, 357.

Letter to Acholius and the other bishops of Macedonia: he condemns the ordination of Maximus the Cynic and exhorts the Macedonians, at the synod soon to be held at Constantinople, to appoint a bishop worthy of that city and to observe the enactments of their forebears against translations of bishops, XIII, 365.

Letter to Acholius, bishop of Thessalonica: Rusticus, the *silentiarius* of Gratian, is commended, and what concerns the ordination of Maximus, etc., is confirmed, XIII, 369.

Letter to Saint Jerome: he submits questions for Jerome to explain and praises his writings, XIII, 371.

To all bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy. He commands that henceforth no one be judged by them on the basis of written accusations, but through a lawful accuser; and that all causes requiring judgment be referred to the apostolic see, XIII, 439.

DEUSDEDIT, pope. Decree that parents may not receive their own children from the sacred font of baptism; otherwise, they are to know that they have created for themselves an impediment to marriage, etc., LXXX, 361.

[Col. 1229] Decree concerning the election of the Roman pontiff, LXXX, 362.

EUGENIUS III, pope.—Letter to Premonstratensian abbots and provosts, that they should assemble once each year at Prémontré for a general chapter, CLXXX, 1017.

Commands Alvisus, bishop of Arras, to decide concerning the marriage of Baldwin of Rispens and Matilda of Albiniac, CLXXX, 1026.

Commands John, archbishop of Braga, to recognize the primacy of Toledo, CLXXX, 1036.

Concerning satisfaction to be rendered to the bishop of Moravia, CLXXX, 1044.

Commands Alvisus, bishop of Arras, to judge between the abbot of Saint Nicholas of Vedogio and the priest of Bafstalms, CLXX, 1053.

Commands Guy, cardinal-priest, to settle a dispute concerning a certain castle which had arisen between canons and certain nobles of Verona, CLXXX, 1054.

Letter to Louis, king of the Gauls, concerning the undertaking of an expedition to the Holy Land, CLXXX, 1064.

Commands archbishops and bishops to bless without delay the elected provosts of the Premonstratensian order as abbots, CLXXV, 1076.

Commands Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, and his successors not to alienate Wincemburg Castle; he forbids the Goslar citizens, who had seized a certain provostship, to be released unpunished, CLXXX, 1082.

Intercedes with Henry, bishop of Moravia, for brethren who had left the monastery on Mount Strahov without permission, CLXXX, 1085.

Letter to the bishops of Angoulême and Limoges, that they should canonically settle the dispute over Roca Boviscurtis between the Cluniacs and the clerics, CLXXX, 1095.

Bull confirming the possessions of the monastery of Crisemone, CLXXX, 1096.

Bull in favor of the monastery of Saint Marian, CLXXX, 1097.

Grants Odo, prior, and the brethren of Saint Martin of the Fields that, as the canons of Blessed Gervasius of Encra die, monks may be substituted there, CLXXX, 1107.

Confirms the possessions of the regular canons of the church of Blessed Peter of Tarentaise and decrees that the regular order according to the Rule of Saint Augustine shall always be observed there, CLXXX, 1114.

Exhorts all God’s faithful established throughout Gaul to undertake the holy war, CLXXX, 1115.

That Abbot Suger should assist, with the king, the monastery of Blessed Medard, burdened by the count of Soissons, CLXXX, 1118.

Concerning the holiness, miracles, and canonization of Emperor Henry, CLXXX, 1118.

To Peter, archbishop of Bourges, concerning primacy in the provinces of Bourges and Bordeaux, CLXXX, 1119.

Concerning Anselm, restored as bishop to the Church of Tournai, CLXXX, 1122–1124.

To Samson, archbishop of Rheims: he rebukes him because he had presumed, contrary to the right of the archbishop of Bourges, to crown the king of the Franks in the city of Bourges; for this reason he forbids him the use of the pallium, CLXXX, 1128.

Confirms the rights of the monastery of Vézelay concerning the election of an abbot and the bearing of the advocate’s office, CLXXX, 1141.

Commands Henry, bishop of Moravia, to admonish Vladislaus, duke of Bohemia, to make satisfaction for the damages inflicted upon the church of Regensburg, CLXXX, 1145.

Praises Bishop Theobald because, on account of the canons’ property seized by citizens, he had forbidden liturgical services in his city, etc., CLXXX, 1149.

Commands certain bishops to compel certain nobles to restore property of the Veronese canons which they had seized, CLXXX, 1150.

To the bishop of Verona: he admonishes him to order that the excommunication pronounced against the enemies of the canons be observed by the priests of Runches and others, CLXXX, 1164.

Commands the bishop of Vicenza to punish the archpriest of Saint Boniface, who had communicated with excommunicated persons, CLXXX, 1165.

Letter to William, count of Nevers, that he cease from harassing the people of Vézelay, CLXXX, 1179–1182.

To Gregory, bishop of Lucca, that he introduce the canons of Saint Fridianus into the church of Saint Pantaleon, CLXXX, 1193.

Confirms the constitution of Pope Callistus II concerning the peace and security of the territory of Trenorc, within specified boundaries marked by crosses, CLXXX, 1201.

Incites people to a holy expedition against the Slavs in Pomerania; he also writes to the king of Spain to prepare war against the Saracens of Iberia, CLXXX, 1203.

To William, count of Mâcon, that he assign the church of Balmes to the Cluniacs and provide assistance, CLXXX, 1227.

[Col. 1230] Bull in favor of the monastery of Tiron, CLXXX, 1228.

Bull for the nunnery of Saint Denis of Montmartre, CLXXX, 1236–1242.

Concerning the dispute between the archbishop of Canterbury and Bernard, bishop of Saint David’s: he commands each to come before him, CLXXX, 1230.

Relaxes the interdict by which he had justly punished churches belonging to the monastery of Balmes, CLXXX, 1251.

Bull confirming the church of Ilbenstadt, CLXXX, 1263.

That certain malicious persons be compelled to make satisfaction for injuries inflicted on the monastery of Cluny according to the decision of the archbishop of Lyons, CLXXX, 1271.

Bull confirming the union of the Savigniac brethren with the Cistercian order, CLXXX, 1282.

Letter to Abbot Suger: he asks which bishops refuse to give him assistance for the defense of the kingdom; a definite place for a council is appointed; concerning the excommunicated duke of Lorraine, CLXXX, 1283.

That henceforth the abbot of Saint Germanus of Auxerre be elected with the counsel of the abbot of Cluny, and that the person elected receive blessing from the bishop of Auxerre, CLXXX, 1294.

Rebukes Theobald, bishop of Verona, because he had lifted the interdict from the city without the canons’ possessions having been restored; he commands him to ensure their restoration, CLXXX, 1298.

Writes to Peregrinus, patriarch of Aquileia, that he is astonished that he had absolved certain knights excommunicated for occupying Church possessions; he commands him to induce them to restore what they took, CLXXX, 1299.

Commands Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, to ensure that estates of Corvey seized by his people are restored, CLXXX, 1300.

To the monks of Corvey: he exhorts them to show humble reverence to Abbot Wilbald, CLXXX, 1306.

Mandate to archbishops, bishops, etc., concerning restorations to be made to the monastery of Lorsch, CLXXX, 1316.

Letter to German prelates: he exhorts them to support King Henry the Younger and to assist him with their counsel and efforts, CLXXX, 1320.

Rebukes the countess of Nevers because she harasses those going to Vézelay, CLXXX, 1324.

That estates of the monastery of Kammin, seized by various persons, be restored, CLXXX, 1331.

Letter to the people of Fulda: he declares void the election they made contrary to his command, and commands them, in the presence of certain abbots whom he names from another cloister, to elect an abbot for themselves, CLXXX, 1334.

Letter to Alfonso, king of Spain, confirming the primacy of Toledo, CLXXX, 1345.

Letter to Abbot Suger concerning the appointment of monks in the church of Saint Genevieve, CLXXX, 1347.

Letter to Humbert, archbishop of Besançon, that he should duly punish contempt of the Roman Church in the priest who had transgressed an excommunication pronounced by him and had stolen the revenues of the monastery of Balmes from the Cluniacs, CLXXX, 1353.

Commands the archbishop of Trier, etc., under penalty of excommunication, to admonish Duke Matthew to destroy a castle built near Toul, CLXXX, 1354.

Prescribes to all the Roman clergy that chaplains shall promise obedience to the rectors of titles or churches, CLXXX, 1358.

That the bishops-elect of Piacenza should receive consecration from the archbishop of Ravenna and his successors, CLXXX, 1370.

To the abbot and monks of Corvey, that the deposed Henry find no place among them, CLXXX, 1380.

Judges the disputes between Ralph, bishop of Orta, and the canons of the Greater Church, CLXXX, 1381.

To Henry, bishop of Moravia, that he absolve Vladislaus, duke of Poland, from excommunication, CLXXX, 1383.

To the abbots of Cuxá, Bisuldun, and others, that they obey the abbot of Saint Victor of Marseilles, upon whom he confers the office of blessing, CLXXX, 1390.

Letter to Bermund, bishop of Béziers: he commands him to permit Trencavel, viscount of Béziers, to build a chapel in his palace, CLXXX, 1397.

To King Conrad. He confirms for his chaplain Thiebald the provostship of Xanten, provided that he relinquish another provostship which he had previously possessed, CLXXX, 1397 and 1402.

To Abbot Suger, that he decide by judicial procedure the case of two excommunicated clerics, CLXXX, 1402.

Suspends the archbishop of Braga from episcopal office unless he render obedience to the archbishop of Toledo, CLXXX, 1405.

[Col. 1231] That Abbot Suger should investigate the case of a priest’s excommunication by the archdeacon and excommunicate those who assaulted the priest, CLXXX, 1406.

To the prelates of Poland: he rebukes them because they do not observe the sentence of interdict pronounced by his envoy; and, that they may repent, he confirms that same sentence, CLXXX, 1408.

Concerning King Louis’s plan for an overseas expedition, CLXXX, 1414.

To Abbot Wilbald, that he excommunicate Godebold, canon of Minden, unless he restore the church of Hemeringen, taken from Everard, CLXXX, 1420.

Letter to King Conrad: he receives favorably his embassy, by which the affairs of Church and kingdom are strengthened, CLXXX, 1422.

To the duke of Burgundy and Henry, bishop of Autun: he rebukes them because they are hostile to the monastery of Vézelay, CLXXX, 1424.

Letter to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, that he restore monks to the Church of Heidenheim after expelling the secular clerics from it, CLXXX, 1439.

To the archbishop of Sens, that he judge the dispute between the bishop of Orléans and the abbot of Vézelay, CLXXX, 1449.

For reconciliation between the king and the bishop of Beauvais, CLXXX, 1436.

Judges the dispute of the clerics of Saint John and Saint Sabina among the Marsicans concerning the consecration of oil, CLXXX, 1474.

Letter to Raymond, archbishop of Toledo: he congratulates him because the archbishop of Braga had submitted himself to his primacy, and rebukes him because he had invaded the latter’s territories and treated him too harshly, CLXXX, 1475.

To Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, that he keep Count Otto excommunicated until he make satisfaction concerning the tithes taken from the monastery of Tegernsee, CLXXX, 1484.

Letter to King Conrad, stating that he had honorably received Conrad’s envoys and had complied in all things with his wishes, CLXXX, 1489.

To Henry, bishop of Liège, that he compel the counts of Looz and Montaigu to restore what they had taken from the monastery of Stavelot, CLXXX, 1490.

That property taken from various monasteries by various devastators be restored under penalty of excommunication, CLXXX, 1491–1493.

Letter to prelates, counts, and barons established throughout Germany, that they support Emperor Conrad on the Italian expedition, CLXXX, 1501.

To the bishop of Langres, that he excommunicate the count of Nevers unless he repent, CLXXX, 1503.

To the archbishop of Lyons, that under threat of excommunication he ensure the restoration to the brethren of Miratoire of property taken by the people of Gignac, CLXXX, 1508.

Letter to Emperor Frederick: he congratulates him on his election, hoping that he will complete what Conrad had begun for the exaltation of the Church, CLXXX, 1522.

Letter to Stephen, archbishop of Metz, that he compel Count Henry of Salm to restore the cell of Asmingia, which he had taken from the abbot of Saint Michael on the Meuse, CLXXX, 1523.

Letter to Count Henry of Salm, that he restore to the abbot of Saint Michael the cell of Asmingia which he had taken, or else be punished by canonical retribution, CLXXX, 1524.

To the bishops of Metz, Verdun, etc., that they restrain Count Rainald of Bar from harassing the church of Saint Michael and compel him, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure, to restore what was taken, CLXXX, 1524.

Bull by which the controversy formerly pursued by the abbess of the Brescian monastery of Saint Julia against the bishop of Cremona concerning the church of Cicognaria is finally settled before the bishop of Reggio, CLXXX, 1533.

To Henry, bishop of Autun, that, when summoned, he appear before the bishop of Langres to answer for the damages inflicted upon the monastery of Vézelay, CLXXX, 1537.

To the convent of Saint Augustine at Canterbury, that they obey Abbot Silvester even if the archbishop refuses to consecrate him, CLXXX, 1549.

To the bishops of Magdeburg, that they not favor the bishop of Zeitz, an invader of the church of Magdeburg, CLXXX, 1543.

Letter to the bishops of Germany: he disapproves the translation of the bishop of Zeitz, transferred to the archbishopric of Magdeburg, CLXXX, 1544.

To Abbot Wibald: he commends to him the case of the bishop of Chur, and charges him to defend ecclesiastical immunities against laymen, CLXXX, 1545.

To Odo, duke of Burgundy, and the Burgundian nobles, that the townsmen of Vézelay be regarded as excommunicated, CLXXX, 1550, 1551.

That the archbishop of Narbonne restrain the bishop of Maguelone and Peter of Verona, hostile to the Cluniacs residing near Montpellier, [Col. 1232] CLXXX, 1533.

To the clergy and people of Toledo, that the Mozarabs obey the archbishop of Toledo and do not differ from him in ceremonies, CLXXX, 1559.

To all the clergy, concerning robbers and violators of churches, and when ecclesiastical burial is to be denied after penance has been performed, unless they give security for restitution of the damage, CLXXX, 1564.

Concerning witnesses to be employed in a case of separation on account of closeness of kinship, CLXXX, 1565.

Rebukes Hugh, archbishop of Vienne, because he inflicts injuries upon Cistercian and Cluniac brethren, CLXXX, 1567.

To John, bishop of Paternò, concerning usury, CLXXX, 1567.

To the bishop of Langres, that he judge those who communicated with the excommunicated people of Vézelay, CLXXX, 1568.

To Peter, archbishop of Bourges: he commands him to restore to the monastery of Saint Denis the church of Casa Major and the property of a deceased priest which had been improperly taken, CLXXX, 1571.

Exhorts the canons of Arras to defend ecclesiastical offices, CLXXX, 1578.

Letter to the clergy and people of Arras: he declares that he approves in advance the sentence which their bishop will pronounce against the heretics of his diocese, and commands them also to obey it, CLXXX, 1579.

To the nuns of Digny: he signifies that he has entrusted their reform to the bishop of Arras, CLXXX, 1580.

Exhorts Count Theodoric of Flanders to restore to Godescalc, bishop of Arras, the people of the village of Marœuil, CLXXX, 1581.

To Sibylla, countess of Flanders, that she dissuade her husband the count from wrongs against Godescalc, bishop of Arras, CLXXX, 1582.

To Samson, archbishop of Rheims, that he withdraw Theodoric, count of Flanders, from inflicting damage upon the bishopric of Arras and, if he does not desist, punish both him and his land, CLXXX, 1583.

To Bernard, archbishop of Tarragona, he again commands that he obey the archbishop of Toledo, CLXXX, 1584.

Bull by which the monastery of Sarlat, founded by the princes Pippin and Charles, is received under Saint Peter’s protection, CLXXX, 1591.

That the decree of Urban II at the Council of Clermont be observed, CLXXX, 1594.

FELIX I, pope.—Letter concerning judgments, accusations, and defenses of the sacred orders, V, 145.

Concerning the authority of the apostolic see and accused bishops, V, 148.

Letter to Bishop Benignus: those err who maintain that the Son does not see the Father because no one has ever seen God; those likewise err who affirm that the Son is less than the Father because the latter is invisible whereas the Son is visible, V, 152.

Letter to Bishop Maximus and the clergy of Alexandria, concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity, V, 155.

FELIX II, Saint, pope.—Rescript to the bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod: that no one accuse a bishop before secular arbitrators; if anyone has a case against a bishop; concerning bishops despoiled of their property or expelled from their sees; that infamous and sacrilegious persons are not to be admitted as witnesses; if a bishop summoned to a council cannot go; concerning cases not contained in the laws or known to be prohibited; concerning accusations against bishops and restoration of their property taken away; who may not accuse or testify; concerning the persons of accusers; concerning primates and metropolitans; concerning accusations against bishops and the unfitness of accusers; who should not be admitted to bring an accusation; that in ecclesiastical matters, after the cause has been stated and concluded, it is permissible to withdraw, which is not permitted in secular matters; concerning accusations against bishops; that cases of bishops are not to be determined without the authority of the Roman pontiff; if a bishop judges himself burdened by fellow-provincials or by his metropolitan; concerning judgments of bishops and the time granted for preparation and appearance; concerning the qualifications required of judges and accusers, XIII, 17–25.

Letter to bishops and the remaining priests of the Lord, concerning the patience to be borne in persecutions and tribulations, XIII, 25.

FELIX III, Saint, pope.—Letter to Acacius of Constantinople: the holy Roman synod desires that he induce Emperor Zeno zealously to correct what he had hitherto done wrongly against the Catholic faith, LVIII, 894.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he pleads for the church of Alexandria; he recalls whatever he had previously said or done for the defense of that Church, in order to rebuke the later expulsion of John, bishop of Alexandria, and the restoration of Peter Mongus, LVIII, 899.

Letter to Peter the Fuller. He shows that Peter had fallen not only into the heresies of Valentinus, Mani, Arius, Sabellius, Apollinaris, and Eutyches, but also into the errors of paganism, which asserts many gods, LVIII, 903.

Peter the Fuller is deposed and anathematized, LVIII, 812.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he announces that Peter the Fuller has been condemned by a sentence of synodical judgment and must therefore be avoided in communion; he exhorts the emperor to expel the deposed Peter from the church of Antioch, LVIII, 918.

Deprives Acacius of priestly office and communion with the faithful, LVIII, 921.

Letter to all bishops: that one rebaptized be received through penance; that a bishop, priest, or deacon, if rebaptized, receive lay communion at death; that a cleric, monk, virgin consecrated to God, or layperson, if rebaptized, be subject to the judgment of the Nicene Council; that persons of either sex of mature age be received through the laying on of hands; that one rebaptized not be received into the clergy; that the bishop of another jurisdiction neither absolve nor receive a penitent, LVIII, 924–927.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he complains that Zeno had violated his legates and advises him to assent to the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius, LVIII, 934.

Letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople, that they not be disturbed by the betrayal of the legates and that they avoid communion with Acacius, condemned by the apostolic see, LVIII, 936.

Letter to the monks of Constantinople and Bithynia: that Tribur, defender of the Church, had been condemned for betrayal, and how they ought to punish their own members who adhere to Acacius, LVIII, 937.

He refutes the arguments offered for Acacius and shows that, as he was justly and rightly condemned, so he can be restored only canonically, LVIII, 944.

Letter to Emperor Zeno. After praising his zeal in the ordination of a new bishop, he exhorts him to agree with the Roman Church in condemning the names of Acacius and Peter—a matter on which the clerical legates had replied that they had received no instructions—LVIII, 969.

Letter to Flavitas, bishop of Constantinople: because his legates had been suspended from communion for replying that they had received no instructions concerning the names of Acacius and Peter, he exhorts Flavitas himself to abstain from their recitation and persuade Zeno to do the same, LVIII, 971.

Letter to Talasius, archimandrite of Constantinople: that neither he nor his monks communicate with the church of Constantinople or its bishop before this has been commanded by the apostolic see, LVIII, 974.

Letter to Bishop Vetranio: recounting the causes of the schism of the Church of Constantinople, he exhorts him to move Zeno to restore union with the Roman Church, LVIII, 955.

That in ecclesiastical matters the royal will must be subordinated to priests, LVIII, 977.

FELIX IV, pope.—Letter to all bishops: that the celebration of Masses should not take place elsewhere than in places dedicated to God unless great necessity compels it; and what ought to be done in cases of doubt concerning a church’s consecration, LXV, 15.

Letter to Sabina: he praises her zeal and devotion toward the Church, and that she puts religion before the honors of lineage and vain pomp, LXV, 22.

FORMOSUS, pope.—Bull confirming the possessions of the Church of Girona, CXXIX, 841.

Letter to Adalgar, archbishop of Hamburg: he decrees that the Church of Hamburg shall have Bremen as an auxiliary until it is able to establish suffragans, CXXIX, 842.

Letter to the bishops of England, that they adhere firmly to the Catholic faith and diligently remove the people from paganism, CXXIX, 847.

GELASIUS I, pope.—Letter to Euphemianus: he writes that no one can be admitted to communion with the apostolic see who has not condemned the name of Acacius. He therefore exhorts him, just as he anathematizes Eutyches and the other heretics, also to anathematize Acacius, LIX, 13.

Letter to Laurentius, bishop of Lignido: upon his elevation to the pontificate, he prescribes, according to the custom of the Roman Church, the formula of faith which all are bound to profess, LIX, 19.

Letter to the bishops of Dardania: he informs them that he has been elected pontiff; he sends them a statement of the Catholic faith and exhorts them not to communicate with Eutychians and to be vigilant in the pastoral office, [Col. 1234] LIX, 23.

Letter to Faustus, legate at Constantinople: that Acacius, lawfully condemned by the apostolic see, having died in excommunication, cannot be absolved and must not be communicated with, LIX, 26.

Letter to Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia: he admonishes him not to allow the Pelagian heresy, condemned by so many pontiffs, to revive, LIX, 30.

Letter to the same person: he writes that he ought not to have wondered that Gelasius had warned him to be vigilant lest the Pelagian heresy sprout again, LIX, 32.

Letter to all bishops throughout Picenum: he refutes the three principal tenets of the Pelagian heresy—first, that infants are born without original sin; second, that they are not condemned for original sin alone; third, that grace is not necessary for salvation and is bestowed according to human merits, LIX, 34.

Letter to Emperor Anastasius: after explaining why he had not written to the emperor, he exhorts him to obey the apostolic see and, once Acacius’s name has been condemned, to ensure restoration of the Churches’ peace, LIX, 41.

Letter to the bishops of Lucania, setting forth certain ecclesiastical institutions, LIX, 47.

Letter to the bishops of Sicily: that the Church’s resources must be distributed among bishops, clerics, and the poor; that dioceses and Church property possessed by bishops for thirty years are not to be taken away from them, LIX, 57.

Letter to the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum: he declares that the bishop of Thessalonica, who had refused to condemn the names of heretics, had been deprived of communion with the apostolic see, and that Acacius, who died in excommunication, cannot be absolved, LIX, 57.

Letter to Aeonius, bishop of Arles: he teaches that mutual charity is to be maintained in the Catholic faith, LIX, 60.

Letter to the bishops of Dardania: he shows that Acacius was lawfully condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see alone, LIX, 61.

He instructs what ought to be answered against the Greeks, LIX, 85.

Letter to the Eastern bishops: that no new synod was needed in the condemnation of Acacius and others; and that Acacius could not absolve Peter of Alexandria without the authority of the apostolic see. Then concerning Catholic bishops expelled from their sees without an examination of their cases, LIX, 90.

Concerning the bond of anathema; that of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon only those approved by the apostolic see are valid; accordingly, concerning the decrees against Acacius, and that Peter of Alexandria could be absolved only by the apostolic see, LIX, 102.

Against Senator Andromachus and the other Romans who had resolved that the Lupercalia should be celebrated according to the ancient custom: he condemns the superstitious celebration of the Lupercalia and proves that Rome’s calamities had arisen not from its discontinuance but from crimes, LIX, 110.

What has been peacefully possessed for thirty years cannot be reclaimed, LIX, 137.

He recounts what assistance he received from Rusticus, bishop of Lyons, and how great were the persecutions he endured from Acacius, LIX, 138.

The body of the Lord is not to be received without the chalice, LIX, 141.

Concerning those who killed their own two bishops, that they should thereafter lack a bishop, LIX, 141.

That bishops may not dare to travel to the imperial court without the authority of the Roman pontiff, LIX, 143.

Concerning slaves ordained without their masters’ consent, LIX, 144.

That a bishop may by no device alienate Church property, and that privileges ought by every means to be preserved intact, LIX, 145.

That property under litigation may not be transferred to any person before the outcome of the hearing, LIX, 146.

That no one communicate with excommunicated persons contrary to ecclesiastical satisfaction, LIX, 147.

A bishop is to be consecrated by his own metropolitan, and he himself by the same one, LIX, 148.

The Church should protect those whom it has received in its own defense, LIX, 149.

Nothing of Church property is to be alienated, LIX, 149.

Absolution is not to be sought when a sentence is rendered unjustly, LIX, 150.

Bishops ought to aid those who seek their protection, LIX, 150.

A cleric is not to be heard before a secular judge, LIX, 151.

A cleric is to be summoned only before the judgment of bishops, LIX, 151.

In the election of a bishop, the parish priest must be present, LIX, 152.

That fugitive slaves ought to seek intercession, not hiding places, at a church against their masters, LIX, 152.

[Col. 1235] The laws of princes or rules of the Fathers must not be disregarded, LIX, 153.

The laws of Roman emperors are to be observed by all, LIX, 153.

He who is frequently thrown to the ground is to be suspended from the governance of the Church, LIX, 153.

What priests have given, succeeding pontiffs must by no means presume to take away, LIX, 154. One does not lie who has no intention of deceiving, LIX, 154.

Roman council under Gelasius, in which seventy bishops distinguished sacred and authentic books from apocryphal ones, in the year of the Lord 494, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, LX, 157.

Decree concerning books to be received and not received, issued at the Roman council by Pope Gelasius with the bishops in the year 496, LX, 164.

Second Roman council, in which Misenus was absolved by Gelasius and fifty bishops, in the year of the Lord 495, LIX, 183.

GELASIUS II, pope.—Letter to the clergy and people of Rome: he commends their constancy against the intrusive antipope, CLXIII, 487.

Letter to Jordan, archbishop of Milan: concerning the restoration of Landulf, CLXIII, 488.

Letter to the Gauls: he commands them to arm themselves against Maurice, bishop of Braga, the antipope intruded into the see by Emperor Henry, CLXIII, 489.

He places Oldegarius, bishop of Barcelona, over the Church of Tarragona, CLXIII, 489.

Letter to Bernard, bishop of Toledo and primate of Spain, concerning Maurice, intruded into the apostolic see, CLXIII, 491.

Letter to the abbots and monks of the greater land: he commands them to cease disregarding the arrangements made by Pope Paschal between themselves and the bishop of Civita, CLXIII, 494.

Confirms the election of the archbishop of Ravenna, the customs of the canons of Lucca and Saint Fridianus, and the possessions of the monastery of Saint Mamianus, CLXIII, 497–500.

To the Christian army besieging the city of Saragossa: he grants indulgence to all who contribute anything to it, CLXIII, 508.

Bull for the monastery of Caunes in the diocese of Narbonne, CLXIII, 511.

GREGORY THE GREAT I, Saint, pope.—Letter to all bishops of Sicily: he declares that he has entrusted his vicariate within Sicily to the subdeacon Peter; he decrees that the bishops of that province meet once each year; he admonishes them what is to be guarded against and what is to be done in council, LXXVII, 441.

Letter to Justin, praetor of Sicily: he exhorts him, with friendliness and seriousness, to devote himself to peace with the priests and justice toward all, LXXVIII, 443.

Letter to John, bishop of Constantinople: he complains that John had sought confirmation of his election from the emperor; he commends himself to John’s prayers, LXXVII, 447.

He unites the desolate church of Minturnae to that of Formiae, LXXVII, 454.

Concerning the transfer of a synagogue of the Jews, if it obstructs the Church’s services, LXXVII, 457.

To John, bishop of Old City: he admonishes him not to continue harassing the monastery, LXXVII, 458.

Letter to Demetrius, bishop of Naples, that he receive certain persons formerly doubtful in faith but now seeking Catholic communion, LXXVII, 459.

To Balbinus, bishop of Roselle: he commands him to visit the church of Populonia and ordain priests and deacons, LXXIII, 460.

Letter to Severus, bishop of Aquileia: he commands him to come to Rome with his followers to be judged in synod, LXXII, 461.

Letter to all bishops of Italy, that the sons of the Lombards baptized in the Arian heresy be reconciled to the Catholic faith, LXXVII, 462.

Letter to Peter, subdeacon, that he provide Marcellus, a servant of the Church, with necessities for food and clothing, and ensure that pastors be appointed in the place and stead of those who have fallen, LXXVII, 163.

Letter to Natalis, bishop of Salona, that he restore Honoratus the archdeacon to his rank; then, if the controversy remains, let them plead the case at Rome, LXXVII, 464.

Letter to Honoratus, deacon of Salona, concerning his dispute with his bishop and the safeguarding of church property, LXXVII, 465.

Letter to Anthemius, subdeacon, instructing him to distribute a specified sum of solidi to certain handmaids of God, to the priest Paulinus, and to two monks, LXXVII, 467.

Letter to John of Constantinople and the other patriarchs: he treats at length of the burden, gifts, and offices of a pastor, [Col. 1236] and finally professes the faith according to the rule of the councils, LXXVII, 468.

Letter to Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch: he complains of the pastoral burden, LXXVII, 479.

Letter to Anastasius, archbishop of Corinth: grievingly announces his own ordination and commends Boniface, defender, LXXVII, 480.

Letter to Sebastian, bishop of Rhizinium, instructing him to ascertain the disposition of the patriarch Anastasius, who had been driven from his see and whom he wished to live with him in his own rank, LXXVII, 481.

Letter to Andrew, *vir illustris*: he laments his elevation to the episcopate and sends a key from the body of Saint Peter, LXXVII, 483.

Letter to John, former consul, patrician, and quaestor: sends a key of Saint Peter and from his chains, LXXVII, 483.

Letter to Romanus, patrician and exarch of Italy, asking that he permit Bishop Alaudus either to be judged in a synod or to return to his own church, LXXVII, 484.

Letter to Venantius, a former monk and patrician of Syracuse: rebukes him for having laid aside the monastic habit; urges him to repent as soon as possible; teaches whose counsels he ought to heed, LXXVII, 486.

Letter to Peter, bishop of Terracina, instructing him to restore a place previously granted to the Jews; those estranged from the Christian religion are to be drawn kindly toward it, LXXVII, 489.

Letter to Malchus, bishop of Dalmatia, instructing him to compel Bishop Stephen to stand trial and to carry out whatever shall have been adjudged, LXXVII, 492.

Letter to Felix, bishop of Messana, directing that Paulinus, a travelling bishop, govern the monastery of Saint Theodore, LXXVII, 493.

Letter to Peter, subdeacon, instructing him to gather monks scattered through Sicily in the Messanan monastery of Saint Theodore, LXXIII, 494.

Letter to Anthemius, subdeacon, instructing him to restrain wandering monks, those pursuing private property, and married monks, etc., LXXVII, 495.

Letter to Leander, bishop of Seville: he laments the episcopal burden; rejoices at the conversion of King Reccared; approves the practice of a single immersion in baptism introduced by the Spaniards on account of the Arians, LXXVII, 496.

Letter to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily, ordering the correction of many acts done contrary to law; determines matters concerning the celibacy of subdeacons, LXXVII, 498.

Letter to all bishops throughout Illyricum, instructing them to receive bishops expelled by enemies and to provide them with necessities, LXXVII, 598.

Letter to Virgilius of Arles and Theodore, bishop of Marseilles: Jews are not to be compelled to baptism but gently encouraged to embrace the faith, LXXVII, 509.

Letter to Honoratus, deacon, concerning what ought to be represented to the emperors on behalf of the inhabitants of Sardinia, LXXVII, 512.

Letter to Anthemius, subdeacon: women are not to live with monks; boys are not to be admitted into monasteries on certain islands before their eighteenth year, LXXVII, 513.

Letter to the monks of the island of Mount Christ: he orders those irregular monks to obey Abbot Horosius, LXXVII, 313.

Letter to Symmachus, defender, concerning the construction of a monastery in Corsica; the correction of monks in Gorgona; and priests’ association with women, LXXVII, 514.

Letter to Felix, bishop of Siponto, instructing him to visit the church of Canosa and ordain there two parochial priests, LXXVII, 515.

Letter to John, bishop of Sorrento, instructing him solemnly to place relics of Saint Agatha in the monastery of Saint Stephen, LXXVII, 515.

Letter to Anthemius, subdeacon, instructing him not to allow either the oppression of the poor or the coercion into slavery of the son of a free woman, LXXVII, 516.

Letter to Severus, bishop, concerning the election of a bishop of Rimini, LXXVII, 517.

Letter to Arcicus, duke, clergy, etc., directing them not to elect Ocleatinus as bishop, LXXVII, 518.

Letter to Gennadius, patrician, instructing him to order the exarch of Africa and Theodore, master of soldiers, to refrain from harassing the poor and the Church, LXXVI, 519.

Letter to Anthemius, subdeacon, directing that the house of Petronius, unjustly entered in title, be restored to his widow Theodora, LXXVII, 522.

Letter to Felix, bishop of Messana, concerning which customs ought to be preserved and which abolished, LXXVII, 522.

To Peter, subdeacon, instructing him to provide an annual allowance for Pastor, whose eyes were infirm, LXXVII, 523.

To Peter, subdeacon: all lawsuits and business of the monastery are to be entrusted to an experienced layman; he is to protect Cyriacus and his wife Joanna, a convert from Judaism to Christianity; the Sicilian bishops are not to come to Rome before winter; and concerning the restoration of the possessions and monies of the Church of Taormina, LXXVII, 525–527.

To Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa: he urges him to curb the attempts of heretics against the Church, etc., LXXVII, 528–529.

He exhorts all the bishops of Numidia to peace, to the defence of the Church, and to concern for their neighbours’ souls; and grants them, out of reverence for ancient law, what he had previously censured—namely, that the senior bishop be elected primate, LXXVII, 531.

That Bishop Martin should transfer in Corsica from the Church of Tainata to that of Saona, LXXVII, 533.
