He exhorts the Church of Mevania finally to agree upon the election of a bishop, LXXVII, 534.

That Lawrence, bishop of Milan, should appoint someone with whom the dispute arising over a demanded sum of money may be settled, LXXVII, 535.

Letter to Hilary, a monk of Africa, instructing that, once a council has been convened as soon as possible, inquiry be made into Argentium, bishop of Lamige, LXXVII, 537.

He warns Peter, notary, that the monks of Tropaea, if they live religiously, are to be assisted in every possible way, LXXVII, 539.

On the occasion of a deadly pestilence, he directs Praejectus, bishop of Narnia, to exhort the citizens to repentance and faith, LXXVII, 539.

He instructs Velox, master of soldiers, to pursue Ariulf, duke of the Lombards, from the rear if he makes incursions into Roman or Ravennate territory, LXXVII, 540.

That the Neapolitans, without delay or discord, should elect a bishop in the place of Demetrius, deposed for abominable crimes, LXXVII, 542.

That Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, should exercise his authority in Sicily, while greater cases are nevertheless reserved, LXXVII, 543.

To Paul, bishop of Naples: in the meantime he is to discharge episcopal duties in such a manner that the testimony and wishes of the Neapolitans may be confirmed, LXXVII, 546.

To the people of Nepi, that they should obey Leontius, who had been sent to them, LXXVII, 547.

Concerning the consecration of an oratory of the Holy Cross, LXXVII, 548.

The see of the bishop of Velletri is transferred to a safer place, LXXVII, 549.

He appoints Paulinus, bishop of Turin, over the Church of Lipari, LXXVII, 551.

That this Paulinus should reside in the Church of Lipari but visit that of Turin at a suitable time, LXXVII, 552.

To Natalis, bishop of Salona: after rebuking Natalis for his continual banquets, he orders him to restore Honoratus, the archdeacon, to his position, LXXVII, 552.

Letter to all the bishops of Dalmatia, explaining what has been done in the case of Natalis and Honoratus, LXXVII, 554, 555.

To Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum: he rejoices that the province devastated by barbarians is being restored under his administration. He commends the administrator of the patrimony and urges him not to assist Bishop Natalis against justice, LXXVII, 557.

To all the bishops of Illyricum, confirming the ordination of Bishop John, LXXVII, 557.

That Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, should carefully examine the priest commended by Felix and, if he finds him worthy of the episcopate, send him to Rome, LXXVII, 560.

Letter to Benenatus, bishop: he entrusts him with visitation of the Church of Cumae, so that he may both protect that church and secure the election from its own clergy of a suitable priest, LXXVII, 561.

He charges John, bishop, with visitation of the Church of Nepi, LXXVII, 562.

To Stephen, chartulary: he is to have two monks, deserters from their profession, confined; he is not to allow new customs to be imposed upon the monastery, LXXVII, 563.

To Justin, praetor: after every suspicion has been laid aside, he is to show complete charity and fitting reverence to Bishop Leo, who has been fully cleared of false accusations, LXXVII, 571.

To John, bishop of Squillace: he directs him to return to the Church of Lissita if it should come about that it is freed from enemies; he is to abstain from unlawful ordinations, etc., LXXVII, 575.

That the clergy and people of Crotone should obey John, their visiting bishop, and request a suitable priest for themselves, LXXVII, 577.

Letter to Felix, bishop: he charges him with visitation of three vacant churches, LXXVII, 581.

He unites the Churches of Cumae and Misenum and appoints Bishop Benenatus as bishop of both, LXXVII, 582.

Letter to John, bishop: concerning the Istrian bishops, schismatics to be compelled to unity, he declares that he will write to the emperor; one who has been ordained is not to be ordained again, LXXVII, 583.

Letter to Columbus, bishop: Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Pudentiana, is, after a council has been assembled, to be deposed if, corrupted by money, he allowed a Donatist bishop to be made in his city; he laments the spread of the Donatist heresy and kindles pastoral zeal lest Catholics be allowed to fall away to it, LXXVII, 588.

Letter to Januarius, archbishop: having heard complaints concerning Bishop Januarius, he sends the notary John to compel the parties to judgment and execute what has been adjudged, LXXVII, 590.

Schismatics boast vainly of persecution; although the Three Chapters were condemned, nothing was changed in the faith, LXXVII, 592.

To Bishop Natalis: the profane banquets in which he indulged and his neglect of sacred reading are not lightly excused in him, etc., LXXVII, 595.

Letter to Peter, subdeacon: he sends Epiphanius, subdeacon, to investigate the sedition stirred up against Bishop Paul; enslaved persons are to be restored to the churches of the city, LXXVII, 603.

To John, abbot: he reproves him because both he and the brethren neglect sacred reading and prayer; he urges him to more careful concern for the souls of the brethren, for guests, and for the poor, LXXVII, 605.

Letter to John, bishop: he deprives him of holy communion because of his unjust condemnation of Bishop Adrian, whom he orders restored to his former position and rank, LXXVII, 607.

To Natalis, archbishop: Bishop Florentius, deposed without a judgment of a council, is to be recalled from exile, and his case reconsidered after bishops have been convened, LXXVII, 612.

Letter to Antoninus, subdeacon, instructing him, if Florentius is acquitted by the assembled bishops, to ensure that all his property is restored, LXXVII, 612.

To Sabinus, defender: Gregory receives and venerates the four councils just as he does the four books of the Gospel; he declares that the faith of Chalcedon was not violated in the Fifth Synod, LXXVII, 613.

Letter to Maximianus, bishop: he is to send to Rome the accusers of the bishop of Agrigentum and documents pertaining to his case, LXXVII, 614.

He exhorts the people of Terracina to obey their bishop Agnellus in all things, LXXVII, 615.

To Peter, subdeacon, instructing him to send relics of Saint Severinus for the preservation of the Church, LXXVII, 618.

He unites the Church of Saint Anthemius to that of Nomentum, LXXVII, 619.

Letter to Peter, subdeacon: Abbot Secundinus is to be deposed for crimes, and Theodosius, requested by the community, is to be ordained, LXXVII, 622.

To Bishop Leontius: while Bishop Castorius is ill and absent, he is to govern the Church of Rimini, LXXVII, 622.

Letter to Magnus, priest: he absolves one whom Bishop Lawrence had formerly excommunicated without merit, etc., LXXVII, 623.

Letter to the priests and clergy of Milan: he does not press for the election of Constantius, though he knows him very well as a friend; he portrays excellently what a pastor ought to be and the character of those who elect him, LXXVII, 626.

To Honoratus, archdeacon: he confirms his absolution, LXXVII, 628.

Letter to Sabinus, defender, instructing him to bring to Rome Bishop Januarius and the priest Epiphanius, accused of crimes, LXXVII, 632.

To Peter, subdeacon: if he judges Deacon Numerius worthy of the episcopate, he is to send him to Rome for consecration, LXXVII, 636.

Letter to Pantaleon, notary: the seducer of a virgin is either to marry her, or, after corporal punishment, be shut up in a monastery, LXXVII, 637.

Letter to Andrew, bishop: he urges him to lay aside the priesthood if he is conscious of sin with a concubine; because he ordered a woman to be beaten with rods, he commands him to refrain from celebrating Mass for two months, LXXVII, 640, 641.

To the clergy of the Church of Salona: he approves the election of Honoratus as bishop, LXXLII, 612.

Letter to Eutyches, bishop, exhorting him to persevere in converting worshippers of idols, LXXVII, 659.

To Chrysanthus, bishop, instructing him to seek a bishop for the Church of Mevania, ordain priests, and there confirm infants, LXXVII, 661.

Letter to all the bishops of Dalmatia: they are not to ordain any bishop at Salona without his consent and permission. Yet if all agree upon someone other than Maximus, he is to be consecrated, LXXXVII, 677.

To Maximinus, bishop: the crime by which a certain man’s wife was abducted and sold to another is to be punished, LXXVII, 681.

[Col. 1239] He removes Maximus, violently intruded, and the bishops who ordained him from every priestly office, until the truth of the imperial command has been established, LXXVII, 690.

Letter to Hospiton, leader of the Barbaricini: he is to support Felix and Cyriacus as they labour to convert the Barbaricini from idolatry, LXXVII, 692.

Letter to the Augusta Constantia: to dissuade her, who requested the head of Saint Paul, he recounts various miracles; finally he promises fragments to be filed from the chains of Saint Paul, LXXVII, 700.

To Narses, patrician: he declares that he will settle the case of the priests with Patriarch John wholly according to the rule of the canons, LXXVII, 707.

Letter to Victor and Columbus, bishops: after a council has been convened, they are to resist the Donatists promptly and resolutely, LXXVII, 709.

To Queen Theodelinda: he laments that she has been led astray by the ignorant; he professes that the faith of the four holy synods, especially that of Chalcedon, is preserved intact in the Roman Church, LXXVII, 712.

Letter to the clergy, order, and people of Orte: he appoints Barbarus as visitor. Above all, he warns them not to elect a lay person as bishop, LXXVII, 716.

To Valentine, abbot: monks are not to bring women into the monastery, etc., LXXVII, 717.

Letter to Boniface, *vir magnificus*: he is to come to Rome, to answer concerning his faith no longer by letter but in person, LXXVII, 717.

To John, bishop of Ravenna: clerics serving churches are not to be placed over monasteries, LXXVII, 721.

Servants of God are to be introduced into the monastery founded by Theodosia, LXXVII, 723.

Letter to Venantius, bishop: priests, deacons, and subdeacons who have stained themselves with the crime of sexual immorality are to remain permanently deposed from their rank; after completing penance, they are to receive communion among the laity, LXXVII, 723.

He congratulates Bishop Dominicus because he has endeavoured with pastoral zeal to restrain the Donatists, LXXVII, 726.

Letter to Cyprian, deacon: he is to pursue the Manichaeans; but the burdens of dues are to be reduced for Jews who have converted to Christ, LXXVII, 729.

Letter to John, bishop of Constantinople: concerning what both he himself and his predecessor Pelagius did in response to John’s usurpation of the title “universal bishop”; he asks him to refrain from it and presses the point with many arguments, LXXVII, 378.

Letter to the Emperor Maurice: he praises the emperor’s zeal for the peace of the Church; portrays the hypocrisy of John, bishop of Constantinople; declares that by the ambitious title which he usurps the whole Church, the venerable synods, etc., are disturbed; and therefore that his pride should be restrained by imperial authority, LXXVII, 744, 748.

To Castorius, notary: he is to urge the people of Ravenna to elect a bishop as soon as possible, LXXVII, 751.

To Romanus, exarch: he is not to protect the priest Speciosus in his resistance to his bishop, nor support nuns who have returned to secular life, LXXVII, 752.

To Severus, bishop: he entrusts him with visitation of the Church of Ravenna, LXXVII, 753.

Letter to Castorius, deacon: he is to investigate the life of the bishop of Pisa and of other priests; if he finds anything untoward, he is to report it, LXXVII, 754.

To Vincomalus, defender: he appoints him defender of the Church, LXXVII, 755.

Letter to Severus, scholar: he is to persuade the exarch to make peace with Agilulf, king of the Lombards, LXXVII, 760.

Letter to the Augusta Constantia: she is to represent to the emperor that Corsicans and Sicilians are unjustly and excessively burdened, etc., LXXVII, 768.

To Leontinus, bishop, concerning the provision of visitation for the Church of Rimini, LXXVII, 774.

He praises certain persons’ zeal for the unity of the Church and urges that they not be deterred from seeking the return of schismatics, LXXVII, 776.

Letter to Vigilius, bishop: he grants him his authority in the kingdom of Childebert; warns him to prevent the stain of simony and to prevent laymen from suddenly becoming bishops, LXXVII, 782.

Letter to Maximus of Salona: accused himself of simony and many other matters, he is summoned to Rome, LXXVII, 695.

To Boniface, bishop of Reggio: he unites the Church of Cassino to his own, LXXVII, 802.

To John, bishop: he absolves John, a priest unjustly condemned, and declares him wholly free from every stain of heresy, LXXVII, 807.

To Candidus, bishop: he is to take monks suitable for the priestly office, with the abbot’s consent, and ordain them priests, LXXVII, 820.

[Col. 1240] To Fortunatus, bishop: if a Jewish or pagan slave desires conversion to the Christian faith, he is to be granted freedom, CXXVII, 823.

Letter to Urbicus, abbot: he is to receive Agatho into the monastery if his wife likewise wishes to convert, LXXVII, 833.

There remain five hundred pages of Letters to various persons, from col. 834 to 1327, which almost all concern the more remote or immediate governance of the Church. Since we have already discussed this Father at sufficient length, we leave them to be turned over in their volume by the diligent reader.

GREGORY II, pope, saint. — Letter to Boniface, priest: grants him authority to proclaim the mystery of the faith to unbelieving peoples, LXXXIX, 495, 501.

Letter to the nobles of Thuringia: praises their constancy in the faith of Christ and exhorts them to obey Boniface, their bishop, LXXVII, 503.

Letter to the whole people of Old Saxony: confirms them in the faith of Christ which they had embraced after abandoning the worship of idols, LXXXIX, 504.

Letter to Emperor Leo the Isaurian, concerning sacred images, LXXXIX, 511 and 521.

He answers Bishop Boniface’s various questions and consultations, LXXXIX, 524.

Letter to Serenus, bishop of Friuli, concerning the prohibition against invading the Church of Grado, LXXXIX, 526.

To Donatus, patriarch of Grado, and his subjects: he announces that the bishop of Friuli has been forbidden to invade other provinces, LXXXIX, 527.

Letter to the bishops of England: recognizes and orders recognition of Tatwine, archbishop of Canterbury, as primate of all England, LXXXIX, 527.

Capitulary given to Bishop Martinianus and others going, with the Lord’s help, into Bavaria, LXXXIX, 331.

GREGORY III, pope. — Letter to Boniface, archbishop: sends him the archiepiscopal pallium and teaches when he ought to use it; grants authority to establish new bishoprics; answers concerning a certain priest and his various questions, LXXXIX, 575.

Letter to all bishops, priests, and abbots: commends to them Boniface as he returns to Germany, that they may assist him and not prevent anyone wishing to join him, LXXXIX, 578.

Letter to the nobles and people of the provinces of Germany: as Boniface returns to them, he warns them to obey him and utterly reject every pagan rite, LXXXIX, 580.

Letter to Charles Martel, mayor of the royal household of France, concerning his undertaking the defence of the holy Roman Church against the Lombard kings, who were harassing it by arms, LXXXIX, 581 and 583.

Letter to Boniface, archbishop of Germany: approves his division of Bavaria into four bishoprics; answers several of his questions; orders a council to be held beside the bank of the Danube, LXXXIX, 583.

Letter to Antony, archbishop of Grado, instructing him to come to Rome for a council, LXXXIX, 586.

GREGORY IV, pope. — Letter to all bishops: Bishop Aldric of Le Mans is not to be accused anywhere other than before the Roman see, and concerning the power of the Roman pontiff, CVI, 853.

Letter to bishops and orthodox faithful: restores the deposed Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, to his former rank, LXXXIX, 858.

GREGORY V, pope. — Bull for the monastery of Subiaco, CXXXVII, 915.

Letter to John, archbishop of Ravenna: restores the Church of Piacenza and subjects Montefeltro to it, CXXXVII, 919.

Letter to Constance, queen of Gaul, instructing that those who had plundered and burned the estates of Bishop Julian be restrained by ecclesiastical and royal authority, CXXXVII, 932.

GREGORY VII, pope, saint. — Letter to Desiderius, abbot: announces that, against his will, he has been appointed in the place of the deceased Pope Alexander; asks him to pray to God for him and to come to him as soon as possible, CXLVIII, 285.

Letters on the same matter to Gisulf, prince of Salerno, and Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, CXLVIII, 285 and 286.

Letter to Rainerius, bishop of Florence: commands that a widow who had married her kinsman be deprived of the gifts and dowry left her by him, CXLVIII, 287.

Letter to Giraldus, bishop of Ostia, and Raimbaldus, subdeacon: recounts the death of Pope Alexander and his own election; warns them to bring the monks and abbot of Cluny to peace, CXLVIII, 288.

Letter to the princes of Spain: announces that he has granted Count de Roccio that part of Spain which he may wrest from the hands of the Saracens; forbids other princes to enter the same region with forces, etc., CXLVIII, 289.

Letter to Guy, count of Imola, instructing him to settle the discord between the archbishop of Ravenna and the citizens of Imola, etc., CXLVIII, 292.

He exhorts Beatrice and her daughter Matilda to avoid simoniacs; announces that he is sending religious men to the king to bring him back to the Roman Church, CXLVIII, 293.

Letter to William, bishop of Pavia: asks him, embracing the decrees of the Roman Church, to contend to the best of his ability against its adversaries, CXLVIII, 294.

To Manasses, archbishop of Reims: he is not to harass the monks of Saint Remigius further, and is to arrange for an abbot to be appointed for them according to canonical enactments, CXLVIII, 295.

Letter to all Christ’s faithful in Lombardy: announces that he has excommunicated Gotefred for simoniacally seizing the Church of Milan; warns them not to agree with him and to defend the faith, CXLVIII, 296.

Letter to Giraldus, bishop of Ostia: he marvels that Giraldus did not inform him of the synod he had convened; says that he is presently unable to answer bishops complaining that Giraldus had deposed them, and that he has absolved the bishop of Auch; orders the bishop of Bigorre restored unless Giraldus finds other crimes in him, CXLVIII, 298.

Letter to the Emperor Michael: he sends Dominic, patriarch of Venice, to deal with him concerning matters which his monks had received in the emperor’s name; he shows himself desirous of making peace with the Church of Constantinople, CXLVIII, 300.

Letter to Rudolf, duke of Swabia: he declares that he does not hate King Henry but rather desires peace with him; asks Rudolf to determine how this may be done, or how not only he and the emperor but also the emperor’s wife and others may meet together; asks him to show himself faithful to the Roman Church and to come to the thresholds of the Apostles, CXLVIII, 302.

Letter to Rainald, bishop of Como: he grieves at his misfortunes and shows himself ready to avenge the wrongs done to him. He exhorts him to come to Rome, both for the sake of making peace with Henry and for the cause of the Lombard bishops, CXLVIII, 303.

Letter to Anselm, bishop of Lucca: he is not to receive investiture of the bishopric from Henry, CXLVIII, 304.

Letter to the people of Carthage: he complains that they have wronged Bishop Cyriacus; exhorts them to repentance, or else threatens them with excommunication, CXLVIII, 305.

Letter to Cyriacus, bishop of Carthage: praises him for patiently enduring the wrongs of Saracens and evil Christians, and for refusing to conduct ordinations in the presence of King Henry; exhorts him to perseverance; he is to pray to God for the African Church, CXLVIII, 307.

Letter to Albert, bishop of Aachen: he praises his religious devotion, of which he had once doubted; exhorts him to oppose simoniacs and give help to Herlembald, CXLVIII, 310.

Letter to the judges of Sardinia: exhorts them, following the example of their forefathers, to show themselves obedient toward the Roman Church; and says that he has imposed many matters for report upon the legate whom he sends to them, CXLVIII, 311.

Letter to Geboaldus, bishop: rebukes him because he does not restrain clerics; warns him to do so, etc., CXLVIII, 313.

Letter to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury: reproves him for allowing a certain Arfastus to trouble the abbey of Saint Edmund; warns him to restrain Arfastus’s audacity in his stead and entreat King William not to grant him any favour; if Arfastus refuses obedience, he orders him and Abbot Baldwin to seek the apostolic see for settlement of their dispute, CXLVIII, 314.

Letter to Arnaldus, bishop of Chartres: he is to restore a certain Isimbard to the care of his abbey, after removal of another intruded abbot, if he finds him deprived for no other fault than that he had travelled to Jerusalem from devotion, CXLVIII, 315.

Letter to the brethren of the monastery of the Blessed Mary: because he judged the privilege of his predecessor false, he is unwilling either to confirm it or grant another; the abbot whom they themselves elected did not seem suitable to him; he reports that he warned him to desist from pre-eminence; nevertheless, he orders them meanwhile to obey him, CXLVIII, 315.

Letter to Remigius, bishop of Lincoln: he bars a murderer from ministry at the sacred altar; nevertheless, if he has done penance, he grants him support from the revenues of the Church, CXLVIII, 316.

Letter to Roderic, bishop of Chalon: he inveighs against Philip, king of the French, [Col. 1242] seller and destroyer of churches; he wishes Roderic to warn him to allow bishops to be canonically elected, CXLVIII, 317.

Letter to Humbert, bishop of Lyons: he directs that the bishop-elect of Mâcon, whether chosen by Humbert or his suffragans, be ordained even against the king’s will; and, if he refuses ordination, be compelled, CXLVIII, 318.

Letter to Countess Aldilasia: he recalls her religious devotion and piety toward holy places and exhorts her always to do better things; he entrusts to her the protection of two monasteries, CXLVIII, 319.

Letter to Wozelin, archbishop of Magdeburg, and others: he complains that war has arisen between them and King Henry; orders them to withdraw from arms until he learns, through his legates, the cause of the dispute, CXLVIII, 320.

Letter to Sicard, archbishop of Aquileia: he summons a council to correct the depraved conduct of princes and prelates; warns him to attend on the appointed day with his suffragans, CXLVIII, 322.

Letter to Jerimorus, bishop of Braga: restores the revenues of the bishopric to the suspended bishop of Braga, so that, laying aside every delay, he may go with the legates of his adversary bishop to the thresholds of the holy Apostles, CXLVIII, 324.

Letter to William, count of Burgundy: warns him, together with certain other princes, to come to the Church’s aid, so that, once the Normans have been pacified, he may be able to assist the people of Constantinople, CXLVIII, 325.

Letter to Countess Matilda: exhorts her frequently to receive the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist and to devotion toward the most blessed Virgin Mary, CXLVIII, 326.

Letter to all Christians: warns them to assist the people of Constantinople, who were suffering many calamities from the Saracens, CXLVIII, 329.

Letter to Arnaldus, abbot of Saint-Sever: rebukes him because, though summoned to a synod, he did not come; confirms, on account of his contumacy, the judgment pronounced against him concerning a certain monastery; warns him to come to Rome if he feels himself aggrieved, CXLVIII, 330.

Letter to Manasses, archbishop of Reims: praises him because he has placed a religious abbot over the monastery of Saint Remigius; grants that abbot authority to administer another abbey if he can bear so great a burden; if he cannot, he orders Manasses to ensure that another abbot is appointed, CXLVIII, 331.

Letter to the canons of Saint Hilary of Poitiers: he orders the observances of the canons of Poitiers to be kept on the feast of Saint Hilary and on All Saints’ Day, CXLVIII, 333.

Letter to Sancho, king of Aragon: commends his observance toward the Roman Church and his effort to have the Roman rite celebrated in his dominion; he does not receive the accusation of a certain absent person, etc., CXLVIII, 339.

Letter to Alfonso, king of Castile, and Sancho, king of Aragon: exhorts them to receive the Roman rite; confirms through his legates the excommunication and deposition of a certain simoniac, CXLVIII, 339.

Letter to the people of Ragusa: rebukes them because, after throwing their bishop into prison, they elected another for themselves; commands that they free him from chains and sends a legate for this purpose; if the matter cannot be brought to completion through that legate, he orders both the bishop and the man elected by them to come to Rome, CXLVIII, 341.

He orders the property of the monastery of Saint Quiricus, which had been taken away, restored to the bishop of Rieti, CXLVIII, 341.

To Giraldus, bishop of Sisteron: he commands him to leave the Church of Croscienza, which he had seized; if he thinks he has any right in that church, he is to come before him, CXLVIII, 342.

Letter to Froterius, bishop of Nîmes: he complains of wrongs done to the monastery and abbot of Saint Giles, in contempt of the apostolic see; orders him to desist, CXLVIII, 342.

Letter to William, count of Die: he sends back the bishop elected by them and consecrated by himself; orders them to obey him, especially in extirpating the simoniacal heresy; threatens the count with excommunication if he will not render justice to the bishop and his Church, CXLVIII, 343.

Letter to William, king of England: commends to him observance toward himself and the apostolic see and exhorts him to defend the Church; announces that he and the Church are involved in great disturbances, CXLVIII, 344.

To Duke Godfrey: he rebukes him because he did not send soldiers in aid of Saint Peter, as he had promised; warns him to send them, CXLVIII, 346.

Letter to Isembert, bishop of Poitiers: he is to give account in a provincial council before the metropolitan concerning the monastery of Nobilly, which the clerics of Saint Hilary complained was being held from them by force; if he feels himself aggrieved, he is to come to Rome before him, CXLVIII, 346.

Letter to the people of Beauvais: he absolves them from excommunication at the prayers of the bishop whom they had offended; warns them to obey him and receive penance from him, CXLVIII, 347.

Letter to Philip I, king of the French: warns him to make reparation for damage done to the Church of Beauvais and imitate his predecessors in defending and enlarging churches, CXLVIII, 348.

Letter to Alfonso, king of Castile: commends Bishop Paul to him and warns him to restore the ancient seat of Paul’s bishopric, CXLVIII, 355.

Letter to the Empress Agnes: gives thanks because she promotes concord in the Church and seeks the restoration of King Henry to the Church’s communion; exhorts her to persevere, etc., CXLVIII, 357.

Letter to the bishops and abbots of Brittany: commands them to come to a synod and prohibit incestuous unions among their subjects, CXLVIII, 359.

Letter to Isembert, bishop of Poitiers: rebukes him for contempt of the apostolic see and wrongs done to apostolic legates; commands him to appear before him; meanwhile declares excommunicated those whose service he used for these acts, CXLVIII, 359.

Letter to Gozelin, archbishop of Bordeaux: warns him to come to Rome or send another who may accuse before him the bishop Isembert, summoned to his presence, of the injuries which Gozelin complained by letter that he had suffered from him; and to declare Isembert, unless he comes as commanded, excommunicated together with his accomplices in the crime, CXLVIII, 362.

Letter to the bishops of the French: recounts the calamities of the kingdom of France and the king’s abominable crimes. He rebukes the bishops for their silence against such crimes; commands them to resist the king; if he refuses obedience, he orders the whole kingdom placed under interdict, and, if the king persists, to be taken from his rule. He threatens the bishops with deposition unless they resist him, etc., CXLVIII, 362–365.

Letter to Geboardus, bishop of Prague: rebukes him for contempt of the apostolic see’s authority, for feigned fidelity, and for fraudulently occupying the possessions of the bishop of Moravia, which he orders restored, etc., CXLVIII, 365.

Letter to Udo, archbishop of Trier: entrusts to him and the bishop of Metz the case pending between the bishop of Toul and one of his clerics, CXLVIII, 370.

Letter to Solomon, king of Hungary: complains that, although the kingdom of Hungary belongs by right to Saint Peter, he received it as a benefice from the king of the Germans; warns him, after correcting his error, to acknowledge it as held from the apostolic see, CXLVIII, 373.

Letter to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, and others: they are to warn clerics to desist from wrongs and make satisfaction for damage done to the monastery of Pully; if they refuse, they are to bar them from entering the church, and, if they persist, subject them to excommunication, CXLVIII, 375.

Letter to William, Count of Poitiers, that, together with the bishops and nobles of the kingdom of France, they should admonish King Philip to desist from throwing the churches into disorder and from plundering; otherwise he threatens to excommunicate the king himself and all who render him obedience, CXLVIII, 376.

Letter to Richer, Archbishop of Sens, that he should ensure that Lanzelin, his parishioner, who had committed many crimes against the Archbishop of Tours, makes fitting amends; if he refuses, he is ordered to exercise canonical censure against him, CXLVIII, 377.

Letter to Hugh of Sainte-Maure, that he should restore to the archbishop the goods of the Church of Tours which he has unjustly retained; and, if he thinks anything is owed to him, should come to Rome with the archbishop’s messenger for the synod; otherwise he is to be excommunicated, CXLVIII, 378.

Letter to Isembert, Bishop of Poitiers; confirms the interdict pronounced against him by his legate, excludes him from participation in the sacred rites until the forthcoming synod, which he is ordered to attend, CXLVIII, 379.

Letter to Gozelin, Archbishop of Bordeaux, and William, Duke of Aquitaine; orders that no one render obedience to the Bishop of Poitiers unless he comes to the synod, as had been commanded him, etc., CXLVIII, 379.

Letter to Liemar, Archbishop of Bremen; inveighs against him because he prevented the legates of the Apostolic See from holding a council as he himself had ordered, and because, when summoned by them to Rome, he scorned to come; therefore he suspends him from office until he comes to Rome for the council, CXLVIII, 382.

Letter to Henry, King of the Romans; rejoices that he has kindly received the apostolic legates and rendered him the service of devoted obedience, and that he is taking pains that simony and clerical fornication be extirpated from his kingdom [Col. 1244], etc., CXLVIII, 384–385.

Letter to Cunipert, Bishop of Turin; reproves him because, having been summoned to a synod, he did not come and caused trouble to the monastery of St. Michael; orders him to attend another synod and not to inflict harm upon the said monastery, CXLVIII, 388.

Letter to Countess Matilda; orders her to separate herself from association with Azo; if she is confident that she can prove him not to be her kinsman, he will investigate his case at the next council, CXLVIII, 389.

Letter to all the faithful; exhorts them to defend Christians who were oppressed by unbelievers in lands beyond the sea, CXLVIII, 390.

Letter to all the faithful, that they should receive his legates with due honor and render them obedience, CXLVIII, 392.

Letter to the people of Fermo and Gubbio; states that he has sent legates for the purpose of ensuring the election of a suitable pastor in their Church; admonishes them to show obedience to the legates, CXLVIII, 393.

Letter to Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, and Berthold, Duke of Carinthia; inveighs against bishops who were disobedient in carrying out the decrees of the Apostolic See concerning simoniacs and fornicating clerics; accordingly he admonishes the dukes on no account to receive any persons known by them to be simoniacs or fornicators, etc., CXLVIII, 397.

Letter to Sancho, King of Aragon; judges it absurd that one born of an illegitimate concubinage should rise to the episcopal rank sought for him, etc., CXLVIII, 401.

Letter to the people of Piacenza; writes that at a synod he has deposed Dionysius, their bishop, and released from the bond of their oath all who had sworn fidelity to him; says that he will ensure that all the faithful assist them in expelling him, CXLVIII, 406.

Letter to the people of Lodi; rejoices in them and their bishop for rising up against the Simoniacal heresy and clerical fornication, etc., CXLVIII, 407.

Letter to Dietwin, Bishop of Liège; rebukes him as a simoniac, and admonishes him to repent, extirpate fornication from the clergy, cease inflicting insults upon the abbot of St. Hubert, and consecrate a certain church, etc., CXLVIII, 412.

Letter to Sichard, Bishop of Aquileia; sets out the statutes enacted at a council against concubinary and simoniacal clerics; orders him to ensure their observance, CXLVIII, 413.

Letter to the monks of St. Denis; exhorts them to concord and peace, while their abbot comes either before the legates or before himself to clear himself of simony, CXLVIII, 415.

On rooting fornication out of the clergy, CXLVIII, 417.

Letter to Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, that, after convening a council of his bishops, he should promulgate and ensure the observance of the decrees of the Apostolic See concerning clerical chastity. He also explains that at a synod he confirmed statutes against simoniacs, CXLVIII, 417.

Letter to Cunibert, Bishop of Turin; reproves him because he harasses the monks of St. Michael, CXLVIII, 419.

Letter to Demetrius, King of the Rus’; writes that, with their consent, he has entrusted the kingdom of Rus’ to their son; shows himself ready for their requests, and asks that they receive his legates kindly, CXLVIII, 425.

Letter to Sweyn, King of the Danes; complains of the disobedience of princes toward the Roman Church; commends him for the due reverence he shows the Apostolic See, etc., CXLVIII, 426.

Letter to the people of Bamberg; states that he has deposed the simoniacal Bishop of Bamberg; forbids anyone to presume to plunder or alienate the goods of that Church, CXLVIII, 427–428.

Letter to Henry, King of the Romans, concerning Hermann, Bishop of Bamberg, anathematized by him, etc., CXLVIII, 430.

Letter to all Christians; enlarging upon the injury done to the Apostolic See, exhorts them to implore divine help, that God may either turn the wicked to repentance or restrain their counsels; and sends them a copy of the king’s anathematization, CXLVIII, 434.

Letter to Henry, King of the Romans; rejoices that the king has entrusted to religious men the cause of the discord between them, and says that by their counsel he will receive him back into the bosom of the Church; exhorts him to act mercifully toward the conquered Saxons and to ensure that another man is canonically substituted in the Church of Bamberg in place of the deposed Hermann, CXLVIII, 435.

Letter to Tedald, cleric of Milan; reproves him because, while a canonically elected bishop was still alive, he had intruded himself into that bishop’s place, etc., CXLVIII, 436–438.

Letter to Henry, King of the Romans; reproves him because he communicates with excommunicated persons; admonishes him, if this is so, to seek absolution from some bishop, etc., CXLVIII, 439.

Letter to Cyriacus, Archbishop of Carthage; since only two bishops are found in Africa, he wishes them to elect another and send him to be consecrated by him, CXLVIII, 449.

Letter to all Christians; complains of King Henry’s faithlessness and of the evils the Church suffered at his hands; admonishes them to call him to true repentance; if he will not listen, to resist him manfully; to admit to the bosom of the Church those who had adhered to the king, if they wish to repent; but shows that those who do not withdraw themselves from communion with the king are to be avoided, CXLVIII, 451.

Letter to Hermann, Bishop of Metz; shows that all who have communicated with King Henry, whether bishops or laymen, are excommunicated; that those who maintain that kings cannot be excommunicated are mistaken, by the authority and examples of holy pontiffs; indeed, demonstrates that pontiffs far surpass kings, etc., CXLVIII, 453.

Letter to the Germans: that they should kindly receive King Henry, excommunicated at a synod and deprived of royal dignity, if he truly repents, after removing evil counselors from him and admitting good ones; also admonishing him not to attack the liberty of the Church. Meanwhile, no bishop is to absolve him until the consent of the Apostolic See is given. If he does not truly repent, they are to elect another suitable king, whom he says he will confirm, yet with the counsel of Empress Agnes, to whom they had bound themselves by oath, CXLVIII, 456.

Letter to Henry, Bishop of Liège; replies that if the Bishop of Utrecht knowingly communicated with the excommunicated king and died without satisfaction, communion cannot be maintained with him even after death; otherwise, he absolves him, etc., CXLVIII, 460.

Letter to the bishops of Tuscany: that all of them, or the two nearest bishops, should meet with the Bishop of Siena, who had communicated with King Henry and sought absolution, and impose penance upon him; when it has been performed, he promises to absolve him. Meanwhile, should he fall into danger of death, he grants him absolution, CXLVIII, 461.

Threatening letter to Richer, Archbishop of Sens, CXLVIII, 462.

Letter to Adela, Countess of Flanders; replies that fornicating clerics ought not to celebrate Masses, but should be expelled from the choir, etc., CXLVIII, 464.

Letter to Robert, Count of Flanders, that he should persecute simoniacal and fornicating priests; inveighs against bishops disobedient to the Apostolic See, CXLVIII, 464.

Announces that King Henry has performed most humble penance, and that, at the supplications of all present, he has absolved him after receiving an oath of fidelity, etc., CXLVIII, 465.

Letter to the people of Chartres, that henceforth they should not receive as bishop Robert, a perjurer and simoniac, and should elect another lawful pastor; if anyone has been made bishop non-canonically, he himself, all his supporters, and those consenting are to be excommunicated, CXLVIII, 468.

Letter to the clerics of Romans; as excommunicated persons, they are not sent greeting and blessing; orders them to appear before the Bishop of Die, so that the case may be examined, etc., CXLVIII, 369.

Letter to William, King of the English; states that the case of the Bishop of Dol, expelled from the episcopate because of his crimes, was handled in such a way that it could not seem capable of more careful handling, etc., CXLVIII, 470.

Letter to the canons of Le Puy; confirms the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the Bishop of Die, the legate, against Stephen, intruder into the Church of Le Puy; therefore, releasing them from every oath sworn to him, orders them not to render him obedience any longer, CXLVIII, 471–472.

Letter to Hermann, Bishop of Metz; entrusts to him the case between the Bishop of Liège and the Abbot of St. Lawrence, CXLVIII, 475.

Letter to Hugh, Bishop of Die; orders that, after a synod of the bishops of France has been convened, the case of the elect of Cambrai be examined. After his election, the latter had received investiture from King Henry, not knowing either that the king was excommunicated or that such investiture had been prohibited by the pontiff, etc., CXLVIII, 476.

Letter to Bernard the deacon and Bernard the abbot, that they should seek safe passage from Kings Henry and Rudolf, so that he may travel into German lands; whichever of the two refuses to grant this is to be excommunicated and forbidden the reins of government, while the one who obeys is to be confirmed in royal dignity, CXLVIII, 478.

Letter to Doge Domenico Silvio and the people of Venice; complains that they communicated with excommunicated persons; sends legates to absolve them from excommunication after they have performed penance, CXLVIII, 480.

Letter to the Spaniards; reminds them that by ancient enactments the kingdom of Spain belongs by right to St. Peter, etc., CXLVIII, 484.

Letter to the canons of St. Martin of Lucca; reproves them because, contrary to his admonitions and after promising satisfaction, they purchased canonries and prebends, etc., CXLVIII, 487.

Letter to the bishops and clerics of Corsica; in fulfillment of his pastoral office sends as legate the Bishop-elect of Sisana, to carry out in his stead matters relating to religion, etc., CXLVIII, 487.

Letter to the Corsicans; rejoices that they wish to recover the island of Corsica, which from ancient times belonged by right to St. Peter, from invaders and restore it to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, etc., CXLVIII, 489.

Letter to the people of Aquileia; writes that among all things he especially desires that in every Church there be elected one worthy to bear the name and hold the office of pastor, etc., CXLVIII, 490.

Letter to the suffragans of the Church of Aquileia; admonishes them to take diligent care that the election of the Bishop of Aquileia, concerning which he sends legates, be canonical, etc., CXLVIII, 491.

Letter to Udo of Trier and the suffragans; states his concern to calm the disturbance of the German kingdom; for this purpose he has sent letters to all princes, that they may bring aid to so great an evil, CXLVIII, 492.

Letter to Rainer, Bishop of Orléans; orders him, within fifty days, to come to the place approved by the bishops of Sens and the other bishops to whom he entrusted the matter, in order to clear himself of the crimes alleged against him, CXLVIII, 494.

Letter to Hugh, Bishop of Die; confirms his excommunication and deposition of a certain young man intruded into the Church of Chartres; for the governance of that church the Abbot of St. Euphemia was being requested from the King of France, etc., CXLVIII, 497.

Letter to Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, and others; accusing their rashness in offending the Holy Roman Church, and providing for their salvation, summons them to a synod, etc., CXLVIII, 496.

Letter to the Germans; says that apostolic legates had been appointed at the Roman synod for the purpose of reconciling peace in the German kingdom; if anyone should presume to hinder them, he excommunicates him, etc., CXLVIII, 500.

States that, following moderation rather than the rigor of the canons, he examined the cases of the bishops of France and Burgundy, etc., CXLVIII, 502.

Letter to Rainer, Bishop of Orléans; rebukes him because, abusing the patience of the Roman Church, he had added crime to crime and squandered almost all the ornaments of his Church; therefore he orders him, etc., CXLVIII, 505.

Letter to Hugh of Cluny, that he should give assistance to the legate whom he sends to the King of Spain, etc., CXLVIII, 506.

Letter to Gausfred and another Gausfred, counts: that they should cause all bishops and abbots of Brittany, and the learned clerics and laymen of the Church of Dol, to assemble for the holding of a council, etc., CXLVIII, 508.

Letter to the Germans; admonishes them neither to favor nor to communicate with those who, against the prohibition of the Apostolic See, attempt to hinder the assembly of bishops and laymen to be held before the apostolic legates concerning the right of Henry and Rudolf in the German kingdom, etc., CXLVIII, 508.

Letter to Henry, Bishop of Liège; accuses him of rashness because he had uttered words against the authority of the Roman Church, etc., CXLVIII, 513.

Letter to Hugh, Bishop of Die: that he should absolve Robert, Count of Flanders, excommunicated by the legate of the Apostolic See and the Bishop of Langres, if he finds that this was not done canonically, or if Robert is willing to make satisfaction, CXLVIII, 516.

Letter to the canons of the Church of Thérouanne: that the canons of the castle of St. Paul be forbidden all entrance into church unless they obey apostolic letters; laymen who do not obey are to be excommunicated, etc., CXLVIII, 517.

Letter to the people of Ravenna; admonishes them to render no further obedience to the Bishop of Ravenna, deposed at the Roman synod for very many crimes; whoever dares to oppose apostolic commands is to be condemned by anathema, CXLVIII, 518.

Letter to the monks of Marseilles; exhorts them to bear the absence of their abbot with equanimity; desires to unite their monastery, like Cluny, to the Apostolic See, etc., CXLVIII, 524.

Letter to Everard, Bishop of Parma; reproves him because he seized an abbot who was coming to a synod; orders him to release the abbot; for this reason he suspends him from episcopal office, CXLVIII, 527.

Letter to the people of Arles; rebukes them because they are moved by almost no concern that their Church has been deprived of a pastor; therefore he sends the Bishop of Gap, so that they may either elect a bishop or promise to accept as pastor whomever he sends to them, etc., CXLVIII, 529–530.

Letter to Arnold, Abbot of St. Sever; states that he has entrusted to the Bishops of Die and Oloron the determination of what ought to be done in the dispute between him and the Abbot of Holy Cross, CXLVIII, 532.

Very many more letters of St. Gregory VII still survive; we omit them, lest we dwell too long upon matters pertaining to this pope, CXLVIII, 534–748.

GREGORY VIII, pope.—He announces his election to the German clergy and exhorts them to devote themselves to an expedition for the recovery of Palestine, CCII, 1537.

To all prelates of Churches, concerning the administration of justice and the settlement of disputes, CCII, 1538.

To all the faithful, concerning the observance of fasting in order to appease God who has been offended, CCII, 1539.

To all Christ’s faithful, concerning the disaster at Jerusalem; admonishes all to perform penance and grants full indulgence to those setting out to war against unbelievers, CCII, 1539.

He takes the monastery of Lucullus under protection and confirms its possessions and rights, CCII, 1543.

He forbids the ancient rights of the monasteries of Savigny to be diminished on the pretext of the Cistercian monks established there, CCII, 449.

To the clergy, governing authority, and people of Bergamo, he commends Lanfranc, bishop-elect, CCII, 1549.

He exhorts the Bishop of Venice to grant the church of St. Bartholomew to the canons of St. Savior, CCII, 1551.

To Emperor Frederick; states that he cherishes counsels of peace toward him and approves the fact that Frederick himself entertains the same, CCII, 1588.

To Folmar, Archbishop of Trier, concerning the calamity of the Eastern Church; rejects harsh counsels and censures against princes and prelates, and rebukes the Archbishop of Trier because he had been harsher than justice allowed, CCII, 1559.

HILARUS, pope.—Letter to Ascanius and the remaining bishops of the province of Tarragona: that no bishop be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan bishop; that no bishop, leaving his own Church, transfer to another; that Irenaeus, removed from the Church of Barcelona, return to his own; concerning the removal of bishops unlawfully ordained; and that there should not be two bishops in one Church; concerning the condemnation of Irenaeus if he does not return to his own church, LVIII, 17.

Letter to Leontius, Veranus, and Victurus, bishops; entrusts to them the controversy between Bishops Ingenuus and Auxanius, and decrees that the city of Cimiez and the fortress of Nice return to the governance of one bishop, LVIII, 20.

Letter to Leontius; admonishes him to send a report concerning Hermes, who was said rashly to have usurped the episcopate of the Church of Narbonne, LVIII, 24.

Letter to bishops of different provinces of Gaul; permits Hermes to preside over the Church of Narbonne, but without the power of ordaining bishops; councils are to be held annually from such provinces as are able, and are to be convened by Leontius; bishops are not to travel to another province without letters from the metropolitan; if they cannot obtain such letters, the Bishop of Arles is to examine the case; concerning the parishes of the Church of Arles, which Leontius claimed back, he remits judgment to the bishops; church estates are not to be alienated unless the reason for their alienation has first been set forth before a council, LVIII, 24.

Concerning Bishop Mamertus, who had ordained bishops for the people of Die beyond his own bounds: Leontius is to examine his case in a synod; no one is to overstep his own boundaries; councils are to be convened annually through Leontius’s efforts; concerning the examination of Mamertus’s case in a synod, LVIII, 27–28.

HONORIUS I, pope.—Letter to Isacius, Exarch of Ravenna; asks that Adaloald, the Catholic king of the Lombards, be restored to the throne, that Ariovald, who had been substituted for him—a perfidious Arian—be expelled from it, and that the Cisalpine bishops through whose agency the crime had been committed be sent to him to receive punishment, LXXX, 469.

Letter to the bishops of Venice and Istria, concerning Fortunatus, Patriarch of Grado, who had been deposed, and Primogenius, substituted in his place, LXXX, 469.

[Col. 1248] Letter to Sergius, Bishop of Constantinople; after affirming the true doctrine of the orthodox faith concerning Christ’s two wills, states why he judges that agreement should be given to Sergius, who enjoins silence regarding novel terms, LXXX, 470.

Letter to Edwin, King of England; exhorts him to persevere in the faith, and, at his request, sends two pallia each to Paulinus and Honorius, metropolitans, so that when one dies the survivor may ordain another in the deceased’s place, LXXX, 476.

Letter to Honorius, Bishop of Canterbury; admonishes him to persevere in preaching the Gospel and sends him a pallium, LXXX, 477.

HORMISDAS, pope.—Letter to Emperor Anastasius; praises him for striving for the Church’s peace, and writes that, when he has learned the reason why Anastasius wishes a council to be convened, he will give him an answer, LXIII, 370.

Letter to Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica; praises his piety and devotion toward the Roman See, LXIII, 372.

Letter to the Emperor Augustus Anastasius; praises the zeal of the emperor, who had announced his wish that a council be convened to settle questions concerning the faith that had arisen in Scythia, and promises to reply through legates, LXIII, 374.

Letter to Emperor Anastasius; says that it is unprecedented for the Roman pontiff to be summoned by the emperor to a council; nevertheless, he will go if the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are not called into question, LXIII, 379.

Letter to Emperor Anastasius; although Anastasius’s deceit had not yet been exposed, he praises his zeal for reconciling peace and admonishes him that, when heresies have at last been condemned, the unity of the Church may take effect, CXIII, 383.

Letter to John, Bishop of Nicopolis; commends his piety; writes that he will communicate in a memorandum that Nestorius and Eutyches must be condemned and how those returning to the faith are to be received, LXIII, 388.

Letter to the synod of Old Epirus; condemns adherents of Eutyches’ errors; exhorts the bishops of Old Epirus to anathematize the heretics by name, LXIII, 391.

Letter to John, Bishop of Nicopolis; since the bishops of Old Epirus had not condemned the heretics by name in their letters, a document is sent to which they must subscribe, LXIII, 392.

Letter to Avitus, Bishop of Vienne; praises in him his zeal to learn the state of the Eastern Church; writes that the legates accomplished nothing because of Greek faithlessness; he intends to send another embassy to them, LXIII, 394.

Letter to Emperor Anastasius; the peace of the Church cannot be restored except by condemning Acacius, LXIII, 397.

Letter to Timothy, Bishop of Constantinople: labor must be undertaken for the unity of the Church, LXIII, 399.

Threatening letter to all heretical bishops of the East: the unity of the Catholic faith must be maintained, LXIII, 400.

Letter to the orthodox Eastern bishops; praises their constancy in the faith and writes that he has again sent legates to Constantinople to reconcile peace, LXIII, 401.

Letter to Bishop Possessor: one must persevere in the Catholic faith, LXIII, 403.

Letter to the people and monks of Constantinople: association with heretics must be avoided and perseverance maintained in the Catholic faith, LXIII, 403.

Letter to Bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus; writes that from John of Nicopolis he learned what the Bishop of Thessalonica had attempted against him, and by this letter entrusts to them the examination of the new case brought before the Apostolic See, LXIII, 404–405.

Concerning John of Nicopolis, LXIII, 406.

Letter to the archimandrites of Syria; consoles and exhorts them to persevere in the Catholic faith, LXIII, 415.

Letter to John, Bishop of Tarragona; gladly heard of his arrival in Italy; approves the letters concerning ecclesiastical institutions issued by him to the Spaniards, and entrusts his vicariate to him, LXIII, 421.

Letter to all the bishops of Spain; concerning the ordination of priests according to canonical statutes; that no payment be received for a bishopric; concerning the annual holding of a council, LXIII, 423.

Letter to Sallustius; Sallustius is appointed vicar of the Apostolic See for the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania, LXIII, 425.

Letter to Emperor Justin; in reply to his letter, commends his concern to reconcile peace, and admonishes him to persist in what he has begun and to have Acacius’s name erased, LXIII, 428.

Letter to John, Bishop of Constantinople: [Col. 1249] while commending him and rejoicing that he has embraced the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy Leo, promises to admit him to the communion of the Church if he erases Acacius’s name from the sacred diptychs, LXIII, 429.

Letter to Caesarius of Arles; teaches that the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum have returned to communion with the Apostolic See after condemning the Eutychian heresy, and after an embassy had been sent to the East, LXIII, 451.

Letter to Justinian Augustus; states that legates are being sent to obtain peace and condemn Acacius, LXIII, 435.

Letter to the same; warns against those who, while accepting the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, refuse to condemn Acacius; commends the legates sent for peace and the union of the Eastern Church, LXIII, 455.

Letter to Empress Euphemia: the emperor is to be exhorted to restore the peace of the Church, LXIII.

Letter to John, Bishop of Constantinople: Acacius must be condemned and a profession of faith delivered into the hands of the legates, LXIII, 438.

Letter to the archdeacon and clergy of Constantinople: now that Catholics have been freed from the harassment of heretics, legates are sent to confirm peace, LXIII, 439.

Letter to Justinian, count of the domestics; hopes that through his efforts the Church will obtain peace, LXIII, 440.

Letter to various persons: the legates are to be assisted in the cause of peace, LXIII, 440–441.

Letter to Germanus and the other legates; wishes to be informed of what they do, etc., LXIII, 452–453.

Letter to Emperor Justin; rejoices that peace flourishes at Constantinople through his efforts, and urges him to ensure the same at Antioch and Alexandria, LXIII, 454.

Letter to John, Bishop of Constantinople; praises him for returning to the unity of the Church; exhorts him to bring about union for the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch, etc., LXIII, 455.

Letter to Justinian; commends him because he assisted Justin in restoring the peace of the Church, and exhorts him to defend that peace completely, LXIII, 457.

Letter to Pomplius; praises him for showing himself devoted to peace, and exhorts him to labor so that complete tranquility may be restored to the Church, LXIII, 457.

Letter to all the bishops of Spain; sends them the profession of John, Bishop of Constantinople, for Eastern bishops who might seek communion with them, LXIII, 459.

Letter to Germanus and the other legates; admonishes them to deal with the emperor and his wife so that all Churches, especially those of Alexandria and Antioch, may be restored to communion with the Apostolic See, LXIII, 461.

Letter to Dioscorus the deacon, that he should consider how those who had condemned the Council of Chalcedon in writing and wished to return to the Church should be received, LXIII, 461–462.

Letter to John and Dioscorus, legates; laments that Bishops Thomas and Nicostratus were not received at Constantinople with due honor, LXIII, 463.

Letter to Emperor Justin, that he should ensure the restoration of Elias, Thomas, etc., to their sees, LXIII, 463–465, 460.

Letter to the legates, concerning what he had heard by report of deeds committed by Eutychians at Thessalonica: Dorotheus and Aristides are to be compelled to come to Rome, LXIII, 467.

Letter to the legates; laments John’s death; and, after Dorotheus has been removed from the episcopate, orders another to be installed in his place, excluding Aristides; Thomas and Nicostratus are to be restored to their churches, LXIII, 469.

Letter to John, Bishop of the Church of Militana; the Church of Constantinople has returned to communion with the Apostolic See, LXIII, 470.

To the bishops of Spain; rejoices over the peace of the Eastern Church, LXIII, 471.

To Justinian; the Scythian monks will not leave Rome before the arrival of the legates; sends relics from the shrines of the apostles, LXIII, 477.

Letter to Bishop Possessor; the Scythian monks, wishing to condemn their errors, are expelled from the city as heretics. The Roman Church does not receive the book of Faustus, LXIII, 490.

To Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantinople; complains that he has neither written nor sent legates, and that Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus have not been restored to their sees; Epiphanius himself must ensure that these matters are carried into effect, LXIII, 493.

Letter to Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica; he must come to Rome to receive Catholic doctrine and clear himself of the charge brought against him, LXIII, 500.

[Col. 1250] Letter to the synod of Constantinople; rejoices that Epiphanius has been elected pontiff, LXIII, 505.

Letter to Emperor Justin: to avoid discord, nothing is to be innovated; he has written to Epiphanius concerning those who may be admitted to communion, LXIII, 510.

Letter to Emperor Justin; the mystery of the Divinity and Incarnation is expounded, LXIII, 512.

Letter to Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantinople; delegates to him the vicariate authority of the Apostolic See in receiving the fallen, LXIII, 515.

Letter to Remigius, Bishop of Reims; assigns him his vicariate in the kingdom of Clovis, king of the Franks, recently converted to the faith, LXIII, 524.

Decree: a presbyter who is confined in a monastery to perform penance is not to be ordained, LXIII, 525.

Decree: it is not lawful to celebrate clandestine marriages, LXIII, 525.

Decree: no altar is to be erected in a consecrated church without the bishop’s permission, LXIII, 526.

INNOCENT I, pope.—To Anysius, Bishop of Thessalonica, confirms the authority over the Churches of Illyricum which Anastasius and his predecessors had granted him, XX, 463.

That no bishop may dare to ordain outside the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop; that, after remission of sins, one who has chosen to wear the military belt is not to be admitted to the clergy; that all disputes or cases arising among clerics of whatever rank are to be decided before the provincials, that is, their own bishops; that major cases are to be referred to the Apostolic See through episcopal judgment; that a cleric may marry a virgin as wife; that a layman who has married a widow, whether before or after baptism, is not to be admitted to the clergy; that one who has taken a second wife must not be ordained a cleric, even if he entered into such a marriage before baptism; that no one may presume to ordain a cleric from another church; that persons baptized among the Novatians or Montanists are to be received only by the laying on of hands; that priests and levites are not to cohabit with their wives; that a monk who wishes to strive for clerical rank must not depart from the former vocation he bore as a monk; that one who has been sexually defiled and wishes to enter the clergy must promise, according to the rule of the ancients, not to take a wife; that members of municipal councils or those occupied in any public duties are not to become clerics; that veiled handmaids of God, if they marry publicly or secretly give themselves to sexual corruption, are not to be admitted to penance unless the man to whom they united themselves has departed from secular life; that handmaids of God not yet consecrated, if afterward they wish to marry, are to be received to penance, XX, 471, 481.

That certain bishops improperly disagree with others because they received converts from heresy; concerning bishops ordained by Rufinus and Minicius, contrary to the canons, in other churches; that the case of Bishop John and of others who refused fellowship in communion be examined; concerning the defective ordinations of many persons: that what has hitherto been usurped be tolerated, but forbidden in the future; that the complaint of Gregory, Bishop of Mérida, be examined; whom it is permitted to admit to clerical rank and what sort of persons are to be chosen, XX, 486, 493.

Letter to Theophilus, Bishop of the Church of Alexandria; he cannot depart from communion with John unless John is condemned by lawful judgment. Theophilus is summoned to a canonical synod, XX, 494–495.

Concerning the incontinence of priests or levites; concerning final penance; concerning administrators, that men are not to live with adulterous wives; that those who compose petitions or criminal accusations are to be held exempt; that those who have undergone divorce following repudiation, if they unite themselves to other marriages, are shown to be adulterers; which books are to be received into the canon, XX, 495–502.

Letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople; declares that only the Nicene canons are to be accepted, and others contrary to them rejected; finally states that it is his concern to have an ecumenical synod assembled, XX, 502–507.

Letter to Rufus, Bishop of Thessalonica; the care of various provinces is entrusted to him, in which he is established as Innocent’s vicar and first among the primates, XX, 315.

On the Paschal calculation for the year 414, XX, 517.

Concerning the reception of clerics known to have been ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation, XX, 519.

That if a priest or any member of the clergy marries a widow or a divorced woman, he loses his office; that if a catechumen had a wife and, after her death, obtained another after baptism, he is not to be a cleric; that persons ordained among heretics are not to be received into the clergy; that crimes or defects are not rightly believed to be removed in ordinations [Col. 1251]; that those ordained by the heretic Bonosus are for this reason received, lest scandal remain in the Church; that in the Church the sin of the people is customarily allowed to pass unpunished; that the Apostolic See had been misled and altered its decision for the better, XX, 526–537.

Concerning Bubalmus and Taurianus, condemned by provincial bishops, whose sentence the Apostolic See undertook to reconsider, XX, 537.

On the condition upon which he grants Acacius communion, XX, 546.

Concerning Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople: communion is not to be restored to him unless he first requests it by a solemn embassy and himself carries out what was done at Antioch—that is, restores John’s name in the sacred diptychs, XX, 544.

Letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch: that the first see of Blessed Peter is remembered as being at Antioch; that, according to the imperial enactments, there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops; that Arian clergy are not to be admitted to their offices, although the Church confirms the baptism administered by them, XX, 547–551.

On giving the kiss of peace after the mysteries have been completed; on names not being recited before the priest’s prayer; that persons ought not to be baptized unless they are sealed by a bishop; that fasting is rightly observed every Saturday; on the *fermentum*, which is to be sent only to the presbyters of the city; on baptized demoniacs; on penitents; on the Epistle of St. James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick is prescribed, XX, 551, 561.—In replying to the bishops of Carthage, he praises and confirms their teaching and judgment against the Pelagian heretics, XX, 582.

He praises the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, both because they judged obstinate heretics to be separated and those corrected to be received, and because, following canons everywhere accepted, they sought the judgment of the Apostolic See in anxious matters. He then demonstrates that the heresy which maintains that a human being can suffice for himself without God’s grace, and denies that baptism is necessary for little children unto eternal life, conflicts with the Scriptures. He orders the authors of these errors and their followers to be cut off from the Church; but, if they condemn their errors, to be received, XX, 589.

He replies to five bishops that he had already made sufficiently known what he thought of their judgment and of Pelagius’s perfidy, etc., XX, 593.

If a husband whose wife had been taken into captivity marries another woman, then, when the first returns, the second woman must be put away, XX, 602.

It is not lawful to encroach upon another’s parish, or to do anything in it without consulting its own bishop, XX, 606.

That Lawrence, bishop of Siena, should ensure the expulsion of heretics following the poisonous doctrines of Photinus, XX, 607.

He pronounces judgment against Arcadius, Arsacius, and Theophilus, XX, 630.

He absolves Arcadius and permits him to receive the sacred mysteries, XX, 635.

INNOCENT II, pope.—He informs King Lothair that Conrad, usurper of the kingdom, has been excommunicated by Honorius; the apostolic legation through Germany is confirmed to Cardinal Gerard, CLXXIX, 53.

He discusses the canonical character of his election, CLXXIX, 55–56.

Letter to Peter, bishop of Beauvais, and the canons: he forbids them to molest the monks of St. Lucian for any reasons known to him, CLXXIX, 74.

He complains of the disobedience of John, bishop of Glasgow, CLXXIX, 90.

Confirmation of the confraternity of the Church of Oxford, CLXXIX, 92.

Letter to Alvisius, abbot of Aquinoinctum: he commands him, despite his refusal, to undertake the care of the Church of Arras, CLXXIX, 93.

He summons Didacus, archbishop of Compostela, to the council to be held at Rheims, CLXXIX, 96.

He confirms the discipline established in the churches of Ramberg by Bishop Otto, CLXXIX, 108.

He informs the clergy and people of Hildesheim that Godehard, a former bishop, has been enrolled among the saints at the Synod of Rheims, CLXXIX, 110.

To Guilenchus, bishop of Langres: that he should not allow Herbert, abbot of St. Stephen of Dijon, to be harassed by the priest Humbert, CLXXIX, 114.

Letter to the bishops of Scotland, concerning the obedience to be rendered to their metropolitan, the bishop of York, CLXXIX, 115.

To Stephen, abbot of Régnier: he exempts the abbots of Régnier from the obedience which they had rendered to the bishop of Autun for the place of Fortum, CLXXIX, 116.

[Col. 1252] To the abbot of Fontenelle, that he should receive blessing from his prelate, etc., CLXXIX, 117.

Letter to the archbishops and bishops of France, that they should defend the nuns of Fontevraud, through two or three suitable witnesses, in recovering their property, CLXXIX, 118.

To Briccius, bishop of Nantes: that he should not inflict injuries upon the monastery of Trénor, CLXXIX, 121.

He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Cîteaux, CLXXIX, 122.

Bull for the establishment of Regular Canons in the monastery of St. Laud of Coutances, CLXXIX, 126.

To those who visit the monastery of Cluny on the day of the dedication of the high altar, he remits forty days of the penance undertaken by them, CLXXIX, 127.

He informs the people of Trier that Albero, whom they had elected, has been consecrated by him and granted the pallium; he admonishes them to obey him, CLXXIX, 131.

To Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny: he newly invests him with the abbey of St. Bertin and commands the monks of the same house to obey him, CLXXIX, 135.

He grants to the canons of St. Alexander at Bergamo certain churches belonging to the Apostolic See, CLXXIX, 143.

He decrees that the monks of the monastery of St. George Major, received under the protection of the Apostolic See, shall henceforth elect for themselves as abbot whomever they judge suitable, CLXXIX, 160.

To Berthold, abbot of St. Blaise: he approves the separation of the Church of Burg from the church of Eggenheim, CLXXIX, 164.

To Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, bishop of Paris: that they should strive to have the honors and goods taken from the subdean of Amélien and his companions restored, CLXXIX, 165.

Letter to archbishops, bishops, etc.: he announces that a certain N., invader of the Church of Oviedo, has been excommunicated by him, CLXXIX, 172.

He adorns Syrus of Genoa, made from bishop into archbishop, with the pallium, and subjects to him the bishops of Mariana, etc., as suffragans, CLXXIX, 174.

To Hugh, duke of Burgundy: he admonishes him to protect Herbert, abbot of St. Denis, against the monks of St. Seine, whom he declares excommunicated, CLXXIX, 176.

He establishes the monastery of Brugnato as an episcopal see, suffragan to the Church of Genoa, CLXXIX, 178.

That all bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway should be subject to Adalbero, archbishop of Hamburg, CLXXIX, 180.

Bull concerning certain bishoprics in Poland and on this side of it subject to the bishop of Magdeburg, CLXXIX, 183.

He reproves Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, and Henry, archbishop of Sens, because they did not more promptly pronounce sentence of excommunication against those who killed the prior of St. Victor, CLXXIX, 191.

Letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, bishop of Paris: what penance the killers of Archembald, subdean of Amélien, are bound to perform in order to make satisfaction and be absolved from excommunication, CLXXIX, 193.

Bull by which the monastery of Frankenthal is established and at the same time received under the protection of the Holy See, CLXXIX, 197.

He invites Geoffrey, archbishop of Dol, his suffragans, and the abbots to come to the Council of Pisa, CLXXIX, 210.

On the parricidal murder of Thomas, prior of St. Victor, CLXXIX, 214.

He exhorts the archbishops and bishops of the German kingdom to observe the privilege of the Roman Church: that major causes be referred to the examination of the Apostolic See, and that all the oppressed may appeal to it without fear, CLXXIX, 226.

To Henry, bishop of Toul: he confirms the agreement made between him and Frederick, count of Toul, CLXXIX, 228.

Bull by which he raises the priory of St. Peter of Nantes to the rank of an abbey, uniting several churches to it, CLXXIX, 237.

He informs the clergy of the Church of Mediolana that Tetald of Medolac has been excommunicated for attacking the church of Virgis, CLXXIX, 240.

He informs Gregory, bishop, and the clergy and people of Bergamo that he has settled the dispute between the canons of St. Vincent and St. Alexander, CLXXIX, 240, 242.

To Albero, archbishop of Trier, against the abbot of St. Maximin, whom, if the allegations are true, he judges ought to be deposed, CLXXIX, 251.

[Col. 1253] Letter to Gerard, abbot of St. Maximin: he accuses him of simony and dissipation of property, CLXXIX, 252.

He praises certain abbots for establishing the discipline of their orders, CLXXIX, 254.

He forbids Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, and his successors to alienate the castle of Winzenburg, CLXXIX, 254.

To Hugh, prior of the Carthusians: he announces that St. Hugh of Grenoble has been enrolled among the saints, and exhorts him to write his life, CLXXIX, 256.

He commands Albero, archbishop of Trier, to compel Brunicus and his sons to restore the estate of Filestanges to the monastery of Romigny, CLXXIX, 256.

Letter to the clergy of Modena: he announces that the consuls of Modena have been excommunicated for attacking the monastery of Nonantola, CLXXIX, 257.

To Berthold, abbot of St. Blaise, concerning the peace to be kept with the monks of Schaffhausen, CLXXIX, 258.

He orders Henry, archbishop of Sens, to abstain from episcopal office, CLXXIX, 254.

To Rainald, archbishop of Rheims: that he should grant to the petitioning people his archdeacon, elected archbishop of Bourges, CLXXIX, 278–279.

Letter to Stephen, king of England: he receives as a special son of Blessed Peter and the Roman Church the king unanimously elected and consecrated, CLXXIX, 391.

To Hugh, archbishop of Rouen: severe in correcting vices, he exhorts him to gentleness, etc., CLXXIX, 304.

Bull confirming the transfer of an abbey from St. Firmin to St. John beside the Scylla, etc., CLXXIX, 308.

To Walter, bishop of Augsburg: he commands that they refrain from harassing the monastery of Benediktbeuern, as a royal monastery, CLXXIX, 326.

He asserts for Albero, archbishop of Trier, and his successors the primacy of Belgic Gaul, and appoints him legate of the Apostolic See, CLXXIX, 331, 333.

Letter to the archbishops of Rheims, Sens, and Tours, whom he admonishes to be gentle and to leave free to those unjustly oppressed the right of appealing to the Apostolic See, CLXXIX, 342.

On the obedience owed to the patriarch of Jerusalem, CLXXIX, 347, 372.

On the excommunication of the consuls of Pistoia, CLXXIX, 376.

To Walter, bishop of Augsburg: he exhorts him to receive Abbot Engescalc of Benediktbeuern with his brethren into favor and communion, CLXXIX, 393.

He informs Abbot Chuunrad and the monks of Fulda that Sturmi has been enrolled among the saints in a council, CLXXIX, 450.

Diploma by which the Church of Ferrara is declared a special daughter of the Roman Church and its county part of the patrimony of St. Peter, CLXXIX, 454.

He exhorts many bishops and counts of Flanders to defend the liberty of the monastery of St. Bertin at Saint-Omer, CLXXIX, 462.

He exhorts archbishops and bishops to protect the churches of the monastery of Monte Cassino, CLXXIX, 478.

He writes to the clergy and laity of the diocese of Hildesheim that no layperson may presume to seize, during life or after death, the movable or immovable goods of cloistered brethren or other clerics, CLXXIX, 488.

To Henry of Sens and Rainald of Rheims, bishops: concerning Abelard and Arnold of Brescia, condemned and to be confined in a monastery, and concerning the burning of their books, CLXXIX, 515.

To Samson of Rheims, Henry, bishop of Sens, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: concerning the condemnation of Abelard and Arnold, CLXXIX, 517.

The nuns of Crisenon are freed, with the pope’s approval, from the lordship of Molesme, CLXXIX, 520.

He forbids Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, to injure the monks of St. Augustine or to exact from them seven denarii for the provision of chrism and holy oil, CLXXIX, 533.

To Stephen, king of England: that he should not allow the monastery of St. Augustine of Canterbury to suffer injuries, CLXXIX, 533.

To the monks of Marchiennes: he declares the censures of the bishop of Arras null and commands them to proceed to the election of an abbot, CLXXIX, 554.

Letter to the bishop of Arras: he reproves him because he has harassed the monks of Marchiennes, CLXXIX, 555.

He grants Henry, bishop of Moravia, leave to preach to the pagans in Prussia; yet he charges him not to neglect the reform of his rebellious people, [Col. 1254] CLXXIX, 564.

He reproves the clergy of the bishopric of Olomouc for celebrating divine offices contrary to their bishop’s prohibition, and admonishes them to obey and revere their bishop, CLXXIX, 565.

He exhorts Count Roboto to restore a certain estate to the Church of Bamberg, CLXXIX, 566.

To Lord Margrave: he exhorts him to restore what had been taken from the monastery of Blessed Peter at Münchstor, CLXXIX, 567.

On the canonization of St. King Edward, CLXXIX, 568.

He guarantees to Abbess Heloise and the sisters of the Paraclete the property granted by the priest Gundric, CLXXIX, 569.

He announces that he has pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the consuls of Montpellier, who, after expelling William, their lord, had withdrawn themselves from allegiance to him, CLXXIX, 561.

He confirms the establishment of the Premonstratensian order in the Secret Valley, CLXXIX, 577.

He informs the bishops of the province of Narbonne that he has commanded them to restrain Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse from bringing aid to his traitors at Montpellier, or else to excommunicate him, CLXXIX, 582.

To the clergy and people of Toulouse, he commends to them Raymond, bishop, who is coming from him, etc., CLXXIX, 592.

He commends to Henry, bishop of Moravia, Cardinal Guy, the legate sent into those regions to correct the enormities of the clergy, asking him to assist the legate with help and counsel, CLXXIX, 597.

To the archbishop of Tours: that he should come to the Apostolic See to answer the bishop of Dol, who complained that he had been deprived of the bishopric of Arles, CLXXIX, 618.

Letter to Stephen, bishop of Paris: that he should absolve the church of St. Geneviève from interdict, CLXXIX, 620.

To Radulf, abbot of Lagny: he accuses him of contempt for the Apostolic See and of dissipating his monastery’s property, CLXXIX, 621.

To the bishop of Cremona: omission of baptism does not harm one who reasonably believes himself to have been baptized, CLXXIX, 624.

He restrains the archbishop and clergy of Lyons, hostile to the Cluniacs and using violence through sworn men, etc., CLXXIX, 632.

To the legate of the Apostolic See: he commands that the men of Montpellier, absolved by him but refusing to render justice to their lord, be again bound by the same bonds of excommunication, CLXXIX, 637.
