INNOCENT III, pope.—It is altogether impossible for us to give, by analytical enumeration, the writings of this pontiff for the government of the Church; for this pontiff has sixteen books of Registers, together with an appendix, a collection of Decretals, and a supplement to the Registers, all of which are contained in volumes CCXIV, CCXV, CCXVI, and CCXVII of the *Patrology*. Everyone can see how great a labor it would be merely to enumerate so many writings, not of small importance and of great authority in the Church. Therefore let the reader himself consult the author.

JOHN II, pope.—Letter of John to Justinian: he asks him to bring back by every effort those whom he knew to be wandering from the straight path of the Catholic faith, LXVI, 17.

Letter to the senators: he confirms the faith concerning Christ’s divinity and incarnation, LXVI, 20.

Letter to the bishops of Gaul: he deprived Contumeliosus, bishop in Gaul, of the episcopate and sent him into a monastery for penance, etc., LXVI, 24.

Letter to Bishop Valerius: he teaches that Christ, according to the nature of his divinity, is equal to the Father, but according to his human nature is less, LXVI, 27.

JOHN III, pope.—Letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. First he rebukes the chorepiscopi, formerly already condemned as rash men, because they arrogated too much authority to themselves in the laying on of hands. Then he shows that Clement I governed the Apostolic See after Peter, and did so by Peter’s own transmission. Finally, he sets forth how great a care and solicitude must be undertaken by one who seeks the flock of Christ, CXXII, 13–18.

JOHN IV, pope.—Letter to the bishops and presbyters of Scotland, concerning celebrating Easter according to Catholic custom and carefully avoiding the revived Pelagian heresy, LXXX, 601.

Letter to Emperor Constantine: an apology for Pope Honorius concerning the one will in Christ, of which his slanderers say that he made mention, LXXX, 602.

Letter to the bishop of Syracuse: that monks may be permitted to appoint priests for their churches, LXXX, 608.

[Col. 1255] POPE JOHN VII.—Letter to King Ethelred of the Mercians and King Alfrid of the Deirans: he admonishes Berthwald, archbishop of Canterbury, to summon a synod and either cause Wilfrid and his opponents to meet or make them hasten to Rome, LXXXIX, 60.

Letter to the bishops of Britain: that all English clerics should wear tunics reaching to the ankles according to Roman custom, LXXXIX, 63.

JOHN VIII, pope.—Letter to Emperor Louis: Rainald, bishop of Château-Félix, is excommunicated, CXXVI, 655.

Those suspected of the murder of a Roman cleric are excommunicated, CXXVI, 656.

To the bishops of Germany and Gaul: he entrusts his authority in Gaul and Germany to Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, CXXVI, 660.

Letter to King Aldephonsus: the Church of Prétensis is made metropolitan of Galicia, CXXVI, 663.

Letter to all Gauls and Germans: concerning the condemnation of Bishop Formosus, the nomenclator Gregory, and others who had been excommunicated at a synod in Rome, CXXVI, 675.

To King Louis: he writes that he cannot settle the disputes between him and the emperor unless he first hears the other party, CXXVI, 680.

Letter to the clergy, etc., of the Church of St. Walva: he inveighs against a certain invader of that Church, while its lawful bishop was still alive, etc., CXXVI, 680.

To the bishops of the province of Bourges: that they should obey Frotanius as their metropolitan, CXXVI, 689.

Letter to Emperor Charles the Bald: at the emperor’s request, because the province of Bordeaux had been devastated by pagans, he transfers Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, to the Church of Bourges, CXXVI, 690.

To Emperor Charles: he recounts the calamities inflicted on the Church by the Saracens and asks the emperor to send aid against them, CXXVI, 696.

To Ursus, duke of Venice: he gives thanks because he obeyed the admonitions of the Apostolic See; he orders the bishops to come to a synod, CXXVI, 701.

He places Bishops Peter and Felix under interdict because they did not render obedience to the archbishop of Grado, and commands them, under penalty of excommunication, to come to Rome for a council; if impeded, he commands them to send representatives, CXXVI, 702.

Letter to Dominic, bishop-elect of Corcella: he inveighs against Bishop-elect Dominic because, though summoned twice, he did not come to Rome; unless he comes on the appointed day, he excommunicates him, CXXVI, 703.

Letter to Bishops Dominic and Leo: he announces that he has excommunicated certain persons summoned to Rome for a council who neglected to come, unless they come by a fixed appointed day, CXXVI, 705.

Letter to Emperor Charles the Bald: because of the most grave dangers threatening both from the Saracens and from certain Christians, he earnestly requests that the promised assistance be sent as soon as possible, etc., CXXVI, 711.

To the bishops established in Emperor Charles’s kingdom: he admonishes them to urge the emperor to bring aid to the Roman Church, CXXVI, 716.

Letter to King Charles: he admonishes him to ensure that goods taken from a monastery of nuns are restored, otherwise threatening him with excommunication, CXXVI, 719.

To Wigro, bishop of Parma: he exhorts him to stir up all whom he can to the defense of the Holy Roman Church and to come to him with his men, so that by common counsel the Saracens may be driven from Italy, CXXVI, 721–722.

Letter to Gregory, imperial tutor: he congratulates him that the emperor has sent a fleet for the Church’s defense against the Saracens and has appointed him commander, CXXVI, 727.

On dissolving the treaty made by bishops with the Saracens, CXXVI, 729–730.

Letter to archbishops and bishops: that they should come to Ravenna for a council; unless they obey, he threatens to excommunicate them, CXXVI, 732.

To the archbishop of Ravenna: he specifies a fixed day on which he is to be present at Ravenna with all his suffragans; if anyone scorns obedience, he threatens him with excommunication, CXXVI, 736–737.

To the Neapolitans: he praises them because, inflamed with divine zeal, they rejected Sergius and elected Bishop Athanasius ruler of their commonwealth; he commands them to obey him, etc., CXXVI, 747.

To the bishop of Embrun: he reproves him because he consecrated another bishop in the Church of Vence besides the one elected by clergy and people; he commands him to come to Rome with both, CXXVI, 750.

To John, archbishop of Ravenna: he describes the evils perpetrated at Rome by Count Lambert, [Col. 1256] and says that he will go to Gaul to seek aid, etc., CXXVI, 756.

To Michael, king of the Bulgarians: he grieves that he follows the Greeks, etc., CXXVI, 758.

To Count Peter: he exhorts him to bring King Michael back to the bosom of the Roman Church, CXXVI, 760, 762.

To Greek bishops and clerics: he declares them excommunicated because, invading the land of the Bulgarians, they had performed unlawful ordinations there, etc., CXXVI, 764.

To Emperor Basil: he grieves that the Church of Constantinople is still afflicted by schism; for this reason he sends legates, CXXVI, 765, 767.

To Anspert, archbishop of Milan: he admonishes him to come as soon as possible to the synod in Gaul with his suffragans, etc., CXXVI, 771.

To all Christians: he excommunicates those who stole his horses and silver vessel unless they restore them within three days, CXXVI, 780.

To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles: that he should come as soon as possible to the synod with his suffragans, CXXVI, 782.

To King Charles: he gives thanks for his observance toward the Roman Church, CXXVI, 785.

To King Charles: he reproves him because, when summoned, he did not come to him as King Louis had done; under penalty of excommunication, he admonishes him to be content with the limits of his own kingdom and inflict no harassment upon Boso, CXXVI, 786–787.

To Theodoric, archbishop of Besançon: he commands him to come as soon as possible and forbids the ordination of a bishop in the Church of Lausanne, because of divisions among the electors, before they have held a conference, CXXVI, 788.

A law concerning sacrilege, added by Pope John to the Gothic laws at the Council of Troyes, CXXVI, 795.

To Count Bernard: he commands him and certain others to come to a synod at which Frotarius, bishop of Bourges, wished to clear himself of the charge of infidelity brought against him, CXXVI, 799.

To the people of Ravenna: he grieves over the death of their bishop and admonishes them to treat the archbishop elected by them with fitting honor, etc., CXXVI, 812.

To Bishops Theodoric and Isaac: he commands them to excommunicate those who had carried off the son of Count Wipert and were devastating that region, CXXVI, 813.

To John, bishop of Pavia: he orders the abductors of a certain Ragibert to be excommunicated, CXXVI, 215.

To Wifrid, bishop of Vence: he forbids a bishop who has communicated with excommunicated persons from celebrating Mass, CXXVI, 816.

He decrees that minors who have killed another person may be ordained after completing penance, CXXVI, 817.

That a betrothed man should not be compelled to marry a wife defiled by another, CXXVI, 817.

To the archbishop of Besançon: he announces that he has absolved Fulcard and his wife from excommunication, CXXVI, 818.

On summoning bishops to Rome for holding a synod, CXXVI, 820, 822.

To King Charles: he exhorts him to send legates and to come to the aid of the Roman Church, CXXVI, 825.

To archbishops and their suffragans: that they should not excommunicate Bicbertinus before the case has been examined, CXXVI, 827.

To King Carloman: that the deacon Cospertus should be appointed bishop in the Church of Vercelli, CXXVI, 830.

To King Charles: he exhorts him to bring assistance as quickly as possible against unbelievers and oppressors of the Church, CXXVI, 831.

To Michael, king of the Bulgarians: he exhorts him to return with his people to obedience to the Roman Church, from which he had departed when deceived, CXXVI, 832.

To Anspert, archbishop of Milan: he reproves him because, though summoned a third time, he did not come to the council, etc., CXXVI, 836.

To Anselm, bishop of Le Puy: a husband who baptized his own son under urgent necessity is not to be separated from his wife, CXXVI, 639.

To the priests and peoples subject to Branimir: he receives them as they return to the bosom of the Roman Church and admonishes them to persevere, CXXVI, 842.

To Michael, king of the Bulgarians: he gives thanks to God because he sent legates to him, ready to receive ecclesiastical teaching and canonical institutions; he exhorts him to return to the Roman Church, etc., CXXVI, 843.

To Airard, archbishop of Auch, and his suffragans: he exhorts them to correct the corrupt morals of the people, especially incestuous marriages, etc., CXXVI, 844.

[Col. 1257] To the clergy of Salona: he admonishes them to return to the bosom of the Roman Church, etc., CXXVI, 846.

To three archbishops: that they should remove the bishop of Nîmes from an unjust invasion of a certain monastery, and, if he does not obey, excommunicate him, CXXVI, 847.

To Michael, king of the Bulgarians: he grieves that he has defected from the Roman Church, to which he admonishes him to return; he shows that the Greeks, though the Bulgarian diocese belongs to the Roman pontiff, hold it contrary to the canons, CXXVI, 448.

To Methodius, archbishop of Pannonia: he commands him to come to him, so that he may learn about his teaching; he forbids Masses to be celebrated in the Slavic language, CXXVI, 850.

To Anspert, archbishop of Milan: he reproves him because he did not obey the Apostolic See, treated its legates unjustly, and celebrated Mass while excommunicated. Therefore he admonishes him to come as soon as possible, either in person or through legates, to the synod in order to clear himself, CXXVI, 850.

To Empress Angelberga: he announces that he is unwilling at present to absolve Archbishop Anspert; but if, at the synod, he clears himself of the charges brought against him, he will then absolve him from excommunication, etc., CXXVI, 851.

To King Louis: he gives thanks for his favorable disposition toward the Roman Church; he exhorts him to come for its defense against pagan incursions and tacitly promises him the empire, CXXVI, 852.

On restoring peace to the Church of Constantinople, CXXVI, 853.

To the people of Constantinople: he commands them, after the schism has been calmed, to return to the unity of the Church and to communicate with Photius, CXXVI, 863.

To Photius, patriarch of Constantinople: he appoints him patriarch of Constantinople provided that he asks forgiveness at the synod; he decrees that henceforth no layman in that Church shall immediately be ordained bishop; he commands that the Bulgarian diocese be assigned to the Roman Church, CXXVI, 870.

To Pulcher, prefect: he reproves him because he neither broke the treaty struck with the pagans nor defended the dominion of St. Peter, as he had promised; he commands him to send back the money given for that purpose, CXXVI, 878.

To Gaiferius: he admonishes him to desist from the injuries he was inflicting on the people of Capua; he announces that he will go into his territories and settle the disputes, CXXVI, 881.

To King Charles: he writes that by letters he summoned him to the City in order to advance him to the empire, and that he hoped to receive aid from him against the enemies of the Roman Church [lacuna]; he asks him to assist the Church, etc., CXXVI, 882–883.

To all the faithful: he commands them to obey the bishop of Pavia, to whom he had granted the power of excommunication, CXXVI, 885.

To King Charles: concerning the deposition of Anspert, archbishop of Milan, and Joseph, bishop of Vercelli, CXXVI, 887.

To the people of Vercelli: he commands them to receive Conspertus, whom he had appointed their bishop, etc., CXXVI, 887.

To the people of Amalfi: he announces that he has excommunicated them until they separate themselves from the pagans; he threatens them with other penalties unless they obey as soon as possible, CXXVI, 889.

To Helmoinus, bishop of Penne: he reproves him because he did not attend the synod; he commands him to come on the appointed day and meanwhile to absolve a certain person whom he had unjustly excommunicated, CXXVI, 890.

To Bishop Paul: he commands that the church situated in the village of Carpana be restored, that a priest be appointed there, and that sacred chrism be sent there every year, CXXVI, 890.

He shows that a woman who had assumed the religious habit under compulsion and threats is not bound to keep her vows; nevertheless, he entrusts the determination of this case to them, CXXVI, 891.

To certain bishops: he commands them to break the treaty made with the Saracens, threatening them with excommunication unless they do so quickly, CXXVI, 892.

To Arpald, bishop of Ascoli: he reproves him because he did not come to the synod, etc., CXXVI, 893.

To Bishop Egilbert: he reproves him because he had communicated with persons excommunicated by the Apostolic See; he commands him not to communicate with the excommunicated, CXXVI, 897.

To Count Eumbert: he threatens him with excommunication unless he restores the property of St. Peter and of Empress Angelberga, CXXVI, 898.

To the people of Amalfi: he admonishes them, having broken their treaty with the Saracens, to return to the bosom of the Church, etc., CXXVI, 901.

To Charles the Fat, king of Italy: he asks him to permit Jerome to retain the bishopric of Lausanne peacefully and to command Hubo to restore the property taken from the Church of Besançon, CXXVI, 901.

Letters of praise to King Charles, CXXVI, 903, 907, 909, 911, 914.

[Col. 1258] To all bishops: that they should come to Rome for a synod, CXXVI, 913.

To Margrave Adalbert: he absolves him from excommunication, CXXVI, 917.

To Attonius: he excommunicates him unless he restores to the Church of Milan the goods he took and returns with his companions to obedience to his bishop, CXXVI, 921.

To Emperor Charles: he informs the emperor that he is suffering such evils from the Saracens that he can endure no longer, etc., CXXVI, 929.

To Constantine, priest: he excommunicates him because, without his permission, he had been promoted by the archbishop of Ravenna to the bishopric of the Church of Faenza; he forbids him to assume administration of that Church until he comes to the Roman synod, CXXVI, 933.

Letter to the bishop of Ficoleno: he entrusts to him the visitation and care of the Church of Faenza, deprived of a pastor, until a new pastor is appointed over it, CXXVI, 934.

To Romanus, archbishop: he commands him, under penalty of excommunication, to come to the Roman synod in order to answer the charges brought against him, CXXVI, 934.

To Emperor Charles: he sends legates to him to correct the evils which, he complains, he endured during the emperor’s reign, CXXVI, 935.

To the people of Ravenna: he commands them to separate themselves from communion with the archbishop of Ravenna, excommunicated in a synod, until they learn that he has been absolved, CXXVI, 935.

To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles: that a betrothed woman should be deprived of communion unless she is willing to abandon her abductor and return to her betrothed, CXXVI, 940.

To Cennemocus, bishop of Vannes: that a priest who is a murderer cannot remain in the priesthood, CXXVI, 941.

To Count Cozilus: concerning those who, having dismissed their wives, contracted other marriages, CXXVI, 942.

To Photius, patriarch of Constantinople: concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, CXXVI, 944.

To Athanasius, bishop of Naples: he absolves him from excommunication, provided that he breaks the pact entered into with the Saracens, etc., CXXVI, 946.

To Emperor Charles: he complains that many possessions of the Roman Church have been seized by a certain Margrave Wido; he asks him to defend the Church, etc., CXXVI, 948.

To Empress Riccarda: he complains that no aid is being brought him against Saracen raids; he asks her to seek help quickly from the emperor, etc., CXXVI, 949.

To the archbishop of Vienne: he reproves him because, after throwing Bishop Optandus into prison, he appointed another in the Church of Geneva, etc., CXXVI, 952.

To Adalbert, bishop of Maurienne: he commands him to come to Rome with the bishop of Grenoble, whom he had treated shamefully, CCXXVI, 953.

To the clergy of Ravenna: concerning a certain Maimbert, whom he had previously ordered to be expelled from the Church of Ravenna, etc., CXXVI, 955, 957.

To the bishops of Britain: what should be done concerning monks ordained by their abbot, CXXVI, 959.

Address to the Fathers of the Second Synod of Troyes, concerning the excommunication of Lantbert, Adalbert, and other followers, CXXVI, 961.

Excommunication against invaders of ecclesiastical property, CXXVI, 962.

Excommunication against Bishop Formosus, CXXVI, 963.

Statute against laymen who take other wives while their wives are living, and against bishops who, out of ambition, move from a lesser to a greater church, CXXVI, 963.

JOHN IX, pope.—Letter to Heriveus, archbishop of Rheims. Reply to inquiries about Northmen recently converted to the faith, some of whom had been baptized and rebaptized and had lived as pagans after baptism: how they should be dealt with, CXXXI, 27.

Letter to Styllianus, bishop of Neocaesarea: he denies him the permission he sought to communicate with those whom Photius had ordained, CXXXI, 29.

JOHN X, pope.—Letter to Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne: he commands him to come to Rome together with Hilduin and Richarius, who disputed concerning the bishopric of Tongeren, CXXXII, 806.

Letter to King Charles III: he informs him of the matter to be handled between Hilduin and Richarius, and that he has also excommunicated Hubert for the dissipation of the Roman Church’s property, CXXXII, 807.

Bull by which, after the monks of St. Laumer had fled before the pagans, he confirms the possessions donated by William, count of Auvergne, CXXXII, 809.

JOHN XII, pope.—How he restrained the people of Subiaco, who were rebellious against the abbot of the monastery of Subiaco and had occupied many [Col. 1259] of its goods, and compelled them to restore everything, CXXXIII, 1019.

On the excommunication of Artald of Rheims and Amblard, archbishop of Lyons, for invading the possessions of St. Symphorian, CXXXIII, 1025.

Letter to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, clergy, and people of Gaul, Germany, and Bavaria: he decrees that the monastery of Magdeburg be transformed into an archbishopric and Merseburg into a bishopric suffragan to the Church of Magdeburg, CXXXIII, 1027.

JOHN XIII, pope.—Bull for the establishment of the archbishopric of Magdeburg, CXXXV, 952.

Diploma by which he deposes and excommunicates Herold, archbishop of Salzburg, and creates Frederick archbishop in his place, CXXXV, 954.

Bull by which he grants Adalbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, primacy among all the prelates of Germany and establishes for him an honor equal to that of the leading bishops of Gaul, CXXXV, 966.

Bull by which he wills that the same Adalbert consecrate all bishops of the Elbe and Saale; and this right shall remain valid for his successors, CXXXV, 967.

Letter to Edgar, king of the English: concerning the expulsion of clerics from the bishopric of Winchester and the introduction of monks, CXXXV, 985.

He excommunicates those who seize the possessions of the monastery of Saint Symphorianus in the diocese of Autun, CXXXV, 987.

Letter to all the bishops of Lesser Brittany: he forbids them to resist the archbishop of Tours until he himself has rendered judgment concerning their dispute, CXXXV, 989.

Letter to Peter, bishop of Pavia: he entrusts the monastery of Saint Saviour at Pavia, founded and endowed by the Empress Adelaide, to the protection, but not to the jurisdiction, of the bishop of Pavia, CXXXV, 995.

JOHN XV, pope.—Letter to all the faithful, concerning the making of peace between King Ethelred of England and Richard, duke of Normandy, CXXXVII, 843.

Bull for the canonization of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, CXXXVII, 945.

Letter to Count Arnulf and others, that they restore to the monastery of Saint-Riquier what they had taken away, CXXXVII, 850, 851.

JOHN XIX, pope.—He invests Peter, bishop of Silva Candida, on receipt of the staff, with the whole territory of all the churches of Galeria, CXLI, 1132.

He restores to Urso, patriarch of Grado, the patriarchate of Grado, which had been reduced, contrary to law and right, under the authority of Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, CXLI, 1140.

Letter to all the bishops of Gaul, concerning the apostleship of Saint Martial, CXLI, 1149.

Letter to Odilo, abbot of Cluny: he reproves him for having refused the archbishopric of Lyons, CXLI, 1150.

Letters of absolution granted to Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, CXLI, 1151.

Letter exhorting all who do good to devote themselves to restoring the Church of Maguelonne, CXLI, 1156.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint), pope.—Letter to the bishop of Aquileia: Pelagians are wrongly received into communion without renouncing their error and professing the faith; he orders a synod to be convened so that a profession of faith may be required of them; what is to be believed concerning Christ’s grace, LIV, 595.

Letter to Septimus, bishop of Altinum: Pelagians are to be received only upon renouncing their error; every cleric must remain in the church in which he was ordained, LIV, 597.

Letter to the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, etc.: no bishop may presume to promote another person’s slave to clerical office; all who have been promoted to the priesthood, whether husbands of widows or men with numerous marriages, are to be excluded from ecclesiastical offices; not only clerics but also Christian laypeople ought not to exact usury, LIV, 610.

Letter to the metropolitan bishops of Illyricum: unlawful attempts contrary to the canons are to be forestalled by admonitions; provincial bishops are to be subject to their metropolitans; graver causes in Illyricum are to be reserved to the Apostolic See, LIV, 915.

Letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica: he urges him, as a good shepherd, by letters to ensure that his fellow bishops are stirred to diligence; he commends observance of the canons; all are to assemble for synods; presbyters and deacons alike, as well as priests, are to be consecrated only on Sundays, LIV, 617.

To the bishops throughout Italy: he warns that his vigilance has uncovered many Manichaeans in the city of Rome and that they too must seek them out with equal diligence, LIV, 620.

Letter to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the day on which priestly or Levitical blessing ought to be celebrated, LIV, 625.

On repeating the sacrifice of the Mass in order to provide for people who arrive later, LIV, 626.

Letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne, concerning the case of Hilary, bishop of Arles, LIV, 628.

Letter to the African bishops of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis: he rebukes ordinations carried out amid disturbance; explains what it means to lay hands on someone hastily; deacons, presbyters, and bishops must be men of only one wife [lacuna]. Concerning Donatus, converted from the Novatians, and Maximus, converted from the Donatists; virgins violated by force ought not to regard themselves as defiled; what is to be done concerning them; ecclesiastical cases are to be referred to the Apostolic See, LIV, 645.

Letter to the bishops of Illyricum: they are not to refuse to come when summoned by Anastasius to a council; no one is to be ordained bishop without the consent of the people; no bishop may claim for himself the cleric of another bishop against that bishop’s will, LIV, 664.

Letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica: the bishops of Thessalonica have always discharged the functions of the Apostolic See; concerning metropolitans; residence, etc.; the continence of subdeacons; the regular holding of provincial councils; the suppression of translations of bishops; fugitive clerics; the summoning of bishops by the metropolitan.

Letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, concerning the errors of the Priscillianists, LIV, 677.

Letter to the bishops of Sicily, concerning baptism: it is to be celebrated not at Epiphany but at the Paschal feast; concerning the preservation of the distinction between times and mysteries; why baptism is administered only at the solemnities of Easter and Pentecost; in necessity baptism is to be administered at any time; concerning a council to be held yearly at Rome, LIV, 695.

Letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against the faithlessness and heresy of Eutyches; concerning Christ’s twofold birth and nature, LIV, 756.

Letter to the Emperor Theodosius: he sends delegates in his stead to the synod at Ephesus, convened on account of Eutyches, LIV, 781.

Letter to the Empress Pulcheria: Christ is a human being of our race; the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches; when the reality of Christ’s flesh is attacked, the whole faith is shaken, LIV, 785.

Letter to the same: he calls upon her zeal against Eutyches; human salvation requires that Christ be not merely human, but human of the same race as ourselves; custom, the condition of the times, and affection for his fellow citizens prevent Leo himself from attending the council, LIV, 789.

Letter to the archbishops, etc., of Constantinople: he denounces the teaching of Eutyches, etc., LIV, 795.

Letter to the Synod of Ephesus: the faith of the Incarnation is proved from Peter’s confession, etc., LIV, 797.

Letter to Julian, bishop of Cos: Eutyches destroys Christian hope and the truth of all the mysteries, LIV, 803.

Letter to Ravennius, archbishop of Arles, concerning Petroniacus, a wandering man falsely claiming to be a deacon: he orders his expulsion from the communion of all churches, etc., LIV, 815.

Letter to the Emperor Theodosius: he asks that a special synod be held in the regions of Italy, etc., LIV, 821.

Letter to the same, concerning the false synod of Ephesus: another general synod against it is to be held in Italy, LIV, 826, 832, 839, 844.

Letter to the Emperor Theodosius: he writes that he adheres to the Nicene faith; Eutyches must be condemned no less than Nestorius; he requests that councils be held within Italy, LIV, 855.

Letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople: he rejoices that they remain always attached to Flavian and resist error; the reality of Christ’s flesh is proved from the mystery of the Eucharist, etc., LIV, 865.

Letter to the Empress Pulcheria: the foundations of the faith are shaken by Eutyches; he desires, with her consent, that a general council be held against him, LIV, 873.

Letter to the people of Arles: he gives his judgment in the longstanding controversy between the Churches of Arles and Vienne, assigning to each its own boundaries, LIV, 881.

Letter to Ravennius, bishop of Arles: he sends him his celebrated letter to Flavian concerning the incarnation of the Word of God against Eutyches, and in defence of the faith, etc., LIV, 886.

Letter to the Emperor Theodosius: he withholds his consent to the ordination of Anatolius of Constantinople; he requires a profession of faith, etc., LIV, 890, 893.

[Col. 1261] Letter to the presbyter Martin: how good it is to suffer for truth, etc., LIV, 899.

Letter to the presbyters Faustus and Martin: he writes that what was done at Ephesus against the faith is intolerable to the Western bishops; both Nestorius and Eutyches serve Antichrist, against whom the Church professes not one nature but that she worships one person, LIV, 901.

Letter to the Empress Pulcheria: he gives thanks that Nestorius and Eutyches have been restrained by her authority, etc., LIV, 909.

Letter to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople: concerning his faith, proved by the writings sent; concerning those who fell into heresy through fear, that they should be received if converted; concerning the names of heretics not to be recited at the holy altar, LIV, 913.

Letter to Bishop Julian: he warns that the fallen ought not to be received into communion unless their faithlessness has been condemned together with its authors, LIV, 917.

Letter to the Emperor Marcian: he rejoices in the preservation of the Catholic faith, for which peace in the empire is rendered in return; action is to be taken only against those who err, not against the faith or the Scriptures, which it is unlawful to interpret otherwise than the holy Fathers did, LIV, 917.

Letter to the Empress Pulcheria, concerning the fallen and Eutyches, LIV, 821, 922.

Letter to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum: he sends him his letter to Flavian, by which he was to be instructed as a legate at the synod; he affirms Christ’s two natures against Eutyches, etc., LIV, 927.

Letter to the Emperor Marcian, concerning the delegates sent to the general council to act in his stead, where everything is to be brought back to unity of faith and peace, LIV, 930.

To the same, concerning the council first convened at Nicaea and later transferred to Chalcedon, LIV, 932.

Letter to the synod: the necessity of the time, etc., prevents him from attending the synod; nevertheless, he will be present through the delegates whom he sends, LIV, 935.

Concerning the celebration of Easter in the following year, 452: unity in its celebration must be preserved, LIV, 945.

Letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning the condemnation of heretics, LIV, 983.

To the same: he sends them a copy of the sentence of condemnation pronounced against Eutyches and Dioscorus, LIV, 987.

Letter to the Emperor Marcian concerning the ambition of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, LIV, 991, 997.

To Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople: he rebukes him for ambition, LIV, 1001.

To Julian, bishop of Cos: the great authority to be accorded to the Council of Nicaea; he reproves him for favouring Anatolius of Constantinople, etc., LIV, 1009.

To Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii: every bishop ought to have recourse to his metropolitan in doubtful matters; a penitent who dies before reconciliation cannot be reconciled after death; reconciliation is not to be denied to anyone at the point of death who seeks it, etc., LIV, 1011.

To Julian, bishop of Cos, concerning the restraint of Palestinian monks because of their violence against Catholics, etc., LIV, 1014.

To the Emperor Marcian, concerning Aetius and Andrew, LIV, 1019, 1023, 1024.

To the Synod of Chalcedon: he agrees with what was established at Chalcedon concerning the faith; what was done there against the Nicene canons is never to be regarded as ratified by him, LIV, 1027.

Concerning perseverance in the faith: heresies, having arisen not without benefit to the Church, are to be suppressed by irrevocable judgment; the Church’s victory over heretics is Christ’s victory, etc., LIV, 1046.

To the Emperor Marcian: care of the Paschal cycle was formerly entrusted to the bishop of Alexandria; what difficulty arose from it, LIV, 1055, 1058.

To the Empress Eudocia, concerning the Palestinian monks: he asks her to devote her care to bringing the Palestinian monks back to faith and peace; having accepted the Synod of Chalcedon, they must denounce both Eutyches and Nestorius if they wish to be considered Catholic, LIV, 1060.

To the monks of Palestine: he warns them that both Eutyches, who confuses the natures in Christ, and Nestorius, who makes the person twofold, are to be detested, etc.; he reproaches these same monks for the scandals arising from their fury, and exhorts them to repent and embrace the common faith, LIV, 1062.

To Julian, bishop of Cos, concerning the restoration of the bishop of Jerusalem and the conversion of the Palestinian monks: he wishes a more careful inquiry to be made into Easter of the year 455, etc., LIV, 1071.

To the Emperor Marcian: he declares that he will gladly receive Anatolius into favour, provided that he satisfy the canons and not undermine the rights of bishops, LIV, 1073.

To Proterius, bishop of Alexandria: bishops must be vigilant lest the unity of faith be violated, etc., LIV, 1075.

To the Emperor Marcian: he promises Anatolius his favour if he repents; he asks that Eutyches, spreading his poison, be relegated in exile to more secluded places, LIV, 1094.

To Euxitheus, bishop of Thessalonica, and others: he exhorts them vigorously to resist the criminal attempts of the Eutychians who had killed Proterius, bishop of Alexandria; they must not permit another synod to be convened, but must uphold their steadfastness in the Chalcedonian Synod, LIV, 1120.

Letter to the Emperor Leo: after the Council of Chalcedon nothing further is to be discussed concerning the faith, etc., LIV, 1127.

Letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, concerning women who, owing to the captivity of their husbands, married others; whether a man who took the place of a captive husband is culpable; the wife must be restored to her first husband; women refusing to return to their first husband are to be excommunicated, etc., LIV, 1375.

Letter to the presbyters, deacons, etc., of Constantinople: he exhorts them to remain steadfast in the faith and separate from the fellowship of heretics; no new judgment is to be instituted; concerning Atticus and Andrew, deprived of the rank of their order, LIV, 1142.

Letter to the Emperor Leo, concerning the Eutychians, etc., LIV, 1148, 1155.

Concerning a presbyter or subdeacon who falsely claimed to be a bishop, and those whom he ordained as clerics; concerning a presbyter or deacon who, once his crime is known, seeks public penance—whether it should be granted to him through laying on of hands, LIV, 1203.

Concerning those who minister at the altar and have wives: whether they lawfully have intercourse with them, etc., LIV, 1204.

Concerning those who take wives after penance or join concubines to themselves, LIV, 1207.

Concerning those abandoned as infants by Christian parents, where it cannot be discovered whether they were baptized: whether they ought to be baptized, LIV, 1208.

Letter to all the bishops of Campania, Samnium, and Picenum: the regeneration of baptism is not to be conferred at every time, but only at Easter and Pentecost, unless dangerous illness intervenes; concerning the penance of the faithful, their confession is not to be made public, LIV, 1209.

To the Emperor Leo, concerning Timothy Aelurus, expelled from the Church of Alexandria, and the election of a Catholic bishop in his place: integrity of faith and moral character alike are required in a priest; the impious Aelurus cannot be restored, even if his faith should perhaps be sound, LIV, 1212.

LEO II, pope.—Letter to the Emperor Constantine: he confirms and approves what was done and determined in the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, XCVI, 400.

Letter to the bishops of Spain: he recounts the proceedings of the Sixth General Council, in which the heretics having been condemned, the Catholic definition of faith concerning the two wills and operations in Christ was promulgated; he transmits it for publication to all, and the bishops themselves are to subscribe to it, XCVI, 411.

Letter to Count Simplicius: he recounts the proceedings of the council, sends the definition for the bishops to subscribe, and asks him to ensure that it is made known to all under his jurisdiction, XCVI, 416.

LEO IV, pope.—Letter to the bishops of Britain: he teaches that simoniacal bishops are to be judged in a council; he then answers: to whom ecclesiastical order belongs; that every parish is to be governed by the oversight of its bishop; that a presbyter is not to be compelled to bring *eulogiae*—blessed bread—to holy councils; that no one is to marry a wife within a prohibited degree of kinship; by what decrees bishops ought to judge, CXV, 667.

LEO VI, pope.—He exhorts Formin, bishop of Zadar, Gregory, bishop of Nin, and the other bishops of Dalmatia to obey John, archbishop of Split; he orders each bishop, and specifically the bishops of Osor, Rab, and Ragusa, to be content with his own boundaries, and Gregory, bishop of the Croats, to remain content with administering the Church of Skradin, CXXXII, 813.

LEO VII, pope.—Letter to Hugh, king of the Franks and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours: he forbids women to be admitted into the monastery of Blessed Martin, CXXXII, 1072.

Letter to the Gauls and Germans: he orders many matters pertaining to discipline to be corrected, CXXXII, 1085.

LEO IX (Saint), pope.—Bull by which he removes the Perugian monastery of Saint Mary of Valle Ponte from the bishops of Perugia, CXLIII, 595.

He subjects the monastery of the Holy Cross, situated at Rome, to Richer, abbot of Monte Cassino, and his successors, CXLIII, 605.

At a synod at Mainz of forty bishops, in the presence of Emperor Henry, he condemns the Simoniacal heresy, etc., CXLIII, 621.

He commands Count William of Nevers, under penalty of excommunication, to restore to the monastery of Saint Bercharius at Déols what he had taken away, CXLIII, 644.

At a synod of forty-five bishops, he inscribes Gerard, formerly bishop of Toul, in the catalogue of saints and orders that he be venerated on 23 April, CXLIII, 644.

Letter to the princes of Britain: he pronounces judgment for the Church of Tours against the Church of Dol; he excommunicates those who resist, the Simoniacs, and those ordained by them, CXLIII, 648.

He releases Edward, king of England, from his vow to go to Rome because of the disturbed state of the kingdom; and commands him to distribute to the poor the money set aside for the journey and to expend it upon building a new monastery of Blessed Peter or restoring an old one, CXLIII, 674.

To all bishops throughout Italy: no one is to give all his possessions to a monastery, but at least half of them to the church to which he belongs, CXLIII, 685.

He commands the bishops of Venice and Istria to render obedience to the patriarch of Grado, whose primacy, granted by the Apostolic See, he had confirmed in a synod, CXLIII, 727.

To Thomas, an African bishop: he shows that the archbishop of Carthage holds primacy over all Africa, etc., CXLIII, 727.

He praises Bishops Peter and John because at his command they held a council concerning ecclesiastical affairs and defended the rights of the archbishop of Carthage against the bishop of Gummi, CXLIII, 729.

Letter to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, against his and Leo, bishop of Acrida’s unprecedented presumptions and excessive absurdities, CXLIII, 744.

He approves the ordination of Peter, bishop of Antioch, if he was promoted according to the canons; exhorts him to safeguard the dignity of his church; approves as identical with that held by the Roman Church the faith which Peter wrote to him, and sends him a summary of that faith, CXLIII, 769.

He congratulates Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, for seeking to reconcile Greeks and Latins; he rebukes him both for trying to subject the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch to his authority, for appropriating to himself the title “universal patriarch,” and for condemning the Roman Church because it consecrates the holy sacrament of the Eucharist with unleavened bread. He proves that Christ consecrated with unleavened bread, CXLIII, 773.

LUCIUS II, pope.—He commands Raymond, bishop of Maguelonne, to pronounce canonical sentence against the count of Gévaudan and others as sacrilegious persons unless they restore to the monastery of Saint Theofred what Bernard, formerly count of Gévaudan, had bequeathed to that monastery by testament, CLXXIX, 844.

He commands Peter of Bourges, Arnold of Narbonne, Raymond of Arles, Pons of Aix, and William of Embrun, archbishops, to ensure the restoration of what had been taken from the monastery of Marseille, CLXXIX, 844.

To Pons, abbot of Vézelay: against the killers of Abbot Artald, CLXXIX, 852.

He informs Gregory, bishop of Bergamo, what he has decreed in the controversy of the canons of Saints Vincent and Alexander, CLXXIX, 859.

To Alfonso, king of Portugal, who had made his kingdom tributary to the Roman Church, CLXXIX, 860.

Bull confirming the ruling of Pope Urban II concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol to the Church of Tours, CLXXIX, 875.

To the bishops of Saint-Brieuc and Tréguier: he absolves them from the obedience promised to the bishop and Church of Dol, CLXXIX, 877.

To Geoffrey, count of Brittany, and Henry his brother: that they not hinder the bishops of Brittany from being subject to the Church of Tours, CLXXIX, 879.

To the count of Nevers: that he restore to Vézelay what he took away, CLXXIX, 888.

To the bishops of Gaul: he forbids churches or chapels to be built in parishes belonging to the monastery of Cluny, CLXXIX, 891.

He commands Gregory, bishop of Bergamo, to compel the priests of his diocese to render loyalty to the churches of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander, CLXXIX, 898.

To the bishops of Arras and Cambrai: that they investigate a matrimonial case and relax the excommunication incurred on that account, CLXXIX, 899.

To the bishops of Arras and Thérouanne: that they ensure compensation for the damages inflicted upon Walter of Waldon while he was on his way to Jerusalem, CLXXIX, 899.

[Col. 1264] He summons Henry, bishop of Olomouc, to Rome on certain ecclesiastical business, CLXXIX, 902, 903.

To Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: that he admonish the count of Nevers not to exact anything from the people of Vézelay beyond what is lawful, CLXXIX, 910.

To Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud: he signifies that he has entrusted the resolution of her controversy with Ulger, bishop of Angers, whether by agreement or judgment, to delegated bishops, CLXXIX, 924.

To the bishop of Burgos in Spain: that he entrust to the Cluniac brothers the reform of the church of Caradigua, CLXXIX, 528.

He commands Otto, bishop of Prague, to protect the monastery of Rajhrad against Duke Vratislav of Brno and other nobles, CLXXIX, 929.

To Peter of Cluny, concerning the subjection of the abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict above the Po to the abbot of Cluny himself, CLXXIX, 930.

The monastery of Saint Sabas is subjected to the Cluniacs in perpetuity, LXXIX, 931.

To the monks of Saint Pancras: he declares void charters by which sons become successors to their fathers in churches, CLXXIX, 934.

LUCIUS III, pope.—He informs Philip, archbishop of Cologne, that he has ordered the provost of Bonn to excommunicate the count of Sayn if he had not compensated the damages inflicted on the monastery of Siegburg, CCI, 1076.

He commands apostolic delegates to investigate the disobedience of the parish priest of the Church of Saint Bartholomew and, if they find it established, to punish him, CCI, 1097.

To Simon, bishop of Meaux: he confirms his statute concerning the residence of those holding benefices in the Church of Meaux, CCI, 1106.

He ratifies the constitution of the canons of Piacenza, CCI, 1126.

To the bishops and clergy of Scotland, concerning the absolution of William, king of Scotland, CCI, 1127.

To Theobald, abbot of Cluny: he decrees that no other order or religious community is to be established in parishes under Cluniac jurisdiction, CCI, 1432.

He commands all prelates of churches to excommunicate those who lay ambushes for monks travelling to the general chapter of Cluny, CCI, 1157.

He commands Stephen, bishop of Autun, and Manasses, bishop of Langres, that nothing be done contrary to the privilege granted to Cistercian monks, CCI, 1161.

He commands the abbots of Vézelay and Flavigny to compel the canons of Chalon and Mâcon to restore to the monastery of Tournus the churches taken from it, CCI, 1171.

He establishes the monastery of Monreale as an archiepiscopal see, consecrates Abbot William as archbishop, etc., CCI, 1778.

He commands the bishops of Cefalù and Patti to obey Richard, archbishop of Messina, CCI, 1183.

Sentence against sacrilegious invaders of ecclesiastical rights, from whom every recourse to appeal is removed, CCI, 1227.

Judgment against robbers who abused the remedy of appeal against ecclesiastical statutes, CCI, 1229.

To Maurice, bishop of Paris, against presbyters accused of fornication, CCI, 1231.

He commands the abbot and monks of Classe to obey the archbishop of Ravenna, CCI, 1244.

He commands the dean and chapter of Rouen, because the archbishop has died, to see to it that William, bishop-elect of Coutances, be consecrated by the suffragan bishops of the Church of Rouen, CCI, 1248.

Statute concerning the oath of beneficed persons regarding residence, CCI, 1253.

He testifies that the churches of Bologna and Modena were consecrated by him, without prejudice to the right of Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna, CCI, 1276.

Decree against heretics, CCI, 1297.

To the chapter of Rouen: he approves the election of the bishop of Lincoln as archbishop of Rouen, CCI, 1300.

He commands the bishops of Patti and Cefalù to obey Richard, archbishop of Messina, CCI, 1315.

He commands the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of the Franks to assist the monks of Saint-Denis in enforcing the monastery’s rights, CCI, 1319.

He commands the bishop of Verona to require laypeople to pay tithes to the canons of Verona, CCI, 1320.

He permits the monks of Saint Remigius, during general excommunications or interdicts, to celebrate the offices with closed doors, CCI, 1324.

To Walter, archbishop of Rouen: none are to be instituted in churches unless they are priests or soon to become priests and are prepared to reside there; nor are persons who are less fit to be instituted, even if presented by patrons, CCI, 1325.

He informs Hartwig II, archbishop of Hamburg, that because of the troubled condition of those kingdoms he has postponed summoning the disobedient bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, CCI, 1356.

He informs the clergy of Rhodigius that he has delegated to the bishop of Passau the case of a new church built by them to the prejudice of the Church of Saint John the Baptist of Costa, subject to the monastery of Saint Cyprian at Murano, CCI, 1364.

MARTIN I (Saint), pope.—Encyclical letter to all Christ’s faithful: a synod assembled at Rome against the heretics Theodore, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, who were anathematized in it, LXXXVI, 120.

Letter to Amandus, bishop of Maastricht: he dissuades him from resigning the bishopric; sends the acts of the Roman synod, that they may be confirmed by the bishops of Gaul in an assembled synod; he urges him to recommend to King Sigebert the sending to the city of bishops who may act as envoys to the emperor, LXXXVII, 136.

Letter to the Emperor Constans: he announces that the heresy of the Monothelites was condemned in the council whose acts he sends, and exhorts the emperor to condemn the same heresy, LXXXVII, 137.

Letter to the Church of Carthage: he approves the confession of faith which they had sent; exhorts them to defend it; sets forth the acts of the Lateran Council against the Monothelites, LXXXVII, 145.

Letter to John, bishop of Philadelphia: he appoints him vicar in the East with power to appoint bishops and presbyters and to restore those returning to the faith after falling away to their former rank of dignity; he disapproves the election of Macedonius and Peter made by heretics; he sends the acts of the council for publication, LXXXVII, 153.

Letter to Theodore, bishop of Esbous: he shows that by his confession Theodore had checked the fury of the heretics, and exhorts him to obey John, bishop of Philadelphia, whom he had appointed vicar, LXXXVII, 163.

Letter to Antony, bishop of Bacatha: since he has now repented, he admonishes him to persist in the Catholic faith and to spare the bishop of Philadelphia, LXXXVII, 165.

Letter to George, archimandrite of the monastery of Saint Theodosius: he praises him for defending the minister of the Apostolic See and urges him to obey the bishop of Philadelphia, LXXXVII, 167.

Letter to Pantaleon: the bishop of Dora, falsely accused by him, had been absolved; those through whom it was brought about that he did not receive the authority of the Apostolic See to ordain bishops and presbyters had sinned; and concerning what should be done with those who had not been canonically elected in the patriarchate of Jerusalem, LXXXVII, 169.

Letter to the illustrious Peter: his integrity of life is commended, and he is exhorted to support the pope’s vicar, LXXXVII, 173.

Letter to the Churches of Jerusalem and Antioch: he announces that the heresy of the Monothelites was condemned in the council, and that the ordinations of Macedonius at Antioch and Peter at Alexandria were wrongly performed; they are to remain steadfast in the Catholic faith and obey John the vicar, to whom he sent the acts of the said synod, LXXXVII, 175.

Letter to Paul, bishop of Thessalonica: because he not only failed, as he had promised, to repent, but also caused the representatives of the Apostolic See to be led into heresy, he is anathematized and deposed, LXXXVII, 181.

Letter to the Church of Thessalonica, concerning Paul’s condemnation and the need to avoid his heresy, LXXXVII, 191.

Letter to Theodore: he recounts what he suffered at Rome, when Calliopas the exarch forcibly seized him there and sent him to Constantinople, LXXXVII, 197, 199, 201.

NICHOLAS I, pope.—Bull for the monastery of Fulda: he commands that an account of the condition of this monastery be rendered to him repeatedly, CXIX, 770.

Letter to the Emperor Michael: he complains that a synod at Constantinople, without authorization from the Apostolic See, had dared to deprive Ignatius of his office and replace him with Photius; he shows that a layman cannot ascend to the rank of episcopal dignity, etc., CXIX, 773.

To Photius: he reserves the entire matter concerning him until the arrival of the delegates, etc., CXIX, 780.

To the bishops established in King Charles’s realm, concerning Ingeltrude, the fugitive wife of Count Boso: they are to excommunicate her if she scorns to return to her husband, CXIX, 780.

To King Charles: he urges him diligently to ensure that Lothair expel Ingeltrude from his kingdom and compel her to return to her husband, CXIX, 781.

[Col. 1266] To Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier: he absolves him and his clergy from an oath, CXIX, 782.

To all the faithful: he teaches that Ignatius was deposed and Photius substituted in the Eastern Church by delegates of the Apostolic See without any consent of his, CXIX, 783.

To Photius: he refutes Photius’s arguments that, by the example of Ambrose, Nectarius, and Tarasius, he had rightly risen from the lay rank to episcopal dignity; he shows that Photius unjustly ascended to that rank both because he was a layman and because Ignatius was still living, CXIX, 785.

Letter to the Emperor Michael: he disapproves the deposition of Ignatius and the promotion of Photius rashly approved by the delegates, etc., CXIX, 790.

That the Lord Jesus Christ suffered only in the flesh; concerning those who say that the divinity is passible and further maintain that in baptism original sin is not remitted to everyone; concerning those who presume to strike a bishop, CXIX, 795.

Letter to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, concerning the divorce between King Lothair and his wife Theutberga, CXIX, 796.

To King Lothair: he sends delegates to convene a synod, at which he orders two bishops from King Charles’s realm to appear, etc., CXIX, 798.

To Charles the Bald, king: that two bishops of his kingdom travel to the synod to be convened at Metz, CXIX, 799.

To the bishops of Gaul and Britain: that they attend the Synod of Metz with the delegates, hear Lothair there, investigate the case of his divorce, and determine it canonically, CXIX, 800.

To the bishops sitting in the Council of Metz: that they examine and decide Theutberga’s case and send him the acts of the council, CXIX, 801.

To Charles the Bald, king, and Queen Ermentrude: he asks them to spare Baldwin, who had abducted their daughter and taken her as his wife, CXIX, 303, 304.

To Stephen, count of Auvergne: he commands him to restore Sigo, bishop of Auvergne, to his church after expelling its invader, and to present himself before the synod of the delegates to answer the charges, CXIX, 805.

To Solomon, king of the Bretons, concerning a renewed examination, before the archbishop of Tours or before the Apostolic See, of the bishops who had been expelled, CXIX, 806.

To Charles, archbishop of Mainz, and his suffragan bishops of Germany: he declares that he has pronounced no sentence against Bishop Solomon; that Abbo’s marriage, contracted in the fourth degree of consanguinity, must be dissolved; and he assigns differing penances for differing sins, CXIX, 809.

To Hincmar, archbishop of Reims: that he restore the deposed Rothad, bishop of Soissons, to his see within thirty days, or come to Rome with him to plead the case, CXIX, 825.

To the bishops of the Synod of Senlis: he annuls the acts of the synod against Rothad; orders that he be recalled from exile and sent to Rome with the synod’s delegates for a reconsideration of the judgment, etc., CXIX, 826.

To Charles the Bald, king: that he have Rothad restored to his former dignity and then permit him to come to the Apostolic See, to which he had appealed, etc., CXIX, 837, 838.

To the bishops established in Lothair’s kingdom: that they urge King Lothair, after removing Hilduin, to whom he had given the Church of Cambrai, to grant freedom to elect a bishop, CXIX, 841.

To King Lothair: that he reject Hilduin, invader of the Church of Cambrai, and permit Hincmar to exercise his privilege in arranging its affairs, CXIX, 842.

To the cleric Hilduin: that henceforth he abstain from the Church of Cambrai, which he had seized, CXIX, 843.

To King Charles: a decree concerning the governance of monasteries is sent to him, to be confirmed under the anathema of all bishops by queens and churches, CXIX, 844.

To the Emperor Michael: concerning the deposition of Photius, the installation of Patriarch Ignatius, and the deposition and excommunication of Bishops Zacharias and Radoald, with chapters appended, CXIX, 850.

To Charles the Bald, king, on behalf of Robert, bishop of Le Mans, against the monks of Saint-Calais, CXIX, 863, 864, 865, 866.

To King Lothair: a bishop is to be elected by apostolic authority, not by royal favour, CXIX, 869.

To Hincmar, archbishop of Reims: he expresses indignation that Rothad was prevented from travelling to Rome; orders that he be sent as soon as possible, and forbids the ordination of a bishop in his place in the meantime, etc., CXIX, 871.

[Col. 1267] Bull for the union of the bishoprics of Hamburg and Bremen, issued in the year 864, CXIX, 876.

To Rudolf, archbishop of Bourges, and his fellow bishops: concerning Theutgaud and Gunthar, condemned by the Apostolic See; he warns them wholly to abstain from communion with them, CXIX, 881.

Absolution and restoration of Bishop Rothad, CXIX, 892.

To Charles the Bald, king: he urges him to support the restored Rothad and to order the return of property taken from his Church, CXIX, 893, 897, 899.

To the archbishops established in Lothar’s kingdom: that they should rebuke Lothar freely and compel him to put away the adulteress whom he keeps, CXIX, 915.

To Louis, king of Germany, and Charles the Bald: he reproves them for not having sent bishops to the city for the synod; urges them to continue warning Lothar about the divorce; concerning bishops to be consecrated in the Churches of Cologne and Cambrai, etc., CXIX, 921.

Letter to the Emperor Michael: he rebukes him for having written many insolent things in pride and arrogance; shows that Ignatius’s deposition was without force, since he had been condemned by suspect, excommunicated, and inferior bishops; recalls much concerning the privileges of the Roman Church; orders Ignatius and Photius, or their representatives if they themselves cannot come, to appear before him, etc., CXIX, 926.

To Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims: he orders a synod to be convened at Soissons concerning Wulfad and his companions, CXIX, 964.

To Festinian, bishop of Dol: he rebukes him for not having written with due reverence, and orders him to recognize the Church of Tours as metropolitan, unless he proves the contrary by authentic documents, CXIX, 969.

To all bishops: he again admonishes them concerning the sentence of excommunication which he had issued against Waldrada and her accomplices, CXIX, 971.

Replies to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, CXIX, 978.

To the Emperor Michael: he urges him kindly to hear the legates; repeats what he had already said concerning Photius, Rhadoald, Ignatius, and Zachary; asks him to order burned the letter full of insults which the emperor himself had sent, etc., CXIX, 1016.

To Photius: he charges him with many crimes committed in usurping Ignatius’s see; proves that he violated both divine and human law; announces that he has been deposed and, if he does not obey the sentence, threatens him with perpetual excommunication until death, CXIX, 1045.

To Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople: he informs Ignatius of everything done in his case since the return of the legates Zachary and Rhadoald, and how Photius was deposed and anathematized in the council together with his followers, while Ignatius himself and his party were restored, CXIX, 1058.

To the Empress Eudocia: he asks her to advocate Ignatius’s cause before the emperor, CXIX, 1063.

To the clergy of Constantinople: condemnation of Photius; repeated condemnation of Gregory, bishop of Syracuse; deprivation of those ordained by Photius; restoration of Ignatius; restoration of bishops exiled by Photius; concerning sacred images, CXIX, 1074.

To the senators of Constantinople: that they should support Ignatius’s cause and abstain from communion with Photius, CXIX, 1089.

To the bishops of the Synod of Soissons: he sharply censures Hincmar for proceeding craftily and evasively in the case of the deposed clerics, and for daring to produce mutilated and corrupt letters of Pope Benedict; he therefore orders the bishops to meet again, etc., CXIX, 1093.

To Wulfad, cleric of Rheims, and his companions: he congratulates them on their restoration, which he ratifies, and warns them not to avenge injuries and especially to show reverence to Hincmar, CXIX, 1112.

To the nobles of Aquitaine: that they should without delay restore the property of Churches which they unjustly retain in whatever fashion, and thereafter abstain from it, CXIX, 1114.

To King Charles: that he should ensure that Lothar restore what he had taken from Helletrude, his sister, widow of Berengar, CXIX, 1115.

To the bishops established in Louis’s kingdom: no one is to be subjected unwillingly to monastic discipline, CXIX, 1120.

To Ado, archbishop of Vienne: concerning the judgments and interdicts of the Apostolic See, CXIX, 1121.

To Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims: concerning the penance imposed on one who had killed a monk who was a priest, CXIX, 1122.

To the same: accuser and accused must both be present, CXIX, 1123.

To Frotary, archbishop of Bordeaux: [Col. 1268] what penance is to be imposed upon invaders of ecclesiastical property, CXIX, 1124.

To John, archbishop of Ravenna: concerning those who, having dismissed their wives, have entered other marriages, CXIX, 1125.

To Adalwin, archbishop of Salzburg: concerning a widow who, after receiving the veil of a nun, returned to marriage, CXIX, 1125.

To the same: that a bishop or cleric must by no means devote himself to hunting, CXIX, 1126.

To Solomon, bishop of Constance: no one is to be condemned unless he has confessed voluntarily or been canonically convicted, CXIX, 1127.

Whether a man may have two spiritual co-mothers; concerning the penance of parricides and incestuous persons; concerning a certain penitent matricide, CXIX, 1127.

Concerning a cleric who kills a pagan, CXIX, 1129.

How wicked it is to unite with blood relatives; that one who kills a pagan in self-defense is to forfeit priestly office; concerning the penalty of a priest who strikes a deacon; and very many other decrees, CXIX, 1131, 1132.

Concerning those who scourge and kill bishops: that a priest who is a murderer is to forfeit priestly office; that, if a bishop has been killed, another is not to be appointed in his place until the perpetrators have been identified and punished, CXIX, 1134.

Letter to Queen Theutberga: he rebukes her for writing against herself, overcome by weariness, and denies that what she proposes can be done—namely, that she may dissolve her marriage for the sake of continence—unless her husband Lothar also promises a celibate life, CXIX, 1136.

To the bishops established in Lothar’s kingdom: he writes for the third time concerning Waldrada’s excommunication; notes their negligence, and orders them to report whether Lothar lives with Theutberga and how he treats her, CXIX, 1139.

To Charles the Bald and others: concerning Theutberga, CXIX, 1142, 1146, 1150.

To Hincmar and the other bishops established in Charles’s kingdom: he explains the causes of Greek hatred and envy against the Latin Church; sends their objections for refutation and asks that whatever they find against them be transmitted to Rome, CXIX, 1152.

To Charles the Bald, king: he asks him to assist the bishops in holding meetings concerning the matter entrusted to them, CXIX, 1161.

To Louis, king of Germany, and others: that he should finally cease intervening for Theutgald and Gunthar, CXIX, 1161, 1163.

He complains concerning Lothar, etc., CXIX, 1163, 1174.

Letter to the bishops sent as legates into Francia: he sends them a memorandum concerning Theutberga’s case, CXIX, 1179.

Letter to King Charles the Elder: concerning the marriage of Charles the Younger, CXIX, 1182.

Decrees: concerning the constitutions of the Church, custom, judgments, the Roman Church and Apostolic See, priests, clerics, monastic vows, laymen, churches, baptism, penance, marriage, impediments to marriage, and wars, CXIX, 1163–1200.

**PASCHAL II, pope.**—To Hildephonsus, king of Spain: that Didacus has been canonically removed from the Church of St. James at Compostela, CLXIII, 33, 34.

He forbids Godinus, bishop of Oria, under penalty of excommunication, to claim for himself the goods of the bishopric of Brindisi, CLXIII, 34.

Bull to Ivo, bishop of Chartres: that no one, upon his death or that of any successor, may presume on any pretext to plunder the episcopal residence, CLXIII, 35.

He commands Ivo of Chartres and Bannon, bishop of Saintes, not to neglect the decree of the Council of Clermont concerning monastic altars, CLXIII, 36.

Bull concerning the union of the Church of Orange with that of Tricastin, and other documents concerning the said union, CLXIII, 38, 58.

Letter to the archbishops and bishops of Gaul: he decrees infamous those bound by a vow to undertake the Jerusalem expedition who withdrew from it, or who shamefully departed from the siege of Antioch; but orders the restoration of possessions to those returning after victory had been achieved, CLXIII, 43.

Concerning the destruction of the Church of Compostela: he forbids the clergy of Compostela, on the pretext of the Jerusalem journey, to abandon their province, CLXIII, 45.

Concerning the consecration of Didacus, bishop-elect of Constantinople, CLXIII, 63, 64.

To the people of Velletri: he repeals the unlawful measures established among them by Guibert and defines their boundaries, CLXIII, 66.

[Col. 1269] To Henry, king of England: against ecclesiastical investitures, CLXIII, 70.

To Didacus, bishop of Compostela: concerning the reform of the corrupt morals of this Church, which had entered it through wars, CLXIII, 79.

To Bernard of Toledo, Gerald of Braga, etc.: he orders them to come to Rome for a synod, CLXIII, 80.

To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: that he should work for the restoration of the English Church and reconcile the king of England with the duke of Normandy, CLXIII, 80.

He commands Peter, bishop of Poitiers, to make satisfaction to Cluny concerning the consecration of the abbot of St. Cyprian, and orders satisfaction to be made to that monastery concerning the abbot of Maillezais, CLXIII, 81.

To the archbishop of Braga and the bishops of Compostela and Tui: that Pelagius’s marriage is not to be dissolved, CLXIII, 87.

To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: that he should stand firm in defending the liberty of the English Church, CLXIII, 90.

To Henry, king of England: against ecclesiastical investitures, CLXIII, 94.

To Bishop Osbern: that monks are not to be forbidden to have in their monastery a cemetery for burying their own members, CLXIII, 95.

Bull concerning the foundation of the monastery of Cheminon, CLXIII, 99.

To Ivo, bishop, and the canons of Chartres: he forbids accepting payment for ecclesiastical benefices or bringing ecclesiastical business before secular authorities, and confirms the excommunication issued by Ivo concerning houses adjoining the church, CLXIII, 100.

To Anselm of Canterbury: investitures are not to be granted to kings or other lay magistrates, CLXIII, 105.

To the same: concerning ecclesiastical investitures, sons of clerics, and the case of the bishop of Wales, CLXIII, 106.

To Gerard, archbishop of York: he warns him to make his profession to Anselm of Canterbury according to the custom of his predecessors, CLXIII, 107.

To Robert, count of Flanders: that the Church should expel the schismatics of Liège who adhere to Emperor Henry, CLXIII, 108.

He commands Gonzalo, bishop of Mondoñedo, either to restore to Didacus, bishop of Compostela, the two archpresbyterates unjustly retained, or to plead his case before Bernard, archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Apostolic See, CLXIII, 113.

To Henry, king of England: on behalf of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, who was lawfully contending with the king concerning ecclesiastical investitures, CLXIII, 119.

He urges Gebhard of Hirsau and the other Catholic abbots and monks throughout Swabia to endure hardships patiently and to honor Gebhard of Constance; he announces that Arnold, the excommunicated invader of the Church of Constance, is excommunicated, CLXIII, 121.

To Welf, duke of Bavaria, Berthold, duke of Swabia, etc.: he calls them back to the Catholic Church, CLXIII, 121.

To the Gauls: he removes the interdict to which the bishop of Autun had subjected the Church of Vézelay, CLXIII, 122.

To Bertrand, count of Toulouse: he rebukes him for invading the borough of St. Giles and displaying altar offerings as though they were merchandise of the populace, CLXIII, 124.

To the archbishops and bishops of the provinces of Rheims, Sens, and Tours: that they should absolve King Philip and his concubine from the bond of excommunication, CLXIII, 128.

To princes, knights, and other laymen throughout Spain and Gaul: concerning an unlawful union, CLXIII, 134.

To Stephen, abbot, and the monks of St. Giles: he declares that he will excommunicate Bertrand, count of Toulouse, and some of his knights unless they desist from the injuries inflicted upon the monastery, CLXIII, 139.

To the monks and other faithful of St. Giles: that no one, without the abbot’s consent, may presume to alienate or defraud anything from altar offerings, CLXIII, 139.

He commands Gisela, abbess of Remiremont, to desist from injuries against the monks of Chaumousey, CLXIII, 140.

He warns Count Eustace to allow Lambert, bishop of Arles, to remain in possession of certain altars, CLXIII, 140.

To Manasses, archbishop of Rheims: concerning the restoration of ten churches to Lambert, CLXIII, 141.

To Lambert, bishop of Arras: concerning certain clerics absolved from excommunication, CLXIII, 141.

To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: [Col. 1270] that supporters of investitures in England were excommunicated at the Lateran Council, CLXIII, 154.

To Robert, count of Meulan: he threatens God’s wrath if he continues persuading the king of England to oppose the Roman Church in investiture cases, CLXIII, 154.

To the clergy of the Church of Paris: he commends to them Galon, made bishop of Paris, who is departing from him, and sends him with the fullest authority, CLXIII, 157.

To Didacus, bishop of Compostela: concerning ministers to be maintained, CLXIII, 170.

To Gonzalo, bishop of Mondoñedo: he states that he has learned that the archpresbyterates of Bisancos, Trasancos, and Salagia belong by right to the Church of Compostela, and commands him no longer to claim them, CLXIII, 170.

To Rothard, archbishop of Mainz: concerning bishops invested by kings, and likewise those consecrated during the time of schism, CLXIII, 174.

To all the Gallican clergy: he recounts Werner’s usurpation of the Apostolic See, CLXIII, 179.

He forbids Abbot Adam and the monks of St. Denis, without the permission of Galon, bishop of Paris, to approach other bishops to receive sacraments, CLXIII, 180.

To Gisela, abbess of Remiremont: under penalty of excommunication, he commands her to desist from harassing the monks of Chaumousey, CLXIII, 182.

To the bishops of Gaul: against the murderers of the abbot of Vézelay, CLXIII, 196.

To Gebhard of Constance and Oderic, bishop of Pavia: not every excommunicated person is to be avoided, CLXIII, 197.

To Hugh, abbot of Cluny: he forbids anyone to exact tolls or anything else from those going to Cluny or returning from it within the designated boundaries, CLXIII, 201.

To William of Sabran and the other associates of Bertrand, count of Toulouse: he calls them to make satisfaction, under penalty of excommunication, for damages inflicted upon the monastery of St. Giles, CLXIII, 202.

To Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, and the bishops of his province: he relates the adulteries of Bertrand, count of Toulouse, and the damages inflicted on the monastery of St. Giles, and urges them to restrain others from aiding or communicating with him and his associates, CLXIII, 203.

To the monks and burgesses of St. Giles: he announces that Bertrand, count of Toulouse, has been excommunicated by him, and orders them, under penalty of excommunication, to abstain from him, CLXVIII, 207.

To Gebhard, bishop of Constance: he rebukes him for attending the consecration of Henry, the invested archbishop of Magdeburg, and for failing to come when summoned to the council, CLXIII, ibid.

To Rothard, archbishop of Mainz: he charges him with certain offenses committed by him, and sends him some extracts from the sacred canons so that he may not henceforth err through ignorance, etc., CLXIII, 214.

To the abbot of St. Pons and the bishop of Elne: that they should not receive persons excommunicated by the bishop of Narbonne, CLXIII, 223.

To Hugh, abbot of Cluny: he places the abbey of St. Walmar under him for reform; its abbots are forever to be appointed by the abbots of Cluny, and any monk may transfer to the monastery of Cluny, CLXIII, 225.

To Adelgot, archbishop of Magdeburg: he summons him to the Apostolic See to render an account of an offense committed, CLXIII, 233.

To Bruno, archbishop of Trier: he entrusts to him the absolution from excommunication of the bishop of Liège, CLXIII, 234.

He assigns to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the monastery of St. Germanus at Auxerre, CLXIII, 235.

He commands Lambert of Arras and John of Thérouanne to judge between the canons of Tournai and the monks of St. Martin, CLXIII, 237.

To several bishops and abbots of Gaul: concerning the legation of the Apostolic See entrusted to Girard, bishop of Angoulême, CLXIII, 240.

To Eustace, bishop of Valence, and Leodegar, bishop of Viviers: that they should restrain Bertrand, count of Toulouse, absolved from excommunication at their prayers, while he was again despoiling the monastery of St. Giles, CLXIII, 242.

To Berengar, bishop of Fréjus, and Leodegar, bishop of Apt: that they should cease attacking the monastery of St. Giles with the count of Toulouse, CLXIII, 243.

To Didacus, bishop of Compostela: that no one is to celebrate Mass upon the altar of St. James except bishops or the seven cardinals, CLXIII, 24.

[Col. 1271] He commands the bishop of Huesca to make satisfaction to the bishop of Barbastro for injuries inflicted, CLXIII, 251.

He commands the Catholic brethren of the Church of Verdun to avoid Richard, the excommunicated bishop, CLXIII, 253.

He urges the abbots and clerics of Guy’s archdeaconry to obey Guy, who had been deposed by Richard, invader of the Church of Verdun, CLXIII, 254.

To the bishops of Anagni and Campania: concerning the canonization of St. Peter, bishop of Anagni, CLXIII, 261.

To Gebhard, bishop of Constance: concerning those communicating with excommunicated persons and how heretics are to be received, CLXIII, 265.

To Didacus, bishop of Compostela: concerning the restoration of the church of St. Michael to Peter the chaplain, CLXIII, 273.

To Peter, bishop of Poitiers: that he should warn Hugh of Lusignan not to delay making amends for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of St. Maxentius, CLXIII, 275.

To Leodegar, bishop of Viviers: he rebukes him for allowing the church of St. Andeolus, assigned by him to the canons of St. Rufus, to be taken from them by his clerics, CLXIII, 280.

To Didacus, bishop of Compostela: he warns that Queen Urraca, daughter of the king of Castile, must, under penalty of forfeiting her kingdom, desist from the incest she entered into by marrying Alfonso, king of Aragon, who was related to her in the third degree of consanguinity, CLXIII, 280.

To Pons, abbot, and the monks of Cluny: he rebukes them for having caused chrism to be consecrated in their monastery, CLXIII, 281.

To the clergy and people of Arles: that they should elect another in place of their bishop Gibelin, transferred to Jerusalem, CLXIII, 282.

He orders the regalian rights to be restored to King Henry by bishops and abbots, CLXIII, 283.

He asks Emperor Henry to order the restoration of goods taken from the Church of Rimini, CLXIII, 288.

To Baldwin, king of Jerusalem: he decrees that, in order to enlarge the boundaries of the diocese of Jerusalem, all cities which Baldwin subdues are to be subject to Jerusalem as their metropolitan, CLXIII, 289.

To John of Tusculum and Leo of Vercelli, bishops and cardinals: he promises to annul and invalidate the concession of investitures made to the emperor, CLXIII, 290.

To Guy, bishop of Vienne: that the investiture of clerics is to be taken away from kings, CLXIII, 292.

To the clergy and people of Arras: he forbids the Church of Arras to be subjected to that of Cambrai, CLXIII, 297.

To Baldwin, bishop of Noyon and Tournai: that he should not allow the brethren of the monastery of St. Martin to be harassed by the clerics of Tournai, CLXIII, 310.

He urges the bishops and princes of Spain to put an end to the overthrowing of churches, killings, robberies, and burnings, CLXIII, 321.

To the clerics of the Church of Tournai: he grants them their own bishop, free from the yoke of Noyon, CLXIII, 532.

To the twelve arbitrators of Arras: that they should decide impartially the dispute between the clerics of the Church of Arras and the monks of St. Vedast, CLXIII, 335, 336.

To John, bishop of the Morini: concerning preservation of the liberty of the monastery of St. Bertin at Sithiu, CLXIII, 340.

To Lawrence, abbot of St. Vitonus: that he should render neither obedience nor communion to the clerics of Verdun, CLXIII, 335.

He urges Didacus, bishop of Compostela, to labor for the restoration of peace, CLXIII, 256.

To Bono the Elder, bishop of Reggio: those born after their godfather or godmother has received children from the font may not marry one another, CLXIII, 369.

To the clerics of Thérouanne: those unwilling to leave their wives are to be deprived of offices and benefices, CLXIII, 369.

He enjoins Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, to undertake nothing against the bishop of Burgos, CLXIII, 376.

To the canons of Lyons: he rescinds the sentence of interdict pronounced by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, upon the churches of the monastery of Savigny, and commands observance of the settlement made by the bishop of Mâcon concerning the castle of Varennes, CLXIII, 370.

To the people of Canterbury: concerning the translation of Ralph from the see of Rochester to Canterbury, CLXIII, 376.

To King Henry and the bishops of England: he reproves them for doing many things wrongly without consulting the pope, CLXIII, 378.

To Guy, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See: that he should end the dispute between the canons of Besançon and those of St. Stephen, CLXIII, 380.

[Col. 1272] He commands Gonzalo, bishop of Coimbra, to return to the obedience of Maurice of Braga, CLXIII, 390.

To Vitalis, abbot of Savigny: he permits the brethren of Savigny to celebrate the divine offices during an interdict, CLXIII, 397.

To the clergy and people of Florence: he declares Innocent to be their bishop and deprives his accusers of offices and benefices, CLXIII, 397.

To the archbishops, bishops, and clergy of England: he announces that he is sending Anselm, abbot of St. Sabas, as legate to England to hold synodal assemblies, CLXIII, 407.

To the Church, king, and people of Jerusalem: he announces that he has restored Arnulf, patriarch, whom his legate had forbidden from exercising episcopal office, CLXIII, 408.

To the clergy of the Church of Augsburg: that their bishop, accused of adultery, has not yet been absolved by him, CLXIII, 412.

To the canons of St. Mary in Porto at Ravenna: that they should observe the rule drawn up by Peter the canon, CLXIII, 414.
