To King Henry of England: in the case of Thurstan, archbishop of York, expelled from his church without judgment, CLXIII, 420.

To Frederick, archbishop of Cologne: he approves the king’s excommunication pronounced by him, and urges him to assist the Roman Church, CLIII, 423.

He urges Conan, count of the Bretons, to compel the monks of Redon to restore Belle-Île to the monks of Quimperlé, CLXIII, 427.

To William, count of Nevers: that he should allow the monastery of Vézelay to remain undisturbed and free, CLXIII, 427.

To the canons of St. Martin: whatever the faithful offer to the Church under the name of an offering belongs to the category of offerings and ought not to be possessed by laymen, CLXIII, 436.

Let him be excommunicated who obtains churches through laymen, CLXIII, 438.

Statute concerning burials and the wills of the deceased, CLXIII, 438.

To Victor of Bologna: monks are not to usurp episcopal rights without the bishops’ consent, CLXIII, 439.

To Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg: that he should examine the case of the abbot of St. Emmeram, accused of simony, CLXIII, 440.

Concerning the bishop of Regensburg, who denies obedience to the Roman Church, CLXIII, 441.

To Henry, bishop of Regensburg: that he should restore the abbot of St. Emmeram; otherwise, let him know that he is under interdict, CLXIII, 441.

To Peter, abbot of Cluny: concerning the prohibition of intincted communion, CLXIII, 442.

**PAUL I, pope.**—He has several letters written to King Pippin and others, all congratulatory, filled with praise and thanksgiving, and urging in various ways the advancement of the glory of the holy Roman Church, LXXIX, 1136–1196.

**PELAGIUS I, pope.**—Letter to Narses: he urges him to provide the legates with help for correcting bishops who disturb the Church, LXIX, 393.

He warns the same man to restrain schismatics, LXIX, 394.

To Narses, the patrician: that he should repress the schismatics by whom he had unjustly been barred from communion, LXIX, 397.

To the bishops of Tuscany: he reproves them for schism, LXIX, 398.

To all the people of God: concerning the Catholic faith, LXIX, 399.

To King Childebert: he pronounces anathema upon those who think otherwise concerning the faith than is contained in Leo’s letters and the Council of Chalcedon, etc., LXIX, 402.

To Sapaudus, bishop of Arles: he delegates to him his authority in Gaul, etc., LXIX, 405, 406.

To King Childebert: he sends his confession of faith and warns him not to allow any discord to be stirred up in Gaul by heretics, LXIX, 408.

He proves that the Father and the Son are one God, LXIX, 419.

**PELAGIUS II, pope.**—Letter to Gregory the deacon: that he should obtain from the emperor assistance against the Lombards, LXXII, 703.

To Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre: he commends the orthodox faith of the Frankish kings and urges him to persuade them not to make an alliance with the Lombards, etc., LXXII, 705.

To John, bishop of Constantinople: he rebukes him for claiming for himself the title of universal bishop, for which reason he had convened a general synod, LXXII, 738.

He disapproves transfers of bishops from one church to another when the Church’s need does not require it, LXXII, 749.

[Col. 1273] To the bishops of Italy: bishops are to be held in the highest honor and cannot be accused by just anyone, LXXII, 755.

To the bishops of Germany and Gaul: that the Roman Church receives nine prefaces to be sung during the solemnities of Mass, LXXII, 758.

**SERGIUS III, pope.**—Letter to Ancelius, bishop of Uzès: he informs him that Pope Formosus has been condemned by him, CXXXI, 272.

He vindicates the rights of the Church of Bremen, CXXXI, 974.

**SERGIUS IV, pope.**—He rebukes Amalric, archbishop of Aix, for harassing the monastery of Montmajour, CXXXIX, 1521.

**SILVERIUS, pope.**—Letter to Vigilius, pseudo-pope: he reproaches Vigilius with ambition for the Apostolic See and the crime of simony, and condemns him by a sentence of anathema, LXVI, 85.

Concerning false witnesses not to be admitted or received against a bishop, LXVI, 86.

**SILVESTER II, pope.**—Concerning the election of Theotard as bishop of Le Puy, CXXXIX, 274.

He sends the sacred crown to Stephen, duke of the Hungarians, whom he also honors with the royal title; by various privileges granted, he establishes the Church of Esztergom as metropolitan of the kingdom, CXXXIX, 274.

Letter to Azelin, bishop of Laon: he summons him, accused of many crimes, to the next synod at Rome, CXXXIX, 277.

Letter to Emperor Otto III: he informs him that he has commended to the bishop of Pavia the monastery of nuns at Pavia called that of Senator, and asks him to confirm this constitution, CXXXIX, 285.

**SIMPLICIUS, pope.**—Letter to Zeno, bishop of Seville: concerning the authority entrusted to him in all the churches of Spain; he appoints the excellent man, the bishop of Seville, vicar of the Apostolic See, LVIII, 35.

Letter to John, bishop of Ravenna: he rebukes John because he had ordained Gregory bishop by using force; he commands Gregory to govern the Church of Modena, having no case against John, LVIII, 35.

Letter to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, bishops: Gaudentius, bishop of Aups, because of illicit ordinations performed, is deprived of priestly office and of a third part of the Church’s revenues, LVIII, 37.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he asks him to restrain by royal power Timothy Aelurus, who was attempting again to occupy the Alexandrian see and secretly disseminate his heresies from Constantinople, LVIII, 38.

He writes to Acacius that he should oppose Timothy by every effort, lest the universal council which Timothy was pursuing before the emperor be held, LVIII, 41.

He commends Acacius because no church in Constantinople had been opened to Timothy Aelurus, and urges him to warn the emperor not to allow the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon to be violated, LVIII, 42.

Letter to the priests and archimandrites of Constantinople: he commends the steadfast faith of the clerics and monks dwelling at Constantinople, because they had not admitted Timothy to communion; he shows that Timothy, repeatedly condemned, must not be heard, LVIII, 43.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he congratulates him on recovering the empire and urges him to restore the Alexandrian bishop to his see and ensure the observance of the decrees of Leo and of the Council of Chalcedon, LVIII, 44.

Letter to the same: he gives thanks that Timothy has been restored to the Church of Alexandria and asks him to order the expulsion of Peter, disturber of that Church, LVIII, 48.

Letter to the same: he writes that Timothy, the Catholic bishop at Alexandria, had sought pardon from him because, through fear, he had recited Dioscorus’s name among the altars; and that he had sent letters to the emperor asking him to keep Peter, disturber of the said Church, at a distance, LVIII, 49.

Letter to Emperor Zeno: he urges him to protect Timothy, restored to the Church of Alexandria through his agency, and to order Peter, disturber of that Church, to be kept at a distance, LVIII, 49, 51.

Letter to the same: he praises the emperor’s diligence in punishing those who conspired at Antioch to kill bishops; grieves that his letters to Acacius were not executed; and approves the election of the bishop of the Church of Antioch, made without observing the decree of the Council of Nicaea, LVIII, 51, 53.

Letter to Acacius: he complains that, together with the emperor’s letters, he received no letter from him; that the emperor sought the installation of Peter, a heretic, as bishop of Alexandria while he himself had been prepared to confirm John; and finally prays that Acacius warn the emperor not to wish to favor a heretic already condemned, LVIII, 56.

[Col. 1274] Letter of Simplicius to Emperor Zeno: he says that he is amazed that Acacius had in no way warned him about the troubles of the Church of Alexandria, and urges him to inform the emperor so that the desired peace may be restored to that Church, LVIII, 59.

**SIRICIUS, saint and pope.**—Decrees: enactment against all heresies; leaven sent by the bishop to priests; Manichaeans driven into exile; Manichaeans are not to receive communion with the faithful; converts among them are to be tested in monasteries and are to receive viaticum at the end of life, XIII, 1128.

Letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona: the manner of receiving heretics into the Church; times and rites for receiving baptism; persons to whom baptism is to be given immediately; apostates are to be cut off from Christ’s body, though pardon is not to be denied at life’s end to penitents; no one may marry another’s betrothed; monks or nuns who violate their commitment to chastity are to be punished; clerical incontinence; the authority of the Old Testament is pleaded in vain; priests and deacons are bound by an indissoluble law of continence; honor is preserved for those who fell through ignorance, but not for others, XIII, 1133–1140.

A priest or deacon who has married twice is not to be ordained; the age of candidates for ordination; a cleric who takes a second wife is to be deposed; what women may live with clerics; promotion of monks to the clergy; no cleric is permitted to perform penance; concerning penitents, bigamists, and husbands of widows, who are not to be admitted to clerical orders, XIII, 1141–1145.

Letter to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica: that no one in Illyricum is to ordain a bishop without Anysius’s consent, XIII, 1148.

Letter to the bishops of Africa: Siricius, with a synod, sets out how much care bishops must take for the Church’s purity; seeking to restore old commands now neglected by some, he determines how bishops are to be ordained; that a cleric may not marry a widow and that one who has married a widow, or who after remission of sins has worn the belt of secular military service, is not to be admitted to the clergy; that no one may ordain a cleric from another church; likewise, concerning persons who have been dismissed and are not to be received; concerning Novatians and Montanists returning to the Church; concerning the continence of priests and Levites; that merciful judgment should not be lacking, XIII, 1155.

Letter to various bishops: that no unworthy person should be made bishop; that the priesthood should not be given to unknown persons; and that neophytes or laymen should not be made priests, XIII, 1164.

Letter to various bishops against the heretic Jovinian and others: he publicly exposes the perverse teaching of Jovinian and his associates, and announces by name the condemnation of its principal authors, XIII, 1168.

Letter to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, and the other bishops of Illyricum: asked for a judgment concerning Bonosus, he does not wish to pronounce one, but orders the judges assigned to him by the Synod of Capua to fulfill their office; meanwhile he confirms that Bonosus was rightly reproved and regarded with horror for his error concerning Mary’s children, XIII, 1176.

Canons: the knowledge of truth is to be sought, and reached by prayers; alteration of traditions leads into heresy; reasons are supplied for questions proposed, XIII, 1181.

Concerning a veiled virgin who changes her commitment: what judgment is to be made; concerning a girl not yet veiled who likewise falls away from her commitment; bishops, priests, and deacons are bound by the law of continence; worshippers of idols, when about to sacrifice to demons, imposed continence upon themselves; one baptized who has fallen into fornication is not to be admitted to the clergy, XIII, 1182–1187.

That there is to be one faith and one tradition; priests may administer baptism outside Easter, but deacons are not granted the same permission; one may not marry one’s wife’s sister; those who have exercised secular jurisdiction are not to be admitted to ministry at the altar; the stain of simony and popular favor in elections must be avoided; one may not marry one’s uncle’s wife; laymen are not to be promoted to the episcopate; no one is to move from church to church; clerics dismissed by their own bishop are not to be received or promoted by others, XIII, 1187–1193.

It is not lawful to conduct ordinations in another’s territory; laymen excommunicated by their own bishop are not to be promoted to the clergy by another, XIII, 1193–1194.

**STEPHEN II, pope.**—Letter to Pippin, king of the Franks: he gives thanks for the promises conveyed through Abbot Droctegang, who had been sent by Pippin to Pope Stephen and had announced that the pope wished to come into Francia, LXXXIX, 993.

Letter to the nobles of the Franks, asking them to support his petition before King Pippin and to lend their aid in undertaking the cause of the Church, LXXXIX, 995.

[Col. 1275] Letter to Pippin and his sons, the kings: since Aistulf delayed to restore the cities and was harassing the Church with fresh attacks, he beseeches the king to bring aid and diligently to fulfill in deed the donation promised to Saint Peter, LXXXIX, 996.

Letter to King Pippin: with the city of Rome besieged by Aistulf and the Lombards, he writes a tearful letter, once again imploring Pippin’s assistance with every entreaty, LXXXIX, 999.

Letter to the Franks, imploring their support against the Lombards, LXXXIX, 1004.

Letter to King Pippin, giving thanks for the liberation of the City and for the benefit bestowed upon the Roman Church; concerning the death of King Aistulf and his successor Desiderius; he asks that Desiderius be commanded, in accordance with the pledge he gave, to restore the remaining cities of the exarchate and Pentapolis not yet returned, LXXXIX, 1007.

Letter to King Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, asking them to compel Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who violated his oath to restore the cities and places granted to him, to do justice regarding what he promised, LXXXIX, 1011.

Decrees.—Concerning a man who, dismissing his slave-woman, married a free-born wife; whether one spouse may be unable to render the marital due; concerning a man who has a wife in his homeland while residing in another region; if someone marries a baptismal or confirmation co-mother; concerning unveiled virgins if they marry; concerning monks and nuns if they enter marriage; concerning a widow who, having received the veil, subsequently marries; whether a healthy man may marry a leprous woman; concerning one who, not knowing by whom he was ordained, celebrated Masses and baptized, then later, after abandoning his office, took a wife, LXXXIX, 1024–1026.

Concerning a priest who, for want of water, baptized an infant in danger with wine; whether it is permissible to baptize with water poured from a shell or the hands; concerning a priest who baptized while knowing neither the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, nor the psalms, and whether he himself was ordained; concerning a priest who added certain words to the baptismal formula and does not know whether the man who ordained him was a bishop, LXXXIX, 1026–1027.

Concerning bishops accused and condemned; priests and deacons accused; a priest whose crime committed before ordination became known; hair not to be worn long by clerics or monks; a woman who married another man when her husband was falsely thought to have died in a foreign province, LXXXIX, 1028.

STEPHEN III, pope.—Letter to Bertrada, queen consecrated to God, asking her to reward Itherius, whom he says had laboured vigorously for the Church’s interests in the duchy of Benevento, LXXXIX, 1248.

Letter to Queen Bertrada and King Charles, concerning Christopher and his son Sergius, who, together with Dodo and other Franks, attempted to kill Pope Stephen, LXXXIX, 1249.

Letter to Kings Charles and Carloman, congratulating them on their reconciliation in fraternal concord; asking them to request that the Lombards restore what they had seized from the patrimony of the Church, LXXXIX, 1251.

To the same persons, earnestly seeks to dissuade them from allowing either of them to marry Desiderius’s daughter, or from giving their sister Gisila in marriage to Desiderius’s son, LXXXIX, 1253.

STEPHEN V, pope.—Letter to Emperor Basil, reproving him for his defense of Photius and refuting the insults directed against the supreme pontiff, CXXXIX, 785.

Letter to the Eastern bishops: when they sought from him a dispensation for the ordination of Stephen, patriarch of Constantinople, because he had been ordained deacon by Photius, he replies and requests further information, CXXXIX, 795.

Letter to Dominic, archbishop of Ravenna, informing him that he had consecrated a bishop for Piacenza, but did not wish thereby to impair in any respect the rights of the metropolitan of Ravenna, CXXIX, 798.

Letter to the clergy and people of Piacenza, giving them Bernard as bishop and commending submission to the metropolitan of Ravenna, CXXIX, 799.

Letter to Amelius, bishop of Uzès, declaring that Gisbert, bishop of Nîmes, will be excommunicated unless he repents, CXXIX, 804.

Letter to Girbert, bishop of Nîmes, warning him not to use force against the monastery of Saint Giles, CXXIX, 804.

Letter to Robert, answering how a cleric whose finger has been cut off may be promoted to ecclesiastical orders, XXIX, 805.

STEPHEN X, pope.—Letter to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: promises assistance to one acting courageously for religion; postpones the cause of the archbishop of Bourges; summons him to Rome for a synod together with his suffragans, CXLIII, 869.

SYMMACHUS, pope.—Letter to Aeonius, bishop of Arles [Col. 1276], directing him and the bishop of Vienne to send reliable persons to Rome, who, informed concerning their controversies, may present their allegations to the Apostolic See, LXII, 49.

Concerning the bishop-elect of Aquileia, to whose election he gives his assent, LXII, 49.

Letter to Aeonius, bishop of Arles: annulling the innovations made by his predecessor Anastasius in the dispute concerning Vienne, he orders the ancient decrees of the Apostolic See to be observed, LXII, 50.

Letter to Caesarius, bishop of Arles: that Church property not be alienated; that no one receive ecclesiastical rank for bribes; that laymen be advanced to the priesthood through the grades; that abductors of widows or virgins be excluded from Church communion; that widows or virgins professing continence not marry; and that no one attain the episcopate by canvassing, LXII, 54–55.

Letter to the bishops of Gaul, confirming the division of the province between the Churches of Vienne and Arles established by Pope Leo, LXII, 64.

Constitution abolishing the law of King Odoacer, contrary to ecclesiastical liberty in the election of a pontiff, and concerning the preservation of Church property, LXII, 72.

THEODORE I, pope.—Letter to Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, accusing him on two grounds: first, because he had not removed from public places the document of Heraclius’s *Ecthesis*, which Pyrrhus had posted; secondly, because he occupied the see of Pyrrhus, who had abdicated the patriarchate under compulsion of hostility, while Pyrrhus was still alive and not yet condemned. He therefore orders a synod to be convened in the presence of his apocrisiaries, so that Pyrrhus’s case may be examined, etc., LXXXVII, 75.

URBAN II (Saint), pope.—Informs the bishop of Salzburg and other bishops of his election as supreme pontiff, and exhorts them to contend manfully for the Church, CLI, 283.

Informs Hugh, abbot of Cluny, that the pontificate has been conferred upon him, and asks him to come to him, CLI, 284.

To the bishops of Vienne, etc., concerning the election of an archbishop of Vienne, since that metropolitan see had long been without a pastor, CLI, 285.

To Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the Church’s distresses and his acceptance of the pontificate, CLI, 286.

Letter to Alfonso, king of Galicia, congratulating him on the Church of Toledo’s liberation from the Saracens, CLI, 289.

Warns the archbishops of Spain concerning the restoration of the primacy of Toledo, CLI, 290.

To the abbots of Pistoia and of Vallombrosa, concerning Wezelo, archbishop of Mainz, deposed for simony, CLI, 294.

Letter to the bishops of Germany, informing them who are to be regarded as excommunicated, CLI, 299.

To Elias, bishop of Bari, concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Nicholas and the dignity and rights of the Church of Bari, CLI, 307.

Letter to Rainerius, priest and legate of the Holy Roman Church, appointing him judge between the bishop of Barcelona and the abbot of Saint-Pons of Tomières, CLI, 314.

Letter to Flotard, abbot of Tomières, exhorting him to make satisfaction for injuries inflicted on the archbishop of Narbonne, CLI, 315.

Commends the archbishop of Vienne and orders restoration of what Artald, provost, had squandered from the property of the Church of Vienne, CLI, 316.

Letter to the suffragans of the Church of Arles, informing them that he has declared void oaths extorted from Bishop Guibelin; he declares infamous those who seize him, CLI, 317.

Letter to Richer, archbishop of Sens: commends to him Ivo, bishop of Chartres; declares Geoffrey anathema-stricken if he attempts to invade the bishopric, CLI, 326.

Letter to Romuald, bishop of the Church of Monopoli: by decision of the Council of Benevento, declares that the bishopric of Monopoli is subject not to the Church of Brindisi but to the Roman See, CLI, 328.

Entrusts the island of Corsica, restored under Gregory VII to the ancient jurisdiction of the Roman Church, to Daibert, bishop of Pisa, and his successors, CLI, 330.

Letter to Berengar, bishop of Ausona, appointing him archbishop of Tarragona, CLI, 331.

To the priors of Vallombrosa and Camaldoli, that they not separate themselves from communion with Pisa, CLI, 333.

Exhorts the bishop of Constance, dukes, and counts to protect the abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour at Schaffhausen against Tato, who was attempting to take away an estate granted to the monastery, CLI, 336.

Letter to Berengar, archbishop of Tarragona, warning him not to act negligently in establishing the Church of Tarragona, and directing him to obey the primate, the archbishop of Toledo, now appointed his vicar throughout Spain [Col. 1277] and in the province of Narbonne, CLI, 346.

Letter to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, reproving them because they allowed a king both to dismiss his wife and to take another, CLI, 554.

Letter to Robert, count of Flanders, directing him to refrain from harassing clerics, CLI, 356.

To the clergy and people of Arras, directing them, having cast off the yoke of the bishop of Cambrai, to elect a bishop to be consecrated by the metropolitan, CLI, 356.

Letter to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, ordering him to consecrate as bishop the man elected by the clergy and people of Arras, CLI, 357.

To Anselm, archbishop of Milan, concerning the reconciliation of the fallen, CLI, 358.

Permission is granted to Guemer of Merseburg for a cleric who had killed a boy by throwing a stone to remain in his order after undertaking perpetual penance, CLI, 338.

That Albert, bishop of Metz, should treat with gentleness a certain priest who had obtained his rank by simony, CLI, 358.

Letter to the princes and people of the Church of Dol, directing them to restore property taken from the Church of Dol, CLI, 359.

To the clergy and people of Amiens, ordering them to obey Bishop Gerewin, who had been cleared of simony, CLI, 362.

Establishes that those who visit the monastery of Saint Mary on specified days shall receive absolution from sins, CLI, 365.

Letter to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, rebuking him because he had not yet consecrated the bishop-elect of Arras, CLI, 366.

Letter to Renaud, abbot of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers, entrusting him with the task of collecting money for the support of the Roman Church, CLI, 369.

The Church of Syracuse is confirmed after Count Roger expelled the Hagarites, under penalty of excommunication against anyone who disturbs it in any way, CLI, 370.

Issues a canonical ruling concerning the king of Aragon, who had pledged in faith to give his niece to a certain knight, CLI, 373.

Letter to the Catholic Saxons, announcing that he had consecrated the bishop-elect of Halberstadt, disregarding the metropolitan of Mainz because of schism, CLI, 375.

To the clergy and people of Halberstadt: praises them for electing another bishop in place of one who had lapsed into schism, and approves the election, CLI, 376.

Letter to Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, enumerating many serious charges on which he was accused; orders him, in order to clear himself, to appear either before Renaud, archbishop of Reims, or before the pope himself, CLI, 378.

That Lambert, bishop of Arras, is henceforth to be obeyed, CLI, 382–383.

Letter to William, count of Poitiers, exhorting him to restore what he took from the monastery of Vendôme, CLI, 384.

Decision concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol to Tours, CLI, 385.

Letter to all bishops throughout Brittany, confirming the judgments of other supreme pontiffs and directing them to obey the archbishop of Tours as metropolitan, CLI, 387.

To Renaud, archbishop of Reims, complaining that he wished Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, already cleared before him of the accusation, to be cleared again, CLI, 388.

Letter to Durand, bishop of Clermont, ordering him to command the canons of Billom to restore the monastery of Saint Lupus to the monks of Cluny, CLI, 392.

Letter to William, count of Toulouse, rebuking him over the expulsion of the abbots of Moissac and Lézat, CLI, 392.

Letter to the bishop of Cahors, ordering him, after expelling Hanaldo, to restore Ausquilinus to the monastery of Moissac, CLI, 393.

Letter to Godfrey, bishop of Lucca, declaring that those who kill excommunicated persons out of zeal for the Church are not to be considered murderers, CLI, 394.

Letter to Robert, count of Flanders, and his nobles, exhorting them to help Lambert, bishop of Arras, recover the Church’s possessions, CLI, 406.

Decree establishing that, after the death of Bishop William, the Church of Orange shall be joined to the Church of Tricastin, CLI, 416.

Apostolic letters confirming the rule of regular clerics established by Peter, bishop of Carcassonne, in the Church of Saint Nazarius and elsewhere, CLI, 418.

The canons of the Church of Canterbury are confirmed in the profession of regular life which they had recently made, CLI, 423.

[Col. 1278] The regular discipline of the canons of the Church of Avignon is confirmed, etc., CLI, 426.

Letter to Guarnerius of Châtillon, ordering him, under pain of excommunication, to release Lambert, bishop of Arras, who had been captured while travelling to a synod, CLI, 429.

Decree concerning the primacy of Lyons, CLI, 438.

Letter to Adhemar, bishop of Angoulême, directing him to compel by the censure of excommunication the monks of Saint Cybard to obey the abbot of Saint John of Angély, CLI, 443.

Letter to the suffragans of the Church of Reims, directing them to obey Manasses, appointed in the place of the deceased Archbishop Renaud, CLI, 443.

Letter to Philip, bishop of Châlons, commending to him and to his brother Hugh, count of Champagne, the monks of Saint Viton of Verdun, expelled by his parishioners from the Church of Saint Nicholas in the wood of Lugolli, CLI, 447.

At the Council of Tours, settles the dispute between the canons of Saint Martin and the monks of Cormery, CLI, 456.

Letter to the canons of Saint Martin of Tours against simoniacs, CLI, 457.

Letter to the bishops of the Franks concerning the refusal to absolve an excommunicated king, CLI, 460.

Against clerics who had violated the cemetery of Saint Orientius, CLI, 464.

At the council held at Nîmes, repealing a command of Gregory VII, forbids the monasteries of Frigolet and Comps to be united; orders each monastery to be governed by its own abbot, CLI, 469.

Letter to Coloman, king of Hungary, against Guibert the antipope, or Clement III, CLI, 480.

Letter to Gebhard, bishop of Constance, directing him to ensure that the monks of Reichenbach restore a certain monk to the monks of Schaffhausen, CLI, 482.

Letter to the people of Bologna, praising their faith and offering remission of sins to all who participate in the war for Jerusalem, CLI, 483.

Letter to Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, concerning the expedition to the Holy Land and taking up the cross, CLI, 485.

That contemners of the canons are to be excommunicated, CLI, 485.

Restores to the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés the monastery of Glanfeuil, adjudged to them, CLI, 489.

Against clerics who had violated the cemetery of Saint Orientius, CLI, 494.

The district of Salmorium is affirmed to belong to the Church of Constantinople, CLI, 494.

Letter to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, directing him to compel the archbishop of Aix to obey his primate, the archbishop of Narbonne, CLI, 496.

Letter to Bernard, bishop of Bologna, commending certain brothers ordained unwillingly by heretics, CLI, 500.

To Peter, bishop of Huesca, establishing the Church of Huesca as the head of the Church of Jaca, CLI, 502.

Writes to William, king of the English, that he should make Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, free in his kingdom and reinvest him with all his possessions, CLI, 506.

Affirms to Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, and his successors the primacy over the provinces of Acerenza and Cosenza, CLI, 507.

To the bishop of Magdeburg, exhorting him not to waver but to persevere in the righteous cause, CLI, 518.

Letter to the bishops of Embrun, Gap, and Digne: before they are reconciled, no one is bound to maintain fidelity to excommunicated persons, CLI, 521.

To Rotger, bishop of Soissons, that regular canons be appointed in parish churches, CLI, 521.

Absolves Petronius, bishop of León, born of a mother not lawfully married, from the bond of this fault, CLI, 527.

Entrusts to Countess Matilda the restitution by the bishop of Mantua of the Church of Saint Florian, for the benefit of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone, CLI, 527.

To the clergy and people of Salerno, concerning ecclesiastical immunity, CLI, 528.

Letter to Godinus, bishop of Oria, ordering him to restore to the city of Brindisi the episcopal see formerly transferred to the city of Oria, CLI, 528.

Letter to Vitalis, a priest of Brescia: mercy may be shown to simoniacs in allowing them to retain their rank, if their lives commend them, CLI, 528.

A wife must not, together with her husband, receive someone’s child at baptism, CLI, 529.

Concerning the validity of baptism and the other sacraments administered by criminal priests, CLI, 529.

[Col. 1279] Permits the infant daughter of Prince Jordan, betrothed against the wishes of her mother and kindred to Renaud, son of Rodel, to be given in marriage to another man, CLI, 534.

Writes to certain regular canons concerning the restoration of canonical discipline, CLI, 535.

Letter to Bernard, archbishop of Toledo: since the legateship has been taken from Richard, bishop of Marseille, Bernard himself is to watch over all matters; the archbishop of Compostela, freed from chains, is to be restored to his office; Bernard is to indicate whom he judges should be entrusted with the legateship, CLI, 536.

Letter to the archbishops and bishops of France, rejoicing that King Philip, who had dismissed his wife and joined himself to an adulteress, had returned to his senses, CLI, 538.

Bull establishing the see of Barbastro, CLI, 539.

Letter to Ingelram, bishop of Laon, exhorting him to restore the altar of Carbonnières to the brothers of Saint Remigius, CLI, 539.

Letter to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, informing him that at last his primacy had been acknowledged at Rome by Raimbert, archbishop of Sens, CLI, 543.

Orders that in the monastery of Saint Peter at Casale there shall always be preserved the same institution of regular discipline which Andrew, the monastery’s founder, had established according to the custom of the brothers of Vallombrosa, CLI, 544.

Concerning the recall of Robert, abbot of Cîteaux, from the wilderness, CLI, 545.

The dispute of the canons of Saint Andrew of Bordeaux with the clerics of Saint Seurin was settled at a Roman council in such a way that the Church of Saint Andrew should have its own cemetery in perpetuity, CLI, 545.

Bull declaring, on the revelation of the most holy Father Benedict and a sign of restored health, that the body of the most blessed lawgiver and patriarch of monks Benedict rests at Monte Cassino, CLI, 549.

Orders the clergy and people of Limoges to obey Bishop Humbald, cleared of simony and restored by the pope to his former standing, CLI, 551.

URBAN III, pope.—To the clergy and people of Split, informs them that he has deferred judgment because the archbishopric of Zadar was vacant, CCII, 1332.

Orders Ralph, bishop of Angers, Maurice, bishop-elect of Nantes, and the abbot of Fougères to expel the abbot of Saint Melaine of Redon, appointed by the count, CCII, 1342.

Bull confirming the judgment issued by Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, abbot of Bonnevaux, concerning disputes between Arducius, bishop, and Count William, CCII, 1343.

Informs the bishops and all persons throughout the province of Canterbury that he has entrusted his authority in their province to Archbishop Baldwin, CCII, 1353.

Confirms the agreement made between the bishop of Saintes and the monks of Aizé concerning the Church of La Rochelle and certain other matters in the diocese of Saintes, CCII, 1368.

Decrees that no prelates may presume to exact procurations from the priories of the monastery of Cluny beyond them, CCII, 1379.

Confirms the statutes of the Order of Arrouaise, CCII, 1399.

To Emperor Frederick, complains concerning injuries inflicted by him upon the Roman Church, CCII, 1410.

To William, king of Scotland, concerning the case of Hugh of Saint Andrews and John, bishop of Dunkeld, CCII, 1422.

Issues mandates to Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow, and to the abbots of Melrose and Newbattle, CCII, 1424.

Writes to Henry, king of England, that he had instructed Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to cause the revenues of Archdeacon Salvaric to be collected and kept intact in his custody, CCII, 1425.

Informs the provosts, etc., of the castle of Valenciennes that he had instructed Roger, bishop of Cambrai, to divide the parish of the Church of Saint Silvatius into three parts, CCII, 1426.

To Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning a church to be built in honour of Saints Stephen and Thomas, CCII, 1443.

Corrects and confirms the decrees of the council held by Peter, archbishop of Split, and his suffragans, CCII, 1446.

Bull for the abbey of Eaucourt [*Exaquiensis*, uncertain], CCII, 1451.

Confirms the customs which the Church of Chartres had rightly employed without interruption for forty years, CCII, 1465.

Exhorts all the faithful throughout the archbishopric of Ravenna and the bishopric of Ferrara to give money to the brothers of Saint Mary of Reno for construction of a bridge over the Reno, CCII, 1466 and 1480.

Makes Henry, archbishop of Bourges, his legate throughout the entire [Col. 1280] province of Bourges, except for the monastery of Dol, CCII, 1475.

Appoints Hugh, dean of Paris, and the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés as judges between the canons of Beauvais and the monks of Saint Lucian, CCII, 1477.

To the abbot and convent of Fécamp, that sons are not to be brought up in their fathers’ churches, but rather removed from them, CCII, 1479.

Orders Hubert, bishop of Aix, not to allow the rights of the canons to be violated by the monks of Saint Peter, CCII, 1484.

Forbids the archpriest and canons of Bologna to inflict injuries upon the brothers of Saint Mary of Reno, CCII, 1485.

To Walter, archbishop of Rouen, that nothing be altered after an appeal, CCII, 1488.

Orders all abbots of the Premonstratensian Order in Germany and Saxony to attend the general chapter of Prémontré every year, CCII, 1488.

To Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, concerning injuries inflicted on the Roman Church by Emperor Frederick, and asking him to interpose himself as a mediator for peace, CCII, 1497.

Reproves Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, because he had inflicted various injuries upon the prior and brothers of the Church of Canterbury and had not attended to their appeal to the Apostolic See, etc., CCII, 1497 and 1499.

To the master and brothers of the Hospitaller cross-bearers of Bologna, approves their order, CCII, 1507.

Orders Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to abandon construction of the new church which, as the monks of Canterbury complained to him, would be detrimental to them, CCII, 1509.

Rebukes the abbots of Battle, Faversham, and Saint Augustine’s because they neglected his commands, CCII, 1511.

Decrees that the Order of Saint Benedict shall be preserved in perpetuity in the monastery of Admont, CCII, 1515.

Most sharply rebukes Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, because he persists both in injuring the monks of Canterbury and in disregarding the pope’s commands, CCII, 1527.

Asks Henry, king of the English, not to permit injuries to be inflicted upon the Church of Canterbury by Archbishop Baldwin, etc., CCII, 1530.

VICTOR III, pope.—Letter to the empress concerning relief from the tribute owed to the Holy Sepulchre, CXLIX, 961.

At the request of Bishop Urso, confirms the possessions of the recently established bishopric of Ravello, CXLIX, 962.

VIGILIUS, pope.—Answers Eutherius’s inquiries concerning the Priscillianist heresy, baptism, consecration of churches, the time of the Paschal day, and the primacy of the Roman pontiff, LXIX, 15.

That baptism must be administered in the name of the Trinity; that there must not be a single immersion in baptism as though it arose from the Lord’s death, LXIX, 200.

Letter to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, replying concerning the penance to be imposed on King Theodoric for contracting an incestuous marriage, LXIX, 21.

Letter to Justinian: when Emperor Justinian had professed the faith in the presence of Vigilius, legitimately elected, he was changed from enemy into defender and from persecutor into preacher, etc., LXIX, 21.

Letter to Menas, bishop, congratulating him on embracing the holy four universal synods after condemning heretics; those who repent of heresy ought to be received, LXIX, 25.

Letter to the bishops of Gaul, announcing that Auxanius had been appointed vicar of the Apostolic See, explaining the functions of that office, and ordering all to obey him, LXIX, 29.

Letter to Aurelian, bishop of Arles: after Auxanius’s death, delegates to Bishop Aurelian his authority in Gaul, LXIX, 37.

Letter to Rusticus and Sebastian, excommunicating them, CXIX, 43.

Letter to Valentinian, bishop of Tomis, concerning the proceedings at Constantinople on the Three Chapters, CXIX, 51.

Letter to the whole Church, setting forth the reasons for his withdrawal to Saint Euphemia and what he did there with Justinian’s legates, and at the same time inserting his confession of faith, LXIX, 53.

Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is deprived of priesthood and communion; the bishop of Constantinople and the remaining bishops who knew of his crime are excommunicated, LXIX, 59.

Letter to Eutychius, commending his faith and consenting that the Three Chapters be dealt with in a council, LXIX, 66.

Constitution concerning the Three Chapters, LXIX, 67.

Oath concerning the Three Chapters, and decree for confirmation of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, LXIX, 121.

Constitution for condemnation of the Three Chapters; definition [Col. 1281] of faith of the holy Council of Chalcedon, LXIX, 143.

VITALIAN, pope.—Letter to Paul, archbishop of Crete, reproving him because he unjustly condemned the bishop of Lappa and did not allow him to appeal to the Apostolic See; restoring the said bishop to his former dignity, he declares void the proceedings taken against him, LXXXVII, 999.

Letter to Vaanes, the emperor’s chamberlain: since John, bishop of Lappa, was condemned contrary to the canons, he desires that Vaanes’s assistance restore him to his church, LXXXVII, 1002.

Letter to Paul, bishop of Crete, ordering him to restore to the bishop of Lappa the churches he had occupied; to correct the deacon who had taken a wife and serves in two churches, etc., LXXXVII, 1003.

Letter to Oswi, king of the Northumbrians, congratulating him on the conversion of the peoples of his kingdom to the faith and on the observance of Easter and the other traditions of the Apostles, etc., LXXXVII, 1004.

WIBERT, antipope: see CLEMENT III, pope.

ZACHARIAS (Saint), pope.—Letter to Boniface, archbishop: approves the bishoprics established in Germany; directs that a synod be held in the kingdom of France, and meanwhile that fornicating and blood-stained priests not be permitted to exercise their office; that Boniface not designate himself a successor unless death is imminent; that the man claiming incestuous marriages had been permitted to him is not to be believed; that pagan rites formerly present at Rome had thereafter been forbidden; and that no faith be given to priests who boasted that they had received permission from the Apostolic See, LXXXIX, 917.

Letter to Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, confirming his episcopal see, established by Archbishop Boniface, LXXXIX, 922.

Letter to the Franks: praises them for what had rightly been established in the synod and exhorts them to continue obeying the admonitions of Bishop Boniface, LXXXIX, 923.

Letter to Boniface, bishop, that baptism administered with faulty words by an unskilled priest is not to be repeated, LXXXIX, 929.

Letter to Pippin, mayor of the palace, and to the bishops, abbots, and nobles of the Franks: 1. concerning the honour of metropolitans; 2. condemned bishops, priests, and deacons; 3. arrogant priests; 4. rural priests; 5. monks and handmaids of God; 6. widows not to be veiled; 7. a layman dismissing his wife; 8. priests and deacons who hold separate assemblies; 9. clerics and monks not remaining in their profession; 10. clerics in parishes, monasteries, and martyria; 11. which clerics ought to abstain from wives; 12. those who dismiss wives or husbands; 13. monks who become clerics; 14. priests and deacons fallen into crime; 15. churches built by laypeople on their own estates; 16. clerics abandoning their own churches; 17. bishops receiving other bishops’ clerics; 18. which clerics may marry wives; 19. that priests and deacons are not to be received without letters of commendation; 20. veiled virgins if they stray; 21. unveiled women if they stray; 22. women who have married two brothers, or men who have married two sisters; 23. those who commit homicide voluntarily; 24. those who commit homicide involuntarily; 25. those who have adulteresses as wives or are themselves adulterers; 26. monks and virgins who do not keep their profession; 27. those who, after undertaking a profession of virginity, marry, LXXXIX, 930–938.

Letter to Boniface, archbishop, concerning the proceedings at the Roman synod against Aldebert and Clement, and concerning the establishment of a metropolitan see at Cologne, LXXXIX, 939.

To the same person, concerning the form and minister of baptism; certain wandering bishops and priests; the heresy of Samson, a Scottish priest, concerning baptism; likewise concerning the priest Vigilius and another of his errors; the metropolitan see established not at Cologne but at Mainz; finally, permits him to choose a successor for himself, LXXXIX, 943.

[Col. 1282] Letter to various bishops of Gaul and Germany, praising their union with one another and with the Roman Church, etc., LXXXIX, 948.

Responses to various questions, LXXXIX, 949.

Letter to Boniface, archbishop: elevation of the see of Mainz into a metropolitan see, LXXXIX, 953.

Letter to the bishops of the Franks, concerning reconciliation of concord and peace between Pippin and Grifo, and restoration of the body of Saint Benedict to the monks of Monte Cassino, LXXXIX, 955.

Letter to Austrobert, archbishop of Vienne, sending him a copy of the synod held at Rome and replying what is to be done concerning bishops ordained for money, LXXXIX, 956.

Letter to Theodore, bishop of Turin, that a son may not marry the woman whom his father received from the sacred font of baptism, LXXXIX, 957.

Three decrees in matrimonial cases, LXXXIX, 939.

ZOZIMUS, pope.—Letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles: 1. that those travelling to Rome or elsewhere from Gaul receive letters of communion from the metropolitan of Arles; 2. that the metropolitan of Arles ordain bishops throughout the province of Vienne and both provinces of Narbonne; 3. that the Church of Arles have its parishes restored to it, XX, 642.

Concerning the case of Caelestius: what was done when the case of Caelestius was reopened at Rome; that, unless within two months persons come who can convict him in person and prove that he thinks otherwise than he professed, he will be absolved, XX, 649.

That Pelagius, by sending letters and a statement of faith, and likewise Caelestius, had cleared themselves; that the accusations of men of such suspect faith ought not readily to be believed; and that those men, when they condemned what should be condemned and followed what should be followed, had never fallen from Catholic truth or the communion of the Church, XX, 954.

Concerning Ursus and Tuentius, bishops unlawfully ordained, that they are nowhere to be received into the Church’s communion, XX, 661.

That the metropolitan of Arles is to have authority to ordain bishops in the province of Vienne and in both provinces of Narbonne, XX, 665.

That Hilary has no legal basis at all for ordaining bishops in First Narbonensis and is not to arrogate anything therefrom to himself, XX, 666.

The metropolitan dignity usurped by Proculus is secured to Patroclus. It belongs to Patroclus to give letters of communion to every member of the Gallican clergy; precipitous ordinations and ordinations by skipping grades are forbidden, XX, 668.

Congratulates him on condemning the heresy of Caelestius, rejecting its slander against himself, and finally approving his own faith; he explains why he is not coming to Rome, XX, 669.

1. That monks or laymen must not attain the high priesthood except through the ecclesiastical grades; 2. that anyone who disregards the prohibited grades shall be subject to the penalty of the higher grade; 3. what periods are fixed for each grade of the clergy, XX, 669.

Against Proculus’s audacity and unlawful ordinations, XX, 63.

That it has been entrusted to Patroclus to receive another bishop in Proculus’s place, XX, 674.

Zosimus, having explained at length the authority of his see, informs the Africans that he did not, as they supposed, give credence to all of Caelestius’s words, nor alter what his predecessor had established concerning him, XX, 675.

Concerning certain rebellious priests and those who joined their association, XX, 679.

Concerning appeals of bishops to the bishop of the Roman Church, and concerning the hearing of the cases of priests and deacons before neighbouring bishops if they have been excommunicated by their own bishops, XX, 680.

Concerning disregard for the rules of judicial procedure, to the extent that priests are judged in the presence of laypeople and an accused person is forced to seek out and bring his adversary to judgment, XX, 682.

[Col. 1283]

CXVIII. INDEX OF DECREES, DECISIONS, CONSTITUTIONS, MORAL PRECEPTS, EPISTLES OF INTERPRETERS OF EVANGELICAL DOCTRINE, ETC., WHICH, HAVING BEEN PROMULGATED BY EMPERORS, KINGS, AND OTHERS FOR THE GOOD OF THE COMMONWEALTH, HAVE HAD FORCE AS LAW AMONG CHRISTIANS; ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY AUTHORS, AND BRIEFLY SETTING FORTH THE PURPOSE OF EACH.

NOTICE.

Whatever imperial decrees, etc., are issued concerning religion, it should be noted that they do not anticipate the judgment of the Catholic Church of God, but follow it. Thus Possidius says of the Emperor Honorius in the *Life of St. Augustine*, ch. XVIII; so that no one should rashly suppose that even then Isaiah’s prophecy concerning Christ’s Church was fulfilled: “Kings shall be your foster-fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers” (Isa. 49:23).

Before proceeding with this Index, therefore, we must answer the apparently religious indignation of certain persons, as though emperors had not kept within the limits of their authority in this matter, but had nearly aspired within the Church to what they once did among the gentiles, when they held the pontificate of pagan impiety. For what, they ask, is it to usurp matters belonging to the priesthood, even in the cause of faith, if not this: to prescribe what ought to be believed; to declare heretics those who think otherwise; to command bishops to subscribe either to dogmas or to condemned persons, threatening deposition—indeed excommunication—if they do not obey; to prescribe to primates what belongs to their office; and so on? Emperors seem to have done precisely this, however religiously they may be praised, when they issued decrees . . .

This complaint is ancient, arising almost with the emperors’ faith itself. The holy Fathers long ago gave a sufficient answer to it when they established that “the world is ruled principally by two powers, the sacred authority of priests and royal power; both, though united in Christ, being apportioned among priests and kings as ministers of God.” Thus two supreme jurisdictions arose, “to each of which its proper measure of power was assigned.” Between the two jurisdictions a sacred compact was entered into, Christ acting as arbiter and reconciler: each was to serve the common Lord in its own sphere, protect his bride, and, with joined forces, overthrow her enemies. For “the King of kings, and likewise Priest of priests, who alone could govern the Church which he redeemed, nevertheless, after raising his humanity into heaven—though by his divinity he would always remain with his own—divided his power for governing that same Church between priests and kings, so that what holy pontiffs taught, most devout kings should themselves fulfil and cause to be fulfilled.”

Certainly, after the Church had cast off the yoke of tyrants, been vindicated into liberty, and turned the emperors’ sword from her own necks against the enemies whom she had formerly endured as unjust persecutors, she obtained, as soon as she made them her sons, most just helpers for the successful conduct of affairs. Kings therefore do not prescribe the form of faith, nor have they ever rightly prescribed it; rather, accepting it from the priests, whose “judgment they follow,” they command peoples to observe it. They do not teach the Church; but, like angels, they defend the gates of God’s city from heretics with a flaming sword. They do not themselves declare heretics those who think contrary to the form of faith; rather, they declare them liable to the penalties of heretics. Nor do they themselves, on their own authority, depose bishops or exclude anyone from the sacraments—for how could they? Rather, they order those deposed and excluded by synods to be driven from their cities lest they create disturbances; and they order them punished by exclusion from others’ society lest the contagion of their poisonous spirit cause harm.

To give a single example: in the case of the Pelagian heresy, the African Fathers themselves, when through delegates of synods they sought decrees of this kind from emperors—the supreme pontiffs themselves, however great the authority in which they flourished—used royal edicts against God’s enemies. The whole sacred clerical order, indeed the universal Church, obeyed those same edicts; against every objection it establishes, and at the same time teaches, what both Christ before his Passion and God at the creation of the world foreshadowed: that the Church needs two swords to frighten the ungodly and two spiritual luminaries to illuminate the world. For, as the Fathers say, one luminary was not enough against all the obscuring mists of error, nor one sword against the unbridled audacity of the ungodly; since an obstinate mind created obscurity for itself and others, while wickedness drew audacity from the patience of the good. This was said long ago with great gravity and truth; and the unhappy experience of our own age confirms it with complete certainty. Hence St. Bernard’s prayer was never more timely: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate. Let those who are united in institutions be united in spirit; let them cherish one another, defend one another, and bear one another’s burdens” (*Letter to King Conrad*, 182, 441; 48, 377).

AETHELRED III, King of the English.—On giving the penny to Holy Church, etc.; on the tithing of thanes, CLI, 1166.—On fasting and cessation from work for three days before the feast of St. Michael, CLI, 1167.—What the king and all the people are to sing daily, CLI, 1107.—On rendering the customary dues of God’s holy Church, CLI, 1167.—That no one be sold outside the country, CLI, 1167.—On confirmations, alms, and restitutions to the Church, CLI, 1169.

AETHELSTAN, King of the English.—Laws concerning the payment of tithes [Col. 1284], the support of the poor, annual almsgiving from royal estates, breaking into a church, sorceresses, moneyers, persons undertaking to submit themselves to ordeal, buying goods on Sunday, perjurers, those who do not enforce these laws, and the lawmakers and place, CXXXVIII, 461–471.

ALEXIUS, Emperor of Constantinople.—Letter to Robert, Count of Flanders, and to all Christians, asking them to bring him assistance against the pagans, CLV, 465.

[Col. 1285] AGRICOLA, Praetorian Prefect.—Edict against the Pelagians, ordering that they be excluded from the city and led into exile, LVI, 492.

ALFRED, King of the Anglo-Saxons.—We give in full the preface or apparatus to his laws, so that everyone may understand upon what foundation they rest. Nothing more fitting could have been chosen, since it is nothing other than the Mosaic laws:

I. The Lord spoke the word to Moses and said thus: “I am the Lord your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt and from its bondage; do not love foreign gods besides me.”

II. “Do not use my name in vain, for you are not innocent before me if you use my name in vain.”

III. “Remember to keep the Sabbath day holy. Work six days, and rest on the seventh—you and your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your beasts, and whoever enters within your gates—for in six days Christ created the heavens, the earth, the seas, and all creatures that are in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord sanctified it.”

IV. “Honor your father and your mother, whom the Lord gave you, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

V. “Do not kill.”

VI. “Do not steal.”

VII. “Do not commit adultery.”

VIII. “Do not bear false witness against your neighbors.”

IX. “Do not unjustly covet your neighbor’s inheritance.”

X. “Do not make for yourselves gods of gold or silver.”

XI. “These are the laws which you must set before them. If anyone buys a Christian slave, he shall serve six years; in the seventh he shall be free without payment. In whatever clothing he entered, in the same shall he depart; if he has a wife, he shall depart with her. But if his master gave him a wife, she and her children shall belong to the master. If, however, the slave says, ‘I do not wish to leave my master, my wife, my children, or my inheritance,’ then his master shall bring him to the service of the temple and pierce his ear with an awl, as a sign that henceforward he is always to be a slave.”

XII. “If anyone sells his daughter into service, she shall not be a slave in every respect as other female servants are. He shall not have power to sell her to a foreign people; but if she does not please him who bought her, he shall dismiss her free to a foreign nation. But if he allows his son to have relations with her, he shall give her a gift; he shall see that she has clothing and the price of her chastity—that is, he shall grant her her dowry. If he provides none of these things, then she shall be free.”

XIII. “If anyone willingly kills a human being, he shall die by death. But if he killed him under compulsion, or unwillingly, or not voluntarily—as though God had thus delivered him into his hand—and had never lain in wait for him, he shall be entitled to his privilege and to the just compensation of the peoples, if he seeks asylum. But if anyone deliberately and willingly kills his neighbor by ambush, you shall drag him from my altar to die by death.”

XIV. “Whoever strikes his father or mother shall die by death.”

XV. “Whoever kidnaps a free person and sells him, and is discovered so that he cannot restore him, shall die by death. Whoever curses his father or mother shall die by death.”

XVI. “If anyone strikes his neighbor with a stone or fist, and he is nevertheless able to walk out leaning upon a staff, he shall provide him with a physician and compensate his labor for as long as he is unable to work.”

XVII. “If anyone strikes his own male or female slave and the person does not die that same day, but survives two or three days, he shall not in every respect be equally guilty, because the slave was his property. But if the slave dies on the same day, then guilt shall rest upon him.”

XVIII. “If anyone, while fighting, injures a pregnant wife, he shall compensate the loss as the laws determine. If she dies, he shall give life for life.”

XIX. “If anyone puts out another’s eye, he shall compensate with his own: tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.”

XX. “If anyone puts out the eye of his male or female slave, and after this act the slave is one-eyed, he shall immediately set that person free; if he knocks out a tooth, he shall do the same.”

XXI. “If an ox gores a man or woman so that they die, it shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; and its owner shall be innocent, if the ox had been dangerous for two or three days and the owner did not know it. But if he knew this and would not keep it confined, and it then kills a man or woman, it shall be stoned and its owner put to death, or his life redeemed by a price, as wise men deem just. If it gores a son or daughter, it shall be subject to the same law. But if it gores a male or female slave, he shall pay the owner thirty silver shillings, and the ox shall be stoned.”

XXII. “If anyone digs a water-pit or opens an enclosure and afterwards does not close it, he shall compensate for every beast that falls into it, and retain the dead animal.”

XXXIII [probably XXIII]. “If one man’s ox wounds another’s ox and it subsequently dies, that ox shall be sold alive and the price divided, as also the flesh of the dead animal. But if the owner knew that the ox [Col. 1286] was dangerous and would not keep it confined, he shall give another ox in its place, and himself retain all the flesh of the dead animal.”

XXIV. “If anyone steals another’s ox and kills or sells it, he shall compensate for it with two oxen and four sheep. If he has nothing with which to compensate, he himself shall be sold for that sum.”

XXV. “If a thief breaks into someone’s house at night and is killed there, the person who kills him shall not be guilty of homicide. But if he does this after sunrise, he shall be guilty of homicide and shall then himself die, unless driven by necessity. If any living thing that he had previously stolen is found in his possession, he shall make double compensation.”

XXVI. “If anyone causes damage to another’s vineyard, field, or any part of his land, he shall compensate as someone appraises it.”

XXVII. “If fire is set to burn a crop, the person who set the fire shall compensate that loss.”

XXVIII. “If anyone deposits money with a friend and that friend steals it, he shall compensate double. But if he does not know who secretly removed it, he shall clear himself by proving that he committed no fraud in this matter. If it was a living animal, and he says that an army took it or that it died of itself, and has witnesses, he need not compensate for it. But if he has no witnesses and the other does not believe him, then he shall take an oath.”

XXIX. “If anyone seduces an unmarried woman and has intercourse with her, he shall compensate her and afterwards take her as his wife. If the woman’s father does not wish to give her to him, he shall pay that sum as a dowry.”

XXX. “Do not permit a woman who is accustomed to harbor enchanters, magicians, and sorceresses to live.”

XXXI. “And if anyone has intercourse with a beast, he shall die by death.”

XXXII. “And if anyone offers sacrifice except to God alone, he shall die by death.”

XXXIII. “Do not oppress a resident alien or stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

XXXIV. “Do not harm or afflict widows and orphans. If you do anything against them, they will cry out to me, and I shall hear them; and I shall kill you with my sword, and make your wives widows and your children orphans.”

XXXV. “If you lend money to your companion who wishes to live with you, do not present yourself to him as an exacting creditor, nor humiliate him with your interest.”

XXXVI. “If anyone has only a simple garment with which to cover and protect himself, and has given it as a pledge, it shall be restored to him before sunset. If you do not do this, he will cry to me, and I shall hear him, for I am very merciful.”

XXXVIII. “Do not slander your lord; do not curse the ruler of your people.”

XXXVIII. “Give to God your tithes and your firstfruits, things that walk and things that grow.”

XXXIX. “Do not eat any flesh left by wild beasts; give it to the dogs.”

XL. “Do not heed the word of a false person, nor listen to him; do not favor his case, nor give testimony after him.”

XLI. “Do not follow the wicked counsel and unjust course of the multitude.”

XLII. “If you come upon anyone’s wandering livestock, even that of your adversary, return it to him.”

XLIII. “Always render just judgment. Do not make one law for the rich and another for the poor, nor one law for a friend and another for an enemy.”

XLIV. “Always avoid falsehood.”

XLV. “Never afflict a guiltless and innocent person.”

XLVI. “Never accept gifts, for they very often blind the judgment of wise men and pervert their words.”

XLVII. “Do not allow a resident alien or stranger, through ignorance, to suffer any injury.”

XLVIII. “Never swear by the gods of the gentiles, nor invoke them for any reason . . .”

These are the laws which almighty God himself spoke to Moses and commanded him to keep. And after the only-begotten Son of God, our God—that is, Christ the Savior—had come into the world, he said that he had not come to violate or abolish those commandments, but to fulfil them in all goodness, CXXXVIII, 447–451.

Now let us come to the ecclesiastical laws of this King Alfred. Those which we shall report have been excerpted from his other civil laws.

Law concerning oaths and pledges, ibid., 452.—Laws concerning sanctuary in churches, violation of surety, ecclesiastical peace, sacrilege, one who removes a nun from a church, ibid., 453.—Laws concerning fornicators, fights, touching a nun, one who entrusts money to monks, a fight involving priests, rape, and one who becomes surety on another’s behalf for something to be rendered to God, ibid., 454.—Laws concerning fighting before a senator, breach of the peace in a town, hereditary land, and observance of feast days, ibid., 455.—Laws concerning love of God and the peace of the Church; those neglecting Christ’s law and worshipping paganism; persons living wickedly in finery; priests falsely proclaiming a feast or fast; priests not seeking chrism within proper limits, or refusing baptism; brothers or kinsfolk committing fornication with one woman [Col. 1287]; an ordained person who forfeits his life; a capital offender wishing to confess to a priest; tithes withheld from God and other restitutions to the Church; those trading on Sundays; those working on Sundays; fasts broken; days on which ordeal and oath are forbidden; that a person convicted of an offence is not to be killed on Sunday; diviners, enchanters, poisoners, perjurers, and the like; and ordained persons or foreigners deceived in any matter concerning money or life, ibid., 455–458.

ALIONORA, Queen of the English.—Letters to Pope Celestine III, imploring his assistance for the liberation of her son Richard, King of the English, CCVI, 1261.

ALIENOR, Queen of England.—Letter to Alexander III, giving thanks for letters sent by the supreme pontiff, etc., CC, 1362.

ALPHONSUS, King of Portugal.—Letter to Pope Lucius II. He makes his kingdom tributary to the Roman Church, CLXXIX, 935.

ALFRED THE GREAT, King of the English.—His laws are the same as those described by us under the article EDWARD THE ELDER, King of the English, CXXXVIII, 459.

AMALRIC, King of Jerusalem.—Letters to Louis, King of the Franks, asking him to come to Jerusalem, CLV, 1265.

On the state of religion in the city of Jerusalem, CLV, 1267, 1269, 1271, 1274, 1277, 1278.

AMALASUNTHA, Queen.—Her praise: “In her is the glory of all kingdoms; in her, the flower of virtues. Whatever brilliance we possess, we receive from her radiance, since she not only brought praise to her parents but adorned human nature itself. Who could adequately declare with what piety and with what weight of character she is endowed? Philosophers, if they were alive, would surely learn new things and admit that their books contained lesser things than those which they would recognize as bestowed upon her. She is acute in deliberation, yet in speech most grave through supreme moderation. This, without doubt, is a royal virtue: to perceive what is necessary more quickly and to break forth into words more slowly. For one does not know how to utter words requiring regret who has first submitted what he is to utter to his own examination. Hence her wonderful learning is spread in great abundance through many languages; her intellect is found so ready for emergencies that it does not appear earthly. In the Books of Kings, the Queen of the South is said to have come to learn Solomon’s wisdom; let princes here hear what they may learn in admiration. Infinite thought is enclosed in a few words, and what others now form only after long deliberation is arranged with the greatest ease. Blessed is the commonwealth that glories in the governance of so great a lady. It was too little that the people should serve under freedom; to such great merits was added the honor of princely reverence being rendered to her. For by this service we rule most worthily. When I obey such great prudence, I second every virtue. Under such a guide we are not burdened with the kingdom; for if anything is unknown to us because of its novelty, her instruction will make it wholly certain for the public good. We are not ashamed to confess the truth. Recognize, princely men, that whatever in us has been able to please more belongs to our most wise lady. For either by questioning her we think better, or by imitating her we advance. Live now happily; live, with God’s help, in concord; and emulate the grace which you know royal concord possesses,” LXIX, 800.

Her laws are the same as the laws of Theodahad, whom she had taken as her partner in rule. See THEODAHAD, King.

ANNA, Queen of the Franks.—Letter for giving thanks to God for the intercession of St. Bernard that had been obtained, CLXXXV, 1632.

ARCADIUS, Emperor.—Constitution against the Donatists, XI, 1192.—Letter to Pope Innocent I, asking him to free himself and Eudoxia from excommunication, XX, 633.—He declares himself innocent of what was done to his envoys or to John; that he has punished those responsible; and accordingly asks that the sentence be relaxed by which he and his wife are excluded from the sacred mysteries, ibid.

ATHALARIC, King.—Confirmation of the senatorial decree against simoniacs, LXVI, 11.—He writes to the senate of Rome that it greatly pleased him that they elected as pontiff the person designated by King Theodoric, LXIX, 748.—He writes to Albienus that he removed the praetorian prefect from office because of misconduct and appointed Albienus in his place, who is highly praised, ibid., 752.—He refers to the pope’s judgment those who bring suit against a Roman cleric; whoever contemns the authority of the Holy See, he wishes both to lose the case and to be punished by a fine of ten pounds of gold, to be distributed to the poor, ibid., 757.—Edict protecting municipal councillors from every injury, with a fine of ten pounds of gold or corporal punishment imposed upon oppressors, ibid., 766.—He ordains that those who, because of the high price of grain, have stored it away shall sell it at a moderate price, ibid., 770.—He remits to all possessors and defenders of the city of Syracuse those burdens imposed on them contrary to custom, granting those harassed by tax collectors leave to complain to the prince, ibid., 774.—He ordains that the edicts promulgated by Theodoric for the regulation of Sicilian morals be observed in such a way that whoever attempts in any degree to violate them shall be held guilty of sacrilege, ibid., 777.—He promulgates decrees against simoniacs according to ancient decrees of the senate, ibid., 777.—He orders that his edict and the senatorial decrees for the eradication of simony be engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of the Basilica of St. Peter, ibid., 781.—Edict against invaders of others’ property; against those posting public notices in a public name; against those fraudulently and perversely obtaining princes’ judgments; against those separating the marriages of others; against adulterers; against those joined to two wives; against male and female concubines; against those extorting gifts by terror; against evildoers; against murderers; against those who appeal a second time from ordinary judges in the same case; and against violators of the edicts both of himself and of Theodoric, ibid., 782.—He writes to the senate of Rome that he has issued an edict of twelve chapters, and orders that it be read in the senate and posted by the urban prefect for thirty days in the most frequented places, ibid., 786.—He writes to all provincial judges that he has decreed that his edict be solemnly read for thirty days in public assemblies, ibid., 786 . . . etc. . . . etc. . . as far as col. 795.

BALDWIN, Count of Flanders.—Letter to the abbot of Cluny, confirming the abbey of St. Bertin, CCXVI, 845.

BLANCESFORT (B. de), Master of the Knights Templar.—Letter to Louis, King of the Franks: excellent hopes are conceived for the advance of successes in the city of Jerusalem and in the neighboring region already captured, CLV, 1269, 1272.
