CLOTHAR II, King of the Franks.—General constitution, LXXII, 1119.

Decree concerning slaves and sanctuaries.

A decree was issued that, since night thieves were not caught at the established watches because, through collusion occurring in various places, they neglected their crimes while carrying out the watches, hundreds should be formed. If anything is lost within such a hundred, the person who lost it shall recover the principal, and the thief shall be pursued. Or, if it appears in another hundred and, though warned, they have neglected the matter, they shall be condemned to five solidi. Nevertheless, the person who lost the principal shall without doubt receive it from that hundred—that is, from the second or third watch. If the track of a thief is established, yet nothing is found nearby through a long search, or if the pursuer apprehends his thief, he shall receive the full composition. But if he is found in a *trustis* [armed association], the *trustis* shall acquire half the composition and exact the principal from the thief. If anyone finds stolen goods in another’s house, where there is a key, the master of the house shall make composition with his life. If anyone is caught with stolen goods, he shall be subject to the aforesaid law. If he is accused on suspicions, he shall come to the *fortis* [assembly or court; reading uncertain]. If misfortune perhaps has taken place, let three persons nevertheless be chosen by each party against the thief, so that collusion may not occur. Concerning slaves of the Church, the fisc, or anyone else: whoever is accused shall come to the *fortis*, or be brought before the people, or be redeemed by his master at his own valuation; for they shall be subject to the ordeal for proof. If any slave belonging to one of the more powerful men, who possess property in various places, is suspected of a crime, his master shall secretly be summoned with witnesses, so that within twenty nights he must present him before the judge [Col. 1291]. If, through intervening collusion, he is not produced within the appointed time, the master, according to his rank, shall make compensation, proportionate to the offense, between the *fredus* [judicial fine] and the *faidus* [feud-composition]. If a slave absents himself before his master has been warned, the master shall restore the principal and surrender the slave; and, when he is found, he shall be given over for punishment. If anyone secretly receives from any thief a composition for property stolen from himself, he shall be subject to both liabilities of the thief. Yet the thief shall be presented to the judge. LXXX, 450.

Let him hasten immediately to restore the principal to the person who lost it and to seek out the thief. If they find him in a *trustis*, he shall claim for himself one half, or the accusation. If it is from the thief’s resources, the person who suffered loss shall be satisfied. For if, in pursuing him, he catches the thief, he shall recover for himself the full composition together with payment, or whatever the loss may have been; but the *fredus* shall be reserved for the judge in whose district it lies. No one shall presume to drag a thief or any other guilty person from the court of a church, as is fitting in the case of the highest bishops. But if there are churches whose courts are not enclosed, a space of land on both sides of the walls, of one arpent, shall be observed as the court. No fugitive outside the aforesaid places shall say that he is leaving for the sake of hired work. If they do so and are caught, they shall be condemned to the punishment they deserve. But if the slave of anyone, abandoning his master, flees to churches, and his master first arrives there, the dispute is set aside; the stolen property shall be restored, so that he may redeem himself by payment of a price. If anyone, when summoned to follow a track or pursue a thief, refuses to come, he shall be condemned to five solidi. We desire that the things which we have ordained in God’s name under the bond of peace be observed forever. We decree this: if any judge presumes to violate this decree, let him know that he is liable to capital danger. When a bishop dies, one who is to be ordained by the metropolitan together with the provincials shall be elected in his place by clergy and people; and, if he is a worthy person, he shall be ordained by the prince’s authorization. Or indeed, if he is chosen from the palace, he shall be ordained on account of his personal merit and learning. No bishop shall choose a successor during his own lifetime; rather, another shall be substituted for him only when he is so afflicted that he cannot govern his Church or clergy. Likewise, no one shall presume, while a bishop lives, to assume his place. If anyone asks for it, it shall by no means be granted him. If any cleric, fortified with whatever rank, despises or bypasses his bishop and goes to the prince or to any powerful persons, or chooses to seek their protection, he shall not be received, except when he appears to be seeking pardon. If, however, he approaches the prince on any matter and returns to his bishop with that prince’s letter, he shall be received as excused. Whoever presumes, after warning by his own bishop, to retain such a person shall be deprived of holy communion. No judge of any rank shall presume personally to compel or condemn clerics in civil cases, except criminal matters, unless the offense is plainly established, with the exception of a priest or deacon. Those convicted of a capital crime shall be proceeded against according to the canons and examined together with the bishops. But if a case stands between a public official and men of the Church, the officials of the Churches on the one side and the public judge on the other, sitting in a public hearing, ought jointly to judge it. Upon the death of anyone intestate, his relatives shall, without opposition, succeed by judgment to his property according to law. The freedmen of any freeborn persons shall be defended by priests in their freedom according to the wording of their charters; nor shall they be judged, or summoned before the public authority, without the presence of the bishop or the Church’s provost. Wherever a new tax has been wickedly added and the people protest, it shall be mercifully corrected after a just inquiry. Concerning toll: it shall be exacted only in those places, or upon those very kinds of goods, from which it was exacted in the time of preceding princes—that is, until the passing of our lords and parents of blessed memory [lacuna]. Jews must not bring public actions against Christians. Therefore, whoever presumes to associate himself with that profit-seeking order shall incur the most severe law under canonical sentence. So that peace and discipline may endure perpetually in our kingdom, Christ being favorable, the rebellion or insolence of evil men shall be most severely repressed. LXXX, 451, 453.

No judge from other provinces or regions shall be appointed in another place; and if he perpetrates any wrong against persons of any condition, he shall be obliged to restore from his own property, according to the order of the law, whatever he has wrongfully taken. Whatever our parents, former princes, or we ourselves have been seen justly to grant and confirm, shall in every respect be confirmed. And whatever any one of the faithful and liegemen, preserving his faith toward his lawful lord, has been seen to lose during an interregnum, we command that he be generally reinvested, without any detriment, in the property justly due to him [Col. 1292]. No one, even by our command, shall presume at all either to carry off or to join in marriage religious maidens and widows, or holy women who have vowed themselves to God, whether they reside in their own houses or are established in monasteries. If anyone obtains an order to that effect, it shall have no force. And whoever presumes, by force or by any means, to carry them off or unite them to himself in marriage shall be struck by a capital sentence. If they contract marriage in a church and the woman carried off, or about to be carried off, appears to consent to this, they shall be separated from one another and deported into exile, and their property shall be joined to their nearest heirs. Bishops or powerful men who possess estates in other regions shall not establish judges or investigating envoys from other provinces, but only persons from the place who receive justice and render it to others. Therefore the agents of bishops or powerful men shall not, under the protection of anyone’s power, exact or take any levy, nor presume by themselves to inflict contempt upon anyone. Fiscal swineherds shall not presume, without the owner’s consent, to enter the woods of churches or private persons with their swine. Neither a free man nor a slave who has not been caught in theft shall be put to death unheard by judges or by anyone whatsoever. And when there is no pasture from which pigs can be fattened, *cellarinsis* [a levy; term uncertain] shall not be exacted publicly. Whoever presumes to violate this ordinance, which we have instituted with bishops and with such great men, our nobles and faithful men, in a synodal council, shall be condemned by a capital sentence, so that others may not commit like acts. We have decreed that this authority or edict, to remain valid in perpetuity, be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand: a certain other special precept for the monastery of Saint-Denis. LXXX, 454.

Law concerning envoys sent throughout the kingdom, so that the people may have peace and justice: concerning abductors, plunderers, thieves, and other evildoers, and concerning every matter of justice. Where the jurisdictions of envoys meet, the envoys shall come together; and if offenders flee from one kingdom into another, or from one missaticum [envoy-district] into another, they shall jointly constrain them. Wherever they flee, a written notice shall be sent there, so that the count may compel them, whether by their allodial land or by whatever means he can, to come there and make amends where they committed the wrong. The envoys are instructed to render justice; and if they do not do so, you yourselves must go. If anyone has need, all shall be ready to help one another. CXXXVIII, 399.

Now we wish to assure you concerning our union, because, Christ being favorable, said the most serene Emperor Clotaire, according to God and for the salvation of the holy Church of God, and for our common advantage and necessity and yours, we wish to join ourselves to you indissolubly in heart and deed, so that we may be one in Christ and you may be one with us. Know that the law which our predecessors—that is, our father and grandfather—granted and maintained for your predecessors, we likewise grant to you; and we wish it to be observed inviolate and uncorrupted in every respect, both at the present time and in times to come. CXXXVIII, 589, 606.

Assembly at Saint-Quentin, CXXXVIII, 650.—Assembly in the synod of Metz, ibid., 653.—Assembly at Saponariae, ibid., 658.—Decrees in the synods of Aachen, ibid., 663, 666.—Decrees in the assembly held in the basilica of Saint Castor at Koblenz, ibid., 669.—Decrees established in the assembly at Sablonariae, ibid., 691.

## CONRAD, Emperor

Letter to Eugenius, requesting confirmation of the election of Wibald, an absent and unwilling man, as abbot of Corvey, and of the union of Keminada and Visbika with the monastery of Corvey, CLXXX, 1613.—He informs Pope Eugenius that his son Henry has been elected king of the Romans by the common acclamation of the princes, and that he himself, having taken up the cross, is preparing for the expedition to Jerusalem, ibid., 1616.

Letters to Pope Eugenius: That he may deign to confer the provostship of Xanten upon his chaplain Theobald, canonically elected, CLXXX, 1623, 1625.—That he may kindly receive Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, and send him back restored to his see.—He commends to him the bishop of Regensburg, who is setting out for Jerusalem, ibid., 1625.—He sends envoys to him and asks that Ellulf, abbot of the monastery of Murbach, be confirmed by him, and that the cleric Otto be absolved.—He commends to him Peter, archbishop of Capua, through whose assistance he had recovered health, ibid., 1627.—He sends to him as envoy Master Henry, notary of his court, ibid., 1628.—That he confirm the election of Herman, bishop of Utrecht, and absolve the count of Ahr from excommunication, ibid., 1630.—Concerning the election [Col. 1293] of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, which he asks to be confirmed, ibid., 1634.—He announces that he is preparing an Italian expedition for the benefit of the Church; and he commends the archbishop of Bremen and Abbot Wibald, ibid., 1635.

## CONSTANS, Emperor

That he supported the party of Athanasius, LXIX, 959.—That he stirred up his brother on behalf of the faith, ibid., 967.

Constantine’s address to the synod held in the palace, concerning peace, VIII, 400.—Address to the assembly of saints: its preface mentions Easter, and that although Christ bestowed many benefits upon humankind, he was ill-treated by them, ibid., 401.—Address to the Church and hearers, asking them to pardon and correct him if he has said anything less than correctly, ibid., 403.—That God is the Father of the Word and maker of all things, and that things could in no way subsist if their causes were different, ibid., 405.—Concerning the error of those who worship images, ibid., 407.—That Christ, the Son of God, created all things and fixed for each person a definite span of life, ibid., 409.—Concerning fate, and that what is said about it is false, ibid., 411.—That in matters which intelligence cannot attain, we must proclaim the wisdom of the Creator and suppose neither chance nor any cause besides God, ibid., 417.—That God abundantly supplies human beings with what is necessary for use, but provides sparingly what serves pleasure, dispensing both for our benefit, ibid.—Concerning the doctrines of philosophers, ibid., 419.—Concerning the Lord’s bodily advent: what it was like and why it occurred, ibid., 425.—That differentiation among created things is necessary; that the inclination toward good and evil arises from human will; and consequently that God’s judgment is necessary, ibid., 437.—That creation is separated by an immeasurable interval from uncreated wisdom, ibid., 438.—What precepts the Saviour delivered, what miracles he performed, and how greatly he benefited his subjects, ibid., 439.—That Christ was foretold, etc., ibid., 443–465.—Thanksgiving, in which he attributes his victories and his remaining blessings to Christ, ibid., 465.—Concerning Christian institutions; that God loves those who pursue virtue; and that one ought to hope for recompense at judgment, ibid., 467.—Concerning the calamitous deaths of the persecutors of the Churches, ibid., 469, 471.—That God was the cause of the emperor’s piety; that we ought to seek prosperous outcomes from God and attribute them to him; but should ascribe adverse events to our own negligence, ibid., 475.—Letter to Pope Melchiades, requesting that a council be assembled at Rome in the case of Caecilian and the Donatists, ibid., 477.—Letter ordering a council of bishops to be held at Rome for the unity and concord of the Churches, ibid., 479.—He orders that leaders of churches be exempt from public obligations, ibid., 481.—He gives money to the churches, ibid.—That the litigating Donatist parties ought to be summoned to a council at Arles, ibid., 483.—Concerning the building and restoration of churches, ibid., 491.—How he suppressed disputes stirred up in Africa, ibid., 495.—That religion began in the eastern regions, ibid.—That, grieving at sedition, he urged peace, ibid., 496.—Concerning agreement in celebrating the Paschal feast, and against the Jews, ibid., 501.—He orders all persons to assent to the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea, ibid., 505.—He orders Arius’ books to be committed to the fire, ibid., 506.—Concerning construction of the Martyrium of our Saviour, ibid., 523.—That Macarius should write to the governors concerning the beauty of the apse, the craftsmen, and the materials, ibid., 527.—He urges the bishops not to remove Eusebius from Caesarea, ibid., 543.—Against images, and concerning the glorification of God, ibid., 547.—He praises Eusebius’ Easter oration, ibid., 451.—Concerning the preparation of sacred codices, ibid., 453.—Edict addressed to Pope Sylvester, ibid., 567.—Autograph treaty of love and concord between Emperor Constantine, holy Pope Sylvester, Tiridates king of Armenia, and divine Gregory, illuminator of the Armenians, ibid., 479.—Letter to Pope Leo II, discussing diverse matters concerning religion, XCVI, 387, 393.—Letters to Athanasius, that he may recall him from exile, XIII, 557.—Letters to the Alexandrian clergy, in Athanasius’ favour, ibid., 560, 561, 563.—He warns the Synod of Rimini not to presume to determine anything concerning the Easterners, who were meeting separately at Seleucia, ibid., 565.—He orders the bishops at Rimini to await his return from the barbarian campaign, ibid., 570.

Concerning the laws which he established for Christians, the alteration of pagan rites, the advancement of Christians, and veneration for religion.—When Constantine had attained sovereignty over the whole Roman Empire, he issued public edicts so that the subject peoples of the East might fearlessly practise the religion of Christ and diligently serve the Deity [lacuna]. Giving thanks to God and claiming nothing for himself, he added: “Because God deigned to have him as a fitting minister of His counsel, and brought him from the British sea to the regions of the East, so that the Christian religion might be increased; and so that those who, for the worship of God, steadfastly remained in the confessions of martyrdom [Col. 1299], might appear more illustrious through His honours.”

Having therefore proclaimed these things, and said much else by which he believed that he could lead his subjects to the worship of religion, he decreed invalid whatever had been conceived or done against religion under the persecutors of the Churches, and granted remission to all who, because of confession of Christ, had been sent to islands or ordered to remain elsewhere against their own will. Those who had been declared infamous on account of religion he released from infamy. He left those discharged from military service free to make their own choice [lacuna]. And after he had recalled all persons to their former liberty and customary honours, he also restored their property to all. If any had been condemned to death and stripped also of their property, he ordered their inheritances to be conveyed to their next of kin; but if none of these existed, he ordered each provincial Church to succeed to the right of inheritance, and that anything of such property taken either by a private person or by the public authority should be restored [lacuna].

These measures therefore pleased the emperor and were confirmed by law, and all was notably completed with an appropriate conclusion. At that time Christians administered all the offices of the Romans; thereafter all persons were forbidden to sacrifice, there was no place for offerings or divinations, and it was no longer permitted to dedicate idols or celebrate pagan festivals [lacuna]. When he had overcome all the wars conducted under him, he, as though repaying Christ, grew more and more fervent in zeal for Christ’s religion. From the land subject to him, he removed from every city a fixed public revenue and distributed it to the provincial churches and clergy, decreeing that this endowment should remain valid forever. To accustom the soldiers to worship God as he himself did, he marked their weapons with the sign of the cross. He decreed that all should have exemption from judicial proceedings and other business on the day called the Lord’s Day—which the Hebrews call the first day, whereas the Greeks assign it to the sun [lacuna]—and that on it they should be occupied only with prayers. He honoured the Lord’s Day because on it Christ rose from the dead; another day because on it he had been crucified.

For he had the greatest veneration for the most sacred cross, both because of the successes which had attended him through its aid in battles fought against his adversaries and because of the sign which appeared, as he thought, to have been divinely shown to him on its account. Finally, by law he prohibited the punishment of crucifixion, which had formerly been customary among the Romans. Moreover, he ordered this sign always to be inscribed and depicted upon the designs of solidi and upon images, as his images decorated with this device still bear witness, etc., etc. [lacuna], LXIX, 891–894.

Constantine’s Letter to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and to Arius, by which he urged them to return to peace, LXIX, 918.---That Constantine caused a council to be held at Nicaea both concerning the Arian controversy and for determining the celebration of Easter, ibid., 920.---Constantine’s letter concerning Arius and his writings, ibid., 934.---Letter to the king of Persia on behalf of the Christians, ibid., 948.---Constantine’s letter summoning the bishops, so that he himself might examine Athanasius’s case, ibid., 952.---That he ordered the Council of Sardica to be convened, ibid., 967.---Letters to Athanasius, that he should come to the emperor himself, ibid., 976.---What Constantius demanded of Athanasius, and what Athanasius demanded of Constantius; and how, when the orthodox bishops recovered their churches, the heretics were expelled, ibid., 979.---Letters in Anastasius’s favour, ibid., 980, 981.---Dialogue between Liberius and Constantius, and how Liberius was sentenced to exile, ibid., 996.---Constantius’s letter to the Council of Rimini, ibid., 1003.

Letter concerning the banishment of Coelestius, the Pelagian heretic, to Volusianus, prefect of the City; concerning the style of this emperor’s letters.---Let this be offered as an example: “Although we long ago ordered that the recent remnants of past superstition, full at that time of vanity, should be corrected, daily reports inform us that matters of greater gravity are occurring.” And since discord has disturbed the minds of the peoples, we command that the measures which we had long ago ordered be repeated. Therefore, once this has been read, let Your Excellency carefully investigate all who envy the piety of God, and immediately cause them to be expelled beyond the walls of the City; yet in such a manner that they are not permitted even to remain within the hundredth milestone. We further command that Coelestius be driven ever farther from the City; for it is clear that, when such persons have been removed from the midst, grace and concord retain their former firmness. Moreover, should anything of the kind henceforth be reported, know that the office of Your Excellency is liable to capital punishment. For we do not allow our commands to remain unpunished through negligent delay in their execution. . . . . . Let what we have ordered be carried out, because this is advantageous to your reputation, LVI, 499.---Letter concerning the dedication of a day to the blessed Apostle Peter, XXX, 227, 228.---Concerning the holding of the ecumenical Council of Nicaea and the closing of pagan temples, XXXI, 1136, 1137.---He recognizes Caecilian as the lawful bishop, XI, 777.---He appoints three bishops from Gaul as judges to decide the case at Rome, together with Miltiades, bishop of Rome, ibid., 782.---Letter [Col. 1300] by which he convokes the Council of Arles, ibid., 785.

DAGOBERT III, king of the Franks.---A judicial settlement asserting the right of the Church of Le Mans to the monastery of Anisolum, LXXXVIII, 1115.

DESIDERIUS, king of the Lombards.---A decree concerning Theodemar, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, for the establishment of territorial boundaries, LXXXVII, 1393.

EDGAR, king of the English.---An edict by which Edwin’s decrees are annulled, property taken from the Church is restored, and Dunstan is recalled from exile.---Charter concerning Oswadeslaw—that is, concerning the expulsion of married clerics and the introduction of monks, CXXXVIII, 485.---On the good reflection of a king, ibid., 490.---By what reasoning, having expelled clerics, he installed monks; because, pierced by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he established an abbot and monks in a new monastery, ibid., 291.---On the anathema of those who plot against monks; on the blessing of those who venerate monks; and what kind of men monks ought to be, and how they ought to live in a monastery, ibid., 492.---On the election of abbots; how a king who venerates an abbot and monks should protect them; how an abbot and monks should rescue a king from demonic temptation; and how a king should defend an abbot and monks from human persecution, ibid., 495.---On the liberty of monastic possessions: that no layman may unlawfully usurp a monastery’s property; on the blessing of those who increase it; on the curse of those who diminish it; in what ways they obey lay authorities; and that no offense can diminish this privilege of the Lord, ibid., 494.---Laws concerning the immunity of the Church and debts owing to it; ecclesiastical dues; tithes; the penny imposed on every household; feast-days and fasting, ibid., 495, 497.

We teach that God’s ministers should serve and minister to God devoutly, intercede for all the Christian people, and be faithful and obedient to their lords; that all persons advanced in rank should assist in a common necessity; and that each should be aid and support to others, both before God and before men, and should also be faithful and true to his temporal lords.---We also teach that each should honour the other; that younger persons should diligently listen to and love their elders; and that elders should diligently instruct their juniors.---We also teach that every year, for every synod, they should have books and vestments for ecclesiastical service, ink and parchment for their enactments, and provisions for three days.---We also teach that every priest going to a synod should have his clerk and a suitable man as attendant, not some unknown person who delights in folly; rather, all should proceed in order and in the fear of God Almighty.---We also teach that every priest should declare in the synod anything that harms him, if anyone has inflicted a serious injury upon him; then all should receive it as though it had been done to them all and should help secure redress, as the bishop determines.---We also teach that every priest should declare in the synod whether he knows anyone in his parish to be rebellious toward God, or to have fallen wickedly into mortal sin and to be someone whom he cannot bring to amendment, or whom he does not dare to correct because of lay persons.---We also teach that no matter between priests should be brought before a secular court; rather, their own fellows should settle and reconcile it, or, if necessary, refer it to the bishop.---We also teach that no presbyter should voluntarily leave the church to which he was consecrated, but should regard it as his lawful wife, CXXXVIII, 499, 503.

Laws concerning churches having cemeteries; boundaries for tithing; persons reluctant to give tithes; those not paying St Peter’s penny; solemnities and observance of boundaries, ibid., 498.---On the rule of life for those initiated into holy orders; on confession, ibid., 503, 511.---How a sick person ought to redeem his fast, ibid., 512.---On magnates, ibid., 512.---He declares that he expelled secular clerics and introduced monks living under a rule, ibid., 519.---Laws addressed to the presbyters of Northumbria, both for correcting their morals and for promoting their ministries, ibid., 521, 525.

EDMUND, king of the English.---Laws concerning the chastity of life of those initiated into holy orders; tithes and ecclesiastical dues, or first-fruits of seed; homicide; one who violated a nun; adultery; the maintenance of churches; perjurers and those who practiced barbarous sacrifices; homicide; one who attacked another in a sacred building or royal town; fines for fighting and homicide; shed blood. He gives thanks because his subjects helped him to rout thieves. How a maiden is to be betrothed and by what rites the proceedings are to be conducted, CXXXVIII, 481.

EDWARD the Elder, king of the English.---Laws concerning the peace of the Church; apostates; correction of those ordained, that is, initiated into holy orders; incest; a person condemned in a capital case who desires a confessor [Col. 1301]; withheld tithes and dues of the Church; persons who conduct their business on the Lord’s Day; fasts; oaths and ordeal; assistance to a severed limb after the third day; sorceresses, diviners, etc.; those initiated into holy orders; and pilgrims, CXXXVIII, 459, 461.

ETHELBERT, king of the English.---Decree that the property of God and the Church must not be taken away; or, these are the judgments established by this king.---The property of God and of the Church shall be compensated twelvefold; the property of a bishop, elevenfold; that of a priest, ninefold; that of a deacon, sixfold; that of a cleric, threefold; violation of the peace of a church, twofold; violation of the peace of a monastery, twofold, LXXX, 346.---If the king summons his people to himself and anyone harms them there, compensation shall be made twofold and fifty shillings paid to the king, ibid., 347.---If the king feasts in anyone’s house and someone there causes damage, compensation shall be made twofold, ibid.---If a free man steals anything from the king, he shall make ninefold compensation, ibid.---If anyone kills a man in the king’s residence, he shall make amends with fifty shillings, ibid.---If anyone kills a free man, the king shall receive fifty shillings as lord, ibid.---If anyone kills the servants of the royal reeve, smith, or cupbearer, he shall pay the customary moderate fine, ibid., 348.---For violation of the king’s protection, fifty shillings shall be paid; if a free man steals anything from a free man, he shall make threefold compensation, and the king shall have the fine and all his goods, ibid.---If anyone has intercourse with the king’s virgin slave-girl, he shall make amends with fifty shillings, ibid.---If she is a willing slave-girl, he shall make amends with twenty-five shillings; if she is of the third rank, with twelve shillings, ibid.---For the king’s female food-provider, compensation shall be twenty shillings, ibid., 348.---If anyone kills someone in an earl’s residence, he shall make compensation with twelve shillings, ibid., 349.---If anyone has intercourse with an earl’s cupbearer-woman, he shall make compensation with twelve shillings, ibid.---For violation of a commoner’s protection, six shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If anyone has intercourse with a commoner’s cupbearer-woman, he shall make amends with six shillings; for another slave-woman he shall pay fifty *sceattas*, and for one of the third rank thirty *sceattas*, ibid.---If anyone is the first to enter another’s house, he shall make amends with six shillings; the second entrant with three shillings; thereafter each with one shilling, ibid.---If anyone lends weapons where there is a brawl, and no harm is done, he shall make compensation with six shillings, ibid.---If robbery is committed, he shall make amends with six shillings, ibid.---But if anyone kills someone, he shall make amends with twenty shillings, ibid.---If anyone kills someone, he shall pay the customary moderate fine of one hundred shillings, ibid.---If anyone kills someone at an open grave, he shall pay twenty shillings, and within forty days shall pay the entire customary fine, ibid.---If a killer leaves the country, his kinsmen shall pay half the customary fine, ibid., 350.---If anyone binds a freeborn man, he shall make compensation with twenty shillings, ibid.---If anyone kills a commoner’s table-companion, he shall make amends with six shillings, ibid.---If, however, a stranger kills the principal table-companion, he shall make amends with eighty shillings, ibid.---If he kills the second, he shall make compensation with sixty shillings; if the third, likewise with sixty shillings, ibid.---If a free man violates an enclosure, he shall make amends with six shillings, ibid.---If anyone takes property kept within, he shall make threefold compensation, ibid.---If a free man climbs over a fence, he shall make amends with four shillings, ibid.---If anyone kills someone, he shall make compensation for each person according to his own rank and with sound money, ibid.---If a free man has intercourse with the wife of a free man, he shall redeem her head-payment, purchase another wife with his own money, and bring her to the other man, ibid., 350.---If anyone pierces the right thigh with a spear, he shall compensate it according to its value, ibid., 351.---If hair is seized, *sceattas* shall be paid as compensation, ibid.---If bone is exposed, he shall pay three shillings, ibid.---If bone is injured, he shall pay four shillings, ibid.---If the bone is completely broken, he shall pay ten shillings, ibid.---If a shoulder is left lame, he shall pay twenty shillings, ibid.---If one ear hears nothing, he shall pay twenty-five shillings, ibid.---If an ear is cut off, twelve shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If an ear is pierced, he shall pay three shillings, ibid.---If an ear is clipped, six shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If an eye is knocked out, he shall pay fifty shillings, ibid.---If the mouth or eye is injured, twenty shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If the nose is pierced, he shall pay fifty shillings, ibid.---If there is one membrane, he shall pay three shillings, ibid.---If both are pierced, six shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If each nostril is clipped, each shall be compensated with six shillings, ibid.---If they are pierced, six shillings shall be paid, ibid., 352.---Whoever cuts off a man’s mouth shall pay twenty shillings, ibid.---For each of the four front teeth, six shillings; for the tooth next to them, four shillings; for the tooth adjoining that, three shillings; and thereafter one shilling for each. If speech becomes worse, twelve shillings; if the jaw is broken, six shillings shall be paid, ibid.---Whoever causes injury to an arm shall pay six shillings. If the arm is broken, six shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If a thumb is cut off, [Col. 1302] twenty shillings; if the thumbnail is cut off, three shillings shall be paid. If anyone cuts off the forefinger, he shall pay eight shillings; the middle finger, four shillings; the ring finger, six shillings; the little finger, eleven shillings, ibid.---For each nail, one shilling shall be paid, ibid.---For a small mole, three shillings; for larger ones, six shillings, ibid.---If anyone strikes another on the nose with his fist, three shillings, ibid.---If there is a wound, one shilling; if he receives a blow from an uplifted hand, he shall pay one shilling, ibid.---If a bruise is black outside the clothes, he shall make amends with thirty *sceattas*; if it is within the clothes, each such injury shall be compensated with twenty *sceattas*, ibid.---If the diaphragm is wounded, he shall pay twelve shillings; if it is pierced, he shall make amends in shillings [amount uncertain], ibid., 353.---If anyone is left lame, thirty shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If anyone wounds the neck, three shillings shall be paid, ibid. If anyone’s genital member is cut off, compensation shall be made with three customary fines; if it is pierced, six shillings shall be paid; if anyone makes an incision, he shall pay six shillings, ibid.---If the thigh is broken, twelve shillings shall be paid; if he becomes lame, his friends must determine the award, ibid.---If a rib is broken, he shall pay three shillings, ibid.---If anyone pierces a thigh, every incision shall be compensated with six shillings; if it penetrates more than a thumb’s breadth, one shilling; for two thumb-breadths, two; beyond that, three shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If a vertebra is wounded, three shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If a foot is amputated, fifty shillings shall be paid, ibid.---If the great toe is amputated, ten shillings shall be paid; for each other toe, half the payment prescribed for the fingers of the hand shall be paid, ibid.---If the nail of the great toe is amputated, thirty *sceattas* shall be paid as compensation; for each of the others, ten *sceattas*, ibid.---If a free woman with flowing hair commits any dishonourable act, she shall make amends with thirty shillings, ibid.---The compensation for a virgin shall be the same as for a free man, ibid.---For violation of the protection of a cupbearer-widow of a noble family, fifty shillings shall be paid; of the second rank, twenty shillings; of the third, twelve; of the fourth, six, ibid.---If anyone marries a widow not under her own legal authority, he shall pay twice the compensation for violation of protection, ibid., 354.---If a man purchases a virgin for a price, she shall be regarded as purchased if this was done without fraud; but if fraud is present, she shall afterward be returned home and her property restored to her, ibid., 355.---If she bears a living child, she shall have half the goods if her husband dies first, ibid.---If she wishes to leave with the children, she shall have half the estate, ibid.---If the husband wishes to retain the children, they shall be as one of his children, ibid.---If he has begotten no offspring, the kinsmen shall have the goods, while she shall have maintenance and her dower, ibid.---If anyone seizes a virgin by force, he shall give one shilling to her possessor, and thereafter redeem her according to the possessor’s will, ibid.---If she has been betrothed to another for a price, he shall make compensation with twenty shillings, ibid.---If she is pregnant, he shall pay thirty-five shillings and fifteen shillings to the king, ibid.---If anyone has intercourse with a slave’s wife while her husband lives, he shall make amends to them, ibid.---If a slave kills an innocent person, he shall make compensation with all his property, ibid.---If a slave’s eye or foot is knocked out, compensation shall be made for its full value, ibid.---If anyone binds another’s slave, he shall make amends with six shillings, ibid.---The fine for a slave’s theft shall be six shillings, ibid.---If a slave steals, he shall make double compensation, ibid.

EDWARD (Saint), king of the English.---Law concerning clerics and their possessions, CLI, 1191.---On the times and days of the king’s peace, ibid.---On the justice of holy Church, ibid.---On all tenants holding from the Church, ibid., 1192.---On accused persons fleeing to a church, ibid.---On breach of the Church’s peace, ibid.---On payment of the Church’s tithes, concerning sheep and piglets, ibid.---On bees and many other small tithes, ibid.---On matters to be subjected, by the king’s justice, to the judgment of iron or water, ibid., 1193.---On St Peter’s penny, ibid.---On the king’s manifold peace and the archbishop’s *manbote*, etc., ibid., 1194.---On treasures hidden and found in the earth, ibid.---What the office of a king is, with the example of Charles and Pippin, ibid.

FERDINAND, king of the Spains.---He accepts the lordship of the pontiff together with his entire kingdom, CC, 1370.

FREDERICK I, emperor.---Decree concerning the elevation and canonization of Saint Charles, XCVIII, 1360.---Letter to Pope Eugenius, informing the pontiff of his election and coronation, CLXXX, 1636.---The pact which he made with Pope Eugenius, ibid., 1638.

FULCHER, administrator of the houses of the Knights Templar.---Letter to Louis, king of the Franks, concerning the irruption of the unbelievers into the Christian host and the lamentable defeat of the latter, CLV, 1273, 1280.

FULCHER, master of the house of Jerusalem.---Letter to Louis, king of the Franks, concerning the condition of the Jerusalem expedition, CLV, 1279 and 1280.

[Col. 1303] GLYCERIUS, emperor.---Edict against simoniacal ordinations, LXXII, 1111.

GRATIAN, emperor.---Letter to Saint Ambrose. He invites him to come to him and confirm him in the faith concerning the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, etc., XVI, 875.---Constitution concerning relapsed persons, XV, 1181.---Law that we should believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one Godhead under equal majesty and in the holy Trinity, LVI, 681.---On those who contend over religion, ibid., 682.---On heretics, especially Arians, Eunomians, and Manichaeans, ibid., 682, 683.

GUDELINA, queen.---She gives thanks to the Empress Theodora concerning her envoy and letters, and writes that she has seen to it that the pope and senate should reply to her by letter. Then she says that she has sent to her an envoy endowed with many virtues and learning, LXIX, 811.---She declares that she and Theodaliad earnestly seek her favour, and asks that they may enter into partnership in her glory, ibid., 812.

GUTHRUM, king of the English.---His laws are the same as those given by us under the heading EDWARD the Elder, king of the English, CXXXVIII, 459.

HENRY I, king of the Franks.---He confirms the donations made by his grandfather Hugh and his father Robert to the monastery of Saint Salvius at Montreuil, CLI, 1025.---Judicial settlement for the monastery of Saint-Médard against Robert of Coudicé, ibid., 1027.---He grants the canons of Chartres the free estate of Unigradum, ibid., 1028.---The king, aided by Abbot Albert in the capture of Châteauneuf, frees his monastery from the yoke of advocates and the vexations of archdeacons, ibid., 1029.---The abbey of Saint Victor of Nevers, rescued from lay control, is restored, ibid., 1032.---Decree by which he abolishes the unjust custom that the gates of the city of Orléans be closed during the vintage season, or guards posted there, ibid., 1036.---He introduces regular canons into the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, restored by himself, ibid., 1037.

HENRY the Younger, king of the Romans.---Letter to Pope Eugenius, in which he excuses the bishop of Mainz for not having attended the Council of Reims, and commends him as he travels to the pontiff, CLXXX, 1618.---He asks for the pontiff’s protection, ibid., 1619.---That he may graciously receive Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and others going to the pope; absolve the duchess of Poland from excommunication; and hold Abbot Wibald in his favour, ibid.

HENRY (Saint) II, emperor of the Romans.---Here we shall recount the manner in which kings proceeded when they issued laws publicly:

“Henry, by the grace of God’s mercy Emperor and Augustus of the Romans. We wish all our faithful, present as well as future, to know that, ever providing what is worthy of the public good, we establish matters with the approval of worthy persons, the faithful of our empire. While we were staying in the city of Strasbourg, which in the common tongue is called Strasburge, reports were brought to us by many persons that very many were then suffering these dangers under a pretext. Therefore, providing fitting relief for all, with the approving testimony of very many faithful standing before us—namely the archbishops of Milan and Ravenna; also the bishops of Strasbourg, Piacenza, Como, Vercelli, Parma, Acqui, Genoa, Luni, and Volterra; likewise margraves and counts of Italy, many nobles, vassals, learned men, and judges—we have, among many measures suited to the commonwealth, inserted certain chapters. We now and henceforth establish, order, and firmly command that these be observed by all subject to our empire and maintained in unwavering observance. These are the matters which we order to be inviolably observed:

“I. Whoever, of whatever nation, has taken or shall take a lawful wife, if it happens that she dies without children born of them both, the husband shall succeed his wife and receive all her goods.---II. Whoever, through greed for property, kills his father or mother, brother or sister, nephew, or any relative, whether by himself or through another, the inheritance of the person killed shall pass to the latter’s other lawful heirs. The killer’s inheritance, however, shall be confiscated to the fisc. The killer himself shall, at the bishop’s direction, be subjected to public penance. But if the person accused of the crime wishes to deny it, he shall fight personally; nor may he appoint a champion for himself, unless decrepit or youthful age, or infirmity, prevents him from fighting.---III. Whoever kills any person during a truce or after the giving of the kiss of peace, and wishes to deny it, shall fight personally and shall not appoint a champion for himself, unless he is in the condition just mentioned. If convicted, he shall lose the hand with which he committed the homicide.”---CXL, 223, 227.

DECREES.---That no member of the clergy may touch a woman; that a bishop may have no woman and may not live with any woman; that the sons of clerics who are servants of the Church shall be servants of the Church, with all their acquisitions; that no judge may promise freedom to sons of clerics who are servants of the Church; that servants of churches may acquire nothing through the hands of a free person; that whoever receives a charter through his own hands shall make a settlement with the Church; that no judge or notary may write charters by which servants of the Church acquire property through the hands of a free person, CXL, 226, 230.---A law that clerics may not dare to swear: that is, it is decreed that no bishop, abbot, presbyter, cleric of any order, monk, or nun, in any controversy, criminal or civil, may be compelled on any ground to take an oath; but they may delegate this office to their qualified advocates, ibid., 230.---Judgment concerning clerical marriage and the pact with Benedict VIII, ibid., 231, 233.---Decree granted to the monks of Saint Remigius, ibid., 237.---Decree of King Henry by which he assigns to Burchard, bishop of Worms, the entire estate that Duke Otto possessed in that city, ibid., 245.---The monastery of Stein, transferred from Duellium, is endowed by Emperor Henry II and subjected to the Church of Bamberg, ibid., 261.---He confirms the foundation of the college of canons in the church of Holy Cross at Liège, made by Notger, bishop of Liège, ibid., 264.---Decree by which he confirms to the Church of Worms all its possessions and adds others, ibid., 268.---He confirms various abbeys to Notger, bishop of Liège, and his successors, ibid., 269.---Decree by which he grants the county of Cambrai to the metropolitan Church of Cambrai and to Bishop Heluin and his successors, ibid., 273.---Letters concerning the bishopric of Bamberg established by him, ibid.---Decree by which he assigns to the Church of Worms everything that Count Becelin possessed as a benefice, ibid., 278.---Decree for the abbey of Saint Apollinaris at Clèves, ibid., 286.---Decree by which he settles the dispute between the Church of Worms and the monastery of Lorsch concerning the forest of Odenwald, ibid., 297.---Decree by which he protects the Church of Worms from the unjust attacks of provincial counts, ibid., 316.---Judgment against the counts and margraves of Este, who refused to obey his authority, ibid., 318.---Grant of King Henry concerning coinage and a market, ibid., 350.---Decrees for the abbey of Protolium and for Hilderad, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, ibid., 354. He confers certain estates upon the Church of Paderborn, ibid., 356.

HENRY III, emperor.---Constitution concerning the oath against vexatious litigation, CLI, 1082.---Assembly at Zurich, at which constitutions are issued concerning despisers of the emperor, poisonings, and forfeiture of benefices, ibid., 1082.

HENRY IV, emperor.---Assembly at Oppenheim, namely the promise that he made to Hildebrand, or Pope Gregory VII, CLI, 1125.---Assembly at Pavia, concerning the command and firm fidelity of Henry IV against the plunderers and raiders of his kingdom, ibid., 1426.---Assembly at Mainz, namely the promulgation of the Peace of God and the oath of the Peace of God, ibid., 1128, 1134.---Constitution of general peace, ibid., 1137.---Constitution of provincial peace and peace in the diocese of Constance, ibid., 1137, 1139.---Assembly at Regensburg, concerning the manner in which advocates are to be supported when they discharge their duties in places assigned to them, ibid., 1140.

HENRY V, emperor.---Concerning tithes and offerings to be distributed to priests, CLX, 236.

HENRY, duke of Saxony.---Letter to Pope Eugenius. He highly praises the merits of Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, and asks that the pontiff confirm the union of Kaminada with the monastery of Corbie, CLXXX, 1621.

HENRY, count of Namur.---Letter to Pope Eugenius, in which he declares himself ready to observe what had been determined at Trier in the pope’s court concerning the dispute between himself and the archdeacon of Verdun, CLXXX, 1622.

HOELIDHA, prince of Wales and of all Cambria.---Seeing that his Welshmen were insolently abusing the laws, he summoned from every hundred throughout his whole kingdom six laymen distinguished for authority and knowledge, and all ecclesiastics holding office—the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and priors of his kingdom—to a place called . . . The king and those assembled remained there throughout the whole of Lent, praying to the Most High by complete fasting, asking grace to do good things according to the king’s purpose. From those assembled the king chose twelve most learned laymen and one most learned cleric to instruct him in laws and customs, so that he might more closely pursue truth and justice; and he ordered these to be written in three parts: the first, the law of his daily court; the second, the law of the country; the third, the practice of both. He ordered three identical books to be made: one always to follow his daily court; another for the court of Dinefwr; and a third for the court of Aberffraw, so that each of the three parts of Cambria might possess a copy of the law ready for use. These laws concerning morals, forty in number and founded upon their own principles, may be read in the volume, CXXXVIII, 471, 479.

HONORIUS, emperor.---Laws renewing penalties enacted against Donatists and other heretics, XI, 1216, 1217, 1218, 1219, 1220.---Law by which he revokes the edict granting freedom to heretics, ibid., 1222.---Against the Donatists, ibid., 1427, 1428, 1430.---Law against those invading churches, XI, 1192.---Laws concerning rebaptizers, ibid., 1204, 1205, 1208, 1216.---On the edict of unity to be published through Africa, ibid., 1311.---Laws establishing many penalties against Donatists, ibid., 1212, 1420.---Letter to Arcadius, ruler of the East: Honorius laments what was perpetrated at Constantinople on Easter Day. The burning of the Temple of Augustus and the senate is the first sign of divine anger. Other things are to be feared unless God is appeased. He cannot remain silent on this matter, lest silence be construed as assent: with what undue haste the sacred bishops were driven into exile while episcopal judgment was awaited. Hence a disturbance of religion was introduced, and a broad field was opened to heresies and schisms, XX, 507.---Letter to Emperor Arcadius, requesting that he order a synod to be convened at Thessalonica and Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, to go there, ibid., 511.---Directive to Pope Boniface, in which the emperor establishes that, if two bishops should again be ordained at Rome, both are to be expelled from the city, ibid., 767.---Decrees concerning bringing the adherents of the heresies of Coelestius and Pelagius before competent judges, LVI, 490, 493.

HUNERIC, king.---His decree sent to Eugenius of Carthage and the other Catholic bishops established throughout Africa, ordering them to come to Carthage to give an account of their faith, LVIII, 213.---That overseas bishops too should be summoned to hold a conference concerning the common faith, ibid., 214.

INGEBURG, queen of the Franks.---Letter to Pope Celestine III, declaring that, while she was neglected, the king attached himself to the daughter of the duke of Merania, CCVI, 1277.

JULIAN the Apostate, emperor.---Rescript in favour of the Donatists, XI, 1179.---How hostile he was to Christians, LXIX, 1033.---That at the beginning of his reign he spared Christians more, ibid., 1034.---That he recalled those whom Constantius had deported, and concerning the persecution of churchmen and the Christian people, ibid.

JULIAN, uncle of Julian the Apostate.---How he closed churches and plundered the ornaments of the Church, LXIX, 1036.

JUNIUS, praetorian prefect.---Edict against Pelagius, LVI, 492.

JUSTINIAN, emperor.---Justinian was born in the year 483. He had as his uncle the Emperor Justin, by whom he was carefully brought up at the Castle of Bederiana and adopted as a son. Before becoming emperor, he married Theodora, a Cyprian by birth, a headstrong woman passionately devoted to the Eutychian heresy. In 518 he was made master of soldiers by Emperor Justin and sent with an army to the East, where he conducted the war against the Persians successfully. In 521 he held the consulship, was soon afterward made patrician, then *nobilissimus*, and finally, in 527, was proclaimed Augustus and began to reign with his uncle. When the latter died in the same year, he thereafter held the empire alone. In 528 he promulgated an edict decreeing that Nestorians and Eutychians, as heretics, should be punished by civil penalties; this was renewed five years later. In 541 he himself condemned Origen by edict and, when a synod was soon afterward held at Constantinople under Mennas, procured the anathematizing of him together with his followers. In 545, by an issued constitution, he condemned the Three Chapters, which the Council of Constantinople likewise did at the end of the following year. In 553 he convened an ecumenical council at Constantinople, in which he requested and obtained from the Fathers the condemnation of the Three Chapters. In 563, when the powers of his mind were failing together with his body, deceived by certain heretics, he issued an edict teaching that Christ’s body, alike before and after the resurrection, was free from corruption and natural affections. He commanded all bishops to subscribe to his opinion; he harshly oppressed the Eastern bishops who appealed to the judgment of Anastasius of Antioch; and he drove Anastasius himself and Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, from their sees because they steadfastly resisted, ordering them to be carried into exile. Devoting himself to such delusions, he died in 565.

There were formerly, and there are still today, persons who unload whole cartloads of slanders and insults upon this prince—for example, Cardinal Baronius. To allow the reader to assess him, certain statements must be set before his eyes: “Justinian,” he says, “was a man utterly unlearned, so much so that he had never even learned the alphabet. A sacrilegious emperor, who stirred up no slight persecution, driven by madness, deranged in mind, corrupted by an evil spirit, agitated by Satan, who dissolved every order in the Church and made the kingdom of heaven into a prison-house of hell.” The sharpness of this criticism smells of an Englishman. Yet very many testimonies of the ancients attest Justinian’s outstanding virtues. Procopius says the following about his learning and piety: “He was accustomed at one time to read through books dealing with divine matters, at another to prolong conversations about the same subjects with bishops and presbyters deep into the night. It was always his practice for many weeks of days before Easter to afflict his body with vigils and fasts more than ascetic, to take food once every two days, to abstain entirely from wine, bread, and other foods, and to be content only with herbs seasoned with salt and vinegar and with water.” Pope Agatho offers this testimony concerning him: “Above all,” he says, “the Augustus Justinian of revered memory was a true champion of the apostolic faith; the soundness of whose faith, insofar as it pleased God through his sincere confession, so exalted the Christian commonwealth, and whose religious memory is still deemed worthy of veneration by all nations. The soundness of his faith, disseminated throughout the whole world by his most august edicts, is praised.”

Decree against heretics, LXIX, 30.—Book against Origen, that is, a treatise against the impious Origen and his wicked opinions, ibid., 177.—Confession of the right faith against the Three Chapters, ibid., 225.—Letter concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and the rest, ibid., 268.—Letter against the impious Theodore and his unjust doctrines, and the letter of Ibas, and other books assailing the Catholic faith, ibid., 273.—Letter to Agapetus. Following the custom of his forefathers, he issued before the newly elected Roman pontiff a profession of his faith, LXVI, 31.—Copy of Justinian’s petitions, ibid., 41.—Second profession of faith presented to Agapetus, ibid., 42.

Novella determining the number of clergy of the most holy Great Church, and likewise of the other most holy churches of this most august City, LXXII, 921.—Novella concerning monasteries, monks, and their superiors, ibid., 926.—Novella on how bishops and the other clergy ought to be brought to ordination, and concerning the expenses of churches, ibid., 936.—Novella concerning the prohibition against alienating or exchanging immovable ecclesiastical property, or giving it to creditors as a special mortgage, since general mortgages should suffice, ibid., 938.—Novella that provincial governors are to be dispatched to their offices without any payment of money, ibid.—Edict addressed to the most devotedly loving archbishops and most religious patriarchs established everywhere, ibid., 957.—Novella concerning the oath customarily rendered by those who assume offices, ibid., 964.—Novella concerning the referendaries of the sacred palace, ibid., 965.—Novella concerning the defenders of cities, ibid., 966.—Novella that clergy may be transferred from one church to another in order to supply the established offices left vacant, ibid., 970.—Novella concerning the Armenians, requiring that they too follow Roman laws in all respects, ibid., 971.—Novella concerning churches established in Africa, ibid., 972.—Novella that Anthimus, Severus, Peter, Zooras, and the remaining heretics be deprived of ecclesiastical rank, ibid., 973.—Sacred constitution against Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zooras, ibid., 975.—Novella concerning the offices or workshops of the City of Constantinople, and requiring that only eleven hundred workshops of the most holy Great Church be exempted; all the rest, to whatever owner they belong, are to bear their customary obligations, ibid., 983.—Novella that Jews, Samaritans, and heretics are not, on grounds of religion and their worship, to be released from curial status, but are to remain subject to curial duties and enjoy none of its privileges. Likewise, that they may give testimony against orthodox persons subject to curial status, insofar as they give distinguished testimony on behalf of the orthodox commonwealth, ibid., 986.—Novella concerning the alienation and discharge of immovable ecclesiastical property, ibid., 987.—Novella that henceforth exchanges of ecclesiastical property are not to be fictitiously made in favor of the most pious emperor and then, by this means, transferred to other lawful persons, but are to be made only to the imperial household. And that perpetual emphyteutic leases may be made from oratories to oratories, provided that a decree is entered, except in the case of this Great Church; yet an emphyteutic lease is not to pass to a private person, ibid., 898.—Novella that documents called *insinuativa* concerning clergy are to be issued in the Great Church, but are in no way to be issued in other churches, ibid., 990.—Novella that sacred mysteries are not to be celebrated in private houses, ibid., 991.—Novella concerning clergy who have abandoned their own churches; likewise concerning those who build oratories, ibid., 992.—Novella concerning funeral rites, and what ought to be done at the burial of the dead, ibid., 995.—Novella concerning property left to the church of Mysia, ibid., 998.—Novella that no one build an oratory without the bishop’s knowledge; that he first determine what will be necessary for the care and establishment of the oratory to be built; that bishops not be absent from their churches; and concerning the alienation of immovable ecclesiastical property, XX, 999.—Novella concerning those who enter monasteries and consecrate their property, and from what time this ought to be valid, ibid., 1000.—Novella that those who practice lust contrary to nature, as well as those who utter blasphemies against God, are to be punished, ibid., 1001.—Novella concerning the courts before which monks and ascetic women ought to litigate, ibid., 1002.—Constitution which frees sons from paternal power through dignities and the episcopal office, ibid., 1004.—Novella that clergy are first to be summoned before their own bishops, and afterwards before civil judges, ibid., 1006.—Novella that governors who delay hearing the allegations of petitioners are to be compelled by bishops to do so; and that, if anyone considers a governor suspect in the hearing of a lawsuit, he may associate with him also the bishop of the city, etc., ibid., 1007.—Novella concerning women of heretical belief, ibid., 1009.—Novella concerning the limitation period for actions belonging to sacred places, ibid., 1011.—Novella concerning the alienation and emphyteutic leasing of ecclesiastical property, ibid.—Novella concerning various ecclesiastical chapters, ibid., 1019.—Novella concerning ecclesiastical canons and privileges relating to the most holy churches, ibid., 1039.—Novella: edict concerning the faith, addressed to the people of Constantinople, ibid., 1044.—Novella concerning monks, ascetics, and their manner of life, ibid.—Novella concerning the Samaritans, ibid., 1050.—Novella concerning the Hebrews, on how they ought to read the Scriptures, ibid., 1051.—Selected laws by which he dealt with affairs of the Church or bore witness to his piety toward God: concerning bishops and clergy, ibid., 1053, 1072.—Concerning episcopal jurisdiction and various chapters relating to pontifical right, care, and reverence, ibid., 1073, 1085.—Concerning heretics, monks, and Samaritans, ibid., 1086, 1088.—Concerning the clarification of the ancient law and the authority of jurists cited in the Digest, ibid., 1089, 1100.—Concerning the office of the praetorian prefect of Africa and the entire condition of that diocese, ibid., 1101.

JUSTIN, emperor.—Letter to Pope Hormisdas. [It reports] that John the bishop, having embraced the Catholic faith, anathematized the heretics, and that the name of Acacius, together with the names of the other schismatics, was erased from the sacred tablets, LXIII, 448.—Since the Church now enjoys peace, prayers are to be offered to God for the emperor, ibid., 450.

CHARLES II, king of the Franks.—Oath in the German language, CXXXVIII, 528.—Concerning diocesan government to be exercised by bishops, and how, ibid., 530.—Concerning the secular and regular government of the Church, ibid., 540.—Concerning various matters relating to church government and the conduct of bishops, ibid., 443–554.

CHARLES II.—Treaty of Strasbourg, CXXXVIII, 527.—Decrees established at the assembly in the royal estate of Cologne, ibid.—Decrees enacted in the synod at Toulouse, ibid., 531.—Decrees established at the assembly in the estate of Théodon, ibid., 533.—Decrees established in the council at the Palace of Verneuil, ibid., 539.

That we may convey some idea of these and similar decrees, let us report certain decrees:

Decrees of the assembly at the estate of Épernay.—Concerning the honor and worship of churches, CXXXVIII, 317.—Concerning the honor of bishops and reverence for the servants of God; concerning justice; that care be taken with those who, through youth or ignorance, err in some respect or disregard the bishops’ admonition, lest they be suddenly or incautiously condemned by anathema; concerning those attempting to be obstinately disobedient to royal authority; concerning precarial grants; hospitals; plunderers; that bishops be allowed suitable time for performing their ministry; that clergy not handle military weapons; that envoys be sent to investigate whether directives concerning church property have been issued for private advantage; concerning the Simoniacal heresy; that no one usurp an episcopal see while its own bishop is incapacitated; that canons sleep within the dormitory; that monks not come to the palace unless on grounds of obedience, abbots excepted; that laypersons not meddle with church tithes; concerning nuns married against authority; concerning the betrothed of others; concerning burials within a church, ibid., 347.—Concerning peace, concord, and unanimity, ibid., 553.

Decrees enacted at the assemblies of Pavia and Marsna, CXXXVIII, 558–575.—Decrees of the assembly at Mainz: namely, concerning harmony among bishops, counts, and faithful men; concerning episcopal authority, ibid., 581.—Concerning the collection of tithes; that no one dare violate immunities, ibid., 582, 583.—That bishops not engage in hunting, ibid., 584.—Concerning the continence of priests; concerning the exemption of priests and deacons, ibid., 585.—Concerning infants smothered [in bed]; adultery; homicide; concubines, ibid., 386, 587.—Concerning servile works not to be performed on Sundays, ibid., 587.—Concerning those who have both a wife and a concubine; concerning the baptism of sick infants; that no priest presume to intrude into another’s parish; that no one solicit another’s cleric; that no priest presume to give gifts in order to seize another’s church, ibid., 587–589.—Decrees in the synod at Verberie, ibid., 595.—Decrees in the synod at Valenciennes, ibid., 599.—Decrees of the assembly at Liège, ibid., 605.—Decrees of the assembly at Attigny, ibid., 607, 609, 617.—Chapters sent from Quierzy to the Franks and Aquitanians, ibid., 631, 637.—Decrees enacted at the assembly of Saint-Quentin, ibid., 650.—Decrees enacted at the assembly of Quierzy, ibid., 651.—Decrees enacted in the council of Metz, ibid., 653.—Decrees enacted at the assembly at Saponariae, ibid., 657.—Decrees enacted at the assembly at Quierzy, ibid., 681.—Decrees enacted in the synod of Pîtres, ibid., 683.—Decrees enacted at the assembly at Sablonariae, ibid., 691.—Treaty of Tusey, ibid., 717.—Decrees enacted at the assembly of Metz, ibid., 731.—Decrees enacted at the assembly at Pîtres, ibid.—Concerning the agreement of Aix, ibid., 741.—Concerning the assembly at the estate of Gundulf, ibid., 745.—Capitulary of Quierzy, ibid., 745, 773.—Concerning the assembly at Attigny, ibid., 751.—Various chapters concerning ecclesiastical persons, ibid., 753, 761.—Concerning the synod at Pontigny, ibid.—Edict concerning the Northman tribute, ibid., 771.—Decrees enacted at the assembly of Furon, ibid., 785.—Decrees enacted at the assembly at Confluence, ibid., 817.

CARLOMAN, king.—“By the common counsel of our faithful men we have decreed that henceforth no one shall commit robbery or consent to one who commits it,” ibid., 791.—“That robbery committed in the past be repaired with every diligence, and that he who committed it undergo the fitting *harmiscara* [penal humiliation].”—“That, if anyone is found committing robbery after this assembly and our ban, the man whose dependent committed it shall bring him before us for lawful redress; but if he cannot bring him, he shall make amends for him according to the statutes of the laws. And all are to know that he who has fled justice is outlawed (*forbannitus*), so that no one may receive him except in order to present him [to justice],” ibid., 791.—Chapters of the same emperor at the Palace of Verneuil, ibid.

LAMBERT, emperor.—Council of Ravenna: “If anyone despises the rules of the holy Fathers and the most glorious emperors, which are established and sacred in their capitularies concerning ecclesiastical tithes, and does not observe them, both the giver and the receiver shall be subject to excommunication by the authority of the holy Apostolic See and the sanction of the holy synod,” CXXXVIII, 809.—“If any Roman, of whatever rank, whether clergy, senate, or any other order, wishes freely to come before the imperial majesty, or, compelled by necessity, wishes to appeal to us, let no one presume to oppose him; nor let anyone presume to invade or plunder their property, or to harass their persons while going, returning, or staying, until the imperial authority is able to determine their causes or persons, whether itself or through envoys. But anyone who attempts to harass them while going, returning, or staying, or to take anything of their property after they have sought protection through mercy, shall incur the indignation of imperial vengeance,” ibid., 811.—“That the privilege of the holy Roman Church, established and confirmed from ancient times by the most pious emperors, be now confirmed likewise and preserved unimpaired as is fitting; and that the holy Roman Church, our mother, be exalted, protected, and defended,” ibid., 811.—“That the synod which [is held] in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, for rooting out certain evils and especially for the cause of . . . by imperial consent,” etc., ibid.

Capitulary.—That a count exercising robbery among his honors be subjected to the law, ibid., 812.—That imperial men hastening to an interview or service of the emperor be content with their own provisions, ibid., 813.—That no count grant the holdings of the Arimanni as benefices to his own men.—That men of counts in no way reside in the houses of Arimanni, but restore the houses of the commonwealth and reside there.—That public notaries in no way be forbidden to register the property of Arimanni whenever this is expedient for them. But if such property has been sold as a means of avoiding military service or a court-session, and the sellers have afterwards ceased to pay the dues on it, both obligations shall be exacted from them as before the registration, CXXXVIII, 813.—That the Arimanni not be compelled to go to court more frequently than is established by law, either by counts or by *sculdais*.—That only envoys of the imperial army exact the ban.—That the *passus* [customary payment] of the emperor be paid by bishops and counts according to ancient custom. But if in recent times a comital fiscal holding has passed into ecclesiastical right, the imperial payment shall be increased from the church in proportion to the diminution of public property.—That every tithe be furnished to bishops or to those appointed by them, and that no one assign it to his own chapel unless perhaps by the bishop’s permission. If this should occur, the offender shall first be subject to human laws; then, bound by the excommunication of the people; and finally the chapel itself, which produces more contention than benefit, shall be destroyed.—That parish churches in no way be granted as benefices to counts, episcopal vassals, or any laymen.—That neither imperial envoy, count, nor judge claim court-session or lodging in the houses of churches, even under pretext of custom; rather, they are to establish houses in public settlements in which they may hold court and lodge according to ancient custom, ibid., 814.—That every parish have an archpriest. “Therefore, because of the continual care of God’s people, we desire archpriests to preside over every parish, who shall not only have care for the unlearned populace, but shall also guard with continual watchfulness the life of those priests who live in lesser churches, and report to their bishop with what diligence each performs the divine office. Nor is a bishop to allege that a parish has no need of an archpriest. If he himself is able to govern it, because he is very capable, it is nevertheless fitting that he share his burdens: as he himself presides over the mother church, so priests should preside over parishes, so that ecclesiastical care may falter in nothing. Yet let them refer everything to the bishop and presume to do nothing contrary to his decree,” ibid.

LANDULF, prince of Benevento.—Constitution with Pope Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 301.

LEOTALD, count of Mâcon.—Donation made by him to the monastery of Cluny, CXXXIII, 841.

LICINIA EUDOXIA, Augusta.—Letter to the emperor Theodosius concerning the disturbance of the Catholic Church, LIV, 861.

LIUTPRAND, king of the Lombards.—Decree establishing the dues to be paid by the people of Comacchio for transporting salt through the ports of Lombardy, LXXXVII, 1343.—Judgment of certain bishops assembled by command of this king to resolve a controversy concerning certain parishes between the bishops of Arezzo and Siena, with a decision in favor of the bishop of Arezzo, ibid., 1354.—The king’s decree concerning that matter, ibid., 1358.

LOTHAIR I, king.—Constitutions of Olonne, A.D. 823, XCVII, 447.—Capitulary issued to bishops, ibid., 455.—Roman Constitution, ibid., 457.—Constitutions at Marengo (825), ibid., 461.—Chapters of Aachen (825), ibid., 463.—Constitutions of Olonne (825), ibid., 473.—Extracted chapters (826), ibid., 481 and 487.—Various other chapters intermingled with the chapters of Charlemagne and Emperor Lothair I, ibid., 489, 675.

LOTHAIR, king of the Franks.—Letter to Pope Nicholas. He complains that the pontiff gives too much credence concerning him to his rivals. He indicates his sorrow at the excommunication of Theutgaud and Gunther. Moreover, clearing himself of all charges, he shows himself ready to refute before the pontiff the slanders of his adversaries, CXXI, 371.—Letter to the same pope. In order to escape the threatened excommunication for association with Waldrada, he announces his arrival at Rome to Nicholas and, to deceive him with false hope, appoints an embassy of bishops to him and promises aid against the Saracens if necessary, ibid., 374.—Letter to Pope Adrian II. On learning of Nicholas’s death, he writes this letter to Adrian, his successor, asking that he obtain from him what he had been unable to obtain from Nicholas: [permission for] his arrival at Rome, ibid., 376.—Charter concerning Saint-Amand granted to the monastery of Cluny in the time of Abbot Maiolus, CXXXVII, 779.—Edict by which he restores to Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, the see and diocese of Rheims, CXXXVIII, 525.—Decrees concerning the good of peace in the exercise of religion, ibid., 554.—Letter to Pope Innocent II. He complains of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, because he demands obedience from abbots, CLXXIX, 669.

Assembly at the estate of Théodon.—Thus this emperor begins his laws: “The holy Church, from its beginning often plunged amid various new disturbances, has never been wholly submerged, Christ its helmsman having been stirred by the prayers of the faithful. And although it was once, as it now appears, almost ruined, it has, by the zeal and devotion of the forefathers of kings, God being its author, been restored in the measure divinely granted. Therefore we render boundless praises to the Lord our God, who has also stirred your hearts to a like purpose and taught and inspired you to desire to walk in the footsteps of your fathers, by which you may attain from a temporal kingdom to an eternal one. We nevertheless offer manifold thanksgivings to your most noble lordship, because, in order to avert danger both from you and from us, and to provide for the common salvation of the whole people, you deem it worthy to pursue the good and acceptable will of God and the divine counsel; and, according to the Lord’s command which says, ‘Ask the priests concerning my law,’ and ‘Ask your fathers, and they will declare it to you,’ to seek this counsel from us—though unworthy, yet vicars of Christ—and with kindly devotion to await it as though it were a severe utterance from the mouth of God himself. The holy Church receives this heavenly gift of your humility with such joy that, even in her consolation, she desires to apply to herself what the Lord says concerning you: ‘Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you’; that is, in place of those forefathers who, with paternal affection, enriched, enlarged, and cultivated her, these sons have been born to you, who in you shall restore, recover, and preserve the paternal gifts, and who, as young men of faithful devotion and good disposition, while I watch over them and extend to them a hand of consolation, shall protect and cultivate them,” CXXXVIII, 535 . . . “let them follow the laws,” ibid., 536 and following.

LOTHAIR II, emperor.—The king’s oath: “And I, insofar as I shall know and reasonably be able, with the Lord’s help, will honor and safeguard each one of you according to his rank and person; and I will preserve him honored and safe without any deceit, condemnation, or deception; and I will preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to him. And to anyone who needs it and reasonably requests it, I will show reasonable mercy, as a faithful king ought rightly to honor and safeguard his faithful men, preserve for each the law and justice appropriate to him in every rank, and grant reasonable mercy to those in need who reasonably ask it. And, so far as human frailty permits, I will not depart from this for the sake of any person through partiality, ill-will, or anyone’s improper persuasion, insofar as God grants me understanding and ability; and if, through frailty, I have been led into acting against this, when I recognize it, I will willingly take care to correct it,” CXXXVIII, 632.—And various ecclesiastical decrees occur from col. 633 to 671, ibid.

Here we shall set down only certain decrees of this king:

Chapters to be observed by all.—“That the abolition of all past evils, hostilities, undermining, evil contrivances and schemes, and injuries mutually committed, be so effected between and among us, and be utterly torn from our hearts with all malice and rancor, that henceforth nothing of these matters come even into memory for the purpose of repaying evil or hostility, reproach or insult.”—“That henceforth, with the Lord’s cooperation, so great a kindness of true charity may always remain among us, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, without deceit or pretense, that no one may betray or give evil counsel against his peer, his kingdom, his faithful men, or anything pertaining to royal safety, prosperity, and honor; nor willingly accept through secret whisperers fabricated lies or detractions,” CXXXVIII, 671 and following, to col. 676.
