LOUIS I, THE PIOUS, king of the Franks.—Capitulary (816), XCVII, 371.—Constitution concerning freemen and vassals, ibid., 371.—Constitutions of Aachen (817), ibid., 373.—Chapters concerning monks (817), ibid., 379.—General Capitulary of Aachen (817), ibid., 393.—Encyclical to archbishops (817), ibid., 417.—Constitution concerning monastic service (817), ibid., 423.—Chapters added to the Welsh law (819), ibid., 437.—Answers given to a certain envoy (819), ibid., 439.—Lombard chapters (819), ibid., 441.—Capitulary of Aachen (820), ibid.—Capitulary at the estate of Théodon (821), ibid., 443.—Capitulary of Attigny (822), ibid., 445.—Precept confirming royal grants to the pope, XCVIII, 579.—Various other chapters intermingled with the chapters of Charlemagne and Emperor Lothair I, ibid., 489, 675.

LOUIS THE PIOUS.—Charter concerning the liberty of the people of Airo and Sagma, CII, 979.—Letter to Magnus, archbishop of Sens. He sends a copy of the rule of canons decreed in the Council of Aachen, CIV, 1309.—Letter to Jeremiah of Sens and Jonas, bishop of Orléans. Memorandum given to them when they were going as legates to Pope Eugenius II at Rome in the affair of images, ibid., 1316.—Letter to Pope Eugenius II. He sends him the acts of the Synod of Paris, ibid., 1317.—Letter to be read generally to the people of God, concerning the convocation of four councils, ibid., 1319.—Imperial letter to be read generally to the people of God, sent from the assembly at Aachen, concerning the gathering of councils of bishops in the four parts of the empire, ibid., 1321.—Letter to Aldric, bishop of Le Mans, concerning certain property alienated from his church, ibid., 1326.—Letter to Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, concerning the collection into one body of those matters which he had found scattered through Greek histories concerning Saint Dionysius, ibid., 1326, 1328.—Precept concerning the mission of Saint Ansgar and his ordination, CXVIII, 1033.

LOUIS II, king of the Franks.—Oath in the Romance language, CXXXVIII, 528.—Certain decrees concerning religion, CXXXVIII, 534.

Assembly at the estate of Épernay. Because the mind of this king had been stirred against the bishops by the faction of certain persons, and the leading men of his kingdom, dissenting from the admonition of those bishops and having removed the bishops from that council, selected from all those chapters only these as to be observed and approved; and they delivered them in writing to the bishops, saying that they had accepted no more of their chapters than these, and that these they wished to observe with the prince.

These are the chapters: concerning the honor and worship of churches; the honor of bishops and reverence for God’s servants; justice; that care be taken concerning those who through youth or ignorance err in any matter or disregard bishops’ admonitions, lest they be suddenly or rashly condemned by anathema; concerning those attempting to be obstinately disobedient to royal authority; concerning precarial grants; hospitals; plunderers; that bishops be allowed suitable time for performing their ministry; that clergy not take up military weapons; that envoys be sent to investigate whether directives issued by you concerning church property have been made for private benefit; concerning the Simoniacal heresy; that no one usurp an episcopal see while its own bishop is incapacitated; that canons sleep within the dormitory; that monks not come to the palace except for obedience, abbots excepted; that laypeople not meddle with church tithes; concerning nuns married against authority; concerning the betrothed of others; concerning burials within churches, CXXXVIII, 547, 554, 557, 564.

Chapters concerning ecclesiastical orders, CXXXVIII, 565, 576.—Concerning harmony among bishops, counts, and faithful men; episcopal authority; and the collection of tithes, ibid., 581, 582.—That no one dare violate immunities; that heirs not divide a church, ibid., 583.—That bishops not hunt; concerning the continence of priests, ibid., 584, 585.—Concerning the exemption of priests and deacons; infants smothered [in bed]; adultery; homicide; concubines; homicides, ibid., 586, 587.—Concerning servile works not to be performed on Sundays; those who have both a wife and a concubine; the baptism of sick infants; that no priest presume to intrude into another’s parish; that no one solicit another’s cleric; that no priest presume to give gifts to seize another’s church, ibid., 586, 587, 588.—Concerning priests who have had marriages; that priests be honored; that festivals may not be celebrated in Lent; that clerics may not attend theatrical entertainments; that Mass may not be sung in a house, ibid., 588, 590.

Laws.—“It has come to our attention that bands of robbers plunder those who travel to Rome for prayer, or who travel through our kingdom for trade; that they sometimes beat or kill them and seize their goods. Therefore we command that our counts and their *sculdais*, joined, if need be, by the vassals of bishops, search with the utmost diligence wherever they hear of such men, seize them, and restrain them. And if they find persons guilty of this crime, they shall inflict upon them, without any negligence, the penalties prescribed by the laws, so that our kingdom may be cleansed of these evildoers and those who come here relying on our protection, whether for prayer or trade, may be safe. Let each one of our faithful men know that any count or public official who gives support to such evildoers or neglects to pursue them shall feel the force of our indignation and be deprived of his own honor,” CXXXVIII, 573.

“But we have also learned that harmful men of this kind conspire together from different places and, passing through various counties, commit plunder and robbery in villages, roads, and forests, robbing and despoiling innocent people. We likewise command that they be diligently sought out, seized, and restrained. If they are found guilty of this crime, let them be subjected without any delay to the legal penalties, so that such disturbance and unjust plundering may be removed from our people, and that all living under our dominion may be permitted to live in safety and peace, in order that the order of the commonwealth, provided for under just administration, may remain secure and tranquil,” CXXXVIII, 574; and other [laws] . . . to 790; and from col. 609 to 622.

“First of all, the faith of priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe; examples must be set forth, so that, as far as he is able, a person may understand the Creator from the creature,” CXXXVIII, 623.

“Second, it must be commanded that the Lord’s Prayer, in which all things necessary for human life are contained, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is wholly contained, be learned by everyone, both in Latin and in the vernacular, so that what is professed by the mouth may be believed and understood in the heart,” CXXXVIII, 623.

“Third, it must be enjoined that suitable responses to priestly salutations be learned, so that not only clergy and persons dedicated to God offer the response to the priest, but all the people ought to respond with one devout voice . . .”

“Fourth, that the creed of Saint Athanasius be learned by priests and recited from memory every Sunday at the first hour,” etc., etc.

There are still other ecclesiastical laws from col. 623 to 631, vol. CXXXVIII.

Letter to the Cistercians concerning the Church and monastery of Fontenay, CLXXXV, 1145.—Letters requesting that the feast of Saint Bernard, abbot, be solemnly observed, CLXXXV, 1653.—Charter concerning the toll at Montreuil and the exactions granted by it to the Church of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1061.—Against heretics commonly called Poplicans, wandering through the regions of Flanders, CC, 1376.—Concerning the murder of Saint Thomas, CC, 1376.—He urges the pontiff to cut off vices by his authority, CC, 1378.

LOUIS IV, king of the Franks.—Precept concerning certain churches and places granted to the monastery of Cluny in the time of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, CXXXIII, 839.

LOUIS VI, king of the Franks (A.D. 1121).—He writes that he will never tolerate the subjection demanded by the primate of Lyons from the archbishop of Sens, CLXIII, 1339.

LOUIS VII, called the Younger.—Letter to his subjects established in the kingdom of France, concerning his capture and release, CLV, 1281.

MACBETH, king of the Scots.—These were the enactments of this king: “Do not summon one initiated into Christ before a secular judge; if he has been summoned and appears, do not judge him, but refer him to the sacred bishops. Freely grant to the shepherds of the churches the tenth part of the produce of the land; and always worship God by customary prayers and offerings. Whoever has contemptuously disregarded the authority of the pontiff throughout an entire year, and has not meanwhile been reconciled, regard as an enemy of the commonwealth; but whoever persists in that obstinacy for two years, punish by the loss of all his property. If anyone accompanies, as a follower, to church, a public assembly, a court, or a market, a person whom he does not otherwise support daily at his own expense or board, let him be liable to capital punishment,” CLI, 1189.

MONAXIUS, praetorian prefect.—Edict threatening exile to adherents of the Pelagian heresy, LVI, 492.

MARCIAN, emperor.—Letter to Leo, archbishop of Rome. A letter in which he informs him that those whom he had sent to him were always received cheerfully; therefore he should deign to come there with all readiness and celebrate a synod; or, if this seems burdensome to him, he should indicate this by letter, so that, after holy bishops have been called together, matters conformable to the faith may be decreed in whatever city is pleasing, LIV, 903.—He rejoices at the strengthening of the faith at Chalcedon and the restoration of peace to the Church; [he states] that the faith was set forth to the synod in accordance with the letters of Pope Saint Leo; he asks that the second place be assigned to the see of Constantinople in accordance with the statutes of the Second and Fourth Synods, etc., LIV, 970.—Letter to Pope Leo, requesting the pope’s confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon as necessary. He praises Leo’s constancy in vindicating the canons and suppressing innovation, LIV, 1017.—Letter to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning the convocation of the Council of Chalcedon. An idea of that emperor may be gained from the following instructions: “Divine matters must be placed before all business. For, with almighty God propitious, we are confident that the commonwealth must both be preserved and improved. Therefore, since certain doubts appear to have arisen in our orthodox religion, as the letter of the most reverend Leo, bishop of the venerable City of Rome, also attests, it has especially pleased our clemency that a venerable synod be celebrated in the city of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, so that, once minds have come together and every truth has been examined, and once the partisan efforts have ceased by which certain persons are known to have troubled the most holy orthodox religion in former times, our true faith may become more manifestly known to the whole age, so that henceforth there may be no doubt or discord. Accordingly, let your holiness hasten to go to the aforesaid city of Nicaea by the first day of September, with such most reverend bishops as you judge suitable and instructed in the orthodox religion from the churches established under the care of your priesthood. Let your religiousness also know that our serenity will attend the venerable synod, unless public necessities keep us occupied on military expeditions,” LVI, 527.

When the most devout and most faithful Emperor Marcian had arrived, he addressed the venerable synod as follows: “As soon as, by the judgment of God, we were chosen for the empire, amid the many necessities of the commonwealth no concern pressed us more strongly than that the orthodox and true Christian faith, holy and pure as it is, should dwell unquestioned in the minds of all. For it is clear that, through the greed or partisan zeal of certain persons, while some during the intervening period held differing opinions and, according to their own will rather than as truth and the doctrine of the Fathers require, misled the peoples, very many have been led into error. For this reason we have endeavoured to convene this holy synod for this very purpose, and seem to have imposed labour upon you: that, once every obscurity and error has been washed away, our religion—pure and holy as it is—may, as the Godhead willed to reveal itself to humankind and as the doctrine of the Fathers shows, be instilled into the minds of all and shine with the light of its truth; and that no one hereafter may dare to dispute otherwise concerning the divinity of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ than the apostolic preaching and the enactments of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, which agree with it, are known to have handed down to posterity. The writings sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople of holy memory, by holy Pope Leo of the city of Rome, who governs the Apostolic See, likewise testify to this.

“Therefore, with party zeal removed, patronage abolished, and greed at an end, let the truth be made known to all. We have wished to attend the synod, following the example of the religious Emperor Constantine, to confirm the faith, not to exercise any power, lest the peoples be divided by the perverse persuasions of others. For the simplicity of some has hitherto been deceived by the talents and excessive verbosity of certain persons; and it is clear that dissensions and heresies have arisen through the wicked insinuations of various people. Our purpose is that the whole people, being of one mind through true and holy doctrine, may return to the same religion and worship the true catholic faith, which you shall expound according to the institutions of the Fathers. Let your piety therefore hasten, in unanimous purpose, so that, just as from the Synod of Nicaea until recent times, after errors had been cut away, the true faith became known to all, so now too, through this holy synod, once the obscurities that seem to have arisen in these few years through the perversity and greed of certain persons have been removed, its decrees may be preserved forever. And it will belong to the divine majesty firmly to keep forever that which we desire to be done with holy purpose.” LVI, 527–530.

Constitution of the same Emperor Marcian concerning the Synod of Chalcedon: “At last that which we had desired with the greatest zeal and prayers has come to pass. Contention has been removed from the orthodox law of Christians. At last remedies have been found for culpable error, and the discordant judgment of peoples has come together into one consensus and concord. For the most religious priests came to Chalcedon from the different provinces, in accordance with our commands, and by a clear definition taught what must be observed in religion. Let profane contention therefore now cease. For he is truly impious and sacrilegious who, after the judgment of so many priests, leaves anything to be determined by his own opinion,” etc. [lacuna], LVI, 547.—Another constitution of the same emperor, addressed to catholic Christians assembled in synod, LVI, 549.—Another of the same concerning the maintenance of the catholic faith and concerning the Eutychians and Apollinarians and their punishments, LVI, 551.

MAXIMUS, emperor.—Letter to Pope Siricius. He promises care for the catholic faith; he pledges that the case of Agriciius, whom Siricius had written was improperly advanced to the rank of presbyter, shall be examined in synod. He again professes his zeal for the catholic faith and sends the records in which the recently exposed crimes of the Manichaeans or Priscillianists are set forth, XIII, 591.

OTTO THE GREAT I.—Decree concerning royal rights granted to Blessed Peter, XCVIII, 625.—That laymen shall not presume, without episcopal permission, to give churches to presbyters or remove them from presbyters, CXXXVIII, 832.—That no layman may dare to demand the services of, harass, or inflict any injury upon a presbyter, ibid.—That the whole Paschal week be celebrated festively; and that on the second, third, and fourth weekdays of Pentecost honour be paid no less solemnly than on the Lord’s Day.—That fasting be observed in the Greater Litany, as in the Rogation days before the Ascension of the Lord, ibid.—That the offerings of the faithful be brought to the altar four times and belong in no respect to lay authority, Scripture saying: “Those who serve at the altar should partake from the altar,” ibid.—That tithes, which the Lord commands to be brought into his storehouse, if they are not rendered to the churches of God but are retained by secular persons through a wicked greed that burns more fiercely than Aetna’s fires, shall not be subject to secular judgments nor debated in secular courts; rather, in holy synod, the [Col. 1314] priests to whose uses they are assigned shall determine by definite enactments what must be done concerning them, ibid.

—That no oppression of virgins or widows, nor abduction, be committed by any persons; and that those who abduct them under the pretext of living together, together with those assisting and conniving with the abductors, if they are clerics, shall fall from their rank, but if laymen, shall be anathematized; and the abductors shall remain forever without hope of marriage. If, after this, they presume to unite themselves, both shall be anathematized, ibid., 833.—That no abbey possessing the right of election in its own right may be given to a monastery or to any person as private property; but abbeys lacking election may, by royal gift and privilege, be transferred to another monastery which stands under the king’s *mundiburdium* [protection], ibid., 834.—If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the office imposed upon him, as is prescribed in the Council of Carthage, chapter 25, ibid.—Bishops, presbyters, and any member of the clergy may not keep hunting dogs or hawks for the love of hunting, as is read in the Council of Toledo, chapter 10. Whoever among such persons delights in this pleasure shall abstain from every ecclesiastical office so long as he remains occupied by that detestable pleasure, ibid.—A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling, if he refuses to desist from this forbidden practice, shall be deposed, as is contained in the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 42, ibid.

—No one remaining in clerical office shall allow a woman brought in from outside to live with him. If any woman, stained by marks of suspicion, attempts to act contrary to this, she shall be beaten with rods and shorn by the bishop or his envoy. But if secular power prevents this from being done, the woman, compelled by royal power, shall be subject to the aforesaid sentence, ibid., 835.—Those fleeing the various affairs of secular life and undertaking the rule of monastic observance may not leave the cloister without permission of their own abbot, but are to devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places in which they renounced the world, as is commanded in the Council of Chalcedon, ibid.—The bishop in whose diocese a monastery is situated must also provide oversight of the monks and, if he finds anything requiring correction, hasten to correct it, ibid., 833.—For clerics wishing to adopt the monastic habit and, in hope of divine reward, to reject secular things and enter a stricter life, the bishop must by no means deny entrance; rather, he should endeavour to exhort them to persevere in such a way of life, as the Council of Toledo provides, chapter 51, ibid., 836.—A nun who of her own free will wishes to bind herself by the purpose of a stricter life shall, with nothing standing in the way, not be prevented by the bishop from accomplishing what she resolved with good intention, ibid.

—That laymen shall not presume to expel presbyters from churches canonically entrusted to them without the knowledge and consent of their own bishop, nor install others in their place; for, just as they are ordained by bishops, so they must receive churches to administer from them, as is found in the Council of Arles, chapter 4, ibid.—That all tithing be under the authority of the bishop; and, if it has been neglected, whatever must be amended concerning it shall be corrected before the bishop or his envoy, ibid.—Bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, as has been established in many councils, must abstain from wives because they handle the divine ministries. Other clerics, when they have reached a more mature age, are to be compelled to continence even if unwilling, ibid., 836.—Agreement with Pope John II, ibid., 838.—Letter to Pope John XII, in which he says that he has heard such obscene things concerning that pope that, if they were said of actors, they would bring shame upon everyone: “Know,” he says, “that you are accused, not by a few but by all, both of our order and of another, of murder, perjury, sacrilege, and incest with your own kin and with two sisters. They say that you have drunk wine in the love of the devil, and that in gambling you have invoked the aid of Jupiter, Venus, and the other demons,” ibid., 845.

OTTO II, emperor.—Edicts: If a dispute arises concerning estates and both parties, or either party, seek to claim the estate by charters or written instruments, and if the person who declares the charter false wishes to establish this by judicial combat, we decree that it shall be so decided. Otherwise, we decree that it shall be determined according to the preceding chapters, CXXXVIII, 849.—Concerning the property of churches, we likewise command that it be done through advocates, ibid., 850.—If there is a dispute concerning investiture of an estate, we likewise decree that it be decided by combat, ibid.—If anyone, in person or through his messenger, deposits anything with another, and the latter, overcome by greed, denies the deposit, if it is valued at twenty solidi, we decree that the truth be decided by combat, ibid.—If anyone says that he made a charter (*cartam*) to someone concerning an estate under compulsion, we decree that the truth be decided by combat, ibid.—Concerning theft or *scachum* [uncertain legal term], if it exceeds six solidi, we likewise command that the truth be found by combat [Col. 1315], ibid.—If anyone finds his horse, other animals, or property in another’s possession, and that person says that he will furnish a warrantor (*warens*), he shall immediately swear that he will bring him to a specified warrantor; nor may he proceed beyond the third warrantor and the third county. If he refuses to do this, he shall lose the property and make composition according to law, ibid.—We permit no layman except counts to have any advocate in ecclesiastical matters alone, ibid.

—Whatever law a man follows, even Roman law, throughout the whole Italian kingdom, we command that he observe all these matters which we have decreed to be settled by combat in these chapters; provided, however, that if youth, old age, or infirmity prevents either party from fighting, he may appoint a combatant for himself, and the other party may do likewise, ibid.—Churches, counts, and widows shall settle the disputes mentioned above by combat through equivalent advocates. All other persons free by birth shall answer and settle matters personally according to the ancient law, ibid.—We absolutely forbid sons of deacons, presbyters, and bishops to be made notaries, *sculdasii*, counts, or judges, ibid.—Command concerning the enthronement of the Archbishop of Magdeburg, ibid., 851.—Edict after the assembly at Pavia: If a disturbance or contest concerning estates arises between churches, other freeborn or free persons, or between a church and an individual, it shall be settled by combat. If one does not dare, his property shall be confiscated and restored to the church or person to whom justice belongs, ibid.

OTTO III, emperor.—“Every day acts are committed against the laws; every day evil men do evil without shame. Therefore by this law, to remain in force forever by God’s favour, we decree that judges may at every season of the year hear cases, decide lawsuits, and end and determine contentious disputes, so that those who offend against the laws every day may every day be struck by the sentence of the law. For those who have never ceased to sin ought not to escape the decree of the law during harvest or vintage time. To do good, speak truth, love justice, and judge rightly is lawful at every time and always will be lawful; for we have learned in catholic teaching that one must never rest from good works but must always rest from evil works. With God as author and by imperial majesty, we decree that this be continually maintained,” CXXXVIII, 853.

“On the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, Sundays, principal feasts, and appointed fast-days, we utterly forbid the carrying out of judicial proceedings and the pursuit of public actions; and we command that Christian solemnities be celebrated with all vigilance,” CXXXVIII, 854.

Decree: “We have learned that bishops and abbots misuse the possessions of churches and assign them by written instruments to various persons, doing this not for the benefit of churches but for money, kinship, or friendship. When their successors are urged both to restore the houses of God and to perform their duty to the commonwealth and the service due to us, they complain that the estates of their churches are being held by others and declare themselves unable to fulfil the commands laid upon them; and the facts prove their claim. Therefore, because the condition of the churches is being destroyed and our imperial majesty suffers no less loss when our subjects cannot render the service owed to us, we establish and confirm by imperial edict that every written instrument—whether it bears the name of a *libellus* or is proved to be an emphyteutic lease—by which anything from the churches of God cannot in any manner be effected, shall expire on the death of the grantor; and he alone who bound and obligated himself by that instrument shall bear the loss. The aforesaid losses shall in no way concern the person who succeeds him in administration; rather, he shall have free authority to restore to the church’s own right all that has been alienated through *libelli* or any other written instruments, and to order it so that it may render service to God and to us.

“For since kings and emperors may not give away what belongs to kingdom and empire beyond their own lifetime, except to churches, how may abbots and bishops distribute the property of churches for the periods of their successors? Every right, law, written instrument, or custom contrary to the welfare of the Church must indeed be made void; nor should those things be confirmed by our authority which tend to bring harm against the author and propagator of the empire. Therefore, in such cases only that written instrument shall be considered law which benefits the Church of God and can in no way harm it. If anyone attempts to act against this our constitution, he shall be judged a rebel and shall be subject to anathema *maranatha*, unless he repents, from all the bishops—and from the presbyters—who subscribed to or gave assent to this edict of our empire. Amen,” CXXXVIII, 855.

PALLADIUS, Praetorian Prefect.—Edict concerning the condemnation to exile of followers of Pelagius’s errors, LVI, 492.

PETER, King of Aragon.—He exhorts Lord Charles [Col. 1316], King of Sicily, not to harass his people, CLXXIV, 1560.

PHILIP THE FAIR, King of the French.—Charter concerning the biennial tithe levied upon the property of the Order of Cîteaux, CLXXXV, 1838.—He announces that he wishes to assist the Abbey of Clairvaux, already so near ruin that divine service there has almost ceased, ibid., 1917.

PIPPIN, prince.—Capitulary of Soissons (A.D. 744), XCVI, 1504.—Capitulary of Vermerie, A.D. 753, ibid., 1506.—Capitulary of Verne (A.D. 755), ibid.—Capitulary of Compiègne (A.D. 757), ibid., 1513.—Assembly of Attigny (A.D. 763), ibid., 1515.—Capitulary, year uncertain, ibid., 1506.—Encyclical concerning the holding of litanies, ibid., 1518.—Aquitanian Capitulary (A.D. 768), ibid., 1509.—Plea by which the estate of Abaciacum in the district of Le Mans and a portion of Sibriacum in the district of Matriacum are vindicated for the monks of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1520.—Writ obtained from Sigobald, abbot of the monastery of Anisole, ibid., 1521.—Royal writ under Boniface concerning the property of the church of Saint Martin, ibid., 1522.—Writ for the monastery of Morbugin, ibid., 1523.—Diploma concerning the fairs of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1524.—Writ confirming the estate of Taberniacum in the district of Paris, ibid., 1526.—Writ concerning the donation to the monastery of Saint-Denis of the castle on Mount Saint Michael in the district of Vienne, ibid., 1528.—Writ by which he restores the estate of Exona to the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1561.—Writ by which he grants the estate of Autmundistat to the Church of Fulda, ibid., 1563.—Writ by which the Forest of Aequalina is granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1565.—Writ declaring the monastery of Saint-Denis immune, ibid., 1566.—Writ confirming the privileges of the monastery of Saint-Denis, ibid., 1567.

PIPPIN, mayor of the palace.—Plea by which he adjudges a *mansus* at Marolium to the monastery of Saint-Denis, LXXXVIII, 1308.

PLACIDIA GALLA II.—Letter to the Empress Pulcheria, in which she condemns the Second Council of Ephesus, LIV, 864.

PULCHERIA, Empress.—Letter to Saint Leo the Great, Archbishop of Rome, asking that a certain synod be held in the eastern regions; and that bishops who had been united with Flavian of holy memory and had been sent into exile should be recalled, and should await the synod’s decision concerning restoration to their churches, LIV, 905.

QUARTUS, Praetorian Prefect.—Edict in the City against the errors of Pelagius, LVI, 492.

RACHIS, King of the Lombards.—Decree determining the boundaries of certain estates belonging to the monastery of Bobbio, LXXXVII, 1376.

RADEGUND, queen.—Letter to bishops concerning the founding of a convent of women in the city of Poitiers, LXXII, 681.

RUDOLF III, King of Burgundy.—He confirms the gifts made to the monastery of Saint Andrew of Vienne by his father Conrad, CLI, 1021.—He grants Anizo, Archbishop of Tarentaise, the county of that city, ibid., 1023.—He grants the church of Saint Nicholas of Polignac to Saint Odilo and the monastery of Cluny, ibid., 1024.

RAYMOND, Prince of Antioch, concerning the miserable condition of the city of Jerusalem, CLV, 1280.

RAYMOND, Duke of Narbonne.—Letter to Louis, King of the French, concerning envoys to be sent to the Emperor at Constantinople, CLV, 1268.

RECCARED, King of the Visigoths.—Edict confirming the Council of Toledo, LXXII, 1121.

RICHARD, King of the English.—Letter to Pope Clement III, informing him of the peace made between himself and King Tancred, CCIV, 1505.

ROBERT, King of the French.—Diploma concerning the election of abbots and the church of Saint Leodegarius of Campellis, CXLI, 945.—Writ confirming the property which Count Burchard and Bishop Rainald transferred to the monastery of Fossatus, ibid., 947.—Writ by which he confirms grants made by earlier kings and others to the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, ibid., 948.—Writ by which he confirms the restoration of the monks of Fécamp made by Count Richard and Richard’s gifts to that place, ibid., 952.—Writ confirming the foundation of the convent of Bellimont near Tours, ibid., 953.—He suppresses the unlawful customs and oppressions of Alfred of Encra, advocate of Corbie, ibid., 955.—Writ by which he grants the chapel of Saint John the Evangelist, situated in the city of Autun, to the monks of Flavigny, ibid., 956.—Writ concerning castles constructed at Mont-Bason and Mirebeau, and providing that no injury thereby be inflicted upon the monks of Cormery, ibid., 957.

RUDOLF I, emperor.—Upon his election as King of the Romans, he asks the congregation of religious for the assistance of prayers to establish the auspices of his empire, XCVIII, 701.—He asks holy virgins for the assistance of prayers for himself and his consort, ibid., 705.—Letter to all the estates of the empire concerning the restoration of peace and requiring them to render him the obedience due to him, ibid.—He thanks Pope Gregory X for graciously hearing his chancellor, sent as envoy, and promises always to render every service to the Roman Church, ibid., 715.—He promises the pope to come to Milan for coronation and gives thanks to God for confirmation of his election, ibid., 731–732.—He promises Pope Gregory to carry out reform against the errant bishops of Germany, ibid., 737.—Letter to the cardinals after the death of Gregory X, asking them to elect a good pontiff, ibid., 718.—He congratulates Pope Innocent V upon his election as Roman pontiff, ibid., 751.—He congratulates the same pontiff upon his papal dignity, commending himself as subject to him, ibid., 755.—He replies to the Archbishop of Salzburg, thanking him for his singular care and vigilance concerning him, ibid., 763.—He informs the Roman pontiff of the notable victory gained over the King of Bohemia, ibid., 789.—He most liberally grants to the Roman Church whatever it has hitherto requested of him, ibid., 794.—He commends the elect of Cologne to the Roman pontiff, ibid., 811.—He commends a certain canon to the Church of Liège and requests that they send him back to the court as soon as possible, ibid., 814.—He writes to a certain archbishop that he should judge rightly and justly, ibid., 825.—He confirms all rights of the Holy See, ibid., 843.—Diploma of the princes of the empire concerning the donation of Emperor Rudolf and the confirmation of the privileges of the Apostolic See, ibid., 869.—Diploma by which Rudolf protects ecclesiastical rights by a strict edict, ibid., 872.

SENATOR, Praetorian Prefect.—Letter to Pope John. He asks to be assisted by the pope’s prayers, admonitions, and corrections, LXIX, 824.—Letter to various bishops: he commends himself to their prayers and asks them to proclaim a fast for the safety of the rulers and the attainment of peace; then he exhorts them to remove all vices far from the people, ibid.—Edict giving many notable and excellent admonitions and promising that he will be a most upright judge, ibid., 834.—Edict against those who had stolen gifts of the king bestowed on churches, ibid., 864.—Letter to Pope John: he asks to be assisted by his prayers, admonitions, and corrections, ibid., 827.—Letter to various bishops: he commends himself to their prayers and asks them to proclaim a fast for the safety of the rulers and the attainment of peace; then he exhorts them to remove all vices far from the people, ibid., 829.—Edict throughout the provinces commanding that taxpayers be warned to pay their customary taxes in three instalments and at appointed times, ibid., 833.—The same: it gives many notable and excellent admonitions and promises that he will be a most upright judge, ibid., 834.—Letter to provincial judges, exhorting them to love justice and make their subjects observe it, ibid., 836.—Edict concerning the *cornicularius* who departs, ibid., 843.—Edict concerning the *cornicularius* who enters office; the *primiscrinius* who departs; the *primiscrinius* who enters; the clerk of records; the office of correspondence; the clerk of the military bureau; the chief of shorthand writers; the sixth *scholarius*; the *prorogativarius*; the *commentariensis*; the *regendarius*; the chief of deputies and Augustales; the departing chief of the *singulares*; the incoming chief of the *singulares*; and the granting of embassies, ibid., 844–845.—Moved by compassion, he frees many persons held in prison, LXIX, 851.—He instructs how *sajones* assigned to chanceries ought to perform their office, ibid., 856.—He commands that peoples and soldiers be kept in duty by judges. He then forbids any house, even his own or the royal house, from being exempted from supplying provisions to troops, ibid., 858.—He threatens penalties to unjust judges and exhorts good ones tirelessly to promote the public interest, ibid., 859.—Edict against those who had stolen gifts of the king bestowed on churches, ibid., 864.

SIGEBERT (Saint), King of the French.—He founds the monastery of Casagonguidinum and appoints Renaclus abbot there, LXXXVII, 319.—He restores to the church of Saint Peter of Trier the cells of Saint Hilary and Saint Eucharius, violently taken from it, ibid., 323.

SISEBUTH, King of the Goths.—On holiness of life and the devout endurance of this world’s miseries, LXXX, 364.—On placing trust in God, ibid., 367.—On his conversion from lay dress to monastic life, ibid., 370, 372.

THEOBALD, Count of Chalon.—Charter by which he confirmed a donation of the monastery of Saint Marcellus of Chalon made to Maiolus, Abbot of Cluny, CXXXVII, 780.

THEODAHAD, king.—He reproves the senators of the city of Rome because, at the very beginning of his reign, they did not counter the fickleness of the populace and vain suspicions, LXIX, 806.—He seeks peace [Col. 1318] from Emperor Justinian through an envoy distinguished for priestly office and renowned learning, ibid., 813.—He tells Emperor Justinian that the senatorial Praetorian Prefect had been sent to the estate of certain nuns, in order that, if the overflow of waters had caused it any injury, he might remit its taxes. He then answers the matters Justinian had written concerning Veranilda, ibid., 815.—He asks the bishops both to assist the envoys he sent to the emperor and to offer prayers to God for him, ibid., 822.

THEODORIC, king.—Letter to Eustorgius, Bishop of Milan. He says that he has restored to his former honour the bishop of Augsburg, falsely accused by clerics, and sends those clerics to Eustorgius that he may restrain them with due punishment, LXIX, 513.—Letter to Bishop Severus. Fifteen hundred solidi are sent through Montanarius, that he may distribute them among provincials who suffered losses through the army, ibid., 548.—Letter to Bishop Gudila. He determines how the dispute between the citizens of Sacerna and the Church is to be settled, ibid., 555.—Edict in which he complains that landholders and town councillors have been oppressed because the leading men did not pay the assessed sum; then he commands anyone who feels burdened for this reason to bring complaints to the king, ibid., 559.—Letter to Bishop Aurigenus. He writes that Julian complains that his wife or property was taken away by the bishop’s dependants; and commands that, if the matter is indeed so, the guilty party be punished as soon as possible, ibid., 584.—Letter to Bishop Peter. He commands him to restore to Germanus the part of the estate which he held, if Germanus is the legitimate son of Thomas; if he refuses to do so, he wishes the case to be summoned to court, ibid., 1341.

THEODORIC, King of the Romans.—Letter to Agapitus, Prefect of the City: he writes that Rome should send its most skilled marble-workers to Ravenna to complete the Basilica of Hercules, LXIX, 512.—He commands Count Felix to restore to the ward Plutianus the property which he had acquired from Neoterius, Plutianus’s brother, less by purchase than by theft; and rebukes him because he had not divided an inheritance equally among equals, ibid., 512–513.—He tells Eustorgius, Bishop of Milan, that he has restored to his former honour the bishop of Augsburg, falsely accused by his clerics, and sends those clerics back to Eustorgius so that he may restrain them with due punishment, ibid., 513.—Letter to Servatus, Duke of Raetia: he commands that slaves taken by the Breonian soldiers be restored without any delay through Miniarius, ibid., 516.—He replies that estates occupied by unlawful claimants must be restored unless a contract or prescription of thirty years stands in the way; and that the killer of a brother must be deported into exile, ibid., 520.—He commands that whoever among the Goths refuses to fulfil his obligation to the fisc shall be compelled to make proper payment, ibid., 521.—He decrees that inquiry be made whether money assigned to the city’s public works was spent upon them in full and without fraud, ibid., 521.—Judges are to be chosen to settle the lawsuit of the patrician men Festus and Symmachus against the patrician Paulinus, ibid., 524.—He establishes that if anyone of the populace inflicts grievous injury upon a senator, he shall know that the Prefect of the City will punish him according to the nature of the deed; and he commands pantomimes to practise their arts in appointed places, ibid., 529.—He instructs the illustrious Agapitus that he has written to the senate and people, and commands that, if any injury is inflicted upon a senator, the offender be immediately punished with the severity of the laws; but if a senator oppresses a freeborn person by wicked killing, he shall immediately incur a fine, ibid., 530.—And there are thus countless letters containing such commands, which are read in that volume, ibid., cols. 531–679.

THEODORIC, King of the Goths.—Order concerning the holding of a council, LXXII, 1111, 1113, 1115.—Law against those priests who presume by direct right either to sell or to give away the property of the Church, ibid., 1117.

THEODOSIUS THE ELDER, emperor.—Constitution against heretics, imposing a gold fine upon Donatists and other heretics, XI, 1192.

THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER.—Edict against the Donatists, XI, 1431.

THEODOSIUS THE GREAT, emperor.—Decree concerning the office of the Count of the Sacred Largesses, XIII, 521.—Decree concerning legal holidays, ibid., 524.—Decree concerning marriage, ibid.—Decree concerning the property of clerics and monks, ibid., 525.—Decree concerning adulteries, ibid., 526.—Decree concerning abduction or the marriage of nuns, virgins, or widows, ibid., 527.—Decree concerning interrogations under torture, ibid.—Decree concerning pardons for crimes, ibid.—Decree concerning those who take refuge in churches, ibid., 528.—Decree concerning performers, ibid.—Decree concerning the catholic faith, ibid., 530.—Decree concerning bishops, churches, and clerics, ibid., 531.—Decree concerning monks and those who dispute about religion, ibid., 532.—Decree concerning heretics, ibid., 533.—Decree [Col. 1319] concerning apostates, ibid., 538.—Decree concerning Jews, worshippers of the heavens (*Caelicolae*), and Samaritans, ibid., 540.—Decree concerning pagans, sacrifices, and temples, ibid.—Letter extending the rights of the Church of Constantinople into Illyricum, XX, 669.—He states that he had commanded the privileges of the Roman bishop in Illyricum to be preserved inviolate, ibid., 770.—Constitution concerning the Manichaeans, LIV, 622.—Constitution concerning the ordination of bishops, ibid., 636.—Rescripts to Palladius, Praetorian Prefect, and Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, concerning expelling from the city the followers of Caelestius and Pelagius, LVI, 490 and 493.—On the manner of believing the mystery of the most holy Trinity, ibid., 681.—Concerning those who dispute about religion, ibid., 682.—Profession concerning the faith, LXIX, 1126.—How he expelled Arians from the Church of Constantinople, ibid., 1127.—How he was hostile to pagans, ibid., 1149.

VALENTINIAN THE ELDER.—Constitution against rebaptizers, XI, 1180.

VALENTINIAN, emperor.—He approves the renewed exile of Ursinus and his schismatic associates, and commands that the one basilica retained by the Ursinians be restored to Damasus, XIII, 126.—Constitution that ecclesiastical persons and the continent may receive nothing from the property of widows, whether by will or gift, ibid., 575.—Edict concerning the consubstantial Trinity, LXIX, 1075.—He approves the election of Siricius, bishop of Rome, ibid., 593.—Constitution concerning certain Pelagians to be summoned by Patroclus, Bishop of Arles, XLVIII, 409.—Constitution concerning the Manichaeans, LIV, 622.—Constitution concerning the ordination of bishops, ibid., 636.—Letter concerning the summoning of the Synod of Chalcedon, LVI, 527.—Concerning belief in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit under one Trinity, ibid., 681.—Concerning those who dispute about religion, ibid., 682.

VOLUSIANUS, Prefect of the City.—Copy of an edict concerning the exile of Caelestius, the Pelagian heretic: “Until now judicial proceedings, friendly to the accused, have kept Caelestius, disturber of the divine faith and public tranquillity, concealed in secret places. Now laws and edicts will pursue him in his absence. First of all, residence in the Eternal City is denied him, so that, if he lodges even in the vicinity, he may not escape the penalty due. On account also of the merit of his rashness and audacity, we warn everyone by the safeguard of this edict not to think that an unjust person ought to furnish a hiding-place to one guilty of crime; for a terrible punishment has been established for him, and whoever judges that a man accused before divine and human law should be concealed in his own house must incur the writ of proscription,” LVI, 500.

VITIGIS, King of the Goths.—Letter to his bishops. He asks them both to assist the envoys whom he sent to the emperor and to offer prayers to God for him, LXIX, 822.

WIDO, king. — We have also been especially pleased to decree that bishops and counts shall be united in their dioceses and counties for the peace and safety of all persons dwelling in their jurisdictions, so that they permit no robber, breaker-in, or incestuous person to remain in their territories or granted jurisdictions. And if they learn that foreigners intend or are obliged to pass by any route through their districts to lay waste this kingdom, they shall send public messengers to meet them, so that they may pass peacefully through their land without plunder; but they shall cause the necessities to be sold to them, not at an excessive price, but according to the usage and custom of the land. If, however, they refuse to comply and commit plundering and robbery, they shall be compelled by the bishop and count of the same place, legally and under our ban, to make restitution for whatever they have taken from another. If they refuse to carry this out, they shall immediately be excommunicated by the bishop. But if it subsequently happens that the count of the place and the people of the land fall upon those robbers, obstruct them, and they are killed, we decree that no feud shall arise therefrom, nor shall compensation ever be demanded for those who fall there. And if the count of that place neglects to fulfil this, he shall be deprived of his own office; and if it is expedient and necessary for a count to summon his neighbor to his assistance, and that neighbor withdraws himself, he likewise shall be deprived of his own office and, in addition, shall pay thirty pounds of silver to the count, CXXXVIII, 801. — Therefore, whenever men of the lay order, both free and enslaved, residing in a county, have been summoned by their own count or by the public authority—that is, by those who administer public affairs—if they withdraw from aiding their own count and do not assist him within that county against raiders who have come into his county, free persons shall pay one third of their movable property; enslaved persons, however, shall be beaten with sixty strokes, provided that it has been proved that notice was given them, CXXXVIII, 801. — There are besides six other decrees dealing with such matters, CXXXVIII, 801, 804.

WILLIAM, count. — Charter concerning an agreement between himself and Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, regarding the monasteries of Mauziac and Celsiniac, CLXXXIX, 1067.

WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR, king of the English. — Admonished concerning the duty of rendering fealty to Pope Gregory VII and of sending money to Rome; he agrees concerning the money, but refuses fealty as an unprecedented requirement, CXLVIII, 748. — That ecclesiastical cases shall be judged by ecclesiastical judges, CXLIX, 1291. — Law concerning the right of the English and ecclesiastical immunity, CXLIX, 1293. — Law concerning the privilege of the king’s men; violators of the public peace; a person accused of theft; and a surety who had assumed responsibility for his conduct, CXLIX, 1295. — Law concerning the apprehension of a thief, the redemption of animals, and goods found by chance, CXLIX, 1297. — Law concerning homicide and the valuation of a head, or *wera*; the persons by whom the *wera* is to be paid; the value of certain animals to be reckoned in assessing the value of a head; an assailant; an inflicted wound; and the valuation of severed limbs, CXLIX, 1299. — Law concerning adultery, a corrupt judge, the purgation of one accused of theft, one who has broken into a house or temple, CXLIX, 1301. — Law concerning St. Peter’s pennies, or the Roman tribute; a woman violated by force and chastity assailed by struggle; those who do not pay the Roman or St. Peter’s tribute; an eye gouged out; and a count’s relief, CXLIX, 1303. — Law concerning the relief of a baron, vavasor, and peasants; and public roads, CXLIX, 1307. — Law concerning a thief; peasants; a pregnant woman condemned to capital punishment; the property of persons dying intestate; an adulteress caught by her father; judgment against an absent associate; judicial proceedings; a pledge; that no one may buy a thing without witnesses; an abandoned suretyship; guests; and servants, CXLIX, 1309, 1317.

[Col. 1319]

CXIX. DISCIPLINARY INDEX. ARRANGED ANALOGICALLY, THAT IS, UNDER VARIOUS HEADINGS, PRESENTING WHATEVER PERTAINS BOTH TO ECCLESIASTICAL AND TO MONASTIC DISCIPLINE, WHILE PRESERVING ALPHABETICAL ORDER WITHIN THE ANALOGICAL ARRANGEMENT.

NOTICE.

In this Index we have established 114 headings, arranged alphabetically by subject. Under each heading we collect works or smaller treatises dealing with the same subject in relation to ecclesiastical discipline, and indicate in brackets the year of each author. At the end of this Index, as in an Appendix, we add three headings comprising everything that pertains specifically to monastic discipline, following the same method; and thus the reader will very easily find what is sought.
