[Col. 1355]

CXXII. INDEX OF ECCLESIASTICAL CENSURES, IN WHICH, ON THE BASIS OF THE FATHERS, THERE IS A SYSTEMATIC DISCUSSION OF EXCOMMUNICATION AND THE EXCOMMUNICATED, IRREGULARITY, SUSPENSION, DEPOSITION, AND INTERDICT.

NOTICE.

This index sets out the various kinds of censures, with the greatest penalty, excommunication, in the first place. Its treatment proceeds as follows:

I. What excommunication is.---II. What its usefulness is.---III. How great is the fear of this penalty.---IV. Its several kinds.---V. Unjust excommunication.---VI. By whom it is to be imposed.---VII. Monastic excommunication.---VIII. The causes for which it is to be imposed.---IX. No communion with the excommunicated.---X. How and when it is to be imposed.---XI. Formulas and rites of excommunication.---XII. Excommunications reserved to the Supreme Pontiff.---XIII. The efficacy of so great a penalty.---XIV. Those who die excommunicated.---XV. Absolution from, and satisfaction for, excommunication.

Thereafter examples of excommunication are mentioned, historical examples directed against:

A. Patriarchs, primates, bishops, etc.---B. Priests and clerics.---C. Emperors and kings.---D. Dukes, counts, etc.---E. Peoples and cities.---F. Distinguished men and women.

In the course of the work are also explained: irregularity, suspension, deposition, and interdict—the penalty by which sacred places are struck. In ordinary usage it is improperly used for the penalty of suspension, by which ecclesiastical persons are punished. Places are interdicted; persons, however, are suspended or deposed.

[Col. 1355] I. What excommunication is.---To excommunicate a cleric is to degrade him, and likewise a layperson: St. Augustine, XL, 271.---What the excommunicator ought to consider: id., XLIV, 62, 94.---No greater penalty exists in the Church: id., XLV, 944.---It is separation from the assembly of the faithful: St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 146.---One prohibited from communion who received the Church’s Eucharist was separated from the body of the Church: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 823.---On the excommunicated: St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 58.---What excommunication ought to be: Anonymous, LXXXVIII, 1067.---On excommunication: St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLIX, 530.---To hand over to Satan is to excommunicate: Collection of Canons, CLIII, 146.---On the sentence of excommunication: *Panormia*, CLXI, 1227.---On excommunication: Paschal II, CLXIII, 758.---On the sentence of excommunication: Innocent III, CCXVI, 1243.

II. What is the usefulness of excommunication?---A lesser severity is sometimes useful: St. Augustine, XL, 199.---It is a remedy against certain grave sins: ibid., 228.---How excommunication is salutary: id., XLIII, 92.---It can be useful: id., XLV, 944.---The bishop should pronounce the lighter sentence of excommunication: St. Leo, LVI, 51.

III. How greatly excommunication is to be feared.---The excommunication of priests is not to be held in contempt: Charlemagne, XCVII, 776.---Whoever transgresses a synodal excommunication has no hope of restoration at another synod: ibid., 804.---Those who despise episcopal correction are excommunicated: Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1102.---Those who hold excommunication in contempt are excommunicated: ibid., 1103.---On contempt for pontifical excommunication: Hincmar, CXXVI, 607.

IV. The several kinds of excommunication.---Whether the excommunication for graver faults of which St. Benedict speaks is ecclesiastical excommunication: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 510.---Major and minor excommunication: St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 543.---What distinction there is between excommunication and anathema: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 591.---Excommunication of the body: St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1106.---On excommunication and anathema: Council of Forojulium, XCIX, 333.

V. Unjust excommunication.---Excommunication cannot take place except against a person accused and convicted: St. Optatus, XI, 106.---It is not to be imposed lightly: St. Jerome, XXXII, 726.---A whole household ought not to be anathematized for one person’s sin: St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1066.---It does not harm a person that human knowledge does not wish him to be recited from the Church’s register: ibid.---If a believer is unjustly anathematized, it harms rather the person who does it than the person who suffers this injustice: ibid., 1068.---Unjust excommunication does not injure innocent persons, but tests them: id., XLIII, 123.---Unjust excommunication does not bind: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 624.---A bishop should not excommunicate rashly: St. Egbert, LXXXVIII, 386.---On just or unjust excommunication, and on the causes and order in which it is to be carried out: Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 936; Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 826.---Unjust excommunication is void and recoils upon its author: St. Agobard, CIV, 300.---On irregular excommunication of parishioners belonging to different bishops: Hincmar, CXXVI, 282.---On those unjustly excommunicated: ibid., 397.---On those who excommunicate unjustly: ibid., 407.---Hincmar of Laon excommunicated parishioners of other bishops without reason: ibid., 572.---Hincmar of Laon unlawfully excommunicated his own parishioners: [Col. 1356] ibid.---Unjust excommunication does not harm the person marked, but the excommunicator: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1295.---Sentences pronounced without reasonable cause have no force: Innocent III, CCXV, 1131.

VI. By whom excommunication is to be imposed.---A monk excommunicates the younger Theodosius: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 516.---To whom excommunication belongs: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 553.---On those excommunicated by their own bishop: Charlemagne, XCVII, 509.---Excommunication approved by the Apostolic See: Hincmar, CXXVI, 612.---John VIII grants the bishop of Pavia the power to excommunicate: John VIII, ibid., 885.---On the power of the Apostolic See in excommunicating King Henry: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 594.---The pope confirms an archbishop’s excommunication: ibid., 624.---Paschal II confirms the excommunication of the priest Ubert: Paschal II, CLXIII, 753.---A heretic cannot excommunicate: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1263.---Innocent approves the excommunication pronounced by Bishop Walter: Innocent III, CCXV, 1077.

VII. Monastic excommunication.---Excommunication is customary among monks: Cassian, L, 16; St. Fructuosus, LXXXVII, 1105.---The causes for which it is incurred: in the Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 501; ibid., 503.---To be excommunicated is to be handed over to Satan: ibid., 510.---On monastic excommunication: ibid., 501; author unknown, LXXXVIII, 976; Anonymous, ibid., 1067; St. Leodegar, XCVI, 378.---On monastic excommunication: Smaragdus, CII, 847; Code of Rules, CIII, 569.---Excommunication from the table: St. Augustine, XLIII, 94.---The nature of excommunication for lighter faults: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 506.---Those who communicated with excommunicated persons incurred excommunication: Cassian, L, 16; Smaragdus, CII, 1108.---Five ways in which one may communicate with excommunicated persons: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 516.---Prayer was made for him: ibid., 520.---The causes for which it is incurred: ibid., 501.---For detraction: ibid., 323.---For an indecent word: ibid., 312.---An abbot introducing women into the monastery: ibid., 337.---For sleeping after the nocturnal office: ibid., 415.---For the vice of private possession: ibid., 556, 561.---Nuns fleeing their monastery: Gallican Liturgy, LXXI, 521.---Fugitive monks: Charlemagne, *Capitularies*, XCVII, 841; Council of Rouen, CCV, 918.---For violation of silence: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 564.---Two monks who castrate themselves are excommunicated: Gallican Liturgy, LXXIII, 968.---Those who take wives are excommunicated together with their households: Council of Rouen, CCV, 918.---Those excommunicated for graver faults are separated from all fellowship and conversation with the brethren: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 512.---They were imprisoned: ibid.---They were sustained on bread and water: ibid., 514.---The vessels they used were either to be broken or distributed to the poor: ibid., 689.---Excommunicated nuns sang the office in another church: ibid., 691.---Those excommunicated for lighter faults neither celebrated Mass nor made an offering at it: ibid., 507.---On the modes of monastic excommunication: St. Donatus, LXXXVII, 294, 295.---How excommunicated monks are to be treated, and concerning the abbot’s care for them: author unknown, LXXXVIII, 976, 978; Smaragdus, CII, 852; Code of Rules, CIII, 1015.---An excommunicated person is to be absolved with the counsel of the brethren, and according to what rite: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 685.---How those excommunicated for a light fault made satisfaction: ibid., 689.---How they are to be absolved: ibid., 690.---Priests are not to absolve monks from excommunication: [Col. 1357] St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 972.---On the satisfaction to be made by the excommunicated: Code of Rules, CII, 1009.

VIII. The causes for which excommunication is to be imposed.---Cases of excommunication: Council of Forojulium, XCIX, 300.

1. It is not to be imposed in order to avenge one’s own injuries: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 591.

2. Against heretics, and against those who refuse to condemn the names of heretics: Gelasius, LIX, 57. Heretics excommunicated in a Roman synod: St. Boniface of Mainz, LXXXIX, 831. Heretics denying true doctrine: Nicholas I, CXIX, 795. Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death: Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1290. Those who err and lead others into error: ibid., 1302. An excommunication pronounced against heretics is to be observed: Innocent III, CCXV, 319.

3. Those who use prohibited books: St. Augustine, LV, 260.

4. Intruded clerics: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 497; St. Adrian, XCIX, 1010; Zachary, XCVIII, 88.

5. Simoniacal clerics: St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 385; Isidore Mercator, CXXXVII, 336; Gratian, CLXV, 226; St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 339.

6. Fugitive monks: Council of Rouen, CCV, 918.

7. Apostate clerics: St. Zachary, XCVIII, 85; Adrian, XCIX, 1050; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1427.

8. Drunken clerics: Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 825; ibid., 833; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1108.

9. The incontinent are excommunicated: St. Augustine, LV, 1094. An abbot introducing women into the monastery: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 501.

10. Clerics appealing to a secular judge: Charlemagne, XCVII, 898. Those who obtain churches through laypersons: Paschal II, CLXIII, 438. Those who transfer ecclesiastical property to laypersons: Council of Rouen, CCVII, 1181. An ecclesiastical person, ecclesiastical persons: Selected Canons, XCIX, 1036. One who brings another before a secular judge: Council of Rouen, CCVII, 1181. Clerics returning to secular military service: Amalarius, CV, 880.

11. A deacon unwilling to return to his own church: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 543. Bishops or clerics neglecting their duties: Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 935; Angelomus, XCVI, 1040. Those ordered to attend a council but refusing to come: Rothad, CXIX, 709. John VIII threatens an archbishop of Milan with excommunication for scorning to attend a synod: John VIII, CXXVI, 817.

12. Bishops or clerics deposed but nevertheless exercising their ministry: St. Zachary, XCVIII, 83. Clerics deserting their bishop: St. Zachary, ibid., 13.

13. Grave sins are to be punished with excommunication: Eugippius, LXII, 865. Anyone is to be degraded and excommunicated for whatever faults: Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 975. Pronounced against various criminals: Council of Rouen, CCX, 481.

14. Idolaters are excommunicated: Adrian, XCIX, 1050.

15. A cleric swearing by created things: Charlemagne, XCVII, 898.

16. Diviners, sorcerers, enchanters devoted to vain auguries: Angelomus, XCVI, 1041; Adrian, XCIX, 1051; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1417; Leo IV, CXV, 668; Council of Rouen, CCVII, 1182.

17. Bigamists: Angelomus, XCVI, 1040; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1304.

18. Adulterers: Hincmar, CXXVI, 101. Those who dismiss their wives without a judicial sentence: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1407; Jun. III, CCXIV, 729.

19. Incestuous persons: Halitgar, CV, 684; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1405; Leo IV, CXV, 668; Nicholas I, CXIX, 819; Hincmar of Laon, CXXIV, 1099.

20. Those associating themselves with consecrated virgins: Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1408; Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 615; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1378. If monks take wives, they are excommunicated together with their households: Council of Rouen, CCV, 918. Against abductors of nuns: John VIII, CXXVI, 815.

21. Detractors, slanderers, and accusers of brethren: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 367; Charlemagne, XCVII, 894.

22. Despoilers: St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 389. Plunderers who do not follow the law: Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 894; Canons of Carthage, XCVI, 1065; Hincmar, CXXVI, 101.

23. Forgers, false witnesses, perjurers, murderers, and arsonists: Adrian I, XCIX, 1062; St. Eugenius II, CV, 646; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1409, 1411; Rothad, CXIX, 722; *Panormia*, CLXI, 1227; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1304; Innocent III, CCXIV, 494, 546; Selected Canons, CXCIX, 1078.

24. Those who lay violent hands upon clerics, monks, or bishops: Eugenius II, CV, 546; Nicholas I, CXIX, 1114, 1134; Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 359; Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1068; Peter of Blois, CCVII, 224; Jun. III, CCXV, 563, 573, 644, 949; CCXVII, 97.

25. Those who do not pay tithes; those who despoil the Church’s possessions or goods: Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 352; St. Theodore, LXXXVII, 102; Marculf, ibid., 949; Charlemagne, XCVII, 833; Penitential Book, CV, 765; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1414; Nicholas I, CXIX, 1114; John VIII, CXXVI, 899, 962; St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 471, 528, 537; Paschal II, CLXIII, 628; Celestine III, CCVI, 1184; Innocent III, CCXIV, 729; CCXV, 1098.

26. Violators of canons and despisers of excommunication: Charlemagne, XCVII, 897; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1102, 1103; Leo IV, CXV, 674.

27. Persons excommunicated for various causes; canons concerning cases of excommunication: XCIX, 1011. A bishop refusing to obey elected judges: Canons of Carthage, XCVI, 1054. Those who consume the blood [Col. 1358] of strangled cattle: Adrian, XCVIII, 383. Those who, because of hatred, do not return to peace: Halitgar, CV, 686. Those opposing the election of the Roman pontiff: Nicholas I, CXIX, 795. Those taking up arms against the kings of England and France: Innocent III, CCXV, 181. Those who do not observe a truce: ibid. Against the bishop of Utrecht for not satisfying the Church’s creditors: ibid., 242.

IX. No communion with the excommunicated.---No communion with the excommunicated: St. Leo the Great, LIV, 374.---Those excommunicated by their own bishops are not to be received by others: id., LVI, 50.---No communion with the excommunicated until their case has been examined in a provincial synod: ibid., 51.---They ought not to be received by other bishops: ibid., 72, 627.---No communion with the excommunicated: id., LIV, 374; LVI, 425, 645, 650.---The penalty of excommunication for those communicating with them: ibid., 660.---Those excommunicated for graver faults are separated from every fellowship and conversation with the brethren: Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 512.---Those communicating with excommunicated persons are excommunicated: ibid., 515.---When it is permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons: ibid., 516.---Five ways in which someone can communicate with excommunicated persons: ibid., 516.---The vessels used by excommunicated persons are either to be broken or distributed to the poor: ibid., 689.---No communion with the excommunicated: St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 819.---One must not pray with the excommunicated: Crisconius, LXXXVIII, 841.---It is not permitted to communicate with them: ibid., 853.---Whoever has once prayed in a house with excommunicated persons is to be excommunicated: Angelomus, XCVI, 1035.---Bishops and clerics who communicate with heretics are excommunicated: Collection of Cambrai, ibid., 1036.---A bishop or cleric communicating with excommunicated persons is excommunicated: Council of Carthage, ibid., 1048.---The alms of an excommunicated person are not to be accepted: Abedoc, ibid., 1297.---It is not permitted to celebrate Mass for them: ibid.---There is to be no communion with them in any way: Capitularies of Charlemagne, LXXVII, 707.---The faithful ought not to receive them: ibid., 772.---That no one is to approach them: ibid., 837.---No communion with those rebaptized: ibid.---They are to be avoided until reconciliation: ibid.---On those who communicate with the excommunicated before a hearing: ibid.---No communion with them: Smaragdus, CII, 1108.---On those who, without the abbot’s command, join themselves to excommunicated persons: Code of Rules, CIII, 1105.---Whoever communicates with an excommunicated person is excommunicated: St. Eugenius II, CV, 645.---It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated laypersons or clerics: Amalarius, ibid., 880; Walter, CXIX, 736; Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1102.---John VIII rebukes Egilbert because he communicated with persons excommunicated by the Apostolic See: John VIII, CXXVI, 890.---Whoever communicates once with an excommunicated person is to be deprived of communion: Apostolic Canons, CXXX, 15.---If an excommunicated cleric or layperson hastens to another city with letters of recommendation, those who receive him are to be excommunicated: Apostolic Canons, ibid., 15.---Those communicating with the excommunicated King Henry are excommunicated: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 458.---With persons excommunicated by the pope, it is permitted neither to communicate nor to remain in the same house: St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 458.---Those who give counsel to an excommunicated person are excommunicated: ibid., 472, 626.---He warns Count Robert of Flanders not henceforth to aid the excommunicated bishop of Thérouanne: ibid., 641.---Book on avoiding the excommunication of excommunicators: Bernald, ibid., 1181.---Book on the law of excommunication: ibid., 1231.---On the baptism of excommunicated persons: ibid., 1255.---Book on avoiding excommunicated persons: ibid., 1231.---Innocent III orders that they warn the duke of Swabia not to render any aid to the excommunicated bishop of Worms: Innocent III, CCXV, 650.---No communion with the excommunicated: ibid., 1530.---On not receiving the excommunicated: id., CCXVI, 564.---On not giving support to the excommunicated: ibid., 596.

X. How and when it is to be imposed.---Excommunication cannot be imposed except upon an accused and convicted offender, St. Optatus, XI, 106.---It is not to be imposed lightly, St. Jerome, XXXII, 726; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 640.---Innocent souls are not to be struck for another’s crime, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 1067.---Excommunication was not imposed where there was danger of schism, ibid., 298.---The separation of false brethren before the time of separation cannot take place without disturbance, id., XXXV, 1799.---Especially when disruption and division of the Church is feared, id., XXXVIII, 51.---One must sometimes prudently refrain from excommunication, lest he who is struck become worse because of the scourge, ibid., 51.---It is not to be imposed except by lawful authority and with judgment, ibid., 900, 1546.---Cases in which excommunication is to be employed, id., XLIII, 92, 93, 95.---What one who excommunicates ought to consider, id., XLIV, 62, 96.---The Fathers preferred that Pelagians be healed within the body of the Church rather than cut off from its body, if necessity permitted, St. Augustine, XLVI, 685, 764, 773.---It is to be imposed after the [Col. 1359] second and third admonition, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 598.---In the guilty, vengeance is not to be inflicted by excommunication, ibid., 624.---No one is to be excommunicated before the case has been examined, John VIII, CXXVI, 827.---One cannot be excommunicated after death, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1288.---Excommunication is not to be imposed lightly, Innocent III, CCXIV, 790.

XI. Formulas and rites of excommunication.---Formulas of excommunication, Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 503; Marculf, LXXXVII, 944.---On the manner of excommunication, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1103; Royal Code, CIII, 985.---On the order of excommunication, Abedoc, XCVI, 1297.---Who ought to be excommunicated and how, Hincmar, CXXVI, 397.

XII. Roman pontiffs reserving certain excommunications to themselves.---Pope Adrian forbids bishops to excommunicate Carloman, Adrian, Letters, CXXII, 1308.---Celestine III grants a privilege for Henry the Lion and his sons: that they may not be excommunicated by any person whatsoever except the supreme pontiff or his legate, Celestine III, CCVI, 1046.---The king and kingdom of Armenia cannot be excommunicated except by special command of Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 1007.---The chapter and abbot of St. John of Sens are granted that no one may pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against that monastery, ibid., 1064.---The dean and chapter of the Duke’s chapel at Dijon are granted that they may not be excommunicated by anyone except in two cases, ibid., CCXV, 343.---Emperor Henry is granted that he cannot be excommunicated except for an enormous offence, ibid., 1316.---Innocent III commands that no one dare excommunicate the monks or chaplains of St. Bertin, ibid., CCXVII, 94.---He commands that the chapel of King John of England and its chaplains may not be excommunicated or placed under interdict without a mandate of the Apostolic See, ibid., 226.

XIII. What is the force of so great a penalty?---The excommunicated person is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, St. Ambrose, XV, 127.---The excommunicated are exposed to every danger and to the teeth of wolves, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 783.---By visible excommunication the excommunicated person is cut off from the body of Christ, ibid., XLI, 674; XLIII, 444.---With excommunicated persons one must not associate even in civil matters, St. Leo, LIV, 50.---Their conversation is to be avoided, ibid., 271, 373, 374.---They have been cast out from the unity of the Church, ibid., 374.---Effects of excommunication, ibid., 640.---The penalty for those associating with the excommunicated, id., LVI, 660.---An excommunicated person cannot exercise or receive sacred orders, Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 511.---The excommunicated were imprisoned; before the offering of the sacrifice of Mass, excommunicated persons were expelled from church, Gallican Liturgy, LXXII, 135.---Eulogiae are not to be given to the excommunicated, ibid., 141.---Those excommunicated by one bishop are to be avoided everywhere by others, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 699.---Entrance into church is everywhere closed to the excommunicated, Honorius I, LXXX, 482.---Let no one approach the excommunicated, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 58.---An excommunicated person ought not to offer [the Eucharist] or baptize, but only pray, Abedoc, XCVI, 1297.---An excommunicated person ought not communicate without permission, Capitularies of Charlemagne, XCVII, 805.---The excommunicated must not be admitted to legal proceedings, Nicholas I, CXIX, 936.---Excommunication accomplishes in the Church what execution accomplished under the old law or under the laws of the commonwealth, Hincmar, CXXV, 705.---Ordination performed by them has no force, St. Bruno of Segni, CLXV, 786.---Persons expressly excommunicated cannot ordain others, ibid., 788.---The excommunicated can neither elect nor be elected, Innocent III, CCXIV, 802.---Sentences handed down by excommunicated judges are invalid, id., CCXVI, 894.---On those who are promoted to ecclesiastical orders while excommunicated, ibid., 1249.---The excommunicated ought not be admitted to accuse clerics, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 367.

XIV. On those who die excommunicated.---Mass ought not be offered for a deceased excommunicated person, Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 511.---Those whom Gregory deprived of communion he did not wish, if the emergency of death pressed, to be deprived of viaticum, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 911.---On those who die excommunicated, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 921; Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 975.---On deceased excommunicated persons, Halitgar, CV, 702.---Excommunicated persons who have shown a sign of repentance are to be buried, Innocent III, CCXVI, 852.

XV. On absolution from excommunication and satisfaction.---On those who are excommunicated, and how they are to make satisfaction, Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 684.---How they are to be absolved, ibid., 690.---An excommunicated person is to be absolved with the counsel of the brethren, and according to what rite, ibid., 685.---How they are to be absolved, ibid., 690.---Formula of reconciliation, Halitgar, CV, 704.---On what grounds unjust excommunications may be lifted, Hincmar, CXXVI, 407.---The pope can absolve persons excommunicated by another, Paschal II, CLXIII, 754.---Those excommunicated by a bishop cannot be reconciled by a priest [Col. 1360], Gratian, CLXXXVII, 1358.---A person excommunicated by the pope must be absolved by him, Council of Rouen, CCV, 437.---On the absolution of the excommunicated, Clement III, CCIV, 1489.---A person excommunicated by a superior prelate cannot be absolved by an inferior unless the case has been investigated, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 138.---The excommunicated are not to be absolved lightly, Innocent III, CCXIV, 195.---He commands the archbishop of Narbonne, after a duly lodged appeal, to revoke actions improperly undertaken and absolve the excommunicated person, ibid., 230.---Sick excommunicated persons are to be absolved as a precaution, ibid., 437.---He commands William, archbishop of Reims, to absolve the count of Flanders from excommunication and interdict, ibid., 582.---Excommunicated persons in whom there were signs of repentance, and through whom it was not their fault that they were not reconciled to the Church, are to be regarded as absolved, ibid., 599.---Excommunicated nuns are to be absolved by their own bishop, ibid., 1030.---Innocent III relaxes the sentence of excommunication by which the archbishop of Messina was bound, ibid., 1030.---Innocent commands that the sentence imposed upon the archbishop of York for violently laying hands on clerics be lifted, id., CCXV, 563.---The same pope commands that the bishop of Toul be absolved from the bond of excommunication, ibid., 659.---Innocent III grants authority to absolve from every excommunication whatsoever, ibid., 670.---Innocent states that the bishop of Halberstadt has been absolved from the bond of excommunication, ibid., 676.---Innocent grants the patriarch of Jerusalem authority to absolve from every excommunication whatsoever, ibid., 670.---He may absolve from the bond of excommunication those who wish to cross over with him, ibid., 752.

XVI. Historical examples of excommunication directed against: A. Patriarchs, primates, archbishops, bishops, etc.

---B. Priests, deacons, clerics, and monks.---

C. Emperors.---D. Dukes, counts, etc.---E. Cities [lacuna] and peoples.---F. Distinguished women.

A. Patriarchs, primates, archbishops, bishops.---If a bishop neglects his diocese, he is excommunicated, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 935.---The excommunication and deposition of the bishops Rodoald and Zachary, Nicholas I, CXIX, 881.---Gregory, archbishop of Syracuse, is anathematized, ibid., 1027.---Photius is threatened with perpetual excommunication, ibid., 1045.---Photius with his followers is anathematized, ibid., 1058.---All who turn away from communion with Ignatius or associate with Photius are anathematized, ibid., 1076.---Excommunication of the apostolic John and other bishops at the assembly at Troyes, Dubious Annals, CXXV, 1288.---John VIII threatens Archbishop Ausbert of Milan with the penalty of excommunication unless he comes to the Roman synod with his suffragans, John VIII, CXXVI, 847.---Excommunication of Auspert, archbishop of Milan, ibid., 819.---He threatens the bishop of Nîmes with excommunication, ibid., 847.---He threatens Anselm of Milan with excommunication unless he returns to obedience to his archbishop, ibid., 922.---He threatens Athanasius, bishop of Naples, with excommunication unless he breaks his alliance with the Saracens, ibid., 922.---Athanasius is excommunicated, ibid., 927.---He orders Archbishop Romanus to come to a synod under penalty of excommunication, ibid., 934.---Excommunication directed against Bishop Formosus, Gregory the nomenclator, and George, master of the soldiers, ibid., 963.---St. Gregory VII announces that he has excommunicated Godfrey because he occupied the Church of Milan simoniacally, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 296.---He confirms the sentence issued by the bishop of Die, legate, against Stephen, invader of a church, ibid., 471.---Gilbert, archbishop of Ravenna, and Tetbald, bishop of Milan, are excommunicated, ibid., 796.---The archbishop of Narbonne is excommunicated, ibid.---Innocent III commands that public excommunication be pronounced against the bishop of Hildesheim, Innocent III, CCXIV, 870.---He commands the archbishop of Split publicly to excommunicate Nicholas, bishop of Forensis, ibid.---Innocent commands that the excommunication of the bishop of Schleswig be publicly announced, id., CCXV, 1316.

B. Priests, deacons, clerics, monks, etc.---A deacon is excommunicated by his priest, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 419.---Likewise a subdeacon by his priest, ibid.---St. Gregory VII does not send a blessing to the clerics of Rome, as though they were excommunicated, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 471.---Confirmation of the excommunication of Hubert the priest, Paschal II, CLXIII, 394.---The abbot and monks of Lorch are suspended on account of excommunication, Innocent III, CCXIV, 873.

C. Emperors and kings.---The younger Theodosius is excommunicated by a monk, Rule of St. Benedict, LXVI, 511.---Nicholas I warns King Charles, under penalty of excommunication, to expel from his kingdom Ingeltrude, the adulterous wife of Count Boso, Nicholas I, CXIX, 781.---One must not associate with the excommunicated Theutgaud and Gunthar, [Col. 1361] ibid., 881.---Hincmar records the excommunication of Odoacer, Hincmar, CXXVI, 245.---On excommunicating Carloman and his accomplices, ibid., 277.---The punishment and salvation of Clement the German, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXXVII, 460.---St. Gregory VII rebukes Henry, king of the Romans, because he associates with excommunicated persons, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 439.---St. Gregory VII excommunicates Henry, ibid., 458.---St. Gregory VII threatens Wezelin with excommunication if he attacks the king of Dalmatia, ibid., 537.---On the authority of the Apostolic See in excommunicating King Henry, ibid., 594.---St. Gregory explains the causes of the excommunication of Emperor Henry, ibid., 671.---Henry, king of Germany; Siegfried of Mainz; William of Utrecht; and Robert, bishop of Bamberg, are excommunicated, ibid., 789.---By sentence of excommunication and interdict, the king of León and the daughter of the king of Castile, united within a prohibited degree, are to be separated, Innocent III, CCXIV, 610.---He commands the archbishop of Sens to publish the sentence of excommunication against those who take up arms against the king of England and the king of France, id., CCXV, 181.---On the excommunication of the king of England, id., CCXVI, 64.---The pope exhorts the Pisans not to give support to the excommunicated Emperor Otto, ibid., 360.

D. Dukes, counts, etc.---Nicholas I warns the senators to abstain from communion with Photius, Nicholas I, CXIX, 881.---Adventius, bishop of Metz, declares to Nicholas I that he does not associate with the excommunicated Theutgaud and Gunthar, Adventius, CXXI, 1146.---Nobles are excommunicated because of seditions, Hincmar, CXXVI, 20.---He threatens Landulf with excommunication unless he obeys the pope’s decrees, John VIII, id., 906.---Priors who seize a bishop not canonically judged are excommunicated, Burchard, CXLVI, 1412.---St. Gregory VII warns Robert, count of Flanders, not further to aid the excommunicated bishop of Thérouanne, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 641.---Innocent III commands William, archbishop of Reims, to absolve the count of Flanders from excommunication and interdict, Innocent III, CCXIV, 582.---Formula for the excommunication of Markward, ibid., 716.---He threatens excommunication to the present and future magistrates, councillors, and consuls of Lombardy if they harass churches and clerics with exactions, id., CCXV, 47.---Innocent III commands that the sentence of excommunication imposed by the bishop of Cambrai upon the count of Namur and others be observed, ibid., 330.---Innocent III commands that the excommunication of Waldemar be publicly announced, id., CCXVII, 280.

E. Peoples and cities.---John VIII excommunicates the Amalfitans until they separate themselves from the pagans, John VIII, CXXVI, 889.---He threatens the Amalfitans with excommunication, ibid., 901.---John VIII commands the inhabitants of Provence, under penalty of excommunication, to restore the property of St. Peter, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 528.---He commands that property of Rorgon, belonging to his brother Hugh and taken away, be restored under penalty of excommunication, ibid., 537.---He absolves the people of Beauvais from excommunication at the request of the bishop whom they had offended, ibid., 339.---Gregory commands the people of Tours and Angers not to associate with the count of Anjou, who had been excommunicated by the archbishop, ibid., 624.---He exhorts the Venetians to guard themselves from excommunicated persons, ibid., 613.---The bishop of Regensburg excommunicates all his citizens, Gratian, CXCIII, 606.---The Albigensian heretics are excommunicated; Celestine III commands the archbishop of Ravenna, under penalty of excommunication, to compel the people of Modena to restore to the monastery of Nonantola what they have taken, Celestine III, CCVI, 1184.---Celestine III threatens the consuls and people of Novara with excommunication, Innocent III, CCXIV, 877.---Innocent III commands the bishop of Modena publicly to excommunicate the people of Cremona, id., CCXV, 21.---Excommunication of certain criminal citizens of Cambrai, ibid., 949.---Innocent III commands that the excommunication against the burghers of Saint-Omer be observed, id., CCXVII, 80.

F. Distinguished women.---Nicholas I commands Hincmar and the bishops of the kingdom to excommunicate Ingeltrude, Boso’s fugitive wife, if she scorns to return to her husband, Nicholas I, CXIX, 780.---Waldrada the adulteress is excommunicated with her accomplices, ibid., 971.---Nicholas writes for the third time concerning Waldrada’s excommunication, ibid., 1140.---Excommunication of Fulcher and Hardoisa because of an incestuous marriage, Hincmar, CXXVI, 277.---Passaguerra is lawfully excommunicated, Innocent III, CCXIV, 337.

Irregularities.---Who are irregular for receiving orders, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 575, 694.---On those who are not to be ordained clerics, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXIV, 25, 27.---Bigamists are not to be admitted to the clergy, Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 846.---He who has taken a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute is not admitted to the clergy, ibid., [Col. 1362] 848.---He who has taken two wives, ibid.---He who has made himself a eunuch, ibid., 849.---Various irregularities, St. Egbert, LXXXIX, 440.---He who has taken two wives or a cousin cannot be a cleric, Angelran, XLVI, 1035.------A bigamist or concubinary, ibid.---Various irregularities, ibid., 1036.---Clerics who abominate the eating of meat, ibid., 1037.---Slaves are not to be ordained, Diplomatic Code, XCVII, 409.---Those rebaptized are not to be ordained, ibid., 805.---Accusers of brethren are irregular, ibid., 894.---Eunuchs, ibid., LXXXIX, 996.---One whose wife has committed adultery, Selected Canons, XCIX, 997.---One who has taken as wife a woman previously defiled, ibid., 998.---Those who are bigamists, ibid.---Those who have had intercourse with a slave-woman, ibid., 999.---Those who have engaged in secular business, ibid.---Defect of birth, ibid., 1000.---Those baptized by heretics, 1002.---Heretics, ibid.---Seditionaries, ibid.---Irregularities, ibid., 1094.---Subdeacons who commit adultery, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1407.---He who after baptism has been joined in a second marriage can be neither bishop, deacon, nor cleric, Apostolic Canons, CXXX, 16.---One who marries an unworthy betrothed woman or a slave-woman, ibid.---One who has taken two sisters in marriage, ibid.---A bishop neglecting his people, ibid., 18.---Bigamists are irregular, ibid., 381, 383.---Why bigamists are altogether excluded from the priesthood, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 240.

The following are irregular.---Bigamists, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 185.---Epileptics, ibid.---Men whose wives are attached to public spectacles, or are repudiated women or slave-women, cannot become clerics, ibid., 193.---He who has mutilated himself, ibid., 302.---Those physically impaired, ibid., 301.---He who deliberately cuts off part of his finger, ibid., 303.---Sons of priests are not to be admitted to sacred offices, ibid., 304.---Simoniacs are in no way to be promoted to orders, ibid., 537.---A simoniac is to be excluded from the helm of the Church, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 86.---Men publicly married ought not be admitted to ecclesiastical dignities, Innocent III, CCXV, 10, 70.---He is irregular who has mortally wounded another, CCXVI, 64.

Suspension and deposition.---What suspension from prayer is, Cassian, XLIX, 105, 172.---Gaudentius, bishop of Aufinium, is deprived of priestly office because of unlawful ordinations which he performed, St. Simplicius, LVIII, 38.---A cleric who made himself a eunuch is to be cast out of the clergy, St. Cresconius, LXXXVIII, 849.---Canons concerning one condemned from office, Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 1017.---Usurious and drunken clerics, those attending banquets or obscene songs, and others like them, are suspended, ibid., 1040.---Canons concerning the deposition of clerics, Angelran, XCVI, 1036.---Usurers, gamblers, drunkards, ibid.---A priest taking a wife, ibid., 1037.---A condemned bishop, priest, or deacon who usurps his former office is never to be restored, ibid., 1039.---A cleric scorning to return to his own parish, Charlemagne, XCVI, 1039.---A cleric devoted to obscene speech or songs at banquets, ibid., XCVII, 898.---A cleric celebrating an office against the will of his bishop, ibid.---Clerics not abstaining from their own wives are suspended from office, St. Zachary, XCVIII, 85.---How and for what offences a person is to be degraded, St. Theodore of Canterbury, XCIX, 1011.---Usurious and drunken clerics, sureties, and those devoted to banquets and obscene songs are suspended, Selected Canons, ibid., 1010.---Rules concerning the deposition and suspension of ministers of the Church who go astray, Halitgar, CV, 687.---Drunkards and fornicators, ibid., 700.---One who negligently loses the sacrifice by accident, ibid., 701.---Priests of depraved life are to be suspended, ibid., 706.---Betrothed or concubinary clerics are to be deprived of office and benefice, Eugenius II, CV, 645.---Gregory IV restores the deposed Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, St. Gregory IV, CVI, 858.---Conspiring clerics, Rabanus, CXII, 1414.---He suspends priests who receive other persons’ clerics and parishioners, Radulf, CXIX, 711.---A priest suspected of the crime of fornication, if found conversing [with a woman] after the first or second admonition, is to be removed from the priesthood, ibid.---Deposition of all persons promoted by Photius to any ecclesiastical order, ibid., 1076.---A homicidal priest ought to be deprived of priestly office, Nicholas I, CXIX, 1134.---Simoniacs are to be deposed, ibid., 1190.---A cleric having intercourse with a veiled woman is to be deprived of his own rank, Isaac of Langres, CXXIV, 1088.---A cleric living dishonourably with women is to be expelled from the clergy, Hincmar, CXXV, 1097.---Deposition of the archbishops Theotgaud and Gunthar, ibid., 1213.---Deposition of Rothald, ibid., CXXVI, 25.---Deposition of Godbald the priest, convicted concerning a woman, ibid., 251.---Deposition of Hincmar of Laon, ibid., 634.---John VIII suspends from celebration of Mass a bishop who had associated with excommunicated persons, John VIII, ibid., 816.---A bishop or priest offering oblations other than wine and bread is to be deposed, Apostolic Canons, CXXX, 116.---A bishop, priest, or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, ibid., 17.---Priests and other [Col. 1363] clerics who lapsed during persecution are to be deposed, Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 261.---The Roman pontiff has the right to depose bishops, St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 407.---That a legate presides over all bishops and can pronounce a sentence of deposition against them, ibid.---The pope can depose absentees, ibid.---Simoniacs are to be deposed, ibid., 414.---The bishop of Dol is removed from the episcopate, ibid., 470.---Simoniacs ought to be deposed, ibid., 738.---The archbishop of Constantinople is deposed by authority of the Roman pontiff, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 125.---A cleric wishing to possess a workshop or tavern is to be deposed, ibid., 229.---He who ordains anyone contrary to the form of the canons is subject to a year’s suspension, ibid., 301.---He who seeks another’s see, after being expelled from it, is also to be deposed from his own, ibid., 738, 762.---Deposition of the abbot of St. William, Innocent III, CCXIV, 1053.---Innocent confirms the sentence of suspension pronounced against the bishop of Béziers by legates of the Apostolic See, ibid., CCXV, 272.

Interdict.---A church is interdicted after bloodshed, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 348.---The church of Rouen [Col. 1364] is interdicted for bloodshed by Bishop Leudovald, ibid., 471.---The basilica of St. Hilary at Poitiers is interdicted because of bloodshed, ibid., 345.---Interdict from water and fire among the Romans, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 214.---An interdict pronounced against the city of Rouen, ibid., CCVII, 1179.---Confirmation of a sentence of excommunication and interdict pronounced by Walter’s authority, ibid.---Divine offices are not to be celebrated in places through which property has been taken from churches, Odo of Toul, CCV, 915.---Divine offices are to cease when someone is buried in a cemetery during an interdict, ibid., 917.---He relaxes the interdict of Cesena, Innocent III, CCXIV, 433.---He threatens the penalty of interdict to laymen exacting tithes from clerics, ibid., 434.---He commands the bishop of Modena to subject the city of Cremona to ecclesiastical interdict, ibid., CCXV, 21.---He threatens the penalty of interdict to King John of England, ibid., 61.---He determines that an interdict imposed by the bishop or chapter of Le Mans against the chapter of St. Peter of the Court is to be observed, ibid., 796.---During an interdict, celebration is not permitted, ibid., 1531.

Volume back matter

[Col. 1363]

ORDER OF THE INDEXES CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME.
